About this text

Toh 6 in the Kangyur is the Vinayakṣudraka-vastu, known in Tibetan as the Dul wa trantsek kyi zhi (འདུལ་བ་ཕྲན་ཚེགས་ཀྱི་གཞི།), rendered in English as The Basis of Minor Vinaya Matters. It is a canonical Vinaya text belonging to the Mūlasarvāstivāda monastic code and deals with a wide range of minor rules and practical regulations governing the daily life of Buddhist monastics, covering topics as varied as tooth-scrapers, robes, bowls, water-strainers, and personal adornments. As the title suggests, it collects miscellaneous disciplinary matters that do not fit neatly into the major categories of the Vinaya but are nonetheless considered authoritative guidance for monastic conduct. This text forms part of the Vinaya section of the Kangyur, the collection of canonical scriptures attributed to the Buddha himself, and opens with the scene of the Buddha residing at Vaiśālī, establishing the narrative frame from which the individual rules and their origins are expounded.

Translation

In the language of India: Vinayakṣudraka-vastu. In the Tibetan language: The Basis of Minor Vinaya Matters. The first section.

Homage to the Omniscient One.

A summary verse of the Basis of Minor Matters:

A tooth-scraper, a monastic robe,
a measuring rod, an elder's body-wash,
an investigation, remorse, and its removal —
these are rightly taught as the basis of minor matters.

A condensed summary verse:

A tooth-scraper, trimming the nails,
a bowl's parts, a mirror-born matter,
a bypath, a water-strainer, pulse soup,
washing the feet, and a knot on the robe.

A summary verse:

A tooth-scraper and white earth,
a fish-scale, a fragrant hand-stamp,
two pillars and two threads,
a wrist ornament, and a ring impression.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Vaiśālī, in the Monkey Pond Hall, the many-storied pavilion. The group of six monks, early in the morning, having divided up their lower robes and their outer monastic robes, and taking their bowls, entered Vaiśālī for the sake of alms. Now, in the interval between Vaiśālī and the many-storied pavilion, the pleasure groves of the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī were filled with flowers and fruit and water in abundance, and with various birds singing — a delightful grove like a pleasure park. Within those groves there were also various implements of sport, of dance, of song, of music, and of bathing set out, and the sounds of all manner of performance were there as well.

The group of six said to one another: "Friends, dear friends — the Blessed One has cited the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī and their pleasure groves as an example for the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Let us go for a while and look at those pleasure groves to see what they are like." And having agreed on this, they entered the pleasure groves. There they saw implements for sport: large arrows and straight ones, various throwing-stones, and various implements for dance, song, and music — lutes, flutes, clay drums, hand drums, beautiful-sounding instruments and many others — and also bathing implements: tooth-scrapers, cleansing powder, various kinds of āmalaka for washing the hair. When they saw all of this, they said to one another: "Friends, dear friends, since there are so many excellent implements here of every kind, should we not do some sport, or dance, or sing, or make music, or bathe?" Some said: "Let us bathe long — the more washing the better." And having agreed, they began rubbing themselves with the tooth-scrapers and set about bathing. Those who were skilled in crafts and in practical arts commenced their bathing, and from those who entered the water there arose a most pleasing sound — like a five-branched melody skillfully played by an accomplished musician.

The great mass of people going along the road heard this sound, and pricking up their ears, they stopped for a moment and said: "O wise ones, let us go to the pleasure groves of the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī where the dancers are dancing!" And those who were attracted by the spectacle quickly set off and entered the pleasure groves. There they came upon the group of six, who had just come out. The group of six said to those people: "Noble ones, in which direction are the dancers dancing?" The people replied: "Wretch, you make no distinction — would a sound like this arise where dancers are dancing? Noble ones, then whose sound was this?" "Wise ones, we were scrubbing our bodies and bathing." "Noble ones, do you contemptible monks torment yourselves with sensual pleasures? You are pressed down by the round of your throat, and you contemptible monks torment yourselves with sensual pleasures. Are you teaching us your way? Say nothing more — we will do you harm." And having threatened them, they set off ahead, entered Vaiśālī, and along the main road and the lanes,

they began to mock them at the crossroads and the lane-junctions. When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter. Whatever fault had arisen came about because the monks were scrubbing their bodies with pumice stones while bathing. Therefore a monk shall not scrub his body with a pumice stone while bathing. If he does scrub in that way, it becomes an offence of wrongdoing. When the Blessed One had declared that a monk shall not scrub his body with a pumice stone while bathing, monks who had cracked heels and went on their alms round in a foul-smelling condition were seen by brahmins and householders, who said: "Noble ones, your feet are cracked and you smell — why do you not cleanse the filth away?" They replied: "Friends, the Blessed One has not permitted it." "Can it be, noble ones, that you will be purified by being mired in filth?" The monks said nothing and, having completed their alms round, they returned to the monastery. Then the monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, what came before was a rule. This is now permitted. Therefore a monk is permitted to scrub his feet with a pumice stone — but not the rest of the body; if he scrubs the rest of the body it becomes an offence of wrongdoing."

The Blessed One was dwelling in Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Monkey Pool. In the morning the monks dressed in their lower robes and outer robes, took up their bowls, and entered Vaiśālī on alms round. They saw a brahmin who had smeared three finger-lines of white clay on himself and was wandering about begging, and he was obtaining a great deal in the way of offerings. The group of six said: "Ananda, Upānanda, this is a good method — let us do the same." And so the next day they smeared three finger-lines of white clay on themselves and went on alms round. Those without faith, seeing this, mocked them and spoke with contempt, saying: "Speak with contempt!" And when the group of six heard this they said: "Wretches, do you not even know to whom respectful address is owed and to whom homage is owed? Those who replied said: "What do you expect of this? Elderly brahmins deserve respectful address, and monks deserve homage — so why do you offer respectful address to monks rather than homage?" The group of six said: "Noble ones, we take you to be brahmins, not monks. That being so, we have not paid homage — please forgive us." And with that, those people said nothing more.

When the monks heard of this they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter. Whatever fault had arisen came about because the monks were drawing three finger-lines. Therefore a monk shall not draw three finger-lines. If a monk draws three finger-lines, it becomes an offence of wrongdoing. When the Blessed One had declared that a monk shall not smear three finger-lines on himself, there was then an occasion when monks, though instructed by a physician, could not get medicine to be absorbed by their bodies. The monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, what came before was a rule. This is now permitted. Therefore what is prescribed by a physician is excepted."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in Prince Jeta's Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. One morning the group of six dressed in their lower robes and outer robes, took up their bowls, and entered Śrāvastī on alms round, when —

They saw a brahmin performing the gestures of Giu Wanggi Thig Le, surrounded by a great crowd of ordinary people who were singing his praises at a festival. The members of the group of six said to one another: "Friend, dear friend, this is a fine method — let us do likewise." Agreeing that they would indeed do so, the very next day they adorned themselves with the marks of Giu Wanggi Thig Le and went out on alms round. Brahmins and householders who saw them mocked them and said: "Speak respectfully! Speak respectfully!" The group of six replied: "You poor wretch — do you not even know to whom respectful address is owed and to whom obeisance is due?" The brahmins and householders said: "What do we want from this? Aged brahmins are the ones to whom respectful address is owed, and monks are the ones to whom obeisance is due. So why do you monks receive respectful address but not obeisance? Noble ones, we take you to be brahmins, not monks. That is why we did not make obeisance to you. Please pardon us." And with that, both sides fell silent.

The monks then reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered it and declared: "Whatever fault has arisen, monks, has come about through adorning oneself with the marks of Giu Wanggi Thig Le. Therefore monks are not to adorn themselves with those marks. If one does so, it becomes an offense entailing a penalty."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks are not to adorn themselves with the marks of Giu Wanggi Thig Le, a monk who had suddenly sustained a wound went to a physician and said: "Good sir, please show me a medicine." The physician replied: "Noble one, anoint the wound with Giu Wang, and you will recover." The monk said: "The Blessed One has not permitted it." The physician said: "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate — he will permit it." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, what a physician prescribes is excepted."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks are not to scrape their bodies with a toothed scraper, the monks began scraping themselves with a fish-scale scraper. The Blessed One declared: "One is not to scrape with a fish-scale scraper. If one does so, it becomes an offense entailing a penalty."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in Prince Jeta's Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six anointed themselves with perfume, then went among the young men and said: "Young men, how does our fragrance smell?" The young men said: "Elders, have you anointed yourselves with perfume?" "We have." "Elders, is it fitting for you to anoint yourselves with perfume?" "Fitting or not fitting, we have done it." The young men mocked and ridiculed them. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered it and declared: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through anointing with perfume. Therefore monks are not to anoint themselves with perfume. If one does so, it becomes an offense entailing a penalty."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks are not to anoint themselves with perfume, a sick monk went to a physician and said: "Good sir, please show me a medicine." The physician said: "Noble one, if you anoint yourself with perfume, you will recover." The monk said: "Good sir, is that something I may do as I please?" The physician said: "Noble one, this is your medicine — no other treatment will cure you." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One,

The Blessed One declared: "Then it is permitted — one may anoint oneself with perfume on a physician's prescription." But when monks had anointed themselves with perfume and were sitting within the Saṅgha, they would teach the Dharma to brahmins and householders who came to visit, and they would also go to the homes of brahmins and householders. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I shall lay down a rule of conduct for monks who carry perfume. A monk who carries perfume shall not, after anointing himself, sit within the Saṅgha; he shall not teach the Dharma to brahmins and householders who come to visit; and he shall not go to the homes of brahmins and householders. But when he has recovered, he shall wash and become free of the scent, and then he may sit within the Saṅgha, teach the Dharma to brahmins and householders who come, and go to their homes. If a monk who carries perfume does not properly observe the rule of conduct as laid down, it becomes an offense entailing a penalty."

Now when faithful brahmins and householders offered perfume to the monks, the monks felt scrupulous and would not accept it. Those donors said: "Noble ones, before the awakened Blessed One appeared in the world, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) were the worthy recipients of offerings. Now that the Blessed One has appeared in the world, you are the worthy recipients. If you will not accept, how shall we from this world accrue merit for the next? Please accept out of compassion for us." They then said: "We shall appeal to the Blessed One." The monks accordingly reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "You may accept it." The monks accepted and then threw the perfume down before those donors. The donors said: "Noble ones, did we not buy this at a fair price? You accepted it and then threw it away!" The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "You should not accept and then discard it; rather, you may apply it as handprint designs on the stūpas of the Tathāgata." The monks took it and applied handprint designs with the perfume on stūpas of hair and nail relics. The donors said: "Noble ones, did you not see the stūpa? We offered it to you alone — we had already made offerings to the stūpas of hair and nail relics before." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Accept it and apply it to the residence halls." The monks applied it to the doors of the residence halls, and the donors, thinking these were fragrant bath-houses, were making prostrations. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Apply it to the interior." The monks applied it directly on the walls, and the same problem arose again. The Blessed One then declared: "Apply it near the joints and near the feet of the columns, and all pleasant fragrances that are beneficial to the eyes may be carried about from time to time — there is no need to be scrupulous about this."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling in the forest of the Fearsome-Looking Grove on the hill of the Jīvaka's Children's Killing — the grove that strikes terror into the heart. At that time a young prince had the handsome Lotus-Decorated Palace decorated and invited the Blessed One, together with his retinue of śrāvaka monks, at midday. The Blessed One was seated on a prepared throne in the upper hall of the Lotus-Decorated Palace. The beloved Ānanda, while eating his meal, leaned a hand against a pillar,

and the Lotus-Decorated Palace shook and swayed. Those who were questioning him said: "Noble one, the young prince Rtogs-byed had the Lotus-Decorated Palace decorated with a hundred and one colors — have you demolished it?" Ānanda replied: "Poor Rtogs-byed became deeply attached to this place and, when he died, was reborn without a fixed destination. And you too, through deep attachment to this place, will die and be reborn among the hungry ghosts with goiters." While these words were being exchanged, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having reflected, said: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through a monk leaning his hand against a pillar. Therefore monks must not lean their hands against pillars. If one does so, it becomes an offense entailing a meeting of the community." Having declared that monks must not lean their hands against pillars, the Group of Six thereupon began leaning against walls, the ground, and others — pressing with fists, elbows, shoulders, the head, the side of the ribs, the back, the waist, the thighs, the knees, the forearms, the feet, staffs, and sticks, and also pressing against others — thereby bringing about that very same fault. The Blessed One then declared: "No one must lean against anything in any such manner." The Group of Six then leaned against walls and the ground and pressed against others, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not lean against others either, in any manner. If one does so, it becomes an offense entailing a meeting of the community."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Group of Six, having entered Śrāvastī in the morning for alms-rounds, saw a brahmin wearing the brahminical cord and wandering about begging, obtaining a great quantity of food and provisions. The Group of Six said among themselves: "Friends, this is an excellent method — let us do likewise." The next day they put on the brahminical cord and went on their alms-rounds. Those of little faith who saw them mocked them and addressed them with derisive politeness — saying, "Speak politely, speak politely!" The Group of Six retorted: "Poor wretches, do you not know to whom one should speak politely and to whom one should bow? They replied: "What do you seek from us? Old brahmins are those to whom one speaks politely, and monks are those one bows to — so why do you monks address others with polite speech rather than bowing? Noble ones, we recognize you as brahmins, not as monks. This being so, we did not bow — please forgive us." And those monks fell silent, saying nothing. When the monks there heard of this, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, having reflected, said: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through monks wearing the brahminical cord. Therefore monks must not put on the brahminical cord. If one does so, it becomes an offense entailing a meeting of the community."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Group of Six, having put on their lower robes and outer robes in the morning and taken their alms-bowls, entered Śrāvastī for alms-rounds. They saw a brahmin adorned with fragrant substances and flowers, his wrists bound with five-colored cords, who had eaten at a festival, his senses satisfied, and was departing from a house. They said among themselves: "Friends, this is an excellent method — let us do likewise." The next day they bound their wrists with five-colored cords and went on their alms-rounds.

When the brahmins and householders saw them, they mocked them and spoke with disdain. When they said "with disdain," the Group of Six replied: "You wretched ones — do you not even know who is to be addressed respectfully and who is to be venerated? The answer is this: elderly brahmins are those to be addressed respectfully, and monks are those to be venerated." They replied: "Then why do you address the monks respectfully rather than venerating them?" The Group of Six said: "Noble ones, we regard you as brahmins — not as monks. That being so, forgive us for not having venerated you." At that, the others fell silent.

At that time, the monks heard of this and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected, and saw that whatever fault had arisen had come about from monks binding their wrists with five-colored cords. Therefore, he declared: "Monks shall not bind their wrists with five-colored cords. If one does so, it becomes an offense."

After the Blessed One had proclaimed that monks shall not bind their wrists with five-colored cords, a certain sick monk went to a physician and said: "Good sir, I have developed such and such an illness — please prescribe a remedy." The physician said: "Noble one, if a cord is recited over with sacred mantras and bound around your wrist, you will recover." The monk replied: "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted this." The physician said: "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate — he will permit it."

At that time, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted to bind a cord on a physician's authority." After the Blessed One declared that a cord may be bound on a physician's authority, the monks bound it at the tip of the right hand — and the very same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "Monks shall not bind it at the tip of the right hand." They then bound it at the upper arm of the right hand — and that same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "It shall not be bound at the upper arm of the right hand." They then bound it at the tip of the left hand — and that same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "It shall not be bound at the tip of the left hand. However, it may be bound at the upper arm of the left hand."

When the monks had recovered from their illness, they discarded the cords carelessly, and non-humans mocked them, saying: "Noble ones, after we cured you, now you show no regard!" At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "They shall not be discarded carelessly. If the illness has not cleared, bind it to the hem of the monastic robe or to a strap. But if one has fully recovered in every respect, place it in a pillar's joint or a crack in the wall."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Group of Six, having put on their lower robes and outer robes in the morning and taken their alms-bowls, entered Śrāvastī for alms-rounds. The brahmins and householders had placed ornaments inside offering trays, and the Group of Six took up foot ornaments and arm ornaments and said: "Friend! Dear friend! How beautiful!" The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, your heads are shaved and your armpits are unshaven — what bodily beauty is there? Without a doubt, you monks have been overcome by the qualities of sensual desire."

They all remained silent. When the monks heard about this, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected that whatever fault had arisen had come from monks adorning themselves with arm ornaments and foot ornaments. Therefore, a monk should not adorn himself with arm ornaments and foot ornaments. If he does so, it constitutes an offense.

The Blessed One was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Those who take what has not been given them broke into the Saṅgha's storehouses and the monks' individual dwelling cells in the monastery, and stole from them. When other monks noticed that even one item was missing, they said: "We did not notice how much was taken from us." At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, permission is granted to keep locks." Once the Blessed One had declared that locks were permitted, the Group of Six fastened locks made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, adorned with various ring-shaped seal ornaments. Then brahmins and householders, seeing this, reached out their hands and said: "Greetings! Good health to you, good health!" Those monks replied: "Noble ones, what is this?" And those laypeople mocked and ridiculed them, saying that the sons of the Śākyan ascetic had fallen away from the conduct of an ascetic and from the conduct of a holy life — that right now these monks were attaching labels to locks and adorning themselves with ornaments. At that time the monks heard about this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk should not keep locks made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal, nor should he keep ring-shaped seal ornaments. However, the five kinds of lock — those made of iron, copper, cane, bone, and horn — are permitted."

The Group of Six painted figures of men and women sleeping together on their locks. Brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, are you who are ascetics tormented by the qualities of sensual desire?" At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "There are two kinds of lock: one belonging to the Saṅgha and one belonging to an individual. On the Saṅgha's lock, a wheel should be drawn in the center, and on the two sides, below deer figures, the name of the owner of the monastery should be written. On an individual's lock, a skeleton or a skull should be drawn."

A summary verse:

Cutting nails, dental cleaning,
āmra fruit and myrobalan,
the eight alms-bowls that were forbidden,
and the two things that were permitted.

The Blessed One was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, he said to the barber: "Good man, go to the Jeta Grove and shave the heads and faces of the noble ones." That man went to the Jeta Grove, and the habitual conduct of the Group of Six was such that at any given moment one member or another of the Group of Six would be at the gate of the Jeta Grove without fail. The venerable Ānanda was walking and sitting within the Jeta Grove, and when he saw that man approaching from a distance, he said: "Welcome! Welcome!"

"You have been gone a long while, like the moon when it disappears. Where have you come from?" The man replied: "The noble householder sent me here to shave the heads and faces of the noble ones." Ānanda asked: "Do you know how to trim nails well?" "This very craft is my trade, noble one." Ānanda looked over, and as the man drew near, Ānanda stretched out his hand. The barber asked: "How shall I trim them, noble one?" "Trim them like the tip of a grain." When the man had trimmed them like the tip of a grain, Ānanda said: "Now make them like the ledge of a fence, like the edge of a razor, like a crescent, and like the first sliver of the new moon." The man did exactly as he was directed in each case. At the end Ānanda said: "Wretch, you know not even the slightest thing! Go and make them exactly even in just this way." And so Ānanda kept the man there until sunset without releasing him.

After sunset the man went to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and Anāthapiṇḍada said: "Good man, how many noble ones' heads and faces have you shaved?" "How could I have shaved the heads and faces of the noble ones? That idle monk Ānanda detained me and had me do every manner of thing with the nails — like the tip of a grain, like the ledge of a fence, like the edge of a razor, like a crescent, and like the first sliver of the new moon — and then said: 'Wretch, you know not even the slightest thing! Go and make them exactly even in just this way,' and now that he has only just let me go, what am I to do?" The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then began to reproach those who had gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, saying: "It seems that those who have gone forth show no restraint whatsoever."

At that time the monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter. Whatever fault has arisen has come about through monks trimming their nails. Therefore a monk must not trim his nails. If he does so, it becomes an offense with consequences.

After the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not trim his nails, the monks kept their nails very long, and when the brahmins and householders saw this they said: "Why do the noble ones let their nails grow so very long? The Blessed One has not permitted it, noble ones. Can you purify yourselves by growing long nails?" At that time the monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The former rule was a prohibition. This now is a permission. Therefore it is permitted: nails are to be trimmed in both ways — like the edge of a razor and like a crescent."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha — everything is exactly as before up to the point: "Do you know how to care for nails, noble one?" "How shall I do it, noble one?" "Make them yellow, red, white, and like the color of gold" — and the man did all of this in every manner. Then Ānanda said: "Wretch, you know not even the slightest thing! Go and make them exactly even in just this way," and now that he has only just let him go, what was there to do? The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then began to reproach those who had gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, saying: "It seems that those who have gone forth show no restraint whatsoever." At that time the monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter.

Whatever fault had arisen came from the monks trimming their nails. Therefore a monk must not trim his nails. If he does, it becomes an offense. The Blessed One declared: "A monk must not trim his nails."

Now, when the Blessed One had given this ruling, those monks who worked with dyes and those who worked with the begging bowl began to get grime under their nails, and their nails became dirty and discolored. They would go out on alms round with their nails in just that state. Brahmins and householders, seeing this, said: "Noble ones, why are your nails so filthy and discolored?" When the monks were questioned in this way, they replied: "Noble ones, why should we clean the filth away? The Blessed One has not permitted it." The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, will you be purified by being mired in filth?" At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In order to remove filth, nails may be filed."

The Blessed One, the buddha and Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove of Veḷuvana. Now King Bimbisāra's regular practice was this: whatever new-season grain or fruit of any kind first appeared, he would offer it first to the Saṅgha, and only after that would he eat it himself. His ministers then presented him with a crop of mango fruits from the trees, and he said: "Go and offer them to the noble ones." When those fruits were eaten up, he said: "Wise ones, what is there to laugh about?" They replied: "Sire, did you not intend to offer them first to the noble ones? But we had already offered them to the noble ones before." He said: "If that is so, I have given the noble ones a garden of a thousand mango trees." The ministers said: "Excellent, Sire — we rejoice in this." He donated a garden of a thousand mango trees for the sake of the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and he also established a seasonal festival there. And just as the crowds of people living in the land of Magadha who came to watch the festival were satisfied by the ripened fruits of the mango trees, so the trees became laden with abundant fruit. When the monks were told to offer this to the Saṅgha, they ate the mango fruits while they were still unripened.

Some time later, a certain border king needed mangoes, and he sent a messenger to King Bimbisāra saying: "Friend, I am in need of mangoes — please send some." Bimbisāra said to the messenger: "Go, ask the noble Saṅgha for however many mangoes are needed." The messenger went to Veḷuvana, but the Group of Six monks, whose regular custom was always to keep the gates of the garden full, were there. The venerable Ānanda was walking about and sitting at the gate of Veḷuvana. The messenger approached him, paid homage, and said: "A certain great king has sent me here on account of mangoes — would you please provide some mangoes for that purpose?" Ānanda replied: "Go, fellow, and take as many mangoes as are needed." The messenger went and looked around the bases of the mango trees, but nothing was visible. He returned and said: "Noble one, there are none." Ānanda took him inside and they went through the entire garden. After they had gone all around the garden, Ānanda said: "Fellow, climb up into this tree." He climbed up but saw nothing. Ānanda said: "Fellow, go along the eastern branches — go along the southern and western branches." He went in all directions, and having done so he came down in dismay and said: "Noble one, did this garden produce no fruit this year?"

"Good fellow, just as the garden bears fruit year after year, so too did it bear fruit this year. Noble one, was it carried off by wind or rain?" "Good fellow, wind and rain did not carry it off. Rather, we ourselves made the mango fruits unripe." He then returned and reported to King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra: "Sire, the noble ones said with their own mouths, 'We ourselves made the mango fruits unripe.'" The king said: "Very well — I need to enjoy them myself," and that man went away.

In due course, when the time of a festival arrived, the crowd of people dwelling in the land of Magadha assembled, and they said: "Noble ones, did the Ānanda Garden produce no fruit this year?" "Good fellows, just as the garden bears fruit year after year, so too did it bear fruit. However, we ourselves made the mango fruits unripe." "Noble ones, all the people of Magadha might have been satisfied with ripe mangoes, yet you made the fruits unripe alone, and in doing so you harmed us — that was not well done." One of the monks replied: "The king did not give this garden to the crowd of people dwelling in Magadha. Rather, it was offered to the community of monks, and therefore we ate as we wished. What business is it of yours?" And those people began to abuse and revile them.

At that time the monks heard of this and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen comes from the monks' eating the mangoes. Therefore monks shall not eat mangoes. If a monk eats mangoes, he commits an offense." The Blessed One declared: "Monks shall not eat mangoes."

Then, when faithful brahmin householders presented monks with the fruits of the sahakāra tree, the monks said: "The Blessed One has not permitted this." Those householders said: "Noble ones, when the awakened Blessed One had not yet appeared in the world" — and so forth, as before, down to — "or please accept them and may you go from this world to the next world." Then the monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted — provided the distinguishing mark is established — and they may be eaten. There is no transgression in this." The distinguishing mark is this: those in which a core has formed.

Other faithful brahmin householders, when presenting monks with ripe fruits of the mango tree — and so forth as before, down to — "or please come from this world to the next, and accept them." Then the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted — provided the distinguishing mark is differentiated — and they may be eaten. The distinguishing mark that is differentiated is this: those in which flesh has formed."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī, a sick monk went to a physician and said: "Good fellow, I am afflicted with such-and-such an illness — please prescribe medicine." The physician said: "Noble one, drink clarified butter, and I will give you a purgative to grease you inside and cleanse you." He drank the clarified butter, but it caused him harm through thirst. The physician came and asked: "Noble one, are you comfortable?" He replied: "Good fellow, thirst is causing me distress." The physician said: "Take some myrobalan fruit," and the monk took some in his hand and sat there.

The physician came again and asked: "Noble one, are you free from thirst?" He replied: "Good fellow, I am not yet free." The physician said: "Noble one, did you not hold the myrobalan fruit in your mouth?" "Good fellow, I am holding it — here it is." "Noble one, chew it." "Good fellow, the Blessed One has not permitted it." "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate — he will permit it." At the words "at that occasion," the Blessed One declared as far as "one should hold it in the mouth." So he put it in his mouth and sat there.

The physician came yet again and asked: "Noble one, are you free from thirst?" He replied: "Good fellow, I am still not free." The physician said: "Noble one, did you not hold the myrobalan in your mouth?" "Good fellow, I have been holding it — here I still am." The physician said: "Noble one, chew it up. Otherwise you will not be free from thirst." He replied: "Good fellow, the Blessed One has not permitted it." "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate — he will permit it."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should chew it up." He chewed it but then spit it out without swallowing it, and his thirst grew worse.

The physician came again and asked: "Noble one, are you free from thirst?" He replied: "Good fellow, it is causing great harm." The physician said: "Noble one, did you not chew the myrobalan?" "Good fellow, I chewed it and then spit it out." "Noble one, why did you not swallow it?" "Good fellow, the Blessed One has forbidden eating at the wrong time." "Noble one, you are a sick man, and your Teacher is compassionate — he will permit it."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, I permit it: the five fruits may be eaten whether at the right time or at the wrong time, whether one is sick or not sick. One should not feel remorse over this." The Blessed One having declared that the five fruits may be eaten whether at the right time or at the wrong time, whether one is sick or not sick, the monks did not know which fruits were the five. The Blessed One then declared: "They are myrobalan (Skt. harītakī), āmalaka (Skt. āmalakī), bibhītaka (Skt. vibhītaka), long pepper (Skt. pippalī), and black pepper (Skt. marica)."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. In the city of Rājagṛha there lived a householder named Shintu Zangpo who was wealthy, of great means, possessed of abundant riches and extensive resources, and who was a devoted follower of the Nirgrantha ascetics (the naked ones). He took a wife from a family of equal rank, and together with her he made merry, enjoyed himself, and reveled in pleasure. While they were thus making merry, enjoying themselves, and reveling in pleasure, there came a time when a being entered his wife's womb.

The Blessed One, one morning, put on his lower robe and outer robe, took up his alms bowl, and set out into Rājagṛha for alms. As he was going about for alms through Rājagṛha, he turned toward the house of the householder Shintu Zangpo. The householder Shintu Zangpo saw the Blessed One from a distance. On seeing him, he took his wife by the hand, went to where the Blessed One was, and when he arrived he addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, this companion of mine has a being that has entered her womb — what manner of child will she bear?"

The Blessed One declared: "She will give birth to a son. He will bring luster to the family line, experience the splendors of gods and humans, go forth into my teaching, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhatship."

He filled the Blessed One's begging bowl with pure and excellent food and drink and offered it. The Blessed One said, "May you be free of illness," received the alms, and departed.

Not far from there, a naked ascetic was sitting. He thought to himself: "The one household that used to give us alms has now been turned away by the ascetic Gautama. Let me go and see what prophecy the ascetic Gautama has spoken."

He went there and said, "Householder, has the ascetic Gautama come? Has he been?" The householder replied, "He has come." The naked ascetic then asked, "And what prophecy did he give?" The householder said, "Noble one, I showed him my wife and asked what kind of child she would bear." The naked ascetic asked further, "And what did he say?" The householder replied, "He said she would bear a son, who would bring luster to the family line, experience the splendors of gods and humans, go forth into my teaching, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhatship."

Now that naked ascetic was skilled in calculation. He took up a white stone pebble and reckoned with it. When he had done so, he saw that everything the Blessed One had prophesied was exactly so. He then thought to himself: "If I praise this fully, the householder will come to have even greater faith in the ascetic Gautama. Therefore I should praise it somewhat and disparage it somewhat." With that thought, he turned away waving his hand sideways.

The householder Shintu Zangpo said, "Noble one, why do you wave your hand sideways like that?" The naked ascetic replied, "Householder, in this prophecy there is some truth and some falsehood." The householder asked, "Noble one, which part is true and which is false?" The naked ascetic answered: "Householder, what he said — that she will bear a son — that is true. What he said — that the son will bring luster to the family line — that is also true, but as for luster: 'luster' is another name for fire. This being of poor fortune will, the very moment he is born, cause the house to burn down. What he said — that the child will experience the splendors of gods and humans — that is false. Householder, have you ever seen or heard of any human being who has experienced the splendors of gods and humans? What he said — that the child will go forth into my teaching — that is true, for when there is nothing to eat and nothing to wear, he will inevitably go forth to the ascetic Gautama. What he said — that the child will abandon all afflictions and directly realize arhatship — that is false. For even now, the ascetic Gautama himself has no arhat who has abandoned all afflictions. To say nothing of his hearers."

The householder Shintu Zangpo became displeased and said, "Noble one, how am I to verify this for myself?" The naked ascetic said, "Householder, we are renouncers who have taken on precepts — you yourself will come to know." Having said this, he departed.

Shintu Zangpo thought, "This too should be discarded," and began to administer something that was not medicine. But because the being in the womb was one in his final existence, even what was not medicine became medicine for him. When Shintu Zangpo began to massage his wife's left flank, the one in the womb moved to the right flank. When Shintu Zangpo began to massage the right flank, the being moved to the left flank. For a being in his final existence, it is simply impossible and out of the question that, before attaining the exhaustion of all defilements, he should perish and be cut off in the intermediate state.

When Shintu Zangpo's wife began to cry from the rubbing of her flanks, the neighbors heard it and came running from all directions, asking: "Learned one, why is the householder's wife crying?" Shintu Zangpo said:

"Without any doubt, the time has come for her to give birth." At that, they went away.

Shintu Zangpo thought to himself: "I cannot kill him here. I will take him out to a deserted place." He led him out to a remote wilderness and tried every means possible to bring about his death, but concealed the fact that he had failed and carried him home. Then he spoke to his friends, relatives, brothers, and neighbors: "Good people, my wife has died." They began to weep and wail, and wrapping the body in blue, yellow, red, and white garments, they carried it to the Cool Grove charnel ground.

When the naked wanderers (Nirgrantha ascetics) heard this news, they were overjoyed, and raising parasols, victory banners, and pennants, they went about the main roads, lanes, crossroads, and intersections of the city of Rājagṛha, proclaiming: "Good people, hear this! The ascetic Gautama predicted of the wife of the householder Shintu Zangpo that she would give birth to a son, that she would illuminate the lineage, that she would enjoy the splendor of gods and men, and that after going forth into his teaching, abandoning all afflictions, she would directly realize arhathood. That very one is now dead and has been carried to the Cool Grove charnel ground. How could branches, leaves, and foliage ever appear on a tree that has no root at all? In a situation such as this, could it be that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not know, do not see, are not aware, or are in any way ignorant?"

But the Blessed One, the Buddha — who had entered into great compassion for the benefit of the world, the sole protector, uniquely courageous, matchless and beyond all duality of speech, abiding in calm abiding and insight, well trained in the three trainings, skilled in the three bases of Vinaya, one who has crossed the four rivers, one whose feet rest firmly on the four bases of miraculous power, one who has long been habituated to the four means of attraction, undaunted by the four fearlessnesses, one who has abandoned the five limbs, one who has truly passed beyond the five destinies, possessed of the six limbs, fully complete in the six perfections, ever abiding in the six, rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, who teaches the noble eightfold path, skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, possessed of the power of the ten powers, whose fame pervades the ten directions, supremely exalted above those who rule over thousands — such Blessed Ones, by the very nature of Dharma, survey the world three times by day and three times by night with the buddha's eye, seeing who is declining and who is flourishing, who has become wretched, who has fallen into misfortune, who has been harmed, who is wretched and fallen into misfortune and harmed, who is inclined toward lower rebirths, who has fallen into lower rebirths, who is falling into lower rebirths — and then draws them from lower rebirths to place them in higher states, liberation, and the fruit. And for whomever the root of virtue has not yet arisen, he causes it to arise; for whomever it has arisen, he causes it to ripen fully; and for whomever it has ripened, he causes it to be liberated. Thus he sets his wisdom-vision into motion.

And again it was said:

The ocean where sea-monsters dwell
may by chance be crossed with the waves of time,
but from the disciples who are to be tamed,
a buddha never lets the moment pass.

Just as a mother watching over her only beloved child
guards even that child's very life,
so too the Tathāgata watches over those beings who are to be tamed,
and likewise guards the continuity of their existence.

Abiding in the cause of omniscience,
the staff of compassion, like a cowherd who has lost a calf,
searches without weariness
for the disciples — those wandering lost on the white road of existence.

The Vinaya: Minor Matters, Volume Two.

Then the Blessed One smiled in a certain direction.

It is the very nature of reality that whenever the blessed buddhas smile, from their mouths there issue rays of light — blue, yellow, red, and white. Some of these go downward, and some go upward.

Those that go downward descend into the hells: Reviving, Black Thread, Crushing, Crying, Great Crying, Hot, Very Hot, Torment Without Respite, Blister, Burst Blister, Gnashing Teeth, Groaning, Lamenting, Split Like a Blue Lotus, Split Like a Lotus, and Split Like a Great Lotus. Into whichever of these are hot hells, the rays arrive having become cool; into whichever are cold hells, the rays arrive having become warm. By this, the particular intensity of those beings' suffering is cut off, and they think to themselves: "O wise ones! Have we died and passed on from here, or have we been born elsewhere?" In order to generate faith in them, the Blessed One sends forth an emanation. When those beings see that emanation, they think and say to one another: "O wise ones! We have neither died and passed on from here, nor been born elsewhere; rather, this is a being we have never seen before, and by his power our particular intense suffering has been cut off." With their minds turned in full devotion toward the emanation, they exhaust the karma that would lead to the experience of hell. They then take up an intermediate-state connection and are reborn among gods or humans who are fit vessels.

Those rays that go upward travel into the realms of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Free from Strife, the Joyful, the Delighting in Creation, the Wielding Others' Creations, the Brahma Heaven, the Brahma Retinue, the Great Brahma, the Minor Light, the Boundless Light, the Radiant Light, the Minor Virtue, the Boundless Virtue, the Abundant Virtue, the Cloudless, the Merit-Increasing, the Great Fruit, the Not Great, the Not Afflicted, the Clear-Seeing, the Graceful Appearance, and Akaniṣṭha — and there they proclaim: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. They also proclaim these two verses:

Rouse yourself and arise!
Strive in the teaching of the buddhas.
Like a great elephant in a house of mud,
vanquish the army of the Lord of Death.
Whoever lives with vigilance
in this Dharma and discipline
shall utterly abandon the wandering of birth
and make an end of all suffering.

Then those rays of light, having circled the great trichiliocosm, follow and trail behind the Blessed One himself. If the Blessed One intends to prophesy the past, the rays dissolve into his back. If he intends to prophesy the future, they dissolve in front of him. If he intends to prophesy rebirth in hell, they dissolve into the soles of his feet. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they dissolve into his heel. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as a hungry ghost, they dissolve into the big toe of his foot. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as a human, they dissolve into his knees. If he intends to prophesy a powerful wheel-turning kingship, they dissolve into the palm of his left hand. If he intends to prophesy a wheel-turning kingship, they dissolve into the palm of his right hand. If he intends to prophesy rebirth as a god, they dissolve into his navel.

If he intends to prophesy awakening as a śrāvaka, they dissolve into his mouth. If he intends to prophesy awakening as a pratyekabuddha, they dissolve into his hair-pores. If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they dissolve into his crown protrusion.

Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm of world-systems three times, circumambulate the Blessed One three times, and dissolve into the mouth of the Blessed One.

Then the venerable Ānanda joined his palms together and addressed the Blessed One with these words:

From his face there issued forth a thousand rays
of brilliant and manifold, many-coloured light,
illuminating all directions round about
just as the risen sun spreads forth its light.

And he continued with these verses:

The buddha, free from wildness, free from dullness and from pride,
the Victor who has tamed all foes, the wanderer supreme,
does not display, without cause, the lotus-petal smile
and lips as white and radiant as a conch.

Therefore, knowing the moment through his own steady wisdom,
for those who earnestly desire to hear the mighty Victor's words,
may the doubts that have arisen be dispelled, I pray,
by the sublime, good, and steadfast speech of the Sage, the highest of the born.

The perfectly awakened buddha, firm as Mount Meru,
does not display a sudden, causeless smile.
O Protector, for what reason have you smiled?
This assembly of beings earnestly wishes to hear.

The Blessed One then declared: "Ānanda, it is indeed so, it is indeed so. Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not smile without cause or condition.

"Ānanda, go and inform the monks: 'The Tathāgata intends to walk through the charnel ground. Whoever among you wishes to walk and go to the charnel ground together with the Tathāgata should take his own robe and come.'"

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command, Blessed One," and, having listened to the Blessed One, went to where the monks were staying. Arriving there, he informed them: "The Tathāgata intends to walk through the charnel ground. Whoever among you wishes to walk and go to the charnel ground together with the Tathāgata should take his own robe and come." All the monks gathered together and came into the presence of the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One — disciplined, with a retinue that was disciplined; peaceful, with a retinue that was peaceful; liberated, with a retinue that was liberated; relieved, with a retinue that was relieved; fully tamed, with a retinue that was fully tamed; arhats surrounded by arhats; free from attachment, with a retinue free from attachment; beautiful, with a retinue that was beautiful — like a noble bull surrounded by a herd of bulls, like a great elephant surrounded by a company of young elephants, like a lion with fangs surrounded by a pride of lions, like a king of swans surrounded by a flock of swans, like a garuḍa surrounded by a flock of garuḍas, like a brahmin surrounded by a company of brahmin students, like a physician surrounded by a company of patients, like a hero surrounded by a company of warriors, like a landowner surrounded by a company of guests, like a merchant caravan-leader surrounded by a company of traders, like a guild-master surrounded by his retinue, like a regional king surrounded by a company of ministers, like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by a thousand sons, like the moon surrounded by a host of stars, like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays of light, like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by a company of gandharvas, like a noble man surrounded by a company of kumbhāṇḍas —

like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a company of nāgas, like Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by a company of yakṣas, like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a company of asuras, like Śakra (Indra) surrounded by the company of the Thirty-Three, like Brahmā surrounded by the company of the Brahma gods, like an unmoving ocean, like a cloud laden with water, like the great elephant-king possessed of no pride, moving with deportment undimmed by his thoroughly tamed faculties, his body adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being, made beautiful by the eighty minor marks, his body haloed in light extending a full fathom around him, his radiance surpassing a thousand suns, good in every aspect like a golden mountain on the move —

he who is endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three bases of mindfulness exclusive to him, and great compassion — proceeded to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove, accompanied by many of the great śrāvakas, all of them learned: Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, Bhadrika, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Yaśas, Gavāmpati, and many other members of the monastic Saṅgha, surrounded by a great multitude of living beings numbering in the hundreds of thousands.

When the Buddha arrived, there were eighteen benefits. What are those eighteen? There is no fear of fire. There is no fear of water. There is no fear of lions. There is no fear of tigers. There is no fear of leopards. There is no fear of the assembled armies of an enemy. There is no fear of thieves. There is no fear of carnivorous beasts. There is no fear of shipwreck. There is no fear of lightning. There is no fear of a false accusation. There is no fear of humans. There is no fear of non-humans. At recurring times one will behold beautiful forms. One will hear pleasant sounds. One will see great light. One will hear those who are omniscient give prophecies. One will be endowed with the enjoyment of Dharma and with the enjoyment of material wealth.

Because the Buddha's arrival causes little harm, many hundreds of thousands of gods and humans followed in the wake of the Blessed One. Breezes also arose from the Cool Grove.

A young man of the warrior caste and two young brahmin boys came out from Rājagṛha and were at play nearby. Of the two, the young man of the warrior caste was a man of faith, whereas the brahmin boy was not. The brahmin boy said to the young man of the warrior caste: "Friend, the Blessed One has prophesied that the son born of the wife of the excellent householder Supriya will become a child of noble lineage, will experience the glory of gods and humans, will go forth into renunciation under my teaching, and, abandoning all afflictions, will directly realize arhathood. Now that that child has died, they are taking him to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove." The Blessed One declared: "It shall not be otherwise." Then the young man of the warrior caste spoke these verses:

The moon together with her host of stars may yet fall to the earth.
This earth together with its mountains and its forests may yet pass into the sky.
The waters of the great ocean may yet run dry —
but it cannot be that the great sage should speak what is untrue.

The brahmin boy said: "Friend, then let us go and visit the charnel ground of the Cool Grove." And as the two of them went, they saw the Blessed One departing from Rājagṛha. The young man of the warrior caste, seeing the Blessed One even from a great distance, again spoke these verses:

The Sage, free of doubt, possessing no agitation —

proclaiming the finest of roars like the lion, king of beasts,
not intimidated by others who speak against him, free of doubt —
thus he goes, surrounded by a multitude of people.
Like a gathering of snowclouds in the direction of the Cool Grove,
a cool and fragrant breeze has arisen —
this is certain to be a great host of gods who have come from their abodes
to investigate the miraculous powers of Śākyamuni.

The king who was Rūpasāra received a prophecy from the Blessed One: "Householder, you will be reborn as the son of the good householder Supriya's wife, your family lineage will blaze forth, you will enjoy divine and human splendors, and then, going forth into my teaching, you will abandon all afflictions and directly realize the state of an arhat." After receiving this prophecy, when the hour of his death arrived, he was carried out to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove. The Blessed One too was heard to have gone together with the community of śrāvaka monks to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove.

On hearing this, the young man of the warrior caste thought to himself: "The Blessed One does not go to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove without purpose, so surely the Blessed One is going there to perform some great act of taming in connection with the wife of the good householder Supriya — let me follow along and see." And so, accompanied by the queen, the young attendants, the ministers, the palace retinue, and the people of the countryside, he departed from Rājagṛha. When the young man of the warrior caste saw King Rūpasāra from a great distance, he again spoke these verses:

This lord and chief among the kings who rules over Magadha,
departing thus from Rājagṛha together with his retinue —
at the sight of this gathering's manifold and excellent wealth,
a feeling of certainty has arisen in my heart.

After the multitude of people watched the Blessed One depart, they parted to make way, and the Blessed One smiled and remained in the midst of the assembled people. When the naked ascetics (Nirgrantha) saw the Blessed One smiling, they thought: "Since the renunciant Gautama smiles in this way and remains in the midst of the many people, this sentient being is surely not going to die." And one of them said to the good householder Supriya: "Householder, this unfortunate sentient being has not died."

He replied: "Noble one, if that is so, what is to be done now in this situation?"

The naked ascetic said: "Householder, I myself have properly taken the precepts of training — you yourself should know what to do."

Then he gathered firewood and placed it within the pyre of the wife's corpse and set it alight. When the entire body was consumed, the womb-vessel remained just as it was. Then the womb-vessel burst open and a lotus emerged. From the heart of that lotus there appeared a fair-formed youth, beautiful and lovely to behold. When hundreds and thousands of living creatures saw him, the utmost wonder arose in them, and the arrogance, pride, and conceit of the naked ascetics were deflated.

Then the Blessed One said to the good householder Supriya: "Householder, take the youth." He looked toward the face of the naked ascetic, who said: "Householder, if one enters into the midst of a blazing conflagration, does one not get burned in every way from every direction?" Having said this, he himself did not take the child.

Then the Blessed One summoned the young physician Jīvaka and said: "Young Jīvaka, take the child." Jīvaka thought: "Since the Blessed One has not appointed me at an improper time or an improper occasion, I will take him." And without hesitation he entered into the midst of the blazing fire and took the child.

By the Victor's command he had entered the mass of fire,
and when he took the child from within the flames,
by the Victor's power the fire was entirely quelled
and in that very instant became cool as a cluster of snowflakes.

Then the Blessed One said to the young physician Jīvaka: "Jīvaka, have you suffered any harm or injury?" He replied: "Venerable one, though I was born in a royal palace and grew up in a royal palace, through the blessing of the Blessed One the mass of fire became cool like the finest sandalwood ground — such a thing as this I had never experienced before."

At that time the Blessed One said to the householder Supriya: "Householder, take the child." He turned away to look in the wrong direction and for a moment made no move to take him, instead looking toward the face of that naked ascetic. The naked ascetic said: "Householder, why say so much? Fire burns everything — that this child of such very poor fortune was not burned goes without saying, but if you bring him to your home, your home will certainly burn and your life too will certainly be cut short." Thinking "there is none dearer to me than myself," he did not take the child.

Then at that time the Blessed One said to Bimbisāra, king of Magadha: "Great King, take the child." With respectful attentiveness the king stretched out his arms, took the child, examined him carefully, and said: "Blessed One, what name shall be given to this boy?" The Blessed One declared: "Great King, since this boy was born from within fire, therefore let this boy's name be given as Agnijāta — Born of Fire."

Then the Blessed One, having understood the dispositions, latent tendencies, constitutions, and natures of that great assembly of ordinary people, taught the Dharma in such a way that those many hundreds of sentient beings, upon hearing it, would each find what was fitting for them. Some directly realized the fruit of stream-entry; some the fruit of once-returning; some the fruit of non-returning; some went forth into renunciation, and by abandoning all afflictions directly realized arhatship. Some engendered roots of virtue that had become warm; some developed the highest intensity of those roots; some developed lesser and middling patience. Some generated the awakening mind of a śrāvaka; some of a pratyekabuddha; and some generated the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Some took refuge and properly undertook the bases of training, and the greater part of that assembly came to rely upon the Buddha, to incline toward the Dharma, and to be supported by the Saṅgha.

Then King Bimbisāra entrusted the boy Agnijāta to eight nurses: two who would carry him and sustain his life, two who would suckle him at the breast, two who would cleanse his impurities, and two who would be his playmates. Those eight nurses nourished and raised him with milk, yogurt, butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and also with the very finest of all other requisites, and caused him to grow swiftly like a lotus dwelling in a pond.

Now, his maternal uncle had taken up his belongings and departed for another region. He had come to know that a being had entered into his sister in the manner that the Blessed One had predicted — that the child would be born, that the family lineage would blaze forth, and that the splendor of gods and humans would be experienced.

"He will go forth into my Teaching, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhathood" — having heard this prophecy, the maternal uncle packed up his goods, collected his price, and traveled to Rājagṛha. There he heard the news that his sister had reached the time of her death. Upon hearing this, he reflected: "The Blessed One had prophesied that the being who entered into my sister would be born as a boy, that the family lineage would blaze forth, that the splendor of gods and humans would be experienced, and that he would then go forth into my Teaching, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhathood. Could the Blessed One's word be false?" And so he asked the members of the household: "I have heard that the Blessed One prophesied of the being who entered into my sister that he would be born as a boy, that the family lineage would blaze forth, that the splendor of gods and humans would be experienced, and that he would go forth into my Teaching, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhathood. I heard that and was filled with joy throughout — and now I hear that she too has reached the time of her death." The Blessed One declared: "Could that be false?"

They then spoke these verses:

The moon together with its host of stars may yet fall to the earth,
this earth with all its mountains and forests may yet travel through the sky,
the waters of the great ocean may yet run dry —
but that the Great Sage should speak falsely can never come to pass.

The word of the Blessed One cannot be false. Indeed, the householder had caused her to die in whatever manner she was to die, and at the time appointed for her death she passed away. But the boy born of her, a mighty one of great power who was cast into fire yet was not burned, is even now being raised in the royal palace."

Upon hearing this, the maternal uncle went to the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po and said: "Householder, you have done something that is not right." "What have I done?" "Deceived by a naked ascetic, you caused my sister — into whom a being had entered — to die in whatever manner she was to die. As for that mighty boy of great power who was cast into fire yet was not burned, who is even now being raised in the royal palace — for the moment there is nothing at all to be done about that. Now, if you take that youth, well and good. But if you do not take him, I will no longer regard you as a kinsman; I will cast aside the genealogical records; and along the highways, at crossroads of three ways, and at crossroads of four ways, I will proclaim the ill-report that the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po killed my sister — that this wife-killer is one with whom no one should consort — and I will also set the king's harm upon you."

Having heard this, the householder was frightened, and thinking, "Given what he has said, he will certainly do this to me," he went to the king, prostrated at his two feet, and said: "O lord, on behalf of my kinsman I would report: if you were now to give that youth, it would be well. But if you do not give him, I will no longer regard you as a kinsman; I will cast aside the genealogical records; and along the highways, at crossroads of three ways, and at crossroads of four ways, I will proclaim the ill-report that the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po killed my sister — that this wife-killer is one with whom no one should consort — and I will also set the king's harm upon you." It was for this reason that the lord gave the youth Meskyes to me.

The king replied: "Householder, it is not I who took the youth Meskyes for you.

The Blessed One entrusted him to me, so if you need the youth, first make a request to the Blessed One on the youth's behalf." And so she went into the presence of the Blessed One, bowed at his two feet, and spoke these words: "Blessed One, my kinsman's message is this: 'If even now you were to give that youth, it would be well. But if you do not give him, I will no longer regard you as a kinsman; I will cast aside the genealogical records; and along the highways, at crossroads of three ways, and at crossroads of four ways, I will proclaim the ill-report that the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po killed my sister — that this wife-killer is one with whom no one should consort — and I will also set the king's harm upon you.' It was for this reason that the lord gave the youth Meskyes to me. Blessed One, if the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po were not to obtain the youth Meskyes, there would arise a situation in which he would vomit hot blood and meet his time of death." Seeing that such a situation indeed existed, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to King Bimbisāra and convey my instruction, saying 'Aroga,' and say this: 'Great King, give the youth Meskyes to the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po. If the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po does not obtain the youth Meskyes, there will arise a situation in which he will vomit hot blood and meet his time of death.' Deliver this message as well."

The venerable Ānanda replied, "Reverend one, I will carry out the command," and having listened to the Blessed One's word, he went directly to King Bimbisāra and spoke to him thus: "The Blessed One addresses you, Great King, with the word 'Aroga,' and declares: 'Great King, give the youth Meskyes to the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po. If the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po does not obtain the youth Meskyes, there will arise a situation in which he will vomit hot blood and meet his time of death.'"

The king said: "Venerable Ānanda, I pay homage to the Blessed One. It shall be done exactly as the Blessed One has commanded." The venerable Ānanda said "Great King, Aroga," and departed.

The king then spoke: "Householder, I have raised this youth and he is dear and pleasing to me, so I shall give him under a binding pledge — on condition that each and every day, three times in each of the three periods of the day, you send him back so that I may see him." The householder replied: "Your Majesty, if I do not send him into your royal presence, into whose presence would I send him? I will send him." And the king adorned the youth with every ornament, placed him upon an elephant, and sent him forth.

Now it is the custom among people of the world that so long as a father is alive, the name of a son is not proclaimed. After some time had passed, the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po met his time of death, and the youth Meskyes came to dwell in his father's house. He developed trust in the Buddha, trust in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

He had a temple built in the direction where his mother had not been killed, furnished it fully with all necessary requisites, offered it to the Saṅgha of the four directions, and thereafter the elders appended to the sūtras the phrase: "The Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Kalandakanivāpa grove."

The servants of the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po who had gone to earn their livelihood in another region learned that the householder Śin-tu Bzang-po had come to his time of death and that the youth Meskyes was now dwelling in his own home.

They heard that he had developed faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and had gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Upon hearing this, those servants filled an alms bowl of finest sandalwood with precious jewels and sent it as a gift to the householder Meskyes.

He hung it at the top of a tall pole and had it publicly announced in these words: "No one is to take this by ladder, by hook, or by grappling device. But if there is among the ascetics (śramaṇas) or brahmins any who has great supernatural power or great might, let one of them take it — whoever does so may carry it off as they please."

Now, certain non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who had risen early in the morning and were going to the riverbanks to perform their ablutions saw this. They came to the householder Meskyes and said: "Householder, what is this?" He explained it to them in full. They said: "Householder, the ascetics who are disciples of the Śākya clan will take it out of devotion to them," and then they went away.

Then, in due course, the elder monks who had entered Rājagṛha for alms rounds saw this. They too came to the householder Meskyes and said: "Householder, what is this?" He explained the matter to them exactly as it was. They said: "Householder, the Blessed One has instructed that monks should make their good qualities known and proclaim their faults — but should one truly display oneself merely for the sake of an alms bowl?" And with that they went away.

Then, in due course, the venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers came to that place. He said to the householder: "Householder, what is this?" The householder told him how things stood. The venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers thought to himself: "If I were to cast off, abandon, and purify the mass of afflictions I have accumulated since beginningless time, the householder would have me compete with the non-Buddhists in supernatural feats — and so for his sake I should please his mind." With that, he stretched forth his arm like an elephant's trunk, took the alms bowl, carried it away, and went to the temple.

The monks said to him: "Elder, how did you come by this alms bowl of finest sandalwood?" He recounted what had happened. The monks said: "Elder, was it fitting for you to display supernatural power before a layman merely for the sake of an alms bowl?" He replied: "Whether it was fitting or not, venerable ones, it is already done — there is nothing to be done about it now."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not display supernatural power before a layman. To do so incurs a serious offense."

Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of alms bowl made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal, and the four kinds made of iron, bronze, copper, and wood: of these, the first four — none of them already obtained is to be kept, and any that have been obtained are to be given up. The last four — none of them not yet obtained is to be obtained; but if one has been obtained, it may be used as a medicine vessel and utilized accordingly.

As for an alms bowl of iron and one of clay — these two are suitable to be consecrated by blessing.

Then, at a later time, the householder Meskyes came to enjoy the splendor of both gods and humans.

Between Rājagṛha and Campā there was a place where dice were played. The keeper of that dice-house came to the hour of death and was reborn as a fierce yakṣa. He then appeared in a dream to his son and spoke these words: "Son, have a yakṣa shrine erected at this place, and hang a bell there and ring it. Whenever anyone who has come to play dice there tries to leave without paying the dice-fee, at that moment let the bell sound, and when they turn back the dice-fee will be collected." With this he made known his instructions.

The son recounted the dream to his friends and companions, his relatives and family members, and when a favorable day arrived — auspicious in terms of the sun, the date, the time of day, the day of the week, the lunar mansion, and the season — he had a yakṣa shrine erected at that place, hung a bell there, and tied it in position.

In the city of Campā, a brahmin had taken a wife from among his own caste. The brahmin's wife reflected: "My brahmin husband, having acquired wealth by this and that means, sits about spending it, doing no work whatsoever — that is not in keeping with my nature." So she went to the market, purchased fine wool, combed and carded it thoroughly, and engaged a skilled weaver, commissioning him to weave one pair of cloth worth a thousand kārṣāpaṇas. She then said to the brahmin: "This pair of cloth is worth a thousand kārṣāpaṇas. Go to the market, and to whoever pays a thousand kārṣāpaṇas, give it to them. If no one pays that price, announce 'This is no marketplace!' and go elsewhere."

He took it and went to the market, but there was no one who would buy it for a thousand kārṣāpaṇas. So he announced "This is no marketplace!" tucked the pair of cloth inside the fold of his sunshade, and set off for Rājagṛha together with some traveling companions.

In due course they arrived at the dice-house. The dice-keeper cut off the road for those travelers and demanded the dice-fee. They paid what was owed and went on their way. But then the bell began to sound, and the dice-keepers said: "Good sirs, the bell is ringing like this, which means that among you travelers, not all have paid the dice-fee properly — someone has slipped away without paying. Collect the dice-fee again!" So they called the travelers back and searched, but there was no one who had not paid. When the travelers departed again, the bell rang once more. Again the dice-keepers called them back and searched, and again there was no one who had not paid. Then the dice-keepers scolded the travelers, saying: "Travelers, are you intending to cheat us today? Why do you keep being called back again and again?"

The dice-keepers then divided the travelers into two groups and separated them. The group that did not include that brahmin departed as they were. When the other group set off, the bell rang just the same. They too were divided and separated into two groups time and again, until in the end the brahmin alone remained behind, and they seized him. He said: "Search me — I have nothing at all." They searched him and found nothing, and let him go — yet the bell rang again. They called the brahmin back once more and said: "Brahmin, the divine blessing of the deity is thus — speak the truth, and we will not collect any dice-fee from you." He replied: "If I speak the truth, will you not take it?" They answered: "We will not take it." He then drew out from inside the fold of his sunshade that pair of cloth and showed it to them. They all cried out in amazement: "So this is how the divine blessing of the deity manifests!" Full of wonder, they unfolded one end of his cloth and displayed it before the deity. The brahmin said: "You were saying you would not collect the dice-fee — yet now are you taking everything?" They replied: "Brahmin, we are not taking it from you.

"Since the deity has displayed such divine blessing, we are merely showing it to the deity — now take it and go." He took it, placed it once more inside the fold of his sunshade, and departed, traveling to the city of Rājagṛha. When he spread out that pair of cloth in the marketplace there, again no one would buy it for a thousand kārṣāpaṇas, and so he declared: "The marketplace of Rājagṛha is no marketplace at all."

Now at that time the young man Agnidatta was riding upon an elephant, having come out from the royal palace, and was making his way through the marketplace toward his own home.
