When he heard this, he had his attendants summon the brahmin and ask him why he was proclaiming the marketplace to be no marketplace. They called him over, and Agnidatta spoke: "Brahmin, why do you proclaim this marketplace to be no marketplace?" He replied: "Householder, because there is no one who will buy this pair of cloth for a thousand kārṣāpaṇas." Agnidatta said: "Bring it and let me see it." The brahmin held it out for him to examine.

Agnidatta said: "Brahmin, that much is indeed fine in appearance, yet of the two pieces of cloth, one has been used and one has not. The unused one is worth five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, and the used one is worth two hundred and fifty." The brahmin asked: "Can it truly be so?" Agnidatta said: "Brahmin, let me show you right before your own eyes." And with that he threw the unused piece up into the open sky — it stretched out and hung there suspended. When he threw the used piece, it immediately fell back down. The brahmin was filled with amazement and said: "Householder, you are a man of great miraculous power and great might."

Agnidatta said: "Look again," and threw the unused one onto a thornbush — it passed over without catching. When he threw the other one, it caught on the thorns. The brahmin was overcome with great wonder, his faith arose, and he said: "Householder, you are a man of great miraculous power and great might — therefore please take it at whatever price you wish." Agnidatta replied: "Brahmin, you are a guest, and so for the sake of honoring you I shall give you a thousand kārṣāpaṇas." He gave him the thousand kārṣāpaṇas, the brahmin took them and departed.

Of the two pieces, Agnidatta gave the used one to a young boy, and made the unused one into a bathing cloth. Then, at another time, King Rūpavanta was sitting atop the upper chamber of his palace, surrounded by an assembly of ministers, when Agnidatta's bathing cloth, which had been set out to dry on top of the building, was carried up into the sky by the wind and fell upon King Rūpavanta. The king said: "Wise ones, from where has this come — such a garment as befits a king?" They replied: "Your Majesty the king, we have heard that when Agnidatta was born from his mother's womb a shower of jewels fell for seven days. If it rains even an ordinary shower upon the king, before long a rain of jewels will fall." The king said: "The Blessed One (the Buddha) prophesied that the householder Agnidatta would experience the splendor of both gods and men. This has come from the sky like a divine garment — when it arrives, make an offering of it." Even as they were saying these words, Agnidatta himself arrived, and the king said: "Young man, the Blessed One prophesied that you would experience the splendor of both gods and men, and here I have this — a divine garment that fell from the sky. Take it with you."

Agnidatta stretched out his hand and thought: "Let me examine it by touching it — perhaps the king will give it to me." When he did so, he perceived at once that it was indeed his own bathing cloth. He smiled slightly and said: "Your Majesty, this is my bathing cloth — the wind has carried it here." The king said:

"Young man, have you now experienced the splendor of both gods and men?" "Your Majesty, I have experienced the splendor of the gods." "Young man, if that is so, why did you not invite me? Your Majesty, I do invite you now." "Go and prepare a feast of yogurt and the like. Whatever feast is proper to offer one who has experienced the splendor of both gods and men — I myself shall come to provide it." The king went to Agnidatta's house and, seeing a group of women assembled on the outside, turned his senses away. Agnidatta said: "Your Majesty, why did you avert your senses?" He replied: "Young man, I did so because of the bride." Agnidatta said: "Your Majesty, she is not the bride — those are the outer retinue of women." This struck the king as utterly astonishing, and when he looked again and still saw that the inner retinue of women was absent, he turned his senses away once more. Agnidatta asked him in the same way, and the king answered in the same way. Agnidatta said: "Your Majesty, those too are not the bride — those are the inner retinue of women." The king's astonishment grew even greater.

The king then saw, before the entrance, an array of mechanical contrivances arranged so as to resemble a pond filled with water and full of swimming fish, all fashioned from the substance of precious gems. Wishing to enter inside, he began to remove his shoes. Agnidatta said: "Your Majesty, why are you removing your footwear?" He replied: "Young man, I intend to step into the water." Agnidatta said: "Your Majesty, this is not water — what appears to be water is in fact a floor of precious gems." He said: "Young man, I see fish swimming there like so." Agnidatta replied: "Your Majesty, those appear to move by means of the mechanical devices." The king was not convinced, and when he tossed a finger-ring, it made a ringing sound and bounced across the surface of the precious-gem floor. The king was struck with wonder, went inside, and took his seat on the lion throne. Then the brides came to bow at his feet, and tears came to their eyes. The king said: "Young man, why are these brides weeping?" He replied: "Your Majesty, they are not weeping — it is that the smell of wood-smoke clings to Your Majesty's divine garment, and it has caused their eyes to water."

"Your Majesty, as you enjoy these divine and human splendors and do not wish to depart, the royal duties and activities have fallen entirely into disarray." Then the young man's ministers said to Māra: "Young man, Your Majesty has gone to Agnidatta's house and appears to have settled there — please rise and return. It has been reported by the ministers that the royal duties and activities have fallen entirely into disarray." He replied: "Young man, can you not manage to conduct the royal business for even a single day?" He said: "Your Majesty, I reckon the heavens to be seven high, yet Your Majesty knows them to be only one." The king looked closely at Agnidatta's face and said: "Young man, is that true?" Agnidatta replied: "Your Majesty, it is indeed only seven." "Then how do you tell day from night?" "Your Majesty, one can tell by whether the flowers open and bloom, by whether the jewels blaze with light or do not blaze, and by whether the birds cry out or fall silent. Some flowers open toward the sky and droop under a canopy; others open under a canopy and droop toward the sky. Some gems blaze toward the sky and do not blaze under a canopy; others blaze under a canopy and do not blaze toward the sky. Some birds cry out toward the sky and fall silent under a canopy; others cry out under a canopy and fall silent toward the sky."

The king was filled with wonder and said:

"Young man, the Blessed One speaks only what is unerring, and things have turned out exactly as the Blessed One prophesied concerning you — no differently." Having said these words, the king departed from Agni's house and left.

The young man Ajātaśatru stole a gem from Agni's house and handed it to a boy, who then went back and sat in the very spot from which it had been taken. Ajātaśatru said, "Boy, take a look at that gem and bring it here." The boy opened a chest and said, "Young master, I do not know where it is." Ajātaśatru began to beat him, and Agni said, "Young man, why are you beating him? Householder, I myself am a thief — but this one is a greater thief still. The gem of yours that I stole was itself stolen by him." The boy said, "Young master, you did not steal it, and he did not steal it either — for he went back and sat in the very spot from which he had taken it." Then he said, "Still, young master, this is your own house, so take as many gems as you need, and as for other goods and valuables, whatever you need, take them freely."

Ajātaśatru thought to himself: "One day, when my father passes away and I become king, I shall take them then." But in time, Ajātaśatru was deceived by Devadatta and, after separating his father — the righteous Dharma-king who ruled in accordance with the Dharma — from his life, he bound the royal crown upon his own head and took the throne. Then he summoned Agni and said, "Householder, since you and I are like brothers, let us divide the houses." Agni thought: "This man has killed such a father as that — the righteous Dharma-king who ruled in accordance with the Dharma — and himself bound the crown on his head and taken the throne. If I defy him, he will kill me too. Yet though he intends to despoil my home, I should give it freely and with a pure heart." Having thought this, he said, "Your Majesty, since this is your domain, what portion do you want? I shall come to your residence; pray come to mine." Ajātaśatru said, "Very well, let it be so." And so Ajātaśatru moved into Agni's home, while Agni moved into Ajātaśatru's home. That glorious mansion vanished from sight, and in its very place there appeared where Agni stood. Seven times in succession it vanished and reappeared, and Ajātaśatru thought: "I have been unable to despoil Agni's gems in this way — I must try another method." He appointed a band of thieves and ordered them: "Go today and steal the gems from Agni's house." They began to climb using ladders, poles, and scaffolding. Now, the wives and attendants of the household were stationed at the base of the upper chambers and saw them, and they raised the cry: "Thieves! Thieves!" When Agni heard this, both in his mind and aloud he said: "May the thieves be frozen in place." And at that very spot, in whatever manner they had climbed, they were fixed there just as they were. When the night had passed and morning came, the assembled multitude of ordinary people saw them and said: "Wise ones, this wicked king has deprived his own father — the righteous Dharma-king who ruled in accordance with the Dharma — of his life, and now he would also destroy our homes. Why should we tolerate this?" Ajātaśatru sent a messenger to Agni saying, "This will bring blame upon me — release them." Agni thought in his mind and said aloud: "May these thieves depart." And they went. Then Agni thought: "He who has done this — who has deprived the righteous Dharma-king, his own father, of his life — will without fail kill me too."

He thought to himself: "The Blessed One has prophesied that I will go forth under his teaching, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhathood." And so, intent on doing exactly this in every way, he gave away all his wealth to those in destitution, to the unprotected, to the poor, and to the sick, leaving those who had been without wealth now endowed with it. Then the householder Agni, turning his face away from friends, kinsmen, relatives, and siblings, went directly to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Agni addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend sir, if it please you, I wish to go forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and attain the state of a monk, and to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One." At this the Blessed One declared, "Come, monk; live the holy life." The very moment these words were spoken, his head was shaved, he was robed in patched cloth, his hands held an alms bowl and a water vessel, his hair and beard were as though trimmed seven days past, and he carried himself in every way like a monk who had been fully ordained for a hundred years.

When the Tathāgata spoke the word "Come,"
He stood there, body clad in shaved head and patched robe,
And in that very moment his faculties became profoundly stilled —
By the Buddha's intention his bodily form was covered.

The Blessed One then pronounced a prophecy over him, and through his striving, effort, and exertion, he moved and then stilled the five-spoked wheel of saṃsāric existence, coming to know it directly. Struck down by the very nature of all formations — that they decline, fall, scatter, and disintegrate — he abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhathood. As an arhat, he was free from attachment to the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold with equal indifference, his mind as even as the sky and the palm of a hand, as even toward a thorn-bush and sandalwood. Through direct knowing he burst open the egg-shell of ignorance, and he attained knowledge, superknowledge, and individual perfect understanding. He turned his back on continued existence, on gain from desire, and on reverence; and the gods, together with Indra and his retinue, came to honor, revere, and speak respectfully of him.

The monks, having arisen in doubt, put all their doubts to the awakened Blessed One to be resolved: "Reverend sir, what action did the venerable Agni perform, such that through the ripening of that karma he was burned together with his mother in a funeral pyre, yet also experienced the splendor of gods and men, and then, going forth under the Blessed One's teaching, abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhathood?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the noble son Agni himself had assembled, fully transformed the conditions for, and brought to full proximity karma that would without fail come to arise — just like a lamp. Could any other person experience individually the karma that Agni himself had done and accumulated? Monks, karma that has been done and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, it is thus: virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been done and accumulated ripens in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases that one has taken up. For:

Even across a hundred aeons,
The karma one has done will not perish;
When the time and conditions are met,
It will bear fruit for embodied beings."

Monks, ninety-one aeons ago in the past, there appeared in this world the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha named Vipaśyin — endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One. Traveling through the countryside together with a retinue of sixty-two thousand monks, he came to the royal palace of Mūlāga and dwelt in the grove of Mūlāga.

At that time in the royal palace of Mūlāga there reigned a king named Bandhumān, a righteous dharma-king who governed justly, whose kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, happy, blessed with good harvests, and filled with many people and townsfolk; a king who caused strife, fighting, quarrels, discord, foreign enemies, domestic disturbances, bandits, famine, and disease to be entirely pacified, and who caused grain, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo to be brought to full abundance.

Now in that place there lived a householder named Anāparin, who was wealthy, of great possessions and extensive resources, with holdings both vast and wide, possessed of the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling Vaiśravaṇa himself in riches. He thought to himself: "Many times I have invited the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin to my home and offered him a meal, but I have never once provided him with all requisites for a full three months. Now let me provide the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin with all requisites for three months."

Having formed this thought, he went to where the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin was, and upon arriving he bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāparin received from the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin a discourse rightly endowed with Dharma — being rightly instructed, rightly encouraged, and rightly gladdened. In many ways Vipaśyin rightly taught a discourse endowed with Dharma, rightly instructed him, rightly encouraged him, and rightly gladdened him, and then remained silent.

Then the householder Anāparin rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in the direction of the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, and addressed the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin with these words: "Blessed One, may it please you to accept, together with the Saṅgha of monks, my offering of robes, food, lodging, medicine for the sick, and medicinal supplies for three months." The perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin granted this to the householder Anāparin by remaining silent.

Then the householder Anāparin, understanding from the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin's silence that he had granted consent, bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, rose from his seat, and departed.

Now King Bandhumān heard that the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, traveling through the countryside with a retinue of sixty-two thousand monks, had come to the royal palace of Mūlāga and was dwelling in the grove of Mūlāga. Upon hearing this he thought to himself: "Many times I have invited the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin to the palace and offered him a meal,

but never for three full months with all requisites. Now I shall provide the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin with all requisites for three full months." With that thought, he went to where the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin was, arrived, bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin taught King Bandhumān a true and proper Dharma discourse, established him in right understanding, praised him rightly, and made him rejoice completely. Having in many ways taught a true and proper Dharma discourse, established him in right understanding, praised him rightly, and made him rejoice completely, he then remained in silence.

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya. The Third Fascicle.

Then King Bandhumān rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned with joined palms toward the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, bowed, and spoke thus to the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin: "Blessed One, would you please grant me leave to offer to you, together with the Saṅgha of monks, robes, food, lodgings, medicinal provisions, and medical supplies for three months? Great King, the householder Anāparin has already invited me first." "Blessed One, if you grant me permission, then however you grant it, I shall follow it in dealing with the householder Anāparin." The Blessed One declared: "Great King, if you would summon the householder Anāparin, then I shall grant it in that same way."

King Bandhumān bowed his head at the feet of the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, rose from his seat, went to his own residence, arrived there, and then had the householder Anāparin summoned by a messenger. He said to him: "Householder, you should know this. From the very first day, I have been offering the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin the midday meal; would it be any hardship to you if after that you were to offer the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin the midday meal?" The householder replied: "Your Majesty, since I was the one who first invited the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin, it is I who wish to offer the midday meal." The King said: "Householder, even if that is so, since you are residing in my territory, it is fitting that I should offer the midday meal first." The householder replied: "Your Majesty, even though I am indeed residing in your territory, it would not be right for a king to obstruct the one who made the first invitation from offering the midday meal. Householder, do not insist on winning the dispute. Rather, let you and the king invite the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin by drawing lots, and whichever of you draws the better lot shall offer the midday meal first, while the one who does not succeed shall offer the midday meal afterward."

The householder Anāparin agreed, saying "I shall do as you say," and that very evening he prepared pure and wholesome food and drink. Rising early the next morning, he spread many seats and set out water vessels. He then sent an invitation to the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin at the time of the midday meal, saying: "Blessed One, please be so gracious as to accept the midday meal. May the Venerable One be pleased to consider that the hour has come." The perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin then dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl and Dharma robes, and, surrounded by the assembly of the Saṅgha of monks, with them going before him, set out for the residence of the householder Anāparin, arrived there, and took his seat on the seat that had been prepared, in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks.

Then the householder Anāparin, perceiving that the Buddha and the rest of the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, served them with his own hands with clean, excellent food and drink and satisfied them. Having many times over served them with his own hands with clean, excellent food and drink and satisfied them, and having perceived that the Blessed One had finished eating and had rinsed his bowl and set it aside, he took a seat lower than that of the others and sat down before the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin in order to hear the Dharma. Then the perfectly complete Buddha Vipaśyin gave a true and proper teaching grounded in the Dharma to the householder Anāparin, led him to a true and proper grasp of it, gave him true and proper encouragement, and gladdened him truly and completely. Many times over he gave a true and proper teaching grounded in the Dharma, led him to a true and proper grasp of it, gave him true and proper encouragement, and gladdened him truly and completely — and then departed.

King Bandhumant, for his part, should be understood as having made an offering of a canopy in the same extensive way as described above. The canopy-offering of the king and of the householder was similarly splendid, yet since there had been neither victory nor defeat in the matter, King Bandhumant sat brooding, absorbed in thought. His ministers asked him: "Majesty, why do you sit thus, brooding and absorbed in thought?" He replied: "Learned ones, if even the townsfolk who dwell in my realm could not surpass the other's canopy-offering in excellence, how could I not sit brooding and absorbed in thought?" They replied: "Majesty, prohibit the sale of timber. The wood of that householder will then run out." The king said: "Learned ones, let those who dwell in my realm not sell timber. Let those who sell timber not remain in my realm" — and the proclamation was made. Accordingly, the householder Anāparin set the canopy in motion with incense-wood, and began to steam cloths soaked in fragrant sesame oil. The entire city of Bandhumatī was filled with delightful fragrance. King Bandhumant asked: "Learned ones, from where does such a delightful fragrance come?" They explained it to him at length. He said: "Am I then without resources? I too shall do likewise." The ministers replied: "Majesty, it would not be fitting for you to do so. This householder has no son; it will not be long before his time of death arrives, and all his wealth will become yours. Majesty, please allow the sale of timber." Thereupon the king permitted the sale of timber.

When the householder Anāparin heard that the king had at first not permitted the sale of timber, he was greatly agitated and uttered harsh words, saying: "With this timber, it would be quite permissible for me to burn even that king Bandhumant together with his mother in a great pyre." The king then sat brooding, absorbed in thought. His ministers asked: "Majesty, why do you sit thus, brooding and absorbed in thought?" He explained it to them in full. They said: "Majesty, do not be displeased. We shall find a way for Your Majesty to get the better of the householder Anāparin."

And so the next day the ministers cleared the stones, gravel, and rubbish from the city of King Bandhumant, sprinkled it with sandalwood water, and placed vessels filled with the most delightful fragrances, hung bunches of silk along with victory banners and pennants, scattered flowers of every variety, and adorned the surrounding courtyard so beautifully that it resembled a pleasure grove — making it fit to be compared with such. Then, on a seat-base adorned with various precious substances, along with a throne of precious materials, cushions, and

splendidly adorned with fine cloths — they arranged abundant food and drink, varied in every way, superbly fragrant, complete with pickled delicacies, and as pleasing as the food of the gods, fit for the Teacher of the three worlds. Having laid out this food and these enjoyments, they addressed King Bandhumant: "We have prepared a city such as this, along with food and amenities such as these — may Your Majesty be pleased." King Bandhumant looked upon it all and was filled with great wonder, and in a mind-stream suffused with that wonder he beheld the perfectly enlightened buddha Namaparīkṣit and then issued an invitation for the noon hour, saying: "Blessed One, we request that you accept our noon-hour offering. Venerable One, please consider that the time has now come." Then the perfectly enlightened buddha Namaparīkṣit put on his robes in the morning, took up his bowl and Dharma-robe, and, fully surrounded by the assembly of monks with the Saṅgha going before him, made his way to the place where King Bandhumant had requested his presence. He arrived and took his seat on the prepared throne in the midst of the assembly of monks. Above the head of the perfectly enlightened buddha Namaparīkṣit, King Bandhumant himself caused the chief of the royal consecration elephants — one bearing a parasol with a hundred spokes — to hold the parasol aloft. Above the monks as well, other elephants were caused to hold other parasols. Over the perfectly enlightened buddha Namaparīkṣit, King Bandhumant's own principal queen was caused to fan him with a fan whose handle was made of gold and jewels. Over the monks too, other members of the queen's retinue were caused to fan them with other fans.

The householder Anāparin appointed a certain man of great discernment and sent him inside, instructing him: "Go in there — observe carefully what kind of noon-hour offering King Bandhumant has presented to the Blessed One and the assembly of monks, and understand it." The man went and looked, and upon seeing such abundance he was filled with great wonder, and his mind, overcome with astonishment, remained right there on the spot. In the same way a second and a third were sent, and they too went and remained right there. Then the householder Anāparin himself went and looked, and upon seeing all that abundance he was filled with great wonder. He thought to himself: "While others can manage such abundance — how could I possibly match the elephants and the queen's retinue?" Realizing this, he returned home, called his gatekeeper, and said: "Hey, gatekeeper — do not turn away any beggars or wanderers who come; give them whatever they desire, but do not let them inside." Having given this instruction, he entered the house of mourning, sat down in a huddled posture, and remained there, the thought gnawing within his mind.

Now the awareness and perception of Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), naturally extend downward, and so he thought to himself: "Among all objects of veneration in the world, the most supreme is the perfectly enlightened buddha Namaparīkṣit, and among all donors, the most supreme is the householder Anāparin — I should go to his aid." With that he transformed himself into a brahmin of the Kauśika clan and went to the dwelling of the householder Anāparin. Arriving there, he called to the gatekeeper and said: "Ho, gatekeeper — go and tell the householder Anāparin that a brahmin of the Kauśika clan has come to the door and wishes to see him." The gatekeeper said: "Brahmin, the householder has instructed me that any beggars or wanderers who come are to be given whatever they desire and not shown inside. What would the householder do for you? Take whatever you need and go." The brahmin said:

"Ho, gatekeeper — I have no other need whatsoever. I simply wish to see the householder himself. Go and tell him."

The gatekeeper went to the householder Anāparin and said: "Sir, a brahmin of the Kauśika clan has come to the door and wishes to see you."

The householder replied: "What? Gatekeeper, did I not instruct you beforehand that if any beggars or wanderers came, you were to give them whatever they desired and not let them inside? What would I do if he came in? Give him whatever he wants and send him on his way. That is what I told you."

"Sir, I told him exactly that, but he said he has no other need whatsoever — he simply wishes to see the householder himself."

The householder said: "Very well, gatekeeper — go and let him in."

The gatekeeper let the brahmin in, and the brahmin said: "Householder, why have you entered the chamber of grief, sitting in anguish with your knees drawn up, your heart sunken within you?"

The householder spoke in verse:

One who cannot dispel my sorrow
should not be told of it.
One who is able to dispel my sorrow —
to that person it is right to speak.

Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) said: "Householder, tell me what your sorrow is, and I will dispel it."

The householder then told him at length. After he had done so, Śakra, lord of the gods, caused the brahmin form of the Kauśika clan to vanish and sat in his own true nature, saying: "Householder, I shall send the divine son Lasthamsadpa to be your companion." And with that he departed.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, went among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and summoned the divine son Lasthamsadpa, saying: "Divine son Lasthamsadpa, go and be a companion to the householder Anāparin."

The divine son replied: "Kauśika, excellent!" And heeding the words of Śakra, lord of the gods, he caused cities to appear that were more beautiful and supremely wondrous than those before. He arranged the halls and thrones of the gods' retinue, and the divine foods were brought forth. Over the head of the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Namapar Zikyi he caused Sāśruṅg — the prince of elephants who had served in the pleasure gardens of Śakra, lord of the gods — to hold a parasol with a hundred spokes. Over the monks he caused other divine elephants to hold other parasols. For the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Namapar Zikyi, Śakra's principal queen, the goddess Bde and others, fanned him with divine fans whose handles were made of gold and jewels. For the monks as well, other assemblies of divine queens fanned them with other fans.

King Nyendan appointed a man of great discernment and commanded him: "Go inside at once, and find out what kind of parasol the householder Anāparin has offered to the Blessed One and the monastic Saṅgha of monks." When this man looked and saw such splendor, he was seized with great amazement, and so struck with wonder did he remain right there on the spot. The king sent ministers, and they too went and remained right there on the spot. He sent a young attendant, and that one too went and remained right there on the spot.

Then King Nyendan himself went there and stood at the door. The perfectly and fully awakened buddha Namapar Zikyi declared: "Householder, you spoke harsh words to King Nyendan, who has realized the truth. He is standing at this door — go and ask his forgiveness."

The householder went to him, asked his forgiveness, and said: "Great King, please come inside and be pleased to perform the serving with your own hands."

When the king entered inside and looked, he saw a divine abundance, and great wonder arose in him. He then said: "The Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha is not something I alone — a mere householder — should be serving with a canopy."

The householder Nyemé then fully satisfied the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Namapar Zik with food befitting such abundance, bowed at his feet, and made this aspiration: "By the root of virtue produced through my having served such a worthy field of merit in this way, may I be born into a lineage that is wealthy, with great riches and abundant enjoyment; may I experience the splendor of gods and humans; may I attain the Dharma in a form such as this; and may I come to please a Teacher such as this, and never displease him."

Monks, the one who at that time and on that occasion was the householder Nyemé — he is this householder Mekye. Because of the karmic maturation of the harsh words that noble son spoke to King Nyendan, who had realized the truth, he was burned in a mass of fire together with his mother for five hundred lifetimes, and he has been burned in a mass of fire again here in this very life. Yet because of the karmic maturation of having served and made aspiration to the Tathāgata Namapar Zik, he was born into a lineage that is wealthy, with great riches and abundant enjoyment; he experienced the splendor of gods and humans; he went forth in my teaching as well; and by abandoning all afflictions he directly realized arhathood. Equal in vigor, equal in strength, and equal in diligent effort to the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Namapar Zik — matching him in every respect — he has pleased me, his Teacher, and has not displeased me.

Monks, therefore the maturation of karma that is purely dark is purely dark; the maturation of karma that is purely bright is purely bright; and the maturation of mixed karma is mixed. Monks, therefore abandon karma that is purely dark and mixed karma, and strive for karma that is purely bright. Monks, you should train accordingly.

Having spoken these words, the monks rejoiced at what the Blessed One had declared.

Summary verse:

Cracked bowls repaired, things used and worn,
small knives and needles, needle-cases too,
seated cushions, and many other things —
all were permitted by the Great Sage.

The setting is Śrāvastī.

At Śrāvastī, the alms bowl of a certain monk cracked, and he took it to a blacksmith's workshop and said: "Good man, please repair this cracked bowl of mine." The blacksmith thought: "These monks press one into unpaid labor but give no wages — no matter what, if I put this off and leave it for a long time, he will eventually come back himself and take it away." So he said: "Noble one, please go and come back tomorrow or whenever — you may come in the morning, or at midday, or in the afternoon," and he began putting him off. Every day the monk went there and grew weary of it. A friend of his saw him and said: "Venerable, since you go there every day like this, is it the house of a relative of yours, or the house of a donor?" The monk replied: "Venerable, it is neither the house of a relative of mine nor the house of a donor. The thing is, my alms bowl cracked and I left it there for repair, and because he keeps putting me off, I go there for that reason." His friend said: "Venerable, have you not heard the saying that craftsmen who tell the truth are rare?"

When the craftsman said, "I do know the craft, but the Blessed One has not permitted it," the monks heard this and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, if there are monks who are craftsmen, I permit them to repair an alms bowl in a secluded place."

That monk went to the craftsman and said: "Venerable, the Blessed One has given permission — please repair this alms bowl." The craftsman replied: "Venerable, this cannot be repaired by bare hands alone; smithing tools are also needed." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I permit smithing tools to be kept for the use of the Saṅgha."

The setting is Śrāvastī.

When the robes of monks needed to be sewn, and they tore them apart by hand, causing damage, the Blessed One declared: "They are not to be torn by hand; they are to be cut with a small knife." When the Blessed One had declared that a small knife was to be used, a certain monk whose robe needed cutting borrowed a knife from a householder, cut the robe with it, and then returned it to that householder. The householder said: "Venerable, keep it — it is yours." The monk replied: "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted this." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, I permit a monk to carry a small knife."

When the Blessed One had declared that a small knife was to be carried, the group of six monks carried knives with handles polished smooth, made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Brahmins and householders said: "Venerable ones, what is this?" They replied: "The Blessed One has permitted knives." The brahmins and householders then said: "You ascetics are tormented by the pleasures of the senses!" At that, the monks fell silent out of embarrassment and said nothing. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk is not to carry a knife with a variegated or ornamented handle made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal. He is to carry an iron small-knife."

When the Blessed One had declared that an iron small-knife was to be carried, the monks carried knives that were far too large. Brahmins and householders said: "Venerable ones, what is this?" "Good sirs, it is a small knife." "Venerable ones, that is a knife — it is not a small knife." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Knives that are far too large are not to be carried." When monks carried knives that were far too small, they could not accomplish any task. The Blessed One then declared: "Three sizes of small knife are to be carried: large, medium, and small. The large one is six finger-widths. The small one is four finger-widths. What falls between these two is the medium."

The setting is Śrāvastī.

When the robes of monks needed to be sewn, the monks tried to sew them using bamboo splints and the quill-shafts of birds' feathers, and these split and frayed. The Blessed One declared: "A needle is to be carried." When a certain monk's robe needed sewing and he borrowed a needle from a householder and sewed it, then returned the needle to that householder, the householder said: "Venerable, keep it — it is yours." The monk replied: "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted this." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, I permit a monk to carry a needle."

When the Blessed One declared that a monk may carry a needle, the Group of Six began carrying needles made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. When brahmins and householders saw this, they asked: "Noble ones, what is this?" The monks replied: "The Blessed One has permitted needles." The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, you śramaṇas are surely afflicted by sensual pleasures." At that, the Group of Six fell silent and said nothing. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk shall not carry needles made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal. Rather, a monk shall carry needles of these four kinds: made of horn, copper, bamboo, or iron."

When the Blessed One declared that a monk shall carry needles of these four kinds, the monks set them down here and there, and the needles became embedded in the ground. The Blessed One then declared: "A needle case shall be carried." The monks did not know what kind of needle case to carry, so the Blessed One declared: "There are two kinds of needle case: one with a hollow tube, and one like a container with a stopper."

When the monks put a small knife into a needle case of the stopper type and it split, the Blessed One declared: "The small knife shall be made in two shapes: like a crow's beak, and like the wing of a white-tailed bird."

The occasion for this rule was at Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One declared that monks shall patch their Dharma robes, the monks stretched the robes out flat on the ground to even them, and the robes became soiled with dust and were damaged by insects. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not lay them on the ground to even them; instead, use a frame." The monks did not know how to make a frame, so the Blessed One declared: "There are two kinds of frame: those made square from wood, and those made square from bamboo."

When the monks pressed them with pegs and the frames split, the Blessed One declared: "Make holes and press them down with wooden pins."

The occasion for this rule was at Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One declared that robes are of three sizes — large, medium, and small — it was found that a frame used for stretching a large robe was not suitable for stretching a medium or small one. The Blessed One therefore declared: "Make several frames."

A summary verse:
Mirror and water,
likewise tooth-wood and the two cleaning sticks,
the topknot and long hair,
the warm gown and the great fever.

The occasion for this rule was at Śrāvastī.

The Group of Six, having put on their lower robes in the morning and taken up their bowls and outer robes, entered Śrāvastī for alms. They saw mirrors and other grooming implements that brahmins and householders had placed on a cloth for sweeping and cleaning. The Group of Six picked up those mirrors, examined their faces in them, and said: "Friend, dear friend — do we not look fine?" The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, your heads are shaved and your armpits are ragged — how could your faces be handsome? These śramaṇas are surely afflicted by sensual pleasures." The Group of Six said nothing in reply. The monks heard about this, reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a monk shall not examine his face in a mirror. If he does, he commits a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk shall not examine his face in a mirror, the monks then began examining their faces in water. The Blessed One declared:

"A monk shall not examine his face in water either." When the Blessed One had declared that a monk shall not examine his face in water, the monks happened to be examining the water, and upon seeing their own faces reflected there they felt remorse. The Blessed One then declared: "There is no transgression in looking at water, a wound, a wrinkle, or a sign of aging, or in examining the state of the body before and after."

The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī.

The Group of Six, having put on their lower robes and taken up their bowls and outer robes early in the morning, set out on alms-round in Śrāvastī. They saw some combs and hairbrushes that the brahmins and householders had placed on top of their clothing bundles. The Group of Six took their combs and combed their hair, then said: "Dear friend, dear friend — how do we look? Are we handsome?" The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, your heads are shaved and your armpits are ragged — how could your hair be beautiful? These śramaṇas are surely afflicted by sensual pleasures." The Group of Six said nothing in reply. The monks heard about this, reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a monk shall not comb his hair with a comb. If he does, he commits a serious offense." The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk shall not comb his hair with a comb, the Group of Six then began combing their hair with a bamboo comb. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not comb with a bamboo comb either. If one does, he commits a serious offense." The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk shall not comb his hair with a bamboo comb, they then made one side into a toothed comb and the other side into a bamboo comb and used it to comb their hair. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not comb the hair with both a comb and a bamboo comb." The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī.

Now, at the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered the Jeta Grove to the community of monks, the buddha and so forth — the rest of this account proceeds just as it was told before, including the one called the sweeper and so on. Ānanda said: "O handsome one, do you know how to arrange a topknot? That noble one is from my own household. Let him try. Noble one, how shall it be arranged?" "Large," he replied. The man arranged a great topknot. Ānanda said: "Cut one side." He cut one side. Then Ānanda said, "The second, the third" — and so on up to "Cut the seventh side" — and he cut up to the seventh side. Ānanda said: "You poor fool, you know nothing at all — do it just as it was before and go," and so on, the rest proceeding just as told before.

The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a monk shall not arrange a topknot. If he does, he commits a serious offense." The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī.

The venerable Vakkha was staying in Kauśāmbī, surrounded by a river, in the wild-boar's cave of the pleasure grove belonging to King Udayana. Then, on another occasion, when the spring season had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, and geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, grouse, cuckoos, and kalavinka birds were calling out in the grove, King Udayana summoned the caretaker of the pleasure grove and said: "Housekeeper, come here. Let us go to the pleasure grove. Clear away all the stones, gravel, and thorns from the ground around the river-encircled perimeter, lay out the pathways, and have the enclosures cleaned. Also drive away any predatory animals."

The caretaker of the pleasure grove replied to King Udayana, saying, "As Your Majesty commands." He cleared away all the stones, gravel, and thorns from the river-encircled perimeter, laid out the pathways, inspected the grove, and drove away the predatory animals. He then went to where King Udayana was and, having arrived, said to him: "May Your Majesty please take note. All the stones, gravel, and thorns have been cleared from the river-encircled ground, the pathways have been laid out, the grove has been inspected, and the predatory animals have been driven away. May Your Majesty know that the time has now come."

Then King Udayana, surrounded by his retinue of queens, went to the pleasure grove, where he experienced delight, sport, and festivity. After a while, he fell asleep.

Now, it is the nature of women to be fond of flowers and fruit, and so the queens' retinue wandered freely through the pleasure grove as they pleased. At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was sitting leaning against a tree, his hair and beard grown long, wearing an old monastic robe and a tattered lower garment.

The queens' retinue saw him sitting there with his hair and beard grown long, wearing an old monastic robe and a tattered lower garment. Upon seeing him, they cried out in alarm: "Oh gods! There is a demon here! Oh gods! There is a demon here!" With that cry of fright, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja rose from where he sat and walked slowly and deliberately into the wild-boar's cave.

The noise awoke the king, who drew his sword and rushed forward, asking the women, "Where is the demon?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it has gone into the wild-boar's cave." King Udayana then took up his weapon, stood at the entrance to the wild-boar's cave, and called out: "Hey, who are you, spirit?"

The reply came: "Your Majesty, I am a renunciant."

"Whose renunciant are you?"

"I am a renunciant of the sons of the Śākyas."

"Are you an arhat?"

"Your Majesty, I am not."

"Then are you a non-returner, a once-returner, or a stream-enterer?"

"Your Majesty, I am not."

"Then have you attained the fourth meditative concentration?"

"Your Majesty, I have not."

"Then have you attained the third, the second, or the first meditative concentration?"

"Your Majesty, I have not."

At this, the king, already further inflamed by jealousy toward the queens' retinue, became furious and said to his ministers: "Hey, wise ones! This ordinary renunciant has behaved improperly with my queens' retinue. Quickly gather a large number of sows here, and have them fill this cave and kill this renunciant."

Now, a deity who dwelt naturally in the wild-boar's cave thought to himself: "It would be wrong if this fierce king were to slay this blameless, faultless renunciant who has come to me for refuge. I must strive to find a means of saving him." With that thought, the deity manifested its own form as that of a great sow and emerged from the cave at the entrance.

The king, delighted by this sight, said to a man nearby: "Go and fetch my horse and bow and arrow." The man brought the king his horse and bow and arrow. The sow then came out from within the pleasure grove and began to run, and as the king chased after it, it led him far away.

Then the retinue of the queen's attendants said to the venerable Vālanasin: "Noble one, this king is fierce, and if he were to slay you it would be most unfortunate. You must leave quickly." The venerable Vālanasin swiftly took up his bowl and robes and departed from that pleasure grove, making his way to Śrāvastī.

When he arrived at Śrāvastī, the monks who saw him said: "Welcome, venerable one, welcome! You have been wandering long, long, like the moon moving through the sky. Where have you come from?" "From Kauśāmbī," he replied. "How has the venerable one fared? How have the venerable ones been keeping?" "The king of Vatsa, Udayana, struck and killed my pupil." "Why so?" And as he was explaining the matter in full, the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then said to one of the monks: "Monk, come here. Go to where the monk Vālanasin is and tell him this: 'The Teacher has said: come into my presence.'" That monk replied, "As you command, venerable one," and obeying the Blessed One's instruction, went to where the venerable Vālanasin was and said to him: "The Teacher has said: come into his presence."

The venerable Vālanasin replied to the monk, "As you command, venerable one," and heeding those words, went to where the Blessed One was. He arrived and bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet, then sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One said to the venerable Vālanasin: "Monk, why did the king of Vatsa, Udayana, strike and kill your pupil?" Vālanasin then explained the matter to the Blessed One in full.

The Blessed One said: "It is because you, foolish man, were excessively attached to that cave that you have come to dwell in such great suffering." And Vālanasin sat in silence.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that a minor fault had arisen among the monks — namely that of allowing hair to grow long — declared: "Therefore, monks shall not let their hair grow long. If they do, it becomes an offense." And when the Blessed One had declared that monks shall not let their hair grow long, the monks who dwelt in hermitages, finding no one to shave them, abandoned their hermitage lodgings and took up lodgings on the outskirts of villages.

The blessed buddhas know while appearing not to know. So the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why have the monks who dwell in hermitages abandoned their hermitage lodgings and taken up lodgings on the outskirts of villages?" Ānanda then explained the matter fully to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, for monks dwelling in hermitages, hair up to the length of two finger-breadths is permitted. For those dwelling on the outskirts of villages, it must be shorter than that."

The origin of this rule was at Śrāvastī. While at Śrāvastī, a sick monk went to a physician and said: "Good sir, please prescribe medicine for me." The physician said: "Noble one, sun yourself and warm your body, and you will recover." The monk said: "Good sir, am I to do whatever I please? Noble one, your medicine — this is the prescription, yet it will not sustain life through any other means." While this exchange was taking place, the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "If the physician says, 'Monk, your medicine is this, and you will not recover by any other means,' then the monk should use the sweat-bath as prescribed."

When the Blessed One had declared that the monk should use the sweat-bath, the monks asked that physician: "Good sir, now that the Blessed One has permitted it, tell us what exactly a sweat-bath is." He replied: "Noble ones, I have read the medical treatise of the wheel-turning king, and the word sweat-bath does appear there, but I have not yet ascertained precisely what kind of sweat-bath it is. Your own Teacher is omniscient — he himself knows it." Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Build a round sweat-bath house." When the windows of those houses did not fit, the Blessed One declared: "Install windows." When the windows were made wide on the outside and narrow on the inside, the Blessed One declared: "Make them narrow on the outside and wide on the inside, in the shape of a sea." When the monks set them too high and it became dark inside, the Blessed One declared: "Do not set them too high." When the monks set them too low and the smoke could not escape, the Blessed One declared: "Do not set them too low." When the monks did not know where to set them, the Blessed One declared: "Set them in the middle."

When sparrows and pigeons entered through the windows, the Blessed One declared: "Fit the windows with lattice screens." When wind and rain-spray came inside, the Blessed One declared: "Fit the windows with shutters." When the wind moved the shutters so that one could not sit comfortably, the Blessed One declared: "Insert pivot-fittings, ceiling pegs, and crossbars."

When the monks were troubled by drafts and the noise of the shutters opening and closing, the Blessed One declared: "Place a dry wooden stick nearby." When the door would not accept a door panel, the Blessed One declared: "Fit a door panel and also a door frame, and fit them with a peephole and a hand-rest as well."

When water was placed on the low side and it became cold, the Blessed One declared: "Build a raised platform inside and place the water vessels on it." When a fire was lit on the ground floor and it cracked and became unsuitable, the Blessed One declared: "Spread out a layer of brick tiles." When the monks spread out the fire and it died, the Blessed One declared: "Once spread out, do not discard it but rake it and let it rest." When the monks did not know how to rake it, the Blessed One declared: "Make an iron rake and use that to rake it."

When the monks entered while the fire was still blazing and became scorched, the Blessed One declared: "Do not enter while the fire is still blazing." When the monks entered and became drunk from the smoke of the fire, collapsing to the ground in a stupor, the Blessed One declared: "Mix flour with mustard oil and pour it onto the fire." When the smell became unpleasant, the Blessed One declared: "Pour incense onto the fire." When smoke caused the monks' eyes to water, the Blessed One declared: "Rinse the eyes with a wash of barley-beer." When they still watered, the Blessed One declared: "Rinse with a wash of āmalaka berry-beer."

When there were no seats and the monks took their own seats away with them, and those seats became smeared with oil, the Blessed One declared: "Place bundles of grass there." When their feet were soiled with dust from being placed on the ground, the Blessed One declared: "Spread grass on the floor."

When dry grass bundles were placed there and caught fire from sparks, the Blessed One declared: "Lay down fresh green grass." When green grass could not be found, the Blessed One declared: "Sweep with water and then lay it down."

When the monks became smeared with grain oil and chaff and husks stuck to their bodies and caused sores, the Blessed One declared: "Use an iron scraper." When the scraper was placed just anywhere and became unsuitable, the Blessed One declared: "Make a hole in the wall, fit a peg, and hang the scraper on it, keeping it away from contact with damp things."

When the scraper became greasy and the monks cleaned it again and again, the Blessed One declared: "Season it with fire." When the monks bathed there and it became muddy and soiled, the Blessed One declared: "Do not bathe there; build a bathhouse and bathe in it."

When those who bathed were troubled by the water, the Blessed One declared: "Dig a bathing pit, heat it with stones, and whoever bathes shall enter the pit while whoever pours the bath water sits at the edge and pours it in." When the pit filled with water, the Blessed One declared: "Make a drain-hole."

When the monks, after bathing, went to the monastery to fetch tooth-cleaning powder, cow dung, and tooth-sticks, the Blessed One declared: "Place baskets filled with tooth-cleaning powder, cow dung, and tooth-sticks in that very place."

When the monks were weakened by the heat of the fire, the Blessed One declared: "Have a boy blow on it." When their hands were scalded from blowing with their mouths, the Blessed One declared: "Use a bellows." When one monk found porridge from the boy's blowing to be far too hot, the Blessed One declared: "Drink it through the bellows tube." When a dressing of salt and leaves was needed and none could be found, the Blessed One declared: "Carry a salt pouch."

When the Blessed One declared that a sweeping task should be done in the bathhouse, the monks did not know who was to do the sweeping, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who lodge together and the attendants shall do it, each one for the other." Thus the bathhouse together with its requisites was approved.

The occasion for the preceding rules was at Śrāvastī.

At that time there was in Vaiśālī a great Licchavi named Mahāsenā who was without deceit or cunning and was by nature straightforward and honest. Each day he would go to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. Once, as he was going into the presence of the Blessed One, a monk who was a dear friend of his — who though born of the earth still wandered about the countryside — arrived in Vaiśālī, and the two of them saw each other on the road. The two said: "Great one, where are you going?" He replied: "Noble ones, I am going to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One." The two said that they knew the venerable Jātanora well, having been with him life after life, and then they said: "Great one, one is to bring a gift of words to the buddha, the Blessed One — do you have some small gift of words?" He replied: "Noble ones, I have none." "Great one, come here. Go to where the Blessed One is, and when you arrive say to the Blessed One: 'Venerable one, it is unsightly and improper that the noble Jātanora should have committed a defeat by engaging in unchaste conduct with my attendant.' And the Blessed One will be pleased with you." He agreed to do exactly as the two asked, and then —

He went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet. He then said to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, it is unsightly and improper that the noble Jātanora should have committed a defeat by engaging in unchaste conduct with my attendant." Having said this, he departed.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, the bowl-overturning ceremony is to be performed against the great Licchavī, and likewise against anyone else of that kind. The ceremony is to be performed as follows: having set out seats, the wooden sounding board is struck, and the monks are properly informed by way of the words of inquiry. When the entire Saṅgha is assembled and in harmony, a single monk, by a motion alone, shall perform the act: 'May the venerable ones of the Saṅgha please hear. Since the great Licchavī has falsely accused the venerable Jātanora, if it is the proper time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, the Saṅgha shall perform the bowl-overturning ceremony against the great Licchavī. This is the motion.' Against the one upon whom the Saṅgha has performed the bowl-overturning ceremony, monks shall not go to his house, shall not make use of his seats, shall not accept alms from him, and shall not teach him the Dharma."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and inform the great Licchavī with these words: 'The Saṅgha has performed the bowl-overturning ceremony against you.'" The venerable Ānanda replied "As you wish, venerable one," and having heeded the Blessed One's command, he went to where the great Licchavī's house was.

At that time the great Licchavī had gone out on some business. Ānanda spoke to his wife: "Sister, where has the great Licchavī gone?" She replied: "Noble one, he has gone out." "Sister, know this: the Saṅgha has performed the bowl-overturning ceremony against you." She said: "Venerable Ānanda, what is called the bowl-overturning ceremony?" "Sister, against the one upon whom the bowl-overturning ceremony has been performed, monks do not go to his house, do not make use of his seats, do not accept alms from him, and do not teach the Dharma. Noble Ānanda, by some stratagem the Saṅgha has cast aside my husband's good name — what offense have we committed against the Saṅgha that on account of it the bowl-overturning ceremony has been performed?" "Sister, your husband went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable one, it is unsightly and improper that the noble Jātanora should have committed a defeat by engaging in unchaste conduct with my attendant.' On account of that he became ashamed and entered the house, and then the venerable Ānanda departed."

When the great Licchavī arrived home, his wife said: "My lord's son, the Saṅgha has performed the bowl-overturning ceremony against you." He said: "Good woman, the bowl-overturning ceremony has been well performed. The bowl-overturning ceremony has been rightly performed. My lord's son, the bowl-overturning ceremony has been well performed. The bowl-overturning ceremony has been rightly performed." Then she asked: "Do you know what the bowl-overturning ceremony is?" "I do not know." "My lord's son, against the one upon whom the bowl-overturning ceremony has been performed, monks do not come to his house, do not make use of his seats, do not accept alms from him, and do not teach the Dharma. My lord's son, did you see the noble Jātanora together with me?" "Good woman, I did not see him." "Then why have you made a false accusation against the noble one?"

"If I likewise seek the forbearance of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, then well and good. But if I do not, you will not allow me into her house." Hearing this, he took it to heart and thought: "Since what she has said will come to pass just as she has spoken, I will go and seek forbearance." So he went before the Blessed One, and upon arriving he prostrated with his head at his feet and spoke these words: "Blessed One, my conduct has been like a single umbrella — I arose early as a Buddhist, and have come to pay reverence at the feet of the Blessed One. At the urging of a friendly monk and of the two earth-born ones, the great one has come here. You went to where the Blessed One was." Then, from that point all the way through "I committed unchaste conduct with my attending woman and incurred a defeat," everything was recited just as before. He then addressed the venerable one: "I ask that you bear with whatever fault I have committed."

Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, toward the great Licchavī, and toward anyone else similarly situated, the bowl-overturning ceremony is to be reversed. The reversal is to be performed as follows. Having set out the seats, the bell is struck, and the monks are properly informed with the words of the motion. Then, once the entire Saṅgha is seated and in harmony, the great Licchavī, having paid reverence, is to sit cross-legged at the edge of the elders' side and, with palms joined, is to say these words: 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. I, the great Licchavī, was deceived by a companion of bad conduct, and I falsely slandered the noble Jātanora. The Saṅgha performed the bowl-overturning ceremony against me. Now that the bowl has been overturned against me, I request the Saṅgha to reverse the bowl-overturning. May the venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, reverse the bowl-overturning for the great Licchavī, out of compassion for me.' This is to be repeated a second and third time. Then the great Licchavī is to be moved from the range of hearing into the range of sight, and a single monk is to perform the act by means of a single motion alone. It is to be done thus: 'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This great Licchavī, who was deceived by a companion of bad conduct, falsely slandered the venerable Jātanora. The Saṅgha performed the bowl-overturning ceremony against him. The great Licchavī upon whom the bowl has been overturned now requests that the bowl-overturning be reversed by the Saṅgha. If it is the appropriate time for the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha consents, may the Saṅgha grant it, and may the Saṅgha reverse the bowl-overturning for the great Licchavī.' This is the motion. To the one toward whom the bowl-overturning has been reversed, monks may go to his house, may make use of his seats, may accept alms, and may teach the Dharma."

Summary verse:
The limb-forms like a mirror,
dance and song and music's sound,
granting applause and tribute of speech —
together with the four concerning the bowl.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time a certain ascetic monk was residing in Śrāvastī. One day, when he was sitting cross-legged and settled, his limbs became fit for service. On another occasion, having made his round for alms and finished the meal, returning from the subsequent alms-round for food, he set down his bowl and robe, washed both feet, sat cross-legged at the foot of a tree, and entered upon mental application. Again his limbs became fit for service, and he acted in whatever way would bring about their pacification.

Because the mind changes quickly, when it was distracted, his limbs again and again became fit for service. Then, when he was utterly gripped by attachment, great aversion also arose in him, and he placed his member upon a stone and struck it with another stone. Tormented by a feeling of pain, he thought to himself: "While I am tormented by painful feelings, how strange it would be if the Blessed One took no notice." Thereupon the Blessed One, by the power of great compassion, came to that place and spoke: "Monk, what is the matter?" The monk explained what had occurred, and the Blessed One declared: "Monk, did I not say that the antidote to attachment is the meditation on the unattractive? The one who should be struck is the deluded one within you, yet you have struck another. What should be beaten is something else, and you have beaten something else." The monk sat in silence. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I guarantee that if you cultivate this one thing, you will become non-returners — and that is mindfulness directed toward the body. Monks, cultivate mindfulness directed toward the body, and I guarantee you will become non-returners. Therefore a monk should beat what should be beaten, and not beat what should not be beaten. If one beats the wrong thing, it becomes a serious offense." The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time there was in Śrāvastī a certain householder who had taken a wife from a family of equal rank, and he played with her, rejoiced with her, and made love with her. Through that play, joy, and lovemaking, a being entered into his wife's womb. Eight or nine months passed, and from the birth there came a boy of beautiful form, handsome and lovely to behold. Later, at another time, having gone forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, he was residing for a short time in a district, carrying his alms-bowl and robe, wandering through the region. While he was wandering about the district, a growth appeared on his face, and he had a physician cauterize it. His face then became unattractive. Later, at another time, he went to Śrāvastī, and a certain monk did not grant him entry. He went to another monk and said: "Venerable, do you not know me?" The monk replied: "If I do not know you, fair-faced one, who are you?" He said: "My name is such-and-such. I am the son of a certain great householder. I went forth right there, and came here from that district." The monk said: "Venerable, you have a fair face and a lovely complexion — why then has your face become unattractive?" When he explained all that had happened, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk's face is like a mirror, therefore a monk should not have a physician cauterize his face. If he does so, it becomes a serious offense." When the Blessed One had declared that a monk should not have a physician cauterize his face, if monks then had need of lancing due to swelling of blood, the monks refrained from lancing. The Blessed One declared: "Lancing may be done — one should have no remorse about this." The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time in Śrāvastī there were two festive assemblies: the merchants' festive assembly and the soldiers' festive assembly. Of these two, the merchants' festive assembly would defeat the soldiers' festive assembly with dance, song, and the sound of music; and the soldiers' festive assembly would defeat the merchants' festive assembly by means of weapons.

Then on another occasion the soldiers' festive assembly said amongst themselves: "Friends, these merchants have defeated us with dance, song, and the sound of music, while we have defeated them by means of weapons. By what means, then, might we also defeat them with dance, song, and the sound of music?" Some among them said: "Just so — we too should train in dance, song, and the sound of music." Others said: "Excellent! But from whom should we train?" And those replied: "The noble group of six are skilled in dance, song, and the sound of music — we should train from them. Since those monks are given to sensual pleasures, if we offer them even a small payment they will surely teach us." The others agreed: "Excellent! Let us give it just so." They went to where the group of six was staying, prostrated at their feet, and said: "Noble ones, please teach us dance, song, and the sound of music." Those monks replied: "Friends, if you give us our customary fee, we will teach you." The soldiers said: "Noble ones, we are poor — we offer you only a physician's fee." And those monks taught them dance, song, and the sound of music.

When the training was complete, the soldiers' assembly defeated the merchants' festive assembly both by means of weapons and with dance, song, and the sound of music. The merchants then said: "Good sirs, formerly you defeated us by weapons, and we defeated you with dance, song, and the sound of music. Now you have defeated us on both counts — what technique have you used?" They replied: "We have now trained." "Trained from whom?" "From the noble group of six." The merchants then said: "The conduct of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyan — it is a mockery. The conduct of the brahmins — it is a mockery. They teach even dance, song, and the sound of music!" And they derided them, they ridiculed them, and they spread slander about them.

At that juncture the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing that whatever fault had arisen among the monks had come about through their teaching dance, song, and the sound of music, declared: "Therefore a monk must not teach dance, song, and the sound of music. If one does so, it will constitute a serious offence."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not teach dance, song, and the sound of music, those festive assemblies forgot this ruling and went once again to the group of six, saying: "Noble ones, even though we are unworthy, please teach us again." Those monks replied: "Friends, the Blessed One has laid down a rule of training that monks must not teach dance, song, and the sound of music — we will not teach you." The soldiers said: "Noble ones, if you will not teach us, then at least come and rehearse along with us." Those monks replied: "Friends, very well — we will come." They went there and rehearsed with them, and the soldiers again defeated the merchants. Then once more — from "the conduct of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyan — it is a mockery, the conduct of the brahmins — it is a mockery" all the way through "they derided them, they ridiculed them, and they spread slander about them" — exactly as before.

At that juncture the monks again reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing that whatever fault had arisen among the monks had come about through their rehearsing dance, song, and the sound of music, declared: "Therefore a monk must not rehearse dance, song, and the sound of music. If one does so, it will constitute a serious offence." When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not rehearse dance, song, and the sound of music —

— rehearsing dance, song, and the sound of music — the good monks again forgot, and they went once more to the group of six monks and spoke accordingly. The group of six replied: "Good fellows, the Blessed One has forbidden it, so we will not rehearse." The group of six then said: "Noble ones, if you would just come and watch, that alone will defeat us." Thinking, "If that is so, let us go," the good monks went there, and the mere sight of those performances filled them with shame. The group of six then derided them, saying: "So much for the monks' way of a wandering ascetic (śramaṇa) in the sons of the Śākyas — the word 'monk' is all it is. So much for the brāhmin's way — the word is all it is. To think they would even come to watch dance, song, and the sound of music!" They mocked them, they ridiculed them, and they spread slander about them.

At that juncture the monks again reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing that whatever fault had arisen among the monks had come about through their going to watch dance, song, and the sound of music, declared: "Therefore a monk must not perform dance, must not take up song, must not make the sound of music, must not rehearse dance, song, and the sound of music, and must not go to watch them. Monks, if a monk studies dance, or studies song, or studies the sound of music, or rehearses dance, song, and the sound of music, or goes to watch them, it will constitute a serious offence."

The Minor Rules of Vinaya. The Fourth Fascicle.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time in Kauśāmbī there lived a householder named Supriya who possessed faith and had good and virtuous intentions. He took a wife from among his equals in lineage, and with her he played, took delight, and made merry. As they played and delighted and made merry together, after some time had passed a being entered the womb of his wife.

The venerable Śāriputra, perceiving that this being was ready to be trained, went to the householder's house, established the good-natured householder Supriya in the going for refuge and in the training precepts, and from time to time visited him. Now after some time had passed, the venerable Śāriputra went alone one day, without an attendant monk. The householder said: "Noble one, do you have no attendant monk?" He replied: "Good fellow, would an attendant monk come to me from a thicket of kāśa grass or a thicket of kuśa grass? Those who prove worthy of someone like you — they alone will become my attendant monks." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is so, then if the being who has entered my attendant's womb gives birth to a boy, I will offer that boy to the noble one as an attendant monk." "Good fellow, may you be free from illness," Śāriputra said, and departed.

In time the householder's wife carried the child for nine full months and gave birth, and the boy who was born had an unfortunate complexion and a small body, yet a beautiful voice. His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day after the birth they held a great birth celebration and set about naming the boy. The relatives said: "Although this boy has an unfortunate complexion and a small body, he is the son of Householder Supriya, and he has a beautiful voice; therefore let this boy's name be Supriya, after the beautiful." And so he was given the name Supriya, meaning "the beautiful." He was cared for and raised and grew to be grown.

Then the venerable Śāriputra dressed himself in his lower robe in the early morning, took up his alms-bowl and his Dharma robe, and entered Kauśāmbī for alms. As he went about collecting alms in Kauśāmbī he came to the home of the householder Supriya, and the householder Supriya, pronouncing the words of welcome, "How good that the noble one has come," greeted him and bowed at his feet. Supriya's wife then filled the alms-bowl with clean and wholesome cooked food and offered it to him. The boy looked into the face of the venerable Śāriputra, and Śāriputra made a gesture to the householder Supriya, whereupon Supriya said to the boy: "My son, even before you were born I had already offered you as a personal attendant to the noble Śāriputra. Go now and accompany the noble one." The being who was in his last existence, following along behind him, was then by Śāriputra given the going-forth and granted full ordination. He received scriptural instruction and, through effort, exertion, and striving, came to know directly that this very wheel of cyclic existence, with its five spokes, whether in motion or at rest, is of a nature in which all formations decay, fall away, scatter apart, and disintegrate. Overwhelmed by this realization, and having abandoned every affliction, he actualized arhatship directly. As an arhat freed from attachment in the three realms, he abided with a mind like a stone of equal weight set against bronze and gold, like space and the palm of the hand in their evenness, like sandalwood soaked and placed aside. He split open the shell of the cave of his rebirth-door, attained the higher knowledges, the superknowledges, and the individual analytical knowledges. He turned his back on gain and honor bound up with existence and desire. He became one worthy of offering, of worship, and of reverent address by the gods together with Indra (Śakra) and their attendants.

Whenever he taught the Dharma with the resonance of his voice, it pervaded everything as far down as the world of Brahmā, and in the streams of many sentient beings it produced virtuous roots conducive to liberation. Indeed, even those sentient beings who belonged to the realm of animal rebirth would prick up their ears and listen to that beautiful sound.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Among my śrāvaka monks of beautiful voice, this monk, Supriya of the beautiful voice, is the foremost. Such is the pleasing quality of his voice and the beauty of his delivery that monks who had not yet parted from attachment would abandon their own affairs and go to listen to him every single day."
