Now, at a certain other time, the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, was riding upon a single great white-lotus elephant, his chief elephant, with the mahout Śrīvarddhana guiding it, and in the early morning hours the two went out to a rocky cliff. At that moment the venerable Supriya of the beautiful voice began to teach the Dharma with the resonance of his voice, and the chief white-lotus elephant heard it. Upon hearing the resonant voice of the venerable Supriya of the beautiful voice, the elephant pricked up its ears and stood utterly motionless. The mahout Śrīvarddhana flapped his hands and feet repeatedly from both sides to urge it on, but still it would not move. The king said: "Śrīvarddhana, the elephant won't come even when struck — what is the reason for this? I cannot fathom it." The king said: "Leave it be; let us see which way it will go." He left it as it pleased, and it turned away from the Jeta Grove and went step by step right to the Jeta Grove, and there at the gate of the Jeta Grove it stood with its ears pricked, listening. When the venerable Supriya of the beautiful voice had finished teaching the Dharma with the resonance of his voice,

Whatever beings have gathered here, whether dwelling on the earth or in the intermediate sky, may they always cherish loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and may they practice the Dharma by day and by night.

With this complete dedication having been made, the chief among the great elephants, the one with a single white lotus mark, knew that the venerable Supriya of the Beautiful Voice had come to the end of teaching the Dharma with the resonance of his voice, and so it went wherever its mind inclined, moving here and there as it pleased.

The king said: "Śrīvarddhana, why does it go wherever it pleases like this?" He replied: "Your Majesty, I beg your pardon — this elephant heard the sounds of a noble one teaching the Dharma with the resonance of his voice, and its mind was captivated; it has lost all self-control." The king said: "Śrīvarddhana, bring the elephant back, seek out that noble one, offer him a robe, and tomorrow morning go to the rocky cliffs." He replied: "As Your Majesty commands." He turned back and went home. The queen Mālyavatī asked him: "My lord, why have you returned?" He told her what had happened, and then said: "Mālyavatī, give me a robe — I will go and offer it to that noble one." She thought to herself: "To think that the noble Supriya of the Beautiful Voice taught the Dharma with the resonance of his voice — he is of unsightly complexion and small of body, and this king is drawn to the grand and magnificent. If the king were to see him, there is a possibility he might lose his faith. I must employ some skillful means." So she said: "Your Majesty, please go to the rocky cliffs. I myself will offer the robe to that noble one." He replied: "Mālyavatī, you too should offer another robe. Would a single robe from both of us impoverish the palace of Kosala?" She said nothing and remained silent, and the king took a robe befitting a great one and went to the Jeta Grove.

At that time the venerable Ānanda was walking back and forth and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove. When the king had dismounted from the elephant and prostrated at his feet with both knees, he said: "Noble one, where is the noble one who was teaching the Dharma with the resonance of his voice earlier tonight?" He replied: "Great king, why do you seek him? You wish to offer him a robe." He thought: "If the venerable Supriya of the Beautiful Voice has been teaching the Dharma with the resonance of his voice — he is of unsightly complexion and small of body, and this king is drawn to the grand and magnificent. If the king were to see him, there is a possibility he might lose his faith. I must employ some skillful means." So he said: "Great king, give it to me, and I will offer it to him on your behalf." The king replied: "Noble one, the Blessed One has praised giving with one's own hand — so please show me him, that I may offer it with my own hand."

At that time the venerable Supriya of the Beautiful Voice was resting in the shade of a tree for his daytime abiding. Then the venerable Ānanda said: "Great king, he is resting there in the shade of a tree — please go." The king went to where he was and looked, and in that moment he saw that he was exceedingly unattractive. Disbelief arose in him; displeased, he turned his face away, threw down the robe, and left.

At that moment the venerable Supriya of the Beautiful Voice spoke these verses:

Those who look upon my form
and follow along after my voice,
those people, governed by desire,
shall not truly see me.

But one who knows inwardly
and does not look to outer things,
one who sees the inner fruit —
that one will be led by the voice alone.

If one knows inwardly,

and sees outward things,
and sees the outward fruit —
that one too will be led by the voice alone.

But if one knows neither inwardly
nor sees outward things at all,
those children utterly bewildered —
they too will be led by the voice alone.

Yet one who knows inwardly
and likewise sees outward things,
that one, firm and inclined toward wisdom,
will not be led by the voice at all.

At that moment the monks were seized by doubt, and they asked the Blessed One, the buddha, to cut through all their doubts: "Venerable one, what karma did the elder, the venerable Supriya of the Beautiful Voice, perform, such that through its ripening he came to have an ugly complexion and a small body yet a beautiful voice?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, know that the son of good family, Supriya of the Beautiful Voice himself, found a collection of karma, gathered conditions like a flame drawing close, and caused things that were inevitably going to arise to be performed and accumulated. Who else but Supriya of the Beautiful Voice himself would experience individually what he has done and accumulated? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

Actions do not decay even across a hundred aeons;
when the gathering and the time arrive,
their fruits will come to be
for those who bear a body.

Monks, long ago in a time that has passed, in this very good aeon, when the lifespan of beings was forty thousand years, there arose in the world a Teacher — a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide who tames persons, a teacher of gods and humans, a Blessed One, a buddha — known as Saṃvartanīya. Having performed all the deeds of a buddha, he passed into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates, like a fire gone out when the fuel is exhausted.

King Bhadra then made extensive offerings to the body of that Blessed One, the buddha Saṃvartanīya, and set about having stūpas built encircling the area, each one a league in circumference, and two and a half leagues high. To carry out this work he appointed a certain labourer — a man of different faith but good disposition, of virtuous intention, and diligent in his labor. There was also another labourer who, upon seeing that such a very great stūpa was being built, began to mock the work, saying to those of discerning eye: "I do not know when this king will ever finish building such an enormous stūpa." At that, the labourer whose wages were being paid said: "Hey, fellow! Why do you mock? If it cannot be done, leave the work alone." The mocker fell silent, and the paid labourer then began to drive him away from the site. The mocker begged his pardon and resumed his work. But the stūpa was not yet complete when the mocker again began to mock, and the paid labourer drove him off again. He then begged pardon very earnestly, resumed his work once more, and in the end there was completed a stūpa so magnificent and inexhaustible to behold that it captivated the eyes and minds of many hundreds of thousands of creatures.

Then the paid labourer, seeing what had been accomplished, felt remorse arise within him, thinking: "While this work was being done, I acted badly toward him by mocking him." He resolved to honour that one in every way, and so from the wages he himself had received he had a golden bell made and, with a mind filled with sincere devotion, hung it upon that stūpa.

Monks, the one who at that time was the paid labourer is none other than this very monk Suvarṇabhadra. And because of the karmic ripening of his having mocked the work done on the stūpa of a perfectly awakened buddha that destroys cyclic existence, he was born with a dull complexion and a small body. And because of the karmic ripening of his having, once faith arose in him, caused a golden bell to be made and hung it upon the stūpa, he came to possess a beautiful voice.

Then the monks again gave rise to doubt, and they put their question to the awakened Blessed One, the cutter of all doubt: "Venerable One, what deed did the long-lived Suvarṇabhadra perform such that his voice filled everything down from the Brahmā world?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, from the point at which this son of good family, Suvarṇabhadra himself, obtained the accumulation of karma, onward through to the point of becoming those results — all of that is just as before.

"Monks, long ago in a time now past, in this very auspicious aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the guide of persons to be tamed, the unsurpassed one, the Teacher of gods and humans — the awakened Blessed One Kāśyapa. He was dwelling near Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park of the sage who speaks truth, residing there in dependence upon that place.

"Between Vārāṇasī and the grove of the sage who speaks truth there stood a mango tree, and in that tree dwelt a male cuckoo bird. At the time when the awakened Blessed One Kāśyapa was going into Vārāṇasī for alms, the bird, regarding him with great attention, let forth a distinctly beautiful and pleasing call, and looked upon him again and again in just that way. Growing satisfied in mind, faith arose in him.

"On another occasion, while giving voice to its call, the bird circumambulated the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa three times, and joy and happiness arose in it, and it then settled once more in that same mango tree. The very moment it alighted, a hawk snatched away its life, and at the moment of death it died and was born as a brahmin skilled in the six branches of learning.

"Monks, the one who at that time was that cuckoo bird is none other than this very monk Suvarṇabhadra. And because of the karmic ripening of his having let forth a beautiful call and performed circumambulation before the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, his voice came to fill everything down from the Brahmā world."

Then the monks again gave rise to doubt, and they put their question to the awakened Blessed One, the cutter of all doubt: "Venerable One, what deed did the long-lived Suvarṇabhadra perform such that through the karmic ripening of that deed he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized arhathood — and was declared supreme among those with beautiful, resounding voices by the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One declared: "That was by the power of aspiration. Where was that aspiration made? In the very teaching of the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa there was a monk who had gone forth, and him the Blessed One Kāśyapa declared supreme among those with beautiful, resounding voices."

Yet in that life, having practiced the holy life for as long as he lived without attaining any accumulation of virtuous qualities, when he came to die he spoke thus: "In the presence of the Blessed One, the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, I practiced the holy life for as long as I lived without attaining any accumulation of virtuous qualities. By this root of virtue of mine — since the Blessed One, the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, gave a prophecy to the brahmin youth Blama saying, 'O brahmin youth, in a future age, when human lives span a hundred years, there will appear a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened buddha named Śākyamuni' — may I go forth in the teaching of that one whose prophecy was given, and by abandoning all afflictions directly realize arhathood. And just as this preceptor of mine was declared by the Blessed One, the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, to be supreme among those with beautiful, resounding voices, so too may I be declared by that Blessed One to be supreme among those with beautiful, resounding voices." By the power of that aspiration so made, he has now gone forth in my teaching, and by abandoning all afflictions has directly realized arhathood. And I have declared this monk to be supreme among those with beautiful, resounding voices.

Monks, therefore the karmic maturation of deeds that are purely dark — from "purely dark" all the way through to "monks, you should train in this way" — is as before.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now it happened that when the monks were reciting the Dharma, they recited it scattering the words about like a shower of pine seeds, while the non-Buddhists recited their texts in a melodious, resonant voice.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada was in the habit of rising early each morning and going to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. One morning, as he was on his way, he heard the non-Buddhists reciting their texts in a melodious, resonant voice. He thought to himself: "The Dharma and discipline of the non-Buddhists is wrongly spoken — and yet they recite their texts in a melodious, resonant voice. My noble ones, on the other hand, when they recite they scatter the words like a shower of pine seeds. This is a matter I must address."

He went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived he touched his head to the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable One, the Dharma and discipline of the non-Buddhists is wrongly spoken — and yet they recite their texts in a melodious, resonant voice. The noble ones, when they recite, scatter the words about like a shower of pine seeds. If the Blessed One would therefore permit the noble ones also to recite the texts in a melodious, resonant voice, that would be excellent."

The Blessed One said nothing, and by his silence gave consent. Understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada touched his head to the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks and declared: "Monks, you are therefore permitted to recite the Dharma in a melodious, resonant voice."

When the Blessed One had declared that the Dharma was to be recited in a melodious, resonant voice, the monks proceeded to recite, chant, and intone the scriptures in melodious, resonant voices, repeating and rehearsing them fully.

Now, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the Jeta Grove, he heard this and said: "Noble ones, what is this — have you set up a musician's lodge in this temple of yours?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks are not to recite scriptures, chant, intone, or rehearse them in a melodious, resonant voice. However, the proper proclamation of the Teacher's qualities and the chanting of texts set to three melodic modes are to be chanted in a melodious, resonant voice."

When the Blessed One had declared that those should be chanted in a melodious, resonant voice, a certain young monk, not knowing how to produce a melodious, resonant voice, proceeded to teach the texts in such a way that, as he taught, it was like scattering a heap of pine cones — all in a jumble. The monks said to him: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has permitted the melodious voice; please let it come forth in a melodious voice." He replied: "Venerable ones, I do not know how to produce a melodious, resonant voice."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should train in the melodious, resonant voice."

When the Blessed One had declared that one should train in the melodious, resonant voice, the monks were practicing the melodious tones in the cloisters, the dwelling halls, and the gateway chambers. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to the temple and, having heard this, said: "Noble ones, if this temple is not a musician's lodge, have you still not dismissed the musicians?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should train in the melodious, resonant voice in a secluded place."

The Blessed One, the buddha Bhagavān, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

A monk was standing and bringing out his alms bowl, and the other monks said to him: "Venerable one, do not bring out the alms bowl while standing." He replied: "What is wrong with it?" They said: "The bowl may break — but what else is wrong?" He fell silent, and at that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "A monk should not bring out the alms bowl while standing. And likewise, for placing it in water, washing it, and drying it — these are to be elaborated upon in full."

Summary verse:

A narrow path, and the three vessels,
not to be placed in a net-like manner,
and the canopy, and the inseparable —
these the Great Sage permitted.

The Blessed One, the buddha Bhagavān, was dwelling among the sons of Śākyamuni, on a frightful forested mountain, the haunt of wild beasts, in the land of crocodiles, in the place of the slaughter of children.

At the time when Prince Youthful Rtogs ldan had a fine mansion called Lotus Palace painted with a hundred and one colors, and had long-fringed cotton cloths spread out in abundance, and invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas for midday, the Blessed One, intending to go to the Lotus Palace, had not yet gone. Prince Youthful Rtogs ldan said: "Blessed One, please come." Yet the Blessed One still had not gone.

When Prince Youthful Rtogs ldan gathered up the cloths, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) heard of this and said among themselves: "Wise ones, the renunciant Gautama is not worthy of such honor."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, if faithful brahmins and householders have laid down long-fringed cotton cloths even on narrow paths and say, 'Noble ones, please come out of compassion for us,' then, in order to overwhelm the non-Buddhists, one should go, bearing in mind impermanence so as to overwhelm them. There is no remorse in this."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Aṅgaspoṅ (Aṅga's Shore), on a mountain infested with crocodiles, a frightening forested hillside and habitat of wild beasts. A monk was walking along carrying his alms bowl in his hand when he turned aside in another direction, and the bowl fell to the ground and broke, thereby becoming an impediment to him. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore a monk should not carry his alms bowl in his bare hand, but should place it in a bowl-bag and carry it thus."

After the Blessed One had declared that a monk should not carry his alms bowl in the bare hand but should place it in a bowl-bag and carry it, the monks put their bowls in bowl-bags and walked along carrying them in their very hands, and that same fault arose again. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not carry the bowl-bag in the hand; one should attach a strap and carry it under the arm."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The monks were wandering through the countryside together with like-minded companions. At a certain point a brahmin who was ill went to a physician and said: "Great master, please prescribe medicine for an illness of such and such a kind." The physician said: "Sir, eat āruṟa fruit and you will recover." The brahmin said: "Where is āruṟa to be found along this road?" The physician said: "These renunciants who are sons of the Śākya are learned; if you ask them, they are likely to have some."

The brahmin went to the monks and asked: "Noble ones, do you happen to have any āruṟa?" They said: "Brahmin, if we do, what is it for?" He replied: "A physician has told me to seek āruṟa. If you have any, I humbly request that you give it to me." One of the monks opened his bowl-bag before the brahmin, and right there was some young bamboo, and right there was a small knife, and right there were cords, and right there were various medicines. The brahmin, seeing this, said: "Noble ones, your way of life is impure! It would be better for me to die than to eat something so impure — eating what is impure is not like that at all!" At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Three kinds of receptacle are to be maintained: the alms-bowl bag, the medicine bag, and the miscellaneous-articles bag."

When the monks attached equal-length straps to all of these, the straps bruised their armpits, and when the Blessed One had declared: "Attach wide straps," they attached wide straps but these chafed them. Then the Blessed One declared: "Fasten a cushioning pad to them, and rub them from time to time with crow-foot grease to make them supple."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A monk found a piece of cloth and thought to himself: "The Blessed One has declared that the three robes are to be cut and stitched." So he took a small knife and needle and went to the foot of a leafy tree. The Blessed One also proceeded in that direction, saw him, and asked: "Monk, what are you doing?"

He replied: "Venerable Blessed One, since you declared that monks are to cut and stitch the three robes, I found this piece of cloth and it seemed suitable for a robe."

Thereupon the Blessed One spoke words of praise for reverence toward the training, and declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, the following five things are not to be woven into cloth: all wool from a young animal, all goat hair, all plain raw cloth, all hemp fiber, and all coarse jute fiber."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk had gone to another monastery on some business, and he was caught there by nightfall. The one in charge of lodgings said to him: "Venerable one, please take a sleeping place." He replied: "I have brought my mat and will not be needing one." The one in charge of lodgings said: "In that case, please take a bed with a frame." He took the framed bed and lay down, but during the night he fell ill, having been afflicted by the suffering of cold. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore a monk must not travel without a sleeping mat. If he does, he commits an offense."

After the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not travel without a sleeping mat, the monks, wishing to return that very same day, would go to other monasteries nearby, go for their daily walking rounds, and go to other villages, and when they brought their mats along on those journeys, the elderly senior monks who were aged and frail, and the sick who could not endure the exertion, became exhausted. Then, in circumstances where it was recorded that even for those journeys where one intends to return the very same day, going without a mat was not permitted, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, when a monk goes to the vicinity or goes on his daily round, he need not carry a mat. When going to another village intending to return the same day, he also need not carry one. When other monks who have no mat go to another village intending to return the same day and circumstances of that nature arise, and night overtakes them there, those who are respectful of the training may borrow a mat for the night from fellow celibates. If one is found, excellent. If none is found, one should fold the upper robe into four layers, lay it down, and pass the night lying on it briefly, but not for a prolonged time."

A certain monk borrowed a mat from another monk, and that monk suffered a nocturnal emission in it and it became defiled. When the same monk then began to return the mat and the owner was unwilling to accept it, the procedure from that point onward is the same as before. The Blessed One declared: "It should be washed and then returned." When that monk washed it and returned it, but the owner still refused to accept it, the procedure up to that point is likewise as before. The Blessed One declared: "Give him the price of cleaning it, or satisfy him in some way."

Monks, other monasteries and

other villages, intending to return that very day, had set out without their three robes, and those who had gone there found themselves in such circumstances that they were forced to spend the night. When, out of respect for the training, they went out at night, they encountered lions, tigers, bandits, and deceivers. On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If those who set out with such an intention are then compelled to spend the night there, they should remain in that place and borrow robes from fellow practitioners of the holy life, then have them consecrated. If those monks do not know how to consecrate borrowed robes, the Blessed One declared: "Consecrate them by means of the mental act of one who previously took them out." These five are accomplished by mental resolve alone: the restoration ceremony, the invitation ceremony, the consecration of robes, the removing of robes, and the inviting of a person as a guest.

When those monks found robes that were worn and unfaded, the Blessed One declared: "If worn and unfaded robes are found, consecrate those worn and unfaded robes. If robes that are unfaded and unworn are found, dye and treat them as appropriate, then consecrate them. If such can be found, well and good. If they cannot be found, consecrate them as they are. Even a layperson's garment may be consecrated, and in doing so one should feel no remorse."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Two monks who had paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One set out for Śrāvastī from the south road. On the way their water ran out, and tormented by the suffering of thirst, they went to the edge of a small pond. One of the two said to the other: "Venerable, you quickly examine the water and drink it." He began to examine it, and when he found that the water was impure, he spoke this verse:

For a thousand hundred thousand aeons
one so rarely comes to see the Guide.
Let me drink of this water now,
and then behold the one who leads.

The other then spoke this verse:

He who feels in his heart compassion for all sentient beings,
who has utterly abandoned all attachment to existence,
by training in this supreme teaching of his
one gives up one's own life, but does not take the life of living creatures.

Then the one who drank the water departed. The one who did not drink roused his diligence and sat down at the foot of a great tree. For as long as his bodily strength remained, he engaged in wholesome deeds, and when at last his bodily strength was exhausted and the moment of death arrived, he was born among the gods of the four great kings. He became a son of the gods, or —

It is the nature of a divine daughter that, not long after she is born, three things arise in her mind: from where she passed away, where she was born, and by what karma she was born. That one saw that she had passed away from among human beings, been born among the gods of the four great kings, and been born there through the mind of manifest faith in the Blessed One.

Then the former monk, now a son of the gods, thought to himself: "It would not accord with my station to attend to my settled dwelling and go near the Blessed One in order to look upon him and pay him homage; I will go near the Blessed One without attending to any settled dwelling, in order merely to look upon him and pay him homage."

So the former monk, now a son of the gods, with his earrings and ear ornaments swaying and spotless, his body adorned with garlands and bracelets, filled his robe with divine flowers — blue lotuses, red lotuses, white night-lotuses, white lotuses, and māndārava blossoms — and with a radiance exceedingly brilliant, in the depths of the night, went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he showered the Blessed One with flowers, bowed his head at the two feet of the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. And it was such that through the shining power of that former monk's radiance, the entire Jeta Grove was suffused with a vast brilliance.

Then the Blessed One, having understood with his mind the former monk's aspiration, his underlying tendencies, his temperament, and his character, and having heard what he had heard, taught Dharma to him as he sat right there on that seat — teaching that causes one to thoroughly and individually realize the four noble truths, just as, by the vajra of gnosis, the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the view that apprehends the self among the aggregates) is shattered while one sits, and the fruit of stream-entry is directly attained.

He then saw the truth, and said aloud three times this solemn declaration to the Blessed One: "This that the revered Blessed One has done for me — not even my father did it for me, not my mother, not a king, not the gods, not my ancestors of former times, not ascetics and brahmins, not the assembly of friends, close companions, and kinsmen. He has dried up the ocean of blood and tears; he has freed me from mountains of bones; he has closed the doors of the lower realms; he has opened the doors of the higher realms and liberation; he has lifted my feet out of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; and he has established me among gods and humans."

Then he also spoke in verse:

By your power I, brimming with pride and laden with many faults,
have had the track to the lower realms blocked and, richly endowed with merit,
have had the path to the higher realms opened — and I myself
have come to reach the further shore of nirvāṇa as well.

Relying on you, supremely pure, today I myself
have obtained a flawless and pure eye,
and rejoicing, have reached the noble, peaceful state of liberation —
I have crossed beyond the ocean of suffering.

You, a sage venerated by beings — asuras, humans, and gods —
freed from birth, aging, sickness, and death,
who sees existence as empty — a rarity supreme —
today there is fruit in my having seen you.

Then, with his robe-end streaming and his garlands hanging free,
he bowed at your feet and joy arose within him,
and circumambulating to the right — the Subduer of Foes —
he rose into the sky, toward the divine world before him.

Then that former monk, the son of the gods, became like a merchant who has found a great profit, like a farmer whose crops have come to fullness, like a hero who has conquered in battle, like a sick man who has been freed from every illness — and in the very same attire in which he had come before the Blessed One, he departed for his own abode.

As for the other monk, he too went straightway to Śrāvastī.

Then, having set down the bowl and robe, he washed his feet and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side.

It is the very nature of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to gladden with genuine gladness a monk who has arrived unexpectedly, saying: "Monk, where have you just come from? Where did you spend the rains retreat?" And so the Blessed One gladdened that monk with genuine gladness, asking him: "Monk, where have you come from? Where did you spend the rains retreat?"

The monk replied: "Venerable One, I have just now come from the south. I spent the rains retreat in the south."

The Blessed One said: "Monk, do you have a fellow monk as a companion?"

"Blessed One, yes."

"Where has he gone? Tell me what happened to him."

Then, at that moment, the Blessed One spoke this verse:

Whoever holds no reverence for my Teaching —
what benefit is it to them to see me?
Even if they look upon me with their eyes,
they neither truly see me nor make true offering.

But the monk who trains in what I teach —
that monk truly sees me.
You, whose wisdom is shallow,
have not seen the Buddha face to face.

Then the Blessed One parted the upper robe from his own body and spoke yet another verse:

Look at this body, monk —
pure, with the color of gold,
born of the ripening of former karma
and arising from father and mother.

One who has not seen the nature of reality
has not seen the fully awakened buddha.
One who has seen the nature of reality
has seen the Great Sage.

Furthermore, one who is steadfast, possessed of a wholesome mind,
and who carefully guards the training —
such a one sees me first
in the form body and in the dharmakāya.

The great being Kāśyapa,
who had transgressed the bounds of training in times past —
even now the ālā leaf has not freed him
from the birthplaces of the nāgas.

The Blessed One then reflected: whatever fault had arisen was due to monks not keeping water filters with them. Therefore monks should keep water filters at hand.

When the Blessed One had spoken the rule that monks should keep water filters at hand, the monks did not know how many kinds of water filters there were. The Blessed One then declared: "There are five kinds of water filters: the triangular water filter, the pot filter with a spout, the ball-shaped filter with a foot, the hanging filter, and the straining filter."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī, two monks who were on bad terms with each other were walking about on tour together. Of these two, one had a water filter and the other did not. The one who had it drew up water and drank, and the one who had none said: "Venerable one, lend me your water filter." The other did not give it, and at that point the second monk was left without. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, therefore a monk should not go on tour together with one with whom he is on bad terms. If such a circumstance does arise, they should ask forbearance of each other and proceed."

The Miscellaneous Matters of the Vinaya, the fifth fascicle.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī two monks were walking about on tour together. Of these two, one had a water filter and the other did not. The one without asked the other: "Do you have a water filter?" The other replied: "I do." But he did not say whether he would lend it or not. Of the two, the one who had the filter drank the water, and the one without said: "Venerable one, lend me your water filter." The other replied:

"Venerable one, you asked me whether I had a water filter, but you did not ask whether I would lend it or not. Since you showed no respect, why should I give you my water filter? I will not give it. Be on your way."

Because he did not give it to him, the other monk was left in difficulty. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk who wishes to travel and who has no water filter should ask his fellow monk: 'Do you have a water filter or not?' If the other says 'I do,' he should say: 'Will you lend it to me or not?' If the other says 'I will lend it,' he may proceed on his journey; otherwise he should not go."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī two monks set out together on tour. Of the two, one had a water filter and the other did not. The one without asked the other: "Do you have a water filter or not?" The other replied: "I do." "Will you lend it to me or not?" "I will lend it."

They set out, and after some time, while they were on the road, some travellers came along. The business for which the monk with the water filter needed it was accomplished by those very travellers. He then began to turn back, and the other monk said to him: "Venerable one, you promised me the water filter — hand it over." The other replied: "Well, if that is so, I gave it to you for straining water — I did not give it to you for absolutely everything and in every circumstance." Since he did not give it, the other was left in difficulty. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"A monk who has no water filter should ask his fellow monk: 'Do you have a water filter or not?' If the other says 'I do,' he should ask: 'Will you lend it to me or not?' If the other says 'I will lend it,' he should ask: 'If you should turn back or go elsewhere, will you lend it or not?' If the other says 'I will,' he may proceed on his journey; otherwise he should not go."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Upavāna asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, is it permitted to go to another monastery or another village without a water filter?" Upavāna replied on his own behalf: "It is not permitted." "If one goes there and will not be left in difficulty, it is permitted."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Upavāna asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, is it permitted for two monks to travel on tour with a single water filter between them?" Upavāna replied on his own behalf: "If they go there and will not be left in difficulty, it is permitted." "Venerable one, is it permitted for many monks, or for members of the Saṅgha, to travel on tour with a single water filter?" Upavāna replied: "If they go there and will not be left in difficulty, it is permitted."

"Venerable one, is it permitted to travel along the bank of a river without a water filter?" Upavāna replied: "It is permitted. For a swift-flowing river, one should examine the water at each league to check that it has not mixed with other water. If it has mixed with other water, one should examine it at whatever point one draws it. For a slow-flowing river, one should examine it bank by bank."

"In this context, a swift river is one whose current runs quickly. A slow river is one whose current runs sluggishly."

"Venerable one, what is the vicinity of the bank?" Upavāna replied: "It is exactly one fathom all around."

"Venerable one, is it permitted to go seeking water that has not been strained and has not been examined?" Upavāna replied: "It is not permitted." "Venerable one, is it permitted to go seeking water that has not been strained but has been examined?" Upavāna replied: "It is permitted, on the understanding that it is pure to the eye."

"Venerable one, is it permitted to go seeking water that has been strained and examined?" Upavāna replied: "It is permitted in the vicinity, all around."

"However, there are five kinds of permissible water: water permitted by the Saṅgha, water permitted by an individual, water permitted by a water-strainer, water permitted by a spring, and water permitted by a well.

Of these, water permitted by the Saṅgha is water that has been strained by a monk appointed by the unanimous consent of the Saṅgha. Such water permitted by the Saṅgha is to be used by monks.

Water permitted by an individual is water that has been rendered completely pure by a monk whose moral discipline is unimpaired, whose view is unimpaired, whose conduct is unimpaired, and whose livelihood is unimpaired. Such water permitted by an individual is to be used by monks.

Water permitted by a water-strainer is water strained through a strainer that has never been impure. Such water is to be drunk.

Water permitted by a spring is water that flows naturally.

Water permitted by a well is water from a well whose water is pure, drawn after sunset and drinkable until the following sunrise. Such water permitted by a well is to be drunk."

When the monks grew confused from examining water for too long, the Blessed One declared: "Examine it only as much as one trusts — just enough to fill a cart of six oxen loaded with bamboo."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the monastery given by the prince Jeta. When faithful brahmins and householders came to offer fingerbowls to the monks, the monks would not accept them. Those donors said: "Noble ones, in the time before the Blessed One, the Buddha, arose in the world, the non-Buddhists were the worthy recipients. Now that the Blessed One, the Buddha, has arisen in the world, you are the worthy recipients. If you will not accept, must we die passing from this world to the next without having made provisions along the good path?" At that point, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Fingerbowls are to be accepted for the sake of the Saṅgha." When the Blessed One had declared that fingerbowls were to be accepted for the sake of the Saṅgha, the monks accepted them, placed them in storage, and ate from them as usual in their begging bowls. When the faithful brahmins and householders saw this, they said: "Noble ones, is there no sign of the fingerbowls we offered?" The monks replied: "Good people, they are in storage." Those donors said: "Noble ones, is there no dwelling place in our homes? We offered them to you — if you were to fully use what we gave, it would become the merit arising from the cause of us having fully given them. Yet you have put them in storage." At that point, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The fingerbowls given by the donors are to be fully used." When the Blessed One had declared that the fingerbowls given by the donors were to be fully used, the monks began to fully use them.

When other brahmins and householders devoted to the Great Vehicle offered large quantities of fingerbowls, and the senior monks — the elder monks — grew weary from washing them, the Blessed One declared: "A fingerbowl attendant is to be appointed." When the Blessed One had declared that a fingerbowl attendant was to be appointed, they were appointed without distinction. Then the Blessed One declared: "A fingerbowl attendant who lacks five qualities is not to be appointed, and one who has been appointed is to be removed. What are the five? Going out of desire, going out of aversion,

going out of delusion, and going out of fear, and not knowing what is and is not proper conduct in the community. A fingerbowl attendant who possesses five qualities is to be appointed, and one who has been appointed is not to be removed. What are the five? Not going out of desire, not going out of aversion, not going out of delusion, not going out of fear, and knowing what is and is not proper conduct in the community."

The appointment is to be carried out as follows. Having assembled in the sitting area, and having struck the wooden sounding board (gaṇḍī), the matter is to be announced to the Saṅgha by means of a question, and when the entire Saṅgha has assembled and is seated, first a motion is to be made: "Does it please the Saṅgha to appoint the one called such-and-such as fingerbowl attendant for the Saṅgha? If it pleases, say: 'It pleases.'" Then a single monk is to make the formal motion and carry out the act: "May the venerable Saṅgha hear me. This monk, called such-and-such, is willing to serve as fingerbowl attendant for the Saṅgha. If the moment is right for the Saṅgha and it consents, may the Saṅgha grant approval: the Saṅgha appoints the one called such-and-such as fingerbowl attendant, and the one called such-and-such, appointed as fingerbowl attendant, will properly manage the fingerbowls for the Saṅgha." This is the motion. The formal act is then to be carried out thus: "May the venerable Saṅgha hear me. This monk, called such-and-such, is willing to properly manage the fingerbowls for the Saṅgha. To that end, the Saṅgha appoints the one called such-and-such as fingerbowl attendant, and the one called such-and-such, appointed as fingerbowl attendant, will properly manage the fingerbowls for the Saṅgha. Those venerable ones who consent to appointing the one called such-and-such as fingerbowl attendant are to remain silent; those who do not consent are to speak." The Saṅgha having consented and approved, the one called such-and-such, appointed as fingerbowl attendant, will properly manage the fingerbowls for the Saṅgha. This is how it is held, by reason of their silence.

When the monks had eaten and gave the leftovers and scrapings directly to the fingerbowl attendant himself, the Blessed One declared: "Those who have leftovers and scrapings are to store them together, and the attendants are to wash them." When the Blessed One had declared that those with leftovers and scrapings were to store them together and the attendants were to wash them, there were other monks who had no attendants and washed the bowls themselves. The Blessed One declared: "Those bowls are to be washed by the fingerbowl attendants alone, and they in turn are to be given the bowls."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six began eating together out of a single black bowl, all six plunging their hands in at once. The bowl caught on their hands and was left dangling. They said to the venerable monks: "Look at the ones doing miracles with the black bowl!" Then they pulled their hands back, it fell and broke. The monks saw them beating it with horse dung and said: "Venerable ones, having done something so unsightly, do you sit there in embarrassment? Look at you laughing!" Those monks replied: "What of it? Have we been drinking ale or eating everything together? So what? Did we not break the black bowl? What violation is there in this? Did the potter die? Is there no clay? It is just something else to be made." They then sat there in silence.

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through the monks eating together. Therefore monks must not eat together. If they do so, it shall constitute an offence."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not eat together, some monks who were travelling — companions who had set out together — began to eat their rice in one place. Because all of those monks had no individual eating utensils, it took each one a very long time to eat in turn, and by the time they had finished the travellers were exhausted, and some thieves fell upon them and robbed them.

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "When one is on the road, if individual eating utensils cannot be found, one may eat together, but each person must put their hand in and take their portion in turn — not all at once."

When the Blessed One had declared that on the road, if individual eating utensils cannot be found, one may eat together, some novices who were present in that place ate together with the monks, and the very same fault arose. The Blessed One declared: "Take a bowl and eat together with them."

There were some others who prepared the food. When they were eating the rice they became separated from the travellers, and the very same fault arose. The Blessed One declared: "Make it into a ball and give it to them."

Some other monks went to the homes of relatives. Their relatives said: "It has been a long time since we ate together; do eat with us." Those monks replied: "You are lay people; we are those who have gone forth into homelessness — it is not fitting for us to eat thus." Those monks, unhappy at this, sat with tears streaming down their faces.

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "If one is invited repeatedly and persistently, one must know the appropriate moment, and wherever it will not appear unseemly in the eyes of others, one may take up the eating utensils and eat there. One need have no regret in doing so."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The group of six monks, wearing a single robe, were seen eating alms food by brahmins and householders, who asked: "Wise ones, who are these people eating rice?" Others replied: "They are ascetics, sons of the Śākyas." Those who saw them mocked them and said: "Wise ones — a teacher such as yours possesses conscience and has shame. How can there be followers of his like these, who are utterly devoid of shame and modesty?"

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through the monks wearing a single robe. Therefore monks must not eat rice while wearing a single robe. If they do so, it shall constitute an offence."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not eat rice while wearing only a single robe, some who were very elderly and frail, and some who were ill and too weak to endure the effort, were unable to eat their rice while wearing their robes. The Blessed One declared: "Those ones may eat rice that has been softened and moistened. One need have no regret in this."

However, there were some others who still could not manage even this. The Blessed One declared: "Those ones may eat in a secluded spot. One need have no regret in this."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The group of six monks were bathing naked in the flooded river. Brahmins and householders who saw them asked:

"Who are these ones bathing naked?" Others replied: "They are monks, sons of the Śākyas." People mocked them, saying: "The Teacher himself is endowed with a sense of shame — how can there be those among his followers who are so utterly devoid of shame and modesty?" When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One reflected and saw that whatever fault had arisen had come from monks bathing naked. Therefore he declared: "A monk must not bathe naked. If one does so, it becomes a serious transgression. One must hold a bathing cloth." When the Blessed One declared that a bathing cloth must be held, the monks wore two lengths joined together. The Blessed One then declared: "It should be a single layer. Whoever has a two-layered one should check the water and wash it clean." Some monks, thinking the three Dharma robes to be unsuitable, did not wear them. The Blessed One declared: "Even those ones may consecrate and hold them." Some others could not find a bathing cloth. The Blessed One declared: "Those who cannot find a bathing cloth should cover themselves front and back with leaves, and bathe in a secluded spot where others will not see and become displeased in faith." When some monks wrung out the bathing cloth, they felt regret. The Blessed One declared: "There are no living creatures in a single layer of cloth, but even so, one should spread out the cloth and then wring it. There is no need for regret in this."

The summary verse:

The bean-sprout dish, what is unsuitable,
the earth, and eating what has been vomited,
eating food that has been selected,
regret, and the greasy-lipped bowl.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The venerable Nāgita was one who ate anything mixed with broth, so he came to be known by the name Nāgita-of-the-broth, or Broth-Nāgita. Then on another occasion he entered the latrine pit, and there he saw the remnant of a bean-sprout dish and an improper thought arose in him: "I have done something improper regarding the rule about seeds." Once, on another occasion, when food made from bean sprouts had been prepared for the Saṅgha, he would not eat it but sat with his bowl covered. Those who were dwelling with him, and his attendants, said: "Preceptor, food made from bean sprouts has come for the Saṅgha — why do you not eat?" He said: "Friends, I have done something improper regarding the rule about seeds." They asked: "Preceptor, what exactly did you do?" He told them what had happened. They too then began not to eat. Their companions and friends asked: "Why are you not eating?" They told them what had happened, and since Nāgita had many followers, the entire Saṅgha ended up not eating on account of him. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is something called dyeing with seed-varieties. If steam has arisen, it counts as having been dyed, and it may then be eaten. There is no need for regret in this."

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The venerable Upananda asked the Blessed One: "Venerable One, if fruit falls in a suitable place from a tree growing in an unsuitable place, may we make full use of it or not?" The Blessed One declared: "Upananda, you may not make full use of it." "Venerable One, then for now — if fruit falls in an unsuitable place from a tree growing in an unsuitable place, may we make full use of it or not?"

"Upananda, you may not make full use of it." "Venerable One, then for now — if fruit falls in an unsuitable place from a tree growing in a suitable place, may we make full use of it or not?" "Upananda, if it has not remained there overnight, you may make full use of it." "Venerable One, then for now — if fruit falls in a suitable place from a tree growing in a suitable place, may we make full use of it or not?" "Upananda, you may make full use of it."

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. A brahmin living at Śrāvastī went begging and obtained a bull. After that he obtained a cow. After that he obtained another bull. And after that he obtained another cow, and in this way his herd of cattle grew large. This brahmin, upon first obtaining the bull, felt it to be auspicious and so let that bull go free. Then at another time, that bull grew old and feeble and infirm, and wanting water it went to the bank of the river Dṛkṣā and wandered into the mud. The venerable Śāriputra also happened to be travelling that road, and seeing the bull he thought: "Does this bull have even a little root of virtue?" And he saw that it did. He then thought: "On whom does it depend?" and concluded: "On me alone." So he pulled it out of the mud and wiped it clean with his hands. Then the venerable one spoke thus: "All formations are impermanent. All phenomena are without self. Nirvāṇa is peace." Having taught these three words of Dharma, he said: "Place your faith in me. If you do so, you will be freed from attachment and released from this birth among animals," and then he departed. Wolves then ate the bull. As it was being eaten by the wolves, it thought: "If this noble one had not come here, I would not have come to such an end." And so, with a mind of pure devotion toward the venerable Śāriputra, it passed from that life and was reborn at Śrāvastī in the family of a brahmin who was diligent in the six duties.

The venerable Śāriputra reflected on what the condition of that bull had been, and he saw the very moment it had passed away. He also reflected on where it had been reborn, and seeing that it had been reborn at Śrāvastī itself in the family of a brahmin who was diligent in the six duties, he went again and again to that household. He established that brahmin together with his wife in taking refuge and in the bases of training. Then at another time he went without a novice attendant following behind him, and the brahmin said: "Noble one, do you not have a novice attendant?" Śāriputra replied: "Good brahmin, are the novice attendants who follow behind me obtained from kuśa grass, or do they arise from kuśa grass? Whatever is obtained from one such as you becomes my novice attendant who follows behind me. Noble one, there is a sentient being in my attendant's womb — if she gives birth to a boy, he shall be your novice attendant who follows behind me." "Venerable one, so be it," said the brahmin, and Śāriputra departed.

Eight or nine months later, she gave birth to a boy with a body like a lump of beef. His relatives gathered and assembled, and on the twenty-first day — being three sets of seven days — after the birth they held a great birth celebration and proceeded to give him a name. What name would they give the boy? The relatives said: "Since this boy has a body like a young bull, let us name him Vatsadāsa," and so he was named Vatsadāsa. He was raised and nurtured, and when he had grown up,

Then the venerable Śāriputra, in the early morning, robed himself and took up his bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. While walking through Śrāvastī collecting alms, he came to that brahmin's house. The brahmin employed the customary greeting of welcome and prostrated at his feet. His wife too offered him clean and well-prepared food and drink, filling his bowl and presenting it to him.

The boy looked up at the face of the venerable Śāriputra, and Śāriputra made a sign to the brahmin. The brahmin then said to the boy: "My son, from before you were born I offered you to the noble Śāriputra to be the novice attendant who follows behind him. Go now with the noble one." That being was one in his final existence. The boy followed after him, and Śāriputra gave him the going forth, conferred full ordination upon him, and gave him instructions. Through diligent and sustained effort, he realized this very fact — that the wheel of cyclic existence moves, yet in this fifth aspect it does not move — and he cultivated the understanding that all formations, by their very nature as reality, are subject to disintegration, to falling apart, to utter destruction. Having abandoned all afflictions, he directly actualized arhathood: freed from attachment and desire in all three realms, his mind like refined and burnished gold, like sandalwood and camphor, equal to the sky and the palm of the hand, having shattered the hollow door-post of ignorance, he attained clear knowledge, the superknowledges, and the individual perfect insights. Turning his back on attachment to existence and gain, and on esteem, he became an arhat worthy of offerings, of prostrations, and of reverent address by the gods of the sense faculties and their attendant deities.

Now this monk had two throats that had arisen from karmic maturation: from one he would vomit, and from the other he would swallow. In the time before the Blessed One had established the training rule regarding eating at wrong times, he would vomit and then swallow again. But after the rule had been established, he would vomit and discard what came up, and as a result his body became emaciated, weakened, scrawny, and his complexion deteriorated.

The awakened Blessed Ones, though they know, still inquire, so the Blessed One asked the venerable Vatsadāsa: "Vatsadāsa, why has your body become emaciated, weakened, scrawny, and your complexion deteriorated?" When Vatsadāsa explained what had happened, the Blessed One declared: "Vatsadāsa, one who has two throats arising from karmic maturation may vomit two or three times, rinse his mouth, and then swallow what remains. He need have no remorse about this." And when other monks ate and then vomited and felt remorse, the Blessed One declared: "If another monk eats and then vomits, he may rinse his mouth. He need have no remorse about this."

At the time when the venerable Vatsadāsa went forth, brahmins and householders began to mock, ridicule, and slander, saying: "The conduct of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākya is degenerate, their celibate conduct is ruined — and now even those of frightful appearance such as Vatsadāsa and the like are being ordained." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Great hearers who are like Mount Meru cause the great mass of ordinary people to lose faith. Therefore, thinking that Vatsadāsa should not be permitted to reside in the central region, he addressed the venerable Vatsadāsa: "Vatsadāsa, from this day forward you shall not reside in the central region but shall instead make use of dwellings and lodgings in the border regions."

"As you wish, Venerable One," said the venerable Vatsadāsa, and having heeded the Blessed One's command, he departed from Śrāvastī and was seen no more. He dwelt in an empty hall of the Śākyas at Śiṃśapā forest.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Among my śrāvaka monks, monks, the foremost in their fondness for dwellings and lodgings in the border regions is none other than the monk Vatsadāsa."

Doubt arose among the monks, and wishing to have all their doubts cut through, they put their question to the Blessed Buddha: "Venerable One, what karma did the venerable Vatsadāsa perform, such that through its karmic maturation he came to have the body of a bull?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the karmas that Vatsadāsa himself performed and accumulated, gathered the requisite conditions, saw those conditions fully come together, and — abiding close like a river — are certain to be experienced. Who else would experience the karmas that Vatsadāsa himself performed? Monks, karmas that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, the virtuous and non-virtuous karmas that have been performed and accumulated ripen in nothing other than the aggregates, sense bases, and elements that have been seized upon.

Over hundreds of aeons
karma does not perish;
when the conditions and the time come together,
it ripens as a fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, long ago, in this very excellent aeon, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha named Kāśyapa arose in the world — accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans, a Blessed Buddha. Under his teaching, a certain one went forth into homelessness. The monk who ordained him was elderly, bent, and frail. One day, while washing that elder's begging bowl, the ordained one heard another monk reciting texts in the distance. Captivated by that recitation, he stole food from his preceptor. Then, at another time, after eating his own food, he washed his own begging bowl and went to where his preceptor was. Seeing that his preceptor was still eating, he accosted him angrily and said: 'Preceptor, are you just sitting there gorging yourself like an old ox?' The elder thought: 'This one is so agitated and quarrelsome that if I say even a little now, it will only stir up greater conflict. I will wait until he is calmer and then speak to him.' So he waited until the other had settled down and then said: 'Venerable one, what did you say?' The other replied: 'I said: are you gorging yourself like an old ox?' — and repeated those same words. Then the elder said: 'Venerable one, do you know who I am? Know well that you, too, went forth under the scriptural dispensation of the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, and I too went forth under that very same dispensation.' The other replied: 'That is so, it is true — and yet I have done whatever is to be done and whatever is being done by one who has gone forth, and therefore I am free from all bondage. You are bound by every fetter. And yet you have spoken this harsh verbal karma. Now you must confess this wrongdoing, that this karma of yours may be fully cut off, fully exhausted, and fully done away with. Confess it as a wrongdoing.' And he confessed it as a wrongdoing."

Through the karmic maturation of the deed of habitually applying the expression "old ox" to an arhat monk, he was born in the existence of an ox for five hundred lifetimes. And through the remaining residue of that very karma, he has now been born as a flesh-and-blood ox as he appears today.

The monks then put a question to the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, what action did the long-lived Ox perform such that, through the karmic maturation of that action, the Blessed One has declared him the foremost among those devoted to remote lodgings?"

The Blessed One declared: "It was through the power of an aspiration. And where was this aspiration made?"

"Under the very scriptural dispensation of the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, this one went forth. Having gone forth, he practiced the holy life for one lifetime and yet did not attain even the slightest accumulation of good qualities. Yet it was the very one under whose dispensation he went forth — the Blessed One Kāśyapa — who declared him the foremost among those devoted to remote lodgings. And so he made this aspiration: 'Though I have practiced the holy life for one lifetime under the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened unsurpassable field of offering, Kāśyapa, and have not attained even the slightest accumulation of good qualities — by this root of virtue, may I go forth under the scriptural dispensation of the one whom the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened Kāśyapa, prophesied to the brahmin youth, his preceptor, saying: "Brahmin youth, in the human lifespan of one hundred years, there will arise a Tathāgata, arhat, fully and perfectly awakened buddha named Śākyamuni" — and having gone forth, may I abandon all afflictions and directly actualize arhatship. And just as my preceptor, the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened Kāśyapa, was declared the foremost among those devoted to remote lodgings, so too may I be declared the foremost among those devoted to remote lodgings by Śākyamuni, the king of the Śākyas.' Through the power of that aspiration, he has now been declared by the Tathāgata to be the foremost among those devoted to remote lodgings."

"Therefore, monks, the karmic maturation of actions that are purely dark is purely dark; the maturation of actions that are purely bright is purely bright; and the maturation of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are purely dark and mixed, and strive for actions that are purely bright. This, monks, is how you should train."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's Grove. The group of six monks were saying "Give this here," "Give from this," picking and choosing as they ate, and their food-taking became quarrelsome and contentious. On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks must not pick and choose what they eat. If they do so, it will become an offense entailing a formal proceeding."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When monks were eating, a bowl that was being held fell onto the base of another bowl; a bowl-base that was being held fell into a bowl. Being troubled by this, they refrained from eating, and on that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, if a bowl that is being held falls onto the surface of a bowl-base, that is to be called a received gift. If a bowl-base that is being held falls into the interior of a bowl, that too is to be called a received gift."

If a bowl that is being held falls into the interior of another bowl, that too is to be called a received gift. If a bowl-base that is being held falls into the interior of another bowl-base, that too is to be called a received gift. Nevertheless, the intention to receive must be present.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Ānanda went to a metal-smith who worked with tin and said to him: "Good man, can you make a tin bowl?" The smith replied: "Noble one, if you yourself will provide the measurements, I will craft it to whatever size you specify." "Make it large." "Noble one, what do you want with a large tin bowl? Do you think that because you are a mendicant I will make it for nothing? Pay the price for it." The smith thought: "What tin work should I put into this?" and so he made him a large tin bowl. Then the smith said: "Make something else too that will fit inside it." He made another, and in the same way continued until the seventh had been made. Ānanda then had a novice carry them, had a net woven from five-colored thread, placed the bowls inside it, arranged them in order, and sent them off balanced on the novice's head — the novice was to go wherever he was invited as a guest. He arrived and spread them out and sat down. The householders and brahmins said: "Noble one, have you spread out a tin-smith's shop?" He replied: "Poor folk, what do you know? Here, take some flour. Here are oil-provisions. Here are cooked rice grains. From the others, take condiments." They said: "Noble one, if it is so, then in a few of the bowls a great quantity of condiment will come — other things too must be set out in the others." But he said nothing. On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about because of monks carrying tin bowls." Therefore a monk must not carry a tin bowl. If he does carry one, it becomes an offense. Excepted are a scraper, a salt-pouch, and an offered drinking cup.

Summary verse: The washing of feet was prohibited; copper foot-scrapers were permitted; likewise a fan and fanning away flies with it.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The place where monks washed their feet repeatedly became filled with insects. When brahmins and householders came to the monastery and saw this, they said: "Noble ones, what is this place that is swarming with buzzing insects?" The monks replied: "We have been washing our feet here." Those people mocked them, saying: "The ascetics (śramaṇas) who are sons of the Śākyas have no sense of cleanliness — they wash their feet again and again in the same spot." On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Do not wash the feet repeatedly in the same spot. Rather, designate a foot-washing place at the southeast corner of the residential building." When the Blessed One had declared that a foot-washing place was to be designated, the monks did not know how to make it. The Blessed One declared: "Make it like a tortoise-shell." When they made it very smooth, the Blessed One declared: "Make it rough." When elderly monks who were frail and infirm were unable to go to that place, the Blessed One declared: "Set out a basin for them." When the monks washed in the basin and it broke and became unusable, the Blessed One declared:

"Set out a copper basin." When the Blessed One had declared that a copper basin was to be set out, the group of six monks set out basins made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. When brahmins and householders saw this, they said: "Noble ones, what is this?" The monks replied: "Good sirs, the Blessed One has permitted a basin." The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, does your ascetic life not hinder you from indulging in pleasures?" And they replied: "It is crushing your throats with a stone." When those monks were thus mocked, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Basins made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli are not to be set out. Instead, a basin made of clay is to be set out." When they set one out in the shape of a drum, it tipped over, and the Blessed One declared: "Make it in the shape of an elephant's foot, with a raised ornament in the center like a fine flower." When they made it very smooth, the Blessed One declared: "Make it rough." When the monks set basins down one after another in a disorderly way, the Blessed One declared: "For the Saṅgha's building, set them out under an awning. For individual residences, set them at the back of the door."

The Blessed One was dwelling in the land of Kauśāmbī, in the pleasure grove of Ghositā. When the hot season arrived, the monks suffered from the heat. They became pale and emaciated, and grew thin, wretched, infested with lice, and haggard. When householders and brahmins saw them, they said: "Noble ones, why have you become pale and emaciated, thin, wretched, infested with lice, and haggard?" When the monks explained how things had come to be, those people said: "Noble ones, do you not carry a fan?" The monks replied: "Good sirs, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The people said: "Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate, so he will grant it." On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Very well then, I permit you to carry a fan." When the Blessed One had declared that fans were to be carried, the group of six monks carried fans with handles polished, ornamented, and finely ornamented with gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. Then, from the point beginning with "brahmins and householders" up through "it is crushing your throats with a stone," the account proceeds as before. When those monks were mocked on that occasion, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Fans with handles polished or finely polished with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal are not to be used. Instead, both types of fans — one made of grass roots and one made from palmyra leaves — may be carried." Then, from the point beginning with "faithful brahmins and householders offering the monks fans of various kinds" up to that point, the account proceeds as before, and the Blessed One declared: "Very well then, I permit you to carry fans on behalf of the Saṅgha."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall by the Monkey Pool. Mosquitoes were biting the monks, and their bodies became covered with welts from the mosquito bites. As they were repeatedly scratching, brahmins and householders said to them: "Noble ones, why are your bodies covered with welts like this?" When the monks explained how things had come to be, those people said: "Noble ones, do you not carry a mosquito-whisk?" The monks replied: "Good sirs, the Blessed One has not permitted it."

"Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate, so he will permit it." On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Very well then, I permit you to carry mosquito-whisks." Once the Blessed One had declared that mosquito-whisks were to be carried, the group of six monks kept whisks with handles made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, and with handles made of tail-hair. As for the brahmins and householders — the rest follows as before. The permitted mosquito-whisks are five in kind: those made of wool, those made of hemp fiber, those made of cotton-wool, those made of cotton cloth, and those made of layered leaves.

The summary verse:

With knotted cloth and body, ladder,
a staff, a net to carry —
shallots were forbidden,
but permitted for the sick.

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that the monks should sweep. Now at that time, a monk was climbing a ladder, and below him a woodworker was sitting. The woodworker saw the monk's groin and genitals exposed and said: "Noble one, since you are possessed of a man's faculties, I would like to salute you as a male." The monk was embarrassed and sat without speaking. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: "Whatever slight fault has arisen has come about from monks climbing ladders without having tucked in their robes. Therefore, when a monk sweeps, he should be made to tuck in his robes before sweeping." Reflecting thus, he declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore, when a monk sweeps, he should tuck in his robes before sweeping." Once the Blessed One had declared that a monk doing the sweeping should tuck in his robes, the monks tucked in their robes before sweeping. Those without faith mocked them, saying: "Noble ones, are you about to wrestle?" The monks replied: "Good friends, we are sweeping." Those people fell silent. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who are climbing the ladder are the ones who should tuck in their robes — not others."

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks carried loads on their bodies, and brahmins and householders mocked them, saying: "Noble ones, we for our part bear loads on our backs for the sake of our parents, our children, and our wives — but for whose sake do you carry loads on your bodies?" The monks replied: "Good friends, we too have the making of offerings to the Teacher, the feeding of the Saṅgha, the tending of the sick, and many such duties to perform." Those people fell silent. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks must not carry loads on their bodies. If they do, it will constitute an offence."

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain. When monks were climbing up and descending Vulture Peak Mountain, they slipped and fell, striking themselves and becoming injured. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks are to carry staffs." Once the Blessed One had declared that monks were to carry staffs, the group of six monks polished staffs made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, and carried ones that were ornamented with elaborate decoration. When brahmins and householders saw this and mocked them, on that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and —

the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, staffs are to be carried by two categories only — those who are old and frail on account of age, and those who are sick and unable to manage."

Once the Blessed One had declared that staffs were to be carried by those two categories — those who are old and frail on account of age, and those who are sick and unable to bear the exertion — those who counted as elderly and those who counted as sick then also took to carrying staffs.
