The Blessed One then declared: "Those who are old and those who are sick are to request the vow of the staff from the Saṅgha, and whoever has been granted the vow of the staff by the Saṅgha may carry a staff."

The request is to be made as follows. The seat is to be prepared, the gong struck, and the monks informed by means of the words of inquiry. When the entire Saṅgha has assembled and is gathered, the elderly monk who is old and frail on account of age, or who is sick and unable to bear the exertion, is to sit quietly at the end of the row of elders, press his palms together, and speak these words:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. I, the monk who am old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so, request from the Saṅgha the vow of the staff. May the venerable Saṅgha, being compassionate, out of compassion grant to me, the monk who am old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so, the vow of the staff."

This is to be repeated a second and third time in the same way.

After that, one monk is to make the request and perform the formal act:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk, who is old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so, has requested from the Saṅgha the vow of the staff. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents, let the Saṅgha grant it. The Saṅgha has granted the vow of the staff to the monk who is old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so."

This is the request. The formal act is to be performed as follows:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This monk, who is old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so, has requested from the Saṅgha the vow of the staff. On that account, if the Saṅgha grants the vow of the staff to the monk who is old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so, then those venerable ones who consent to granting the vow of the staff to the monk who is old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so, should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha has consented and granted, and has given the vow of the staff to the monk who is old and frail on account of age, or sick and unable to bear the exertion, called so-and-so. Since no one has spoken, it is held to be so."

Whoever has been granted the vow of the staff by the Saṅgha may carry a staff, and in this matter there is to be no regret.

The Vinaya of Minor Matters, the sixth fascicle.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain. Elder monks — the elders — and those suffering from wind-illness (a humoral disorder), when climbing and descending Vulture Peak Mountain, slipped and fell, striking themselves and becoming injured. Their water pots, clay vessels, and broad-mouthed pitchers also broke. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks are to carry nets." Once the Blessed One had declared that monks were to carry nets —

The group of six monks carried nets made from cords of five different colors, and brahmins and householders, upon seeing this, mocked and derided them. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not carry a net made from cords of five different colors; it is to be made from a single color." Once the Blessed One had declared that nets made from a single color were to be carried, elderly and frail monks and those suffering from wind-illness also began carrying nets. The Blessed One then declared: "Even elderly monks and those suffering from wind-illness must request from the Saṅgha the vow pertaining to the net, and whoever has been granted the vow pertaining to the net by the Saṅgha may carry a net."

The request is to be made as follows. A seat is prepared, the wooden sounding board is struck, and the monks are assembled by means of the inquiry formula, so that the entire Saṅgha is convened and seated. The elderly monk — one who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness — sits respectfully at the end of the row of elder monks, joins his palms together, and speaks these words:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. I, the elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so, request from the Saṅgha the vow pertaining to the net. May the venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, take me under their compassionate care and grant the vow pertaining to the net to me, the elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so."

This is repeated a second and third time.

After that, a single monk makes the motion and performs the formal act. "May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. This elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so, requests from the Saṅgha the vow pertaining to the net. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha and they consent, may the Saṅgha approve it, and may the Saṅgha grant the vow pertaining to the net to the elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so. This is the motion."

The formal act then proceeds as follows. "May the venerable Saṅgha please hear me. The elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so, has requested from the Saṅgha the vow pertaining to the net. Therefore, if the Saṅgha grants the vow pertaining to the net to the elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so, then those venerable ones who consent to granting the vow pertaining to the net to the elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so, should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak."

The Saṅgha having consented and approved, the Saṅgha has granted the vow pertaining to the net to the elderly monk who is old and frail, or who suffers from wind-illness, named so-and-so. It is thus held, by reason of the silence. Whoever has been granted the vow pertaining to the net by the Saṅgha may carry a net, and in this regard there is no ground for regret.

As for certain other monks who needed both a staff and a net, the monks gave them the vow pertaining to the staff and the vow pertaining to the net separately. The Blessed One then declared: "The vow pertaining to the staff and the vow pertaining to the net are to be granted together at the same time, as before."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk who was staying at Śrāvastī ate garlic, then went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, and having prostrated at the Blessed One's feet with his head, sat to one side. The Blessed One then spoke to that monk:

"Monk, monk, lend your ear to the teaching of Dharma and listen well." That monk prostrated at the Blessed One's feet with his head and sat to one side. The Blessed One then began to teach him Dharma. Yet the more the Blessed One taught that monk, the more the monk thought, "It would not be right for me to ask the Blessed One a question and trouble him," and so he looked away to one side. A second and a third time the Blessed One said to that monk: "Monk, monk, lend your ear to the teaching of Dharma and listen well." Yet that monk, a second and a third time, looked away in the other direction, then prostrated at the Blessed One's feet with his head and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Now, since the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are fully aware yet feign ignorance, the Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why does that monk look away in the other direction no matter how I teach him Dharma?" Ānanda replied: "Reverend One, that monk ate garlic." The Blessed One then said: "Ānanda, monks who eat garlic create an obstruction to the Noble Truths. So it is, Blessed One. Ānanda, if this monk had not eaten garlic today, then today itself he could have shattered the twenty peak-summits of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection with the vajra of wisdom, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Therefore, from this day forward monks shall not make full use of garlic, or shallots, or chives. If they do make use of them, it shall be a serious offense."

At that time the venerable Śāriputra was gathered in that very assembly and was sitting there. He thought: "If this monk does not see the Noble Truths today, perhaps he will see them tomorrow," and so he entered into a state of mind considering this — yet he did not see it. Śāriputra then examined through the fourth dhyāna of the pinnacle of existence how much time must pass before the monk would see them, and also entered into that state of mind to consider it — yet still he did not see it. The venerable Śāriputra then arose from that meditative absorption and spoke in verse:

Having abandoned this supreme leisure here in this very place,
this one will never in this life ever see
the Noble Truths here — there is a state
from which there is no seeing them again.

The Blessed One then, knowing the venerable Śāriputra's mind through his own mind, said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, do not venture into the domain of a buddha. This is a time beyond the domain of the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. At a future time there will arise a Teacher, a Tathāgata, an arhat, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, a buddha and Blessed One known as 'One Who Overwhelms All.' Under that one's teaching, this monk will go forth, abandon all afflictions, and directly realize arhatship." Having said this, the Blessed One reflected: "Whatever slight fault has arisen has arisen from the monk's eating of garlic. Therefore monks shall not eat garlic. If they do eat it, it shall be a serious offense."

Having declared that monks shall not eat garlic, a certain monk who was ill went to a physician and, after requesting treatment, said: "Good sir, I have contracted such-and-such an illness — please prescribe medicine for it." The physician said: "Noble one, take garlic and you will recover." The monk replied:

"Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The physician replied: "Noble one, this is your medicine — no other remedy can cure you." At that point the monk spoke to his fellow monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "If a physician says to you, 'Monk, this is your medicine — no other remedy can cure you,' then you may eat it, and you need feel no remorse in doing so."

When the Blessed One had declared that an ill monk might eat garlic on a physician's authority, the ill monk, having eaten the garlic, continued to make full use of the monastery — the dwelling places and the bathrooms — and entered there as before. He went among the Saṅgha. He taught the Dharma to brahmins and householders who came to visit. He made prostrations at the stūpa. He went on alms rounds to the homes of brahmins and householders. He sat in gardens, assembly halls, temples, and other public places crowded with people. The brahmins and householders, catching the smell, criticized and reproached him, saying: "The monks, sons of the Śākyan, have fallen away from the conduct of wanderers and from the conduct of the pure — now even those who have gone forth eat garlic."

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "I shall establish a code of conduct for a monk who eats garlic. A monk who eats garlic must not, while still eating it, make full use of the monastery, nor the dwelling places, nor enter the bathroom area, nor go among the Saṅgha, nor teach the Dharma to brahmins and householders who come to visit, nor make prostrations at the stūpa, nor go on alms rounds to the homes of brahmins and householders, nor remain in gardens, assembly halls, temples, or other public places crowded with people. He shall eat it in some remote direction where, if others see him, no lack of faith will arise. When the task is finished, he shall stay in that same place for seven days. For a sore on the face, three days. For a cold sore, one day. After that he shall bathe, wash his robes as well, and fumigate them with incense. Only then, when the smell is gone, may he enter the monastery and do whatever else was previously permitted."

A monk who eats garlic and properly undertakes the code of conduct thus established — if he does not abide by it, he incurs a serious offense.

Here ends the first section of the minor offenses.

The summary verse is:

With heated water, a razor, an umbrella,
cotton cloth, and ornamental trimmings —
accepting, assembly, bathing,
urine, and moving through a doorway.

The summary verse:

With heated water, a razor, and wrapping cloth,
and likewise giving itself,
a seat and a single grass mat,
residing in a house, and not sharing.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, belonging to Prince Jeta. At the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of the four directions, he sent a barber with the instruction to shave the hair and beards of the noble ones — and what follows is as before up to that point.

Ānanda said: "Good sir, do you know how to shave hair with heated water?" The man replied: "Noble one, that is precisely my trade." Ānanda said: "Good sir, if that is so, come here and shave it." The man shaved with the heated water. Ānanda said: "Shave it again." The man shaved again. Then he said:

"Shave it again." He shaved it again. And so, continuing in this way until the sun set without letting the man go, Ānanda then said: "You poor fellow, you know nothing at all — just do it evenly as it is and be off," and so on, just as before up to that point.

The Blessed One declared: "A monk must not shave with hair-scissors. If a monk shaves with hair-scissors, it becomes an offense." After the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not shave with hair-scissors, some monks sustained wounds on their heads, and when the razor touched them during the course of treating those wounds, the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Around the wound one may shave with hair-scissors, and the remainder is to be shaved with a razor."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada again sent a barber, and so on, just as before up to that point. Ānanda said: "Good sir, do you know how to shave the hair around the private parts?" The man replied: "Noble one, that is precisely my trade." Ānanda said: "If that is so, come here and shave it." The man said: "Noble one, how shall I shave it?" Ānanda said: "Good sir, shave it neatly." The man began to shave, and Ānanda said: "Good sir, do it like this." The man did so. Then Ānanda said: "Now do it like this as well," and kept the man without letting him go until the sun set. People condemned, sneered, and disparaged them, saying: "The conduct of the ascetics, the sons of the Śākyan, is degraded; their brahminical conduct is degraded — now they even have the hair around their private parts shaved." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore a monk must not shave the hair of the private parts. If a monk shaves the hair of the private parts, it becomes an offense."

After the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not shave the hair of the private parts, some monks developed wounds in the private area, and those monks, feeling remorse, did not shave the hair. Other monks developed parasites, and because of the harm from these, they were unable to perform virtuous activities. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk may show the affected area to elder monks, and for the sake of a wound or parasites one may shave the hair of the private parts — one need not feel remorse about this."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada again sent a barber, and so on, just as before up to that point. Ānanda said: "Good sir, do you know how to shave the armpit hair?" The man replied: "Noble one, that is precisely my trade." Ānanda said: "If that is so, come here and shave it." The man said: "Noble one, how shall I shave it?" Ānanda said: "Good sir, shave it neatly." The man began to shave, and Ānanda said: "Good sir, do it like this." The man did so, and Ānanda said: "Now do it like this as well." The man was kept without being let go until nightfall. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked him about it, and so on, just as before up to that point. The man reported what had happened, and while people were condemning them, the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks must not shave the hair of a layman's body. If a monk does so, it becomes an offense."

The Blessed Buddha was then dwelling at Vaiśālī in the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pool. After the Blessed One had declared that monks must not shave the hair of a layman's body, wounds appeared on the thighs of some monks, and other monks were afflicted with insects, so that because of these conditions they were unable to engage in virtuous activity. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "For the sake of a wound, or for the sake of insects, the hair of the body may be shaved. One need feel no remorse regarding this."

The Blessed Buddha was then dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Six Group monks were lying together on a single couch, and lying there they made noise, played, chattered, laughed, jostled one another, and struck each other on the body. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: "Whatever faults have arisen have come about from monks lying on a single couch together. Therefore I shall not allow a monk to lie on the same couch with another monk." Having thus reflected, he declared to the monks: "Monks, from this day forward a monk must not lie on a single couch together with another monk. If one does so, it becomes an offense."

After the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not lie on a single couch with another monk, a large number of monks went wandering through the countryside and set out on a journey. They went to a certain rocky hillside, and when they arrived there they found couches. They gave up the couches to one another, saying: "These are too few. Bring more as well." The others said: "Noble ones, we have many people sleeping on each single couch of ours. Please take turns on yours, and let two or three sleep on each one." Those monks replied: "If the Blessed One has not permitted two or three to lie on a single couch, how may we do so?" The others said: "Noble ones, there are no other couches here." When they said this, the monks fell silent, unable to speak. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those monks who are conscientious, who feel remorse, and who desire training shall establish mindfulness and, placing a folded robe or the bowl as a divider in the middle of the couch, sleep thereon. One need feel no remorse regarding this. As for a grass mat in place of a couch, and other such things, the same rule applies."

The Blessed Buddha was then dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A large number of monks went wandering through the countryside and set out on a journey. They went to a certain rocky hillside, and there they received lodging from a householder. The cold season having arrived, they obtained robes. The brahmins and householders, thinking "These are monastics," took pity on them and gave them robes. Each one wore what he had received and slept, while other monks were afflicted by the cold. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not keep what each has obtained for oneself alone; rather, all must share together. Whatever single item is found should be spread over all of them in order of seniority, as much as can be covered."

At some point they went to another rocky hillside, and there they found a single robe and spread it over themselves. A close friend among them put it on and went for a walk. The monks, suffering from the cold, said to him: "Venerable Ānanda, we are suffering from the cold, yet you alone wear it and walk about?" He replied: "Did I forbid you? Why don't you walk as well?" When the monks had passed the night suffering from the cold, they reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Whoever is walking must distribute the robe among the persons present and then walk. If others walk wearing it without sharing, it becomes an offence."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The cold season having arrived, the monks were huddled together, overcome by the affliction of the cold. At one point a householder, the benefactor Anāthapiṇḍada, came to the monastery. Seeing them, he said: "Noble ones, why do you huddle together, abandoning your diligent recitation of scripture and the practice of virtue?" They replied: "Householder, those who are at ease can attend to Dharma, but we are suffering greatly from the cold." He then went home and sent five hundred bolts of fine cloth. The monks divided up these household robes and went outside, and brahmins and householders who saw them exclaimed in surprise: "Noble ones, what has happened to you?" They replied: "We were cold and divided the cloth among ourselves. Venerable sirs, please say nothing of this." When those people began to mock them, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks must not divide household robes as they are. If such a circumstance arises, one must first cover them with a layer of saffron-coloured robe cloth and then distribute them." The Saṅgha did likewise in wearing them, and then the Blessed One declared: "For the Saṅgha, one must place the cloth underneath and cover it from above and then distribute it. Otherwise it becomes an offence."

The summary verse:

An umbrella, a worldly javelin throw,
joining and stitching, likewise forest fire,
paths without a dwelling-place,
and sharing shares — one does not walk in these.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who dealt in robes, making and selling cloth. On one occasion he came to obtain a great quantity of robes, and he thought: "What means could I use so that I might gain merit and yet also accomplish what I need?" Being a man of faith, the thought arose in him: he would invite the buddha and the monastic Saṅgha of monks, spread robes as seat-coverings, and offer a midday meal. He reasoned that in this way the robes would be fully used, and by fully using the robes and fully enjoying the meal, he would gain great merit. Thinking thus, he invited the buddha and the monastic Saṅgha of monks to his home for the midday meal, set out pure and excellent food, and placed robes upon the seats. When the meal was arranged and the Blessed One was invited by the invitation, the monastic Saṅgha of monks went, but the Blessed One remained in the monastery and received alms-food. Now, the Blessed Buddhas remain in the monastery and receive alms-food for five reasons. What are those five?

to settle into proper meditation indoors, to teach the Dharma to the gods, to visit the sick, to inspect the lodgings, and to establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the śrāvakas. In this particular instance, the Blessed One, the buddha, wishing to establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the śrāvakas, remained in the monastery and received alms-food.

Now, as the monks were walking along the road, rain fell, and their robes became soaked and clung to them as they stood there. Seeing how each monk's robe clung to him in just that way, producing a kind of transparent outlining of the body, the brahmin was disturbed and said: "You have rendered my gifts unfit to be gifts. Take these robes and just share them among yourselves." When this happened, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, since that brahmin gave them in a state of faithlessness, they must not be accepted." Then, once he had calmed down and again offered the robes with a mind of faith, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, now that the brahmin has offered them with a mind of faith, they may be accepted. Having accepted them, make them proper and distribute them."

When the monks had accepted them, the brahmin said: "Well done, noble ones — it is worthy of a lineage that wields a canopy!" At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If that is so, I permit it: monks may carry a canopy."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks might carry a canopy, the group of six monks had canopy shafts made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya), and crystal, and others made of variegated and polished materials, while the canopy itself was made of white cloth and peacock feathers. When brahmins and householders saw this, they said: "Noble ones, what is this? The Blessed One has permitted a canopy. Noble ones, you ascetics (śramaṇas) — are you afflicted by a craving for the pleasures you desire? Why do you carry canopies like these?" They replied: "We crush the throats of our enemies underfoot and are indeed afflicted by the desire for pleasures." When people were thus insulting them, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Such canopies as those must not be carried. However, two kinds of canopy may be carried: one made of grass and one made of leaves."

When the Blessed One had declared that two kinds of canopy might be carried, the group of six monks made extremely long canopy shafts, raised those shafts upright, and went into the town. Brahmins and householders, seeing them, rose and looked about wondering: "Is some wealthy man coming, or a merchant chief, or a caravan leader, or who?" Some craned their necks, and when they actually saw who it was, they became faithless. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Canopy shafts must not be made extremely long. Rather, a shaft of just the canopy's own measure may be fitted, and one must not go into a village carrying a canopy."

When the Blessed One had declared that one must not go into a village carrying a canopy, it came to pass that a considerable number of monks were traveling together through the countryside on a shared errand, and their road happened to pass through a village. They thought: "The Blessed One has declared that one must not go into a village carrying a canopy, so we should bypass the village." And so they set the village aside.

Being separated from his companions, he was distressed and overcome. At that point, the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the road happens to pass through the middle of a village, one may tilt the canopy to the side and proceed. There is no need to feel regret about this."

Those who were on alms rounds had entered upon their rounds when rain fell and their robes were soaked through with rainwater. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One on alms rounds may fit the canopy shaft to an appropriate length and then set out. Once out, if the rain stops, one must leave the canopy at the first house one comes to, then proceed onward, and later retrieve it and go on one's way."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park of Prince Jeta.

Now, from the southern lands there came a wandering debater named Bright World-Hurler, who traveled about the countryside and arrived at Śrāvastī. He rested, then went to the venerable Kauṇḍinya and, having arrived, said: "Monk, I possess certain letters received from my teachers, and for that reason I wish to hold a discussion with you." Kauṇḍinya said to him: "Brahmin, I am not one who seeks out discourse. Be on your way."

Then the venerable Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, Bhadrajit, Vimala, and Gavāṃpati went to that place, and each of them said the very same thing.

Next, the venerable Śāriputra went to that place and, having arrived, said: "Monk, I possess certain letters received from my teacher, and for that reason I wish to hold a discussion with you." The venerable Śāriputra reflected: "Does this wanderer have even a little root of virtue, or does he not?" He saw that he did. He then considered: "On whom does this depend?" And he saw that it depended on himself. "By my speaking, is there somewhat of the Dharma-Vinaya that can tame him?" He saw that there was. "In how many days could the assembly gather?" Knowing that it could be convened within seven days, he said: "Very well, let it be so. But where shall the debate take place?" "In a large open space," said the wanderer. Having agreed to the terms of the debate, they established which side would speak first and which second, and who would present the opening position and who would present the opposing view.

The venerable Śāriputra said: "Since you are the one who has come unexpectedly, you yourself should take the first position." The wanderer stated the first position, and the venerable Śāriputra, having listened and repeated it back, declared: "That argument of yours is improper. It is not sound. It does not hold." He leveled these criticisms. The wanderer stated it again, and each time the venerable Śāriputra left it without conceding.

Now that wandering debater from the southern lands named Bright World-Hurler had come to Śrāvastī and entered into debate with the venerable Śāriputra, and when it was announced all around that seven days had now passed, many hundreds of living beings gathered — some out of amazement, and others assembled urged by roots of virtue from former lives. The venerable Śāriputra reflected: "Have those who can be tamed by my speaking gathered?" He saw that they had gathered. Then the venerable Śāriputra spoke the teaching in full, and that wandering debater was utterly defeated. He then became filled with faith and said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if I may obtain the going forth and the full ordination as a monk in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, I shall practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the venerable Śāriputra granted him the going forth and the full ordination, and gave him instruction. Through his striving, effort, and exertion, the rest follows as before, from "knowing this very wheel of saṃsāra in its fifth part, moving and unmoving" down to "he came to speak with reverence."

Then those in the assembly were filled with great amazement, saying: "The noble Śāriputra has defeated such a great debater as this."

Then the venerable Śāriputra, having understood the aspirations, latent tendencies, elements, and natures of those in the assembly, taught the Dharma in accord with them. Many hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, upon hearing it, attained a great and distinguished realization — as follows: some directly realized the fruit of stream-entry; some the fruit of once-returning; some the fruit of non-returning — and so the passage continues as before, down to "they inclined toward the Saṅgha."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, in all cases no one will become like the monk Śāriputra, or even comparable to him. Therefore, permit it — monks may study the treatises of outsiders such as worldly logic and debate. The Blessed One has declared that monks may study the treatises of outsiders such as worldly logic and debate." When the Blessed One had declared this, even monks who were childish, confused, or unclear all studied without distinction. The Blessed One then declared: "Those who are able to defeat the arguments of opponents may study the treatises of outsiders such as worldly logic and debate — but not those who are childish, confused, unclear, or unskilled." Those among them who were capable then applied themselves with diligence. The Blessed One declared: "Divide the day into three parts. In two of the three, read the scriptural words of the Buddha; in the third, study the treatises of outsiders." When the Blessed One had declared "divide it into three parts," the monks then studied by the measure of years and months. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, since life is but a moment, it was not with years and months in mind that I spoke — rather, divide a single day into three parts." The monks then recited the treatises of outsiders during the bright period, and during the other periods recited the scriptural words of the Buddha. The Blessed One declared: "During the bright period, recite the scriptural words of the Buddha — not the treatises of outsiders."

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Śāriputra had given the going forth to two brahmin youths, Devadatta and Vālendriya, and had set them to reciting sūtras. At some point, they went wandering through the countryside, made their way to a certain rocky cliff, and there great offerings and great honor came to them, and the two settled there. Through the force of their former habituation, they composed the scriptural words of the Buddha with metrical arrangement, words, and order, and recited them as a chant. One of the two died. The other forgot the text, and since no offerings came from his recitation, he wandered from place to place and eventually returned to Śrāvastī. Having rested and recovered, he went to where the venerable Kauṇḍinya of complete knowledge resided, paid homage, and said:

He asked the venerable elder, "Please lend me the recitation."

The elder said, "Good, my son — learn the recitation just so," and began to chant together with him. After reciting a short portion he said, "Elder, you have made an error by not reciting at length."

The monk replied, "My son, I have learned it just as it is."

The young monk prostrated with his head at the elder's feet, then went to where the venerables Aśva, Bhadra, Revatī, Mahānāman, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and the noble Hastaka were staying. He arrived, prostrated at their feet, and said, "Elder, please lend me the recitation."

Each one replied, "Good, my son — learn the recitation just so," and each in turn began to chant together with him. After each had recited a short portion he said, "Elder, you have made an error in your recitation."

Each replied, "My son, I have learned it just as it is."

He prostrated at each one's feet, then made his way to where the venerable Śāriputra was staying. He arrived, prostrated at the venerable Śāriputra's feet, and addressed him thus: "Preceptor, please lend me the recitation."

He replied, "Good, my son — learn the recitation just so." They began to chant together, and as they recited at length, the venerable Śāriputra also recited at length. Then the young monk said, "Preceptor — all those monks made errors, but you alone recited without fault."

The venerable Śāriputra replied, "You foolish one — you yourself recited incorrectly; the monks recited without fault." Having said this to him, he fell silent and said nothing more.

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: whatever slight fault has arisen here has come about because of monks reciting the scriptures of the Buddha with metrical arrangement, words, and set order. Therefore monks shall not recite the scriptures of the Buddha with metrical arrangement, words, and set order. If a monk recites the scriptures of the Buddha with metrical arrangement, words, and set order, it becomes a serious offence. If the established words are those of the region, the established words of the language, or the established words of the district, there is no transgression.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Group of Six, even in their old age, continued to behave recklessly and with levity. The monks said, "Venerable ones, even with your grey hair you still will not let go of this levity?" Without a word they drew together to one side and said, "Ānanda and Upānanda — these black-bowled, rope-belted paupers should be made unwelcome." While they were thus busying themselves looking for an opportunity, the elder monks and the senior monks went off to the monastery quarters and commenced their meditation and recitation.

Then the Group of Six set fire to the forest from three sides and gathered together on one side. As the monks came to harm from the forest fire, they began to flee as far as their legs would carry them. The Group of Six called out, "Elders, why are you hurrying away like that? Venerable ones, can you not see the forest fire?" And they engaged them in a bit of conversation, saying, "Elders, did the Blessed One teach the Vinaya only for pleasant conditions?"

Thereupon the others said, "Venerable ones, surely you did not deliberately harm us? You wretches — you told us to make ourselves unwelcome!" When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks shall not set fire to a forest. If one does so, it becomes a grave offence."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī an elder monk and a junior monk were traveling together on a journey. The elder had many vessels and many possessions, while the junior was unknown and had nothing beyond his three robes. The elder said, "Venerable one, I am tired — please carry my robe bundle for a while and come along." The junior replied, "Elder, if it would not be an imposition, may I make a small request for a moment? Venerable one, please scold me on this point. Elder, do you not see the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha? What use is this foolish load of possessions? Good sir, if disrespect is acceptable for a moment, I would ask you this: are you my preceptor or my teacher? For what reason do you guide me?" The elder said nothing, and the elder thought to himself, "I should make this poor fellow unwelcome."

When the two of them arrived at the monastery, there was a rule in place that one was not to spend even a single night there without arranging lodging in advance. The one in charge of lodging told them to look for sleeping places, and the elder accepted one. The junior said, "Venerable one, since I have not arranged lodging, I request lodging," and he went to the elder of the Saṅgha, bowed at his feet, and said, "Elder, please provide me with lodging." The elder asked, "Good sir, with whom did you come?" "Elder, with a certain senior monk." "Good sir, that senior elder of the Saṅgha said that he has dismissed me from his company — go back to him and request lodging from that very one." So the junior went to the others, but they all refused him in the same way. And so it was that when morning came, he went to that elder's own door and knocked, saying, "Elder, homage to you. I am he who is called such-and-such a name. May you be free of illness. Elder, since there is a rule established that one may not stay here even a single night in this monastery, please provide me with lodging." The good man replied, "It is well that the Saṅgha has established such a rule. Had they not done so, I would have had a plan: I have many vessels and many possessions, and am I not the elder? Even if you have shown disrespect, it is proper that you stay, and one who offers lodging — you should pay him your respects." The junior was left speechless and said nothing.

When his lodging had thus been cut off, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One shall not travel on a journey without arranging lodging. A monk shall not be fierce like a lion. And the Saṅgha shall not establish rules that would harm the monks. For if a monk travels without having arranged lodging, or acts fierce like a lion, or the Saṅgha establishes such a rule, all of it becomes an offense."

The Blessed One, accompanied by his attendant the venerable Nāgapāla, traveled through the country of Magadha and arrived at the city of Śāketa, where he took up residence at Śāketa in the dwelling of the yakṣa Bakula. Then one night toward dawn, while it was dark and drops of rain were falling here and there and lightning was flashing, the Blessed One was walking on a walking path that had no roof over it. By the nature of things, attendant monks of Blessed Buddhas do not enter inside to settle down for as long as the Blessed Buddhas themselves are not inside and properly settled. The awareness and perception of Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, extends downward, and so he thought to himself —

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śāketa, in the dwelling of the yakṣa Bakula on the hill of Śāketa. One night toward dawn, while it was dark and drops of rain were falling here and there and lightning was flashing, he was walking on a walking path that had no roof over it. Venerable Nāgapāla, perceiving that he himself ought to go to the Blessed One there, manifested a fragrant chamber made of lapis lazuli, went to where the Blessed One was, and sat walking behind the Blessed One's feet as he walked on his walking path. At that time, the people of the land of Magadha would frighten crying boys and girls by invoking the name of the yakṣa Bakula. Then Venerable Nāgapāla thought to himself: "Alas, the Blessed One has been walking for so long on a walking path with no roof over it — he must have been frightened by the yakṣa Bakula into doing so." Realizing this, he reversed his robe and, having wrapped it differently, sat at the side of the walking path, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Bakula, Bakula! Ascetic, I am the yakṣa Bakula." Thereupon the Blessed One said to Venerable Nāgapāla: "You foolish man — can you really think to frighten a Tathāgata with the yakṣa Bakula? Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and fully awakened buddhas are free from fright and shame. There is nothing by which a Tathāgata could be made to flinch, shrink, or have the hair of his body stand on end." At that, Śakra, lord of the gods, became displeased, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable one, can there really exist a person of this kind in this Dharma-Vinaya?" The Blessed One replied: "Kauśika, stay where you are. The Gautama lineage is vast — this one too will in time become one who possesses the fully purified Dharma." The Blessed One then reflected and, knowing that whatever fault had arisen had come about for the monks through the reversing and rewrapping of the robe, he addressed the monks: "Monks, the foolish Nāgapāla reversed and rewrapped his robe and said to the Tathāgata: 'Bakula, Bakula! Ascetic, I am the yakṣa Bakula.' Therefore, monks must not reverse and rewrap the robe. If one wears it so, it incurs a serious offense." The Blessed One declared: "Monks must not reverse and rewrap the robe. If one wears it so, it incurs a serious offense." And when he had so declared, the monks who were staying at Valgu came upon some reversed-robe wrappings there, and lice got into them. In the situation where the monks fell ill from eating lice, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One may sit with the robe reversed and rewrapped, and one may lie down in it; but one must not tear it apart."

Summary verse:

A strip of wool cloth, and a robe,
and likewise the finest of robes,
a buckle-eye, a buckle-support, a knot,
and waistbands — these make three.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, if a wool-strip garment has been completed, it is permitted both for the Saṅgha and for an individual." The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, as before, and declared: "If a robe has been completed, it is permitted both for the Saṅgha and for an individual." The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, as before, and declared: "If a finest robe has been completed, it is permitted both for the Saṅgha and for an individual."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now at that time there was a monk in Śrāvastī who was an alms-round practitioner. One morning he put on his lower robe and his outer robe, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to go on alms round. As he was walking about on alms round, his outer robe became loose. He quickly set his bowl down on the ground, adjusted it, and tucked it back in. The brahmins and householders who saw this mocked him, saying: "The monks, sons of the Śākyan, have no sense of decorum — they set their bowls down just anywhere." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not set his bowl down just anywhere. If a monk sets his bowl down just anywhere, it becomes an offense. However, in order to protect the outer robe, a robe-loop should be attached." The monks attached one, but the robe then wore out. The Blessed One declared: "Run the strap through the loop and hang it from the shoulder." The monks ran the strap through and attached it, but because there was no robe-knot it would not stay fixed and became a source of fault. The Blessed One declared: "A knot should be made."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now at that time there was a monk in Śrāvastī who was an alms-round practitioner. One morning he put on his lower robe and outer robe, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to go on alms round. As he was walking about on alms round, his lower robe came unwrapped. He quickly set his bowl down on the ground and readjusted it. The brahmins and householders who saw this — and what followed — is as stated before. The Blessed One declared: "In order to protect the outer robe, three kinds of belt should be worn: a plain sash, a cord sash, and one with a stick-fastener."

This is the Vinaya: Minor Bases, the Seventh Fascicle.

Summary verse:

The Teacher was dwelling at the Śākyan seat;
ornamental trim and dangling fringe,
crescent shapes and gold thread —
all variegated patterns were prohibited.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at the Nyagrodha Grove pleasure garden in the Śākyan seat. At that time, the household steward of the great man Śākya passed away, and a group of people dwelling in the rocky hills went to the great man Śākya and said: "Lord, your household steward has died — please appoint another steward." Now there was a brahmin youth sitting near him, and the great man Śākya said to him: "Brahmin youth, go for now; when another steward has been sent, I will let you know." That youth went and, having administered affairs properly and in accordance with custom, he offered a great abundance of tribute and extra gifts. The great man Śākya then said: "Brahmin youth, in gathering this tribute and these extra gifts in such abundance, you surely did not harm the people?" The youth replied: "Lord, this tribute and these extra gifts were obtained by legitimate means; I did no harm to the people." The great man Śākya then said to the group of people dwelling in the rocky hills: "Good people, surely this brahmin youth did no harm to any of you? The tribute and extra gifts were obtained by legitimate means — he harmed no one." And so he installed that youth as steward of the rocky hills region. Now, since the world desires prosperity and is averse to hardship, another brahmin gave his daughter to him in marriage, and that man, together with her, began to track the days, the lunar dates, and —

the seasons — and after a short while he took her as his wife. Together with her he played, rejoiced, and made merry. From their playing, rejoicing, and merrymaking, a baby boy was born. When the boy was born, they held a great birth-celebration and gave him a name befitting his lineage. Again, from their playing, rejoicing, and merrymaking, a baby girl was born. For her birth-celebration too they made great festivities and gave her the name Candravatī. They raised and nurtured her until she grew up, and she became so accomplished, well-mannered, graceful in her gait and bearing, that she was pleasing to all the people dwelling in the rocky hills.

Then, some time later, that brahmin youth fell ill. Though he was treated with medicines of roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, the illness did not subside. The steward of the rocky hills spent everything that had been paid to him as tribute and given as extra gifts, and he took out further loans — yet he did not recover, and he died there on the spot. The people dwelling in the rocky hills came to that great man Śākya and said: "Sir, the steward has passed away." He said to them: "Wise ones, was there tribute and extra gifts paid to him?" "Sir, a great deal was paid to him, but he spent it all on remedies for his illness, and when he still did not recover, he also took on other debts." "Whatever small remainder there may be, let the son pay off that debt." "Sir, there is nothing at all remaining; as for his household, there is his wife, his son, and his daughter, and his daughter is accomplished, well-mannered, and graceful in her gait and bearing, so that she is pleasing to all the people dwelling in the rocky hills."

The great man said: "Wise ones, let his wife and son go wherever they please, and bring that daughter here." And so they released his wife and son to go wherever they pleased, and brought the daughter to the great man's residence. Now, there was an elderly wife of the great man Śākya whose two tasks were preparing food and gathering flowers, and she said: "Master, I am very old now and can no longer manage these two tasks. Please appoint this Candravatī as my companion in service." And so he appointed her as her companion. The old woman said to her: "Candravatī, you go to the pleasure grove and gather flowers. I will prepare the food." Candravatī went to the pleasure grove, gathered flowers, wove them carefully into a garland, and went to the great man's residence. When he saw her, he was delighted and said: "Excellent! Set it down." Then he said this to the elderly wife: "Why were there few flowers before, yet so many today?" She replied: "Before, when your kinsmen came and asked me for some, I gave them to those people; this one gives to no one. But I am old and my eyes are dim, whereas she has sharp eyes and is skilled at gathering." He said: "If that is so, let her stay in that pleasure grove and live there." So he had her established there in that very pleasure grove, and because she was always weaving fine garlands of flowers, she became known as Mālyavatī, "the Garlanded One."

On another occasion, she had taken her meal from the house and gone to the pleasure grove, and the Blessed One was also going on his alms round. She saw the Blessed One and found she could not look her fill at him; filled with great ease and profound joy, she contemplated and thought: "It is certain that because I did not serve such a truly worthy recipient of offerings, I have come to be in such a condition as this. Therefore, if only the Blessed One would accept alms from me —"

"I shall offer alms to the Blessed One," she thought. And at such a moment, the awakened buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know nothing that is unknown to them, see nothing that is unseen by them, are aware of nothing that is unrecognized by them, and have nothing whatsoever of which they are unaware. Thus, beginning from "because the awakened buddhas, the Blessed Ones, by the very nature of reality..." down to "ripens as a fruit for embodied beings," all of that is as before.

Then the Blessed One, in order to take her under his care, held out his alms bowl and declared: "Sister, if you have anything to give, place it in this bowl." With very great faith she offered her alms to the Blessed One, prostrated at his two feet, and made this aspiration prayer: "By this root of virtue, may I never again become a slave or one who is poor."

Now it happened that a brahmin astrologer who was a friend of her father saw her and said: "Girl, where have you come from?" "From that very cliff," she replied. "Whose household are you staying with?" He said: "You are dwelling in a place of little fortune — you have been made a slave of the householder Mingchen." "Where did your father go?" "He died." "And where did your mother and brothers go?" "I do not know where they have gone." He said: "Mālyavatī, you are not fit to be a slave. Stretch out your hand and let me look." She stretched out her hand, and he looked, and then he spoke this verse:

She upon whose palms
the mark of the iron wheel is found —
though born into the lineage of slaves,
she shall be taken as a queen's consort.

She whose face is full and bright,
with the bearing of the lord of swans —
though born into the lineage of slaves,
she shall be taken as a queen's consort.

She upon whose soles
the marks of a city's gate and a horse's descent are found —
though born into the lineage of slaves,
she shall be taken as a queen's consort.

"Do not be downcast — go on your way. You will not remain a slave; you will become a queen."

From there she went to a pleasure grove. Prasenjit, the king of the realm of Kosala, had gone out in pursuit of game, and his horse had bolted, carrying him off alone to a place among the yellow-robe wearers. Wandering here and there, he arrived at the pleasure garden of the householder Mingchen. He asked the girl: "Whose pleasure garden is this?" She replied: "It belongs to the householder Mingchen, a divine patron." He dismounted from his horse and said: "Girl, bring water so I may wash my feet." She went very swiftly to the pond and fetched water that had been warmed by the rays of the sun. He washed his feet and sat for a short while, then said: "Girl, bring water so I may wash my face." She skimmed the surface of the water with her hand, took water that was neither too warm nor too cold, and with it he washed his face. He said again: "Girl, I am thirsty — bring water to drink." She stirred the water and took it in a vessel made of cool leaves, and the king drank it and said: "Girl, are there three ponds in this pleasure garden? You have brought water of three kinds." She replied: "Divine patron, there is only one pond here; there are not three." He said: "Then how did you bring water of three different kinds?" She explained what she had done, and the king said: "Very well, I should ask you about this: why did you bring water of three different kinds?" She replied: "Divine patron, the first time I sought warm water: it was in order to bathe your royal feet and ease them. The second time I sought water that was neither too warm nor too cold: it was because both heat and cold are harmful to the eyes. Having stirred the water and sought what was very cool, I brought it in order to free you, divine patron, from thirst." He thought to himself: "This girl is clever," and recognizing this, he said: "Girl, you are capable and skillful. Since I need my feet massaged, rest here a while."

She massaged his feet, and because his body was endowed with a pleasing tactile quality, the moment she touched them he fell asleep. When he had fallen asleep, she thought to herself: "This king has many enemies. If while he is sleeping someone were to harm him, it would certainly bring disgrace upon my master." And so she barred the door and sat keeping watch.

After some time, word passed from one to another, and the four-limbed host of the army arrived at that pleasure grove and called out for the door to be opened. She did not open it. The king was awakened by the noise of the commotion and said: "Girl, what is that?" She replied: "Divine patron, some people are calling out asking that the door be opened, and they have named your title as well." He said: "Girl, who barred this door?" "Divine patron, I barred it." "Why did you bar it?" "Divine patron, it occurred to me: this king has many enemies, and if while he lay sleeping someone were to harm him, it would certainly bring disgrace upon my master. For that reason I barred the door." He said: "Wise girl, I wish to ask you about this matter I am uncertain of. First, tell me — what is your relationship to the great Śākya clan chief?"

She replied: "I am a maidservant sent in service by him." He said: "You are not a maidservant sent in service by him. You are surely his own daughter. Speak truthfully." She remained silent and said nothing. The king then said: "Girl, go to the great Śākya chief's quarters and say to him: 'King Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, is staying in your pleasure grove.'"

She went quickly, and said: "Lord, the king of Kośala, King Prasenajit, is staying in your pleasure grove." When the great Śākya chief heard this, he had food and drink and perfumes and garlands prepared, and surrounded by a great number of people he went to the pleasure grove. There they exchanged the pleasantries of greeting with words of "Welcome," making one another fully glad. Then the king bathed and ate, they conversed, and after sitting together for a little while, he said: "Great Śākya chief, what is this girl's relation to you?" "Divine patron, she is a maidservant sent in service by me." "She is not a maidservant sent in service by you. She is your own daughter. Give her to me." He replied: "Divine patron, there are other Śākya daughters more distinguished than she. Please take one of those. Why would you want her?" The king said: "It is this very one I need. Give her to me." He replied: "Divine patron, if that is truly so, I will present her to you in the proper manner." "Then do so."

The great Śākya chief then had the city adorned, and having decked the girl with every ornament, he set her upon an elephant and had a proclamation announced at the main roads, the market streets, the crossroads, and the intersections, where the citizens of the city had gathered and crowds of people had come from various regions — calling out: "Know all who have understanding: the daughter of the great Śākya chief, the garland-wearing Phreng-ldan-ma, has been presented as chief queen to King Prasenajit of Kośala." And thus the general populace came to know that she had been presented as chief queen to King Prasenajit of Kośala.

Then King Prasenajit of Kośala took her with great splendor and magnificence and led her to Śrāvastī. When her father heard that "my son has taken a maidservant as his junior wife," jealousy arose in him and he thought: "Either she is truly not that man's daughter, or else I have been deceived into thinking so, and it has turned out that she was born of a slave-woman's union."

He brooded over this, keeping it within himself. Then the king spoke to Phreng-ldan-ma: "Phreng-ldan-ma, go and bow at the feet of the maidservant." She went and took hold of that woman's two feet. Now, that woman possessed a most exquisite touch, and from the mere contact of Phreng-ldan-ma's hands she stirred in her sleep and awoke, thinking: "From such a touch as this, belonging to the daughter of a woman who eats grain, the lineage of Kośala will flourish and grow great."

At that time King Prasenajit of Kośala had two chief queens: Gyal-rik Yar-tsul-ma, of royal lineage, and Phreng-ldan-ma. Whenever the king was together with Phreng-ldan-ma, she would praise Gyal-rik Yar-tsul-ma, saying, "Such a one as she is truly beautiful." And Yar-tsul-ma would say, "O lord, when shall I be able to see her?" The king replied, "Wait but a little while; it will not be long before you see her." And so she remained, full of longing. Likewise, whenever the king was together with Gyal-rik Yar-tsul-ma, she too would praise Phreng-ldan-ma, saying, "Phreng-ldan-ma also possesses such an exquisite touch." And Yar-tsul-ma would say, "O lord, when shall I be able to see her?" The king replied, "Wait but a little while; it will not be long before you see her." Thus, the more the king stirred their wonder, the more each of them grew eager to meet the other.

Then, some time later, the season of spring arrived. The trees in the groves burst into bloom, and in those garden parks filled with the calls of geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, red-legged partridges, cuckoos, and shang-shang-teu birds, the king set out surrounded by his retinue of queens. Since women delight in flowers and fruit, they began to wander through those various garden parks. Gyal-rik Yar-tsul-ma grew tired and weary, and leaned against an aśoka tree to rest there. Then Phreng-ldan-ma caught sight of her. Seeing how beautiful she was, Phreng-ldan-ma took her for a tree goddess and immediately bowed at her feet. The very moment Phreng-ldan-ma's hand touched her, she fell asleep.

Then, when the king began praising Phreng-ldan-ma to Yar-tsul-ma, Yar-tsul-ma said, "O lord, when shall I be able to see her?" The king replied, "You have already seen her." "O lord, I do not remember." "I shall remind you. Well then — do you remember the one who took hold of your feet with both hands?" "O lord, was that the goddess Phreng-ldan-ma?" "It was." "O lord, for you to have left behind a queen possessed of such exquisite touch and to have come to me — truly you love me and hold me dear."

Likewise, when the king began praising Yar-tsul-ma to Phreng-ldan-ma, she said, "O lord, when shall I be able to see her?" The king replied, "You have already seen her." "O lord, I do not remember." "I shall remind you. Do you remember the one before whom you bowed as she leaned against the aśoka tree?" "O lord, was that Yar-tsul-ma?" "It was." "O lord, for you to have left behind a queen of such beauty and to have come to me — truly you love me and hold me dear."

At that time King Prasenajit of Kośala had those two chief queens, Gyal-rik Yar-tsul-ma and Phreng-ldan-ma. Of these two, one was proclaimed the supreme among those possessed of beauty of form, and the other was proclaimed the supreme among those possessed of exquisite touch, and this report spread in all directions. The monks were seized by doubt, and they put their doubt before the Blessed One, the Buddha, the dispeller of all doubts:

"What was it that Phreng-ldan-ma and Yar-tsul-ma had done, such that through the karmic maturation of those deeds one became supreme among those possessed of exquisite touch, and the other became supreme among those possessed of beauty of form?"

The Blessed One declared: "O monks, it is they themselves who accumulated the collections of karma, who thoroughly transformed the conditions, who performed and gathered deeds that will inevitably arise, abiding like a flame. Could anyone other than themselves experience individually what they themselves have done and accumulated? O monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Yet wholesome and unwholesome karma that has been performed and accumulated does ripen in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

Even across a hundred aeons,
karma does not perish.
When conditions are assembled and the time arrives,
it ripens as fruit for embodied beings.

O monks, in a time long past, in a bygone age, there was a brahmin who dwelt upon a rocky mountain. He took a wife of equal birth, and together with her he played and rejoiced and took his pleasure. Through their play and rejoicing and pleasure, a son was born. Again they played and rejoiced and took their pleasure, and from that a daughter was born. They raised and nurtured them, and they grew up. After some time, that brahmin died together with his wife, and that brahmin's son, separated from his parents, came to delight in solitude. He took his sister and went to dwell in a forest hermitage, and there the two of them began to live on roots, trunks, flowers, and fruits."

The Blessed One declared: "O monks, a black serpent has five faults. What are the five? It is wrathful, it bears grudges, it is venomous, it does not requite what is done for it, and its poison is sharp. In the same way, certain women also have five faults. What are the five? They are wrathful, they bear grudges, they are venomous, they do not requite what is done for them, and their poison is sharp. O monks, this is what is meant by the sharp poison of women: women are for the most part possessed of excessive attachment and desire.

Now the sister of that brahmin's son was tormented by afflictions, and she said: 'Brother, I cannot bear the hardship of living in this hermitage on roots, trunks, flowers, and fruits. I am going out to the edge of the village.' He took her and went to the edge of the village, and there she entered a brahmin household to beg. As she begged alongside her sister-in-law, calling out together, a brahmin heard them, came out, and said: 'Do wandering ascetics also travel with their wives?' She replied: 'This is not my husband's wife — she is my sister. I have given her to no one and have not given her away to anyone.' The brahmin said: 'If that is so, why will you not give her to me?' She answered: 'It is because she has renounced that ignoble, sinful dharma.' But tormented by the desire of craving, she said: 'Brother, do you think there is no hardship in living in the hermitage on roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits? It was in order that you might abandon afflictions without hardship that I spoke to you thus. Please give her to this brahmin.' He replied: 'That would be contrary to the Dharma, and so I will not give her to you — it is for you yourself to know your own mind.' When that brahmin came to understand her and her intentions, he took her as his bride with great and abundant wealth and brought her into his own home. Then her brother said to him:"

"Brother, come here — please vow to remain together with her as her head of household." He replied: "Sister, I have no interest in seeking sensual pleasures. If you permit me, I shall go forth into renunciation." She said: "Make a promise: if you come to visit me from time to time, I give you my permission." He replied: "Excellent — so be it." Having received her permission, he went forth into renunciation among the sages. Because he had already generated roots of virtue, without a teacher he directly realized the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening and actualized solitary awakening face to face. Then he thought: "I promised my sister that I would come to her — therefore I must go to her." And so he went to her.

Upon arriving, he began to perform miracles: blazing fire, brilliant light, falling rain, and flashing lightning. Ordinary people are swift to gain faith in miraculous powers, and so she fell at his feet like a tree cut at its roots and said: "Brother, have you attained such an extraordinary distinction of qualities?" "I have." "If that is so, then you are one who seeks alms; I too am one who seeks merit — therefore please remain right here, and I will offer you alms." He replied: "Sister, you are dependent on another. Ask your husband." She said: "Very well, so be it." And she said to her husband: "My lord's son — my brother who has gone forth into renunciation has become a great being accomplished in ascetic practice. If you permit it, I wish to invite him for alms for three months." He replied: "Good woman, if he had not gone forth and we had had to support him against our will — well, he has now gone forth and become a great being accomplished in ascetic practice, so what need is there even to speak of it? Go and invite him." So she invited him for alms for three months.

Now that brahmin had another wife, a second one. She thought: "We share property in common, and if she is making merit in this way, why should I not do the same?" And she said to her: "Co-wife, your brother is also my brother-in-law in precisely the same way, so please offer one bowl of food to him, and I will also offer one bowl of food." She replied: "Excellent — so be it."

The sister of the pratyekabuddha, in order to protect his mind, wrapped fine and abundant food of excellent texture in inferior food and presented it to him, saying: "Co-wife, rejoice! I offer my brother-in-law food of this kind." The other replied: "Excellent!" and rejoiced. Then she too, likewise in order to protect his mind, wrapped fine food of excellent color in inferior food and presented it to him, saying: "Co-wife, you rejoice as well — I too offer our brother-in-law food that is fine and of excellent color, just like this."

Monks, what do you think? The one who was the sister of the pratyekabuddha — she who offered him excellent food of fine texture wrapped in inferior food — that very one is the goddess Mālyā. Through the karmic maturation of that deed she performed, that of offering him excellent food of fine texture wrapped in inferior food, for five hundred lifetimes she was endowed with excellent texture, and throughout that time she became supreme among those endowed with excellent texture. The other one — she who offered the pratyekabuddha excellent food of fine color wrapped in inferior food — that very one is the noble lady Āyuśmāna of royal lineage.

Through the karmic maturation of that deed — she who offered the pratyekabuddha excellent food of fine color wrapped in inferior food — for five hundred lifetimes she was endowed with good form, and throughout that time she became supreme among those endowed with good form.

O monks, it is thus: the karmic maturation of deeds that are purely dark is purely dark — and so on, as before, down to: O monks, train yourselves in this way.

At another time, the goddess Mālyā conceived a child. On the very same day that she conceived, the wife of a brahmin who was her neighbor also conceived. From the very day she conceived, she was afflicted by suffering. When nine months had passed, the goddess Mālyā gave birth to a boy who was handsome, pleasing to behold, and beautiful. A great birth-celebration was held for this newborn, and when the time came to give the boy his name, the king said: "Go and present him to his grandmother; she shall give him his name."

The ministers took the child and went to her presence and said: "O goddess, the king requests that you bestow a name upon the young one."

She replied: "O wise ones, did I not say from the very beginning that this daughter of Zunmā would cause the lineage of Kosala to flourish?"

The ministers said: "Indeed so. And since from the very moment of his birth the goddess was calling him 'noble-born,' we therefore give the young one the name Āryajāta." And so his name was fixed as Āryajāta.

On the very same day that the young Āryajāta was born, the son of the brahmin's wife was also born. When their kinsmen had come and assembled, and after seven times three — twenty-one days — a great birth-celebration was held, and when the time came to give the boy his name, some among them said: "On the very day this one entered his mother's womb, his mother was afflicted by suffering, and after his birth she has known only suffering; therefore the boy's name shall be 'Affliction to His Mother.'" And so his name was fixed as Mātṛdatta.

The young Āryajāta was entrusted to eight nurses: two who suckled him with milk, two who held him in their arms and kept him alive, two who bathed away his impurities, and two who played with him. Those eight nurses raised and nourished him — with milk, curds, butter, melted butter, and the essence of butter, along with other principal and excellent requisites — like a lotus dwelling in a pond.

When he had grown to maturity, he studied the written arts, and having mastered writing, he became proficient in these eight branches of examination: the examination of precious gems, the examination of wood, the examination of land, the examination of cloth, the examination of elephants, the examination of horses, the examination of women, and the examination of men. He became expert in analysis and in reading, his conduct was clear, and he was skilled in the ways of every aspect. He was then anointed by the king from the crest of the head, after the manner of royal consecration, as lord of the realm, possessing might and diligence, having brought the great earth-circle under his sway. The crafts and vocational arts practiced by those who dwell there are as follows: riding atop elephants, riding horses, the methods of chariot-driving, the methods of the sword, drawing the bow, shooting forward, shooting backward, the method of guiding with an iron hook, casting the lasso, the method of discharging a ballista, modes of gripping, modes of stance, the topknot, striking at range, striking so that a sound rings out, striking at a vital point, striking without missing, striking with great force, cutting, wounding, and —

— the five techniques of cutting: in all these he became skilled. Although the boy suffered harm, he was entrusted to the eight mothers — and from that point, as stated before, down through "like a lotus dwelling in a pond," it is as in the preceding passage.

Now, at such time as he had grown to maturity, he was trained in letters and became skilled in the Brahmin view, the Brahmin conduct, the Brahmin rules of behavior, the Brahmin standards of purity, the Brahmin modes of deportment, the grasping of balls of food, the taking up of earth, the taking up of ash, the sacred syllable Om, the sacred syllable Bho, the Veda of formal proclamation, the Veda of burnt offering, the Veda of poetry, the Veda of statecraft and protection, the making of the sage Gārgya, the making of Māthara, the examination of earthquakes, the examination of the atmosphere, and the six terminal duties of Brahmin work: performing burnt offerings, causing others to perform burnt offerings, reciting, causing others to recite, giving, and receiving.

Then at a certain later time, the noble young man and his mother went out together to drive away deer in the mountains. A dog gave chase and ran off with something in its mouth, and they wandered here and there until they came to the pleasure garden of the Śākyas dwelling in the yellow-robed community. The man who guarded the pleasure garden spoke to the Śākyas dwelling in the yellow-robed community: "Good sirs, the noble young man, with a dog running off with something in its mouth, has come into your pleasure garden." Those men arose with indignation and said: "Good sirs, if that is how things are, the time has come — go and kill that interloper." And so, having divided up the task accordingly, they set out. But the elder Śākyas, upon seeing them, said: "Young men, where are you going?" Those men replied: "The noble young man has come into our pleasure garden — we are going to kill him." The elder Śākyas said: "Young men, this was an accident; bear with his fault in some measure and turn back." And they turned back.

Meanwhile, the four-division army host of the noble young man, having heard from one to another, came searching and arrived at the pleasure garden, and the four-division army host surrounded the pleasure garden on every side. The man who guarded the pleasure garden then spoke to the Śākyas dwelling in the yellow-robed community: "Good sirs, the four-division army host of the noble young man has come to the pleasure garden, and the elephants and horses with their unclean matter have rendered the entire pleasure garden unfit." At this they became exceedingly indignant, and breaking the word of the elder Śākyas, they set out to kill the noble young man. When the noble young man heard that the Śākyas of the yellow-robed community were coming to kill him, he left a man in place and said: "Come now, fellow — I will go on ahead. Whatever the Śākyas dwelling in the yellow-robed community say, report it back to me." When the Śākyas of the yellow-robed community arrived at the pleasure garden and the noble young man was nowhere to be seen, those men asked his servant: "Where has the son of the maidservant gone?" He replied: "He has fled." Some among them said: "If we had seen him, we would have cut off his hands." Others said: "If he had not fled, we ourselves would have cut off his feet." Others still said: "We for our part would have separated him altogether and in every way from his life — but since he has fled, what is to be done now?" They gave instructions to their hired men: "Sweep out the pleasure garden, and where the maidservant's son has gone, scrape away the ground in that direction and cover it over with fresh earth."

As for those sections of the wall they had been leaning against, let others scrub those spots thoroughly; then wash them down with milk-water, sprinkle them with fragrant water, and adorn them most beautifully with perfumes, flowers, and the like." The servant did exactly as instructed.

Then that man, having seen how everything had turned out, went before the noble-born one, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. The noble-born one said: "Well now, young man — what do the Śākyas dwelling in Kapilavastu say?" He replied: "Whatever Your Lordship may say to him, the curse of one who petitions a god shall not fall on him — let it fall on those very people instead. But, Your Lordship, please make it known only to the extent of what needs to be known." Understanding that the moment was right, he recounted it all in detail. Then he spoke to the people of his household: "Wise ones, the moment my father passes away and I become king, the very first thing I must do is to separate those people from their lives. You must urge forward everything that has been set in motion. As for the Śākyas dwelling in Kapilavastu, I will face them down." They agreed.

Mālagandhā said: "Excellent, excellent! Your Lordship, this too you shall certainly accomplish. Virtuous people stand firm in their pledges." He replied: "I do not know how soon I shall become king." Mālagandhā said: "Do not think that way. The aged king will not linger long before departing to his divine abode, and then you yourself will become king. When one serves desire, there is no evil deed one will not commit."

So it was that from among the five hundred ministers of Prasenajit, king of Kośala, the noble-born one began to dismiss the ministers one by one, and all of them departed from his presence, save only Dīrghacārin. That chief of ministers, being the one closest to the sovereign's heart, did not depart.
