Then, some time later, Dīrghacārin came before the noble-born one on some matter, and the noble-born one said to Dīrghacārin: "If I am to take revenge on the Śākyas of Kapilavastu by making use of a plot to kill King Prasenajit, tell me when I shall become king." Dīrghacārin replied: "Your Lordship, why do you seek to generate demerit? The aged king will not linger long before departing to his divine abode, and the kingship will pass to no one other than yourself. As for Dīrghacārin, I say this to you alone — do not repeat it to anyone." His Lordship said: "But what have I done wrong? How could I tell this to anyone?" And with that he departed.

At that time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Śākyas, in the Śākya town called Meḍuludī. Then King Prasenajit of Kośala mounted a fine horse, with Dīrghacārin as his charioteer, and as they were traveling through the countryside they came to a certain city. There King Prasenajit caught sight of a secluded forest grove at the edge of a park — a lodging place set apart, free from wicked people, well suited to solitary retreat and proper composure within. Upon seeing it, he said to Dīrghacārin: "Dīrghacārin, the Blessed One is dwelling in just such a place as this — a forest grove at the edge of a park, secluded, free from wicked folk, suited to solitary retreat and proper composure within. If I were to pay attendance on the Blessed One from time to time, that would be good. Tell me, Dīrghacārin — where is the Blessed One now dwelling? Have you heard?" He replied: "Your Lordship, I have heard. The Blessed One is dwelling among the Śākyas, in the Śākya town called Meḍuludī. Your Lordship, how far is it to the Śākya town of Meḍuludī?"

"Your Lordship, it is a little more than three leagues away." Dīrghacārin then respectfully heard King Prasenajit of Kosala and said: "As your Lordship wishes, let the chariot be brought to that place — to the Śākya town of Meḍuludī." And so, having had the chariot brought and going by carriage as far as the road was passable, he alighted from the carriage and entered the park of Ānanda on foot.

At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in a great hall, staying there through the day with the door closed. King Prasenajit of Kosala saw many monks walking in the open walkway outside the great hall. He went up to those many monks and addressed them thus: "Venerable ones, where is the Blessed One staying?" The great king was told: "Great King, the Blessed One is staying in this very great hall, resting through the day with the chamber door shut. Great King, if you wish, go to that great hall with the door shut, and when you arrive, knock gently and softly on the door panel — the Blessed One will open it."

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala removed his five royal insignia — the diadem, the parasol, the sword, the jewel-handled fly-whisk, and the embroidered shoes — and gave them to Dīrghacārin, turning his face away. Dīrghacārin then thought to himself: "The king has placed upon me the five royal insignia — the diadem, the parasol, the sword, the jewel-handled fly-whisk, and the embroidered shoes — and has turned his face away. The king must wish to conduct some private business; I should remain right here."

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala went to that great hall with the door shut. He knocked gently and softly on the door panel, and the Blessed One opened the door. King Prasenajit of Kosala then went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One's two feet, covered them with his face and hands, and spoke these words: "Blessed One, it has been a long time since I have seen you. Sugata, it has been a long time since I have seen you."

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to King Prasenajit of Kosala: "Great King, why do you show yourself even more humble than the most humble before the Tathāgata?"

"Venerable Blessed One, I have faith in the Dharma arising from the Dharma itself. Therefore I think: the Blessed One is the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha; your Dharma and Vinaya are well taught; and the Śrāvaka Saṅgha is well entered upon the path."

"Great King, what is the nature of this faith you have in the Dharma?"

"Venerable One, I have observed here certain learned ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins who are arrogant in their learning, skilled in disputation, and accounted by ordinary folk as inspiring childlike wonder and awe. I have seen how these men, by their own wisdom and eloquence, shatter the positions of others and reduce their theories to nothing, and then proceed to disparage them, saying among themselves: 'Let us go to that wise Gautama and put such-and-such questions to him. If he fails to give a prophetic answer, we shall debate him, and if he answers in such-and-such a way, then we shall say to him thus:'

saying: 'O Gautama, this of yours is improper. This is unbecoming. This is untenable.' But having prepared all those questions they had planned to put, they came into the presence of the Blessed One, and before they could even begin to pose them — let alone actually pose them — they fell silent and did not speak. Instead, they simply gazed upon the Blessed One's face and reflected upon it, thinking: 'The Blessed One Gautama alone knows what is to be known; he sees what is to be seen.' Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, here I have observed certain learned ascetics and brahmins who are arrogant in their learning — and what follows is the same as before, up to the point of 'I have seen some of them.' Having prepared all those questions, they went to where the Blessed One was and, having arrived, put their questions to him before they were even fully posed, and the Blessed One, while they were still putting their questions without having completed them, gave a prophetic answer that fulfilled them completely. Delighted and pleased by having their questions thus answered prophetically, those people went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks, and undertook the training precepts as well. Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma — and what follows is as before.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, here I have observed certain learned brahmins and householders who are arrogant in their learning — and what follows, up to 'I have seen some of them,' is as before. Having prepared all those questions, they went to where the Blessed One was and, having arrived, put their questions to him in full. The Blessed One gave them a complete and prophetic teaching on the Dharma. Delighted and pleased by that prophetic teaching, those people requested from the Blessed One the going forth and full ordination as monks, and the Blessed One granted them the going forth and conferred full ordination upon them. Having thus gone forth and been fully ordained, having attained arhatship and experiencing the joy and bliss of complete liberation, they reflected to themselves: 'We were indeed improper. We were utterly improper. Formerly, when we were not yet true ascetics, we claimed to be ascetics. When we were neither true brahmins nor arhats, we claimed to be arhats. Now at last we truly are ascetics, brahmins, and arhats.' Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma — and what follows is as before.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, here I have observed certain ascetics and brahmins who are thin and emaciated, gaunt of flesh, slight and feeble in frame, of poor complexion —

whose faculties were impaired, and who were disagreeable to look upon with the eyes of the many. Having seen them, I thought to myself: 'Are these wise men practicing the holy life against their will? Or has some long illness overtaken them? Or might it be that they have committed some evil, unwholesome action in secret and are now concealing it? For indeed, these wise men are pale and gaunt, their flesh wasted and poor, slight and feeble in body, their faculties impaired, and disagreeable to look upon with the eyes of the many.' I approached them and, having approached, spoke to them thus: 'Wise ones, why have you become pale and gaunt, your flesh wasted and poor, slight and feeble, your faculties impaired, and disagreeable to look upon with the eyes of the many?' They replied to me, Great King, that desire afflicts them. Venerable One, at that I thought: 'If, by obtaining, partaking of, and accumulating desired objects, one were to become fair of form, pleasing to behold, and beautiful, then I — Prasenajit, King of Kosala — would become the fairest of form, the most pleasing to behold, and the most beautiful, for I, Prasenajit, King of Kosala, obtain the five qualities of sense-pleasure to my heart's content and with ease. But since it is precisely because of obtaining, partaking of, and accumulating desired objects that one does not become the fairest of form, the most pleasing to behold, and the most beautiful, therefore I have seen that the Saṅgha of monks (śrāvakas) of the Blessed One is very fair of form, their faculties flourishing, their faces radiant, their complexions entirely pure, their minds free of anxiety, living in complete dependence on others — and therefore they are able to practice, for as long as they live, the holy life unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and perfectly cleansed.' Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma — and what follows is as before.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, here I have seen how those who come to me for the sake of wealth quarrel with one another over the basis, the grounds, and the purpose of their desires — mothers with their children, children with their mothers, fathers with their children, children with their fathers, brothers with their sisters, sisters with their brothers, and friends with their friends; to say nothing of person against person, they quarrel and dispute. And when they quarrel and fall into contention, the mother speaks ill of the child, the child speaks ill of the mother, the father speaks ill of the child, the child speaks ill of the father, the brother speaks ill of the sister, the sister speaks ill of the brother, the friend speaks ill of the friend — to say nothing of person against person.

Furthermore, here I have seen two monks who, having quarreled with other monks over some matter, surrendered their training and fell away. Yet in no manner whatsoever did they speak ill of the Buddha, nor did they speak ill of the Dharma or the Saṅgha. Rather, they reproached only themselves, saying: 'We two are inferior here, lowborn, and lacking in merit — we were unable to practice, in the presence of the Blessed One and for as long as we live, the holy life unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and perfectly cleansed.' Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma — and what follows is as before.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, here I, Prasenajit, King of Kosala, have those who are to be executed put to death, and when it comes to those who are to be released, I have the power to release them —

when those of great clans, like great śāla trees, come before me on their own affairs, and when great brahmins, like great śāla trees, and great householders, like great śāla trees, come before me, they do not wait until I have finished speaking but interrupt me again and again with their own words, and I think to myself that I shall speak without discourtesy and without disrespect. Yet, Venerable One, there was once an occasion when the Blessed One was seated in the midst of a retinue of many hundreds, teaching the Dharma, and at that time there was not even the sound of a cough, not even the sound of a clearing of the throat. Then a certain person let out a cough, and another person said to that one, "My friend, you are making noise with your mouth. The Blessed One teaches the Dharma in a way that is sweet beyond sweet, like one who satisfies with honey." When this was said, that person fell completely silent. At that, I thought to myself: "How great is the power and how great is the miraculous ability of the Blessed One — that here, right now, he tames his assembly with the sweet Dharma, without punishment and without weapons. How wonderful!" Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma — and what follows is as before.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, here, when I encounter certain ascetics and brahmins, I deprive them of wealth — and after eight or nine months of their living the holy life, they cast off those appearances, those signs, those marks, and, equipped and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, they indulge, they delight, and they engage in pleasure. Venerable One, yet the śrāvakas of the Blessed One whom I see here practice the holy life for as long as they live — unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and perfectly cleansed — up to the very end of their lives. Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma — and what follows is as before.

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, the Eighth Fascicle.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, I give to certain trusted and long-standing sages, Dāna and the others — I give them wealth, I give them renown, and I even give them my life — yet they do not think to render to the Blessed One what they render to me in the same way. Venerable One, there was once an occasion when I wished to examine certain trusted and long-standing sages, so I left the midst of my retinue and went off to a secluded corner, thinking: "Let me see how these ones turn their feet — toward the Blessed One's side or toward my side." Those sages then praised the buddha in many words and with many ways of speaking, and praised the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and they turned their heads toward the side where the Blessed One was, and turned their feet toward the side where I was. At that, I thought to myself: "How great is the miraculous ability and how great is the power of the Blessed One — that those to whom I give wealth, to whom I give renown, and to whom I even give my life, do not think to repay the Blessed One as they repay me. How wonderful!" From that point on — Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma — and what follows is as before.

Venerable One, I have yet another faith that has arisen from the Dharma. Venerable One, I am a man of the land of Kosala, and the Blessed One is also of the land of Kosala.

My family lineage is the warrior caste (kṣatriya), and the Blessed One's family lineage is also the warrior caste. I am old, aged, burdened with years, having reached eighty years of age. The Blessed One too is old, aged, burdened with years, his body having reached eighty years of age. Venerable One, I am a king of the warrior caste, anointed from the crown of the head. The Blessed One is the unsurpassed king of the Dharma. Venerable One, this too is a faith in the Blessed One that has arisen from the Dharma, and so I think to myself: the Blessed One is a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened buddha; his Dharma and Vinaya are well proclaimed; and the Saṅgha of śrāvakas has entered well upon the path.

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, having spoken at length before the Blessed One on many aspects of the Dharma, prostrated at the Blessed One's feet and departed. Not long after King Prasenajit of Kosala had gone, the Blessed One perceived this and addressed the monks, saying: Monks, you should take up, learn by heart, and master the various Dharma categories of manifold teachings. And why? Monks, the various Dharma categories of manifold teachings have meaning, have Dharma, have pure conduct; they lead to direct knowledge, they lead to perfect awakening, they lead to nirvāṇa. Therefore, a son of good family who has gone forth in faith should take up these various Dharma categories of manifold teachings, master them thoroughly, and in that way hold them, retain them, and recite them.

Now, King Prasenajit of Kosala had been sitting a long time listening to the Dharma in the presence of the Blessed One. Prince Viḍūḍabha, who had been waiting there for some time, then mounted his chariot and departed for Śrāvastī. Prasenajit had left Viḍūḍabha in charge of the kingdom. Mālikā and Vāsabhā-khattiyā asked Viḍūḍabha: "Where is the king?" They were told: "He is residing in the village of Medaḷumpa." So they set out on foot for the village of Medaḷumpa.

After King Prasenajit of Kosala had listened to the Dharma and emerged from the assembly hall, Prince Viḍūḍabha was nowhere to be seen. He asked the monks: "Noble ones, where has Prince Viḍūḍabha gone?" They replied: "He departed just a moment ago by chariot." The king then went on foot. Now the Blessed One had already set out for Rājagṛha at an earlier time. Along the road the king encountered Mālikā and Vāsabhā-khattiyā, and he asked them: "Why have you come here on foot?" They replied: "Your Majesty, Prince Viḍūḍabha has placed Viḍūḍabha in charge of the kingdom and departed; and we, where else should we go but to follow the king?" The king said: "Mālikā, you have already enjoyed your reign as queen — go now and enjoy your son's reign. As for me, I will go to Rājagṛha with Vāsabhā-khattiyā." At that, Mālikā turned back weeping and lamenting with piteous cries. Then King Prasenajit of Kosala set out together with Vāsabhā-khattiyā and gradually made his way to Rājagṛha. Wandering here and there, he came and sat in Ajātaśatru's pleasure garden. He said to Vāsabhā-khattiyā: "Vāsabhā-khattiyā, go and tell King Ajātaśatru that King Prasenajit of Kosala is sitting in the pleasure garden."

She told King Ajātaśatru: "Your Majesty, King Prasenajit of Kosala is sitting in your pleasure garden and wishes to have an audience with you."

Upon hearing this, Ajātaśatru was alarmed and said: "Wise ones, that king commands a great army — if he has come so suddenly, has not any one of you noticed?" The minister Vāsabhā-khattiyā said: "Your Majesty, what army does he have? His son has expelled him from the kingdom, and he has come here with only a single attendant." Ajātaśatru said: "Then the king is welcome. As for me, I shall stay in the quarters of the young." He then said to his ministers: "Wise ones, it would not be fitting for me to receive a king who has been consecrated as sovereign over the kṣatriya clans with no honour and no proper reception. Therefore, today beautify the city and beautify the roads." They cleared the city of stones, gravel, and weeds — and so forth, as before, up to the passage: "like the pleasure garden of delight among the gods."

Then, after the roads and the city had each been made especially beautiful and distinguished, a proclamation was sounded: "Let all the people — those dwelling in Rājagṛha, those in the palace environs, and those who have come from various lands — hear this! King Prasenajit of Kosala is seated in the pleasure garden. Go forth together with your lord, bearing parasols, victory banners, and flags to receive him."

Then King Ajātaśatru, with many thousands of chariots preceding him and accompanied by a fourfold army, went to meet King Prasenajit of Kosala. But Ajātaśatru had been delayed too long on the way, and Prasenajit, exhausted from the hardship of the journey, had gone to a certain enclosure of a thicket not far at all from the pleasure garden. There the bushes filled the entire hollow of the thicket with their shade. He then ate the roots and leaves of the plants in that hollow, and being utterly parched, went to the bank of a pool and drank his fill of water. When he rose, his hands were trembling and his legs would not bear him, so he stumbled and fell onto the road where the chariots pass, and there, his face filled with the dust churned up by wheels, he passed away from this world.

King Ajātaśatru went into the pleasure garden and, thinking to find him, searched about but could not. He dispatched mounted messengers in all four directions to search, and one of those messengers went to the enclosure of the thicket and asked the bushes there: "Ho there! Has anyone come into this pleasure garden?" "Yes — he took the shade of that bush, went along this path to the pool, and left." Following that trail, the messenger found him lying dead on the chariot road. He then told King Ajātaśatru: "Your Majesty, in the direction of a certain chariot road, he has passed away." The king cried out, "Alas!" and surrounded by many hundreds and thousands of people, went in that direction. When he saw the corpse, which was exceedingly unpleasant to behold, he said once more to his ministers: "Wise ones, it is not agreeable to me that this king — consecrated as sovereign among the kṣatriya clans — should have passed away in my realm. Take him with great honour and convey him to the cool grove of the charnel ground. I too will go to the Blessed One to request that offerings be made over his remains." They accordingly conveyed him with great honour to the great charnel ground of the cool grove.

King Ajātaśatru then went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, and bowing his head at the feet of the Blessed One, spoke these words: "Venerable One, King Prasenajit of Kosala has passed away in my realm — what manner of offerings shall I make over his remains?" The Blessed One declared: "Great King, honour the body with the fullest offerings that lie within your power and your means."

Then the king made great offerings over his remains. Afterward he went again into the presence of the Blessed One and addressed him: "Venerable One, what action did King Prasenajit of Kosala perform such that, by the karmic maturation of that action, he found himself at the end of a mountain pass, overcome by hunger, his limbs stiff and swollen, and passed away before his time?"

The Blessed One declared: "The very actions accumulated and gathered by King Prasenajit himself, having met with the right conditions, will ripen without fail — abiding close like a shadow that never departs, and arising inevitably to be experienced by none other than himself. Great King, the actions one has performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, whatever virtuous and non-virtuous actions have been performed and accumulated ripen solely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

Even through a hundred aeons,
actions do not perish.
When conditions and the time converge,
they ripen as fruit for embodied beings.

Great King, once upon a time there was a brahmin who dwelt in a mountain pass. He took a wife of equal caste, and with her he sported and delighted and enjoyed pleasure. While they sported and delighted and enjoyed pleasure together, a son was born to them, and in the fullness of time they raised and nurtured him until he grew up. One day the son went out begging and found a bowlful of grain husks in the mountain pass. He said to his mother: 'Please keep this for me while I wash and return.' He gave it to her and went off to bathe.

Now, when buddhas have not appeared in the world, there arise in this world pratyekabuddhas — those who have compassion for the base and the lowly, who are devoted to solitary forest dwelling at the edge of the world, and who are the sole field of merit for the world. One such pratyekabuddha, wandering and traveling through the land, came to that mountain pass. He stayed there for a while. In the morning he dressed in his lower robe and his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and entered the mountain pass for his alms round, coming step by step to that very house. The brahmin woman, seeing his beautiful form and beautiful mind and so forth, felt her heart filled with joy and offered the pratyekabuddha that entire bowlful of grain husks. Now, these great beings teach the Dharma through their body, not through speech. So he spread his wings like a king among geese and rose up into the open sky, displaying various miraculous feats.

Ordinary beings are quick to develop faith upon seeing miraculous power. He then alighted, touching the ground with his feet, as smoothly as a tree cut at the root falls. And he regarded her with compassion and went on his way.

In due course the brahmin boy returned and said: 'Mother, please give me that bowl of grain husks.' She replied: 'Son, rejoice! I offered it to a renunciant of peaceful nature who had come seeking alms.' At this, overcome by hunger, he fell into suffering and distress of mind, and said: 'Since that renunciant ate it, why did his arms not stiffen and swell so that he died before his time?'

Great King, what do you think? That brahmin boy — he is none other than King Prasenajit of Kosala in this very life. At that time, through the karmic maturation of having spoken harsh words to a pratyekabuddha, he was born in the hells for many years, for many hundreds of years, for many thousands of years, for many hundreds of thousands of years. And by the remainder of that same karma, six times his arms stiffened and swelled and he passed away before his time."

And from that time until now, seven times in all his arms stiffened and swelled, and he passed away before his time by that alone.

Therefore, Great King, from the passage beginning 'those actions that are entirely dark' to 'one must strive toward those that are entirely bright' — you should train yourself accordingly, Great King — all of this is as stated before.

Then King Ajātaśatru, full of sincere faith in what the Blessed One had declared, rejoiced, and bowing his head to the feet of the Blessed One, withdrew from his presence.

Then Virūḍhaka said this to the noble Ajātaśatru: "My lord, while your father still reigns as king and the royal consecration has not yet been conferred upon you, when the time comes for me to become king, I shall make the Śākyas bow their heads. That shall be the first thing I do." Having uttered these great and powerful words befitting a bull among men, he declared it with finality and proclaimed it with a lion's roar in the midst of the assembly. "Was this your intent? Now the time for it has come."

Ajātaśatru replied to him: "Whatever Virūḍhaka has said — all of it, shall it really be done? That matter is past; let it go. The affairs of a king and the deeds of a king will come to ruin."

Virūḍhaka said: "My lord, virtuous men are firm in their pledges. Therefore please let me carry out what I vowed. As for Virūḍhaka — set that aside for now. It will not be difficult."

Ajātaśatru said: "My lord, since this was a vow made at the very beginning, I will certainly not stop you. Whether today is a good time, or a moment hence is good, or an hour hence is good — even the umbrella of merit is good. So it is fitting, my lord, that you depart this very day, without requiring those gods to lay out a reception."

Then Virūḍhaka, the noble one, deceiving Ajātaśatru, armed a fourfold host — the assemblage of elephants, the assemblage of cavalry, the assemblage of chariots, and the assemblage of infantry — and set out from Śrāvastī toward Kapila, intending to slay the Śākyas dwelling there.

Now at such a moment, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess not even the slightest lack of knowledge, lack of vision, or lack of understanding. Knowing that the karma of the Śākyas dwelling in Kapila would not be made fruitless, and moved by that knowledge, the Blessed One set out from Śrāvastī toward Kapila ahead of them all.

The Blessed One, traveling along the road, sat cross-legged in the midday resting beneath a certain śākoṭaka tree whose bark was peeling and unpleasant, whose leaves were sparse, and whose shade was meager.

King Virūḍhaka the noble one saw the Blessed One from afar. Seeing him, he went to where the Blessed One was and addressed him thus: "Venerable One, if there are other trees with pleasant leaves and fuller shade, why has the Blessed One abandoned those and chosen to sit under this śākoṭaka tree with its peeling bark, its unpleasant appearance, its sparse leaves, and its meager shade?"

The Blessed One declared: "Great King, the shade of one's kinsmen is cool."

Virūḍhaka thought: "The Blessed One looks upon his kinsmen with compassion and love. Alas, the Blessed One truly acts with love toward his kinsmen." Recognizing this, he turned back from that very place.

The Blessed One then reflected: "If the Śākyas dwelling in Kapila are struck by Virūḍhaka's army before they have seen the truth, they will not become vessels fit to realize the truth." Knowing this, he set out traveling through the lands of the Śākyas, journeying to Kapila and dwelling in the Nyagrodhā park there.

The Śākyas dwelling in Kapila heard that the Blessed One, who had been traveling through the lands of the Śākyas, had arrived there and was residing in this very Nyagrodhā park. And upon hearing this, they went to where the Blessed One was, and arriving there —

they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, touching their heads to the ground, and took their seats to one side. The Blessed One, knowing their dispositions, latent tendencies, constitutions, and characters, then taught them the Dharma in such a way that they would come to realize the four noble truths. Upon hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained a great distinction: some directly realized the fruit called stream-entry, and some the fruit called once-returning — and so on as before, down through "those who are destined for the Saṅgha."

Now Virūḍhaka, seeing a noble-born man, said to him, "God, why have you come back?" The man replied, "Virūḍhaka, the Blessed One has regard and compassion for his kinsmen. Alas, because the Blessed One has compassion for his kinsmen, the great king has spoken these words to them: 'The cool shade of a kinsman is a kinsman's shade.' This has entered my heart and settled there. Let the Śākyas dwelling in Kapila go free; do not slaughter them." Virūḍhaka replied, "God, the ascetic Gautama has gone beyond attachment. Those who are beyond attachment do not look upon their kinsmen. Therefore today, whether it be the divine sun, or a mere moment of time, or a star, or a parasol of merit — all are equally fine. Today, go to the territory of Kapila." But that man, having been misled and seized by a companion of unwholesome intent, equipped the fourfold army — the host of elephants, the host of cavalry, the host of chariots, and the host of foot soldiers — and marched to the territory of Kapila, setting up his encampment not very far off.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, touching his head to the ground, and taking a seat to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend One, I have heard that the deluded fellow Virūḍhaka, equipping the fourfold army — the host of elephants, the host of cavalry, the host of chariots, and the host of foot soldiers — has come to the territory of Kapila in order to massacre the Śākyas dwelling in Kapila. For that reason I should like, along with an army and its mounts, either to dispatch him to another world-realm, or to hurl him beyond the surrounding mountains, or to encircle the city of Kapila with an iron palisade, or to encircle it with an iron net." The Blessed One replied: "Maudgalyāyana, it is so. It is indeed so. You could do what you have described — encircle it, as before. And yet, the Śākyas dwelling in Kapila have themselves accumulated the assemblage of karma, the condition has fully matured, it draws near like a welling flood, and those actions that will inevitably ripen — the karma they have done and accumulated — who else would experience it? Monks, the actions one has done and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of wind. But the virtuous and non-virtuous actions one has done and accumulated ripen in those very aggregates, elements, and sense bases that one has appropriated.

Even across hundreds of aeons,
karmic actions do not perish.
When the conditions and the time are met,
they ripen as results for embodied beings.

Maudgalyāyana, the world is governed by karma, born from karma, living out karma's portion, relying on karma. Whoever has performed a virtuous or a sinful action becomes an heir to that karma. Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, one should incline toward wholesome karma."

Then the venerable Maudgalyāyana bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed.

The Śākyas dwelling at Kapilavastu heard that the man Virūḍhaka, born of a woman of low birth, was coming with a fourfold army — a host of elephants, a host of cavalry, a host of chariots, and a host of foot soldiers — to put them to death. Upon hearing this, they too equipped a fourfold army — a host of elephants, a host of cavalry, a host of chariots, and a host of foot soldiers — and arrayed themselves against Virūḍhaka to do battle. Yet because they were seers of truth, they would not kill even slightly. Instead, they drove back his men with sticks and whips, cut bowstrings, ropes, and cords, and shot arrows at ear-ornaments. Having broken apart the armor of Virūḍhaka's army, they entered Kapilavastu, shut the gates, and manned the ramparts.

Virūḍhaka's forces, having been repulsed in their hostile advance, came to the mother of Virūḍhaka and said, "Mother, do you not see? The Śākyas are going to destroy us — make way and let us pass." She replied, "My lord, do not be troubled. The Śākyas dwelling at Kapilavastu are seers of truth; they are unable to bring themselves to part even a living creature — even an insect — from its life. And this is evident from the fact that they have not killed even a single one of our men." He was taken in by this and sat in silence, saying nothing.

The Śākyas then established a rule among themselves: "Friends, none among us shall strike Virūḍhaka or his army. Whoever strikes them is no kinsman of ours and no Śākya."

At that time there was a certain Śākya named Śambhaka who was sitting alone on a cliff, off by himself, intent on some business of his own. He had not heard the rule the Śākyas had established. Being an ordinary person, he heard the news that Virūḍhaka had come to Kapilavastu to kill them, and that he was sitting in a great open quarter. On hearing this, seized by anger that had erupted and pervaded him, his mind disturbed, he charged into Virūḍhaka's army. There he killed many among the populace, and left some barely alive.

Virūḍhaka then, greatly troubled, said, "Mother, do you not see? You told us that these people are seers of truth and would not part even an insect from its life. Yet this one alone has killed so many of our people in this manner. If all of them were to come at once, not a single one of our beings would survive — what more need be said? We have been constrained by time; let us turn back for now."

She said, "My lord, the Śākyas enacted a rule of this kind among themselves: none among us may strike Virūḍhaka or his army; whoever strikes him is no kinsman of ours and no Śākya. He did not hear this pledge, and so now there is ground for him not to be counted among them."

Then Śambhaka went to the gate of Kapilavastu, sat down, and said, "Friends, open the gate and let me in." They replied, "You have broken our rule; from this point on you are neither our kinsman nor a Śākya. How can we allow you inside? Be gone." He said, "I did not hear your rule — but what is the use of speaking at length?"

"If I have violated your rule, send my retinue back out and I shall go elsewhere." They sent his retinue out, and he led them to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, Śākya Śambhaka addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Venerable One, please grant me some token by which I may act in your service." The Blessed One gave him strands of hair, nail clippings, and teeth produced by his miraculous power. Śambhaka took these and went to the land of Kudara. There the people heard that one called Śākya Śambhaka, endowed with diligence, strength, and all the excellent qualities of a great champion, was coming, desiring the kingship of their land. Hearing this, they began to deliberate. The wise men said among themselves, "We have heard that one called Śākya Śambhaka, endowed with diligence, strength, and all the excellent qualities of a great champion, is coming to our land. Let everyone gather here for now — shall we go to meet him or not?" All of them assembled together for the time being and remained there.

Meanwhile, Śambhaka left his retinue to one side, dressed himself in the manner of a minister's attendant, and went to them. They greeted him with words of welcome, exchanged pleasantries, and then asked, "Where have you come from?" He replied, "Śākya Śambhaka, endowed with diligence, strength, and all the excellent qualities of a great champion, desires the kingship and wishes to come here. He has sent this letter — open it and read it." They said, "There is not even a seat — where should we place it?" At that he drew his sword from its scabbard, chopped a flat stone into pieces, and said, "Place it on this." Seeing this, they looked at one another with astonished eyes and said, "Good man, how many men like you does he have?" He replied, "Wise ones, I am only his attendant — what am I capable of? He has many other brave warriors." Hearing this, they were filled with awe and said to one another, "Wise ones, if the attendant of such a man is like this, what must his other men be like? Let him come — we will make him our king." They read the letter and sent back a reply: "It is good that you are coming. We trust in this and will act according to your command." Śambhaka took the reply letter and arrived together with his retinue and all their best possessions, coming to the land of Kudara. The people there received him with great honor and established him on the throne. The proclamation spread everywhere: "Śākya Śambhaka has been enthroned over the kingdom!" And so he came to be known by the name King Śambhaka, King Śambhaka. There he had a shrine made for the hair and nail clippings of the Blessed One, and it came to be known as the Śambhaka Shrine, the Śambhaka Shrine.

His wife was a woman without faith. She was, however, his chief queen, and so he could not slight her in the least. He gave orders to his ministers: "Have the hermitage guarded." They guarded the hermitage, and from that time on no wild animals were killed there.

Ārya-jaṭa harmed his mother and said to her, "Now that you have harmed her, the Śākyas have shut the gates and enclosed the grounds, and they dwell there at ease. What do you want to do, hemmed in as you are by time's certainty?" He replied, "My lord, would a single enemy destroy an entire city? I, living in the royal palace, have heard that —"

"The wise accomplish their aims through five means: conciliation, lavish giving, deception, all-round practice, and fifth, armed force."

And so, he said, "Consider sowing division among them." Ārya-jaṭa sent word to the Śākyas: "O wise ones, I bear you no attachment and no anger, yet there is a small matter of personal dignity that concerns me. Once I have settled it and obtained what I need, open the gates quickly, that I may leave at once." The Śākyas said among themselves, "O wise ones, shall we assemble and open the gates, or shall we deliberate on whether to leave them closed?" They all gathered together, and some said, "Open them." Others said, "If we open them, it will not go well." Then some said, "O wise ones, some say open the gates; others say it will not go well if we do. Therefore, if you wish, cast lots, and whatever the majority desires, let that be done." So they began to cast lots.

At that moment Māra the evil one thought to himself: "Many times I have sought an opportunity and looked for a flaw in the ascetic Gautama, following him again and again, yet never found an opening. Now I realize I can drive a wedge between his kinsmen." So he manifested himself in the visible form of an aged Śākya and sat at the end of the row of elders. He was the first to draw a lot, and seeing that an elder Śākya had drawn, all the others drew as well.

Then one of single mind sent word to Ārya-jaṭa: "Enter." He entered with his fourfold army and, having entered, declared, "I have driven a wedge between the Śākyas. I have utterly abandoned the Śākyas." The very instant those words had left his mouth, armed men began slaughtering the Śākyas on all sides, and a great outcry arose.

Hearing the great cry of the name Śākya, a kinsman was seized with distress born of love for his kin, and quickly, quickly went to Ārya-jaṭa and said to him, "Noble god, grant me a boon worthy of your nobility." He replied, "Tell me what boon you ask." The man said, "Noble god, grant fearlessness to my kinsmen." Ārya-jaṭa replied, "I will not grant fearlessness to your kinsmen. But you and your retinue may come out." The man said, "Noble god, for as long as I remain submerged in the water, grant fearlessness to those who come out." Ārya-jaṭa then looked toward his ministers, and they said, "Noble god, this great name is both your mother's kinsman and your father's friend, so it is fitting that you grant him this boon." He replied, "If that is so, I grant it at once."

The one who bore the great name Śākya, his mind distressed with grief born of love for his kin, his heart moist with compassion, went to a pool of water. Beside that pool stood a sāla tree whose branches dipped into the water of the pool. He clung to those branches, submerged himself, and remained submerged until his very life was spent.

Now, among those Śākyas dwelling in the dwelling of the yellow-robed ones, those who had not participated in the communal act — some left the dwelling of the yellow-robed ones and went out wandering as wanderers; some went to Nepal; some went to various villages, market towns, royal territories, and one palace or another.

Those who had participated in the communal act came out through the eastern gate of the ground of the yellow-robed ones and entered from the south; came out from the south and entered from the west; came out from the west and entered from the north; came out from the north and entered from the east. The ministers said, "Noble god, alas, the Śākyas are being cut down! Alas, the Śākyas are being cut down! Right now, those who enter through the eastern gate come out in the south; those who enter through the south come out in the west —"

those who enter from the west come out in the north; those who enter from the north come out in the south.

The noble one spoke: "Wise ones, look — it has been a long while since that ancestor sank beneath the water." The ministers went at length to inspect the pool, and by that point the time had already passed. They returned and reported to him: "Noble god, the time has passed." Then, surrounded by a great plain on all sides, he spoke: "Wise ones, prepare your seats. Until a rain of blood falls on the great highway, we shall not depart from this place. When brave men are slain, it is the natural order that little blood flows." The ministers began to deliberate among themselves: "Wise ones, if this being is one who commits sinful deeds and holds firm to his oath, how could so much blood possibly come from here? Let us send for some lacquer." And so they took lacquer and poured many hundreds and thousands of jars of lacquer-water onto the great highway.

The noble one thought to himself: "My oath is now fulfilled; I may go." Then that benighted and ignoble man killed seventy-seven thousand Śākyas, and the great majority of them were those who had seen the truth. Having slaughtered that multitude of beings, he took five hundred youths and five hundred maidens and went to the pleasure garden of the wandering non-Buddhist (tīrthika) teachers, a place called the Sow's Abode.

Mālanod said: "Noble god, you have fully nurtured your enemies. Why leave these enemies alive? Kill them." The noble one handed them over to the executioners and commanded: "Have these ones trampled by elephants." The executioners began to drive the elephants at them, but the youths and maidens pressed the elephants back on their haunches and began to pass one another hand to hand along the elephants' backs.

Mālanod said: "Noble god, do you see, do you behold, how these ones are getting the better of you? If you leave them alive, will they not do you harm?" "Mālanod, you are right. Ask how they are to be killed, then tell me." He replied: "Noble god, put them in a pit and from above crush them with iron beams. Do as that dictates." So he had them put into the pit and from above crushed them with iron beams.

Then two of them escaped and went before the Blessed One. When they arrived, the Blessed One covered them with his begging bowl, and they died right there. When the Śākyas were slaughtered, the Blessed One's head became very painful.

Then that benighted and ignoble man said to a certain man: "You there — go, take a seat before the Tathāgata, and whatever the Blessed One says, listen and then come back and report it to me." Having said this, he departed. That man went and took his seat before the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, bring me a bowl of water." Ānanda offered a bowl of water to the Blessed One. The Blessed One poured just two or three drops of water into it, and from within the water they hissed and sputtered, bubbling with steam, and produced a sound.

The monks, having witnessed this marvel, were filled with faith, and they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Reverend Blessed One, what deed was performed such that by the ripening of that deed the Blessed One's head has become painful? And as for those Śākyas who dwelled among the yellow-robed ones — what transgression did they commit in a former time? They had done no wrong, they had caused no harm, and yet they were killed by that benighted and ignoble man."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, come — in that very place where the pig-park pleasure grove of the wandering non-Buddhist ascetics is located, where that deluded and ignoble man killed the Śākyas, I shall there and then prophesy the deeds of both those Śākyas and myself." "Reverend one, so be it," said the monks, and they listened, deferring to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One set out for that place — the pig-park pleasure grove of the wandering non-Buddhist ascetics — accompanied by a great many monks. A brahmin of ignoble birth and low lineage caught sight of the Blessed One from quite a distance, and having seen him, addressed the Blessed One in these words: "O Gautama! That deluded and ignoble man has separated from life those Śākyas who dwelled among the yellow-robed ones, who had committed no wrong and done no harm — he has produced a great deal of demerit."

The Blessed One replied: "Brahmin, it is so. It is indeed so. Because that deluded and ignoble man has separated from life those Śākyas who dwelled among the yellow-robed ones, who had committed no wrong and done no harm, he has produced a great deal of demerit."

Then, as the Blessed One arrived at the pig-park pleasure grove of the wandering non-Buddhist ascetics, those Śākyas who had been cut down by the iron swords and in whom a little spark of life yet remained — when they saw the Blessed One, they cried out in pitiful voices. The Blessed One then went to one side, and where a seat had been spread he sat down. Having sat, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, these Śākyas who dwell among the yellow-robed ones have now, for the third time, raised a great cry — the very same cry as when, in former times, they were fishermen catching fish for the sake of fish, and when, as bandits, they were the same ones who destroyed villages, and now, as those who dwell among the yellow-robed ones and have been left with barely a thread of life remaining by that deluded and ignoble man, they face death and move toward it. In the bursting forth of all these cries there is not the slightest difference, distinction, or variation — they are the same.

"Monks, what do you think? Have you ever seen or heard of a butcher — one who, from that trade, with that craft and that livelihood, rides upon an elephant, or rides upon a horse, or travels in a carriage, or goes about attended by a retinue of men, or comes to dwell having accumulated vast and abundant heaps of wealth?" "Reverend one, no." "Monks, excellent, excellent! I too, from a butcher who with that trade" — and so forth as before, through "comes to dwell having accumulated vast and abundant heaps of wealth" — "have neither seen nor heard of it. And why is that? Because butchers deliberate with evil intention, and therefore such a one does not come to ride upon an elephant or ride upon a horse or travel in a carriage or go about attended by a retinue of men, and does not come to dwell having accumulated vast and abundant heaps of wealth.

"Furthermore, monks, what do you think? Among those who kill chickens, kill pigs, who are fishermen, who snare game, who trap birds, who sell straying donkeys, who kill cattle — from that trade" — and so forth as before, through "comes to dwell having accumulated vast and abundant heaps of wealth — have you seen or heard of such a thing?" And so on as before. "And why is that? Because one who kills cattle deliberates with evil intention, and therefore such a one does not come to ride upon an elephant" — and so forth as before, through "does not come to dwell having accumulated vast and abundant heaps of wealth" — as stated before.

Monks, even among those who have taken birth in the animal realm, if one deliberates with an evil intention, one will not come to ride upon an elephant, ride on a horse, travel in a carriage, or journey accompanied by a small retinue with all its trappings, nor will one come to dwell having accumulated vast and abundant heaps of wealth. How much less, then, is it possible for a deluded, ignoble, base-born man, overcome by the splendor of moral discipline that has been shattered, to ride upon an elephant, ride on a horse, travel in a carriage, or journey accompanied by a small retinue — to say nothing of dwelling having accumulated vast and abundant heaps of wealth. That simply has no basis whatsoever.

Monks, this very clan of Kosala will, within seven days, have its lineage cut off, as if smitten by a serpent's gaze. And that deluded, ignoble, base-born man, along with his mother and with harm done to her, will, within seven days, be consumed by fire, crying out in lamentation, and will be born in the great hell of Avīci.

Monks, therefore train yourselves thus: "If one should not harbor an evil thought even toward a piece of firewood, how much less toward a body possessed of consciousness." Monks, you should train yourselves in exactly this way.

Then the monks, having doubts arise, presented all their doubts to the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubt. They asked: "Venerable One, what karma did these five hundred Śākyas commit such that, through the karmic maturation of that action, they were killed by that deluded, ignoble, base-born man, having done no wrong and having caused no harm? And at the time the Śākyas were slaughtered, the Blessed One too was struck by a severe headache."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, these very things, and the karma I myself have performed and accumulated — the conditions fully assembled, present like a creditor who has reached the threshold — will without doubt come to arise. Who else but oneself could experience the karma one has performed and accumulated? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in nothing other than the appropriated aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense sources (āyatanas) themselves.

Even across a hundred aeons,
actions never come to naught;
when the assembly of causes meets the time,
their fruit ripens for those who bear a body.

Monks, in a time long past, five hundred fishermen dwelt on the bank of a river. They saw two great fish swimming together in the great ocean and then entering that river. Filled with delight, the fishermen ensnared them in a great net. When they saw the bodies of the two fish they began to deliberate: "Friends, how should we proceed with these? These bodies are so very large that if we kill them the flesh will not be manageable — it will rot. So what should be done?" Some said, "What is there to do? Let us kill one and tie up the other and keep it." Others said, "But that one too is enormous, and since it too cannot be managed, let us tie it to a stake, cut off the flesh while it is still alive, and sell it piece by piece." They all agreed: "Good — let it be done so." And as they began to do this, the fish, as they were being cut, began to cry out in their own voice. The suffering of those fish was heard by a young boy who was the child of a fisherman, and he felt delight arise in him at the sound.

Then when the two fish were being cut in this way, they gave rise to the following thought: "We have done no wrong and caused no harm, yet these men have killed us in this fashion. Therefore, wherever these men too have done no wrong —"

may they be killed without having done wrong and without having caused harm."

Monks, what do you think? Those two fish are none other than these very ones: Āryaskanda and Mālāgandha. And those five hundred fishermen are none other than these five hundred Śākyas. By the karmic maturation of the act whereby those two killed the fish in that manner, these five hundred Śākyas — having done no wrong and caused no harm — are now being killed by Āryaskanda and Mālāgandha, crying out as iron shafts press down upon them. As for the fisherman's boy, that was none other than myself at that time, in that life. By the karmic maturation of the act of generating delight when the fish were killed, even now I, having attained perfect and complete awakening, am struck by a severe headache. Had I not attained an accumulation of qualities such as this, I too would have received karmic results of that very kind.

Monks, hear also what the Śākyas who dwell in the borderlands have done. Monks, long ago, five hundred bandits waylaid travelers on a road, seized their goods, and went to plunder in a rocky mountain gorge. They robbed and plundered every gathering of people dwelling in that rocky gorge. Two householders climbed up to a high ledge and sat there, and the bandits called out to them: "You there — come down! Vanish without a trace!" The two replied: "As long as we live, we will not come down." The bandits then stripped away most of the grass and wood, set that ledge alight, and the two — tormented and consumed by the pain of the heat — gave rise to this thought: "We have done no wrong and caused no harm, yet these men are killing us; therefore may these men too — having done no wrong and caused no harm — be killed."

Monks, what do you think? Those two householders are none other than these very ones: Āryaskanda and Mālāgandha. And those five hundred bandits are none other than these five hundred Śākyas. By the karmic maturation of that act — the act of separating those people from their lives though they had done no wrong and caused no harm — now Āryaskanda, joining with Mālāgandha, has separated these five hundred Śākyas from their lives though they had done no wrong and caused no harm.

Monks, thus it is: the karmic maturation of utterly dark actions is utterly dark; the maturation of utterly bright actions is utterly bright; and the maturation of mixed actions is mixed.

Therefore, monks, abandon utterly dark actions and mixed actions, and strive after utterly pure and bright actions. Monks, you should train yourselves accordingly.

After killing the Śākyas in this way, Āryaskanda went to Śrāvastī. Upon entering the city, he went to the palace in the pleasure garden of the royal prince Jeta, where he played, rejoiced, and made merry with women, without a man in sight. Āryaskanda saw this and said: "Good sirs, who is it that plays here?" The ministers replied: "It is the royal prince Jeta, my lord." He said: "Good sirs, summon him." They summoned him, and Āryaskanda said: "Prince Jeta — I have come after killing my enemies. Are you here amusing yourself?" Jeta replied: "My lord, who are your enemies?" "The Śākyas." "If the Śākyas were your enemies, then what manner of friends did you have?"

He said: "Good sirs, this one too is entirely on their side — he must be killed." And so they killed him. When his time had passed, he was reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Before the sound of his human music had even ceased, the sound of divine music arose.

Then the Blessed One spoke verses concerning this event:

One who has made merit rejoices here and rejoices hereafter;
in both places one rejoices.
Seeing the ripening of one's own karma, one rejoices and is supremely glad,
and rejoices again at having gone to a good destiny.

One who has made merit is pleased here and pleased hereafter;
in both places one is pleased.
Seeing the ripening of one's own karma, one is pleased and supremely content,
and is pleased again at having gone to a good destiny.

Then the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, I have not understood the meaning of these verses." The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, the young royal prince Jeta, innocent and without harm, was separated from his life by the arrogant-born man (Āryaskanda), a being of delusion — and before the sound of his human music had ceased, the sound of divine music arose. Reflecting on that, I spoke thus: from 'One who has made merit rejoices here and rejoices hereafter' to 'and is pleased again at having gone to a good destiny.'" When the Blessed One said this, Āryaskanda sat there in silence.

Then at some later time, Āryaskanda was boasting and preening himself in the midst of his queen's retinue, arrogant and full of pride, saying: "I am powerful, heroic, and diligent, and I have crushed my enemies — who is there equal to me?" Then the five hundred Śākya women whom Āryaskanda had taken captive spoke a verse in reply:

Those whom you claim to have crushed
are sons of the Victor, children of the Śākyas,
bound by the restraint of their training.
What right have you to speak thus here?

When they said this, he flew into a rage and ordered his ministers in verse:

Just as the daughters of nāgas, when nāgas are killed,
are shrouded in clouds filled with venom —
cut off the hands and feet of these women,
then quickly release their kinsmen after them.

The ministers cut off the hands and feet of those five hundred Śākya women at the bank of a red pond. The place came to be named "the hollow of the hand, the hollow of the hand," and the elders likewise, at the opening of sūtra passages, inserted the phrase "the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, at the bank of the pond of the hollow of the hand."

The Minor Vinaya Matters, ninth fascicle.

When those women were experiencing pain that was unbearable, harsh, burning, and disagreeable, they thought: "We are in unbearable, harrowing, and wretched agony — can it be that the Blessed One has not taken notice of us?" In such a situation, there is not the slightest thing that the Blessed Buddhas do not know, do not see, do not comprehend, or fail to understand. Then, moved by great compassion, the Blessed One made his way to that place, and he saw that all those women were sitting there helpless. Seeing this, the Blessed One gave rise to a worldly resolve of mind. It is the nature of reality (dharmatā) that whenever the Blessed Buddhas give rise to a worldly resolve of mind, even creatures as small as ants and insects know it through the Blessed One's intention and mind. But when they give rise to a transcendent resolve of mind, even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know the Blessed One's intention and mind through their own minds — let alone the creatures born in the animal realm: what need is there even to speak of them? The Blessed One considered:

"How wonderful!" the Blessed One thought inwardly, just as the divine daughters Bhadra and the others were coming, bearing robes and water. The moment the Blessed One formed this resolve, the divine daughters Bhadra and the others took five hundred pairs of linen cloth and drew water from the great unheated lake Anavatapta, then went to where the Blessed One was. When they arrived, they prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet, touching their heads to the ground, and said: "Venerable One, we have come to offer these five hundred bolts of cloth and water for bathing." The Blessed One replied: "Go, and let the Śākyan women breathe freely. Once they have done so, wash their feet and hands and clothe them in the garments." "It shall be done as you command, Venerable One," they said, and thereupon washed the feet and hands of those women and dressed them in the robes. Then they prostrated at the Blessed One's feet, touching their heads to the ground, and took their seats before the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then, through his miraculous power, cut the stream of suffering of those five hundred Śākyan women. Having cut it, he declared: "Sisters, these karmic deeds that you yourselves have performed and accumulated, gathered together, brought to full ripeness in their conditions, dwelling close as though at the bank's edge — they are bound to arise without fail. Who else could experience the karma that you yourselves have performed and accumulated? Sisters, apply yourselves to virtue." Having said this, the Blessed One departed.

They, their minds filled with clear faith toward the Blessed One, passed from that life and were reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. It is the nature of reality that when a divine son or divine daughter has been born not long before, three recognitions arise: from where one has passed away, where one has been reborn, and by what karma. They saw for themselves that they had passed from among human beings, been reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and that the karma responsible for this was the clear faith they had directed toward the Blessed One.

Then those five hundred gods who had formerly been the Śākyan women occupied with their weaving thought to themselves: "It would not be right for us to wait a number of days before going to see the Blessed One. Come, let us go this very day — without delay — to see the Blessed One." And so those gods who had been the weaving Śākyan women adorned themselves, their sparkling earrings and earrings gleaming, their bodies decorated with garlands and armlets, and that very night they filled their laps with divine flowers — utpalas, lotuses, kumudas, white lotuses, and māndāravas — and illuminated the whole of Prince Jeta's Grove with a great radiance. They scattered those flowers over the Blessed One and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One, knowing their intentions, their latent tendencies, their spiritual faculties, and their natures, taught them the Dharma in such a way as would lead them to realize the four noble truths. Hearing this, they shattered with the vajra of wisdom the mountain peak of the view of the transitory collection, twenty heights high, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truths, they uttered this inspired utterance three times: "Such healing as the Blessed One has administered to us — this our mothers have not done for us, nor our fathers, nor kings, nor gods, nor the assembly of our own people and dear kinsmen, nor our ancestors of former times, nor ascetics and brahmins. He has dried the ocean of blood and tears, freed us from the mountain of bones, closed the doors to the lower realms, opened the doors to higher states and liberation, and set us in order among gods and humans."

They then spoke again:

Through your power, the paths to the lower realms,
So terribly hard to bear and fraught with harm, are cut.
The doors to higher states are opened; we have gained
Great merit and attained the path to nirvāṇa.

By drawing near to you, today we are freed from fault,
We have gained eyes utterly pure and perfectly clear,
Attained the noble state of joy and peace,
And crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.

Among wandering beings, honored by asuras, gods, and humans,
Free from the faults of birth, aging, and death,
Seeing existence as empty — a thing most rare to find —
O Sage, today there is fruit in having seen you.

Then those of Śemoḍo who had arisen in joy
Prostrated at the two feet of the Blessed One,
Circumambulated the Subduer of Foes,
And departed once more in the direction of the divine world.

The monks, having grown uncertain, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubt: "Venerable One, what karma did those five hundred Śākya women perform, such that their hands and feet were cut off? What karma did they perform, such that they were born among the gods? And what karma did they perform, such that they came to see the truth in the presence of the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One declared: "O monks, these very ones performed and accumulated karma" — and from that point through the passage "ripens as a fruit for embodied beings," it is as before.

"O monks, long ago, in this very good eon, at a time when human life spanned twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and completely awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide for those to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a blessed one — a Teacher by the name of Kāśyapa. These women had gone forth under his teaching. At that time, these women habitually used the words 'handless' and 'footless' toward monks who were in training and beyond training. Through the karmic maturation of that action, they were born for many years in the hells. Through the remainder of that very karma, for five hundred lifetimes they had their hands and feet cut off, and even up to the present they have had their hands and feet cut off. The karma of having turned their minds with full sincerity toward me ripened as birth among the gods. The fact that they received the scriptural transmission at that time, and recited and chanted it, is what caused them to see the truth in my presence.

"O monks, therefore, for those whose karma is exclusively dark" — and from that point through the passage "strive diligently; O monks, you should train in just this way," it is as before.

Then that man came to Viḍūḍabha, and Viḍūḍabha said: "Ho there, man — what did the Blessed One say?" He replied: "My lord, from the mouth of the Blessed One came these words: 'In seven days from now, Viḍūḍabha, the king of Kosala, will meet his end, struck down like a serpent's gaze.'" And he said: "Viḍūḍabha, together with his mother's harm, will fall like one consumed by fire into the great hell of Avīci, the Unceasing."

Upon hearing this, Viḍūḍabha rested his cheek in his hand and sat absorbed in his own thoughts. His mother, Mālagandha, said: "My lord, why do you sit with your cheek resting in your hand, lost in thought?" He replied: "Mālagandha, the Blessed One has declared: 'In seven days, Viḍūḍabha, together with Mālagandha's harm, will fall like one consumed by fire into the great hell of Avīci, the Unceasing.' How then can I not sit lost in thought?"

She replied: "My lord, one who does not offer a seat to a brahmin who has come — even that person, when he reflects, thinks of a hundred thousand ruinations."

"He killed that many friends and companions of the ascetic Gautama — need one even speak of it? Let him say what he will, or let others say what they will. Nevertheless, let the king have a pavilion built in the pleasure grove, standing on a single pillar in the middle of the water. Let the king go there and remain for seven days in the sky, and when the seven days have passed, let him return to Śrāvastī." He replied, "So be it," and together with the queen's retinue he went there and took up residence.

When one day had passed, Mālagandha said: "My lord, one of the seven days in the sky has passed. Six days remain. Once the six days have passed, you are to depart for Śrāvastī." And from the second and third day on through to the seventh, she said likewise: "My lord, today you are to depart for Śrāvastī."

Now an ill omen arose. Women are fond of adornment, and so the ladies of the queen's retinue said to one another: "Sisters, since today we must set out for Śrāvastī, let us put on our ornaments." And they began to adorn themselves. One among the queen's retinue had set a crystal gemstone on the top of a tent-panel and was putting on her ornaments. Just then the ill omen cleared, and rays of sunlight struck the crystal, which burst into flame, and the fire spread to the tent-panel, and from there to the pavilion, and the queen's retinue fled.

Viḍūḍabha and Mālagandha also began to flee just as foretold, but spirits had already blocked all the exits. Viḍūḍabha spoke the words exactly as foretold: "Mālagandha, burn!" She replied: "Your majesty too!" And crying out those very words, they were born in the great hell of Avīci, the Unceasing.

Thereupon the Blessed One spoke these verses concerning what had come to pass:

One who has done evil burns here; he burns hereafter; he burns in both.
He burns and is utterly consumed, seeing the karmic ripening of his own deeds.
Having gone to an evil destiny, he burns again.

One who has done evil grieves here; he grieves hereafter; he grieves in both.
He grieves and is utterly tormented, seeing the karmic ripening of his own deeds.
Having gone to an evil destiny, he grieves again.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda addressed him: "Reverend sir, I do not understand the meaning of these verses."

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, that man of delusion, Viḍūḍabha, together with Mālagandha, was consumed as if by fire and gone to the hell of Avīci, the Unceasing. With that in mind I spoke, from 'One who has done evil burns here' through 'Having gone to an evil destiny, he grieves again.'"

Now at the time when Viḍūḍabha had slaughtered the Śākyas, the daughters of the Śākyas, seeing the ornaments of the dead, began to weep. They thought: "The Śākyas had faith in the noble ones; let these ornaments be offered to the noble ones." And so they gave those ornaments to the monks.

But the group of six monks put on those ornaments and entered the region of Serkya. When the daughters of the Śākyas saw this, they wept just as before and said: "Noble ones, we offered these for a good purpose, and yet this fault has come of it!" And the monks said nothing.

At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered: "Whatever fault has arisen comes from the monks having worn ornaments." Therefore a monk shall not wear or sport ornaments,

and he shall not sport or wear pendants, crescents, gold thread, or any ornament whatsoever. If he does so, he incurs an offence entailing censure.

The summary verse:

Receiving and the training rule,
incense, yellow orpiment, and salve,
alms-bowl and cup, raw grain,
white butter, grain-oil, and ointment.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In a certain rocky region there lived a householder who had taken a wife of equal station and was sporting with her, delighting in her, and enjoying pleasures with her. At a later time his relatives all passed away, his wealth was exhausted, and his possessions were spent. He thought to himself: "Now that I am old I cannot acquire wealth, I have no possessions, and my relatives have all passed beyond their time. I will go and take the going-forth." And so he said to his wife: "Good woman, now that I am old I cannot acquire wealth, I have no possessions, and my relatives have all passed beyond their time. I tell you this and then go to take the going-forth."

Now, that householder was straightforward, yet he lived his life as a wanderer, always looking at other men. So she said: "Master, do as you see fit — but come to see me from time to time." He promised to do so, then went to the Jeta Grove. He approached a certain monk and said: "Noble one, I wish to go forth." The monk replied: "Well-favored one, your courageous aspiration is good and excellent. The Blessed One has declared that one who is wise and truly sees five benefits is worthy to aspire to the going-forth. What are those five? One who is wise and truly sees that one will thereby obtain one's own unconfounded aim is worthy to aspire to the going-forth. One who is wise and truly sees that those who have been one's servants, employees, laborers, dependants, and those without freedom will come to venerate and praise one is worthy to aspire to the going-forth. One who is wise and truly sees that one will attain the accomplishment of nirvāṇa and the highest happiness is worthy to aspire to the going-forth. One who is wise and truly sees that even if one fails to attain the accomplishment of nirvāṇa and the highest happiness, one will be reborn among the gods is worthy to aspire to the going-forth. And one who is wise and truly sees that going-forth is praised in many ways by the buddhas and by those who have gone perfectly well — the most excellent among the holy disciples of the buddhas — is worthy to aspire to the going-forth."

Having spoken thus, the monk said: "You have aroused the mind in a way that is good and excellent. Go forth into this Dharma and Vinaya that has been well proclaimed!" And so he gave him the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon him.

Then, after two or three days, having trained him in the conduct of daily life, he said: "Well-favored one, wander through broad Śrāvastī — which deer do not avoid as they avoid hunters — going for alms in your accustomed domain, your native land, and living by what you receive." The next morning, having put on the lower robe and the Dharma-robe and taken up the alms-bowl, he entered Śrāvastī to go for alms. As he was wandering for alms, he caught sight of a woman who resembled his former wife, and he thought to himself:

"My former wife has come to see me since I went forth. She made a vow on account of that, and so I have only just now gone forth — I shall stay a little while, so that she will not be displeased, and then go on as I must."

With this thought he finished his alms-round and went to the Jeta Grove.

He stayed there for a short while and then said to the preceptor: "Preceptor, I have a former acquaintance who came to see me after I took the going-forth, and she bound me with a vow on that account. Please grant me leave to go to her." The preceptor said: "Go then, son — and guard your mind." He replied: "I shall guard it," and departed, making his way gradually to that rocky cliff.

When she saw him from a good distance away, she went out joyfully to meet him with quick steps and said: "Welcome, noble son! Well come indeed — it has been a long time and now I see you!" And she began to touch him. He said: "What are you doing? Take off the Dharma-robe and let me rest and stretch out on a bed." He said: "Do not touch me." "Why? The preceptor instructed me to guard my mind against you." She said: "Noble son, guarding your mind is up to you — have I forbidden it? What is to stop you?" And she took his Dharma-robe, spread out a seat, washed his feet, and massaged them.

Then, after she had bathed him, she gave him food, and she too sat down there to eat. He said: "What are you doing?" She said: "Noble son, it has been a long time since you and I ate together." He said: "The preceptor instructed me to guard my mind against you." She said: "Noble son, guarding your mind is up to you — have I forbidden it? I have not. It has been so long since you and I ate together — certainly you must eat." And so she ate with him.

Then she prepared a bed and said: "Noble son, lie down here and recover the rest of sleep that you have long been missing." He washed his feet and lay down, and she too began to lie down right there beside him. He said: "What are you doing?" She said: "Noble son, it has been a long time since we lay together — do not scold me." He said: "The preceptor instructed me to guard my mind against you." She said: "Noble son, guarding your mind is up to you — have I forbidden it? You and I have not lain together for so long — certainly I shall lie here." He was unable to resist.

Then he thought: "If I take hold of her by the neck, she will come under my power." And so he seized her by the neck — but women are a poison to the touch, and from that mere contact he committed transgression.

After remaining there for a long while, he said: "Good woman, I must go." She thought: "Whatever secret has passed between him and me, the monks do not know of it, and so I will let many laypeople know of it. Then, shamed by them, he will have to come back." With that thought she said: "Noble son, before you go, please gather up some provisions for the road — coins and kārṣāpaṇas." He said: "Good woman, monks do not touch silver and gold — how am I to take them?" She said: "Noble son, I will arrange it so that you do not have to touch them at all — just let me gather them." And so she bundled the coins together, tied them up, and fastened them to the base of the monk's staff. Those intoxicated by pride, those intoxicated by craving, have not even the slightest restraint — and so he picked it up and went, making his way gradually back to Śrāvastī.

Now as for the conduct of the Group of Six: one of the Group of Six, seeing that the gate of the Jeta Grove was not empty, went to where the venerable Ānanda was walking and sitting at the gate of the Jeta Grove. Catching sight of him from a great distance — his eyebrows hanging low, like a flower of dishevelled hair — the monk thought to himself: "Here comes an elder monk; I shall go and meet him." And so he went to meet him, saying: "Welcome, Elder! Welcome!" At this, the other said: "Homage to you, Teacher! Homage to you!" Hearing this, the venerable Ānanda thought: "My, this one is an old fellow — he does not know who is a teacher and who is a preceptor. Let me first ask him where he has come from." And so he asked: "Old fellow, where have you come from?" The other replied: "Teacher, I was in a certain place before, in a certain lodging, and I have come from there."
