Ānanda said: "Good, old fellow — you are one who guards what has been done. And guarding what one has done is praised by the wise." The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, train yourselves thus: you shall guard what has been done, feel what has been done, and not waste even the smallest good deed — to say nothing of a great one." "Did you see your former wife?" "Yes, I saw her." "Was she well?" "She was well." "Old fellow — what was that thing hanging from the base of your staff?" "Teacher, she gave me some kārṣāpaṇas tied up in a bundle of old cloth." "Old fellow, look at you — you have made merit: you have seen your former wife, and you have obtained provisions besides." "It is thanks to your kindness, Teacher." The monk thought: "There may be more I can learn from this; let me question him on everything." And so, speaking to him with gentle words, he asked him about everything. Since the old fellow was by nature straightforward, he recounted to him exactly what had happened. The monk said: "Old fellow, tell all of this to your preceptor — your preceptor will be pleased." The old monk, having been deceived in this way, recounted exactly what had happened to his preceptor. The preceptor in turn told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, this deluded man's bodily conduct has lapsed, but his intention has not lapsed. A root downfall has occurred. Therefore, from now on, promulgate in full the four conditions that entail a root downfall immediately upon ordination, so that this transgression will not occur again."

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there lived a monk named Priyadatta who constantly practised meditative concentration at forest-edge lodgings in remote places; and so his name became known as Dhyāyin Priyadatta — Priyadatta the Meditator. Whenever he sat cross-legged and meditated, the gods of Māra's host would harass him. On one occasion, as he sat cross-legged, a goddess of Māra's host came and sat upon his crossed legs. Since a woman is a poison to the touch, she engaged in sexual intercourse with him. The moment the act was over, it struck him like a poisonous thorn, and with a mind aroused he thought: "I have engaged in sexual conduct, in the act of sexual intercourse — I have fallen into ruin." But then he thought: "The intention with which I held on has not for one moment been held by me willingly. Let me go before the Blessed One — if I still have the fortune to continue, I will remain; if not, I shall live as a layman." With this thought, he picked up his robes with his right hand —

— and with his left hand he covered his private parts, his face flushed with shame and his cheeks wet with tears, he made his way to where the Blessed One was.

At that time the Blessed One was seated on a prepared seat in the midst of a vast retinue of many hundreds and thousands of monks, and he was teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One saw the venerable Nandaka while he was still far off. Seeing him, he reflected: "If I do not speak to Nandaka now, there is a danger that he may vomit hot blood and die on the spot." With this thought, the Blessed One spoke these words to the venerable Nandaka: "Nandaka, it is good that you have come. But why does your face flush with shame?"

Nandaka replied: "Reverend sir, I who was formerly Nandaka am now one without joy. I am one without gladness."

"Nandaka, why do you speak like that? What have you done?"

"Reverend sir, without surrendering my training I engaged in unchaste conduct, in the act of sexual intercourse — yet I did not do so with even a single moment of willing intent to conceal it."

"Nandaka, are you willing to train in the precepts for as long as you live?"

"Blessed One, I am willing."

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, although the monk Nandaka engaged in what was not to be engaged in, since he did not do so with even a single moment of willing intent, this has not become a defeat for him. Monks, to Nandaka and to any other who is like him in this way, give the training-vow for as long as he lives. And it is to be given in this manner: set out the seats, strike the wooden signal board, summon all the monks with the words of inquiry, and when the entire Saṅgha is assembled and seated, let the monk Nandaka perform prostrations in order of seniority, and then, crouching down at the end of the senior monks, let him join his palms together and say these words:

'May the venerable Saṅgha please listen. I, called the monk Nandaka, without surrendering my training engaged in unchaste conduct, in the act of sexual intercourse, yet I did not do so with even a single moment of willing intent to conceal it. I, the monk Nandaka, request from the Saṅgha the training for as long as I live. May the venerable members of the Saṅgha, out of compassion, please take me under the wing of their compassion and grant me, the monk Nandaka, the training for as long as I live.'

This is to be said a second time and a third time in the same way."

After that, the monk Nandaka is to be removed from among those who are within earshot and placed among those who are within eyeshot. One monk then makes the motion and performs the act. The motion is as follows:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please listen. This monk Nandaka, without surrendering his training, engaged in unchaste conduct, in the act of sexual intercourse, yet he did not do so with even a single moment of willing intent to conceal it. This monk Nandaka requests from the Saṅgha the training for as long as he lives. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and they consent, may the Saṅgha please grant it. This is the Saṅgha's granting to the monk Nandaka of the training for as long as he lives. This is the motion."

The act is then performed as follows:

"May the venerable Saṅgha please listen. This monk Nandaka, without surrendering his training, engaged in unchaste conduct, in the act of sexual intercourse, yet he did not do so with even a single moment of willing intent. This monk Nandaka requests from the Saṅgha the training for as long as he lives. In consequence, the Saṅgha grants the monk Nandaka the training for as long as he lives. Those venerable ones who consent to the granting to the monk Nandaka of the training for as long as he lives — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak. This is the first recitation of the act."

The second and third recitations of the act are to be performed in the same way. The Saṅgha having consented and granted, the Saṅgha has bestowed the training upon the monk Nandaka for as long as he lives. Since no one spoke, it is held to be so.

I shall now set forth the rules of conduct to be observed by a monk upon whom the training has been bestowed. A monk upon whom the training has been bestowed must not perform the acts of one who is junior toward a monk who abides in his natural standing — that is, he must not speak respectfully to him, must not bow down to him, must not rise to meet him, must not join his palms in greeting, and must not perform acts of service. He must not sit on the same seat. If he does sit, he must take a seat that is lower. He must not walk in the same procession. If he does walk, he must shorten his steps. The novice who follows behind him must not go to the houses of monks who abide in their natural standing, or to the houses of brahmins and householders. If he does go, he must send the novice ahead. He must not sleep under the same cover. He must not give the going-forth. He must not give full ordination. He must not grant a residence. He must not appoint anyone to act in the capacity of a novice. He must not perform the act of requesting. He must not perform the request-and-two and the request-and-four. He must not commission others to perform acts. He must not be a teacher of nuns. Even if he was previously appointed, he must not instruct the nuns. He must not raise objections against a monk on grounds of impaired moral discipline, impaired view, impaired conduct, or impaired livelihood. He must not seek to extract instruction from him.

These apply to the restoration ceremony, the invitation ceremony, the act of requesting, the request-and-two, and the request-and-four.

In the morning, before others, he must rise and open the doors. He must clear away the lamp vessels. He must sweep the shrine-hall. He must dust with a cloth. He must smear the floor with a good fresh coating of fresh cow dung. He must sweep the toilet rooms. He must set out earth, leaves, and water — cold or warm as the season requires. Then he must clean the rinsing basin. Knowing the proper time, he must set out the seats. He must place the incense burner and incense nearby. If he is able to proclaim the qualities of the Teacher, he must do so himself. If he is not able, he must request the speaker to do it. He must attend to the distribution of food, and once the food has been assigned, he must go up to the roof of the building and strike the gong. In the hot season, he must fan the monks with a fan. Then, after all who are fully ordained, and before those who are not yet fully ordained, with calm and composed conduct, cultivating the perception of himself as a monk, he must take his meal. When the business of the meal is done, he must confine himself to his dwelling and cell. He must relinquish his claim to the bowl stand. Knowing the proper time, he must sweep and clean the Tathāgata's hair and nail reliquary shrines, and smear them with a good fresh coating of fresh cow dung. When it is time for the assembly to gather, he must arrange the seats and place the incense and incense burner. He must proclaim the qualities of the Teacher. He is to say to the venerable Saṅgha: "May the Saṅgha please listen. Today is the first day of the Saṅgha's month. For the sake of the shrine-hall's lord and the deities of the shrine-hall, please recite the verses." Then he must announce the date of the sun. If he is unable to do so, he must entrust it to a monk.

When the monks would not assign him a dwelling, the Blessed One declared: "Assign him a dwelling." When they would not give him his share of goods received, the Blessed One declared: "Give him his share of goods received." When he would not make effort on the side of virtue, the Blessed One declared: "He must make effort on the side of virtue." This is the conduct prescribed for him, and it continues for as long as he has not entered the path. Entry upon the path, in this context, means the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravas).

Through strenuous effort and exertion he understood this very fifth part of the wheel of saṃsāra — whether it moves or is still — and, meditating on how all conditioned phenomena, by virtue of their very nature of reality (dharmatā), decay, fall apart, disintegrate, and utterly collapse, he abandoned all afflictions and directly actualized arhatship. He became one who is free from attachment to the three realms, equal to gold and dung alike, equal to the sky and the palm of the hand, like sandalwood and a foul-smelling weed, one who has shattered the enclosure of the egg-shell of ignorance, who has obtained knowledge, the higher knowledges, and individual precise understanding, who has turned his back on attachment to worldly gain and on veneration, and who is to be worshipped, honored, and respectfully addressed by gods — both those of the primary faculties and those of the secondary faculties. Though he had attained arhatship, he remained as before, continuing to conduct himself in the same way. The Blessed One then declared: "Let him be seated in order of seniority, and whatever has been prohibited, the monks who remain of their natural disposition shall observe accordingly."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the bamboo grove, the Kalandaka park. The venerable Pilindavatsa's companions — those who had taken the going-forth under him and who always lived in celibacy in like manner — went to him and inquired: "Elder, are you well?" He replied: "Friends, I am ill and unwell." "Elder, what ails you?" "Friends, I have a chest ailment." "Elder, please take some medicine." "Friends, I used to rely on the smoke of a particular plant in the past." "Elder, why do you not rely on it now?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." The monks then made the matter known to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, I permit it: a sick monk may inhale the smoke of that plant." The Blessed One having declared that a sick monk may inhale the smoke of the plant, the monks did so — and it was done improperly. The Blessed One then declared: "Make a hole in a bowl, fit another bowl over it, and inhale through that." Still it was done improperly, and the Blessed One declared: "Inhale through a tube." They inhaled through tubes of bamboo — and that same problem arose again. The Blessed One declared: "One must not inhale through a tube of bamboo; rather, make a metal smoking pipe." They made them too short, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not make them too short." They made them too long, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not make them too long; make them twelve finger-breadths in length." They made them sharp-edged, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not make them sharp." They made them rough, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not make them rough." They left them lying about on the ground, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not set them down loosely; put them in a container and keep them there." When they put them in a container and placed them on the ground, the Blessed One declared: "Do not place the container on the ground; rather, hang it on a peg or on a cloth rack." When they carried them about tucked in their robes, the Blessed One declared: "Coat them with butter or oil and store them. When the need arises and they have been used, wash them." The Blessed One declared: "Do not wash them; instead, pass them through fire — that itself is their cleansing."

Summary verse:

What has been accumulated, ointment for bathing, and nasal pouring used and drinking cups,
What curves and water sources there are, and water and the place for washing —
these are the topics here set forth.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

A sick monk went to a physician and asked him to show him a good medicine. The physician said: "Noble one, bathe with an accumulated-herbs bath and you will recover." The monk replied: "Noble one, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The physician said: "Your Teacher is compassionate, so he will permit it."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If a physician prescribes it, one may bathe with an accumulated-herbs bath. In doing this bathing, one should feel no remorse."

When the Blessed One had declared that one may bathe with an accumulated-herbs bath, the monks, not knowing what an accumulated-herbs bath actually was, went again to the physician. The monks said: "Noble one, since the Blessed One has given permission, please show us what an accumulated-herbs bath is." The physician replied: "Noble ones, I myself do not know it precisely. From the medical literature of my tradition of the wheel-turning physicians, there is something called an accumulated-herbs bath, but I do not know exactly what it is. However, your Teacher is omniscient, so he himself knows it — go and ask him directly."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The roots, stems, flowers, and fruits of wind-releasing plants — these are to be boiled and used for bathing."

The monks boiled these and bathed with them, and their skin became rough. At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Apply oil to the body." When they had applied it, the oil was so excessive that the bedding became unsuitable for use. The Blessed One declared: "Wash it off by counting as a bath." Even so their skin remained rough, and the Blessed One declared: "Into the last water-pot, pour two or three drops of grain oil."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the garden of the kalandaka birds.

The venerable Pilindavatsa, from the time he went forth in renunciation and onward, was always ill. Those who lived the holy life equally came to him and asked: "Elder, are you comfortable?" The venerable one replied: "Friends, I am ill and uncomfortable." "Elder, what ails you?" "Friends, I have a cold." "Elder, please take some medicine." "Friends, in the past I was accustomed to performing nasal-pouring. The Blessed One has not permitted it." "Elder, why do you not do it?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, permission is granted: the practice of nasal-pouring may be performed."

When the Blessed One had declared that nasal-pouring may be performed, the monks at first poured it in the same way as the pouring itself was done. The Blessed One declared: "Do not pour it in that manner." The monks poured it using a leaf tube, and the same fault arose. The Blessed One declared: "Do not pour it using a leaf tube." The monks poured it using the corner of a monastic robe, and the same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "Do not pour it using the corner of a monastic robe. Instead, use a nasal-pouring implement." The monks made a nasal-pouring implement with a single spout. The Blessed One declared: "Make the nasal-pouring implement with two spouts." The monks made the spouts sharp, and the Blessed One declared:

"Do not make the spouts sharp." The monks poured the nasal medicine without having washed their hands. The Blessed One declared: "One should wash one's hands, receive it properly, and then pour it."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka. The Venerable Pilindavatsa, from wherever he had gone forth, had up to that time always been sick, and those who were living the holy life in conformity with celibacy went to him and asked: "Elder, are you comfortable, are you well?" He replied: "I am sick; I am not well." "Elder, what is your illness?" "Venerable ones, it has been permitted." "Elder, please take a little medicine." "Venerable ones, I am holding a drinking bowl that was given to me previously." "Elder, why do you not hold it now?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, let one hold a drinking bowl that has been permitted and given."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka. Relatives of the Venerable Pilindavatsa came, and he taught them the Dharma. They then went home and said to their wives: "The noble Pilindavatsa has taught the Dharma in a fine and beautiful way, and we came here having listened to him." Their wives said to them: "Then you have come with the fruit of the buddha's arising." Why did they say that? "Because you listened to the noble Pilindavatsa teaching the Dharma in a fine and beautiful way. Why do you not listen?" "We are people of modest standing; we are shy. However, if the noble one were to come here and teach, we too would listen." "If that is so, let us invite the noble one." They said: "Excellent." They went to him and said: "Noble one, the women wish to hear the Dharma." He replied: "Wise ones, let them listen and take it in. Did I forbid them?" They said: "Noble one, we are shy speaking on behalf of the women. We came to say that if the noble one would come here and teach, we would also listen." He replied: "Wise ones, I am too ill to go and teach." "Noble one, we request that you ride a palanquin and come. If the fair-faced Blessed One has not permitted it, how can you go?" At that point the monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, let it be permitted to travel by palanquin."

When the Blessed One had declared that one might travel by palanquin, the Venerable Pilindavatsa, with his attendants and personal servants around him, mounted the palanquin and set out to teach the Dharma. The Group of Six saw this, and they asked his attendants and personal servants: "Wise ones, who is this travelling?" They replied: "It is the preceptor." "Has the Blessed One permitted the palanquin?" "He has." "The Blessed One's intention is good — because these Śākyan pleasure-folk cannot travel on foot, he has shown consideration for us in every way." Once they had gone, the Group of Six said among themselves: "Friends, dear friends, why are we left out? Let us also ride palanquins." "Yes, splendid, let us do the same." So they had palanquins made, adorned with tails and bells and the like, and mounted them. They then entered the main street, riding about in a manner that assumed a lordly status over the world, and the brahmins and householders said: "Wise ones, what is this?" "The Blessed One has permitted riding." "Noble ones, has he permitted you renunciants also to partake of sensual pleasures?" But they said nothing at all.

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A sick monk must not travel by riding. If a sick monk travels by riding, it will constitute an offense. Nevertheless, there are two cases in which riding is permitted: one who is feeble with old age, and one who is ill and cannot manage the journey on foot."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there lived a faithful householder who went to the Jeta Grove together with a brahmin woman of no faith, and the faithful one began pointing out the surrounding grove to her. As the two wandered about, they came upon some excrement at the base of a tree. The brahmin woman said: "Friend, these renunciants, the sons of the Śākya, have no cleanliness whatsoever — they defecate and urinate at the base of flowering and fruit-bearing trees." The other replied: "Friend, the great ones themselves would not do such a thing; it must certainly have been done by some layperson." As they were speaking thus, an old monk who had wrapped his head in a cloth began to defecate at the base of a tree. The faithless brahmin woman, seeing this, said: "Friend, did you not just say it was done by a layperson? Look — a renunciant with his head wrapped in cloth, defecating at the base of a tree!" The faithful one was ashamed and sat there saying nothing at all. The brahmin woman then reported the incident to the monks. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered it: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through monks defecating at the base of trees. Therefore monks must not defecate or urinate at the base of trees. If they do, it will constitute an offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not defecate or urinate at the base of trees, the monks set out along the road and came to a remote place. There some monks needed to defecate. Others who needed to urinate, thinking that these trees had leaves and branches, refrained from both defecating and urinating, and as a result they fell ill. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Trees in the wilderness that have leaves and branches — there one may defecate and urinate, and there should be no regret about this."

When the Blessed One had declared that defecating and urinating might be done in the wilderness, the monks who lived near towns did not do so. In time the spring season arrived, and as they defecated and urinated during the day the ground became soiled. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted: one may defecate and urinate at the base of thorny trees, and there should be no regret about this."

When Upananda made the enclosure of a hermitage unsuitable for use by fouling it with excrement, the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not defecate or urinate where there is green grass." The monks then defecated and urinated in places where there was no green grass, and those places became filled with filth. When brahmins and householders saw this, they mocked and reviled them, saying: "Look how these renunciants, the sons of the Śākya, have a fine custom — just as they all gather together to eat, so too they defecate and urinate." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted: a latrine pit should be made."

The monks set about building a latrine house on the north and west sides, but not knowing how it should be constructed, they asked the Blessed One, and he declared: "A latrine pit should be of two kinds: one resembling a small house, and one resembling an open shed. The house-type is made square, with a crossbeam in the middle, and an opening is cut in it with a wooden frame fitted around it. The shed-type is constructed with the beams projecting outward, and thorny plants are grown beneath it. On the latrine site, above the pit of the latrine, footrests should be placed. There should also be a place set aside for a rinsing pot and a communal water ladle. The door should be hung so it closes downward, and both a door bolt and a door latch should be fitted. If someone has entered inside, the one waiting outside should make a sound; and if the person is still inside, one may enter only if it is all right to do so. The person inside should also make a sound. If it becomes malodorous, the one responsible for maintaining the building should clean it each day, and earth and leaves should also be kept on hand. Therefore a latrine pit together with its surroundings is hereby permitted."

Now follows the Vinaya section on minor matters, the tenth fascicle. Its summary verse reads:

A site for urination, vessels and utensils,
And delight in the Teacher himself,
Five foods, and milk,
Curds, solid food, and what was permitted.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When the Blessed One had declared that a latrine pit together with its surroundings should be made, the monks urinated right in that same latrine area, and other monks were distressed by the smell of the excrement and were obstructed from passing through that way. The Blessed One then declared: "There should be a separate place for urination." The monks did not know in which direction or in what manner to make it, and the Blessed One declared: "Nearby that same spot, make one of the shed type: fit a wooden surround and install both a door bolt and a latch. Everything else about the urination place should be done just as before with the latrine."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. During the hot season a certain brahmin was so parched with thirst that, yearning for water, he entered the monastery. He went up to a certain monk and said: "Venerable monks, if you are thirsty, please give me some water." The monk took up his rinsing vessel and went to him and said: "Brahmin, drink." The brahmin said: "Noble one, a vessel for cleansing is quite a different thing. Oh my! Leave your water vessel aside. Is there any harm in pouring water for a wandering ascetic or a brahmin? Are you not thereby earning merit?" At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A communal water vessel for the Saṅgha should be provided."

When the Blessed One declared that a communal water vessel for the Saṅgha should be provided, a certain householder heard that the Blessed One had permitted a communal water vessel for the Saṅgha. He had a stock of pottery vessels made by potters piled up inside the monastery. From that supply, those who lived in the garden as well as other laypeople took away whatever they wished and departed. Because the monks did not stop them, those vessels were exhausted. The monks then said to that householder: "Good sir, the vessels have run out; please give others." He said: "Noble ones, I offered a great many — why did they disappear so quickly?" When they told him how it had come about, he said: "Noble ones, whatever was simply thrown away and lost — that was not well done.

When he said, "I did not give those to the laypeople," the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "One must not simply throw things away and let them be lost. Rather, a keeper of vessels and utensils is to be appointed." When the monks appointed one without discrimination, the Blessed One declared: "One who lacks the five qualities should not be appointed as keeper of vessels and utensils, and if already appointed should be removed. What are the five? He is led by desire, led by aversion, led by delusion, led by fear, and does not know what vessels and utensils have been distributed and what have not. One who possesses the five qualities should be appointed as keeper of vessels and utensils, and if already appointed should not be removed. What are the five? He is not led by desire, not led by aversion, not led by delusion, not led by fear, and knows what vessels and utensils have been distributed and what have not."

"The appointment is to be carried out as follows: after seats have been arranged and the wooden signal-board struck" — and so forth, as before, down to "and let him consent" — "You, named so-and-so, do you consent to serve as keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha? If you consent, let him say, 'I consent.'"

After that, one monk is to make a motion and carry out the formal act: "May the venerable Saṅgha hear me. If the monk named so-and-so consents to serve as keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha, and if the time is right and the Saṅgha approves, may the Saṅgha grant its consent; and the Saṅgha shall appoint this monk named so-and-so as keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha. This monk named so-and-so shall be keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha. This is the motion."

"The formal act is also to be performed thus: May the venerable Saṅgha hear me. This monk named so-and-so consents to serve as keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha. Therefore the Saṅgha shall appoint this monk named so-and-so as keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha. Those venerable ones who approve of appointing this monk named so-and-so as keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha shall remain silent; those who do not approve shall speak. The Saṅgha has consented and approved; the Saṅgha has appointed this monk named so-and-so as keeper of vessels and utensils for the Saṅgha. So it is held, since no one has spoken."

That keeper then gave the old vessels and utensils to the monks and gave the new ones to the laypeople. The Blessed One declared: "New ones are to be given to the monks, and old ones to the laypeople." That keeper, having given some to the laypeople, did not reclaim them, but did reclaim them from the monks. The Blessed One declared: "What has been given to the laypeople may be reclaimed, but not what has been given to the monks." When vessels were left outside and became scattered about, the Blessed One declared: "A storeroom for vessels and utensils is to be made, and the vessels and utensils made by potters are to be kept there."

When the Blessed One had declared that a storeroom for vessels and utensils was to be made and the pottery kept there, it so happened that a traveler arrived from the north. He supplied the Saṅgha with all manner of provisions for three months. Then he thought: "Why should I serve the Saṅgha with inferior provisions? Rather, I shall serve them with my own vessels and utensils." With that in mind, he set out a great many bronze vessels and utensils. He then made an offering feast to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks for three months, providing abundant provisions. At the end of the feast he took his leave and departed.

When he departed, he donated all those bronze vessels and utensils to the Saṅgha. The monks stored them in that same storeroom together with the pottery made by the potter. The bronze vessels and utensils shifted against the pottery and broke it. The Blessed One then declared: "The bronze vessels and utensils are to be kept separately, and the pottery made by the potter is likewise to be kept separately."

Now it happened that a brahmin, suffering from thirst, came in distress to the Jeta Grove and went to the quarters of a certain monk, where he said: "Venerable monk, I am thirsty — please give me water." The monk gave him a water pot and a cord. The brahmin said: "Noble one, what am I to do with these? Please give me water." The monk replied: "Brahmin, water that is lifted by a rope is not available here." The brahmin said: "Noble one, you have entered upon the path of benefiting all sentient beings — how could it be unsuitable for you to keep water readily at hand?" The monk replied: "The Blessed One has not permitted it."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The Saṅgha may keep water at hand." The monks then placed it here and there in the corridors, in the dwelling rooms, inside the assembly hall, in the gate-house, and on the stairways. The Blessed One declared: "It is not to be placed here and there in the corridors, in the dwelling rooms, inside the assembly hall, in the gate-house, and on the stairways. Instead, a water-house is to be built."

When the Blessed One had declared that a water-house was to be built, the monks did not know in which direction or what form it should take. The Blessed One declared: "Inside the assembly hall, on the south and west sides, a water-house is to be built."

When it became dark inside, the Blessed One declared: "Windows are to be fitted." When mud accumulated, the Blessed One declared: "A brick floor is to be laid and a drain hole fitted. A door is to be fitted, and a door panel and its frame are also to be installed." When the water pots were placed directly on the ground, the Blessed One declared: "They are to be placed on wooden stands." When there were no wooden stands, the Blessed One declared: "Brick platforms are to be made, and the pots placed on top without resting them against the wall." When the water inside the pots went bad, the Blessed One declared: "The pots are to be washed from time to time." When the monks did not know with what to wash them, the Blessed One declared: "A wooden scrubber — either a piece of wood with a pumice stone attached, or a bundle of thick leaves, or a bundle of cotton cloth tied together — may be used to scrub and wash them." Nevertheless, the water continued to go bad. The Blessed One declared: "Half the pots are to be washed while fresh water is poured into the other half." When the Blessed One had declared that water was to be poured in, the monks did not know who should pour it. The Blessed One declared: "Those who are in residence are to pour the water."

Accordingly, the water-house along with its furnishings was permitted.

The Blessed One, the awakened Bhagavān, was residing in Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodhā Grove. Then the great Prajāpatī Gautamī came with five hundred followers to where the Blessed One was, and arriving there, she bowed her head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. As Prajāpatī Gautamī sat there, from the passage beginning "The Blessed One addressed her with words in keeping with the Dharma" up to "The Blessed One was refreshed," everything proceeds as before.

Then the great Prajāpatī Gautamī spoke these words to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One live long, and may the Great Sage dwell for an aeon."

Hearing the voice of the great Prajāpatī Gautamī, the five hundred nuns likewise said in the same words: "May the Blessed One live long, and may the Great Sage dwell for an aeon." The yakṣas of the earth heard the voice of the five hundred nuns and cried out and sang: "May the Blessed One live long, and may the Great Sage dwell for an aeon." The voice of the earth-dwelling yakṣas was heard by the yakṣas of the sky, by the gods of the realms of the Four Great Kings, by the gods of the Thirty-Three, by the gods Free from Strife, by the gods of the Joyful Heaven, by the gods of the Heaven of Delight in Emanation, and by the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations. In that very instant, in that very moment, in that very flash — in an instant, in a moment, in a flash — the sound spread all the way to the Brahmā world, and the gods of the Brahmā realms cried out and sang: "May the Blessed One live long, and may the Great Sage dwell for an aeon."

Then the Blessed One addressed the great Prajāpatī Gautamī with these words: "Gautamī, you have caused a hindrance to many sentient beings. Your voice was heard by the five hundred nuns, who thereupon raised the same cry; and through the voice of those five hundred nuns, the earth-dwelling yakṣas, the sky-dwelling yakṣas, the gods of the realms of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-Three, the gods Free from Strife, the gods of the Joyful Heaven, the gods of the Heaven of Delight in Emanation, and the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations heard it, and in that very instant, in that very moment, in that very flash — in an instant, in a moment, in a flash — the sound pervaded all the way to the Brahmā world, and the gods of the Brahmā realms likewise raised that same cry. Yet, Gautamī, one should not pay homage to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha in that manner — to pay homage in that way is not to pay homage well."

"Venerable One, how then should one pay homage to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha? How should homage be paid so that it is homage well paid?"

"Gautamī, one should pay homage to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha in this way: 'May my Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of hearers, be in harmony, rejoicing together, without dispute, of one mind, reciting in unison, blended like water and milk, and may the teaching of the Teacher shine forth with clarity.' To pay homage in that way to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha is homage well paid."

At that point a monk spoke these verses:

The great Prajāpatī Gautamī, sovereign of beings,
bowed at the feet of the Teacher,
and prayed: "May my Blessed One live long;
may the Great Sage dwell for an aeon."
She addressed the Teacher with those words,
and the Teacher replied to his disciple thus:
"Gautamī, the homage you have paid
is not homage to the Tathāgata.
How should one possessed of wisdom
pay homage to the Tathāgata
so that it is homage truly well paid?
Teach me, I ask, what I should know.
Those who strive with energy, who are themselves diligent,
who steadily and firmly surpass the other shore,
hearers who dwell in harmony, viewing one another as kin —
that is homage to the buddha."

The great Prajāpatī Gautamī reflected: "The Blessed One has spoken in praise of a harmonious Saṅgha. Therefore, for as long as the Blessed One remains and the Saṅgha of monks is in harmony, I shall pass completely into nirvāṇa." Realizing this, she rose from her seat, turned to face the Blessed One, joined her palms, and bowed.

She said to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, I wish to pass into nirvāṇa deliberately and of my own accord." When she had spoken, the Blessed One sat in silence. The great Prajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Blessed One a second time and a third time: "Venerable One, I wish to pass into nirvāṇa deliberately and of my own accord." And the Blessed One sat in silence a second time and a third time. Then the great Prajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Blessed One once more: "Venerable One, I wish to pass into nirvāṇa deliberately and of my own accord." When she had spoken, the Blessed One said to her: "Gautamī, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa?" "Blessed One, it is for the sake of your passing into nirvāṇa." "Gautamī, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa?" "Sugata, it is for the sake of your passing into nirvāṇa." "Gautamī, if you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa — all conditioned phenomena are of such a nature; what need have I to speak of it?" The five hundred nuns too bowed their heads to the Blessed One's feet and said: "Venerable One, we also wish to pass into nirvāṇa deliberately and of our own accord." The Blessed One declared: "Gautamīs, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa?" "Blessed One, it is for the sake of your passing into nirvāṇa." "Gautamīs, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa?" "Sugata, it is for the sake of your passing into nirvāṇa." "Gautamīs, if you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa — all conditioned phenomena are of such a nature; what need have I to speak of it?"

Then the great Prajāpatī Gautamī, rejoicing and delighting in what the Blessed One had said, bowed her head to the Blessed One's feet and departed. The venerable Ānanda, Anupama, Selā, and the venerable Ānanda of the eastern quarter went to where the venerable Ānanda was, and having arrived they bowed to his feet and said to him: "Venerable One, we wish to pass into nirvāṇa deliberately and of our own accord." "Gautamīs, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa?" "Venerable Ānanda, it is for the sake of your passing into nirvāṇa." "Gautamīs, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa?" "Venerable Ānanda, it is for the sake of your passing into nirvāṇa." "Gautamīs, if you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa — sisters, conditioned phenomena are of such a nature; what need have I to speak of it?"

Then the great Prajāpatī Gautamī together with her retinue of five hundred nuns bowed their heads to the feet of the elder monks and elders and went to the rains-retreat hall. There, having examined the nature of the assembly of three groups, she taught the Dharma in such a way that over seven days, through whatever she taught, the great multitude of sentient beings attained great distinction. Then, in an open and spacious spot, she sat with her legs half-crossed in the midst of the community of nuns. The nuns likewise sat in the same manner.

Then the great Prajāpatī Gautamī entered into a meditative absorption of the following kind: having settled her mind in equanimity, she rose from her seat, became invisible, soared aloft into the sky to the east, and displayed the four kinds of deportment — walking, standing, sitting, and lying — and then also entered into the fire element. Having entered into the fire element, from the body of the great Prajāpatī Gautamī rays of many varied colors blazed forth — blue and yellow and

red and white and crimson and crystal-colored — and displayed pairs of miraculous transformations: from the lower part of her body flames blazed forth, while from the upper part of her body streams of cool water flowed; and then from the upper part of her body flames blazed forth, while from the lower part of her body streams of cool water flowed. Just as she had done in the eastern direction, so too she did in the southern, western, and northern directions. In this way she displayed all four varieties of miraculous transformation through supernatural power in the four directions, and then she entered into meditative absorption in the first dhyāna. The five hundred nuns likewise entered into meditative absorption in the first dhyāna. Rising from the first dhyāna, she entered the second; from the second, the third; from the third, the fourth; from the fourth, the base of infinite space; from the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness; from the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness; from the base of nothingness, she entered into the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then, rising from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, she re-entered the base of nothingness; from the base of nothingness, the base of infinite consciousness; from the base of infinite consciousness, the base of infinite space; from the base of infinite space, the fourth dhyāna; from the fourth, the third; from the third, the second; from the second, she entered meditative absorption in the first dhyāna. Then, resting in the first dhyāna itself, she passed completely into nirvāṇa. The five hundred nuns likewise, having entered meditative absorption in the forward sequence and the reverse sequence in the same manner, resting in the first dhyāna itself, passed completely into nirvāṇa.

The moment the great Prajāpatī Gautamī, mother of beings, passed into nirvāṇa, the great earth trembled, shooting stars fell, the horizon turned red, and the sounds of divine music arose in the sky.

Then the monks who were practicing meditation on the terraced slopes of Mount Meru, and also those in towns and villages and districts, in royal palaces, and in remote and secluded dwellings — feeling the great earth tremble, they wondered why it was shaking. And when they saw that the great Prajāpatī Gautamī, mother of beings, together with her retinue of five hundred, had passed completely into nirvāṇa, they thought to themselves: since the foster-mother of the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, we should go and devote ourselves to making the finest offerings to her body. And so, taking fragrant wood, they went to the summer pavilion of the great Prajāpatī Gautamī.

The Blessed One too, together with the great śrāvaka Kuṇḍinya the All-Knower, the great Kāśyapa, Lāṅgika, Nāmavān, Aniruddha, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, and also together with the great community of monks, went to the summer pavilion of the great Prajāpatī Gautamī. Likewise, the king of Kośala, Prasenajit, surrounded by his queen's retinue and by young nobles, ministers, townspeople, and country folk; the householder Anāthapiṇḍada surrounded by his retinue; Mṛgāramātā Viśākhā; the elder sage Ṛṣidatta; Purāṇa; and other assemblies of people who had come from various regions — all went to the summer pavilion of the great Prajāpatī Gautamī.

Then King Prasenajit, with five hundred cushioned couches adorned with jewels and various silks, with incense, fragrant perfumes, flowers, garlands, parasols, victory banners, pennants, and

offered various kinds of music. Then the venerable Ānanda, Avighna, Nandaka, and Sundarananda raised up the litter of the great Prajāpatī Gautamī, and the Blessed One supported it with his right hand. The remaining monks likewise raised up the litters of the remaining nuns. Then, having performed a great offering, they carried the litters and set them down in an open space of ground at some distance. The Blessed One then removed the outer robes from the bodies of the great Prajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred nuns, and declared to the monks: "O monks, look upon the great Prajāpatī Gautamī and these five hundred nuns — though they have reached one hundred and twenty years of age, there is not a single wrinkle on their bodies, not a single white hair; behold them as though they were girls of sixteen."

Then the king of Kośala, Prasenajit, together with the queen's retinue, young nobles, ministers, townspeople, and country folk, piled up heaps of fragrant wood of various kinds and cremated the great Prajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred nuns. The Blessed One taught on the nature of impermanence and then departed for the monastery. Having arrived, he took his seat on the prepared throne in the midst of the monks' assembly. Seated there, he declared to the monks: "O monks, in regard to saying 'May there be recovery' when a fainting has occurred — there are faults such as these, and others besides. Therefore a monk must not say 'May there be recovery' when a fainting has occurred. If he says it, it becomes a serious transgression."

The monks, having arisen in doubt, asked the buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubt: "Venerable One, what karma did the great Prajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred nuns perform, such that, though they had reached one hundred and twenty years of age, there was not a single wrinkle on their bodies, not a single white hair, and they appeared as girls of sixteen?"

The Blessed One declared: "O monks, the great Prajāpatī Gautamī and those five hundred nuns themselves assembled an accumulation of karma, transformed the conditions, abided like a flame, and brought about what would certainly be experienced. The karma accumulated by the great Prajāpatī Gautamī and those five hundred nuns — who else could experience the ripening of it individually? O monks, accumulated karma does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, the virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens in the appropriated aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas). As it is said:

Even through hundreds of aeons,
karma does not perish;
when the conditions and the time arrive,
it ripens as fruit for embodied beings.

"O monks, in the distant past, in this very auspicious aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Teacher called Kāśyapa appeared in the world." — and so on as before, up to: — "and he dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park at the Sages' Discourse in the city of Vārāṇasī.

"When the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa had performed all the deeds of a buddha and passed completely into nirvāṇa — the nirvāṇa without remainder, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted — at that time a king called Kṛkī performed bodily offerings to his body, and at the four crossroads of the great highway erected a stūpa of one league in circumference and half a league in height, made of the four precious substances."

The queen Dampa and the other five hundred women of King Kṛkī — when they had grown old and wrinkles and grey hair had appeared on their bodies and the king had cast them aside, they began to speak among themselves. "Friends, why has the god cast us aside?" Some of them said, "What is there to reflect upon? We have grown wrinkled and grey-haired, and that is why we have been cast aside." Others said, "That is so. But now what shall we do regarding the god? There are other women who still possess beauty and youth; he will surely be taking his pleasure and delight with them. Therefore let us go to the stūpa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, pay homage, and make an aspiration prayer: 'May we, from this point forward throughout saṃsāra, never be reborn with wrinkles and grey hair on our bodies.'" They said, "Excellent! Let us do just so." And so they made offerings at the stūpa of the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa — with fragrant substances, garlands, unguents, parasols, victory banners, and pennants — and having hung beautiful bunches of various flowers fragrant and fresh, and charming garlands, they made this aspiration prayer: "By the root of virtue that we have accumulated through making offerings to the Blessed One, the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, the unsurpassed field of merit, may we never develop wrinkles or grey hair on our bodies even when we have lived to one hundred and twenty years of age."

Monks, what do you think? Those five hundred women — the queen Dampa and the rest — who were the attendants of King Kṛkī, those very same ones are these five hundred nuns, headed by the Great Mistress of Beings. By the karmic maturation of that deed — of having made offerings at the stūpa of the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa and having made aspirational prayers — they are such that even now, having been born and reached the age of one hundred and twenty, they have no wrinkles or grey hair on their bodies, but appear like girls of sixteen.

Monks, therefore, from the passage beginning "Those whose karma is thoroughly dark" — it should be sought out thus, and the remainder is as before, up to "Thus, monks, should you train." When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said and praised it with delight.

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk who falls unconscious should not be revived by anyone calling out to him, there was in Śrāvastī a certain householder who had taken a wife from an equal family. He would sport with her, delight in her, and take his pleasure with her. Though they sported and delighted and took pleasure together, there was neither son nor daughter. When old age came upon him, his wealth and property were exhausted, and he said to his wife: "My good woman, I am old and poor, with neither son nor daughter, and so I shall go to the Jeta Grove and go forth." She said, "Sire, please do so, please go forth." He went to the Jeta Grove and went forth.

Some time later, his former wife came to visit him, and when he fell unconscious, no monk called out to revive him. Then his former wife took up some earth with her left hand, rubbed it along the joint, and said, "May he live for a long time." The monks then began to investigate the matter, and she took him by the hand, drew him out, and said —

"Son of a king, you have gone forth among enemies. This Jeta Grove is not empty of five hundred yakṣas wearing blue garments, and it was I alone who revived you — that is why they did not carry off your vitality. Stay here, I urge you; come away to your own home." So saying, she took him by the hand and departed.

The monks said to him, "Old man, do not go." But he continued on his way and would not stay. The monks seized him by one arm and pulled him back, and he cried out, "It hurts, it hurts!" At that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Ask him in which arm the pain is. If he says, 'In the arm you are holding,' then he definitely wants to go — release him entirely in all respects. If he says, 'In the arm my former wife was holding,' then he does not want to go, and you should not release him."

"However, monks, the old man is one whose intention is to stay alive, and therefore when an old man falls unconscious, you should call out to revive him."

The monks asked him, "Old man, which arm hurts?" He replied, "Venerable ones, the one you are holding." They released him, and he went to his own home. That very matter became an obstacle to his going forth and receiving full ordination and becoming a monk.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there was a faithful layman who went to the Jeta Grove together with an unfaithful brahmin woman. When the layman fell unconscious, no monk called out to revive him, but that same brahmin woman revived him and said, "Friend, you have faith in enemies. This Jeta Grove is not empty of five hundred yakṣas wearing blue garments, and it was I alone who revived you — so do not let them steal away your vitality; come back this way." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, laypeople are ones whose intention is to stay alive, and therefore when a layman falls unconscious, you should call out to revive him."

"Furthermore, monks, when an elder falls unconscious, a junior should rise and pay respect; and when a junior falls unconscious, the elder should say, 'Be well.'"

The Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park in the Ṛṣipatana grove. At the time when the Blessed One introduced the group of five monks, who were endowed with certainty, into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, those monks did not know what they should eat as supplementary food and what they should eat as regular food. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there are five kinds of supplementary food: root food, stem food, leaf food, flower food, and fruit food. The five kinds of regular food are: flour, grain porridge, hot cooked rice, meat, and oil-bearing foods."

When they still did not know what the condiments were and what could be eaten, the Blessed One declared: "Milk, yogurt, fresh butter, ghee, fish, meat, dried meat, and whatever else is suitable — even if it is simply moistened with water, it may be consumed. Monks, anything moistened is restorative."

Verses in summary: the bolt of the door and the handle, the lattice of the windows,

the lower hinge and the upper hinge, the waist-bar, the dry wooden peg.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The monks were building dwelling-houses but were not fitting them with doors. The Blessed One declared: "Doors are to be fitted." The monks fitted doors but did not insert door-panels, and those who had entered into meditative concentration and recitation were visible to all. Brahmins and householders saw them, came close, and addressed them in conversation, so that their one-pointed mental composure was lost. The Blessed One declared: "Door-panels are to be inserted." The monks inserted door-panels, but since the handles had no eye-holes bored in them, it was difficult to distinguish them. The Blessed One declared: "Eye-holes are also to be bored into the handles." When these were opened, a noise arose. The Blessed One declared: "A piece of leather is to be inserted." Since no window-lattices had been fitted, it became pitch dark. The Blessed One declared: "Window-lattices are to be fitted." When they were fitted too low, thieves and miscreants were able to enter. The Blessed One declared: "They are not to be fitted too low." When they were fitted too high, the same problem arose. The Blessed One declared: "They are to be fitted in the middle." The monks made the inner recess narrow and the outer opening wide. The Blessed One declared: "The outer recess should be narrow and the inner opening wide, fitted in the shape of the ocean." Birds and pigeons entered. The Blessed One declared: "A net is to be made." The monks made a net, but since they had not inserted a door-sill, snakes, scorpions, insects called traymabuka, and trailata entered. The Blessed One declared: "A door-sill is to be inserted." The monks inserted a door-sill, but it did not hold at the bottom. The Blessed One declared: "A lower hinge is to be inserted." When the monks inserted the lower hinge, it was not suitable for resting on top. The Blessed One declared: "An upper hinge is to be inserted." When the monks inserted the upper hinge, the wind blew it open. The Blessed One declared: "A waist-bar is to be inserted." When the monks inserted the waist-bar, it was difficult to cut and difficult to remove. The Blessed One declared: "A dry wooden peg is to be held in place, and with it the bar may be cut and removed."

Verses in summary: the tool, the iron mallet, the bowl, the wooden fan, the stone pestle, the chair, the backrest, the axe, and the water vessel.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared that an eye-hole for the handle was to be bored into the door-panel. The monks then bored into the door-panel with an awl, and the door-panel split. The Blessed One declared: "The door-panel is not to be bored into." Since the Blessed One had declared that the door-panel was not to be bored into, the monks affixed the eye-hole and pulled it, but it was unstable and came out. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted: a tool is to be held in place, and with it an eye-hole is also to be bored into the socket."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Pilindavatsa — from the passage beginning "the venerable Pilindavatsa, from the time of his going forth," down to "reverend ones, I am ill and unwell" — the earlier portion proceeds as before. "Venerable one, what is your illness?" "Reverend ones, I have a wind ailment." "Venerable one, please take some medicine." "Reverend ones, in former times I would heat an iron mallet, steep it in water, and steam my body with it."

"Elder, why do you not heat it?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then I hereby permit it. One who has a wind ailment may heat an iron mallet, steep it in water, and steam the body with it."

When the Blessed One had declared that the iron mallet was to be heated, the monks were unable to lift it out once it had been heated. The Blessed One declared: "Grasp it with an iron chain." When the monks placed the iron chain in the fire as well, it too became hot. The Blessed One declared: "Do not put it in there directly. Place it inside a wet cloth and use that to handle the heated iron mallet."

The monks made the iron mallet ready by smoothing it with a grass called uṣatu. The Blessed One declared: "It is not to be smoothed down. The heated mallet itself is what is suitable."

The monks were heating the water first by full use, and afterwards by letting it cool to a suitable temperature. The Blessed One declared: "First heat the water to a suitable temperature, and afterwards heat it further for full use."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. The venerable Pilindavatsa — from the passage beginning "the venerable Pilindavatsa, from the time of his going forth," down to "reverend ones, I am ill and unwell" — the earlier portion proceeds as before. "Elder, what is your illness?" "Reverend ones, I have this and that ailment." "Elder, please take some medicine." "Reverend ones, in former times I would hold a medicine bowl." "Elder, why do you not hold one now?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it."

At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then I hereby permit it. One may hold a medicine bowl."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A householder built a steam-house for the Saṅgha, and after spreading charcoal inside and leaving it there, the Blessed One declared: "It is to be swept out."

When the Blessed One had declared that the charcoal was to be swept out, the monks did not know how to sweep it. The Blessed One declared: "Make an iron dustpan and use that to sweep it out." When the Blessed One had declared that an iron dustpan was to be made, monks in remote monasteries had no such thing available. At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Let them have a wooden dustpan made to use." When the Blessed One had declared that a wooden dustpan was to be made, the monks did not know what form the dustpan should take. The Blessed One declared: "Make the head thick, then smear it with mud and clay, and use it to sweep up the charcoal."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk, being ill, went to a physician and said: "Good sir, such and such an illness has come upon me; please prescribe a medicine." The physician said: "Noble one, do this and that, and you will recover." The monk needed a mortar for preparing the medicine, so he went to a householder and asked for one, and the householder gave him one. After preparing the medicine, the monk returned the mortar to that same householder, and the householder said: "Noble one, please keep it yourself." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said:

"Noble one, if that is how it is, then so be it — please go."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may keep a mortar." When Mṛgāra's mother Visākhā heard that the Blessed One had permitted monks to keep mortars, she presented five hundred iron mortars. The monks did not know what to do, and the Blessed One declared: "Distribute them in order of seniority."

When the Blessed One had declared that they were to be distributed in order of seniority, on that occasion when the youngest monks had not yet received theirs, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Give a stone mortar to those who have not yet received one."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk slept on the ground, and his food did not digest. He went to a householder and borrowed a couch, and lying on it he recovered; he then returned it to the householder. The householder said: "Noble one, please keep it yourself." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is how it is, then so be it — please go." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may keep a couch."

When Mṛgāra's mother Visākhā heard that the Blessed One had permitted monks to keep couches with decorative legs, she presented five hundred couches with decorative legs. The monks did not know what to do, and the Blessed One declared: "Distribute them in order of seniority."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk needed a backrest. He borrowed one from a householder, used it for his need, and returned it. The householder said: "Noble one, please keep it yourself." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is how it is, then so be it — please go." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may keep a backrest."

When Mṛgāra's mother Visākhā heard that the Blessed One had permitted monks to keep backrests, she presented five hundred backrests. The monks did not know what to do, and the Blessed One declared: "Distribute them in order of seniority."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk had a worker who was employed in the kitchen, and that worker needed an axe. The monk borrowed one from a householder, the work was done with it, and it was returned. The householder said: "Noble one, please keep it yourself." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is how it is, then so be it — please go." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may keep an axe."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk's couch top broke, and he borrowed a plank from a householder;

The work was done with it, and it was returned. The householder said: "Noble one, please keep it yourself." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is how it is, then so be it — please go." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: monks may keep a peg."

A summary verse:

A peg and three kinds of ladder,
a latch and an interior support-bar,
wood, stone, and earthen
tread-boards — three kinds of ladder are permitted.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk's chair leg broke and he needed a peg, so he borrowed a peg from a householder; the work was done with it, and it was returned. The householder said: "Noble one, please keep it yourself." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is how it is, then so be it — please go." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may keep a peg."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Eastern Park, in the mansion of Mṛgāramātā. The Blessed One instructed the monks that they should assist with building walls, and the monks accordingly helped to build stūpas and temples. When the mansion of Mṛgāramātā had been built to a great height and it became necessary to plaster it, the monks did not know from what they should do the plastering. The Blessed One declared: "Plaster it from a ladder." When the Blessed One had declared that they should plaster it from a ladder, the monks did not know how many kinds of ladder there were. The Blessed One declared: "There are three kinds of ladder: one of wood, one of rope, and one of bamboo."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Kapilavāstu in the Nyagrodhā Park. The Blessed One had a younger brother, a monk named Nanda, whose body was golden in colour and who bore thirty of the eighty minor marks of a great being, yet who was four finger-breadths shorter than the Blessed One. Nanda had a wife named Sundarī — beautiful of form, lovely, pleasant to behold, charming to men — and toward her he felt intense attachment, clinging, infatuation, the casting off of restraint, swooning, excessive longing, and passionate desire.

The Blessed One, knowing that the time had come to tame him, dressed in his lower robe in the morning, took his alms bowl and outer robe, and set off for alms at Kapilavāstu accompanied by the śramaṇa Nanda walking behind. While making his alms round in Kapilavāstu he headed toward the dwelling of Nanda, and when he arrived and stood at the door he sent forth rays of light the colour of molten gold, so that the whole house appeared like liquid gold. Nanda thought: "Surely the Blessed One has come — that is why my house appears like liquid gold." He sent a man, saying: "Go and look — who is at the door?" When the man came back out and saw the Blessed One, he went quickly inside and said: "Master, the Blessed One has come and is standing at the entrance." Nanda, filled with reverence, began to go out. Then Sundarī thought: "If he goes before the Blessed One, the Blessed One will certainly ordain him." So she grabbed the hem of his robe and said: "My lord, do not go — stay here."

He said: "Let me go — I will pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and return." She put a mark on him and said: "My prince, if you come back having dried off this mark, I will give you authority over five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." He replied: "Very well — let it be so." She bound him to this promise and let him go. He went, paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, took the Blessed One's alms-bowl, and returned. Then, as he emerged carrying the alms-bowl filled with clean and fine food and drink, the Blessed One did not stop to accept it himself but continued on, and signaled to the venerable Ānanda not to take it either. For the blessed buddhas are difficult to approach and difficult to endure, and so no one was able to say to the Blessed One, "Please accept this." Then, when Ānanda began to present the offering, Nanda said: "Please offer it to the very one from whom you received it." Ānanda lost his nerve. So he took the Blessed One's alms-bowl and followed after him. The Blessed One had gone to the monastery and was seated there, and Nanda presented the alms-bowl. Then the Blessed One performed the act of eating, and declared to Nanda: "Nanda, eat what remains in the alms-bowl." Nanda replied: "As the Blessed One wishes." The Blessed One gave him what remained in the alms-bowl, and Nanda ate it. After he had eaten, the Blessed One declared: "Nanda, why do you not go forth?" For the Blessed One had not broken a single word of Dharma across all those generations — not with parents, not with teachers, preceptors, or others in the role of spiritual guides. So Nanda said: "Blessed One, I will go forth." Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and have Nanda's hair and beard shaved." The venerable Ānanda, having heard this command from the Blessed One, said: "As the reverend one commands," and went to find a barber and had him begin to shave. But Nanda threatened the barber: "Hey, barber! Before long I will become a wheel-turning king who rules by the power of his might. If you shave my hair and beard, I will cut off your arm at the elbow." The barber, terrified, set down his razor and sat still. The venerable Ānanda reported this to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One himself went to where the venerable Nanda was and asked: "Nanda, will you not go forth?" He replied: "Blessed One, I will go forth." Then the Blessed One himself poured water over his head from a water vessel, and the barber shaved away his hair and beard. And Nanda thought to himself: "For now I will go forth out of reverence for the Blessed One, and when night has passed I will leave." So when night had passed he set out. But the Blessed One conjured a great chasm. Nanda thought: "My beautiful wife is now far away, and I will surely die here in this desolate place — I will go when morning comes." And so, agonizing over thoughts of that most lovely one, he passed the night in misery. The Blessed One, knowing his mind, said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell Nanda to guard the house." Ānanda went and relayed the Blessed One's instruction to the venerable Nanda: "The Blessed One commands you to guard the house." Nanda asked: "Reverend Ānanda, what is this thing called 'guarding the house'? What exactly does one do?" Ānanda replied: "The venerable Nanda is to do the work of the monastery. After the monks have gone out for alms, he should first sweep the monastery clean, then clean up the cow-dung and maintain the grounds, and guard the monastery." The monks then said:

"Whatever there is to be announced, let it be announced. Whatever incense, flowers, fragrant substances, and so forth there may be, let those also be distributed to the Saṅgha. In the evening the doors are to be closed, and in the morning they are to be opened. The latrines and the urinals are also to be cleaned. And whatever other duties are connected with the monastery, those too are to be carried out."

Nanda replied: "Reverend Ānanda, I shall do exactly as the Blessed One has commanded."

Then in due course, one morning the monks put on their lower robes, took up their bowls and outer robes, and went into the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Nanda thought to himself: "I will go and sweep the monastery." He took up a broom and began to sweep. The Blessed One, at that very moment when Nanda was sweeping a courtyard, blessed a second broom so that it became full.

Nanda thought: "I will put down this broom and go," but he could not put down his broom and began to shake it out. Before it was empty, he thought: "I will go and close the doors of the cells," and so he began to close the doors of the cells. But the Blessed One blessed things so that the very moment Nanda closed the door of one cell, another flew open, and Nanda grew weary. He said to himself: "When I become king, I will build a monastery far grander than this."

Then he thought: "I will go down a side path," and he went down a side path. The Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of Nanda's mind, went along that very path. Nanda saw the Blessed One from a great distance, and seeing him, he swiftly ran to a nearby tree with thick, hanging branches and hid beneath it. The Blessed One then blessed the branches of that tree so that they rose upward.

The Blessed One then said: "Nanda, where are you going? Come here."

Nanda was speechless, and with a mind full of shame he followed behind the Blessed One.

The Blessed One reflected: "This one is so intensely attached to his beautiful wife that he must be separated from her." Knowing that he should separate Nanda from her, the Blessed One stayed as long as he wished in the city of Śrāvastī, then set out toward Śrāvastī and arrived there directly.

Now the mother of Sundarī, wife of Mṛgāramat, had heard that the Blessed One's younger brother named Nanda, whose body was golden in color and who bore thirty of the thirty-two major marks of a great being, falling four finger-breadths short of the Blessed One, had come there together with the Blessed One, and she thought: "When will I get to see him?"

The Vinaya, Minor Matters. The Eleventh Fascicle.

Then, on another occasion, the venerable Nanda, one morning having put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. He went straight to the house of the mother of Sundarī, wife of Mṛgāramat. When he saw her beautiful form and radiant complexion, he thought: "This must surely be the Blessed One's younger brother Nanda." And filled with faith, she touched his feet and paid homage. When she touched his feet, since the touch of a woman is a thing that stirs the passions, he was overcome by desire, and his semen was released and fell onto the top of Sundarī's head. Now, since awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, possess the quality of never forgetting, the Blessed One blessed the matter so that it became turushka (a fragrant resin). Nanda thought: "From where could turushka resin have come here? Surely the noble Nanda has lost an impure substance. And the Blessed One, possessing the quality of never forgetting, has blessed it as turushka resin." Realizing this, she was filled with joy and cried out in delight: "O the Buddha! O the Dharma! O the Saṅgha!"

"How wonderful! The Dharma is indeed well proclaimed, and thus even I — along with the noble Nanda and others who are strongly given to passion — practice the holy life." This she declared aloud, again and again.

Then the venerable Nanda thought to himself, "Can it be that no offense against the Saṅgha has arisen for me?" and remorse arose in him. At that point he reported the matter to the monks, and the monks brought it before the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, for this monk Nanda, who is excessively given to passion, there is no offense. Therefore I permit it, and those who are of such a nature — that is, excessively prone to passion — should carry a receptacle for the outflow. They need not feel remorse over this."

When the Blessed One had given the ruling that those excessively prone to passion should carry such a receptacle, the monks did not know from what skin it should be made. The Blessed One declared: "It should be made from the skin of a goat, a deer, or a mouse." When they stored these as they were, they became unpleasant in smell. The Blessed One declared: "Wash them, knead them, and dry them." While they were washing and drying them, some monks, upon seeing women, emitted semen, and their lower garments became soiled and stained. The Blessed One declared: "Make two and dry one while wearing the other." For some monks, so much semen was produced that it soaked through. The Blessed One declared: "Stuff those with cotton wadding." When the monks stuffed them with pigs' bristles they were caused discomfort. The Blessed One declared: "Stuff them with sand or earth." While the monks were wearing these and eating food and making prostrations before a stūpa, the Blessed One declared: "Set that aside in a private place, then having bathed, eat food and make prostrations at the stūpa."
