Then, on another occasion, the venerable Nanda was seated on a flat stone in a certain place, and he called to mind the beautiful Sundarī, and began to draw her likeness on that stone. The venerable Mahākāśyapa also came to that place and, seeing him, said: "Venerable Nanda, what are you doing?" He replied: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, I am drawing the likeness of Sundarī." Mahākāśyapa said: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a monk's activities are two: meditative concentration and recitation. Are you here drawing your own wife? He said nothing." At that time the venerable Mahākāśyapa brought the matter before the Blessed One. The Blessed One, reflecting on the matter, recognized that whatever fault had arisen had come about through the drawing of a likeness, and declared to the monks: "Monks, the deluded man Nanda, with a mind attached to Sundarī, drew the picture. Therefore monks must not draw pictures. A monk who draws a picture commits a serious transgression." The Blessed One thus declared that monks must not draw pictures.

Furthermore, monks must not anoint or smear the stūpas of a Tathāgata's hair-relics or nail-relics with perfume, nor scatter perfume upon them. The Blessed Ones, the buddhas, ask questions while already knowing the answer — and so the Blessed One questioned the venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, why is it that monks do not anoint or scatter perfume upon the stūpas of a Tathāgata's hair-relics and nail-relics?" At that, the venerable Ānanda gave a detailed account to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Very well then, I permit it. You may anoint and scatter perfume upon them — but you must not draw images of sentient beings."

The Blessed One then reflected: "This foolish man Nanda is still full of attachment to Sundarī and his mind is bound to her. I must devise a means to help him." Knowing this, he spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do you see the fragrance of the mountain incense rising?" "Venerable one, I do not see it." "In that case, take hold of the lower hem of the Tathāgata's robe." And he took hold of the lower hem of the Blessed One's robe.

Then the Blessed One rose into the middle of the sky like a king among geese spreading its wings, and passing through the upper sky he arrived at Mount Fragrance, wafted with sweet scent. And so, traveling together with the venerable Ānanda, going here and there, they came to stand beside a saha tree, where a young female monkey was roaming about as she pleased. She caught sight of the Blessed One and gazed at him without distraction.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do you see this young female monkey?" "Blessed One, I see her." "Ānanda, what do you think — between this female monkey and Sundarī, which is more beautiful, more lovely, more delightful to behold?" He replied: "Venerable one, this female monkey does not come within one hundredth of the Śākya girl Sundarī, not within one thousandth, not within one hundred-thousandth — she is not to be reckoned, counted, compared, calculated, set as an example, or set as a basis in relation to her. Venerable one, the Śākya girl Sundarī is a match for the daughters of the gods."

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, if that is so, take hold of the lower hem of the Tathāgata's robe." He took hold of the lower hem of the Blessed One's robe. Then the Blessed One rose into the middle of the sky like a king among geese spreading its wings, passed through the upper sky, and arrived directly in the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods.

Then the Blessed One, dwelling in the Joyful Grove pleasure garden, said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and look upon the gods of the Thirty-Three." And so Ānanda went and looked upon the gods there — their sport and joy and delight, their places of happiness, the pleasure gardens, the Joyful Grove, the various chariots, the mingling and gathering and assembly, the beautiful Dharma and all the rest. And as he looked, seeing each one more splendid and more excellent than the last, he went about the beautiful city in wonder.

Going on from there and looking around, he saw a palace in which there were no god-sons at all, filled entirely with goddesses. He asked the goddesses: "In all the other palaces, the god-sons and goddesses together fill them with sport and joy and pleasure — what is the reason that in this palace there are no god-sons?" They replied: "The Blessed One's younger brother, named Nanda, who has been practicing the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One — when he passes from this life he will come here. That is why this palace has been reserved, and we too remain here, waiting for him."

Hearing this, Nanda was filled with delight, gladness, and great joy, and he returned before the Blessed One. The Blessed One said to him: "Did you see the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three?" He replied: "Blessed One, I did see them." The Blessed One said: "Tell me what you saw there." When Nanda had described in full what he had seen, the Blessed One said: "Nanda, did you see the goddesses?" "Blessed One, I did see them." "Nanda, what do you think — who is more beautiful, lovely, and fair to behold: the Śākyan girl Sundarī, or those goddesses?" He replied: "Venerable One, Sundarī the Śākyan girl does not come within even a hundredth part of those goddesses — not within a thousandth, not within a hundred-thousandth, not by count, by reckoning, by fraction, by calculation, by comparison, or by cause."

"Nanda, this being so, dwelling in the holy life brings benefits such as these and others as well. Rejoice in this, and practice the holy life — and you shall experience the splendor of the gods."

At this, Nanda consented in his mind to the Blessed One's words and sat silent.

Then the Blessed One disappeared from the realm of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and departed for Śrāvastī.

From that time on, the venerable Nanda practiced the holy life with delight in the divine world in view.

Then the Blessed One, knowing his state of mind, addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and convey to the monks this instruction: 'Monks, none of you shall sit together with Nanda on the same seat, walk together with him on the same walking ground, place a robe on the same robe-rack as his, place a bowl on the same bowl-stand as his, or place water on the same water-stand as his. You shall not recite together with him, and you shall not chant together with him.'"

"Venerable One, I shall do as you command," said the venerable Ānanda, and having listened to the Blessed One he conveyed this to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has spoken thus: 'Venerable ones, you shall not sit together with Nanda on the same seat' — and so on, all as before, down to 'you shall not chant together with him.'"

"Venerable Ānanda, so be it. As the Blessed One has commanded, so shall it be done." And they did not sit with him on the same seat, did not walk with him on the same walking ground, did not place a robe on the same robe-rack, did not place a bowl on the same bowl-stand, did not place water on the same water-stand, and did not recite or chant together with him.

Because the monks had shunned him in this way, the venerable Nanda felt deeply distressed, ashamed, embarrassed, and mortified.

Then at a certain later time, when the venerable Nanda was doing work with robes together with a great many monks at the service hall, Nanda thought to himself: "These monks have shunned me, it seems. Now, this venerable Ānanda is my own younger brother — would even he shun me?" Realizing this, he went and sat down beside him. But the venerable Ānanda rose up very quickly and moved away.

Nanda said to him: "If it is right for these fellow practitioners of the holy life to shun me for now, you are my own younger brother — why would you shun me?"

He replied: "Venerable Nanda, that is true — and yet you have entered upon one path, and we too have entered upon a path, and so there is indeed reason to shun you."

Nanda said:

"Venerable Ānanda, tell me: what path have you entered upon, and what path have I entered upon?"

He replied: "You practice the holy life out of delight in the realm of the gods, while we practice the holy life with the aspiration for nirvāṇa."

When these words were spoken, Nanda was filled with deep despondency.

Then the Blessed One, knowing Nanda's state of mind through his own awareness, said to the venerable Nanda: "Nanda, have you seen the hells?"

"I have not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "Take hold of the hem of my robe." And Nanda took hold of the hem of the Blessed One's robe.

The Blessed One then led the venerable Nanda and departed to the hell realms. Standing a little to one side, the Blessed One said to the venerable Nanda: "Nanda, go and look at the hells."

Nanda looked. He saw rivers without fords, forests with leaves like swords, charnel grounds, smoldering fires, and in those various regions, one more terrible in its particular sufferings than the next — utterly unbearable. Going into those hell realms, he saw sentient beings enduring all manner of specific sufferings: being hauled up and cut down and shattered. Some had their eyes and teeth gouged out by dryness; some were being devoured by buzzards; some had their legs hacked off with axes; some were being skewered with short spears, great arrows, and single-pointed weapons; some were being beaten with iron hammers; some were being placed inside great iron cauldrons that blazed, burned fiercely, and burned on every side, their flames merging into one, and were being boiled within them. Having seen those many and varied specific sufferings, Nanda moved to another area. There he saw a great iron cauldron boiling, and seeing it he felt no joy. He asked the hell guardians: "O knowers, what is the reason that sentient beings are placed in all the other iron cauldrons while this one stands here boiling but empty?"

They said: "One called Nanda, the younger brother of the Blessed One, who delights in the realm of the gods, practices the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One. When he dies, he will come here — and for that reason this cauldron is being kept ready. We too are stationed here, waiting for him."

Upon hearing this, Nanda was seized with terror and dread and revulsion, his hair standing on end. Thinking, "Right now I am about to be cast in — I must flee at once!" he ran and ran as fast as he could, and arrived before the Blessed One breathless and disheveled, his face dark, and said:

The Blessed One said: "Nanda, have you seen the hells?"

Half-dead with fright, his tongue faltering, speaking words of pity in a slow, faint, subdued murmur, he said: "I have seen them, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "Tell me what you saw there." And Nanda reported in full what he had seen.

The Blessed One then said: "Nanda, for one who practices the holy life with the aspiration for the realm of the gods there are faults such as these and others besides. Therefore you should delight in nirvāṇa, not delight in the realm of the gods."

Nanda sat there silently, his mind overwhelmed with shame.

The Blessed One then vanished from the hell realms and proceeded to the Hot Springs of the Sages near the city of Campā.

Then at another time the venerable Nanda, rising from his afternoon meditation together with five hundred monks, went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Those five hundred monks likewise prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One, knowing that the Saṅgha of monks was seated to one side, spoke to the venerable Nanda: "Nanda, I shall teach you the Dharma — namely, the Dharma discourse called 'Entering the Womb,' good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end, excellent in meaning, excellent in word, unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, perfectly cleansed, revealing the holy life. Listen to it well and hold it in mind." "Venerable one, I shall do as you command," said the venerable Nanda, and he attended to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke as follows.

"Nanda, what are the conditions under which entry into a mother's womb occurs, and what are those under which it does not? Nanda, it is like this: the parents must be attracted to each other and have come together; the mother must be in her fertile season; and the gandharva (Skt. gandharva) must also be present and ready to enter. Nanda, the word 'gandharva' is the designation for a being of the intermediate existence (Skt. antarābhava). It comes in two kinds: one of fair appearance and one of dark appearance. The intermediate existence of beings destined for the hell realms is of dark appearance — like, for example, a charred tree-stump. The intermediate existence of those going to an animal birth is like the color of smoke. That of hungry ghosts is like the color of water. The intermediate existence of humans and gods is like the color of gold. That of gods dwelling in the form realm is white. Gods dwelling in the formless realm, being without form, have no intermediate existence at all.

"Some beings of the intermediate existence have two hands and two feet; some have four feet; some have many feet; and some have no feet at all. A being of the intermediate existence takes on whatever form corresponds to the destiny it is to be born into through its previous karma. Every being of the intermediate existence is endowed with the supernatural power of moving through the air, and possesses, as it were, the divine eye.

"As for the mother being in her fertile season, Nanda, 'fertile season' means a particular time and period. Nanda, some women enter their fertile season for three days, or five days, or seven days. Others, through the power of causes and conditions, remain in their fertile season for a long time, and their fertile season may even come around again and again.

"Among these, women who are afflicted, who are of poor constitution, who are troubled, and who have eaten food and drink of poor quality — their fertile season does not last long, and it quickly comes to an end and passes. Nanda, it is just as when water is poured onto rough, coarse ground: it quickly dissipates and disappears. In the same way, for women who are afflicted, of poor constitution, troubled, and who have eaten food and drink of poor quality, the fertile season likewise does not last long and quickly comes to an end and passes.

"On the other hand, women who possess well-being, who have abundant comfort, who are not troubled, and who have eaten food and drink of good quality — their fertile season lasts long and does not quickly come to an end and pass. Their fertile season and —

their fertile season also arrives at the proper interval.

"Nanda, it is just as when water is poured onto smooth, soft ground: it does not quickly dissipate and disappear. In the same way, for women who possess well-being, who have abundant comfort, who are not troubled, and who have eaten food and drink of good quality, the fertile season likewise lasts long and does not come to an end and disappear. Their fertile season and their fertile season arriving at the proper interval both occur.

"Nanda, if semen comes from the father but not from the mother, then at that time no entry into the womb will take place. If it comes from the mother but not from the father, then at that time no entry into the womb will take place. If it comes neither from the mother nor from the father, then at that time no entry into the womb will take place.

"If the mother has become impure while the father has become pure, or if the father has become pure while the mother has become impure — and at that time the mother's womb is obstructed by wind, or obstructed by bile, or obstructed by phlegm, or obstructed by blood, or obstructed by fat; or it is filled with mucus; or it has been altered by medicine; or it is similar in the middle to an ant's waist; or it is like the mouth of a drum; or it is like the middle knob of a door-bar; or it is like the bolt of a door; or it is like a door-horse; or it is like a thorn; or it is like a leaf; or there has grown inside it something like a lump; or it is deep below; or it is deep above; or it is unsuitable as a vessel for the womb; or blood flows from it; or it is short; or it is like the beak of a crow; or it is spread wide to the left; or spread wide to the right; or spread wide above; or spread wide below; or it is raised; or it is sunken; or it is collapsed; or it has only the semblance of a mark; or it is unsteady; or it is defective; or its position has shifted; or it has been eaten by insects called besaraka — then at that time no entry into the womb will take place.

"If the father and mother are known to be potent but the gandharva (gandharva) is known to be weak, then at that time no entry into the womb will take place. If the gandharva is known to be potent but the father and mother are known to be weak, then at that time no entry into the womb will take place. If all are known to be weak, and moreover the father and mother have not performed and accumulated the karma that would result in finding a child, and the gandharva has likewise not performed and accumulated the karma that would result in becoming a father or mother, and the two minds of the gandharva — whether a male mind or a female mind — neither one has been placed in proximity, then at that time no entry into the womb will take place.

"If all are known to be potent, but the father and mother have not performed and accumulated the karma that would result in finding a child, and the gandharva has likewise not performed and accumulated the karma that would result in becoming a father or mother, and the two minds of the gandharva — whether a male mind or a female mind — neither has been placed in proximity, then at that time no entry into the womb will take place.

"Nanda, how then does entry into the mother's womb come to take place? Nanda, in this case the father and mother come together in desire and union; the mother is fit and is in her fertile season; the gandharva is present nearby and has the wish to enter; semen comes from both father and mother; and both father and mother are pure. At that time the mother's womb is not obstructed by wind, not obstructed by bile, not obstructed by phlegm, not obstructed by blood, not obstructed by fat; it is not filled with mucus; it has not been altered by medicine; it is not similar in the middle to an ant's waist; it is not like the mouth of a drum; it is not like the middle knob of a door-bar; it is not like the bolt of a door; it is not like a door-horse; it is not like a thorn; it is not like a leaf; nothing like a lump has grown inside it; it is not deep below; it is not deep above; it is not unsuitable as a vessel for the womb; blood does not flow from it; it is not short; it is not like the beak of a crow; it is not spread wide to the left; it is not spread wide to the right; it is not spread wide above; it is not spread wide below; it is not raised; it is not sunken; it is not collapsed; it does not have only the semblance of a mark;"

it is not wobbly; it is not defective; it has not been displaced; it has not been eaten by the creature called a besaraka.

If the father and mother are renowned as being of high standing, the gandharva too is renowned as being of high standing. If the father and mother are renowned as being of low standing, the gandharva too is renowned as being of low standing. When all are renowned as being of high standing, and the father and mother have also performed and accumulated the karma that results in obtaining a child, and the gandharva has likewise performed and accumulated the karma that results in becoming a father or mother, then, if the gandharva keeps in mind whichever it may be of the two minds, a male mind or a female mind, it will enter the mother's womb.

Nandaka, when a gandharva is about to enter the mother's womb desiring to do so, it possesses an inverted mind and a wrongly oriented pride, and through the force of the causes and conditions of its former karma, it acquires these ten false perceptions, each arising separately in each birth: the perception of warmth, the perception of sunlight, the perception of wind, the perception of rain, the perception of drizzle, the perception of cold, the perception of an unpleasant region, the perception of a red wind, the perception of heavy rain, and the perception of a great crowd of common people making a clamor.

Nandaka, after those perceptions have arisen and are present, when these other ten false perceptions arise inwardly in birth, they arise thus: the thought "I am entering my own house," the thought "I am climbing up into a fine mansion," the thought "I am going down into a multi-storied building," the thought "I am ascending a throne," the thought "I am entering a heap of grass," the thought "I am entering a pile of leaves," and the thought "I am going toward dense grass, or a thick forest, or the gap in a wall, or the foot of a wall." Nandaka, dependent upon whichever of these perceptions it may be, the gandharva enters the mother's womb, and having been born there, the soft and tender body comes to be fully formed.

Nandaka, as to that, the soft and tender body is not to be regarded as being the impure substance of the father and mother, nor is the soft and tender body other than the impure substance of the father and mother. Nandaka, nevertheless, dependent upon that very impure substance of the father and mother, through the assembling of causes and conditions, the soft and tender body arises, and thus the semen and blood serve only as its object of focus and its support, and nothing more.

Nandaka, take for example how, dependent on milk, and dependent on the pot, and dependent on the churning stick, and dependent on the effort arising from a person, butter comes forth from milk. Nandaka, in that case one does not observe the butter separately in each of those, yet, Nandaka, dependent upon that very milk, through the assembling of causes and conditions, the butter comes forth, and thus milk serves only as the object of focus and support of the butter, and nothing more.

In the same way, the soft and tender body is to be regarded as arising from the impure substance of the father and mother; the soft and tender body is not other than the impure substance of the father and mother, and yet it is not that either. Nandaka, nevertheless, dependent upon that very impure substance of the father and mother, through the assembling of causes and conditions, the soft and tender body comes to be fully formed, and thus the semen and blood serve only as its object of focus and its support, and nothing more.

Nandaka, take for example how, dependent on green grass, a worm is born. Nandaka, in that case the worm is not to be regarded as being the green grass, nor is the worm to be regarded as other than the green grass. Nevertheless, dependent upon that very green grass, through the assembling of causes and conditions, a worm is born possessing the power of a matching color, and by that power of color the worm in its very nature becomes like a green leaf. Nandaka, in the same way, the soft and tender body is not to be regarded as being the impure substance of the father and mother, nor is the soft and tender body other than the impure substance of the father and mother.

Nandaka, nevertheless, dependent upon that very impure substance of the father and mother, through the assembling of causes and conditions, the great elements of the sense faculties come to be fully established.

Nandaka, consider, for example, how a worm is born in dependence upon cow dung. Nandaka, in that case the worm is not to be regarded as being the cow dung, nor is the worm to be regarded as other than the cow dung. Nevertheless, dependent upon that very cow dung, through the assembling of causes and conditions, a worm is born possessing the power of a matching color, and by that power of color the worm in its very nature becomes yellow.

Nandaka, in the same way, the soft and tender body is not to be regarded as being the impure substance of the father and mother, nor is the soft and tender body other than the impure substance of the father and mother. Nevertheless, dependent upon that very impure substance of the father and mother, through the assembling of causes and conditions, the great elements of the sense faculties come to be fully established.

Nandaka, consider, for example, how a worm is born in dependence upon cedar wood. Nandaka, in that case the worm is not to be regarded as being the cedar, nor is the worm to be regarded as other than the cedar. Nevertheless, dependent upon that very cedar, through the assembling of causes and conditions, a worm is born possessing the power of a matching color, and by that power of color the worm in its very nature becomes red.

Nandaka, in the same way, the soft and tender body is not to be regarded as being the impure substance of the father and mother, nor is the soft and tender body other than the impure substance of the father and mother. Nevertheless, dependent upon that very impure substance of the father and mother, through the assembling of causes and conditions, the great elements of the sense faculties come to be fully established.

Nandaka, consider, for example, how a worm is born in dependence upon curds. Nandaka, in that case the worm is not to be regarded as being the curds, nor is the worm to be regarded as other than the curds. Nevertheless, dependent upon those very curds, through the assembling of causes and conditions, a worm is born possessing the power of a matching color, and by that power of color the worm in its very nature becomes white.

Nandaka, in the same way, the soft and tender body is not to be regarded as being the impure substance of the father and mother, nor is the soft and tender body other than the impure substance of the father and mother. Nevertheless, dependent upon that very impure substance of the father and mother, through the assembling of causes and conditions, the great elements of the sense faculties resembling those of the father and mother come to be fully established.

Nandaka, in that soft and tender body arisen from the impure substance of the father and mother, the earth element (Skt. pṛthivīdhātu) is present as solidity, the water element as moisture, the fire element as warmth, and the wind element as lightness and movement.

Nandaka, if in that soft and tender body arisen from the impure substance of the father and mother the earth element were present but the water element absent, it would become dry and would crumble apart, like a handful of flour or a handful of ash.

Nandaka, if in that soft and tender body arisen from the impure substance of the father and mother the water element were present but the earth element absent, it would dissolve away by moisture, like oil or water.

Nevertheless, because the water element is held together by the earth element it does not fall apart, and because the earth element is bound by the water element it does not dissolve.

Nandaka, if in that soft and tender body arisen from the impure substance of the father and mother the earth element and the water element were present but the fire element absent, it would become moist, it would decay, and it would putrefy. Nandaka, just as in the last month of winter a piece of meat, lacking the fire element, becomes moist, decays, and putrefies, in the same way, Nandaka, if in that soft and tender body arisen from the impure substance of the father and mother the earth element and the water element were present but the fire element absent, it would become moist, it would decay, and it would putrefy.

Nandaka, if in that soft and tender body arisen from the impure substance of the father and mother the earth element, the water element, and the fire element were present but the wind element absent, it would not stir, and it could not grow, expand, and develop. Yet, Nandaka, these very elements — the four great elements (mahābhūtas) that arise from within, aroused inwardly, produced by the karmic maturation of previous actions, present and mutually conditioning, having come together — being supported by the earth element, cohered by the water element, ripened by the fire element, and set in motion by the wind element, they grow, expand, and develop.

Nandaka, just as when a butter-lamp carrier, or the student of a butter-lamp carrier, heats sugarcane juice that has been clarified, and then with the breath drives it through the hollow stalk of a lotus root, those very things grow, expand, and develop — in the same way, Nandaka, these very elements — the four great elements that arise from within, aroused inwardly, produced by the karmic maturation of previous actions, present and mutually conditioning — being supported by the earth element, cohered by the water element, ripened by the fire element, and set in motion by the wind element, they grow, expand, and develop.

Nandaka, that soft and tender body should not be regarded as being the impure substance of the father and mother. It is not from the father's loins. It is not from the mother's womb. It is not from that karma. It is not from that cause. It is not from that condition. Yet, Nandaka, in dependence upon that very impure substance of the father and mother — through the coming together, the assembling, the arriving, and the becoming manifest of the causes — dwelling in the womb is accomplished.

Nandaka, just as seeds that are intact, sound, not broken open, not punctured, not split, not rotten, and not damaged by wind and sun, when sown in a moist patch of ground, a meadow, or in a well-ploughed good field, and well irrigated — from those seeds, through the power of causes and conditions, the sprout, the leaf, the stalk, the pith, the flower, and the fruit gradually and manifestly come to be — Nandaka, in that case the sprout and the rest are not those very seeds, nor, apart from those seeds, do the sprout and the rest arise without cause and without condition. Rather, they arise from the assembling of causes and conditions. In the same way, Nandaka, the soft and tender body should not be regarded as the impure substance of the father and mother. It is not from the father's loins. It is not from the mother's womb. It is not from that karma. It is not from that cause. It is not from that condition. Yet, Nandaka, in dependence upon that very impure substance of the father and mother — through the coming together, the assembling, the arriving, and the becoming manifest of the causes — dwelling in the womb is accomplished.

Nandaka, just as a man with good eyes, wishing to produce fire in the proper way, takes a fire-crystal, holds it up toward the sun, and then placing well-dried powder of cow dung there, produces fire — Nandaka, fire is indeed present in those causes, yet if those causes were set aside, fire would not arise from no cause and no condition. Rather, fire arises from the assembling of causes and conditions. In the same way, Nandaka, in dependence upon that very impure substance of the father and mother — through the coming together, the assembling, the arriving, and the becoming manifest of the causes — dwelling in the womb is accomplished.

Nandaka, as for that which is the soft and tender body arisen from the impure substance of the father and mother — this is form (rūpa). The feeling, perception, and formations that arise together with it, along with consciousness — these are name. This name, taken together with the form just described, is reckoned under the designation name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Nandaka, this is so: that name-and-form is no more than just that and nothing beyond. Nandaka, I do not praise even the slightest accomplished existence.

I do not praise even a single moment of accomplished existence. And why is that? Because accomplished existence is suffering. Just as even a small amount of vomit is foul-smelling, so too even a single moment of accomplished existence is suffering.

Nandaka, in this regard: the arising of form, its abiding, its becoming manifest, and its emergence; the arising of feeling, perception, and formations; and the arising, abiding, becoming manifest, and emergence of consciousness — that arising is suffering, that abiding is disease, and that emergence is old age and death.

Nandaka, what pleasure could there be in dwelling in the womb of a mother who harbors accomplished existence? Nandaka, in the first week, one dwells within the slimy, impure, putrid, and blazing mire of the womb, with all the faculties of the body in pain, in great hardship, oppressed and afflicted, and that consciousness — with its one flavor of suffering — becomes a viscous mass in the mother's belly.

Nandaka, what is the nature of that viscous mass? Nandaka, the nature of the viscous mass is like the surface of whey-water or curds — such is the nature of the viscous mass. It dwells there for seven days, and throughout those seven days it is tormented, wholly tormented, heated, wholly heated, and utterly burning. The earth element is present as solidity, the water element as moistness, the fire element as heat, and the wind element as lightness and motion.

Nandaka, in the second week, one dwells within the slimy, impure, putrid, and blazing mire of the womb, with all the faculties of the body extremely heated, unbearably intense, oppressed and afflicted, and that consciousness — with its one flavor of suffering — is struck by the inner winds of the womb, born of the ripening of previous karma, called "gathering," and through their touch that pain of the womb becomes a firmer mass. Nandaka, what is the nature of that firmer mass? Nandaka, it is like solidified curds or butter — such is the nature of the firmer mass. It dwells there for seven days, and throughout those seven days it is tormented, wholly tormented, heated, wholly heated, and utterly burning. The earth element is present as solidity, the water element as moistness, the fire element as warmth, and the wind element as lightness and motion.

Nandaka, in the third week, one dwells within the slimy, impure, putrid, and blazing mire and mud of the womb, with all the faculties of the body extremely heated, unbearably intense, oppressed and afflicted, and that consciousness — with its one flavor of suffering — is struck by the inner winds of the womb, born of the ripening of previous karma, called "storehouse-door," and through their touch that pain of the womb becomes a lumpy mass. Nandaka, what is the nature of that lumpy mass? Nandaka, it is like a fine copper needle or a tiny worm — such is the nature of the lumpy mass. That pain of the womb dwells there for seven days, and throughout those seven days it is tormented, wholly tormented, heated, wholly heated, and utterly burning. The earth element is present as solidity, the water element as moistness, the fire element as warmth, and the wind element as lightness and motion.

Nandaka, in the fourth week, one dwells within the slimy, impure, putrid, and blazing mire of the womb, with all the faculties of the body extremely heated, unbearably intense, afflicted and oppressed,

and in suffering. In that being possessed of a single consciousness, winds arise within the mother's womb — winds born from the karmic maturation of prior karma, called the "inward-drawing" winds — and through them the one dwelling in the womb becomes a rounded mass. Nandaka, what is the nature of that rounded mass? Nandaka, it is like a lump of curd or a nodule of butter — such is the nature of the rounded mass. That being dwells there for seven days, and throughout those seven days it is tormented, wholly tormented, heated, wholly heated, and utterly burning. The earth element is present as solidity, the water element as moistness, the fire element as warmth, and the wind element as lightness and motion.

Nandaka, in the fifth week, winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there — winds born from the karmic maturation of prior karma, called the "gathering" winds — and through these, five signs appear on the body of that thorn of the womb: the signs of the two shoulders, the signs of the two thighs, and fifth, the sign of the head. Nandaka, just as when the seasonal rains fall in summer, shoots first spring forth from piles of wood, so too, for the one dwelling in the womb, winds arise within the mother's womb — winds born from karmic maturation, called the "gathering" winds — and through these, five signs appear on that being's body: the signs of the two shoulders, the signs of the two thighs, and fifth, the sign of the head.

Nandaka, in the sixth week, winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there — winds born from the karmic maturation of prior karma, called the "wide-spreading" winds — and through these, four signs appear on the body of that thorn of the womb: the signs of the two forearms and the signs of the two lower legs. Nandaka, just as when the summer rains fall, shoots of dark-blue grass first grow, so too, for the one dwelling in the womb, winds arise within the mother's womb — winds born from the karmic maturation of prior karma, called the "wide-spreading" winds — and through these, four signs appear on the body of that thorn of the womb: the signs of the two forearms and the signs of the two lower legs.

Nandaka, in the seventh week, winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there — winds called the "all-turning" winds — and through these, four other signs appear on that being's body: the broad signs of the two palms of the hands and the broad signs of the two soles of the feet. Nandaka, it is like a heap of hollow reeds or a heap of fish scales. So too, within the mother's womb, four signs appear on the body of that thorn of the womb dwelling there: the signs of the two palms of the hands and the signs of the two soles of the feet.

Nandaka, in the eighth week, winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there — winds born from the karmic maturation of prior karma, called the "wholly-turning" winds — and through these, twenty signs arise on the body of that thorn of the womb: the signs of the ten fingers of the hands and the signs of the ten toes of the feet. Nandaka, just as when the summer rains fall, the root-bases of trees first spring up, so too, within the mother's womb, twenty signs arise on the body of that thorn of the womb: the signs of the ten fingers of the hands and the signs of the ten toes of the feet.

In the ninth week — the seventh day of the ninth week — within the mother's womb, nine signs arise on the body of that thorn of the womb: the signs of the two eyes, the signs of the two ears, the signs of the two nostrils, the signs of the two lower openings, and the sign of the mouth.

Nandaka, in the tenth week — the seventh day of the tenth week — winds called the "stable" winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, born from the karmic maturation of prior karma, and through these, solidity and heaviness come to pervade the body of that one dwelling in the womb.

In that very same week, winds called the "all-opening" winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, and these fill that one dwelling in the womb — fill it completely, fill it entirely. Nandaka, it is just as a bladder or bellows when fully inflated.

Nandaka, in the eleventh week — the seventh day of the eleventh week — winds called the "horse-making" winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there. Through these, the interior of that one dwelling in the womb becomes hollow, and the nine apertures of its body open. To whatever degree the mother moves, stirs, and shifts — whether she exerts herself strenuously or her body is thrown about — to that very degree the interior of the one dwelling in the womb becomes hollow, and those apertures are fully formed.

Nandaka, when those winds called the "horse-making" winds travel upward, they produce the upper apertures; when they travel downward, they produce the lower apertures. Nandaka, it is just as when a skilled smith or a smith's apprentice takes a smith's bellows and works it with both hands — just as the bellows moves with each working — so too, those winds called the "horse-making" winds, when traveling upward, produce the upper apertures, and when traveling downward, produce the lower apertures. Nandaka, once those horse-making winds have opened those sense bases, they cease to exist in that very place.

Nandaka, in the twelfth week — the seventh day of the twelfth week — winds called the "crooked-opening" winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there. These form the intestines and the mesentery on the right and left sides of the belly of that one dwelling in the womb. Nandaka, it is just as the rootlet-tendrils at the base of a lotus are intertwined — bound inward, coiled and twisted — so too, they come to rest, supported by the body.

Then, in that very same week, winds called the "hair-producing" winds arise, and through these, no more and no fewer than three hundred and thirty joints are produced on the body of that one dwelling in the womb, and through the power of the wind, one hundred and one vital points come to rest, supported by the body.

Nandaka, in the thirteenth week — the seventh day of the thirteenth week — hunger and thirst arise in the one dwelling in the womb within the mother's belly. Whatever the mother eats and drinks, its essence enters through the navel of that one, and by that, the one is nourished there.

Whatever food and drink the mother of that one consumes —
by that, the one dwelling in the mother's womb
is sustained and nourished there.

Nandaka, in the fourteenth week — the seventh day of the fourteenth week — winds called the "channel-opening" winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there. Through these, nine hundred channels are produced on the body of that one dwelling in the womb: two hundred and twenty-five on the front of the body, two hundred and twenty-five on the back of the body, two hundred and twenty-five on the right side of the body, and two hundred and twenty-five on the left side of the body.

Nandaka, in the fifteenth week — the seventh day of the fifteenth week — winds called the "lotus" winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there.

Through these, twenty channels are produced on the body of the one dwelling in the womb. Nandaka, of these, five channels are on the front of the body, five channels are on the back of the body, five channels are on the right side of the body, and five channels are on the left side of the body. These channels have many names and various names, and many colors and various colors. There are those called "companions," those called "the powerful," those called "the stable," and those called "the mighty." In color, there are blue, yellow, red, white, a tawny color like raw wool, variegated, the color of butter, the color of yogurt, the color of oil from grain, those pervaded by unripe bile, and those pervaded by ripe bile.

Nandaka, each of these twenty channels has forty encircling channels surrounding it, making those channels eight hundred in number. Nandaka, of these, two hundred arise on the front of the body, two hundred on the back of the body, two hundred on the right side of the body, and two hundred on the left side of the body. Two hundred belong to the companions, two hundred belong to the powerful, two hundred belong to the stable, and two hundred belong to the mighty.

Nandaka, each of those eight hundred channels has one hundred encircling channels surrounding it, making those channels eighty thousand in number. Nandaka, of these, twenty thousand arise on the front of the body, twenty thousand on the back of the body, twenty thousand on the right side of the body, and twenty thousand on the left side of the body.

Nandaka, moreover, at the root of each of those eighty thousand channels there are many pores and various pores — some channels have one pore, some have two pores, some have three, some four, some five, some six, and some have seven pores. Nandaka, it is just as the roots and stalks of a lotus have many pores and various pores — some with one pore, some with two, some with three, four, five, six, and some with seven pores. In the same way, Nandaka, at the root of each of those eighty thousand channels there are likewise many pores and various pores — some with one pore, some with two, some with three, four, five, six, and some with seven pores.

Nandaka, each of those channels connects individually to each separate hair follicle.

Nandaka, on the seventh day of the sixteenth week, winds called the "deathless" winds arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there. Through these, they fully set in place, establish, position, correctly place, and individually arrange the two sense bases of the eye of the one dwelling in the womb. And they also fully set in place, establish, position, correctly place, and individually arrange the two sense bases of the ear, the two sense bases of the nose, the opening of the mouth, the throat, the hollow around the heart, and that which digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and that in which it abides, and that through which it is expelled downward.

Nandaka, just as a skilled potter or a potter's skilled apprentice takes a well-kneaded lump of clay, places it on the wheel, and fully sets in place, establishes, positions, correctly places, and individually arranges the shape of a vessel — in the same way, Nandaka, those winds born from karmic maturation likewise fully set in place the two sense bases of the eye of that one,

establish, correctly place, and individually arrange the two sense bases of the ear, the sense bases of the nose, the opening of the mouth, the throat, the hollow around the heart, and that which digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and that in which it abides, and that through which it is expelled downward.

Nandaka, on the seventeenth week — that is, the week that is seven days times seventeen — winds known as "the face of the draw-string" arise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there. Those winds thoroughly purify, individually arrange, fully set in place, distinctly arrange, and completely establish the two sense bases of the eye of that one dwelling in the womb; and they also thoroughly purify, fully set in place, distinctly arrange, and completely establish the two sense bases of the ear, the sense bases of the nose, the opening of the mouth, the throat, the hollow around the heart, and that which digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and that in which it abides, and that through which it is expelled downward.

Nandaka, consider this example: a skilled boy or girl takes a mirror disc that is not yet fully clean, and with a hand holding ash, or fine earth, or sesame oil, or a cloth moistened with fermented grain-water, polishes it, wipes it all over, thoroughly cleanses it, and makes it brilliantly clear.

This is the twelfth fascicle of the basis of the minor Vinaya.

Nandaka, in just the same way, those winds born from karmic maturation likewise thoroughly purify, fully set in place, individually arrange, firmly establish, distinctly arrange, and correctly place the two sense bases of the eye, the two sense bases of the ear, the sense bases of the nose, the opening of the mouth, the throat, the hollow around the heart, and that which digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and that in which it abides, and that through which it is expelled downward.

Nandaka, on the eighteenth week, winds known as "the stainless" arise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there. Those winds render all those sense bases thoroughly pure and thoroughly cleansed. Nandaka, consider this example: when the disc of the sun or the disc of the moon is covered by great clouds and a great wind scatters those clouds, it becomes thoroughly pure and thoroughly cleansed. Nandaka, in just the same way, on the eighteenth week as well, when the winds known as "the stainless" arise within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, those winds render all that one's sense bases thoroughly pure and thoroughly cleansed.

Nandaka, on the nineteenth week, the one dwelling in the womb obtains, within the mother's womb, four sense faculties: the sense faculty of the eye, the sense faculty of the ear, the sense faculty of the nose, and the sense faculty of the tongue. The three faculties — the sense faculty of the body, the faculty of mind, and the faculty of the life-force — were obtained by that one at the very moment of entering the womb previously.

Nandaka, on the twentieth week, winds known as "the firm" arise for the one dwelling in the womb. Those winds, in dependence upon the left foot of the one dwelling in the womb, generate twenty bones; in dependence upon the right foot, they generate twenty bones. They generate the four bones of the ankle, the two bones of the lower leg, the two bones of the knee, the two bones of the thigh, the three bones of the hip joint, the eighteen bones of the spine, the twenty-four bones of the ribs, and the three bones of the waist. In dependence upon the left arm they generate twenty bones; in dependence upon the right arm they generate twenty bones. They generate the two bones of the shoulder,

the four bones of the forearm, the seven bones of the chest, the seven bones of the collarbone region, the breastbone, the two bones of the jaw, the thirty-two bones of the teeth and their roots, and the four bones of the skull.

Ānanda, consider a sculptor or a sculptor's skilled apprentice: he binds together solid pieces of wood with cord and thereby fashions figures of various colors and shapes. In just the same way, Ānanda, those winds born of karmic maturation bring about the formation of a body of bones such as this.

Thus, Ānanda, at the twentieth week — the twentieth seven-day period — there arise, apart from the small bones that come together in clusters and the fine ones, two hundred of the great bones.

Ānanda, at the twenty-first week — the twenty-first seven-day period — winds called "the arising of all" rise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, and these generate flesh upon the body of that one dwelling in the womb. Ānanda, consider a plasterer or a plasterer's skilled apprentice: using well-prepared clay, he plasters the foundation of a wall. In just the same way, those winds of arising generate flesh upon the one dwelling in the womb.

Ānanda, at the twenty-second week, winds called "the all-victorious" rise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, and these generate blood in the one dwelling in the womb.

Ānanda, at the twenty-third week, winds called "the holder of purity" rise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, and these generate skin upon the body of the one dwelling in the womb.

Ānanda, at the twenty-fourth week, winds called "the all-floating" rise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, and these bring clarity and smoothness to the skin upon the body of the one dwelling in the womb.

Ānanda, at the twenty-fifth week, winds called "the carrier of dissolution" rise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, and these bring clarity and smoothness to the flesh and blood upon the body of the one dwelling in the womb.

Ānanda, at the twenty-sixth week, within the mother's womb, hair of the head, body hair, and nails begin to grow upon the one dwelling there, and each of those hairs of the head, body hairs, and nails is individually connected to its own root channels.

Ānanda, at the twenty-seventh week, winds called "the great medicinal offering" rise from within the mother's womb for the one dwelling there, and these bring clarity and smoothness to the hair of the head, the body hair, and the nails of the one dwelling in the womb.

Ānanda, however, if that being was previously enmeshed and entangled in a web of wrong views tinged with blue and yellow, if it grasped at all manner of possessions, and if, by not listening respectfully to its teachers, it committed and accumulated non-virtuous, unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind — and if those actions now become manifest for the sake of karmic ripening — then even though it may be reborn among human beings in like measure as others, it will arrive in a condition described by this verse on bodily form:

Long and short, connected,
likewise manifold in number,
even and broad and rough,
tall and dark — these are what appear beautiful.

Whatever features are beautiful when long will become short for that one; whatever features are beautiful when short will become long for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when thick will become thin for that one; whatever features are beautiful when thin will become thick for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when joined will become disjointed for that one; whatever features are beautiful when disjointed will become joined for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when numerous will become few for that one; whatever features are beautiful when few will become numerous for that one.

Whatever features are beautiful when even will become uneven for that one; whatever features are beautiful when uneven will become even for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when broad will become narrow for that one; whatever features are beautiful when narrow will become broad for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when firm will become soft for that one; whatever features are beautiful when soft will become firm for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when low will become high for that one; whatever features are beautiful when high will become low for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when dark will become pale for that one; whatever features are beautiful when pale will become dark for that one.

Moreover, Ānanda, to whatever degree that person has committed and accumulated wicked, non-virtuous karma, to that very degree he will become dull-witted and mute, unpleasant to behold, deformed, with impaired hearing, with an impaired tongue, with a contracted mouth, and with withered hands; he will come to resemble hungry ghosts and will be unlike ordinary human beings. His own relatives and blood-kin will not want him, will find him unpleasant to behold, and will come to have the quality of being avoided — to say nothing of how other people will regard him. Whatever he accomplishes in the world through body, speech, and mind will be entirely unworthy of being received by the world and will not come to fruition. Ānanda, why is this? It is because, having committed and accumulated wicked, non-virtuous karma, he becomes such as this.

Ānanda, if, on the other hand, that person has abandoned the stain of miserliness and is endowed with generosity, and through respectful attendance upon a teacher has performed and accumulated wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind — then if that too were to come to fruition, and he were to arrive at a human rebirth a hundredfold equal in fortune to this, then whatever features are beautiful when long will become long for that one; whatever features are beautiful when short will become short for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when thick will become thick for that one; whatever features are beautiful when slender will become slender for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when joined will become joined for that one; whatever features are beautiful when disjointed will become disjointed for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when numerous will become numerous for that one; whatever features are beautiful when few will become few for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when even will become even for that one; whatever features are beautiful when uneven will become uneven for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when broad will become broad for that one; whatever features are beautiful when narrow will become narrow for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when firm will become firm for that one; whatever features are beautiful when soft will become soft for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when low will become low for that one; whatever features are beautiful when high will become high for that one. Whatever features are beautiful when dark will become dark for that one; whatever features are beautiful when pale will become pale for that one.

Moreover, Ānanda, to whatever degree that person has performed and accumulated wholesome karma, to that very degree he will become handsome, beautiful, pleasing to behold, and endowed with a complexion of the highest bloom. He will be desired and found pleasing by other people — to say nothing of his relatives and blood-kin. Whatever he accomplishes in the world through body, speech, and mind will all be worthy of being received by the world and will come to fruition. Ānanda, why is this?

It is because that one has performed and accumulated wholesome karma that it is thus.

Ānanda, if the being is to become a boy, it will sit crouched and huddled on the right side of the mother's womb, covering its face with both hands and looking back toward the mother's spine, resting on top of the bladder, covered by the stomach, supported by the membrane, and bound as though tied with five cords or transfixed on a post. Ānanda, if the being is to become a girl, it will sit crouched and huddled on the left side of the mother's womb, covering its face with both hands and looking toward the mother's belly, resting on top of the bladder, covered by the stomach, supported by the membrane, and bound as though tied with five cords or transfixed on a post.

Ānanda, if the mother eats excessively, this harms the being dwelling in the womb; and if she eats too little, this likewise harms the being dwelling in the womb. In the same way, eating food that is excessively oily, excessively coarse, excessively cold, excessively hot, excessively salty, excessively sour, excessively sweet, excessively bitter, excessively spicy, or excessively pungent will all cause harm to the being dwelling in the womb. Engaging in sensual activities, running excessively, moving quickly, jumping, or swimming will disturb the being entering into existence and cause harm to the being dwelling in the womb; and sitting near a fire or sitting crouched and huddled will likewise cause harm to the being dwelling in the womb. Ānanda, the being dwelling in the mother's womb endures suffering that is intense, sharp, hot, and thoroughly disagreeable.

Ānanda, if even those beings who are named as migrating to a good destiny experience suffering of this kind, what need is there even to speak of the beings who have fallen into bad destinies, miserable destinies, and ruinous rebirths — into the hells? Their suffering cannot even be given as an example.

Ānanda, what benefit is there in dwelling in the womb for one who is seeking existence? Ānanda, on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh week, eight inverted perceptions arise for the being dwelling inside the mother's womb: the perception of a house, the perception of a vehicle, the perception of a pleasure grove, the perception of a multi-storied building, the perception of a pleasure garden, the perception of a throne, the perception of a river, and the perception of a pond.

Ānanda, on the twenty-ninth day of the seventh week, winds arise within the mother's womb for that being, called "the winds that thoroughly cleanse." These thoroughly cleanse and clarify the skin color of the body of that being dwelling in the womb. For some, the skin color — being dark through the ripening of karma, appearing dark in color, seemingly dark, and emitting a dark light — is thoroughly cleansed and clarified. For some, the skin color — being a dusky blue, appearing dusky blue in color, seemingly dusky blue, and emitting a dusky blue light — is thoroughly cleansed and clarified. For some, the skin color — being coarse, appearing coarse in color, seemingly coarse, and emitting a coarse light — is thoroughly cleansed and clarified. Likewise, for some the color is oily, for some white, and so forth as before, described as "of a white color" and so on. For some, the skin color is like the color of the bark of kuśa grass — appearing in color like the bark of kuśa grass, seeming to be like the color of the bark of kuśa grass — and the skin is thoroughly cleansed and clarified so as to emit the color of kuśa-bark.

Ānanda, on the thirtieth day of the seventh week, winds arise within the mother's womb for that being, called "the iron-gate winds." These thoroughly cleanse that being's body, including the hair of the head, the body hair, and the nails.

and thoroughly clarified. For some, the hair of the head, the body hair, and the nails become dark — a dark color. For some, they are yellowish — a yellowish color, rough, of a rough color, oily, of an oily color — and these are thoroughly cleansed and clarified.

Ānanda, on the thirty-first day of the seventh week, the being dwelling in the womb will grow and expand within its mother's belly. Ānanda, in just the same way, on the thirty-second day, the thirty-third day, and the thirty-fourth day of the seventh week, the being dwelling in the womb will grow and expand within its mother's belly.

Ānanda, on the thirty-fifth day of the seventh week, the being dwelling in the womb will come to possess all its major and minor limbs, within its mother's belly.

Ānanda, on the thirty-sixth day of the seventh week, the being dwelling in the womb wishes to emerge and feels displeasure at remaining there.

Ānanda, on the thirty-seventh day of the seventh week, the being dwelling in the womb, within its mother's belly, will obtain the three accurate perceptions: the perception of impurity, the perception of foul odor, and the perception of emergence.

Ānanda, on the thirty-eighth day of the seventh week, winds called "the limb winds" arise within the mother's belly for the being dwelling in the womb. These turn that being about, bring its two hands together, and place it at the gateway of the mother's womb. Then, by reason of that being's karma and its fruits, winds called "the downward-facing winds" arise. These raise its feet upward and lower its head downward, and push it in the direction of the mother's urinary passage.

Ānanda, if that being had previously performed and accumulated sinful, non-virtuous karma that would lead to death within an earlier womb, then its feet become reversed, or its hands become reversed. Unable to emerge in the reversed position, its life faculty is cut off.

Thereupon, skilled women or young persons expert in the care of the newborn anoint their hands with butter or grain-oil, or smear them with a well-prepared ointment of the śalmali plant, and fit onto that same hand a blade with a thin, well-sharpened edge, exceedingly sharp, like a razor. That womb — which is like a drain, utterly nauseating and foul-smelling, a dark cavity, damp and moist, the constant dwelling-place of many hundreds of thousands of species of worms, perpetually requiring cleansing, thoroughly putrefied by filthy fluids, blood, impurities, and pus, rotting and decaying all around, shrouded in the hide of a bladder-sac that is terrifying to behold when stretched out, and arisen from the karmic maturation of past actions — into the channel of that wound-cavity of the body they insert the hand, gently softened with butter, grain-oil, and a śalmali-plant ointment, and having carefully palpated the being dwelling within the womb, they cut it into pieces and extract it. On that basis, both the mother and child who desired the birth will experience intense, acute, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering, and tormented by those feelings they may die, or they will experience the suffering of near-death.

Ānanda, if that being had previously performed and accumulated virtuous karma that would lead to a long life, then it will not fail to emerge, and will not remain unable to come forth; its life faculty will not be cut off. And on that basis, its mother will not experience so much as a single moment of intense, acute, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering.

When the thirty-eighth week has passed, the being emerges from the mother's belly with great suffering, great intensity, great acuteness, and great unbearability. Ānanda, birth is utterly painful.

Ānanda, immediately upon emerging, two perceptions arise for that being:

"A boy has been born," or "A girl has been born."

Ānanda, immediately upon the birth of a boy or a girl, if that newborn is picked up by hand, it experiences from that very basis intense, harsh, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering individually. If it is picked up in cloth, it experiences from that very basis intense, harsh, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering individually. If it is held in the lap, or placed on a bed, or on a small cot, or on the ground, or on a flat plank of wood, or in a covered place, or in an uncovered place, or placed in shade, or touched by sunlight, or touched by wind, it experiences from that very basis nothing but feelings of suffering individually — experiencing their very intensity, their very harshness, their very unbearability, and their very disagreeableness.

Ānanda, consider this example: a freshly flayed ox-hide — if it is left leaning against a wall, then whatever creatures live on walls will feed upon it. If it is placed against a tree, or a pile of grass, or left suspended in open air, then whatever creatures inhabit those places will feed upon it. Ānanda, whatever that freshly flayed ox-hide is set against, the creatures dwelling there will devour it, and from that very basis it experiences intense, harsh, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering.

Ānanda, in exactly the same way, when a boy or a girl has just been born, if that newborn is picked up by hand, it experiences — as was said before, from "feelings of suffering" all the way through to "disagreeable" — exactly those things individually. If it is wrapped in cloth, or held in the lap, or placed on a bed, or on a small cot, or on the ground, or on a flat plank of wood, or in a covered place, or in an uncovered place, or placed in shade, or touched by heat, or touched by cold, it experiences from that very basis nothing but suffering individually — experiencing its very intensity, its very harshness, its very unbearability, and its very disagreeableness.

Ānanda, even if a newborn child is merely touched by gentle water, it experiences from that very basis nothing but suffering — from "suffering" all the way through to "nothing but disagreeableness" — individually.

Ānanda, consider this example: a man afflicted with leprosy, with a weeping body, a body inflamed, a body decaying — one who is suffering, whose faculties have deteriorated — if he is struck with a whip, he experiences nothing but suffering individually, experiencing its very intensity, its very harshness, its very unbearability, and its very disagreeableness.

Ānanda, in exactly the same way, even if a newborn child is merely touched by gentle water, it experiences from that very basis nothing but suffering individually — experiencing its very intensity, its very harshness, its very unbearability, and its very disagreeableness.

Ānanda, born in this way, arisen in this way, fully manifest in this way — from that point onward it is nourished, sustained, and kept alive by the impurity of its own blood. Ānanda, in this noble Dharma discipline, that impurity of blood is to be understood as mother's milk.

Ānanda, when wandering in saṃsāra, what pleasure is there for one who desires existence and is thus endangered by manifold sufferings? For a body born in such a way, arisen in such a way, seven days after birth eighty thousand kinds of parasitic worms will arise, and they will devour every part of that sentient being's body. Ānanda, among those parasitic kinds: the kind called "hair-eaters" dwell at the roots of the hairs and feed upon the hairs. The second two kinds — those called "stick-shaped" and "large-headed" — dwell on the head and feed upon the head. The kind called "eye-devourers" dwell at the eyes and feed upon the eyes. The four kinds called "wanderers," "givers,"

"Orderly" and "Full" dwell on the brain and feed upon the brain. The kind called "Eye-of-Thought" dwells at the eyes and feeds upon the eyes. The kind called "Storehouse-Door" dwells at the nose and feeds upon the nose. The two kinds called "Thrower" and "Setter" dwell at the lips and feed upon the lips. The kind called "Honey-Petal" dwells at the teeth and feeds upon the teeth. The kind called "Wooden-Door" dwells at the roots of the teeth and feeds upon the roots of the teeth. The kind called "Needle-Mouth" dwells at the tongue and feeds upon the tongue. The kind called "Sharp-Lip" dwells at the base of the tongue and feeds upon the base of the tongue. The kind called "Handed" dwells at the palate and feeds upon the palate. The two kinds called "Water-Net" and "Half-Curved" dwell at the fingers and feed upon the fingers. The two kinds called "Dangling" and "Fully Dangling" dwell at the wrists and feed upon the wrists. The two kinds called "Shoulder" and "Near-Shoulder" dwell at the shoulders and feed upon the shoulders. The two kinds called "Digger" and "Near-Digger" dwell at the sides and feed upon the sides. The two kinds called "Wrathful" and "Great Wrathful" dwell at the heart and feed upon the heart. The two kinds called "Conch" and "Conch-Water" dwell at the flesh and feed upon the flesh. The two kinds called "Colored" and "Powerful" dwell at the blood and drink the blood. The two kinds called "Hero" and "Scented-Door" dwell at the lymphatic channels and feed upon the lymphatic channels. The two kinds called "Low" and "Hollow-Mouthed" dwell at the spine and feed upon the spine. The kind called "Fat-Colored" dwells at the fat and feeds upon the fat. The kind called "Bile-Colored" dwells at the bile and feeds upon the bile. The kind called "Pearl" dwells at the spleen and feeds upon the spleen. The kind called "Great Pearl" dwells at the kidneys and feeds upon the kidneys. The kind called "Not-Yet-Come" dwells at the liver and feeds upon the liver. The four kinds called "Water-Mixture," "Great Water-Mixture," "Needle-Mouth," and "Great Needle-Mouth" dwell at the intestines and feed upon the intestines. The five kinds called "Moon," "Moon-Face," "Moon-Light," "Moon-Light-Face," and "Vast" dwell at the right lung and feed upon the right lung. The other kinds called by that same name dwell at the left lung and feed upon the left lung. The four kinds called "Sequential-Piercer," "Forward-Piercer," "Hard-Piercer," and "Firm-Piercer" dwell at the bones and feed upon the bones. The four kinds called "White," "Near-White," "Strength-Robber," and "Smooth" dwell at the channels and feed upon the channels. The four kinds called "Lion," "Powerful," "Muddy," and "Flower-Taker" dwell at the stomach and feed upon the stomach. The two kinds called "Stable" and "Near-Stable" dwell at the bladder and feed upon the bladder. The four kinds called "Worm-Mouth," "Aggregate-Face," "Net-Mouth," and "Render" dwell in the urinary tract and feed upon the urinary tract. The four kinds called "Ill-Sounding," "Great Ill-Sounding," "Drawer," and "Possessed-of-Slime" dwell in the digestive tract and feed upon the digestive tract. The two kinds called "Diseased-Mouth" and "Terror-Maker" dwell at the thighs and feed upon the thighs. The two kinds called "Leprous" and "Near-Leprous" dwell at the knees and feed upon the knees. The kind called "Root-of-Stupidity" dwells at the calves and feeds upon the calves.

The kind of worm called "Black-Head" dwells at the toes and feeds upon the toes.

Nanda, this body is thus gnawed day and night by eight hundred kinds of worms, and because of that it becomes tormented, utterly tormented, feeble, and afflicted. Nanda, arising from that very basis, one comes to experience, individually experience, feel, and fully feel torment, utter torment, and complete torment of body; and one comes to experience, individually experience, feel, and fully feel torment, utter torment, and complete torment of mind. One comes to experience, individually experience, feel, and fully feel bodily fever, exhaustion, and complete burning; and one comes to experience, individually experience, feel, and fully feel mental fever, exhaustion, and complete burning. When even physicians are bewildered by this and do not know how to compound the medicine for it, Nanda, what pleasure can there be in clinging to existence in cyclic existence, which is threatened in this way by so many sufferings?

Nanda, since the body arises in this way and is fully constituted in this way, afflictions of the following kinds appear in it: affliction by gods, affliction by nāgas, affliction by asuras, affliction by wind-gods, affliction by garuḍas, affliction by gandharvas, affliction by kinnaras, affliction by great serpents, affliction by yakṣas, affliction by rākṣasas, affliction by hungry ghosts, affliction by flesh-eaters, affliction by elemental spirits, affliction by the pot-bellied ones, affliction by the decaying ones, affliction by the bodily decaying ones, affliction by the blind decaying ones, affliction by the withering ones, affliction by the maddening ones, affliction by the shadow-oppressors, affliction by the sweating ones, affliction by birds, affliction by wild animals, affliction by those of the sky-corner, affliction by lords of livestock, affliction by māmō spirits, affliction by the grinning ones, affliction by the skeletal ones, affliction by the weakening ones, affliction by the moon, affliction by the sun, and affliction by the stars. When such afflictions as these arise in the body, Nanda, what pleasure can there be in dwelling in the womb of a mother who is seeking existence?

Nanda, one who is born in this way, fully constituted in this way, is produced, sustained, and nourished by one's mother's own filth of blood. Nanda, a mother's breast-milk, in the noble Dharma-Vinaya, is called just this: "filth of blood."

Nanda, one who dwells in that way in the place of the womb of a mother seeking existence, born in that way, arisen in that way, fully constituted in that way — what pleasure can there be in eating coarse food in that way? Even if one is cared for excellently and comfortably, one lives at most a hundred years, or perhaps a little longer. Half of that is covered over by sleep. Ten years pass in childhood. At twenty one is old. And one is cut down by grief, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and distress; one is cut down by the many hundreds of manifold diseases arising from the body. Nanda, diseases of the body arise that are exceedingly difficult to bear, and when tormented by them, living beings even wish to die.

Nanda, the life of embodied beings at the present time is utterly unbearable, brief, and wretched; it is attended by suffering and leads onward to the next life. Therefore one should practice virtue and live the pure spiritual life, for there is no one who is born and does not die. Yet people at the present time abide heedlessly with respect to practicing what is meaningful, practicing Dharma, practicing merit, practicing virtue, and practicing what is wholesome and good. It is through karma that virtuous and non-virtuous actions are performed here.

Nanda, dwell with mindfulness and heedfulness. In the end you will come to regret it: you will be separated from everything desirable, pleasant, joyful, and agreeable. Separation and parting are utterly inevitable.

Nanda, embodied beings are those for whom karma is their own possession, karma is their inheritance, and karma is their refuge. Whether karma is virtuous or sinful, whatever actions they perform, they become heirs to precisely those actions.

Nanda, one who lives for a hundred years passes through ten phases of life, each experienced in turn. In the first phase one is a helpless infant lying on one's back. In the second phase one is a youth given to play. In the third phase one sporadically indulges in sensual pleasures. In the fourth phase one is possessed of strength and enthusiasm. In the fifth phase one is possessed of wisdom and courage. In the sixth phase one is possessed of mindfulness and has a discerning nature. In the seventh phase one's steadiness reaches its full measure. In the eighth phase one's steadiness is like that of a king. In the ninth phase one is old and bent by age. In the tenth phase one's life is exhausted and one is subject to death. And so, Nanda, one who lives for a hundred years passes through each of those ten phases in turn.

A life of one hundred years amounts to three hundred seasons of life: one hundred seasons of winter, one hundred seasons of spring, and one hundred seasons of summer. A life of three hundred seasons amounts to one thousand two hundred months: four months of winter, four months of spring, and four months of summer. A life of one thousand two hundred months amounts to two thousand four hundred fortnights: eight fortnights of winter, eight fortnights of spring, and eight fortnights of summer. A life of two thousand four hundred fortnights amounts to thirty-six thousand days. One who lives thirty-six thousand days consumes seventy-two thousand meals, not counting the intervals when no meals are taken. The occasions when one does not eat are these: when one does not eat out of anger, when one does not eat out of contentment, when one does not eat out of suffering, when one does not eat even though food is obtained, when one does not eat because food is not obtained, when one does not eat because one is asleep, when one does not eat because one is keeping a fast, when one does not eat because one is carried away in play, and when one does not eat because one is distracted by activities. Totalling together all meals eaten and all meals not eaten, and including mother's milk, the sum comes to seventy-two thousand.

Nanda, in this way the years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, meals, and meal intervals of those mortals who live for a hundred years have been set forth.

Nanda, for one born thus and come forth thus, with a body thus fully constituted, there arise in the body diseases of the following kinds: headache, eye disease, ear disease, nasal disease, tooth disease, throat disease, heart disease, catarrh, cough, scabies, foot disease, leprosy, tumors, fine pustules, mottled skin, amnesia, seizure, gout, night-sweat, dropsy, hiccup, nausea, jaundice, diarrhea, fever, virulent fever, vomiting, shortness of breath, wasting disease, hunger and thirst, vertigo, swelling, lipoma, bile disease, inflammation, infectious disease,

one-day fever, two-day fever, three-day fever, four-day fever, continuous fever, fever of the limbs, fever of the ribs, fever of the heart, pain in the limbs, pain in the ribs, pain in the heart, and pain in the joints. Nanda, for one constituted in such a way, there arise one hundred and one diseases arising from wind, one hundred and one diseases arising from bile, one hundred and one diseases arising from phlegm, and one hundred and one diseases arising from their combination.
