When these are totaled, four hundred and four diseases arise within the body. Nanda, this body is subject to disease, subject to eruptions, subject to pain; it does not last long; it is subject to destruction, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, no-self; it has rivals and adversaries; its breathing is labored; and it is subject to transformation.

Nanda, when sentient beings are born, they come to experience, to individually experience, to feel, to individually feel the suffering of having their hands cut off; the suffering of having their feet cut off; the suffering of having their ears cut off; the suffering of having their lips cut off; the suffering of having their tongues cut off; the suffering of having their heads cut off; and the various sufferings of being bound with unwanted restraints, with iron, with a neck-yoke, with arms pinioned behind the back, and with the fivefold binding. They come to experience, to individually experience, to feel, to individually feel various intense, harsh, unbearable sufferings that reach unto death: being rolled on a grindstone, being pierced with sharp stakes, being impaled on a wooden stake, being boiled in copper, and the like. They come to experience, to individually experience, to feel, to individually feel the sufferings of being killed, bound, beaten, threatened, starved, and thirsted; and various sufferings arising from frost, rain, horseflies, mosquitoes, wind and sun, and the touch of venomous snakes.

Nanda, thus, when sentient beings are harassed and utterly overwhelmed by such sufferings, and when those who relentlessly seek, who pursue, who thoroughly search for rooted suffering — suffering sought after — cling again and again to that pursuit, there arise for them intense, harsh, unbearable, disagreeable physical and mental sufferings that torment and afflict. Nanda, therefore: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, separation from what one loves is suffering, meeting with what one does not love is suffering, and not obtaining what one seeks and desires is also suffering. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

Nanda, know that each of the four postures — walking, sitting, standing, and lying down — is in its own way suffering. When a practitioner of meditative concentration examines those postures and their intrinsic nature: if one were to pass the entire day walking and were never to stand, never to sit, never to lie down, one would experience in that walking nothing but suffering — one would individually experience and feel its intensity, its harshness, its unbearability, its disagreeableness — and no perception of pleasure would arise with respect to that walking. If one were to pass the entire day sitting and were never to walk, never to stand, never to lie down, one would experience in that sitting nothing but suffering, and would individually experience and feel its intensity, its harshness,

its unbearability, its disagreeableness — and no perception of pleasure would arise with respect to that sitting. If one were to pass the entire day standing and were never to sit, never to walk, never to lie down, one would experience in that standing nothing but suffering, and would individually experience and feel its intensity, its harshness, its unbearability, its disagreeableness — and no perception of pleasure would arise with respect to that standing. If one were to pass the entire day lying down and were never to walk, never to stand, never to sit, one would experience in that lying down nothing but suffering, and would individually experience and feel its intensity, its harshness, its unbearability, its disagreeableness — and no perception of pleasure would arise with respect to that lying down.

Yet, Ānanda, it is because each successive suffering of those postures is interrupted that a perception of pleasure arises upon the arising of a different and distinct resting-point of suffering. And yet, Ānanda, when that arises, only suffering arises, and when it ceases, only suffering ceases. When it arises, it is formations alone that arise, and when it ceases, it is formations alone that cease. The Tathāgata, having thoroughly understood in his mind the continuity and interconnection of formations, declared to sentient beings the nature of death and rebirth. Ānanda, all formations are impermanent and unstable. All formations are oppressive and subject to change. Therefore, Ānanda, it is fitting to become disenchanted with all formations and fitting to seek liberation from them.

Ānanda, even among those who hold the perception that they are bound for a fortunate destiny, there arise such extremely unbearable, dreadful, contemptible, indescribable, deceptive, and manifold forms of suffering. What need then is there even to speak of those born in the hells, among animals, or in the realm of hungry ghosts? It is exceedingly difficult to give even an illustrative example to convey what their forms of suffering are like.

Ānanda, there are four ways of entering the womb. What are the four? In this world, some enter the mother's womb with full awareness, remain in the mother's womb with full awareness, and emerge from the mother's womb with full awareness. This is the first way of entering the womb. Ānanda, furthermore, some enter the mother's womb with full awareness, remain in the mother's womb with full awareness, and emerge from the mother's womb without full awareness. This is the second way of entering the womb. Ānanda, furthermore, some enter the mother's womb with full awareness, remain in the mother's womb without full awareness, and emerge from the mother's womb without full awareness. This is the third way of entering the womb. Ānanda, furthermore, some enter the mother's womb without full awareness, remain in the mother's womb without full awareness, and emerge from the mother's womb without full awareness. This is the fourth way of entering the womb.

How is it that one enters the mother's womb with full awareness, remains in the mother's womb with full awareness, and emerges from the mother's womb with full awareness? In this world, some person is by nature endowed with moral discipline — possessed of virtuous qualities, inclined toward virtue, consistently engaged in virtue, holding many restraints, given to much reflection, dwelling in heedfulness, and possessed of great wisdom — and at the time of death, whether that person is one who has not yet attained any result, or a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner who dies having had but a single intervening life: though touched by intense, harsh, unbearable, disagreeable, and life-taking feelings of pain at the moment of death, that person, supported and sustained by those virtuous qualities, does not lose mindfulness,

and passes the time of death without losing mindfulness. Thereupon, without losing mindfulness, with full vigilance, that person enters the womb of a mother. Having entered there, what comes to be is this: karma as one's own possession, born of karma, partaking of the inheritance of karma, relying upon karma, done by intention, arising through dependent origination — a womb intensely hot; karma as one's own possession, partaking of the inheritance of karma, relying upon karma, done by intention, arising through dependent origination; dependent upon māra, a vessel of māra, the home of māra; a treasury of every impurity; unstable; of a deceptive nature; leading fools astray; a mechanical contrivance of bones strung with sinews; enveloped in a net of channels; wrapped in flesh, blood, and fat; covered over by nothing more than skin; bristling with a host of lice, and destined to grow hair, nails, teeth, and bodily hair — clinging to pride, the conceit of "I," thinking "this is mine"; seized by ego-clinging and the sense of "I"; overtly addicted; without self-mastery; saturated and oozing with the damp seepage of rotting filth, with grease, pus, sweat, saliva, bile, phlegm, lungs, intestines, the small intestine, the spleen, the bladder, filled completely with many forms of impurity; the habitat of many thousands of species of worms, possessed of two extremely foul-smelling orifices; furnished with many holes and cavities in the bones; slimy with urine, brain, and cerebellum, and the drippings of the assembly of limbs — lying beneath the stomach on the hollow floor of the belly, its face turned toward the spine, its back presented to the skin of the abdomen, swallowing and swallowing in fine, grinding fashion with the double row of teeth what food arrives month by month with the monthly flow, in the form of predigested nourishment; moistened from below by the filth of the wound of the mouth and by saliva, pressed from above by the cerebellum; nourished by the taste of food resembling vomit as it enters through the navel opening within the belly; and thus gradually transforming into something soft and tender, then something firming and hardening, then something thickening, then rounding out, taking on the form of limbs sprouting hands and feet. The hands, feet, and flanks are wrapped in a membrane of raw flesh, foul-smelling beyond endurance like a used rag. It moves about here and there in utter darkness. It is touched by the tastes of food — bitter, sour, acrid, salty, hot, and scorching like tongues of flame. It is nourished by unclean fluid as though by a grub-releasing vessel. It enters into the mire of impurity, oozing and blazing. The vital faculty is unstable. It is burned on all sides, through and through, utterly tormented, by the inner fire of the mother's body — burned everywhere and entirely, heated everywhere and entirely, scorched everywhere and entirely — and it experiences great, intense, harsh, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering. In whatever way the mother is still, moves a little, or moves fully about, or carries a heavy burden, or stretches her body, in just those ways that person, as if bound by five bonds and thrust into a pit of smoldering fire, experiences great, intense, harsh, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering that are hard to illustrate by comparison. Yet while dwelling thus in the abode of the mother's womb and beset by suffering, because the faculties are keen, mindfulness is not lost.

Among those dwelling in the mother's womb, moreover, there are some who, through the power of causes and conditions of previous karma, experience a reversal in the womb and come to feel discomfort while dwelling there. When the mother consumes and drinks what is discordant — something excessively cold, or excessively hot, or excessively sour, or excessively sweet, or excessively pungent, or excessively sharp, or excessively scorching, or excessively rough, or excessively salty; or when she is struck by indigestion from drink, or by indigestion from food; or when she is frequently ill, or speaks excessively,

or is greatly sorrowful, or excessively attached, or fatigued, or struck — then by those causes her body comes to be harmed. When her body is harmed, what depends upon it, namely the one dwelling in the womb, is also harmed. Being harmed there and threatened by extreme suffering, it stirs, and through that stirring it becomes reversed.

Thereupon a woman skilled in midwifery, or a young nurse, anoints her hand with a little warm water, white butter, and sesame oil, and introduces it into that great mechanism of bones — that opening which is like a cesspit: foul-smelling, stinking, unbearable, pitch-dark, filled with slimy mud, home to many hundreds of thousands of worms, constantly dripping and in perpetual need of cleansing, filthy, tainted with blood and serum and festering throughout, in a state of utter decay, swarming with flies, dreadful to behold, covered in the membrane of the birth canal. She slowly and gently feels her way and correctly repositions the child just as it was.

When she so repositions it, groping with a hand anointed with a little warm water, white butter, and sesame oil, the one dwelling there experiences a great feeling of suffering that is intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable. To give an analogy, Nanda: if a young man of noble family, whose body is extremely tender by nature, were to have all his limbs and minor limbs cut with a razor sharp enough to shave hair, and were then smeared all over with a fierce medicinal substance, an extremely intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable great feeling of suffering would arise in his body. In just the same way, Nanda, when that hand anointed with a little warm water, white butter, and sesame oil gropes about, an intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable great feeling of suffering arises in the body. Yet even when these intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable great feelings of suffering born from tactile contact arise in the body of the one dwelling in the womb, the mindfulness of that being does not deteriorate on account of having keen faculties. Thus it is that the being dwells in the mother's womb with full awareness.

Then, once all the limbs and minor limbs have formed, the wind born from the maturation of previous karma, by the force of causes and conditions, propels the being — with feet raised upward, head turned downward, and both hands drawn in — so that it is squeezed, pressed, and thoroughly crushed by the two mechanisms of bone at the opening of the bladder: that place of putrefaction, decay, collapse, unbearableness, foul smell, stench, pitch-dark darkness, dreadful to behold, smeared with excrement and urine, tainted with foul odor, constantly dripping with blood and serum. All the bony protuberances of the body's limbs become like one raw wound and turn blue. All the sense faculties of the body burn. The body is befouled by the extremely foul impurity of the womb. The mouth, throat, and heart dry out from thirst. Afflicted and tormented, dwelling in an unbearable state — then, propelled by the wind born from the maturation of previous karma through the power of causes and conditions, the being emerges, just as with great difficulty anything whatsoever emerges. The very moment it emerges, if the outer wind touches it — like the touch of a fierce medicinal substance on a raw wound — or if it is touched by a hand or by cloth, it experiences an intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable great feeling of suffering, as though being cut by a sword. And yet even when threatened by such suffering, the mindfulness of that being does not deteriorate on account of having keen faculties. Thus it is that the being emerges from the mother's womb with full awareness.

Therefore, Nanda, since entering the mother's womb is suffering, dwelling there is suffering, and emerging from the mother's womb is also suffering —

Nanda, what pleasure is there in dwelling in the mother's womb, longing as one does for existence? How is it that one enters the mother's womb with full awareness, dwells there with full awareness, and yet emerges from the mother's womb without awareness?

In this regard, there are some who are ordinary persons by nature and who are naturally endowed with moral discipline, who possess wholesome qualities, who are inclined toward virtue, who practise virtue in all things, who are richly endowed with restraint and discernment, who abide in heedfulness and are free from remorse — or those who are stream-enterers. When such a person, having reached the time of death — whether one who will be reborn seven more times, or one who is born from noble family to noble family, or a once-returner, or one who will die in an intermediate state — is sustained and stabilized in those wholesome qualities at the moment of death, even though they are touched by feelings of suffering at death that are intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable, that rend the life-force, their mindfulness does not deteriorate. And so they die without their mindfulness deteriorating. Thereafter, without mindfulness having deteriorated, they enter the mother's womb with full awareness.

Having entered there, as was described earlier from the passage "let it be known as one's own karma" up through "nourished by fluids like a creature in a net, gone into a swamp blazing with foul filth, the life-faculty unstable, scorched on all sides by the fire within the mother's body" — they are burned, utterly burned, completely burned, and experience a great feeling of suffering that is intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable. And according to whatever movement, every movement, and complete movement of the mother, they are correspondingly bound by the five bonds and experience a great feeling of suffering that is intense, rough, unbearable, disagreeable, and beyond compare, as though thrust into a pit of smouldering embers. And yet, dwelling thus in the mother's womb and threatened by such suffering, their mindfulness does not deteriorate.

Among those dwelling in the mother's womb, there are also some for whom, through the power of causes and conditions from previous karma, the womb becomes inverted and dwelling in the womb becomes uncomfortable. As described earlier from the passage "when the mother eats or drinks something discordant, extremely cold or extremely hot" — if she is struck, jostled, or beaten, those causes harm her body. When harm comes to her body, harm comes as well to the being depending on her who dwells in the womb. When harmed there and threatened by intense suffering, it stirs, and through that stirring the womb becomes inverted. Thereafter, a woman who is experienced or a young midwife skilled in obstetrics, having coated her hand with warm water, white butter, and sesame oil, as described from that passage up through "massages it and repositions it properly in place" — when it is massaged by a hand coated with warm water, white butter, and sesame oil, the being experiences a great feeling of suffering in the body that is intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable.

Nanda, consider, for example, a youth of noble family, exceedingly tender in constitution, whose limbs and secondary limbs are all cut with a sharp razor fit for shaving hair, and whose body is then anointed all over with a fierce caustic substance — such a person would experience in the body a great feeling of suffering that is intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable.

The minor Vinaya matters. The thirteenth fascicle.

In just the same way, Nanda, when that being is massaged by a hand coated with warm water, white butter, and sesame oil, there arises in its body a great feeling of suffering that is intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable. Even though those great feelings of suffering arising from the painful contact that afflict the body of that being dwelling in the mother's womb — feelings so intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable — arise in this way, its mindfulness does not deteriorate. Thus it is that the being dwells with full awareness in the mother's womb.

Then, once all the limbs and secondary limbs have fully formed, the being dwells in a womb that is a festering place of urine, a site of falling filth, unbearably foul-smelling, rank, dark, and terrifying to behold — smeared with excrement and urine, oozing with impure odors, and with wounds that constantly seep blood and lymph. A wind born from the karmic maturation of past karma pushes the feet upward and the head downward; with both arms drawn in, the being is pressed and crushed on all sides by the two wheels of bone. Great feelings of suffering — intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable — afflict it, and every limb of the body, like a wound that is raw and exposed, becomes bruised and livid, while all the sense faculties of the body burn with heat. The womb's utterly defiling impurities wrap around the body; thirst parches the lips, the throat, and the heart. Dwelling there in that wretched, pathetic misery, unbearably afflicted, the being is at last expelled by the wind born from the karmic maturation of past karma, through the force of causes and conditions, emerging with terrible difficulty. The very moment it emerges, the contact of the outer wind upon its raw body — like that of a sharp-edged substance, or the touch of a hand, or the touch of clothing — is experienced as a great feeling of suffering that is intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable, like being cut by a blade.

When afflicted by such suffering, because its faculties are only of middling strength, the being's mindfulness deteriorates and the mind is struck with confusion. Thus it is that, unlike the entry into the womb, the departure from the mother's womb occurs without full awareness.

Nanda, in this way, entering the mother's womb is suffering, dwelling in the mother's womb is suffering, and departing from the mother's womb is also suffering. Nanda, what pleasure, then, is there in wishing for continued existence and in dwelling in the place of the mother's womb? How is it that one enters the mother's womb with full awareness, dwells in it without full awareness, and departs from it without full awareness?

Here, there are certain ordinary persons who are by their very nature endowed with moral discipline, who possess virtuous qualities, who aspire to virtue, who practice virtue throughout, who have many vows and much discernment, who dwell in heedfulness, who are free from regret — or who have entered the stream of liberation. If such a person, having reached that point, is either a seven-times-returner, or one who is born from noble family to noble family, or a once-returner, or one who has an intervening existence of a single life and makes their death, then the stability of those very virtuous qualities, even when contacted by the intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering at the moment of death — feelings that strip away the life-force — will not cause the mindfulness to deteriorate. That person passes away with mindfulness unimpaired, and then with mindfulness unimpaired enters the mother's womb with full awareness. Having entered there, dwelling in the womb in accordance with karma — the womb itself being born by karma, sustained by karma, supported by karma, created by intention, arising through dependent origination — that place is supremely hot.

It is a place where one dwells in accordance with karma, is born by karma, supported by karma, created by intention, arising through dependent origination. It is dependent upon māra, a vessel of māra, a home of māra, a treasury of all that is impure, unstable, possessed of a deceptive nature, capable of leading children astray. It is a mechanical contrivance of bones, wound around by a lattice of tendons and ligaments, encased in a net of channels and veins, wrapped in flesh, blood, and fat, covered over with nothing but skin. It is an assemblage of impurities heaped together. Hair, nails, teeth, and body hair grow and appear on it. It is attended by conceit — the pride that thinks "I am" — and by the grasping of self and mine, made manifest through clinging. Without independence, it is moistened and soaked by the putrid moisture of the nasal discharge, along with the impurities of fat, lymph, and sweat.

It is filled entirely with bile, phlegm, lungs, intestines, the omentum, the spleen, the bladder, and a great many kinds of impurities. It is the dwelling place of many thousands of kinds of worms. It possesses two openings of extreme foulness. It has the many hollow cavities and channels of the bones. There, in the lower cavity beneath the stomach, the face turned toward the spine and the back exposed to the skin of the belly, drenched and sodden in a swamp of urine, brain fluid, and marrow — month after month, as the months and nights pass, the food of the womb is ground exceedingly fine by the two rows of teeth, chewed over and over, then swallowed. From below it is moistened by the filth and discharge of the lower wound, dampened by saliva. From above it is pressed upon by the cerebral matter. The flavor of the food, which is like vomit, enters through the navel passage within the belly, and it is nourished and transformed entirely in substance — soft and tender, then firming, then hardening, then rounding out, becoming the very form of limbs and members. The hands, feet, and flanks, wrapped in a casing of raw flesh, stink like a freshly turned field, fetid, unbearable, groping about in pitchy darkness. It is touched by the tastes and vapors of food — sour, rough, salty, hot, and scorching as a tongue of fire. It is nourished by the impure fluid of the womb as though by a wet-nurse. It enters into the interior of a seething swamp blazing with burning, festering impurity. The life faculty is unstable. The inner fire of the mother's body scorches it on all sides, torments it utterly, consumes it completely, heats it through and through, scalds it everywhere, burns it entirely. And so it comes to experience great, intense, rough, unbearable, disagreeable feelings of suffering.

In whatever way it remains without moving, or moves about, or turns completely, or carries a heavy burden, or hangs suspended — in just that way it is bound by the five bonds, and experiences great, intense, rough, unbearable, disagreeable feelings of suffering beyond all comparison, as though it had been thrust into the pit of a smoldering fire.

While abiding thus within the mother's womb, beset by suffering, its mindfulness becomes impaired.

Among those dwelling in the mother's womb, moreover, some, through the force of causes and conditions from previous karma, come to lie transversely in the womb, bringing discomfort to the one dwelling within. If the food and drink consumed by the mother prove unsuitable — whether extremely cold or extremely hot — or if she experiences excessive attachment, agitation, or receives a blow, these causes will harm her body. And when her body is harmed, the being that depends upon her and dwells within the womb will likewise be harmed. This much as before.

Then the birth goes awry. Thereupon a woman who is knowledgeable, or a midwife skilled in care, anointing her hands with warm water, ghee, and grain oil, presses in and draws the child down by manipulation. When she presses in and draws the child down using hands anointed with warm water, ghee, and grain oil, the being comes to experience great, intense, rough, unbearable, disagreeable feelings of suffering in the body.

Ānanda, consider this example: the body of a young man of good family, extremely tender in nature, is cut in all its major and minor limbs by a sharp razor fit for shaving hair, and then smeared all over with a potent bodily medicinal substance — from this there would arise in the body great, intense, rough, unbearable, disagreeable feelings of suffering.

Ānanda, in just the same way, when the one dwelling in the womb is pressed upon and drawn down by hands anointed with warm water, ghee, and grain oil, the body comes to experience great, intense, rough, unbearable, disagreeable feelings of suffering.

rough, unbearable, and disagreeable. When those great, intense, rough, unbearable, and disagreeable feelings of suffering arising from painful contact strike the body of the one dwelling in the womb, because the faculties are dulled, mindfulness deteriorates and the mind becomes impaired. Thus it is that one enters the mother's womb without clear awareness, dwells in the mother's womb without clear awareness, and emerges from the mother's womb without clear awareness.

Ānanda, how is it that one enters without clear awareness, dwells without clear awareness, and emerges without clear awareness? In this world, there are those who by their very nature are of broken moral discipline, possessed of unwholesome qualities, inclined toward the unwholesome, habitually engaged in the unwholesome, abundantly without restraint, abundantly without discernment, dwelling in heedlessness, grasping at all manner of possessions, miserly, fearful, covetous, malicious, holding wrong views, and prone to remorse. When the time of death arrives, those unwholesome qualities, having become firmly established, are encountered as intense, rough, unbearable, disagreeable feelings of death's suffering that tear away the life-force. Then mindfulness deteriorates and the mind becomes impaired. At that point, this consciousness that is of one flavor with suffering — what is it? What is its nature? What is this self? From where did it die and transmigrate, from where did it come, and where will it be born? — all of this is not known. Thus it is that one enters the mother's womb without clear awareness, dwells in the mother's womb without clear awareness, and emerges from the mother's womb without clear awareness.

Ānanda, since entering the mother's womb is suffering, dwelling in the mother's womb is suffering, and emerging from the mother's womb is suffering — Ānanda, what satisfaction can there be for one who delights in continued existence in saṃsāra, who takes pleasure in dwelling in the mother's womb, that place beset by so much suffering?

Ānanda, although birth is thus afflicted and oppressed by so much suffering, human existence is still extraordinarily difficult to obtain, even across hundreds of thousands of millions of eons. Ānanda, when the gods are passing away, other gods urge them, saying: "Go to the world of the happy destinies and there establish yourselves firmly and with discernment." Ānanda, what is the world of the happy destinies for the gods? It is birth as a human being — so extraordinarily difficult to obtain is it. Therefore, a life of leisure and full endowment is extraordinarily rare and difficult to find.

Hell-beings are purely and entirely in suffering, purely and entirely in intensity, purely and entirely in roughness, purely and entirely in unbearability, purely and entirely in disagreeableness — Ānanda, they cannot even serve as an analogy for suffering. Hungry ghosts (pretas) are malicious, their minds afflicted, their minds ungentle, possessed of deceit and cunning, rough, harmful, their hands smeared with blood, disagreeable, obscured, naked, ugly in form, frightful, oppressed by the suffering of hunger and thirst. The gods are ever in fear — subject to the suffering of death and transmigration, of falling and transformation, of separation from what is beloved, and ever under the power of sorrow. As for sentient beings born in the animal realm, there is no limit to their number — Ānanda, there among them there is no acting for true benefit, no accumulation of merit, no practice of Dharma, no engagement in virtue, no pursuit of what is good and wholesome.

They devour one another — the stronger among those sentient beings eating the weaker. Ānanda, among the sentient beings born in the animal realm, there are also those who are born in darkness, who age in darkness, and who meet their time of death in darkness. And who are these? They are such creatures as beetles, flatworms, long-proboscised insects, those whose food is sesame husks, the worm called traima-buka, the worm called traila-ta, and whatever other sentient beings are born in darkness, age in darkness, and meet their time of death in darkness. In this regard, an ordinary, childish person who lacks learning, who is excessively attached to the flavor of what is old and rotten, and who has engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, will be reborn sharing the same lot as such sentient beings — and those beings are born in darkness, age in darkness, and meet their time of death in darkness.

Ānanda, among the sentient beings born in the animal realm, there are also those who are born from a body, who age upon a body, and who meet their time of death upon a body. And who are these? They are such creatures as lice, nits, left-coiling worms, mites, and whatever other sentient beings are born from a body, age upon a body, and meet their time of death upon a body. In this regard, an ordinary, childish person who lacks learning, who follows after the flavor of what is old and rotten, and who has engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, will be reborn sharing the same lot as such sentient beings — and those beings are born from a body, age upon a body, and meet their time of death upon a body.

Ānanda, among the sentient beings born in the animal realm, there are also those who are born in water, who age in water, and who meet their time of death in water. And who are these? They are such creatures as fish, turtles, frogs, young crocodiles who kill, the creature called luka, and whatever other sentient beings are born in water, age in water, and meet their time of death in water. In this regard, an ordinary, childish person who lacks learning, who follows after the flavor of what is old and rotten, and who has engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, will be reborn sharing the same lot as such sentient beings — and those beings are born in water, age in water, and meet their time of death in water.

Ānanda, among the sentient beings born in the animal realm, there are also those who, catching the scent of excrement and urine, think "I will eat this, I will drink this," and run toward it, roaming about in that way. And who are these? They are such creatures as goats, sheep, crows, pigs, dogs, foxes, ravens, monkeys, flies, and whatever other sentient beings catch the scent of excrement and urine, think "I will eat this, I will drink this," and run toward it, roaming about in that way. In this regard, an ordinary, childish person who lacks learning, who follows after the scent of such things, and who has engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, will be reborn sharing the same lot as such sentient beings — and those beings catch the scent of excrement and urine, think "I will eat this, I will drink this," and run about, roaming in that way.

Ānanda, among the sentient beings born in the animal realm, there are also those who gather dry and fresh grass with the tip of the tongue, cut it with the sharpness of their teeth, and eat it. And who are these? They are such creatures as elephants, horses, rhinoceroses, cattle,

donkeys, deer, buffalo, wild boars, and any other sentient beings that gather dry and fresh grass with the tip of the tongue and cut and eat it with the sharpness of their teeth.

Ānanda, saṃsāra is thoroughly bad, exceedingly thoroughly bad. All of it burns, blazes on every side, blazes up completely, and has become a single mass of flame. Ānanda, furthermore, all of it — the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind; forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, and mental phenomena — all of it burns, blazes on every side, blazes up completely, and has become a single mass of flame. And by what does all of it blaze on every side, blaze up completely, and become a single mass of flame? It blazes by the fire of attachment, the fire of aversion, and the fire of delusion. It blazes on every side through birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, mental distress, and anguish. It blazes on every side through suffering — so it has been taught.

Ānanda, one who is lazy, who is afflicted through and through by wicked, unwholesome phenomena, who continues in further existence, whose karmic maturation is suffering, and who will be subject to birth, aging, and death in future lives — one associated with such things abides in suffering. But Ānanda, one who has set forth with diligence, who possesses power, who is endowed with diligence, who is joyful, who is firm in overcoming whatever stands before them, who is not timid, and who does not abandon effort in wholesome phenomena — such a one abides in happiness.

Therefore, Ānanda, you should train thus: Even if only skin, sinews, and bones remain in this body, even if the flesh and blood wither away from this frame — never mind, for one who has set forth with diligence, who possesses power, who is endowed with diligence, who is joyful, who overcomes whatever stands before them, who is firm, who is not timid, and who does not abandon effort in wholesome phenomena must not abandon diligence in the interval before attaining what is to be attained. Train in this way, Ānanda.

Ānanda, I do not quarrel with the world; it is the world that quarrels with me. Why is that? One who speaks the Dharma does not quarrel with anyone. I do not quarrel saying "It is I." It is not through adopting views by way of speculative tolerance, nor through the form of one who has the fortune — rather, I speak only what I myself have seen, known, fully and perfectly awakened to, and directly realized.

Ānanda, what do you think? Would a Tathāgata speak words by which he could be held to be otherwise? Venerable one, he would not. Ānanda, excellent, excellent! For a Tathāgata to speak words by which he could be held to be otherwise — that is not possible, that has no occasion. Ānanda, the Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks the Dharma, speaks suchness, speaks without distortion. The Tathāgata has long desired the benefit of the world, desired its happiness, desired its accomplishment and happiness. He knows the path, has accomplished the path, teaches the path, proclaims the path, and guides beings fully along the path. The Tathāgata is an arhat, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha, one perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide who tames those who are to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One, a buddha.

Ānanda, the world lacks faith, is boiled up by the senses, looks only at what is immediate, is drawn to what is ready at hand, has great conceit, has gathered little — it does not make things easy but through hardship strains in every way after itself.

Ānanda, scripture is not even needed, nor is wisdom needed. Understand directly just what you yourself see with the eye of flesh.

By examining thoroughly just what one sees, one will attain liberation.

Ānanda, do not go by faith in me. Do not go by affection. Do not go by what you have heard. Do not go by reasoning about appearances. Do not go by regarding someone as a contemplative. Do not go by tolerating or approving a contemplative's view. Do not go by reverence for a contemplative. Do not go by thinking, "This contemplative Gautama is my teacher." Rather, Ānanda, go off alone to a secluded place and reflect on those Dharmas by the direct knowledge of which I myself have become a perfectly and completely awakened buddha. Incline toward them. Comprehend them closely. Practise them again and again. And whatever Dharmas, when made directly manifest and brought to completion, allow one to dwell as one's own island, as one's own refuge, as a Dharma-island, as a Dharma-refuge, as an island that is no other, as a refuge that is no other — dwell in them.

Ānanda, how does a monk dwell as his own island, his own refuge, a Dharma-island, a Dharma-refuge, an island that is no other, a refuge that is no other? Ānanda, here a monk, endowed with ardour, with mindfulness and vigilance, having set aside covetousness and mental discomfort toward the world, dwells contemplating the body as body with respect to the inner body, dwells contemplating the body as body with respect to the outer body, dwells contemplating the body as body with respect to both inner and outer body. He dwells contemplating the body as phenomena of arising. He dwells contemplating the body as phenomena of the passing away of what arises. The mindfulness that there is a body is established in him just so — to the extent needed for bare knowing, bare seeing, and bare recollection — and he dwells unattached, not clinging to anything whatsoever in the world.

Ānanda, in the same way a monk, endowed with ardour, with mindfulness and vigilance, having set aside covetousness and mental discomfort toward the world, dwells contemplating the body as body with respect to the inner body, and with respect to both inner and outer body. He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings with respect to inner feelings, outer feelings, and both inner and outer feelings. He dwells contemplating mind as mind with respect to the inner mind, the outer mind, and both inner and outer mind. He dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena with respect to inner phenomena, outer phenomena, and both inner and outer phenomena. He dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena of arising. He dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena of the passing away of what arises. The mindfulness that phenomena exist is established in him just so — to the extent needed for bare knowing, bare seeing, and bare recollection — and he dwells unattached, not clinging in the slightest to anything in the world. Ānanda, it is in this way that a monk dwells as his own island, his own refuge, a Dharma-island, a Dharma-refuge, an island that is no other, a refuge that is no other.

Ānanda, consider a person who is unswaying, without deceit, upright, of a stable nature — if I were to teach him inwardly, he would be able to know and prophesy all evenings; if I were to teach him in the evening, he would be able to know and prophesy all mornings.

Ānanda, my Dharma is well taught, rightly seen, free of sickness, uninterrupted, leading to closeness, meaningful for those who see it here and now, to be individually understood by the wise. This scripture is such that when the Teacher becomes directly manifest, when the sacred Dharma is brought close, when one will pass completely into nirvāṇa, when one proceeds to perfect awakening — these are to be understood by the Sugata himself and their essence is to be drunk by the Teacher.

Therefore, Ānanda, you should look to your own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both, and train individually and perfectly in each. By all means, let my going forth have been purposeful and fruitful, and

may its karmic maturation become a source of happiness. And those who have made full use of the robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites supplied on account of illness — so that the service rendered to them may become, by all means, of very great fruit, very great benefit, very great majesty, and of wide extent — this, Ānanda, is how you should train.

Whatever form one delights in, whatever form one cherishes with fondness — toward that form there arise change, alteration, grief, lamentation, suffering, unhappiness, and distress. A form in which these would not arise — not a single one have I ever rightly discerned.

Ānanda, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?

Impermanent, Blessed One.

That which is impermanent — is it suffering or not suffering?

It is suffering, Blessed One, for whatever is impermanent has the character of becoming suffering.

Then how could a learned noble śrāvaka affirm of it: "This is mine," "This I am," "This is my self"?

Blessed One, it could not.

Ānanda, what do you think? Are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?

Impermanent, Blessed One.

That which is impermanent — is it suffering or not suffering?

It is suffering, Blessed One, for whatever is impermanent has the character of becoming suffering.

Then how could a learned noble śrāvaka affirm of them: "This is mine," "This I am," "This is my self"?

Blessed One, it could not.

Ānanda, therefore, whatever form there is — of whatever kind — whether past, future, or presently arisen; whether internal or external; whether coarse or subtle; whether inferior or excellent; whether far or near — all of it should be seen as it actually is with genuine wisdom thus: "This is not mine. This I am not. This is not my self."

And whatever feeling there is — of whatever kind — and whatever perception, whatever formations, whatever consciousness — whether past, future, or presently arisen; whether internal or external; whether coarse or subtle; whether inferior or excellent; whether far or near — all of it should be seen as it actually is with genuine wisdom thus: "This is not mine. This I am not. This is not my self."

When a learned noble śrāvaka sees in this way, they become disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Being disenchanted, they become free from attachment. Being free from attachment, they are fully liberated. Being fully liberated, the knowledge arises: "My defilements are exhausted. The holy life has been lived. The task is done. There is no knowing of further existence beyond this" — and thus the gnosis of liberation is seen.

When this enumeration of the Dharma was taught, the Venerable Ānanda's Dharma eye — pure and stainless — arose with respect to all phenomena. And five hundred monks were fully liberated in mind from the defilements, without remainder.

The Blessed One spoke thus; the Sugata having said this, the Teacher then spoke further:

Ānanda, in a mind not in equipoise,
all the aggregates come to exhaustion,
yet pure gnosis does not arise.
Therefore, take up diligence earnestly.

Contemplate again and again, each in turn,
the aggregates as they arise and dissolve.
When purity is genuinely produced,
all the gods rejoice.

One who keeps company with suffering, with companions, with association —

who rises to attend and pay homage, and who is given goods and honor in verse —
abandon all such delight, Ānanda.
One who dwells in a house is likewise not truly a householder.
If you do not mingle with either,
you will bring suffering to its end.
Thus you shall reach the final goal.

At first it becomes a glutinous mass,
then from that it becomes a foam-like substance.
From the foam-like substance it becomes a hardening form.
From the hardening form it becomes rounded.
From the rounded form, four limbs arise,
and the head as well.
From karmic causes there emerge
the various joints and bones.

The skull holds nine bones,
and the bones of the cheeks are two.
The teeth number thirty-two,
and the roots of the teeth are thirty-two.
The throat, and those near the ears,
the nose, the palate above,
and the chest without its cartilage —
those bones number twenty.

The bones of the eye sockets number four,
and likewise the bones of the forehead number four.
In the right and left shoulders together,
the bones number fifty.
The bones of the chest are eight,
and within that, the vertebrae are thirty-two.
The bones of the ribs along the back
number thirty.

On the two sides, along the right ribs,
there are thirteen rib-bones.
Likewise on the left side,
there are again thirteen.
These together make twenty-six.
The third joints have three joints each,
the second joints have two,
and the remaining ones have no joints at all.

In the right and left thighs,
the bones number sixty-five.
In this body altogether, the bones
number one hundred and eight —
so the perfectly awakened buddha, supremely knowing,
declared, with the seal of truth.

Below, from the soles of the feet,
up to the brain above —
this body that one so closely relies upon
is as wretched as a mud-worm's dwelling.

Not held together by pegs and fasteners,
but covered over with flesh and blood,
like a puppet joined by a conjurer's strings
to a wooden machine —

so too this body is strung together by sinews,
wrapped separately in moist skin,
furnished with the great wounds of nine openings,
reeking with the stench of impurity and rot,
and dripping and oozing on all sides.

Just as a storehouse is packed full
with various grains and provisions,
so too this body
is a source of manifold decay.

This body, like such a machine of bones,
is a rotting thing without essence.
Yet the childish are heedless of it —
know it to be utterly without attachment.

Sweat and saliva and mucus,
phlegm and pus and blood,
liver and bile and fat,
discharge, brain and cerebellum,
heart and intestines, kidneys,
the impure lungs and bladder,
grease and hair and spleen,
entrails and membranes —
this is a collection of manifold rot,
a vessel that is the source of such things.

This sinful body is a source of great terror;
know it to be like an enemy.
Like an old, crumbling city,
this body of decay is wretched indeed.

Compounded things, by day and by night,
disintegrate and utterly collapse.
This city with its walls of bone,
plastered over with flesh and blood —
within it, attachment, aversion,
delusion, and concealment arise.

This city walled with bones,
smeared with flesh and blood,
within and without, at all times,
is tormented openly by the unfriendly.

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the venerable Ānanda and those five hundred monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had taught.

Then the Blessed One composed the sūtra on entering the womb for the venerable Nanda, and having freed him from the wilderness of cyclic existence, established him in the utterly complete attainment of peace and happiness — nirvāṇa.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, among my monks who restrain the doors of the senses, the foremost is this: the monk Nanda." Then the venerable Nanda, having attained arhatship and experiencing the joy and happiness of liberation, spoke at that moment these verses:

One who has been nurtured with clean bathing,
with food, with anointings of oil,
and sheltered beneath a parasol —
such a one has known many pleasures.

The monks, having arisen in doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, who cuts through all doubt: "Venerable one, what karma did the venerable Nanda perform and accumulate such that, through the ripening of that karma, his bodily complexion has become like the color of gold, and he is adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being? And yet the Blessed One is four finger-breadths taller than him. And from his intense attachment to sensual pleasures, the Blessed One forcibly separated him and, freeing him from the wilderness of cyclic existence, established him in the utterly complete attainment of peace and happiness — nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, karma that Nanda himself performed and accumulated, a collection obtained, conditions fully ripened, dwelling nearby like a creditor — it was inevitable. Who else could experience karma that Nanda himself performed and accumulated? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element; rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases:

Even through hundreds of eons,
karma does not perish.
When the gathering and the time have come,
it ripens as fruit for those who have bodies.

"Monks, in a past age, when the lifespan of beings was eighty thousand years, there appeared in the human world a Teacher, a buddha, a Blessed One — fully endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans — named Vipaśyin. His retinue consisted of six hundred and twenty thousand monks. As he was traveling through the regions, he came to the royal palace called Bandhumat and dwelt in the Bandhuma Grove. The younger brother of the house to his right had become intensely attached to sensual pleasures. The perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin forcibly separated him from those pleasures, freed him from the prison of cyclic existence, and established him in the utterly complete attainment of peace and happiness — nirvāṇa.

"At that time, in the royal palace of Bandhumat, a king named Bandhumat was exercising royal dominion. The royal kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, and happy; the harvests were good; it was filled with people and a great population; strife, dispute, conflict, and disturbance were at peace; bandits and disease were absent; rice, sugarcane, cattle, and water buffalo were abundant. He was a righteous king who administered affairs in accordance with Dharma and in the proper manner.

"The younger brother of the house to his right had become intensely attached to sensual pleasures. King Bandhumat heard that the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, together with his retinue of six hundred and twenty thousand monks, had arrived here and was dwelling in the Bandhuma Grove. Hearing this, together with his queen's retinue, the young men, and the ministers —

— together with the townspeople, they went to where the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin was. And the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, having heard what had occurred, taught such Dharma as was fitting to King Bandhumat, together with the queen's retinue, the young men, the ministers, and the townspeople, so that they attained great distinction.

Now the younger brother of the house to the king's right, being intensely attached to sensual pleasures, had not come out from his house. So the sons of the ministers, the sons of the royal attendants, and the other younger companions went to him and said: "Friend, the king has gone with the queen's retinue, the young men, the ministers, and the townspeople to visit the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin. You, who have obtained a human birth so rare and exceedingly difficult to find, are intensely attached to sensual pleasures and have not come out from your house." When they had spoken these words to him and he felt shame in his heart, he joined their company and went to where the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin was.

Now when the younger brother of the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin saw that they were leading this man there by taking hold of his face, he asked: "Why are they leading him like this, holding him by the face?" They then told him in detail what had happened. He said: "Friends, I too am actually the younger brother of the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, and just as he was, I myself was intensely attached to sensual pleasures. But the Blessed One, the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, forcibly separated me from that and rescued me from the wilderness of cyclic existence, establishing me in the utterly consummate attainment and happiness of nirvāṇa. It is for this very reason that some persons who are deluded must be treated in just this way. You have done well in bringing him here. Now lead him before the Blessed One, and without doubt he will find faith in the Blessed One."

Then they brought him before the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, and the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin taught him such Dharma as was fitting. Having heard it, he found faith in the Tathāgata Vipaśyin. He rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, joined his palms together, bowed in the direction of the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, and then addressed the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin with these words: "Blessed One, would you please consent, along with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, to accept a bathing ceremony at my bathhouse?" The perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin consented by remaining silent.

Knowing from his silence that the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin had consented, he was overjoyed and delighted at the teaching. He prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed, going to where King Bandhumat was. He arrived, prostrated with his head at the king's feet, and then addressed King Bandhumat with these words: "Your Majesty, I have invited the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas, to accept a bathing ceremony at my bathhouse, and he has consented by remaining silent. Since he is worthy of honor, it would be fitting, for his sake, to beautify the city through which he will pass as he enters it, and to beautify the roads along his route."

King Bandhumat thought: "If that is so, then I shall beautify the city and the roads along which the Blessed One will pass as he enters the city."

Realizing that the Blessed One had indeed tamed even this one who was so difficult to tame, King Bandhumat said: "Well done, younger brother! You go and make the preparations. I myself will beautify the city and the roads."

Filled with joy and delight, the king's younger brother bowed his head at King Bandhumat's feet, rose from his seat, and departed.

King Bandhumat then issued an order to his ministers: "Wise ones, proclaim it throughout the city that tomorrow the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin will enter the city of Bandhumat. Therefore, let all of you who dwell in the city, and all the multitudes of people who have come from various regions, beautify the city and the roads, and let each of you greet him with adornments befitting your own means."

The ministers listened to King Bandhumat and made the proclamation in these words: "Hear this, wise ones — you who dwell in the city, you townspeople, and all the multitudes who have come from various regions! By the king's command: the Blessed One, the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin, will enter the city of Bandhumat. Therefore, let all of you who dwell in the city, and all the multitudes of people who have come from various regions, beautify the city and the roads, and let each and every one greet him with adornments befitting your own means. Thus does the king command."

They cleared the city of stones, gravel, and rubbish. They sprinkled it with sandalwood water and set out censers with fragrant incense. They hung many silk banners, raised victory standards and flags, and scattered flowers of many kinds, making the city as lovely and delightful as the pleasure groves of the gods. The roads were made even more beautiful than that. There too they prepared warm water scented with various fragrances, as well as sesame oil. The bathhouse was swept clean, seats were arranged, and all was made ready to welcome the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin as he entered the city.

Then the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin arrived, attended by King Bandhumat's queen and her retinue, by princes, ministers, townspeople, and a great multitude of other folk who had come to escort him, and he entered the royal palace of Bandhumat in supreme splendor.

Then the king's younger brother, his faith having arisen, invited him to enter the bathhouse. Once he had entered and the bathing had begun, the king's younger brother beheld the body of the buddha Vipaśyin, golden in hue like burnished gold, adorned throughout with the thirty-two major marks of a great being. Seeing this, his faith deepened further. When the bathing was complete, he touched his head to the Blessed One's feet and made this aspiration: "By the root of virtue I have generated through performing this service for so worthy a field of merit, may I too, just as this great being's body is golden in hue, and just as he has forcibly separated this younger brother of his from his intense attachment to sensual pleasures, led him forth into the going-forth, freed him from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and established him in the utterly final accomplishment and bliss of nirvāṇa — may I likewise become the younger brother of just such a Teacher, and if at that time I too should happen to be deeply attached to sensual pleasures, may that Blessed One then forcibly separate me from them, lead me forth into the going-forth, free me from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and establish me in the utterly final accomplishment and bliss of nirvāṇa."

Now, monks, what do you think? King Bandhumat's younger brother at that time — he was none other than the noble son Ānanda himself. And at that time, having bathed the perfectly and fully awakened Vipaśyin with the bathhouse bathing,

through the karmic maturation of that aspiration he had made, he became the younger brother of the Tathāgata, and his body too became the color of gold. And I indeed forcibly separated him, led him forth into the going-forth, freed him from the wilderness of saṃsāra, and established him in the utterly final accomplishment and bliss of nirvāṇa.

Then the monks, having grown uncertain, put all their uncertainty to the Blessed One, the buddha, requesting: "Venerable one, what action did the long-lived Ānanda perform, such that through the maturation of that karma the thirty major marks of a great being have visibly come to perfection in him?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is this very one who performed and accumulated the karma, who gathered the accumulation, who fully transformed the conditions, and who came to abide as though at the water's edge. Could whatever karma this very one performed and accumulated be experienced by anyone else? Monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed and accumulated ripens solely within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

Though hundreds of aeons pass away,
karma is never lost.
When the time and conditions come together,
it ripens as fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, long ago in the past, on a certain mountain crag there lived a wealthy householder of great riches and abundant possessions. He had a pleasure grove adorned with flowers, fruits, and various roots, well supplied with water, and ornamented with many kinds of trees — a grove suitable for those who have gone forth. In an age when no buddhas had appeared in the world, there arose in that world solitary buddhas, compassionate toward the poor and destitute, who delighted in dwelling in remote and isolated lodgings, and who each appeared as a singular field of merit for the world.

Then a certain solitary buddha, wandering through the countryside, came to that mountain crag. As he was seeking a dwelling and moving about here and there, he entered that pleasure grove. The grove-keeper greeted him with the respectful salutation of welcome and had him settle there.

That night the solitary buddha entered into meditative absorption on the element of fire, and the grove-keeper, seeing him, was filled with the greatest wonder, thinking: "This one who has gone forth is of such great majesty — accomplished in the discipline of austerities." Rising that very night, he went to the householder and said: "Master, please be glad! In your pleasure grove there has entered a one who has gone forth, a great being accomplished in the discipline of austerities. He has illumined that entire pleasure grove throughout the night."

Hearing this, the householder was filled with great joy. He went out at length, touched his feet to the ground, and said: "Noble one, you seek alms, and I seek merit. Please remain in this very pleasure grove. I shall provide you with alms."

The solitary buddha accepted, and dwelling there he experienced the bliss of meditative concentration, liberation, meditative absorption, and meditative attainment. After residing there for a short while, he reflected: "Whatever I was to obtain by means of this decaying body, I have already obtained. Now I shall enter into the expanse of the peace of nirvāṇa." Knowing this, he performed miracles of blazing fire, radiance, falling rain, and flashing lightning, and then passed into the nirvāṇa without remainder, beyond all residual aggregates, into the expanse of complete nirvāṇa.

The fourteenth fascicle of the foundation of the minor rules of Vinaya.

Then that householder gathered fuel of all kinds of fragrant wood and burned it, and extinguished those firewoods with milk.

He placed those bones in a golden urn, built a bone-stupa, and erected parasols, victory banners, and pennants. Having erected them, faith arose in him, and he then anointed the stupa with saffron and made thirty handprint offerings of fragrant substances. Monks, what do you think? That householder is none other than this son of good family, Priya, and it was he who, at that time and on that occasion, built the stupa for the pratyekabuddha, erected parasols, victory banners, and pennants, arose in faith, anointed it with saffron, and made thirty handprint offerings of fragrant substances. Through the karmic maturation of that action, thirty of the major marks of a great being have come to be perfected in him.

Then the monks, having grown uncertain, requested the Blessed One, the buddha who cuts through all doubt: "Venerable One, what action did the long-lived Priya perform such that, through the karmic maturation of that action, if he had not gone forth into renunciation, he would have wielded the kingdom of a wheel-turning king who rules by force?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, whatever actions this son of good family Priya performed and accumulated, assembled and completed, drawing near like a crossbow bolt ready to fly — it is certain that the ripening of those actions will be experienced by him. By whom else could actions performed and accumulated be experienced? Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Yet the virtuous and non-virtuous actions that have been performed ripen in none other than the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As it is said:

Even across a hundred aeons,
actions do not perish.
When conditions are gathered and the time arrives,
they ripen as fruits for those who have bodies.

Monks, in a previous time, in this very Fortunate Aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher — a Tathāgata, arhat, fully and perfectly awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha and Blessed One — by the name of Kāśyapa appeared in the world. He dwelt in the city of Varanasi, in the Deer Park forest called Ṛṣivadana. At that time and on that occasion there was a king in Varanasi named Kṛkī who ruled over the kingdom — prosperous, flourishing, happy, with good harvests, filled with people and populous — and governed in accordance with the Dharma, as stated before in full. That king had three sons: the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.

When the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa had accomplished all the deeds of a buddha and passed into the expanse of nirvāṇa without remainder, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted passing beyond all residual aggregates, King Kṛkī, after making offerings to his body, built a stupa constructed of four precious substances, measuring one league in circumference and half a league in height. As for erecting a parasol over it: King Kṛkī's middle son arose in faith and affixed a medium parasol. Monks, what do you think? King Kṛkī's middle son is none other than this son of good family, Priya, and it was he who, having arisen in faith at the stupa of the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, affixed a medium parasol. Through the karmic maturation of that action, he carried out the rule of a wheel-turning kingdom by force for two thousand five hundred times,

Had he not gone forth into renunciation at this present time, he would even now be ruling a wheel-turning kingdom by force. Then the monks asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, what action did the long-lived Priya perform such that, through the karmic maturation of that action, the Blessed One declared him supreme among those who guard the gates of the sense faculties?" The Blessed One declared: "It was through the power of an aspiration. And where did he make that aspiration?" "Monks, this one had gone forth into renunciation under the teaching of the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa. The one under whom he went forth — the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa — declared him supreme among those who guard the gates of the sense faculties. Yet for as long as he lived the holy life, he did not attain even a portion of the assembly of qualities. Then, at the time of his death, he made this aspiration: 'In as much as I have lived the holy life for the full span of my life before the supreme worthy recipient, the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, yet have not attained even a portion of the assembly of qualities — by this root of virtue, may I, just as the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, declared my preceptor supreme among those who guard the gates of the sense faculties, now go forth under the teaching of the one whom that buddha prophesied to the brahmin youth Blama, saying, "O brahmin youth, when the human lifespan is one hundred years, there will arise a Tathāgata, an arhat, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha, Śākyamuni" — and, having gone forth, may I abandon all afflictions and directly realize the state of arhat. And just as the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, declared my preceptor supreme among those who guard the gates of the sense faculties, may I likewise be declared supreme among those who guard the gates of the sense faculties by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the great sovereign of the Śākyas.' It is through the power of that aspiration that the Tathāgata has now declared him supreme among those who guard the gates of the sense faculties. Monks, therefore, one should train beginning from the passage 'those who make karma altogether dark' down through 'monks should train in this way,' just as before."

The setting is Śrāvastī. A certain monk went to a physician and said: "Good sir, I have an illness of such and such a kind; please prescribe a medicine." The physician said: "Noble one, please take a medicinal enema, and you will recover." The monk said: "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The physician said: "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate; he will permit it." The monk then related this to the other monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a sick monk may take a medicinal enema by prescription of a physician."

The setting is Śrāvastī. The Blessed One declared: "When monks build a monastery of five stories, the latrine is to have seven stories and the cooling chamber above the gatehouse is also to be seven stories. When monks build a monastery of three stories, the latrine is to have five stories and the cooling chamber above the gatehouse is also to be five stories." Then, since the monks did not know from which side to ascend, the Blessed One declared: "There are to be three kinds of stairway: wooden stairs, earthen stairs, and stone stairs. Monks, at the top, stone; in the middle, earth; at the bottom, wood — set these and then ascend." The Blessed One then declared:

"At the bottom, stone; in the middle, earth; at the top, wood — set these and then ascend."

This concludes the second chapter on minor matters, on the doors.

Summary verses:

The robe, the drying-rack, the inner room, and the sweeping,
the fine dwelling, salt, the gourd,
the face-cloth and the covering cloth,
the portable bed, the mat, and the razor.

Further summary:

The measuring-stick for the robe,
the tablets and the dust-broom,
the very act of smoothing the ground,
and the patches together with the patch-tent.

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The Blessed One had declared that monks must keep the three robes that have been sewn. The monks then began to sew the robes in a mesh pattern, and by doing so they made the panels and half-panels uneven. At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not sew the panels and half-panels unevenly in a mesh; rather, sew them evenly." Not knowing how to make them even, the Blessed One declared: "Cut a measuring-stick for the panels and half-panels, and sew by that measure."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The monks sewed the patches of the robe unevenly, and these turned out unsightly. At that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Sew the patches evenly." When the Blessed One had declared that the patches should be sewn evenly, the monks did not know how to do so, and the Blessed One declared: "Cut a measuring-stick for the patches, measure by it, and then sew." When the Blessed One had declared that the patches should be stitched using the measuring-stick, the monks made the patches oversized. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not make the patches oversized. There are, however, three sizes of patch: large, medium, and small. The large is four finger-widths, or the full width of a crow's wing. The small is two finger-widths, or the full width of a thumb's belly. The medium is between these two."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The monks were sewing robes on dusty ground, and these became soiled. The Blessed One declared: "Smear on a clay paste and then sew the robes." When the Blessed One had declared that the robes should be sewn after applying a clay paste, and none could be found, the Blessed One declared: "In that case, sprinkle and sweep that spot, and then sew."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The monks made the legs of their seats sharply pointed, and these tore up the ground in a way that was improper. The Blessed One declared: "Do not make the legs of seats sharply pointed; rather, cut them rounded." When even this proved improper, the Blessed One declared: "Place them on a bundle of thatch, or wrap them with strips of cloth."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. Now at Śrāvastī there lived a brahmin who, having gone out on some business and wandered here and there, by midday was utterly exhausted. He entered the Jeta Grove and there saw a fine seat laid out and food set ready.

Seeing it, he was filled with reverent faith. The robe that brahmin wore was one suited to a great elder, and he offered it to the edge of the elder's seat as a cushion to sit upon. Then at another time it became soiled, and the verger placed it at the edge of the junior seat. Some time later, the brahmin entered the assembly hall and, not finding that robe at the elder's edge, looked along the rows and went to the junior's edge, where he saw that it had become soiled and been placed there. He thought to himself: "If this robe was suited to a great elder, I should first look into what cause has brought it to such a condition." He waited a little while, and presently the verger arranged the seats in order and began to dust them off. The brahmin then understood: "This is the cause by which the robe has become soiled." He said to the verger: "Noble one, do you not even know this much — that one should sweep by striking the ground and then arrange the seats in order? Moreover, you have made my robe dirty." The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Sweep by striking the ground and then arrange the seats in order."

The verger then laid out the sleeping mats on seats that were full of dust, and the very same fault arose. The Blessed One declared: "Shake out the seats and then lay the sleeping mats upon them." The verger did not know what to shake them with, so the Blessed One said: "Shake them with a cloth." When he shook them with a good cloth, the Blessed One declared: "Shake them with a coarser one." The verger shook them with a coarse cloth, and when that cloth became old and worn beyond repair, he discarded it. The Blessed One declared: "In that case, cut it into strips and patches, tie them around a stick, and use it to shake." When even that was too worn to use further and was discarded, the Blessed One declared: "Even when it is too worn to use further, do not throw it away — mix it with heavy or wet clay and plaster it into the gaps of pillars or the holes in walls, and the merit of the donor will thereby increase for a long time."

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. At that time, a certain young monk was pacing back and forth in meditation in a certain spot, and the ground was worn bare by the dragging of his feet. A householder who was wandering here and there reached that place and thought to himself: "Given that things have come to this condition, one wonders what state this noble one's feet must be in." He said: "Noble one, what has worn this away so completely?" The monk replied: "Householder, it is from my pacing back and forth." The householder said: "Noble one, given that things have come to such a condition, what must your feet look like? Let me look at your feet." The monk showed him his feet, and the householder, seeing them, felt compassion arise and said: "Noble one, I shall lay stone paving on this ground here — please gather comfortably." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate; he will grant permission." Then and there the householder reported the matter to the monks. The monks asked the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, I grant permission: stone paving may be laid on the meditation walkway of a monk who is striving with diligence." The householder laid the paving, and the monk began pacing back and forth along it. Presently that stone paving split into two pieces.

One piece of it lay to one side, the other piece lay elsewhere. When the householder came and saw that one piece of the stone paving lay to one side and the other lay elsewhere, he said: "Noble one, since the paving has come to be in this condition, what harm would there be in joining the pieces together with clamps?" The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "What that householder says is true. Therefore, the pieces may be joined together with clamps, and pegs may be used to fasten them. When the paving becomes very old and worn, and is difficult to repair, then plaster or mud should be mixed and spread over it. The merit of the donor will thereby grow for a long time."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk went to a physician and said: "Good sir, I have developed such-and-such an illness; please prescribe medicine." The physician said: "Noble one, do such-and-such, and you will recover." The monk needed a container for the medicine the physician had prescribed, so he went to a certain householder and requested one. That householder gave him a container with a lid. After using the medicine, the monk returned the container, along with its lid, to that same householder. The householder said: "Noble one, please take it and keep it." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is so, then leave it and go."

The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, I grant permission: a monk may keep a container together with its lid."

A summary verse:

For robes placed inside and out on racks,
and likewise for tent poles, cords and strings,
for lamps, and for the walkways of the cloister —
the robes are to be marked with their distinguishing sign.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.
