The monks were leaving their robes lying about at random, and they became soiled with dust and eaten by insects. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Robes must not be left lying about at random. Rather, they must be placed on robe racks." The monks bored holes in the walls and inserted pegs for the robe racks, and the walls crumbled. The Blessed One declared: "Holes must not be bored in the walls. Rather, when the wall of a temple is being built, hooks should be set in from the outset, and the pegs of the robe rack should be inserted into those." When the Blessed One said that holes for robe rack pegs should be made in the temple, many were made all around, and the Blessed One declared: "Just as they are made in the temple, so they may also be made in the surrounding cells."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that robes were to be placed on robe racks. Forest-dwelling monks, however, could not find robe racks. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those monks may hang their robes on tent poles and place them there." When others had no tent poles either, the Blessed One declared: "Those monks may tie a cord and place their robes on that."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared that robes were to be given distinguishing marks and that the Dharma was to be listened to at night, and —

The monks began giving the gift of listening to the Dharma at night. Now, at the time of listening to the Dharma, a snake came, and a young monk who saw it was startled and cried out, "Friends, move back! Move back!" The other monks, being ordinary persons, were also startled, and they disrupted the Dharma teaching. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The Dharma teaching is not to be interrupted. Instead, teach the Dharma by the light of a lamp." When the Blessed One had declared that the Dharma was to be taught by the light of a lamp, the monks taught the Dharma by lamplight on summer nights. But living creatures flew into the lamps, and so the Blessed One declared: "A lamp house is to be made." The monks did not know how to make a lamp house, and the Blessed One declared: "Make a framework of bamboo strips and cover it with white cloth." When white cloth could not be found, the Blessed One declared: "Cover it with gauze." When that too could not be found, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, make one with a hundred holes." The monks did not know what a hundred-hole lamp house should look like, and the Blessed One declared: "Have a potter make a vessel from wet clay and pierce it with a hundred holes. If no potter is available, take a broken potsherd or the base of a broken pot — anything suitable that is broken — and make it with a hundred holes. Then light a lamp and cover it with that."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. When the season of heat arrived, the monks were tormented by the warmth, their bodies aching, their flesh wasting, their color becoming pale and wan and sallow. Since buddhas, the Blessed Ones, ask questions knowing full well the answers, the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why is it that the monks now have aching bodies, wasting flesh, and color that has become pale and wan and sallow?" At that time Ānanda reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit a cloistered walkway to be built around the dwelling." The monks did not know how to build it, and the Blessed One declared: "It is to be made with three sides." They then built a wall on the inside and a row of pillars on the outside, and the Blessed One declared: "Place the row of pillars on the inside and build the wall on the outside." Because no windows were installed, it became hot inside again, and the Blessed One declared: "Windows are to be installed." They installed them too low, which caused the very same problem, and the Blessed One declared: "Install them higher." Having installed them too high, the Blessed One declared: "Do not install them too high; rather, install them level with the seat." When sparrows and pigeons entered through the windows, the Blessed One declared: "The windows are to be fitted with lattice screens." When wind and rain caused damage, the Blessed One declared: "Shutters are to be fitted to the windows." When the monks closed the shutters while eating their meals and it became pitch dark inside, the Blessed One declared: "During the time of eating, the shutters are to be opened." When monks in the heat of the season were reading aloud, reciting, engaged in analytical discussion, or working on their robes, or were thoroughly exhausted from their labors, they were permitted to sit there wearing only their sweat cloth and their lower robe.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The Blessed One had given the going forth and full ordination to Ānanda, and then led him, suffused with the fragrance of mountain incense, to the gods of the Thirty-Three and to the beings in the hells, before bringing him back again to Śrāvastī. Because this had happened suddenly, not all the monks recognized him. Seeing his body — radiant in color like gold, its marks shining forth brilliantly — they thought the Blessed One had departed, and even the elder monks, the senior ones, rose to their feet. When everyone came to know who it was, regret arose, and at that moment the monks appealed to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, this is the Teacher; this is someone else — in order that each may be easily distinguished, Ānanda and any other such person should have a mark sewn onto his robe."

The summary verse:

Monks who are to be expelled,
tooth-wood of three kinds,
those who are novices about to be expelled,
and those who are never to be expelled at all.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At the time when the monks dwelling on the bank of the river Sundarī first applied themselves with effort, exertion, and striving through the use of water vessels and pots, and thereby abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship, the conduct and the practice of those monks inspired faith in a great many people. The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, those people in whose village district the monks dwelling on the bank of the river Sundarī reside — those people have gained excellent gain."

The venerable Ānanda, who was attending upon the Blessed One and dwelling in his presence, understood through the Blessed One's intention — whether indicated by a sign or by direct speech — and sent word to those monks saying: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One wishes to speak of your virtues and to look upon you; it would be fitting for you to come."

When they heard this, they discussed it among themselves: "We are told that the Blessed One wishes to speak of our virtues and to look upon us — how then shall we go?" Some said: "What need is there to deliberate? Arhats do not engage in deliberation before their wisdom perceives." But others said: "That is well, yet let us go accompanied by a great assembly of people." And so they spoke to the monks: "Venerable ones, be informed: the Blessed One wishes to speak of our qualities and to look upon us, and he is coming to see you — it is fitting that you come." Those monks said: "Venerable ones, if that is so, we too shall go. Let it be done." And so they set out together with them, and gradually made their way to Śrāvastī.

Then in the garden of Anānda, a great and loud noise and the sound of a large crowd arose from the visiting monks and the resident monks greeting one another with genuine joy. The Blessed One heard the great and loud noise and the sound of the large crowd in the garden of Ānanda. And since the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, ask while already knowing, the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "What is this great and loud noise and the sound of a large crowd that is heard in the garden?" Ānanda replied: "Blessed One, it is because the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī have come here together with a great many monks, having brought along many people."

"That," replied Ānanda, "is the great and loud noise and the sound of a large crowd that is heard — the sound of the resident monks and the visiting monks rejoicing with one another in genuine joy."

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī: 'Monks, the Blessed One bids you leave this place at once and not remain here.'"

"As you command, Blessed One," replied the venerable Ānanda. Having heard the instruction of the Blessed One, he went to the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī and said these words: "Venerable ones, know this: the Blessed One bids you leave this place at once and not remain here."

Understanding that they had been dismissed by the Blessed One, those monks took up their bowls and robes and departed, wandering through the countryside.

A second time and a third time the Blessed One addressed the assembled monks: "Monks, the people in whose village fields the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī have been staying — those people have truly found a good find" — and the passage continues as before, down through "it is fitting that they should come," just as above.

When those monks were talking among themselves, they said: "Why does the Blessed One wish to praise us and look upon us with favor, yet still he dismissed us? Before, he dismissed us because we had attached ourselves to many people. But now let us go away by ourselves alone, without attaching ourselves to anyone." And so, having resolved to go entirely unattached, they made their way straightaway to where the Blessed One was, bowed with their heads at his feet, and sat down to one side.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and in one assembly hall prepare seats for the Tathāgata and for the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī."

"As you command, Blessed One," replied the venerable Ānanda. Having heard the instruction of the Blessed One, he arranged seats in one assembly hall for the Tathāgata and for the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī, then went to where the Blessed One was, bowed with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the seats in one assembly hall for the Blessed One and for the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī have been prepared. Now may the Blessed One consider that the time has come."

Then the Blessed One went to the assembly hall where the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī were. Having arrived, he washed his feet outside the hall, entered the assembly hall, and sat down cross-legged on the prepared seat, straightened his body upright, and settled his attention directly before him.

The monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise went to their own assembly hall. Having washed their feet outside the hall, they entered and took their places, each reclining on his own couch.

Then the Blessed One entered into the first meditative concentration, and the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī also entered into the first meditative concentration.

The Blessed One arose from the first meditative concentration and entered into the second, the third, the fourth, and then into the meditative absorption of the base of boundless space, the base of boundless consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither perception nor non-perception. The monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise arose from the first meditative concentration and entered into the second, the third, the fourth, and then into the base of boundless space, the base of boundless consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither perception nor non-perception.

Then the Blessed One arose from the base of neither perception nor non-perception and entered into the base of nothingness, and the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise arose from the base of neither perception nor non-perception and entered into the base of nothingness.

The Blessed One arose from the base of nothingness and entered into the base of boundless consciousness, then the base of boundless space, then the fourth meditative concentration, the third, the second, and the first. The monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise arose from the base of nothingness, entered into the base of boundless consciousness, then the base of boundless space, and then entered into the fourth meditative concentration, the third, the second, and the first.

Then the Blessed One thought to himself: When I enter into the first meditative concentration, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī also enter into the first meditative concentration. When I arise from the first and enter up through the base of neither perception nor non-perception, they too arise from the first and enter up through the base of neither perception nor non-perception. When I arise from the base of neither perception nor non-perception and enter into the base of nothingness, they too arise from the base of neither perception nor non-perception and enter into the base of nothingness. When I arise from the base of nothingness and enter back down through to the first meditative concentration, they too arise from the base of nothingness and enter back down through to the first meditative concentration. Now then, by means of these modes, these signs, and these reasons, I shall remain in that first meditative concentration which surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having perfected it and abiding in it.

Then the Blessed One, by those very modes, those signs, and those reasons, remained in that first meditative concentration which surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, having perfected it and abiding in it.

Then the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī thought to themselves: Venerable ones, be aware of this. The Blessed One is now abiding in his own way of abiding, so let us also abide in our own way of abiding. And so they began to abide each in his own way of abiding.

Then, early the next morning, the Blessed One arose from that meditative absorption and took his seat on the prepared seat in the midst of the monastic community of monks.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his outer robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke these words to the Blessed One: Reverend Blessed One, you have again and again been pleased to praise and look upon the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī, and

yet the Blessed One had not been genuinely pleased with them. The Blessed One declared: Ānanda, the Tathāgata was genuinely pleased with the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī with a noble, genuine pleasure. Reverend One, what constitutes noble, genuine pleasure in the noble Dharma and Vinaya? How did the Blessed One express genuine pleasure with a noble, genuine pleasure?

Ānanda, in this case I went to the temple where the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī were staying. I washed my feet outside the temple, entered the temple, arranged the prepared seat, and sat down cross-legged, holding my body upright, with mindfulness established before me. The monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise washed their feet outside the temple, entered the temple, arranged their own prepared seats, sat down cross-legged, held their bodies upright, and established mindfulness before them.

When I entered into the first meditative concentration (dhyāna), the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī also entered into the first meditative concentration. When I arose from the first meditative concentration and entered into all the absorptions up through the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise arose from the first meditative concentration and entered into all the absorptions up through the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. When I arose from the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entered into the sense base of nothingness, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī also arose from the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entered into the sense base of nothingness. When I arose from the sense base of nothingness and entered, as before, into all the absorptions back down to the first meditative concentration, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise arose from the sense base of nothingness and entered, as before, into all the absorptions back down to the first meditative concentration.

Then I thought to myself: when I enter the first meditative concentration, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī also enter the first meditative concentration. When I arise from the first meditative concentration and, as before, enter all the absorptions up through the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī also arise from the first meditative concentration and, as before, enter all the absorptions up through the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. When I arise from the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and enter the sense base of nothingness, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī also arise from the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and enter the sense base of nothingness. When I arise from the sense base of nothingness and, as before, enter all the absorptions back down to the first meditative concentration, the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī likewise arise from the sense base of nothingness and, as before, enter all the absorptions back down to the first meditative concentration. Now therefore, by these qualities, these signs, and these reasons, I shall dwell having perfected and established in the first meditative concentration that which surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. And so by these qualities, these signs, and these reasons I did dwell having perfected and established in the first meditative concentration that which surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Then the monks from the bank of the river Sundarī thought to themselves: Venerable friends, the Blessed One is presently dwelling in the way of his own abiding,

and we too should dwell in the way of our own abiding. And so they too began to dwell in the way of their own abiding.

"Ānanda, this much is genuine noble joy in the noble Dharma and discipline, and through such genuine noble joy one has been made to rejoice genuinely. Venerable one, genuine noble joy in the noble Dharma and discipline is good. Venerable one, genuine noble joy in the noble Dharma and discipline is excellent — the Blessed One has caused the monks on the bank of the river Sundarī to rejoice genuinely with genuine noble joy. The Blessed One has caused the monks on the bank of the river Sundarī to rejoice genuinely with genuine noble joy."

When this report spread and was heard by the brahmins and householders living in the surrounding area, they came to see what had happened. As they drew near, the monks began to teach them the Dharma. While they were teaching the Dharma, a foul smell came from their mouths, and those people looked at one another and asked: "Noble ones, where does this foul smell come from?" The monks replied: "Venerable friends, it comes from our mouths." The people said: "Noble ones, do you not discard your tooth-wood?" The monks replied: "Venerable friends, we do not discard it." "Noble ones, why? Has the Blessed One not permitted it?" "Noble ones, would you become pure by not eating tooth-wood?" The monks said nothing.

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the brahmins and householders have spoken well. Therefore I permit monks to discard tooth-wood. And why? Monks, tooth-wood has five qualities. What are the five? It draws out bile; it draws out phlegm; it draws out wind; it removes foul smell from the mouth; and it improves the eyesight. Monks, tooth-wood is also beneficial for the eyes."

When the Blessed One had said that monks should discard their tooth-wood, a young monk was sitting in a non-secluded place and had just begun to discard a small piece of tooth-wood when the Blessed One happened to approach in that direction. Upon seeing the Blessed One the monk's hair stood on end, and he thought to himself: "For me to be eating tooth-wood openly before the Blessed One's eyes is not fitting on my part." And with that it became lodged in his throat and neck. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess the quality of never being forgetful. The Blessed One then pressed down upon the monk's head with his left hand — the hand that bears the wheel, the auspicious marks, and the swastika, born from many hundreds of meritorious deeds, which gives relief to those in fear — and with a crooked finger of his right hand drew it out from his mouth together with blood. He then said to the monk: "Monk, what is this?"

The monk at that moment reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected, understood that whatever slight fault had arisen had come about from a monk eating tooth-wood while sitting in a non-secluded place, and declared to the monks: "Monks, a certain young monk of some seniority was sitting in a non-secluded place and ate a small piece of tooth-wood, and a fault such as this befell him. Therefore a monk must not sit in a non-secluded place and eat tooth-wood — not even a small piece. If a monk sitting in a non-secluded place eats tooth-wood or uses it as a small piece, it becomes a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had said that a monk must not sit in a non-secluded place and eat tooth-wood,

Some junior monks, sitting among the elder monks, began eating tooth-wood, and the Blessed One declared: "Junior monks must not sit among the elder monks and eat tooth-wood. Nor indeed should they eat it in a non-secluded place. However, there are three things that should be done in seclusion: defecating, urinating, and eating tooth-wood."

When the Blessed One had said that a monk must not eat a small piece of tooth-wood, the Group of Six began eating very long pieces. When the other monks saw this, they rebuked them, saying: "Venerable ones, what surplus are you cutting off? What surplus is there in this? You saw that when a monk ate a small piece of tooth-wood, the Blessed One saved him from dying from it — and now you want our alms-bowls and robes? There are other advantages to this too: blowing soot under a pot and striking ascetics." Those monks said nothing and remained where they were.

Then the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not eat tooth-wood that is excessively long. If a monk eats tooth-wood that is excessively long, it becomes a serious offense."

The Vinaya of Minor Matters, the fifteenth bundle.

When the Blessed One had said that a monk must not eat tooth-wood that is too long, the monks did not know how much was the proper amount to eat. The Blessed One declared: "There are three sizes of tooth-wood: long, medium, and short. Long is twelve finger-widths. Short is eight finger-widths. Medium is anything in between."

When the Blessed One had said that tooth-wood should be eaten in secluded spots, monks who were sick or elderly and infirm were unable to go to a secluded place. The Blessed One declared: "They may set out a spittoon."

Some monks placed spittoons next to their couches in the same way, and when these were knocked over by a foot the floor became unsuitable. The Blessed One declared: "Place ones like elephant's feet."

Others could not find a spittoon. The Blessed One declared: "They may eat at the entrance to a water-hole."

When monks were eating at a spot far too distant from the entrance of a water-hole, the Blessed One declared: "One should sit within a cubit's distance of the entrance to the water-hole and eat there."

When the Blessed One had said that monks should eat tooth-wood, some monks ate the tooth-wood without scraping the tongue, and that same fault arose. The Blessed One declared: "After eating tooth-wood, one should scrape the tongue."

When the Blessed One had said that after eating tooth-wood one should scrape the tongue, the monks did not know with what the tongue was to be scraped. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted to hold a tongue-scraper."

When the Blessed One had said that one should hold a tongue-scraper, the Group of Six used tongue-scrapers made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. When brahmins and householders saw this, they said: "What is this, noble ones? The beautiful Blessed One has permitted tongue-scrapers. Noble ones, are you ascetics tormented by the qualities of what you desire?" Those monks said nothing and remained where they were.

Then the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Four kinds of tongue-scraper are permitted: bone, copper, iron, and tin."

When monks made them sharp, the Blessed One declared: "They must not be made sharp."

When the Blessed One had said that four kinds of tongue-scraper are permitted, some monks were unable to obtain them, and —

the Blessed One declared: "Those who are unable to obtain them may use a tooth-stick itself, chewing one end to scrape the tongue."

When monks chewed a tooth-stick and used it without cleaning it to scrape the tongue, and this was reported, the Blessed One declared: "One should chew the tooth-stick, scrub it back and forth against itself, and then scrape the tongue."

When monks, having used a tooth-stick, discarded it silently without making a sound, and it struck those residing in the monastery on the head, they complained, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not discard it thus silently; one should make a sound when doing so."

Now, when monks discarded tooth-sticks by making a sound, some also discarded in the same silent manner whatever excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, vomit, or loose stool there was, and the same fault arose from this. The Blessed One declared: "Whatever excrement, urine, and all such things there are, one should make a sound and then discard them."

When the Blessed One had said that tooth-sticks may be used, some monks who had set out on a journey found that in certain directions there were no trees, leaves, or branches, and being unable to find a tooth-stick, they fasted. The Blessed One declared: "One must not fast. Instead, one should take tooth-stick powder, or rinse the mouth with the paste made from it, wash three times, and then eat. One need feel no remorse about this."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. The venerable Śāriputra had two novices: Cunda and Śroṇagṛhīta.

On another occasion, when the venerable Śāriputra was preparing to go on a regional tour, he said to the novice brothers Cunda and Śroṇagṛhīta: "Novices, I am going on a regional tour — will you stay, or will you come?" The venerable Cunda said: "Preceptor, I shall go along with you alone." Śroṇagṛhīta said: "Preceptor, I shall remain right here." The venerable Śāriputra said: "Śroṇagṛhīta, if that is so, in whose care shall you be left?" He replied: "Preceptor, please entrust me to the venerable Cāraka; I shall be in his company." Śāriputra said: "Śroṇagṛhīta, that one is of bad conduct and behaves badly everywhere — will he not harm you?" He replied: "Preceptor, he dwells toward me as a father and mother; how could he do me harm?"

So Śāriputra entrusted him to Cāraka and set out on the regional tour. Śroṇagṛhīta then came out of the monastery, and Cāraka said to him: "Śroṇagṛhīta, do this and this." He replied: "I will not." Cāraka grew angry and said: "You fool, if you will not do even this much, what else will you do?" He replied: "Are you my teacher? Are you my preceptor? I will not do it." Cāraka grew even angrier, seized him by the throat, and expelled him from the monastery. Śroṇagṛhīta sat weeping at the gate of the Jeta Grove.

The great Gautamī, the mother of beings, came to the Jeta Grove with five hundred attendants to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and she saw him weeping and said: "Noble Śroṇagṛhīta, why do you weep?" He replied: "Gautamī, I have been expelled." She asked: "By whom?" He said: "By the venerable Cāraka." She thought to herself: "Whoever turns his back and abandons a son of the Buddha — that is no concern of mine," and so they gathered around him and surrounded him.

Then Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, came to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and he too began to question him: "Noble Śroṇagṛhīta, why do you weep?" He recounted what had happened, and —

He too thought to himself: "Whoever turns his back and abandons a son of the Buddha and a grandson of the Buddha — that is no concern of mine," and so he too gathered around him and surrounded him.

Shortly thereafter, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and he too began to question him: "Noble Śroṇagṛhīta, why do you weep?" Śroṇagṛhīta recounted what had happened. Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself: "Whoever turns his back and abandons a son of the Buddha, a grandson of the Buddha, and a king — that is no concern of mine," and so he too gathered around him and surrounded him.

At that very moment, a great tumult arose in the Jeta Grove — a loud uproar and the clamor of a great multitude of people. Since buddhas, the Blessed Ones, always know while feigning not to know, the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, what is this loud uproar in the Jeta Grove, this clamor of a great multitude?" Ānanda then related the full circumstances to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, are monks expelling a monk from the Saṅgha's monastery?" "Blessed One, they are expelling him." The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, a monk has authority over his own dwelling cell, but not over the Saṅgha's monastery. Therefore a monk must not expel another monk from the Saṅgha's monastery. If he does so, it becomes a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not expel another monk from the Saṅgha's monastery, the monks who were living together with the offending monks and those who were their attendants did not say so much as a word to them, so that those monks were neither brought under control nor subdued. The Blessed One then declared: "Apply the act of exclusion (Sanskrit: taghanīyakarman) to them."

When the Blessed One declared that the act of exclusion should be applied, the monks did not know how to apply it, and so the Blessed One declared: "Exclusion consists of five things: not speaking to them, not instructing them, not sharing resources with them, cutting off any wholesome undertaking on their part, and blocking their lodging."

As for not speaking — one must neither speak to them nor speak with them at all. As for not instructing — one must neither give them instructions nor offer them guidance. As for not sharing resources — one must not accept service from them for oneself, nor enjoy material goods from them, nor receive from them the sharing of Dharma. As for cutting off any wholesome undertaking — whatever wholesome activity they have begun must be interrupted. As for blocking their lodging — one must not allow them to appear at or enter a dwelling.

When the Blessed One had declared that the act of exclusion should be applied, the monks applied it indiscriminately to all. The Blessed One then declared: "The act of exclusion should be applied only to a fellow-resident or an attendant who possesses five qualities. What are the five? Lack of faith, laziness, being difficult to admonish, lack of respect, and keeping company with bad friends. Monks, it is only one who possesses all five of these qualities to whom the act of exclusion is to be applied; one who possesses only some of them is not to have it applied."

Then the Blessed One declared: "If someone possesses even one of these five qualities, the act of exclusion should be applied to him as well." When exclusion had been applied and others began to receive the excluded monk back, the Blessed One declared: "Preceptors and teachers must not receive back one who has been excluded. If they do so, they will incur the heavy offense of coming close to causing a schism." The Blessed One declared: "No one must receive back a fellow-resident or an attendant upon whom the act of exclusion has been applied.

If they do so, they will incur the heavy offense of coming close to causing a schism." Because no one received them back, those monks became very discontented. Some went away to another region, and some abandoned the teaching. The Blessed One then declared: "A monk skilled in reconciliation should be appointed." But they appointed someone without skill, and when he went to them and said, "Venerable one, your preceptor says please come back," this only made the excluded monks more arrogant. The Blessed One then declared: "One who is skilled in reconciliation, chosen by his own discernment, should be appointed." But when he sought consent from all without distinction, their virtuous qualities did not grow, and some new members also abandoned the teaching. The Blessed One then declared: "Consent should be sought from one who possesses five qualities: one who has faith, one who has undertaken diligence, one who is respectful, one who is easy to instruct, and one who has a spiritual friend."

The Blessed One further declared: "Monks, after seeking consent from one who possesses all five of these qualities, consent may then be sought from one who possesses any one of the five." "If a monk who is unfit to be ordained is ordained, it becomes an offense entailing serious transgression. If a monk who is fit to be ordained is not ordained, it becomes an offense entailing serious transgression. If consent is not sought from one from whom it should be sought, it becomes an offense entailing serious transgression. If consent is sought from one from whom it should not be sought, it becomes an offense entailing serious transgression. In such cases, consent should be sought from one who possesses any one of the five qualities mentioned above. If it appears that the mind will become favorable, consent should be sought. If it appears that the mind will not become favorable, consent should not be sought. From one who possesses all five qualities, consent should definitely not be sought; if consent is sought, it becomes an offense entailing serious transgression. If the one from whom consent is not to be sought is a novice, give him water, a ball of food, an upper robe, and a lower robe, and send him away. But if he is one who is fully ordained or one who desires full ordination, give him five requisites and send him away; do not send him away empty-handed."

The condensed summary verse:

Fine dwelling, platform, likewise
railings, lattice, and corbel,
broom, and pinnacle,
placing pinnacle and railing.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared that among the various dwelling places, a place at the foot of a tree is suitable and easy to obtain, and that a monk who dwells there and has gone forth and received full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya becomes a proper monk. If something better is obtained, then a cell, a front room, a multi-storied dwelling, or the like may be used. The monks then went about building dwelling cells, and the Blessed One declared: "Build fine dwellings." But when the Blessed One said "Build fine dwellings," the monks did not know how to do so. The Blessed One declared: "Lay a foundation seven or eight courses of bricks high, with a platform reaching to knee height, and set column bases in place. On top of that, arrange a row of columns. On top of the columns, set the column caps. On top of the column caps, place the rafters. On top of the rafters, lay flat planks. Cover all of that with bricks. Then plaster it over with powdered brick. This is how a fine dwelling should be built." After the Blessed One had declared this and the monks had built fine dwellings, they built them without railings. The Blessed One declared: "Build railings." But when the railings were built, they fell down. The Blessed One declared: "They should be fitted together and fastened with iron pegs."

When the monks were eating in the fine dwelling, sparrows and pigeons were pecking at them. The Blessed One declared: "Screens should be put up." When the Blessed One declared that screens should be put up, the monks did not know what kind to make, so the Blessed One declared: "There are five kinds of screens: those made from hemp, those made from muñja grass, those made from balvaja grass, those made from kuśa grass, and those made from cord." When the monks did not know on which side to fasten them, the Blessed One declared: "Fix them well with hooks projecting from the four corners." When they attached wooden hooks, these cracked in the sun and rotted in the rain, and the Blessed One declared: "Iron ones should be attached." Crows, sparrows, and pigeons then stopped coming, and the Blessed One declared: "On one side, a crow-hole should be made, and it should be open only at mealtimes; after the monks have eaten, it should be closed again."

While a monk was eating, a dog approached, and thinking to himself that it would certainly bite him if he did not give it something, he waited for a moment, expecting to give it food; but the monk did not give it anything, and that moment passed beyond its proper time. Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A food rack should be set out for animals."

When the Blessed One had declared that a food rack should be set out for animals, a certain monk who was staying at a hermitage gave the rack of food to some foxes and drove away the crows. The crows became angry and, speaking in their own crow language, told the leader of a band of thieves: "That monk has a great deal of gold." The leader of the band of thieves was skilled in the language of crows, and he began to beat the monk. The monk said: "Good man, why do you beat me?" The man said: "Noble one, give me the gold you have." The monk said: "Good man, where would I get wealth in gold? Do not beat me without cause." The man said: "You have gold — give it to me. If you do not hand it over, I will kill you." The monk said: "Good man, if you have been deceived by one thing, tell me — who said this to you?" The leader of the thieves said: "The crows said it." The monk said: "Good man, those crows are angry with me." And he then explained what had happened. The leader of the thieves said: "Noble one, if you had not spoken the truth to me plainly, I would have killed you."

Thereupon the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "This flaw arose from setting out only one rack; therefore, for the sake of all sentient beings, a food rack that is comfortable for all should generally be set out."

When the fine summer dwelling became full of water, the Blessed One declared: "It should be drained." When the Blessed One declared that it should be drained, the monks did not know how to do it, and the Blessed One declared: "Between the columns, it should be cut through with flat planks." When they were cut through everywhere it became completely dark, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not cut it through everywhere; rather, leave spaces for light." When no timber was to be found, the Blessed One declared: "It may be cut with a saw or an axe." When these were cut through, they rotted in the water, and insects also got in, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "They should be set in place every four months and then removed."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada was in the habit of rising early each morning and going to the Jeta Grove to pay his respects to the Blessed One, sweeping it himself as he went.

Then on another occasion the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was occupied with some pressing business and did not come. The Jeta Grove went unswept, and the ground was covered with fallen leaves. The Blessed One, while walking in meditation, saw this. Having seen it, he thought to himself: "Alas — even if Śakra (Indra), the sovereign of the gods, were to come bearing a broom, his garments fragrant with the scent of the Himalayas, it would be presumptuous." For it is the nature of reality that whenever the blessed buddhas give rise to worldly intention, the very insects and creatures sense it through the Blessed One's mind and thought. And when the buddhas give rise to a mind that transcends the world, even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know it through the Blessed One's mind and thought — so what need is there to speak of the creatures born in animal existences? Śakra, the sovereign of the gods, reflecting on why the Blessed One would give rise to a worldly intention, saw that he wished the Jeta Grove to be swept. Śakra, knowing the Blessed One's mind and thought, then took five hundred brooms soft as wool to the touch and placed them before the Blessed One.

Then, in order to show sentient beings who desire merit a basis for the accumulation of merit, the Blessed One himself took up a broom and set about sweeping the Jeta Grove. Seeing the Blessed One doing so, the great śrāvakas — Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Nāmadru, and others — likewise took up brooms and swept. Then the great śrāvakas, together with the Blessed One, swept the Jeta Grove and went to the dwelling house. There, in the midst of the community of monks, a seat having been spread, the Blessed One took his seat.

Seated, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, there are five benefits in the act of sweeping. What are the five? One's own mind becomes thoroughly clear; the minds of others become thoroughly clear; the gods are pleased; the roots of virtue that give rise to beauty are accumulated; and at the dissolution of the body, one will be reborn among the gods of the higher realms, the happy destinies."

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada arrived at that spot. He heard how the Blessed One, together with the great śrāvakas, had swept the grove himself, and he thought: "How could I walk upon the very ground swept by the Blessed One together with the great śrāvakas?" The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, feeling a sense of shame welling up in his heart, remained where he stood and did not go forward.

Now the blessed buddhas, even while knowing something, may act as though they do not know, and so the Blessed One asked the monks: "Monks, who is that?" The monks replied: "It is Anāthapiṇḍada, Blessed One. Having heard that the Blessed One himself swept the grove together with the great śrāvakas, he is too embarrassed to come before the Blessed One, and has dropped his walking staff and stands there with a sense of shame."

Then the Blessed One said to him: "Householder, you should recite and take to heart the teaching of the Buddha. For the blessed buddhas revere the Dharma, and the Dharma is the teacher even of the arhats."

Then Anāthapiṇḍada, chanting verses aloud, approached and drew near before the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One instructed him thoroughly with talk rich in Dharma, drew him fully into it, praised him fully, and gladdened him fully. Having instructed him thoroughly with talk rich in Dharma, drawn him fully into it, praised him fully, and gladdened him fully, the Blessed One departed.

The monks, having given rise to doubt, asked the buddha, the Blessed One, in order to have all their doubts cut through: "Venerable Blessed One, it is wonderful that, having arisen to reverence and respect for the Dharma, he praised the Dharma in that way."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, that the Tathāgata, who here and now is free from attachment, free from aversion, free from delusion — fully liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and anguish — who, through omniscience and the wisdom that knows all aspects, has gained mastery over all objects of knowledge, that such a one should arise to reverence and respect for the Dharma and thus offer praises of the Dharma — what is so wonderful in that? Rather, monks, listen well and take to heart what I shall tell you: what is truly wonderful is what happened in a time past, when I had not yet been liberated from attachment, aversion, and delusion, from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and anguish, and yet for the sake of the Dharma entirely gave up my own life. I shall now tell it.

Monks, in a time long past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there reigned a king named Brahmadatta. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, and happy; the harvests were good, the people were many, the population was great; strife, quarrel, tumult, and uproar were thoroughly stilled; there were no robbers; rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo were abundant. He was a righteous king who governed in accordance with the Dharma, ruling by Dharma.

That king was faithful, of wholesome and good intention, devoted to the benefit of himself and others, compassionate, a great-souled one who loved the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects like a mother toward her child, giving everything, relinquishing everything — he engaged in great generosity.

Then at another time he was enjoying himself, delighting, and taking pleasure together with his noble queen. As they were thus enjoying themselves, delighting, and taking pleasure, the queen conceived a being within her womb, and she felt a wish to hear well-spoken words. She said so to the king, and the king summoned the astrologers and asked them about it. They replied: 'Your Majesty, this is the power of the being conceived in her.'

Then the king, wishing to obtain well-spoken words, sent a hundred thousand gold coins and had messengers circle through towns, villages, districts, and the palace precincts, yet well-spoken words were not to be found.

In due course, nine months being complete, the queen gave birth to a son — handsome, pleasing to behold, beautiful, of golden complexion, with shoulders like a canopy, long-armed, with a broad forehead, arched eyebrows, a high nose, endowed with all limbs and minor members. Twenty-one weeks of seven days after the birth, a great naming ceremony was held, and they set about giving the boy his name. The ministers said:"

"Because it was on account of the god for whom, from before his very birth, a search was made for well-spoken words, let the boy's name be Seeker of Well-Spoken Words." And so the name Seeker of Well-Spoken Words was given to him.

The boy Seeker of Well-Spoken Words was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him, two to suckle him, two to bathe him, and two to play with him. These eight nurses raised and nourished him on milk, yogurt, fresh butter, melted butter, clarified butter, and other finest provisions of every kind, so that he grew as a lotus grows in a pond. Yet even when he had grown great, when a search was made for well-spoken words, they were not to be found.

His father then passed away, and the kingdom was placed in his hands. He spoke to his ministers: "Lords, I have need of well-spoken words. Search for well-spoken words." The ministers then sent a hundred thousand gold coins and circled through all the towns, villages, districts, and palace precincts of Jambudvīpa, yet well-spoken words were not to be found. They reported this to the king, and the king was seized with longing, consumed with hope of hearing well-spoken words.

Śakra, the lord of gods — whose knowledge and vision penetrate below — saw that the king was suffering on account of well-spoken words, and thought to himself: "I should go to comfort the king." Then Śakra, lord of gods, transforming himself into the form of a yakṣa, with hands, feet, and eyes made ugly and repellent, sat down before the king. At that moment he spoke in verse:

Practice the Dharma of right conduct.
Practice it; do not practice wrongdoing.
One who practices Dharma abides in happiness
In this world and in the next.

The moment the king heard that verse, joy and great joy arose in him, and he said to the yakṣa: "Mysterious one, speak that verse again! Speak it again — I wish to hear it." Then the yakṣa said to the king: "O god, if you do what I tell you, then I too will do whatever you command." The king said: "Speak — what is it?" The yakṣa said: "For seven days, pile up logs of śāla wood in a fire-pit, and if at the end of that time you cast yourself into it, then afterward I will speak the verse."

The moment the king heard this, he rejoiced and said to the yakṣa: "So be it." Then the king proclaimed throughout all the land: "In seven days the king will cast himself into the fire-pit for the sake of hearing well-spoken words; those who wish to witness this wonder — let them come." Then many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered, and in the sky too many hundreds of thousands of gods assembled, knowing the purity of the bodhisattva's elevated aspiration, and stationed themselves there to witness the wonder.

Then the yakṣa rose into the sky and said to the bodhisattva: "Great king, act according to your vow." Then the king appointed his eldest son over the kingdom, asked forgiveness of his ministers, the townspeople, and the people of the land, and while the crowd of people breathed out with held breath, he drew near to the fire-pit and spoke in verse:

Here at this fire-pit, whose terror is great
and whose light is like the rays of the rising sun,
for the sake of Dharma I shall leap in without fear for my life,
with a mind of certainty.
By the power of my merit, may this fire-pit too become filled with lotuses —

cool as a lake of water infused with sandalwood and blue lotus —

Having said those words, the bodhisattva leapt into the fire-pit, and the very instant he leapt in, that fire-pit turned into a lake. Then Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, seeing that miraculous display which made the king's wonder equal among gods and humans alike, caused the form of the yakṣa to disappear and sat there in his own form. At that moment he spoke in verse:

Practice the Dharma that is well practiced;
do not practice that which is wrongly practiced.
One who practices the Dharma abides in happiness
in this world and in the next.

The bodhisattva then took hold of those verses, wrote them on golden tablets, and sent them to all the towns, villages, districts, and royal palaces throughout Jambudvīpa.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, what do you think? The one who was the king at that time and on that occasion — that was I. And if even then I gave up my life completely for the sake of the Dharma, what need is there to speak of the present? Therefore, monks, you should train in this way: hold the Dharma in reverence, regard it as supreme, take delight in it, and honor it. You should dwell in dependence upon the Dharma, having revered it, regarded it as supreme, taken delight in it, and honored it. Monks, you should train in exactly this way."

When the Blessed One had spoken those words, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada (the benefactor of the poor).

The Blessed One declared that there are five benefits of sweeping, and upon hearing this, the monks — the elder monks among them — abandoned their meditation and their recitation and set about sweeping the Jeta Grove. The Blessed One declared: "I spoke with the monk in charge of duties in mind, not with the elder monks." Nevertheless, a monk's two tasks, having gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, are these: meditation and recitation. The Blessed One declared: "I spoke with the attendant monk in charge of duties in mind." Since that monk was unable to sweep the entire Jeta Grove, the Blessed One declared: "Whatever area the monk in charge of duties is able to sweep, he shall sweep, and on the eighth and fourteenth days the wooden board shall be struck and the entire Saṅgha shall sweep together."

When the Blessed One declared that the wooden board should be struck on the eighth and fourteenth days and the entire Saṅgha should sweep, some monks, holding no broom in hand, spoke ill of the task and did the work poorly. The non-humans dwelling in the Jeta Grove and other monks as well were reproached. The Blessed One then declared: "One should sweep while speaking words of resolution that accord with the Dharma, or one should sweep in noble silence." When the monks had swept the Jeta Grove and sat there with their bodies soiled by dust, those of little faith saw them and mocked them. The Blessed One declared: "Having swept and set aside the broom, those who wish to bathe may bathe. Those who do not wish to bathe should wipe the body with water, wash the hands and feet, and then enter. That same one should inspect the sleeping quarters during the day." When the entire Saṅgha had done so and inspected in that way, the Blessed One declared: "The entire Saṅgha need not inspect; rather, those who are appointed to look after the lodgings shall do the inspection." The Blessed One declared: "After sweeping, one should recite the words of the buddha while going along."

The monks, seeing that a shadow had fallen there, felt it would be improper to walk in that direction, and so they did not go. The Blessed One declared: "One should recite the words of the buddha while walking along; there is no need for remorse in this."

When the shadow of the bathhouse, of an image, or of the central pole of a stūpa fell in that direction, the monks again felt remorse and did not traverse it. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, shadows are unstable. In such cases as well, one should recite the words of the buddha while traversing. There is no need for remorse in this."

Now, the king of Kera sent two of his Kera-born servant boys as a gift to King Prasenajit of Kosala. One of these was called Servant Boy and the other was called Skyongwa. Of the two, Servant Boy was skilled in the service of food and drink, while Skyongwa was skilled in the service of lodgings and bedding.

The people who lived in the border regions were mostly by nature given to greed, and whenever the two went to the market, they would snatch fish, meat, and oil from the local people and eat them, and those people would beat them for it. The two then reported to the king: "Your Majesty, when we went to the market today and tried to take just a small portion of fish, they soiled us and nearly killed us."

King Prasenajit had it proclaimed by drum that no one was to beat Servant Boy or Skyongwa, though people should guard their own goods. After this proclamation, whenever the two went to the market, the people, upon seeing them, would hide their own goods.

Then one day, after growing weary from his royal duties, the king lay down to rest. Servant Boy and Skyongwa were kneading his feet and waiting at his side. They roused the king, and Servant Boy said to Skyongwa: "Skyongwa, has His Majesty fallen asleep?" Skyongwa replied: "He has fallen asleep." The king, having heard this, thought to himself: "These two certainly wish to exchange some private words." He then feigned sleep and remained still. Servant Boy said to Skyongwa: "Skyongwa, does the next world exist or not?" Skyongwa replied: "Servant Boy, the next world does indeed exist, I think." Skyongwa then said: "Servant Boy, are there arhats in the world?" Servant Boy replied: "There are indeed arhats in the world, I think."

When the king had heard all of this, he thought to himself: "These two are both practicing such wrong views — one holds the view of permanence, and the other holds the view of annihilation."

And so it came to be widely known throughout the land that of the two Kera-born boys belonging to King Prasenajit of Kosala, one held the view of permanence and the other held the view of annihilation.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada raised a great lion's roar before the assembly with these powerful words: "Whoever in this world acts in a human way and does good deeds in my home shall, upon the breakup of the body, be reborn in a good destiny, in the higher realms among the gods." King Prasenajit thought: "When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada comes here, I shall arrange some means by which to present these two boys to him."

Then on another occasion the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to the king's presence. One of the boys set out a seat for him and, thinking the time had come, went back out and began playing with the other children. The king, knowing that boy had gone, thought: "This is the very moment those two have arranged to present him." He quietly instructed the doorkeeper: "Do not let the Servant Boy who came out from the householder Anāthapiṇḍada's quarters back inside."

The doorkeeper did not let him back inside. When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat to leave, he looked around and the king said: "Householder, where is the boy who arranged the seat for you?" The householder replied: "Your Majesty, please accept the Servant Boy and the Guardian as my gift and take them with you." The householder accepted this before the king's face, and then thought: "Why has the king given me these two boys?" He thought further: "These two hold wrong views, and the king wishes to test me through them." So he led the two of them home, called his steward, and said: "Good man, give these two whatever they desire." Then he went out to the marketplace and said to the assembled people: "Whatever the Servant Boy and the Guardian take, give it to them, record the price, and I shall pay double." Whatever the two took from the steward's hand, they received in full, and being pleased they said: "Good man, if you give us everything we have taken, who instructed you to do so?" He replied: "The householder instructed me to do exactly that." They thought: "The householder treats us just as our own parents would — we shall receive whatever we have taken." Then on another occasion, when the two went out to the marketplace, the assembled people called out and gave things to them — some saying, "Take what you like from us," and others likewise saying, "Take from us." The two said: "Wise ones, when you saw us before, you hid things away from us; now you call out and give them freely — what is the reason for this?" The people replied: "Before, you would snatch and eat things. Now the householder is paying double the price." The two thought: "The householder exerts himself greatly for our benefit." So they went to the householder and said: "Householder, please give us some work to do." He replied: "Friends, stay here — there is indeed work." After some time had passed, on another occasion the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took the Servant Boy and the Guardian with him to sweep the Jeta Grove. When they arrived and had begun the sweeping, something came up for him, and he said: "Servant Boy and Guardian, something has come up for me. You go on ahead and sweep in the direction of the Jeta Grove." As they began to sweep, the Blessed One blessed it so that, as when a sweeping cloth is inexhaustible, in just that way it did not come to an end, and because of their affection for the Lord they could not bring themselves to stop. Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, leave the remnants of the alms-bowl for the Servant Boy and the Guardian." And Ānanda left the remnants of the alms-bowl for them. When they put down the sweeping cloth and it continued to remain inexhaustible just as before, the two remained there working until nightfall. Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, call the Servant Boy and the Guardian to come before me." And to the monks he said: "Monks, I have spoken to you of not being indifferent to virtue and of confessing misdeeds and dwelling accordingly. However, because the Servant Boy and the Guardian must be freed from wrong views, whoever among you has attained the absorptive dwelling in equipoise by which they abide — let that one make it known to them through that very absorptive dwelling." Venerable Ānanda replied: "Reverend one, it shall be done as you say." Having heeded the Blessed One's words, Ānanda said to the Servant Boy and the Guardian: "Come before me alone." And to the monks he said: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared from his own mouth that I, monks —

"It shall be done as the Blessed One has declared," replied Venerable Ānanda. Then, at the first watch of the night, he began to display miraculous powers: some blazed with fire, some crackled with lightning. The Servant Boy and the Guardian asked: "Noble Ānanda, what is this?" He replied: "These are arhats at play with their supernormal powers." They said: "Ānanda, since there are arhats in this world, surely these cannot but appear directly before our very eyes — what is there to doubt about this?" And of those two, whichever one had held the view that there are no arhats in the world was freed from that view, and attained the right view that there are indeed arhats in the world.

Then, at the middle watch of the night, the Blessed One aroused in his mind the worldly intention that Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) and Brahmā and the other gods would come. Now, as concerns the passage beginning with "When the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arouse in their minds the worldly intention" and ending with "Śakra and Brahmā and the other gods, knowing the Blessed One's intention through his mind, proceeded into the Blessed One's presence" — all of that proceeds as before. By their power, a vast radiance arose. The Servant Boy and the Guardian asked: "Noble Ānanda, what is this?" He replied: "These are Śakra, Brahmā, and the other gods who have come into the Blessed One's presence. There is another world beyond this one — surely these cannot but appear directly and vividly — what is there to doubt?" And of those two, whichever one had held the view that there is no world beyond was freed from that view, and the right view that there is indeed a world beyond was born in them.

Faith having arisen in them, they went to where the Blessed One was, and having gone there, they touched their heads to the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One, having understood their dispositions, latent tendencies, constitutions, and natures, taught them the Dharma of such a kind that they would realize the Four Noble Truths. Having heard this, the Servant Boy and the Guardian struck down with the vajra of wisdom the mountain peak of the view of the transitory collection — twenty heights high — and directly manifested the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, they touched the Blessed One's feet and implored him: "Reverend one, if we may obtain the going-forth and full ordination in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya and receive the status of monks, we wish to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One." The Blessed One addressed those two: "Servant Boy and Guardian, come, practice the holy life" — and by this utterance of "Come, monks," he fully ordained them.

The moment the Blessed One spoke, they found themselves with their heads shaved, robed in patched cloth, bowl in hand, water-pot borne, their hair and beards cut — appearing as though seven days had passed since the shaving, and comporting themselves like monks who had been fully ordained for a hundred years.

When the Tathāgata spoke the word "Come,"
their heads were shaved and their bodies clothed in patched robes;
in that instant their faculties were perfectly stilled,
and through the Buddha's intention their outer form was transformed.

The basis for the minor rules of the Vinaya.

The sixteenth fascicle.

The Blessed One gave instruction to the two of them, and through their earnest and sustained effort they abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. As arhats, they were free from attachment to all three realms — their minds even and equal, like clay and gold, like open sky and the palm of the hand, like a mongoose and sandalwood. They had split open the shell of the egg of ignorance, attained clear knowing, higher knowledge, and the four kinds of individual discriminating awareness; they had turned their backs on attachment to existence, to gain, and to honor; and they had become worthy of veneration, reverence, and respectful address by the gods of the sense faculties and the faculties' near-dependents.

Now when the Blessed One ordained those servants and herdsmen, King Prasenajit lost faith, thinking: "It is not a good thing that the Blessed One has done — ordaining servants and herdsmen; these are people who practice every manner of wrong view." The Blessed One, perceiving with his wisdom that King Prasenajit had lost faith in those great hearers who were like Mount Meru, thought: "I must therefore proclaim their virtues."

With that intention the Blessed One remained silent, and then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and sat to one side. Once he was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with a Dharma discourse that was genuine, led him to genuine acceptance, genuinely praised him, and genuinely gladdened him; and in many ways with such a Dharma discourse he taught genuinely, led him to genuine acceptance, genuinely praised him, and genuinely gladdened him — and then remained silent.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned to face the Blessed One with palms pressed together in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, would you grant permission for me to offer tomorrow's noon meal to the community of monks together with the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One remained silent, and by that silence gave his assent.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that permission had been granted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had taught, expressed his delight, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to where the two — the servant and the herdsman — are staying, and when you arrive, say this to them: 'Tomorrow, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepares the noon meal, the two of you are to arrange the water for rinsing.'"

"Venerable one, it shall be done as you say," said the venerable Ānanda. Respectfully complying with the Blessed One's instruction, the venerable Ānanda went to where the venerable servant and herdsman were staying and said to them: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has spoken from his own mouth and commanded: 'Tomorrow, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepares the noon meal, the two of you are to arrange the water for rinsing.'"

They replied: "Venerable Ānanda, it shall be done exactly as the Blessed One has commanded."

And they thought to themselves: "Why has the Blessed One, leaving aside the elder monks, commanded us alone to arrange the water for rinsing tomorrow? Surely he intends to proclaim our virtues before the meal is consumed — he wishes to fulfill the Teacher's intention completely."

That very night the householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepared the food and drink, clean and well-arranged, and rose early the next morning to set out the seats. He set out the water vessels, and then sent a messenger to the Blessed One, saying: "Lord, the food and drink have been prepared at the noon hour. May the Blessed One please take notice that the time has now come." And so he announced the hour.

Then the Blessed One, in the forenoon, donned his robe, took up his bowl, and surrounded by the assembly of monks, with the community of monks going before him, proceeded to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, going directly to the place. Upon arriving, he took his seat on the appointed seat in the midst of the community of monks.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sent a messenger to King Prasenajit, saying: "My lord, I have invited the buddha and the community of monks to the noon meal. It would be fitting for you to come and rejoice in this." At that, the king, accompanied by his queen's retinue, his youths, and his ministers, came to the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to rejoice at the noon gathering, and they sat down, paying homage in order of seniority.

Then the Venerable Śroṇa, sitting at the elder's end, blessed the stream of water just as one pours water from the younger end. The Venerable Pāṃśukūlika likewise blessed the stream of water just as one pours water from the elder end. King Prasenajit thought to himself: "Which among the monks is displaying these miraculous powers before the Teacher?" And following the stream of water, he went to the younger end, and at a certain moment he saw the Venerable Pāṃśukūlika. Then, following the stream of water back again, he went to the elder's end, and at a certain moment he saw the Venerable Śroṇa. He was utterly astonished, bared his upper body, extended his right hand, and exclaimed aloud: "Wonderful — the Buddha! Wonderful — the Dharma! Wonderful — the Saṅgha! Wonderful — that the Dharma has been so well proclaimed! Even now, here among us, Śroṇa and Pāṃśukūlika and others who hold mistaken views have attained qualities such as these!"

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, knowing that the Blessed One and the community of monks were comfortably seated, with his own hands served them with food and drink, clean and well-prepared, satisfying them fully and completely, in all respects filling them to contentment. After serving them fully and repeatedly with his own hands with food and drink, clean and well-prepared, and satisfying them and filling them completely, he informed the Blessed One that the noon meal was done, and perceived that the Blessed One had covered his bowl and withdrawn his hand. Then he took a low seat and sat before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma.

Thereupon the Blessed One instructed, guided, inspired, and gladdened King Prasenajit and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with a discourse in harmony with the Dharma, and then rose from his seat and departed.

The monks were filled with doubt, and put to the Blessed One, the buddha, all their doubts to be resolved: "Venerable one, what karma did Śroṇa and Pāṃśukūlika perform such that they were born in an outlying borderland, with one holding the view of eternalism and the other the view of annihilation? And what karma did they perform such that they went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized the state of arhatship?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the karma that Śroṇa and Pāṃśukūlika performed and accumulated in former lives in other existences" — from the passage beginning "Having obtained a gathering" through "ripening as a fruit for embodied beings" — is as before.

"Monks, long ago in this very auspicious age (kalpa), when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there was a Teacher named Kāśyapa" — from that passage through "a sage who speaks in the deer-forest grove" — is as before.

In the teaching of that Teacher, these two went forth. But then the two of them went to an outlying borderland and, without any master's instructions, aroused in themselves a mental engagement in meditation. There, with what they had not understood, they conceived a perception of having understood. Then, at the time of their death, they arrived at wrong views concerning the transcendence of the world. Damaged by those wrong views, the two said: "We have been deceived by the perfectly complete buddha Kāśyapa. If for the time being there is no arhatship for us in which the afflictions are abandoned, let there at least be something of the sort for others." Monks, what do you think? Those who, having gone forth in the canonical teaching of the perfectly complete buddha Kāśyapa and having gone to an outlying borderland without instructions, aroused that mental engagement in meditation — those very ones are these same servants and attendants here. And because they went to that outlying borderland, aroused in themselves a mental engagement in meditation without instructions, and thereby obtained wrong views — through the karmic maturation of that action they were born among the lower realms, and for many years were born in outlying borderlands, becoming holders of wrong views. Right down to the present they have still been born in outlying borderlands and held wrong views.

However, because these two, at that time, had recited the scriptures, chanted them aloud, and trained in understanding the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), the sense sources (āyatanas), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and what is possible and what is not possible — by virtue of that, they went forth in my teaching, abandoned all afflictions, and directly realized the state of arhatship.

Monks, there are these faults — and others as well — in meditating without a master's instructions. Therefore a monk should not meditate without a master's instructions. A monk who meditates without a master's instructions will come to ruin.

Monks, therefore, the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is itself wholly dark; the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly bright is itself wholly bright; and for mixed actions the maturation is likewise mixed. Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are wholly dark and mixed, strive for actions that are wholly bright. This is how you, monks, should train."

The origin story takes place in Śrāvastī. A householder there had a squirrel come to live in his park. A monk was also there, and from the intense heat of fever he had become pale and dry, his body wasted, wretched, and thin. He said to the householder: "Please let the householder know; I will go elsewhere." The householder replied: "Noble one, I hope I have caused you no trouble at all." The monk said: "Householder, there is no trouble at all — but the time of fever has come upon me, and the squirrel in that place is a bother." The householder said: "Noble one, please stay. I will have an underground chamber made for you." The monk replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted this." The noble one said: "The Blessed One is compassionate — he will permit it."

At that time the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then I grant permission: let a monk have an underground chamber made." When the Blessed One declared "I grant permission: let him have an underground chamber made," the householder had an underground chamber built. During the rainy season it became damp, and the monk went to the householder and said:

"Householder, know that I will go elsewhere." The householder said: "Noble one, surely you are not inconvenienced?" The monk replied: "Householder, I am not at all inconvenienced, but I cannot stay in this damp underground chamber." The householder said: "Noble one, if that is so, then please allow me to have a roof made and remain here." The monk replied: "The Blessed One has not permitted this." The householder said: "The Blessed One is compassionate — he will permit it."

At that time the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then I grant permission: let a monk have a roof made." When the Blessed One declared "I grant permission: let him have a roof made," the householder had a roof built. When it collapsed, the Blessed One declared: "A railing is to be erected." When that too shifted, the Blessed One declared: "Support beams are not to be used; instead, it is to be fastened with iron nails."

A summary verse: Salt, and a hollow-stemmed container, a covered medicine bowl, a parting board and a cross-beam, a foot-rest and a mortar.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Cool Wood. The venerable Pilindavatsa, from the time he went forth until now, was always ill. The celibate practitioners went to him and asked: "Elder, are you well?" He replied: "Friends, I am ill and unwell." They asked: "Elder, what did you take as medicine before?" He replied: "Friends, it was salt." They asked: "Elder, if that is so, why do you not take it now?" He replied: "Friends, the Blessed One has not permitted it."

At that time the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then I grant permission: salt is to be taken as medicine." When the Blessed One declared that salt was to be taken as medicine, the monks stored it in small heaps and it spoiled. The Blessed One then declared: "It is not to be stored in small heaps; rather, it is to be stored in a hollow container." The monks stored it in hollow bamboo stems, and when those became saturated, the Blessed One declared: "It is to be stored in a horn container." The monks put it inside a horn flask, and it acquired an unpleasant smell. The Blessed One then declared: "It is not to be put inside a horn flask; rather, it is to be washed with cow's urine and dye and then put inside." The narrative occasion is in Rājagṛha.

When the Blessed One declared that salt was to be stored inside a horn container, the son of the venerable Pilinda put salt inside a horn container and left it uncovered, so that dust got in. At that time the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A lid is to be put on it." When the Blessed One declared that a lid was to be placed on it, the monks did not know how to make one. The Blessed One declared: "Make a second piece identical to that very horn, and place it as a paired horn-lid."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Cool Wood. The venerable Pilindavatsa, from the time he went forth until now, was always ill. The celibate practitioners went to him and asked: "Elder, are you well?" He replied: "Friends, I am ill and unwell." They asked: "Elder, what did you formerly use to hold medicine?" He replied: "Friends, it was a medicine bowl." They asked: "Elder, if that is so, why do you not use one now?" He replied: "Friends, the Blessed One has not permitted it."

At that time the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Therefore I permit it: a monk may hold a medicine bowl."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's grove. At that time there was a householder in Śrāvastī who had taken a wife from an equal family. He sported with her, delighted in her, and enjoyed her company.
