From their sporting, delight, and enjoyment together, a son was born; they raised him, cared for him, and he grew up. In due course he went forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and he had obtained a throne and couch but no bed-mat. Some time later the householder went to the Jeta Grove and, seeing his son lying on an empty throne without a bed-mat, said to him: "Son, these monks have bed-mats — why do you have none?" The son replied: "Father, these monks have been gone forth for a long time and that is how they obtained bed-mats, but I have only just now gone forth and so I have not yet obtained one." The father said: "Son, if that is so, I will send you a blanket; spread it out here as a mat." The son replied: "The Blessed One has not permitted it." The father said: "Son, the Blessed One is compassionate — he will permit it."

At that point the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may spread out a blanket." When the Blessed One had declared that a monk may spread out a blanket, that monk used the blanket without spreading it out, and it became soiled. Some time later the same householder also came to the monastery, saw the soiled blanket, did not recognize it, and said: "Son, you have become quite deserving of great merit! Father, have you found another blanket besides this one? How fortunate to have found another, father! Son, why has this one become so soiled?" "Father, because I used it without spreading it out." "Son, have you thus made this fine garment, fit for a great person, unsuitable? Alas, it would have been better had you spread it out and then used it."

At that point the monks made the request to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not use even a person's parti-colored cloth without spreading it out; if one does, it constitutes a serious offense."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in Prince Jeta's grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When the Blessed One declared that the gift of Dharma-listening was to be given, the Dharma-speaker sat on a lion-throne with his feet dangling down. The Blessed One declared: "A foot-rest is to be provided." When the Blessed One had declared that a foot-rest is to be provided, the monks did not know how to make one. The Blessed One declared: "For a throne that is firm and solid, make steps of ivory. If it is moved about repeatedly, make a small wooden seat." When it became difficult to move, the Blessed One declared: "Fit iron roller-wheels to the four base legs and, holding it by those, move it about as desired."

Merit-wishing monks, and faithful brahmins and householders, anointed the foot-rest with fragrant hand-impressions and with perfumes, and the Dharma-speaker was reluctant and would not set his feet upon it. The Blessed One declared: "Place a layer of leaves or grass on top of it, and having placed it, then set the feet upon it — there is no need to be reluctant about this."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the pleasure garden of Prince Jeta. The Blessed One declared that a foot-rest should be placed at the lion throne. But monks dwelling in forest hermitages had no foot-rests, and as they taught the Dharma with their feet hanging down, they became fatigued. At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "They may place a stone."

Summary verse:
A wiping cloth, a lion-throne cloth, a spittoon,
a body-wiping cloth, a long basin,
a strainer, a burning lens,
a cushion-layer, and a flat board.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Squirrel-Feeding Park. From the time the venerable Pilindavatsa (Skt. Pilindavatsa) had gone forth until now, he had been continuously ill. Those living the holy life (brahmacarins) came to him and asked: "Elder, are you comfortable?" He replied: "Friends, I am ill and not comfortable." "Elder, what did you use before as a remedy?" "Friends, a face-wiping cloth." "Elder, why do you not use one now?" "The Blessed One has not permitted it." At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted — one may keep a face-wiping cloth."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Rājagṛha at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the Squirrel-Feeding Park. When the summer season arrived, the venerable Pilindavatsa became feverish and fell ill. He became pale and wan, his bodily flesh wasted away, and he grew thin, frail, and emaciated. Those living the holy life came to him, and seeing his bodily condition, they said: "Elder, why have you become pale and wan, your flesh wasted away, thin, frail, and emaciated?" He replied: "Friends, because of fever my body has come to this state." "Elder, what did you use formerly in the summer season?" "Friends, a linen cloth." "Elder, if that is so, why do you not use one now?" "Friends, the Blessed One has not permitted it." At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted — a monk may keep a linen cloth."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the pleasure garden of Prince Jeta. A monk fell ill with a cold and cough and spat on the ground, making both sides of his sleeping mat unsightly. In the morning, one who had been dwelling with him rose early, entered the dwelling, made his obeisance, enquired after his illness, and then departed. As he bowed, the spittle-residue touched his forehead, and the monks saw this and said to him: "Friend, where did your forehead come into contact with this spittle?" He replied: "I thought perhaps the preceptor who was ill with the cold had not spat on the ground — let me check," and he entered the dwelling, where he saw that spittle had been spat on both sides along the edge of the sleeping mat. He reported this to the monks, and they criticized, rebuked, and reproached the ill monk, saying: "How could it come to this? Monks are making the permitted dwelling of the Saṅgha unseemly with their spittle." At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not spit on the ground near a monk's sleeping mat and bedding. When making obeisance in the dark one should not bump one's head against the other person's body; rather, one should make obeisance with words alone. And if there is something to be attended to, one should inquire about that also with words alone."

Furthermore, whoever has a cold or is coughing up phlegm should keep a spittoon close at hand. When monks spat into bowls and stirred up the contents, making them greatly unpleasant, the Blessed One declared: "A spittoon should be provided together with a stand, or alternatively a large bronze vessel should be set out." When the monks placed bronze vessels of just any kind close by, these too were stirred up and the same fault arose, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "Something shaped like an elephant's foot should be set out." When others were spitting and thorns rose upward from below, the Blessed One declared: "The surface should be spread with a mat." The monks not knowing what to spread it with, the Blessed One declared: "Wood shavings, or else sand." When flies gathered there, the Blessed One declared: "They should be shooed away." When an unpleasant smell arose, the Blessed One declared: "It should be washed out from time to time." When the monks washed it out without drying it and living creatures appeared, the Blessed One declared: "After washing it out, it should be dried." When certain other monks vomited up phlegm and remained in a pitiable state until it was dry, the Blessed One declared: "Those who are gravely ill should keep two spittoons close at hand."

When monks in the assembly halls were reciting, chanting, or meditating, they would drool, and being mentally distracted, would spit carelessly. The Blessed One declared: "One must not spit carelessly near one's bedding and sleeping mat. However, four spittoons of the Saṅgha should be placed at the four corners by the pillars of the assembly hall, and while one is reciting, chanting, or meditating there, one should practice mindfulness and then spit into those."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Śrāvastī. At that time the Venerable whose paternal kinsman had, through five hundred lifetimes, died in hells and been reborn in hells, and who had then returned and been reborn here — from the time of his childhood he had been a householder, deeply attached to household life, delighting in the joy of play and intent on earning a livelihood, so that no recollection directed toward the hells had ever arisen in him. At another time, having gone forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, when the Blessed One was teaching about hells, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, and humans in such and such passages of the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, that monk, upon hearing the discourse on hells, vividly experienced the sensation of hell, and blood poured from every single pore of his body; his robes became stained with it, and a foul odor arose. At that time the monks informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted — monks should wear a cloth wrap around the body." When the Blessed One had declared that monks should wear a cloth body-wrap, those monks wore it on the outside of their robes, and the same fault arose again, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "It should be worn on the inside." When, by wearing it on the inside alone, they chafed and wounds appeared, the Blessed One declared: "One must not drag it against the bare skin alone; rather, having rinsed it with warm water, one should gently wash and cleanse it." The cloth body-wrap should also be washed from time to time to remove the pus and blood, and it should furthermore be dyed with coloring.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the abode of the kalandaka birds. The Venerable Pilindavatsa (Skt. Pilindavatsa), from the time he went forth and onward, was always ill. Those who were living the holy life (Skt. brahmacarya) alongside him came to him and asked —

"Venerable one, are you well? Is your countenance pleasant?" "I am ill and not well."

They asked him: "Venerable one, what did you use before to make fire?" "Friends, an iron fire-pan with a long handle." "Venerable one, if that was so, why do you not use one now?" "Friends, the Blessed One has not permitted it."

At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may keep an iron fire-pan with a long handle."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When monks were paying homage at a stūpa, mud and mire clung to their feet. The Blessed One declared: "Scrape it off." They did not know from what to scrape it, so the Blessed One declared: "Use a wooden scraper, and then apply powdered wood-ash and smear it with stone-ash." The courtyard around the stūpa became large and insufficient, so the Blessed One declared: "Scrape within a fathom of the enclosing fence." Still it was not enough, so the Blessed One declared: "If it is not sufficient, scrape as far as the flat paving-stones." That too was not enough, so the Blessed One declared: "Place wooden scrapers at intervals." When mud and mire collected in the corridors of the monks who were dwelling at the gateways, the Blessed One declared: "There too, proceed in the same sequence."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. There was a householder in Śrāvastī who had arranged for a garden hut to be built, and one monk was staying there. When the cold season arrived, he was afflicted by the cold and became pale and thin, his body wasted away to a pitiful state. He went to that householder and said: "Householder, please be informed — I will go elsewhere." The householder said: "Noble one, have you not a little time to spare?" He replied: "I have not the slightest trouble to spare, yet I am oppressed by the cold." The householder said: "Noble one, please stay. I will give you a fire-crystal." He replied: "Householder, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The householder said: "Noble one, the Blessed One is compassionate — he will grant it."

At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit it: a monk may keep a fire-crystal and use it to kindle fire and perform fire-related tasks."

That householder gave the fire-crystal to the monk, who used it to kindle fire and perform fire-related tasks. Now it happened that five hundred bandits were going to work in a rocky crag, and they went in that direction. They said to that monk: "Noble one, afflicted by the cold as we are, is there fire here?" He replied: "Friends, there is none." "Noble one, how do you perform your fire-related tasks?" "Friends, I kindle fire with a fire-crystal and perform fire-related tasks." "Noble one, where is that crystal?" "Friends, it is right here in this direction." They looked at it, then went to the rocky crag, carried out their work, and returned, saying: "Friends, let us go and take that crystal from the noble one." They went to him and said: "That fire-crystal — friends, it is right here in this very place." They took it and left.

Again the monk was afflicted by the cold and went to that householder, saying: "Householder, please be informed — I will go elsewhere." He said: "Noble one, have you not a little time to spare?" He replied: "Householder, I have not the slightest trouble to spare, yet I am oppressed by the cold." He said:

"Noble one, did I not give you a fire-crystal? Householder, you did give it. But those thieves took it. A gem of that quality, fit for a great one — and you hand it over to thieves like that. Ah, but you did leave it in an isolated spot."

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Gems of that kind should not be shown to those who take what is not given. However, they may be entrusted to a fire-tender. A water-crystal is just like a fire-crystal in this regard."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park belonging to Prince Jeta. The group of six monks were sending their robes to a laundryman to be washed. Then at some point a festival took place at Śrāvastī, and the brahmins and householders of Śrāvastī sent their brightly colored garments to the laundryman to be washed. The venerable Ānanda, toward sunset, took one saffron robe and went to the laundryman's place, saying: "Good man, please wash this robe." The laundryman replied: "Noble one, today I have a great many lay garments to see to — please leave and come back tomorrow; I will wash it then." Ānanda grew angry and began to threaten him. The laundryman said: "Noble one, what cause is there to threaten? If you cannot wait, leave it and go — I will wash it in the morning." Ānanda left the robe and departed. Then, distracted by the commotion of Ānanda's outburst, the laundryman bundled that robe into a bundle of garments and placed it among the brightly colored clothes. After some days had passed, the brightly colored garments had dyed it all mottled. The laundryman slapped his hand against his cheek and sat there, inwardly distressed. The crowd of people became displeased.

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing that this had fallen upon the brahmins and householders and caused them to lose faith, declared to the monks: "The saffron robe that the monk Ānanda sent to the laundryman to be washed has been made mottled by the brightly colored garments. Therefore, monks must not send their saffron robes to a laundryman to be washed. If a monk sends his saffron robes to a laundryman, it will become an offense."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks must not send their saffron robes to a laundryman to be washed." Whereupon the group of six monks began sending white garments instead. The laundryman carelessly beat them on a washing board and washed them, with the result that some garments tore and some frayed at the edges. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, therefore monks must not under any circumstances send garments to a laundryman."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park belonging to Prince Jeta.

The Blessed One having declared that monks must in all cases not send garments to a laundryman, the group of six monks went to the laundryman's washing place, wrapped their heads in their robes, and crouching down muttering to themselves in the manner of laundrymen while washing their own garments — this was seen by brahmins and householders, who became displeased.

At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks must not go to a laundryman's washing place and, crouching and muttering to themselves in the manner of laundrymen, wash their own garments. A monk who goes to a laundryman's washing place

and, crouching and muttering to themselves in the manner of laundrymen, washes his own garments, is guilty of an offence.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, belonging to Prince Jeta. When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not go to a laundryman's washing place and wash their own garments in the manner of laundrymen, crouching and muttering to themselves, the group of six monks began washing their garments on flat wooden boards, and that same fault arose again. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks must not wash garments on flat wooden boards. However, they may wash their own garments by gently agitating them back and forth in a basin with a little soft water." When the Blessed One had declared that they should wash garments by gently agitating them back and forth in a basin, certain other monks were unable to wash with both hands, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who are unable to wash with both hands may wash with both feet." When certain others were unable to wash with either both hands or both feet, the Blessed One declared: "For those, let others be permitted to wash on their behalf."

A summary verse:
A mat of straw, and a snake's slough,
a chisel, contrition itself,
a basin for dye and a dye vat wall,
and four kinds of dye-paste — these are the topics.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, belonging to Prince Jeta. When monks had bathed and then put on their Dharma robes while their bodies were still wet, those robes became mottled and developed an unpleasant odor. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted for monks to use a body-drying cloth." When the Blessed One had declared that they may use a body-drying cloth, certain other monks did not have one, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who do not have one should for the time being sit squatting, dry their bodies with a bathing cloth, and then put on their Dharma robes." When monks' sandals became dusty, the monks beat them clean, but when they beat them the sandals split and the fastening threads broke. The Blessed One declared: "Monks must not beat their sandals." When the monks washed them with water, that too proved unsatisfactory, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks must not wash sandals with water; rather, they should wipe them with a water-dampened cloth and polish them. Therefore it is permitted to use a sandal-polishing cloth."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in the land of Campā on the bank of the pond of the sage Gagā. In the land of Campā there was a nāga-girl (nāga daughter) named Campā who was faithful and of good, virtuous intention, and her son was a faithless, undisciplined young man. She caused him to listen properly to the Dharma, saying: "Son, go to the presence of the noble ones and listen to the Dharma — it will become a source of merit for you." He was accordingly brought to listen and entered among those who had sat down in their natural manner of dress to hear the Dharma. A certain young man saw him and was alarmed, and called out, "Venerable ones, behind you — behind you!" Hearing this, those monks who had not been freed from attachment were alarmed, and those men seized the nāga's son by the neck, tied him with a rope attached to his tail, and hurled him from the top of the assembly hall. His mother saw this and said: "Son, did you hear the Dharma from the noble ones?" He replied: "Mother, may no one ever become a noble one of that sort! What did they do to you?" He then recounted what had happened to him.

She said to him: "Son, those very ones are noble ones. Had others caught sight of you, you would have been killed." At that he said nothing more.

At that, the young nāga men burst into laughter and began to taunt him, calling out again and again, "Sore throat! Sore throat!" And because they all called out this mockery at him, his body became pale and thin, his flesh wasted away wretchedly, and his neck shriveled and dried up.

Then his mother said to him: "Son, why has your body become so pale and thin, your flesh wasted away wretchedly, your neck shriveled and dried up?" He replied: "Mother, these young nāga men keep taunting me and crying out, 'Sore throat! Sore throat!' — there is no escape from it, no help for it."

"Son, you went in your own natural form, and so this situation has come about. Had you gone in an emanated form, they would not even have been able to attach a rope to your tail. Now go in an emanated form and listen to the Dharma, and all will go well for you. However, if you listen in your own form, simply remain where you are and listen from there."

But he, lacking faith, did not agree to this, and said nothing further to his mother.

Then he thought to himself: "The noble ones tying a rope to a young nāga's tail will also obstruct those who wish to hear the Dharma. This, then, is what I must do." And so, before dawn broke, he went to where the Blessed One was, and arriving there, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

At that moment, by the power of the complexion of the young nāga daughter of the nāga Campā, the entire bank of the sage Gārgā's pond was suffused with a great radiance.

Sitting to one side, the young nāga daughter of the nāga Campā addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, I have a son who is without faith. I granted him permission to properly receive the hearing of the Dharma, and he went to hear the Dharma from the noble ones. The noble ones attached a rope to his tail, threw him out, and his throat was injured. Then the young nāga men taunted him over and over, crying, 'Sore throat! Sore throat!' When he was thus tormented in that way, his body became pale and thin, his flesh wasted away wretchedly, his neck shriveled and dried up. O Blessed One, please think with compassion: may you issue just a small admonishment to remind the noble ones not to tie ropes to young nāgas' tails."

The Blessed One, by remaining silent, gave his consent to the nāga daughter of Campā. Then the nāga daughter of Campā bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and vanished from that very spot.

Then the Blessed One, when that same night had passed, sat down upon the seat that had been spread for him in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, last night the nāga daughter of the nāga Campā came to where I was, and arriving there she bowed her head at my feet and sat down to one side. At that moment, by the power of the complexion of the young nāga daughter of Campā, the entire bank of the sage Gārgā's pond was suffused with a great radiance.

"Sitting to one side, the nāga daughter of Campā addressed me with these words: 'Venerable One, I have a son who is without faith. I granted him proper permission to receive the hearing of the Dharma, and he went to hear the Dharma in the presence of the noble ones. They attached a rope to his tail and threw him out; his throat was injured. Then the young nāga men taunted him, crying out, "Sore throat! Sore throat!" When he was thus taunted, his body became pale and thin, his flesh wasted away wretchedly —'"

"Alas, when his throat had become sore and thin — O Blessed One, please, out of compassion, give some instruction to remind the noble ones so that the noble ones will no longer attach a rope to a young nāga's tail." Thus she spoke.

Therefore, monks, since it is neither seemly nor fitting that the gods themselves should now taunt the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyas, saying, "Alas, the renunciants who are sons of the Śākyans have utterly deteriorated from their virtuous qualities" — therefore a monk must not attach a rope to a young nāga's tail. However, if a young nāga is seen, one should make a snapping sound and say: "Good sir, do not remain on the path where you may be seen." If he is not on the visible path, then well and good. But if he is there, one should gently take a dry stick, insert it into a pot or clay vessel, make a hole in it, close off the opening, and pull the nāga out with it. If no dry stick is available, one may use a reed, an iron tong, or a pair of tongs tied around the neck to pull him out. If no reed, iron tong, or pair of tongs is available, one should wrap cloth around the loop of a cotton rope or hemp rope, use that to catch him, then place him in a pot and remove him.

The monks did accordingly, removed him, and threw him into the forest. But he, enraged, burned down the forest with fire, and in that same place he too was burned up. Then the Blessed One declared: "One must not throw them into the forest." The monks threw him into an open area, and without a moment's pause an animal carried him off. Then the Blessed One declared: "One must not turn it away immediately from that very spot; rather, having placed it in an open area, one should remain there until it has entered its proper abode."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. In Rājagṛha there lived a householder who was skilled in the working of stone. He would fashion stone chips and sell them. At another time, he had accumulated much gain, and he thought: "What is the means by which I might both accrue merit and at the same time come to accumulate much gain?" Since he was a man of faith, he thought: "I shall invite a monastic Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at their head to my home, and offer them a meal prepared from the earnings from my stone chips — thereby I shall accrue merit, and my gain shall also increase." The passage from there up to "he went to where the Blessed One was" and onward to "he remained seated in the middle of the monastic Saṅgha of monks, where seats had been laid out" — all this is as before.

Then, having discerned that the Buddha and the monastic Saṅgha of monks were sitting comfortably, the householder served them personally with his own hands, providing clean and pure food and provisions, satisfying them fully and abundantly — in many ways he served them personally with his own hands, providing clean and pure food and provisions, satisfying them fully and abundantly. Having served them thus, perceiving that the Blessed One had finished eating and had drawn back his hand from the bowl, he took a low seat and sat before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One expressed his rejoicing in that act of giving with these words of rejoicing:

Among offerings, the fire sacrifice is supreme.
Among metrical compositions, the Sāvittī verse is supreme.
Among humans, the king is supreme.
Among rivers, the ocean is supreme.
Among stars, the moon is supreme.
Among luminaries, the sun is supreme.
Above, below, and in all directions —
Of all the destinies of beings there are,
In the world together with its gods,
The perfect buddha is the supreme worthy of honor.

Up to this point, and then after he had caused him to rejoice thoroughly, he rose from his seat and departed — all this is as before.

He then invited the buddha and the rest — the monastic Saṅgha — to his home, and after he had served them there, he began to scatter gravel and sand in order of seniority as they walked about. The monks felt remorse and would not accept it. The Blessed One declared: "It has been completely purified by a layman — with that understanding, you should receive it; there is no cause for remorse in this."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the prince Jeta's grove.

The Blessed One declared that dyeing work should be done. When the monks boiled the dye, it was curdled because it contained whey, and when cooked it turned foul and became unsuitable. The Blessed One then declared: "Dry it first and then boil it."

The monks dried it in the sun, but it shrank and became too small. The Blessed One declared: "Do not dry it in the sun."

The monks then dried it in the shade, but the wind carried it away. The Blessed One declared: "Do not dry it in the shade; rather, dry it where there is partial sunlight."

The monks put the dye and the robes together in the same water and boiled them, and the robes became ruined. The Blessed One declared: "Boil the dye separately."

The monks boiled it once only and then discarded it. The Blessed One declared: "Boil it up to three times before discarding it."

When the monks boiled it up to three times, they kept everything in a single vessel. The Blessed One declared: "Keep them in separate vessels."

The monks did not know which was the first, which was the second, and which was the third. The Blessed One declared: "Write on them: 'This is the first, this is the second, this is the third.'"

The monks put the robes directly into the dye itself. The Blessed One declared: "Do not put the robes directly into the dye; instead, pour the dye into a basin and rub the robes in it."

A monk rubbed a robe in dye that was far too wet, and it washed out. The Blessed One declared: "Do not rub them when they are far too wet."

The monks rubbed the robes when they were far too dry, and the robes became mottled. The Blessed One declared: "Do not rub them when they are far too dry; rather, rub them when they are of just the right moisture."

The monks dried the robes on the ground, and the robes became soiled with dust. The Blessed One declared: "Do not dry them on the ground."

The monks laid down grass and dried them on that, but the dye ran to one side. The Blessed One declared: "Hang them on a drying line and dry them there."

When the monks laid the robes on the line in that way, the dye did not set evenly in the middle. The Blessed One declared: "Tie cords at the corners, spread them on poles, prop them up, and dry them thus."

When the monks rubbed the robes, they did not turn them over, and the dye ran to one side and was absorbed unevenly. The Blessed One declared: "Turn them over again and again."

Some other patched robes were very large and would not fit on the drying line. The Blessed One declared: "Lay down grass and dry them on it, turning them over again and again."

The monks applied fresh dye to old robes and old dye to fresh robes. The Blessed One declared: "Apply fresh dye only to fresh robes, and old dye only to old robes."

The monks dried the new robes in the shade and the old robes in the sun. The Blessed One declared: "Dry the new ones in the sun and the old ones in the shade."

The monks applied the first dye first, then the second beneath it, and then the first dye again on top — resulting in the first dye being in excess. The Blessed One declared: "Apply the first and second dyes first, and only afterward apply the third."

The monks did not soak the robes in water, and the robes became mottled. The Blessed One declared: "They are to be soaked in water."

The monks soaked them in water on that very same day, and the Blessed One declared: "Soak them the following day."

While some other monks were doing dyeing work, wind and rain arose, and the monks, not knowing where to dry the robes, piled them on top of one another. The Blessed One declared: "When wind and rain arise, do the dyeing work inside a hall."

When the Blessed One had declared that the dyeing work should be done inside a hall when wind and rain arise, the monks did the dyeing inside the hall. The hall walls became heavily stained and streaked with dye, and some brahmins and householders who saw this said: "Noble ones, where does all this blood come from?" The monks replied: "This is not blood — we were doing dyework here." Those people said: "We thought it was blood." Thereupon the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Plaster that area with cow dung or mud."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered the Jeta Grove to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, the thought arose in him: "Since I offered the Jeta Grove to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, the walls there are unadorned with paintings, and it would be good to ask the Blessed One's permission and paint them." With that in mind, he went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, paid homage at the Blessed One's feet by bowing his head, and sat down to one side. Having sat to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the walls here have no paintings on them. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I would now wish to have the walls painted." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, you have permission — have it done."

When the Blessed One had declared that the walls should be painted, the monks did not know how to make multicolored paintings, and so they asked the Blessed One. The Blessed One had given permission to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and declared that the walls should be painted — "With which of many colors should we paint?" The Blessed One declared: "Monk, it is excellent, excellent that you asked what the householder Anāthapiṇḍada did not know to ask. Paint using all four colors: every shade of blue, every shade of yellow, every shade of red, and every shade of white."

This is the Vinaya, the Minor Matters, the seventeenth fascicle. In summary:

The utensils of those who do plastering work,
Stools with holes,
The receiving of washcloths and hair,
Rosaries, needles, and combs.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder at whose home an almsman came regularly from time to time, and that man went for refuge and was established in the training precepts. On another occasion, praises were recited to him regarding the seven objects that generate merit through material things, and he said:

The noble one said, "I shall perform whichever of the seven meritorious works produced from material things I am able to." The almsman said, "Householder, very good — do exactly so." The noble one said, "What shall I do?" The almsman said, "Householder, build a monastery for the Saṅgha." The noble one said, "I have kārṣāpaṇas, but I have no one to assist me in the Dharma work." The almsman said, "Householder, give the kārṣāpaṇas, and I shall be your partner in the Dharma work." The noble one said, "Very good," and gave him the kārṣāpaṇas one by one.

The almsman thought to himself, "This money belongs to the monks of the four quarters who practice the holy life, so how can I use it? I shall set it aside for now and ask others to take it up." And so he deposited the kārṣāpaṇas in a strongbox and kept them there.

Some time later, the householder thought, "The noble one is building my monastery; let me go there and see what is being done." He went, and when he arrived he could see nothing at all being done. He said, "Noble one, has not even a little of my monastery been built?" The almsman said, "If there is not even the procurement of building materials for the monastery to begin with, what is to be done?" The noble one said, "Alas! Where are the kārṣāpaṇas?" The almsman said, "They are in the strongbox." The noble one said, "Please use those very funds to procure the building materials." The almsman said, "Householder, how can I use money belonging to the monks of the four quarters for procuring building materials?" The noble one said, "But this monastery too is being built solely for the monks of the four quarters — what contradiction can there be? Let us ask the Blessed One." The almsman said, "Noble one, please do so."

The householder then reported the matter to the monks, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Let the building materials be procured from those very funds, and let there be no regret about this."

While that almsman was building the monastery and also going on his alms round, the householder said, "Noble one, since you are building the monastery and still going on your alms round, why not take your alms from these very funds, and I shall give you additional kārṣāpaṇas as well." The almsman said, "Householder, how can I take alms from building-fund money?" The noble one said, "I give this with an easy and open mind — what contradiction is there in this?" The almsman said, "Let us ask the Blessed One." The noble one said, "Please do so."

The householder reported the matter to the monks, and the monks presented it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "One who is engaged in building work shall take his alms solely from the building fund."

When the Blessed One had declared that one engaged in building work should take his alms solely from the building fund, he began eating very bad food. The Blessed One declared, "You must not eat excessively bad food." He then began eating excessively refined food. The Blessed One declared, "You must not eat excessively refined food either; rather, you should use the fund only up to the level of an equivalent from another monastery."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk suffered from diarrhea and had to go repeatedly to the latrine, which exhausted him greatly. At that time the monks presented the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Make a stool with a hole." When the Blessed One had declared that a stool with a hole should be made, the monks without distinction bored holes in stools with knives. The Blessed One then declared, "Only in one that is fastened with a hidden joint or fastened with a cord shall a hole be bored from beneath. One that is fastened with a peg shall have a hole bored in it and then be bound." When he defecated, he suffered pain in the tailbone.

The Blessed One declared, "Place a leaf cushion on that side." When the defecation fell to the ground, the Blessed One declared, "Place a chamber pot underneath." When they set it too high, the Blessed One declared, "It shall not be set too high." The pot became foul-smelling, and the monks removed it and threw it away and set out another, but that one also became foul-smelling. They threw that one away too, and when they could not find another, the Blessed One declared, "Do not throw them all away. Keep two: wash one and dry it, and do the same with the other. But if it comes about that they cannot be found in pairs, place a woven-leaf mat over the top of it and defecate upon it, and then set out another of the same kind." When the Blessed One declared that the pot should be washed, they washed it, but it still became foul-smelling. The Blessed One then declared, "Anoint it with sesame oil." Yet it still became foul-smelling, and the Blessed One declared, "Anoint it with mustard oil."

The Blessed One declared that the sick monk should be attended to, and upon hearing this, both senior monks and junior monks came to his side. The junior monks paid homage to him, and since the sick monk had to pay homage in return to the senior monks, he became distressed. The Blessed One then declared: "One who is ill shall not pay homage. One who is ill shall not receive homage. One who is ill shall not claim homage as something due to oneself. From one who is ill, homage shall not be appropriated as something due to oneself. If one who is ill pays homage, or receives homage, or claims homage as something due to oneself, or appropriates homage from an ill person as something due to oneself, one incurs an offense."

The venerable attendant then addressed the Blessed Buddha: "Blessed One, you have declared that one who is ill shall not pay homage, shall not receive homage, shall not appropriate homage, and shall not have homage appropriated from one who is ill. Reverend Sir, how many kinds of illness are there?" The attendant replied: "There are two kinds of illness — illness from food, and illness from impurity. Illness from food is distress caused by eating tooth-cleaning sticks, food, drink, fruit, roots, and the like. Illness from impurity is the attending to excrement and urine, and the cleaning of unclean places in order to wash them."

The Blessed Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, at the prince's park.

The venerable attendant then addressed the Blessed Buddha: "Reverend Sir, the brahmin Padmahṛdaya has made this request to the Blessed One: whenever you, Gautama, see me mounting a carriage, taking the reins, raising a whip, or speaking in a loud voice, please acknowledge my homage at that moment; and whenever you see me standing in a doorway, removing my shoes, or stepping aside from the path, or stretching out my hand, please acknowledge my homage at that moment; and whenever I come from within a gathering, rise from my seat, or am struck by the topknot or by an umbrella, please acknowledge my homage at that moment — this is what he has requested. Reverend Sir, is such a manner of paying homage reckoned in the noble Dharma-Vinaya?" The attendant replied: "The attendant did not perform a physical homage. What the attendant did was merely a word of reverent speech, while the bodily bow and the verbal utterance — that constitutes an offering. However, in the noble Dharma-Vinaya there are two forms of homage: the five-limbed prostration, and the embrace at the hands."

The case is at Śrāvastī. The monks, the very same ones who, while wearing their Dharma-robes, were having their hair and beards shaved, wore those same robes while eating their meals, wore those same robes while paying homage to the Teacher,

provoked the scorn of those without faith, who said: "The monks, the disciples of the Śākyan, are without cleanliness. The very same robes they wear while having their hair and beards shaved, those same robes they wear while eating their meals, and those same robes they wear while paying homage to the Teacher." On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not wear the Dharma-robes while having one's hair and beard shaved. Rather, one should hold a hair-catching cloth, and having spread it out, shave the hair." When the Blessed One had declared that a hair-catching cloth should be held, some monks had none to hand. The Blessed One then declared: "Those who have none shall wrap the body in a sweat-cloth and then shave the hair." After the monks had shaved their hair and beards and then went about as before, brahmin householders (brāhmaṇas and gṛhapatis) mocked them, saying: "The ascetics who are disciples of the Śākyan are without cleanliness, for after the work of the razor they do not bathe." On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "After the work of the razor, one shall bathe." Some other monks were old, decrepit, and weak. Others were ill and could not endure the preparation for bathing. Others had no water available. The Blessed One declared: "Those monks shall wash just the five limbs."

The Blessed One, the fully awakened buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's grove. Faithful brahmin householders offered garlands of flowers to the monks, but the monks did not accept them. The brahmin householders then said: "Noble ones, at the very time one speaks of the Blessed One, the fully awakened buddha — do we not come from this world to the next with the stock of virtue exhausted? Please accept them" — and so on, as before. On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "It is therefore permitted to accept garlands of flowers." The monks accepted them and then threw them down right in front of those same donors. The donors mocked them, saying: "Noble ones — these we purchased at great price, so why have you accepted and then discarded them?" The Blessed One declared: "They must not be discarded." The monks placed them on stūpas enshrining the hair and nails of the Tathāgata, and the donors said: "Do the noble ones not see that we have stūpas enshrining the hair and nails of the Tathāgata? We have given these to you, yet you have first offered them at the stūpas enshrining the Tathāgata's hair and nails — that is precisely right." The monks accepted the garlands and placed them at the doorway of the dwelling. Faithful brahmin householders, seeing them, thought it was a toilet and paid homage accordingly. The Blessed One declared: "They must not be placed at the doorway of the dwelling; they shall be placed inside." The monks placed them directly opposite the door, and this produced the very same fault. The Blessed One declared: "All fragrant things, since they are beneficial to the eyes, shall be placed in a secluded corner and preserved." When the Blessed One had declared that they were to be placed in a secluded spot and preserved, the monks did not know how to store them properly. The Blessed One declared: "On the inner side, a pin or thorn shall be driven in, and they shall be hung upon it."

The summary verse:
A fine seat and a backrest,
an anointing vessel, a bowl with a hole,
three containers for grain and oil,
a rope for wringing, and a well.

The Blessed One, the fully awakened buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's grove.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "When the Saṅgha has the means, fine seats may be given to it, but they shall not be given to individual persons. When the Saṅgha has the means, backrests may be given to it, but they shall not be given to individual persons."

The Blessed One, the fully awakened buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's grove.

Faithful brahmins and householders offered perfume to the monks, but the monks did not accept it, whereupon those donors said: "Noble ones, when the Blessed One, the fully awakened buddha, has not appeared in the world" — and so on as before, up to the point where the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted. Perfume may be accepted." The monks accepted it, and then threw it down right in front of those very donors. The donors then reproached them, saying: "Noble ones, we purchased this at great price, and you accepted it only to throw it away!" When the matter was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "They shall not throw it away."

The donors then offered perfume to a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata, and said to the monks: "Noble ones, do you not see the stūpa of the hair and nails of the Tathāgata? We are offering this to you, but we already made our first offering to the stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails." The monks accepted it and placed it at the door of the residence hall. Faithful brahmins and householders, seeing it there, thought it was a fragrant bathing room and brushed their feet against it. The Blessed One declared: "It shall not be placed at the door of the residence hall; rather, it shall be kept inside."

The monks then placed it directly opposite the door, and the same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "It shall not be placed directly opposite the door. However, since all fine fragrances are beneficial to the eyes, one should draw a line of fragrance with the perfume alongside the window recess, and it should be carried about from time to time."

Other faithful donors invited monks to their homes, offered them a feast, and had lines of perfume drawn on the monks' feet. The monks did not accept this, and those donors said: "Noble ones, those who are devoted to brahmins offer them garlands and perfume first, and the brahmins accept and apply them to their heads and bodies. We, having devotion to you, offer this to your feet — what contradiction could there be? Please accept." When the matter was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "Offerings made to the feet are to be accepted as one's own."

The monks accepted the perfume and then threw it down right in front of those very donors. The donors exclaimed: "Alas, noble ones! Please go to the monastery and make yourselves comfortable. Though faith arose in us in the way it did, now the opposite of faith has arisen too." When the matter was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "They shall not throw it down in front of those very donors."

The Blessed One, the fully awakened buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's grove.

The monks were placing their bowls down carelessly, so that the bowls were being damaged. When the matter was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "Bowls shall not be set down carelessly. Rather, a bowl-niche shall be made in the wall, and bowls shall be placed there."

The monks then dug into the wall. The Blessed One declared: "One shall not dig into the wall. However, at the time when the wall of a monastery building is being constructed, a bowl-niche shall be built into it at that time. Likewise, this shall be done in the case of the surrounding residential quarters as well."

The Blessed One had declared that bowls are to be placed in the bowl-niche. When the monks who were dwelling in remote monasteries had no bowl-niche, the Blessed One declared: "Let them make a peg of wood or twisted cord, smear it with cow dung or clay, and place the bowl upon it." When dust carried onto the bowl became a problem, the Blessed One declared: "A cover matching it in size shall be made for it." When monks placed their bowls on the ground, the Blessed One declared: "One shall not place a bowl on the ground. Rather, it shall be set leaning against a rope or a tree branch."

When the monks went wandering through the countryside, they carried their bowls and went out. Some faithless people mocked the noble ones, saying: "Look — are these home-builders, or monkeys carrying things off?" When the matter was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "Whenever one goes anywhere, one shall not carry the bowl-stand along. Rather, wherever one goes, a separate one shall be left there."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk was wandering through the countryside and came to a rocky cliff. He took lodging in a certain house, washed his feet, and began to rub them with sesame oil. Just then a woman arrived carrying sesame oil, and the monk stretched out his hand. She said: "A noble one who begs yet has no vessel — how can that be? Oh, would you please fill your sesame-oil container for yourself?" He replied: "Sister, the Blessed One has not permitted it." She said nothing more to this and departed. When the matter was then reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "In that case, permission is granted: one may fill a sesame-oil container."

After the Blessed One had declared that a sesame-oil container may be filled, the venerable Nandaka's two novices took a sesame-oil cask and went out to collect sesame oil on alms round. A woman came carrying sesame oil, and when she saw the two novices holding the sesame-oil cask, she struck her chest and said: "Noble ones, who is it that will fill this for you?" They replied: "Poor woman, first set down whatever you yourself have given. The remainder — look — the faithful brahmins and householders will fill it." She said nothing more and left. When the matter was then reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared: "Monks shall not fill a sesame-oil container that is excessively large."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks shall not fill an excessively large sesame-oil container, the monks filled one that was excessively small, and this proved insufficient for what was needed. The Blessed One then declared: "One shall not use an excessively small one either. Rather, sesame-oil containers are of three kinds: large, medium, and small. The large holds a full pha (a standard measure); the small holds half a pha; and the medium is what falls between these two."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. An elder monk and a younger monk set out together on the road. As they walked along they were exchanging words that were not wholesome. A faithless yakṣa overheard them and thought: "These two śramaṇas (Skt. śramaṇa), sons of the Śākyas, go about exchanging unwholesome words — I shall dim their radiance." And so the yakṣa followed along behind the two of them. Then the yakṣa thought again: "What is past is past. But if they now speak further unwholesome words, I will certainly dim their radiance."

While the faithless yakṣa was thus thinking and following along behind the two monks, another yakṣa who had faith arrived in that direction and asked the first, "Friend, where are you going?" The faithless yakṣa told him what had happened. The faithful yakṣa said: "Friend, these monks are men of ascetic practice. They go along speaking Dharma talk without interruption. What have the monks done to you? Leave it alone. Let us walk along exchanging words of genuine mutual delight." The faithless yakṣa replied: "Friend, I will certainly not let these two go — come, let us follow them." The faithful yakṣa, knowing it was time to restrain him, followed along together behind the two monks.

Now, as the two monks continued on their way speaking nothing but unwholesome words, they came to a fork in the road. One of the monks went toward the Jeta Grove, and the other went toward the mansion of Mṛgāramātā. The younger monk bowed his head at the feet of the elder and said: "Venerable one, I am going to the mansion of Mṛgāramātā. Please be heedful, and may you go in good health." With that he departed.

Then the faithless yakṣa raised up his hair on end and made to dim the elder monk's radiance. But the faithful yakṣa said: "Friend, do not be so rash. The two of them spoke Dharma. When one said, 'May you be in good health,' health is the supreme gain; and when one said, 'Be heedful,' heedfulness is the root of all virtuous qualities. Indeed, the Blessed One himself declared:

Heedfulness is the ground of the deathless;
heedlessness is the ground of death.
The heedful do not die;
the heedless are as if perpetually dead.

So said he, and with this the faithful yakṣa turned the other back.

The faithful yakṣa then thought: "This is exactly what I should do," and went to where the Blessed One was. He arrived, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Seated there, the yakṣa addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Venerable Blessed One, there ever dwells here a yakṣa who has no faith in the Blessed One's teaching — a vile being, a fierce yakṣa. Venerable One, those who do have faith are very few. Venerable Blessed One, the fierce yakṣa who lacks faith in the Blessed One's teaching and ever dwells here are very many. Venerable One, these noble ones go along speaking unwholesome words, and others follow in their wake. Alas, Blessed One, out of compassion please offer some counsel by which the noble ones would not go along speaking unwholesome words with others following in their wake, and by which the noble ones would be mindful."

The Blessed One said nothing to the yakṣa and remained silent. Then the yakṣa, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had given his assent, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Not long after the yakṣa had gone, the Blessed One, knowing this, had a seat arranged in the midst of the assembly of monks and took his seat. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I have heard from a yakṣa that when monks go along the road speaking unwholesome words, faithless yakṣas seek an opportunity and watch for a weak point."

"Monks, those who have gone forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya — for them to speak unwholesome words is neither seemly nor fitting. Therefore I shall establish rules of conduct for monks when they set out on the road. A monk who sets out on the road shall travel in one of two ways: either speaking on the Dharma, or observing the noble silence. At a place of rest, he shall recite a sacred verse. At a river crossing, he shall recite a verse addressed to the spirit of that river and its deity. At whatever place he takes lodging, he shall recite the third of the Anumodanā verses."

"If a monk who has set out on the road does not properly take up and practice the rules of conduct as established, he shall be guilty of an offence."

The Blessed One, the buddha Bhagavān, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time monks had taken up their robes — robes dyed in colour and completed — slung them over their shoulders, and set out on the road, but the robes became spoiled by dust and grime. The Blessed One then declared: "They should be rolled up and carried that way."

When the Blessed One had said "roll up the robes and carry them," the monks, not knowing how a robe-roll should be made, the Blessed One declared: "Take a length of cloth three cubits long and one and a half cubits wide, fold it in two, and stitch it together."

When the monks turned the ends outward, the roll became like an elephant's trunk. The Blessed One declared: "Do not turn the ends outward; turn them inward at the centre."

When they did not sew the edges and dust got in just the same, the Blessed One declared: "Make something like a net of thread, and then run another thread through it."

When some monks placed the robes they were wearing underneath and pulled the others to the top, and then, opening the roll again and again, they came undone, the Blessed One declared: "Place the robes that are being worn on top, and put the remaining ones underneath."

The Blessed One, the buddha Bhagavān, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time some bandits had waylaid some travellers, shooting at each other, while those who fled took refuge in their own villages. The bandits bound their prisoners tightly, and then, themselves without shelter and tormented by thirst, went searching for water from one place to the next until they found a well somewhere and went to it. The bandit chief said: "Friends, look here for a water-vessel and a rope." They looked, but there was no rope and no water-vessel. The chief said: "Friends, if any travellers come along, take their rope and water-vessel, climb a tree, and keep watch." They climbed a tree and began to look, and from quite a distance they spotted some monks approaching. They said: "Chief, a number of Śākya-sons are coming." He said: "Friends, since they are wise, they will certainly have a carrying rope and a water-vessel." They said: "Chief, if they have them, so much the better; but if they do not, we will slit their bellies and drink their blood." Having made this plan, they waited.

The monks arrived. The bandits asked: "Venerable ones, we are thirsty — do you have a carrying rope and a water-vessel?" The monks replied: "Virtuous ones, we do not."

The bandits became enraged and reached for their weapons. Now, a senior monk (sthavira) in the Saṅgha who was an arhat began to reflect: "Why are these men enraged and reaching for their weapons?" He looked, and he saw that they wanted to kill the monks. He said to them: "Venerable ones, why have you become enraged?" They told him what had happened. He said: "Venerable ones, be at ease — there is a way. Sit down here and drink water." They sat down, and the monks knotted together their carrying rope, lower robes, and sashes, lowered the alms-bowl into the well on this line, drew up water, and gave it to them to drink. Once all the bandits had drunk their fill, they said: "Noble ones, if you had not given us water, we would have killed every one of you. How wonderful — please do keep a carrying rope with you." The monks replied: "Venerable ones, we will do so." The bandits bowed and departed.

The monks too drank as much water as they wished to be satisfied, filled their water-pots and pitchers, and set out, gradually making their way to Śrāvastī. The monks performed the customary welcome greeting of "Welcome, well-come," and then asked: "Venerable ones, did you travel comfortably?" The monks told them everything that had happened. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, I permit it — monks may keep a carrying rope." When the Blessed One had said that monks may keep a carrying rope, the monks began keeping extremely long ones. The Blessed One declared: "One must not keep an extremely long one." They then kept extremely short ones. The Blessed One declared: "One must not keep an extremely short one either. Rather, three lengths of carrying rope are to be kept: long, medium, and short. The long is one hundred and fifty cubits; the short is one hundred cubits; and the medium falls between these two." The Blessed One having said that three lengths of carrying rope are to be kept, the monks kept them. Then, in another region where water was also scarce, monks set out carrying their ropes, and the Blessed One declared: "Carrying ropes are to be kept adapted to the various localities."

The summary verse reads:

Razor-honing and nail-cutting,
medicinal thorns and thorn-wood sticks,
the application of ointment to different kinds of blisters,
and what has been thoroughly refined with fragrance.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A monk's hair had grown very long. He went to a barber and said: "Good man, please cut my hair." The barber thought: "These Śākyan monks are shameless — they have you do work without any payment. If I cut this one's hair and word gets out, others will come too." He kept putting him off for a long time, setting him aside, thinking that the monk himself would lose interest and go away. So the barber gave him an appointment, saying: "Noble one, come back tomorrow — morning or afternoon, whichever you prefer, or at midday." The monk was put off in this way and kept going back again and again. A monk who was a close friend of his saw him going back again and again and said: "Venerable one, why do you keep going there? Is that a relative's house or a family home?" He replied: "Venerable one, it is neither a relative's house

nor a family home — but my hair has grown very long, and I spoke to that barber as follows: 'Please trim my hair, which has grown so long, and it will accrue as merit for you.' Yet he kept putting me off with appointments and would not cut it." The friend said: "Venerable one, have you not heard it said that it is rare to find a craftsman who speaks the truth? Even though he is skilled at cutting hair, the Blessed One has not given permission for it." The monk then related this matter to the other monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "In that case, permission is given. A monk who is skilled in it may cut hair in a secluded place, and there should be no regret in this." The Blessed One having declared that a skilled monk may cut hair in a secluded place, monks went to that monk and said: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has given permission — please trim your hair." He replied: "Venerable ones, it is well that the Blessed One has given permission, but must one trim it with a finger? One also needs a razor, a whetstone, scissors, and tweezers." He said this to the monks at that time, the monks again reported to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, permission is given — barber's implements may be kept for the sake of the Saṅgha."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Kapilavatthu in the Nyagrodha Grove, the pleasure park. When the Blessed One ordained members of the Śākya clan who were living at Kapilavatthu one by one, those who were ordained were by nature very young. They went to sleep exposed and uncovered without any bedding, and they slept that way. Sleeping thus uncovered, their constitutions became unbalanced and they grew feverish, so they went to a physician and said: "Good sir, our bodies have grown feverish — please prescribe a remedy." He said: "Noble ones, please come, and lie and sit as you normally do." They came, and when he saw how they were lying exposed and uncovered, he said: "Noble ones, because you are sleeping uncovered, your constitutions have become unbalanced and you have grown feverish. You should use bedding and sleep wrapped up." They replied: "The Blessed One has not given permission for that." He said: "Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate — he will grant permission." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One at that time, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, permission is given — one may insert bedding and sleep on it." They inserted bedding and slept on it, but still did not recover, so they again spoke to the physician. He said: "Noble ones, you should sleep with stuffed mattresses inside." They replied: "Good sir, the Blessed One has not given permission for that." He said: "Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate — he will grant permission." The monks then reported this at length to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, permission is given — monks may keep stuffed mattresses." When the Blessed One had declared that monks may keep stuffed mattresses, the monks did not know what kind to make. The Blessed One declared: "That cloth should be made four cubits long and one cubit minus a span wide, and stitched; it should then be filled with tree-cotton and used as a mattress."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka park. The passage beginning with "Venerable Pilindavatsa had gone forth" and ending with "Elder, what did you keep?" is as before. He replied: "Venerable ones, I kept mud that had been asked for and given." The Elder asked: "But why did you not keep it now, Venerable one?" He replied: "The Blessed One has not given permission."

The monks then requested this of the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A sick monk may keep mud that has been asked for and given. There is no fault in this."

Here ends the third section of the bases in the minor Vinaya.

The summary verse is:

The elder who was helped, the sick, the inferior pig,
The drawing, the absent bowl,
The one who took up residence, and the wood that was grown.

The second summary verse is:

The elder's entreaty, another's turn,
The restoration ceremony with its interval,
The two kinds of drink,
And the temple at all times.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared: "Every half-month, at the time of the restoration ceremony, the recitation should be performed." When the monks did not know who should perform the recitation, the Blessed One declared: "The elder of the Saṅgha should perform the recitation."

After the Blessed One had declared that the elder of the Saṅgha should perform the recitation, the elder of the Saṅgha took up performing the recitation at the time of the restoration ceremony every half-month. But on a certain occasion, an elder residing in another temple was unable to perform the recitation. The monks said to him: "Elder, the restoration ceremony is approaching — why do you not think of this?" He replied: "Venerable ones, what am I to do if I am unable?"

The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the elder of the Saṅgha is unable, the second elder should perform the recitation."

After the Blessed One had declared that the second elder should perform the recitation, there was on a certain occasion another temple where even the second elder was unable. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If even the second elder is unable, the third elder should perform the recitation."

After the Blessed One had declared that the third elder should perform the recitation, there was on a certain occasion another temple where even the third elder was unable. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If even the third elder is unable, the monks should take turns and perform the recitation."

After the Blessed One had declared that the monks should take turns and perform the recitation, the monks began to take turns performing the recitation. But among those taking turns in rotation, the turn fell on some who were capable and on some who were not. When it fell on a capable monk, he would perform the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra every half-month on the appointed turn. When it fell on an incapable monk, he would say on his appointed turn, "I do not know it — what am I to do?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "He should delegate his turn to whichever monk is capable."

After the Blessed One had declared that the incapable monk, when his turn comes, should delegate to another, there was on a certain occasion another temple where the monk to whom the incapable one's turn had been delegated also declined. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "He should delegate permanently to whichever other capable monk there is."

The Blessed One declared: "Every half-month, the elder of the Saṅgha should perform the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra. If he is unavailable, the second elder should do so. If he too is unavailable, the third elder should do so."

If he too is unavailable, one should recite the text by turns as a choral recitation, or else delegate to whichever other capable monk there is. This was so declared.

Now in another temple there was no one at all who had memorized the Prātimokṣa sūtra in full. The elder of the Saṅgha recited the four rules entailing defeat, and the monks then performed the Poṣadha ceremony based on the remainder. The monks reported this to the Blessed One at that time, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not hold the Poṣadha in that way. Rather, whoever has memorized whatever section should recite that section. If the elder of the Saṅgha has memorized the four rules entailing defeat, he should recite those. Another should recite the thirteen rules requiring a formal meeting of the Saṅgha. Another should recite the two rules of indeterminate cases. Another should recite the thirty rules involving forfeiture. Another should recite the ninety rules of transgression. Another should recite the four rules requiring individual confession. Another should recite the rules of the many trainings. And another should recite the seven rules for settling disputes. If the Poṣadha is joined together in this way, I shall not say that it constitutes an interruption of the Poṣadha." The occasion for this ruling was at Śrāvastī.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "You have declared, Venerable One, what is permitted at the proper time, and you have also declared what is permitted at an improper time. What, Venerable One, is what is permitted at the proper time, and what is what is permitted at an improper time?" The Blessed One replied: "What has not yet been fermented is what is permitted at the proper time. What has been fermented and mixed with water is what is permitted at an improper time." The occasion for this ruling was at Śrāvastī.

The group of six monks, being of evil intent, occupied temple buildings improperly out of miserliness, claiming exclusive use for all seasons, claiming use by turns of residence, claiming use for alternating periods, or claiming prior use by having their footprints already there. As for how they claimed exclusive use for all seasons, it was by saying: "This is my winter temple. This is my spring temple. This is my summer temple." That is how they claimed it for all seasons. As for how they claimed use by turns of residence, it was by saying: "This is my temple for tomorrow. This is my temple for the day after. This is my temple for the day after that." That is how they claimed use by turns. As for how they claimed use for alternating periods, it was by saying: "I am staying here in the morning. I am staying here in the afternoon." That is how they claimed it for alternating periods. As for how they claimed prior use by footprints, it was by saying: "This is my teacher's temple, my preceptor's temple, the temple of one who resides with me, the temple of my attendant, the temple of one I converse with, the temple of one who visits me." That is how they claimed prior use by footprints.

The monks who dwelt in various localities arrived and found themselves without accommodation. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One at that time, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, one must not exclusively occupy the temple buildings of monks by claiming them for all seasons, by turns of residence, for alternating periods, or by having footprints there. If one does so, it becomes a serious offense."

Verse summary:
Enclosures and wooden fences,
roads and wells and Kārttika,
Dharma robes washed and dried,
the ritual portions and the brahmin.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's pleasure garden. At the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, people of the world went and came to the Jeta Grove with great joy and celebration, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself:

"My temple has become a great thoroughfare, and so, if the Blessed One would permit it, I shall enclose it with a fence." Having thought this, he went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he touched his head to the feet of the Blessed One in homage, then sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, this temple has become greatly exposed, and so, if the Blessed One would permit it, I would enclose it with a fence." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, in that case you are permitted to do so. Enclose it."

He enclosed it with a fence, and then, when the time of the rains retreat arrived, the Jeta Grove became completely flooded with water.

Now at the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, he saw that the Jeta Grove was entirely filled with water. He thought to himself: "I enclosed the Jeta Grove with a fence but did not install a drainage outlet, and that is why it has become filled with water like this. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I shall install a drainage outlet." He then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, I enclosed the Jeta Grove with a fence but did not install a drainage outlet, and so it became filled with water and I came to see this. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I would install a drainage outlet." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, in that case you are permitted to do so. Install it."

He installed the drainage outlet. Then cattle came and came again, rubbing their bodies against the wall and boring through it with their horns. At the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw this, he thought: "I enclosed the Jeta Grove with a fence but did not weave a wooden lattice, and that is why cattle come and rub their bodies against it and bore through it with their horns. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I shall weave a wooden lattice around it." He went to where the Blessed One was and, upon arriving, touched his head to the feet of the Blessed One in homage, then sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, I enclosed the Jeta Grove with a fence but did not weave a wooden lattice, and cattle came and came again, rubbing their bodies against it and boring through it with their horns. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I would weave a wooden lattice." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, in that case you are permitted to do so. Weave the wooden lattice."

He wove the wooden lattice, but then those who take what is not given broke apart the wooden lattice and stole the wood. On another occasion, as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was walking along, he saw that the wooden lattice had been broken apart in various places and the wood stolen. He thought: "I enclosed the Jeta Grove with a fence and wove a wooden lattice, yet it has been broken apart in places and the wood stolen. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I shall surround it with a wall." Having thought this, he went to where the Blessed One was and, upon arriving, touched his head to the feet of the Blessed One in homage, then sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, I enclosed the Jeta Grove with a fence and wove a wooden lattice, but because I did not surround it with a wall it was broken apart in places and the wood stolen. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I would surround it with a wall." The Blessed One declared:

"Householder, in that case I permit it. Surround it with a wall." And he surrounded it with a wall.

The occasion for the next rule took place at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī there was a nun named Kārtikā whose hair had grown very long. She went to the barber's shop and said, "Good man, please trim my hair. It will be a source of merit for you." The barber thought to himself: "The ascetics who are sons of the Śākyans are quite demanding, and these nuns likewise put people to work without any payment. If I trim this one's hair, others will keep coming as well. I'll put her off for a long time and she herself will lose interest and give up."
