So he set an appointment for the noble nun, telling her to come in the morning, or at midday, or in the afternoon. She was kept going back and forth by his excuses again and again. A nun who was a friend of hers saw her going back and forth repeatedly and asked her: "Noble one, why do you keep coming here again and again? Is this the house of a relative of yours, or of your family?" She replied: "Noble one, this is neither the house of a relative nor of my family. However, my hair has grown very long, and I went to the barber and said, 'Good man, please cut my very long hair; it will be a source of merit for you.' But he did not cut it and kept making appointments." The other nun said: "Noble one, have you not heard that craftsmen rarely speak truthfully? She may be skilled at cutting hair, but the Blessed One has not granted permission for this." At that point she reported the matter to the nuns, the nuns reported it to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a nun who is skilled in this may cut hair in a secluded spot."

After the Blessed One had declared that a skilled nun may cut hair in a secluded spot, that same nun went to the nun Kārtikā and said: "Noble one, the Blessed One has given permission. Come here and have your hair trimmed." Kārtikā replied: "Noble one, if the Blessed One has given permission, that is excellent. But how is one to trim it with fingers alone? For this one needs a razor, a whetstone, scissors, and tweezers." She then reported this to the nuns, the nuns reported it to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "In that case I permit it. The nuns are to keep a set of razor implements on behalf of the Saṅgha."

The Vinaya of Minor Matters, the Eighteenth Fascicle.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At the time when the Blessed One gave going forth to Ānanda, Bhadrā sent robes both stitched and fully stitched to Śrāvastī. Venerable Ānanda then distributed the stitched and fully stitched robes that had been washed, cleaned, and prepared, and holding an alms bowl that sparkled, he sauntered in front of the monks with an air of conceit. The monks informed the Blessed One of this, and the Blessed One, reflecting on the matter, understood that whatever fault had arisen had come from the monks wearing stitched and fully stitched robes. He then addressed the monks: "Monks, because of this, that foolish person Ānanda distributed the stitched and fully stitched robes that had been washed and cleaned, took up a sparkling alms bowl,

and sauntered in front of the monks with an air of conceit — this is neither seemly nor appropriate. Therefore, a monk must not keep stitched and fully stitched robes. If he keeps them, he commits an offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not keep stitched and fully stitched robes, faithful brahmin householders and lay householders came to offer stitched and fully stitched robes to the monks, but the monks would not accept them. The householders then said: "Noble ones, in the times when no buddha, no Blessed One, has appeared in the world, it is the non-Buddhists who are proper fields of giving. Now that the Blessed One has appeared in the world, you are the proper fields of giving. If you will not accept, shall we have no way to accumulate virtue for the journey from this world to the next?" Upon hearing this, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, accept them with permission, and having accepted them, shake out the shine and use them fully. If they cannot be shaken free of shine by hand, the Blessed One declared: place them in soak and shake out the shine that way." If when soaked and placed thus the shine could still not be removed entirely, the Blessed One declared: "Scrub them in water." If the monks scrubbed them in water and still the shine could not be removed, the Blessed One declared: "If it still cannot be removed even after doing all that, then use them fully — there is no need for remorse in this matter."

Likewise, when faithful brahmins and lay householders offer stitched and fully stitched robes to the Saṅgha, those too should be used fully, following this same procedure in sequence.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park belonging to Prince Jeta. At that time the brahmins and lay householders of Śrāvastī had gathered and assembled in a meeting hall, and were exchanging conversation of this kind among themselves: "The renunciant Gautama, the Blessed One, is not by nature one who distributes, and his hearers too are not by nature ones who distribute. In that case, even those shaven-headed renunciants who are non-Buddhists would be more fitting — not these ones."

Then one brahmin spoke up: "As for whether the renunciant Gautama is by nature one who distributes or not, and whether his hearers are by nature ones who distribute or not — let tomorrow make that clear to you directly." They agreed, saying: "Very well, do it and let us see." He then took a length of cloth and went to the Jeta Grove. He set the cloth down at the edge of the old-age hall and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks of the four directions, saying: "Noble ones, I offer this length of cloth to the Saṅgha — please do with it as you see fit." The senior elder of the Saṅgha replied: "O great brahmin, may you be free of illness. May this act of giving adorn your mind, furnish your mind with what it needs, complete the gathering of meditative practice, bring you attainment of the highest aim, and grant you the robes of gods and humans." The brahmin then bowed his head in a polite gesture and departed.

The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell the monks that this length of cloth was offered by the brahmin in order to test us. Therefore you should divide it equally, and some should receive a full share, some should be listed as receiving it, and some together —

and some should use it to make a tent of robes." The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you wish, Reverend One," and having listened to the Blessed One, he conveyed those very words to the monks: "The Blessed One has declared that this length of cloth was offered by the brahmin in order to test us. Therefore you should divide it equally — some should receive a full share, some should be listed as receiving it, some together, and some should use it to make a tent of robes." The monks replied, "Venerable Ānanda, we shall do exactly as the Blessed One has declared," and they divided it and distributed it in that very way.

Now, the brahmin had risen early and was standing at the gate of Śrāvastī. When the monks, having divided their lower garments that morning, took up their bowls and outer robes and set out to enter Śrāvastī for alms, the brahmin said to them, "Noble ones, what have you done with the cloth I offered to the Saṅgha?"

One monk replied, "Great brahmin, the Saṅgha divided it equally and distributed it. My own share — this is what I received as a full portion." Another said, "Mine was listed as received." Another said, "Mine was placed together with another's." And another said, "Mine was made into a tent of robes."

The brahmin then thought to himself: "Those who say that the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan have no custom of sharing things — well, a flash of surprise has just struck me, for these great ones do indeed have a custom of sharing. I shall go forth among them alone." Faith arose in him, and he went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him thus: "Reverend One, if I may go forth and receive full ordination in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and so obtain the state of a monk, I shall live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

The Blessed One declared, "Excellent! Excellent, brahmin! The resolve you have generated is good, and going forth is supreme. A wise person who sees five benefits ought rightly to be devoted to going forth alone. What are the five? A wise person who sees that he will attain the unsullied accomplishment of his own goal ought rightly to be devoted to going forth alone. A wise person who sees that even those who were his slaves, his employees, those who acted on his instructions, those who were under his authority, and those who worked for his pleasure will themselves become worthy of offerings and worthy of praise ought rightly to be devoted to going forth alone. A wise person who sees that he will attain the unsurpassed accomplishment and bliss of nirvāṇa ought rightly to be devoted to going forth alone. A wise person who sees that even if he falls short of attaining the unsurpassed accomplishment and bliss of nirvāṇa, he will be reborn among the gods ought rightly to be devoted to going forth alone. And a wise person who sees that going forth has been praised in many ways by the buddhas and by the noble ones — the holy śrāvakas of the buddhas who have entered [the path] rightly — ought rightly to be devoted to going forth alone. Therefore, go forth well."

The Blessed One then called out, "Come here, monk," and thereby conferred on him the going-forth and full ordination, and gave him instructions.

By striving and applying himself with vigor, he came to understand this very wheel of saṃsāra — both its moving and its stationary parts — as one fifth, and he realized that all aspects of the formations are subject to deterioration, downfall, dispersion, and destruction by their very nature. Having abandoned all afflictions, he directly actualized arhathood. He was an arhat, free from attachment throughout the three realms — equal in composure, like clay and gold; equal in composure, like the sky and the palm of the hand; equal in composure, like leather and sandalwood. Through knowledge he had torn open the hollow cave-door of ignorance. He had attained supernormal cognitions and the four individual discriminating awarenesses. He had turned his back on existence, on material gain, and on honor. He became one to be revered, praised, and addressed with respect by the gods, together with Indra and those in his retinue.

The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, for one who is restrained there are these benefits, and there are others as well. Therefore, monks, if a gain of food arises, divide it equally, even if it be only the leaves of a grain plant. If a gain of cloth arises, divide it equally, even if it be only the wick of a butter lamp."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who was devoted to purity and who wished to go forth. He thought: "I shall go forth into the teaching of whichever one whose purity brings contentment to my mind." He wandered to the dwellings of the non-Buddhists, but their purity did not bring contentment to his mind. He then thought: "I have visited all the non-Buddhists, and none of them has brought contentment to my mind. Now then, the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, remain. Let me go and visit them." With this in mind he went to the Jeta Grove.

Just then he saw the venerable Śāriputra taking up his begging bowl and setting out to go to the latrine. He thought: "This one is the foremost among the śrāvakas of the śramaṇa Gautama. Let me watch and see just how he conducts himself regarding purity." He followed along behind him.

Now, since arhats do not engage their unintentional primordial wisdom in seeing, the venerable Śāriputra entered into deliberate attention and, knowing that this brahmin was following him, he thought: "Why is the brahmin following behind me? He must wish to see how I attend to purity." And he again turned his attention to consider: "Does this man have any root of virtue, or not?" He saw that he did. He then considered: "On whom does it depend?" and he saw that it depended on himself alone.

Having reflected thus, Śāriputra removed his sandals and set aside his outer robe. He then placed seven mounds of earth on one side, seven mounds on another side, and two mounds of earth on yet another side. Then, taking three mounds of earth, he began to relieve himself in such a way that the brahmin could see. After finishing, he wiped himself with one mound of earth, and washed with two. Then he rose slowly and came to that place, and with his left hand washed with seven mounds of earth. Then he washed with both hands together using seven mounds. Then he scrubbed from his shoulders downward with one mound of earth. Having washed his hands, he then washed his begging bowl with the second. Then he rose slowly, and with calm deportment he put on his robe and washed his feet.

When the brahmin saw this, he became filled with faith. He thought: "A single mound of earth used by the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, is supreme — not even a hundred of the non-Buddhists can equal that." Knowing this, he touched his head to the feet of the venerable Śāriputra and addressed the venerable Śāriputra with these words:

"O noble Śāriputra, if I may obtain the going forth and full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and thereby receive the status of a monk, I will practice the holy life in the presence of the noble Śāriputra."

Śāriputra said: "Excellent, brahmin! The intention you have aroused is good, and the going forth is supreme. The Blessed One himself, with the wisdom that sees five benefits, declared that one ought to be devoted to the going forth alone" — and so on as before, up to — "the buddhas, and the noble śrāvakas of the buddhas who have entered correctly, those holy persons, have praised the going forth in many ways; and with the wisdom that sees this, one ought to be devoted to the going forth alone" — thus he spoke.

And so he gave him the going forth and full ordination well, bestowed instruction upon him, and that one, through earnest and sustained effort, came to know this very wheel of cyclic existence with its five parts — both moving and unmoving — as before, up to: "he came to speak with respect."

Then the monks, having grown uncertain, asked the Blessed One, the buddha, to cut through all their doubts: "Venerable One, behold how the elder Śāriputra caused this brahmin of pure conduct to arise in faith, freed him from the wilderness of cyclic existence, and established him in nirvāṇa — in accomplishment and happiness unsurpassed, utterly supreme, and final."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, not only now — hear also how in times past he turned this man away from theft and established him in the five bases of moral discipline. Monks, long ago there was a brahmin who lived on a rocky crag. He took a wife from among those equal to his own station, and together with her he took pleasure, rejoiced, and made merry. While they were taking pleasure, rejoicing, and making merry in this way, at another time a living being entered into the wife. Eight or nine months passed, and she gave birth to a girl who was beautiful of form, pleasing and lovely to behold. After giving birth, he held a grand celebration lasting twenty-one days — seven times three — and gave her a name befitting her lineage. He raised and nurtured her, and she grew to adulthood.

Then one day five hundred bandits came to that rocky crag, intent on plunder. Their leader was tormented by thirst and entered the brahmin's home. As soon as he entered, he saw the girl. He said to her: 'Girl, give me water.' She replied: 'Wait just a moment.' She said nothing more, but quickly blew out the lamp. The bandit chief gazed at the girl and reflected. The girl, having blown out the lamp, was looking into the water. The bandit chief said: 'Girl, what are you looking at?' She said: 'I am looking at the water.' He said: 'What is there to look at in that?' She said: 'Because bubbles or strands of hair are coming in.' He said: 'Girl, I have entered here in order to harm you, and I intend to pour poison for you — yet you speak to me thus!'

She then spoke these verses:

Those deceitful ones who seize what belongs to others —
whatever deed it is that bandits do,
whether they do it or whether they do not,
I myself must ever guard the Dharma.

He was greatly pleased and said: 'Girl, if I were to make you my sister, what would you do? Tell me.' She replied: 'If you were to generate attachment to the wealth of others, and were then struck by an arrow and died, I would be desolate with the suffering of separation from my brother and would cry out in grief — I would not rejoice. Therefore a brother who is a thief — such a one as that — I do not need.'

'Therefore, if you are able to take up fully the five bases of moral training, then I will make you my sister.' Though he was unwilling, she spoke in a pleasing, agreeable manner, and he became greatly delighted and eager to become her brother. He said: 'Sister, excellent — let it be so.' She turned him away from banditry and established him in the five bases of moral training.

Monks, what do you think? The leader of that band of bandits at that time and place — he is none other than this brahmin here. The brahmin's daughter at that time and place — she is none other than the monk Śāriputra. And even then, as now, Śāriputra turned that one away from theft and established him in the five bases of training. Now, too, having purified and inspired him with faith, he has freed him from the wilderness of cyclic existence and established him in the utterly final nirvāṇa — the accomplishment and supreme bliss that is the absolute culmination.

Monks, thus there are these and other benefits of purity. Therefore, monks, just as Śāriputra did, practice purity in that same manner.

The summary verse:

Patches and arm-cloths and sweat-cloths,
nuns and the months,
residences with six furnishings,
and three ways of sitting on a seat.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the monks were using robes distributed in due season without taking care of them, and as a result the stitching at the edges frayed apart. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: 'Frayed edges of robes are to be patched.' When the Blessed One had said that frayed edges of robes were to be patched, the monks applied patches; yet the threads continued to fray. The Blessed One then declared: 'Patches are to be applied at intervals throughout.'

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared: 'An outer robe is to be cared for as one would care for one's skin.' Now certain monks had no other suitable robe to wear, and so they wore the outer robe all the time; in the heat of summer it became soaked with perspiration from the armpits, grew soiled and dank, and developed an unpleasant odor. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: 'A sweat-cloth is to be inserted at the armpit side.'

When the Blessed One had declared that a sweat-cloth was to be inserted at the armpit side of the outer robe, the monks did not know what kind of sweat-cloth to make. The Blessed One declared: 'A piece of cloth that is half a cubit wide and one cubit long — that is to be inserted on that side.' The monks sewed it in. The Blessed One declared: 'It is not to be sewn in.' When it became soiled, the Blessed One declared: 'It is to be washed from time to time and turned.' The monks inserted it on one side only. The Blessed One declared: 'It is to be inserted on both sides.' When the Blessed One had declared that it was to be turned, the monks dyed it saffron. The Blessed One declared: 'It is not to be dyed saffron; it is to be turned by wringing it out.'

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who had taken a wife from a family of equal rank.

He played with her, delighted in her, and sported with her in joy. While they were playing, delighting, and sporting together, at another time a being entered into his wife's womb. Nine months passed, and she gave birth to a daughter. A great birth celebration was held, and the girl was given the name Candramāsā, "Moon-Month." She was raised and nurtured until she grew up.

Then at another time, the Great Mistress of Creatures Gautamī went forth and received full ordination. After that, the Great Mistress of Creatures Gautamī, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred, went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, and bowed with her head to the Blessed One's two feet, then sat down to one side.

Once she was seated to one side, the Blessed One properly instructed, properly guided, properly exhorted, and properly delighted the Great Mistress of Creatures Gautamī with a Dharma-endowed discourse. Having properly instructed, properly guided, properly exhorted, and properly delighted her with a Dharma-endowed discourse in many ways, he then fell silent.

Thereupon the Great Mistress of Creatures Gautamī rose from her seat, turned and faced toward the Blessed One with hands pressed together in reverence, and said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you have taught the Vinaya of monks to the monks. Pray, out of compassion, may the Blessed One also teach the Vinaya of nuns to the nuns."

The Blessed One declared: "Gautamī, for a Tathāgata to teach even a single phrase at a time — that is not the proper way, and there is no occasion for it. However, if there are some nuns who are willing to take up what I teach in one recitation, then I shall teach it in that manner."

Then at that very moment the nun Candramāsā assembled together and sat there. The nun Candramāsā rose from her seat, turned and faced toward the Blessed One with hands pressed together in reverence, and said this to the Blessed One: "The Blessed One has spoken once. I wish to receive and hold it; please teach it."

Thereupon the Blessed One taught her, and she retained what was spoken in that single recitation.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, among my śrāvaka nuns, the foremost in retention of what has been heard is this very nun Candramāsā."

The Blessed One then reflected: "Everywhere, a nun such as Candramāsā, or even one who resembles Candramāsā, will not easily arise. Therefore monks should also take up the Vinaya of nuns and retain it, and should teach it to the nuns, giving it as well to those who recite and those who inquire."

With this in mind, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, though the nun Candramāsā has received the Vinaya of nuns taught in a single recitation tomorrow, nonetheless, since everywhere a nun like Candramāsā or one resembling her will not arise, monks too should take up the Vinaya of nuns, retain it, teach it to the nuns, and give it to those who recite and those who inquire."

The Blessed One then said: "One should cultivate the two qualities of calm abiding and special insight by relying on moral discipline and abiding in moral discipline." And the nun Candramāsā, in accordance with the Vinaya, by relying on moral discipline and abiding in moral discipline, strove and exerted herself through the practice of meditative concentration and recitation. She came to know directly that this very fifth portion of the wheel of cyclic existence — whether moving or unmoving — and understood by its very nature of reality that all formations are subject to deterioration, downfall, disintegration, and destruction.

Having abandoned all mental afflictions, she directly realized arhathood. The arhat nun, freed from attachment to the three realms, her mind equal to gold and butter, equal to the sky and the palm of a hand, comparable to heartwood and sandalwood, had torn open the dark cavern of ignorance with the light of wisdom. She had attained the higher knowledges and the individual perfect insights. She had turned her back on craving, gain, and honor. She came to be venerated, revered, and spoken of with reverence by the gods of the faculty realms and the realms close to them.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Among my śrāvaka nuns, the foremost in great wisdom, great eloquence, and retaining what she has heard is none other than the nun Candramāsā."

The monks, having given rise to doubt, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One, to resolve all their doubts: "Venerable Blessed One, what karma did the nun Candramāsā perform, such that through the karmic maturation of that action she came to possess great wisdom and great eloquence, and such that the Blessed One also proclaimed her foremost in retaining what she has heard, and such that having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One she abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhathood?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it was the nun Candramāsā herself who performed and accumulated the karma — from the passage beginning 'she obtained a retinue' down to 'ripening as fruit for embodied beings' — just as before."

"Monks, in a past age, ninety-one great aeons ago, when the lifespan of beings was eighty thousand years, a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly complete buddha arose as a Teacher in the world — endowed with knowledge and feet, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide and driver of persons to be tamed, Teacher of gods and humans — by the name of the Blessed One buddha Vipaśyin. He traveled with a retinue of sixty-two thousand monks to Rājagṛha at Jīvaka's mango grove, and dwelt there in that grove.

"At that time there lived in Rājagṛha at Jīvaka's mango grove a householder who had taken a wife from an equal family. He sported with her, delighted with her, and enjoyed her company. While they were sporting, delighting, and enjoying each other's company, after some time a being entered the wife's womb. After nine months had passed, a daughter was born. A great birth feast was held, a name befitting the family was given, and she was raised and reared until she had grown up.

"Now that householder was a man of faith, and at the time of the pravāraṇā ceremony he took the girl and went to the nuns' rains-retreat dwelling. He performed the pravāraṇā for the community of nuns with various implements such as needles and knives, and so forth, offering them individually to the nuns of the Saṅgha.

"The girl, seeing the beauty of the occasion, gave rise to faith, and said to her father: 'Father, I too would like to perform the pravāraṇā for the community of nuns.' The householder replied: 'Daughter, excellent — do perform the pravāraṇā just so.' She then performed the pravāraṇā for the community of nuns with distinguished gifts of needles, knives, gold, iron, and other implements. With intense and powerful delight, she went from the eldest to the last, prostrated at their feet, and made this aspiration: 'By this wholesome root of generating the mind of awakening and giving away things to be given, may I come to possess great wisdom and great eloquence, and may I retain what I hear.'

"Monks, what do you think? The daughter of that householder — she is none other than the very nun Candramāsā herself."

By this very act — having performed the pravāraṇā for the community of nuns of the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Vipaśyin with distinguished gifts of needles, knives, gold, iron, and other implements, and having made the aspiration, 'By this wholesome root of generating the mind of awakening and giving away things to be given, may I come to possess great wisdom and great eloquence, and may I retain what I hear' — through the karmic maturation of that deed, she has now come to possess great wisdom and great eloquence, and retains what she hears.

Furthermore, she went forth under the scriptural teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, and though during that life she practiced the holy life for a full lifespan, she did not attain even a single collection of virtuous qualities. The preceptor under whom she went forth was designated by the Blessed One, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa, as supreme among those who retain what they hear. And so she made this aspiration: 'Although I practiced the holy life for an entire lifetime before the Blessed One, the perfectly and completely awakened, peerless field of offerings, Kāśyapa, without attaining even a single collection of virtuous qualities, by this wholesome root may I — just as my preceptor was designated by the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa as supreme among those who retain what they hear — likewise be designated by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the chief of Śākya kings, as supreme among those who retain what they hear.' Through the power of that aspiration, she has now been designated by the Tathāgata as supreme among those who retain what they hear.

Therefore, monks, from the passage beginning, 'The karmic maturation of those that are wholly dark is likewise wholly dark; the karmic maturation of those that are wholly bright is likewise wholly bright,' strive accordingly. Monks should train in just that way — and all that follows is as before.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park of Prince Jeta. At that time a young monk was traveling together with another monk, and they arrived at Śrāvastī. The other monk went to the fine lodging house of Mṛgāramātā, while the young monk went to the Jeta Grove and sought lodging with a monk there. He sat for a little while in that monk's presence and then said: 'I left my bowl and robe in a certain great assembly hall and have come here; I will retrieve them and return.' The other monk said: 'Go, child, and come back quickly.' He replied: 'Teacher, what would you have me do there? I will come back quickly' — and having prostrated at his feet, he departed and proceeded in due course to that assembly hall.

Now, the community had established a rule that no one was to spend even a single night in that assembly hall without the community's permission to reside there. Having duly obtained permission from a monk to lodge there, he slept that night. At dawn he thought: 'Let me go and look in on the teacher,' and so he went to the teacher's lodging, knocked on the door, and offered his respects. 'Are you well?' he asked. 'Child, I am ill; I am not well.' The young monk then thought: 'To go off and abandon a sick teacher — that is not right for me.

The Blessed One had also, for this very reason, granted permission for them to lodge together in order to care for one another in illness. It was with that in mind that he had tended to the teacher, thinking: 'When he recovers, I will go.' Having nursed him back to health, the young monk said: 'Venerable sir, please be informed that I shall take my leave.' The teacher replied: 'Child, I wonder whether you are slightly unwell?' 'Venerable sir, there is not the slightest thing wrong with me. However, I did not come here to reside; I came only to retrieve the robe and bowl I had left behind. The community has established a rule that no one is to spend even a single night in the assembly hall without the community's permission to reside there. It was for that reason that I properly obtained permission to lodge, and then, when you fell ill, I thought: "To go off and abandon my teacher — that is not right for me. The Blessed One, for this very reason, granted permission for them to lodge together in order to care for one another in illness. So I will care for the teacher, and when he recovers I will go." Now that you have recovered, venerable sir, please be informed that I shall take my leave.' 'Excellent, excellent, venerable one. Continue to dwell just as you have entered upon the path, and let those who share quarters with you and those who serve as attendants fulfil their duties toward their preceptors and teachers. If they fulfil them in that way, then — just as the blue lotus (utpala) arises from the water — virtuous qualities will grow and flourish. Noble one, be heedful, and go.' The young monk paid his respects and proceeded in due course to the Jeta Grove. When his own teacher saw him, he said: 'Welcome, venerable one. Why have you been so long in coming?' The young monk recounted all that had happened. The teacher said: 'Excellent, excellent, venerable one. Continue to dwell just as you have entered upon the path, and let those who share quarters with you and those who serve as attendants fulfil their duties toward their preceptors and teachers. If they fulfil them in that way, then — just as the blue lotus arises from the water — virtuous qualities will grow and flourish.'

Now that monk was seized by doubt. He wondered: 'Is that same lodging-place sufficient, or must another be given?' And so he raised the matter with the monks, and the monks asked the Blessed One about it. The Blessed One declared: 'Monks, he obtained only a temporary permission to lodge. Therefore that very same lodging-place is sufficient; no other is needed.'

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī a young monk had lodged with a monk who was a renunciant, and the young monk thought: 'The Blessed One has said that to ordain monks, to give them full ordination, and then to give them no instruction and no guidance — that is worse than butchering them.' And further: 'Even an attendant is like a student in this regard. Since I too am a renunciant, I should entrust this one to someone who will give something.' Thinking thus, he went to a certain monk and said: 'Please teach this young venerable one.' The monk replied: 'If you will serve me, then on that condition I will teach him.' The young monk said: 'I respectfully ask to be taught.' And so he began to train under him.

At another time the young monk fell ill, and the teacher with whom he had lodged nursed him in his sickness. Then at yet another time, when that very teacher with whom he had lodged fell ill, the young monk did not look in on him — and likewise did not look in on him even after three times had passed. Then the teacher said to him: 'Venerable one, go to someone else and take up residence there.' The young monk replied:

"Noble one, I have come to you alone, and I am not lacking in anything." The teacher replied: "Venerable one, it is true that you lack nothing. Yet I was in want, and when you fell ill I nursed you through your sickness — so when I fell ill three times over, why did you not look in on me even once? Go, and take up residence with someone of your own kind who would give lodging to one as disrespectful as you."

The young monk had no reply and sat in silence. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One who lodges with a preceptor must attend upon the preceptor."

Then at another time the reading-teacher fell ill, and the young monk did not look in on him. When the reading-teacher had recovered, the young monk went to him and said: "Teacher, please assign me a text to recite." The teacher replied: "Venerable one, when I was ill you did not look in on me even once. Go, and learn from someone who would take on a pupil as disrespectful as you."

Again the young monk had no reply and sat in silence. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must attend upon one's reading-teacher."

After the Blessed One had declared that one must attend upon one's reading-teacher, it came about at yet another time that both the reading-teacher and the residential preceptor fell ill at once, and the young monk did not know whose attendance he should give first. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If one is able, one should attend upon both. If one cannot, one should attend upon the residential preceptor — for one may reside without a reading-teacher, but one may not reside without a residential preceptor."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the prince Jeta's grove. A certain person who wished to go forth came to a monk, and that monk gave him the going-forth and performed his full ordination, then left to wander through the provinces. As for the residential teacher who had remained with him, he had gathered him only with material things and not with Dharma, so that young monk took up residence with someone else.

Now the Blessed One had taught the four bases of attraction: giving, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and consistency of purpose. Because this monk gathered his student through both Dharma and material things, that student kept watch over the teacher at all times and held him constantly in mind.

In due course the preceptor of that young monk had wandered through the provinces as he pleased and then returned to Śrāvastī. When those who were newly leading the holy life saw him coming, they rose from their seats. Those who were elder monks received him with the customary greeting of "welcome." But that same young monk who had lived with him did not rise from his seat.

The other monks said to him: "Venerable one, when your preceptor arrives, some of those leading the holy life rise to their feet, some come forward openly to greet him, and some receive him with the words 'welcome.' Since they all conduct themselves thus, it is not fitting that you, seeing him, should not rise from your seat."

He replied: "Was it he who ordained me through material generosity, or through Dharma? Remembering that, why should I rise?" They said: "Venerable one, say no such thing."

Did not the Blessed One also declare: "The person in dependence upon whom another person, trusting in the Dharma-Vinaya as taught by the Tathāgata, has shaved hair and beard, donned the ochre robe, and gone forth from home into homelessness with genuine faith — that person can never easily be repaid by that other person for as long as life lasts, not even with robes, alms food, medicines for illness, bedding, and requisites"?

The other monks said to him: "Venerable one, saying such a thing is not fitting." He had nothing to say in reply and sat there in silence.

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Co-residents and attendant monks must rise from their seat the moment they see their preceptor. The moment a preceptor is seen there must be no remaining seated."

When the Blessed One had declared that no one was to remain seated the moment a preceptor was seen, certain others came who were unable to sit with a preceptor — they would arrive, sit for a short while, and then leave. Some of them would scold the preceptors and teachers, while others would be pleased with them. Those toward whom there was scolding would receive no lodging allocation going forward, nor would such a monk take them under his own care. Those toward whom there was pleasure he would take under his care — but then those previous teachers would fall into dispute and depart, and even they would not be taken in. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Even toward those who are unable to sit with a preceptor, everything is to be done; and toward the previous teachers too, everything is to be done. Nevertheless, one should make it one's chief concern to please both parties, and one should consult both. If in every single matter it is the preceptors who are present, then it is to them that one should address one's questions."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the monastery of Prince Jeta. A monk gave lodging to a certain young man. That young man spent half a month there, and when the time of the restoration ceremony came he went to his host and said: "Teacher, I pay homage to you. I request that you bless the restoration ceremony." The monk said: "Good sir, how could I become your teacher?" The young man said: "Because it is to you yourself that I was assigned as a lodger." The monk said: "Good sir, one who assigns a lodger to someone as disrespectful and impudent as you — understand it was he who did so, and make your request to him." The young man had nothing to say in reply and sat there in silence.

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, perceiving that some slight fault had arisen, reflected that it had arisen from monks not attending upon their preceptors and teachers at the three times of day. Therefore, thinking that co-residents and attendant monks should go to visit their preceptors and teachers at the three times of day, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore co-residents and attendant monks should go at the three times of day to visit their preceptors and teachers."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the monastery of Prince Jeta. A monk gave lodging to a certain young monk and raised him like a son. On another occasion that young monk prepared to go on a journey through the region and said: "Teacher, I pay homage to you. Please take note: I am going to travel through the region." The teacher said: "My son, are you not the least bit unwell?" He replied: "Teacher, I am not in the least unwell. Yet I am eager to travel through the region and shall return again."

The teacher said: "My son, if you have a change of heart along the way, then turn back." The young monk replied: "Teacher, very well — I shall turn back," and departed. Before long, he did have a change of heart along the way, and he thought: "My teacher has provided me with all my requisites, yet I left — that was wrong. I shall turn back." So thinking, he returned, and when the teacher saw him he said: "My son, why have you come back? Have you forgotten something?" He replied: "Teacher, I have forgotten nothing at all. Yet I thought: 'My teacher has furnished me with all my requisites — what purpose is there in going?' And so I have returned." The teacher said: "My son, if you have turned back, that is good. Your teacher is none other than myself." Then the teacher thought: "Is it sufficient that this one simply stay here, or should I give him instruction from the outset?" He then raised the matter with the monks, and the monks put it before the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, if the preceptor has not dismissed him yet the attendant has, it is said that the lodging-arrangement is not broken. If the preceptor has dismissed him yet the attendant has not, it is said that the lodging-arrangement is not broken. If neither the preceptor nor the attendant has dismissed him, it is said that the lodging-arrangement is not broken. If both the preceptor and the attendant have dismissed him, then it is to be said that the lodging-arrangement is broken."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there was a certain teacher living among the assembly of monks who set many young men to studying. On another occasion that teacher fell ill, and yet those monks did not look in on him again; and even when he fell ill a second and a third time, those monks still did not look in on him. Then on another occasion he recovered, and his attendants came to him. One said: "Teacher, please give me a recitation lesson." Another said: "Please give me a lesson in question and answer." Yet another said: "I request instruction." The teacher replied: "Venerable ones, I was ill three times over and not once did any of you look in on me — so go to such a disrespectful person as yourselves to receive teachings and recitations." Then the monks put the matter before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "You must attend upon the reading-teacher." When all of them had done so, their accumulation of virtue diminished, and the Blessed One then declared: "Do it in turns." When they began doing it in rotation, they said to an elderly monk who was staying there: "Elder, tomorrow it is your turn." He replied: "Venerable ones, should I serve the teacher by turns? I shall serve him by myself alone. The rest of you may set your minds at ease." They said: "Elder, if that is how it is, excellent." And since the Blessed One has also said, "Whoever attends upon the sick attends upon me," the elder said: "Noble one, you should do so." He then began to tend to the sick monk, and that monk recovered. Knowing the state of his own body, the monk said: "Teacher, please give me a teachings-lesson." The elder replied: "It is not yet your turn; wait a while." Again he said: "Teacher, let there be a recitation and a question session." Again the elder replied: "It is not yet your turn; wait a while." Then the monk said: "Teacher, if tending the sick is my turn, while reading and recitation are the turns of those others — please understand why I say this." The elder replied: "My son, stay here until everything is done."

He said nothing and remained silent. At that time, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One who is constantly serving others should not become displeased, and should give to others their scripture lessons, recitations, and question sessions."

When both skilled and unskilled monks were reading together, and scripture lessons were given to the skilled ones in a way that caused harm to the unskilled, the Blessed One declared: "Scripture lessons, recitations, and question sessions should be given to them as well, according to occasion."

Summary verse: Abandoning the sick, the preceptor, the half-month arrival, and the one who conducts the reading of the assembly — these are correctly taught as the summary topics.

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks went to the house of a noble family. Those hosts brought out a chair and said: "Noble ones, please be seated as you like." All of them sat down at once and the chair broke. The monks struck one another with horse-whips. Other monks came there, and seeing what had happened, one said: "Venerable ones, why did you behave in such an unseemly manner — was it to cause laughter?" The group of six replied: "Did someone drink wine? Did someone eat garlic? Did they do these things too? What else was done? Was the chair broken? Was the wood used up? Are the woodworkers dead?" The others, displeased, said nothing and remained silent. At that time, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, six should not sit on a single chair." When the Blessed One had declared that six should not sit on a single chair, five sat on it and the same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "Five should not sit on it either." Four sat on it and the same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "Four should not sit on it either — and furthermore, three should not sit on a large seat; two may sit on a medium seat; and one only on a small seat."

Summary verse: The attendant to the sick, climbing a tree, receiving full ordination while leprous, and cutting off a hand — these are correctly taught as the summary topics.

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Neyaka, a novice, wished to receive full ordination. He approached the monk who was to perform the act of full ordination, and the monk who would train him privately, and he petitioned the monks who were to come to the assembly. The novice then took his robe and mat, went ahead to the assembly hall, swept the assembly hall, and arranged the seats. But the monks did not come. As Neyaka looked around, he saw a flowering tree and said: "Novice, gather flowers from that tree and distribute them to the monks." He climbed up but did not get a firm footing, fell, and broke his arm. That very injury became an obstacle to his receiving full ordination as a monk. At that time, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Just as the eldest son of a wheel-turning king, who is worthy of receiving consecration, has not yet been consecrated and therefore must be guarded and tended during that interval, so too a novice who wishes to receive full ordination from a monk must likewise be guarded and tended. Therefore a monk must not allow a novice who wishes to receive full ordination to climb a tree. If he permits it and the novice climbs, it becomes a serious transgression."

The Minor Vinaya. The nineteenth fascicle.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. There was a man of the Kosala kingdom in the service of King Prasenajit who was known as "the Great Inner Chamberlain." On another occasion the king became displeased with him, and he thought to himself: "Kings are difficult to please no matter what one does. I will go and take ordination." And so he went to the Jeta Grove. Now it was the practice of the group of six monks that one or another of them would never leave the gate of the Jeta Grove unattended, and so the venerable Nanda was sitting at the gate. Since Nanda had known this man before, he greeted him as he approached, saying the customary welcome: "Great one, it has been a long time — like the moon that has stayed away — where have you come from?" The man replied: "Noble one, one who is seen again and again becomes contemptible; it is good to be seen after a long absence. Noble one, what need has brought you here?" "Noble one, the king is difficult to please. I am unable to satisfy the god — and so I will go forth into ordination." "Great one, your intention is good — excellent! Renunciation is supreme. The Blessed One himself, beginning with 'He perceived five benefits' and ending with 'Going forth has been praised in many ways by the buddhas, by the noble śrāvakas of the buddhas who have entered properly, and by noble, holy persons' — just as before." "Then go forth well!" And so that man went forth and received full ordination.

The king then said to his ministers: "Wise ones, if the Great One is not to be seen, he must have died." They replied: "Your majesty, he has not fled anywhere, but at your majesty's command he went to the Jeta Grove and took ordination." "Who ordained him?" "The venerable Nanda did." Upon hearing this the king became furious, and he sent a messenger to Nanda, saying: "Noble ones, did you ordain one who had been expelled by us? If you ordain the Great One, then I will have you, the venerable noble-born one, the one with the garland, and the rainy-season women all ordained too, and you yourselves can govern the kingdom!" Nanda sent this reply: "Your majesty, come here. You, the venerable noble-born one, the one with the garland, and the rainy-season woman — all of you take ordination, and I myself will govern the kingdom. Did I deceive your Great One or anyone else and ordain them? Whoever comes to the Jeta Grove and petitions me — those I ordain." When the king heard this he became displeased. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, perceiving the fault, considered: "Whatever small fault has arisen here has come about through monks' ordaining those expelled by the king. Therefore monks must not ordain those expelled by the king." And he declared to the monks: "Monks, the deluded man Nanda ordained a minister, and the king has become displeased. Therefore, monks must not give full ordination to one who has been expelled by the king."

Whenever someone wishing to go forth comes to any monk, that monk must ask whether the person has been expelled by the king. If he gives full ordination without having asked, he commits a serious offence. When the Blessed One had declared that one expelled by the king must not be ordained, some came from distant regions, some came whose background was unknown, and some came who had not been granted permission. The monks were uncertain and did not ordain these people either. Then the Blessed One declared: "Those who come from distant regions, those whose background is unknown, and those who have not been granted permission — these may be ordained; one should not feel remorse in such cases."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana), the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, the benefactor of the destitute. The venerable Nanda shaved his hair and beard, and shortly thereafter, early in the morning, he put on his Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī for alms. As he proceeded gradually along the street, there happened to be a brahmin teaching the brahminic sacred texts to about five hundred brahmin youths. This brahmin was fierce, dissolute, and rough, and he said to one of the brahmin youths: "Hey, brahmin youth — can you jab the top of this shaven-headed ascetic's head with a shoulder-pole?" The youth replied: "If the master goes first, I'll follow." And so he went over to Nanda and struck his head with a shoulder-pole. The venerable Nanda turned around and looked at the brahmin, whereupon the brahmin grew all the more enraged and said: "Strike the brahmin youth again!" The youth struck him twice more with the shoulder-pole, and the venerable Nanda thought: "I looked back — whatever comes of it, let it be." And he went on his way.

He arrived at the Jeta Grove, finished the business of the meal, washed his alms bowl, and said to the monks: "Venerable ones, do not go to the great main thoroughfare." The monks asked: "Why?" He told them: "There in that street a fierce, dissolute, and rough brahmin is teaching the brahminic sacred texts to about five hundred brahmin youths, and he jabbed me twice with a shoulder-pole." They said: "What was your offence in this?" He replied: "Venerable ones, one thing was an offence, and the second was not. How was the first an offence and how was the second not? Without any provocation he jabbed me with a shoulder-pole, and I turned and looked back at him — that was the offence. That he then jabbed me a second time after I had turned to look at him — that was not an offence." The venerable Ānanda heard this and said: "Noble one, what are you saying?" Nanda replied: "It is nothing of consequence, great one." Ānanda said: "Noble one, I have heard it; please tell it again." Nanda recounted what had happened, and Ānanda, shaking his head three times, thought: "I will go and confront him and be displeased." Thinking thus, he shaved his head again, anointed it with sesame oil, washed it, and early in the morning put on his lower robe, took up his alms bowl and Dharma robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. As he proceeded gradually along the street, the brahmin was distracted elsewhere and did not see him. But as the venerable Ānanda began to walk right in front of him, the brahmin saw him and said to a brahmin youth: "Brahmin youth, go and jab the head of this shaven-headed ascetic with a shoulder-pole." The venerable Ānanda, hearing this, said: "Why send the wretch? Come yourself!" When these words were spoken, the brahmin grew furious and went himself and jabbed Ānanda with a shoulder-pole. Ānanda then seized the brahmin by the arm and said: "Shall I strike back — or shall we go to the king's palace?" And grasping the brahmin by the arm, he dragged him along.

He then called over those brahmin youths, and they too seized the brahmin's other arm and dragged him along. The venerable Ānanda, possessed of great physical strength, took those five hundred brahmin youths and the brahmin and dragged them to the gate of the king's palace, where he sat down.

Now it is the nature of things that whenever the group of six monks sat in anger at the gate of the king's palace, the palace of King Prasenajit would begin to tremble. The king looked and saw this, and said to a man: "Go and look — it seems some of the noble group of six have come to the gate." The man went and looked: the venerable Ānanda was sitting at the gate with some five hundred brahmin youths. He returned and told the king: "Your Majesty, the noble Ānanda is at the royal gate." The king said: "Invite him inside." Ānanda came in and said: "Your Majesty, had the noble Ānanda not gone forth into homelessness, what would he have become?" "A noble wheel-turning king." "And what would I have become?" "A minister, noble one." "Your Majesty, you granted monks as servants for princes and nuns as attendants for the queen's retinue. And yet, treating us in this way, a single brahmin has struck Your Majesty and jabbed the teacher Ānanda twice with a shoulder-pole, and when I became angry at this he struck me too with a shoulder-pole."

The king, furious, issued a command to his ministers: "Go and cut off that brahmin's hand." They took him and went to the marketplace. When the brahmin's father and mother heard of this, they gathered with friends, siblings, and relatives, and went weeping to the marketplace speaking soft and piteous words and wailing "O my child!" There, together with the crowd, they spoke to the minister: "Good sir, since this brahmin has committed an offense against a god and since cutting off a hand is appropriate, yet as this brahmin earns his living by his hands, it would be fitting to cut off his left hand." So they cut off his left hand. Then, some time later, that same brahmin was seen going about with his left arm bandaged, writing and teaching the brahmin youths with his right hand.

Some time after that, Ānanda saw this, grew very angry, went before the king, and said: "This is a king's happiness? If the firm fruit of a royal command is reduced to this, then even that is nothing to His Majesty." The king said: "Noble one, what has happened?" Ānanda replied: "Your Majesty, that brahmin's hand was not cut off." The king summoned his ministers and said: "Did you not cut off that brahmin's hand?" The minister replied: "Your Majesty, it was cut off." "Then why does the noble Ānanda speak thus?" The venerable Ānanda said: "Your Majesty, that brahmin goes about managing things with his right hand and has the brahmin youths learning their texts." The minister said: "Your Majesty, the brahmin's father and mother petitioned that since this brahmin earns his living by his hands, the left hand should be cut off — and on account of that I cut off his left hand." The king said: "If his parents caused his left hand to be cut off, I shall have his right hand cut off — go and cut it." The minister went before him and cut off his right hand, and the brahmin sat there with both arms hanging useless.

As he sat there in pain, the venerable Ānanda said: "Brahmin, why do you sit there with your arms dangling, without beating us with a shoulder-pole?" The brahmin was humbled and his arrogance and pride were broken; he sat saying nothing. Then brahmins and householders began to mock, revile, and slander the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyans, saying: "Those sons of the Śākyan have no compassion — even after punishing him by amputation they still seek to cut further." It was at this juncture that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One considered the matter and concluded that whatever fault had arisen came from allowing monks to proceed with the cutting off of hands. He therefore thought: "Monks must not cut off hands and feet," and he addressed the monks accordingly: "Monks, this foolish companion has done what is not the work of a śramaṇa. That those who have gone forth into my teaching should engage in such conduct is neither fitting nor appropriate. Therefore monks must not cut off hands and feet. If they do so, it shall become a grave offense."

The monks then raised a doubt, and submitted every aspect of that doubt to the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, at that time the brahmin was protected by the venerable Gavampati, while it was his companion Upananda who entirely abandoned him."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, listen now — it was not only in the present that Gavampati protected and Upananda abandoned. Even in the past it was so. Monks, in former times there was a pleasure grove adorned with a variety of trees, rich in flowers and fruit and water, where a hermit (ṛṣi) dwelt, living on fruit, roots, and water, dressed in grass mat and bark, sitting beneath a wood-apple tree and attending to his own spiritual purpose. From above, a monkey flung a wood-apple fruit, which struck the hermit on the head, and the hermit recited these verses:

What would cause your undoing —
that I shall not do;
what would cause your undoing —
that is exactly what you yourself are doing.

Now, a hunter who had been staying with that hermit had gone out and lost track of his quarry, and so made his way to that dwelling. The hermit had left the foot of the wood-apple tree and gone elsewhere on some business. The hunter, not seeing him, looked around and sat down at the foot of that very wood-apple tree. The monkey then hurled a wood-apple fruit at the hunter's head. The hunter had no hat, and the fruit struck his skull; the pain and distress caused by the blow made him look upward. The moment he caught sight of the monkey he was enraged, and notching a poisoned arrow to his bow, he shot it into the monkey's vitals. The monkey fell to the ground and died.

Monks, what do you think? The hermit of that time and place was none other than this very monk Gavampati. The monkey of that time and place was none other than this very brahmin. The hunter of that time and place was none other than this very Upananda. Even then Gavampati protected, and Upananda abandoned. So too in the present: Gavampati protects, and Upananda abandons."

The summary verse:

Bad lineage and Ācāra together;
a patched robe, contempt,
a fine border region and Supriya,
taking the bowl with a sense of ownership;
Aparājita and Candrarakṣitā —
each stole the cloth of the other's ward.

This summary verse is to be expanded in full exactly as it appears in the second root defeat, with no difference whatsoever.

The summary verse:

Pigs, sugarcane,
a palm tree, a dark Dharma robe, Gavampati;
a vessel smeared with lard,
a fat bowl — beloved of Subhaga.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time a famine struck, and some thieves stole pigs, drove them into a dense thicket, and slaughtered them there. Having killed them, they ate the good meat and discarded the heads, the bones, and the innards.

The practice of the Group of Six was to rise early in the morning, climb up onto a rooftop, and look out in all four directions. Wherever they saw smoke rising or vultures circling, they would all gather and head there. Rising early one morning, they climbed up onto a rooftop and began looking out in all four directions. When they spotted smoke and circling vultures inside a dense thicket, they said to one another: "Friends, there is smoke rising and vultures circling inside that thicket — there may well be something to be found there; let us go."

They went there quickly and found pig heads, bones, and discarded innards. They said to one another: "Friends, we have found something like a windfall — let us cook it and eat it." As they were gathering these things up and boiling them, the owners of the pigs came searching and arrived on the scene. When they saw the Group of Six eating the pork, they said: "Noble ones, even while bearing the victory banner of the holy life, do you do such things as this?" The monks replied: "Good sirs, if we were fit to kill, could we not slaughter fine, fine game and eat good meat ourselves? Why should we gather and boil heads, bones, and innards? These things were stolen and eaten by someone who had not been given them, and then thrown away — we have merely picked them up as one picks up a windfall." The pig owners said: "Noble ones, even if that is so, you are nonetheless those who have gone forth into renunciation, and this is not fitting," and with that criticism having been voiced, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, a monk must not pick up a windfall of that kind. If he does, it becomes an offense requiring expiation."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Those who take what is not given stole sugarcane, ate it, and then discarded the roots, the small stalks, and the shoots. The Group of Six, wandering about and teasing one another, went in that direction. When they saw these remnants, they said to one another: "Friends, here is something like a windfall — let us pick it up." As they began to do so, the guards of the sugarcane came searching and arrived on the scene. When they saw the Group of Six picking up the sugarcane roots, small stalks, and shoots, one of them said: "Noble ones, even while bearing the victory banner of the holy life, do you commit such sinful acts?" The monks replied: "Good sir, if we were fit to take what is not given, could we not choose carefully and pluck fine sugarcane, or even scatter jewels, pearls, and other precious things? Someone who takes what is not given stole the cane and ate it — we have only now gathered up the roots and the small tips and stalks." The guards said: "Noble ones, even if that is so, you are nonetheless those who have gone forth into renunciation, and this is not fitting." The monks sat there without saying anything further, and then the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, a monk must not pick up a windfall of that kind. If a monk does pick up such a windfall, it becomes an offense requiring expiation."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Those who take what is not given stole palm fruits, carried them into a dense forest, chose the best ones and ate them, and discarded the refuse. The Group of Six, wandering about and teasing one another, went in that direction. When they saw these remnants, they said to one another:

"Joyful and Delight-in-Joy, let us gather these windfalls as though they were rags." When they began to gather them, the guardian of the palm grove arrived on his rounds and saw the Group of Six picking up the crown cuttings and dregs of the palm trees. He said: "Noble ones, kings among the ascetics of the forest! Though you wear the marks of renunciation, do you still perform such sinful deeds as these?" They replied: "Good fellow, if we were permitted to take what is not given, could we not simply choose and select fine palm fruits, and indeed scatter abroad jewels, pearls, and other precious things? Some thieves stole these things by taking what was not given, and we have merely gathered up what they left behind." The guardian replied: "Even if that is so, you who have gone forth into renunciation — this is not fitting." They said nothing further and sat there quietly.

At that juncture, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks must not pick up windfalls of that kind. If a monk does pick up such a windfall, it becomes an offense requiring expiation."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time in Śrāvastī there was a young incense-seller who had a fine woolen shawl, and he had become extremely attached to it. Then on another occasion he fell ill, and, as much as those dear to him would mourn for other possessions, for this shawl there was no grief. Though medicines were made from roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, none of them availed him. When the time came that he understood the state of his body, he gathered his relatives and said: "When I die, do not cremate me; instead, wrap me in this shawl and cast me out in the charnel ground." They sighed and said: "Do not be afraid — not everyone who is struck by illness dies; some recover." But when his life ran out and he perished, and neither care nor tending helped, he died. Because of his intense attachment to the shawl, he was reborn among the hungry ghosts who possess dangling gullets. His relatives wrapped the corpse in blue, yellow, red, and white cloth, wound that very shawl around it, and cast it in the charnel ground.

A group of monks saw this and said to the monk who worked in the charnel ground — whose name was Nāgānanda — "Venerable one, the young incense-seller has died; his relatives wrapped him in a shawl and cast him in the charnel ground. Go and pick up that windfall of rags." He quickly went to the charnel ground and took up the shawl, whereupon a non-human being said to him: "Noble Nāgānanda, do not carry off my shawl." Most who dwell in charnel grounds are brave of heart, so he said to the being: "Wretch, because of your extreme attachment to this shawl you were reborn among the hungry ghosts with dangling gullets. Do you now wish to be reborn in hell as well? Let it go!" Yet the being would not release it. So great was the being's attachment that it struck the monk with its fist, snatched the shawl back, and carried it off. The monk went to the Jeta Grove.

The being followed him, wailing, crying out all the way: "Noble Nāgānanda, please give back the shawl!" He ignored it and entered the Jeta Grove. Now in the Jeta Grove there dwelt gods, nāgas, and yakṣas who had faith in the Buddha, and the being, being of scant power, was unable to enter. It remained at the gate of the Jeta Grove, wailing. The Blessed Buddhas, though they know all, feign not to know, and so the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why is there a non-human being at the gate of the Jeta Grove?" Ānanda replied:

"Venerable Nāgānanda has taken its shawl." The Blessed One considered the matter, thinking: "This non-human being is crying as it does from such intense longing, and there exists the possibility that, if it does not recover the shawl, it will vomit hot blood and die." With that thought, he spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to the monk Nāgānanda and give this non-human being back its shawl. If the shawl is not given to it, it will certainly vomit hot blood and die. When you give it, tell it to move on ahead. When it has gone to the charnel ground, tell it to lie down, and when it lies down, drape the shawl over it." The venerable Ānanda replied: "As you command, venerable one." He listened to the Blessed One and went to where the venerable Nāgānanda was, and when he arrived he said to him: "Venerable Nāgānanda, please take note. The Blessed One has declared from his own mouth: give this non-human being back its shawl. If you do not give it the shawl, it will certainly vomit hot blood and die. When you give it, tell it to move on ahead. When it has gone to the charnel ground, tell it to lie down, and when it lies down, drape the shawl over it. That is what was declared." The venerable Ānanda conveyed exactly what the Blessed One had said.

The venerable Ānanda then departed, and Nāgānanda said to the non-human being: "If you want the shawl, move ahead and I will give it to you." It moved ahead. Then he said: "If you want the shawl, lie down." It lay down, and he draped the shawl over it. The non-human being then pressed and kneaded him with its foot, and since he was endowed with power, he was overpowered by it.

This matter was then reported to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, one should not hesitantly take or give a corpse's garment. If one is to take it, one should go from the feet to the head and take it. Whoever gives it should also go from the head to the feet and give it. Monks, there are five faults in a corpse's garment: it is of poor color, it has an unpleasant smell, it is old and worn, it is full of lice, and it is not tolerated by yakṣas. Nevertheless, a shroud-gatherer should not take a corpse's garment as long as the wound has not opened." The Blessed One declared that one should not take garments from a corpse before the wound has opened.

Then the group of six took a dog with them and went out, and those without faith, seeing them, said: "Noble ones, why are you leading a dog out to the wilderness? Are you going to take a life?" These monks gave back an impertinent reply. The matter was then brought before the Blessed One by the monks, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not go about leading a dog."

Then those monks used a weapon to open a wound and took the garment. The Blessed One declared: "One should not open a wound with a weapon and take it. However, once maggots and ants have fed upon it, then one may take it." Those monks took it and wore it just as it was. The Blessed One declared: "One should not wear it just as it is. Rather, one should leave it in an isolated place for seven or eight days, and when it has been dried out by wind and sun, one should wash it, boil it, and then wear it." Those monks put it on and entered the temple, prostrating before the stūpas. The monks then brought this before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"I shall establish a code of conduct for monks who are charnel-ground dwellers. A monk who is a charnel-ground dweller, having taken a corpse's cloth, should not go to a temple. He should not prostrate before stūpas. Even if he does prostrate, he should not approach within one armspan of the stūpa. He should not make use of dwelling quarters. He should not sit on a bed or seat. He should not sit within the Saṅgha assembly. He should not teach the Dharma to brahmins or householders who have come and arrived. He should not go to the homes of brahmins or householders. If he does go, he should remain at the door. If a householder says, 'Noble one, please come inside,' he should say, 'I am a charnel-ground dweller.' If the householder then says, 'Noble one, such ones as yourself, who have properly undertaken the qualities of training, have entered the home — would it not be that my gains are well gained?' then he may enter, but he should not sit on a seat. If the householder says, 'Noble one, please be seated,' he should say, 'I am a charnel-ground dweller.' If the householder then says, 'Noble one, such ones as yourself, who have properly undertaken the qualities of training, who use the seat and dwell in the home — would it not be that my gains are well gained?' then he may sit there, and need not feel regret about it. If a monk who is a charnel-ground dweller, having properly received the code of conduct just as it has been established, does not put it into practice, he commits an offense."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the pleasure grove of Prince Jeta. Some monks were leaving needles and blades scattered about in disarray, and these were being swallowed by rats. The monks then brought this before the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not leave them scattered about in disarray; rather, one should store them in a container." When the Blessed One had declared that they should be stored in a container, the monks did not know what kind of container to make. The Blessed One declared: "Smear a piece of cloth with monkey fat, and place the needles and blades inside it."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the pleasure grove of Prince Jeta. At Śrāvastī there was a nun named Pom Gamo. At a certain time, another nun, faint with thirst and wishing to drink water, went to her and said, "Noble sister, I am thirsty — please lend me your drinking bowl." She replied, "It is right here — go fetch it yourself." The other nun took it and went, but it slipped from her hands, fell, and broke, and she sat there in silence. At another time, Pom Gamo remembered this, went to that nun, and said, "Noble sister, please return the bowl you took." The other replied, "Noble sister, I am sorry, but it slipped from my hands and broke. I will buy another and offer it to you." Pom Gamo said, "Give me that very one" — and she harassed and tormented her over it for a long time. At that time the nuns reported this to the monks, and the monks brought it before the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter, and understood: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through nuns drinking from a bowl. Therefore nuns should not drink water from a bowl." He then declared to the monks: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through nuns drinking water from a bowl. Therefore nuns should not drink water from a bowl, and neither should they eat or drink other things from it. If a nun drinks water from a bowl or eats or drinks anything else from it, she commits an offense."

The summary verse:

Taking a picture-fort, fire, and —

bathing, obstruction, and a bowl —
not leftovers, a bowl as base,
feet not placed, and sandals too.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada (Anāthapiṇḍada, the householder known as "feeder of the destitute"). At the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of the four directions, the thought arose in him: "Without paintings it is unattractive. Therefore, if the Blessed One permits it, I shall have it painted." Knowing this, he went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada spoke these words to the Blessed One: "Reverend Sir, this Jeta Grove, being without paintings, is unattractive. For that reason, if the Blessed One permits it, I would have it painted." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, in that case, permission is granted — have it painted."

Having declared permission to paint it, Anāthapiṇḍada also gathered pigments and summoned the painters, and said to them: "Friends, the Blessed One has granted permission. Therefore, using these pigments, paint the Jeta Grove." They said: "Householder, for the painting, tell us: in which location should what be painted?" He replied: "Friends, I do not know — wait while I ask the Blessed One." They said: "Householder, very well — please do so, and we shall wait." He then went before the Blessed One, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and submitted: "Blessed One, I have gathered the pigments and summoned the painters. They ask through me: 'Householder, in which location should what be painted?' Therefore, out of compassion, may the Blessed One please declare in which location what should be painted." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, if that is so, then go and have the following executed: At the outer gateway, a yakṣa (yakṣa) holding a staff. In the gatehouse, a great miracle scene and the five-part wheel of cyclic existence. In the cloisters, a garland of the Jātaka stories. At the door of the bathing chamber, yakṣas holding garlands. In the monks' residence halls, elder monks engaged in establishing the Dharma. In the pantry area, yakṣas holding food. At the door of the storehouse, yakṣas holding iron hooks. In the water hall, nāgas (nāgas) holding vases, adorned with various ornaments. In the bathing house or the warming room, stories drawn from divine sūtras, or alternatively, stories of the hells.
