In the infirmary, the Tathāgata acting as nurse to the sick. At the latrine site, a charnel ground that inspires great dread. At the door of the dwelling rooms, paint skeletons and skulls." The Blessed One then said: "Reverend Sir, I request this." The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having listened to the Blessed One, had everything executed exactly as specified.

Then, at the time when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had the Jeta Grove painted, some monks who were residing there carelessly lit fires, and the smoke damaged the paintings and rendered them unsightly. At that occasion, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, I grant permission for a fire room. Any monk who needs a fire should light it in the fire room — not in a good dwelling. Lighting a fire in a good dwelling would create a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that fires should be lit in the fire room and not in a good dwelling, some other monks who were residing there fell ill and suffered from cold. The Blessed One declared: "Those monks who suffer from cold may light a smokeless fire outside the assembly hall or beside a pond, and place a warming vessel inside."

The monks then bathed in a good dwelling and damaged the paintings. The Blessed One declared: "Do not bathe in a good dwelling. Rather, bathe in one corner of the pond that does not fall within the Teacher's line of sight, or else build a bathhouse and bathe there."

When the ground became muddy, the Blessed One declared: "Spread a layer of pig bristles in that area."

When water pooled up, the Blessed One declared: "Dig a drain channel for the water."

Having declared that a drain channel should be dug, the mouth of the drain became blocked. The Blessed One declared: "Clear it regularly, and bathe right at the mouth of the drain channel."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At Śrāvastī, the son of a brahmin fell ill and went to a physician and said: "May you be blessed! May you be blessed!" The physician replied: "Good sir, please say what you wish." The man said: "I myself have no desire for merit whatsoever, yet my son has been struck by such and such an illness — please prescribe a medicine for him." The physician was a person of faith, and so he said: "Brahmin, go to the presence of the noble ones and request water from their alms bowls. Have him bathed in that, and he will recover." The brahmin said, "May you be blessed!" and set off for the Jeta Grove.

Now the behavior of the group of six monks was such that whichever one of them it happened to be never left the gate of the Jeta Grove unoccupied. The venerable Nanda was standing at the gate of the Jeta Grove when he saw that brahmin and said: "Great brahmin, welcome! Welcome! You are like the moon — it has been a long time since you came from afar. Noble one, I pay homage to you. It is good to see you after such a long time — if one sees a person again and again, one comes to look down on them. For what purpose have you come?"

"Noble one, my son has been struck by a very serious illness. The physician has indicated that I should take water from the alms bowl of the noble ones, bathe him in it, and he will recover. I have come here for the purpose of obtaining water from an alms bowl — please grant me some."

He replied: "So you have come here for water from an alms bowl! Noble one, yes, that is indeed the purpose. If that is so, wait here, and I shall fetch you water from the alms bowl." Saying this, he went inside.

He ate his meal, washed his alms bowl, and poured into it a small amount of bones, raw meat, fish scraps, a grain-paste gruel, flour, bark fibers, and dregs. Then he came back out and said: "Brahmin, take this alms bowl water."

When the brahmin saw it, he said: "Noble one, this is like the water used to wash a corpse — it is impure and it is not fitting to bathe my son in such a thing."

The venerable Nanda said: "You who possess such faith — your son is already cured."

The brahmin then became incensed. At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter. Whatever slight fault had arisen had come about because monks were discarding the leftover rinse water from their alms bowls.

For that reason, the Blessed One considered that monks should not discard the leftover rinse water from their alms bowls, and he declared to the monks: "Monks, for this reason a monk must not discard the leftover rinse water from his alms bowl. If he does so, he commits an offense. However, I shall establish a code of conduct for monks who give away alms-bowl water: a monk who gives away alms-bowl water shall wash the alms bowl three times, then shall praise the alms-bowl water by reciting a verse from the sacred scriptures over it, and only then give it away. If a monk who gives away alms-bowl water does not properly take up the code of conduct as it has been established, he commits an offense."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the pleasure grove of Prince Jeta.

Some monks placed their alms bowls on the ground as a base and ate their meals, and when brahmins and householders saw this they reproached them, saying: "The ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan are unclean — they place their alms bowls on the ground as a base and eat their meals." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the reproach of the brahmins and householders is fitting. Therefore a monk must not place his alms bowl on the ground as a base and eat. If a monk places his alms bowl on the ground as a base and eats, he commits an offense."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Vaiśālī, in the Monkey Pond Pavilion, the many-storied building.

Some monks ate their meals without removing their sandals, and when brahmins and householders saw this they reproached them, saying: "The ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan are unclean — they eat without removing their sandals." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the reproach of the brahmins and householders is fitting. Therefore a monk must not eat without removing his sandals. If a monk eats without removing his sandals, he commits an offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not eat without removing their sandals, the monks took off their sandals and began to eat, and in the course of this some fell ill. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who are sick may eat without removing their sandals, and in this regard there is no cause for remorse."

Summary verse:

Without an alms bowl, and with a famous elder,
during the rains retreat, and without a fixed dwelling,
and for five years having one and the same source of support,
the lungs, the back, the waist, and the head.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the pleasure grove of Prince Jeta.

A certain person who had been ordained by Ānanda had not previously set an alms bowl in readiness. So when the time for the monks' meal arrived, all the monks washed their own alms bowls, set them on the ground as a base, and went to pay their respects at the stūpa. He then thought: "There are so many alms bowls here — surely whoever takes any one of them will eat from it and then set it back in the very same place. Therefore I too shall take one for now and put it back afterward." With that thought, he began to take the alms bowl of the elder Kuṇḍinya, who is known as Ājñāta Kuṇḍinya. Then another monk said to him: "Venerable one, this alms bowl belongs to the elder Ājñāta Kuṇḍinya — do not take it." He set it down, and then reached for the alms bowls of the venerable Aśvajit, the venerable Bhadrika, the venerable Vāṣpa, the venerable Mahānāman, the venerable Gavāmpati, the venerable Vimala, the venerable Gavāmpati, the venerable Subāhu, and

he began to reach for the alms bowls of certain other monks. The monks said to him: "Venerable one, if you have no alms bowl, who gave you full ordination without an alms bowl?" He replied: "The preceptor Nanda did." The monks reproached him, saying: "Who but someone of utterly depraved conduct would ordain someone without an alms bowl?" At that juncture the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not confer full ordination on one who has no alms bowl. To do so constitutes an offense. One who confers full ordination must ensure that the candidate is provided with the six requisites."

The venerable Upāli then addressed the Blessed Buddha with this question: "Blessed One, if monks were to confer full ordination on someone who has no alms bowl, should the ordination be called a full ordination? Upāli asks: is it a full ordination? Those who perform the ordination incur an offense." He continued: "Blessed One, if monks were to confer full ordination using a small alms bowl, a large alms bowl, or a clay alms bowl, should it be called a full ordination? Upāli asks: is it a full ordination? Those who perform the ordination incur an offense."

At that time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Prince Jeta's park. At that time, a man known as a notorious thief was caught in the act of stealing. He dropped the stolen goods and fled. Exhausted from his flight, he sat down in a thoughtful daze beside a roadside tree along the path to the Jeta Grove, leaning his arm against its trunk. The venerable Upāli, having dressed in his lower robe early that morning and taken up his alms bowl and outer robe, was setting out toward Śrāvastī to go on alms round. He saw the man and said to him: "Venerable one, who are you?" The man replied: "Noble one, I am a destitute man with no one to protect me — I have nothing at all." Upāli said: "Good friend, if that is so, why do you not go forth into the renunciant life?" The man replied: "Noble one, since you yourself have gone forth, let me speak plainly for a moment: I am known as a notorious thief — who would ordain me? The teaching of the Blessed One is opened by compassion, but would anyone truly ordain me?" Upāli said: "Take heart. I will ordain you." The man replied: "Noble one, excellent — I will go forth."

Upāli then gave him the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon him, and said: "Good friend, a deer does not rear a deer. Make your living on alms rounds through the wide reaches of Śrāvastī, your own domain, your home territory." He then dressed in his lower robe that same morning, took up his alms bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī to go on alms round. While he was going about on his alms round, the brahmins and householders recognized him. Some of them said: "Wise ones, this is the notorious thief — and he has gone forth!" Others said: "The Dharma of the Śākyan ascetics is fine indeed: they even ordain notorious thieves. These people go about the houses by day disguised in the equipment of alms-seeking, then come back at night to steal."

At that juncture the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about from monks ordaining someone who is a notorious thief. Therefore monks must not ordain one who is known as a notorious thief." Having reflected thus, he declared to the monks: "Monks, the reproach of the brahmins and householders has indeed reached us. Therefore a monk must not confer full ordination on someone who is known as a notorious thief."

When the Blessed One declared that a monk must not confer full ordination on one who is known as a notorious thief, the monks did not ordain even those who were not manifestly thieves, and their going-forth and full ordination were thereby obstructed. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One who is manifestly a thief must not be ordained; one who is not manifestly so may be ordained. Therefore, when someone who wishes to go forth approaches any suitable person, that person must ask him: 'Are you not someone known as a notorious thief?' If one confers ordination without asking, it becomes an offence."

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, the Twentieth Fascicle.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time a number of monks were residing together at a certain dwelling. When the residential preceptor of that place passed away and those monks did not know to whom they should make a request for their immediate needs, nor with whom they should reside, they reported the matter to the monks. The monks then reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those monks should seek another monk by relinquishing the assignment of a monk, relinquishing the dwelling, relinquishing the bedding, and relinquishing the attendant. If one is found, that is well. If none is found, those monks must not remain in that dwelling until a second observance day, for if they do remain it becomes an offence."

Other monks at a certain place wished to commit to spending the rains retreat with a particular residential preceptor, but that preceptor also passed away, and those monks did not know how to proceed. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those monks as well should seek another monk by relinquishing the assignment of a monk, relinquishing the dwelling, relinquishing the bedding, and relinquishing the attendant. If one is found, that is well. If none is found, those monks must not make a commitment to enter the earlier rains retreat at that place; if they do make such a commitment, it becomes an offence."

Other monks at a certain place had already committed to spending the earlier rains retreat with a particular residential preceptor, but that preceptor also passed away, and those monks did not know how to proceed. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those monks as well should seek another monk by relinquishing the assignment of a monk, relinquishing the dwelling, relinquishing the bedding, and relinquishing the attendant. If one is found, that is well. If none is found, those monks must not remain there; they should go elsewhere and commit to entering the later rains retreat for the nearby preparations of the second period. If they remain there, it becomes an offence."

Other monks at a certain place wished to commit to spending the rains retreat with a particular residential preceptor, but that preceptor also passed away, and those monks again did not know how to proceed. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those monks as well should seek another monk by relinquishing the assignment of a monk, relinquishing the dwelling, relinquishing the bedding, and relinquishing the attendant.

If another monk is found, that is well and good. If one is not found, those monks should not commit to spending the earlier rains retreat there, for if they do commit, it will become an offence.

Other monks at a certain place had committed to spending the later rains retreat with a particular residential preceptor, and that preceptor also passed away, and those monks likewise did not know how to proceed. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those monks should remain for up to two months inquiring of one another and examining each other individually. After the two months have passed, they should seek another monk by relinquishing the assignment of a monk, relinquishing the dwelling, relinquishing the bedding, and relinquishing the attendant. If one is found, that is well and good. If one is not found, those monks should not remain in that place until the second restoration ceremony, for if they remain, it will become an offence."

Other monks at a certain place had been given the going forth (pravrajyā) and full ordination by a particular monk, and that preceptor passed away, and those monks as well did not know how to proceed. From that point onward, everything is to be stated just as before, up through what is said regarding the preceptor.

The Blessed One Śākyamuni was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At a certain place called Riyor, a householder who lived there had a temple built, filled it with all manner of requisites, and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions. Then at some later time, that householder was arrested at the royal palace, and the monks heard of this. Upon hearing it, they abandoned the temple and fled, and those who received without giving — taking what belonged to the Three Jewels — stole it. Then at some point the householder was released, and the monks heard that the owner of the temple had been set free, and they went to that householder. The householder had already heard beforehand how the monks had abandoned the temple and fled, and that those who received without giving had stolen what belonged to the Three Jewels, and so he reproved them: "Noble ones, why did you flee?" They replied: "We heard how you were arrested at the royal palace, and upon hearing that we became frightened and fled." The householder said: "Noble ones, even if I was arrested at the royal palace, why should you flee on that account? If my relatives were not arrested, would they not have provided you with requisites?" The monks had no answer and said nothing. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not flee in that manner. However, one should ask the relatives of the owner of the temple: 'Since the owner of the temple has been arrested in the royal palace, are you able to provide us with our alms-round requisites?' If they can provide them, that is well and good. If they cannot, one should go on alms-round and remain there for up to five years. If after five years the owner of the temple is released, that is well and good. If he is not released, then, having performed a motion-and-one-proclamation act, one should stay for another five years together with those who maintain the subsidiary temples surrounding that temple and who have separate acquisitions and separate restoration ceremonies. The act is to be performed as follows: in the subsidiary temples, bedding is to be set out, the gong is to be struck, and the monks are to be properly informed by means of the words of inquiry; then, with the entire Saṅgha assembled and convened, one monk should make a motion and perform the act.

'May the venerable Saṅgha please hear.

The king has seized ownership of a certain great temple. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and they are willing, let the Saṅgha give its consent, and let the Saṅgha make that temple one that shares acquisitions and has a separate restoration ceremony from these temples. This is the motion. The act is to be performed as follows: May the venerable Saṅgha please hear. The king has seized ownership of a certain great temple. Therefore, if the Saṅgha were to make that temple one that shares acquisitions and has a separate restoration ceremony from these temples, then let those venerable ones who are willing that that temple share acquisitions and have a separate restoration ceremony from these temples remain silent, and let those who are not willing speak. The Saṅgha has consented and agreed, and the Saṅgha has made a certain great temple one that shares acquisitions and has a separate restoration ceremony. Thus, since no one has spoken, so it is held.

If, in that way, the owner of the temple comes to those who have remained for up to ten years, that is well and good. But if he does not come, bedding, vessels, and utensils are to be placed in the subsidiary temples surrounding that temple, the inner door is to be closed, and one should depart. When the owner of the temple eventually releases it, the articles that were deposited in the subsidiary temples are to be retrieved and given back to that same place. If the monks residing in the subsidiary temples hand them over, that is well and good; but if they do not hand them over, they will be guilty of an offence.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park of Prince Jeta. The group of six monks were seen carrying loads with their bodies by brahmins and householders, who then mocked them, saying: "Noble ones, we are householders living at home, and yet we carry loads with our bodies for the sake of our fathers and mothers, sons and daughters, male servants and female servants, laborers, dependants, kings, gods, the spirits of the deceased, ascetics, and brahmins. For whose sake do you carry loads? They sit there saying nothing." On that occasion the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the mocking by the brahmins and householders is entirely appropriate. Therefore, monks must not carry loads with their bodies. If a monk carries a load with his body, he will be guilty of an offence." When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not carry loads with their bodies, the group of six then began carrying loads on their backs, on their hips, under their arms, and on their heads, thereby incurring that very same fault. The Blessed One then declared: "One must not carry a load on the back, on the hip, under the arm, or on the head. If one does so, one will be guilty of an offence."

Summary verse:

Dwelling place and six utensils,
then seizing from that place,
enticing and taking, the five,
and cooking shelter, doorway, and place of walking.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park of Prince Jeta. At that time a brahmin who wished to go forth came to the Jeta Grove, and he saw a number of monks carrying their alms bowls in their hands, holding rinsing vessels, and setting out for alms. He thought to himself: "Let me ask where these people are going." So he asked them: "Noble ones, where are you going?" They replied: "Brahmin, we are going for alms." He then asked: "Do all monks go for alms?" They replied:

"As for monks who have spiritual friends among brahmins, brahmins and householders bring alms to the monastery and offer them there. Those who have no such friends go for alms."

He thought to himself: "What difference is there between going forth among the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan? I too should go for alms in the same way." Then he thought again: "First let me ask another monk whether they have gone forth on the basis of alms alone, or whether there is something else as well." So he went to a monk, and that monk welcomed him properly with the full customary greeting for a visitor, and then said: "Brahmin, from where have you come, and why have you come here?" He replied: "Noble one, I came simply to see you; but first I wish to ask what you have gone forth on the basis of." The monk said: "Brahmin, excellent, excellent! Your thinking is sound — sit down and we shall speak." The brahmin who wished to go forth paid homage at the monk's feet and sat before him. The monk said: "Brahmin, these four are the prescribed supports in which, within the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya as proclaimed by the Blessed One, one goes forth, receives full ordination, and stands as a monk. Brahmin, what are the four? The Blessed One declared that among robes, a cast-off rag robe is suitable and easy to come by; abiding in that, a monk who has gone forth and received full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya becomes a true monk. Among foods, alms; among lodgings, the foot of a tree; and among medicines, fermented urine that has been discarded — these are suitable and easy to come by. Abiding in those, a monk who has gone forth and received full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya becomes a true monk. Brahmin, these are the four prescribed supports the Blessed One has established for us; abiding in these, we who have gone forth and received full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya become true monks."

The brahmin said: "Noble one, who could sustain life on these supports? I had come here thinking to go forth, but since going forth is so arduous, I pay my respects and take my leave." So saying, he departed.

Now that very matter became an obstacle between going forth, receiving full ordination, and becoming a monk. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever slight fault has arisen has come about from proclaiming the four supports only to those who have not yet gone forth. Therefore a monk should not proclaim the four supports to one who has not gone forth or has not received full ordination. Only at the time when one has gone forth and received full ordination should the four supports be proclaimed. To proclaim the four supports to one who has not gone forth and not received full ordination constitutes a serious transgression."

The occasion is at Śrāvastī.

At Śrāvastī a householder who lived there took a wife from a family of equal rank, and he sported with her, delighted in her, and enjoyed her company. From his sporting, delighting, and enjoying her company — as described before — a child was born, given a name befitting the family, and was raised and grew up. Then at another time the father passed away, and the son thought: "Father has passed away, and matters have become difficult. I shall go to the Jeta Grove and go forth." So he went to the Jeta Grove.

The conduct of the Group of Six is this: one or another of the Group of Six would keep the gate of the Jeta Grove unguarded. The venerable Ānanda was sitting at the gate, and when he saw the young man approaching he said: "Welcome, good-looking one! It has been a long while — where have you come from?" The young man replied: "Noble one, it is good to see someone after a long time, but seeing them again and again leads to contempt. Nevertheless, noble one, I wish to go forth — please ordain me." Ānanda said: "Good-looking one, your intention is excellent, and going forth is the highest thing. The Blessed One has said that a wise person who sees five benefits should be disposed to go forth" — and so on, from that point up to "the buddhas and the noble persons who have genuinely entered upon the path, the blessed disciples of the buddhas," just as before. "Therefore, go forth and be well ordained. However, for that one needs the six requisites — do you have the six requisites?" "Noble one, what are those six requisites?" "Good-looking one, they are: the alms bowl, the water strainer, the three robes, and the sitting cloth." "Noble one, I do not have them." "Good-looking one, I too do not have them at hand — go for now, and I will seek out the six requisites."

The young man then left his father behind and went to his relatives. When they heard that the boy was about to go forth, they took a wife for him. Meanwhile the venerable Ānanda set down the six requisites and entered Śrāvastī for alms. While doing so he saw the young man in the street and said: "Good-looking one, I have obtained the six requisites — come here, let us go and take them." The young man replied: "Noble one, I too have obtained six requisites." Ānanda said: "Good-looking one, what sort of things?" The young man replied: "Noble one, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind." Ānanda said: "Good-looking one, what does that mean?" The young man replied: "Noble one, my relatives have taken a wife for me — how then can I go forth now?"

That very matter became an obstacle to his going forth and to his receiving full ordination and becoming a monk. At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, I permit that one may confer going forth and full ordination after the six requisites have been set aside. Since going forth, receiving full ordination, and attaining the status of a monk in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya is something difficult to obtain, let the six requisites be sought out one by one and then, once set aside, returned."

The occasion is at Śrāvastī.

At that time a great many monks were travelling through the countryside on a journey, and some thieves attacked them and took what they had stolen away, bringing it to the Jeta Grove to sell. The very monks who had been attacked then arrived there, and recognizing their own alms bowls and robes, they cried out: "O wise ones, these men have stolen our alms bowls and robes! Seize the thieves! Seize them!" Upon hearing the outcry, the thieves became frightened and fled. The monks took back their own alms bowls and robes respectively, but then they sat uncertain whether these items were now allowable for them or not. At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "These belong to whomever they were taken from, and therefore they should not be regarded as suspect." After the Blessed One had declared, "These belong to whomever they were taken from," some other monks, while travelling through the countryside on a journey, were spotted by thieves, and the thieves began to attack them —

The thieves touched with their hands as many of those monks' alms bowls and robes as there were, then abandoned them without a glance and left, so that the monks ended up bereft of their alms bowls and robes. At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "For as long as the thieves have taken and carried off the items and the continuity of their handling has not been broken, one must not disregard them." After the Blessed One had declared, "For as long as the thieves have taken and carried off the items and the continuity of their handling has not been broken, one must not disregard them," those very thieves carried off what they had seized and entered Śrāvastī, where they began selling it in the market. The monks recognised what had been seized, and having recognised it, they brought those thieves before the royal court. There the thieves were made to suffer acutely with various kinds of pain — execution, imprisonment, mutilation, fines, and the like. At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not denounce them at the royal court. Rather, one should first speak to them with the Dharma and urge them. If they do not give the items back, one may recover them by paying half the price. If they still do not return them, one should pay the full price and take them back — for monks, alms bowls and robes that have been well made are difficult to come by." The context is Śrāvastī.

Monks abandoned dry excrement, tooth-cleaning sticks, painting-palette scrapers, and the like without looking back at them, and when some monks did not pick them up out of scrupulousness, those things were in that very place eaten away by water. At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Taking with five kinds of mental engagement is allowable — namely, taking with the thought that the person is a friend, or agreeable, or a senior, or one to be remembered, or that upon hearing of it they will be pleased. That is a proper taking, and one should feel no remorse over it." The context is Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One declared that the work of dyeing should be done. The monks dyed robes in the gatehouse and in the walking-meditation areas, and those robes were hit by dust and soaked by dirty rain. At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The dyeing work should be done inside the monastery." When the monks began doing the dyeing work inside the monastery, the brahmins and householders saw that the runoff from the dye pools appeared blood-red and said: "Noble ones, are goats and sheep being slaughtered over here?" The monks replied: "Friends, we have been doing dyeing work here, so here there is dye-water." Those people said: "Noble ones, if the dye has gone into the soil and appears unpleasant to the senior monks, please pour it out on the ground." At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Apply it layer upon layer." When they applied it everywhere in that way, the stone floors became unusable. The Blessed One then declared: "If there are stone floors, wash them. Otherwise apply it layer upon layer."

The summary verse:

Permission to plant trees was granted,
along with nameru robes,
and the long-tailed garment — in verse
these are gathered and summarised correctly.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the place where the kalandaka birds stay. At the time when the Blessed One established Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), in truth on Vulture's Peak, King Bimbisāra arranged a festival there, and all the crowds of people dwelling in the land of Magadha assembled there.

Vulture's Peak was rocky and bare of trees, and the crowds of people dwelling in the land of Magadha were scorched by the heat and said, "Noble ones, please grow trees here." The monks replied, "Friends, the Blessed One has not permitted it." The people said, "Noble ones, what objection could there be to this?" The monks remained silent. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, permission is given — trees may be grown." When the Blessed One had declared that trees were to be grown, the monks planted trees and watered them, but the trees dried up just as before.

The following year, when the crowds of people dwelling in Magadha came again and were equally tormented by the heat, they said, "Noble ones, did you not plant those trees?" The monks replied, "Friends, we planted them, but because we did not tend them they did not thrive." The people said, "Noble ones, if your own parents had planted you and then failed to tend you, you too would not have thrived. Please do tend them." The monks again reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not plant trees and then abandon them to wither; one must tend them." When the Blessed One had declared this, the monks did not know how to tend the trees. The Blessed One declared: "At regular intervals you should water them." The monks took this instruction alone to heart, and their wholesome activities fell into neglect. The Blessed One then declared: "This should not be made the sole occupation. At times wash the hands; at times wash the feet; at times chew tooth-sticks; at times wash the begging bowls; at times bathe. That will count as tending them." In the winter season the trees were scorched by frost, and the Blessed One declared: "Cover them with straw." When the monks covered them with straw, the trees were scorched by a forest fire. The Blessed One declared: "Surround them with a fence." When the wind did not reach them the trees were burned by heat, and the Blessed One declared: "Make ventilation holes in the fence." During the rains retreat the monks sat with water flooding all around them, and the Blessed One declared: "In the rainy season, breach the wall and drain the water away." The monks abandoned the trees before they had grown large, and the trees dried up as before. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I shall establish a rule of conduct for monks who plant trees. A monk who plants trees: if he has planted a flowering tree, he must not leave until it has flowered; if he has planted a fruit tree, he must not leave until it has fruited." When the Blessed One had declared that a monk who plants trees must not leave before the flowers or fruit have formed, certain monks had long journeys to make and did not know how to fulfil this obligation. The Blessed One declared: "They may entrust the tree to the caretaker of the monastery or to a monk who can be contacted, and then depart — there is no transgression in this."

The narrative setting for what follows is Rājagṛha. King Śreṇya Bimbisāra sent a precious gem as a gift to King Prasenajit. King Prasenajit gave it to the venerable Pilindavatsa. The venerable Pilindavatsa put it on and went to stay at a forest dwelling.

The thieves had heard exactly what had happened — that King Śreṇya Bimbisāra had sent a precious gem to King Prasenajit, who had given it to the venerable Pilindavatsa, and that he was wearing it while staying at a forest dwelling — and they began to deliberate among themselves. Some said: "What need is there to scheme? Let us simply go there and rob him." They went, knocked softly at the door, and the venerable Pilindavatsa asked, "Who is there?" They replied, "Noble one, we are thieves." "What do you want?" "Noble one, the precious gem." "Very well, good fellows — if that is the case, stretch your hands through the window." One of them extended his hand, and the venerable Pilindavatsa blessed the gem, saying, "May it not cut, may it not burn, and may it not be exhausted when drawn upon," and then passed a portion of it out through the window. The thieves pulled and pulled, making a heap of it, and tried to drag it away — but they could not exhaust it. When they tried to cut it with a weapon, it would not be cut; when they tried to burn it with fire, it would not burn. Then they said, "Noble Pilindavatsa, what use do you have for us? Let us go." He replied, "Deluded fellows, since you yourselves have not attempted anything against me, how could I have attempted anything against you? If it was by your own strength, your own diligence, and your own superior force that you dragged it, how could I not let it go?" They said, "Wise ones, since the noble Pilindavatsa is of great miraculous power and great might, if we do not depart before he summons those who might seize us, it will not go well for us — let us flee!" And so they fled.

At that time the monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: whatever slight fault had arisen had arisen from a monk of that kind wearing a precious gem and staying at a forest dwelling. Therefore a monk should not bring such precious gems to a forest dwelling. Reflecting thus, he declared to the monks: "Monks, what the monk Pilindavatsa did — wearing such a precious gem and staying at a forest dwelling — was improper. Therefore a monk should not wear such a precious gem and stay at a forest dwelling. If he does so, he incurs an offense. However, if a monk who is living at a forest dwelling happens to possess such a precious gem, he should leave it in a household."

When the Blessed One had declared that such a precious gem should be left in a household, another monk who was staying at a forest dwelling and who had received a gem befitting a great person left it in a household — and then insects infested it. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "It should be placed inside a box sealed with nāmeru wood. If that cannot be found, it may be placed inside any wood, or wrapped in leaves of the vāśaka plant or in arista leaves, one layer after another, and kept in that way." When placing it layer by layer was not feasible, the Blessed One declared: "If the means are not at hand, place it on top and dry it out from time to time."

The narrative setting for what follows is Śrāvastī. On the occasion when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered a meal in the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, the Teacher would come at that time in due season, together with the elder monks and elder nuns, to receive reverential salutation.

Then on another occasion, during winter, some monks were overcome by the cold and huddled in their dwellings lying and sitting still. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having come to the Jeta Grove to pay reverential salutation at the feet of the Teacher, saw those monks sitting there facing away from the wholesome direction, and said: "Noble ones, why do you sit facing away from the wholesome direction in the teaching of the Strenuous One?" They replied: "Householder, we are overcome by the cold." Without another word he paid reverence at their feet and departed. He went home and sent five hundred robes to the Saṅgha. The monks trimmed the edges and dyed them with other colors and wore them as they pleased.

Then again, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came to pay reverential salutation at the feet of the Teacher, he looked into the monks' dwellings and those robes were nowhere to be seen. He said: "Noble ones, since those robes are not to be found, where have you put them?" They told him what had happened. He said: "Noble ones, you have wasted robes of a quality fitting for a great one. Alas! Please keep such things for a good long while and keep them in good order." They sat there without the confidence to say anything. On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit the Saṅgha to keep new robes for a long time, a good long time, before wearing them."

Here ends the Fourth Gate of the Bases of the Minor Vinaya.

The verse of summary:

The body, the discourse, the buddha,
renunciation, and the deceased,
monks outside the boundary —
together with the occasion for a feast and its cause.

A further summary verse:

A corpse is to be cremated;
the stūpa of Śāriputra's son;
the festival to be held there;
and the merchant of conch shells and dried fish.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain householder was living in Śrāvastī. He took a wife of equal birth, and from that point onward — "together with her," and so forth — she gave birth to a son. A great birth celebration was held for seven days, twenty-one days together, a name was given in keeping with the family lineage, and he was raised and nurtured until he grew up — all as before down to "and he became grown."

Then on another occasion, having gone forth into renunciation in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and his physical constitution being unbalanced, he fell ill. Though he was treated with medicines of roots, stems, flowers, and fruits, none of them helped, and his time passed. The monks cast him aside near a road, together with his bowl and his Dharma robes.

Then some brahmins and householders walking along that road saw him, and some among them said: "Friends, a son of the Śākyas has passed beyond his time." Others said: "Come, let us go and look." They went and saw him, recognized who he was, and said: "Friends, this is the son of such-and-such a great householder. Having gone forth among the Śākyan renunciants, the sons of the ascetic Śākya, the shelterless ones, he has come to such a state as this. Had he not gone forth among them, his relatives would have tended to him."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, therefore I permit: monks shall perform the last rites for a deceased monk." When the Blessed One had declared that monks should perform the last rites for a deceased monk, the monks did not know how those rites were to be carried out, and so the Blessed One declared:

"He is to be cremated." When the Blessed One had declared that cremation was to be performed, the venerable Upāli addressed a question to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, you have said that there are eighty thousand species of worms in this body — what of those?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, they are born when the person is born, and they die when the person dies. Nevertheless, the openings of the wounds should be examined and then the cremation carried out."

When the Blessed One had declared that cremation was to be performed, there was no wood available. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then cast the body into a river." When there was no river either, the Blessed One declared: "Dig the earth and inter the body within it."

In the rainy season the ground became waterlogged and the wood became infested with living creatures. The Blessed One then declared: "Go to a dense spot, lay the body with the head pointing north, place a bundle of grass beforehand, lay the body on its right side, cover it with a mass of grass or leaves, dedicate the merit, give the gift of hearing the Dharma continually for the three successions, and then depart."

The monks departed accordingly, and brahmins and householders then mocked them, saying: "The renunciants, the sons of the Śākyan, carry out a corpse and walk away without washing — they have no cleanliness." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "You should not depart in that manner; you should wash." When all of them began to wash, the Blessed One declared: "Not all need wash. Those who have touched the body should wash together with their robes. The others need wash only their hands and feet."

When those monks then failed to pay respects at a stūpa, the Blessed One declared: "You should pay respects at the stūpa."

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka bamboo grove. The venerable Śāriputra and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in the course of their wanderings, would at various times pass through the hells, pass through the animal realms, pass through the realm of hungry ghosts, pass through the realm of the gods, and wander among human beings.

On one occasion the two of them, while wandering through the hells, descended into the great Avīci hell. There the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, please bring relief to the beings of the hells." The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied: "So be it — I shall bring them relief," and deferring to the venerable Śāriputra, he rose into the sky and began to pour down a continuous stream of rain the size of chariot axles. But that water was dried up in mid-air by the flames of the Avīci fire.

The venerable Śāriputra then said: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, please rest. I shall bring them relief." Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied: "Excellent — please do so, and bring them relief," and the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana stood by. The venerable Śāriputra entered into the meditative absorption known as "inspired concentration," and by means of it cooled that great Avīci hell, cutting off the stream of suffering of the beings within it.

Then the two of them, while teaching the complete Dharma to those with wrong views, took on a great bodily form, and saw that the tongue of that being was being pierced by five hundred ploughshares. That being said: "Noble Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if you would go to Jambudvīpa, please convey my words to those of pure conduct: I taught the Dharma falsely and deceived great multitudes of people.

"Whatever precepts they received from me and put into practice — for those very practices their tongues are pierced by five hundred ploughshares; and just as you have desecrated my reliquary stūpa in whatever manner you have done, so too have I come to suffer unbearable anguish in exact proportion. Tell them to stop doing so from this day forward." This was the message he asked them to convey.

The venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, completing the task, accepted this in silence without saying anything further. Then the two of them departed from Avīci hell unseen and traveled to Rājagṛha.

When the two of them arrived at Rājagṛha, some wanderers carrying staffs and wearing topknots came out and confronted them. Some among them said: "Friends, let us beat these ascetics, these sons of the Śākyas!" Others said: "It would not be right to beat them outright — find a pretext first and then beat them." They agreed: "So be it."

The venerable Śāriputra had gone on ahead. Those men came up to him and said: "Noble Śāriputra, among the wandering ascetics are there any true ascetics?" He replied in verse:

Among wandering ascetics, there is no true ascetic.
Among the Śākyas, there is.
Among arhats, there is none possessed of attachment.
Among the foolish worldly folk — none at all.

Not grasping the meaning of that verse, they said: "Friends, this one has praised us! Let him go without saying another word," and off he went.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana came along behind, walking slowly, slowly, weighed down by the ripening of former karma that was close upon him. Seeing him, those men said: "Noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, among the wandering ascetics are there any true ascetics?" He replied: "Friends, how could there be true ascetics among wandering ascetics? It is the Blessed One who has proclaimed: in this teaching there is the first ascetic, the second ascetic, the third ascetic, and the fourth ascetic — whereas outside this teaching there are neither ascetics nor brahmins. Those who loudly proclaim themselves superior to us are utterly devoid of ascetics and brahmins." And he thus proclaimed the lion's roar rightly in the midst of the assembly.

He continued: "Moreover, your teacher was born into the great Avīci hell. Through teaching the Dharma falsely, he took on a great body, and his tongue is being pierced by five hundred ploughshares. He sent this message to me: 'I taught the Dharma falsely to those of my companions in the holy life, thereby deceiving great multitudes of people. Whatever precepts they received from me and put into practice — for those very practices their tongues are pierced by five hundred ploughshares; and just as you have desecrated my reliquary stūpa in whatever manner you have done, so too have my sufferings become unbearably intense in exact proportion.' This is what he asked me to tell you."

At these words they flew into a rage and said: "Friends, this wretch has not only abused us, he has spoken ill of our teacher as well — what is to be done?" Then some among them said: "What is there to do about it? Just smash his head and be done with it." Others said: "We told you so before — beat him, beat him! You were the ones who said, 'Find a pretext first and then beat him.' Well, now he has spoken against us and our teacher — the deed is accomplished by his own words!" And with that they shattered his limbs and joints like reeds in mud and went away.

The venerable Śāriputra, wondering what was keeping the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, turned back and looked — and there he saw him collapsed on the ground, his limbs and joints shattered like reeds. He said: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, what has happened to you?" He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, it is karma exhausting itself — what else could it be?" The venerable Śāriputra then said:

"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana — were you not declared the foremost among those with miraculous powers by the Blessed One? How has it come to this?" He replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, when I am so crushed by karma that I cannot even remember the word 'miracle,' what need is there to speak of miraculous powers?"

Then the venerable Śāriputra placed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana inside his outer robe, as one would a small child, and carried him to the assembly hall. When the monks saw such a dreadful sight, they were alarmed and gathered around, asking the venerable Śāriputra: "What is this?" He replied: "The wandering mendicants armed with clubs and shaved-headed topknots have done this to the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana," and he set him gently down on the ground.

The monks said: "Was not the venerable Śāriputra — was not the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana declared by the Blessed One to be the foremost among those with miraculous powers?" He replied: "Yes, he was declared so, venerable ones — but look at the force of karma. He who stirred, thoroughly stirred, and completely stirred the palace of Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, named Vaijayanta, with the great toe of his right foot — he who was declared by the Blessed One to be the foremost among those of great miraculous power and great might — today, crushed by karma, cannot even remember the word 'miracle,' let alone miraculous powers."

Thereupon those monks in whom the noble path had not yet arisen, disheartened and deeply grieved, went to dwell in forest glades, jungle groves, and remote lodgings at the foot of trees, and began to rouse their minds to earnest effort.

And the report spread through every quarter of the city of Rājagṛha: "The wandering mendicants armed with clubs and shaved-headed topknots have beaten the great noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana and shattered his limbs and joints like reeds in mud; the noble Śāriputra has placed him inside his outer robe as one would a small child and has carried him to the Bamboo Grove; only a little life remains in him, and it will not be long before he passes away." When this report became known, many hundreds of thousands of living beings gathered in the Bamboo Grove.

The ministers of King Ajātaśatru came and reported to him: "Your divine majesty, the great noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana has been beaten by wandering mendicants armed with clubs and shaved-headed topknots; his limbs and joints have been shattered like reeds in mud; the noble Śāriputra has placed him inside his outer robe as one would a small child and has gone with him to the Bamboo Grove; only a little life remains in him, and it will not be long before he passes away."

When the king heard this he was enraged, and said to them: "Wise ones, seek out those wandering mendicants armed with clubs and shaved-headed topknots!" And together with his queen's retinue, his princes, and the people of the palace court, he went to the Bamboo Grove.

As the great crowd of people saw the king, they parted to make way. His eyes filled with tears, and with compassion in his voice, his words heavy with sorrow, he gently asked: "Great noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana — what is this?" He replied: "Great King, karma has consumed me — what else could it be? Was not I, noble one, declared by the Blessed One to be the foremost among those with miraculous powers? Great King, that is so — he did declare it — but karma has crushed me so utterly that I cannot even remember the word 'miracle,' let alone miraculous powers. The Blessed One never speaks in two voices. The Blessed One himself proclaimed:

Even across a hundred aeons of time,
actions do not waste away or come to nothing.
When causes ripen and the moment arrives,
their fruit matures for those who bear a body.

This teaching stands confirmed." At that, the king wiped away his tears with the hem of his garment, summoned all the physicians, and commanded them.

"Wise ones, if the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana is not healed within seven days, your authority shall be stripped from you." With that command given, he also entrusted the matter to his ministers and departed. The wanderers carrying staffs, those who wore topknots, had also heard this, and they fled. The physicians began to deliberate among themselves: "Wise ones, the king has spoken in such terms — how are we to accomplish this? The noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana is old, and every one of his limbs and joints has been shattered like reeds. How can we possibly heal him? He himself is mighty, possessed of great miraculous powers — let us go to him for refuge." Some of them said, "Good — let us do exactly that." And so they all gathered together and went before the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. They prostrated at his two feet and said, "Noble one, the king has commanded us thus: 'If the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana is not healed within seven days, your authority shall be stripped from you.' Since you are old, we have no means to restore you as you were before. But you yourself are possessed of great miraculous power and great might — please act in such a way that our authority is not stripped from us." He replied, "Wise ones, if that is so, then go now and tell King Ajātaśatru this: 'The noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana himself will enter Rājagṛha for alms in seven days.'" Overjoyed, they prostrated at his feet and went before King Ajātaśatru, where they touched their heads to his feet and said, "Your Majesty, the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana himself will enter Rājagṛha for alms in seven days." The king was greatly delighted and said, "Wise ones, if that is so, excellent! When the seven days have passed, the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana himself, by his own miraculous powers, dispelled his discomfort entirely, and entered Rājagṛha to collect alms.

Now, the gnosis of arhats operates by intention: the venerable Śāriputra contemplated why the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, though gravely ill, had himself entered Rājagṛha for alms, and he perceived that he wished to pass fully into nirvāṇa. Because Śāriputra's own stream of being was suffused with the habitual tendencies of their friendship, he himself fell ill that very same day. He thought: "If the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana is to pass fully into nirvāṇa, what am I to do remaining here? I shall pass into nirvāṇa before him." And so he journeyed from Rājagṛha to the town of Nālā. There the venerable Śāriputra, in the town of Nālā in the land of Magadha, was attended by those who cared for him, calling for a monk to tend to him, while he lay in great pain and suffering from a severe illness. Then the venerable Śāriputra passed fully into nirvāṇa from that very illness. And the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana also went to the city of Kalasikā, and that same afternoon passed fully into nirvāṇa. At the time when the venerable Śāriputra passed fully into nirvāṇa, some eighty thousand monks who were for the most part possessed of spiritual powers likewise passed fully into nirvāṇa. And at the time when the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana passed fully into nirvāṇa, again some seventy-seven thousand monks who were for the most part possessed of spiritual powers likewise passed fully into nirvāṇa. Then the one who had been attending to him performed bodily veneration before the relics of the venerable Śāriputra, and taking those relics, together with his begging bowl and his Dharma robes, he set out traveling in the direction of Rājagṛha, journeying by stages until he arrived at Rājagṛha.

The attendant of the monk set down the begging bowl and the Dharma robes, washed his feet, and went to where the venerable Ānanda was staying. Upon arriving, he bowed his head to the feet of the venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the attendant of the monk said this to the venerable Ānanda: "May the venerable Ānanda please take note: my preceptor, the venerable Śāriputra, has passed fully into nirvāṇa, and here are his relics, his begging bowl, and his Dharma robes."

Then the venerable Ānanda, bringing the attendant of the monk with him, went to where the Blessed One was staying. Upon arriving, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the attendant of the monk came here to me and said this: 'May the venerable Ānanda please take note: my preceptor, the venerable Śāriputra, has passed fully into nirvāṇa, and here are his relics, his begging bowl, and his Dharma robes.' And upon hearing this, venerable sir, my body became as though scorched, I lost my bearings, and even the Dharma I had known seemed to slip away."

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, the twenty-first fascicle.

Ānanda: "Did the monk Śāriputra pass into nirvāṇa taking with him the aggregate of moral discipline?" "Venerable sir, he did not." "Did he pass into nirvāṇa taking with him the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the wisdom of the vision of liberation?" "Venerable sir, he did not. And nor did he pass into nirvāṇa taking with him those teachings that I myself have fully awakened to through direct knowledge, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right abandonments, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven limbs of awakening, and the noble eightfold path." "Venerable sir, it is not that the venerable Śāriputra passed into nirvāṇa having carried off the aggregate of moral discipline — he did not. Nor the aggregate of meditative concentration — he did not. Nor the aggregate of wisdom — he did not. Nor the aggregate of liberation — he did not. Nor did he pass into nirvāṇa having carried off the aggregate of the wisdom of the vision of liberation — he did not. And nor did he pass into nirvāṇa having carried off those teachings that the Blessed One himself has fully awakened to through direct knowledge, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right abandonments, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven limbs of awakening, and the noble eightfold path — he did not. Nevertheless, the venerable Śāriputra was one endowed with moral discipline, learned in much teaching, contented, of few desires, dwelling in seclusion, having aroused diligence, established in mindfulness, possessed of meditative equipoise, possessing wisdom — wisdom that is swift, wisdom that is quick, wisdom that is sharp, wisdom of renunciation, wisdom of discernment, wisdom that is great, wisdom that is vast, wisdom that is profound, wisdom that is without equal, wisdom that is like a precious jewel. He was one who rightly teaches, who rightly leads others to receive the teaching, who rightly encourages, who rightly delights. One who rightly teaches, rightly leads others to receive,

rightly praises with true and heartfelt delight. When teaching the Dharma to the four assemblies, he was inexhaustible. When I, the Venerable one, recall the Dharma of the Venerable Śāriputra, and those enjoyments of Dharma that were his, then on account of the complete nirvāṇa of the Venerable Śāriputra, I am filled with grief and utter lamentations.

Ānanda, do not grieve, do not be dejected, do not lament. Whatever is born, come into being, made, compounded, intended, or arisen through dependent origination — that has the nature of disintegration. That it should not disintegrate when possessed of those conditions — where could that be? It is impossible.

Ānanda, have I not taught you from the very beginning that all things dear to us, beloved, pleasing, and agreeable will become separated, lost, parted from, and no longer ours?

Ānanda, consider this simile: the highest branch of a great tree possessed of roots and heartwood, with trunk, leaves, foliage, flowers, and fruit — it is the first to fall. The highest peaks of a great mountain of precious gems are likewise the first to crumble. So too, among the Saṅgha of monks dwelling with the Buddha and the other elders, the monk Śāriputra has passed into complete nirvāṇa. In whatever direction the monk Śāriputra dwelt, in that direction I find my concern to be but small — for I see the direction where the monk Śāriputra dwelt as not empty.

Therefore, Ānanda, do not grieve, do not be dejected, do not lament. Whatever is born, come into being, made, compounded, intended, or arisen through dependent origination — that has the nature of disintegration. That it should not disintegrate when possessed of those conditions — where could that be? It is impossible.

Ānanda, have I not taught you from the very beginning that all things dear to us, beloved, pleasing, and agreeable will become separated, lost, parted from, and no longer ours?

Therefore, Ānanda, whether I am present now or have passed beyond, dwell with yourselves as your own island, yourselves as your own refuge, the Dharma as your island, the Dharma as your refuge, no other island, no other refuge.

And why is that? Ānanda, whether now or after I have passed beyond, those who dwell with themselves as their own island, themselves as their own refuge, the Dharma as their island, the Dharma as their refuge, no other island, no other refuge — these shall be the highest among my monks who wish to train.

And how does a monk dwell with himself as his own island, himself as his own refuge, the Dharma as his island, the Dharma as his refuge, no other island, no other refuge? Here, a monk dwells contemplating the body as body internally, having overcome covetousness and discontent with regard to the world, abiding with ardor, vigilance, and mindfulness. He dwells contemplating the external body, and the body internally and externally; the internal feelings, external feelings, and feelings both internal and external; the internal mind, external mind, and mind both internal and external; the internal phenomena (dharmas), external phenomena, and phenomena both internal and external — contemplating each as phenomena, having overcome covetousness and discontent with regard to the world, abiding with ardor, vigilance, and mindfulness.

Ānanda, in this way a monk dwells with himself as his own island, himself as his own refuge, the Dharma as his island, the Dharma as his refuge, no other island, no other refuge.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having openly praised what the Blessed One had said, rejoiced in it, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

How the crowds of people dwelling in Rājagṛha roamed about armed with clubs and staves, and, with those weapons, broke the limbs and lesser limbs of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana like the joints of a reed — and how the noble Śāriputra, saturated with the habitual tendencies of friendship and affection for him, passed away in the village — so too, when in the morning the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had fully passed into nirvāṇa, word reached him that the great one had gone to the village of Kalasikā and there had fully passed into nirvāṇa.

At that interval, the monks were seized by doubt, and in order that all doubt might be cut through, they addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable sir, what deed had the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana done, that through the karmic maturation of that deed, those wandering ones armed with clubs and staves should have broken his limbs and lesser limbs like the joints of a reed?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the deed that this very monk Maudgalyāyana performed and accumulated — 'the karma has been done and gathered, the conditions have been fully transformed, it abides close at hand like a glowing flame, it will certainly arise, it will ripen as a fruit for embodied beings' — all this is as stated before."

"Monks, long ago in a past time there was a brahmin who dwelt in a certain mountainous region. He took a wife from among those of equal birth, and with her he sported, rejoiced, and delighted in pleasures. While they were thus sporting, rejoicing, and delighting, at another time a being entered into his wife's womb. After eight or nine months had passed, a boy was born. On the twenty-first day — that is, within three weeks of seven days — the birth feast was held in full; he was named, raised, and nurtured, and in time he grew great.

His father took that wife of his and sported with her, rejoiced, and delighted in pleasures, and became deeply attached to her as well. But his mother constantly stoked him with harsh and unpleasant words, speaking ill of him. He repeated these to his husband, and in this way that husband was deceived: the son came to have no great love for his mother and would contradict everything she did.

Then the son said to his wife: 'Is it on account of her that you are so attached to me that you oppose me?' She fell silent, saying nothing.

The son's wife then thought to herself: 'Though this venomous creature grows old and passes on, she will not relinquish even the smallest attachment to her own husband, and she insults my husband.' Realizing this, she began to look for an opportunity.

In time, at another moment, when the mother had bathed, adorned her body with perfumes and flowers, and before the sun had set, she lay with the husband in secret without the household members noticing. Then that daughter-in-law led her husband away and arranged matters so that he went in that direction. And then — the father and the mother were seen lying together in secret.

The son thought: 'This creature — while accusing me of being deeply attached to women — has herself, even now without ceasing, lain in secret before the sun has set, without any regard for the household members.'

Thinking this, he became enraged and spoke a harsh verbal act, saying: 'Is there no one who will break the limbs and lesser limbs of these two like the joints of a reed?'"

The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, what do you think? The one who at that time and in that period was born as the brahmin's son — that one is none other than this very monk Maudgalyāyana. Because he became agitated in mind and uttered a harsh verbal act against his father and mother, through the karmic maturation of that deed his limbs and lesser limbs have been broken like the joints of a reed for five hundred lifetimes. Now, having reached his final existence, his final abiding, his final body, his final self,"

even among those possessing miraculous power, he was proclaimed supreme — and yet his limbs and lesser limbs have been broken like the joints of a reed. Therefore, monks, the karmic maturation of deeds that are utterly dark is utterly dark; the karmic maturation of deeds that are utterly bright is utterly bright; and the maturation of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandoning deeds that are utterly dark and deeds that are mixed, strive toward deeds that are utterly bright. Monks, you should train yourselves accordingly."

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Then the monks made this request to the buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, the wanderers carrying staffs and wearing topknots let the venerable Śāriputra pass away, while they beat the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. We ask the Blessed One to look upon this."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, this is not so only now. Even in times past, Śāriputra was let pass and Maudgalyāyana was beaten. Listen to how this came about. Monks, long ago, some boys and girls who were at play saw two brahmin boys and said to them: 'We shall beat those brahmin boys.' Then someone said: 'Before beating them, let us ask them a question. If they please us with their answer, we will not beat them; otherwise we will.' So they asked one of the brahmin boys: 'When is it cold?' That one thought to himself: 'With what sort of intention are these ones asking me this? I know they want to beat me without any pretext,' and so he spoke in verse:

Whether it be cold or whether warm,
when the wind arises and blows upon one,
there is cold when wind strikes,
and without wind, no cold.

When they had dismissed him and asked the other one, that one replied: 'Is it not plain? It is the cold of winter.' And so they beat him.

Monks, what do you think? The one who was let pass — that was none other than this very Śāriputra. The one who was beaten — that was none other than this very Maudgalyāyana. Even at that time Śāriputra was let pass and Maudgalyāyana was beaten. And now again Śāriputra is let pass and Maudgalyāyana is beaten.

Now listen to yet another account of how Śāriputra was let pass and Maudgalyāyana was beaten. Monks, long ago, some boys and girls who were at play along a dried riverbed saw a śālmalī flower being carried along by the current, and they saw two brahmin boys coming." From here onward it unfolds as before: "They asked one of the brahmin boys: 'What is this that the water carries?' That one thought to himself: 'With what sort of intention are these ones asking me this? They want to beat me without any pretext'" — and so on as before. He too replied in verse:

Cut down by one of great strength,
in quest of what is sure to arise,
think not of it as a śālmalī tree —
think of it as a lotus on dry land.

When they had dismissed him and asked the other one, that one replied: 'Can you not see? It is plainly a śālmalī flower.' And so they beat him.

As for what you think, monks — and so forth, as before in full.

Thereafter, the Blessed One, having remained in Rājagṛha as long as it pleased him, set out journeying toward Śrāvastī and traveled on until he arrived there by stages. In Śrāvastī he resided in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. And it was there that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada learned that the noble Śāriputra had passed into complete nirvāṇa,

and that the noble Śāriputra's relics were in the hands of the venerable Ānanda. Upon hearing this, he went to where the venerable Ānanda was staying, and arriving there, he prostrated with his head at the venerable Ānanda's feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the venerable Ānanda: "May the noble Ānanda take note. The noble Śāriputra has long been dear to me, agreeable to me, a teacher to me, one whom I hold in remembrance. He has now passed into complete nirvāṇa. Please give me those relics of his that are in your possession, and I will perform a relic offering for his relics."

Ānanda replied: "Householder, he too has long been dear to me, agreeable to me, a teacher to me, one whom I hold in remembrance. And so I myself am making a relic offering for his relics."

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Blessed One was staying, and arriving there, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, may you take note. The noble Śāriputra has long been dear to me, agreeable to me, a teacher to me, one whom I hold in remembrance. Those relics of his that are in the venerable Ānanda's possession — may the Blessed One direct that they be given to me. I wish to perform a relic offering for his relics."

Then the Blessed One summoned the venerable Ānanda by messenger and declared: "Ānanda, give the relics of the monk Śāriputra to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and let him perform offerings for them. Brahmins and householders are faithful on account of this kind of matter. Moreover, Ānanda, you have not thereby benefited my teaching or repaid your debt to it — not by this much alone. Therefore, go forth, receive full ordination, provide lodging, set yourself to the purposes of the ascetic life, and let people recite and hold whatever arises from it, and teach it — by this much you will have benefited my teaching and repaid your debt to it."

Then, acting on the Teacher's word, the venerable Ānanda gave the relics of the venerable Śāriputra to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. He did so because, in all the times when the Blessed One was formerly a bodhisattva, he had never once broken the word of those who stood in the position of parents, preceptors, teachers, or other spiritual guides.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took the relics of the venerable Śāriputra, went to his own home, placed them up high in the finest part of the house, and together with his household, his friends, his relatives, and his kinsmen, began to perform offerings with lamps, incense, flowers, scents, garlands, and unguents.

The assembly of people dwelling in Śrāvastī heard how the noble Śāriputra had passed into complete nirvāṇa in a village in the land of Magadha, and how the noble Ānanda had collected his relics and given them to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and how he had placed them in his home and, together with his household, his friends, his relatives, and his kinsmen, was performing offerings with lamps, incense, flowers, scents, garlands, and unguents.

Likewise, Prasenajit, the king of the land of Kosala, also heard the news. Together with his queen Vāsuladattā, the royal lady Āvanti, the brahmin Giribhadra, his elders, his mother Sagā of the Mṛgārin lineage, and many other faithful people, he took offerings and went to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. There they began to make offerings with the various offering articles, and some among them attained an accumulation of virtues in that very place.

Now at a certain point the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had a little business to attend to somewhere, and he went out, locking the door behind him. Many ordinary people then arrived in the same way, and when they saw that the door was locked, they began to revile, reproach, and disparage him, saying: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has locked the door and gone away, and by doing so he has created an obstacle to our accumulation of merit."

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada returned from that errand, and the people inside said to him: "A great crowd of people came bearing offering articles, but when they saw the door was locked, they reviled, reproached, and disparaged you, saying that you had locked the door and gone away and thereby created an obstacle to their accumulation of merit."

When he understood that this matter was his own responsibility, he went to where the Blessed One was. Upon arrival, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, he spoke to the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable One, a great crowd of people filled with deep faith in the noble Śāriputra came bearing offering articles and assembled at my home. I had gone out, having locked the door for a moment to attend to a small piece of personal business. When they found the door locked, they reviled, reproached, and disparaged me, saying that I, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, had locked the door and gone away, thereby creating an obstacle to their accumulation of merit. Therefore, Venerable One, if the Blessed One would permit it, I should like to build a great stūpa for the noble Śāriputra in a wide and open space, and to allow the great crowd of people to make offerings there freely."

The Blessed One declared: "Householder, it is permitted. Go ahead and do so."

When the Blessed One had thus declared it permitted, he did not know how to proceed. The Blessed One then declared: "Build it step by step with four tiers of steps, and upon that place a vase-base. Then make a vase, a harmikā, a life-pole, and canopies — one, two, three, or four — up to thirteen, and place a rainspout."

When the Blessed One had described how such a stūpa should be built, the householder did not know whether a stūpa of that form was intended only for the noble Śāriputra, or for all noble ones. At that juncture, the monks asked the Blessed One about this, and the Blessed One declared:

"Householder, a Tathāgata's stūpa is to be made complete in every respect. For a pratyekabuddha, no rainspout is to be placed. For an arhat, there are four canopies. For a once-returner, three. For a twice-returner, two. For a stream-enterer, one. The stūpa for virtuous ordinary persons is to be a mound. The Blessed One has declared: this is the form of stūpas for noble ones, and such is the form for ordinary persons."

When he still did not know in what location and where to build it, the Blessed One declared: "Just as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana sat in the presence of the Tathāgata, so too should the stūpa of one who has passed into complete nirvāṇa be built."

Furthermore, the stūpas of the elders (sthaviras) are to be arranged in order of seniority. For virtuous ordinary persons, the stūpa is to be placed outside the monastery's assembly hall.
