The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then addressed the Blessed One: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I shall hold festivals for the stūpa of the noble Śāriputra." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, you have permission. Do so."

Just as King Prasenajit of Kosala, upon hearing that the Blessed One had granted the householder Anāthapiṇḍada permission to hold festivals for the stūpa of the noble Śāriputra, thought, "I too should assist in this," and had the following proclamation announced: "O wise citizens dwelling in Śrāvastī, and all the companies of people who have come from other regions, hear this! Whoever comes bearing provisions to the festival of the stūpa of the noble Śāriputra shall face no tax, no toll, and no ferry charge. Let them come here freely and at ease."

During this interval, five hundred merchants who had returned to Śrāvastī with great wealth gained from the ocean also heard the king's proclamation throughout Śrāvastī, which ran: "Whoever comes bearing provisions to the festival of the stūpa of the noble Śāriputra shall face no tax, no toll, and no ferry charge. Let them come here freely and at ease."

Upon hearing this announcement, they reflected: "Even though this king abides in the fruit of his own merit, he is never satisfied with merit — he gives gifts, he accumulates merit. Why then should we not give gifts and accumulate merit?" Their minds became supremely joyful, and at the time of the festival they offered conches, jewels, pearls, and the like. When the monks did not know how to proceed with these offerings, the Blessed One declared: "Whatever is from the offerings — let those be offered to the image of the Blessed One seated in the shade of a rose-apple tree. A portion is to be set aside for the proper maintenance of Śāriputra's stūpa, and the remainder is to be divided among the assembled Saṅgha. These offerings are for the stūpa of Śāriputra, not for a Tathāgata's stūpa — therefore one need not feel regret."

Condensed summary in verse:

Reproach, recollection itself,
finding occasion, and speaking out —
reciting scripture and the restoration ceremony,
and the invitation ceremony are what is established.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks, having seen, heard, or suspected a fault, reproached the monks. When those monks were reproached on the grounds of what had been seen, heard, or suspected, they stood as if ashamed. Standing thus in shame, they became pale and thin, languishing and physically unfit, and they lost their activities of teaching the scriptures, reading, recitation, yoga, and inward proper mental engagement. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter. He discerned: "Whatever drawback has arisen has come from monks reproaching other monks on the grounds of what they have seen, heard, or suspected. Therefore monks shall not reproach other monks on the grounds of what has been seen, heard, or suspected. If a monk does reproach another monk on the grounds of what has been seen, heard, or suspected, he commits an offense involving a meeting of the assembly."

As for those who carry out such reproach — how one recollects it, how one finds occasion —

— making someone not speak, imposing a formal recitation of scripture, setting aside the restoration ceremony, and setting aside the invitation ceremony: these are all similar. All the summary verses are to be recited as before.

The summary verse:

Named for the Buddha's marks, and
Conduct none of the venerable may engage in,
Devising expedient means, lack of faith,
And the Vinaya in brief: this is the summary.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the deer park of the Sages' Speaking, the Grove of Isipatana. Then the Blessed One spoke to the five monks:

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This is the noble truth of suffering' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path, the noble path leading to the cessation of suffering' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of suffering is to be fully known through direct knowledge' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned through direct knowledge' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be directly realized through direct knowledge' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of the path, the noble path leading to the cessation of suffering, is to be cultivated' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of suffering has been fully known through direct knowledge' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned through direct knowledge' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been directly realized through direct knowledge' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, when, with regard to these things never before heard by me — 'This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, the noble path, has been cultivated through direct knowledge' — I attended to them properly, vision arose. Knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization arose.

"Monks, so long as, with regard to these four noble truths, in their three rounds and twelve aspects, such vision had not arisen — such knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization had not arisen — for as long as that was so, I had not been released, had not fully emerged, had not been freed, had not been utterly liberated from this world with its gods, its māras, its Brahmā, with its assemblies of ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans —

— and had not dwelt abundantly in a mind free from error. For so long as that was so, I did not know that I had fully awakened to the unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. But, monks, from the moment that, with regard to these four noble truths, such vision had arisen in me — in their three rounds and twelve aspects — such knowledge, understanding, intelligence, and realization had arisen — from that moment I was released from this world with its gods, its māras, its Brahmā, with its assemblies of ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans; I had fully emerged, was utterly liberated, and dwelt abundantly in a mind free from error. From that moment I knew that I had fully awakened to the unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening.

While this exposition of the Dharma was being taught, the vision of the Dharma arose in the venerable Kauṇḍinya and in eighty thousand gods — a vision pure and unstained, free from all dust and defilement.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Kauṇḍinya: "Kauṇḍinya, have you understood all the Dharma?" "I venerate you, Blessed One." "Kauṇḍinya, have you understood all the Dharma?" "I venerate you, Sugata."

Because the venerable Kauṇḍinya had understood all the Dharma, he came to be known by the name Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya — Kauṇḍinya Who Has Understood.

At the moment the venerable Kauṇḍinya understood all the Dharma, the yakṣas (Skt. yakṣa) dwelling on the earth raised up their voices and proclaimed aloud: "Friends, the Blessed One, for the benefit of the many and the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, the benefit, and the happiness of gods and humans, has turned the wheel of Dharma in accordance with Dharma — a turning that no ascetic, no brahmin, no god, no māra, no Brahmā in this world has ever turned in accordance with Dharma — turning it three times, in its twelve aspects, here in the deer park at Isipatana near Vārāṇasī. The ranks of the gods shall increase, and the ranks of the asuras shall dwindle."

The yakṣas of the earth raised their cry, and the yakṣas moving through the middle sky heard it; they in turn raised their voices and proclaimed it aloud. From them it was heard by the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, then by the gods of the Thirty-Three, then by the gods of the Realm Free from Strife, then by the gods of the Joyful Realm, then by the gods who Delight in Creation, then by the gods who Wield Power over Others' Creations — and in that very instant, that very moment, that very flash of time, the sound rose all the way to the Brahmā world. And the gods of the Brahmā realm raised up their voices and proclaimed aloud: "Friends, the Blessed One, for gods and humans" — and so on, just as before — "has turned the wheel of Dharma, here in the deer park at Isipatana near Vārāṇasī, in its twelve aspects, three times over, in accordance with Dharma. The ranks of the gods shall increase, and the ranks of the asuras shall dwindle."

Because the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma in accordance with Dharma — turning it three times, in twelve aspects, here in the deer park at Isipatana near Vārāṇasī — this exposition of Dharma is therefore called the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

When the Blessed One had turned the wheel of Dharma in the mindstreams of those five monks and they had thus become, through full ordination, the very substance of the monkhood, they then, addressing the Tathāgata, began to use expressions of intimacy and tenderness toward him, calling him "venerable one." And the Blessed One addressed them thus: "Monks, do not address the Tathāgata with expressions of intimacy and tenderness and —"

"— calling him 'venerable one' at every turn. Monks, why is this? Whoever uses expressions of intimacy toward the Tathāgata, or expressions of tenderness toward him, or calls him 'venerable one' at every turn — for that deluded person this will bring harm over a long time, will bring no benefit, and will bring suffering. The Blessed One reflected: whatever fault has arisen has arisen from monks using expressions of intimacy toward the Tathāgata, expressions of tenderness toward him, and calling him 'venerable one' at every turn. Therefore a monk must not use expressions of intimacy toward the Tathāgata, expressions of tenderness toward him, or call him 'venerable one' at every turn, for to do so would constitute a serious offense." With this thought in mind, the Blessed One declared to the five monks: "Monks, therefore a monk must not use expressions of intimacy toward the Tathāgata, expressions of tenderness toward him, or call him 'venerable one' at every turn; to do so would constitute a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not use expressions of intimacy toward the Tathāgata, expressions of tenderness toward him, or call him 'venerable one' at every turn, for to do so would constitute a serious offense — it then came about that junior monks were addressing senior monks by name or by clan, and calling them 'venerable one' at every turn. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A junior monk must not address a senior monk by name or by clan. However, the two forms of address 'venerable one' and 'reverend one' may be used at every turn. If a junior monk addresses a senior monk by name or by clan, it will constitute a serious offense."

The occasioning incident is from Śrāvastī. The full account of what is found in Śrāvastī — concerning a monk who was scheming and a nun named Gosomā who in various ways would go wandering through the households in a manner that caused many people to lose faith — is as it appears in the detailed analysis.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Kuśinagara in the twin sāla trees in the forest near the stronghold of the Mallas. At that time, when the hour of the Blessed One's passing into nirvāṇa had come, he declared to the monks: "Monks, I have taught the Vinaya in extensive detail, and I have not taught it in brief. Now listen well and take to heart what I am about to say. Monks, whatever I have neither previously permitted nor prohibited — if it is improper, conducive to impropriety, and inconsistent with what is allowable, then it must not be practiced on the grounds that it is not allowable. But if it is proper, conducive to propriety, and consistent with what is allowable, then it may be practiced on the grounds that it is allowable, and one need not feel regret in doing so."

Summary verse:

Things that are abandoned: what is torn,
refuge for bees,
worn-out cloth and winnowing baskets,
stiff outstretched things, and many more.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, in the park of Prince Jeta. A monk came to cast off his monastic robe, and having done so he sat to one side of the elders and cast it before the Saṅgha. The steward of the Saṅgha thought: "This is property that belongs to the Saṅgha; it should be distributed after being put out." He had it put out and distributed to the Saṅgha, whereupon that monk was left destitute. Then the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One reflected that whatever fault had arisen had come about because a monk had cast off his robe and given it to the Saṅgha. He therefore thought: "A monk should not give his cast-off robe to the Saṅgha," and he declared to the monks: "Monks, a monk cast off his robe and gave it to the Saṅgha, and the steward of the Saṅgha had it distributed. Therefore a monk should not give a cast-off robe to the Saṅgha; rather, he should give it to an individual person. Even if it was given out of ignorance, the Saṅgha should not distribute it. If a monk gives his cast-off robe to the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha distributes it, both parties incur a serious transgression." The Blessed One declared: "A monk should not give a cast-off robe to the Saṅgha; rather, he should give it to an individual person."

After the Blessed One had thus declared, another monk came to cast off a monastic robe, and he gave it to a monk who did not know what to do with it. That monk took it and said nothing. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Another monk should indicate the matter to him. If he gives it back, well and good. If he will not hand it over, it should be taken by force and consecrated by blessing. Since the robe was cast off in order to make it available for use, the cast-off robe should not be kept permanently; rather, it should be returned to the one who cast it off."

The setting for this was Vaiśālī.

During the summer season, mosquitoes bit the monks, and they scratched themselves all over with their nails, so that from time to time drops of blood and sores appeared. Brahmins and householders saw the monks in that unsightly bodily state and said to them: "Noble ones, how did your bodies come to be in such a condition?" The monks described what had happened, and the brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, will you not keep mosquito nets? If the Blessed One, who has a beautiful complexion, has not permitted it, how can you keep them? But your Teacher is compassionate, so he will grant permission." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Very well then, I permit it. Monks should keep mosquito nets."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks might keep mosquito nets, the monks did not know what kind to keep. The Blessed One declared: "A cloth four cubits in length and two cubits in width should be hung over a wooden frame and covered from above, and a cloth twelve cubits around should encircle it on all four sides." The monks made the cloth without any opening left, whereupon mosquitoes entered from inside. The Blessed One declared: "It should be kept with the remaining cloth, and that cloth should be wrapped around from inside." The monks, having made the mosquito net, lifted the cloth from one side to enter, whereupon the Blessed One declared: "A door-flap should be made." The monks made the door-flap straight across, and the Blessed One declared: "It should be made as a cross-over flap." When it was hot, the Blessed One declared: "In that same place a fan should be set." When mosquitoes entered from below, the Blessed One declared: "It should be covered with a mat, and in whatever manner mosquitoes bite, all means to deal with them are permitted." The setting for this was Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One had declared that water should be sprinkled, and when the monks held water containers in their hands they became fatigued. The Blessed One declared: "They should be attached to a pole and the sprinkling done that way." When the monks attached them to a pole and sprinkled in that way, they still became fatigued, and the Blessed One declared: "Three sticks should be used together." When the monks attached them to three sticks and it would not stand steady, the Blessed One declared:

"Their holes should be bound together with cord or with small nails, and the water strainer placed on top. When the monks set up the water strainer and poured water, it spilled on the ground, and the Blessed One declared: "Be mindful not to let it spill on the ground, and pour carefully." When the monks placed the jar without a base support and it tipped over, the Blessed One declared: "A base support should be inserted." When another monk among them began to draw water, and at that moment the water strainer was not yet fitted, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A filter should be inserted." When the monks did not know what to insert, the Blessed One declared: "Sand or cow dung." But still it would not strain properly, and the Blessed One declared: "A vessel to support the strainer should be filled." When the Blessed One had declared that a vessel to support the strainer should be filled, the monks did not know how it was to be held, and the Blessed One declared: "There are two kinds of vessel for supporting the strainer: one made of copper and one made of clay." When the monks held the strainer-support vessels in their hands and became fatigued, the Blessed One declared: "The one made of copper should be hung at its hole on three sticks by means of a soft iron chain. The one made of clay should be hung at its hole by means of a cord." When other water strainers would not let the water pass through, the Blessed One declared: "They should be struck repeatedly with a mallet." When the monks, upon inspecting a jar that was not full while drawing water, could not discern any living creatures in it, the Blessed One declared: "Fill the jar full, let it stand until the water is still, and then examine it." When the jar was filled and dust had entered it from above, the monks did not remove it and so could not discern any living creatures, and the Blessed One declared: "Remove the dust and then examine it." When the monks pointed out living creatures with the tip of a finger and the creatures moved but could not be seen with the naked eye, the Blessed One declared: "They should be pointed out with the tip of a small stick, the tip of a blade of grass, or any other fine point." When the monks drew water out of the water strainer itself and the living creatures were harmed by being crushed and pressed, the Blessed One declared: "A draining strainer should be fitted." When the monks fitted one of the sort that, when filled and released, comes back full again, the Blessed One declared: "Fit one of the sort that, when filled and released, comes back empty." When some others lacked a draining strainer, the Blessed One declared: "Let them attach a cord to the water strainer, and release it in such a way that when filled and sent down it comes back empty." When the monks, after drawing water, did not wash, rinse, squeeze, dry, or fold the water strainer, the Blessed One declared: "After drawing water with the water strainer it should be washed, rinsed, squeezed, dried, and folded." When the monks were straining the Saṅgha's water with the water strainer and the greater part of the monks' Saṅgha grew weary, the Blessed One declared: "If the greater part of the monks' Saṅgha is involved, either have many water strainers filled, or alternatively fill a jar-strainer fitted with a spout." When the Blessed One had declared that a jar-strainer fitted with a spout should be used for straining, the monks did not know what such a jar-strainer looked like, and the Blessed One declared:

"It should be made from clay or copper in the shape of a pot, and holes like the heart of a lotus should be pierced in it. To gather those holes together, one large hole should be bored above them. To collect them further still, a spout should be inserted. Then it should be covered on top with cloth, the water strained through it, and that cloth too should be rinsed, washed, and dried."

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, the twenty-second fascicle.

When monks were discarding lice, grass, and other living creatures from a height, those creatures lost their senses and were harmed. At that time the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not throw any living creature from a height. When they were throwing them wherever they happened to land, the Blessed One declared: "One must not throw them just wherever they happen to land. Lice should be put back into the seam of the garment. If that cannot be found, let them be placed in the groove of a pillar or in a crack of a wall. Grass should be placed in the direction of a blue-green meadow. If that cannot be found, then in a cool spot. Other living creatures too should be released into their own proper habitat."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, is it permissible to use water that has been strained without examination?" "It is not permissible if Upāli has not examined it with his eyes." "Venerable one, is it permissible to use water that has been strained after examination?" "It is permissible, since Upāli has examined it with his eyes." The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One declared that the Saṅgha that had committed to a rains retreat should distribute robes. When Prasenajit, King of Kosala, heard this, he offered robes to the Saṅgha. Likewise, Queen Mālikā, the Kṣatriya lady observing the rains, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the brahmin Jīvaka, the elders, the diviners, and many others offered robes. The monks, having consecrated one robe each, began returning the remainder to those same donors. The donors said: "These noble ones — we have offered these to the Saṅgha, so how can we take them back?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, these should be accepted with permission, and once accepted, many monks should be appointed to distribute the stored goods. Let one robe be distributed after another in the manner previously appointed. The remainder should be set aside, and since this is the acquired property to be divided among the Saṅgha that has committed to the rains retreat, the assembled Saṅgha that has committed to the rains retreat should divide it as they see fit, and in this matter there should be no regret."

The summary verse:

No gift after I have passed,
one who has dedicated it dying,
one to whom it was entrusted dying,
what has come, and regret.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain householder living at Śrāvastī took a wife from the same social class, and with her he played, rejoiced, and took his pleasure. From their playing, rejoicing, and taking pleasure together, in time three sons were born. The youngest of these went forth in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. Then at another time he went wandering through the provinces. While he was wandering through the provinces, his father fell ill, and though he was treated with medicines of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, the illness did not subside. When the moment came that he felt death approaching, and it was clear he would die before long, he called his dear friends, his relatives, his elder and younger brothers, and

the household intimates together, and spoke to those two sons: "Sons, whatever little there is in my house, take it all and come." They heeded his words and came, bringing everything. Then he spoke to his dear friends, his relatives, his elder and younger brothers, and the household intimates: "Good people, listen well. Of my three sons, the two elder ones are here before you. As for the youngest, he has gone forth among the ascetics of the Śākyas. Therefore, let all the wealth, whatever little there is in my house, be divided equally among them." Having said this, and knowing that all that is accumulated is exhausted in the end, that what has risen high must in the end come down, that what has gathered must in the end separate, and that the end of the living is death, he passed on at the appointed time. Wrapped in blue, red, yellow, and white shrouds, he was carried to the charnel ground and cremated. His sons performed the rites of mourning and lamentation and remained there.

Now when that son — the one who had gone forth — heard that his father had died, he thought: "I shall go back, preach the Dharma to my mother and my elder brothers, and console them in their grief." He stayed in the provinces as long as he wished, and then, taking up his alms bowl and Dharma robes, he set out wandering toward Śrāvastī and arrived there in due course, journeying stage by stage. He left his Dharma robes and alms bowl in the Jeta Grove, and after resting there to recover from the weariness of the road, he went to his own home. When the members of the household saw him, they wept. Hearing their weeping, the household intimates gathered, and some among them wept aloud while others filled with tears.

Because he was a worldly person, on hearing the great crowd of people lamenting together he too sat with eyes brimming with tears. Then one of the women among the household intimates said to him: "Child, do not grieve. Your father performed meritorious deeds and has gone to the realm of the gods. Your father also gathered your dear friends, your relatives, your elder and younger brothers, and the household intimates, and gave you as well a third share of the wealth."

He reflected: "The Blessed One has taught that there is no such thing as someone who has passed on saying, 'Give this to such a person.' Understanding that this is exactly what the Blessed One meant by those words, I am not weeping on that account. Rather, it was my father's hardships on my behalf that caused these tears to fall against my will. The Blessed One taught that parents labor hard for their children — carrying them, nursing them, raising them, and showing them the many wonders of Jambudvīpa. Even if one were to carry one's father on one shoulder and one's mother on the other, honoring them for a full hundred years, or even if one were to install them as lords and masters of this great earth with all its jewels, pearls, beryl (vaiḍūrya), crystal, coral, silver, gold, precious stones, topaz, rubies, and all that is auspicious — even so, by that alone a son would not have benefited his father and mother, nor repaid the debt he owes them. But whoever leads parents who lack faith into the fullness of faith, who praises them, tames them, settles them, and firmly establishes them; and whoever leads parents who are deficient in moral discipline into the fullness of moral discipline, who leads those given to timidity into the fullness of generosity, and who leads parents deficient in wisdom into the fullness of wisdom — who praises them, tames them, settles them, and firmly establishes them — by that alone does a son truly benefit his father and mother and repay the debt he owes them." So it was taught.

Furthermore, the Blessed One forbade the practice of saying "give it to so-and-so after I am gone," declaring that such a statement does not constitute a gift. The woman in question said nothing at all about it.

On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, I did not frame this teaching with the layperson in mind, but rather with the one who has gone forth in mind. A householder dies still bound by attachment, whereas one who has gone forth does not. Therefore, when a layperson thinks, 'after I am gone, give this to so-and-so,' that does constitute a gift. But it does not apply to one who has gone forth. The gift should be accepted, and once accepted, one may enjoy and make full use of it as one wishes."

The case arose in Śrāvastī.

A monk dedicated robes to another monk. Having made this dedication, the one who received them passed away before the appointed time, and his fellow monks carried them off to be cremated. In the meantime, the dedicating monk took those robes from the deceased's cell and placed them in his own cell. When the other monks returned from performing the funeral rites and came back to the monastery, the duty-officer inspected the deceased's cell and found only a bowl, the three robes, and a water-strainer. He brought these to the assembly of elders, and the monks said to the one who had made the dedication: "Venerable one, did you take these three robes and bring them here? And if there are other items that were rendered suitable as robes, bring those as well." He replied: "There is nothing else in his cell beyond what is here." The monks said: "Venerable one, ask the elder known as the Senior Monk who was his close companion." He asked that monk, who replied: "I took them. He had dedicated them to me."

On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, for the purpose of making things acceptable I permit the dedication. You should address the one who took those robes thus: 'Present those gains from the belongings of the deceased to the Saṅgha and be satisfied with your own share.'"

The case arose in Śrāvastī.

Another monk dedicated robes to a fellow monk, and the one to whom they were dedicated passed away before the appointed time. The monks carried him to the cremation ground, burned him, and on returning brought those robes to the assembly of elders. The monks asked the one who had made the dedication: "To whom do these belong?" He replied: "These are mine, yet I dedicated them to him." The monks did not know how to resolve the matter, and so on that occasion they reported it in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, although for the sake of making things acceptable I permit the dedication, the robes nonetheless belong to the one who made the dedication."

The case arose in Śrāvastī.

Another monk dedicated robes to a fellow monk. The one to whom the robes were dedicated then fell ill. He thought: "That monk dedicated robes to me. Though I am ill, I shall go and claim them by my own authority." He went to that monk and said: "Noble one, you dedicated robes to me — give them to me now." When this was reported to the monks, they did not know how to deal with it, and so on that occasion the monks reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the situation.

The fault that arose was this: the monk had trusted in that particular monk alone and brought the robes, and the dedication was made in the presence of that monk alone. Therefore, the Blessed One reflected: a monk should not make a dedication in the presence of the very monk toward whom he has directed his trust and brought robes. Having so reflected, he declared to the monks: "Monks, for this reason, a monk must not dedicate robes in the presence of the very monk toward whom he has directed trust and for whom he has brought them. If the dedication has not been made directly before him, then no offense is incurred thereby."

The case arose in Śrāvastī. Another monk dedicated robes to a certain monk. The one to whom the robes were dedicated was a quarrelsome person, ever picking quarrels with the monks. He then made trouble with a different monk and set off to leave. The monk who had dedicated the robes to him began trying to prevent him from going, saying, "Venerable one, do not go," and he seized him by the arm. The man could not be made to stay. He was turned back again and again. Then one of the monks said to him, "This venerable one is a quarrelsome fellow who constantly causes trouble for the monks — let him go." The other monk replied, "It is not for another's sake that I am not letting him go. Rather, I dedicated my own robes to him, and I am holding on to them." When this was reported to the monks, they reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Even if the monk one trusts in is on the far side of the ocean, one may still direct one's trust toward him, make the dedication, and take the robes. One should feel no remorse about this." And the Blessed One declared: "Even if the monk one trusts is on the far side of the ocean, robes may still be dedicated to him."

Then another monk dedicated robes to a monk who was residing in a very distant land. That monk died, and the dedicating monk only learned of the death after a considerable time had passed. He was stricken with remorse. He spoke of this to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "At the moment one hears of the death, one should dedicate the robes to another. One should feel no remorse about this."

A summary verse:

One who resides outside the boundary
must not present faith-offerings or give.
One must not do so between one another,
nor during the Restoration nor the Invitation ceremony.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada (Anāthapiṇḍada, the "Feeder of the Destitute," was the great lay patron who donated the park). The Group of Six monks, though residing outside the boundary, were presenting faith-offerings. When this was reported to the monks, they reported the matter in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One who resides outside the boundary must not present faith-offerings."

Then, following the Blessed One's declaration that one who resides outside the boundary must not present faith-offerings, some other monks went outside the boundary. While they were away, some Saṅgha business arose, and the Group of Six monks took faith-offerings from those who had gone outside. When this was reported to the monks, they reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not receive faith-offerings from monks who have gone outside the boundary."

Following the Blessed One's declaration that one residing outside the boundary must not present faith-offerings and that one must not receive faith-offerings from monks who have gone outside the boundary, the Group of Six monks, while residing outside the boundary, began presenting offerings to one another — Gāvampati to Nandika, Nandika to Gāvampati, Udāyin to Canda, and Canda to Udāyin —

and Gāvampati to Nandika, and Nandika to Gāvampati. When this was reported to the monks, they reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks must not present faith-offerings to one another. If they do so, it becomes an offence." The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One declared that at the time of the fortnightly restoration ceremony (poṣadha) the Prātimokṣa sūtra should be recited, the Group of Six, while residing outside the boundary, offered their intention and declaration of purity for the ceremony. When this was reported to the monks, the Blessed One declared: "One who resides outside the boundary must not offer intention or declaration of purity for the restoration ceremony." Following this declaration by the Blessed One, some other monks went outside the boundary. When they had gone out and then came back, the Saṅgha assembled wishing to perform the restoration ceremony, and the Group of Six received from those monks their intention and declaration of purity. When this was reported to the monks, the Blessed One declared: "One must not receive intention or declaration of purity from monks who have gone outside the boundary."

Following the Blessed One's declaration that one residing outside the boundary must not present faith-offerings or a declaration of purity, and that one must not receive faith-offerings or a declaration of purity from monks who have gone outside the boundary, the Group of Six, while residing outside the boundary, continued to present faith-offerings to one another — Nandika to Nanda, Nanda to Nandika, Udāyin to Canda, Canda to Udāyin, Gāvampati to Nandika, and Nandika to Gāvampati — and when this was again reported to the monks and they reported it to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks must not present to one another intention or declaration of purity for the restoration ceremony. If a monk presents to another monk intention or declaration of purity for the restoration ceremony, it becomes an offence." The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

When the Blessed One declared that a monk who had undertaken the rains retreat must perform the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā) on the basis of three grounds — what was seen, what was heard, and what was suspected — the Group of Six, while residing outside the boundary, presented faith-offerings and declarations of purity for the invitation ceremony in full, just as if it were a restoration ceremony.

The summary verse:
Counting monks, toilet wood, and whatever one wishes,
Sitting on one seat, dwelling in a house,
And novices newly joined — these are not to be present.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. There was a brahmin residing at Śrāvastī who had gone outside for some small errand and made his way to the Jeta Grove. After a moment he thought to himself, "I wonder how many monks are residing here," and so he asked the monks: "Noble ones, how many monks are dwelling here?" They replied: "Brahmin, we do not know." The brahmin said: "If you know the count of the market quarters in the capital of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, how is it that you do not know the count of your own monks?" They said nothing in reply, and the brahmin went away. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you must count one another."

When the Blessed One declared that the monks must count one another, the monks counted by saying "one" and so on. Later, forgetting this, they heard the Blessed One declare: "You must not count by saying 'one' and so on." When the monks then tried to count by raising fingers, they still forgot, and the Blessed One declared: "You must not count by raising fingers." After the Blessed One had declared that monks must not count by saying 'one' and so on, and must not count by raising fingers, the monks did not know how they were to count. At that point the monks asked the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Tally-sticks are to be prepared and distributed, and after they are distributed, counting is to be done. When the count is complete, one should announce to the Saṅgha: 'There are so many monks.'"

When the Blessed One declared that tally-sticks were to be prepared, the monks did not know for which day, month, or year the sticks were to be distributed. The Blessed One then declared: "The tally-sticks are to be distributed at the time of the invitation ceremony at the end of the rains retreat."

Now, when the Blessed One had declared that monks were to be counted, there was a householder living in Śrāvastī who would come regularly to the Jeta Grove. He saw the monks there striving in the practice of meditative concentration, of recitation, and of the yoga of mental cultivation, and from their conduct, their comportment, and their practice he gained faithful confidence. He thought to himself: "For now, let me first ask how many monks there are here, and afterward invite them and offer them a meal." He asked the monks: "Noble ones, how many monks are residing here?" The monks replied: "So many." He then paid homage at their feet and departed, went to his own home, and said to his household: "Go! Prepare a meal for a monastic Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha — prepare food for so many monks." They replied: "Master, that is good; we will do exactly so." They then began to prepare honey, molasses, sugar, and the like. The householder also gathered his friends, relatives, and family members, and when all was prepared, he set out together with them to the Jeta Grove. Starting from the eldest, he paid homage at the feet of the monks, and then said to the monastery steward: "Noble one, a great householder wishes to invite the monastic Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha tomorrow at midday. Please convey this message." The steward made the announcement, the monastic Saṅgha of monks consented, and the householder paid homage at their feet and departed.

However, some other monks who were wandering on tour had also come to Śrāvastī. That same evening the householder prepared a clean and plentiful meal with food and provisions, rose early the next morning, set out seats and placed out water vessels, and then sent a messenger to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the midday meal is now prepared. May the Blessed One be pleased to consider that the hour has come." This was conveyed at the midday hour.

The monks in the early morning, having adjusted their robes, took their alms bowls and Dharma robes and set out for the householder's home. The Blessed One remained in the assembly hall and was summoned at the midday hour.

Awakened ones, Blessed Ones, remain in the assembly hall and are summoned at the midday hour for five reasons. What are the five? They wish to settle properly within; they wish to teach the Dharma to the gods; they wish to inspect the lodgings; they wish to attend to the sick; and they wish to establish rules of Vinaya training for the hearers. In this case, the Blessed One, wishing to establish rules of Vinaya training for the hearers, remained in the assembly hall and was summoned there at the midday hour.

That householder had set out seats in proportion to the number of monks in the Saṅgha and had prepared food accordingly. But when he saw that the monks were exceedingly numerous, he said, "Noble ones, I laid out seats for exactly as many monks as you told me there were, and I prepared food to match — yet far more monks have come."

The monks replied, "Householder, be glad that these additional monks have arrived unexpectedly."

He said, "Noble ones — alas! You should have told me that other monks were also coming. I would have prepared more food and laid out more seats." The monks fell silent, having no confidence to say anything further. And then some of the last to arrive had nothing at all, while the monks ate only what they could scrape into their mouths, struggling as it was shared out among them.

At that point, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "The monk who is the duty-officer shall, upon learning how many unexpected monks have arrived, announce this to the householder-patrons. Other monks who come only at mealtime — the Blessed One declared that these too shall be announced. Other monks who arrive late, beyond the first announcement — the Blessed One declared that these too shall be announced. Furthermore, I shall establish a rule of conduct for the senior monk of the Saṅgha's community. The senior monk of the Saṅgha shall inspect the Saṅgha of monks, and if the monks are many but the food is little, he shall say to the donor, 'Honored sir, the food is little and the monks are many — please serve them in turn by going round.' But if the food is much and the monks are few, he shall say, 'Honored sir, the food is plentiful — please serve them in turn as much as is available.' If the senior monk of the Saṅgha does not properly take up and apply the rule of conduct thus established, he incurs an offense."

The narrative occasion is in Śrāvastī.

Then the venerable Śāriputra, in the early morning, robed himself, took up his bowl and robes, and entered Śrāvastī on alms-round. Having made his way through Śrāvastī on alms-round, he went to where Queen Mālinī was and, having arrived, began to teach her the Dharma. While he was teaching her the Dharma, Queen Mālinī heard the sound of song and music coming from the direction of Mṛgāra's mother Sādhā, who was carrying medicine for the ailing Saṅgha of monks and making her way toward the Jeta Grove. She asked, "Noble one, whose is that sound of song and music?"

He replied, "Queen, it is Mṛgāra's mother Sādhā, carrying medicine for the ailing Saṅgha of monks — that sound belongs to her."

She said, "Noble one, if that is so, it would be fitting for me to have it announced to the Saṅgha of monks in my own name, saying: 'Queen Mālinī has offered medicine to the Saṅgha of monks.'"

He replied, "Queen, very well. The Blessed One himself has said, 'Whoever tends to the sick tends to me.' Therefore, let it be announced to the Saṅgha of monks in your name." So saying, he wished Queen Mālinī freedom from illness, rose from his seat, and departed.

He then went to the monastery, sat at the end of the row of elders, and said, "Queen Mālinī has offered medicine to the Saṅgha of monks. Whoever wishes for whatever medicine — go and ask for it." When the duty-officer made this announcement, the monks said:

The venerable Cāraka said, "Did the Blessed One not declare that there are ten faults in going to the royal palace? How then should we transgress our training for the sake of medicine?" Having no answer to this, he said nothing, and not a single monk requested medicine from Queen Mālinī.

After some time, the venerable Cāraka himself went to where Queen Mālinī was. She said to him, "Noble one, did you not distribute medicine for the sick in the name of the Saṅgha of monks?" "Queen, I did." "Noble one, if that is so, why have the monks not come?" "Queen, did the Blessed One not declare that there are ten faults in going to the royal palace? How could the monks come here?" "Noble one, if that is the case, how am I to arrange this?" "Queen, if you were to place the kārṣāpaṇas in the hands of a marketplace merchant, then whatever medicine any monk wishes for, he may request it from him."

She replied, "Noble one, excellent — let it be done so." She placed the kārṣāpaṇas in the hands of a marketplace merchant and said, "The noble ones will not come to the royal palace; therefore, whatever any monk wishes for, give it to him." The merchant received the kārṣāpaṇas at the queen's command and set them aside.

The monks then entrusted the kārṣāpaṇas to a certain large perfume-seller's stall belonging to the goddess Mālinī, instructing her: "Whatever any monk wishes for, you are to give it to him." Hearing this instruction, they left, thinking she would do so.

Then certain monks came and said, "Good woman, prepare for us dried broth, broth, and meat, and give it to us." Others said, "Give us broth and dried meat." Yet others said, "Give us raw meat broth and lard." She was troubled by all this and said, "Noble ones, I am neither a soup-maker nor a meat-preparer. Please take this money and go, and let whoever wants whatever arrange it for themselves." They said, "Good woman, the Blessed One has not permitted monks to handle money." She replied, "Noble ones, I am a perfume-seller living by trade in the marketplace — if it comes to this, my livelihood will be ruined."

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Trusting in the patron, one may take the kārṣāpaṇas and make whatever use of them one wishes. There is no fault in this."

The setting for this is Śrāvastī.

The group of six monks were sitting together on one seat with laypeople. Faithful brahmin and householder devotees saw this and mocked them, saying, "Noble ones, you have gone forth and lead the holy life — how is it that you sit on the same seat together with those who enjoy sensual pleasures?" When the monks said nothing in response, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is fitting that the faithful brahmins and householders mocked them. Therefore, monks must not sit on the same seat together with laypeople; if they do, it becomes an offense. The Blessed One has declared that one must not sit on the same seat together with laypeople."

When it was then seen by lay practitioners that the monks were sitting on the same seat together with novices, they said, "Noble ones, you have received full ordination — how is it that you sit on the same seat together with novices?" The monks said, "Venerables, these are not laypeople — these are renunciants; what transgression is there in this?" When they said nothing further in response, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "One must not sit on the same seat together with one who has not received full ordination." When the Blessed One had declared that one must not sit on the same seat together with one who has not received full ordination, senior monks began sitting on the same seat together with junior monks, and the junior monks showed disrespect toward the senior monks on that account. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Senior and junior monks must not sit on the same seat together. However, one may sit on the same seat together with one who is in the intermediate period of three years. One who has not yet completed a year and one who has completed three years may sit together; one who has completed one year and one who has completed four years, and similarly up to one who has completed nine years and one who has completed twelve years, may also sit together."

When the Blessed One had declared that one may sit on the same seat together with one who is in the intermediate period of three years — that one who has not yet completed a year and one who has completed three years may sit together, that one who has completed one year and one who has completed four years, and similarly up to one who has completed nine years and one who has completed twelve years, may also sit together — the monks would not sit together with those in the intermediate period of three years even inside a layman's house, and as a result those monks went without seats. The Blessed One then declared: "Inside a layman's house, one may sit together even with one's preceptor and abbot — there is no cause for remorse in this."

The summary verse:

Not giving a novice a cushioned stool,
not correcting a novice in speech,
not administering an oath or making one kneel,
and not eating tiger-food.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When the Blessed One declared that seats should be arranged for listening to Dharma, the novices sat on cushioned stools and listened to the Dharma. They fell asleep there and in that very place lost control of their urine and feces, and the cushioned stools became soiled. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not give novices cushioned stools."

When the Blessed One had declared that one must not give novices cushioned stools, the novice known as Śāradvatīputra's (Śāriputra's) charge went to hear the Dharma, and the monks gave him a plain stool. He said, "Venerables, why do you give me a plain stool?" They said, "The Blessed One has forbidden cushioned stools for novices." He said, "Venerables, do you think I too would commit that offense?" The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "To those novices who are established in mindfulness, one may give a cushioned stool; to others, one may not."

The setting is Śrāvastī.

There was a monk who had a novice, and he reprimanded him harshly. The novice sat weeping at the gate of the Jeta Grove. Since one or another of the group of six was always to be found at the gate of the Jeta Grove, the venerable Ānanda, who was sitting at the gate, saw him and said, "Novice, why do you weep?" He said, "Venerable Ānanda, my abbot has reprimanded me harshly." He said, "Come here, my child — I will ensure that you are not lacking in your almsbowl, your robes, your straining cloth, your bowl, your belt, and whatever else you are in need of," and he led him to his dwelling.

The Blessed One declared that one must not harshly rebuke and then simply abandon the novice, but that he should instead be recalled. The monk accordingly sent another monk to that novice, who spoke to him. The novice replied, "What do I need an abbot for? My friend Ānanda has provided me with all my requisites — I will not go." The monk began to mock him, to slander him, and to revile him, saying, "The one I ordained has been won over by a companion." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "A monk must not draw away another's novice. If he draws him away, it becomes a grave offence close to creating schism."

The origin of this rule was at Śrāvastī.

Members of the group of six would renounce their vows wherever and whenever it suited them — renouncing before the Buddha, renouncing before the Dharma and the Saṅgha, renouncing before their teachers and their abbots. When brahmin and householder devotees observed this, they said, "Venerable sirs, even we householders do not renounce the Teacher, yet you who have gone forth — how is it fitting that you renounce the Teacher in this way?" When those monks sat in silence, the other monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the reproach of brahmin and householder devotees has truly struck home. One who has gone forth is of sincere intention. Therefore a monk must not renounce his vows. If a monk renounces them, it becomes an offence entailing a serious breach."

The origin of this rule was at Śrāvastī.

Members of the group of six, wherever and whenever they wished, would make a pack of their almsbowl, their robes, their straining cloth, their bowl, their belt, and whatever other requisites of a renunciant they had. When brahmins and householders saw this, they mocked them, saying, "Noble ones, why are you bundling up your almsbowl and other requisites as laypeople do? That is not fitting." Those monks replied, "Have you eaten garlic? Have you drunk ale? What impropriety is there in this?" And they sat in silence. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the reproach of brahmins and householders has truly struck home. Therefore a monk must not make such a bundle of his requisites. If a monk makes such a bundle, it becomes an offence entailing a serious breach."

The origin of this rule was at Śrāvastī.

The conduct of the group of six was as follows: they would rise before dawn, climb to the roof, and look out in all four directions — wherever they saw smoke rising or vultures circling, they would quickly set off at a brisk pace for that place. Then one day a companion of theirs rose before dawn, went up to the roof, and began to look. He saw vultures wheeling in the distance, flying far and farther away. Then he saw that a tiger had hidden a carcass somewhere in a dense forest, and he was delighted. He took it and went to the Jeta Grove. The tiger, following the scent and tracking him, began to make a commotion at the gate of the Jeta Grove. Now, the blessed buddhas, even when they already know something, feign not knowing, and so the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda, "Why is the tiger roaring?" Ānanda replied, "Venerable sir, it is because the venerable one's companion has come seeking the carcass that the tiger had hidden." The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, does a monk eat a tiger's carcass? It is fit only for a wild beast to seek out. Ānanda, the king of beasts, the lion, kills noble and noble prey, eats fine flesh, drinks pure blood, and then leaves the remainder behind. A tiger, however, hides carcasses away. Therefore a monk must not eat a tiger's carcass.

To eat it would constitute a grave offence. Furthermore, O monks, I shall establish a rule of conduct to be observed by the senior resident of a Saṅgha residence: the senior resident monk of a Saṅgha residence, when distributing meat, must ask, 'Is this not a tiger's carcass?' If he takes it without asking, he incurs a grave offence.

The summary verse:

When the tooth-wood sticks are distributed,
the two friends who concealed themselves,
the reversal of the shares received,
and matters such as these are the subject.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, belonging to Prince Jeta. On a certain hillside there was a monastery. One day Nanda and Upananda were wandering and exploring in the countryside, and they went to that hillside. While they were there, a gain accrued to the Saṅgha. Since those two were practitioners of wrongful conduct, no monk had gone to summon them. Then Upananda said to Nanda, "Teacher, these arrogant ones with their black bowls filled to the brim are harassing us. Let us hide and watch how they divide up whatever they get." Nanda replied, "Good, let us do just that." They hid themselves and watched as the Saṅgha divided the gains. When the distribution was finished, those two came forward and said, "Venerable ones, divide the Saṅgha's gains that have come in." The monks replied, "Where have you come from only now? The time for distributing those gains has passed." Those two said, "Are you the ones who are supposed to divide? You may have divided it, but it was wrong to divide it. Did you make the announcement and then divide?" At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "When gains are to be distributed to the Saṅgha, make the announcement to the Saṅgha that no monk is to go anywhere, and then distribute the gains." The monks collected those gains back together. After collecting them, they announced to the Saṅgha that when the Saṅgha's gains were to be distributed no monk was to go anywhere, and began to divide them. Nanda and Upananda hid themselves just as before.

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, twenty-third fascicle.

When the Saṅgha had finished distributing those gains, those two came again and said, "Venerable ones, give us our share of those gains." The monks said, "Where have you come from only now? The time for distributing the gains was when the announcement had been made to the Saṅgha." Those two replied, "Even if you made the announcement, you cannot divide it away from us — it was wrong to divide it. Did you sound the gong (gaṇḍī) after making the announcement?" At that point the monks again reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "After making the announcement, sound the gong and then distribute the gains to the Saṅgha." The monks again collected the gains back together, and after collecting them, made the announcement just as before, sounded the gong, and began to divide. Those two hid themselves exactly as before. When the distribution of those gains was finished, they came again and spoke exactly as before. The monks replied, "We made the announcement to the Saṅgha and we sounded the gong — where have you come from only now?" Those two said, "You made the announcement and sounded the gong, but did you distribute the tooth-wood sticks? You cannot divide it away from us — it was wrong to divide it." When this was said, the monks again reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "After making the announcement, sound the gong, distribute the tooth-wood sticks, and then divide the gains."

The monks again collected those gains. Having collected them, they made the announcement, sounded the gong, distributed the tooth-wood sticks, and were just beginning to divide the gains — whereupon those two hid themselves exactly as before. When the distribution of the gains was finished, those two came forth and spoke exactly as before. The monks said, "Venerable ones, how do you dare make such a claim to the Saṅgha? We made the announcement to the Saṅgha, sounded the gong, and distributed the tooth-wood sticks — from where have you come only now?" Those two replied, "Venerables, never mind the gains. If that is so, then tell us: in what manner did we make a claim to the Saṅgha? If you made the announcement, sounded the gong, and distributed the tooth-wood sticks — did you then show us our share? That is all. Even without any gains, we would still go on our way." When this was said, the monks again reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "After making the announcement to the Saṅgha, sounding the gong, and distributing the tooth-wood sticks, show the share of anyone who is absent, and then make the division. Whatever share belongs to one who comes only after the division is complete — gains shall not be given to that person. If the division is made in this way, it is a proper division, and there shall be no remorse in this. A monk must not deliberately stir up such trouble for the Saṅgha. If a monk deliberately does stir up trouble for the Saṅgha, it becomes a serious offense."

The basis of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

At a certain time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, and had it painted inside and out with various and distinct colors. When the multitude of people dwelling at Śrāvastī heard how the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had painted the Jeta Grove inside and out with various and distinct colors of excellent quality and made it supremely magnificent, many hundreds of thousands of living creatures came near to the Jeta Grove to see it.

Now at that time a brahmin was residing at Śrāvastī. The king, his ministers, and the townspeople looked upon this brahmin with admiration and said, "This brahmin is handsome," and so he received a considerable gift fitting for one of high standing, from the royal palace. He shared out that gift and went to the Jeta Grove to see the spectacle. The moment he saw it, an immense faith arose in him, and he offered that entire gift to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions.

The Blessed One had said, "Whenever gains of cloth arise, divide them equally, down to even what is enough for the wick of a lamp." So the monks cut the cloth into strips and divided it equally. The brahmin thought, "That gift was one of great worth. Let me offer the noble ones some kārṣāpaṇa coins and receive it back." So the next morning he rose early and went to the Jeta Grove. At the gate of the Jeta Grove many monks were sitting. He addressed them: "I pay homage to the noble ones. May the great brahmin be in good health. That gift which was offered to the noble ones — what have you done with it?" The monks replied, "Great brahmin, rejoice! We have divided it equally." One said, "I used my share to mend my hat." Another said, "I used mine to mend my short shoes." Another said, "I used mine to patch my upper robe." Another said, "I used mine to wipe out my begging bowl." Then he said —

"Noble ones, something befitting the great gift would be to exchange those kārṣāpaṇas and divide the kārṣāpaṇas among yourselves." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, what the brahmin says is true. Therefore, whatever gain of robes of that kind has come to the Saṅgha, it should be exchanged for kārṣāpaṇas, and those kārṣāpaṇas should be divided."

Summary verse:
The five unsuitable kinds,
the prohibition of shoes,
shoes of bear hide,
and the layers upon them.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six said: "Friend, dear friend! If we were to go through all of Śrāvastī to every last person without exception and set up a round of meals, those royal elephant-trainers would give us nothing at all. Let us go and stir up a little trouble." Some of them said: "Good — let us do so; but we should devise a plan. What shall we do? Let us make shoes from a lion's hide, divide them up, go and sit in the place where the elephants walk, and startle the elephants." Others said: "First let us go and ask them, and if they refuse to give anything, we can do that afterward." So the next morning they rose early, went to those elephant-trainers, and said: "Friends, you brutes! Will you not pay us the price of our meals?" The trainers replied: "Noble ones, what do we owe you? Why should we pay you the price of meals?" The group of six measured them up and left.

Then, just as they had planned, they made shoes from a lion's hide, divided them among themselves, went and sat down in the place where the elephants were accustomed to walk, and when the elephants caught the scent of the lion they panicked, lost control of their bowels, and began to bolt. The royal elephant-trainers tried to hold them with their iron hooks, thrusting with all their might, but could not restrain them. The group of six called out: "Venerable ones, do not let them go! Do not let them go!" The trainers replied: "Noble ones, if we cannot hold them, how can we not let them go?" The group of six said: "Then will you pay us? Noble ones, if you accept this arrangement, all the better. Venerable ones, if you promise to give us the price of our meals, we will pay you back." The trainers replied: "Noble ones, we are destitute." "Is that so?" And with that, they moved off to a direction away from the elephants' path and sat down there; no longer catching the lion's scent, the elephants stood still. The elephant-trainers said: "Noble ones, do you know any incantations?" "Friends, we know no incantations." "Noble ones, then how did you stop them?" The trainers described what had happened, and those trainers then said: "See what harm you have done! If these excellent royal elephants with their superb limbs were to have strayed off into the forest, would you not have done great injury to the king?" The group of six sat there smiling, saying nothing in reply.

The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter: "Whatever fault has now arisen has come about because monks wore shoes of lion's hide. Therefore monks should not keep shoes of lion's hide." Having so considered, he addressed the monks: "Monks, therefore a monk should not keep shoes of lion's hide. If a monk keeps shoes of lion's hide, he incurs a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks should not keep shoes of lion's hide, the group of six then began to keep shoes of tiger's hide. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore monks should not keep shoes made from the hides of any of the five kinds of animals possessing claws and fangs: the trained elephant, the trained horse, the lion, the tiger, or the bear. Monks should not keep shoes made from the hides of these five animals possessing claws and fangs."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks should not keep shoes made from the hides of the five animals possessing claws and fangs, the venerable Upavāna asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, are there yet other animals possessing claws and fangs? Should shoes made from their hides likewise not be kept?" "Shoes made from the hides of those animals likewise should not be kept; if kept, one incurs a serious offense."

The setting for the next rule is Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī a certain monk was afflicted with an illness of swelling sores. He went to a physician and said: "Revered sir, I am afflicted with swelling sores; please prescribe a medicine." The physician said: "Noble one, tread upon shoes of bear's hide and you will recover." The monk replied: "The Blessed One has not permitted this." The physician said: "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate; he will permit it." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore it is permitted: a monk afflicted with the illness of swelling sores may keep shoes of bear's hide."

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk afflicted with swelling sores may keep shoes of bear's hide, it happened that many layers could not be obtained. The Blessed One then declared: "If many layers cannot be obtained, one may fasten a single upper layer with a piece of felt."

Here ends the fifth chapter from the Vinaya on minor matters.

The summary verse is as follows:

By hide of leopard, of bright fine-cloth, harsh,
of servant, and likewise of bark,
of one who has fallen, of a merchant,
and of a monk who does not discard the remainder.

The further summary verse:

The lining of those hides, with cording,
and likewise inner toe-piece and heel-piece,
with long handle and with short handle,
and those with a strap — these should not be made.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When the Blessed One had declared that monks should not keep shoes made from the hides of the five animals possessing claws and fangs, the group of six stitched shoes using the lining of those hides, and on account of that very fault the Blessed One declared: "One should not stitch shoes using their lining." When the Blessed One had declared that one should not stitch shoes using their lining, the group of six stitched shoes using leather cording from those hides, and on account of that very fault the Blessed One declared: "One should not stitch shoes using leather cording from those hides." When the Blessed One had declared that one should not stitch shoes using either their lining or their leather cording, the group of six made inner toe-pieces from those hides, and on account of that very fault the Blessed One declared: "One should not make inner toe-pieces from those hides." When the Blessed One had declared that one should not make inner toe-pieces from those hides, the group of six made heel-pieces from those hides, and on account of that very fault the Blessed One declared: "One should not make heel-pieces from those hides." When the Blessed One had declared that one should not make inner toe-pieces or heel-pieces from those hides, the group of six made shoes with long handles from those hides, and on account of that very fault the Blessed One declared:

"One should not make shoes with long handles from those hides." When the Blessed One had declared that one should not make inner toe-pieces, heel-pieces, or shoes with long handles from those hides, the group of six made shoes with short handles from those hides, and on account of that very fault the Blessed One declared: "One should not make shoes with short handles from those hides." When the Blessed One had declared that one should not make shoes with short handles from those hides, the group of six made shoes with tassels from those hides, and on account of that very fault the Blessed One declared: "One should not make shoes with tassels from those hides."

Summary verse: Vairocana, all desires, the Saṅgha's heating and craft-training, giving food to the unprotected, children, the temple — and excellence.

Intermediate summary verse: The birth, the great king, and his own power; likewise the white man, the renunciant, the viceroy; the buddha-realm itself, and the supreme limb; likewise the dream, the earth-holder, the birth and the dwelling.

When the bodhisattva, the Blessed One, was dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, he surveyed the world through the five surveys — the survey of lineage, the survey of time, the survey of place, the survey of clan, and the survey of women — and, having stirred the six gods of the desire realm three times and indicated the form of a great elephant, he entered his mother's womb. At that moment the great earth shook mightily, and this entire world was pervaded by a great radiance that surpassed even the power of the brilliant hues of the gods of the Heaven of Thirty-Three. The darkness — the dense, impenetrable gloom — that lies between world and world, where the sun and moon, though possessed of such great miraculous power and such great might, cannot illuminate with their light, was likewise at that moment pervaded by that great radiance. Those sentient beings who had been born there and could not see even their own hand held before them, they too, by that light, saw one another; and those with understanding knew: "Look, other sentient beings too have been born here! Look, other sentient beings too have been born here!"

At the time when the bodhisattva, the Blessed One, was born, the sons of the four great kings were also born: in Rājagṛha the son of King Mahāpadma was born; in Śrāvastī the son of King Brahmadatta; in Vaiśālī the son of King Anantamekhalin; and in Kauśāmbī the son of King Śatānīka was born. When the bodhisattva was born, this great earth appeared like molten gold, and each king thought to himself, "This is the power of my son! This is the power of my son!" — and each of them, separately, gave him a name.

King Mahāpadma spoke: "Wise ones, when my son was born he made the world shine like the form of the sun; therefore I give the youth the name Rūpasāra, 'Essence of Form.'"

King Brahmadatta Long-flight spoke: "When my son was born the valleys appeared clear and brilliant; therefore I give the youth the name Jayaprabha, 'Victorious Radiance.'"

King Anantamekhalin spoke: "When my son was born the world was illuminated by a most excellent light; therefore I give the youth the name Suprabha, 'Excellent Light.'"

King Śatānīka spoke: "When my son was born the world was illuminated as though the sun had risen; therefore I give the youth the name Udaya, 'Rising.'"

At that time, in the Rikṣavana forest, there dwelt a sage named Śvetakarṇa, skilled in the destruction and the arising of this world. He had a nephew named Nālada, who came repeatedly to visit him. Whenever Nālada came, the sage would constantly speak to him of destruction and arising. Having heard these teachings on destruction and arising, Nālada grew weary and, right there in that place, went forth into renunciation.

Then, at another time, Nālada saw the cave of Śvetakarṇa pervaded by a vast and spreading light. Upon seeing it he spoke in verse:

Have all the suns together
risen here at once?
Like this — mountains and cave ablaze,
burning with rays of light!

Śvetakarṇa replied in verse:

The sun's light is warm; this light is cool.
Since it enters and illumines the body here,
this is certainly the light of the Mighty One —
the great radiant bodhisattva
has beyond all doubt emerged from the womb.
This is that bodhisattva's light,
stainless upon his arising.
All three worlds spread out
resemble gold.

Nālada said: "Master, if that is so, come this way! Let us go and behold the bodhisattva!"

He replied: "Son, at this very moment the bodhisattva is attended by those celebrated as greatly powerful among the gods, surrounded by the greatly powerful, and it is not easy for us to see him. We shall go at the time when he has gone to the palace, received his name, and come back out."

On the very day the bodhisattva was born, five hundred male attendants and five hundred female attendants were born and brought along; five hundred she-elephants and five hundred wild mares were also born and followed; and five hundred treasuries opened and became manifest. The ministers reported to King Śuddhodana: "Blessed one, whose face the gods delight to see, please be of good cheer! At the birth of the youth these many things have come to be: five hundred male attendants and five hundred female attendants have been born; five hundred she-elephants and five hundred wild mares have followed; and five hundred treasuries have opened and been displayed."

King Śuddhodana heard this and a feeling of joy arose in him. He spoke: "Wise ones, at the birth of the youth all my aims and the fullness of all my deeds are accomplished; therefore I give the youth the name Sarvārthasiddha, 'All Aims Accomplished.'" And so the bodhisattva received this name, Sarvārthasiddha.

The bodhisattva was placed in a palanquin adorned with the four precious substances, surrounded by many thousands of sentient beings, and with great honor from gods and humans he entered the city of Kapilavastu. When the bodhisattva entered the city, the proud Śākyas were speaking noisily all at once, while those who held themselves to be restrained sat in silence, composed like sages. Then King Śuddhodana spoke:

"Since these proud Śākyas were speaking noisily all at once, yet when the youth entered the city they fell silent, composed like sages, therefore let the youth's name be proclaimed Śākyamuni, 'the Sage of the Śākyas.'" And so the bodhisattva received this second name: Śākyamuni.

Now among the Śākyas there dwelled a permanent yakṣa by the name Śākyavarddhana, "the Increaser of the Śākyas." Whenever a son or a daughter was born among the Śākyas, the child was first brought to bow at the feet of the yakṣa Śākyavarddhana. So King Śuddhodana spoke: "Wise ones, let the youth now be brought to bow at the feet of the yakṣa Śākyavarddhana." When the ministers led him before the yakṣa, the yakṣa Śākyavarddhana caught sight of the bodhisattva from a great distance. Upon seeing him, the yakṣa rose up, striding forth with long, sweeping steps, went to receive the bodhisattva, and bowed at his feet. Then King Śuddhodana spoke: "Wise ones, the yakṣa Śākyavarddhana himself has bowed at the youth's feet. Therefore this youth is a god above gods, and so let the youth's name be proclaimed Devātideva, 'God above Gods.'" And thus the bodhisattva received his third name: Devātideva, "God above Gods."

Then King Śuddhodana presented the bodhisattva before the brahmins, the masters of bodily marks, and the astrologers, and said: "Wise ones, a youth who possesses certain signs will follow one of two paths of a great man and none other. If he remains a householder dwelling at home, he will become a wheel-turning king (cakravartin), victorious in the four directions, a righteous king of Dharma, possessing the seven precious treasures.
