And those seven precious treasures are these: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious woman, the precious householder, and seventh, the precious minister. But if with faith he shaves his hair and beard, dons the ochre robes, and goes forth from home to homelessness, he will become renowned throughout the world as a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha. Does he possess the thirty-two marks of a great man?" They replied: "Sire, it is just as you say. The youth possesses those signs through which one becomes a great man in one of two ways and no other" — and so they declared, from "the youth possesses those signs through which one becomes a great man in two ways and no other" up to "he will become renowned throughout the world, and he possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man."

Then Nālada spoke: "Master, the bodhisattva has gone to the city of Kapilavastu and his names have been bestowed. Come now, let us return and behold him." He replied: "Good, child. Let us do so." The two then set out by means of their supernormal powers — but through the power of the bodhisattva, those supernormal powers were rendered ineffective, and they entered the city of Kapilavastu on foot alone. They went to where King Śuddhodana's palace was, and having arrived, they stood at the gate of the royal palace.

Then the sage Nārada said to a man: "Friend, please go and announce to King Śuddhodana that the sage Nārada wishes to see him and is standing at the gate." The man went and announced: "Sire, the sage Nārada wishes to see the king and is at the palace gate." The king replied: "Wise ones, quickly invite the sage Nārada inside." When he entered, King Śuddhodana received him with the proper courtesies of welcome, offered a ceremonial gift to his feet, and had him seated upon a lion throne.

Then King Śuddhodana, touching his two feet, spoke: "Great sage, for what reason have you come?"

He then spoke in verse:

Great king, I have come wishing to behold your son —
I have come desiring to see him,
the guide, the lord of the world,
the Sage whom I long to behold.

King Śuddhodana said: "Great sage, the young one is asleep."

Nārada replied: "Then let me behold him as he sleeps."

King Śuddhodana said: "Great sage, very well — please go and look."

Nārada went and saw the bodhisattva gazing at forms without blinking his eyes. Upon seeing this, he spoke in verse:

A pure thoroughbred of noble lineage,
like one lying down at the midnight hour,
does not long keep sleep in his eyes —
for those who pursue purposeful aims do not linger in sleep.

Having said this, he asked: "O king, were those young brahmins, the astrologers, and the stargazers shown to him?"

Nārada said: "Great sage, they were shown to him."

"And what did those gods and seers prophecy?"

King Śuddhodana replied: "They said he would become a wheel-turning king (cakravartin)."

Then Nārada began to examine the bodhisattva from head to toe. As he beheld the marks of a buddha upon the bodhisattva, he fell into this contemplation: "In how many years, having seen the marks of a buddha upon this bodhisattva, will he attain the nectar of immortality?" And he perceived that at the age of twenty-nine he would go forth from the home life, and that after six years of austerities he would attain the nectar of immortality. Then, turning his contemplation upon his own stream of being, he saw that he himself would die in the interval, and the craving for existence in the desire realm arose in him. With eyes filled with tears, he spoke in verse:

The minds of those who reason and speculate err.
At the end of time there will be no wheel-turning king.
This one of supreme merit is a treasury of Dharma;
victorious over all faults, he will become a buddha.

By those who discern only the lesser marks of a great being,
he is proclaimed sovereign lord over the four continents.
He whose marks shine forth completely, the Lord of Sages, the perfect buddha —
this most excellent of men will turn the wheel of Dharma.

Then the king, seeing Nārada's eyes filled with tears, felt embarrassed and displeased, and in turn spoke in verse:

Men and women who encounter him
will not grow weary but will find delight.
This beautiful one, the giver of joy — you have seen him here.
Why then do your eyes brim with tears?

Surely my young one faces no danger,
nor is his life drawing near its end?
Therefore quickly tell me this good news.
Your mournful expression makes me tremble.

Nārada then spoke in verse:

Even if upon this earth from the sky
a fierce and terrible rain of vajras were to fall,
not a single hair of the great Sage's body
could be made to move.

Driven by a great storm-wind,
unbearable and keen and utterly sharp weapons,
the venom of vicious serpents and most terrible poisons —
were they to fall upon the young one's body, they could not harm him.

O lord of men, I weep because I, having encountered
this supreme treasury of the highest Dharma,
will die without accomplishing my purpose —
I will not attain peace. Seeing my own failing,
for that reason I weep.

Those in the world who, at the proper time,
hear the Dharma of this incomparable and peerless teacher,
and having heard, go to supreme peace —
they are joyful, full of merit, free of disease.

King Śuddhodana, upon hearing that the bodhisattva would attain the nectar of immortality, sat in silence without a word.

Now Nārada the white-clad sage — having become corrupted through wrong views, he had entered into great falsehood and the constant practice of deceit — spoke: "O king, the gathered people dwelling in your city may think: 'Alas, it is wrong that the white-clad sage Nārada should come on foot to the city of the Śākya land.' But I have long aspired, out of compassion for beings, to come on foot to the city of the Śākya land, and indeed I have come on foot. Please grant that the city be beautified by the mere fact of my coming on foot."

King Śuddhodana gave orders to his ministers: "Wise ones, have the white-clad sage Nārada depart the city on foot. Let the city and roads be made beautiful. Have the drums beaten, proclaiming aloud: 'Let all who dwell in the Śākya land, the assembled peoples, and those who have come from various regions, as well as others, ask: Who is the white-clad sage who departs the city on foot?'" The ministers, saying "As the king commands," had the city of the Śākya land cleared of stones, gravel, and clods of earth. They sprinkled it thoroughly with sandalwood water, placed bowls fragrant with perfume, hung many silk pennants, raised victory banners and flags, scattered flowers of many kinds, and made the city as beautiful and joyful as the pleasure groves of the gods — indeed more delightful even than a divine park of delight. They made the city and roads beautiful, then sounded the drums, proclaiming: "Let all who dwell in the city, the inhabitants of the palace, and the assembled peoples who have come from various regions hear this! The king has commanded: 'Tomorrow, the white-clad sage Nārada departs the city of the Śākya land on foot. Therefore all of you — ask who he is!'"

When morning came, the white-clad sage Nārada departed the city of the Śākya land on foot, escorted with great honor by many thousands of the finest of men.

He went some distance away, and there he gave rise again to meditative concentration and accomplished miraculous powers. But then, his karma having fully ripened and been exhausted, he was struck by illness. Though he was treated with medicines of roots, stems, flowers, leaves, and fruits, that illness did not subside.

Nāḷada, knowing the condition of his own body in its final stage, bowed at his feet and said: "Master, all who have gone forth to whatever degree seek nectar and search for nectar. Therefore, if you have found the nectar, I pray you share a portion of that nectar with me."

He replied: "My child, though I too, having gone forth, seek nectar and search for nectar — I have not found it. Nevertheless, you should go forth in the presence of the youth born among the Śākyans. Do not take pride in your clan, do not take pride in your lineage, do not take pride in being a brahmin's son. With that humility, practice the holy life — and so you will attain the nectar."

Then he spoke these verses:

All that is gathered must reach its end.
All that is high must come to fall.
All meeting must end in parting.
All that lives must end in death.

And so he met his time, in accordance with the nature of the hour.

Nāḷada performed the bone-rites for his bones, and then went to the city of Vārāṇasī, where he dwelt among the sages. And since Nāḷada was kin to Nārada through his bones, his name came to be the sage Nāḷada.

The youth Suprabhā was entrusted to eight nurses: two who would carry him in their arms and sustain him, two who would suckle him, two who would cleanse him of impurity, and two who would be his companions in play. These eight nurses reared and nourished him with milk, curds, fresh butter, clarified butter, the essence of butter, and other principal provisions and necessities, so that he grew and flourished like a lotus dwelling in a lake.

When he had grown to adulthood, he was instructed in letters, numerals, calculation, accounting, and the royal consecration poured upon the head of the kingly lineage. The various crafts and occupations of those who had attained lordship over the land and power over the realm, and those who abided in the settled domain of the great earth, were as follows: riding on the neck of an elephant, riding a horse, the handling of chariots, the handling of swords, archery,

pulling back, thrusting forward, the method of steering with an iron hook, the casting of a lasso, the hurling of a great arrow, cutting, splitting, the manner of seizing, the manner of stepping, striking at the crown, striking at a distance, striking so as to make a sound, striking a vital point, striking without missing — in all these formidable arts he became skilled, and he also became accomplished in the five fields of knowledge.

Now, whenever the bodhisattva sported in the play of youth, the young prince Rab Snang likewise sported in youthful play. When the bodhisattva was consecrated as crown prince, the young prince Rab Snang was likewise consecrated as crown prince.

When the bodhisattva, having seen an old person, a sick person, and a dead person, felt weariness and renounced sixty thousand women — including those known as Sā Tsho Ma, Ri Dags Skyes, Grags Dzin Ma, and the rest — and at midnight went to dwell in the forest of austerities, then, in the presence of the ascetics who had freed themselves from the coarser and subtler forms of existence, he proceeded from freedom from attachment to the desire realm (kāmadhātu), through freedom from attachment to the form realm (rūpadhātu), and — in the matter of the excellent conduct of the son of Raṅs Byed — freedom from attachment all the way up to the sphere of nothingness (ākimcanyāyatana) within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). Thinking that since he had not yet found liberation through scriptural transmission, it was fitting to undergo austerities, he practiced austerities for six years, and yet did not attain any exceptional realization. Then he breathed comfortably in and out as he pleased, ate coarse food with rice and warm gruel, anointed his body with white butter and sesame oil, and bathed in water neither too cold nor too warm. He proceeded to the village called Sde Grong, and from the maidens Dga Mo and Dga Stobs he received sixteen portions of milk-porridge sweetened with honey, pressed into essence, and consumed them. Praised by Nāgarāja the Black, the king of nāgas, he received fresh grass from the auspicious grass-seller, and went to that very place, the foot of the tree of awakening. Arriving there, he spread the grass in an undisturbed and unentangled manner, sat down, crossed his legs, straightened his body, set his awareness in direct presence, and resolved in his heart — and also declared aloud — that until he attained the exhaustion of all defilements, he would not uncross his legs:

"Until I have found the exhaustion of all defilements,
I shall not unfold my crossed legs."

When the Blessed One vanquished Māra, together with his host of sixty myriads of demon troops, with the weapon of loving-kindness, and thereby obtained unsurpassed wisdom; when at Brahmā's urging he proceeded to the region of Vārāṇasī and, reciting three times, turned the wheel of Dharma in twelve aspects in accordance with the Dharma — at that time the young prince Rab Snang was likewise consecrated as a great king.

At that time, in the noble realm of Ārya, there was a king named Rab Snang, a Dharma-king, whose kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, happy, with good harvests and many people, filled with humans; and quarrels, disputes, conflicts, and the disturbances of conflict were thoroughly pacified; there was no banditry, and no illness. He governed in accordance with the Dharma, ensuring abundance of sālu rice, sugarcane, and mahā. By his power he always rejoiced greatly in festivals.

In that city of the noble realm there were the five sense faculties and the five proximate faculties. Five hundred streams flowing from five hundred ponds flowed into the very place called the Beautiful Palace of the King.

King Rab Snang had five supreme-limbed elephants: the elephant Dam Bu's Mountain, the great elephant Mo Bzang Ldan, the female elephant Ocean-Footed, the horse Kha Dog Mgrin, and the one called Phar Ma Pa Kha. Of these, Dam Bu's Mountain could in a single day cover a distance of one hundred leagues. Mo Bzang Ldan could cover eighty leagues. Ocean-Footed could cover seventy leagues.

The horse Kha Dog Mgrin could cover fifty leagues, and Phar Ma Pa Kha could cover twenty leagues.

With all such abundance and perfect prosperity, the king was struck by a condition called "sleeplessness from unbalanced elements." The king loathed butter and was fond of alcohol, so when the physicians prepared clarified butter blended with various special medicinal substances and offered it to him to drink, he would not drink it. If the consort's retinue, the young men, the ministers, or the people of the palace household tried to offer him butter, he would grow ever more enraged, and whoever so much as uttered the word "butter" he would have beheaded and thrown to the ground. Because of his sleeplessness, during the first watch of the night he would sport and take pleasure with the consort's retinue. During the second watch, he would inspect the elephants and horses. During the third watch, he would go to those of his subjects who tended the fires and ask, "Who is stoking the fires right now?" Whoever failed to answer on the first asking, he would let pass. Whoever failed to answer on the second asking, he would also let pass. But whoever failed to answer on the third asking, he would have beheaded and thrown to the ground. Because of this, the name by which he had been known, King Rab Snang, came in time to be replaced from all sides by the name the Fierce King Rab Snang, Grim Rab Snang the Fierce.

On another occasion he said to the consort's retinue: "Women, I tend the fires — why do you not tend the fires?" They replied, "Your Majesty, we too will do so when our turn comes." They tended the fires for a little while and then said, "Your Majesty, if we were to tend them always, this is not our duty — it is not our task, for we must guard Your Majesty's heart; this work of stoking falls on no ordinary person." He said, "If this is not your work, then whose work is it?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it belongs to the young men." He dismissed them and went to the young men and said, "Young men, I tend the fires — why do you not tend the fires?" They replied, "Your Majesty, we too will do so when our turn comes." They also tended the fires for a little while and then said, "Your Majesty, if we were to tend them always" — and from the passage "what are the duties of a king" up to "in five places," just as before — "this work of maintaining the kingdom is not our task." He said, "If this is not your work, then whose work is it?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it belongs to the ministers." He dismissed them and went to the ministers and said, "Wise ones, I tend the fires — why do you not tend the fires?" They replied, "Your Majesty, we too will do so when our turn comes." They also tended the fires for a little while and then said, "Your Majesty, if we were to tend them always, ruling the kingdom in accordance with the Dharma — this work of stoking falls on no ordinary person; this is not our task." He said, "If this is not your work, then whose work is it?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it is the work of the town guild." He dismissed them and went to the town guild and said, "Wise ones, I tend the fires — why do you not tend the fires?" The town guild replied, "Your Majesty, we too will do so when our turn comes." They also tended the fires for a little while and then said, "Your Majesty, if we were to tend them always, engaging in battle alongside those who attack Your Majesty and those who counterattack — this work of stoking falls on no ordinary person; this is not our task." He said, "If this is not your work, then whose work is it?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it belongs to the townsfolk and the villagers." He dismissed them and went to the townsfolk and

He went to the townsfolk and said, "Wise ones, I tend the fires — why do you not tend the fires?" They replied, "Your Majesty, we will do so when our turn comes." He then appointed them to tend the fires constantly, and they divided the duty among themselves in rotation and began to take their turns.

Now, at a certain point the turn fell upon a young incense-seller. He feared that the fierce king would kill him, and so he sat in distress, resting his chin on his hand and brooding inwardly. A friend of his saw him brooding and said, "Friend, why do you sit resting your chin on your hand and brooding?" The young man told him what had happened. Near that friend's home there was a certain guard, and the friend said to the young man, "Friend, you have a guard living near your home — why don't you commission him?" The young man replied, "Friend, just as my own life is precious to me, his life is equally precious to him — why would he do my errand?" The friend said, "Friend, give him some kārṣāpaṇas and without fail he will tend the fires." So he commissioned the guard, and the guard said, "Give me five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and I will tend the fires." The young man promised, "I will give them." Then the guard said, "For now, give me two hundred and fifty. As for the remainder — if I return alive, give it to me then; but if not, it is yours to do with as you wish." The young man said, "Very well, let it be so," and gave him the two hundred and fifty kārṣāpaṇas. The guard took them and went to the market, where he bought a great quantity of meat and ale.

Then the fierce king Rabhasprabha invited all the household servants as guests, fed them, and poured out as much ale as they wished. He said, "Wise ones, when the fire-tending duty falls on me, tell me what the behavior of this king is like." They told him everything about how things actually were. He said, "Wise ones, remember that I have done you a small service." They replied, "O lord of the earth, you have fed us and quenched our thirst, and we have not yet finished drinking — why should we not remember? Tell us what you need done." He said, "If I fall asleep while on fire duty and the king sends the fire-watchers around, please wake me." They said, "Very well, we will do so." He then wrapped his lower robe around himself and began tending the fires — and overcome by deep drowsiness, he lay down and fell asleep.

As it happened, that same king, during the first watch, had taken pleasure and delight together with the retinue of his queens. In the middle watch he had reviewed the elephants and horses. When the final watch came and he began to inspect the fire-tenders, those servants roused the guard, saying, "O lord of the earth, the king is coming — get up!" He leapt up at once and sat there just as he had been, with his lower robe wrapped around him.

The king called out, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard thought to himself: "If I answer only this first call and fail to answer thereafter, this king will surely cut off my head without a second thought and cast it to the ground." Knowing this, he said nothing. The king called out a second time, "Who is tending the fires?" Still he said nothing. The king called out a third time, "Who is tending the fires?" Only then the guard spoke: "It is I, O lord of the earth." The king said, "Guard, what do you have in mind?" For though his intentions were base, he was a man well versed in the lore and tales of the world. The guard replied, "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought."

The verse summary is as follows:

An owl, a crane, muñja grass,
a black thing, burning, a pot,
salt, powder, death,
a pit, a snare, an earthen vessel — these are inauspicious.

What sort of worldly thought, O lord of the earth, is the guard thinking?

"Your Majesty, an owl with feathers and an owl without feathers, when weighed on a scale, come out exactly equal. That is most remarkable, O lord of the earth. Can this truly be so?" "Guard, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day the guard came bringing an owl, and before the king weighed it with its feathers, then plucked out its feathers and weighed it again — it was exactly the same. The king said, "Guard, what is the reason for this?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is because the feathers catch the wind." The king said, "Guard, you are a learned man." The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

The guard waited until dawn had not yet broken, then at first light anointed his head and departed from the royal palace. The incense merchant's boy also gave him those two hundred and fifty kārṣāpaṇas. In the kingdom of Kośala, whatever person's turn it was received five hundred kārṣāpaṇas from him as payment, and so that person always tended the fires in his stead. Again the king, just as before, called out, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard replied as before, "Your Majesty, it is I who do so when it is my turn." The king said, just as before, "Guard, what are you thinking?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." The king said, "Guard, what sort of worldly thought are you thinking?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, those birds called cranes — when one gives them milk mixed with water, they drink the milk and leave the water behind." "Guard, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day the guard came bringing a crane, and before the king mixed milk with water and poured it out before him — the crane drank the milk and left the water behind. The king said, "Guard, what is the reason for this?"

The Vinaya of minor matters. The twenty-fourth section.

The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is because there is sourness in its beak, and by that sourness, as it drinks, the milk it desires curdles and separates from the water." The king said, "Guard, you are a learned man." The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king, just as before, called out, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard replied as before, "Your Majesty, it is I who do so when it is my turn." The king said, "Guard, what are you thinking?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." The king said, "Guard, what sort of worldly thought are you thinking?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, muñja grass that has been beaten with a mallet and muñja grass that has not been beaten — when placed on a scale, they come out exactly equal." "Guard, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day the guard came bringing muñja grass and demonstrated before the king exactly as described — and everything was just as he had said. The king said, "Guard, what is the reason for this?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is because beating it with the mallet compresses the air within it." The king said, "Guard, you are a learned man." The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king, just as before, called out, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard replied as before, "Your Majesty, it is I, the guard." The king said, "Guard, what are you thinking?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." The king said, "Guard, what sort of worldly thought are you thinking?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, the creature called the black-headed spider monkey — its body and its tail are of exactly the same length." "Guard, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day he brought a black-headed spider monkey and demonstrated it before the king exactly as he had described, and everything proved to be just so. The king said, "Guard, how did you know this?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, when this creature entered its burrow I observed its tail reaching the opening at the same moment as its head." The king said, "Guard, you are a learned man." The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king called out as before, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard replied as before, "Your Majesty, it is I, the guard." The king said, "Guard, what are you thinking?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Guard, what sort of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, among the wing-feathers of a bird that has been singed, however many are scorched, exactly that same number are unscorched." "Guard, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day he demonstrated it before the king's very eyes, and everything proved to be just so. The king said, "Guard, how did you know this?" "Your Majesty, I had counted them beforehand." The king said, "Guard, you are a learned man." The guard replied, "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king called out in the same way, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard replied as before, "Your Majesty, it is I, the guard." The king said, "What are you thinking?" "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Guard, what sort of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, if a full pitcher of water is poured into a full pitcher of sand, all that water will be absorbed within it." "Guard, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day he demonstrated it before the king's very eyes, and everything proved to be just so. The king said, "Guard, how did you know this?" "Your Majesty, it is because sand is born from water." The king said, "Guard, you are a learned man." "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king called out in the same way, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard replied as before, "Your Majesty, it is I, the guard." The king said, "Guard, what are you thinking?" "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Guard, what sort of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, if a full measure of water is added to a full measure of salt, the result will be nothing more than a full measure of water." "Guard, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day he demonstrated it before the king's very eyes, and everything proved to be just so. The king said, "Guard, what is the reason for this?" "Your Majesty, it is because salt comes from water." The king said, "Guard, you are a learned man." "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king called out in the same way, "Who is tending the fires?" The guard replied as before, "Your Majesty, it is I, the guard." The king said, "Guard, what are you thinking?" "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Guard, what sort of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, if a full measure of water is added to a full measure of flour, the mixture will be neither loose nor stiff." "Guard, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, you shall see it with your own eyes." "Well done, guard."

The next day he demonstrated it before the king's very eyes, and everything proved to be just so. The king said, "Guard, what is the reason for this?" "Your Majesty, we guards are those who sift flour, and I have observed this many times." The king said, "Guard, you are a man of mindfulness." "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king called out in the same way, "Who is tending the fires?"

He replied in the same manner as before. "Your Majesty, it is I, the earth-holder." The king said, "Earth-holder, what are you thinking?" "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Earth-holder, what kind of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, if a dead man and a living man were placed on the two pans of a scale, they would not balance." "Earth-holder, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, I shall demonstrate it before your own eyes." "Well done, earth-holder."

The next day he demonstrated it before the king's very eyes, and everything proved to be just so. The king said, "Earth-holder, what is the reason for this?" "Your Majesty, a dead man is no longer a man, and so his vital lustre has been taken from him." "Earth-holder, you are a knowledgeable man." "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king called out in the same way, "Who is tending the fires?" He replied in the same manner as before. "Your Majesty, it is I, the earth-holder." The king said, "Earth-holder, what are you thinking?" "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Earth-holder, what kind of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, when a pit is dug, if the very same earth taken from it is put back, it will not be level." "Earth-holder, can this truly be so?" "Your Majesty, I shall demonstrate it before your own eyes." "Well done, earth-holder."

The next day he demonstrated it before the king's very eyes, and everything proved to be just so. The king said, "Earth-holder, what is the reason for this?" "Your Majesty, a dead man is no longer a man, and so his vital lustre has been taken from him." "Earth-holder, you are a knowledgeable man." "Your Majesty, it is by your gracious command." And the king said nothing more.

Again the king called out in the same way, "Who is tending the fires?" He replied in the same manner as before. "Your Majesty, it is I, the earth-holder." The king said, "Earth-holder, what are you thinking?" "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Earth-holder, what kind of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, when a weaver weaves cloth day and night, I cannot tell where it has gone." "Ah, earth-holder, the curious thing is that one does not know where it goes." "Your Majesty, it has become ground." "Ah, earth-holder, look at that — it has become ground indeed."

Again the king called out in the same way, "Who is tending the fires?" He replied in the same manner as before. "Your Majesty, it is I, the earth-holder." "Earth-holder, what are you thinking?" "Your Majesty, I am thinking a worldly thought." "Earth-holder, what kind of worldly thought?" "Your Majesty, when a potter makes vessels day and night, I cannot tell where they have gone." "Ah, earth-holder, the curious thing is that one does not know where they go." "Your Majesty, they have become ground." "Ah, earth-holder, look at that — they have become ground indeed. Earth-holder, you are a knowledgeable man, and if you know everything, what is the reason for this sleeplessness of mine?" "Your Majesty, grant me freedom from fear and I will speak." "Earth-holder, I grant you freedom from fear — speak without anxiety." "Your Majesty, you were born of evil." "Earth-holder, are you speaking ill of me?" "Your Majesty, do not say such a thing. How have I spoken ill of Your Majesty? I have not spoken ill. I shall demonstrate it before Your Majesty's own eyes." "Well done, earth-holder."

He then filled a freshly dug pit with dry ox dung, spread a bed over it, and the next day told the king, "Your Majesty, please sleep on this bed." The king lay down there, and as soon as he lay down he fell fast asleep. When he awoke, he said, "Earth-holder, have you seen?" The earth-holder, understanding that he had demonstrated his point before the king's eyes, went to the queen's retinue and asked the queen mother directly: "Mother, tell me truly and without falsehood — from whom was I born?" "Your Majesty, I will speak. Grant me freedom from fear." "Mother, I grant it." "Your Majesty, your father, accompanied by a great retinue of the queen's ladies-in-waiting, had gone away to some region, and at that time I found myself with the marks of pregnancy. When I was bathing because of those signs of pregnancy, I saw a wicked man, and a thought arose in me: 'If only this were a male child, I would enjoy the pleasures of desire with him in delight and happiness.'

That man became a male child, and with him I enjoyed the pleasures of desire in delight and happiness. From that union you were born."

He thought to himself: "This king-holder of the land is a learned man. If he knows this about me, and I have granted him freedom from fear, it would not be right to kill him — yet I must ensure he tells no one else. Therefore I will give him a reward and banish him from the realm." With that thought, he gave the man five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and expelled him from the country.

Here ends the summary verse: Jīvaka, Golden Light, the Ela leaf, the Nala, the renunciant with hair, food, grain, butter, and vessel — these are the final ones.

The fierce king Pradyota thought to himself: "This illness of mine has become severe at its root; I should gather physicians and have them examine me." He therefore assembled all the physicians dwelling in his realm and said: "Learned ones, examine me regarding this illness of mine." They replied: "Your Majesty, we do not have the capacity to examine you. However, in the city of Rājagṛha there is the son of King Bimbisāra, the king of physicians, named Jīvaka. If Your Majesty were to have him examine you, he would have the capacity." He then sent a letter to King Bimbisāra: "Send the king of physicians, Jīvaka, here — or else I shall come myself. Prepare herbs and equipment." When King Bimbisāra read the letter, he was alarmed; he rested his hand on his cheek and sat absorbed in thought. He reflected: "If I do not send Jīvaka, and that king summons whatever he requires by force, I too shall become the object of his reprisal — that would not be good." Seeing the king's distress, the king of physicians Jīvaka approached and, paying homage at his feet, said: "Your Majesty, why do you sit with your hand resting on your cheek, absorbed in thought?" He replied: "My son, you have trained in such a craft as this — and now harm has come of it." Jīvaka said: "How has harm come?" When the king explained what had happened, Jīvaka said: "Your Majesty, please command me; I will go and attend to him." "My son, that king is fierce — why does he keep killing sentient beings? Would he not kill you?" "Your Majesty, what sort of physician would I be if I cannot protect myself? Please send me without apprehension." He replied: "My son, if that is so, then go — but take care that my retinue, the queen's attendants, the young men, the ministers, the people of the palace, and the crowds who come from various lands do not fall into grief." Jīvaka said: "Your Majesty, why has this come about? I will be able to protect the mind of the patient." The king said nothing more.

Jīvaka then asked the messenger: "Fellow, what are the king's habits like, and what sort of illness has afflicted him?" The man explained in detail what had occurred. Jīvaka then mixed butter infused with the color, scent, and taste of liquor, performed auspicious, fortunate, and propitious rites, assembled his companions, kinsmen, and younger brothers, and set out for the realm of the noble king. Arriving at the border town of Kanyākubja, he heard that the king of physicians Jīvaka had come and was making his way to the realm of the noble king. A young physician dwelling there took a single āmalaka fruit, went to him, and the two rejoiced in one another's company. Jīvaka said: "Brother in the Dharma, what sort of illness has afflicted the fierce king Pradyota? Have you not examined him?" He replied: "That king is afflicted by an illness of sleeplessness. When butter benefits him, he has an aversion to butter; he delights in liquor and is violent —

Whoever were to speak the name of butter in his presence would have their head struck off on the spot and cast to the ground — and so, in their terror, they would all flee. Who then could dare to examine him?" Jīvaka said: "For this reason, I have come carrying butter that has been boiled with the color of liquor, the smell of liquor, and the taste of liquor. When I give you the signal, you must give the king that measured portion of butter. I shall go before him first; you, meanwhile, attend to him for a time. Once he has recovered, I will give you an exceedingly great reward, and I will continue to give it." The young physician said: "Excellent! Let us go," and the two set off together.

Jīvaka gradually drew near the realm of the noble king. King Pradyota, the fierce one, heard that Jīvaka, the king of physicians, had arrived, and he thought: "He is a prince as well as the king of physicians; he should come into the city with honor and ceremony." With this in mind, the king had the city adorned and the roads made beautiful, and setting out with the queen's retinue, the young attendants, the ministers, and the palace household to receive him, he welcomed Jīvaka, the king of physicians, who entered the city surrounded by many thousands of people.

After arriving, Jīvaka rested from the weariness of the road and stayed for a short while. Then King Pradyota the fierce said to Jīvaka: "My affliction of sleeplessness has become greatly aggravated — examine me." Jīvaka replied: "I shall do so, Your Majesty, but in treating this illness the remedies are to be found in many different lands and many different places. Some medicines I know of but others do not; some others know of but I do not; some both I and others know of; some are to be found in distant places, and some close at hand. Therefore, Your Majesty, please grant us the use of the excellent great elephant Bhadravatī as we require." The king said: "Jīvaka, do so exactly as you see fit," and he commanded the elephant keepers: "Let Jīvaka use the excellent great elephant Bhadravatī as he pleases; do not hinder him." He likewise commanded the ministers and the palace gatekeepers: "By day or by night, whether Jīvaka rides the excellent great elephant Bhadravatī coming or going, do not obstruct him — let him pass and return at will, as he desires." The ministers, the gatekeepers, and the elephant keepers all replied: "As Your Majesty commands."

The king of physicians Jīvaka mounted the excellent great elephant Bhadravatī and began accustoming his eyes to the sight. Sometimes he went out in the morning and returned in the afternoon; sometimes he went at midday and returned in the afternoon; sometimes he went in the afternoon and returned after the evening watch — and in this way, by going and coming, he built up the king's trust and confidence.

The king said: "Jīvaka, examine me." Jīvaka replied: "Your Majesty, please bathe first." When the king had bathed, he asked again: "Jīvaka, now that I have bathed, what should I do?" Jīvaka replied: "Your Majesty, please take your meal." When the king began to eat, Jīvaka said: "Your Majesty, I have brought a very choice drink from the land of Magadha; if Your Majesty will accept it, I offer a small portion." The king said: "Jīvaka, excellent — let us have a look at it." Jīvaka gave the signal to the young physician to administer that measured portion, and the young physician gave the measured portion, and the king drank it. The moment he had drunk it, he fell into a deep sleep. Jīvaka then mounted the excellent great elephant Bhadravatī and fled.

When the king awoke at midnight, the burning sensation of the butter came upon him.

He called to someone: "Hey, send for the physician Jīvaka!" The man had poured melted butter over his head and then cut it off at the neck and thrown it to the ground. He searched everywhere but could not find Jīvaka, so the messenger reported back: "Your Majesty, he is nowhere — he has certainly fled." The king, now furious, said: "Hey, send for my messenger-crow!" and the man summoned him. The king said: "Listen, messenger-crow — go quickly, mount the elephant Damburi, take Jīvaka by the neck, bring him here, and cut off his head. But if that trickster gives you even a little something, do not accept it. Go and search at once." The messenger-crow, heeding the wrathful King Pradyota's command, quickly mounted the elephant Damburi and set off in pursuit.

When the crow saw Jīvaka enter a grove of emblic myrobalan trees, he called out: "Jīvaka, Your Divine Honour, come here this instant." Jīvaka replied: "Ah, crow, how long a journey — come rest a moment; eat some myrobalan." The crow said: "The king has ordered me: 'That man is a trickster — do not accept so much as a scrap from him.'" Jīvaka said: "Well then, crow, if that is so, you eat half and I will eat half." The crow thought: "He says eat half — but what kind of trick could there be in just the half?" and so he reasoned and replied: "Jīvaka, you may give me mine to eat." Jīvaka ate half of the myrobalan, then cut the remaining half with a fingernail that he had packed full of powder, and handed it over. The crow ate it — and immediately, from both ends, he was drenched through and through, for it was laced with a powerful purgative. Jīvaka then placed him with some hill-folk and instructed those hill-folk: "Wise ones, the three most prized possessions of King Pradyota are: the elephant Damburi, the great she-elephant Bhadravatī, and this messenger-crow. Treat him here with this remedy, nurse him back to health, and he will recover. Otherwise the king will surely destroy you all." Having said this, he departed. They tended him and he recovered, and they went on their way.

The king too, treated by the young physician with the remedy as prescribed, likewise recovered. In time the messenger-crow gradually made his way back to the king's presence, and the king questioned him: "Crow, why did Jīvaka flee? If he fled, that was wrong of him. But crow — if he had been captured, what would I have done to him?" The crow answered: "Your Majesty, you would have cut off his head at the neck and cast it to the ground." The king said: "Majesty, the king of physicians who healed both Your Majesty and me — to kill such a one is not fitting." The king said: "Crow, if that is so, then what shall be done with him?" "Your Majesty, give him a generous reward — that is best. Do likewise."

The king then sent Jīvaka a letter: "Jīvaka, physician-king, why did you flee? Come back; you will be rewarded — take your reward." Jīvaka sent back a reply: "Your Majesty, by your kindness there is enough wealth in my home. Yet if Your Majesty would truly think of me, it would be fitting to bestow honour upon the young physician who treated Your Majesty." The king gave many gifts to that young physician. To Jīvaka he also sent a great robe of fine linen, a hundred thousand cubits in length. Jīvaka thought: "This robe befits a king. To whom should I give it?" He reflected: "The Blessed One is by his very nature my father — I shall offer it to him." And so he offered it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, make this into a Dharma-robe and offer it back to me." The Venerable Ānanda took it, and as he did so, he saw that the three Dharma-robes of the Blessed One were already more than sufficient. As he set about the task, from those robes of the Blessed One there emerged three Dharma-robes and —

— a full upper robe together with an under-robe for the Venerable Ānanda, and a sweat-cloth for Sāṅkāśya also arose.

Now, in the Joyful Heaven (Tuṣita), a riddle was spoken by the buddha, and it went like this:

What king is it who, when attached, is covered in dust,
yet when without attachment, becomes free of dust?
Who here would speak of such attachment?
How does a foolish one grieve?
How does a wise one rejoice?
By abandoning what one possesses,
who here is said to have accomplished peace?

This was written down. At any time when a buddha, a Blessed One, has not appeared in the world, no one is able to grasp these questions, nor is anyone able to explain their meaning. Even at a time when a buddha, a Blessed One, has appeared in the world, though the questions can be grasped, their meaning cannot be explained.

Now, at a certain time, a lord of yakṣas named Son of Vaiśravaṇa went into the assembly of the gods of Tuṣita on some errand, and there he saw those questions that had been posed. Struck with wonder, he took hold of them but was unable to penetrate their meaning. He carried them to the Palace of the Spreading Willows, wrote them on a board, and set them there.

At that time, in a place called Resting-Stone, there dwelt a king of nāgas named Elā's Wing, who had long held this aspiration in his heart: "When will I ever see a buddha, a Blessed One?" A friend of his, a yakṣa named Golden Light, went on some errand to the Palace of the Spreading Willows of the yakṣa lord Son of Vaiśravaṇa, and there he saw those questions written on the board. He took them, memorized them thoroughly, and began to analyze them — yet he could not penetrate their meaning. He brought them to Resting-Stone, gave them to the nāga king Elā's Wing, and said: "Friend, these questions were spoken by a buddha. No one has yet understood their meaning. Take these and a hundred thousand gold coins, and travel through villages, towns, and royal courts, announcing: 'Whoever is able to explain the meaning of these questions — to that person I will give a hundred thousand gold coins and honor them with the highest respect.' If anyone can explain them, give him the hundred thousand gold coins. If no one can, then proclaim that it is no village or town, and go on elsewhere."

He took them, memorized them completely, and then, having transformed himself into the form of a brahmin youth, he took the hundred thousand gold coins and traveled through villages, towns, and royal courts, eventually reaching Vārāṇasī. There, on the broad roads of Vārāṇasī, at crossroads of four and three ways, he addressed the gathered wise residents of Vārāṇasī and the crowds of people who had come from various lands: "I have brought these questions; whoever is able to explain their meaning — to that person I will give these hundred thousand gold coins and honor them with the highest respect."

Some claimed to be learned, others were seized with wonder, and though many hundreds and thousands of living beings assembled, none was able to explain the meaning. He then began to announce that it was no village or town. At that point the brahmins and householders dwelling in Vārāṇasī said: "Do not yet proclaim that it is no village or town. Let the renunciants and brahmins who dwell in forest hermitages and who are truly honored by our people come first — and only afterward proclaim that it is no village or town."

He asked: "Who are they?"

"Nālandā and others," they replied.

He agreed that this was the right course, and so —

He waited, and after some time Nālandā arrived. Nālandā sat before him and said: "Great sage, I have come bringing these questions. To whoever is able to explain their meaning, this hundred-thousand in gold will be given, and he shall be honored with great veneration."

Nālandā read them through and said: "The brahmin youth Legky did just so and spoke accordingly. How long ago? Twelve years have passed." "Great sage, that time is long." "Six years." "Still long." "Three years." "One year." "Six months." "Three months." "One month." "Half a month." "Seven days have passed." "Great sage, Legky, do it in that very way — wait until then," he said. And so he waited.

Now, Nālandā's closest companions were the five monks, and so he went to them and said: "Wise ones, a brahmin youth has come to me with these questions and a hundred thousand in gold, saying that whoever can explain the meaning of these questions shall receive this gold and be honored with great veneration. But since these questions are numerous in meaning yet few in words, and since they are difficult to penetrate, how is one to resolve this?" They replied: "Go to Nālandā — go and ask the Buddha, the Blessed One." "Wise ones, has the Buddha, the Blessed One, appeared in the world?" "He has." "Where does he dwell?" "In the forest of the Ṛṣipatana, the deer park," said the sage.

He arose with joy and delight, and swiftly, swiftly, made his way to where the Blessed One was. And Nālandā beheld the Blessed One — his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being, beautified by the eighty minor marks, encircled by a fathom of radiance, shining with a light exceeding that of a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, glorious on all sides. Just as one who has accumulated roots of virtue beholds a buddha for the very first time, or as one who has trained the mind in calm abiding for twelve years, or as a childless person who finds a child, or as a poor person who discovers a treasure, or as one who delights in sovereignty and is anointed with the power of kingship — the joy of beholding was not like a faint or ordinary delight. Having seen him, he went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side.

As he sat to one side, the Blessed One, perceiving his intention, his disposition, his constitution, and his character, taught Dharma of such a kind that he would come to realize the Four Noble Truths. Upon hearing this, the sage Nālandā shattered with the vajra of gnosis the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection, and directly actualized the fruit of stream-entry.

Having seen the truth, he bowed at the feet of the Blessed One and implored him: "Venerable one, if I may obtain the going-forth and full ordination as a monk in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya — the state of a fully ordained monk — I wish to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

The Blessed One declared: "Nālandā, you have pledged to explain the meaning of those questions to that brahmin youth. Therefore go back, first discharge that prior commitment, and afterward go forth."

He replied: "Venerable one, though I have obtained such a collection of qualities, if I am unable to set forth the meaning of those questions before him, what purpose would be served by going there?"

The Blessed One declared: "Nālandā, go, approach him, and say these words: 'Speak those questions aloud for now.'" And whenever he recites these words —

What king, the sovereign lord, is he?
When there is attachment, dust is there.
When dust is absent, freed from dust he is.
Who in this world is called "attached"?
How does the foolish one fall into sorrow?
How does the wise one come to joy?

"When one is freed from its possession, that is called accomplishment and bliss." When those words have been spoken, you should then say: "Sixth — the sovereign lord and king: when there is attachment, dust is there; when dust is absent, freed from dust he is. When attached, the childish one is so called here. The one of wicked mind falls into sorrow in that way; the wise one comes to joy in that way. When one is freed from the possession of this, that is called accomplishment and bliss."

If he says, "I do not understand the sign," then say to him:

One who knows what is well spoken is to be prized.
One who knows both learning and meditative absorption is to be prized.
For any person who has become doubtful and negligent,
not knowing — for such a one, hearing is of little benefit.

If he should say, "You speak the words of the buddha, yet no mark of distinction appears in you. My mind is dull in this matter — quickly resolve my doubt," then pluck a blade of grass with your fingernail before him.

If he asks, "Has the buddha, the Blessed One, appeared in the world?" say, "He has appeared."

If he asks, "And where does he dwell?" say, "In the forest of the deer-haunting sage, he speaks."

"Venerable one, so be it," said the noble youth Nālandā, and, following the Blessed One's instruction, he went to where the brahmin youth was and said to him: "Brahmin youth, recite those questions for now."

Then the brahmin youth recited the verse:

What king, the sovereign lord, is he?
When there is attachment, dust is there.
When dust is absent, freed from dust he is.
Who in this world is called "attached"?
How does the foolish one fall into sorrow?
How does the wise one come to joy?
When one is freed from its possession,
what is that called accomplishment and bliss?

He replied:

Sixth — the sovereign lord and king:
when there is attachment, dust is there;
when dust is absent, freed from dust he is.
When attached, the childish one is so called here.
The one of wicked mind falls into sorrow in that way;
the wise one comes to joy in that way.
When one is freed from the possession of this,
that here is called accomplishment and bliss.

The brahmin youth said: "Great sage, I do not understand the sign."

He replied:

One who knows what is well spoken is to be prized.
One who knows both learning and meditative absorption is to be prized.
For any person who has become doubtful and negligent,
not knowing — for such a one, hearing is of little benefit.

The brahmin youth said: "Nālandā, you speak the words of a buddha, yet no mark of distinction appears in you. My mind is dull in this matter — quickly resolve my doubt."

Then Nālandā plucked a blade of grass with his fingernail before him, and the other said: "Nālandā, has the buddha, the Blessed One, appeared in the world?"

He replied: "Brahmin youth, he has appeared."

"Where does he dwell?"

"Right here in this land of Vārāṇasī."

"In what direction?"

"In the forest of the deer-haunting sage, he speaks."

The brahmin youth thought to himself: "If I reveal my own lineage to him, he will look down on me. But if I go in the guise of a brahmin youth, the brahmins who dwell in Vārāṇasī and who possess the three Vedic knowledges — or those who say a brahmin youth of high birth has gone to the presence of the ascetic Gautama — will lose their faith. And if I go in my own guise, I have many enemies among the nāgas, and some of them will come and do me harm on the way. Therefore I shall manifest myself in the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch and go before the Blessed One."

Then the nāga king, through the power of Elā, manifested himself in the form of a wheel-turning monarch. Seven precious jewels were arrayed before him; nine hundred and ninety million troops of the city's army surrounded him; a thousand sons, adorned with ornaments of various precious things, encircled him like a crescent moon. Non-Buddhists, ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute of every kind —

a thousand of the foremost among men followed behind. Above, an umbrella with a thousand spokes was held aloft, and a radiance of a thousand rays of sunlight illumined everything, outshining even the glorious palace adorned with the moon, the planets, the stars, and their constellations, its brilliance surpassing all. In this manner he proceeded to where the sage was speaking.

Now at that time the Blessed One was seated before a retinue of many hundreds, teaching the Dharma. The members of that assembly, from a great distance, caught sight of Elā, the nāga king. Upon seeing him they were struck with wonder, their eyes wide open, and various thoughts arose in their minds. Some said, "Friends, from where has this king come?" Others said, "Friends, whoever possesses such complete and perfect wealth — this is no ordinary king; this must be some lord of the earth, a sovereign of the land." Still others said, "This is no king at all — this is Śakra, lord of the gods, who has come here to behold the Blessed One." And those who were under the sway of attachment, upon seeing him, gave rise to longing, thinking, "Oh, when shall I too become like this?"

While they were thus thinking in many different ways, Elā the nāga king proceeded to where the Blessed One was and arrived there. He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Blessed One addressed Elā the nāga king in these words: "You foolish man — you transgressed the boundaries of the training laid down by the perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, and were consequently reborn in the wretched state of a nāga. Do you now wish to deceive my retinue as well? Enough of this — drop the emanation and come in your own proper form."

He replied, "Venerable One, I have many enemies among the nāgas, and some of them might do me harm."

Then the Blessed One addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi (the vajra-holder): "Vajrapāṇi, go and guard Elā the nāga king." "Venerable One, so be it," said the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi, and heeding the Blessed One's word, he took upon himself the task of guarding Elā the nāga king and followed along behind him.

The Minor Bases of Discipline. The Twenty-Fifth Fascicle.

Then Elā the nāga king departed from the presence of the Blessed One and manifested himself in his true form. His tail rested at Rājagṛha, while his seven heads lay at Vārāṇasī. On each head, through the ripening of past karma, ela trees had grown, and they were entirely filled with many hundreds of thousands of kinds of insects; many swarms of flies were buzzing and settling; an ooze of foul and extremely pungent smell, of pus and blood, dripped down.

Then, having transformed his body in the same way that sentient beings avert their eyes when they see something repulsive, he proceeded to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. The members of the assembly, upon seeing the body of Elā the nāga king, beheld something utterly repulsive and thoroughly terrifying, frightful and distressing to those not yet free from attachment, vast and cracked, rough, without lustre, and displaying many differences in color and shape. Seeing this they were alarmed, and addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is this utterly terrifying thing that has come into the Blessed One's presence?"

The Blessed One replied: "Monks, this is the very one who, bearing the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch, came before me, and toward whom you gave rise to attachment, captivated by the distinguishing features of the gates of saṃsāra. This body he now bears is the intrinsic result, fully accomplished through the fault of undesirable karma. The earlier form was an emanation."

Upon hearing this, those who had experienced discomfort of mind, finding that karma cannot be escaped, sat in silence and said nothing.

Then the nāga king Elapatra addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, I beg you to grant me a prophecy. Sugata, I beg you to grant me a prophecy."

The Blessed One declared: "Lord of nāgas, when the lifespan of human beings reaches eighty thousand years, at the time when human beings are capable of living eighty thousand years, a Teacher named Maitreya, a Tathāgata, an arhat" — and so on as before, through "the Teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One, will arise in the world" — "he will grant you a prophecy."

Then the nāga king Elapatra bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and vanished from that very spot.

The monks were seized by doubt, and they addressed the Buddha, the Blessed One, who dispels all doubt: "Venerable One, what karma did the nāga king Elapatra perform and accumulate such that, through the ripening of that karma, he was born in the lowly birthplace of nāgas with a cardamom tree growing from his head, so that he is filled by many hundreds of thousands of kinds of insects, swarmed over and fallen upon by many swarms of flies, dripping and oozing with the flowing suffering of the stench and foul smell of pus and blood — and experiences suffering such as this?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, karma that has been done and accumulated by the nāga king Elapatra — who else would experience it? Monks, karma that has been done and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been done ripens solely within the very aggregates, elements, and sense bases that have been appropriated.

Though a hundred aeons pass,
karma is never lost or wasted.
When the conditions are assembled and the time arrives,
it ripens as a fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in this very good aeon that has gone before, when the lifespan of living beings was capable of supporting twenty thousand years, there arose in the world a Teacher named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. He resided and dwelt in the Deer Park forest of the seers (Ṛṣipatana) near the city of Vārāṇasī.

One man went forth into homelessness under that one's teaching, became a monk (bhikṣu) versed in all three collections of scripture, and in a secluded spot made himself a walking path beside a cardamom tree. While he was walking there, the branches of the cardamom tree struck him on the forehead, and he felt irritated by this. On another occasion, as he was walking, weary from meditation, and the branches again struck his forehead, he became enraged, cut the tree down, chopped it into pieces with both hands, threw it away, and said: "This thing has neither life nor breath — what offense did the Blessed One Kāśyapa see in it that he made it a basis for training?" And with these words he angrily broke his vows, abandoned his training, left the body, and was reborn among the nāgas, with a cardamom tree growing from his head, filled by many hundreds of thousands of kinds of insects, swarmed over and fallen upon by many swarms of flies, dripping and oozing with the stench and foul smell of pus and blood.

Monks, what do you think? The monk of that time, versed in the three collections, who had gone forth — that very one is this nāga king Elapatra. It was he who, having gone forth under the teaching of the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha Kāśyapa, fell into fierce rage and abandoned his training, and through the ripening of that karma was reborn among the nāgas.

with a cardamom tree growing from his head, filled by many hundreds of thousands of kinds of insects, swarmed over and fallen upon by many swarms of flies, dripping and oozing with the stench and foul smell of pus and blood.

Monks, just as the karmic maturation of actions that are wholly dark is itself wholly dark, so too the maturation of actions that are wholly bright is itself wholly bright, and the maturation of mixed actions is itself mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are wholly dark and mixed, and strive for actions that are wholly bright alone. Monks, you should train in this way.

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Then the sage Nālada went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One with his head, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the sage Nālada addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, I have now broken my former vow. Venerable One, if I may obtain going forth and full ordination and the state of a monk in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, I wish to lead the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

The Blessed One said to him, "Monk, come here — live the holy life!" And by that word of the Blessed One, "Monk, come," he was immediately ordained: his hair was shaved, he wore the patchwork robe, he held in his hands a begging bowl and a water vessel, his head and beard were shorn, and he came to abide in the conduct of one who has been fully ordained for seven days, yet was as one who had maintained it for a hundred years.

By the Tathāgata's word "Come here," his form was transformed — hair shaved, body clad in the patchwork robe — and through the Buddha's intention his bearing was changed; in an instant he abided with faculties perfectly stilled.

When the Blessed One had ordained the venerable Nālada with the words "Monk, come here," those who led the holy life did not know by what name to call him, and the monks asked the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, his clan is that of the Kātyāyanas, therefore call him the Son of Kātyāyana." The monks then began to call him the Son of Kātyāyana, and the name Son of Kātyāyana became established.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Son of Kātyāyana: "Son of Kātyāyana, this world mostly relies upon two things: existence and non-existence. Son of Kātyāyana, this world is mostly bound by the aggregates and by clinging, and relies upon existence and non-existence. Son of Kātyāyana, those things that become latent as the underlying tendency of mental grasping — toward these one does not assert 'self,' does not take them up, does not abide in them, does not cling to them.

Son of Kātyāyana, when arising occurs, this suffering arises; when ceasing occurs, this suffering ceases.

Son of Kātyāyana, if regarding this there arises in you a knowledge that is without doubt, without wavering, not dependent on another — then, Son of Kātyāyana, this alone is right view, and this alone is what the Tathāgata designates as right view in his designating.

Why is this? Because, Son of Kātyāyana, one who sees, just as it truly is, with correct wisdom the true arising of the world does not conceive of non-existence with respect to the world. And one who sees, just as it truly is, with correct wisdom the true cessation of the world does not conceive of existence with respect to the world."

"Son of Kātyāyana, the Tathāgata, without relying on those two extremes, teaches the Dharma to the world by the Middle Way, thus: Because this exists, that arises; because this has come to be, that is born. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance, formations arise; conditioned by formations, consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense sources; conditioned by the six sense sources, contact; conditioned by contact, feeling; conditioned by feeling, craving; conditioned by craving, grasping; conditioned by grasping, becoming; conditioned by becoming, birth; conditioned by birth, aging and death, grief, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation all arise. In this way there comes about the arising of this entire great mass of suffering.

Because this does not exist, that does not arise; because this ceases, that ceases. That is to say: when ignorance ceases, formations cease; when formations cease, consciousness ceases; when consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases; when name-and-form ceases, the six sense sources cease; when the six sense sources cease, contact ceases; when contact ceases, feeling ceases; when feeling ceases, craving ceases; when craving ceases, grasping ceases; when grasping ceases, becoming ceases; when becoming ceases, birth ceases; when birth ceases, aging and death, grief, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation all cease. In this way there comes about the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering."

Then the venerable Kātyāyana, having seen the truth, and having known through this very instance the wheel of cyclic existence in its five aspects of movement and non-movement, and having comprehended that all conditioned phenomena are by their very nature subject to decay, falling away, dissolution, and destruction, abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. He became an arhat: free from attachment to the three realms, his mind equal and steady like refined gold, like the expanse of space and the open palm of a hand, like sandalwood and the cool of shade; through knowledge he shattered the hollow gateway of ignorance; through direct knowledge he attained the individual perfect cognitions. Turning his back on attachment to continued existence and gain, and on the seeking of honor, he came to be venerated, revered, and respectfully addressed by the gods of the surrounding heavens together with their lords.

The Blessed One addressed him, calling out "Son of Kātyāyana," and from that point on his name became known as Kātyāyana the Great.

Now at a certain later time there appeared in the realm of the noble Aryans a fierce man roaming about bent on battle, and the fierce king Rabsnang sat stricken with grief together with his queen, the prince, the ministers, and the people of the palace retinue. Some among them said, "May the gods please be propitiated." Others said, "Please send for the brahmins." And others said, "Please seek out whatever ascetic or brahmin dwelling nearby who is honored as a being of virtue." The fierce king Rabsnang commanded those in charge of the gates: "Wise ones, if any ascetic or brahmin, whoever it may be, who is capable of bringing the plague to an end should come here, report that person to me."

In such an occasion as this, the blessed buddhas have not the slightest lack of knowing, not the slightest lack of seeing, not the slightest lack of awareness or understanding. The blessed buddhas possess great compassion; they have entered upon the path of benefiting the world; they are the sole protector, uniquely courageous, without equal, speaking nothing twofold, abiding in calm abiding and insight.

skilled in the three elements of taming beings, one who has crossed the four rivers, one in whose soles the four legs of miraculous power rest perfectly, one long accustomed to the four means of attraction, one who has abandoned the five limbs, one who has utterly transcended the five destinies, one possessed of six limbs, one in whom the six perfections are perfectly complete, one rich with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening, one who teaches the noble eightfold path, one skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions, one possessed of the power of the ten powers, one whose renown pervades the ten directions, one supremely distinguished by sovereignty over a thousandfold — such blessed buddhas, by the very nature of reality, three times by day and three times by night, look upon the world with the eye of a buddha, perceiving who is in decline and who is thriving, who has come to poverty, who has fallen into distress, who is being harmed, who has fallen into poverty and distress and harm, who is inclining toward the lower realms, who is descending into the lower realms, who has fallen into the lower realms, who is to be drawn out from the lower realms and established in the higher realms and liberation, whose root of virtue has not yet arisen and is to be caused to arise, whose root of virtue has arisen and is to be fully ripened, whose ripened virtue is to be brought to full liberation, who is sinking in the mire of desire and is to be drawn out by hand, who is deprived of the noble wealth and is to be established as one who commands the lordship of noble wealth, and for what world, adorned by the arising of buddhas, a fruitful outcome is to be brought about — and so their gaze of primordial wisdom is set in motion.

It was said:

The ocean, home of sea-monsters, may be overturned by the waves of time,
yet for the sons who are to be tamed,
the buddhas never miss their moment.

Just as a mother gazes upon her only beloved child
and guards that child's very life,
so too the Tathāgata gazes upon the beings who are to be tamed
and guards the stream of their being.

Abiding in the stream of omniscience,
with the hook of compassion traversing the difficult expanse of cyclic existence,
he searches, without weariness, for the wandering sons who are to be tamed,
as a mother cow searches for her lost calf.

The Blessed One then considered: among those to be tamed — the fierce king Rabsnang, together with his queen's retinue, the young nobles, the ministers, and the assembled people dwelling in the noble realm — and he saw that it was the great monk Kātyāyana who was the one to tame them.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the venerable great Kātyāyana: "Kātyāyana, attend to the fierce king Rabsnang of the noble realm, together with his queen's retinue, the young nobles, the ministers, and the assembled people dwelling in the noble realm."

"Venerable one, I shall do so," said the venerable great Kātyāyana, and having listened and obeyed the Blessed One, when that very night had passed, he dressed in his robe and lower robe in the early morning, took up his bowl, and set out to seek alms in Vārāṇasī. Having made his alms-round in Vārāṇasī and completed the business of the meal, setting aside the acceptance of further food, he folded his bedding just as it was, took up his bowl and robe, and departed, travelling together with five hundred attendants toward the noble realm.

At that time, in the region of Kanyākubja, there lived a brahmin who had previously been a householder friend of the venerable great Kātyāyana, and this brahmin's daughter, who possessed exceptional beauty, was given the name Śrāvaṇī in keeping with the name she had borne in former lives. Now as it happened, a master of dance came from the south and, seeing that her hair was excellent, went to the brahmin and said to him: "O great brahmin, give me this girl's hair."

The brahmin said: "I will give you a thousand kārṣāpaṇas." But the master of dance replied: "We are brahmins; it is not fitting for us to sell hair — how then could we sell hair?" And so the master of dance left without another word.

The next day that brahmin passed away. His wife then heard how the venerable great Kātyāyana, together with his five hundred attendants, was staying not far from there and wished to travel on to the noble realm. Grief-stricken and distressed at the loss of her husband, when she heard that the venerable great Kātyāyana was coming, she sat with her cheek resting in her hand, lost in her own thoughts. The daughter with the beautiful hair saw her mother sitting in this way, and asked: "Mother, why do you sit with your cheek in your hand, lost in thought?" The mother replied: "Daughter, the noble great Kātyāyana — the younger companion of your late father — is staying not far from here. He wishes to travel on to the noble realm. Your father has passed away, and the situation of our household has become such that when someone who has come from afar arrives, we are unable even to offer him alms for a few days. That is why." The daughter said: "Mother, if that is so, let the master of dance buy my hair for a thousand kārṣāpaṇas right here and now, and with that very sum offer alms to the noble great Kātyāyana. My hair will grow back, so please do not grieve." Hearing these words, which arose from such faith, the mother said: "Good, daughter — do just that." She went to where the master of dance was and upon arriving said: "Master, if you will weigh out a thousand kārṣāpaṇas for my daughter's hair, take it now and give us the thousand kārṣāpaṇas." The master of dance replied: "Sister, at the time I needed those things, but now I do not. Nevertheless, I will take it for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." The brahmin woman said: "Master, please accept it — take these." And so he took them.

By this time the venerable great Kātyāyana had arrived in the region of Kanyākubja and was sitting in a secluded, open place. Then the brahmin woman set out with a brisk step, went to where the venerable great Kātyāyana was, and spoke to him thus: "Noble great Kātyāyana, would you kindly come tomorrow at mealtime to take your midday meal at my home?" He replied: "Brahmin woman, my retinue is made up of ordinary people, quite numerous." She asked: "Noble one, how many are in the retinue?" "Brahmin woman, my retinue numbers five hundred." She said: "Excellent, noble one — I shall indeed do so. Please grant your consent." And the venerable great Kātyāyana accepted by saying nothing in refusal to that brahmin woman. When the brahmin woman understood that the venerable great Kātyāyana had accepted by remaining silent, she bowed at his feet, rose from her seat, and departed.

That very evening she prepared clean and pure food and drink, and the next morning rose early and arranged seats, set out water vessels, and went to invite the venerable great Kātyāyana, saying: "Noble one, the midday meal is prepared — please consider that the time has come." She then formally announced the hour.

The following morning the venerable great Kātyāyana dressed in his robe and lower garment, took up his bowl, and surrounded by many monks, with the monastic Saṅgha of monks preceding him, he went to the place the brahmin woman had designated. Upon arriving he took his seat on the spread seat in the midst of the monastic Saṅgha. Then the brahmin woman, knowing that the great Kātyāyana and the rest of the monastic Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, with her own hands served clean and pure food and drink, and satisfied them fully and gave them their fill.

In many ways she served clean and pure food and drink with her own hands, fully satisfying them and seeing that they were well supplied. When the venerable great Kātyāyana had eaten his meal and she perceived that he had set aside his bowl, she placed a low seat before the venerable great Kātyāyana and sat down to hear the Dharma.

Then the venerable great Kātyāyana, wishing to teach the Dharma to that brahmin woman, said to her the following: "O daughter of a brahmin, you with the hair — what is she doing?" She replied, "Noble one, her conduct has been remiss. Since arhats do not engage primordial wisdom without prior reflection, he considered the conduct of the girl with the hair and then said: "Brahmin woman, call that girl of wholesome intention." When she was called, she came out of the house, and with intense faith prostrated at the feet of the venerable great Kātyāyana and sat to one side. The brahmin woman then said, "Noble one, this girl with the hair has abandoned evil and is your spiritual daughter. Therefore, whatever may be done, when we inquire of you and only you in this matter, please tell us to whom we should give her." She replied, "The brahmin woman has asked something improper, and it does not befit one who has gone forth. Nevertheless, this girl will come to obtain five hundred pieces of intimate adornment, five hundred pieces of outer adornment, and five hundred of the finest things in the village."
