She said, "Noble one, we brahmins are poor — how would we obtain all of these?" He replied, "Brahmin woman, do not say such a thing. Because this girl has acted with intense faith toward the excellent field of merit, she is known to have great power of merit. All of this will certainly come to her, so do not lament." And at that she said nothing more.

The venerable great Kātyāyana then taught that brahmin woman and her daughter in many ways with talk that accorded with the Dharma, fully instructing them, fully engaging them, fully praising them, and fully delighting them. Having fully taught, fully engaged, fully praised, and fully delighted them in many ways with talk that accorded with the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed, and in due course arrived at Śrāvastī.

At the moment he entered the city, half of the plague sickness was stilled. And the gatekeeper reported to the king: a certain ascetic bearing signs and marks of the gods never before seen, accompanied by five hundred attendants, had arrived — and the very moment he arrived, half of the plague sickness was stilled.

The king said, "Good people, show him honor." The brahmins said, "O lord, because we have striven at the ritual of pacification day and night, it is through our power that half of the plague sickness has been stilled; without delay everything will be fully pacified before long." The monks meanwhile said, "May the fierce king, Glorious Light, be freed from sickness," and said nothing more and left.

The king said to his ministers, "Wise ones, the gatekeeper says that a certain ascetic bearing signs and marks of the gods never before seen has arrived here with a retinue of five hundred, and the very moment he arrived, half of the plague sickness was stilled. And the brahmins say: 'O lord, because we strove at the pacification ritual from morning to night, it is through our power that half of the plague sickness was stilled.' If it is not known whose power this truly is, then today let these ascetics and brahmins be given poor cooked rice and broth, the food of the filthy quarter where elephants are washed, and after they have eaten and come back out, ask them both what sort of meal they had." "As your lordship commands," he replied, and —

Following the ministers' instructions, seats were spread in a filthy quarter where elephants are washed, and the ascetics and brahmins were given food. Once they had eaten and come back out, the doorkeeper asked the brahmins: "O great brahmins, with what sort of meal did the god satisfy you?" At that, they grew angry and said, "The king and all his conduct are devoted to what is contrary to the Dharma. He satisfied the brahmins with dirty cooked rice of inferior grain, two-legged legumes, and coarse broth." And at that they said nothing more.

The doorkeeper then went and asked the monks: "Noble ones, with what sort of meal did the god satisfy you?" They said, "A generous giver gave the gift, and the recipients ate it. The great elements were satisfied, and the day's sustenance was taken in." The doorkeeper reported this to the king: "Your lordship, the brahmins said such-and-such, and the monks said such-and-such."

The king then commanded his ministers: "Wise ones, now give them both excellent clean food in a clean quarter that is no place where elephants are washed, and ask them the same question again." They spread seats for both groups in a clean quarter no place where elephants are washed, and satisfied them with fine food. When the doorkeeper asked them the same question, the brahmins said: "The king is an anointed sovereign of the warrior caste, consecrated from the crown of the head, and he gave whatever food one could desire and satisfied us fully. These brahmins say that this royal palace, seen now and then from the edge of its gateway, has sometimes seemed inferior and sometimes fine — so do not mock us!" And at that they said nothing more.

The doorkeeper then went and asked the monks, and they said exactly as they had before. The doorkeeper reported this to the king in just the same way. The same procedure applied to the washing place of elephants was then applied in turn to the washing place of horses, to the ash-heap, and to clean and agreeable places.

King Candragupta reflected: "I understand that the monks are worthy recipients of gifts, while the brahmins are not." Faith arose in him, and he went directly to where the venerable Mahākātyāyana was staying. He prostrated himself with his head at the venerable Mahākātyāyana's feet and sat to one side. As he sat there, the venerable Mahākātyāyana gave King Candragupta thorough instruction in Dharma-filled discourse, led him to thoroughly receive it, offered him thorough praise, and gladdened him thoroughly. With many categories of Dharma-filled discourse he gave thorough instruction, led him to thoroughly receive it, offered thorough praise, and made him thoroughly joyful. Then he sat in silence.

Then King Candragupta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned and faced the direction of the venerable Mahākātyāyana with palms joined, and said: "Noble Mahākātyāyana, would you grant that tomorrow, together with the community of monks, you accept a noon meal within my household?" The venerable Mahākātyāyana gave his consent to King Candragupta by remaining silent. Then King Candragupta, understanding by the venerable Mahākātyāyana's silence that consent had been given, prostrated with his head at the venerable Mahākātyāyana's feet, rose from his seat, and departed.

That very evening King Candragupta arranged clean and excellent food and drink, and rising early the next morning, spread seats and set out water vessels.

He then sent word to the venerable Mahākātyāyana with this invitation: "Noble Mahākātyāyana, the seats have been arranged; please be aware that the hour has now arrived."

The venerable Mahākātyāyana, in the early morning, robed in his outer and inner garments and taking up his alms bowl, set out surrounded by the community of monks, with the monastic Saṅgha preceding him, and proceeded to the residence of King Candragupta. Upon his arrival, seats had been spread in the midst of the monastic Saṅgha, and he took his seat. Then music was struck up, and dancers began to perform dances of many kinds. The venerable Mahākātyāyana and the monks restrained their sense faculties and remained composed.

When the sound of those songs, dances, and music had subsided, King Candragupta said: "Noble one, was the dancing good? Were the songs pleasing?"

The venerable Mahākātyāyana replied: "Great King, it was for those who heard or saw them."

The king said: "Noble one, if those who had withdrawn their sense faculties inward did not see, how then did they not hear?"

Mahākātyāyana said: "O King, do you have anyone who would not recoil from killing a man? If so, noble one, what do you wish of such a person?"

The king replied: "Take that man and fill a vessel with sesame oil to the very brim — so full that a crow could drink from it — and have him carry it. Send him to tour all the fine districts and bring it back here. Meanwhile, station an executioner behind him, sword raised, and give him this instruction: 'If even a single drop of sesame oil falls to the ground, this executioner with his raised sword will cut off your head at the neck and cast it to the ground.' Then have varied music played before him and have various dances performed in front of him. After that, you will believe me."

King Candragupta did precisely as had been described, step by step. He then asked the man: "Well, fellow — was the dancing good? Were the songs pleasing? Was the music pleasant?"

The man replied: "O King, it was for those who saw or heard them."

The king said: "Come now — if those who had withdrawn their sense faculties inward could not see, how did they not hear?"

The man said: "O King, I thought to myself: if even a single drop of sesame oil were to fall from this vessel to the ground, that executioner with his raised sword would cut off my head at the neck and cast it to the ground. In terror of dying, I fixed my mind one-pointedly on the vessel of sesame oil, straining my eyes to watch it — so how could I possibly have seen or heard anything?"

The king fell silent, having nothing to say.

The venerable Mahākātyāyana then said: "O King, did you see?"

"Noble one, I did see."

"O King, that man, for the sake of the suffering of a single life, kept himself from distraction and maintained constant vigilance. We monks, having taken up the training precept of abandoning the watching and listening of musical performances, need we even speak of watching or listening to dances, songs, and music? For it is a cause of suffering across many lifetimes — that would simply be out of the question."

King Candragupta, convinced by the sight of the vessel of sesame oil, and filled with heightened faith, together with his retinue of queens, young princes, ministers, and the people of the royal household, personally served Mahākātyāyana and the rest of the monastic Saṅgha — who were seated at ease — with clean and pure food and drink from his own hands, satisfying and refreshing them fully. Again and again he served them with clean and pure food and drink from his own hands, satisfying them completely.

When the meal was properly concluded, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, perceiving by the shadow of the sun's position that it was time, and knowing that his alms-bowl had been washed and returned, took up a seat lower than Mahākātyāyana's own and sat down before the Venerable Mahākātyāyana. Having sat down, he spoke to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana as follows: "Noble one, was there anyone else who, as I have done, satisfied your retinue of five hundred with pure and wholesome food?"

Mahākātyāyana replied: "You who have surpassed many gods — what is so remarkable about the fact that you satisfied my retinue of five hundred with such food? When I was coming here, a girl living in the hills sold her own hair and thereby satisfied my retinue of five hundred with food of this very kind. That, I tell you, is far more remarkable and wonderful than what you have done."

King Candragupta reflected: "A woman who sold her hair for five hundred kārṣāpaṇas — where in the world, even among the gods, could there be such a woman?" He thought, "In short, I must find her." But since the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was difficult of approach, the king could not ask him directly where in the hills this girl was. Instead he gave instructions to those of his men who lived by selling curds: "Good sirs, seek out along whatever road Mahākātyāyana came by some girl living in the hills who sold her hair and today provided pure food to the noble Mahākātyāyana along with his retinue of five hundred — find her and bring her back for my sake. Such is the king's command."

His men who lived by selling curds obeyed King Candragupta's order and searched in due course. They went to Kanyākubja and searched for her there. After searching and resting from the fatigue of the road, they went to the house where that brahmin woman lived, and standing at the doorway called out, "May there be auspiciousness! May there be auspiciousness!"

The brahmin woman said, "Good sirs, what do you wish?"

They said, "The girl with the hair."

The brahmin woman said, "For whose sake do you come?"

They said, "For the sake of King Candragupta, O brahmin woman."

She replied, "Good sirs, very well — but the bride-price for her will be considerable."

They said, "Sister, how much is required?"

She replied, "Five hundred intimate ornaments, five hundred outer ornaments, and the five foremost towns."

They conveyed this matter to King Candragupta, telling him the price the brahmin woman was asking. The king sent back his reply: "Good sirs, find out the full amount of the girl's bride-price, and pay it all." They received the command, and the king fixed the day of the month, the auspicious moment, and took her as his bride with great splendor and wealth.

On the very day he went to Magadha, throughout Magadha all the people everywhere became completely calm and at peace, and from that time the place came to be known as "the Peaceful."

Here ends the twenty-sixth fascicle of the Vinayakṣudrakavastu.

The summary verse is as follows:

Birth, and the one sustained by curds, and the son of Kātyāyana,
the peaceful one, the merchant, the battle,
the chanter before the assembly, and the goddess Tārā,
the lute-player, the hair-cutting,
and the episode of the skeleton —
all these are rightly gathered into this chapter.

At that time in Magadha there lived a merchant's son who took a wife from a family equal to his own, and he would sport with her, delight in her, and take pleasure with her. After sporting and delighting with her for a little while, he loaded up his goods and went off to another region. His wife, tormented intensely by affliction from eating fine and delicious food and wearing fine clothes —

One day she went up to the roof and gazed out in every direction. Some time later, the fierce king Rānaprabhā came riding past on an elephant, passing close by her house. She threw a garland of flowers toward him, and it landed on the fierce king Rānaprabhā's shoulder. He looked up, and there he saw her — young, in the full bloom of youth, supremely beautiful by virtue of her exceptional complexion and figure, standing at the edge of the parapet, glancing sideways with a sidelong gaze, her bearing suffused with desire. Seeing her, his mind became utterly captivated, and he called out to her, "If that is so, come down!" She replied, "O lord, come up here to me in secret." And indeed, overcome by passion, he was unable to turn back. He dismounted from the elephant, entered her house, sported with her in joy and delight, and she conceived a child.

Now, some women of discerning nature possess five qualities found in none other. What are those five? They know when a man is attached to them and when he is not; they know the right time and can tell by the signs of their monthly cycle; they know when conception has occurred; they know from whom conception has occurred; and they know whether a boy or a girl has been conceived.

She reported to the king exactly what had happened, saying, "O lord, I have conceived." The king gave her a pearl necklace and told her, "If a boy is born from you, give him this pearl necklace and send him to me. But if a girl, she shall be yours alone." With that he departed.

When the signs of pregnancy appeared, the merchant sent a letter: "I too am coming in comfort; do not be unhappy — take care." When she received this she was frightened, and she reported the matter to the king, saying, "O lord, my husband is drawing near — what am I to do?" The king sent word back to her: "Do not be unhappy, take care; I shall arrange for him to travel far away." And so the king said nothing further on the matter.

The king sent word to the merchant: "I require such-and-such goods — do not return without finding them." To obtain these, the merchant set out on a long and distant road.

Nine months having passed, a boy was born, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold. The woman filled a box with butter and honey, laid cotton-wool inside, placed the infant upon it, wrapped him in white cloth from above, set the pearl necklace upon him, sealed the lid, and affixed a wax seal to the box. She then instructed her maidservant, "Take this box and go; set it down at the city gate of the royal capital, placing it in a circle of lamps; and once you have set it there, stand to one side until someone takes it up." The maidservant did exactly as she was told.

Not long after, cattle passing along that road gathered around the box and stood surrounding it. Meanwhile, the fierce king Rānaprabhā was sitting up in his fine pavilion together with his tranquil queen, and he saw those cattle standing clustered together. He instructed his cowherds, "Good men, go see what that is that the cattle are encircling." They looked and reported, "O lord, there is a box sealed with a wax seal." The king said, "Bring it here." The tranquil queen made a request: "O lord, whatever contents the box may hold, pray grant them to me." The king replied, "Excellent — let it be so." When the box was brought before the king, he opened it and looked, and there he saw a pearl necklace and a child.

He recognized the pearl necklace and the thought arose in him, "This child is mine." He entrusted the child to the tranquil queen, saying, "This is your son." She asked, "O lord, what name shall we give this boy?" He replied, "This boy was nurtured by the cattle, and so let his name be Gopalaka — Keeper of Cattle." And thus the boy was named Gopalaka. From that time on, because the tranquil queen had raised him, she too came to be known as the Mother of Gopalaka.

At that time, in the land of Droṇaprāsāda, a king named Padmahṛdaya was ruling the kingdom — and from "the prosperous" down to "he ruled the kingdom in accordance with the Dharma" is as before.

In his land the rains fell in their season, the trees bore flowers and fruits without cease, the harvests were good, and even beggars found food easily. Then, at a certain later time, King Padmahṛdaya went up to the roof of his palace and was seated there surrounded by a company of ministers. He spoke to the ministers: "O wise ones, is there any other king in whose land the rains fall thus in their season, the trees perpetually bear flowers and fruit, the harvests are good, and even beggars always find food easily?" They replied, "O lord, in the land called Ārya-rājya under King Ugraprabha, it is said the rains fall in their season, the trees perpetually bear flowers and fruit, the harvests are good, and beggars always find food easily." He said, "O wise ones, if that is so, then arm the fourfold host of troops, and let us go to destroy that kingdom." They armed the fourfold host of troops, and King Padmahṛdaya set out with that fourfold host toward Ārya-rājya, advancing by stages until he arrived in the land of King Ugraprabha.

When he began to attack, the people dwelling in that land sent word to King Ugraprabha: "A great army has been gathered by one called King Padmahṛdaya from another land, and he is coming to conquer this realm." King Ugraprabha then armed his own fourfold host — the corps of elephants, the corps of cavalry, the corps of chariots, and the corps of foot soldiers — and marched out to do battle with King Padmahṛdaya.

Then King Padmahṛdaya seized the entire corps of elephants of King Ugraprabha, and seized the corps of cavalry, the corps of chariots, and the corps of foot soldiers as well. He captured, bound, and overpowered King Ugraprabha and routed him in battle. In the rout and the general scattering on all sides, the ministers and the rest of the troops and people fled into Ārya-rājya and gathered at the edge of the enclosure, where they sat. The king himself, entirely alone, went to a certain mountain cave.

In that mountain cave there was a farmer named Kṣetraka who was plowing his field. He saw the king and said, "It is being proclaimed that the hero of the market — King Padmahṛdaya — captured, bound, and overpowered King Ugraprabha and routed him in battle. Is that true?" The man replied, "It is true, friend. Though you live in this land, King Padmahṛdaya who has come from another land has captured, bound, and overpowered him and routed him in battle. Whatever the ministers and generals of that king are like — if I were to become a minister of his, I could swiftly, and without delay, seize King Padmahṛdaya by the neck, bring him to Ārya-rājya, and present him." So the man was speaking these words as he sat there.

His wife, a woman named Riktrödma, came carrying food. She dug up the earth, laid down leaves, washed her hands, and set about eating. She looked at the king and said, "Oh, hero of the market, you are weary and tormented by hunger and thirst. Though what we have to eat and drink is meager, and affliction diminishes our strength, please do not hold back — come, draw near, and partake of whatever there is." At these words, King Ugraprabha thought to himself, "If I do not eat, I shall starve and die." Realizing this, he dismounted from his horse, washed his hands and feet, took the saddlecloth from the horse, spread it on the ground, and sat down. Having sat, he began to eat with the thought of sustaining his life.

Then the woman poured beer from a bowl that was chipped at the rim. The king thought to himself, "The bowl is chipped, but I shall drink from the side that is not chipped." Now, kings are endowed with wisdom and possess excellent character, and so he thought further, "If I drink from the side that is not chipped, she may feel embarrassed, thinking, 'He drank from the unbroken side,' and she may shun me. It would be far better for me to drink from the very side from which she herself drank." And so he drank from that very same side. The man, Namdö Gyi, observed this and thought to himself, "This hero of the market is a man of no pretension at all — he drank from the very same side of the bowl from which I drank. I should make him a lasting friend, one who will not soon be parted from my household and way of life." And so he said to his wife, "Good woman, this hero of the market is a friend of my heart. Take him home, give him a proper welcome and bath, and feed him food. Give his horse fodder and provisions as well." She took the king home, welcomed him properly, gave him a bath, fed him food, and gave the horse fodder and provisions.

Now, certain mountain cliff-dwellers called Gyabrak Kyaseng had gathered against King Padmahṛdaya, and, descending from their mountain cliff valleys, they began to ravage the lands of King Padmahṛdaya. His ministers sent him a letter saying, "Your Majesty, the divine mountain cliff-dwellers Gyabrak Kyaseng have attacked and devastated the divine lands. Please give thought to what is to be done." Within the letter they also wrote a verse:

Just as you have striven with great diligence
to destroy the lands of your enemies,
so too please, Your Majesty,
act in the same way to protect your own realm and its borders.

King Padmahṛdaya read the letter and thought, "If I return the same way I came, the people of the world will think that King Padmahṛdaya has been defeated and has therefore turned back." Deciding that he would go to meet his friend one last time before departing, he sent word to King Ugraprabha: "Dear friend, what is done is done — what has become ash is ash. Now please come out. I shall do nothing whatsoever to you. Otherwise, we would simply part by embracing each other at the neck and going our separate ways." When the ministers heard this message, they thought, "If we send word that the king is not here, we may find an opportunity — let us try something deceptive." And so they sent him a letter: "Dear friend, even if that is so, we view the king with suspicion, like a crow, and so he will not come out. Your ally's son, the young prince Langkyong, will come — please hand authority over to him and depart." King Padmahṛdaya handed authority over to the young king Langkyong, encircled him with a royal escort, and then departed for Döjok. The ministers then said:

"Wise ones, King Padmahṛdaya has been put at ease and has gone to the land of Döjok — now let us go in search of the god." So saying, they sent mounted messengers out in every direction.

When King Tumpo Rabnang heard that King Padmahṛdaya had encircled the noble king with a royal escort and then departed for the land of Döjok, he spoke to a farmer named Namjé: "Namjé, I am free from fear, and for that reason I shall go to the noble king. If you come to the noble king's realm, come to my house."

Namjé replied: "Hero of the marketplace, I do not even know your name — how then could I come to your house?"

The king said: "Namjé, even if you do not know my house, never mind — when you arrive in the noble king's realm, simply ask whichever of the many horse-owners lives there, and come." So saying, he departed and journeyed gradually until he reached the land of the noble king. There he instructed the gatekeeper: "Hey, if someone comes asking which house belongs to the one with many horses, bring that person to me." Then he entered the house.

Some time later a festival came to the land of the noble king, and the crowds of people who lived in that region all went out to it. The farmer's wife, Ritrömma, said: "My lord's son, a festival has come to the land of the noble king and those crowds of people are going out to it — let us go too, enjoy the festival, and also catch a glimpse of the one with many horses."

He replied: "Good woman, can everything that the hero of the marketplace said really be true? One should consider three possibilities: that he was defeated, that he fled, or that he has fallen from his kingdom."

She said: "My lord's son, if that is how it is, very well — let us go, enjoy the festival, and then return." He agreed: "Good woman, fine — let us do just that." The two of them set out and journeyed gradually until they reached the noble king's realm. Namjé asked the gatekeeper: "Hey, which is the house of someone called the one with many horses?" The gatekeeper led him and his wife to the presence of King Tumpo Rabnang. The king greeted them with the full ceremony of welcoming guests who have come from afar, and then addressed Namjé directly: "Namjé, have you come?" Namjé answered: "Your Majesty, I have arrived."

Now the king was wearing plain, ordinary clothes, and because he had a crown bound on his head Namjé did not recognize him as the king. But when the king descended from his lion throne, Namjé recognized him, and together with his wife he prostrated at the king's feet.

King Tumpo Rabnang received them with great honor, led them into the queen's retinue, had them bathed and given a change of clothes, provided them with food, and also gave them a sleeping chamber. He then instructed the ladies of the queen's retinue: "These two are my father and mother — therefore you are to attend upon them with food, drink, bedding, seats, male and female servants, working people, attendants, and all necessary provisions." Thinking that the king was honoring and venerating them, all the ladies of the queen's retinue, the young men, the ministers, and every person of the palace household began to wait upon them.

After sitting for a while, the farmer Namjé spoke: "Your Majesty, please hear me. I am here, and being in your royal presence is not difficult." The king replied: "Namjé, stay right here and let us hold the kingdom together." Namjé said: "Your Majesty, what use would it be for someone like me, a farmer, to take hold of a kingdom?" The king said: "Namjé, at that time you yourself said: 'If I were that king's minister, or —'"

"— if I were made a general, I would swiftly and without delay seize King Lotus-Heart by the throat and drag him away to be taken to the noble king." When I said I could not do it, what kind of thing was that? And he had nothing more to say.

Now, King Tumpo Rapnang had five hundred ministers, and the king had them nurse Söpa back to health. When they had nursed him and he had recovered, he came to be known by the name Söpa, meaning "the recovered one." At another time the king asked him: "Söpa, how are you faring? Your Majesty, how are things with me? The ministers are treating me with contempt." The king replied: "Söpa, if that is the case, then when counsel is being taken on matters that concern them, you too shall enter into it, and no one will treat you without respect." Söpa said: "Your Majesty, what use is there in a farmer like me entering into councils?" The king commanded: "Söpa, do it just so, and all the ministers will come to show you respect." And at that Söpa said nothing more.

Some time passed, and then King Tumpo Rapnang was sitting surrounded by his assembly of ministers. Wishing to have Söpa speak, he first sent his own thoughts ahead and asked the ministers: "Wise ones, how should this matter be handled?" Some of them said: "Your Majesty, we would do such-and-such." The king replied: "This matter should not be handled that way." Others said: "Your Majesty, for this matter we would do such-and-such." The king replied: "This matter should not be handled that way either." Then the king asked Söpa how this matter should be handled, and Söpa said: "Your Majesty, this matter should be handled thus. If it is done in that way, things will go well." The king did accordingly. The ministers said among themselves: "The king has acted in accordance with this man's counsel, so we must not fail to show him respect," and they began to treat him with deference.

Again the king asked Söpa: "How are you faring?" He replied: "Your Majesty, how should things be? At first I had no house." The king commanded his ministers: "Wise ones, give Söpa a house." They replied: "Your Majesty, there is a certain great minister whose time of service has passed, and his house stands empty, along with his household and dependents." The king commanded: "Give that house to Söpa, complete with a wife and possessions," and they gave him that house together with a wife.

Again the king asked Söpa: "Söpa, how are you faring?" He replied: "Your Majesty, the servants of the household keep treating me with contempt, saying: 'This man is a farmer.'" The king said: "Söpa, if that is the case, then whenever you wish to bathe, at that time send word to me, and when you have finished bathing, announce that you are coming. And do the same when you wish to eat: send word to me a second time, and when you have finished eating, announce that you are coming. And then I myself will come to your house, and when I arrive I will eat together with you from one vessel." Söpa said: "Your Majesty, I am a subject and you are the lord. It is not fitting that I should eat together with you as one. That would not be proper." The king replied: "Söpa, if I grant you this, what contradiction is there in it? You eat, and if you do so, they will come to show you respect," and having said this, Söpa accepted and said nothing more.

Then the king sent a messenger to Söpa at the time of his bathing, saying: "Söpa, there is something I need of you — come quickly." Söpa went to the king's presence and said:

"I have some small need of Söpa — tell him to come quickly," the king declared. Söpa said: "Very well, my lord, I will wash and come — go ahead." And the messenger went back.

Some women of Söpa's wife's retinue then began to gossip: "Sisters, look at that husband of ours, the farmer — he is so shameless! See how he dismisses even the king's command." At this, some said: "Sisters, those who are born of low family will grow arrogant even over barley." Others said: "Sisters, wait and see: what goes up high must fall, so without any doubt the king will ruin this one," and so they spoke.

When Söpa had finished bathing and had begun to eat, the king sent a second messenger to him saying: "There is some small matter I need Söpa for — he has not arrived, so let him come at once." The messenger went to him and delivered the message just so. Söpa said: "Good fellow, go on your way — I will eat and come." Before long the king himself arrived and said: "Söpa, have you eaten?" Söpa replied: "Your Majesty, I have not." The king said: "Söpa, will you not play host to me?" Söpa replied: "Your Majesty, I will be your host — please take your meal." The wives thought: "He is laughing and joking together with the king!" and were so astonished that they began to stare fixedly.

The king washed his hands and feet and began to eat together with Söpa. When the wives saw this, they were alarmed and spoke among themselves: "Sisters, we scorned this man as nothing but a farmer, and look — there he sits eating with the king himself. Now, some said: "Sisters, what is to be done about this?" Others said: "What is there to be done? The king eats together with him, and if we have not shown him respect and the king comes to know of it, he will certainly harm us. What is done is done. From now on let us never be disrespectful toward him." Others said: "Good — let it be so." And though they felt ashamed and unhappy, they did not gainsay that counsel.

Later, the king asked Söpa: "How do you find yourself? How are things, Your Majesty? That father-in-law of yours has been extremely contemptuous toward me." The king replied: "Söpa, he may not be capable of doing as you wish, yet all of it depends on you alone — you yourself know what to do." Söpa said: "Your Majesty, if that is so, please grant me one thing — do not rebuke me for it." The king said: "Excellent — do it just so."

Some time later Söpa was passing through the market. There he saw two children who had been separated from their parents, wandering as they pleased wherever they liked, having found their daily food and now playing cheerfully in an alleyway.

Then a serving woman carrying a water jar came walking along that road, and one of the boys said: "Friend, look — this one has punctured the jar with a dry needle." She replied: "If you had made a hole with a dry needle, that would be no great wonder. That I have plugged the leak with this wet needle — that is the great wonder!" He said: "Very good, do it just so," and the boy plugged it with the dry needle, while the other stopped the leak with a wet one.

When Söpa saw this he was greatly astonished, and thought: "If the two of them cooperate, they could be capable of healing flesh." He called out: "Hey children — whose are you two?" The two replied: "Your Majesty, we have been separated from our parents and are from somewhere or other, searching for our daily food." Söpa said: "If that is so, why not stay with me?" They replied: "Your Majesty, we will gladly come."

Nevertheless they had a request: "What work of yours do you wish us to do?" He replied: "There is nothing at all to be done — simply let them become accustomed to this very cesspit and leave them there. However, I want you to do one thing for me: whenever someone joins me in eating, the two of you are to fill that person's mouth with filth steeped in excrement." The two of them said: "Your Majesty, we shall gladly do just so."

Some time later, when he began dining with someone for whatever reason, the two of them filled that person's mouth with filth steeped in excrement, and that person, choking on it, wiped his lips in disgust and fell silent, unable to utter a word.

The king then went to attend to the patient, and asked: "Patient, how are you faring?" The patient said: "Your Majesty, how am I faring! That household servant of yours insulted me by saying I was a farmer's man." The king replied: "Patient, if that is so, then whenever I go into the inner quarters of the queen's retinue, you are to come there and ask, 'Where is the king staying?' If they say, 'He is staying within the queen's retinue,' then say this: 'If he resides and remains within the queen's retinue, the king's affairs and the king's business will fall into ruin.' And furthermore, if you see my bed and throne there, sit down on them, and I shall wash your feet." The patient replied: "Your Majesty, you are the lord and I am the subject — how could that be fitting? That would not be proper at all." The king said: "Patient, if that is what I wish, what objection can you have to it? In that way, all of them will show you respect and attendance." The patient accepted and everything was gradually carried out accordingly. He was told to rest a while on the king's very own bed and throne, and he lay down there, and fell asleep on the spot. When the king came back out and asked, "Who is this?" they replied, "It is the patient, Your Majesty." The king said: "Has no one washed his feet? Bring water and come — I will wash his feet," and the king washed his feet. The attendants, though uneasy and reluctant, began to wait upon him.

Now King Rāpana (Raudra-prabhā) was violent in nature and consumed with lust for women. So it was that on another occasion he went up to the rooftop of the fine palace together with the sons of ministers, the young courtiers, and sat with them in improper conversation, asking the wise men: "In which village, town, or region are the women beautiful?" Some said: "Your Majesty, the women of Kānyakubja are beautiful." Others said: "Your Majesty, the women of Campājika are beautiful." Others said: "Your Majesty, the serpents that are fierce and fine." Others said: "Never mind the women living in other cities — right here in this very noble land there dwells one called Suvarṇā the beauty, and whoever sees her sees a goddess worthy of the veneration of the thirty-three, endowed with form, complexion, youth, and figure such that, as the brilliance of sunlight overwhelms the glow of stars dwelling in the celestial palace of the gods, so is she." When the king heard the description of her form and the qualities of her youth, he desired all the more to go to another man's wife. He disguised himself and that very evening took five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and went to her house. She received him with every welcoming courtesy befitting his arrival, and then entrusted him to her daughter, the maidservant. "Daughter, go and rub this noble young man down and bathe him. Mistress commands it so." The daughter obeyed Suvarṇā the beauty and began to rub down King Raudra-prabhā.

While she was rubbing him down, another man also arrived there carrying five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, and he said to Suvarṇā the beauty: "Come, let us take our pleasure together." Now the practice of Suvarṇā the beauty, who lived by her body, was this: if one man had come inside and then another came, she would kill the first and take her pleasure with the second. The maidservant looked upon King Raudra-prabhā — his form and the beauty of his youth — and thought to herself, "Even a young man of royal birth like this one will be killed by this woman who practices every manner of wickedness," and she wept. As she wept, drops of her tears fell upon the body of King Raudra-prabhā. He looked up and saw the girl weeping, and said, "Girl, why do you cry?" She replied, "My lord, do not ask." The king grew suspicious and asked again, "Girl, why are you crying? Speak plainly and without shame." And she told him everything in full.

King Raudra-prabhā then said, "Girl, is there any means by which I might escape from here?" She replied, "This house is surrounded on all sides by the madam's men carrying drawn swords, so there is little hope — yet there is one direction. It is unclean, so it may be improper to mention it." The king said, "Girl, clean or unclean, speak — and save my life." She said, "In this direction there is a drainage channel, and it has been fastened shut with an iron peg. If you can pull it out, open it and flee." The king said, "Girl, show me which direction that is — I can pull it out." And she showed him that direction.

Now, adjacent to the house of that courtesan lived the house of a brahmin astrologer. At that moment the brahmin had come outside to urinate, and his wife had also come out carrying water to rinse. The brahmin looked up at the stars and, seeing that the omens were inauspicious, said to his wife, "Brahmin lady, the stars are inauspicious — I fear that the portent of the gods is most dreadful." She replied, "Brahmin, do not say such things — the king will be displeased." He said, "Brahmin lady, we ourselves dwell safely under the king's protection, and therefore I do not approve of these words — yet I say them nonetheless."

All of this the king overheard. Then the king began to work at pulling out the iron peg, but he could not move it. He gathered his full strength and forced it loose and pulled it free, and at that very moment his bowels gave way, and he went forth together with that discharge. The brahmin said to his wife, "Brahmin lady, that dreadful and fearful portent of the god of which I spoke — it has passed. The king is alive, our power and authority remain great." Meanwhile, the king, still dripping with filth as he was, made his way to Queen Śāntā. She asked him what had happened, and he told her how it had all come to pass. Queen Śāntā, her eyes filled with tears, pressed her body against his with a clump of reeds, rubbed him down with a clump of reeds, bathed him with water scented with various perfumes, and dressed him in fitting garments.

The next morning he sat in his place of business and said to his ministers, "Wise men, summon the astrologers." They summoned the astrologers, and the king asked them, "Wise men, how did last night pass for me?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it passed just as it ought for a king of royal lineage, anointed with the consecration poured upon the crown of his head, ruling the earth according to the Dharma." The king said, "Wise men, in a certain large district there lives a brahmin astrologer — summon him." And they sent the king's men to fetch him.

They went there and announced to the brahmin, "The king summons you." He replied to his household members, "Wise men, do as the king has commanded — I will come to attend upon the king," and sent them back. When they returned, the brahmin's wife said, "Brahmin, before this I told you not to speak of the king becoming furious and angry, yet you would not listen to my words — and now it has come to pass." He said to the brahmin woman, "All will turn out well — do not be anxious," and with that he composed himself and went before the king.

The king, seeing him from a great distance, called out words of welcome — "It is good that you have come!" — and said, "Master, it is good that you have come — please be seated here." Gladdened, the brahmin offered the king a prayer of victory and long life, then sat where he had been directed. The king waited a short while and then said, "Master, do you know my omens?" He replied, "I shall probe and divine it for the king's pleasure." "Master, how did last night pass for me?" "Your Majesty, what appeared threatening and terrifying by way of some dreadful portent, yet you are a man of great merit, and because of that you fainted and escaped from among your enemies." The king was pleased and said to his ministers, "What the master has said is precisely so — it is exactly as he states and nothing other." Then the king said, "Master, tell me what excellent gift I should give you." He replied, "Please allow me first to consult with my household members, and I will make my request afterward." The king said, "Master, very well — do so." The brahmin took his leave and departed, going home to his own house. He called his household members together and said, "If the king is resolved to give me an excellent gift, tell me what each of you desires." The brahmin's wife said, "Brahmin, first ask yourself what you desire." He replied, "Brahmin woman, I desire five excellent townships." She said, "Brahmin, if that is so, then I desire a hundred cows." The son said, "Father, I desire a chariot of the finest sandalwood." The daughter said, "I desire jeweled earrings with pendant loops." His maidservant Kyedma said, "If you all have such desires, then I desire a fine flat stone."

The brahmin thought to himself: "I will ask the king for the gift in the melody of verse — I shall not do it in the common way of others." With that in mind, he composed the verse in his thoughts and went before the king, saying:

"Your Majesty, hear what we desire. I seek five cities; my brahmin wife seeks a hundred cows; the son seeks a fine sandalwood chariot; the daughter desires jeweled earrings; and my maidservant Kyedma — she too desires a fine flat stone."

The fierce king Rabsang replied to him in verse in kind:

"To you I grant five excellent townships; to your wife, a hundred cows; to your son, a chariot adorned with horse-drawn glory; to your daughter likewise, earrings; to your maidservant Kyedma, who sought a fine flat stone — may that hope of hers too bear fruit, and let every wish be fulfilled just as desired."

Then the king gave him the gift he had desired, and said, "Master, now enter my service and counsel me in affairs of state." He replied, "Your Majesty, I am a brahmin, and that is not my proper domain." The king insisted upon it earnestly and had him brought before him.

Now some time passed, and there came to the fierce king Rabsang certain grey-robed forest ascetics. He commanded the officer who greeted them, "Go and drive those ascetics away." So the officer mustered the fourfold army — the divisions of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry — put on their armour, and went. They drove those ascetics away, and afterward seized their encampment as well.

They were also made to hand over the tribute and the head-tax before they departed. When the king had nursed her back to health, he laid the grey-robed ascetics low in defeat and seized their encampment, and word came that they had been made to hand over the tribute and the head-tax as well. Upon hearing this, he went out to meet them with the fourfold army. Now after some time, within that encampment he caught sight of a girl who had been struck and bruised by the rocky crags of the mountain. He saw her, and asked the physician, "Is there anyone living with this physician who enjoys pleasures together with him?" The physician replied, "Your Majesty, it is not only for pleasure that I have her. Whoever has been granted her favors and then seeks her from behind — there is one present who would make him neigh like a horse." The king said, "Physician, can that really be so?" He replied, "Your Majesty, it will be demonstrated before your very eyes." The physician entrusted the girl to the healers and said, "Learned ones, I shall prepare all the medicines; you examine her." They examined her, and she recovered from her illness. Then gradually, through the excellence of the various medicines, she grew beautiful in form. The physician took her as his own daughter and gave her the name Tārā, the Daughter of the Grey-Robed One. The physician instructed the girl, saying, "Daughter, I am going to summon the god here within the hour — adorn yourself with all your ornaments and present yourself to the god." But she sat there saying not a word. The physician said to the king, "Does Your Majesty not see how the god has utterly cast aside my embarrassment?" The king replied, "Physician, how could I look, when you have not called?" He said, "Your Majesty, if that is the case, I shall invite him now. Excellent — a kindness has been done." The physician prepared food and drink fit for a king, had the house swept and cleaned, and came to the king's dwelling. He then wiped the king with fine cloths fit for royalty, bathed him with water perfumed with many fragrances, anointed him with various unguents, dressed him in many fine garments, offered him refreshments fit for a king, and sat conversing with him. Then from behind a curtain she tossed out a shuttlecock, and he deflected the curtain, and said, "Please return the shuttlecock." At that moment the king caught sight of her — young in years and beautiful. The instant he saw her, desire arose in him, and he said, "Physician, whose daughter is this?" "Your Majesty, she is my own daughter." "Physician, has she been given to anyone?" "Your Majesty, she has not." "Physician, if that is so, why will you not give her to me?" "Your Majesty, I wish to present her." So the fierce king Rabsang took her as his queen with great and splendid wealth. Since it is the very nature of things that what is new eclipses all that is old, the king gazed upon her alone, his mind filled with desire, neglected other affairs, and attended only to her. The physician thought to himself, "Now is the time to fulfill the vow I made before," and spoke these words to the girl: "Daughter, are you able to have this king ride on your back and make him neigh like a horse?" She laughed a little and replied, "Father, wait but a moment — I shall see whether it is possible or not."

The Vinaya: the Section on Minor Matters. The twenty-seventh bundle.

Now women, being skilled without having been trained, spread out a soiled garment and lay and sat upon a latticed couch. The king said, "My queen, what is the meaning of this?" She replied, "Your Majesty, the gods are in turmoil." He said, "What have you done to the gods?" She said, "Your Majesty, when the god sent my father, the grey-robed forest ascetic, away in defeat, I prayed to the gods in order to pacify the matter,

"If my father, having accomplished his purpose rightly, returns in victory, then he who took me in marriage shall mount my back, and I grant him the right to make the sound of a horse." This was the vow I made, and so I was offered to the god. Since the retinue of the god's queen is vast, I could by no means have failed to fulfill this vow. Those who are enslaved by the attachment of desire will stop at nothing." The king then said, "O goddess, since you prayed on my behalf and for my sake, fulfill everything and rest at ease." She said nothing further.

King Pracandarabha said, "O goddess, why do you not speak? Is there perhaps something more you prayed for, goddess?" She replied, "There is nothing further from the god — yet at that time I vowed that I would have the brahmin reciter chant an auspicious blessing of the gods, and that a lute-player would take up the lutes." He said, "O goddess, that too is easy enough — there are brahmin reciters — but a lute-player must be sought." She said, "Then, O god, please be so good as to seek a lute-player." At that time a man from the provinces, a landowner, came to Āryarāja carrying a basket. He was so completely overcome by attachment and desire for a courtesan that he sold everything in the basket, ate with her, and grew all the more attached. All the hired servants he had with him abandoned him and fled. She then said to him, "Son of a lord, I am not a farmer, I am not a merchant, and I am not a village person traveling with a basket to another region. Otherwise, living is sustained by whatever one finds from people such as you, so give me kārṣāpaṇas, or else open the door to another man." He replied, "Dear woman, I have no kārṣāpaṇas. But if I had kārṣāpaṇas, who would there be more worthy than you to give them to? Yet since you are dear to me, stay here and do not drive me away. If you do what I say, then I shall truly know that you hold me dear." She said, "Very well, I bow my head to that." He relieved himself and placed a twig of cypress upon the excrement, saying, "If you love me, pick up this cypress twig." As she began to pick it up, he smeared a lump of dung upon her and offered it to her, saying, "Do even beggars behave like this? Filth — I shall not sit together with you. Get out!" And with that he drove her from the house.

Now he was a man skilled in the lute, and he set about making his living by playing the lute. The king said to the nurse, "Your daughter prayed to the gods in this manner. Now that I have brahmin reciters, who shall play the lute?" She replied, "Your Majesty, there is a landowner who makes his living playing the lute — cover his eyes with a cloth and bring him inside." The king said, "Excellent, nurse — do exactly so and bring him in."

The king and the reciter ascended to the top of a seven-storied palace, and the reciter was told everything that had come to pass, yet he said nothing. The nurse covered the landowner's eyes with a cloth and placed him at the top of the seven-storied palace.

The daughter of the grey-robed ascetic, Tārā, having made all auspicious, propitious, and fortunate arrangements, and having dressed in white garments, mounted on the back of the king. The brahmin reciter began to chant the auspicious blessing. The landowner took up the lute. King Pracandarabha began to make the sound of a horse. The landowner then thought to himself:

"This building is seven stories high — how could anyone escape on horseback from up here? Without doubt, some woman has mocked a man like me who has fallen under a woman's sway." Thinking this, the landowner took up those words as a song:

Just as the branches of a pine are bent and bowed,
just as the branches of a pine are bent and bowed,
so too this matter is much the same —
so too this matter is much the same.

He sang on, not picking up the lute again, repeating the song again and again without interruption, speaking those very words of the song. The king then asked him: "Good fellow, what is the meaning of that song?" The landowner recounted everything that had come to pass. The king then thought, "He has seen through what I did — I must send him away from the land." So the king gave him five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and banished him from the country.

On another occasion, the royal reciter said to the king: "Sire, you have done something improper — kings ought not to fall under the sway of women." At those words the king said nothing whatsoever in reply.

The next day the king said to his attendant: "If today that brahmin were to be made to have his head shaved by his own wife, could you manage it?" The attendant looked around for a moment and said, "I can, Sire." The attendant then went home and said to his wife: "My dear, the brahmin reciter said such-and-such to the king, and now the king has commanded me to bring about an arrangement of this kind — to have that brahmin's head shaved by his own wife. Can you contrive it?" She replied: "My lord's son, what need is there to ask? Just watch and see — it has already been done." He said: "My dear, if that is so, very well. A cunning wife is cunning indeed." And so she began to befriend the brahmin's wife.

When the two of them had grown fond of one another, she said to the brahmin's wife: "My friend, my husband loves me deeply and does whatever I say." The brahmin's wife replied: "My friend, you imagine she can bear it? How could you possibly have the same power over your husband as he has over you?" The attendant's wife said: "My friend, if you think your husband is under your power, go ahead and shave his head." Emboldened by this taunt, the brahmin's wife said, "My friend, just wait and see!" — and with that she put on a soiled garment and lay down on a cot with a net canopy.

The reciter asked: "Brahmin's wife, what does this mean?" She replied: "Brahmin, I have angered the gods." He said: "Brahmin's wife, is there no one in your house? Whatever vows you made to the gods — fulfill them all, and you will be well." She said nothing. The reciter said: "Brahmin's wife, what did you vow to the gods?" She replied: "Brahmin, at the time when you were living as a brahmin and the god called to you, I prayed to the gods: 'If my husband returns home safely, I will shave his head and offer his hair to the gods.' And after that, fortune arose for you as well. But I forgot the vow, and now the gods are angered — in short, I am perishing." He said: "Brahmin's wife, that prayer you made to the gods was made on my account, so fulfill it — pray to the gods and accomplish everything." So she conveyed to the attendant's wife: "My husband says to pray to the gods and do it all." And she in turn sent word to the attendant: "My lord's son, the reciter's wife says to me: 'I made my husband agree, and he says — pray to the gods and do everything.'"

The attendant then spoke to the king: "The matter of the gods has been accomplished, my lord. The reciter has conveyed his compliance to me — please be informed of this." The king said: "That compliance was done for my sake — never mind, let it go." Before long, the reciter came to the king and said: "My lord, I will do something for the gods and I wish to come and visit the gods' presence in six months." The king said: "Good — do it just so." He went home and had his head shaved. But after shaving his head he simply stayed indoors. His wife sent word to the attendant's wife: "Friend, that husband of mine has had his head shaved." And she in turn informed the attendant. The attendant then spoke to the fierce king Prabha, who was greatly pleased and gave the order: "Summon that reciter."

The attendant then taught two young boys a song with these words:

Where there is a woman fair of form,
noble-born and continuing her line,
there, without a horse, a horse-sound rings —
look, O reciter, at your shaven head.

When the reciter came before the king wearing a hat, the two boys began to sing:

Where there is a woman fair of form,
noble-born and continuing her line,
there, without a horse, a horse-sound rings.

And then one of them snatched off the reciter's hat and sang:

Look, O reciter, at your shaven head.

At that, great laughter broke out. The reciter felt deeply ashamed, hung his head and left in disgrace, chin dropped to chest.

When the attendant had gotten what he needed from this, he began to harass them, saying: "Whoever falls under a woman's power like this — how can the king's interests be served?" The king then said to the reciter: "Learned one, are you capable of harassing that attendant?" He replied: "My lord, I will look for a chance — whether by day or by night — and do it." The attendant had a nephew who was skilled in illusion, and the attendant said to him: "If this uncle-by-marriage, the attendant, is put to shame before the king and his retinue, and if you are capable of humiliating him over it, then I shall be repaid in flesh." The nephew said: "Let me look and see whether it is possible or not, and then I will do it." Using illusion, he conjured a guest; from a pile of cloth he conjured a house; and from a skull-bone he conjured the merchant's wife — beautiful, lovely, and ravishing to behold.

Now it was the king's custom that whenever a guest arrived, the king himself would cut a gambling portion for him, or else he would send the attendant. The attendant began cutting gambling portions for those guests, and he asked the guests: "Good people, which is the merchant's house?" They pointed and said: "It is this house, my lord." He entered it. Before long he saw the merchant's wife — beautiful, lovely to look upon, entrancing to the senses, stirring to the mind. The moment he saw her, desire arose in him. He said: "Good woman, if I enjoy pleasure with you, I will cut no gambling portion for the guests." She replied: "Young lord, if you do it in that way, then let it be — but only enjoy pleasure at night." Through illusion she appeared to him that night. He enjoyed pleasure with her, and after a time he embraced her around the neck and fell asleep. Then the illusionist withdrew the illusion, and there was the attendant, asleep and lying with his arms wrapped around a skeleton's neck amid a pile of cloth. The reciter then said to the king: "My lord, look at the condition to which the attendant has been brought by the gods."

The king went, having assembled many hundreds of thousands of living creatures to witness the scene. The king then woke the attendant by rattling a rattle, and when he had roused him he said: "Tell me — did you even eat the flesh of the woman with whom you took pleasure?" At that the attendant was seized with tremendous shame, rose up, and thought to himself: "If this king keeps questioning me while I am alive, then whatever comes of it, I would rather die by my own hand." Then he thought again: "To kill myself by my own hand is going too far. I will instead take ordination before the noble great Kātyāyana." With that he went to wherever the venerable great Kātyāyana was staying, and when he arrived he said to the venerable great Kātyāyana: "Noble one, I wish to go forth — I beg you, please ordain me with the going forth." Kātyāyana then gave him the going forth, conferred full ordination upon him, and had him recite the scriptural transmission that flows from one to the next.

The fierce king Prabhaśvara, finding him gone, became displeased. He had him removed from the going forth and reinstated in his former position exactly as before.

Now a summary verse:

The cowherd and the hunter himself,
the women and the king of the land of the dead,
the one given by the god of wealth, and Prabhaśvara,
the king who went to Śilānikṣepa,
and the one who dreamed a dream — these are the last.

The fierce king Prabhaśvara, as he sat upon his great bed, gave rise to this thought: "If I were to pass away, would young Govarddhana be capable of ruling the kingdom, or would he not?" He thought further: "I should put this to the test for a while." He summoned the young man and said to him: "Son, there is a small matter to attend to in the queen's retinue. I will be inside the queen's retinue for seven days. In that interval, you act as king." Having so instructed him, the young man performed the duties of king while the fierce king Prabhaśvara remained within the queen's retinue.

Young Govarddhana, training himself well in the language of those who bring cases forward and those who oppose them, had the king's men who acted as go-betweens approach the men and women brought before him and ask each one individually: "Sir, do you desire this woman?" and of the women: "Do you desire this man?" — and if they showed mutual desire for one another, he then declared to the ministers: "Wise ones, if these two desire each other, why should I refuse them? Let no one under my rule say even a word against them living as they please together." Toward those who brought tribute payments he kept close and attentive watch.

When seven days had passed the king came out and asked the attendant: "Tell me, attendant — is young Govarddhana capable of ruling the kingdom after I am gone?" The attendant replied: "Your majesty, though lightning strikes above, those who act as go-betweens will flourish." The king said: "Attendant, what exactly is meant by acting and not acting as a go-between?" The attendant explained what the matter was, and the king thought: "Is this young man free of jealousy concerning other men's wives? Or does he hold the same attitude toward his own wife as well? I should test this." He instructed a territorial lord, saying: "Go, territorial lord, and enjoy pleasure together with young Govarddhana's wife." The territorial lord covered both ears and said: "Your majesty, this is ruination through wickedness!" The king said: "Territorial lord, the king's business stands as I have stated — go. If you do not proceed in order, the king's business will be undermined." The man replied: "Your majesty, though I will do it, I have no appetite for such a deed — but I will do it out of fear." The king said: "Then do it just so. When the time comes, territorial lord, what method will you use?" The man replied: "Your majesty, I will prepare a spread of refreshments near her gathering place, offer them to her, become acquainted with her, and then carry out the royal command."

The king gave him funds, and with those funds he gathered goods and spread out a market stall. One of the handmaidens of the cowherd's wife came to buy incense sticks at the stall. The territorial lord asked the girl: "Young woman, for whom are these incense sticks?" She replied: "For the cowherd's wife, my mistress." "What is her name?" "Her name is such-and-such." The territorial lord said: "My own mother bears that very same name — she is like my mother," and he then discounted the price of the incense sticks and gave her a generous measure of goods. The cowherd's wife asked the girl: "Before, with that same amount of money you brought back only a little — why now have you brought back so much?" The girl told her everything as it had happened. The cowherd's wife said: "Excellent! He is like a son to me." This went on a second and a third time, and she grew fond of him.

On another occasion the territorial lord said to the girl: "Tell your mistress that I wish to come and pay my respects many times over." The girl did so, and the cowherd's wife said: "Good — tell him to come here." The girl conveyed this, and he came, bringing gifts of fragrant goods. He embraced her and wept. She asked: "My son, why do you weep?" He answered: "Dear lady, my own mother was of exactly your appearance and bearing, and it is for that reason that tears have come to me." She said: "My son, I myself am your mother — you are my son, so do not weep," and she grew all the more fond of him.

Some time later, when the cowherd's wife had gone off in one direction, he called her back and said: "Young woman, come and bow at your uncle's feet." She came. The cowherd's wife asked: "Mother, what is this girl's name?" "Her name is such-and-such." "Mother, my daughter-in-law also bears the same name and has the same appearance — she is my daughter-in-law!" He replied: "Excellent, my child."

When the two of them had grown intimate with each other, the territorial lord feigned illness and lay as if sick. The girl came to buy goods, and the territorial lord's young man said to her: "Young woman, my master is suffering from a certain illness — will the lady not come? She does not know he is sick." The girl replied: "I will do it." The cowherd's wife then came to visit and asked: "My son, how are you?" He said: "Dear lady, there is a peculiar heaviness in my body." She said: "My son, consult a physician and have an examination done." He replied: "Dear lady, this is not an illness that can be healed by examination. There is something here that will cause me to die from this illness alone." She said: "My son, what do you have in mind — what means might cure this illness?" He said: "Dear lady, there is indeed a means by which it could be cured, but it is unattainable." She said: "My son, say what it is that is unattainable — everything will be provided." He said: "Dear lady, if I could enjoy pleasures together with the cowherd's queen, then this bodily heaviness would be healed."

At this she flew into a violent rage and said: "You wretch — you are finished! Do you want to enjoy pleasures together with the king's queen?" And she cursed him roundly, rose, and left.

Now, the territorial lord was a crafty man. He wrote down all his possessions in a register, and in that register he wrote the following: "Should I die, all my goods belong to the cowherd's wife."

He sent that register to her, and when she read it her anger subsided. She thought: "He has gone to such lengths just to win me over — if he comes now, he will love me all the more." And so, since it is in the very nature of women to be like this, she thought: "It would be wrong for him to die — I should help him." With that she summoned the girl and recited at length the praises of the territorial lord, then said: "My girl, your thread — is it still in that condition? Has it improved at all? And has a doctor been consulted? Has an examination been made?" He said: "My lady, his illness is of a curious kind — there is indeed a condition in which that very illness will bring him to his end. However, he says: 'If I could enjoy pleasures together with the bride, then I would survive.'" At this she flew into a rage and said: "You wretch — is he at death's door, and he still wants to enjoy pleasures with the king's queen?" He said: "My lady, do you know from whom your own garment was born?" She said: "I do not know." "That girl was born from a wicked man who became a king and held a great army. Your husband too is the son of a merchant who will in turn become a king. You too should enjoy pleasures together with him, and whatever son comes from you will also become a king." So she was deceived by him, and she agreed. Then he sent word to the territorial lord's boy: "Son, this girl has agreed, but she may yet cause you harm, so be alert to the timing and come quickly."

The territorial lord sent a message to the king: "Your god's wish is accomplished — but please, for a little while, do not send the cowherd away." The king thought: "After I am gone, the young cowherd will become king, and after him his son will be king. If a son is born to the cowherd's wife by the territorial lord, that son would become king. Therefore I must give him a medicine of such a kind that the territorial lord's faculties cannot become seed." With that in mind, he sent him certain pills that prevent the faculties from becoming seed, and sent word: "Territorial lord, at the moment when you enjoy pleasures together with the young cowherd's wife, you are to eat these pills."

He also instructed the cowherd: "There is a small matter of business to discuss — do not go home just yet." And so he stayed. The territorial lord ate the pills that prevent the faculties from becoming seed, then enjoyed pleasures with the cowherd's wife, and exhausted with the bliss of desire, fell asleep with his arms wrapped around her neck.

The king thought: "He has enjoyed pleasures with her and gone — I should send the young man home now." So he said to the young cowherd: "Son, the bride will be displeased — do not stay long, go home." When he arrived home, he found his wife sitting together with another man, and he saw the arm of that territorial lord hanging loosely. He folded that arm up, thinking: "Some people are going to notice this," and covered them with a garment.

The territorial lord slept on until dawn broke. When the sun rose he woke up, and wondering whether he had been seen or not, he ran off. The king said to the cowherd: "Son, last night in my dream I saw your wife enjoying pleasures together with another man." The god replied: "What your majesty saw in a dream, I witnessed directly, in person." "How so?" And he then recounted in full how it had come about.

The king said: "Son, are you not jealous?" The god answered: "I am not, my lord." "Son, why is that?" "My lord, I naturally remember my past lives. In another life of mine long ago, I was a merchant captain's wife —"

That merchant captain had fallen into ruin and set out for another land, and I said to him, "My lord, I too shall come with you." He replied, "Who will look after you here?" He refused to take me along, and I wept. The dairy folk then said to me, "Merchant captain's wife, why are you crying?" I told them what had happened, and they said, "Lead the merchant captain here and we will look after you," whereupon he brought me along. But as we traveled the road, some five hundred brigands appeared and fell upon those travelers, slew the merchant captain, and those five hundred brigands used me for their pleasure. When they found another woman among the travelers they had killed, I thought, "This one will become my rival," so I threw the old one away and that very instant perished.

My lord, seeing that I was used for pleasure by five hundred brigands and yet was not satisfied, what jealousy could I possibly feel toward women? My lord, moreover, anyone in the world who places trust in women is a fool. It is only right that women place trust in men.

The king said: "Son, that is exactly so. Women ought to place their trust in men."

In the land of Āryāvarta there lived a hunter whose wife was beautiful and lovely to behold, and he was deeply attached to her. He thought: "If I leave my wife and go off to dwell in a forest retreat, she will end up enjoying pleasure with another man. But if I do not go, I am a hunter — I make my living by taking others' lives and sustaining myself by killing. I am not a farmer, I am not a merchant, and no one else will support me either, so I will certainly starve to death. So I had better take my wife with me as I go." He took his wife, went to a forest retreat, built a leaf shelter in a certain spot, and stayed there. He would choose the finest wild game, kill it, sell the good meat, and make his living that way.

Then one day the ferocious king Rabsang went out on a hunt, and his horse bolted and galloped off in that direction. The hunter recognized the king, and knowing that the horse had bolted, used all manner of welcoming words to attend to him, and the king dismounted and sat down at the foot of a tree.

The hunter thought: "My due — the tribute of game flesh I owe the royally consecrated king of the warrior caste — is no debt yet fallen due, so I shall bring him some other game not yet owed." He strung his arrow, took his bow in hand, and went off in pursuit of the game.

King Rabsang, ferocious as he was, caught sight of the hunter's wife, who was beautiful and in the full bloom of youth. Overpowered by the force of violent affliction, he gave rise to lustful desire and at once committed adultery with that hunter's wife on the spot. When the hunter had killed the game and was returning, he came upon his wife in the very act of being violated. Now, among the reasons for anger, anger on account of women is the decisive kind, and so he fell into fury and thought: "This wicked-times king who has transgressed the royal law — I will kill him." Then again he thought: "Should I kill him merely on account of a woman?" While he was turning this over in his mind he had not yet decided, when he came face to face with a lion, and the lion killed him. Because he had aroused a mind of loving-kindness toward King Rabsang, he was reborn, upon dying, among the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings. King Rabsang thought: "I have enjoyed this woman, and when her husband's time is past and he is gone, to abandon her would not be proper on my part" —

and so he kept her close and stayed there conversing pleasantly with her. After some time, his ministers, young men, and the troops of the town began searching here and there and made their way to that place. They asked: "Your Majesty, to whom does this woman belong?" He replied: "I am the king — who would present a woman to me? From this day forward, place her among the queen's retinue." And they placed her among the queen's retinue. The king then departed with his army and cavalry and train of attendants as he pleased, and proceeded to the Noble Kingdom; and there the queen's retinue grew very large indeed.

The Blessed One then said: "I have not rightly seen even a single phenomenon that changes as swiftly as the mind." When King Tumpo Rabsang saw how vast the queen's retinue had become, he thought: "If that afflicted hunter took just one wife to a remote wilderness and could not even keep her safe, what need is there to speak of my guarding a retinue of queens so exceedingly large?" And so he had it proclaimed throughout the Noble Kingdom in these words: "Listen, all you wise people dwelling in the Noble Kingdom, all you city-dwellers, and all you crowds of people who have come from various lands. I am sending the queens of my retinue to enjoy themselves however they please. Whoever fully enjoys the company of the queens shall be said to have done well." And to the queen's retinue he also issued this command: "You too, each of you, go and enjoy yourselves with other men, and any woman who does not return when the drum is beaten will have her head cut off from her shoulders and flung to the ground."

Now since all women desire men, what need is there to speak of the king's own retinue of queens? They roamed everywhere throughout the Noble Kingdom, and each woman, upon seeing whatever man she saw, began to amuse herself with him. However, Śānti, the wife of the cowherd Balangskyong, and Drölma, the daughter of the gray-robed ascetic, out of their especially deep affection for King Tumpo Rabsang, did not lose their respect for the king and did not go. The king said to Śānti: "Śānti, you too, go and amuse yourself with other men." She replied: "Your Majesty, I was sent by a god — I will not amuse myself with another man." He then said to Drölma, the gray-robed ascetic's daughter: "You, go!" Now she was young and of an unsteady nature, and so, desiring another man, she consented and went down the street.

As she was wandering about, she saw a perfume-seller's apprentice boy and said to him: "Come, let us amuse ourselves together." He replied: "First hold this lamp for me while I finish reckoning these accounts, and then afterward we shall amuse ourselves." So she held the lamp and stood there. The perfume-seller's boy was busy calculating: "I made this much profit from this, and this much is to be given to such-and-such a person," and he gave her no thought at all — and so it went on until dawn came. When the drum was beaten at the royal palace, the daughter of the gray-robed ascetic set the lamp down on the ground and left. He said: "Stay and amuse yourself!" She replied: "How should I amuse myself? The king has established this law: any woman who does not return when the drum is beaten will have her head cut off from her shoulders and flung to the ground. The drum has now already been beaten — do I have two heads that I should go?" And so she returned without having amused herself at all.

The king asked: "Drölma, did you amuse yourself?" She replied: "Your Majesty, I did not." "Why not?" he asked.

She told him what had happened, and the king said nothing more.

Once again the king made the same proclamation by drum, and the announcement spread everywhere: "King Fierce Blazing Light grants, as his queen's retinue desires, the enjoyment of men." The son of the king of Kauśāmbī heard how King Fierce Blazing Light had granted the enjoyment of men as his queen's retinue desired. Having heard this, he said to Śabara: "Śabara, it is proclaimed that King Fierce Blazing Light grants the enjoyment of men as his queen's retinue desires. Let us go together and enjoy ourselves with the retinue of Queen Fierce Blazing Light." Śabara said: "Your Majesty, King Fierce Blazing Light is your longstanding enemy — he has been trying to kill you — and if you go there and meet with him, there is every reason to fear harm." The prince replied: "Śabara, there are foolish men in this world, but you stay here — I shall go." Śabara said: "If Your Majesty is determined to go, though Your Majesty may have no fear, it is still fitting to take care." Now the son of the king of the East was extremely lustful toward women, and so, dismissing Śabara's words, he went to the Noble Palace. There the daughter of the gray-robed ascetic saw that he was handsome, fine-looking, and beautiful. Seeing him, she said: "O prince, come here — let us enjoy ourselves together with Drölma, daughter of the gray-robed ascetic." He said: "You make the bed." She replied: "You make the bed." And since both of them were haughty and full of pride, the son of the king of the East did not make the bed, and the daughter of the gray-robed ascetic, Drölma, likewise did not make it. They went on saying "You make it — I will not," until dawn came. When the drum was beaten at the royal palace, the daughter of the gray-robed ascetic, Drölma, left. The son of the king of the East said: "Stay and let us amuse ourselves!" But the daughter of the gray-robed ascetic, Drölma, said: "How am I to amuse myself? The king has established this law: any woman who does not return when the drum is beaten will have her head cut off from her shoulders and flung to the ground. The drum has already been beaten — do I have two heads that I should stay?" And so, without having amused herself at all, she pulled the ring from the finger of the son of the king of the East and left.

The king asked: "Drölma, did you amuse yourself?" She said: "Your Majesty, I did not." "Why did you not amuse yourself?" She recounted everything that had happened, then displayed the ring and said: "Your Majesty, I have come bearing this ring of his."
