King Fierce Blazing Light read the inscription on the ring and summoned Gosā, saying: "Gosā, the son of the king of the East arrived here with a great army and no one noticed. He desired my queen's retinue — how is it that you let him slip away?" Gosā replied: "Your Majesty, he arrived here undetected — what can be done about that now? But if he comes again, he will not be tolerated."

Thereupon King Fierce Blazing Light again made the same announcement by drum. The son of the king of the East heard it in the same way and said to Śabara: "Śabara, it is proclaimed again that King Fierce Blazing Light grants the enjoyment of men as his queen's retinue desires. Come along — let us go and enjoy ourselves with the retinue of Queen Fierce Blazing Light." But Śabara said: "Your Majesty, last time you went there undetected and returned safely. But now King Fierce Blazing Light is prepared and ready — it would be better not to go."

The Eastern king's son said: "Among the men who bear weapons there are some who are careless and inattentive — I will go." And so he went, and the weapon-bearing men had also been sent out by the king's order. The son of the king of the East made his way gradually into the royal city and entered a certain house. The guards there — men armed with drawn swords — had surrounded it on all sides, and he gave them this instruction: "Good men, if a woman comes out, let her pass. But if a man comes out, do not let him go."

Śabara perceived what was happening and thought to himself: "That I abandoned my lord in his hour of need — leaving him to his fear and anxiety about the king's terrible wrath — that was not right on my part." And so he dressed the king in ordinary women's clothing and ornaments, then had him carry a water pot and drew a garment over his head with a spindle, and, teasing him playfully, said: "God, if you do not bring water to drink and do not come back, the river will carry you off!" — and with that he pushed him outside. The king's men thought he was just a maidservant being sent on an errand and let him go. Śabara then threw the water pot down by a small pond and fled.

When the guards checked that house and realized in a moment that he had escaped, they seized Śabara, brought him before King Fierce Blazing Light, and said: "Your Majesty, this man-god sent away the son of the king of the East." Śabara said: "Your Majesty, I had used his food and clothing for myself, and that I sent him away was the right thing for me to do. But in his case — he had used your food and clothing for himself, and then when he was sent away he simply wandered off and deserted you. That was not right." When Śabara said this, King Fierce Blazing Light became furious with the guards and said: "Guards! Was it right that the son of the king of the East be allowed to slip away with what my queen's retinue desired? Therefore, if you bring the son of the king of the East back here right now, all will be well. But if you do not bring him, I will cut you down with a heavy punishment." Terrified, they sat there scheming about how to capture him.

Before long a master of the art of mechanical automata (yantra) came from the south. The guards asked him: "Good man, are you able to construct an automaton of such and such a kind?" He replied: "Your Majesty, I will undertake it gladly." The guards hid the lead elephant — the great elephant known as the Hill of the Muddy Reed — in a secluded place, and had it cried out through the royal city: "The lead elephant, the great elephant of the Hill of the Muddy Reed, has fled!" At that moment the sound of this proclamation spread in all directions far and wide. Then the guards said to the master of automaton-craft: "Make an automaton of just this kind!" And he built an automaton made to look exactly like the Hill of the Muddy Reed, the great elephant, placed five hundred men inside it, and loaded it with a great quantity of elephant dung and water. Then he instructed those men: "By whatever means, drive this automaton in such a way that it appears before the eyes of those who dwell in the vicinity of Kauśāmbī. If the son of the king of the East comes forth with a fourfold army, do not give him into their hands. But if he comes alone, seize him by both hands and bring him back here without delay." Those men drove the automaton along so well that it looked convincingly like the vicinity of Kauśāmbī, and the cowherds, cowherd women, grass-cutters, wood-cutters, those who lived by the road, and wayfarers all stared wide-eyed in astonishment and gathered around to look. Some among them said: "Good people, this is the rogue lead elephant!"

Others said: "This is no rogue elephant — it is the chief of the herd of King Tumpo Rabnang of the noble realm of Ārya, the one named Damburi Mountain, who ran away; that is what has come here."

Then some of them went to the king of the East and announced: "Your Majesty, the one that had been the chief of the elephant herd of King Tumpo Rabnang who dwells in the noble realm, the one named Damburi Mountain who had fled — by the power of Your Majesty's merit, it has arrived here, appearing like many hundreds and thousands of living creatures." When the son of the king of the East heard this, joy and gladness arose in him. He beat the drum of rejoicing, had the pair of conches sounded, and commanded his general: "Go, array the fourfold host of troops, and have the city drums beaten with this proclamation: to all who dwell in the city and to all the multitudes of people who have come from various lands, the king goes to take hold of the elephant chief Damburi Mountain — come, bearing all manner of weapons and ropes!" The general arrayed the fourfold host of troops and had the city drums beaten with this proclamation: "Listen, all you wise ones who dwell in the city, all who dwell in the palace and its environs, and all the multitudes of people who have come from various lands — the king commands: the king goes to seize the elephant chief Damburi Mountain; come, bearing all manner of weapons and ropes!" And so it was proclaimed.

Then the son of the king of the East set out toward the elephant chief Damburi Mountain together with the fourfold host of troops and many thousands of the finest men. The operators of the automaton drove it in such a way as to make it appear that the fabricated likeness of the elephant chief Damburi Mountain was beginning to flee, and so they drove the automaton forward. The ministers said: "Your Majesty, you yourself are skilled in the rites of elephant-keeping; please devise a means to make this elephant flee, and apply it yourself." The king commanded his general: "You keep the fourfold host of troops back — I myself will approach it by skillful means." The general held the fourfold host of troops back, and the king himself began to approach, playing a pleasing lute melody and drawing near. The operators of the automaton drove it so that the automaton went straight toward the son of the king of the East and came to rest there. Then those five hundred men emerged from the automaton and seized him. Having seized him, they placed him inside the automaton, and drove it away as swiftly as the force of the wind. The son of the king of the East had been taken.

"The son of the king of the East has been taken!" — when the ministers spread this cry on all sides, the many hundreds and thousands of living creatures and the fourfold host of troops began to give chase. When they had passed beyond a certain critical distance, the general said: "Wise ones, the king has already been taken away — think of some other plan and turn back." And they all turned back.

The son of the king of the East was brought to the noble realm and looked after. He was then presented to King Tumpo Rabnang, and it was said: "Your Majesty, this is the son of the king of the East." The king beat the drum of rejoicing, had the pair of conches sounded, and gathered the many suffering living creatures of villages, towns, market settlements, and roadsides. Then he commanded the keepers: "I am releasing the son of the king of the East — tend to him." The ministers said: "Your Majesty, this prince is skilled in the rites of elephant-keeping; if he is killed, the tradition of elephant-keeping will be lost. Therefore, for the time being, Your Majesty should please learn the rites of elephant-keeping from him."

"We shall do just as Your Majesty commands." The king said: "Keeper, if that is so, then learn the rites of elephant-keeping from him. But once I have learned the rites of elephant-keeping from him and he has become my teacher, how could I then have my own teacher put to death?" The keeper said: "Your Majesty, the same fault would fall upon me as well — that would not be right." The king said: "Keeper, if that is so, who should be made to learn from him, so that I may then learn from that person?" The keeper said: "Your Majesty, your daughter Norha Jin is without idleness, possessed of diligence, learned, and accomplished. Have her be the one to learn from him, and she in turn shall teach Your Majesty."

The fierce king Rab Nang then said to Norha Jin: "My daughter, that man has eighteen ugly marks, yet he is skilled in the rites of elephant-keeping. Therefore, you shall separate yourself from him by a screen, learn the rites of elephant-keeping from him, and afterward teach them to me. You must not look at him at all — if you see him, bad luck will befall you, and you will die." And so she separated herself by a screen and began to learn the rites of elephant-keeping from him.

Jungwa Chang thought to himself: "If His Majesty searches for me and I am still alive, I should think of a means of escape. If, however, I have died and passed my time, another will be consecrated as king." He then spoke to his sister, whose name was Sertrengchen, who was even more skilled in deception than Jungwa Chang himself: "Sister, go to the Noble Kingdom, make haste there, and search everywhere for the king. If he is still alive, think of some means of his escape. If he has died and passed his time, let another be consecrated as king." She said nothing in reply to this, accepting it in silence, and then, disguising herself in the garb of a wanderer, she set out for the Noble Kingdom.

She sat at the king's gate and asked the king's men: "Good people, is the son of the king of the East alive or dead?" The king's men said: "Ask the monk who is just inside — what harm did he do to you?" She said: "Good people, he separated my husband and children from their lives and seized all my goods and wealth." They said: "That monk has not yet passed his time. He is teaching the rites of elephant-keeping to the king's daughter Norha Jin." In the same way she asked the king's men at the four gates of the palace, and in each case they gave the same reply.

By those very stratagems she gained entry inside. When she saw the son of the king of the East, she looked in all four directions and quietly asked: "Is His Majesty still alive?" And he too, feeling shame and inward unhappiness, looked in all four directions and said: "Sister, you are alive." Having thus made direct contact, she used another stratagem and, catching sight of Norha Jin, said: "My daughter, from whom are you learning the rites of elephant-keeping?" She replied: "There is an old woman possessed of eighteen ugly marks, and I am learning from her, separated by a screen." He said: "There is no one here whatsoever who possesses eighteen ugly marks. The one from whom you are learning is the son of the king of the East — handsome, beautiful, lovely to behold, endowed with all fine marks. Who has deceived you with such a tale? If you do not believe me, open the screen and look." Upon hearing a description of his form and his youth, she felt faith arise, opened the screen, and saw him. The very instant she saw him, she was agitated by desire as though stirred by the force of a gust of wind, and she said: "Old woman, whatever you have said may be as it is, but there is a request I have to make."

"Will you arrange for me to meet with him?" The old woman replied: "Daughter, I will accomplish exactly what you wish. Wherever one wanders, it is difficult enough to encounter a man such as this — how much more need be said of your bringing such an improper request to me!"

The Vinaya, the fourth, resides here.

The Minor Vinaya Topics, the twenty-eighth fascicle.

"Your desire shall be fulfilled — you will meet with a king, a sovereign of the royal lineage, anointed by consecration from the crown of the head. I will arrange your meeting with him." She then brought her together with the son of the eastern king. Dattā (Nora Lhé Jin) and he became deeply attached to one another. Suvarṇamālā (the Golden Garland One) maintained the liaison while the god lived on. The fierce and brilliant king sent word to Dattā: "The princess is to be taught the elephant ceremony." She then concealed her five ornaments, dressed herself in ragged clothing, took the name Vasantī (the Spring One), and went to the royal capital in the guise of a madwoman. There in the great roads, the market streets, the crossroads, and the three-way junctions, she ran and leaped about, calling out the mad words: "I am Vasantī — how delightful!" Those who recognized her as the one maintaining the liaison she rewarded with ornaments, and they took them and went away without saying a word. Those who did not recognize her dismissed her, thinking: "This one is mad." Wherever she entered — the royal palace, its environs, and fine houses — she found food, flowers, and clothing, and she secretly made common counsel with the eastern prince.

When another time came, Dattā said to the son of the eastern king: "My lord, if my father notices, flee here quickly." He replied: "My lady, if it should come to that, go to your father and say this: 'Father, I have learned the elephant ceremony, and yet I see no work to be done with it. For that reason, please grant me a fine, well-trained elephant to do with as I please, so that I may practice with it and examine its capabilities.'" She went and spoke to the king accordingly. King Caṇḍapradyota then commanded the elephant keepers: "Knowledgeable ones, give the princess Dattā the fine, well-trained she-elephant to do with as she pleases, and let her ride it to examine its capabilities." They gave it to her to do with entirely as she wished, and together with the son of the eastern king, she mounted it and began plotting escape. Sometimes she went out in the morning and returned at midday; sometimes she went at midday and returned in the afternoon; sometimes she went in the afternoon and returned in the evening; sometimes she went in the evening and returned at midnight; sometimes she returned at the third watch of the night; sometimes at the fifth watch; sometimes in the small hours; and sometimes at the breaking of dawn.

When the eastern prince, who maintained the liaison, had described the plan of escape to her, she began removing the elephant's dung. The grooms said: "Vasantī, what is this for?" She replied: "Knowledgeable ones, I have made this an offering to the king — take it there, and it will become sacred food." At that they laughed, thinking: "This one is mad," and said nothing more. She then carried the dung and hung it on the branches of trees along the road to Kauśāmbī. Then she began filling pots with the elephant's urine and carrying them away. The grooms asked the same question as before. She replied: "Knowledgeable ones, I have made this an offering to the king — this will become a libation there." They laughed in the same way, thinking: "She is mad," and left it alone.

She likewise carried it and hung it on the branches of trees along the road to Kauśāmbī.

Now, the prince of King Śarva, along with Holder-of-the-Bow and Golden-Garland, had set a time, agreeing to assemble at a certain place on a certain great day of the sun. The prince of King Śarva mounted the great elephant Bhadravatī, who had been given by the god of wealth, and set off toward that place. Holder-of-the-Bow and Golden-Garland likewise mounted that same elephant, and as they went along enjoying pleasant melodies, the prince of King Śarva took up a musical refrain, and Holder-of-the-Bow, delighted, broke into song:

Bhadravatī and Sweet-Voiced,
Dhanavardhana and Śarva's son,
Golden-Garland and Spring-Blessed —
all these journey toward the same aim.

Whatever time it is when they return, may that time come swiftly. Whatever final moment there may be, may it also pass —

and he spoke to fierce King Pradyota, who had revived him: "Revived one, Dhanavardhana — what has become of him now?" The revived one began to search, but could not find him, and so he said to the king: "The prince of King Śarva seized the great elephant Bhadravatī and fled, taking Dhanavardhana with him." The king was startled and said: "Revived one, go quickly — mount the marsh-land elephant and bring back Śarva's son and Dhanavardhana." He mounted the marsh-land elephant and chased them for a long distance.

He pursued them and caught up with them. Then Holder-of-the-Bow untied the bundle of the elephant's dung, and the marsh-land elephant began trying to eat it. For as long as it was eating, the great elephant Bhadravatī gained a distance of ten leagues. Again the marsh-land elephant caught up with them, and Holder-of-the-Bow poured out a single pot of the urine, and the marsh-land elephant began trying to drink it. For as long as it was drinking, the great elephant Bhadravatī gained another ten leagues, and they passed into foreign territory. The revived one then thought: "This is foreign territory; I will lose the marsh-land elephant too if I go further" — and at that decided it was hopeless, and turned back.

King Pradyota asked: "Revived one, what news?" He replied: "Your Majesty, there is nothing for it — they have fled." The king rested his hand against his cheek and sat sunk in thought.

The prince of King Śarva, having recovered from his brush with death, came to Kauśāmbī and gave gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, friends, brothers, and kinsmen, held a great feast, and together with Dhanavardhana played and rejoiced and took pleasure in merriment.

On another occasion, the two of them went up to the roof of a fine mansion and sat there exchanging private conversation. He said: "My lady, you too were stolen away from me by that trick." She said: "My lord, and you likewise were seized and held by my father through his stratagem." He said: "My lady, if your father is not summoned here and put to work learning the rope-maker's trade, then I am no longer the son of King Śarva" — and she, though angry, said nothing.

King Śarva said to Holder-of-the-Bow: "Are you able to dispel my displeasure? My lord, what should I do?" She said: "Seize King Pradyota by the neck, bring him here, and put him to work learning the rope-maker's trade." He said: "My lord, when you seized Dhanavardhana and the great elephant Bhadravatī, that in itself was sufficient to dispel your displeasure. Nevertheless, if you have truly thought this through and insist upon it, I will do it" — and so saying, she made preparations for caravans traveling to the noble realm and inspired the caravan leader with enthusiasm.

A courtesan of fine form and youthful beauty, adorned with varied ornaments, was made to pose as the caravan leader's wife, and they made their way gradually through villages, towns, districts, and royal palaces, surveying the markets as they went, until they arrived in the noble realm.

King Pradyota heard that a wealthy caravan leader had arrived, possessed of great riches. Being covetous by nature, he went himself to inquire of the travelers: "Friends, which is the caravan leader's house?" They pointed it out to him, and the king went there. Standing at the door, he asked where the caravan leader was. They replied: "He has just gone out." He said: "Then who is inside?" They answered: "The caravan leader's wife is within." He pushed the door wide open and entered, and the moment he did so he beheld the caravan leader's wife — a woman of such surpassing beauty and youth that she outshone every woman in all the noble realm. The sight of her kindled in him a fierce passion, and he said: "Fair one, share pleasure with me, and I will give you the caravan leader's dice." She replied: "If that is so, sit here on this bed." Now there is nothing a man corrupted by attachment will not do, and so he sat down there — whereupon the king's men blocked the door, bundled him into a palanquin, lifted it on the shoulders of four men, and singing as they went, they carried him out through a single gate and into the noble realm.

Some among the onlookers clapped their hands, some laughed, and some sang this song:

The moon was swallowed by the wasps.
Vaiśravaṇa's steward drove him on.
Earth and forest soared into the sky.
The courtesan led Pradyota away.

The inhabitants of the noble realm wondered why the merchants were saying such things. But the travelers came out through a different gate, cut short their disguises, fled, and made good their escape. The scouts, meanwhile, searched in all directions for the king, and in this way they eventually made their way back to Kauśāmbī.

The ministers said to King Śarva: "May the king rejoice — King Pradyota has been brought here and captured." King Śarva commanded: "Friends, seize him today and set him to learning the rope-maker's trade. As for King Pradyota's arrival here — let it be established as law that the god Dhanavardhana has given this, and that no one is to say a word about it."

Now some time after this, King Śarva's son Dhanavardhana was seated up on the roof of a fine mansion together with his companions when King Pradyota came out through the door of the weaving workshop on some errand. King Śarva caught sight of him and said to Dhanavardhana: "That man over there — do you know who he is?" Dhanavardhana looked for a long time and, recognizing the king from his bare crown, sat there with tears streaming down his face. He thought to himself: "This wicked king has brought my father to such a condition as this. If I do not kill this wicked king, I am no son of Dhanavardhana. And I will kill him in such a way that he himself does not know he has been killed."

Now that king too was a man of sharp mind, and perceiving that Dhanavardhana was angry, he summoned his attendant and gave instructions: "Attendant, go and make peace with the enemy — gain his trust — and then release King Pradyota, bathe him, feed him, honor him with great ceremony, and escort him back to the noble realm." The attendant carried out this command and escorted him back to the noble realm.

Dhanavardhana thought to himself: "If I begin plotting to kill him here, that deceitful one will see through it and we shall come to blows — so let me distract him for a little while." And so he engaged him with some light conversation, with laughter and play, and —

— distracted him with pleasures and merriment.

Now, there was a queen who was wearing soiled garments and lying on a net-covered cot. The son of King Śarva spoke to her: "My lady, what is the matter?" She replied: "My lord, the gods are in turmoil." He said: "My lady, can you not calm them? Let someone else fulfill whatever vow you have made." She replied: "My lord, the vow I have made cannot be undone. When my father took my lord captive and kept him confined, I made a vow to my lord, saying: 'If my lord and I might travel together in safety and happiness to Kauśāmbī, then there, for seven days, my lord and I shall eat no food together, and when the seven days have passed, my lord shall be wrapped in flower garlands from the tips of his toes to the crown of his head and seated at the gate of the enclosure; and I, having completed my austerities, shall give food to a thousand brahmins and honor them with great ceremony and reverence.' That was the vow I made. But now the retinue of the queen's household has grown very large, and I was wondering to myself why things would be done in this manner — and in short, my lord, it has been lost." The king replied: "My lady, the request you made to the god was in truth made entirely on my account. Be at ease — everything shall be accomplished." With that, she rose, tied two young dogs at the gate of the enclosure, and from that time forward, day by day, fed them ever-increasing portions of meat, however much they were capable of eating. Once the two young dogs were able to eat that much meat, she remained with the king for the full seven days — and during those seven nights she herself ate only at night. As for King Śarva's son, out of his attachment to that wife, he did not eat for seven days, and as a result his complexion became pale and wan, his flesh wasted, his vitality diminished, and he grew haggard and faint.

When the seven days were complete, Dhanavardhana gave instructions to those skilled in threading and stringing flower garlands: "Have those well-acquainted with the matter quickly bring fragrant, beautiful flowers and come here." He also gave instructions to the one who held the provisions: "Today the god's austerities are fulfilled — adorn the city beautifully and prepare food for a thousand brahmins, together with the king, the queen, the retinue, the young attendants, the ministers, and the assembled citizens of the city." As for the other ministers, so that they would notice nothing, he assigned them to various other tasks in various other places. The keeper of the provisions, being close to the king and devoted to him, cleared the city of stones, pebbles, and gravel, sprinkled sandalwood water all about, set out censers of sweet-smelling incense, raised banners and victory standards, hung strings of pearls, swags of silk, and tinkling ornaments, and spread flowers of every kind in profusion, making the whole place as delightful and joyous as the pleasure gardens of the gods. Throughout every quarter and every corner, various sounds of music were proclaimed, and dancers, poets, and skilled performers of every kind began to dance and perform.

When this great festivity and commotion was at its height, Dhanavardhana had King Śarva's son wrapped in flowers from the tips of his toes to the crown of his head and pushed off the top of the enclosure wall. Scarcely had he fallen before he was alive no longer — the dogs left nothing but a skeleton. Then crows, vultures, jackals, and other creatures that feed on human corpses fought over what remained.

All of Kauśāmbī resounded with a great cry: "The god has fallen from the top of the enclosure wall while gazing out at the beautiful city — and the dogs have eaten him!" At that, some wept, some rejoiced, and some sat in indifference.

Some among the people began to loot and plunder. When the great clamor broke out, the monks who had been residing in Kauśāmbī each fled for themselves: some went to Śrāvastī, and some went to one distant place or another. At that point, the commander-in-arms, the other ministers, the leading men of Kauśāmbī, the brahmins, and the householders quieted the uproar. Then the commander-in-arms began a thorough investigation into how the king had come to go to the top of the enclosure wall, and how the dogs came to be gathered at the foot of that wall. Through this investigation the truth came to light: Dhanavardhana had used a stratagem to commit the murder. Enraged, the commander-in-arms had Dhanavardhana locked inside a house of lac and burned alive.

The monks were filled with doubt, and in order to resolve all their doubts they put a question to the buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, what deed had King Śarva's son done, such that through the ripening of that karma he was devoured by dogs and died before his time?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, King Śarva's son accumulated a mass of karma and, like conditions ripening as they do, what was resting close at hand inevitably came to pass — for what he had done and accumulated was inescapable. Monks, by whom else could what King Śarva's son had done and accumulated be separately experienced? Monks, the karma that has been done and accumulated does not ripen in the outer element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, the virtuous and non-virtuous deeds that have been performed ripen solely within the acquired aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas). As it is said in verse:

Even across hundreds of aeons,
karma does not perish.
When the conditions and the time converge,
the fruit ripens for embodied beings.

Monks, long ago there was a reciter of vedic texts who lived near a certain mountain. At a time when no buddha had appeared in the world, a pratyekabuddha — one who takes compassion on the impoverished and the lowly, who delights in remote dwelling places at the forest's edge, and who serves as a singular field of generosity for the world — was wandering through the regions and arrived at that mountain. He stayed there for one night. The following morning, that reciter of vedic texts donned his lower robe and outer robe, took up his alms bowl, and entered that mountain village to collect alms. As the man came out again with his dog on a leash, he set the dog upon that great and venerable pratyekabuddha — who was utterly blameless and would harm no one.

Now monks, what do you think? That reciter of vedic texts was none other than King Śarva's son himself. Through the ripening of the karma of having set a dog upon that blameless, harmless pratyekabuddha at that time, in that place, he was devoured by dogs and died before his time five hundred lifetimes in succession — and even now he has been devoured by dogs and died before his time.

Therefore, monks, the ripening of karma that is wholly dark is itself wholly dark; the ripening of karma that is wholly bright is wholly bright; and the ripening of what is mixed is itself mixed. Therefore, monks, having abandoned karma that is wholly dark or mixed, strive exclusively for karma that is wholly bright. Monks, you should train accordingly."

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, those monks rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.

After King Śarva's son had died, a king who was fierce, radiant as the sun, and without rival came to rule as king in his place.

Then, at another time, he came up to the roof of a fine mansion and sat surrounded by a throng of ministers, and they spoke words that were not proper. They said: "O wise ones, in what town, city, or place is there a beautiful courtesan?"

The ministers replied: "O king, if you must know, there is a courtesan of beauty and youth who is skilled in the sixty-four arts, and there is no one on earth who, upon seeing her, would not instantly become enamored. There she is, constantly at the pleasure quarter."

King Rabhasa Prabhā, upon hearing of her beauty and youth, became instantly smitten and said: "Whatever care is taken, it is useless. I must go to take pleasure with a woman of that kind. Go to the pleasure quarter and take delight with her."

One of those present said: "O king, the one known as Lotus-Hearted has long been your enemy, your opponent, your adversary. He is always at the pleasure quarter. If you go there, he will certainly bring ruin upon you."

The king replied: "There may well be faint-hearted men among people, but you stay here. I shall go."

That one said: "If it is the king's pleasure, the king knows best — yet it would be wise to be careful."

But King Rabhasa Prabhā, being gripped by lust for the woman, did not heed those words. He mounted his finest elephant named Dambha and set out for the pleasure quarter. Proceeding along the way, he arrived at Sandal Wood Mountain, and there he left behind his finest elephant Dambha and proceeded on to the pleasure quarter. Then, removing from the neck of a young hill-man a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand, he went into the dwelling of the beautiful woman who lived by her form, and there he played with her, rejoiced with her, and took pleasure with her.

The brahmins and householders who dwelt in the noble realm of Āryā, wise men all, began to wonder where the king had gone since he was nowhere to be seen. Some of them said: "What is strange about this? He is simply somewhere out of sight and will appear again soon. He has not gone anywhere." Others said: "He has a great retinue of queens, so why would he come outside? He is taking his enjoyment and amusement privately within the queen's quarters." Some said: "Why doubt it? Come, let us go and inquire of the minister." Some said "Very well, let us do so," and so they all gathered together and went to the minister and asked: "Minister, where has the king gone, since he cannot be found?"

He replied: "Wise ones, you will see him before long."

They asked: "Minister, when will we see him?"

He said: "After twelve years have passed."

They grew angry and said: "Minister, you speak that way only because you surely intend to kill the king and seize the royal throne for yourself. Therefore, let us say this: if within seven days the king is found alive, then well and good; but if he is not, then we shall consecrate another as king."

With that, he said nothing but rested his cheek in his hand and sat sunk in thought. The mother of Balaṅkya, who was tending cattle nearby, heard this and called to him and asked: "Minister, why do you rest your cheek in your hand and sit sunk in thought?"

He replied: "O goddess, when the brahmins say such things to me, how could I not sit sunk in thought?"

She said: "Minister, if that is the case, go and place barley-flour mixed with butter and honey into a golden vessel and pour it in, and then —"

— place it before whichever horse-herder is familiar with horses, and say these words: 'Whatever horse eagerly goes to set down stones, let it eat of this, which has been mixed with butter and honey.' Do it in just that way, and whichever fine horse eats it, let me know." The minister did exactly as instructed, but not a single horse showed any eagerness to eat.

In another quarter there was a horse that was lean and bony, its body covered in sores, that ate dung, breathed with difficulty, and had a broken ear. The minister went to it, sat down before it, and said: "Whatever horse eagerly goes to set down stones, let it eat of this, which has been mixed with butter and honey." And that horse ate it all up.

The minister went back and told the mother of Balaṅkya, the cattle-tender, what had happened. She said to him: "Go, minister, and groom it. And if when you are grooming it the horse is unruly, do not be afraid — just summon your courage. No one can make a fool of one who has the strength of heart." He went and began to groom it, and as he was doing so, the horse transformed itself into a terrifying form and said: "Hey, you there — have you ever before seen a horse of this kind?" The minister drew his sword from its scabbard, pointed it, and said: "Hey, demon of a horse! Of all the riders you have carried, have you ever seen a whip like this?" The horse replied: "No, indeed, I have not seen that before." Then the minister said: "Hey, demon of a horse, if for now you will not be disobedient, well and good. But if you are, I shall cut off your head from the neck and throw it to the ground." The horse replied: "Hey, you there — if that is so, then swear that you will not bring me back here, and I will go." The minister said: "Excellent — I wish it to be so, done just like that." He mounted the horse and rode off, and in due course arrived at the land of setting-down-stones.

The fierce king Rab-snang saw him and said: "Has the minister come?" The minister replied: "Yes, Your Majesty, I have come." The king asked: "And for what purpose?" The minister then recounted everything that had happened. The king said: "Minister, for now take your ease for seven days, and when the seven days have passed, know that the time has come." With that, the minister spent seven days in good cheer and enjoyment together with a woman of gracious appearance who sustained him well. When the seven days had passed, he set out.

He went to a jungle hill and began to groom the great elephant, the chief bull of the herd. While he was grooming it, the elephant cried out. Not far away there lived a blind brahmin astrologer, who heard this, and said: "According to the cry of this great bull elephant, it will go from here and, traveling a hundred leagues to the south, will drink from the great ocean."

Then King Rab-snang and the minister mounted the great bull elephant of the jungle hill and rode off. Before long, in one place, the legs of the jungle-hill elephant crushed the unfired vessels of a potter who was sitting there, and the potter began to lament. The minister said: "Those who live at others' expense shall come to this." King Rab-snang, upon hearing this, thought: "The minister is mocking me with that. Does he think that I alone live at others' expense?" He thought this but said nothing and rode on.

Then in another place, the legs of the jungle-hill elephant broke the egg-filled nest of a dung beetle that had been built in the middle of the road, and that one too began to lament. The minister said: "Those who conduct themselves outside their proper domain shall come to this." King Rab-snang again felt a thought arise and considered: "Again the minister is mocking me. Does he think a prostitute is outside my proper domain?" He thought this but said nothing and rode on.

They descended further to a tree on the jungle hill, and —

a snake that was lurking in the branches of that tree struck and began to swallow King Rab-snang. After a moment the minister saw this, drew his sword from its scabbard, cut the snake into pieces, and threw it on the ground. As it writhed and convulsed, the minister watched and said: "Those who pursue what should not be pursued shall come to this." King Rab-snang, as before, felt a thought arise and considered: "Now for the third time he has mocked me. Does he think a prostitute is not what I should be pursuing?" He thought this but said nothing and rode on.

At another time, a hare of the jungle hill leapt across their path. The king tried to catch it but could not, and the minister said: "Your Majesty, a brahmin astrologer (jyotiṣa) has prophesied that this creature, after travelling a hundred leagues, will go and drink from the great ocean to the south. That is why it sprang quickly to grasp a tree branch — release the elephant, I say!" And with that, the creature swiftly seized a branch of the tree. The minister too grasped a branch of the tree, and so the jungle hill passed beneath them and was gone.

The king said to the minister: "Go and tell her quietly, without her noticing, that the god has come and is resting in the pleasure grove."

He went and told her this, and she was delighted and sat in silence without a word. The king also began to enter through a gap in the fence. Just then two girls came out to relieve themselves, and one of them said: "Friend, I hear the god has come!" The other replied: "He entered through a gap in the fence." The king heard this and thought: "I told the minister to tell her without her noticing, yet he has gone and told every soul in the house." Furious, he recalled everything the minister had done and began to seek a grievance against him.

"Minister! You have set yourself to harm me. Do I survive by my children alone? Why do you in one place mock me with the saying 'Those who are sustained by children shall come to this'? Is a prostitute not within my proper domain? And yet in another place you mock me with 'Those who act outside their proper domain shall come to this.' And is a prostitute not what I should be pursuing? And yet in still another place you mock me with 'Those who pursue what should not be pursued shall come to this.' And even now, while I sit here in the pleasure grove, I commanded you to go and tell her quietly, without her noticing, that the god has come and is resting in the pleasure grove — and you went and told every soul in the house! You have set yourself to harm me."

Suspicious and displeased, the minister spoke in order to be believed: "May I perish by my own wickedness if I have at any point mocked my lord the god. In what manner did I mock him? As for what my lord says — that in one great place I spoke the words 'Those who are sustained by children shall come to this' — in that direction some unfired pottery vessels of a potter were smashed by the legs of the jungle hill, and that potter began to grieve. From that I reflected and said: 'Those who are sustained by children shall come to this.' As for what my lord says — that in another great place I spoke the words 'Those who act outside their proper domain shall come to this' — in that direction the dung-beetle's nest filled with eggs was crushed by the legs of the jungle hill, and that creature too began to grieve.

From that I reflected and said: 'Those who act outside their proper domain shall come to this.' As for what my lord says — that in another great place you said to me, 'Those who pursue what is not worth pursuing shall come to this' — in that direction a snake was dwelling on the branch of a tree, and it reared up and began to devour a god. I then drew my sword from its scabbard, cut it into pieces, and it fell to the ground. From that I reflected and said: 'Those who pursue what is not worth pursuing shall come to this.'

As for your saying, 'Without my knowing it, arrange for me to be stationed in the pleasure grove of the gods at Śānti,' and that you then reported this to all the household — even in that, my lord, if I arranged it in complete secrecy, how could I have set about harming a god?

The king said: Physician, since you have answered every one of my charges well, you need not be distressed. Nevertheless, when I went to place the stone, there were certain brahmins who had begun to consecrate another man as king, and now is the time to destroy them. Let them be killed.

The physician said: My lord, let those brahmins be set aside for now. As for those spies, I shall have them put to death.

The king said: Physician, how can they be killed?

The god said: My lord, I will devise a means to entrap them.

The physician said: Very well, do so.

The physician then went to a certain young man in his entourage who was skilled in incantation and knowledgeable in spells, and said to him: These spy-women are killing many people — is there any method for catching them?

He replied: Father, what is to be done? I can catch them.

The son said: Excellent.

He then transformed something in a man's hand to look like a blue lotus flower, handed it to the man, and said: Go, fellow, go out to the marketplace and sit there. Whoever laughs upon seeing what is not bought for a price — ask that person's name and write it on a tablet.

The man took it, sat there, and for whoever saw it and did not buy it for a price but laughed — he asked that person's name and wrote it on the tablet. In this way he asked the names of five hundred spy-women of the noble king and wrote them down.

He then showed the list to the physician, and the physician in turn showed it to the king.

The king said: Physician, how shall all these many spy-women be dealt with?

The physician said: My lord, please ask me for the method by which those women are to be put to death, and set your mind at ease.

The king said: Physician, good — you yourself know it.

He then set up an enclosure on one side of the noble king's compound, and had it announced by proclamation: By the pledge of the mother of the gods, let all the she-demons dwelling in the noble king's realm gather in the courtyard of the enclosure.

And they thought:

"If we go to the pledge-gathering in the courtyard of the divine retinue's compound, they will give us many fine things" — thinking this, even those who had been staying hidden came forward out of greed for the reward and revealed themselves, and more than five hundred she-demons gathered in the courtyard of the compound.

Then the head herald's son bound them all with the noose of a spell, and the physician had their mouths covered and gagged. The king then summoned the brahmins dwelling in the noble realm and declared: "O wise ones, if this many spy-women are killed, great demerit will be incurred. Therefore, so that I may be freed from that wilderness of cyclic existence, assemble each day in the courtyard of the compound and eat your fill." And they, rejoicing and expressing their blessings, agreed to this.

The fierce king Radiant Light then commanded the herald: "O good man — every brahmin who has eaten their fill in the courtyard of the compound and then departs, you shall duly count them and report to me." The herald replied: "My lord, it shall be so. I beg to report as commanded." The king also commanded his ministers: "O wise ones, give abundant food to all the brahmins dwelling in the noble realm who come to eat in the courtyard of the compound, for brahmins are for the most part driven by their bellies" — and hearing that the king had ordered this done, they all came and set to eating.

When they had eaten and were leaving the courtyard of the compound, the herald counted them, and without exception eighty thousand brahmins had come out. He then reported to the king: "My lord, without lack or surplus, eighty thousand brahmins are present." The king then thought: "What method can be used to cut off all their heads at once?" And he commanded those who lived by the chopper's trade: "Behind each brahmin as he eats, station one executioner holding an unsheathed sword — and at the moment I say the word 'milk,' let all their heads be cut off at once."

The fierce king Radiant Light did exactly that. Of all the brahmins dwelling in the noble realm, the full eighty thousand who had gathered in the courtyard of the compound — those seized by the noose of the Lord of Death — were all beheaded at that moment by this device. Thus eighty thousand brahmins from among those dwelling in the noble realm were slain by King Radiant Light.

After he had slain them, that night as he lay in his great bedchamber, he heard in a dream six sounds from below the earth and six sounds from the sky, and he saw eight kinds of dream-visions.

What were the six sounds from below the earth? They were these: "six," "not," "self," "evil," "mind," "we, these ones here" — these are the opening syllables of six verses, as given below.

From "six," the verse runs:

For sixty thousand years,
and for six thousand hundreds —
the torment of beings burning in hell:
when will that ever reach its end?

From "not," the verse runs:

Boundless — where could any bound be seen?
Neither you nor I ourselves
shall ever come to perceive a bound.
Thus was this sinful deed done.

From "self," the verse runs:

We built up our wealth and goods
by means both favourable and foul.
Others take delight in that ease,
while we ourselves inherit only suffering.

From "evil," the verse runs:

The life we led here was wretched and vile.
What we possessed, we never gave away.
When wealth and goods were ours to enjoy,
we did no good for ourselves.

From "mind," the verse runs:

Deceived by mind,
and led astray by ignorance —
born now in hell among its beings,
who is there to blame but ourselves?

From "we, these here," the verse runs:

We, these here, went on to happy destinies,
performed many virtuous deeds,
and having thus accumulated merit,
those wholesome acts shall lead us to the higher realms.

As for the six sounds in the sky, they are as follows: "All," "Who," "Whatever," "Now," "Those," and "These" — these are the opening syllables of the six verses.

From "all," the verse runs:

All has been drawn out and spent,
and only the bare essence remains.
The king has grown miserly with even that essence,
and, finding no joy in it, has abandoned hope.

From "who," the verse runs:

Whoever, by foul and dishonest means,
might contrive to obtain even a single eye —
by that very act, such a one
would deliver my children and myself from suffering.

From "whatever," the verse runs:

In this pond, from its many
fish and turtles that fill it,
frogs may well make their living now,
but I shall not abandon my home.

From "now," the verse runs:

Those blind afflictions (kleśas) that trampled me underfoot
upon the savage mountain —
they are now without any protector.

From "those," the verse runs:

From that fine lake, cool
and sweet waters
will be found with ease.
I, for my part, am glad to be there now.

From "these," the verse runs:

These ones, having bathed and eaten,
go wandering from place to place,
while I, seized by a net,
wonder what evil deed I committed in the past.

Now, what are the eight dreams? They are as follows: his body anointed with white sandalwood; red sandalwood scattered over him; fire blazing upon his head; two snakes hanging from both armpits; two fish licking both feet; two geese flying up into the sky; a dark mountain approaching from in front; and clusters of foam swirling and dispersing upon his head.

He awoke from that sleep in a state of terror, alarmed and with his hair standing on end, and he thought: "Surely, on account of this, I shall not lose the kingdom, nor shall my life be cut short." He then summoned those brahmins who were versed in the interpretation of dreams, and related the dreams to them. They deliberated among themselves and concluded: "Although the god has seen favorable signs in these dreams, they ought not to be praised. For if they are praised and this turns out badly, it will bring ruin to whatever brahmins remain, leaving not one of them behind." Having reached this judgment, they spoke: "O God, your dreams are not auspicious."

He replied: "Wise ones, what will come of them?"

They said: "On this account, O God, you will either lose the kingdom or your life will be cut short."

The king said: "Wise ones, is there any means by which I shall neither lose the kingdom nor have my life cut short?"

They replied: "O God, you have committed a great evil — you caused the slaying of eighty thousand brahmins. On account of that, if you act accordingly, there is one means."

When he heard of the killing of the brahmins, his heart trembled throughout, and he said: "Wise ones, tell me what must be done."

They replied: "O God, have a pond dug in the pleasure garden, and once it is dug, grant it with a lining of powdered stone. Then have the five finest limbs nourished there, along with a chanter, an unweaned mother cow, a freed brahmin girl, and young cowherd boys — have them slaughtered and placed within it. Bathe in their blood; then emerge from the pond, press both knees to the ground, lick the feet of the brahmins — and by doing so, you shall not lose the kingdom,

and it shall not become an obstacle to your life." The king reflected: "If I slaughter the five finest limbs I have nourished, and the chanter, and the unweaned mother cow, and the freed brahmin girl, and the young cowherd boys, what will be the use of my remaining king?" With that thought, he spoke to the brahmins: "Wise ones, I have heard what you have said. Give me a little time, for I must think before I act." The brahmins departed, and the king sat with his arms resting on his knees, sunken in his own thoughts. The unweaned mother cow saw him there and said: "O God, why do you sit with your arms on your knees, lost in thought?" He told her everything that had come to pass, and she replied: "O God, those brahmins are always in the habit of giving improper counsel — what could they know? Go instead and present your question to the great noble one, the son of Kātyāyanī." He said: "Excellent, excellent, O Peaceful One! You have pointed me in time to the great noble one, the son of Kātyāyanī — I shall go." And so he went to where the venerable one, the son of Kātyāyanī, was staying. Having arrived, he bowed his head to the feet of the great venerable son of Kātyāyanī and sat to one side.

Sitting to one side, the fierce king Suprakaśa spoke these words to the great venerable son of Kātyāyanī: "Master, great son of Kātyāyanī — last night, as I lay in my great bed, I heard in a dream six sounds from the earth below and six sounds from the sky above, and I saw eight dreams. What were the six sounds from the earth? They were these: 'Six,' 'Not,' 'Self,' 'Evil,' 'Mind,' 'We these.' These are the first syllables of six verses. And the verse beginning with 'Six' runs:

For sixty thousand years,
and for six thousand centuries,
beings tormented in the hells —
when will they ever reach the end?

The verse beginning with 'Not' runs:

Without end — how could there be a view of an end?
Neither you nor I myself
shall ever come to perceive that end.
Thus has this evil karma been done.

The verse beginning with 'Self' runs:

We pursued our pleasures
by every favorable and unfavorable means;
others rejoice and delight in happiness,
while we have become the heirs of suffering.

The verse beginning with 'Evil' runs:

Here our livelihood was wretched;
we did not give away what we possessed.
Though we had wealth and riches,
we did no good for ourselves.

The verse beginning with 'Mind' runs:

Deceived by the mind,
bound by ignorance —
for those who are born in the hells,
who will be their protector?

The verse beginning with 'We these' runs:

We these ones went to a happy destiny,
performed many virtuous deeds,
then made merit,
and those who did what was auspicious went to the higher realms.

And what were the six sounds from the sky? They were these: 'All,' 'Who,' 'Whatever,' 'Now then,' 'Those ones,' 'These here.' These are the first syllables of six verses. The verse beginning with 'All' runs:

All has been drawn out and spent;
only the bare essence remains.
The king, grudging even that essence,
has abandoned hope through joylessness.

The verse beginning with 'Who' runs:

Whoever with wicked ways of grasping
would gain even a single eye —
by that one, both my sons and grandsons
and I myself have been freed from suffering.

The verse beginning with 'Whatever' runs:

This pond, though it be filled
with many fish and turtles,
I shall live on frogs for now,
but I shall not abandon my dwelling.

The verse beginning with 'Now then' runs:

The verse beginning with 'Now then' runs:

Those blind ones who, on the fierce mountain,
trample me underfoot with their feet —
those very ones shall now
be left without a protector.

The verse beginning with 'Those' runs:

From this fine lake, those ones
shall find cool and sweet water
easily obtained —
and I too rejoice in that now.

The verse beginning with 'These' runs:

These ones, having bathed and eaten,
go off in every direction.
I, caught in a snare —
what evil did I do before?

Now, what are the eight dreams? They are as follows. He anointed his body with white sandalwood; he was sprinkled with red sandalwood; fire blazed on his head; from both armpits hung two snakes; two fish licked both his feet; two geese flew up into the sky; a black mountain approached from the front; and he saw a mass of frogs scattering at the blows of otters upon his head. He woke from sleep in terror, overcome with anxiety, his hair standing on end, and he thought: "I wonder whether, on account of these signs, I shall lose my kingdom or meet with an obstacle to my very life." He thought: "If I were to present this matter to the great noble Kātyāyana, I wonder whether he would know whether, on account of these signs, I shall lose my kingdom or meet with an obstacle to my very life."

The venerable great Kātyāyana said: "Great King, have you related these sounds and these dreams to any other person?" He replied: "Noble one, I have related them." "To whom?" "To the brahmins." "And what did they foretell for you? Relate in full what transpired." He replied: "Great King, those brahmins always delight in sensual pleasure and desire a divine world — what do they know? You have heard some good sounds and seen some good dreams. Do not be afraid! On account of these signs, you shall not lose your kingdom, nor shall any obstacle come to your life."

"Why is that so? Great King, as for the six sounds from below the earth that you heard in your dream — what are they an omen of? Six kings before you, having ruled their kingdom by both Dharma and non-Dharma, passed away from their bodies and were reborn among the beings of the hells."

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya. The twenty-ninth fascicle.

Now, one of those beings, oppressed by the suffering of hell, uttered this verse:

For sixty thousand years,
for six thousand years,
those tormented in the hells —
when at last will any of them reach the end?

The second spoke this verse:

A limitless limit — where could such a boundary be?
Neither you nor I together
shall ever come to perceive any end.
Such is the evil karma we have made.

The third spoke this verse:

The wealth we gathered
through both harmony and discord —
others rejoice in it with pleasure,
while we have become heirs to suffering.

The fourth spoke this verse:

Here, where our lives are wretched,
we gave away nothing of what we had.
When wealth was still there,
we brought no benefit even to ourselves.

The fifth spoke this verse:

Deceived by mind,
led astray by ignorance —
for those born into the hells,
who is there to be their protector?

The sixth spoke this verse:

Let us, once gone to a happy destiny,
perform many virtuous acts,
and then, having made merit
and done what is auspicious, go to the higher realms.

These, then, are the omens of those sounds.

Great King, you ask of whose omen are the six sounds you heard from the sky. There is a woodworm living in the ridgepole of your house. It has eaten away everything that is not the heartwood, leaving only a little heartwood remaining. Displeased with its situation there, it spoke this verse:

All the sapwood has been hollowed out and taken;
only a little heartwood is left.
O King, the worm, finding no joy
in the heartwood, has abandoned hope.

That was the first sound from the sky. Therefore you should remove that beam and replace it with another.

Great King, there is also this: your horse-keeper, the one called Gnyerlen, went to the nest of a crow, and when eggs appeared he smashed them. Because of this the crow was separated from her young and became distressed. Crying out in grief with a sound of lamentation, she slowly spoke this verse:

Whoever, with wicked and dishonest ways,
procures even a single eye's worth —
by that one, both my children
and I myself have been freed from suffering.

That was the second sound from the sky. Do not have him punished.

Furthermore, there is in your home a pleasant ornamental pond, one that was full to the brim with water just at the depth a crow could drink from, and in which many fish, tortoises, and frogs lived. A single otter was there eating the fish, and now it has dried up and become waterless. The otter, seeing things come to this pass, was displeased and spoke this verse:

This pond was once filled
with many fish and tortoises.
Now I may yet live on frogs,
but I will not abandon this place.

That was the third sound from the sky. Have that pond refilled with water.

Furthermore, in your realm there is a mountain called Tumldän. On it there lived a bull elephant and a blind cow elephant. These two had a single calf, which tended to their needs. When it went out to find food for the two of them, it joined up with another cow elephant. You had it lured away by a stratagem and brought back and kept tethered. It grieved for its mother and father, refused to eat grass or drink water, and thinking of them with sorrow and displeasure, it spoke this verse:

Those blind and afflicted ones on the mountain Tumldän,
who once fed at my feet —
they are now left without a protector.

That was the fourth sound from the sky. It is wrong that the one who cared for its parents should perish. Release it.

Furthermore, there is a deer that has been caught and is kept in your home. Separated from its herd, it remembered the deer of the forest wilderness and spoke this verse:

From a good lake there,
the water is cool and sweet
and easily found.
Even now I rejoice to think of that place.

That was the fifth sound from the sky. Release it.

Furthermore, there are some geese that have been caught and are kept in your home. Seeing the geese flying through the sky, they were displeased and spoke this verse:

These others, having bathed and fed,
go wherever they will, in every direction.
I am caught in a trap —
what evil did I do in the past?

That was the sixth sound from the sky. You should release those as well. These are the omens of those sounds.

Great King, you ask what foretoken the eight dreams you saw represent.

As for what you saw — your body anointed with white sandalwood — a great fine bolt of cotton cloth is on its way to you as a gift from the king of the northern continent, and it will arrive within seven days. Your first dream was the foretoken of that.

As for what you saw — red sandalwood scattered over your body — a precious cow is on its way to you as a gift from the king who holds your treasury lands, and it too will arrive within seven days. Your second dream was the foretoken of that.

As for what you saw — fire blazing on your head — a golden garland is on its way to you as a gift from the king of the land of Yavana, and it too will arrive within seven days. Your third dream was the foretoken of that.

As for what you saw — two snakes hanging from both your armpits — a pair of swords is on its way to you as a gift from the king of China, and it too will arrive within seven days. Your fourth dream was the foretoken of that.

As for what you saw — two fish licking both your feet — a pair of jeweled shoes is on its way to you as a gift from the king of Siṃhala, and it too will arrive within seven days. Your fifth dream was the foretoken of that.

As for what you saw — two geese flying through the sky — a pair of horses is on its way to you as a gift from the king of Vaṅgāla, and it too will arrive within seven days. Your sixth dream was the foretoken of that.

As for what you saw — a black mountain coming toward you from the front — a chief elephant is on its way to you as a gift from the king of Kaliṅga, and it too will arrive within seven days. Your seventh dream was the foretoken of that.

As for what you saw — crabs scattering about with their heads broken open — this means that you will come to learn of the death of Gopālā's mother. You must not give rise to ill thoughts even toward the brahmins.

When these words were spoken, King Radiant Light felt joy, delight, elation, gladness, ease, and mental happiness, as though he had regained his life after losing it. Rejoicing in what the venerable great son of Kātyāyana had explained, he bowed his head to his feet, rose from his seat, and departed.

He went to his own home and carried out everything exactly as the venerable great son of Kātyāyana had said: he installed a different person in the funeral litter, he did not allow the horse-keeper to go on tending the horses as before, he filled the pond again with water, and he released the elephants, the deer, and the geese.

Seven days later, all the gifts that had been foretold arrived, and finding himself thus enriched he was filled with mental happiness. He developed deep and open faith toward the venerable great son of Kātyāyana and thought to himself: whatever wealth, power, and prosperity exist in my home, all of it has come about through reliance on the noble great son of Kātyāyana. Therefore I shall first send him this great fine bolt of cotton cloth, and afterward I shall offer him the kingdom.

With that thought he spoke to a man: "Here, friend — take this great fine bolt of cotton cloth and present it to the noble great son of Kātyāyana." The man took the great fine bolt of cotton cloth and gave it to the noble great son of Kātyāyana.

Then Gopālā's mother passed away. And he spoke to the daughter of the śramaṇa woman, Tārā, to the young Gopāla, to the attendant, and to the one leading in front:

"Wise ones, the kings who hold sway over many lands have sent these gifts to me. Take them as you each desire."

Then Gopālā's mother, Śivā, took the golden garland; the daughter of the śramaṇa woman, Tārā, took the precious coral; the young Gopāla took the two horses; the attendant took a pair of swords; the one leading in front took a pair of jeweled shoes; and the chief of the elephants that remained was taken by the king.

Then King Pradyota, having distributed among the five foremost attendants all the precious things, went to where the venerable great son of Kātyāyana was, and having arrived he prostrated with his head at the venerable great son of Kātyāyana's feet and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Pradyota spoke to the venerable great son of Kātyāyana thus:

"Noble one, you are a healer and one who holds dear. Therefore I pray that out of affection you would accept the royal domain and exercise it — please receive the kingdom."

The venerable great son of Kātyāyana replied: "Great king, the Blessed One has prohibited monks from ruling a kingdom."

The king said: "Noble one, if that is so, then please fully enjoy every sensual pleasure I can offer."

He replied: "Great king, the Blessed One has also prohibited every sensual pleasure."

The king said: "Noble one, if that is the case, then please accept and fully enjoy material wealth and the finest material provisions that I can offer."

He replied: "Great king, let me first put this to the Blessed One and then act accordingly."

The king said: "Noble one, please do so."

At that time the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now at such a moment as this, the awakened Blessed Ones possess not the slightest unknowing, not the slightest unseeing, not the slightest unawareness, not the slightest non-discernment. The Blessed One perceived: "The monk, the great son of Kātyāyana, does not seek material wealth and the finest material provisions for his own sake; yet he does this intending to benefit beings of future generations." With that intention he gave rise to a worldly thought.

By the nature of reality, at the very moment the awakened Blessed Ones give rise to a worldly thought, even living creatures such as ants know it through the Blessed One's mind. When he gives rise to a supramundane thought, even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know it through the Blessed One's mind — so what need is there to speak of those reborn in animal destinies? In this matter, what arose was a worldly thought corresponding to and meeting the minds of both the Blessed One and the venerable great son of Kātyāyana.

Then the Blessed One and the venerable great son of Kātyāyana each actualized the divine eye and divine ear and thereby entered into mutual seeing and hearing.

Then the venerable great son of Kātyāyana addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend One, is it permissible for a monk to accept material wealth and the finest material provisions on behalf of the Saṅgha?"

The Blessed One declared: "Great son of Kātyāyana, for the sake of compassion toward beings of future generations and in order to increase the wealth of donors — it is permissible. Therefore material wealth and the finest material provisions may be given to the Saṅgha, but not to individual persons. Of these, 'material wealth' refers to villages and fields; 'the finest material provisions' refers to cattle, water buffalo, goats, and sheep."

Then the venerable great son of Kātyāyana, having put this to the Blessed One, spoke to King Pradyota thus:

"Great King, the Blessed One, out of compassion for beings of future generations and in order to increase the wealth of donors, has granted material wealth and the finest material provisions to the Saṅgha."

Thereupon King Pradyota, taking his lead from the venerable great son of Kātyāyana, had a temple built fully equipped with all furnishings, and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions; and he offered material wealth and the finest material provisions as well.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "O monks, among my lay devotees, among those who first gave all desired things to my śrāvaka Saṅgha, the foremost is this very one: the noble king Pradyota. O monks, among my lay devotees, among those who first offered cooked food to my śrāvaka Saṅgha, the foremost is this: Bimbisāra, the artisan-king of Rājagṛha. O monks, among my lay devotees, among those who first offered lodgings to my śrāvaka Saṅgha, the foremost is this: Anāthapiṇḍada, the householder of Śrāvastī. O monks, among my lay devotees, among those who first built a temple for my śrāvaka Saṅgha, the foremost is this: Supriya, the householder of Vārāṇasī."

A summary verse:

Pradyota, the supreme illuminator of all desires,
Bimbisāra, the artisan, the cook for the Saṅgha,
Anāthapiṇḍada, the lodging-giver and feeder of the shelterless,
And Supriya, the excellent one of the temple.

Now King Pradyota, among his queens' retinue, took his meals in turns: on one day in the presence of the cowherd woman Śāntā, and on another in the presence of Tārā, daughter of the wandering ascetic.

Then on another occasion, while he was eating in the presence of the cowherd woman Śāntā, the king, fond of curds, was holding a bowl of curds from Śāntā's herd and was sitting before the meal. Just then Tārā, daughter of the wandering ascetic, came from that direction; she was wearing a jeweled necklace, and at her arrival there appeared, as if a flash of lightning had burst forth, a radiance illuminating the king together with the cowherd woman Śāntā.

Śāntā, seeing that radiance, was astonished and said: "My lord, what is this? Has a bolt of lightning suddenly appeared, or has someone lit a flame?" She replied: "This radiance is neither the light of lightning nor the light of a lamp; rather, it was Tārā, daughter of the wandering ascetic, who came from that direction, and she was wearing a jeweled necklace — this is the light of that."

"You were foolish to give away such a precious jeweled necklace and take a gold garland in its place. Is there no gold garland in my house? Or is this how one born of a low lineage behaves? How disgraceful."

She replied: "My lady, how could she have had such wisdom? Without any doubt it was you yourself who showed her, saying 'accept the precious necklace,' and that is why she took it."

The king said: "I did not tell her that — she took it of her own accord."

"You said it."

"I did not say it."

The two fell to quarreling, whereupon Śāntā struck her on the head with the bowl of curds. The king, his crown altogether shattered, had his skull cracked open. She touched it with her hand and thought: "My skull is also cracked; my brains are also seeping out — she has already killed me. So long as I have life, I shall kill this woman." Having resolved on this, she gave an order to her attendant: "Attendant, go and kill the cowherd woman Śāntā once and for all."

The attendant thought: "She has been so terribly wronged that, being completely overcome with fury, she is saying this much — but I must not kill immediately. Once she has cooled from that state of being overwhelmed, I must understand what she truly intends; then, perhaps, the killing may proceed. For now let me place her somewhere secluded." Thus reasoning, he said:

"Indeed, Your Majesty, I sought her out and killed her." So saying, he placed her in a secluded spot.

When the king had recovered from his state of being utterly beside himself, he spoke: "Attendant, what of Śāntā, the cowherd woman?"

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, you yourself commanded me, saying, 'I bid you send Śāntā the cowherd woman away and have her killed.' And so I killed her in accordance with Your Majesty's command."

The king said: "Attendant, well done. Now then — I, and Tārā the daughter of the weaver, and the young Gopāla, and even the herald too shall go, and you yourself, having bound on a crown, shall take the royal throne and rule. As for that woman — because she showed me disrespect, I thought to press her down hard and afterwards be glad of it; but you have killed her outright in an instant."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, there is a meaning conveyed by the words of certain wise men here — a meaning that even through example becomes fully apparent. Please therefore first hear the example. It is summarised thus:

A hawk and a heron,
something hard to obtain, and deception,
insatiability, and one overcome by sleep —
these are properly gathered in a concise summary.

The summary itself:

Hawks and monkeys in this world
and the blind — these are the last.

In former times there was a great king. On a mountain slope, remote from human habitation and free of danger, adorned with a forest of various trees, roamed lions, tigers, bears, cats, deer, and wild boars. The place was attended by many kinds of flocks of birds. In one particular spot, a living creature called a thī-ba had made its nest in a great tree. It filled the nest with ripe fruits and said to its mate: 'Dear one, you must not eat these fruits. For now, sustain yourself on whatever else is at hand. When the wind blows hard and adverse conditions arise, then these are to be eaten.'

The mate replied: 'Good — so it shall be.'

In time, the fruits dried out from the wind and the sun, and the nest became cramped. Then the thī-ba said: 'Dear one, did I not forbid you, saying you must not eat these fruits, that you should eat them only when wind blows or adversity comes? Then why have you eaten them?'

The mate replied: 'I have not eaten them.'

The thī-ba said: 'I filled this nest and left it so. If you did not eat them, then why has this nest become cramped?'

The mate replied: 'I do not know why the nest is cramped. I have not eaten a single one of the fruits from it.'

As they went back and forth, each saying 'You ate them' and 'I did not eat them,' a quarrel broke out, and the thī-ba seized his mate by the beak, took her life, and she hung there dead in that very spot.

After some time had passed, a great unseasonable rain fell, and the nest filled up again, just as before, with those same fruits. The thī-ba then thought: 'This nest is full of fruits again — and so she did not eat them.' He began to beg her forgiveness:

'Beautiful spotted one, forgive me —
you did not eat these things,
yet for some wrong done to my nest
I beg you, please forgive.'

Then the god spoke these verses:

The thī-ba who roams the forest,
with dappled wings and red eyes,
killed the very one he loved,
then in his dull mind grieves — to what end?

Just as the thī-ba, acting rashly,
killed here his beloved, faultless one,
then in dull bewilderment mourns her, calling her 'dear' —
so he approaches her and begs her to forgive his wrong.

Just so the king, acting carelessly,
killed here Śāntā who was pleasing to his heart,
then in dull bewilderment mourns her, calling her 'dear' —
so he approaches her and begs her to forgive his wrong.

This is what I have to say, Your Majesty. I think the meaning you have spoken corresponds to exactly this example."

The attendant continued: "Furthermore, Your Majesty, there was a householder who, when summer had passed and the season of autumn had come, gathered up a load of pulses and set out for his field."

He set down his load of pulses at the foot of a tree and went aside to relieve himself. Just then a monkey came down from that tree, took a double handful of pulses, and climbed back up. As it was climbing, a single pulse fell and dropped to the ground. The monkey thereupon cast away the whole double handful of pulses it was holding and began searching for that single pulse. Seeing this, the householder took a stick and struck it, and at that moment a deity spoke this verse:

Who throws away a double handful
to search for a single grain —
this monkey, so richly endowed with company,
is foolish indeed. What a pity!

The attendant then said: "This, Your Majesty, is what the deity declared. And the meaning the deity spoke — that he who killed the cowherd's mother and then wishes to beg her forgiveness — I believe corresponds exactly to that example."

The king said: "Attendant, with a single word alone you have killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

The Teacher, a person without equal,
speaks but one word, and one word only.
Since what he speaks is certain truth,
my mind in this cannot change."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have made me blind."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

In this world, together with its gods and humans,
two kinds of blind are held for certain:
those who are blind by nature from birth,
and those who do not abide in the Dharma.

And in both this world and the next,
there are yet two more who are blind:
one in whom a sinful view is present,
and one who does not rely upon the law."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have made me desolate."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard the verse on the three kinds of desolation?

A river without water is desolate.
A city or district without travelers is desolate.
Even if a woman has ten brothers,
without a husband she is desolate."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have made me good for nothing whatsoever."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard that there are three things in the world that are good for nothing whatsoever?"

The king said: "Attendant, what are those three?"

The attendant replied:

"A white-ashed horse presented as tribute,
a festival held with no one there,
a woman who brings ruin to her household —
these three are good for nothing whatsoever."

The king said: "Attendant, you killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, without having made use of her."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Clothes used for wiping soot,
shoes used for cleaning and washing,
and the retinue of a king's queen —
all go to waste without being enjoyed.

And those are not the only three, Your Majesty — there are three more:

The blossoms of a forest tree,
the youth of one who lives in austerity,
and the wives of chariot-masters —
all go to waste without being enjoyed."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you deserve to be beaten with a club."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

A carpenter who makes rough joints,
a tailor who cuts his thread too long,
a charioteer who is short of sight —
these three deserve to be beaten with a club.

And those are not the only three, Your Majesty — there are three more:

A messenger who plays the go-between,
an envoy who is employed as a spy,
and a woman who acts as a seductress —
these three deserve to be beaten with a club."

And those are not the only three — there are three more:

A cowherd who wanders through the village,
a woodcutter who roams through the forest,
and a son-in-law who is forever coming to visit —
these three deserve to be beaten with a club.

The king said: "Attendant, you killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, with a single blow."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

A king speaks once and that is final,
a daughter is given in marriage once and that is final,
