and the sight of a noble one is granted once and that is final —
these three each happen but once."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have brought sickness upon yourself."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

One who wears armour of many different kinds,
a herdsman with a short rope but many cattle,
and an old man who takes a young wife —
these are they who have brought sickness upon themselves."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have shamed me."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

One who chatters and babbles without end,
another who wears shabby, wretched clothing,
and one who eats by stealing and scrounging —
these three are worthy of contempt and shame."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have set an enemy upon me by means of a net."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Fish are to be caught with a net,
mountains are to be climbed with a net of ropes,
and all one's aims are to be accomplished by one's network —
these three are to be done, net by net, through connections."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are a child."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Placing trust in one who is unfamiliar,
relying on one who is unsuitable,
and abandoning everything in a fit of doubt —
these are the three defining marks of a child."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are one who drives away friends."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Not spending time with one's friends at all,
or on the other hand clinging to them far too much,
and asking favours of them at the wrong time —
by these things one drives friends away."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are a base person."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Always coveting the wealth of others,
stirring up trouble for one's own desires,
and likewise taking delight in others' suffering —
these three are the marks of a base person."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are to be executed by the wheel of a chariot."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

A painter who does not know how to apply colours,
a mechanic who does not know how to fix the axle,
and a wrestler's son who does not know how to throw his opponent —
for one who is to slay, there is always the means to do it without fail."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are a deceiver."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

A woman who has passed through three husbands,
a monk who has come back from outside,
and a bird that has escaped from a trap — these three:
among deceivers, that last is the most devious of all."

In summary:

What is hard to obtain, what is distinct, and what is singular,
what is accumulated, and likewise what is discordant —

what is beaten, what is absent, and what is discordant — these are without purpose.

The attendant said: "Your Majesty, you have killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā — the one that was hard to obtain."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

A horned rabbit is hard to find,
a feathered tortoise is hard to find,
a courtesan who sits alone,
and a miser who speaks straight — these are hard to find."

The king said: "Attendant, you killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, for someone else's sake."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

One who accepts what is forced upon him, a guarantor,
and the four great ones among the treacherous —
a fool who flatters: these four
are unfit for another's purposes."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have left me alone."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

At birth, one is born into this alone.
Likewise at death, one dies in this alone.
It is as a lone person that one experiences suffering here.
In saṃsāra, there is no companion."

The king said: "Attendant, you killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā — she who had accumulated stores."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Fish eggs and mango blossoms,
the striving of one whose aim has turned to sorrow —
like an autumn cloud, for example:
even what has been accumulated comes to nothing."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have become one who is discordant."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

The sun is discordant with shadow,
light is discordant with darkness,
day is discordant with night —
Dharma and what is not Dharma are always discordant."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you deserve to be beaten."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Garments, when beaten, become soft.
Donkeys, when beaten, become swift.
Women, when beaten, come under control.
Drums, if not beaten, will not make a sound."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you deserve to be destroyed."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Wind destroys bubbles.
The sound of a crowd destroys a song in just the same way.
Keeping company with a bad person,
and ugliness — these destroy virtue."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are not fitting."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

A king who speaks falsely,
a physician who speaks out of turn, a renunciant who quarrels,
and a wise man who is utterly confused —
these four are not fitting."

The king said: "Attendant, you killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, for no purpose."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this verse?

Lighting a lamp in daytime is without purpose.
Rain falling on the ocean is without purpose.
Giving a feast to one who is sated is without purpose.
Keeping company with a bad person is without purpose."

In summary:

Deceiving, watching, wrongdoing, expulsion,
fear, sending away in disgust,
craving, acting without thought, grief and its attendants —
these were properly proclaimed to the assembly.

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are a deceiver."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard that there are four kinds of deceivers? What are the four?

Instructing one who does not wish to learn,
explaining to one wearied by sleep,
seeking a purpose from one who seeks no purpose,
and dividing what belongs to the powerful —
these are the four."

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you deserve to be watched."

The attendant replied:

"Your Majesty, have you not heard:

On the field of battle, watch the hero;
for unbearable poison, watch the mantra;
at the time of eating and drinking, watch the kinsman;
and to grasp the meaning, watch the wise.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have done wrong."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

A householder who is lazy — that is wrong.
One gone forth who holds no proper vow — that is wrong.
A king who behaves negligently — that is wrong.
And a scholar who sows discord — that too is wrong.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are to be expelled."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

An unskilled driver breaks the cart.
Overloading with a heavy load kills the ox.
Nursing too eagerly kills the calf.
Staying too long in a relative's home drives away the young wife.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you fill me with dread whenever I see you."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

There is the wasp, and the water-blister,
third, the silk-cloth moth,
and fourth, the wet leather shoe —
these make one dread what is not truly dreadful.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, the absence of the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, displeases me."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

A monkey is displeased in the village.
The crocodile that kills children is displeased in the mountains.
The thief is displeased in the house of the ascetic.
And the mouse is displeased in its own home.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are to be dismissed."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

For the sake of a clan, one individual is dismissed.
For the sake of a village, a clan is dismissed.
For the sake of a realm, a village is dismissed.
And for one's own sake, a realm is dismissed.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, my craving cannot be cut."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

One who has no root, and another man's wife,
drinking water with only one hand,
and wine poured by another —
these are things whose craving cannot be cut.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, you killed the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, without having given it any thought."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

A king who gives no thought to the royal treasury,
one who sets out on a road without thinking of bandits,
a woman at the hearth who gives no thought to fire,
and one gone forth who gives no thought to material gain —

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are a cause for grief."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

An aged person of attachment — cause for grief.
A woman who has not become good — cause for grief.
An aged courtesan — cause for grief.
And a violent one who has gone forth — cause for grief.

As a summary verse:

One who is never satisfied by looking, one who seems agreeable in mind,
one whom it is wrong to cherish, and wealth,
one whom it is wrong to speak to, one full of hatred,
a friend without protection — these are to be relied upon by the resolute.

The king said: "Attendant, you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā — one who was never satisfied by looking."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

The lord of elephants, and a king,
the ocean, and Mount Meru,
and a buddha — the highest of all speakers —
these are things that are never satisfied by looking.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā — one who was agreeable to my mind."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard:

A woman of beautiful form, of good lineage,
who brings pleasure and extends the family line,
in the prime of youth — these five qualities
make a woman agreeable to a great king's mind.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, by killing the cowherd's mother, Śāntā, I shall not play together with you."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

A child, a snake, a frog,
a woman of loose conduct,
and a friend whose love is impermanent —
these are not things to play with.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you have stolen my wealth."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

Musicians, soldiers,
physicians, thieves, and herdsmen —
these will take a person's wealth
even when that person is in a weakened state.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are not fit to be spoken to."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

One who is far too rich and one who is far too poor,
one who is lowly and one who is far too exalted,
one who is far too distant and one who is far too near —
these six are said not to be fit to speak with.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, I bear you deep enmity."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

One who gives without being seen to do so, who acts in opposition,
who fails to act in accord and broadcasts one's faults,
and who, having given, gradually takes back what was given —
these are the signs of one who bears deep enmity.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, I have been left without a protector."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

A senior monk, an aged king,
one whose counsel is improper and brings no ease,
and one who harms one's teacher —
these six are said to be without a protector.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are not fit to be befriended."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

A jester, a dancer,
a messenger, a prostitute, one addicted to alcohol,
a eunuch, and likewise one of wicked disposition —
with these one should not make friends.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, you are not to be trusted."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

Water that ebbs by only a neck's breadth, a horse,
an elephant, a monkey, a black snake,
one whose hair stands on end, one whose brow is furrowed,
and one with sparse facial hair — in these one should place no trust.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

Now in summary:

Sleeplessness, unwished-for things,
a mind tormented from all sides, material things,
and likewise compassion, the crow,
and finally, strength — these are the means of repelling.

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, I cannot sleep."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard this:

Wanton conduct, illness from emaciation,
being struck by cold sickness, suffering,
a troubled mind intent on gain, exertion,
and fear — in all these forms,

sleep does not come. In this world
these eight are by their very nature suffering.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, I am in a state of unwished-for things."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard of the eight unwished-for things? What are these eight?

Illness, old age, and death,
separation from the pleasant, meeting with the unpleasant,
hail, lightning, and impermanence —
these eight are what the world wishes for least of all.

Has your Majesty not heard this?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed my cowherd's mother, Śāntā, a mind tormented from all sides has arisen in me toward you."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard of the nine things that subdue a tormented mind? What are these nine, Your Majesty?

One thinks: 'This person wishes to harm me, does not wish me benefit, does not wish me happiness, does not wish me comfort, does not wish me success and well-being — this one has done, is doing, and will do what I wished against me.' And then one thinks further:

'How could it ever come to pass that, just as this has befallen me through another, I should bring about exactly the same to that other — for that would be wrong?' And thinking thus, one dispels the tormented mind that has arisen toward that person.

This is the case of one who wishes to harm me, does not wish me benefit, does not wish me happiness, does not wish me comfort, does not wish me success and well-being — one who wishes harm to that person, does not wish benefit, does not wish happiness, does not wish comfort, does not wish success and well-being; one who has done, is doing, and will do harm to that person. And yet one thinks:

'How could it ever come to pass that, just as this has befallen me through another, I should bring about exactly the same to that other — for that would be wrong?' And thinking thus, one dispels the tormented mind that has arisen toward that person.

This is the case of one who wishes to harm me, does not wish me benefit, does not wish me happiness, does not wish me comfort, does not wish me success and well-being — yet who wishes that other person well, wishes them benefit, wishes them happiness, wishes them comfort, wishes them success and well-being; one who has done, is doing, and will do good to that person. And yet one thinks:

'How could it ever come to pass that, just as this has befallen me through another, I should bring about exactly the same to that other — for that would be wrong?' And thinking thus, one dispels the tormented mind that has arisen toward that person.

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed Śāntā, the cowherd's mother, you are without compassion."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard of the ten who are without compassion — the butcher, the poultry-seller, the pig-seller, the fisherman, the deer-hunter, the fowler, the rabbit-snarer, the thief, the executioner, and the slaughterer of cattle?"

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed Śāntā, the cowherd's mother, you are like a crow."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard it said that one who possesses ten qualities is like a crow? What are these ten? Your Majesty: one who snatches, one who speaks harshly, one who breaks things off abruptly, one who steals, one who is ungrateful, one who is without compassion, one who takes what is not given, one who hoards, one who is hard to satisfy, and one who is dissolute."

The king said: "Attendant, because you killed Śāntā, the cowherd's mother, you are one who turns things away."

The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, have you not heard it said that there are ten who turn things away? What are these ten? Your Majesty: the sun, which turns things away; the moon, which turns things away; fire, which turns things away; water, which turns things away; a young woman, who turns things away; a wife, who turns things away; a brahmin, who turns things away; a naked ascetic, who turns things away; a monk, who turns things away; and fallow ground, which turns things away.

As for the sun being one who turns things away: when the sun comes in winter it does not bring warmth, yet when it comes from a great distance in summer it does bring warmth — this is why the sun is called one who turns things away.

As for the moon being one who turns things away: when the moon is in its waning phase all people bow to it, yet when it has become completely full in every aspect no one bows to it — this is why the moon is called one who turns things away.

As for fire being one who turns things away: fire burns the very thing that is burning into fire itself — this is why fire is called one who turns things away.

As for water being one who turns things away:

water in a winter pond, though cold, is not fit to drink; water in a well, though warm, is fit to drink; water in a summer pond, though warm, is fit to drink; water in a well, though cold, is not fit to drink — this is why water is called one who turns things away.

As for a young woman being one who turns things away: when she has not yet been given away in marriage she delights in a wealthy household, yet when she has been taken to that wealthy household she also grows fond of her own home and weeps — this is why a young woman is called one who turns things away.

As for a woman being one who turns things away: when she is young and pleasing to look upon she goes about with her body covered, yet when she is old and no longer pleasing she goes about with it uncovered — this is why a woman is called one who turns things away.

As for a brahmin being one who turns things away: when a brahmin is a child and desire and attachment have not yet arisen he practises the holy life of celibacy, yet when he has come of age and desire and attachment have arisen he indulges in sensual pleasures — this is why a brahmin is called one who turns things away.

As for a naked ascetic being one who turns things away: when a naked ascetic is at home he sits dressed in robes, yet when he goes out into his domain he goes about naked — this is why a naked ascetic is called one who turns things away.

As for a monk being one who turns things away: when he is young and in the prime of life and is able to digest what he has eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, those things are not to be had; yet when he is old and unable to digest what he has eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, those very things are obtained in abundance — this is why a monk is called one who turns things away.

As for mud being one who turns things away: when mud is wet it floats upon water, yet when it dries it sinks — this is why mud is called one who turns things away.

Thirtieth fascicle of the Vinaya, the section on minor matters.

The king said: I have heard and understood all of this — enough. Now answer me this directly: by what power did you kill the herdsman's mother, who had not been subdued? He replied: O king, how could I ever have had the power to subdue the herdsman's mother? O king, it is rather that this great noble Kātyāyana is a śrāvaka of one who is a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, tamer of persons to be tamed, a charioteer, unsurpassed, Teacher of gods and humans — a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha who, by the power of wisdom unobstructed, turns the wheel like a wheel-turning monarch, and whoever is endowed with what that one possesses roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and is endowed with the ten powers. What are those ten? O king, the first is this: that one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, what is a basis as a basis and what is not a basis as not a basis — that, O king, is his first power. Endowed with that power, he roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly. Furthermore, O king, that one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, in terms of basis, ground, cause, and karmic maturation, the deeds and the Dharma rightly undertaken by sentient beings in the past, the future, and the present.

That one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, in terms of basis, ground, cause, and karmic maturation, the deeds and the Dharma rightly undertaken by sentient beings in the past, the future, and the present — that, O king, is his second power. Endowed with that power, he roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, that one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, the defilement and the purification, as they are established and as they are clarified, of the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), liberations, meditative absorptions (samādhi), and meditative attainments. That one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, the defilement and the purification, as they are established and as they are clarified, of the meditative concentrations, liberations, meditative absorptions, and meditative attainments — that, O king, is his third power. Endowed with that power, he roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, that one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, whether the faculties of other sentient beings and other persons are superior or inferior. That one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, whether the faculties of other sentient beings and other persons are superior or inferior — that is his fourth power. Endowed with that power, he roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, that one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, the diversity of the inclinations of other sentient beings and other persons. That one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, the diversity of the inclinations of other sentient beings and other persons — that, O king, is his fifth power. Endowed with that power, he roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, that one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, what is called the variety and multiplicity of world-realms. That one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, what is called the variety and multiplicity of world-realms — that, O king, is his sixth power. Endowed with that power, he roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, that one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, the path that leads everywhere. That one fully and correctly knows, just as they are, the path that leads everywhere — that, O king, is his seventh power. Endowed with that power, he roars the lion's roar in the great and lofty station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, that one recollects his many former lives in their various aspects — one life, two lives, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred lives, a thousand lives, a hundred thousand lives, many hundreds of lives, many thousands of lives, many hundreds of thousands of lives, an aeon of dissolution, an aeon of formation, an aeon of both dissolution and formation, many aeons of dissolution, many aeons of formation,

many aeons of both dissolution and formation — and recollects them, thinking: "In such and such a place my name was this, my clan was such, my lineage was such, my food was such, the pleasure and suffering I experienced were such, my lifespan reached this far, my stay lasted as long as this, and when that end of life came to pass, those sentient beings arose there. I passed away from that existence and was born in such and such a place. From there too I passed away and was born here." In this way he recollects his many former lives in all their aspects, together with their places and directions.

Having thus recollected his many former lives — from "recollecting even one life" all the way through "was born here" — with their many aspects, together with their places and directions: this is the eighth power of that god. Endowed with that power, he takes on the magnificent station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, with the divine eye — purified and surpassing human capacity — that one sees sentient beings dying and being born: fair in form and ugly in form, fortunate and unfortunate, high and low. He fully understands, exactly as it is, how sentient beings pass on in accordance with their karma: those who go to a happy destination and those who go to a bad destination. He fully understands, exactly as it is: "These sentient beings are endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind; they have slandered the noble ones; they hold wrong views; and having taken up actions and dharmas rooted in wrong view, at the breaking up of the body after death they will be reborn in a bad destination, a bad realm, a fallen state — in the hells. And these sentient beings are endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind; they have not slandered the noble ones; they hold right views; and having taken up actions and dharmas rooted in right view, at the breaking up of the body they will be reborn in a happy destination, a higher realm, among the gods."

From "the divine eye" through "reborn among the gods in a happy destination, a higher realm" — all of this is as before. This is the ninth power of that god. Endowed with that power, he takes on the magnificent station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

Furthermore, O king, that one — for the sake of the exhaustion of all defilements, and in this very visible existence alone — realizes through direct personal knowledge the undefiled liberation of mind and the liberation of wisdom, enters into them, and brings them to completion, and declares: "My defilements are exhausted. The holy life has been demonstrated. What had to be done has been done. I shall not know another existence beyond this." From "the undefiled liberation of mind and the liberation of wisdom" through "I shall not know another existence beyond this" — all is as before. This is the tenth power of that god. Endowed with that power, he takes on the magnificent station of the finest bull of the herd, turns the wheel of Brahmā, and roars the lion's roar in the midst of the assembly.

When these words had been spoken, King Prabhāsa sat in silence, utterly speechless. Gośa thought to himself: "The god sits in silence, saying nothing at all — how much longer must this cow-herder's mother remain uncalmed?" And so he took her by both arms and led her forward, and she bowed at the king's two feet in prostration.

She approached the king to beg his forgiveness and sang these verses:

O god, O lord of human beings, behold how here the way of the Dharma of permanence is traveled and traveled again, truly and rightly. Patience is the foremost virtue of kings, O god — please extend your forgiveness for the transgression of the cow-herder's mother.

She is a precious jewel of excellent speech, a wonder for the world to behold. If you, who even tame great elephants, have not yet seen or heard her — what need is there to speak of a woman's slight offense? Endowed with form and qualities that do not stray from you, she has been and will be your devoted queen, before as now. For the sake of the king alone, O god, please grant full forgiveness to this cow-herder's mother — thus did she speak.

The king, in response to her plea, spoke again in verse:

This you have spoken, and spoken well — you have said it with deep affection for me. Therefore I grant you the gift of Kanyākubja, and I forgive, from my heart, even the offense against Śiva.

Here ends the reply.

The summary verse:

Ugraśena, with the golden vessels,
Bhaddā the luminous, and the forest-dweller,
The life-giver, the medicine of fruits,
And many in his retinue who caused offense.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Vaiśālī in the Pavilion with Many Storeys on the bank of the Monkey Pool. At that time a large assembly of brahmins and householders had gathered and were seated in a gallery, speaking among themselves in conversation of this sort: "Learned ones, the ascetic Gautama and his śrāvakas are greatly filled with desire. The non-Buddhists are not so," they said.

Now at that very gathering, the householder Ugraśena was also seated in that assembly. Then the householder Ugraśena addressed the many brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī with these words: "Learned ones, wait a moment. I will show you, face to face, whether the Blessed One has great desire or little desire, and whether his śrāvakas have great desire or little desire." And having said that, he had vessels of gold, silver, vaiḍūrya, and crystal filled and loaded, then went to where the Blessed One was and, going there, exchanged with the Blessed One various pleasant and appropriate words of greeting and celebration, and sat down to one side.

As he sat to one side, the Blessed One taught the householder Ugraśena thoroughly with a Dharma talk, fully guided him, fully encouraged him, and filled him with joy. In many different ways, using words in accord with the Dharma, he taught him thoroughly, fully guided him, fully encouraged him, and filled him with joy — and then remained in silence.

Then the householder Ugraśena rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and turning toward the Blessed One with palms pressed together in reverential salutation, said to the Blessed One: "Might the Blessed One be pleased to consent to come to my home tomorrow at mealtime together with the monastic Saṅgha of monks?" The Blessed One consented to the householder Ugraśena's request by remaining silent.

Then the householder Ugraśena, knowing from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been granted, praised what the Blessed One had said, rejoiced, and rising from his seat, departed.

He then invited the non-Buddhists as well, saying: "Learned ones, tomorrow I have invited the buddha, the Blessed One, along with the monastic Saṅgha of śrāvakas, to my home at mealtime — come you also to that place for the meal." And he invited the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī likewise: "Learned ones, I have invited the buddha, the Blessed One, along with the monastic Saṅgha of śrāvakas, and —"

"— and the non-Buddhists have been invited to my home tomorrow at midday; come you also at that time to be of company." Then he went to his own home and gave instructions to those in his household who prepared food, saying: "Learned ones, prepare a great abundance of pure and varied food." And they prepared a great abundance of pure and varied food.

Then, the following morning, the householder Ugraśena rose early, arranged seats, set out water vessels, and sent word to the Blessed One announcing the midday hour: "Venerable One, you were invited for midday — now that the time has come, may the Blessed One be pleased to know that the hour is at hand."

Thereupon the Blessed One, in the time of the morning, donned his under-robe and outer robe, took up his alms bowl, and went to the place to which the householder Ugraśena had directed him. Having arrived, he took his seat on the prepared cushion at the head of the monastic Saṅgha of monks.

Then the householder Ugraśena, together with the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, began serving the buddha and the members of the monastic Saṅgha of monks with vessels of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal.

At that point the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and announce to the monks that the householder Ugraśena is serving with vessels of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal as a way of testing them — let none among you monks accept any of them." The Venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One's words, assented, saying "As you instruct, Venerable One," and then went and announced to the monks: "Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared that the householder Ugraśena is serving you with vessels of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal with a mind intent on testing you — let none among you monks accept any of them." Having been so informed, the Venerable Ānanda said, "As the Blessed One has commanded, so shall we do: we shall not accept them" — and indeed they did not accept them.

Then the householder Ugraśena, perceiving that the buddha and the monastic Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, served them himself by hand, thoroughly satisfying and replenishing them with an abundance of pure and varied food and drink. Many times over, serving them himself by hand with an abundance of pure and varied food and drink, he thoroughly satisfied and amply served them all. When he knew that the Blessed One had finished eating and had covered his bowl and withdrawn his hand, Ugraśena placed a low seat before the Blessed One and sat down in front of him to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One thoroughly taught the householder Ugraśena with discourse in accord with the Dharma, thoroughly guided him to receive it, thoroughly praised him, and thoroughly gladdened him. Many times over he thoroughly taught him with discourse in accord with the Dharma, thoroughly guided him to receive it, thoroughly praised him, and thoroughly gladdened him. Then, having spoken the dedication of merit, he rose from his seat and departed.

Thereafter, certain of the untamed non-Buddhists sat about making a clamour, grumbling in all directions. The householder Ugraśena then instructed his gatekeeper: "Good steward, if any non-Buddhist attempts to leave by the gate carrying a vessel of gold, silver, vaidūrya, or crystal, do not give it to him. If he says 'The householder gave it to me,' reply: 'The householder gave it to you for the meal — he did not give it to you to keep.' And if he still will not hand it over, beat him and take it back."

The man obeyed the householder Ugraśena's instruction. Then the householder Ugraśena began distributing vessels of gold, silver, and vaidūrya to the non-Buddhists, and a great uproar and commotion broke out, with some crying, "Householder, give me something made of gold!" and others, "Give me something made of silver!" and so on, all clamouring together. A brawl then broke out among them, and they began striking one another with fists, slaps, sticks, cudgels, and clods of earth. The householder Ugraśena had them threatened, overpowered, and by the device of separating them, compelled each to sit down and eat in his own place. Whoever had eaten his fill from whatever vessel then tried to leave taking that very vessel with him, and the gatekeeper moved to seize them. They protested: "Hey, steward — the householder gave it to us, so why are you stopping us?" He replied: "The householder gave it to you for the meal — he did not give it to you to keep. Hand it over at once." When they refused to give it back, the gatekeeper beat them, and a tremendous outcry arose, so that all the great multitude of men, women, boys, and girls residing in Vaiśālī gathered together.

The householder Ugraśena, seeing those disagreeable scenes, spoke these words to the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī: "O you of discernment, have you observed the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks and śrāvakas, and the distinction they display?" They replied: "Householder, we have indeed observed it." He then said: "O you of discernment, see how the Blessed One is of few wants, and his śrāvakas likewise are of few wants — whereas these non-Buddhists, who are criticized in the Dharma and Vinaya as people of many wants, are not like that at all."

Thereupon, many who had lacked faith in the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks and śrāvakas came to have faith. Even among the neutral bystanders, some developed faith in the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then went to the meeting hall, washed his feet, and took his seat on the seat that had been prepared for him in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, since there are these and other benefits to knowing moderation, a monk must not eat from vessels of precious materials — gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, and the like. If he does, it becomes a serious offence. The Blessed One declared that monks must not eat from vessels of gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, and so forth, from vessels of precious materials."

Now because of such other monks who were free from faults, ordinary people who had gone to the abodes of gods and nāgas were invited to eat there. But in those divine and nāga dwellings there were only vessels of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal, fashioned by the power of their own merit, and no other vessels were to be found. The monks regretted this and did not eat.

On that occasion the monks informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, in a place where no other vessel can be found, I permit you to eat from vessels of gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, and the like — you need feel no remorse about this."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder — wealthy, of great property, possessed of vast resources and extensive holdings, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa (the god of wealth), a rival to Vaiśravaṇa in riches. He had taken a wife from a family of equal rank, and with her he sported and took delight and enjoyed himself.

From that sport and delight and enjoyment, at a certain time a being entered into that wife's womb. From the very day that the being entered her womb, her complexion became radiant and lovely. Eight or nine months passed, and she gave birth to a daughter — beautiful of form, fair to see, lovely to behold, endowed with all her major and minor limbs. At the moment of her birth, that household blazed with light like the rays of the sun, and throughout all of Śrāvastī the news spread: "A great householder's daughter has been born — beautiful of form, fair to see, lovely to behold, endowed with all her major and minor limbs — and at the moment of her birth, that household blazed with light like the rays of the sun." On hearing this, many hundreds of thousands of living beings, filled with wonder, gathered at that householder's home.

Now, a brahmin astrologer had come from another region, and he too gathered there out of wonder. He gazed at the child carefully, then said to the assembled people, "O wise ones, have you seen this girl?" They replied, "We have seen her." He said, "O wise ones, this girl will without doubt take delight and find enjoyment in the company of five hundred men." They answered, "Given how beautiful this brahmin's girl is in her form, she will certainly, without fail, take delight and find enjoyment in the company of five hundred men."

And throughout all of Śrāvastī the report spread: "A householder's daughter has been born — beautiful of form, fair to see, lovely to behold, endowed with all her major and minor limbs — and at the moment of her birth that household blazed with light like the rays of the sun; and an astrologer has prophesied that this girl will take delight and find enjoyment in the company of five hundred men." Everyone who heard the news came there as well.

After twenty-one days — three sets of seven — a great birth-celebration was held, and it came time to give the girl her name. The relatives said, "At the moment this girl was born, the household blazed with light like the rays of the sun. Therefore let the girl's name be Prabhāvatī — Radiant with Light." And so she was named Prabhāvatī.

Prabhāvatī was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry her in their arms, two to suckle and nurse her, two to bathe and cleanse her, and two to play with her. These eight nurses reared and raised her on milk, yogurt, clarified butter, fresh butter, the very essence of butter, and other excellent and choice provisions, so that she grew and flourished like a lotus in a pond.

When she came of age, she was endowed with beauty, the flush of youth, grace, and the particular excellence of artistic accomplishments, and she was as lovely in that household as a forest goddess amid a forest in full bloom. Such were her beauty, her youth, her complexion, her bearing and deportment that she captured the minds even of sages who had renounced attachment by the ordinary worldly path — to say nothing of those people who, from beginningless time, have accumulated the pervasive practice of affliction and who are intoxicated with the pride of caste, form, youth, and wealth. That householder himself, together with his household retinue, applied himself to guarding her and did not even sleep at night.

The king of the land of Kośala, Prasenajit, together with his queens' retinues, his young princes, his ministers, his palace attendants, and also kings and sons of ministers dwelling in outlying regions,

Though the heralds and others had been sent to summon her, since the astrologers had prophesied that the girl Śrī-prabhā would live in joy together with five hundred men, there was fear that she might be regarded as belonging to the world at large, and so no one came to take her away. Even so, men would sit at the latticed windows, the ordinary windows, on the balconies, and on the rooftops of her house, gazing at her and hoping to win her. When the householder saw her conduct, he began offering her to others of equal birth who had not even sought her — yet not a single one of them would accept. The householder, seeing that no one at all wanted her, grew disheartened and abandoned all his other affairs, consuming himself with thoughts of how to give her away. His body became pale and wan, his flesh wasted, and he was reduced to a gaunt and emaciated state.

Now at that time there lived in Śrāvastī a certain householder — wealthy, possessed of great riches, and of ample means — who had taken a wife from a family of equal standing, but she died by her own karma. Similarly, a second wife, and then from the third to the seventh, each likewise died by her own karma. Because those wives had performed deeds that caused them to be short-lived, and because he had performed deeds that caused him to be fined and penalized for it, he had come to bear the name "Wife-killer, wife-killer." When he sought a wife from others, they said, "Why should our daughter be killed?" When he then tried to seek widows, they too said, "Why should our body be cast away on your account?" — and every one of them refused him. And so, having cut off all hope of ever getting a wife, he began to keep company with wandering ascetics (śramaṇas), brahmins, wanderers, and mendicants.

Now, his father was a lay practitioner who had gone for refuge to the Buddha, and that son thought: "If my father is a Buddhist layman, what do I need with wandering ascetics, brahmins, wanderers, and mendicants? I should attend upon the Blessed One's hearers, serve them, and then right there go forth into the renunciant life." With this in mind, he began going again and again to the Jeta Grove.

After some time a friend saw him and said, "Friend, if you go again and again to the Jeta Grove, surely you would do well to make the effort to go forth." The man replied, "Friend, even if I had not gone forth, why should I go forth? I took one wife and she died by her own karma. Likewise a second, and then from the third to the seventh — all died by their own karma. They had performed deeds that caused them to be short-lived, and I had performed deeds that caused me to be penalized, so that my name has become 'wife-killer, wife-killer.' I have lost all heart. It is my father's custom to attend respectfully upon the monks. If I do not do this, whom else should I serve?" The friend replied, "Friend, even granted all that, you must without fail produce a son — otherwise your lineage will be cut off. Why not seek a girl from another family?" The man said, "Friend, what use is that? Every family I have approached says: 'Why should our daughter be killed?'" The friend said, "Friend, if that is the situation, what harm is there in seeking a widow?" The man replied, "Friend, if I were to seek widows, they too say: 'Why should our body be cast away on your account?'" The friend said, "Friend, if that is so, why not seek Śrī-prabhā?" The man replied, "Friend, she is known throughout the entire world — would she be taken to the house of some lowly courtesan?" The friend said, "Friend, since you are a person of faith, go and invite a monk from your household to come and seek her."

"Friend, even if she will not give — friend, just ask! Her father is grieving and dejected, so he will give her." The man went to that householder's house, and the householder said to him, "Be well! Be well!" The householder asked, "What do you want?" "Śrī-prabhā." "She is given." And so the man, with his great wealth, took her as a bride. He gave her the keys — both the keys and the crooked keys — and established her as mistress of the household. He said to her: "Good woman, according to the custom of our family lineage, the Teacher, the Buddha, and the monks are the fitting recipients of our generosity, so you too should serve them accordingly." She replied: "My lord, well and good — I shall do exactly so."

Each day the monks came to that householder's house to eat, and Śrī-prabhā herself waited upon them and served them with her own hands. Now, when she saw those monks who were distinguished in complexion, in form, and in the excellence of their youth, conceptual thoughts arose in her. As these thoughts about them multiplied, a feeling of pleasure arose in her mind.

Then the householder had some business to attend to in a certain hill country. He said to his wife: "Good woman, I must go somewhere in a remote hill region on a matter of business. While I am away, continue to offer food and hospitality to the worthy recipients just as before." She replied: "Son of a noble house, I shall do exactly so before you have gone." She also said to the monks: "Noble ones, I must attend to some business in a remote hill region and will go there. In my absence, please come and take your meals here at my table just as before." They replied: "Householder, go, and may you be in good health. We will come and eat." And so he went to that hill country village.

The monks then continued to come to his house to take their meals. Śrī-prabhā, thinking to herself, "My husband is absent," began to display before the monks the guile of a woman, the deceit of a woman, and the wiles of a woman. The monks, finding fault with one another on this account, took counsel together, saying: "What should be done about this?" Some of them said: "What is there to be done? We simply need not come tomorrow." Others said: "We, the venerable ones, are mendicants — tomorrow we will simply go on our alms round." Yet others said, "Very well, let us do just that," and so from the very next day they began going on alms rounds.

When some time had passed, the householder returned and asked Śrī-prabhā: "Śrī-prabhā, have you been feeding the worthy recipients?" She replied: "They came on the first day, but after that they never came again." He thought to himself: "She must certainly have displayed feminine guiles before them, failed to honour them properly, and out of embarrassment they stopped coming." He went to them and invited them again. They replied: "Householder, we are mendicants — we shall go on our alms rounds." He said: "Noble ones, please come at my request. Such a fault will not occur again." They consented, and he prostrated at their feet and departed.

The next morning the monks came to his house. The householder had Śrī-prabhā stay inside the house, shut the outer door, and left her there. He himself then began to wait upon the monks and serve them with his own hands. But now Śrī-prabhā, sitting inside the house, conceived thoughts about those monks who were eating — thoughts about a certain noble person's feet, how such they were; his calves, how such they were; his thighs, how such they were; his waist and flanks and back; his belly; his face; his teeth; his lips; and —

his nose; his eyes; his brow; his head — how such they were — she so dwelt in conceptual thought about each of these things that the fire of attachment at the tenth ground blazed up, and fanned by the blast of the wind of conceptual thinking, it flared and consumed her, and she died on the very spot.

When the monks had eaten, expressed their thanks, and departed, the householder opened the door and called out, "Śrī-prabhā, come — come and eat." But there was no one to answer, for her time had passed. When he went inside, he found her lying collapsed on the ground. He thought to himself, surely she has only fallen asleep — and began to rouse her. But after a moment he saw that her time had indeed passed. His face turned dark, his beard disheveled, and he said to the people of the household, "Wise ones, look upon me, wretched one that I am, parted from a wife so precious and rare. Tell her friends and companions, her brothers and sisters and kinsmen that Śrī-prabhā has passed from her time." They raised a lament; some threw themselves on the ground and wept; others grasped the householder by his hands and feet and wept. Friends and companions, brothers and sisters and kinsmen uttered cries of sobbing. Because the householder had a great circle of his own people and associates, and they wept throughout all that time, by the time the sun had set they adorned her with blue, yellow, red, and white cloths and, with great honour, carried her to the charnel ground.

Now it happened that some five hundred wild men had gone out to a mountain pass, found goods and profit, and were returning, and drew near to that charnel ground. A man living in the city saw them and thought: the great crowd of people who went out from the city to escort Śrī-prabhā to the charnel ground — if those wild men were to harm them wrongfully, it would be terrible. He went quickly and warned the great crowd of people, saying, "Wise ones, some five hundred wild men are very close by — flee!" Those people set guards to attend to the funeral rites later, and then, just as Śrī-prabhā had been laid out adorned with a wealth of ornaments, perfumes, incense, cloths, powders, a parasol, victory banners, and pennants in all their glory, they abandoned her as though casting her aside, set the people fleeing, and entered the city. Shortly after, those wild men arrived at that very place, and the guards fled. The wild men saw her lying there so splendidly adorned and were supremely astonished. They then stripped away her robes and examined her, and seeing the youth and beauty of her form they were overcome with desire. They said among themselves, "Wise ones, wherever one wanders, there is nothing but enjoying pleasure with a woman like this" — and they enjoyed pleasure with her, and they set down five hundred kārṣāpaṇas. And word spread everywhere that five hundred men had given five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to the corpse of Śrī-prabhā and taken pleasure with it.

The monks were seized with doubt, and to resolve that doubt they presented it to the Blessed One, the Buddha. "Venerable One, what karma did the householder's wife Śrī-prabhā perform, such that through the ripening of that karma she was endowed with radiance and, just at the moment of birth, illuminated the entire house with light — and yet even in death five hundred wild men gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and took pleasure with her?"

The Blessed One declared, "Monks, the karma performed and accumulated by Śrī-prabhā, the householder's wife, the resources she gathered, the conditions she fully transformed, and what abided near her like a weapon's thrust — these are indeed determined.

Monks, the karma performed and accumulated by Śrī-prabhā — could any other person experience its ripening? Monks, karma performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma performed and accumulated ripens solely in the appropriated aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense sources (āyatanas).

Even across hundreds of aeons,
karma is never lost or wasted.
When conditions gather and the time arrives,
it ripens as fruit for those who bear bodies.

Monks, long ago in this very fortunate aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there arose in the world a Teacher named Kāśyapa — one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a fully awakened buddha, a Blessed One. He resided near the city of Vārāṇasī, in the deer park called the Grove of Sages Who Speak Truth. At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Kṛkī was ruling the kingdom — a kingdom prosperous, flourishing, joyful, with good harvests, full of people and a great population, where fighting, quarrelling, internal strife, and all disturbances were thoroughly pacified, free of disease, and rich in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo — a dharma-king who ruled in accordance with Dharma.

When the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa had performed all the deeds of a buddha and passed into nirvāṇa — into the expanse free of any remainder of aggregates, like a fire extinguished when its fuel is spent — King Kṛkī, together with his queen, his young prince, his ministers, and the people of the royal palace, paid great honour to the Teacher's relics, performed the relic worship, and erected a stūpa of four precious substances, one league in circumference on all four sides and a half-league in height.

At that time, a merchant's daughter arose in faith and hung a mirror on the central pole of the stūpa. Monks, what do you think? That merchant's daughter who, having arisen in faith toward the stūpa of the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa, hung a mirror on the central pole — she is none other than this very householder's wife Śrī-prabhā. Through the karmic ripening of that act — having hung a mirror on the pole of the stūpa of the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha Kāśyapa — she was born endowed with radiance, life after life, and at the very moment of birth illuminated the entire house with light. Now hear also the explanation of how, after death, five hundred men gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and took pleasure with her.

Monks, long ago in the city of Vārāṇasī there was a king named Brahmadatta who was ruling the kingdom — a kingdom prosperous, flourishing, joyful, with good harvests, full of people and a great population, where fighting, quarrelling, internal strife, and all disturbances were thoroughly pacified, free of thieves and disease, rich in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo — a dharma-king who ruled in accordance with Dharma. At that time, in Vārāṇasī, there lived a woman who made her living by her beauty, named Sudarśanā — beautiful, lovely, pleasant to behold, agreeable to the minds of men — who had formerly been enjoyed by the maternal uncles of King Brahmadatta.

Now, on another occasion, five hundred pleasure-seekers gathered together much food and drink and went to a pleasure grove. There they conferred with one another, saying, "We have arranged all the pleasures of the pleasure grove, yet we have no woman. Let us go and invite some courtesan." They agreed: "Yes, let us do so. Whom shall we invite?" "Sudarśanā." They went to Sudarśanā and said, "Sudarśanā, come here. Come to the pleasure grove." She replied, "If you give me a thousand kārṣāpaṇas, I will go — otherwise, no." They said, "Take five hundred kārṣāpaṇas now, and after we have enjoyed your company we will give you the other five hundred." She said, "Very well, let it be so." They gave her five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, and she said, "Today, then — having adorned yourself with perfumes, garlands, and fine garments — come." And they departed.

Then regret arose in her. She thought: "If I spend time in pleasure with these five hundred pleasure-seekers, what will become of my standing? I have already accepted five hundred kārṣāpaṇas — what am I to do now?" Then this thought arose in her mind: "Since I was formerly taken up entirely by the king's maternal uncle, it is to him alone that I shall look for protection, to no one else." So she sent no servant-girl in her own place, but herself went to the king's maternal uncle and spoke these words: "I am in a bad situation. I have accepted five hundred kārṣāpaṇas from these five hundred pleasure-seekers. Now if I were to enjoy their company, all five hundred of them together — what would become of my standing? Since you have formerly taken me as your own, it is fitting that you protect me from them. Please speak on my behalf."

The girl went to him and spoke, and he — relying on the king — had her snatched away from them.

Now, at that time when buddhas do not appear in the world, inferior pratyekabuddhas arise — those who are compassionate toward the impoverished, who delight in remote and secluded dwellings, who are the sole field of generosity in the world. And so a pratyekabuddha was wandering through the regions and came to Vārāṇasī, that great being, peaceful in nature, and seeking utter seclusion, he came to that very pleasure grove. The five hundred pleasure-seekers saw him — beautiful in body and beautiful in mind — and thought to themselves: "Wherever we may wander, one should serve such a field of merit as this." Consulting one another, they filled his bowl with clean and excellent food and drink and offered it to him. Now, that great being teaches the Dharma not by word but by body. So he rose visibly into the sky above, performing miracles — blazing, shining, sending down rain, flashing lightning, and so on. Ordinary people, inspired by these miracles, fell at his feet like trees cut at the root, and made this aspiration: "By this root of virtue which we have created through serving such a perfect field of generosity as this, may we — even those of us who live by our bodies — upon dying, come to give five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and enjoy pleasure."

Monks, what do you think? She who was called "Sudarśanā, she who lives by her body" — she is none other than this householder's wife, Prabhāvatī (Odbzangma), right here. And those five hundred pleasure-seekers of that time and that occasion are none other than these five hundred ruffians here.

Through the karmic maturation of the aspiration they made after offering alms to the pratyekabuddha at that time and on that occasion, as they have wandered in saṃsāra, for five hundred lifetimes they have given five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and enjoyed pleasure — and now, having become the householder's wife, she will continue to give five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and enjoy pleasure until the moment of her death.

Thus it is, monks: the karmic maturation of those who are wholly dark is itself wholly dark; the karmic maturation of those who are wholly bright, and of those who lead others, is likewise wholly bright and fit to lead. Therefore, monks, abandon actions that are wholly dark and those that lead downward, and strive only in actions that are wholly bright. Monks, you should train accordingly.

Whatever slight fault arose in the Blessed One's consideration was the result of going to such a household. Therefore, knowing that monks should not go to such households, the Blessed One declared to the monks: Monks, a monk who sees the householder's wife Prabhāvatī may give rise to a thought and die of it. Therefore, monks, a monk should not go to a household in which such a fault as this may arise. If a monk goes to such a household, it will be an offense.

The setting is in Rājagṛha.

There was a monk who had gone forth into renunciation, and who again and again went to a secluded dwelling place to practice meditative concentration. There a goddess of the class of Māra waited, hoping to lead him into improper conduct, but she failed. She said: "Noble one, I will not rest until I harm you!" He replied: "Sister, I am a monk who observes the moral discipline — what power do you have to harm me?" She retorted, "We shall see!" and devoted herself to seeking an opportunity against him.

On another occasion, he untied the knot of his patched robe at the knee and fell asleep. The goddess thought: "Now is the time to roast this one's flesh," and taking him up, she dropped him on the upper story of the pleasure palace of King Rūpavadana, who was sleeping there. He awoke with a start and, seeing her, asked: "Who are you?" She said: "A wandering ascetic." "Which wandering ascetic?" "A wandering ascetic among the sons of the Śākyan." "Noble one, how did you come to be here?" He told her what had happened. She then said: "Noble one, why do you dwell in such a dangerous and treacherous resting place? If the Blessed One does not gain his trust, I will have you killed, or you will be expelled from the teaching." He said nothing.

At that moment the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter: whatever slight fault arose was the result of a monk dwelling in such a dangerous and treacherous resting place. Therefore, knowing that a monk should not dwell in such a dangerous and treacherous resting place, the Blessed One declared to the monks: Monks, the slander of King Rūpavadana has struck. Therefore a monk should not dwell in such a dangerous and treacherous resting place. If a monk dwells in such a dangerous and treacherous resting place, it will be an offense.

The setting is in Rājagṛha.

At that time a young monk was afflicted by a disease called "the fruit of wrong food and conduct," and tormented by that illness he was vomiting, while the monks sat around him. Then the king of physicians, Jīvaka, arrived and asked: "Noble ones, what is this?" The monks replied:

"Jīvaka, this young monk has been struck by a disease. Please examine what the illness is and what treatment should be applied." Jīvaka looked at him and said: "Noble ones, it is an abscess. Lancing it will be beneficial." The monks said: "If that is so, then lance it." He lanced it, and after the procedure had begun, he left without completing the dressing. The monk became gravely ill, and the monks said: "Let whichever venerable one is skilled attend to the dressing." Then another young monk did the dressing. Jīvaka thought: "I ought not to return without having dressed the wound of that noble one," and so he turned back and asked: "Noble ones, which noble one was it whose abscess I lanced?" The monks replied: "What does it matter? Noble one, we shall have the dressing seen to." Jīvaka said: "The dressing has already been done." "Noble one, by whom?" "By this young monk here." "Noble one, let us look at how it was done." He went to the monk's side and examined the wound, and seeing that the dressing had been done well, he said: "Noble one, the dressing is excellent. Even in my absence, please continue to do likewise in the future." The monk replied: "Jīvaka, even performing this without my having received permission is something — why speak at all of formally doing so? It has not been determined whether the Blessed One has permitted or forbidden it." Jīvaka said: "Noble one, the Blessed One is compassionate — why would he not permit it?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, whichever monk is skilled is hereby permitted to perform the dressing." Now that the Blessed One had declared that whichever monk is skilled is permitted to perform the dressing, they began doing so in the corridors, beside the ponds, in the gatehouse, and on the steps. The Blessed One declared: "Do it in a secluded place. If done elsewhere, it will be an offense."

The setting is in Śrāvastī.

Faithful brahmin and householder devotees came to the monastery and said to the monks: "Noble ones, if I am afflicted by such-and-such a disease, what food should I seek? What medicine should I take?" They asked about dietary practice, and those monks who did not know said nothing at all, while those who knew fell into doubt and remained silent. The brahmin and householder devotees departed dissatisfied. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, whichever monk is skilled is hereby permitted to teach dietary practices and medical treatments. One should have no regret in doing so."

The setting is in Śrāvastī.

At the time when the Blessed One displayed the great miracle (mahāprātihārya), the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) were overcome and humbled, gods and humans were filled with delight, and noble persons were gladdened. At that time, non-human beings dwelling in various lands came to Śrāvastī from villages, hamlets, districts, and royal palaces, and from other world-realms as well. Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and the Kośala king Prasenajit, the queen Mālikā, the noble woman Viśākhā, the brahmin ascetic Dīrghanakha, elderly persons, the mother of Mṛgāra, and many other devotees came to Śrāvastī with reverent faith in the Blessed One, and there, with material gifts and honors of worship, the great multitude of people was brought to complete satisfaction.

This is the Vinaya of Minor Matters, the thirty-first fascicle.

Upon witnessing such excellent abundance, some of the non-human beings rejoiced right there on the spot, while others departed and returned to their own dwelling places.

Those who remained and rejoiced — when desire arose and their minds became entirely bound by sensual attachment, they would take on the appearance of the husbands of women whose husbands had gone out on business, manifest in that guise, and sport in pleasure with those women. From those women, boys and girls were then born as the result of that union, coming into the world with unpleasant limbs, eyes, and bodies. Some were dark-skinned with red eyes. Some had large heads and small bodies. Some had yellowish heads. Some had green hair. When their mothers saw them, they were terrified and abandoned them — some in the space between the houses, some in the direction of the thickets — and the non-human beings sustained those children with their own non-human essence. Some were born not clearly appearing in human form, and when they had grown up they would manifest changes. These too were abandoned at the main crossroads, and they also were nurtured by the non-human beings with their essence.

The conduct of the Group of Six monks was such that they would ordain all such beings and confer full ordination upon them, and so long as those ordained ones did not know that their co-resident was one of bad conduct, they lived together with them. But when it became known, the monks who were of naturally upright conduct would separate from them, and thereafter at the times indicated by the Teacher they would depart accordingly.

Now one day, the Venerable Ānanda rose early in the morning, put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and entered Śrāvastī on alms-round. While walking on the alms-round he saw a being with green hair, and he thought: "This one will not be snatched away by those with black bowls. If someone were to ordain this one, I shall take him forth." With this thought he went up to him and asked: "Good sir, to whom do you belong?"

The other replied: "Noble one, there is no one at all I belong to. I am without a protector."

Ānanda said: "Good sir, if that is the case, why do you not go forth?"

The other replied: "Noble one, who would take forth one such as me with green hair?"

"Good sir," said Ānanda, "the teaching of the Blessed One is opened wide by compassion. If no one else will take you forth, come here — I shall give you ordination. Let us go."

At that the being's heart was gladdened, and he went to the Jeta Grove, where Ānanda took him forth and conferred full ordination upon him.

After a few days, having taught him the principles of proper conduct, he gave him his charge: "Good sir, deer do not feed deer. Śrāvastī is both a broad domain of your own and a land of your fathers, so sustain yourself by going about for alms."

He did not like this, and so the very next morning he put on his lower robe, took up his outer robe and bowl, and entered Śrāvastī on alms-round. Now it happened that a woman came out carrying alms food she had collected, and when she saw him she beat her breast and cried out: "Noble one, you with the green hair — who ordained you?"

He replied: "Sister, the preceptor Ānanda ordained me out of compassion."

She said: "Who but someone of bad conduct could so degrade and mar the beauty of the Blessed One's teaching!" Others likewise mocked him, and those faithless, fault-finding people in the main roads, at crossroads, and at triple junctions called out: "The discipline of the ascetics, the sons of Śākya, is worn threadbare! Even the brahma-conduct is worn threadbare!"

It was at this time, while such ill repute was being spoken — that people were now ordaining even those with green hair — that the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "Whatever fault has arisen has come about through monks ordaining persons of that sort. Therefore a monk should not confer ordination on persons of that sort." Knowing this, he declared to the monks:

"Monks, the mockery of brahmins and householders has fallen upon us. Therefore a monk must not keep in his vicinity a retinue that brings the retinue into disrepute. If a monk does keep in his vicinity a retinue that brings the retinue into disrepute, it will become a serious offence."

When the Blessed One had declared that a monk must not keep in his vicinity a retinue that brings the retinue into disrepute, the monks did not know what kind of retinue brings the retinue into disrepute. The Blessed One declared:

"Monks, a retinue brings the retinue into disrepute by two means: by lineage and by marks.

"As for by lineage: it is by any lineage whatsoever — lowly, base, impoverished, utterly destitute, wretched, lacking sufficient food and drink. When those born from such lineages are ordained by monks, that is the case of bringing disrepute by lineage.

"As for what is meant by marks, it is as follows:"

Yellow hair and green hair,
and likewise red hair,
white hair among men,
elephant-like hair, and no hair at all —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

A swollen head or an elephant-like head,
a shrunken head or a flat head,
the head of a donkey or of a pig,
or a person who has two heads —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

Ears like an elephant's or like a horse's,
ears like a cow's or like a monkey's,
ears like a donkey's or a pig's,
a single ear or no ears at all —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

Eyes extremely red or extremely large,
eyes that are small or exceedingly yellow,
eyes of glass and protruding eyes,
a single eye or no eyes at all —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

A nose like an elephant's or like a horse's,
like a cow's or like a monkey's,
noses like a donkey's or a pig's,
a single nostril or no nose at all —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

Lips like a horse's or an elephant's,
lips like a cow's or a monkey's,
lips like a donkey's or a pig's,
a single lip or no lips at all —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

Teeth like an elephant's or like a horse's,
teeth of a cow or of a monkey,
teeth like a donkey's or a pig's,
a single tooth or no teeth at all —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

A neck that is short or extremely long,
pig-eyed, or hunchbacked,
with genitals that are mutilated or shrivelled,
with a single testicle or none at all —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

Extremely tall or extremely short,
withered, or racked by excessive fatigue,
of a complexion that is the fourth colour,
with skin that hangs loose or is rough, or with prominent teeth —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

With a hand severed or a foot severed,
with fingers rounded and webbed,
with no lips, a body covered in marks,
extremely old or extremely young —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

Lame and limping in the lower body,
with fingers missing, hunchbacked, a dwarf,
with a goitre, or mute,
bent and leaning on a support, with club feet —
persons of such kind
were rejected by the great sages.

One with leprosy, with boils, with cataract,
with a swollen throat, scrofula, or crooked limbs,
and indeed any other disease whatsoever —
all such were rejected by the great sages.

Worn out by journeys and by burdens, a woman —

a slave woman, a kept woman,
a pledged woman — these and others with damaged limbs:
all such were disruptive to the retinue.

As for the one who is supremely beautiful,
the perfectly pure candidate for full ordination,
the fully awakened Buddha, the Blessed One, discerned this well
and declared it by the mark of truth.

Upananda of the green hair — at the time when his hair too had been sold into the hands of a dancer, the monks made a report to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore a monk must not sell hair. If one does so, it becomes a serious offense."

The summary verse:

A slave, a kept woman,
an occasion, a petition,
a great miracle and one of good repute,
an entire army, and a mountain of worms.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upananda had two novices: one who was a slave and one who was kept. These two were intimate with each other, conversing freely, speaking in each other's presence, exchanging words, and companions to one another. One of the two said to the other: "You should take full ordination, and I will serve as your preceptor and perform your attendant duties." The other said exactly the same thing in return. Since each was deferring to the other in this way, neither of the two received full ordination.

Then the venerable Upananda went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. The venerable Upananda then said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, is it proper for two persons to be fully ordained by means of one preceptor, one teacher, and one formal act?" The Blessed One replied: "Upananda, it is proper." "Of those two, which is the elder?" "Neither is." "Venerable one, is it proper for three persons to be fully ordained by means of one preceptor, one teacher, and one formal act?" "Upananda, it is proper." "Of those, which is the elder?" "None is." "Venerable one, is it proper for four persons to be fully ordained by means of one preceptor, one teacher, and one formal act?" "Upananda, it is not proper. Why? Because the assembly performing the formal acts of the assembly is itself irregular — it is contradictory for the Saṅgha to be fully ordained by the Saṅgha, and if the Saṅgha were to perform full ordination for the Saṅgha it would become seriously contradictory."

The venerable Upananda then performed full ordination for those two together by means of a single formal act. Not knowing to whom among the two they should bow, what duties should be assigned to each, and how gains should be received, the venerable Upananda reported this at length to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "The two must not bow to each other. As for gains, they should be received according to whoever came first. The one who came later should be appointed junior in duties, and gains should be distributed to him later."

The occasion for this was at Śrāvastī.

The venerable Upananda asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, in the future there will arise monks who are forgetful and of weak memory. If they are unable to find, in whatever monastery, town, or village they reside, which sūtra was taught and what rule of training was established, how shall they proceed? Furthermore, if sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are lost to transmission, how shall they proceed? Moreover, with respect to prior instructions given by kings, householders, and male lay practitioners concerning a monastery, and concerning a king, a city, a town, a householder, and

the lay practitioners whose names were forgotten — how shall those monks proceed?"
