The Blessed One declared: "Upananda, those who have forgotten the name of the monastery and so forth may invoke either any one of the six great cities, or else the place where a Tathāgata resided on many occasions. If the name of the king is forgotten, it shall be Prasenajit. The name of the householder shall be Anāthapiṇḍada. The name of the laywoman shall be Mṛgāramātā Viśākhā. The former traditional seat shall be Vārāṇasī. The king shall be Brahmadatta. The householder shall be Saṃgharakṣita. The laywoman shall be declared to be the wife of the householder Poṣadhajāta. If the sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are forgotten, they shall be written on tablets and preserved, and in this one should have no regret."

The buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. Kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, townsfolk, countryfolk, the wealthy, merchants, and caravan leaders paid him honor, held him as supreme, paid him homage, and made offerings to him; and thus the Blessed One obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines as remedies for illness, along with all requisites. The tīrthikas, however, were not honored, held as supreme, paid homage, or offered reverence by kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, townsfolk, countryfolk, the wealthy, merchants, or caravan leaders; and thus they did not obtain robes, alms-food, bedding, medicines as remedies for illness, or any requisites.

Then the evil Māra thought to himself: "For a long time I have been looking for an opportunity against the ascetic Gautama but have not found one. Now I shall look for an opportunity against the tīrthikas." At that time, Pūraṇa and the other six teachers — those who arrogated to themselves omniscience without truly being omniscient — were dwelling in Rājagṛha. Then the evil Māra manifested himself in the very appearance of Pūraṇa and went to the son of the dark-roaming god Kāḷa, and upon arriving before the son of that dark-roaming god, he displayed miraculous feats of blazing, radiance, rainfall, and flashing lightning. The son of the dark-roaming god Kāḷa said: "Pūraṇa, have you attained such a collection of qualities as this?" "I have." In the same way, he also went before Sañjaya's son Vairatīputra, before Ajita Keśakambala, before Kakuda's son Kātyāyana, and before Nirgrantha's son, and before each he displayed those miraculous feats of blazing, radiance, rainfall, and flashing lightning, and each of them said: "Pūraṇa, have you attained such a collection of qualities as this?" "I have."

In the same way, manifesting himself in the appearance of the son of the dark-roaming god Kāḷa, he went before all of them; and then, likewise manifesting himself in the appearance of Ajita Keśakambala, he went before all of them and said: "Have you attained such a collection of qualities as this? I have" — and so forth, as before. In the same way, manifesting himself in the appearance of Sañjaya's son Vairatīputra, he went before all of them — and so forth, as before. In the same way, manifesting himself in the appearance of Kakuda's son Kātyāyana, he went before all of them — and so forth, as before.

In the same way, manifesting himself in the appearance of the Nirgrantha's son, he went before all of them — and so forth, as before. Each of them then thought to himself: "All of these, apart from me alone, are of great power and great supernatural ability."

Then, at another time, the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa assembled and gathered in a council hall, and there they raised conversation of this kind: "Friends, in former times kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, townspeople, country folk, the wealthy, merchant chiefs, and caravan leaders honored us, paid homage to us, and venerated us, and thereby we obtained robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal remedies for the sick, and requisites. Now they no longer honor us, no longer attend upon us, no longer revere us, no longer venerate us" — and so on through to: "and we no longer obtain robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal remedies for the sick, and requisites" — all as before. "Friends, the śramaṇa Gautama is honored and paid homage" — and so on through to: "the śramaṇa Gautama obtains robes, alms-food, lodgings, medicinal remedies for the sick, and requisites" — all as before. "Friends, therefore let us challenge the śramaṇa Gautama to a contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities and supernatural powers. If the śramaṇa Gautama displays one miraculous display of superhuman qualities and supernatural powers, we will display two; if he displays two, we will display four; if he displays four, we will display eight; if he displays eight, we will display sixteen; if he displays sixteen, we will display thirty-two — however many miraculous displays of superhuman qualities and supernatural powers the śramaṇa Gautama displays, we will display them doubled and tripled."

Then the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa went to wherever King Bimbisāra was, and having greeted the king and exchanged pleasantries, they said this: "Your Majesty, we claim to possess supernatural powers and to be endowed with gnosis. The śramaṇa Gautama likewise, we believe, claims to possess supernatural powers and to be endowed with gnosis. Therefore it would be fitting that both those claiming to be endowed with gnosis together display miraculous displays of superhuman qualities and supernatural powers. If the śramaṇa Gautama displays one, we will display two" — and so on through to "we will display them doubled and tripled" — all as before. "Please also invite the śramaṇa Gautama to the second half of the day; we too shall come for the second half of the day."

Then the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra the artisan — Śreṇya — spoke to the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa: "Well then, shall you likewise challenge the Blessed One to a contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities and supernatural powers?" When the king spoke these words, they went off.

Now at another time, the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra the artisan — Śreṇya — departed from Rājagṛha and went into the presence of the Blessed One in order to see him and pay him respect. They intercepted the king on his road and greeted him and exchanged pleasantries, then said: "Your Majesty, we claim to possess supernatural powers and to be endowed with gnosis" — and so on as before.

"— displaying the miraculous display of superhuman qualities two-fold and three-fold: let the ascetic Gautama be invited to the latter half of the contest; we too will come to the latter half" — and so on as before.

The king said: "Enough of this for now. If you say this sort of thing a third time, I shall have you driven out and sent away." He had them turned back, and they departed.

When they returned to their own place, they deliberated again: "Sages, it is said that the king of Magadha, Bimbisāra the artisan — Śreṇya — is inclined toward the ascetic Gautama, and that in Śrāvastī there is a king of Kosala named Prasenajit who is, as it were, a bystander. When the ascetic Gautama comes to Śrāvastī, let us issue a challenge to him there regarding the miraculous display of superhuman qualities."

Then after some time the Blessed One stayed in Rājagṛha as long as he wished, and then set out travelling through the provinces in the direction of Śrāvastī. While he was making his way progressively through the provinces, he arrived at Śrāvastī and dwelt there in the Jeta Grove — the pleasure grove of Anāthapiṇḍada — belonging to the prince Jeta.

Then the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa likewise followed after the Blessed One and went to Śrāvastī. When they too arrived at Śrāvastī in due course, weary from the road, they rested, then went to the place where the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, was. They greeted the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, with lengthy salutations, and said: "Your Majesty, we claim to possess supernatural powers and to be endowed with gnosis. The ascetic Gautama too, we believe, claims to possess supernatural powers and to be endowed with gnosis. Because of this, it is fitting that those who claim gnosis together with one who claims gnosis should display the miraculous display of superhuman qualities. If the ascetic Gautama displays the miraculous display of superhuman qualities once, we will display it twice; if the ascetic Gautama does so twice, we will do so four times; if the ascetic Gautama does so four times, we will do so eight times; if the ascetic Gautama does so eight times, we will do so sixteen times; if the ascetic Gautama does so sixteen times, we will do so thirty-two times — whatever the miraculous display of superhuman qualities the ascetic Gautama may display, we will display the miraculous display of superhuman qualities two-fold and three-fold beyond it. Let the ascetic Gautama be invited to the latter half of the contest; we too will come to the latter half."

The king of Kosala, Prasenajit, said: "Sages, if that is so, wait while I petition the Blessed One about this." They replied: "Your Majesty, please do so; we will wait."

Then the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, went to where the Blessed One was, touched his head to the feet of the Blessed One in homage, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Venerable One, these non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are challenging the Blessed One to a contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities. Therefore, may the Blessed One please display the miraculous display of superhuman qualities. May the Blessed One please defeat the non-Buddhists. May the gods and humans be made glad. May the holy ones rejoice." When he had spoken these words, the Blessed One declared to the king of Kosala, Prasenajit as follows:

"Great King, I do not teach the Dharma to the hearers in this way: 'Monks, display for these brahmins and householders who have come here the miraculous display of superhuman qualities that surpass the human.' Rather, I teach the Dharma to the hearers in this way: 'Monks, do not be indolent in virtue. Confess wrongdoing and be purified of it.'"

The king of Kosala, Prasenajit, then addressed the Blessed One a second and a third time with these words: "Venerable One, since these non-Buddhists are challenging the Blessed One to a contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities, may the Blessed One please display the miraculous display of superhuman qualities. May the non-Buddhists be defeated. May the gods and humans be made glad. May the holy ones rejoice."

The Blessed One declared to the king of Kosala, Prasenajit, a second and a third time: "Great King, I do not teach the Dharma to the hearers in this way: 'Monks, display for these brahmins and householders who have come here the miraculous display of superhuman qualities that surpass the human.' Rather, I teach the Dharma to the hearers in this way: 'Monks, do not be indolent in virtue. Confess wrongdoing and be purified of it.'

There are five things that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, perform without fail. What are these five? They cause sentient beings, without distinction of earlier or later, to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. They confer empowerment upon the hearers who have accumulated wholesome roots, empowering them as regents. They establish father and mother in the truth. They display the great miraculous performance at Śrāvastī. And they tame all those whom a buddha is to tame.

Reflecting on where the previous perfectly and completely awakened buddhas had displayed the great miraculous performance, the Blessed One saw that it was at Śrāvastī. And reflecting on how much time it would take for the great assembly of people to comprehend it fully, he knew it would be after seven days had passed. He then declared to the king of Kosala, Prasenajit: 'Great King, go and make the necessary arrangements and preparations.' 'Blessed One, how much time?' 'Great King, seven days.'"

Then the king of Kosala, Prasenajit prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, withdrew from the presence of the Blessed One, and went to the non-Buddhists and said: "The Blessed One will display the great miraculous performance in seven days. Whatever preparations and arrangements you need to make, do so."

The non-Buddhists deliberated among themselves: "Friends, the ascetic Gautama will either flee or he will seek allies. If he seeks allies, how are we to counter him?" They said to one another: "Friends, the ascetic Gautama will certainly seek allies. So if that is indeed what happens, we too shall seek allies."

Now at that time in the city of Kuśa there lived a wanderer called Supriya — old, bent, and worn — who was honored, attended upon, venerated, respected, and revered as an arhat by the warriors of the city of Kuśa. Having conferred among themselves, the non-Buddhists went to him and said: "Supriya, you and we are fellow practitioners of the holy life. We implore you: be an ally to us against the ascetic Gautama in the contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities." He replied:

"Friends, you have done wrong in challenging the ascetic Gautama to a contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities. Why? Because his miraculous power is great, his might is great." "How do you know this?" "It is a well-founded assertion. What reasoning supports it?"

"Friends, during the time when the ascetic Gautama had not yet appeared in the world, I used to dwell by day on the bank of the great lake called Anavatapta, and after taking my alms-round I would go to the great lake Anavatapta to eat. There, as I sat in one quarter, the gods dwelling at Anavatapta would pour water over me and offer it as a gift. Yet when the ascetic Gautama appeared in the world, his foremost śrāvaka — the one called Śāriputra, the one who urges the ascetic's monks — would come to the great lake Anavatapta carrying a cloth-fan. Those same gods dwelling at Anavatapta would wash that cloth-fan of his and present it as an offering, and they would then pour the water from the washing upon their own heads. For this reason, you have done wrong in challenging one whose very disciple is so incomparably exalted above us — you have done wrong in challenging him to a contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities."

The non-Buddhists said among themselves, "This one too is on his side; let us go and seek others elsewhere." Then, treating him with customary shows of respect while inwardly dissembling, they departed. They sat down in another secluded place and deliberated: "Friends, how should we go about seeking other allies?"

Some of them said, "In the city's pleasure grove there dwells a great one possessed of the five higher knowledges. Go to him — he will become our ally." Others said, "He will not be able to help. But in the forest of ascetics there dwells a great one called the Great Ascetic who possesses the five higher knowledges. Go to him — he will become our ally."

Now at that time, in a mountain valley adorned with forests of many kinds of trees, lovely with springs of water, flowers, fruits, and roots in abundance, and beautified with streams and lakes, there lived some five hundred seers, most of whom possessed the five higher knowledges. Among them, one seer possessing the five higher knowledges had come to the vicinity of the city, and as he wandered about, he happened to come to where those non-Buddhists were gathered. They greeted him with the customary welcome, saying "Well come!" and asked him, "Where have you come from?" He told them all that had transpired. They felt heartened and went along with him. After taking mutual delight in one another's company and resting from the weariness of the road, they said: "Friends, you and we are fellow practitioners of the holy life. Since we are challenging the ascetic Gautama to a contest of the miraculous display of superhuman qualities, please be our ally as well." The seers replied: "Very well, let it be so — but first, show us a sign."

Those non-Buddhists departed, having pleased the seers with respectful and agreeable speech.

Now, in that same period, a younger brother of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala — a young prince by the name of Nagnaja — adorned with garlands of scent and flowers, had passed below the royal palace on his way down, when one of the king's consorts, from the upper terrace of a fine chamber above, dropped a flower garland which fell upon his body. Another person saw this. Since in the world there are those who are friendly, those who are hostile, and those who are indifferent, that person reported it to a minister. The minister then informed the king: "Majesty, the young prince Nagnaja has been intimate with the royal consort."

Since kings act without proper investigation, the king issued an order to his ministers: "Wise ones, dispatch the young prince Nagnaja at once and have him rendered without hands and feet." They dragged him to the marketplace, cut off his hands and feet, and left him there, while his kinsmen, their eyes filled with tears, and great crowds of other people as well, all gathered around him and sat watching.

It was then that some tīrthikas arrived in that same place. His kinsmen addressed them and asked: "Noble ones, please make a truth declaration so that the limbs and members of the young prince Nagnaja may be restored to what they were before." At that, the tīrthikas, having no confidence, rose up and departed without saying a word.

It was then that the venerable Ānanda, while wandering on his alms round, came to that place. His kinsmen said to him: "Noble Ānanda, please make a truth declaration so that the limbs and members of the young prince Nagnaja may be restored to what they were before." He replied: "Friends, I will go and ask the Blessed One." At this they breathed a sigh of relief, saying: "Now he is saved!"

The venerable Ānanda went without delay to Śrāvastī, set down his alms bowl, approached the Blessed One, and reported the matter to him at length. The Blessed One then declared: "Ānanda, go and let the kinsmen of the young prince Nagnaja position his limbs and members in their proper place, and then make a truth declaration in this manner:

By the truth and the truth declaration through which, among all sentient beings — those without feet, those with two feet, those with four feet, those with many feet, those with form, those without form, those with perception, those without perception, and those that are neither with nor without perception — the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha is proclaimed the highest; and through which, among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, the state free of attachment is proclaimed the highest; and through which, among all assemblies, multitudes, congregations, and retinues, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's śrāvakas is proclaimed the highest; and through which, among all those who abide in moral discipline, vows, austerity, and the holy life, the noble Vinaya of which the noble ones delight is proclaimed the highest: by this truth and this truth declaration, may the limbs and members of the young prince Nagnaja be restored to what they were before.

And they will be restored to what they were before."

The venerable Ānanda respectfully accepted the Blessed One's words just as he had spoken them, and the kinsmen, having positioned the limbs and members in their proper place, then began to make the truth declaration in this way, from the words "By the truth and the truth declaration through which, among all sentient beings — those without feet" all the way through to "may the limbs and members be restored to what they were before by this truth and truth declaration, through which the noble Vinaya in which the noble ones delight is proclaimed the highest" — just as before. And through the power of that truth declaration, his limbs and members were restored to exactly what they had been before. The crowd of people opened their eyes wide in amazement, and a great cry went up: "Wonderful! The noble Ānanda has defeated the tīrthikas!"

Then the venerable Ānanda led the young prince Nagnaja to where the Blessed One was, and arriving there, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One, "Venerable sir, the young prince Nagnaja is here." Thereupon the young prince Nagnaja bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

The Blessed One, having understood the prince's disposition, his latent tendencies, his elemental constitution, and his inherent nature, then taught the Dharma suited to him. The moment the young prince Nagnaja heard it, he directly realized the truth and actualized the fruit of non-returning, and he also attained miraculous powers.

Then Prasenajit, king of Kosala, heard that the noble Ānanda, by performing the truth declaration exactly as told, had restored the limbs and members of the young prince Nagnaja to what they had been before. Hearing this, he went to where the young prince Nagnaja was, and upon arriving, said to him: "Young man, come — return home." The prince replied, "Your Majesty, I wish to attend upon the Blessed One and shall remain right here." "Very well, do as you please," said the king, and he had lodgings prepared for him within the Ānandavana grove. While he was dwelling there, his scattered limbs and members rejoined one another, and so the place came to be called the Grove of Rejoining — the Khaṇḍānandavana.

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala went to where the Blessed One was, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Prasenajit of Kosala said to the Blessed One: "If the Blessed One would permit it, I wish to build a hall for the display of the Great Miracle along the entire road from Śrāvastī to the Jeta Grove." The Blessed One declared, "Well done, great king — do so! There, without doubt, a great assembly of people will gather."

And so King Prasenajit of Kosala, along the entire stretch from Śrāvastī to the Jeta Grove, had the ground thoroughly cleared and prepared a hall for the display of the Great Miracle. The hall was draped with hundreds of thousands of cloth canopies arranged in tiers; it was sprinkled with fragrant sandalwood water; vessels of sweet-smelling incense were set out; banners and victory standards were raised; clusters of silk streamers were hung; flowers of many kinds were scattered — all so that the place was made as delightful as the pleasure groves and gardens of the gods. And for the Blessed One, he also had prepared a golden lion throne adorned and ornamented with vajra, lapis lazuli, emerald, coral, wish-fulfilling gems, pearls, the crystal andara stone, great blue sapphires, and rubies.

The lay supporters of the tīrthikas likewise constructed six halls of their own, draped with cloth befitting their respective resources, and set out six seats. The tīrthikas then came early, surrounded by their own retinues, and sat there. They sent a messenger to the king saying, "Your Majesty, we are present — please invite the ascetic Gautama."

When the king heard this, he set out for the hall of the Great Miracle together with his queens, his young courtiers, and the people of the palace. From there he said to the brahmin youth who served as his chief minister: "Brahmin youth, come here — go to where the Blessed One is dwelling." The minister went, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and inquired after his health on the king's behalf, asking: "Is there little discomfort? Little weariness? Are you at ease? In good health? Are you in a state of strength and comfort? Is nothing troubling?" Then he said further: "Venerable sir, those tīrthikas have assembled and are present. Please, Blessed One, be mindful that the time has come."

"So be it, Your Majesty" — thus the brahmin youth who served as chief minister received the command of Prasenajit, King of Kosala, and went to where the Blessed One was dwelling. On arriving, he and the Blessed One exchanged various pleasant and cordial words with one another, and then he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin youth who served as chief minister said to the Blessed One: "Gautama, Prasenajit, King of Kosala, bows his head to the feet of Gautama and inquires after his health: Is there little discomfort? Little weariness? Are you at ease? In good health? Are you in a state of strength and comfort? Is nothing troubling?" And he added: "May you be well, brahmin youth who serves as chief minister of Prasenajit, King of Kosala. From Prasenajit, King of Kosala: Gautama, those tīrthikas have assembled and are present in the Hall of the Great Miracle. Please, Blessed One, be mindful that the time has come." The Blessed One declared: "Minister, go ahead — I too shall come." The brahmin youth who served as chief minister departed.

Then the Blessed One, blessing himself just as the king of swans stretches forth its wings, rose into the middle of the sky. Countless hundreds of thousands of living beings opened eyes of wonder and cried out "Aha!" in sounds of astonishment and amazement, gazing upward as he descended from the sky into the Hall of the Great Miracle. When Prasenajit, King of Kosala, saw this arrival, his mind was filled with wonder and faith, and he said to the tīrthikas: "Behold — the Blessed One has already displayed the supreme superhuman miracle-display transcending the human. Now your turn has come: you display yours." They replied: "Your Majesty, with this great assembly of people gathered here, whose is this great miracle — is it the ascetic Gautama's, or is it ours? Whose is it? Let someone determine that."

Then at that very moment, by the miraculous power of Cullapanthaka of the Jeta Grove, a mango tree arose fragrant with the scent of mountain herbs, wreathed in many white mango branches, leaves, and petals, with many flocks of birds giving voice — and he set it to the north of the Hall of the Great Miracle. The king saw this too, and joy arose in him. He said to the tīrthikas a second time: "Behold — the Blessed One has already displayed the supreme superhuman miracle-display transcending the human. Now your turn has come: you display yours." They replied: "Your Majesty, did we not already put this question to you? With this great assembly of people gathered here, whose is this great miracle — is it the ascetic Gautama's, or is it ours? Whose is it? Let someone determine that."

Then at that very moment the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, by his miraculous power, took the wish-fulfilling tree of the gods of the Thirty-Three and set it to the south of the Hall of the Great Miracle. When Prasenajit, King of Kosala, saw this as well, great delight and joy arose in him, and he said to the tīrthikas a third time: "Behold — the Blessed One has already displayed the supreme superhuman miracle-display transcending the human. Now your turn has come: you display yours." They replied: "We did ask, Your Majesty. But now we ask a third time: Your Majesty, with this great assembly of people gathered here, whose is this great miracle — is it the ascetic Gautama's, or is it ours? Whose is it? Let someone determine that."

Then many hundreds and thousands of living beings who were delighted to behold the Blessed One's great miracle-display gathered there, and many hundreds and thousands of gods gathered in the midst of the sky. The Blessed One washed his feet outside the hall, entered the hall, sat upon the prepared seat, and entered meditative absorption in the element of fire. From within the crevice of the door a beam of light emerged and began to burn all the tīrthikas' tents of the great miracle-display. The tīrthikas said: "Your Majesty, now that the ascetic Gautama's tents of the great miracle-display are burning and ablaze, surely if the ascetic Gautama is here in time he will extinguish them." But the king said nothing, sitting silently with the thought held inwardly to himself. Likewise, Queen Vimalā, the noble lady of the kṣatriya caste Yārtsulma, the brahmin soothsayer Jyin, and Nyingpa, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and the female lay practitioner Migdak Dré'i Masa, and many other faithful ones, and some who remained neutral — all likewise said nothing and sat in silence. But the tīrthikas and their disciples became exceedingly delighted.

Then that fire burned away every impurity of the tents of the great miracle-display and then subsided of its own accord, so that — by the power of the buddhas, the power of a buddha, and by the power of the gods, the power of a god — the tents of the great miracle-display stood immaculate, clear, and beautiful. Then again the king, filled with joy and happiness as if rescued from the loss of his own life, addressed the tīrthikas, saying: "Behold — the Blessed One has already displayed the supreme superhuman miracle-display transcending the human. Now your turn has come: you display yours." But they, having no boldness, said nothing and sat in silence.

Then the Blessed One, with deliberate intention, placed his right foot inside the privy, and the earth shook in six ways: this great earth trembled, trembled all around, trembled all around and thoroughly; it quaked, quaked all around, quaked all around and thoroughly — so that when the east rose high the west sank low, when the west rose high the east sank low, when the north rose high the south sank low, when the south rose high the north sank low, when the center rose high the edges sank low, and when the edges rose high the center sank low.

That earthquake stirred the hermits dwelling in the pleasure grove amid the Himalayan ranges. They said to one another: "Wise friends, those brahmins who practice brahmahood equal to ours are displaying their signs — let us go and see them." And having said so, they set out. The Blessed One, seeing that they were to be tamed, spread forth rays of light with a brilliance surpassing a thousand suns, the color of refined gold, so that the entire distance from the Blessed One to those hermits was transformed to the likeness of pure molten gold.

Those hermits then beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One: as beautiful as the disc of the sun rising for the first time; like a heap of refined gold nuggets piled together; with the luster of a mass of kurandaka flowers and a cluster of campaka blossoms; with a voice deep, stable, and clear as a rain cloud, as the ocean, as the finest of swans, and as the sound of a drum — pleasing and sweet to hear; adorned with a treasury of whiteness like the fresh foam of an ocean of milk on the side that falls away, like a garland of pearls, like the root-tendril of a lotus, like a white goose, like kunda flowers, like a mound of crystals; abiding in an inconceivable and boundless assemblage of wondrous qualities beyond all reckoning —

free from the blemish of the swamp of defilement that delights in the joys and pleasures of existence and in the mire of attachment to honor and veneration; renowned as one adorned with the ornament of unsurpassable wisdom, utterly perfected, accumulated over measureless ages; whose two feet are touched by the jeweled sprouts of the crowns of the lord of gods (Śakra, Indra); revered by gods, asuras, humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, mantra-holders, and serpentine beings worthy of worship — in brief, that body, excellent and beautiful, was seen adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and ornamented with the eighty minor marks, encircled by a fathom-wide halo of radiance, his brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns, altogether beautiful to behold like a moving mountain of precious jewels.

Just as a sentient being who has accumulated the roots of virtue sees a buddha for the first time — like one who has cultivated the mind of calm abiding for twelve years, or a childless woman who finds a child, or a pauper who discovers a treasure, or a prince long eager for the throne who is at last consecrated as king — yet not quite like any of these, those sages prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, touching their heads to the ground, and then sat to one side.

The Blessed One, knowing their intentions, their underlying dispositions, their elements, and their natures, taught Dharma of such a kind as would lead them to realize the Four Noble Truths. Upon hearing it, they shattered with the vajra of wisdom the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a substantial self), and they directly actualized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, they rose from their seats, joined their palms and bowed in the direction where the Blessed One was, and addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Venerable One, if we might receive the status of monks — going forth and receiving full ordination — in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, we wish to lead the holy life of brahmacarya in the presence of the Blessed One."

The Blessed One gave them the going-forth and full ordination, and they received his instructions. Through zealous and sustained effort, they came to know this very fifth part of the wheel of saṃsāra — its moving and its still — and to understand that all formations are characterized by disintegration, downfall, dispersion, and destruction. Having abandoned all afflictions, they directly actualized arhatship itself.

Those arhats were free from attachment and desire in all three realms; they were impartial toward gold and clods of earth, toward the sky and the palm of the hand, toward sandalwood and dung. By wisdom they shattered the hollow throat of the cave of ignorance. They attained the superknowledges (abhijñā) and the individual perfect understandings (pratisaṃvid). They had turned their backs on attachment to existence and gain, and on the receiving of gifts and service. They came to be honored, revered, and respected by the gods together with Indra and Upendra.

Then the Blessed One, attended by a retinue of five hundred arhats surrounding him like the orb of a full moon, went to that hall of great miracles and arrived there, and in the midst of an assembly of many hundreds of thousands he took his seat upon a lion throne.

Then the laywoman Rdzuʼphrul len ma went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, she prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him thus:

"Blessed One, please be without even a small concern. I shall display before the tīrthikas the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, the great miracle of supernatural power, and I shall put the tīrthikas to flight. I shall gladden the gods and humans. I shall delight the noble persons."

The Blessed One then declared:

"Rdzuʼphrul len ma, have no concern whatsoever. Although you are indeed capable of displaying before the tīrthikas the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, the great miracle of supernatural power, of putting the tīrthikas to flight, of gladdening the gods and humans, and of delighting the noble persons — nevertheless, these tīrthikas will not summon you to the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma. They will summon me to the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, and so I myself shall display to them the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma. For if you were to display before them the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, the tīrthikas would say: 'The ascetic Gautama possesses no miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma — yet this śrāvaka laywoman, Rdzuʼphrul len ma, one of such great supernatural power and such great might, displays the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma together with us.' Therefore remain seated just as you are."

And she remained seated just as she was. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the novice monk Kulabhadra, the novice nun Amogha, the nun Utpalavaṇṇā, and likewise most of the others who possessed supernatural powers — all were the same.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One thus:

"Blessed One, please be without even a small concern. I shall display before the tīrthikas the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, the great miracle of supernatural power, and I shall put the tīrthikas to flight. I shall gladden the gods and humans. I shall delight the noble persons."

The Blessed One then declared:

"Maudgalyāyana, have no concern whatsoever. Although you are indeed capable of displaying before the tīrthikas the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, the great miracle of supernatural power, of putting the tīrthikas to flight, of gladdening the gods and humans, and of delighting the noble persons — nevertheless, these tīrthikas will not summon you to the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma. It is I whom they have summoned to the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, and so I myself shall display to them the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma. For if you were to display before them the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, the tīrthikas would say: 'The ascetic Gautama possesses no miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma — yet this śrāvaka monk Maudgalyāyana, one of such great supernatural power and such great might, displays the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma together with us.' Therefore remain seated just as you are."

And he too remained seated just as he was.

Then the Blessed One addressed Prasenajit, the king of Kośala:

"Great king, who is it that has requested the Tathāgata to display the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma before the tīrthikas?"

Thereupon Prasenajit, king of Kośala, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One thus:

"Venerable Blessed One, it is I who request you to display before the tīrthikas the miraculous performance of superhuman Dharma, the great miracle of supernatural power, to put the tīrthikas to flight, and to"

"bring joy to gods and humans, and to gladden the hearts of noble beings — it is I who make this request. This will be for the long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness of the multitude of beings, including ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans."

Upon this request, the Blessed One gave his consent to Prasenajit, king of Kośala, by remaining silent. Prasenajit, king of Kośala, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been granted, remained seated in his place.

Then the Blessed One, entering into that meditative absorption wherein he would be invisible from his own seat as he remained in equipoise, rose visibly into the sky to the east and there performed the four deportments — walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Entering into the meditative absorption of the fire element, from the body of the Blessed One, the Buddha, there streamed forth rays of many colors: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and the color of crystal. In the miracle of the twin display, from the lower part of his body fire blazed forth while from the upper part a stream of cool water flowed down; and then fire blazed from the upper part while a stream of cool water flowed from the lower part. As it was to the east, so too to the south, west, and north: having displayed in all four directions the fourfold miracle of supernatural power, he gathered in the display of miraculous power and then took his seat upon the lion throne.

The Blessed One then addressed Prasenajit, king of Kośala: "Great king, this miraculous power of the Tathāgata is held in common with all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

The Blessed One then put this question: "Great king, who is it that has requested the Tathāgata to display before the tīrthikas and the assembly of people the supreme great miracle?"

Thereupon Prasenajit, king of Kośala, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable Blessed One, it is I who have requested the Blessed One to display before the tīrthikas and the assembly of people the supreme great miracle, to put the tīrthikas to flight, to bring joy to gods and humans, and to gladden the hearts of noble beings. This will be for the long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness of the multitude of beings, including ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans."

Upon this request, the Blessed One gave his consent to Prasenajit, king of Kośala, by remaining silent. Prasenajit, king of Kośala, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been granted, remained seated in his place.

The thirty-second fascicle of the Minor Bases of Discipline.

Then the Blessed One touched the earth with his hand — that hand marked with a wheel, with auspicious signs, and adorned with a webbed pattern, born from many hundreds of meritorious deeds, granting relief from fears — and he roused within himself a worldly intention, thinking: "Even if the nāgas were to come bearing a lotus-wood wheel the size of a chariot wheel, fitted with a thousand petals, made entirely of gold, with streams of jewels and dewdrops of vajra, it would still be manageable."

Now it is the very nature of reality that when the blessed buddhas rouse a worldly intention, even small creatures such as ants and worms come to know the mind and thought of the Blessed One; yet when they rouse a supramundane intention, not even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are able to know the mind and thought of the Blessed One.

To say nothing of the nāgas who had taken birth in the animal realm — as the Blessed One touched the earth, they saw that he was displaying a great miracle. They carried a lotus the size of a chariot wheel, with a thousand petals, made entirely of gold, with streams of jewels and dewdrops of vajra, and emerged from beneath the ground. The Blessed One then took his seat at the heart of that lotus.

Thereupon, to the right and left of the Blessed One, a great multitude of other lotuses just like it arose, and upon each of them emanation buddhas (nirmāṇakāyas) took their seats. To the right and left of those in turn, still other such lotuses appeared, and upon them yet others — and so it continued, all the way to the realm of Akaniṣṭha, with emanation buddhas filling the expanse without limit. Among those buddhas, some blazed with light, some shone with radiance, some caused rain to fall, some sent forth lightning, some proclaimed omniscient prophecy, some posed questions, some gave replies, some paced in walking meditation, some sat cross-legged, some stood, some remained seated, and some lay in repose — and through this, a blessing was granted such that even young children could behold the body of the Buddha without obstruction.

Witnessing this great miracle, Prasenajit, king of Kosala, together with the retinue of the queen, the princes, the ministers, the people of the royal court, and the many hundreds of thousands of living beings who had come from various lands, and the many hundreds of thousands of gods in the midst of the sky — all gazed upon the Blessed One's great miracle with unblinking eyes and paid homage to him without cease. The gods dwelling in the sky beat their drums. In every quarter, great kettledrums were struck, conch shells were blown, and all manner of musical sounds arose; some sang and some danced.

Even the creatures belonging to the animal realm felt joy arise in their hearts and called out in many varied sounds and voices, each according to its own kind: horses neighed, elephants trumpeted, donkeys brayed, cattle lowed, and peacocks cried. Joy and great delight arose in all beings, gods and humans alike, and they became eager to make offerings to the Blessed One.

Then the gods scattered divine flowers — utpala, lotus, kumuda, white lotus, and māndārava. They also scattered divine powdered agaru, powdered saffron, powdered sandalwood, and divine garments, and all the humans and non-humans did likewise.

When this great festival arose, the Blessed One himself, in order that those to be trained might understand, declared these verses:

One should strive and renounce,
and exert oneself in the Buddha's teaching.
Like a great elephant at a house of reeds,
one should crush the hosts of the lord of death.

Whoever practices this discipline of Dharma
with care and diligence,
having utterly abandoned the wandering of birth,
will bring suffering to its end.

Then all the remaining emanation buddhas likewise declared these verses in unison:

So long as the sun has not yet risen,
fireflies glow bright in the darkness.
But when the sun rises in the sky,
the fireflies grow dim and their brightness is gone.

So long as the Tathāgata has not yet appeared,
logicians shine bright and stand in the fore.
When the perfectly awakened Buddha illumines the world,
the logicians grow dim — they are not his disciples.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "O monks, the great miracle is about to disappear — take note of these signs."

The moment the Blessed One had spoken these words, the great miracle instantly became invisible. As soon as it vanished, Prasenajit, king of Kosala, addressed the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) with these words: "The Blessed One has now displayed the great miracle — the supreme wonder surpassing all human mastery. Now it is your turn: let each of you demonstrate what you can."

Then Pūraṇa Kassapa, saying nothing at all, passed the matter on to the son of the wanderer Kṛṣṇadeva. He in turn passed it to Vijayaputra, son of Smarā. He passed it to the one with matted hair, disciple of Ajita. He passed it to the one with dark hair, son of Kātyāyanī. He passed it to the naked ascetic, son of Jñāti. And when it came back again to Pūraṇa Kassapa, not a single one of them spoke. Even when the king addressed them two and three times, they simply kept passing it one to another, saying nothing — each retreating into himself, shrinking down, hanging their heads in shame, without a word of confidence, crushed inwardly with dismay.

Then Vajrapāṇi the yakṣa thought to himself: "These foolish men have long been challenging the Blessed One, and so now I must find a way to make them scatter and flee." To this end he sent down a fierce downward wind and a driving rain of such force that the great miracle hall became utterly invisible to their eyes. Some fled in terror and took shelter in the clefts of mountains; some in thickets of grass; some in dense forests; some in the assembly hall; and some in temples.

The Blessed One, meanwhile, remained seated within his own great miracle hall, and he declared these verses:

People seized with fear and panic
mostly go for refuge to mountains,
to forests and sacred groves,
to trees, and to stūpas.

That is not the foremost refuge,
that is not the supreme refuge —
relying on such refuge,
one is not fully freed from all suffering.

But whoever, at any time, goes for refuge
to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
and, with wisdom, truly contemplates
the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones —

suffering, the origin of suffering,
the genuine transcendence of suffering,
and the noble eightfold path
that leads to the bliss of nirvāṇa —

that is the foremost refuge,
that is the supreme refuge —
relying on that refuge,
one is fully freed from all suffering.

Then the Blessed One, having discerned the intentions, latent tendencies, faculties, and natures of the assembled gathering, taught the Dharma accordingly — a teaching such that, upon hearing it, many hundreds of sentient beings attained great distinction. Some directly realized the fruit of stream-entry; some the fruit of once-returning; some the fruit of non-returning; some abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. Some generated the mind of awakening aimed at the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; some aimed at the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and some generated the awakening mind (bodhicitta) aimed at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. The great majority of the assembly was thereby established as those who inclined toward the Buddha, who entered into the Dharma, and who took refuge in the Saṅgha.

Then the Blessed One rightly instructed that assembly with a Dharma discourse, rightly led them to receive it, rightly praised and gladdened them, and then rose from his seat and departed.

Thereafter the disciples of Pūraṇa Kassapa asked him: "Master, please tell us — what is the real nature of things?" In response he told some of his disciples this: "My son, this is the way it is: the world is permanent — that is the true reality." But to others he said: "It is impermanent."

To yet others he said: "It is both permanent and impermanent." To others: "It is neither permanent nor impermanent." To some he said: "It has a limit." To others: "It is limitless." To others: "It both has a limit and is limitless." To others: "It neither has a limit nor is limitless." To some he said: "The life-principle and the body are one." To others: "The life-principle is one thing and the body is another." To some he said: "A Tathāgata exists after death." To others: "A Tathāgata does not exist after death." To others: "A Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death." To others: "A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death — this alone is true; everything else is delusion." And so each was deceived in a different way, with one view after another.

Overwhelmed with shame, Pūraṇa Kassapa hung his head and, tormented by the fire of grief and wishing to cool himself in water, went to a pond. There on the road a eunuch saw him and spoke these verses:

Like a buffalo whose horn-tip has been broken,
you wander along, lusterless — where have you come from so far?
Not knowing the Dharma of the Śākyan,
you flounder about shamelessly like a donkey.

He too replied in verse:

Before me stands the lord of death himself,
and in my body there is neither strength nor striving.
All things rest on pleasure and on suffering —
I am released. I go now to make my joy.
Those who are scorched by the blazing rays of the sun,
their body and mind utterly tormented and exhausted —
tell me quickly: where is that cool and excellent pond
free of weeds, that I may find refreshment there?

The eunuch replied in verse:

O wretched and sinful man, no excellent person you —
have you not seen the superb little pond
adorned like a lotus lake with geese,
whose water is wholly pure as glacial streams?

He replied again in verse:

You are neither a man nor a human woman.
Give me a sign, show me the way,
to that pond filled with good water, cool water —
for I go there to cool my burning.

Then, turning off the road and leaving his companion behind, Pūraṇa Kassapa went to the bank of the pond, tied around his neck a clay pot filled with sand, and sank beneath the water. There and then his time was spent.

Thereafter his disciples asked one another: "Did any of you see the Master?" They replied: "We did not see him." "Who among you received a final teaching from the Master?" At that, some said: "O wise ones, our Master taught us: 'The world is permanent — this alone is true; everything else is delusion.'" Others said: "We were taught: 'It is impermanent.'" Yet others said: "We were taught: 'It is both permanent and impermanent'; 'It is neither permanent nor impermanent'; 'It is limitless'; 'It has a limit'; 'It both has a limit and is limitless'; 'It neither has a limit nor is limitless'; 'A Tathāgata exists after death'; 'A Tathāgata does not exist after death'; 'A Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death'; 'A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death — this alone is true; everything else is delusion.'"

Then they all said: "O wise ones, see how it is — being taught in such varied ways, we have all come into disagreement with one another. Come then, let us search everywhere for the Master and ask him what the truth of things really is." And so they set out.

Along the road they saw a young woman, and they asked her in verse:

O wearer of the Dharma robe,
you who eat the fare of ascetic practice —
Pūraṇa Kassapa, who departed from here,
noble one, did you not see him?

She replied in verse:

That unfortunate one, that hell-being,
who walks with arms stretched out —
Pūraṇa Kassapa was distracted by the water
and now sits there with his limbs turned white.

They then replied in verse:

O wearer of the Dharma robe,
one who is capable of Dharma practice —
what you have said is not well said.

"Good woman, do not say such things!" She too replied in verse:

One in whom the signs of manhood have arisen —
what wise man in the world
would forever be seen by the world
wandering naked through the town,
examining his male members from the front?
One whose Dharma is of such a kind —
let King Vaishravana
have him cut down with an arrow shot from a crossbow!

With that, they went away without saying another word and arrived at the pool. There they saw him — his completing vessel filled with sand and tied around his neck — dead, his time having passed. Those among them who had wished to take up the training said, "This one truly has it right; all the others are confused," and they too tied vessels filled with sand around their necks and died on the spot. The remainder turned back and went to dwell in the borderlands.

Now, when the Blessed One — the peerless tamer of persons, who turns the wheel without obstruction by the power of the unimpeded, who had fully awakened to unsurpassed and perfect awakening and was turning the wheel of Dharma — when all the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) challenged him to a contest of superhuman miracles, miracles of superhuman Dharma surpassing that of ordinary people, the Blessed One utterly defeated them all, turned their backs, and left them without confidence, and they came to dwell in the borderland regions. There the monks became uncertain, and they asked: "Venerable one, the Blessed One, having fully awakened to unsurpassed and perfect awakening, challenged all the non-Buddhists to a contest of superhuman miracles surpassing ordinary human Dharma, utterly defeated them all, turned their backs, and left them without confidence — we have witnessed this. We marvel at it greatly."

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, now I am free from attachment, free from aversion, free from delusion, fully liberated from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation — omniscient, knowing all aspects, having mastery over all that is to be known, the peerless tamer of persons. Having fully awakened to unsurpassed and perfect awakening, I utterly defeated all the non-Buddhists, turned their backs, and left them without confidence. What is so wondrous about that? In times past, when I was not yet free from attachment, not yet free from aversion, not yet free from delusion — not yet liberated from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation — even then, I defeated these six teachers together with their retinues, turned their backs, left them without confidence, routed them, and drove them to dwell in the borderland regions. Listen well to that account and take it to heart.

"Monks, long ago in times past, in a land called Uttarakuru, there was a king named Janaka — a passage beginning with 'whose kingdom was prosperous and flourishing' and ending with 'he came to undertake' — and so forth in full. Then King Janaka took as his queen a woman who was beautiful, lovely, and fair to look upon. He sported with her, delighted in her, and enjoyed her company. In time, a being entered into the queen's womb, and when nine months had gradually elapsed, she gave birth to a boy who was beautiful, lovely, and fair to look upon. When that boy was born, the regions of Uttarakuru became rich in good harvests, food, and drink in abundance, and the gods sent rain at the proper times, and the winds arose seasonably, so that food and drink were ever plentiful. Then a great birth-festival was held for the young prince,

When the king was pondering what name to give the young prince, he reflected that at the time of the prince's birth, food and drink in the region had become plentifully abundant. For that reason he gave the young prince the name Abundant Food and Drink. The young prince was then entrusted to the care of eight wet-nurses. When he had grown older, he was set to learning letters, and before long he had mastered them completely. In the crafts appropriate to his lineage as well, he became proficient in no long time — all of which should be told in full, as described above. That young prince too was brave, unfaltering, and ferociously fierce.

Then the queen, made proud by her son, became thoroughly disobedient to the king, his father, and took to thwarting him. By that cause the king was afflicted with displeasure. When the ministers perceived his displeasure, they said to him, "Sire, why have you become displeased?" The king said, "My queen, made proud by her son, no longer obeys my commands at all and takes to thwarting me. That is why I have become displeased."

Then the ministers said, "Sire, if she will not act according to your commands, we shall take another queen, and that one will be brought under control, while you, Sire, will once again enjoy happiness together with another." The king said, "From where shall she be taken?" The ministers said, "We shall take her from the king of the south." The king said, "If he and I are not friends, how can she be taken from there?" A minister said, "This southern king, if allied through marriage from youth, will become a friend. Therefore let your Majesty be at ease and leave no care for this — we shall accomplish it."

Then the ministers went directly to that southern king, and they pleased him greatly. He said to them, "I shall make a pledge and give my daughter, but only if a certain nephew of mine is given the means of succession to the throne — if that is so, then I shall give her." They replied, "So it shall be done." The king said, "First, proceed accordingly with that king — and if he is able to fulfill the pledge as made, then she shall be given thereafter."

Then the ministers bowed to him and said, "Sire, regarding the granting of the means to act as regent, since it has been made the trust of the ministers, should there be a nephew of yours, he will certainly be given the regency." And thus it was obtained. The southern king accepted her as his bride with great festivity, and together with that king he sported, rejoiced, and enjoyed delight.

Then that queen, being exceedingly devoted and careful, so greatly pleased the noble king that the king said to her, "What boon shall I grant you?" She joined her palms together and said, "If the Sire would grant me an opportunity, then let the son I have borne be given the regency." The moment the king heard those words, he was struck as though pierced by a weapon, and he fell silent. He thought to himself: I opened the way to grant her a boon, and she has now made such a request of me. And yet this son of mine, Abundant Food and Drink, is brave and diligent, fair of form and lovely to look upon, born fittingly of noble lineage, my one and only son — how then could I send him away and grant the means of kingship to another? What am I to do about this? And so doubt arose and he fell into brooding.

After a while the ministers, perceiving that the king was ill at ease, asked him, "Sire, what are you thinking?" The king told them the matter plainly: "I opened the way to grant the queen a boon, and she petitioned me, saying that if she were to have a son, he should be granted the regency — and on account of this I have become troubled within myself."

Then the ministers said, "Sire, in this too do not be distressed.

"We took this prince from a king beneath the sun who made such a solemn oath — but, Sire, whether a child will come or not, and whether it will be a boy or a girl, no one can yet say. Please, for now, grant the regency to whoever seeks it first."

Then the king ordered that it be done accordingly.

Some time later, the queen conceived and, when the nine months were complete, she gave birth to a son, handsome, beautiful, and lovely to behold. A great birth celebration was held, and they proceeded to give the boy a name. "What shall this young man be called?" The king, Skyed-pa, reflected: "Because even before this child was born he was ardently desired and celebrated as heir to the royal throne, his name shall therefore be Rgyal-srid-la-Mngon-par-dga'-ba — 'Rejoicing-in-the-Royal-Throne.'" He was then entrusted to eight wet-nurses, and they raised him on milk, honey, and clarified butter, bathing, washing, and massaging him; yet even when he had grown to maturity, he was not installed as regent.

Then the maternal grandfather, the king beneath the sun, sent a messenger to King Skyed-pa with the following words: "If my grandson Rejoicing-in-the-Royal-Throne is not installed as regent, I shall arm my fourfold military force and march against you." Upon hearing the messenger's words, the king was overcome with fear and sat in distress and discomfort.

When the ministers perceived that King Skyed-pa was frightened and displeased, they said, "Sire, why do you appear so troubled?" Skyed-pa replied, "The king beneath the sun has sent a messenger on his grandson's behalf, and that messenger has said this: 'If my grandson is not installed as regent, I shall come and depose you as king and install my grandson in your place.'"

Then the ministers said, "Sire, grant the regency to Rejoicing-in-the-Royal-Throne, and as for the boy's food and drink, we shall have it poisoned." But King Skyed-pa said to the ministers, "Do not speak such lawless words as these! Here one may hear of a son killing his father, but not of a father killing his son — I will absolutely not do such a thing."

The ministers said, "If you will not kill him outright, then let us have him dismembered." King Skyed-pa replied to the ministers, "If he is dismembered, that amounts to killing him." Then the ministers, having heard the king's words, said to him, "Sire, what else can be done with him? Let him be banished." The king said, "How can one be banished who has committed no offence?"

The ministers said, "There is no need to wait long or to delay. Grant Rejoicing-in-the-Royal-Throne the regency for now, and first find a pretext to lay fault at the boy's door — then the boy himself will seek his own food and drink."

Then King Skyed-pa waited for an auspicious and fortunate day under a propitious sun and, having pronounced blessings and good omens, granted the regency to Rejoicing-in-the-Royal-Throne.

When the boy heard that the regency had been granted, he thought: "The king has cast me aside — what use is it for me to remain here any longer? They will come to kill me." He went to his mother's presence, recounted the unhappy news, and said, "Please know that I am going to the land of the five kings."

Then she, intoxicated with manifold sufferings, overwhelmed by the anguish of separation from her son, took him by the neck and embraced him, and with a voice full of compassion she cried out and lamented:

He who slept at ease upon the great and fitting bed,
adorned with its coverlet of fine cotton cloth —
my only son now wanders alone upon the bare ground.

How did he lie, with his robe spread out to one side?
He who lay in ease upon the bed, awakened
by the sounds of many kinds of music and song —
how can a body so radiant rejoice in the forest
when touched by cold or burning water?

He who once enjoyed the food and drink granted by the king,
who used carriages and mounts and traveled in the finest conveyances,
who was attended by perfumes, ornaments, and fine garments —
by whose power does he now wander in suffering?

He who, meeting with the world and its crowds of people,
was honored fittingly by hearts and ears alike
with joined palms, the beat of drums, and melodious songs —
where does he now wander, tormented by thirst?

Then the young man spoke:

Who is there who knows only happiness forever?
Who is there who knows only suffering forever?
Who is there who has never tasted unhappiness?
And who is there for whom nothing will ever be obtained?

By the power of change, people know happiness and suffering —
like the wheel of the constellations turning in the sky.
There is no joy without happiness, and no sorrow without pain.
This is the sign that the lord of men follows the way of his kind.

Having made his mother understand these and many other such points, he set out for that place where the five kings had their territories. He arrived near a village, and being tired in body and hungry, he lay down to rest in the shade of a tree.

After some time had passed, a group of scouts from the territory of the five kings came that way on some business for the king, and seeing him lying and resting in that shade, they said among themselves: "This man is so fine of form, so handsome to behold, so tall and firm and well-proportioned, with such a broad chest and long arms — who could he be?" They roused him and asked whose son he was. He replied: "I am called Bzabtung, the son of the king who founded the land of the noble body. I have come with a certain purpose." And he told them all that had come to pass.

Then those scouts took the prince and brought him before the king of the five territories, and presented Bzabtung to him, saying: "Your Majesty, this man is called Bzabtung, the son of the king who founded that realm. His father banished him for such-and-such a cause, and so he has come here." Bzabtung then gave the king of the five territories a full and detailed account of everything.

He also spoke these words in verse:

He is the very son of the lord of men —
this prince who is the equal of a sovereign god,
endowed with form and with all excellent qualities —
and having lost the royal domain, he has come here.

Then the king of the five territories embraced him around the neck, spoke to him many delightful and comforting words, filled his heart with joy, and gave him daughters and lands as well.

And so the two of them passed time together in play, in joy, and in pleasurable enjoyment, until after a while the queen of all the people became with child, and when the nine months were complete, she gave birth to a boy — beautiful of form, handsome to behold, lovely, with a countenance like that of a seated lion, with long arms and a chest like a lion's. A great birth celebration was held, and when they came to give the boy a name, they thought: "My own name is Bzabtung, so let this one be called Bzabtung the Many." Then the young Bzabtung the Many was entrusted to eight wet nurses, who anointed, wiped, bathed, and nourished him with milk, honey, and white butter, and when he had grown to maturity, the boy was sent to school to learn letters.

Now Bzabtung his father was struck by illness. Despite the efforts of physicians, medicines, and attendants, he could not be healed, and he passed beyond his time. When he passed away, the king's daughter was overwhelmed with profound grief, and she wept and lamented.

Then the king of the five territories reflected —

"The wishes of most women are to desire a man, so I shall give her to one," he thought, and he presented her, together with young Bzabtung the Many, to the herald. Thereafter the herald experienced great joy together with her. After some time, a crow was crying out near the herald's house. A brahmin astrologer who happened to be passing by heard it and declared, "Whoever eats the flesh of this bird will become a king." These words were heard by the herald, and he questioned that same brahmin further. He then caught the crow, killed it, and said to his wife, "Cook this crow at once — I will return from the royal palace." And so he went to the royal palace.

Meanwhile young Bzabtung the Many came home from school, hungry, and his mother was nowhere to be seen. He thought, "What have we cooked? What is there to eat?" For a moment he looked about, his mother being absent, and he spotted a crow's head turned upward in a pot. He then cut off the head right there as it sat in the pot, and ate it. When the mother returned, she asked him, "Who ate the head?" He replied, "I ate it myself." She gave him food and sent him back to school. When the herald came home and asked to eat, the crow's neck was missing. "What happened to the neck?" The wife said, "The boy ate it." The herald then ate the remainder of the crow and reflected: "Will becoming a king come from having eaten the whole crow? Or might one still become a king from eating it incompletely?" Doubt arose in him, and in order to resolve his doubt he used a stratagem to summon that same brahmin astrologer. He said, "O great brahmin, you said before that whoever eats this crow will become a king — does that apply even if one has eaten it incomplete, or only if one has eaten it whole?" The brahmin replied, "Even if the parts are not complete — whoever ate the head of that bird will become a king. Or alternatively, if someone kills the one who ate its head and then eats that head, that very person will become a king."

Then the thought arose in the herald's mind: "If I kill this boy and eat his head, and his mother discovers it, she will not allow the killing or the eating. So first let me sound out his mother's own feelings about this." He approached her with many sweet words and said, "Good woman, would it be better if you became queen, or would it be better if your son became king?" She looked carefully from the corners of her eyes, considering, and thought: "If she says it would be better for the son to become king, this man will turn away from me — so no matter what, I shall say what agrees with him." And so she said, "It would be better if you became king."

Now that woman was clever and wise and discerning. She had reflected: "He is nursing a grudge over the crow's head, and is scheming to kill my son. Now the moment has come — I must protect my son at all costs." She secretly told her son, "What you did in eating the crow's head was something ill done. Leave this land quickly! Go to the kingdom where your grandfather rules as king — there you will find your own people. Stay safely there." When she had said this, he fled and made his way into the highlands.

Weary and afflicted by poverty and thirst, his body tormented, he spread out a garment beneath a tree in a pleasure grove near a certain border region and lay down resting. At that time, the one who had rejoiced in royal sovereignty was struck by illness, and physicians, medicines, and attendants could not cure him, and he died — and the royal line was extinguished. It is the very nature of kingship that so long as no other person has been consecrated as king, the body of a king is not removed.

Meanwhile the ministers, others in the king's service, the brahmins, and the omen-readers set out searching in all directions, saying to one another, "If we find some being renowned for great merit, we shall place him upon the royal throne." In their search they came upon, at the foot of a tree outside the city, a handsome youth, beautiful and pleasing to behold, fine-looking as a lion at first sight, who was lying resting there — and although the sun had moved, the shadow of the tree had not shifted to the east, but stayed upon his body.

When the six ministers saw this they were filled with wonder and said, "We have seen no being endowed with the power of merit greater than this one who is renowned for great merit. Moreover, he is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold, and possesses the marks of a great being. He is worthy to be placed upon the royal throne." Having reached this single firm conclusion, they called out, "Young man, rise up!" He rose and asked, "Why do you rouse me? What is it for?" They replied, "To make you king." He said, "Do you rouse a sleeping king in this way?" The ministers asked, "Then how should we rouse you?" The youth replied, "One should be roused by the sounds of song, cymbals, and music — not without them."

When they heard this, they thought: "This one has not come from a low lineage; surely he was born of a high lineage." So they asked him, "Who are you? Whose son are you?" Then that youth raised his face like a lion and declared his lineage: "The son of the one called 'King who Gives Rise to the Noble Ones' is Bha-tung. The son of that Bha-tung is called Bha-tung Mangpo — and that is I."

Then the six ministers broke into smiles and said, "We have found our own youth!" And right there on that spot, surrounded by a great gathering of people, led forward with songs, cymbals, the sounds of music, and auspicious proclamations, he was brought into the city and consecrated as king. Because he had repaired the broken royal line, he was known henceforth by that epithet alone — "the one who restores" — and the name Bha-tung Mangpo, whatever it had been, ceased to exist.

Then, as he began to govern the kingdom, the ministers thought him a mere boy and held him in contempt, so that he had no real power whatsoever.

Later, at another time, King Bha-tung Mangpo went on a tour of inspection of the realm. Having surveyed the villages, the towns, and the mountain districts, he asked, "To whom do all these villages, towns, and mountain districts belong?" They all replied, "They belong solely to those six ministers." He pondered alone: "Whomever I ask — from each and every direction — they all say the same. So it seems I am master only in matters of food and clothing, and nothing else." Recognizing this himself, the thought sank into the ocean of his heart and he reflected: "What is to be done?"

While he was thinking thus, a god spoke to him: "O King, do not be dismayed. In your own realm there is a mountain district called 'Full Mountain.' In it there is a village headman called Gangpo who has a son called Great Medicine. Appoint him as your minister. He will make the realm his own and present it to you, and you will come to have benefit, happiness, and all that you desire." Such was the command.

Then Bha-tung Mangpo sent men to search in the mountain district called Full Mountain for the village headman called Gangpo, and commanded them to find out whether or not Gangpo and his wife had a son. They went and when they found him and asked, he said, "My wife has a son."

They returned and reported to the king: "The one in the northern region is indeed there, and moreover his wife is pregnant."

Then the king sent a letter summoning Gangpo, and with friendly words gave him the mountain district Full Mountain, commanding him: "From this day forward, fully care for and protect the child who is now in the womb of your own daughter-in-law, and see to it that no limb of that child is harmed in any way."

When the nine months were complete, she gave birth to a boy who was handsome, beautiful, and lovely to behold. A great birth celebration was held with whatever was available, and they asked, "What name shall we give this boy?" The mother spoke: "I had long been afflicted with illness, and physicians, medicines, and attendants were unable to calm my disease. But from the very moment this boy entered my womb, my illness was calmed. Therefore I shall name him Great Medicine."

She spoke in verse:

Among all medicines,
my son is the great medicine.
He is a medicine beyond the physician —
and so his name is Medicine.

Then Great Medicine was carried on his father's shoulders to be taken to a pond in the middle of the marketplace for bathing. Along the way he saw a piece of fish lying on the ground. Thinking it was a jewel, Gangpo began to pick it up with his big toe from the ground. Just then Great Medicine said:

Dear father Gangpo, thinking a jewel has fallen,
you fix your gaze unblinking on a piece of fish,
you look at it and then imagine it a jewel.
Dear father Gangpo, understand — it is no jewel.
It is nothing but a red piece of fish to be kicked aside.
Dear Vaiśravaṇa's son, do not act heedlessly.

Then they went on to the pond. Gangpo set Great Medicine and his clothes at the pond's edge and entered the water to bathe. On the surface of a lotus there sat a water-bird, and thinking to catch that water-bird, Gangpo approached it — whereupon it flew away. Great Medicine then said:

A water-bird sat upon a lotus.
The bird took flight and the lotus was stirred.
A water-bird upon a lotus —
dear father, look, it flew away for a moment.

Then on another occasion Gangpo carried Great Medicine on his shoulder to bathe in the Ganges River. He set him and his clothes at the river's edge and entered the water to bathe. He saw a pot being carried along in the current of the Ganges, and upon the pot sat a goose. Seeing this, Great Medicine said to his father:

The Ganges carries along a pot.
Upon that pot sits a goose.
Dear father, look for a moment —
the pot and the goose together, carried by the Ganges.

Then on yet another occasion they again went to the Ganges River wishing to bathe. He set Great Medicine at the water's edge and entered the water to bathe. After a while he saw a fleece being carried along downstream in the current of the Ganges, and upon it sat a crane. Seeing this, Great Medicine said:

The Ganges carries along a fleece.
Upon it likewise sits a crane.
The fleece and the crane together —
dear father, look, carried by the Ganges.

After that, Great Medicine was playing with other children. After some time the children gathered and made him their king. He in turn appointed some as ministers, and he played and remained together with them.

Now, it happened that an elderly brahmin was travelling along the road together with his young wife, who was in the bloom of youth, heading to another region, when the brahmin went off to relieve himself. A rogue then approached the woman and said to her: "Good lady, where has your father gone?" The woman replied, "What do you mean?" The rogue said, "Surely that man must be your grandfather." She replied, "What are you saying?" The rogue said, "Then surely he must be your great-grandfather." The woman said, "He is neither my father, nor my grandfather, nor my great-grandfather — he is my husband." At this the rogue laughed a little and said, "You fool, are you not ashamed to say 'he is my husband' in front of your friends or other respectable people? Do you not see that this blessed earth is filled with men who are like the form of a god? Such beauty as yours is being wasted. Come, let me be your husband and we shall go off together. And if the old brahmin puts up a fight over you, you need only declare before a great crowd of people that I am your husband."

With that, she went off with the rogue. When the brahmin finished relieving himself and rose up, he could not find her. After a while he climbed to the top of a high mound and looked out, and saw her going along in the company of another man. The brahmin ran after them and seized her by one arm. The rogue likewise seized her by one arm. The brahmin said, "Why are you taking away my wife?" The rogue said, "If this were your wife — good heavens, you are deluded! She is mine." The brahmin also said, "She is mine." And the two of them struggled over her right there on the road, pulling her back and forth. Since the rogue was in the prime of youth, he was stronger and pulled her away from the brahmin and seized her.
