The brahmin, utterly defeated, was then taunted by the brahmin's wife with the words, "Arrow reversed!" At that moment, Great Medicine was playing with the children in the wilderness. The cry "Arrow reversed at the brahmin's wife!" reached the ears of the children. The children then said, "Oh, Great Medicine, you say you are our king, yet when your father the brahmin is called out and shamed as 'arrow reversed at the brahmin's wife,' why do you not protect him from this danger?" Great Medicine then went to the children, directed them, and said, "Come, bring everyone." The children gathered them all together and came. Someone asked, "What is the matter?" The brahmin said, "I, who am without allies and of little standing, have had my wife stolen away by this powerful rogue." The rogue said, "He is lying — this woman is my wife." The woman too declared, "This man here is my husband," and affirmed that he was none other than the rogue.

Great Medicine, recognizing that the brahmin was suffering an unjust and dejected defeat, thought to examine the matter, and said, "Good sir, where did you come from when you first met this woman?" The rogue said, "I came from a dyer's house." Great Medicine asked, "And what did you eat and drink there?" He replied, "I had meat, oil, a sweet dish, and beer."

Thus ends the thirty-third bundle of the basis of the Vinaya of minor matters.

Great Medicine said, "If that is so, vomit — and we shall see whether it is true or false." When told this, the rogue put his fingers in his mouth, and when he vomited, nothing of the kind of food described came up.

Great Medicine then asked the brahmin where he had come from. The brahmin said, "I came from a dyer's house."

Great Medicine asked, "And what did you eat and drink there?" The brahmin said, "I ate flatbread, cooked grain, dried curd, and barley broth." When told to vomit, he vomited, and everything he had eaten and drunk appeared plainly before them.

Having seen this, Great Medicine concluded that it was the rogue who had deceived the young woman and stolen the brahmin's wife. He beat the rogue with a stick and his fists, dug a pit deep enough not to collapse, buried him up to his neck, and wrote across his forehead in peacock bile: "Whoever steals a woman in this manner shall be punished by Great Medicine with a penalty of this kind." Then, just as he had done with the woman-stealer, he had some five hundred thieves seized — those who had stolen children, oxen, goats, thread, and the like — and beat them with sticks and fists, buried them up to their necks in the earth, and wrote their names on them in peacock bile, adding: "Whoever else commits theft shall be punished by Great Medicine in this manner."

Now it happened that the six ministers had been seen by the king consuming the country's revenues, and the king thought to himself, "Let me go and see what Great Medicine is doing now." He told his ministers, "I am going to chase a deer," intending to visit the rocky cliff village. He feigned a deer hunt, gathered a large retinue, and set out toward the rocky cliff village. When the rogue buried up to his neck in the earth saw the king coming, everyone around began calling out "The king! The king!" When the king heard this cry he could not make out who had spoken, and though he looked all around, the sound continued. Then one of the rogues caught sight of the king and called to him. The king looked, and when he read what was written on the board in peacock bile he saw: "Whoever steals a woman, steals a child, steals an ox, steals a goat, or commits such offenses shall be punished by Great Medicine with a penalty of this kind." When Great Medicine and the children saw the king coming, they all ran away.

The king observed what had been done there, and his heart was pleased. He thought: "Though these are children, looking at what they have done, there is nothing wrong in it." And so the king had them all released and sent them away.

When Pūrṇakacchana heard that the king was coming, he welcomed him with water-filled vessels, a parasol, banners, victory standards, and the like. The king reassured him, saying, "Have no fear," and then said to Pūrṇa, "Bring your son and let me see him." Pūrṇa replied, "Your Majesty, since the child is very young, I would not presume to bring him before the king." The king again said, "Bring him." So the father brought the boy, and when the king looked at him he saw a handsome, fine-looking, excellent, and courageous child, though still a boy who had not yet fully grown. The king gave the father many instructions and commands, then departed.

Some time later, the king thought, "I shall question Great Medicine to test the full extent of his wits." The king sent a messenger from his palace to the headman Pūrṇa at the rocky cliff village of Pūrṇakacchana, with the message: "Send me here a rope made of sand, one hundred arm-lengths long." The messenger went to the rocky cliff village, came before Pūrṇa, and delivered the royal command: "Send a rope made of sand, one hundred arm-lengths long." When the village headman Pūrṇa heard this, he was deeply disturbed and distressed, filled with fear and alarm. He said, "In all my life I have never seen or heard of such a thing, and now a disgrace like this is being sought from me." He was utterly miserable.

The great physician asked Pūrṇa, "Father, what is wrong? Why are you displeased?" The father said to his son, "Even though I myself have never heard of or seen such a thing, the king intends to punish me by some means, though I do not know what." Then the great physician said, "Bring that man to me, and I will send a reply to the king who sent him." The father brought the messenger, and the great physician said to the messenger, "Do not forget to deliver this my request to the king. We who dwell here in the countryside are rough in mind, unskilled and foolish, so forgive us. If the king commands that it be loaded, we wish to load it. If the king wishes it sent, let a deity send us a sample rope one arm-length long, and from that sample we will measure it out a hundredfold — even a thousandfold — load it onto the rock face, and dispatch it." The messenger went and reported to the king, saying, "Your divine majesty, this is what has been said." The king asked, "Who said this — Pūrṇa, or his son?" The messenger replied, "Your divine majesty, it was the young great physician who said this." At that, the king was filled with wonder and reflected, "This is truly a sign from the gods. It is clear that this one will cause my kingdom to flourish."

Then again, at a later time, the king, wishing to test the great physician, sent a messenger to Pūrṇa at the rocky cliff village of Pūrṇakacchana with the following command: "Send me a load of rice that has not been struck even by a rice stalk, that has not been broken into pieces, that is cooked neither inside the house nor outside, neither by fire nor without fire, that is brought neither by road nor off road, that has not been touched by sunlight nor by shadow, sent neither by a woman nor by a man, carried neither by mount nor on foot." Carrying the king's command, the messenger traveled through villages, towns, and settlements in turn until he came to the rocky cliff village and, arriving there, called out to Pūrṇa. He exchanged various pleasant words with Pūrṇa, and then relayed the king's words in full and said, "The king has issued this command." The moment Pūrṇa heard those words, he was deeply and utterly displeased, and the great physician asked him, "Father, what is wrong? Why are you unhappy?" Pūrṇa replied, "Son, how should I not be distressed? The king has sent a command of this kind." "What kind?" asked the physician. Pūrṇa then described everything in detail just as it had been said. Then the great physician said, "Father, do not be unhappy. I will manage all of it."

The great physician then dried rice in the sun, gathered a large number of men and women together, gave each person a few grains of rice and instructed them to remove the husks with their fingernails without breaking the grains. Those grains, removed unbroken, were to be poured into a pot and cooked on the threshold of the doorway, neither by fire nor without fire — for on its one side it was over fire, and on the upper side it was cooked by the sun. As for bringing it neither by road nor off road, the instruction given to the man was: let one foot go on the road and one foot go off the road. As for carrying it neither in sunlight nor in shadow, the instruction to that man was: tie the pot to the tip of a staff, wrap it in a thin cloth, and go. As for carrying it neither by mount nor on foot, the instruction given to that man was: put a shoe on one foot and leave the other foot bare, and go. As for sending it neither by a man nor by a woman, it was entrusted to a hermaphrodite. That person brought it and came before King Ajātaśatru, and the king questioned the person, who then explained everything in detail to the king.

When the king heard this, he was delighted, and he asked whether it was Jīvaka himself who had devised and sent the message, or whether it had been the great physician. The messenger replied that it had been sent by the great physician. The king then said: "That great physician possesses understanding, resourcefulness, proper method, and correct procedure." Some time later, the king dispatched another messenger with this instruction: send a pleasure grove with a park, fruit trees, and a pond. The messenger went to the town of Pūrṇakaṭcha, and conveyed to Jīvaka the king's words: the king commands that you send something that has a pleasure grove, a park, fruit trees, and a pond. When Jīvaka heard this, he was displeased, and he fell to wondering how on earth he could manage it, having never before seen a pleasure grove of that kind. Then the young great physician noticed that his father was troubled, and the great physician asked: "Father, what is it that displeases you?" Jīvaka replied: "Son, how could I not be displeased? The king has sent this command: send something that has a pleasure grove, a park, fruit trees, and a pond — but how in the world am I to put such a thing together?" The great physician said: "Father, do not worry. I will do whatever will please the king." He then called the messenger and said: "Go back and report to the king as follows: these cliff-side pleasure groves have nothing particularly fine to recommend them; how, then, could they be sent to the king? Let the king send one of the pleasure groves of the royal palace; Father will observe how such a pleasure grove is arranged, learn from it, and then afterward send one modeled on it." The messenger was sent back and duly reported to the king exactly what had been said. The king was pleased and asked whether this had been Jīvaka's own idea or whether it was the great physician who had suggested it. The messenger replied that it was the great physician's message. The king said: "Truly, that young one is possessed of wisdom." Some time afterward, the king sent a messenger of the same kind, with instructions to go to that town of the cliff country and send back a tree that was one year old yet bore both blossoms and fruit. The messenger went and conveyed this to Jīvaka, who fell into worried thought as before and was displeased. Seeing this, the great physician said: "Father, do not be displeased — this matter is not difficult." He then cultivated a castor-oil plant, and when it produced both fruit and blossoms within its first year, sent it off. When the king saw it, he was amazed, and he said to the messenger: "Was this Jīvaka's idea, or the great physician's — whose was it?" The messenger replied that it was the great physician's. "Excellent, excellent!" said the king, and sat in silence, saying nothing more. Some time later still, the king had five hundred oxen driven to Jīvaka in that town of the cliff country, with these instructions: feed them grass to fatten them, then milk them and from that milk produce curd, butter, fresh butter, and whey, and send all of it back. The messenger obeyed the king's command, went gradually to the town, and summoning Jīvaka with words that won his trust, told him: "The king has had these five hundred oxen driven here, and instructs you to fatten them on grass, then produce from them milk, curd, butter, fresh butter, and whey, and send it all back." When Jīvaka heard these words, he was disheartened and said to the other townspeople: "The king is certainly going to have me put to death by some such stratagem — he has issued a command to take milk from the bulls." He sat there deeply agitated. The great physician said: "Father, do not be displeased — I have already thought of an answer, and I will find a way to please the king while also making certain that none of this has to be done."

Then the great physician trained two servants and sent them off, saying: "Go to a place not far from the king in the great city. Find a hollow in a tree, wrap yourselves in cloth, and roll back and forth on the ground as though weeping. And you, boy, make supplication in all directions, scatter flowers, incense, and offerings of parched grain to the ten directions, and say aloud: 'May this father be well, prosperous, and auspicious, and may a son be born to him.'"

The two servants did exactly as they had been taught. They went from the village of Pūrṇakaccha to a place near where the king was born, sat down not far off, and did as they had been instructed — lamenting and weeping and so forth. And the boy called out: "O whoever in this world protects the world, guard my father, and may he be well, prosperous, and auspicious, and may a son be born to him!" King Prasenajit heard this and sent a man to find out what was happening.

The man went and looked, and saw a large-bodied man rolling back and forth on the ground, weeping. He also saw the man's son making supplication to Yama, the king of the nāgas, the gods of rest, Vāsava, and the lords of the gods. When they asked him why, the boy said: "I am doing this so that a son may be born to my father." They went back and reported to the king, and the king summoned the two servants. The boy said exactly as before: "May a son be born to my father." Then the king laughed and said: "I have never heard or seen anywhere that a son is born from a man." Then the boy replied: "Your Majesty, is that not exactly what you yourself have just said?" "Indeed it is." The boy then said: "In that case, why did you have five hundred oxen driven to the village of Pūrṇakaccha in the hills and send word that milk, curd, fresh butter, and whey should be produced from them? If you say that oxen can give birth and bear young, then where have you seen it, and where have you heard of it?"

At this the king laughed and asked: "Whose is this clever mind — is it the father's, or is it the great physician's, or whose?" The messenger replied: "Your Majesty, it is the divine great physician's." The king and his ministers were filled with great wonder.

Then, at a later time, the king, wishing to test him, sent a messenger with a monkey, and the messenger went to the village of Pūrṇakaccha in the hills with instructions: "Tell Gaṅgapa to keep this monkey unrestrained and unenclosed, to let it roam freely without shelter or confinement." The messenger duly went to the village of Pūrṇakaccha in the hills and delivered the order to Gaṅgapa: "You are to keep this monkey, and if it escapes through any negligence on your part, you will be punished most severely in body." When Gaṅgapa heard this he was frightened. He thought: "All of this is manageable, but this one is not. For the king to give me such a command — not even a god could make this easy." He sat there in great distress.

The great physician saw that his father was in distress and said: "Do not be displeased." He had the monkey tethered to a post by day and let it go wherever it wished in the open, and at night he had it surrounded by twenty men, with five men to each torch held at each watch, one man holding each limb, and one man constantly riding on the monkey's back. By such means twenty men kept watch over it with no shelter whatsoever.

King Prasenajit sent a man to observe Gaṅgapa and see how he was keeping it. The man observed and reported to the king: "Your Majesty, the physician is doing it by means such as these." The king said: "If it is guarded like that, it cannot escape — but question one of those men." The minister asked: "Which one should be questioned?" The king replied: "Question the one who rides on top at night."

"When the others have fallen asleep, bring him here." This was said, and the king then had the man who rode on top brought forward, and that man too came, leading the monkey.

When dawn broke, Gaṅgapa said that the monkey had escaped. The man who had been riding on top was terrified, thinking, "My life is now forfeit," and he began to wail and lament, saying "What shall I do? What shall I do?" — sitting there in utter misery. The great physician saw him sitting thus in wretchedness, and he too began to turn the matter over in his mind. "All those measures," he thought, "can be accomplished through clever means — but no means for this one appears to me." He said nothing, for he too was afraid. Yet, pondering a stratagem, he said to his father: "If you are able to accomplish this aim, there is one way." The father asked: "What is it?" The great physician replied: "Only if you are willing to bear some slight humiliation to yourself will the aim be accomplished." Gaṅgapa then said: "Do whatever will ensure that I am not deprived of my livelihood."

Thereupon the great physician shaved his father's head in seven furrows, tattooed his scalp with designs using ink, indigo, white pigment, and the like, seated him on a donkey, and proceeded gradually toward the great city. Everywhere the announcement was cried out: "The great physician is coming!" And this too became known: "He has shaved his father's head in seven furrows, mounted him on a donkey, and is coming!"

When the king and his ministers heard what had happened, they said: "He is learned! He is wise!" — and the praises spread everywhere. And yet: "If he is so excellent, why has he done this unseemly thing?" Then the king, filled with curiosity, went out together with his ministers and retinue to meet the great physician. "Is what they say true — or is it a lie?" When the king and his retinue witnessed the scene with their own eyes, the ministers said to the king: "Your Majesty, we praised the great physician, calling him learned, clear-sighted, and wise — and yet he has done a thing like this. Is it possible?" At that, the king asked the great physician directly: "Great Physician, why did you treat your father with such humiliation?" He replied: "Your Majesty, this is not humiliation — it is homage. I desired to obtain far more from my father than my father had given me, and so I paid him this full and distinguished honour." The king said: "Which is better — you or your father?" He replied: "I am good; my father is bad." The king said: "I have never heard or seen anywhere that a son surpasses his father — for it is the father who makes the son famous, while it is the mother who nurses, raises, and protects him. Therefore I, for my part, have always thought that the father must be the better one." Then the great physician said to the king: "Your Majesty, please understand clearly whether or not the father is truly as I have said." Both the king and the ministers declared: "It is so, and not otherwise." Thereupon the great physician touched the king's feet and said: "Your Majesty, if that is indeed so, then the monkey Your Majesty gave us to guard has escaped. Since both Your Majesty and the ministers have just now praised the father as supremely good — and the father of that monkey is this very donkey here — please accept it in exchange." Then the king and the ministers, hearing how he had deployed such a stratagem through those very words, were struck with wonder and exclaimed: "Extraordinary! How clever, to accomplish both the fitting and the unfitting in such a manner!" Fully understanding this, the king was delighted and joyfully conceived a great happiness, and he adorned him with ornaments of many kinds and bestowed upon him the authority of a minister. To the father as well he gave that clifftop village.

The intermediate summary verse:

The one laden with sand, the fruiting tree,
the castor plant, the ox,
the monkey, and the man who went there —
to him the minister's stratagem was given.

Then, when the great physician had been granted the authority of a minister and reflected with complete ease of mind on what was to be done and how to serve the king's interests,

Throughout the entire city the fame was proclaimed that the great physician was a man of intelligence and skill. Then, after some time had passed, a brahmin spent a great deal of wealth on the wedding gifts for a bride he had taken, and having lived together with her for a long while, he thought to himself: "I have spent a great deal of wealth on wedding gifts for this wife of mine, and now there is no great prospect of wealth increasing, and it would not be good to remain idle at home." So this brahmin, who had memorized many recitations and was versed in the branches of the priestly arts, went to another region in order to acquire wealth through his mastery of learning. As he traveled on, going gradually from place to place, he found five hundred gold coins buried in the ground, took them up, and returned home. He thought: "If I bring wealth home openly she will not let me into the house." For who can know the workings of a woman's mind? The brahmin's wife was fair of form and beautiful to look upon, and being of such good appearance, he thought it quite possible that while he was away she had become attached to some other man. So he waited until nightfall, went to the charnel ground, dug a hole at the foot of a nyagrodha tree, placed the coins inside, and when day broke he went home. His wife indeed had become attached to another man, a brahmin named Karṇabhadra, and at that very moment the two of them had eaten fine food together, anointed their bodies with sweet-smelling perfume, and were lying in bed taking pleasure in each other's company. When the brahmin arrived at his own house and called out for the door to be opened, his wife said, "Hey — who are you?" He gave his own name, and she herself let out sounds of delight and welcome, roused Karṇabhadra from his sleep, hid him under the bed, then came to open the door. She made a show of affection toward her husband, received him warmly as he entered, opened the door weeping, embraced him by the neck, and offered him gifts and honor. She gave him warm food. While the brahmin was eating, he thought to himself: "She has certainly become attached to another man — why else would food like this be prepared so late at night?" Now he was by nature a straightforward and simple man, so she asked him, "Dear husband, is it not a lucky day, or has some festival come along, or a city celebration, that such food as this should appear?" He replied: "A deity appeared to me and told me that your husband is coming today, so I prepared all this in readiness for you." The brahmin exclaimed, "How wonderful! I must be a man of great merit indeed — a deity appeared even in my wife's dream!" He ate the meal, washed himself, lay down in bed, and the two of them spoke affectionately with each other: "Are you well, or have you suffered any trouble?" Then his wife asked, "My lord, did anything of any significance come your way?" He replied: "A little something did come." Then his wife spoke in a roundabout way, saying, "Listen to what he is saying." Karṇabhadra spoke, saying: "If you don't show me those five hundred gold coins, where have you put them?" He said: "Be patient — they are here." "But where have you put them?" He replied: "I will show you tomorrow." Then the woman said: "You and I share one body — why keep secrets?" The brahmin, being simple and straightforward by nature, said: "I buried them outside the city." The woman then said: "Listen here, Karṇabhadra — tell me exactly where you buried them." The brahmin replied: "I dug a hole at the foot of the nyagrodha tree in the charnel ground and buried them there." At that point the brahmin's wife patted and stroked her husband along the way as he went to lie down, and said, "You too are weary — now go to sleep." When she perceived that he had fallen into sleep, she said to Karṇabhadra: "Go quickly and do what you have heard."

Then Karṇabhadra crept out stealthily and left the house, making his way to the charnel ground. Just as he had been told, he took the jewels from the foot of the nyagrodha tree in the charnel ground and went to Karṇabhadra's own home.

The next day the brahmin went to look, and going to the charnel ground he found nothing in that spot. He beat his head and chest and came home, and his wife, his kinsmen, his other friends, and his brothers and sisters asked him what was wrong. He said that he had taken five hundred gold coins and brought them there, and at a time when no one was passing along the road he had dug a hole in the charnel ground, buried them, and gone home — yet today when he had gone back to look they were nowhere to be found.

They then told him to go to the great minister, saying: "That chief minister is learned and wise, skilled at investigation and examination, and able to reason out the meaning of affairs. Go to him for help. Even if it seems impossible, there may be a way — no other refuge presents itself." So the brahmin went to the great minister with tears streaming down his face, weeping, and after offering salutations and wishing him long life, he appealed to him, saying: "My lord, I brought the coins and came there, and at a time when no one was passing along the road I dug a hole in the charnel ground, hid them, and went home. Today when I went back they were gone."

The chief minister, the great minister, sat silent for a moment without speaking, and then asked the brahmin: "In which direction did you place them? At what time? Was anyone seen nearby, or is there any indication that you spoke of it to someone?" The brahmin then told him exactly how everything had happened.

The great minister, thinking to himself that the brahmin's wife had clearly developed attachment to another man and that this was certainly her trick, said to the brahmin: "To put your mind at ease — do not be troubled. If the coins are not found, I will give you the equivalent from my own wealth." He then, having reassured the brahmin, asked: "Is there a dog at your house?" The brahmin replied that there was. The minister instructed him: "Go and invite eight brahmins as guests. You yourself should invite four of them, and you should also have your wife invite four. And then have this said: 'If I return home safely and auspiciously, I have vowed before the god Indra (Śakra, lord of the gods) to give food to eight brahmins.' Then when you bring them home, come first from my presence with this man, and when they go inside, station him at the door. When they are eating, do not let him do anything — just place him in front. And you yourself should watch for the signs: observe which brahmin the dog approaches and around which one's legs it wags its tail. The behavior of dogs is such — instruct him accordingly."

He further instructed him: "Direct it so that the wife serves that brahmin woman, not the brahmins themselves. And the man you station there should observe this: when the brahmin's wife is serving, notice which one she catches the eye of and gazes at with a lingering look, which one she laughs with and exchanges words with, and which one she serves with special attention — make sure these are noted clearly."

After these instructions were given —

The brahmin stationed that man at the doorway. He instructed the brahmin woman: "You yourself call in the brahmins that I have invited as guests" — and then he too called in those he himself had invited. As they entered one by one, the dog looked on. When a certain Raṇabadra arrived, the dog looked at him, then dropped its ears and wagged its tail, and following him inside, let out a sound of joyful recognition. The king's man thus knew that this was the one called Raṇabadra.

Then, when the serving of the meal was observed, the brahmin woman came forward to serve, and she made a slight flick of an eyebrow to Raṇabadra, let her gaze linger on him, chatted and laughed with him in particular, and served him with special attention. The king's man then reported to the Great Minister exactly what he had witnessed, saying, "My lord, this is the state of affairs." The Great Minister, hearing this at once, dispatched the king's man with orders to seize Raṇabadra.

When he was brought before him, the Great Minister instructed him: "Is it the way of brahmins to plunder another's wealth? Return what you have taken." The man replied, "May this wrongdoing be pacified — I do not want it to remain with me." The Great Minister then ordered his men: "Throw this wicked one into prison and press him hard until the bones come out of him." Threatened in such a manner, Raṇabadra was seized with extreme terror and anguish, and cried out: "Save me, O god! I will return it!" He then went to his own house and brought back the earring just as it had been, along with the five hundred antique gold coins that had been bound with it, and presented everything to the Great Minister. The Great Minister in turn restored them to the brahmin.

The brahmin was overjoyed, his mind filled with delight. He then reflected to himself: "All of this — the recovery of my five hundred antique gold coins and the earring that I had lost — is entirely due to the power of the Great Minister. How shall I show him proper respect and repay his kindness? The Great Minister is kind to me, and I must repay him in kind." Thinking thus, he took half of the antique gold coins and went to the Great Minister's presence, presenting them to him and saying, "Please accept this gift." The Great Minister accepted it, then gave it all back to him. Word of this deed spread throughout that city. The king, his ministers, and the citizens all proclaimed far and wide: "This man is endowed with wisdom!" And they thought to themselves: "We are truly fortunate to have a minister of such quality."

Now at a certain time, another man had gone to a foreign land on some business of his own. On his return, he arrived at the bank of a pond and, opening his traveling food-bag, took out his provisions and ate. Having eaten, he went out to relieve himself in the open air without closing the bag. While he was sitting there, a poisonous and deadly snake crept into the food-bag. When the man returned, without checking inside he tied the bag closed, slung it over his shoulder, and proceeded toward the great city. Along the way, a diviner pronounced an omen, saying: "Young man of good family, you are on the verge of losing your life." The man turned back and looked. Then, having heard those words, he was seized with regret: "Why did I not question that diviner?" Filled with doubt, he said to himself — and spoke aloud — "I will not go home until I have gone to the minister, the Great Minister, and asked him about this matter." He went to the presence of the Great Minister and —

"When I was on my way to the city, a diviner gave this prophecy," he said, and recounted those matters in full. "I did not question him at the time, and so it is to you that I put the question."

The Great Minister asked where he had come from, and the man told him in detail exactly what had happened.

The minister thought: "If a venomous snake is found inside a bag, this truly is dangerous — and that is surely why the diviner spoke as he did."

Then the Great Minister, in full view of a great crowd of people, declared: "Open that bag — from a distance, with a stick — and the truth will become known at once." When this was done, from within the bag the venomous creature raised its head, flicked its tongue, and writhed as it emerged. The Great Minister said: "There — that is the danger you suspected."

Thereupon the Great Minister, wishing to inspect the territory, had his four-division army equipped and set out. When he surveyed the villages, towns, and markets, he asked: "To whom do these villages, towns, and districts belong?" The local landholders replied: "This one belongs to such and such a great minister; these belong to those," and so on.

The Great Minister investigated and observed, and came to see that the entire realm had been seized by the six ministers, and that the king who had engendered the realm held authority over nothing more than his food and drink.

Then the Great Minister inquired of the gods of the celestial villages and of the cliff-towns and cities whether they would submit. As to what the king should do, the kindly-disposed gods had revealed this to him: "In the cliff-town of Pūrṇakaccha there lives a son of a man named Gaṅgapa — appoint him, O Great Minister, as your great chief minister. When the territories have been developed and enriched, they will be offered up to you, and at that time you yourself will become a king with dominion over all."

So it had been prophesied. "For this reason, and because you will have need of things in just this way, I have kept you these years in the womb, nourishing you with the provisions of ease. Now, if you are appointed chief of ministers, then — showing the gods' words and your own capability to me — bring it about, by whatever means, that I become a sovereign king."

The Great Minister then bowed to the king and said: "Set your mind at ease, Your Majesty; I shall do whatever is needed to please the gods."

The Great Minister then set the leading figures of those territories, villages, towns, and cliff-settlements at odds with one another, separating them one by one, saying: "I shall act in whatever way makes you favor me." Those ministers, being exceedingly greedy, levied unlawful fees and irregular dues, and this caused harm — the minister made this known to each of them. "If you act according to my words, I shall have it brought to light and see that the fees are levied rightly; beyond that, I shall provide for your ease and maintain you with all the provisions of comfort. By every means, bring about discord among yourselves."

Having thus set them at odds, he instructed them: "Even if the king and the ministers come to hear of it, do not fall under their authority — not until I myself arrive. Say only this: 'We submit to the authority of our chief, the Great Minister, and to none other.'"

Having first applied intelligence of this kind, he stirred all those territories into discord and had it sustained — and so the royal commands were cut short.

Then those ministers presented themselves before the king, and —

In this way, the king Skyedpa dispatched those six ministers together with a great force of fourfold military strength, yet even so they were unable to subdue so much as a single fortified mountain village. Messengers were then sent to the king, reporting: "If Your Majesty himself does not come, we cannot bring these people under control." The king then came in person, yet still not a single fortified mountain village could be subdued. Many were killed in the fighting, and both the king Skyedpa and the six ministers grew deeply displeased.

At that point the people of the fortified mountain villages said to one another: "If the Great Minister were to come here, and we listened to his words and acted according to his authority, our being at odds with King Skyedpa would not truly be our own doing — it is the ministers who have been harming us." Thereupon the king sent a messenger to the Great Minister, saying: "We have been unable to travel to the territories ourselves — please come here." As soon as the Great Minister saw that letter, he came before the king. Upon seeing him arrive, all the local people bowed to him, and he said to them: "Do not be afraid." He had taxes levied in accordance with the law. He gave comfort and relief to the lowly, the destitute, and those without protection. To the country-dwellers and city-dwellers alike he showed equal honor and affection — as though they were his own parents, brothers, and kinsmen — and he embraced them warmly. All the elders, young men, and women of those territories came to look upon the Great Minister as their own son or maternal uncle. He brought joy and contentment to everyone, and in time gathered all the territories together as one, and returned with King Skyedpa to the royal palace. Through deeds such as these, his fine reputation spread even to other kings.

The king, greatly pleased, gave his own daughter to the Great Minister as wife, and together they enjoyed the pleasures of life in full. Then, from another land, a king who had fallen on misfortune came before King Skyedpa. The king Skyedpa, having no desire to receive him, sent him on to the Great Minister. Out of compassion the Great Minister took him in and gave him provisions. Later, a brahmin came, and having borrowed a measure of grain from him, the Great Minister agreed and entrusted it to a creditor, promising to repay on the following day — yet it was not repaid.

Then, at a later time, the king was sitting in a place where many people came to pay homage, surrounded by ministers, city-dwellers, and country folk. He said to the ministers: "A secret — to whom should one speak it? In whom should one place trust?" The ministers fell to pondering this. Among them, one said it was fitting to tell a friend; another said a man should tell his wife; another said his mother; another said his sister and father; and still another said his brother — and so others spoke in those ways. The king then asked the Great Minister: "Since others have spoken as they thought fit, why have you not spoken?" The Great Minister replied to the king: "Your Majesty, I have thought to myself this: a secret is not right to tell to anyone at all — how much less to one's wife. I shall demonstrate this openly before Your Majesty's very eyes."

Then, some time later, the king's peacock went missing. The Great Minister had it found, concealed it in another place, and obtained a different peacock that resembled it. He then asked his wife: "Have you heard, my dear, that a peacock has gone missing from the royal palace?" She replied: "Yes, I have heard it."

The Great Minister instructed his wife: "Tell no one whatsoever — cook this quickly and eat it." She then thought to herself: "Look at how this village man from the rocky crags is eating the king's peacock. My father trusts this man greatly, yet he is doing something that harms the king." Some time later, the Great Minister dressed a prostitute in all the adornments of a queen and had her enter among his women. He then told his wife: "This is a certain queen of the king's — I trust her greatly. If you love me, do not tell anyone." At this, the king's daughter thought: "This woman is consorting with the Great Minister," and in her anger a quarrel arose within her. She went to her father and slandered him, saying: "My father has no discrimination in these matters whatsoever. That man came from the base village people of the rocky crags, and yet he has been made the foremost minister and all the king's affairs have been entrusted to this wicked one — how is that fitting? Let things be restored to what they were before, as in former times." She went and spoke to her father: "How is it fitting, father, that without examining this wicked man's character, you made him the foremost minister and placed your trust in him? For he is in this way intimate with one of the king's queens — associating with her under the title of 'Your Majesty's queen.' Furthermore, he ate the king's peacock. He receives and entertains those who come from foreign lands and supplies them with all necessities. And yet, father, you are always saying that you are very fond of this Great Minister, and that there is no one more pleasing to you than he — let such things not be done, and please find out what the truth of the matter is." Upon hearing these words, the king had his executioners summoned in order to examine the matter.

The executioners then placed a garland of karavīra flowers about the Great Minister's neck, beat drums with a sound like the braying of an ass, abused him with harsh words, bound him, and sentenced him. Men who were like the servants of the Lord of Death, bearing weapons, led him toward the charnel ground — and yet no one moved to kill him. The townspeople and those from the countryside wept tears from their eyes and, suffering as if their own son were being slain, let out cries of lamentation and prayed to the gods. To such an extent had the Great Minister been close to the poor of the royal lineage and had shared out his wealth and given to them — and so those people said to the king's men: "You are killing him for our sake; go back, all of you."

The Vinaya Kṣudraka-vastu, thirty-fourth fascicle.

Now, as he emerged from the city, a brahmin named Mongtul grasped him by the hem of his robe and said: "You once promised to give me a measure of barley — give it and be on your way." At that place the Great Minister spoke in verse:

A king becomes no true friend.
With an outcast there is no fellowship.
To women one does not reveal secrets.
The flesh of a peacock one does not eat.
From the brahmin Mongtul
not even a measure of barley shall be claimed.

Having spoken these words, he departed. Then the executioners said: "Great Minister, if you have such knowledge and excellent discernment, why do you not appeal?" The Great Minister replied: "I do not appeal — but then again, what would be the use of appealing?" They said: "We, your lordship, do not appeal either — but we speak out of necessity, being ourselves oppressed by suffering. And what is it?" They said: "The line 'A king becomes no true friend' — explain it at length." He then said again: "If your lordship would hear a request, please listen for a moment. When I said 'A king becomes no true friend,' formerly — whether it was a village of the gods, a city, or a settlement — there was none who was not subject to him; and as for the meaning of why you spoke those words, you simply did not understand it." Having said that, they went on.

They said to the king: "What great medicine is superior to vitality? Please grant us permission to recite it back." Then the king called them and questioned them. They said: "As for the food, drink, and clothing that were yours — from those you came to rule over this realm of the gods, the kingdom, the army, the treasury, and the troops. If I had done likewise, then without any thought of you repaying what you had previously done for me, the god cast me out to be killed. For that reason I said: 'A king becomes no true friend.'

"As for the saying 'A candāla has no friend' — the god, this candāla bereft of bed and clothing, thought: 'If the king provides me with the means of livelihood, I shall live by that.' And so he came before the god, but the god did not fully receive him. Thinking 'I am impoverished' and 'I am a wanderer from the land,' I shared what I had, and it is on that account that he is now well off. Yet today he has set out to have me killed — and for that reason I said: 'A candāla has no friend.'

"As for the saying 'One should not tell one's secrets to women' — once the king was seated within his assembly and spoke these words: 'To whom should one entrust one's confidence?' The ministers then said: 'To one's father, one's mother, one's sister, and one's companions' — each naming whomever he would speak to. The god then said: 'One should tell it to one's wife, for a wife is half of one's own body, and therefore one should tell her.' Thereupon I thought: 'I shall bring this matter before the god's eyes,' and so in order to test him, I hid the king's peacock and took another peacock to present. From among the royal garments, I took an ornament from a rather shabby one and hung it around the neck of a certain courtesan and left it in a house, and invited the god to look at that courtesan as well.

"The king then had both the garment and the courtesan brought and placed side by side. When both were examined, their marks, color, manner, and shape were identical, and not the slightest difference could be detected in either one. Having thus investigated, the king understood inwardly that I, the great physician, was without fault.

"As for the words:

Do not become attached even to a measure of barley
belonging to a dull-witted brahmin —

when the god sent me to be killed and I was being led away by the executioners, that one gave me a measure of barley. For the sake of that measure of barley he seized the hem of my garment — and it is for that reason I said those words.

"Then the king, all these matters having been demonstrated plainly before him, rejoiced, released me, and honored me with great honor." Thereupon he prostrated before the king and said: "Your majesty, have you seen through the secrets of women? As for your daughter — there is no need for her to come to me. Nevertheless, I shall take a female companion whose lineage, form, conduct, and wisdom are like mine." With the king's leave, he himself took on the appearance of a brahmin — in his right hand he held a water-pot with a bird atop it, he adorned his body with a fly-whisk to beautify it, he clothed his body in the hide of a forest antelope, he painted three stripes on his face — and set out thus for the densely forested mountains and valleys to seek a girl. After some time, it grew dark midway on the road in a certain village. Presently a brahmin asked him: "Where do you come from?" He answered: "From the noble land of Āryāvarta." "Where are you going?" "To the dense forest." "Do you have the acquaintance of anyone at whose house to lodge?" He replied: "No." The brahmin then took him home and entertained him hospitably with generous and fitting provisions.

He also warned the brahmin's wife, saying that she ought not to give herself over to attachment to another man. The next morning, after asking for directions and setting out, the brahmin said to him: "Friend, this house of mine — whenever you pass this way going to and fro, treat it as your own home." He replied, "I shall do so," and departed.

After some time, at a certain point along the road, there was a barley field. There he saw a girl who was beautiful of form and pleasing to behold, of noble family, and possessed of great gentleness. Upon seeing her, his mind became attached to her. He then asked: "Dear one, who are you? Whose are you? What is your name?" She replied: "Sa-ga." "And whose are you?" She said: "I belong to him who provides wood for all the village."

The great physician thought to himself: "If this girl is of fine form, let me first test her intelligence to see what it is like." He then entered the barley field and, raising his arm as if to throw it up, kicked the barley stalks with his foot. At that, Sa-ga said: "Good sir, just as you threw your arm, so too throw your two legs." He thought: "This girl is clever."

Then he spoke to her with a laugh: "Young woman, you are wearing a very large ear-ornament — a ring and a pendant — quite weighty indeed." Sa-ga replied: "Sir, it is to cover both ears." Then the great physician said: "The girl is of fine form, pleasing to behold, and beautiful." Sa-ga replied: "It is by the kindness of the village masters." After sitting a while, he said: "Go to your father's house." The girl replied: "I am able to make a single road into two — I gather the branches of thorn-bushes and block the path, so that people must make a second way around. Go to your mother's house as well." "Where has your mother gone?" "She has gone to the field for seed grain."

"Will you be my wife, girl?" The girl replied: "If the village masters consent." He said: "Show me which road through the dense forest is comfortable and direct." Again he said in verse:

Through the dense forest's tangled paths,
where no thorns snag and no thicket stands,
smooth, comfortable, and straight —
show me from which way I should go.

She then showed him a roundabout road, but herself ran ahead by another way. She removed her clothes at a small pond, closed one eye, and sat there — as if she did not know him, or perhaps did not. She blew one breath and sat still. Again she said in verse:

Leave by the road where you shall eat,
abandon the road where you shall not eat,
and, having left the rest behind,
proceed into the forest of grain.

The great physician then traveled by the road she had indicated. After some distance, he recognized her from afar and said in verse:

One who wears no woven woolen cloth,
who wears unwoven, unspun cloth instead,
the beautiful one with a left eye — from which way
is she who goes to the flower-village? Show me.

Then the girl laughed a little and said in verse:

Here on the left-hand road and trail
where rabbits may be found,
and the blossoms of the palāśa tree bloom fully —
from there, let the brahmin proceed.

He went on and on until he arrived, but when he reached the home of Sa-ga's father, her parents were not to be found. He then spoke to the village masters: "If you will permit it, I shall take Sa-ga as my wife." No sooner had those words been spoken than all the village masters replied with one voice, rebuking him: "You shameless, wretched, begging brahmin! How dare you beg for our Sa-ga, who is like a daughter of the gods! Get out of this village at once! Shall we set untamed dogs on you?" And they drove him away with abuse.

He was chased away by those people and went to her very presence. Sa-ga saw him coming from afar and said: "Welcome — it is good that you have come."

The great physician then reported to her the words the village masters had spoken — that they had beaten him off like a fly.

Sa-ga said: "How did you put it to them, and by what means did you speak?"

The great physician then recounted the exchange just as it had occurred.

Sa-ga then said to the great physician: "Noble brahmin, do not be discouraged. I shall do as you have done in seeking to win a girl. Act as you acted."

The brahmin said: "What else can be done?"

The girl said: "First, come close and enter my presence. Then, in keeping with that agreement, proceed accordingly. Once the agreement is settled, invite them as guests and give a feast with food and drink. After that, whatever it is you need to do, do it."

He went and, just as she had instructed, gave the village masters a feast in the manner of various kinds of food. Then he rose and formally asked for Sa-ga, and they consented, saying: "Today we shall fulfill whatever you have wished in your heart." Having arrived at an agreement of that kind, just a short while later her parents arrived. The great physician and the village masters then appealed to her parents, saying: "This matter should be considered." The village masters then said: "What is there to consider? He is a young brahmin of good form and pleasing to behold, learned in many treatises, and accomplished in the Vedas and their auxiliary branches — he will not fail in anything. Give her to him." The great physician then summoned the brahmin assembly and the girl was formally given in marriage.

On another day, the groom and the bride were called, honored with ceremony, dressed in fine clothes, and made to sit together; then they set out for the house of the one who causes the body to flourish.

On the way there, a certain brahmin gave a feast on the occasion of the fourteenth and offered a full measure of barley as a sacrificial gift. That brahmin then tucked the full measure of barley into the hem of his garment and went to a friend's house, where he knocked at the door.

A brahmin woman inside said: "Who is that?"

He said: "I am your husband's household friend."

She said: "The master of the house is not here, and there is no one else at home; it would not be proper to let another man enter the house in the absence of the master. Go find another house."

Then the great physician thought: "Why is she not letting me in?" and on reflection, he saw that she was letting another man in on one side. The great physician then said: "It is entirely fitting that she would not let me in."

While he was thinking this, just then that brahmin arrived from another village and called at the door. Hearing the sound of the dog, she was displeased and wondering what to do, she let him come in.

Then the two of them went inside together and settled in comfortably.

After a while, the great physician said to the brahmin woman: "Where shall I put this barley?"

The brahmin woman said: "On the ground over there."

The brahmin said: "Mice will eat it." And so he searched under the bedding and in all the corners of the house, but it was nowhere to be seen. Then, shortly after, a storage vessel appeared on one side, and he thought: "There it is."

The great physician then said: "Pour the barley into this vessel."

The brahmin woman said: "My precious goods are in there — how can you pour barley into it?"

He said: "Brahmin woman, that wretched pot — move it into any suitable vessel." And so the barley was poured in there.

The great physician also said: "Otherwise, mice will spoil the barley, and that is why it should be poured in here."

Then the brahmin woman, suddenly understanding with certainty, cried out in fear and alarm: "This vessel too will become wet, and the barley will be spoiled!"

The great physician then said to the brahmin woman: "You need have no worry at all — I shall arrange things in such a way that it will not get wet, and the barley will not be spoiled either." With that, he rose, turned a deer skin inside out and outside in, and hung it doubled around his neck as a sacred offering-cloth. He then said, "The vessel will be dry," and began to heap in ox-dung and pieces of wood.

Then the brahmin woman, clearly perceiving the suffering that had arisen from separation from what she loved, thought, "This will soon be gone," and sent an urgent message to the rat's household, saying: "Come quickly — let it be arranged thus!"

Her father, the moment he heard, went immediately and said to the great physician: "I will buy this item at whatever price you ask." The great physician replied: "Look carefully and take note. What is the arrangement? It is five hundred gold coins — no less than that." Even as he said these words, he was also arranging oil lamps around the vessel. The father thought to himself: "This matter should not be spoken of abroad." He then opened the house door, and with great physical strength lifted the vessel and carried it to his own home.

The very next day, the great physician gave one hundred gold coins to that householder and told him: "Your wife is such-and-such a person" — relating to him those domestic matters — "and therefore you should be on your guard." He then entrusted the remaining four hundred gold coins to the brahmin and said: "Go to the forested and overgrown place and give these to Sāgā, wherever she is encamped. Tell them: I am not a brahmin — I am the great physician, the finest minister of the king who nourishes the Noble Ones, and I have come solely to find this token. Therefore, care well for the girl." Having said this, he flung those gold coins, sent a letter along with them, and went to the court of the king who nourishes the Noble Ones.

That brahmin then went to the forested and overgrown place and gave Sāgā the letter and three hundred gold coins. When Sāgā had read the letter, it said in verse:

Of the four portions due,
if even one is not delivered,
take a wooden skewer unasked
and let it be plunged into him there.

Seeing that one hundred gold coins had not arrived, Sāgā searched for a long while under the bed. Then he said: "What are you looking for there?" The brahmin replied: "Word came from around the palace saying that when the king's men arrive they will cause harm — seize them! — and that is why I was searching for someone to take as a substitute." Sāgā took him up and said to the brahmin: "Whoever such a person might be, if she does not recognize him, let his foot be placed here for a moment first, to see whether it fits or not." The brahmin, intending to test his suspicion, placed his foot inside, and Sāgā drove a long nail into it. The brahmin said: "Why are you seizing me?" Sāgā replied: "Because when four hundred were to be sent to him, you withheld one hundred."

The brahmin was then filled with amazement and thought: "The great physician and this one — they must be demons. Two great demons have assembled in one place." With that thought, he handed over the remainder.

Just then the parents arrived. The letter was shown to them, and it was announced: "This is not a brahmin — this is the great physician, the finest minister of the king who nourishes the Noble Ones." Hearing this, the parents, the girl, and the members of her family all rejoiced greatly, saying: "We have made alliance with a great man. We are meritorious and made pure by this — now our lineage has been received by the great physician." From that time on, Sāgā was attended with the most excellent care in the form of massage, bathing, food and drink, clothing, and ornaments, and before long she became a person of exceptionally fine and beautiful form.

Then the great physician traveled to the city, and the king heard that he had arrived. The king and all the senior ministers were filled with great joy when they learned that the great physician had come.

King Skyed pa said: "How did you come to find her?" He replied: "I found myself a bride." The king said: "What is she like?" The great physician said: "She is beautiful of form, lovely and fair to behold, and richly endowed with intelligence — she has fallen to my lot as my daughter-in-law. And yet, O king, may I ask whether you yourself would take her?" The king then said: "Who other than I should fall to your lot? For you are the foremost of ministers. Therefore, take her with such wealth as will cause her to delight in me in every way." Saying "As the king commands, so it shall be," the great physician, surrounded by an assembly of ministers and accompanied by brahmins, householders, and other invited crowds of people, along with a great multitude of elephant-riders, cavalry, charioteers, and infantry, went to the forested woodland home of Gyopo (the hunter). There a great wedding was performed, and in due course he brought his new wife to the city, where she lived together with him in play, joy, and festive pleasure.

Now at that time, five hundred merchants from the north arrived in the region of Lus 'phags (Uttarakuru), traveling by horse caravan, and came to the court of King Skyed pa. In that place there were five hundred courtesans disposed and suited to the manners, conduct, form, and grandeur of the place — skilled in flattery, adornment, the arousing of delight, in song, in dance, in platforms for display, and in clever conversation — and these five hundred stripped bare of their goods all the merchants who arrived and came there. Having heard that the party of merchants from the north had arrived, each of the courtesans undertook to entertain one merchant each, drew them close, and with them engaged in play, joy, and festive pleasure. Now among those merchants, the one who was their caravan leader was a man of prudence and care, and he did not join in reckless sport with the rest. The one who was the chief among all those courtesans desired that caravan leader, yet the caravan leader would not comply. She then gathered the merchants together and entreated them: "Please bring about a reconciliation between me and the caravan leader." The merchants and the courtesans thereafter arranged a daily round of wagers, so that he might not fall under the power of recklessness. Then that courtesan came herself and engaged the caravan leader in flattery and banter. The caravan leader said: "Since you cannot deceive me, why do you torment yourself?" She replied: "If I were to deceive you, what would a wise man give?" He said: "I will give five excellent horses. But if you fail to deceive me, I will henceforth follow you without a single karṣāpaṇa (a coin of currency) to my name." She then made her scheme and tried with all her effort, but was unable to prevail.

After some time the merchants said to the caravan leader: "The chief courtesan of the city is unattainable — let us behave then as the world behaves." The caravan leader then said to them: "Friends, in a night dream I enjoyed her fully." The merchants spread this tale abroad, and she had the caravan leader seized by the king's men, saying: "You enjoyed yourself with me as you desired — now give me the five excellent horses." The caravan leader said: "You wicked woman, are you saying I lied?" And so the two of them quarreled and went to the royal palace. There the king together with his retinue held court from the opening of proceedings until the sun set in the west, yet not one side was defeated, nor the other either.

The king and all his ministers, wearied and threatened by hunger, said they would deliberate further the next day, and each went home to his own dwelling.

That evening the great physician went home and Sagā asked him: "Your Highness's son — why was there a delay today?" The great physician told her at length the whole story of how the case had proved impossible to decide. Then Sagā said: "That you, with your perfect powers of analysis and resolution, could not settle this case — that is the nature of your being male, it seems." The great physician replied: "Well then, could you settle it?" She said: "Indeed I could. Watch what my mind is capable of." She then said: "Go and have the five excellent horses tied up at the edge of the pool, and have the king and his ministers also assemble at that place and be given a meal. If the courtesan says they had intercourse — the two of them together — then say the five horses are to be taken. But if she says the intercourse took place in a dream, then show her the reflections of the horses in the water. If she says, 'What do I need with these, which cannot be taken?' then say: 'Just as these cannot be taken, so too the pleasure enjoyed in a dream is like them in precisely that way.'" Hearing this, the great physician himself was filled with wonder.

The next day the king assembled and the ministers gathered, and the five excellent horses were led to the pool. There the five excellent horses were tethered and a meal was provided. Then the great physician settled the case exactly as Sagā had shown him, and the king and the ministers and the members of the court, hearing it, were filled with wonder. The king said: "O great physician, this verdict that has just now been pronounced — if there is something that does not perplex me, and my ministers, and other people besides — it has come about through your skillful means." The great physician replied: "This was Sagā's skillful means; it was she who also showed the verdict." At that the king and the ministers and the other assembled people were filled with wonder and said: "How very wise is Sagā, daughter of the carpenter! Sagā is truly intelligent!" And her fame spread through every land.

Then a merchant from the northern regions presented the king with two wild geese as a gift, saying: "Your Majesty, these wild geese are said to be female — but as to which is the mother and which the offspring, that no one has been able to determine." The king and his retinue were once again vexed, and in exactly the same manner the great physician put the question to the carpenter's daughter Sagā and described the difficulty of determining which was male and which was female at length. Then Sagā thought for a moment and said: "That you, one who is a minister — or rather the minister of a great and learned king — you who are adorned with such perfect powers of analysis and resolution, should ask me about such a matter: do you truly not know?" She said: "Take a wisp of soft wool or a tip of lampwick, or the tip of a reed, wrap it in cotton or wool, and stroke both their backs with it. Whichever one cannot bear the touch — that one is male." The next day it was done accordingly, and the king was delighted.

Then at another time, merchants from the south arrived carrying a sandalwood log, but they could not tell which end was the root and which was the top. Just as before, the prince's wife was asked about it, and she said: "Cast it into the pond, my lord, and whichever end sinks — that is the root."

This too filled the king with delight, and when the assembled people heard of it they were filled with wonder. The thought arose in the king's mind: "I should find out which among my ministers is skilled and knowledgeable in the assessment of precious jewels." He had a jewel fastened to the tip of a victory banner atop a multistoried building, and below that building lay a pond. The king made a solemn pledge that whoever could identify that jewel would receive it as a gift. Those who entered the pond and reached up to take the jewel, grasping at it, could not obtain it.

Then the carpenter's daughter Sagā was told of this, and she said: "Look upward, my lord. That which is fastened to the tip of the victory banner — it is only its reflection appearing in the water below. One must take it from the tip of the banner itself." The next day it was done accordingly, and the king asked: "Whose solution was this?" When told it was Sagā's solution, the king was pleased and praised her, saying she was supremely skilled in every respect.

Now the six ministers came to know that Sagā was exceedingly beautiful of form, and they conceived a plan among themselves: "Let us seduce her with jewels, silver, lapis lazuli, gold, coral, rubies, crystal, and the like, and then meet with her alone." But nothing came of it. As they kept speaking of this among themselves, one of them spoke to the physician and said: "You know the custom of this land — if any young and beautiful woman is seduced by another's husband, consider what that is like." The physician replied: "This is the way of all people. Men pursue all women, yet it is women themselves who must be discerning about it. If a woman is wise, it cannot be done."

Then Sagā said: "My lord, if someone were to make improper advances toward such a person, or do her some harm, would that not put them in danger?" The physician replied: "Be careful in what you do." Then Sagā said: "Pretend to say, 'Yes, it is I who will do it,' and then carry it up to a certain height. Otherwise, feign agreement and sit." She herself then sent a reply through each of the messengers who had come from those ministers: "While it is disagreeable to be forced by you messengers in this way, I will offer whatever service has been commanded." She then made a wooden effigy in the likeness of the physician, wrapped it in cloth, and laid it in a bed. She also said separately to each of them: "The physician is unwell. Come at such and such a time, at such and such a time, and let no one come seeking him, but do so covertly." Then she had six large boxes made and placed one in each of her six rooms. When they came, she placed them one by one into the boxes, bound them fast, and the following day announced with a proclamation that the physician had died.

Upon hearing this, the royal consort together with her retinue, and likewise the assembled populace, were stricken with great grief. Lamenting, "We are now bereft of such a being," they plunged into an ocean of sorrow and cried out with voices of compassion. But the carpenter's daughter Sagā had the six ministers, bound well in their boxes, brought before the king, and announced: "The divine physician has in fact passed beyond his time. Here, sealed with his own seal, are his possessions — his lapis lazuli, gold, silk, jewels, and the like." Then the king spoke.

"He died today, and today these were delivered to me." So saying, the king was overcome with profound grief.

But at that very moment the great physician himself appeared from another place, adorned with flowers and smiling, and went to the royal palace. He bowed before the king and said: "Has Your Majesty accepted any marriage contract that I, your servant, failed to approve with loving consent? The king replied: "I have not taken one myself — they were brought here from your own house." Then the physician spoke in verse:

Great king, the divine physician
has departed to the world beyond.
These are his treasures and possessions —
may the lord of men be pleased to receive them.
I, the great king's servant, am destitute,
for I have been separated from my spouse and home.
Having been thus despised and wronged,
they now come to rob me of my wealth.

Then the great physician also demonstrated the excellence of the chief ministers' reasoning and discernment. When king Skyedpa looked up, he saw the six ministers with their hair and beards shaved off and their four limbs bound and folded. He laughed, and said to the great physician: "Great physician, tell me — whose stratagem was this?" The physician replied: "It was Sagā's," and recounted everything in full detail.

Then the king reflected: "How remarkable is the intelligence of this woman! How remarkable her steadiness! How remarkable her discernment! She has reduced these chief ministers to such a state!" Delighted, he honoured her greatly. And throughout all the provinces the fame spread abroad: "Such is the wisdom of Sagā, the carpenter's daughter."

The summary verse:

Just as I too was healed by the physician,
food and reward were given to dog and cattle.
The oath-stone, the musical instruments —
all like a false udumbara flower.
Even the necklace was lost,
and the secret of the mynah bird was told.
This is the verse-summary of the second middle tale.

Now, the king came to know that Sagā was learned and wise, and he thought: "The great physician, endowed with merit, has found such an intelligent wife." Then the king said to the great physician: "If it pleases you, I too would like to seek and take a wife as wise as this for myself — it would be of great benefit for the affairs of the household, and moreover for the affairs of the outer royal palace." The great physician asked: "Where shall I seek her?" The king then said: "I have heard that the daughter of the king of Ngalen, named Menden, is beautiful and lovely in form, and moreover is endowed with mindfulness and vigilance, and has wisdom of the same calibre as Sagā. Go and take her as a bride." The great physician replied: "Your Majesty, if I am to devise a stratagem in this matter, that kingdom is like an enemy beyond your Majesty's borders. I shall first seek out a means." Then king Skyedpa dispatched the minister-envoys, and they set out on the mission.

When the king of Ngalen assembled his ministers and asked them what should be done, they replied: "King Skyedpa has in the past not heeded the royal command, and there are those who would bring this matter under the power of strife. Let him grant a little time first, for us to determine what to do." Having been given that time, they set a certain great date, combined it with a brief interval, and said: "Let them come to receive the bride." Then they departed and informed king Skyedpa that the princess Menden had been obtained for him. As for when she was to be fetched — they reported the reply: "Come on such and such a great date combined with the brief interval."

Shortly after that time, the king of Ngalen began preparations for sending the bride: all manner of food and drink were readied, but every kind of food and drink was mixed with poison, and he dispatched messengers with orders that no one should escape alive from the expedition of king Skyedpa.

When this was learned, the great physician said to king Skyedpa: "Your Majesty, this must not be done in haste. And why is that?

"And why is that? He is a king who dwells beyond the boundaries of the divine realm, one with whom there is constant conflict and with whom this king has long been at odds. Let this be investigated."

The king said: "Whom shall we send to investigate?" The physician replied: "May Your Majesty rest at ease. I have here a parakeet of mine named Caryāprakāśa — clever, bright, and agreeable — whom I shall send there. He will speak with everyone and then return."

"Let it be done." So Caryāprakāśa went there and thought: "Whom shall I approach, and with whom shall I keep company and converse?" He looked all around but saw no one at all. He then thought: "By what worldly convention shall I act?" Presently he entered the royal palace, and looking about, he spotted between the rafters a mynah bird sitting there. He went to her, and the two of them, delighting in each other's company, took mutual pleasure together. He then asked her: "Where do you come from?"

The parakeet said: "I come from the northern king named Śibi. I guard the pleasure grove. My wife — a fine mynah bird, well-formed, gentle, congenial, pleasing, and sweet-spoken — was carried off violently by another, and so I am tormented with grief, wandering to and fro, and have come to your side. Dear one, could you not become my wife?"

The mynah said: "I had not heard nor seen that the parakeet's wife was a mynah bird. Be that as it may, I have heard it said by the wise that the parakeet's wife is none other than a parakeet itself."

Thereupon, speaking and pursuing his intention just so, Caryāprakāśa played with her, made her joyful, and sported together with her in delight.

Then the parakeet Caryāprakāśa, while in the royal palace, saw many foods being prepared — things called the finest honey, and treats called "sorrow-free sweets," and fried puffed grain being stirred abundantly, and many dishes made of raw sugar — and he said to the mynah: "Why are all these being prepared? Might we obtain some?"

Then he spoke to the mynah in verse:

"These many dishes set in heavy crocks,
all being stirred and made ready —
might some of them be ours?
Speak to me softly, dear mynah."

The mynah replied:

"Parakeet, you clever Caryāprakāśa,
these porters laden with heavy loads,
all this that is being stirred and made —
none of these foods are for you.
All of this, for the sake of Skyedpa,
has been mixed entirely with poison."

Then Caryāprakāśa, having sent his understanding ahead, spoke again to the mynah with a skilful stratagem:

"If sounds like these were to spread
in every direction — that Lnalen's own daughter
has been given to Skyedpa —
then whose words would be true,
and whose words would be just as they are?"

The mynah said:

"You clever parakeet, Caryāprakāśa —
that wrathful one will not give her;
those with wicked minds
strive only to slay him."

Having heard all this, Caryāprakāśa turned back. What he had seen and heard, grasped and understood, was as fully accomplished as a merchant who has found and obtained the object of his quest.

For the sake of Śibi he spoke to the mynah:

"I have found a wife just right for me —
a mynah who speaks so gently —"

"So that the king of Śibi may know,
noble one, I shall go."

The mynah said:

"If the lord's son departs,
let the king of Śibi be informed,
and in no more than seven days
let him come to know.
Let the king of Śibi know as well
my lineage and clan
and my resources, just as they are.
I too, for my part, will not betray you hereafter."

Having gone and arrived, the minister Smanchen reported everything at length to the minister of state. Then Smanchen informed King Skyedpa. Upon realizing that the enemy would not come of his own accord, the king of Lnalen armed his fourfold host — his corps of elephants, his corps of cavalry, his corps of chariots, and his corps of foot soldiers — and marched to the presence of King Skyedpa, surrounding King Skyedpa's palace.

Then the foremost of ministers, Smanchen, reflected: "If I cannot break through and fight alongside him, what is to be done? I must drive a wedge." So he sent lavish gifts of every variety to the five hundred ministers of the king of Lnalen and sowed division among them. Having sown that division, King Skyedpa sent an envoy to the king of Lnalen, saying: "It is not that I am unable to fight you — but you and I are kin, and since you yourself are the one who is a kinsman, I will not cross you. Nevertheless, know this well: whether you live or die is in my hands. Even though I have the power, I will not cross you. But if you are in doubt, examine whether those gifts were indeed sent to your chief ministers." The envoy, together with the gifts, was then seized.

That very evening the king of Lnalen departed and went to his own home. When it was reported as true that those five hundred ministers had been put to death and that their sons had been installed as ministers, joy arose among King Skyedpa and those with him. Smanchen too, upon hearing that they had been killed, thought, "I have accomplished such deeds as these," and was glad.

After they had been killed, Smanchen submitted to the king: "Now I myself will go in person and ascertain whether we have gained the victory or not." So saying, he set out with his own army to the territory of the king of Lnalen. The king of Lnalen said: "Come inside the city." He replied: "I will remain right here in this pleasure grove. However, if I am definitely to come inside, I wish to come to the residence of a great chief minister." Thereupon the king of Lnalen grew suspicious, thinking, "Why does he speak in this manner? Surely there is yet someone who is driving a wedge between me and my ministers." He sent word back: "If it pleases you so, stay just where you are."

His ministers then conferred among themselves: "The one who has managed to convey all our counsel to our master's ears — it is none other than this Smanchen. Let us therefore call to mind our old grievance, press the king by all means to hold firm, and ensure that this man does not go back." They assembled and said to the king: "Whoever has devised such a stratagem of mind — that is the doing of this great minister Smanchen. King Skyedpa himself cannot harm the other side directly. Therefore, while Smanchen is here present with us, we others will go from here to King Skyedpa's side." The king said: "Well spoken."

Then, arming his fourfold host — the corps of elephants, the corps of cavalry, the corps of chariots, and the corps of foot soldiers — they marched to the palace where the king resided. King Skyedpa too made preparations. And Smanchen came to know that the king of Lnalen had set out by the main road toward King Skyedpa's territory.

He stayed there for a short while, and came to know that somewhere in a great distant quarter there was a treasury of the king, and that in that treasury there dwelt a princess called Smanldenma, the king's own daughter. Then he took a lady of the inner retinue, settled the escort outside, and straightway entered the royal treasury. He opened it up, took the princess along with the wealth — the valuables and the gold — equipped his fourfold host, and went by a different road to King Skyedpa's presence.

Then King Skyedpa, his ministers, the townspeople, and all the others rejoiced greatly, saying that a great deed had been accomplished, and they performed many acts of celebration and festivity.
