When the chief minister of the king of Lnalen arrived in turn, Smanchen had already taken the princess and the treasury, abandoned those palaces of the king, and departed for his own land. King Skyedpa, for his part, took the princess as his bride amid auspicious ceremonies, and he made merry with her, rejoiced, and lived in delight.

Thereupon the king of Lnalen sent a messenger to the princess Smanldenma, saying: "Find out and report back to me whose stratagem this was, who devised it, who caused this division, and what the meaning of these deeds is. Examine it and send word."

She examined the matter and sent a messenger back. It was a myna bird, known in the language of humans as Chösal, belonging to Smanchen — and it had worked all this out.

Then the king of Lnalen declared: "By all means send Chösal back to me." Chösal was caught at great effort and dispatched to him. But the king, consumed by anger, had it tortured in manifold ways and ordered it killed.

Then Chösal prostrated at the king's feet and petitioned him: "My lord, just as you killed my father and grandfather, please permit me to be killed in the same manner. If that is how it is to be, then kill me thus." And the king consented.

Chösal asked him: "In exactly what way were my father and grandfather killed?" He was told: its tail was bound with raw cotton wool, it was smeared with sesame oil, set ablaze, and released. It then flew up into the sky, set the entire royal palace ablaze all round, and plunged into the water.

After that it went to King Skyedpa's presence. Smanchen also questioned it: "From where have you come here?" It made known everything that had happened, and Smanchen was delighted.

Then the king of Lnalen, consumed by anger, sent another letter: "This one has caused harm in such and such a manner — send it back without fail." It was caught again and dispatched. The king of Lnalen in his rage had its feathers plucked, put it in a cage of bones, and had it cast outside, saying: "Go on your way." A hawk then carried it off.

But Chösal made a petition to the hawk: "Eating me will last you but a single day's meal, whereas if you release me, I will provide you with as much food and provisions of every kind as you need for day after day in the same measure." The hawk, having sworn a trustworthy oath on this, released it.

Chösal then said: "Set me down in a great and distant quarter, at the royal temple there." The hawk did so, and Chösal went to the temple and entered a hollow in it. The next day, brahmin priests came there to make offerings to the deity. They wiped the image clean and were engaged in offering incense, flowers, divine cakes, and torma. Then Chösal spoke: "O brahmins, repeat these words of mine to the sinful king, the king of Lnalen. 'These and these offenses that have been committed — it is I who brought this harm. If you do not act in accordance with my words, I shall come again.' In this manner, day by day, red flesh and sesame and —"

thick rice porridge, a small bowlful, was offered as a divine cake. And from that time on she made plans. She went and conveyed the message into the heart of the king of Lnalen. The king, for that very purpose, took up the making of divine cakes and torma-offerings. Each day, the king, his ministers, and the court attendants came forward and prayed, asking the deity whether such-and-such should be permitted or not, and the reply was always, "Do so."

In this way, much time passed. The mynah bird Chösal grew feathers and became able to fly, and she conceived the wish to leave. She then spoke these words: "Thus to me — you, together with your military forces, your queens, your princes, and your ministers, all bowing your heads, shall come before me. Grant me your pardon and your permission." She conveyed this to the king, and the king did so. All of them, bowing their heads, went to where the deity was, touched their foreheads to its feet, and begged forgiveness. Then the mynah bird soared up into the sky and recited this verse:

The doer is repaid in kind —
look back, and the scorned one scorns in turn.
Here it was one alone, a despised one,
who swept out every last queen perfectly.

Having spoken these words, she then went to the Great Physician. When the Great Physician had not seen Chösal for quite a long time, he asked where she had gone. She told him at length, saying, "I carried out such-and-such schemes." The Great Physician was delighted and gladdened, and told the king, explaining how the mynah bird Chösal had done all this. The king too was filled with the greatest joy and said, "How wonderful — to meet one so purely skilled as you is a mark of good fortune."

Then, at a later time, the king formed the thought that he wished to test which of his ministers was the most capable. He summoned them and gave each one a dog, commanding them: "Within such-and-such a time, make all of these speak in the human tongue." They took the dogs home and tried to feed and raise them, but while they could teach them to recognize food, they could not get them to speak in the human tongue.

The Great Physician took his dog home, went inside, and tied it to a stake not far from his throne. Whenever the Great Physician's food was set out and prepared — various eatables, dishes, and broths — the dog would look on but could not take any. Then he gave it a small amount of something unpleasant, not enough to kill it nor to restore it, leaving it wasted, famished, and thin.

Then the king ordered that all the dogs be brought before him to see whether they had been trained or not. Since those ministers knew no method, they had been unable to train them. The Great Physician too was told, "Bring yours — whatever state it is in," and so he came before the king. When the king looked, the dog was thin and famished. The king asked, "Why is it so thin?" The Great Physician replied, "My lord, I gave this one whatever I ate and whatever I desired." The dog then spoke up: "The lord lies — I am starving; he has killed me with hunger." The Great Physician then submitted, "This is how I made this one speak in the human tongue." The king was greatly pleased.

Then again, at a later time, wishing to fatten the sheep, the king commanded, "Give these sheep delicious food and drink, and make them plump and full of vigor without fat." The five hundred ministers, knowing no method, simply fed the sheep well and made them fat. The Great Physician, however, placed delicious food before them and then fashioned a likeness of a wolf from wood and set it in front of the sheep. When the sheep saw it they were terrified, and so they did not put on fat but became full of vigor.

When they all looked, the others had become sleek in coat and heavy with fat. But the Great Physician's sheep were seen to be free of fat and full of vigor, and the king was pleased and praised him, saying, "Well done — wise man!"

Then at a later time, wishing to test who was truly clever, the king had the five hundred sons of those ministers invited to a garden for a meal. They were eating, drinking, and at their ease when he began a conversation filled with marvels, saying, "Let each of you tell a wondrous tale, or speak of something remarkable you have heard or seen at home." In their friendship they told one another every marvelous thing they had, and spoke of what they had seen at their own homes and in other directions. Then the boys urged the son of the Great Physician, saying, "You too must speak." So the boy said, "In the home of the Great Physician there is a stone — it alone serves as a support — and when it is placed on water it floats back and forth, bobbing and dipping, and performs all manner of tasks." The boy then told those at his own home what he had described, saying, "A marvel such as this exists at our house and nowhere else." They took him at his word from then on, and when he told them, "In our house there is a stone that floats and moves on water," they replied, "We have never seen or heard of anything like a stone floating and moving on water." So he and the others wagered five hundred gold coins. Then the youth went to his father and told him what had happened and how he had wagered against them. His father said, "Son, do not show it to them yet." When they came and it was not shown to them, the five hundred gold coins were won. Then the Great Physician caught some monkeys, trained them in music, and said to his son, "Now go to the garden feast. Bring up the earlier conversation, and when they ask you what marvels you have seen or heard or what is to be found at home, say: 'You made me lose the wager twice already. In my house there are performing monkeys — skilled in song, skilled in dance, skilled in drumming.'" He instructed him thus. The boy, weaving this in among other topics, said, "I have seen such a thing and it exists." Then they said, "We have never seen or heard of monkeys performing music." He said, "If I show you, what will you give me?" They replied, "We already gave you five hundred gold coins before. Now you would wrongly and improperly say such a thing again — if you still fail to show us, we wager one thousand gold coins; but if you show us, we will pay you." Having made this wager, he led the monkeys to the royal palace. He drove the monkeys into the king's palace and displayed before the king every manner of song, dance, and drumming. Thereupon they gave him one thousand gold coins. The king too was filled with wonder, saying, "Such things I have never before seen or heard." Then the king, the ministers, and the townspeople all exclaimed, "Behold — in all things, this one alone is wise and possessed of intelligence!" Everyone paid their respects to the Great Physician.

Now in the land of Videha there was a brahmin who had taken a wife of equal birth, and together they sported and lived in full enjoyment. After some time the brahmin's wife conceived, and when nine months had passed she gave birth to a girl who was lovely in form and beautiful to behold. That brahmin had mastered the Vedas and their branches to perfection, had mastered the eighteen branches of the fields of knowledge, and was sharp in mind and wisdom. He thought, "Whoever resembles me and studies and recites in my presence — to such a one I will give this girl."

A great birth-celebration was held for the newborn, and when they deliberated on what name to give her, they named the girl Udumbārikā. She was nursed and raised until she grew up.

Now another brahmin had a son who was ugly in complexion, unpleasant in form, swarthy in colour, and inauspicious in marks — one who bore the eighteen inauspicious signs. From the very moment of his birth, even his own parents, finding him so unattractive and displeasing, gave him a name that reflected his ugly appearance. He was nursed and raised until he grew older, but his father, thinking it shameful to teach a son of such ugly appearance and feeling it would not be worthwhile, did not teach him.

When the ugly boy had grown older and wished to study, since his father would not teach him, he thought, "I shall go to another region," and went to another brahmin. The brahmin boy rose and said: "I am the son of the brahmin named such-and-such. I have come to you for the purpose of studying under you, and I request that you teach me." The other brahmin likewise granted him the opportunity. Before long, that brahmin had taught everything he knew to the ugly one, and the ugly one had mastered it all. Then the teacher thought: "I made a solemn pledge to give the girl Udumbārikā to whoever would study in my presence and whose learning would become equal to mine. Now this ugly brahmin has studied with me and his learning has indeed become equal to mine. Though he is unpleasant to look at, I cannot do otherwise. And yet, if I give her to him, that will be disgraceful to me and my ancestors, and it will be unseemly in the eyes of the world — other brahmins too will reproach me." Then, deciding he must nonetheless honour his pledge as he had given it, he adorned the girl Udumbārikā with all her ornaments and gave her to the ugly brahmin boy. He accepted her, yet could not bring himself to live with her in happiness.

He then came to his own home, and thinking there should be rejoicing and festivity, he brought her to his own house. But Udumbārikā, whenever she looked upon his ugliness, felt no pleasure, thinking: "I am endowed with good form, while this one has a swarthy complexion and bears all eighteen inauspicious signs — to be joined to a husband like this is a disgrace." Then the ugly one took her and they set off toward his homeland, but provisions ran out along the way. They reached the bank of a certain pond, and both were sitting there hungry, when a companion of his stirred some flour into water with a stick and began to drink it. She too, tormented by hunger, asked him to let her up. The ugly one then took a handful of flour, drank it himself, and told Udumbārikā, when she said she too was deeply tormented by hunger, "Here, at least drink some water," yet when she asked him, he replied to the woman: "It is not permitted by the ancient sages skilled in Dharma for a woman to drink such a water-gruel; therefore I will not give it to you." And he gave her none.

Then, as no rain had fallen, they wandered through a wilderness, tormented by hunger. The two of them found the carcass of a dog, and the ugly one roasted it, ate of it himself, and when Udumbārikā too asked him for some, he again said: "The sages have not permitted this for women," and gave her none. He tormented her with the suffering of hunger, leaving her, like a lizard, to starve unfed.

She thought: "What fault of mine did my parents see, that they gave me to one such as this?" And she spoke at length to her parents in her mind, reproaching them in many ways.

Then, as the two of them wandered on, they came upon a ripe udumbara fig tree. The ugly one climbed it and sat eating, whereupon Udumbārikā said: "Do not eat alone — throw some down to your poor wife as well." He ate the ripe ones himself, but threw down only the unripe ones.

She threw down none of the ripe ones to her, yet she gave her the ripe ones too — but by force. The ugly one then said to her, "If you want the ripe ones, climb up yourself and pick and eat them." Compelled by the pangs of hunger, she climbed hard up into the udumbara fig tree and sat there eating. And the ugly one thought to himself: "A merciless one like me has no merit — what need is there to say he would look after a wife like this? She is not even fit to look at me." With that, he came down from the tree, surrounded the base of the udumbara fig with thorny branches, and abandoned her there and went away.

Then it is further told. The two of them walked on through the forest and saw a ripe udumbara fig tree. He climbed it just as before and sat eating, giving her nothing. The sweet-spoken woman spoke to him, saying: "I too have grown hungry — my lord, give me some as well." He replied to her with harsh words: "Wicked woman, if you want to eat, climb up yourself." She too, pressing herself hard, climbed the great tree. Seeing her climb, he came down, surrounded the base of the trunk with branches, and went away.

Now at that very time and moment, King Udayana had gone out hunting deer and came in that direction. And she was left there, tormented by the suffering of separation from her husband — with no one coming, no one to call out to — sitting alone in the wilderness, weeping most pitifully and piteously. Then, as King Udayana pursued the deer in that direction, he heard her voice — someone in the wilderness, crying out in such pitiful, heartfelt lamentation. He thought to himself: "Who is this, lamenting so piteously alone in the wilderness? I must investigate." He followed the sound and came to where Udumbārikā was. He saw a woman of exceedingly fine eyes, beautiful of form and lovely to behold, like a goddess of the forest. He said: "O beautiful one — are you a goddess, a female yakṣa, a gandharva woman, or a daughter of the gods? What are you? For what purpose have you come to this place?" he asked.

And it is further told in verse:

O you of exceedingly beautiful eyes, enchanting, adorned and covered with every ornament —
With the melodious voice of a goose and anklet-rings,
Like lightning amid great clouds,
Blessed with a shapely navel and fair complexion —
Are you a goddess, a nāga woman,
A gandharva, a human, or what?
Tell me clearly what you are when I ask you thus.
Let me know you in this way.

Then, when the king had asked her thus, she answered in these words:

I am no goddess, no nāga woman,
No gandharva, no human woman —
O great king, I am a human being,
One separated from her husband.

Then he brought her down from the tree, and right there they lay together. King Udayana, the great lord of the earth, that lord of men, was captivated by her. He placed her upon his chariot and brought her to the city, and together with her he enjoyed himself in pleasure and delight.

The brahmin, alone on the road, repented, thinking: "It was wrong of me to abandon my wife in the wilderness and go — I must return and bring her back." And so he went back to where Udumbārikā had been, but she was nowhere to be found. Then he heard from another that King Udayana had taken her away and made her his queen. Hearing those words, his mind was once again pierced with great suffering. He went to the king's gate but was not allowed inside. Looking on from outside, he saw the king's retinue carrying stones to work. He thought: "I will take up stones and go along with these workers." So he picked up stones and entered the king's palace. He looked, and there was his wife, sitting with the king, rocking back and forth a hundred times in intimate closeness. He thought to himself: "My wife is with this man — by what means could I speak with her?"

He said:

The base is made of gold —

set in eights, a delight to behold —
does my lovely one not love me?
The carpenter picked up a stone.
There in that place, when I spoke,
a woman said it was not right to drink flesh,
and even now I remember those words —
she who discards and sets down this one.
The udumbara tree,
and you, my pleasing one, asked me —
born on the banks of the Gaṅgā,
let the carpenter take up a stone;
stirred by a frog with a wooden stick —
tell me now the answer to what was asked.
A woman said it was not right to drink,
and that is why she is set here.
The one of vast learning who speaks on many things,
speak now for the sake of the countless rays of gold —
does my lovely one not love me?
Master, take up a stone;
the unripe ones you threw at me,
the ripe ones you yourself ate.
Even those harsh words I remember.
Here one sits having cast off the owl.
From the mountain peak he cast me away,
and poison too shall I eat, O brahmin woman —
I come for your sorrow.
Let the carpenter take up a stone;
push me from the mountain peak.
The brahmin shall indeed eat poison —
when I wished, you did not wish it.
The owl made its home there.

Then, as the two of them exchanged these words back and forth, suspicion arose in the king's mind. He said: "Goddess, whatever the two of you are saying to one another — I cannot make it out. Speak clearly so that I may hear what is being said." Since the king was under the power of a woman, the woman Udumbārikā told the king everything that had happened, in full detail. "This is my husband. My parents gave me to him as his wife. He is a learned brahmin who knows all the branches of learning."

Then the king said to the goddess: "What is to be done? How is his mind to be pleased? Should you go and stay with him?" She replied: "I shall act in such a way that he will not desire me, that his spells will not work against me, and that I will not come under the power of the brahmin's mantras." She said: "I shall do it thus."

The king then related the whole situation to the Great Physician. The Great Physician said: "I shall act in such a way that the goddess cannot be separated from you." He asked: "How is it to be done?" The Great Physician replied: "This brahmin's power is limited and not extensive, and the queens are extremely majestic and radiant. Therefore I shall do the following: have him made to choose among the queens, and he will not be able to recognize her." Having said this, the Great Physician made the king understand the plan.

They called the brahmin over and asked him: "What is the carpenter looking for? Why have you come to the king's palace?" He replied: "My wife was brought here by the king's desire, and so I have come seeking her." The Great Physician said: "Do you recognize your own wife?" The ugly-featured one replied: "I do." The Great Physician then warned him: "Five hundred queens will be placed before you. If you take hold of any queen other than your own, your body will be cut to pieces with weapons." He agreed: "I shall do as you say."

Then King Prasenajit dressed all the queens in every adornment and commanded them: "Come before me — make sure there are differences in the ornaments." Then, in the place where the path of the food offering was visible, he adorned the goddess Udumbārikā like the queen of Śakra (Indra) and placed her at the head of all the queens, so that she came before the king just as she were surrounded by divine maidens. The Great Physician placed the brahmin in front of the assembly and commanded him: "If you recognize your own wife, take hold of her from among them."

Then, when that brahmin saw Udumbārikā and the other queens all adorned with every ornament, he sat rooted to the spot as though struck by a serpent-charmer's spell. Just as one cannot bear to gaze directly at the open sun, so he sat staring at them all. Then he noticed, following behind the others, a servant woman resembling a demoness, walking in the rear of another queen — and he seized her by the hand, declaring: "This is my wife." The Great Physician said: "If that is she, then take her." And he led the servant woman away, reciting:

One of the finest takes a fancy to one of the finest.
One of the middling takes a fancy to one of the middling.
Even to the stooped one my heart is drawn.
O beautiful one — I am like a demon, and you too are a demoness.
As demonesses delight in the forest of the gods, come hither, demoness!
I too am demon-like, so let the two of us delight together.

Having spoken thus, he went away.

Now, some time later, the king became enraged at his chief minister, the Great Physician, on account of some fault and dismissed him. One day the king went with his queens to the royal garden and there spent the whole day sporting and taking pleasure together with the queens. Then one queen removed her pearl garland of a hundred thousand strands and hung it on a branch of an aśoka tree; and in the midst of her sporting with the king, she forgot that pearl garland of a hundred thousand strands. The king then returned to the palace together with the queen. At midnight that queen remembered that the pearl garland had been left behind in the very garden. A monkey had taken the garland and placed it in a treetop.

Then the king commanded his servants to go quickly to the garden and bring back the pearl garland. When they went there, they did not find it. After a while, a beggar who had gone into the garden searching for scraps of food discarded by others found some such scraps on the ground, ate them, and was leaving the garden — whereupon the king's men seized that beggar and commanded him: "No one else is to be seen here; hand over the pearl garland." He replied: "I did not take it and I have not seen it. I am a beggar; I came in here to search for leftover food." They beat him with fists and clubs and threw him into prison. There, tormented by hunger, he thought to himself: "If I do not devise some stratagem here, I shall starve and die." He then said to the prison guards: "It is true that I took that pearl garland — but I gave it to a certain merchant's son of such-and-such a name." When the king's men heard this, they summoned that person too and had them both bound to the pillory. Then food of many kinds arrived from the merchant's son's household, and when he was about to eat it the beggar urged him to share. The merchant's son shoved him away and said: "You are surely plotting to steal from me so as to oblige me to feed you — I will give you nothing," and ate by himself.

After that, the merchant's son was gripped by intestinal discomfort and asked him: "Go and relieve me" — meaning, attend to him. The other replied: "I am not one to listen to your words — I will not go." Thereupon the merchant's son addressed him with soft and conciliatory words, winning his confidence, and the one with the discomfort was duly relieved of it.

The next day the merchant's son sent word home: "From today onward, bring food here for the two of us." The beggar's comfort improved, and he thought to himself: "Before, even when I wandered through every city I could not find enough to fill my belly — yet now here I have food to eat,

and fine drink to satisfy me — yet a single companion is not enough for me; I shall bring in a courtesan as well." He then sent word to a courtesan that she too was among those who had been carrying off goods, telling her to be seized, and the king's men had her imprisoned there as well. Together the four of them ate fine food and drank fine drink, and he spoke again: "Even if I could not escape from a situation like this for twelve years, it would still be worth it." And so it went as they continued to enjoy themselves — yet later desire arose in him again, and he thought: "This one courtesan alone is not enough for me; when desire is upon me and I want to experience great pleasure, I should bring in a musician as well." The beggar then said to a musician, "This one too has carried off a pearl necklace," and thereupon the king's men likewise imprisoned the musician there as before. So the merchant's son, the courtesan, and the musician were together in the prison, living in comfort and merriment, enjoying themselves fully.

Some time passed, and his companions petitioned the beggar: "Whatever it takes, find a way to free us. If you free us, you will want for nothing — we will see to it." He agreed that he would do so. He thought to himself: "No one else can manage this — only a great physician can," and with that conviction he said to the others: "Nothing but a great physician can get our people out of this prison — no other way have we seen." He then told the king's men: "The son of a great physician is also involved in this." The king's men brought him in and had him imprisoned there as well.

When the great physician heard that his son had been thrown into prison, he thought: "No matter what it takes, I cannot fail to go to the royal palace on his account — and if I do not go, my son will suffer." So he went to the royal palace. Arriving there, he addressed the king: "Your Majesty, a command has come down upon me: my son has done what great wrong to Your Majesty that he has been placed in prison?" The king replied: "A pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand was lost in the pleasure garden, and that beggar says he went there — that is the reason." The physician listened carefully to the full account of their scheme, and then said: "Your Majesty, these persons have not been sought out by anyone else; I ask that those I have named be released." And they were released.

Then the physician went to the pleasure garden. Someone who had previously been present there was asked where he had been staying, and pointed out the direction, saying, "He was sitting at the foot of a tree." The physician looked at that tree and saw a female monkey sitting at its top. He thought: "This creature must have taken the pearl necklace — I must devise some stratagem to lure her down." He then petitioned the king: "Your Majesty, please come here together with the queen." The king came with the queen to that pleasure garden and took his place there. The physician said: "Your Majesty, if the queen adorns herself with ornaments, the monkey will put on ornaments too." The female monkey, sitting there at the treetop, then put on the pearl necklace. The physician said: "If the queen dances," and when she danced, the monkey too sat at the treetop and danced — but the pearl necklace did not fall from her neck, for the monkey watched whatever people did and how they were dressed, and imitated them exactly. The physician said: "Your Majesty, if the queen bows her head and dances, that too would be fitting." The king ordered it done; the queen bowed her head and began to dance, and the monkey likewise bowed her head and danced — and the pearl necklace fell from her neck.

The king, overjoyed, embraced the great physician about the neck, honored him, and bestowed wealth upon him.

Then the six ministers gathered together and conferred: "In former times, and in times before that, the king treated us with honor, held us as superiors, esteemed us, and revered us. Now this man — a dull-witted villager from the crags, come from a family of hungry folk — has cast all of us out from our place of dignity. What is to be done about him?" Then one of the ministers spoke: "In the past, we went against one another separately, and that is what rendered us powerless. Therefore, let us now go together to the pleasure grove. Let us go there, swear oaths to one another, place our trust in one another, and become allies. If we do so, the king will grow fond of us again, and the great physician will cease to shun us and will come to rely on us once more." They all agreed, gathered together, and went to the pleasure grove.

As they set out, the great physician saw them. He thought to himself: "These men have never before assembled all together like this and gone off somewhere — something unusual is being planned." Growing suspicious, he sent a servant woman named Mātarā to follow after them secretly and find out what they were deliberating, what they were saying, and what they were doing.

The six ministers arrived at the pleasure grove, made alliance with one another, and said: "If we rake up one another's faults and expose one another's secrets, we will never come to trust each other. So let it not be so." Another said: "Agreed." Then one of them said: "I have eaten the king's peacock." Another said: "I have lain with the king's queen." Another said: "I too have had such a thought in mind." And thus those six confided their secrets to one another and ate together from one vessel.

Mātarā heard all of this and reported it to the great physician. The great physician then went before King Prasenajit and told him everything: "Your divine ministers behave in this manner — such are their discipline, their cleanliness, and their conduct."

King Prasenajit came to understand and, having perceived all this clearly, resolved to rid himself of them, saying: "Ah — these ministers of mine have acted so improperly! Let them this very day be expelled to wherever they have no power," and so he banished them and drove them out.

The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, what do you think? The great physician of that time and that occasion was none other than myself. The king Prasenajit of that time — that is the monk Śāriputra here present. And those six ministers of that time are these six teachers of today. Even then, serving as ministers, they were driven out and stripped of their domain. And now, after I have fully awakened to the unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening, they have been defeated by my miraculous powers and wonders and expelled to the borderlands.

Therefore, monks, you should strive diligently to rely upon a true spiritual friend — one from whom wisdom, learning, and the highest gnosis arise. Cultivate such qualities as will lead to such attainment.

When the Blessed One displayed the great miracle, bringing the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) to silence by every means, gladdening gods and humans, and delighting noble beings — at that very time, craftsmen residing in various regions, from villages, towns, and palace courts, came to Śrāvastī from all those places, went forth into the renunciant life, along with their sons, daughters, wives, and still others — friends and relatives —

Brothers and sisters searched for one another and came to Śrāvastī. When they met, those who had gone forth said to the ones who had remained behind: "Noble ones, you have come here — but now that we have gone forth and settled here, who will provide for our livelihood?" And the others replied: "Stay right here, and train right here." The renunciants answered: "Very well, we shall do so," and entered upon the training.

Before long, brahmins and householders also arrived, and when they saw what had happened, they cried out in dismay: "All these craftsmen have gone forth — who will do our work?"

When this was reported by the monks to the Blessed One, the Blessed One reflected that for one who holds such an intent — namely, a vessel of such a kind — this would be an occasion for fault. Therefore, considering that from such a stream of being one should not take on conduct of that kind, he declared to the monks: "Monks, it is fitting that those brahmins and householders bring their complaint. Therefore, monks, one should not take on conduct of that kind from a stream of being of such a kind. If monks were to take on conduct of that kind, it would become a transgression." The Blessed One declared: "Do not take on conduct of that kind from such a stream of being."

After some time, another physician went forth and was travelling through the countryside and came to Śrāvastī. The monks there said to him: "Venerable one, please examine and treat this sick monk." But that person replied: "The Blessed One has not permitted it — the instruction was that from such a stream of being one should not take on conduct of that kind. Why then should I treat him?"

When this was reported by the monks to the Blessed One, the Blessed One accordingly granted permission, declaring: "When a physician has gone forth into the renunciant life, let him practise the art of incision and treatment. As for one who was formerly a scribe, let him practise with a reed pen. And when a barber has gone forth, let him practise the cutting of nails."

The Vinaya on Minor Matters, the thirty-fifth fascicle.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī, at the time when the Blessed One displayed the great miracle, bringing the non-Buddhists to silence, gladdening gods and humans, and delighting the minds of many people. At that time, the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of hearers, was held in very great gain and honour. The Blessed One then, reflecting that he should cut off the arising of gain and honour, went to the realm of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Near the white stone slope, among the trees — the pārijāta and the kovidāra — not far off, he entered the rains retreat. There the Blessed One taught the Dharma to his mother, who had given him birth, and to the other gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

At that time, the great Maudgalyāyana entered the rains retreat in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada at Śrāvastī. Then the four assemblies went to where the venerable great Maudgalyāyana was. They bowed at his feet with their heads touching the ground and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana instructed those four assemblies with Dharma talk rightly given, rightly roused, rightly exhorted, and rightly gladdened. With Dharma talk in its many expressions rightly given, rightly roused, rightly exhorted, and rightly gladdened, he then fell silent. Thereupon the four assemblies rose from their seats, draped their robes over one shoulder, and with palms joined in reverence, bowed toward where the venerable great Maudgalyāyana was —

they said to the venerable great Maudgalyāyana: "Venerable one, great Maudgalyāyana, have you heard where the Blessed One has entered the rains retreat at present?" He replied: "I have heard that the Blessed One has entered the rains retreat at the heaven of the Thirty-Three, not far from the white rock called Pāṇḍukambala, near the trees called Pārijāta and Kovidaraka, and that he is teaching Dharma to his mother and to the gods of the Thirty-Three."

Then the four assemblies, delighted and rejoicing at what the venerable great Maudgalyāyana had said, bowed at his feet with their heads touching the ground, rose from their seats, and departed.

Three months then passed for the four assemblies. The venerable great Maudgalyāyana went to where they were. They bowed at his feet with their heads touching the ground and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana instructed those four assemblies with Dharma talk rightly given, rightly roused, rightly exhorted, and rightly gladdened. With Dharma talk in its many expressions rightly given, rightly roused, rightly exhorted, and rightly gladdened, he then fell silent. Thereupon the four assemblies rose from their seats, draped their robes over one shoulder, and with palms joined in reverence, bowed toward where the venerable great Maudgalyāyana was, and spoke to him thus:

"Venerable one, great Maudgalyāyana, please take note of this: it has been a long time since we have seen the Blessed One, and we are exceedingly thirsty with longing to behold him. We wish to see the Blessed One. If it be fitting and good in the eyes of the venerable great Maudgalyāyana, would you please go to where the Blessed One is, approach him, and on our behalf bow at the feet of the Blessed One and inquire: 'Is the Blessed One's discomfort little? Is he free from discomfort? Does he arise quickly? Is he well? Does he have strength? Is he at ease? Is his illness slight? Does he dwell in comfort? Has he become comfortable?' And please also say this: 'Venerable sir, the four assemblies of Jambudvīpa wish to see the Blessed One. Venerable sir, the humans of Jambudvīpa do not possess the supernatural powers and might to ascend to the abode of the gods of the Thirty-Three and come into the presence of the Blessed One to see and pay reverence to him. As for those gods of the Thirty-Three — if they have the supernatural power and might to descend to Jambudvīpa and come into the presence of the Blessed One to see and pay reverence to him — it would be good if you would say: If the Blessed One would be pleased in his compassion to depart from the abode of the gods of the Thirty-Three and come to Jambudvīpa, that would be excellent.'"

When they had said this, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana granted the four assemblies his consent by remaining silent. Then the four assemblies, understanding from his silence that the venerable great Maudgalyāyana had given his consent, bowed at his feet with their heads touching the ground, rose from their seats, and departed.

Then, knowing that the four assemblies had not gone far after departing, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana entered into a meditative absorption of such a kind. And just as he stilled his mind and entered that absorption, it was as when a strong man extends an arm that had been drawn in —

or as when a drawn-in arm is extended — in just that way, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared at the dwelling of the gods of the Thirty-Three, near the trees of white coral, the Pārijāta and the Kovidaraka. And there, not far off, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana saw the Blessed One seated before many hundreds and thousands of divine attendants, teaching the Dharma. Seeing the Blessed One thus seated before many hundreds and thousands of divine attendants and teaching the Dharma, Maudgalyāyana smiled and said: "Blessed One, it is just as it is here — being in the company of many gods, just as with the four assemblies of Jambudvīpa."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought of the venerable great Maudgalyāyana, spoke to him as follows: "Great Maudgalyāyana, it is not that you arrange this yourself. Rather, whenever I think 'I shall come,' at that moment I come; and whenever I think 'I shall go,' at that moment I go. Knowing my mind through my mind, I come and go."

Then the venerable great Maudgalyāyana went to where the Blessed One was, bowed at his feet with his head touching the ground, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana looked over all the divine assembly and said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this divine assembly has gathered here in great variety. Among those assembled, there are those who, being endowed with knowledge of and faith in the Buddha, have passed from the body and been born here. And among those assembled, there are also those who, being endowed with knowledge of the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the moral discipline esteemed by noble ones, have passed from the body and been born here."

And so it was: Great Maudgalyāyana confirmed that this diverse divine assembly had gathered and was present. Among that divine assembly, there were those who, endowed with knowledge of and faith in the Buddha, had passed from the body and been born there. And there were also those who, endowed with the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the moral discipline esteemed by noble ones, had passed from the body and been born there.

Then Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, rejoiced in what the Blessed One and the venerable great Maudgalyāyana had said, and spoke these words to the venerable great Maudgalyāyana: "So it is, so it is indeed, venerable great Maudgalyāyana. Just so — this diverse divine assembly has gathered and is present. Among this divine assembly there are those who, endowed with knowledge of and faith in the Buddha, have passed from the body and been born here. And there are those who, endowed with the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the moral discipline esteemed by noble ones, have passed from the body and been born here."

Then another divine youth, rejoicing in what the Blessed One, the venerable great Maudgalyāyana, and Śakra, lord of the gods, had said, spoke these words to the venerable great Maudgalyāyana: "So it is, venerable great Maudgalyāyana. So it is indeed — this diverse divine assembly has gathered and is present. Among this divine assembly there are those who, endowed with knowledge of and faith in the Buddha, have passed from the body and been born here. And there are those who, endowed with the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the moral discipline esteemed by noble ones, have passed from the body and been born here."

Then at that moment one of the gods rose from his seat, arranged his outer robe over one shoulder, turned to face the Blessed One, joined his palms together in homage, and said: "Blessed One, I, being endowed with knowledge of and faith in the Buddha, passed from the body and was born here." And another spoke likewise, saying: "I, in the Dharma; I, in the Saṅgha —"

"I, endowed with the moral discipline esteemed by noble ones, passed from the body and was born here." Then many hundreds of thousands of gods, one after another, received from the Blessed One the prophecy of their stream-entry, and in that very moment became invisible.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, perceiving that the assembly of gods had dispersed, rose from his seat, arranged his outer robe over one shoulder, went to where the Blessed One was, joined his palms together in homage, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, the four assemblies from Jambudvīpa bow their heads at the Blessed One's feet and inquire: Is there little affliction? Is there no affliction? Are you in good health? Are you vigorous? Are you at ease? Are there few ailments? Do you dwell in comfort? Are you well?"

The Blessed One replied: "May you, Maudgalyāyana, and the four assemblies of Jambudvīpa likewise be well."

Then the venerable one said: "Blessed One, the four assemblies of Jambudvīpa wish to behold the Blessed One. They say this: 'Blessed One, the people of Jambudvīpa do not possess such miraculous power and might as to ascend to the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods in order to see and pay homage to the Blessed One there. But the gods of the Thirty-Three do possess such miraculous power and might as to descend to Jambudvīpa and come into the Blessed One's presence to see and pay homage to him. Therefore, Blessed One, it would be good if, out of compassion, you were to come down from the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods to Jambudvīpa.'"

"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, go to Jambudvīpa and announce to the four assemblies: 'The Blessed One will, seven days from today, come down from the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods to Jambudvīpa, to the city of Sāṃkāśya, to the forest of Apaṇajarī, to the foot of the udumbara tree.'"

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard this from the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and entered into meditative absorption of just such a kind. And the manner of his mind's settling in absorption was this: just as a strong man might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm, so did the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana vanish from the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods and arrive in Jambudvīpa.

Then the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having come to Jambudvīpa, announced to the four assemblies: "Hear this — the Blessed One will, seven days from today, come down from the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods to Jambudvīpa, to the city of Sāṃkāśya, to the forest of Apaṇajarī, to the foot of the udumbara tree."

Then, when seven days had passed, the four assemblies took perfumes and ointments and set out for the city of Sāṃkāśya. And the many people dwelling in Sāṃkāśya cleared the city of stones, weeds, and rubbish, sprinkled it with sandalwood water, and hung festoons of sweet-smelling incense; they raised victory banners and divine pennants, draped silken streamers, and scattered flowers of every kind. The place was transformed into something like a divine pleasure garden — a grove of delight — and seats were set out and arranged in an open, unobstructed expanse of ground.

Then the Blessed One rightly taught, rightly exhorted, rightly inspired, and rightly gladdened the gods of the Thirty-Three with a discourse on the Dharma. Then, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three, he vanished from the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods and descended to the Yāma heavens. There the Blessed One rightly taught the gods of the Yāma heavens with a discourse on the Dharma —

rightly exhorted, rightly inspired, and rightly gladdened them. Then, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three and the Yāma gods, he vanished and proceeded in just the same way to the Tuṣita heaven. In like manner he proceeded onward through the heavens of those who Delight in Emanation, those who Wield Power over Others' Emanations, the Brahmic orders — the gods of Brahmic Retinue, the gods of the Brahmic Attendants, and the Great Brahmic gods — then the gods of Minor Radiance, Immeasurable Radiance, and Resplendent Radiance, then the gods of Minor Virtue, Immeasurable Virtue, and Complete Virtue, then the Cloudless gods, the gods of Increasing Merit, the gods of Great Fruit, the gods who are Not Great, the Untroubled gods, the gods of Fair Appearance, the gods of Great Vision, and finally to Akaniṣṭha, where dwell the gods inhabiting the desire realm and those inhabiting the form realm alike.

Then the Blessed One rightly taught the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven with a discourse on the Dharma, rightly exhorted them, rightly inspired them, and rightly gladdened them. He then vanished from Akaniṣṭha and proceeded to the abode of the gods of Fair Appearance. In reverse order, he descended step by step through the ranks of the gods — those inhabiting the desire realm and those inhabiting the form realm together — down as far as the level of the gods of the Thirty-Three.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra, king of heaven), addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, are you descending to Jambudvīpa? O Kauśika, by what means do you descend — by miraculous power, or on foot?"

"O Kauśika, on foot," he replied.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, instructed the divine son Sarvārthasiddha: "Sarvārthasiddha, conjure three stairways — one of gold, one of lapis lazuli, and one of crystal."

Sarvārthasiddha replied, "O Kauśika, excellent indeed!" And having heard the command from Śakra, lord of the gods, Sarvārthasiddha conjured three stairways — one of gold, one of lapis lazuli, and one of crystal.

The Blessed One then descended by the stairway of lapis lazuli. Brahmā, lord of the assembly, came down the golden stairway from the right side, holding a thousand jeweled fans, accompanied by the gods of the form realm. Śakra, lord of the gods, came down the crystal stairway from the Blessed One's left side, holding a parasol with a hundred spokes, accompanied by the gods of the desire realm.

Now the Blessed One had considered the following: if he were to descend on foot, the non-Buddhists would say, "The ascetic Gautama went to the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods by miraculous power, but upon seeing beings of enthralling beauty he lost his power and descended to Jambudvīpa on foot." And if he were to descend entirely by miraculous power, then the deeds performed by the All-Accomplished One would come to nothing. He therefore resolved: "Let half the descent be on foot, and half by miraculous power."

And so the Blessed One descended alternately — now a step on foot, now a step by miraculous power. Within twelve leagues below, the smell of human impurity rose up, and the gods could not bear it. The Blessed One then manifested the fragrance of sandalwood and gośīrṣa-sandalwood, so that the odor of humanity was overcome.

The Blessed One then considered further: "If men were to behold divine sons and women were to behold divine daughters, it would inevitably come to pass that they would vomit warm blood and die on the spot. How then shall I bring about such a miraculous display that men may behold the divine sons and women may behold the divine daughters?" And so the Blessed One manifested precisely such a miraculous display — that men could see the divine sons, and women could see the divine daughters.

At that very moment, the Venerable Subhūti was sitting beneath another tree, spending the midday hours in repose.

The Venerable Subhūti saw the Blessed One descend from the realm of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three to Jambudvīpa, together with supreme riches and splendor. Having seen this, he thought to himself: "These gods, great as their miraculous powers and might may be, have nevertheless left the Blessed One behind and returned each to his own dwelling place. And these people here will pass away when a hundred years have gone by. The Blessed One too will pass into complete nirvāṇa, and all of this great wealth and abundance will utterly cease to be, in every way, for everyone. In this regard, what the Blessed One has so well declared is precisely this: all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, not to be relied upon, subject to change — one should be satisfied with all conditioned phenomena, for it is fitting to be wearied by them, fitting to be without desire for them. Knowing that one must attain liberation, one should apply the mind to the five appropriating aggregates as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self."

He then entered upon that very contemplation — turning the mind to the five appropriating aggregates as impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless. And by having turned the mind to the appropriating aggregates in this way as impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless, through the aspect of impermanence he shattered — as with a vajra of gnosis — the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection that had arisen upward, and thereby actualized the fruit of stream-entry.

Then, having seen and understood the truth and possessed of faith, he swiftly unfolded his crossed legs, placed his right knee upon the ground, and made obeisance to the Blessed One.

Now the nun Utpalavarnā thought to herself: "When the Blessed One descends from the Heaven of the Thirty-Three to Jambudvīpa, by what means might I be the first to pay homage to him? If I were to go just as I am, people would say 'A wandering ascetic woman has merely touched the head,' and since gods and men, great and many, surround the Blessed One and would not allow one to pass within, I shall go by miraculous power." So she manifested herself openly in the guise of a wheel-turning king (a universal monarch), led at the front by the seven precious treasures, attended on all sides by seventy-nine hundreds of thousands of ministers of supreme strength, encircled like the orb of the moon by a thousand sons adorned with ornaments of every variety, followed in procession by a thousand tīrthikas, brahmins, the destitute, the lowly, and the foremost among men, bearing over her head an umbrella with a hundred spokes, dazzling and radiating a thousand rays like the light of the sun, and accompanied by the moon, the stars, and a magnificent palatial hall — outshining them all in splendor — she proceeded to where the Blessed One was.

When that retinue then saw the nun Utpalavarnā from a distance, they were struck with amazement. They gazed at her with fixed eyes and their thoughts turned in many directions. Some said, "Where has such a king as this come from?" Others said, "There is no army as splendid as this anywhere upon the land of a king — this must truly be a wheel-turning king who has come from another world to behold the Blessed One." And seeing the wealth and splendor of that wheel-turning king, they thought with longing, "Oh, may we too accomplish something of this kind!" and they opened a way for her.

At that moment the Venerable Śāriputra was sitting within that assembled retinue. He said: "This is not a wheel-turning king — this is the nun Utpalavarnā, who has come by miraculous power to behold the Blessed One."

They replied: "Noble one, how is it that you know this to be the nun Utpalavarnā?"

He said: "Because of the exceedingly fragrant scent of the blue lotus — it is Utpalavarnā who has come by miraculous power into the presence of the Blessed One."

The nun Utpalavarnā then drew back the miraculous display she had manifested and went to where the Blessed One was. She bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the nun Utpalavarnā: "Nun, go — do not sit here before me. It is not fitting for a nun to perform miracles in the presence of the Teacher."

Dismissed by the Blessed One, she moved away and sat to one side.

The Blessed One reflected: "Whoever, being a nun, displays miracles in the presence of the Teacher, that is a basis for an offence. Therefore, nuns should not perform miracles in the presence of the Teacher." With this in mind, he addressed the monks: "Monks, it is not fitting for a nun to display miracles in the presence of the Teacher. Therefore, let nuns refrain from displaying miracles in the presence of the Teacher. A nun who displays miracles in the presence of the Teacher will incur a transgression."

Now, some among those who had seen the nun Utpalavarnā in the form of a wheel-turning king's splendour had given rise to attachment to human existence. Others, who had seen her in the form of the miraculous splendour of the gods, had given rise to attachment to divine existence. The Blessed One therefore taught the Dharma to that assembled retinue in such a way as to turn them back from rebirth as gods or as humans. Upon hearing it, some among them realized the fruit of stream-entry (Skt. srotāpatti). Some realized the fruit of non-return. Some realized the fruit of once-return. Some, having abandoned all afflictions, realized arhatship. Some aroused the mind of awakening aimed at the awakening of a śrāvaka; some, at solitary awakening; and some, at unsurpassable and perfect complete awakening. Some produced roots of virtue that had reached the level of heat. Some reached the summit; and some produced the lesser and middling forms of patient acceptance. The greater part of that assembled retinue was established as inclining toward the Buddha, falling into the Dharma, and thoroughly falling into the Saṅgha.

Thereupon the Blessed One, on account of this, spoke these verses:

Better than winning grounds one by one,
better than going again among the gods,
better even than attaining meditative absorption —
the fruit of stream-entry is supreme.

The Blessed One then thoroughly instructed, thoroughly exhorted, thoroughly praised, and thoroughly gladdened that assembled retinue with words of Dharma. He rose from his seat and departed.

The monks, having given rise to doubt, asked the Blessed One, the Buddha, to cut through all their doubt: "Venerable one, we observed that the Venerable Śāriputra recognized the nun Utpalavarnā by her scent."

The Blessed One replied: "Monks, this is not only so at present. In times past as well, Śāriputra recognized her by her scent. Therefore listen, monks. In former times there lived in the city of Camkarmojik a certain merchant. He took a wife of equal station and enjoyed himself with her in sport and pleasure. While they were thus sporting together, his wife became with child. That merchant then made ready to sail across the great ocean, and said to her: 'My dear, I am taking goods and departing for another land. Be diligent in managing the affairs of the household.' She said to her husband: 'If that is so, then take me along as well.' He replied: 'My dear, who would serve you there?'"

She sat there weeping. When the servants asked the merchant why his wife was weeping, he replied: "She wishes to come with me. I have not taken her, and that is why she weeps." The servants then said to the merchant: "Then why not take her? Who here will serve her? There is no fault in it, merchant — take her along, and we will attend to her." So he took her, and they set out in due course and entered upon the great ocean. But while they were on the great ocean, a large sea-creature resembling a water-serpent or a great fish struck the ship unseasonably, and the merchant perished there in that very moment. His wife clung to a plank, and the wind carried her along in due course until she came to the island of Kāśeru. There the king of birds, Śubhapakṣa — Splendid-Wings — dwelt, and he took her as his consort. Nine months passed, and she gave birth to a son, fair of form, lovely to behold, and beautiful in every way. Thereafter, she and the bird-king Splendid-Wings sported together in great delight. Through that sport she gave birth to a bird, a young Splendid-Wings. Then in time the bird-king Splendid-Wings passed away. When all the birds had gathered, they installed the son as king in the rightful succession of Splendid-Wings his father. His mother said to him: "Now that you have been installed as king in your father's succession, you must let your elder brother here rule as human king of Camkarmojik." He replied: "So it shall be done."

At that time the king of Camkarmojik was a man called Brahmadatta, and the realm was prosperous, flourishing, comfortable, with good harvests and many people. Yet it was troubled by conflict, dispute, strife, and discord. So in order to accomplish that purpose, at a gathering the wife of the bird-king Splendid-Wings seized her son by the hand, cast him into the great ocean, and then adorned his elder brother with all ornaments and placed him upon a lion throne. She then said to the ministers: "This is your king. Should anyone do him even the slightest harm, I shall deal with them in such a manner." They were afraid and obeyed her words. And because they told this to no one else, the people of the world assumed that he was none other than Brahmadatta himself.

He said to the bird-king: "Brother, keep an eye on me from time to time." And the bird-king replied: "I will watch over you well."

Then at a later time a she-buffalo belonging to King Brahmadatta gave birth to a calf, and the calf became stuck at the mouth of the womb. When the ministers reported this to the king, he said: "Have it brought to the queen's quarters, and let the queens free it from this affliction by the power of a truthful declaration." So it was brought to the queens' quarters, and the queens made aspirational prayers through truthful declarations — yet even so they were unable to free the calf from its affliction, and a great and terrible cry arose. Not far from the royal palace there lived a certain cowherdess who heard this sound and asked someone: "What is this great terrible cry from the royal palace?" When it was explained to her what had happened, she said: "I will make an aspirational prayer through my own truthful declaration and free it from its affliction." And she went to report this to the ministers.

The ministers brought her into the queens' quarters, and she made an aspirational prayer through a truthful declaration. "If it is true that I have had only one husband and have never known a second man, then by the power of this truthful declaration, may the cow be swiftly freed from her affliction." When she had made this aspirational prayer through a truthful declaration, the calf emerged from the cow but became stuck at the tail. The cowherdess burst out laughing, and the queens asked her: "What is this — that you cannot even bear so much as this?" She replied: "I had taken a small infant boy onto my lap, and when he urinated and the urine ran down to my private parts, I felt pleasure at that — it is for that reason that I am stuck at the tail." She then told exactly what had happened, and thereupon the tail was freed. The ministers reported to the king: "Your Majesty, the cow has given birth to the calf." When asked who had freed it from its affliction, they explained what had taken place. The king reflected: "It is certainly the case that all my queens have become corrupt in their moral discipline, and it is the cowherdess who, by making an aspirational prayer through a truthful declaration, freed it from its affliction." He gave the order: "Go and summon that cowherdess." They summoned her, and the king asked her: "Is it true that you freed the cow from its affliction by means of a truthful declaration?" "It is true, Your Majesty." The king thought: "A daughter born of such a woman would herself be of such a character." And thinking, "If she has a daughter, I shall take her as my queen — let me ask straightaway," he said: "Do you have a daughter?" "I do, Your Majesty." "What is her name?" "Your Majesty, her name is Śoṣumā." "To whom has her mother given her, or has she not been given?" "Your Majesty, she has not been given to anyone." "Well then, if that is so, offer her to me — I shall take her as my queen." "As Your Majesty commands." She gave her consent, and the king joined her in a great and splendid gathering and took her as his bride.

The king then thought: "If I keep this woman here in the company of my queens, she will certainly become corrupt in her moral discipline." So he told the king of birds, the Golden Wing (Suparṇa), what had occurred and gave him this command: "Take her by day to the island of Kāśeru, and bring her back at night." The Golden Wing replied: "Very well, it shall be done as you say." He was bound to the bird of Golden Wings, and thus she was taken there and brought back again. By day she was taken to the island of Kāśeru, and by night she was brought back to the capital. On the island of Kāśeru there was a sweet-smelling flower called the timarī, and garlands of it were sent every single day to King Brahmadatta. Now at Khorumo Jig there lived another brahmin youth, and one day he went into the forest to gather wood. While he was there, a kinnara woman caught sight of him and drew him into a cave and kept him there. She sported and played with him in complete delight. When he went out one time to gather flowers and fruit, the brahmin youth covered the mouth of the cave with a great flat stone so that she could not move it. After some time had passed, she gave birth to a son by that brahmin youth, and wherever the child went he moved with great speed, so he was given the name Swift-Goer. The brahmin youth would constantly speak before the child of the qualities of the land of Khorumo Jig, saying: "In the city of Khorumo Jig there are such-and-such qualities and things of this kind." When the child asked him: "Father, what land are you from?" he replied: "I was born in the land of Khorumo Jig." The father said: "If that is so, then why do you not flee?" He replied: "Son, when your mother went out to gather flowers and fruit, the mouth of this cave was blocked by a great flat stone, and so —"

"I am unable to move it, so how could I flee?" he said. The child replied: "Father, I myself will shift it. Son, excellent! Train yourself in lifting stones," he said. On the first day he lifted a small stone. On the second day, one larger than that. On the third day, one larger still. In this way he trained until he was able to lift a great flat stone. Then the child said to the father: "Throw aside the flat stone and flee, and be gone." But the father said: "Son, even your mother, who went out to gather flowers and fruit, will soon return, and if she finds me gone she will without fail make the two of us suffer for nothing." The child said: "Father, whatever causes her not to return quickly, that I shall arrange." "Son, excellent!" Then the child came back carrying flowers and fruit, and the father kept placing them into the child's mouth, again and again, tossing them in. The mother asked: "Son, why do I keep putting things into your mouth and throwing them away?" He replied: "Mother, you are lazy. When you go nearby, you bring back flowers and fruit all covered in frost and snow, and they are not sweet — I cannot eat them. That is why I throw them away. Mother, tomorrow I will go far away. Nearby there is nothing sweet, so tomorrow I will go far away." She said: "Good, then tomorrow do as you like, and eat what is sweet." After that, the next day she went a very long way off. Swift-Goer said to the father: "I have sent her far away. Now is the time to flee." The father said: "Son, excellent! Throw aside the flat stone." The child threw aside the flat stone, and together with Swift-Goer they fled and arrived at the city of Khorumo Jig.

Now the mother had gone a great distance carrying flowers and fruit, and when she finally returned and looked, the cave was empty. She sat weeping, and her companion, seeing her, asked: "Why are you crying?" She told her: "Sister, that brahmin youth took my son too and fled." Her companion said: "Sister, he is a human being — what grief is there in that among humans? Do not grieve that he does not dwell with you. As for me, I gave him not even a little livelihood. Sister, what shall you give? Pass it into my hand — if you find one, give it." She gave her a lute, saying: "Play this and live by it. Do not touch the highest string of the instrument, lest it become a cause of wrongdoing." She took it and went away.

As for the brahmin, he entrusted the boy Swift-Goer to many brahmin youths who were studying, saying: "Teach this brahmin youth," and had them instruct him in reading. The boys memorized their lessons, and whenever any of them was not reciting, at that moment he would go out to urinate. However swift-footed Swift-Goer was, when a great distance had passed and the boys were no longer reciting, they went to urinate. When Swift-Goer had gone very far away, his mother's companion saw him and asked: "Boy, what news is there to tell?" He replied: "What kind of news? I am tormented by hunger and thirst." She said: "Boy, your mother is in grief, sitting and weeping — why do you not go to her? I am unable to speak together with that wrathful woman. Son, but if you will not go, I will give you a livelihood — do not give it to anyone else. Here it is — do not give it to anyone." She gave him the lute, saying: "Play this and live by it. So that it does not become a cause of wrongdoing, do not touch the lowest string of the instrument." She replied: "Good, mother, I will do just so." She took it and went among those brahmin youths. They asked: "Boy, why did you delay so long in coming, and who gave you that lute?" He replied:

"My mother's friend saw me and gave me this lute." They asked: "Boy, do you know how to play the lute?" He replied: "I do. Watch." He took it up and played it, singing as he played. He did not touch the lowest string of the instrument, and they asked: "Boy, why do you not touch the lowest string?" He said: "Ah, if one touches that, it will become a cause of wrongdoing." They said: "What wrongdoing could there be in a brahmin boy's touching it?" — and they touched it, whereupon they all leapt up and began to dance. When they had danced, they became exhausted, and toward evening they came to the teacher's house. He asked: "Boys, why have you come so late?" They told him everything that had happened in detail. He quickly asked that brahmin boy: "You — do you know how to play the lute and sing?" He replied: "I do." "Then, brahmin boy, let the lute be heard — play it." He took it up and began to play and sing, and he did not touch the lowest string. The teacher asked: "Brahmin boy, why do you not touch the lowest string?" He replied: "Teacher, if one touches that, it will become a cause of wrongdoing." The teacher said: "Brahmin boy, what wrongdoing could there be in touching it? Touch it." He touched it, and the brahmin, together with his wife, leapt up and began to dance. The whole house shook from their leaping and was ruined. In the ruin, all the clay pots and vessels were smashed. The brahmin flew into a rage and seized that brahmin boy by the throat and threw him out. Having been thrown out, he took up the lute and entered upon a livelihood of playing it.

Some time later, a group of about five hundred merchants prepared a vessel to set out across the great ocean, and set sail for it. They said among themselves: "When we enter the great ocean, let us take along a musician who can lift our spirits." One of them asked: "Whom shall we take?" Another said: "Let us take the brahmin boy called Swift-Going." Some agreed: "Excellent, let it be so." And they brought the brahmin boy Swift-Going along and entered the great ocean. When they had gone out into the great ocean, someone said: "Swift-Going the musician, let the lute be heard — play it." He took up the lute and began to play and sing, and he did not touch the lowest string of that lute. The merchants said: "Swift-Going, why do you not touch that lowest string?" He replied: "Ah, if one touches that, it will become a cause of wrongdoing." They said: "Brahmin boy, what wrongdoing could there be? Touch it." He touched it, and a great wave surged up, the ship capsized and was wrecked, and those merchants perished before their time. But he, by the power of his former karma, seized hold of a plank and a swift wind carried him to an island. There he sat in another grove, and when there was no other person about, he saw a certain woman of the crocodile kind, and he lay down together with her. By day he spent his time together with Swift-Going; by night he consorted with King Brahmadatta. She asked: "Fair one, where do you go at night?" Since she had become intimate with him, she told him everything. She then said: "Fair one, even so — take me too when you flee." He replied: "My lord, I shall gladly take you. Tell me your name." He said: "Fair one, my name is Swift-Going. Tell me your name." She replied: "My lord, my name is Crocodile-Woman."

He then began to devise a plan involving stones. On the first day he took a small stone and rode upon Swift-Going's wings. On the second day he carried two stones of that size. On the third day he carried three stones of that size, and so on until he was carrying a weight equal to that of a man. Then he mounted Swift-Going's wings together with Swift-Going and flew away. As they went, Śoṣumpa said: "My lord, you must not open your eyes — there will be harm." So he shut his eyes. When they were close to the point where Nāmakhormo was about to fall away beneath them, he heard the clamour and noise of a great multitude of people. He thought: "Now I may look." When he opened his eyes, his eyes came out and he was rendered blind. Śoṣumpa set him down in a pleasure grove and went inside among the wives of King Brahmadatta.

Some time later spring arrived. The trees were in blossom, and in a dense forest filled with the calls of geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, śārikā birds, cuckoos, and the creatures that live by living — surrounded by Brahmadatta's consorts, Queen Brahmadatta went together with Śoṣumpa to the pleasure grove. Now the brahmin's son, Swift-Going, smelt the fragrance of tīmira flowers and, having taken them up, thought to sing a song of that kind. Borne along on the wind, it carried the fragrance of tīmira flowers — in the place where Śoṣumpa dwells, among the kāśeru groves.

When King Brahmadatta heard this, he said to the consorts: "Find out who is singing here." They said: "There is a man deprived of his god-eyes, who is here in this pleasure grove singing." The king summoned him and asked: "Young man, was it you who sang?" He replied: "Sire, it was I who sang." The king said: "Young man, sing again — I will listen again." He thought: "It is not another's — it is what I myself sang, and it was pleasing to hear. Therefore the king wishes to hear it, and perhaps I may gain some small benefit." So he sang:

Borne along on the wind,
the fragrance of tīmira flowers —
in the place where Śoṣumpa dwells,
among the kāśeru groves.

The king asked: "Young man, how far is it from here to these kāśeru groves?" He replied in verse:

A hundred leagues from here
lie the waters of the great ocean.
There dwells Śoṣumpa,
in the kāśeru groves.

Then King Brahmadatta answered him in verse:

If this Śoṣumpa, who delights my heart,
were seen or heard by you to have any flaw,
speak too of whatever marks are on her body.

He in turn replied in verse:

A svastika mark is on her thigh,
her breasts curve round upon her,
and the tīmira flowers
are strung along the back of your beloved.

The king thought: "This one has conducted himself badly. I have no need of him — I shall give him to the blind one." But then growing further angry, he spoke in verse:

I shall give you Śoṣumpa,
adorned with every ornament —
mount a donkey, and depart
from the city with all haste.

In his anger the king had Śoṣumpa and the blind man put together upon a riding donkey and expelled them. The blind man led her, and they wandered here and there. When the sun set they arrived at a village on a rocky cliff and spent the night in an empty shrine. That night some five hundred wild men came to plunder the village on the rocky cliff. The many people dwelling in the village of the rocky cliff became aware of this and raised a general alarm, and the villagers of the rocky cliff captured and routed the wild men. Their leader, however, was not caught, and he entered that very shrine.

The villagers of the rocky cliff surrounded that very shrine on all sides, and the leader of the wild men barred the door from within. The villagers called out: "Who is in there?" The brahmin's son Swift-Walker replied: "We are travelers." They said: "Let this wild man come out. You yourself have surely been made to suffer for nothing." The leader of the wild men said to Śoṣumpa: "What use is this blind man? Drive him off and the two of us will enjoy each other fully." She replied: "Good sir, please do as you like. As for me, I am yours." And then she and the leader of the wild men threw the blind man from the top of the cliff wall, whereupon the villagers of the rocky cliff cut off his head and threw it away.

The next day, as the leader of the wild men led her and they were going, they came to the river Kāradā and found no boat for crossing. He said: "Fair one, this river Kāradā is full of water, and you cannot cross it adorned with all your ornaments. You wait here and bathe while I take your ornaments across. I will come back and carry you over afterward." She agreed and said, "So be it, I will bathe," and gave him all her clothing and ornaments. Then she entered the water and sat there naked. When he had gone to the middle of the river, she began to feel regret, thinking: "Has he not stolen my ornaments and clothing and gone without returning?" And she spoke in verse:

This river Kāradā is full of water.
To you, fair one, I gave all my goods.
Now doubt has arisen in my heart.
O wicked one, do not deceive me!

He too replied in verse:

You, no friend, have slain an old friend.
That man is now as nothing.
Therefore it is hard to trust you.
Will you not slay me too?

And with that he stole them and fled. She, still naked, crouched down inside some thick grass. Just then an old fox came along the bank of the river Kāradā carrying a piece of meat, and a large fish, leaping out of the water onto dry land, fell there. The fox dropped the meat and ran after the fish, but the fish jumped back into the river. And a crow swept up the meat. Thus losing both, the fox sat with its ears drooping in regret. Śoṣumpa, sitting inside the thick grass, saw this and spoke in verse:

The piece of meat was seized by the crow.
The fish escaped into the river.
Both are now beyond reach.
Why should the fox not be sorrowful?

The fox looked in all four directions. It saw no one. Then it spoke in verse:

No wild men dance here,
and songs do not delight me either.
Who is it that dwells within the grass
to mock and laugh at me?

She answered: "Uncle, it is I, Śoṣumpa." The fox was angered and thought: "This wicked woman knows how to taunt me," and spoke in verse:

Your husband was slain by you yourself.
Because the mouse fled away,
both were lost to you.
Why should the wicked woman not grieve?

She replied in verse:

I will go to my own home
and take an excellent husband there.
Once a husband has been found,
one need not cast shame upon one's lineage.

The fox spoke in verse:

When the Gaṅgā flows back upstream
and crows turn the color of yogurt,
when such fruit appears,
only then will you truly be a woman of virtue.

When someday a crow and an owl,
having made their dwelling on a single tree,
dwell together in happiness,
then, at that time, virtue will be yours.

When someday a snake and a mongoose, both —

dwelling together in a single burrow,
dwelling there in happiness and contentment —
then, at that time, virtue will be yours.

When someday a tortoise's wool
has been well spun and fashioned
into a winter garment —
then virtue will be yours.

When someday from a gnat's kneecap
a ladder has been well constructed
and set up as a stairway to the heavens —
then, at that time, virtue will be yours.

When someday upon the stalk of a jasmine plant
a bridge has been well built
and an ox-cart passes over it —
then, at that time, virtue will be yours.

When someday even in the middle of the ocean
a fine fire blazes brightly
and people enter into it —
then, at that time, virtue will be yours.

When I have finished mocking you, woman, that will be the end of it. Now, if I am to restore you to your former place, what will you give me in return? The woman said to that fox: If you, dear one, restore me to my former place, I will give you a piece of meat every single day. The fox said: Very well then, watch carefully.
