Enter the river, submerge yourself up to your neck in the water, face east, and remain there. I will make supplication to the god. The fox then went near the royal palace and addressed the deity thus: O god, this woman is virtuous and truthful and is practicing austerities; she is one who is fit to be summoned quickly. Upon hearing this, King Brahmadatta, who was skilled in the language of foxes, commanded his minister: I have heard that on the bank of the river Karanadana a woman is practicing austerities. Go and bring her here. The attendants dressed her in fine garments and ornaments and brought her, and the king restored her to her former place. Each day she gave the fox a piece of meat. She gave it for a certain period of time, and then she stopped giving it. The fox, sitting near the royal palace, threatened the woman, saying: If you give me a piece of meat, well and good. If you do not, I will give you a sound thrashing and restore you once again to your former place as before. Hearing this, the woman was frightened and again began giving the fox a piece of meat each day.

Now, monks, what do you think? That woman at that time and on that occasion was the nun of blue-lotus complexion. That swift-footed one at that time and on that occasion was the monk Utpalā. At that time and on that occasion, he knew her by her scent, and even now he knows her by her scent.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the monks rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had taught.

The Thirty-Sixth Fascicle of the Miscellaneous Matters of the Vinaya.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, on the bank of the river Vaṅgumatī, certain monks, by means of a compound of clay pills and a purgative preparation, abandoned all afflictions and directly attained arhatship. At that time the Blessed One declared to the monks: Therefore, monks, strive, be diligent, make effort with this very compound of clay pills and a purgative preparation, just as those monks on the bank of the river Vaṅgumatī strove, were diligent, and made effort. Monks, do not be slothful in diligence. Monks, if one is slothful in diligence, one will be finished, along with all that has passed.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing in the dense forest of Rikāta, near the town of Kīṭa. At that time, in Rikāta, monks Thāskaryesd and Nābso and —

— the reddish-brown monks were staying there. These monks engaged in, arranged, and deliberately attended the following kinds of fights and contests: wool-sheep fighting, horse fighting, chariot fighting, ram fighting, staff fighting, fist fighting, bull fighting, buffalo fighting, goat fighting, cock fighting, dog fighting, quail fighting, partridge fighting, crane fighting — and they set women, men, youths, and girls to competing in tests of strength, and they abused, reviled, and spoke ill of faithful brahmins and householders, saying: "Why should one give alms or make offerings to this bald-headed ascetic who, though he has gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, goes about arranging wool-sheep fights and the like?" When this had happened, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the brahmins and householders are right to criticize. Therefore, monks, they must not be allowed to arrange fights involving wool-sheep and the like, nor even to watch them. If monks arrange fights involving wool-sheep and the like, or arrange for others to do so, or watch them, they will be finished, along with all that has passed."

In brief: what was asked in full
and answered by the nun who had entered confinement —
those deeds too are to be performed.
The nun who has descended again.

The awakened one, the Blessed One, was residing in the Nyagrodha pleasure grove at Kapilavāstu. Then Gautamī, the great Progenitress, together with five hundred Śākya women, went to where the Blessed One was, bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet, and took a seat to one side. Seated to one side, Gautamī, the great Progenitress, was taught the discourse of Dharma, rightly exhorted, rightly encouraged, and rightly gladdened by the Blessed One. Having been rightly taught, rightly exhorted, rightly encouraged, and rightly gladdened through the discourse of Dharma in its many aspects, and the Blessed One then remaining silent, Gautamī, the great Progenitress, rose from her seat, turned to face the Blessed One, joined her palms together, paid homage, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, if there were an occasion for women to attain the four fruits of the ascetic life, may the Blessed One please permit women to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to conduct themselves in the manner of nuns, and to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One." To this the Blessed One replied to Gautamī, the great Progenitress, with these words: "Gautamī, in just this way, wearing the white robes of a laywoman for the rest of your life, practice the holy life that is in all things complete, entirely pure, and entirely perfected — and it will be for your long-term benefit, welfare, and happiness." Gautamī, the great Progenitress, again a second and a third time addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, if there were an occasion for women to attain the four fruits of the ascetic life, may the Blessed One please permit women to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to conduct themselves in the manner of nuns, and to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

The Blessed One, a second and a third time, addressed Gautamī, the great Progenitress, with these words: "Gautamī, you should, in exactly this way, for as long as you live, shave your head and wear stitched robes, and for as long as you live practice the holy life that in that alone is entirely perfected, entirely pure, and entirely purified — and it will be for your long-term benefit, welfare, and happiness."

Then, since the Blessed One had refused three times, Gautamī, the great Progenitress, bowed her head to the feet of the Blessed One, paid homage, and departed from his presence.

Thereupon the Blessed One remained in the settlement of the Śākyas as long as he wished, then took up his bowl and robes and traveled onward through the country toward Nādikā, and came to dwell at the Guñja residence at Nādikā.

When Gautamī, the great Progenitress, heard that the Blessed One had remained in the settlement of the Śākyas as long as he wished, had taken up his bowl and robes, and was traveling through the country toward Nādikā, she, together with five hundred Śākya women, at once cut off her own hair and distributed robes of the Dharma among them. With their heads shaved and wearing stitched robes, they followed after the Blessed One, walking in his wake, and set out.

The Blessed One, having traveled through the country of the Vṛjis, arrived at Nādikā and resided there at the Guñja residence.

Then Gautamī, the great Progenitress — her body weary, her body aching, her body exhausted, covered in dust — went to where the Blessed One was and arrived there. She bowed her head to the feet of the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side.

Having stood to one side, Gautamī, the great Progenitress, was then thoroughly shown, thoroughly urged, thoroughly encouraged, and thoroughly gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on Dharma. After being thoroughly shown, thoroughly urged, thoroughly encouraged, and thoroughly gladdened with a discourse on Dharma in many ways, the Blessed One remained in silence.

Then Gautamī, the great Progenitress, rose from her seat, pressed her palms together in reverence toward where the Blessed One was, paid homage, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, if there were an occasion for women to attain the four fruits of the ascetic life, may the Blessed One please permit women to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to conduct themselves in the manner of nuns, and to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

The Blessed One then addressed Gautamī, the great Progenitress: "Gautamī, you should, in exactly this way, in just this manner, for as long as you live, with your head shaved and wearing stitched robes, practice for as long as you live the holy life that in that alone is entirely perfected, entirely pure, and entirely purified — and it will be for your long-term benefit, welfare, and happiness."

Gautamī, the great Progenitress, again a second and a third time addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, if there were an occasion for women to attain the four fruits of the ascetic life, may the Blessed One please permit women to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to conduct themselves in the manner of nuns, and to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

And when she had so spoken, the Blessed One a second and a third time addressed Gautamī, the great Progenitress: "Gautamī, you should in exactly this way, in just this manner, for as long as you live, with your head shaved and wearing stitched robes, practice what in that alone is entirely perfected, entirely pure, and —

entirely pure, the holy life. And this will be for your long-lasting benefit, welfare, and happiness."

When the Blessed One had refused Gautamī, the great Progenitress, a second and a third time in exactly this way, she sat down to one side of the outer gatehouse and wept, shedding tears. The venerable Ānanda then saw Gautamī, the great Progenitress, sitting to one side of the outer gatehouse, weeping and shedding tears. Seeing this, he said to her: "Gautamī, why are you sitting to one side of the outer gatehouse, weeping and shedding tears?"

She replied: "Venerable Ānanda, it is because the Blessed One has not permitted women to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to conduct themselves in the manner of nuns, and to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

"Gautamī, remain here. I shall petition the Blessed One."

Then the venerable Ānanda went to where the Blessed One was and approached him, bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet in reverence, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if women are capable of attaining the four fruits of the ascetic life, may the Blessed One please permit women to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, to conduct themselves in the manner of nuns, and to live the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, do not petition me to permit women to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, to receive full ordination, and to conduct themselves in the manner of nuns. And why not? Ānanda, if women go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, this Dharma and Vinaya will not long endure.

It is like this, Ānanda. Consider a household in which there are many women and few men — it will be plundered and utterly ruined by thieves and robbers. In just the same way, Ānanda, if women go forth into the Dharma and Vinaya, this Dharma and Vinaya will not long endure.

Or consider this, Ānanda. When an excellent field of rice and sālu grain is struck by an overwhelming hailstorm, that very rice and grain becomes damaged, completely ruined, and unsuitable by reason of what is contrary to its nature. In just the same way, Ānanda, if women go forth into the Dharma and Vinaya, this Dharma and Vinaya will not long endure.

Or again, Ānanda. Consider a prosperous householder-farmer whose excellent sugarcane is afflicted by the blight of rust-disease — the sugarcane becomes unsuitable and is entirely wasted and ruined. In just the same way, Ānanda, if women go forth into the Dharma and Vinaya, this Dharma and Vinaya will not long endure.

Nevertheless, Ānanda, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing, I now establish eight chief rules by which women must train for as long as they live.

It is like this, Ānanda. Consider a householder-farmer who, when autumn has passed and the harvest season has come, builds a dike to dam a river or an irrigation channel — the water that is held back will not overflow the dam. In just the same way, Ānanda, I now establish these eight chief rules in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in them for as long as they live.

What are the eight?"

Ānanda, women must clearly understand that going forth and receiving full ordination from among the monks is what constitutes becoming a fully ordained nun. Ānanda, I now establish this as the first chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, nuns must seek instruction and scriptural transmission from the monks every fortnight, in accordance with the Teacher's word. Ānanda, I now establish this as the second chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, nuns must not enter the rains retreat in a place where there are no monks. Ānanda, I now establish this as the third chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, at the close of the rains retreat, a nun must perform the invitation ceremony before both communities regarding three matters: what was seen, what was heard, and what was suspected. Ānanda, I now establish this as the fourth chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, a nun must not speak of, nor bring to mind, any lapse in ethical conduct, any lapse in view, any lapse in behavior, or any lapse in livelihood on the part of monks. A nun is not permitted to speak of or call attention to any such lapses in ethical conduct, view, behavior, or livelihood on the part of a monk. As for monks speaking of and calling attention to such lapses on the part of nuns — there is no prohibition against that. Ānanda, I now establish this as the fifth chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, a nun must not speak harsh words to a monk, must not be angry with him, and must not be contemptuous of him. A nun is not permitted to speak harshly to a monk, to be angry with him, or to be contemptuous of him. Ānanda, I now establish this as the sixth chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, if a nun has transgressed a chief rule, she must perform a fortnight's probationary conduct to satisfy both communities. Ānanda, I now establish this as the seventh chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, a nun who has received full ordination — even if she has completed a hundred years — must speak words of welcome, offer praise, rise to her feet, join her palms together, and make prostration to a monk who has only just received full ordination. Ānanda, I now establish this as the eighth chief rule, in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.

Ānanda, if the great lady Gautamī sincerely takes up and diligently upholds these eight chief rules, that itself shall constitute her going forth, that itself her full ordination, and that itself her status as a fully ordained person.

Thus the Blessed One declared. Then the venerable Ānanda, greatly rejoicing and delighted at the words of the Blessed One, prostrated with his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

He then went to where the great lady Gautamī was, and said to her the following: "Gautamī, it has been granted that women may go forth, receive full ordination, and be established as fully ordained nuns in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. However, Gautamī, the Blessed One has established eight chief rules in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in these for as long as they live, and must do so diligently. Venerable Ānanda has spoken. Please hear what he said. Gautamī, the Blessed One declared the following. 'Ānanda, women are to understand that, from monks, they receive going forth, full ordination, and establishment as fully ordained nuns. Gautamī, this is the first chief rule that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.' Gautamī, the Blessed One then further declared: 'Ānanda, a fully ordained nun must, twice each month, seek from monks the scriptural transmission of the Teacher's instruction. Gautamī, this is the second chief rule that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.' Gautamī, the Blessed One then further declared: 'Ānanda, a fully ordained nun must not enter the rains retreat in a place where there are no monks. Gautamī, this is the third chief rule that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.' Gautamī, the Blessed One then further declared: 'Ānanda, a fully ordained nun who has completed the rains retreat must perform the invitation ceremony before both communities — the Saṅgha of monks and the Saṅgha of nuns — on the three grounds of what was seen, what was heard, and what was suspected. Gautamī, this is the fourth chief rule that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.' Gautamī, the Blessed One then further declared: 'Ānanda, a fully ordained nun must not discuss or bring up matters concerning a monk who has violated ethical conduct, who holds a wrong view, who has engaged in wrong conduct, or who maintains a wrong livelihood. Ānanda, a fully ordained nun is not permitted to discuss or bring up such matters concerning a monk who has violated ethical conduct, who holds a wrong view, who has engaged in wrong conduct, or who maintains a wrong livelihood. Ānanda, however, it is permitted for a monk to discuss and bring up such matters concerning a fully ordained nun who has violated ethical conduct, who holds a wrong view, who has engaged in wrong conduct, or who maintains a wrong livelihood. Gautamī, this is the fifth chief rule that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.' Gautamī, the Blessed One then further declared: 'Ānanda, a fully ordained nun must not speak harsh words to a monk, must not become angry at him, and must not scold him. Ānanda, a fully ordained nun is not permitted to speak harsh words to a monk, to become angry at him, or to scold him. Gautamī, this is the sixth chief rule that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.' Gautamī, the Blessed One then further declared:

'Ānanda, a fully ordained nun who has emerged from under the preceptorship must conduct herself in a pleasing manner toward both assemblies of the Saṅgha for a fortnight in turn. Gautamī, the Blessed One has established this as the seventh chief rule in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.' Gautamī, the Blessed One then further declared: 'A fully ordained nun who has been fully ordained for a hundred years must speak pleasing words to, praise, rise before, join her palms toward, and bow down to a monk who has only just received full ordination. Gautamī, this is the eighth chief rule that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing. Women must train in it for as long as they live.'

The Blessed One then further declared: 'Ānanda, if Gautamī the Great Lady takes up and earnestly upholds these eight chief rules, then for her this itself shall count as the going forth, this itself as full ordination, and this itself as the status of a fully ordained nun.'

The venerable Ānanda then said: 'Venerable one, these eight chief rules that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing — women must train in them for as long as they live — I accept these with speech, with mind, and even with the crown of my head.

Venerable Ānanda, it is just as when a daughter of the warrior class, or a daughter of the brahmin class, or a daughter of the merchant class, or a daughter of the common class, well bathed, well anointed, with her hair and nails dressed and wearing white garments, is offered by someone a garland of blue lotus flowers, or a garland of campaka blossoms, or a garland of jasmine flowers, or a garland of atimuktaka flowers — she would receive it joyfully with both hands and place it upon the crown of her head, the highest of all limbs. In just the same way, venerable Ānanda, these eight chief rules that the Blessed One has established in order to restrain women and prevent them from transgressing — women must train in them for as long as they live — I accept these with speech, with mind, and even with the crown of my head.

And since the Blessed One has now been pleased to grant Gautamī the Great Lady, through her acceptance of these chief rules, the going forth and full ordination and the status of a fully ordained nun, the venerable Upāli then said to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you declared that if Gautamī the Great Lady takes up and earnestly upholds these eight chief rules, that itself shall count as the going forth, that itself as full ordination, and that itself as the status of a fully ordained nun — but how then are other women to go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the status of fully ordained nuns?"

The Blessed One declared: 'Upāli, other women shall be given the going forth and full ordination in successive order.' When the Blessed One had declared that other women should be given the going forth and full ordination in successive order, the monks did not know what the successive procedure should be, and those monks therefore asked the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: 'Gautamī the Great Lady together with the other five hundred Śākya women have gone forth, received full ordination, and become fully ordained nuns by virtue of their acceptance of the chief rules.'

As for other women, the procedure is as follows in successive order. One who wishes to go forth shall come before any fully ordained nun she chooses, who shall then ask her about the obstructing factors and receive her. Having received her, the nun shall give her the three refuges and the five training rules that form the basis of a laywoman's practice.

What are the three refuges? The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

What are the five training rules? They are the complete abandonment of taking life; of taking what is not given; of sexual misconduct through desire; of false speech; and of the state of heedlessness that arises from intoxication by fermented or distilled liquor. Having thus fully abandoned that state of heedlessness caused by intoxicating fermented or distilled liquor, the formula is as follows: 'I, who am called such-and-such by name, from this day forward and for as long as I live, fully abandon taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the state of heedlessness caused by intoxicating fermented or distilled liquor.' In this same manner the taking of refuge and the giving of the training rules shall be performed.

First, let her make prostration to the Teacher. Then let the fully ordained nun who is giving the refuge and training rules allow her to make prostration and join her palms together. After that, she shall speak these words:

'Noble one, please hear me. I, who am called such-and-such by name, for as long as I live take refuge in the Buddha, who is supreme among two-footed beings. I take refuge in the excellent and holy Dharma, which is free from attachment. I take refuge in the excellent Saṅgha, which is supreme among assemblies. I request the noble one to hold me as a laywoman for as long as I live.' This shall be done a second and a third time in the same manner.

Then the five training rules shall be given: 'Noble one, please hear me. Just as those noble arhats have for the duration of their lives abandoned taking life and fully refrained from it, so too I, called such-and-such by name, from this very day forward and for as long as I live, abandon taking life and fully refrain from it. By this first rule I follow, accomplish, and carry out the training of those noble arhats. And just as those arhats have for the duration of their lives abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct through desire, false speech, and the state of heedlessness caused by intoxicating fermented or distilled liquor, and have fully turned away from it, so too I, called such-and-such by name, from this day on and for as long as I live, abandon taking what is not given, sexual misconduct through desire, false speech, and the state of heedlessness, and have fully turned away from the state of heedlessness caused by intoxicating fermented or distilled liquor. By these five rules I follow, accomplish, and carry out the training of those noble arhats.'

The preceptor shall then say: 'It is well.' And the laywoman shall say: 'Excellent!'

Then a fully ordained nun shall be appointed to make the announcement within the assembly of nuns. The one so appointed shall ask that fully ordained nun: 'Did you question her about the obstructing factors?' If the announcement is made without having asked, it shall constitute a transgression. The appointed nun shall then, whether the assembly of nuns is gathered together or whether they are in their individual dwelling places, proclaim the following:

'Hear me, noble assembly of nuns. This person, called such-and-such, who is a householder clothed in white with uncut hair, seeks going forth from the preceptor called such-and-such. If this person called such-and-such — who has cut her hair, put on ochre robes, and with genuine faith has gone forth from home into homelessness under the preceptor called such-and-such — seeks to achieve the status of going forth and full ordination and becoming a fully ordained nun in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, going from the household life to homelessness, then…'

If she herself declares 'the obstacles are fully purified,' then let her receive going forth. And all should say: 'Then, since they are fully purified, let it be so.' If they speak accordingly, it is well. But if they do not speak, there will be a transgression.

Then a request is to be made to the preceptor nun: 'Venerable preceptor, please give your attention. I, called such-and-such, request of you, the venerable preceptor, through the acharya nun: may the venerable preceptor become my preceptor. I request going forth from the venerable preceptor.' This is repeated a second and third time in the same way. At the third recitation, the word 'from the preceptor nun' is to be said. The preceptor nun says 'It is possible,' and the novice candidate says 'Excellent.'

Then the preceptor nun is to request the hair-cutting nun to cut the candidate's hair. The hair-cutting nun asks: 'Sister, shall I cut your hair?' If she says 'Cut it,' the hair is cut. If she says 'No,' say to her: 'Then leave from here.'

The fully ordained monks assign to the hair-cutting nun the following duty to perform directly in that way: if the candidate becomes cold after the hair-cutting nun has attended to her in this way, she is to be bathed with warm water; if she is warm, she is to be bathed with cool water. Then in a single moment, after drying the water from the body, she is to put on the lower robe. When the lower robe is being put on, the candidate's sex characteristics are to be examined, to determine whether she is without characteristics, or has ambiguous characteristics, or is hermaphroditic.

If the hair-cutting nun, having taken up the duty to perform directly in that way, does not carry it out, there will be a transgression.

Then the going forth is to be carried out. First, the candidate is caused to prostrate before the Teacher. After that, she is caused to prostrate before the preceptor nun. She is then made to sit cross-legged in front of her, caused to join her palms together, and thereupon she is to speak these words:

'Venerable preceptor, please give your attention. I, called such-and-such, for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, who is supreme among two-footed beings. I take refuge in the holy Dharma, which is free from attachment. I take refuge in the supreme Saṅgha, which is the highest among assemblies. Following in the going forth of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Śākyamuni — the Lion of the Śākyas, the King of the Śākyas, the Chief — I have gone forth and renounce the marks of a householder. I take up the marks of one who has gone forth.'

This is repeated a second and third time. The preceptor nun says 'It is possible,' and the one who has gone forth says 'Excellent.'

Then the preceptor nun is to request a fully ordained nun who is skilled in imparting the training rules of a novice nun. Whoever is requested should cause the candidate to prostrate before the Teacher, seat her cross-legged in front of her, cause her to join her palms, and then impart the taking of refuge and the training rules of a novice nun.

'Noble one, please give your attention. I, called such-and-such, for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, who is supreme among two-footed beings. I take refuge in the holy Dharma, which is free from attachment. I take refuge in the supreme Saṅgha, which is the highest among assemblies. I request the noble one to accept me as a novice nun for as long as I live.'

This is repeated a second and third time. At the third recitation, the words 'the acharya nun' are to be said. The acharya nun says 'It is possible,' and the novice nun says 'Excellent.'

After this, a fully ordained nun is to measure the shadow and is to state the person's name, the day and night portions, and the time.

Then the ten training rules are to be given:

'Noble one, please give your attention. Just as the noble ones, the arhats, have throughout their lives abandoned the taking of life and turned back from the taking of life, so too I, called such-and-such, from this day forth, for as long as life lasts, abandon the taking of life and turn back from the taking of life.'

By this first training rule, just as the noble ones, the arhats, have trained, practised, and acted, so too shall I follow in their training, accomplish it, and carry it out.

Furthermore, just as the noble ones, the arhats, have throughout their lives abandoned taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, grain-based alcohol and fruit-based alcohol, the intoxicants that lead to heedlessness, singing, dancing, playing instruments, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, and cosmetics, high beds and large beds, eating at improper times, and accepting gold and silver, and have turned back from accepting gold and silver — so too I, called such-and-such, from this day forth, for as long as life lasts, abandon taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, grain-based alcohol and fruit-based alcohol, the intoxicants that lead to heedlessness, singing, dancing, playing instruments, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, and cosmetics, high beds and large beds, eating at improper times, and accepting gold and silver, and I turn back from accepting gold and silver. By these ten training rules, just as the noble ones, the arhats, have trained, practised, and acted, so too shall I follow in their training, accomplish it, and carry it out.

The acharya nun is to say 'It is possible,' and the novice nun is to say 'Excellent.'

If the one who resides as a householder has completed ten years of age, or if she is a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, she is to be given the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them for a period of two years. It is to be given in the following way.

The assembly of nuns is to gather and convene. She is to be allowed to bow to the assembly, and even if there are as few as twelve nuns gathered, she is to be seated cross-legged before the eldest and is to make a request of the preceptor nun. She is to be allowed to bow to the preceptor nun, to sit in a low posture, and to join her palms. If the preceptor is a preceptor nun, she is to make the request in these words: 'Please attend, Preceptor. I, called such-and-such, request of the preceptor nun — may you, Preceptor, become my preceptor nun. I request of the preceptor that I be fully allowed to take up the vows of the training.' If she is an acharya nun instead, the request is to be made in these words: 'Please attend, Acharya. I, called such-and-such, request of the acharya — may you, Acharya, become my preceptor nun. I request of the acharya that I be fully allowed to take up the vows of the training from the preceptor nun.' Likewise this is done a second and a third time. On the third repetition, one says 'preceptor nun.' The preceptor nun is to say 'It is possible,' and the student is to say 'Excellent.'

Then the vows of the training are to be requested. The candidate should attend and say: 'Noble members of the Saṅgha, I, called such-and-such, for the sake of the matter — stating her name — request full ordination from she called such-and-such. I, called such-and-such, with the preceptor nun called such-and-such, request of the noble Saṅgha the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them for a period of two years. May the noble Saṅgha, out of compassion and for the sake of that compassion, grant to me, called such-and-such, a householder of ten years' standing, or a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them.' Likewise this is to be done a second and a third time.

After this, one nun who has received the request is to perform the act. The candidate should attend: 'Noble members of the Saṅgha, she called such-and-such, a householder who has completed ten years of age, or a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, requests of the noble Saṅgha of nuns the training in the six rules and the six accompanying rules for a period of two years.

If the noble Saṅgha of nuns is agreeable and the time is right, let the noble Saṅgha of nuns grant permission, and let the noble Saṅgha of nuns confer upon her called such-and-such, a householder who has completed ten years of age, or a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, with the preceptress called such-and-such, the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them for a period of two years from the Saṅgha of nuns. This is the motion. The act is to be performed as follows. 'Noble members of the Saṅgha of nuns, she called such-and-such, a householder who has completed ten years of age, or a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, with the preceptress called such-and-such, requests of the noble Saṅgha the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them for a period of two years. On her behalf, the noble Saṅgha of nuns is requested to confer upon her called such-and-such, a householder who has completed ten years of age, or a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, with the preceptress called such-and-such, the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them for a period of two years from the Saṅgha of nuns. Those among the noble members of the Saṅgha who are agreeable to conferring upon her called such-and-such, a householder who has completed ten years of age, or a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them, should remain silent. Those who are not agreeable should speak.' She called such-and-such, a householder who has completed ten years of age, or a young woman who has completed eighteen years of age, has been conferred the training in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them by the noble Saṅgha of nuns. The noble Saṅgha of nuns has consented and granted this by remaining silent. This is accordingly held to be so.

Then the six rules and the six rules that accompany them are to be taught to her in detail. What are the six? They are:

She shall not go alone into a village,
she shall not ford to the far bank of a river,
she shall not make physical contact with men,
she shall not dwell together with a man,
she shall not act as a go-between,
she shall conceal no wrongdoing.

These are the six rules of the scriptural teaching
proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

And what are the six accompanying rules? They are:

She shall not take hold of gold and the like,
she shall not shave the hair of the secret place,
she shall not dig the earth,
she shall not, out of foolishness, cut green grass,
she shall not eat food before receiving it as an offering,
she shall not eat food that has been set aside.

These six accompanying rules
the Sugata has not permitted.

When she has trained for two years in the six rules and the six rules that accompany them, she is then to be given the vow of full ordination into the celibate life in proper order. First, the preceptress should prepare the five robes and the bowl, then instruct her privately, and then request a nun to perform the act. After that, when the Saṅgha of nuns has assembled and gathered, and when the assembly consists of at least twelve nuns, the candidate should bow three times to the assembly and then make a request to the preceptress. If she is indeed the preceptress, the request is made in these words: 'Please give heed, preceptress. I, called such-and-such, request of the preceptress that she become my preceptress. Preceptress, please become my preceptress. I request full ordination from the preceptress.' If she is likewise requesting from a preceptress-teacher, she should make the request in these words: 'Please give heed, preceptress-teacher. I, called such-and-such, request from the preceptress-teacher that she become my preceptress. Preceptress-teacher, please become my preceptress. I request full ordination from the preceptress-teacher through the preceptress.' Likewise this is done a second and a third time.

Then the robes are to be consecrated with blessing. 'Please give heed, preceptress. These robes of her called such-and-such are consecrated as paired garments and are the completed robes to be worn throughout.' Likewise a second and a third time. In the same way this is done for the upper robe and

the middle robe, the skirt, and the perspiration cloth are likewise consecrated with blessing.

Then the alms bowl is to be shown to the assembly of nuns. The nuns are to say: "The alms bowl is good." Then the alms bowl is consecrated with blessing. "Please give heed, preceptress. This alms bowl of her called such-and-such is the vessel of a sage; it is consecrated as a vessel to be lifted and used as a receptacle for eating at all times." Likewise a second and a third time.

After that, from the place of hearing, she is to be led away and set apart in a place of seeing, with her palms pressed together, shown to those assembled. Then the acting nun is to say: "Designate someone to reveal the secret matters to her called such-and-such." Whoever is appointed, let her say: "I am called such-and-such." Then the acting nun is to say: "First, win her confidence. She called such-and-such — with the preceptress called such-and-such — with her called such-and-such as the revealer of secret matters, having won confidence: if she has consented, say that she has consented."

Then the acting nun is to make a brief application. "Heed this, noble assembly of nuns. I, called such-and-such, am preceptress. She called such-and-such, whose secret matters are to be revealed by me called such-and-such, has consented. If the time is right and the noble assembly of nuns is agreeable, may the noble assembly of nuns approve, and may the noble assembly of nuns — with the preceptress called such-and-such — reveal the secret matters to her called such-and-such. This is the application."

Then the nun who reveals secret matters is to have her sit cross-legged before her, let her press her palms together, and say to her: "She called such-and-such, listen. This is your time of truth; this is the proper time. Whatever I ask you, answer without embarrassment: to what has occurred, say that it occurred; to what has not occurred, say that it has not occurred — answer without error.

"Are you a woman? — I am a woman.

"Are you a laywoman of twelve years, or a young woman who has reached the age of twenty? — I have reached it.

"Are you furnished with the five Dharma robes and an alms bowl? — I am furnished.

"Are your parents and your husband living? — Have your father, mother, and husband given permission?

"Are you not a slave girl? Not one who has been seized? Not one who was purchased? Not one who has been sold? Is there no dispute? Are you not one who has been stolen away? Is there no attachment of another? Are you not a magical emanation? Not an animal? Not one who has been troublesome to the king? Not one who has a quarrel with the king? Not one who performs acts harmful to the king? Have you not yourself performed or caused to be performed acts harmful to the king? Are you not one who is not at peace? Not one afflicted by grief? Not pregnant? Not without the feminine characteristic? Not possessed of both characteristics? Not a person with a festering wound? Not one who constantly bleeds? Not one without blood? Not one who has only the mark? Have you not deceived a monk? Have you not killed your father? Not killed your mother? Not killed an arhat? Have you not, with malicious intent, drawn blood from the body of a Tathāgata? Are you not a tīrthika adherent? Are you not one who goes over to the tīrthikas? Are you not one who bears the banner of a thief? Not one who abides as a thief? Not one who lives separately? Not one who does not abide?

"Have you previously gone forth into the homeless life? — If she says, 'I have gone forth,' say: 'In that case, go back.' If she says, 'I have not gone forth,' then: Have you, having now gone forth, been practicing the holy life properly? — I have been practicing it. Have you requested from the assembly of nuns the training in the six rules and the six rules to be followed for two years? — I have requested it. Have you trained for two years in the six rules and the six rules to be followed? — I have trained. Has the vow that generates the holy life been conferred upon you by the assembly of nuns? — It has been conferred."

"Has the assembly of nuns performed for you what was to be done beforehand?" — "It has been performed." "Have you shown respectful regard toward the assembly of nuns?" — "I have shown respectful regard." "Are you fully pure of the impediment-factors?" — "I am fully pure." "Do you have any debt to others, whether great or small, that remains unpaid?" "What is your name? What is your preceptress's name?" — "My name is such-and-such." Stating her name for the purpose of the matter: "My preceptress's name is such-and-such."

"You, named thus-and-such, listen. There are bodily afflictions that may be harmful to the female body, and they are as follows: leprosy, skin eruptions, scabies, open sores, fever, dappled flesh, emaciation, convulsions, severe itching, nausea, vomiting, haemorrhoids, epidemic illness, foul breath, intoxication, urinary obstruction, fatigue, stupor, difficulty breathing, coughing, wasting disease, loss of memory, trembling, white disease, swollen feet, nocturnal discharge, tumors, blood disease, bile disease, anal fistula, indigestion, burning sensations in the limbs, burning sensations in the sides, deterioration of the bones, severe fever, quartan fever recurring every day, every second day, every third day, every fourth day, daily fever, aggregative fever, chronic fever, and fever accompanied by exhaustion and collapse. Are there any such bodily afflictions of this kind, or other afflictions harmful to the body, that you have on your person?" — If she is fully pure of them, instruct her privately in this way: "Just as I asked you, speak the same inside the assembly. Remain here and do not come until you are called." Then the one who teaches privately shall sit by the path and say these words: "Listen, noble one: I have taught and questioned you, named thus-and-such, regarding the impediment-factors, and you have said, 'I am fully pure.' Shall I go in?" All the nuns should then say: "If she is fully pure, come forward." If that is said, it is well. If it is not said, she will be accompanied by a transgression.

Then the officiating nun shall place her in front and confer upon her the vow that generates the holy life. "Attend, noble assembly of nuns! I, named thus-and-such, request full ordination from the preceptress named thus-and-such. I, named thus-and-such, request from the noble assembly of nuns the vow that generates the holy life" — stating the matter by name — "my preceptress being named thus-and-such. May the noble assembly of nuns confer upon me, named thus-and-such, the vow that generates the holy life, out of compassion, for the sake of compassion." Likewise a second time, likewise a third time.

Then the officiating nun, having received the petition, shall perform the act. "Attend, noble assembly of nuns! This one, named thus-and-such, requests full ordination from the one named thus-and-such; this one named thus-and-such, whose preceptress is named thus-and-such, requests from the noble assembly of nuns the vow that generates the holy life. If it is the proper time for the noble assembly of nuns, and if they consent, let the noble assembly of nuns give their assent. I, named thus-and-such, shall ask in the midst of the assembly about the impediment-factors. This is the petition."

"You, named thus-and-such, listen. This is the time for truth; this is the time for accuracy. Of everything I ask you, speak without concealment: what has occurred, say it has occurred; what has not occurred, say it has not occurred, without error. Are you a woman?" — "I am a woman," says she —

"Does your body suffer from such a disease or any other?" — and she says, "It does not." This completes the section up to that point.

Then she should make the petition. "Listen, noble assembly of nuns. This one, named thus-and-such, seeks full ordination from the preceptress named thus-and-such. She is either a householder of twelve years' standing, or a young woman who has completed twenty years of age. She possesses the five Dharma-robes and the alms-bowl as well. She declares herself to be entirely pure of the impediment-factors. She, named thus-and-such, with the preceptress named thus-and-such, asks the noble assembly of nuns for the vow that generates the holy life. If it is the proper time for the noble assembly of nuns, and if they consent, let the noble assembly of nuns assent. Let the noble assembly of nuns give to her, named thus-and-such, with the preceptress named thus-and-such, the vow that generates the holy life. The preceptress is named thus-and-such. This is the petition." The formal act is performed in this same manner.

"Listen, noble assembly of nuns. This one, named thus-and-such, seeks full ordination from one named thus-and-such. She is either a householder of twelve years' standing, or a young woman who has completed twenty years of age. She possesses the five Dharma-robes and the alms-bowl as well. She declares herself to be pure of the impediment-factors. She, named thus-and-such, with the preceptress named thus-and-such, asks the noble assembly of nuns for the vow that generates the holy life. The noble assembly of nuns is to give to her, named thus-and-such, with the preceptress named thus-and-such, the vow that generates the holy life. Those among the noble assembly of nuns who consent to granting the vow that generates the holy life to her, named thus-and-such, with the preceptress named thus-and-such, let them remain silent. Those who do not consent, let them speak. The noble assembly of nuns has given to her, named thus-and-such, with the preceptress named thus-and-such, the vow that generates the holy life. The noble assembly of nuns has consented and approved by remaining silent. So it is held to be."

After that, the entire assembly of monks gathers and is seated — a minimum assembly of ten monks — and the entire assembly of nuns gathers and is seated — a minimum assembly of twelve nuns. Before the officiating monk, she is placed on a bundle of grass or a cushion with a proper covering, and with palms pressed together she requests full ordination from both assemblies.

"Listen, both venerable communities. I, named thus-and-such, for the sake of the matter — naming the preceptress by name — seek full ordination from the preceptress named thus-and-such. I, named thus-and-such, request full ordination from both communities. May both venerable communities fully ordain me. May both venerable communities lift me up. May both venerable communities take me under their care. May both venerable communities show me kindness — for those who are kind, out of kindness." This is to be done three times, in this same way, a second and a third time.

After that, the officiating monk makes the petition: "Listen, both venerable communities. This one, named thus-and-such, seeks full ordination from the preceptress named thus-and-such. She, named thus-and-such, with the preceptress named thus-and-such, requests full ordination from both communities. If it is the proper time for both communities, and if they consent, let both communities assent."

"I will now question this candidate about the impediment factors in the presence of both venerable communities. This is the petition.

You, named thus-and-such, listen. This is your moment of truth; this is the proper time. Whatever I ask you, answer without embarrassment: if it occurred, say it occurred; if it did not occur, say it did not occur — speak without error.

Are you a woman? I am a woman.

Are you a lay resident of twelve years of age, or a young woman who has completed twenty years? I have completed them.

Are you provided with the five robes and the alms bowl? I am provided with them.

Are your father, mother, and husband living? They are living. Have your father, mother, and husband given their consent? They have given consent.

Are you not a slave? Not a slave. Are you not a kidnapped person? Not a kidnapped person. Are you not a purchased person? Not a purchased person. Are you not a sold person? Not a sold person. Are you free of attachment? Free of attachment. Are you not an emanated being? Not an emanated being. Are you not one cherished by the king? Not one cherished by the king. Are you not in enmity with the king? Not in enmity with the king. Are you not one who performs acts harmful to the king? I am not. Have you not caused harm to the king, or caused harm to be done to him? I have not. Are you not rebellious? Not rebellious. Are you not one consumed by grief? Not consumed by grief. Are you not pregnant? Not pregnant. Are you not without the female sex organ? I am not without it. Do you not have a double sex organ? I do not. Are you not one with a blocked organ? Not blocked. Are you not one who perpetually flows with blood? Not so. Are you not one without blood? Not so. Are you not one who possesses only a mark? Not so. Have you not deceived a monk? I have not. Have you not killed your father? I have not. Have you not killed your mother? I have not. Have you not killed an arhat? I have not. Have you not, with malicious intent, drawn blood from the body of a Tathāgata? I have not. Are you not a tīrthika (non-Buddhist adherent)? I am not. Are you not one who goes over to the tīrthikas? I am not. Are you not one bearing the banner of a thief? Not so. Are you not one who dwells as a thief? Not so. Are you not one who remains separately? Not so. Are you not one who is without a proper residence? Not so.

Have you previously gone forth into renunciation? If she says, 'I have gone forth,' then say: 'In that case, proceed.' If she says, 'I have not gone forth,' then ask: 'Have you now gone forth into renunciation? I have. Have you properly observed the celibate life? Have you been given by the community of nuns the training in the six rules and the six consequential rules for two years? They have been given. Have you trained for two years in the six rules and the six consequential rules? I have trained. Has the community of nuns conferred upon you the restraint that produces the celibate life? It has been conferred. Has the community of nuns performed for you the preliminary acts? They have been performed. Have you gained the approval of the community of nuns? I have gained it. Are you fully purified of all the impediment factors? I am fully purified. Do you have any debts to others, whether many or few? I am free of them.'

What is your name? What is the name of your preceptress? My name is thus-and-such. Speaking the name explicitly for the sake of clarity, the name of my preceptress is thus-and-such.

You, named thus-and-such, listen. There are bodily ailments that may afflict the female body. They are as follows: leprosy, swelling, consumption, eye disease, fever, mottled-flesh disease, emaciation, epilepsy, severe trembling, vomiting, hemorrhoids, hiccups, contagious fever, foul breath, madness, exhaustion, dizziness, burning fever, coughing, difficulty breathing, wasting, forgetfulness, chronic sores, white disease, swollen feet, nocturnal eruptions, tumors, blood disease, bile disease, rectal hemorrhoids, goiter, heat of the limbs, heat of the sides, dissolution of the bones, severe epidemic fever, intermittent fever occurring on the first day, on the second day, on the third day, on the fourth day, daily intermittent fever —"

— congregate fever, intermittent fever with exhaustion, and constant fever — and all other such bodily illnesses and bodily harms that may afflict your body: tell us truthfully and accurately whether they are present or not."

The Vinaya on Minor Points, fascicle thirty-seven.

Then the monk who makes the request, having obtained permission, shall perform the act. "Hear me, venerable ones of both Saṅghas. This one here, called such-and-such, requests full ordination from both Saṅghas with the preceptress called such-and-such. She who is called such-and-such, with the preceptress called such-and-such, requests full ordination from both Saṅghas. She is a woman; she possesses the faculties of a woman. Whether she is a woman who has lived in a household for twelve years or a young girl who has completed twenty years of age, she has the five Dharma-robes and the alms bowl. Her father, mother, and husband have given their consent. The impediment-factors are entirely pure. She has practiced the holy life well. The community of nuns has imposed upon her the training in the six qualities and the six accompanying qualities for two years. She has trained in the training of the six qualities and the six accompanying qualities for two years. The community of nuns has given her the vow that produces the holy life through the three factors. The community of nuns has already performed the preliminary acts for her. The community of nuns has been satisfied. Declaring herself that the impediment-factors are pure — this one called such-and-such, with the preceptress called such-and-such, requests full ordination from both Saṅghas. If the time has come for both Saṅghas and they consent, both Saṅghas should remain silent, and both Saṅghas should grant full ordination to this one called such-and-such with the preceptress called such-and-such. This is the motion. The act shall be performed as follows."

"Hear me, venerable ones of both Saṅghas. This one called such-and-such, with the preceptress called such-and-such, requests full ordination from both Saṅghas. She who is called such-and-such, with the preceptress called such-and-such, requests full ordination from both Saṅghas. She is a woman; she also possesses the faculties of a woman. Whether she is a woman who has lived in a household for twelve years or a young girl who has completed twenty years of age, she has the five Dharma-robes and the alms bowl. Her father, mother, and husband have given their consent. The impediment-factors are entirely pure. She has practiced the holy life well. The community of nuns has imposed upon her the training in the six qualities and the six accompanying qualities for two years. She has trained in the training of the six qualities and the six accompanying qualities for two years. The community of nuns has given her the vow that produces the holy life. The community of nuns has already performed the acts required for her. I have satisfied the community of nuns. Declaring herself that the impediment-factors are pure — this one called such-and-such, with the preceptress called such-and-such, has received full ordination from both Saṅghas. The community of nuns hereby grants full ordination to this one called such-and-such with the preceptress called such-and-such from both Saṅghas. If both Saṅghas have granted full ordination to this one called such-and-such with the preceptress called such-and-such and both Saṅghas consent and agree, let the venerable ones remain silent. Those who do not consent should speak. This is the wording of the first act. In the same way, the wording of the act is to be spoken a second time and a third time."

Such-and-such, with the preceptress called such-and-such, has received full ordination from both Saṅghas. Since both Saṅghas consent and agree and remain silent, it is accepted as so.

Then the shadow is to be measured. Since the nuns were measuring the shadow with a long measuring rod, the Blessed One declared that one should not measure the shadow with a long rod. And since they measured with the foot, the Blessed One declared that one should not measure with the foot. One should measure with a wooden rod of four finger-widths. The span of that rod shall be called a person's measure. After that, you should know the seasons. There are the winter season, the spring season, the summer season, the end of the rains retreat, and the long season. The winter season is four months. The spring season is four months. The summer season is one month. The end of the rains retreat is one day. The long season is three months less one night. You should also know the times of day: first dawn, middle dawn, last dawn, before sunrise, at sunrise, one-eighth of the day after sunrise, one-quarter of the day after sunrise, before midday, at midday, past midday, the afternoon quarter, the afternoon eighth, at sunset, before sunset, before the stars rise, and when the stars rise.

Then the three foundations are to be spoken. "You who are called such-and-such, listen. The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha, knowing and seeing, declared these three foundations to a nun who has gone forth and received full ordination. If a nun abides in these, she, having gone forth and received full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, shall become truly established as a nun. What are the three? The first is dust-heap robes within the class of Dharma-robes — that which is permitted and fitting. If one abides in this, a nun, having gone forth and received full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya and thereby becoming truly established as a nun, may by means of dust-heap robes be content. Venerable one called such-and-such, do you accept this as sufficient from this day forward for as long as you live?" She should respond, "I accept." If one obtains more, the additional acceptable robes are: silk, cotton, coarse cloth, bark-cloth, linen, hempen cloth, cotton cloth called ami-la, so-mi-la, a woven fabric the color of a lac-insect resembling the color of a crimson worm, fine Kāśī cloth, fine zarma cloth, fine wool called dugulaka, and fine cotton cloth called kotampaka. Whatever other suitable robe-material one obtains, whether from the Saṅgha or from an individual, from these you should take what you need and be satisfied. Do you take a solemn vow regarding such a foundation?" She should respond, "I also take a solemn vow."

"You who are called such-and-such, listen. Within the class of food, alms-food is what is permitted and fitting. If one abides in this, a nun, having gone forth and received full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, shall become truly established as a nun. Do you, called such-and-such, accept alms-food as sufficient from this day forward for as long as you live?" She should respond, "I accept." If one obtains more, additional allowable foods are: cooked rice, sour gruel, porridge, regular meals, meals to which one is invited, meals offered on the spot, prepared foods, the festival of the fifth, the eighth-day meal, the fourteenth-day meal, and the festival of the fifteenth. Whatever other suitable alms-food one obtains, whether from the Saṅgha or from an individual — from these too you should take what you need and be satisfied. "Do you take a vow regarding such a foundation?" She should respond, "I take a vow."

"You who are called such-and-such, listen. The permissible medicines are those that have been boiled and then discarded. If you abide by this foundation, you will become a fully ordained nun — one who has gone forth and received full ordination in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. You who are called such-and-such, do you from this day forward for as long as you live take a vow of contentment with medicines that have been boiled and cast away?" She should respond, "I accept." If one obtains more, additional allowable medicines are: butter, oil, honey, molasses, root medicines, trunk medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, fruit medicines, those taken in the morning, those taken in the evening, those taken on the seventh day, and those taken for life. Whatever other suitable medicines of this kind one obtains — whether from the Saṅgha or from an individual — from these too you should take what you need and be satisfied. "Do you take a vow regarding such a foundation?" She should respond, "I take a vow."

"You who are called such-and-such, listen. The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, having known and seen, proclaimed eight grounds of defeat for nuns who have gone forth and received full ordination. If a nun commits any one of them — the very instant she commits and enacts it — she is no longer a nun, no longer a female renunciant, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas. She loses the status of a nun and loses the status of a female renunciant. She is gone, expelled, fallen, defeated — one who has incurred a defeat — and she cannot be reinstated as a female renunciant. It is like the top of a palm tree that has been cut down: it cannot grow green again, cannot sprout, cannot grow, cannot increase. There is no possibility of its ever growing tall again. In exactly the same way, if a nun commits any one of those eight grounds — if she commits and enacts any one of those eight grounds — the very instant she commits and enacts it, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female renunciant, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas. She loses the status of a nun and loses the status of a female renunciant. She is gone, expelled, fallen, defeated — one who has incurred a defeat — and she cannot be reinstated as a female renunciant.

"You who are called such-and-such, listen. What are the eight? The Blessed One, in numerous categories, has blamed sensual desire, calling it clinging, attachment, intention, fondness, dwelling, certainty, and deep infatuation; while renouncing sensual desire he has praised, extolled, commended, proclaimed, encouraged, glorified, and declared it as something to be specially praised — returning it, exhausting it, being free of attachment, being noble, being thoroughly pacified, being extinguished. You who are called such-and-such — even if, from this day forward, with a mind of attachment you were to gaze eye-to-eye at a man with a desirous mind and not look away, how much more so would it be to engage with him in the act of unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse. The Blessed One has also declared: if a nun, without having surrendered her training or declared her training to be weak, and without having formally prepared the ground — even with one born in an animal realm — commits the act of unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse in any such circumstance whatsoever, and if a nun commits and enacts it, the very instant she commits and enacts it, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female renunciant, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas. She loses the status of a nun; she loses the status of a female renunciant. She is gone, expelled, fallen, defeated — one who has incurred a defeat — and she cannot be reinstated as a nun. It is like the top of a palm tree that has been cut down: it cannot grow green again."

It cannot grow green again, it cannot flourish and spread. In just the same way, if a nun commits and enacts such a circumstance as this, the very instant she commits and enacts it, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female renunciant, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas. She loses the status of a nun; she loses the status of a female renunciant. She is gone, expelled, fallen, defeated — and she cannot be reinstated as a female renunciant.

Therefore, from this day forth, you are to take up with enthusiasm the refraining from this act, the not committing of it, the not engaging in it, and the giving it up entirely. Guard your mind. Be mindful, be heedful, be diligent. Ask whether she refrains from such a thing as this, and let her say that she does refrain from it.

Now, you whose name is so-and-so, listen. The Blessed One has, in many categories, condemned the taking of what is not given. The giving up of taking what is not given he has praised, encouraged, extolled, and proclaimed. Therefore, from this day forth, you whose name is so-and-so, even if you would not take so much as a sesame husk that belongs to another without stealing intent — to say nothing of five māśas or more than five māśas, as the Blessed One has taught — if a nun, whether dwelling in a village or in a remote place, takes by theft what is known to belong to another, to whatever amount, and is on that account seized by a king or his minister and killed, or bound, or expelled, and they say to her: "You are a thief, you are a fool, you are ignorant, you are a thief" — if she commits and enacts such a circumstance as this, the very instant she commits and enacts it, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female renunciant, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas — and all the rest as before, up to: be mindful, be heedful, be diligent. Ask whether she refrains from such a thing as this, and let her say that she does refrain from it.

Now, you whose name is so-and-so, listen. The Blessed One has, in many categories, condemned the taking of life. The giving up of taking life he has praised, encouraged, extolled, and proclaimed. Therefore, you whose name is so-and-so, from this day forth, even if you would not intentionally deprive even an insect of its life — to say nothing of a human being or one who has come to be in a human body — as the Blessed One has taught: if any nun, whether in regard to a human being or one who has come to be in a human body, intentionally deprives that person of life with her own hand, or provides a weapon for that purpose, or procures a weapon for that purpose, or urges that person toward death, or praises the virtues of death, saying to him: "O man, living as you do in such sinful, impure, wretched circumstances — what is the use of living? For you, sir, death is better than life" — thinking this in her mind, if she urges him toward death in many ways with this thought fixed in her mind, or if she praises the virtues of death, and by such means that person dies — then if a nun commits and enacts such a circumstance as this, the very instant she commits and enacts it, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female renunciant, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas, and she loses the status of a nun — and all the rest as before, up to: be mindful, be heedful, and be diligent. Ask whether she refrains from such a thing as this, and let her say that she does refrain from it.

Now, you whose name is so-and-so, listen. False speech the Blessed One has, in many categories, condemned. The giving up of false speech he has praised, encouraged, extolled, and proclaimed. Therefore, you whose name is so-and-so, listen: even for the sake of play as a child, one should not knowingly speak falsehood —

— how much more so to falsely claim, as though one possessed it when one does not, the superhuman Dharma of one's spiritual teachers. The Blessed One has declared: Moreover, whatever nun does not directly know, does not comprehensively know, and does not possess — yet falsely claims, as though she possessed it when she does not, to have realized, to have seen, or to have attained contact with the noble distinction that is the superhuman Dharma of one's spiritual teachers — and when asked what she knows, says "I know this, I see this" — if what she claims to know is: "I know suffering, I know the origin of suffering, I know cessation, I know the path" — and if what she claims to see is: "I see gods; I see nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas (Skt. garuḍa), gandharvas (Skt. gandharva), kinnaras (Skt. kinnara), great serpents, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas (Skt. kumbhāṇḍa), and putrefying bodies. The gods see me; the nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and putrefying bodies also see me. I hear the voices of gods; I hear the voices of nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and putrefying bodies. The gods also hear my voice; the nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and putrefying bodies also hear my voice. I go to visit gods; I go to visit nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, great serpents, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and putrefying bodies. Gods come to visit me; nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, great serpents, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and putrefying bodies also come to visit me. I converse with gods, converse with all of them, delight in each of them, and constantly dwell together with them. The nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, great serpents, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and putrefying bodies converse with me, converse with me about everything, delight in me, and constantly dwell together with me. Gods converse with me, converse with me about everything, delight in me, and constantly dwell together with me. The nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, great serpents, kinnaras, flesh-eaters, hungry ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, and putrefying bodies also constantly converse with me about everything, delight in me, and constantly dwell together with me" —

— and if, without having attained it, she says "I have attained the perception of impermanence," or perceives what is impermanent as suffering, perceives what is suffering as selfless, perceives food as disagreeable, perceives the entire world as something to be disenchanted with, perceives it as a basis for recognizing faults, perceives it as something to be abandoned, perceives it as separation from attachment, perceives it as cessation, perceives it as death, perceives it as impure, perceives it as turning livid, perceives it as festering, perceives it as decaying, perceives it as being devoured by worms, perceives it as bloated, perceives it as eaten away, perceives it as red and bloody, perceives it as scattered, perceives it as a heap of bones, perceives it individually as emptiness — and without having attained it she says "I have attained" the first meditative concentration, the second, the third, the fourth, loving-kindness,

compassion, joy, equanimity, the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception — and without having attained it she says "I have attained" the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-return, the fruit of non-return, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of former lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, exhaustion of the outflows, arhatship, cultivation of the eight liberations, and liberation from both aspects — if a nun engages in and carries out conduct of such a kind, the moment she has so engaged and carried it out, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female contemplative, no longer a daughter of the Śākyan. She will have lost the substance of a nun and the substance of a female contemplative. She is without it. She is expelled. She has incurred a downfall. It is a defeat. She cannot be restored to the state of a female contemplative. It is like the top of a palm tree that has been cut: it cannot turn green again, cannot sprout again, cannot grow and spread. In the same way, if a nun engages in and carries out conduct of such a kind, the moment she has so engaged and carried it out, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female contemplative, no longer a daughter of the Śākyan. She will have lost the substance of a nun and the substance of a female contemplative. She is without it. She is expelled. She has incurred a downfall. It is a defeat. She cannot be restored to the state of a female contemplative.

Therefore, from this day forward, you should refrain from such conduct, not fall into such engagement, and with swift and earnest resolve to abandon such conduct, guard your mind, be mindful, be heedful, and be diligent. If there is anyone who does not engage in conduct of this kind, or who says "I do not engage in it," then announce: "Let she who bears such-and-such a name hear this."

The Blessed One has declared: if a nun, acting out of attachment and having become attached, takes pleasure in touching and fully contacting from the waist down to the knee together with a man who is born — if a nun engages in and carries out conduct of such a kind, the moment she has so engaged and carried it out, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female contemplative, no longer a daughter of the Śākyan — from that point up to and including the injunction that she should refrain from such engagement, and with swift resolve to abandon such conduct, guard her mind, be mindful, be heedful, and be diligent. If there is anyone who does not engage in conduct of this kind, or who says "I do not engage in it," then announce: "Let she who bears such-and-such a name hear this."

The Blessed One has declared: if a nun, acting with attachment and having become attached, together with a man exchanges words of flattery, plays, laughs, shows pride, runs, makes bodily contact, exposes herself at an appointed time or on an impulse, sets up a signal, or whether the man comes or goes takes pleasure in it — if she is such a one, leans her body toward him, and has become subject to a man in that manner, being endowed with those eight such qualities, and a nun engages in and carries out conduct of such a kind, the moment she has so engaged and carried it out, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female contemplative, no longer a daughter of the Śākyan — up to the point where she should refrain from such engagement, and with swift resolve to abandon such conduct, guard her mind, be mindful, be heedful, and be diligent. If there is anyone who does not engage in conduct of this kind, or who says "I do not engage in it," then announce: "Let she who bears such-and-such a name hear this."

The Blessed One has declared: if a nun knows that another nun has previously committed a defeat and no longer remains in good standing, and when that nun has died, or has returned to lay life, or

has fled to another district — after that, she should speak thus: "Noble ones, I previously knew that such-and-such a nun had committed a defeat and no longer remained in good standing." If she then acts and conducts herself in a manner befitting that same category of offense — that same conduct involving the transgression of a nun — then the moment she so acts and conducts herself accordingly, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female contemplative, no longer a daughter of the Śākyan, and so on as before, up to the point where she should refrain from such engagement, and with swift resolve to abandon such conduct, guard her mind, be mindful, be heedful, and be diligent. If there is anyone who does not engage in conduct of this kind, or who says "I do not engage in it," then announce: "Let she who bears such-and-such a name hear this."

The Blessed One has also declared: if a nun knows that a certain monk has performed an act for which he is to be expelled by the assembled Saṅgha of monks, and the assembled Saṅgha of nuns has also imposed a vow of not paying homage to him — and yet, while that monk is lying down with his hair unbound, she goes to prostrate herself before the Saṅgha by lying flat, bowing down with her body stretched out; she prepares to rise; she shows readiness to make obeisance; she sits within his boundary and requests his approval — and all this she does knowingly — then she should be told the following: "Noble one, do not lie prostrate with your hair unbound, and do not, while rising, prostrate yourself before the Saṅgha by stretching out flat. Do not prepare to rise. Do not show readiness to make obeisance. Do not sit within the boundary and request approval. I will see to it that your alms-bowl, your robes, your strainer, your cup, your waist-band, your reading, your recitation, your meditative mental engagement, and whatever else concerns you, noble one — all of these I will arrange so that they are not left unattended." The nuns should then instruct that nun in these words: "Noble sister, that monk has performed an act for which the assembled Saṅgha expelled him, and the assembled Saṅgha of nuns has also imposed upon him a vow of not receiving homage. Yet that monk, while lying down with his hair unbound, has others prostrate themselves before the Saṅgha by stretching out flat; he prepares to rise; he shows readiness to make obeisance; he sits within the boundary and requests approval — all this knowingly.
