Noble sister, do not speak to him thus: 'Noble one, do not lie prostrate with your hair unbound, and do not, while rising, prostrate yourself before the Saṅgha by stretching out flat. Do not prepare to rise. Do not show readiness to make obeisance. Do not sit within the boundary and request approval. I will see to all of this for you — your alms-bowl, your robes, your strainer, your cup, your waist-band, your reading, your recitation, your meditative mental engagement, and whatever else concerns you, noble one — all of these I will arrange so that they are not left unattended.' Noble sister, abandon the words and the course that follow from what has been abandoned, and let go of that path." If the nuns admonish that nun in this way and she abandons the matter, that is good. But if she does not abandon it, she should be admonished and instructed a second and a third time. If after being admonished and instructed a second and third time for the purpose of causing her to abandon the matter she does abandon it, that is good. But if she does not abandon it, and instead follows after what the nun has abandoned and conducts herself in a manner befitting that same category of offense, then the moment she so conducts herself, she is no longer a nun, no longer a female contemplative, no longer a daughter of the Śākyan, and so on as before, up to the point where with swift resolve to abandon such conduct she should guard her mind, be mindful, be heedful, and be diligent. If there is anyone who does not engage in conduct of this kind, or who says "I do not engage in it," then announce: "Let she who bears such-and-such a name hear this."

These eight are the chief rules (Skt. gurudharma) that the Blessed One — knowing and seeing, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha — has laid down for women who have gone forth and received full ordination as nuns, in order to restrain them and prevent transgression. Women are to train in these for as long as they live.

What are the eight? She who bears such-and-such a name, being a woman who has gone forth and received full ordination among the monks and thereby become established in the substance of nunhood, should clearly understand this. She who bears such-and-such a name: the Blessed One has laid down, as the first chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, that women are to train in this for as long as they live. Nuns are to seek, every fortnight, the instruction that shows them the teaching from the community of monks. She who bears such-and-such a name: the Blessed One has laid down, as the second chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, that women are to train in this for as long as they live. A nun must not enter the rains retreat in a place where there are no monks. She who bears such-and-such a name: the Blessed One has laid down, as the third chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, that women are to train in this for as long as they live. When a nun has emerged from the rains retreat, she must make the invitation ceremony before both communities in three respects: what was seen, what was heard, and what was suspected. She who bears such-and-such a name: the Blessed One has laid down, as the fourth chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, that women are to train in this for as long as they live. A nun must not speak of, or make mention of, a monk's lapse in moral discipline, lapse in view, lapse in conduct, or lapse in livelihood. A nun who speaks of or makes mention of a monk's lapse in moral discipline, lapse in view, lapse in conduct, or lapse in livelihood is not permitted to do so. A monk, however, is permitted to speak of and make mention of a nun's lapse in moral discipline, lapse in view, lapse in conduct, or lapse in livelihood. This is what the Blessed One has laid down for she who bears such-and-such a name, as the fifth chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, and women are to train in this for as long as they live. A nun must not speak harshly to a monk, must not be angry toward him, and must not upbraid him. A nun who speaks harshly to a monk, who is angry toward him, or who upbraids him, is not permitted to do so. She who bears such-and-such a name: the Blessed One has laid down, as the sixth chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, that women are to train in this for as long as they live. If a nun has incurred a chief rule, she must perform the probationary practice before both communities for a fortnight. She who bears such-and-such a name: the Blessed One has laid down, as the seventh chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, that women are to train in this for as long as they live. A nun who has been fully ordained for a hundred years must pay courteous respect, offer praise, rise, join her palms in reverence, and bow down before a monk who has only just then received full ordination. She who bears such-and-such a name: the Blessed One has laid down, as the eighth chief rule for women in order to restrain them and prevent transgression, that women are to train in this for as long as they live.

"Have you received and will you observe these eight chief rules?" "I will observe them." "She who bears such-and-such a name, listen. The Blessed One has connected the following four, just as the preceding ones, until they are known by a perfectly awakened buddha. What are the four? From this day forward, she who bears such-and-such a name: do not speak back against one who has spoken ill of you; do not be angry in return against one who is angry with you; do not strike back against one who has struck you; do not revile in return one who has reviled you.

She who bears such-and-such a name, listen. You formerly wished, saying: 'May I go forth and receive full ordination in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and may I come to the full status of a nun.' That wish is now fulfilled: you have gone forth and received full ordination, with a preceptress endowed with moral discipline, an ācārya endowed with moral discipline, and both communities of the Saṅgha assembled, by means of the motion and the fourfold act, without anything to be done and without anything to be set aside. You have gone forth and received full ordination.

She who bears such-and-such a name, listen. The training that a nun who has been fully ordained for a hundred years observes — that same training must also be observed by one who has been fully ordained just today. And the training that one who has been fully ordained just today observes must also be observed by one who has been fully ordained for a hundred years. You who are equal in moral discipline, equal in training, and equal in the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra — from this day forward you must give satisfaction to each other, and must not give dissatisfaction to each other. From this day forward you must regard your preceptress as a mother, and your preceptress must likewise regard you as a daughter. From this day forward you must attend upon your preceptress for as long as you live, and your preceptress must likewise attend upon you for as long as you lives. From this day forward you, reverencing with fear and living a holy life equal to that of your teacher, must show courtesy to senior nuns, nuns of middle standing, and newly ordained nuns alike.

She who bears such-and-such a name, from this day forward receive scriptural transmission, learn by heart, and recite. Become skilled in the aggregates (skandhas), skilled in the elements (dhātus), skilled in the sense bases (āyatanas), skilled in dependent origination, skilled in what is a proper case and what is not. Do not relax your diligence toward attaining what has not yet been attained, realizing what has not yet been realized, and manifesting what has not yet been manifested. These things I have set forth to you as the basis of training in what is great and foremost. All the rest your ācārya, your preceptress, your co-ācārya, your co-preceptress, your speaker, your general speaker, your praiser, and your friend will likewise teach you. Every fortnight, listen to the reading of the Prātimokṣa sūtra."

In this way, upon full ordination:

You are now fully ordained
in the supreme teaching of wisdom.
A precious human opportunity, so hard to find —
do not be disheartened by it.

You went forth from what is good,
received full ordination from what is pure.
The buddha called Satya,
having fully known this, has declared it so.

"She who bears such-and-such a name, having received full ordination, conduct yourself with heedfulness."

The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time, when the Blessed One, the Buddha, had given full ordination and the status of nuns to Gautamī, the Great Progenitress, and to the five hundred Śākya women who came with her, accepting the chief rules as their vow — at that very time those women gave full ordination and the going-forth as nuns to other women as well. And those in turn gave it to yet others. In this way the community of nuns became numerous and continued to grow. Then the elder monks and elder nuns went to where Gautamī, the Great Progenitress, was, approached her, and addressed her as follows.

"Alas! These elder nuns — those monks who are newly ordained, who are of middle standing, or who are juniors who have not been long since ordained, they should salute one another in order of seniority." When these words were spoken, Gautamī, the Great Progenitress, said to those nuns: "Sisters, wait here. I shall go and ask the noble Ānanda, and it shall be done accordingly." And so Gautamī, the Great Progenitress, went and spoke to the venerable Ānanda. When she had spoken, the venerable Ānanda said to Gautamī, the Great Progenitress: "Gautamī, wait here. I shall go and ask the Blessed One." And having said this, he went to where the Blessed One was. Upon arriving, he bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: "Alas, Blessed One! Among these elder monks and elder nuns, those monks who are newly ordained, who are of middle standing, or who are juniors not long since ordained — it is said they should not salute one another in order of seniority. How is this to be?" The Blessed One then declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do not speak such words again. And why? If, Ānanda, women had not gone forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, then devout brahmins and householders would still fill begging bowls with alms and offer them warm to the monks. If, Ānanda, women had not gone forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, then devout brahmins and householders would lay down fine uncut cloth with long fringes in the road and say: 'Monks, please walk upon this cloth with the long fringes that we have spread out; this will be for our long-lasting benefit, welfare, and happiness.' If, Ānanda, women had not gone forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, then devout brahmins and householders would scatter upon the ground the finest hair grown on their limbs and say: 'Monks, please walk upon this hair; this will be for our long-lasting benefit, welfare, and happiness.' If, Ānanda, women had not gone forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, the radiance of my śrāvakas — who, being of great power and great miraculous ability, would outshine the moon and sun — how much more would they outshine the tīrthikas! If, Ānanda, women had not gone forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, my teaching would have remained for a full thousand years, without fault and without decline.

Therefore, Ānanda, let even a nun who has been fully ordained for a hundred years perform acts of respectful greeting, praise, rising, joining the palms together, paying homage, and so forth toward a monk who has just been fully ordained."

The setting was at Śrāvastī. Among the nuns there are deeds to be performed by an assembly of four, deeds to be performed by an assembly of five, and deeds to be performed by an assembly of twelve. These became numerous deeds to be performed before the assembled community of both orders. Carrying out so many deeds became an obstacle to teaching, reciting, chanting, yoga, and mental practice. The monks who were in that situation informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One permitted the deeds of full ordination and

apart from the deeds to be performed in common, the deeds of the monk-fathers are to be performed separately, and the nuns are likewise to perform theirs separately." This was declared by the Blessed One.

The setting was at Śrāvastī. At that time in Śrāvastī there was a certain householder who had taken a wife of equal rank and lived with her in pleasure and delight. Through their pleasurable and delightful life together, after some time his wife conceived, and nine months having passed, she gave birth to a daughter. The very moment she was born, the father passed away. The mother raised her and brought her up, and when the girl had grown, the mother too passed away. Then some time later, the nun Sthulanandā was out on her alms round and happened to see the girl on a street. She asked, "Girl, whose are you?" The girl replied, "Noble one, I belong to no one — I have no protector." Sthulanandā said, "If that is so, girl, why do you not go forth into the religious life?" The girl asked, "Who would give me the going-forth?" Sthulanandā said, "I will give you the going-forth, girl — come along." "Excellent," said the girl, and she went with her to Sthulanandā's dwelling, where Sthulanandā gave her the going-forth. But the girl, tormented by affliction, later disrobed. Sthulanandā was again out on her alms round, and when she saw the girl she asked, "How are you living, girl?" The girl bowed at her feet and said, "Noble one, I live in suffering." Sthulanandā said, "If that is so, girl, why do you not again go forth?" The girl said, "Noble one, who would give the going-forth to one who has once disrobed?" Sthulanandā said, "Shall I give you the going-forth again, girl?" "Excellent," the girl replied. So Sthulanandā ordained her again, and when the girl went out on the alms round, the brahmins and householders who saw her mocked her, saying: "The female disciples of the Śākya monks practice the holy life wearily, wearily — they practice the Dharma while worn out." The nuns, having witnessed this, told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: "The fault that has come into view here is that nuns who have disrobed are being ordained again. Therefore, intending that nuns who have disrobed should not be ordained again," he declared to the monks: "Monks, the brahmins and householders mock them with reason. Therefore, a nun who has once disrobed, being without power, shall not be given the going-forth by a nun. If she is given the going-forth, there is an offense."

This is the basis in the Vinaya of minor matters, the thirty-eighth fascicle.

In summary:

She who sneers and lusts greatly,
who reviles and mocks again —
the nun who mocks the monk:
she is a nun, a novice nun.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada (the benefactor of the unprotected). At that time in the town of Khormo Jig there was a householder named Gautama, wealthy, of great possessions and resources. He had taken a wife of equal rank and lived with her in pleasure and delight. At one point he loaded up goods and went to the village of Donjog, where he visited the house of another householder. That householder greeted him with words of welcome and they rested. Through mutual affection that householder of Donjog and the householder Gautama became friends. The householder Gautama sold his goods, took up his return goods, and went back to the city of Khormo Jig. The householder of Donjog too, at a later time, loaded up goods and came to Khormo Jig, and likewise went to the householder Gautama's home.

He greeted him with words of welcome and delight, saying, "Have you come in comfort?" and they rested. The two of them grew deeply fond of one another. The householder of Donjog said to the householder Gautama, "Friend, after the two of us have passed on, what means is there to ensure that the friendship between our children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and great-great-grandchildren will never be broken?" Gautama replied, "Friend, well said — I have been thinking the very same thing. Therefore, let us betroth them before any children are even born. If a son is born to me and a daughter to you, you shall give her to my son; and if a son is born to you and a daughter to me, I shall give her to your son." The other replied, "Friend, excellent — let it be so." And so the householder of Donjog and the householder Gautama pledged to one another that they would betroth their children before any were born. Then the householder of Donjog sold his goods, took up his return goods, and went back to Donjog. There he lived with his wife in pleasure and delight, and after some time his wife conceived. When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a boy. For twenty-one days — three sets of seven — a great birth-feast was held in lavish celebration, and the child was given a name befitting his family lineage. When the householder of Khormo Jig heard that a son had been born to the householder of Donjog, he thought, "My friend has had a son, and that boy may well become my son-in-law, so it is fitting that I send him clothes and ornaments." He sent the child clothes and ornaments, and wrote a letter to the householder of Donjog saying, "Friend, I have heard that a son has been born to you. I am overjoyed that my friend has had a son, and I send these clothes and ornaments for the boy — please accept them." The other read the letter and sent a reply, and the householder Gautama read it, hoping that a daughter would be born to him, and continued to live with his wife in pleasure and delight. As they lived thus in pleasure and delight, his wife conceived, and when nine months had passed, she gave birth to a daughter. The girl was beautiful and lovely to behold, yet she was somewhat thin and slight of build. For twenty-one days — three sets of seven — a great birth-feast was held in lavish celebration, and they turned to the matter of giving the child a name. They asked, "What shall this girl be called?" The relatives replied, "This girl is thin and slight, and she is the daughter of the householder Gautama — therefore let this girl's name be Gauthami the Thin." When the householder of Donjog heard that the householder Gautama of Khormo Jig had had a daughter, he thought, "My friend has had a daughter, and that girl is surely destined to become my daughter-in-law — it is right that I send her clothes and ornaments." He wrote to the householder Gautama: "Friend, I have heard that a daughter has been born to you. I am greatly delighted that my friend has had a daughter, and I send these clothes and ornaments for her — please accept them." The householder Gautama read the letter and wrote back in reply: "What our dear friend has done is excellent. We made this alliance before the children were born, and now that a daughter has been born she shall be taken as bride." The householder Gautama then read that letter, and he had the girl instructed in the training proper for women. Likewise, the householder of Donjog had his son instructed in his training, and entrusted the boy's education to women who had formerly lived as courtesans, saying, "Let this girl be taught her proper training."

She began instructing him. When she had taught him with words for some time, he said, "I have learned my lessons — now I shall go." The woman said, "My son, learn them well. Do not go yet." He replied, "Mother, I have learned them well. I am going." She picked up a bundle of lac and said, "If you insist on going and leaving me behind, I will strike myself on the head." He said, "Mother, do not do that — I will not go," and he stayed.

Then she said, "Wretch! You claim to have learned your lessons from me, yet you do not even know this much — you would strike your own head for the sake of another's son. You are no person of sense. Stay until such time as you say, 'Mother, I will go.'" He agreed to stay a while longer.

When he still insisted on going, she said, "If you are so set on going and leaving me behind, I will throw myself into a well." He said, "Mother, if that is so, I will not go — please do not do it," and he stayed.

Again she said, "Wretch! You claim to have learned your lessons from me, yet you do not even know this much — why would you throw yourself into a well for the sake of another's son? If you cannot stay, then I myself can sit by a well with its rope and pulley and stay there. You are no person of sense. Stay." He agreed to stay a while longer.

Then she said, "Son, since time drags on like this while you sit here, cook some porridge, drink it, and be on your way." He stayed, and she cooked the porridge and set it before him. Into the bowl she put butter and honey, he drank it, and then vomited it back into the very same bowl. She poured it back into the same cup and said, "Son, come here — drink this." He said, "Mother, this is vomit — how can I drink it?" She pretended to weep, and when the neighbors heard her they all gathered and asked, "Why are you crying?" She told them everything in detail, and they said to the boy, "She prepared this porridge for your sake — why will you not drink it?" He said, "But this is vomit — how can one drink vomit?" He turned away, beat his chest, and sat there weeping.

The neighbors began saying, "Why did she vomit into it?" The neighboring households of that area pressed the boy hard, and he began to drink. At that moment she seized him by the hand, slapped him across the face, and declared: "Wretch! You claim to have learned your lessons from me — how have you learned them? Even though you saw with your own eyes that it was vomit, you were about to drink it. You are no person of sense." With that, she drove him out and sent him away.

Some time later he set out with five hundred merchants, carrying goods to trade, and went into the middle of a district. In front of those merchants he kept slandering women, one occasion after another. They then went in a group to the Āvantī quarter. Now, those merchants had previously enjoyed themselves freely and consorted with the courtesans there. But because of their association with him they too began speaking ill of women and stopped going to any courtesan's house. The courtesans then took counsel with one another.

One of the courtesans spoke up: "Distinguished friends, merchants from the district of Roḍa used to come here and consort with us freely. Now they have all become dispassionate and not one of them consorts with us anymore." Another said: "Distinguished friend, I have heard that the caravan leader of that group is very skilled in the rites of seduction and deals with women most adeptly. Because of their association with him, they all refuse to consort with us." Then an old courtesan among them said: "Girls, is that person a man, or is he not?" They replied: "Distinguished friend, he is a man — fully possessed of a man's faculties." She said: "If that is so, can you arrange for my daughter to win him over — and if she succeeds, will you make her your madam?" They said: "It would not be fitting for that." She then said: "If she cannot win him over, what will you give?" She replied: "I will give you five hundred kārṣāpaṇas." They said: "Excellent! Let it be so."

The old woman then rented a house near them and gathered there a great many vessels and household goods. The caravan leader's boys came and visited, and they borrowed the vessels. She asked them: "Boys, who are you?" They replied: "Mother, we are the boys of the caravan leader from the district of Roḍa." She said: "Boys, my own son too is a caravan leader. He has taken his goods and gone to another district, and I thought that his boys, just as you do now, must be borrowing vessels from others in the same way. Therefore, all the vessels and household goods here in this house — use them all just as you wish, as though they were your own." From then on they came each day and took the vessels.

One day the caravan leader asked them: "Who gives you vessels and utensils every day?" They told him: "Caravan leader, there is a certain mother of a caravan leader staying here. She says: 'My son too has taken his goods and gone to another district, and his boys will certainly be borrowing vessels from others just as you do — therefore, all the vessels and household goods in this house, use them all as you please, just as if they were your own.' That is what she tells us, and so we come and borrow vessels and goods each day." When the caravan leader heard this, affection arose in him, and he said: "If you are on such friendly terms with her, then she is like a mother to me as well."

The boys said to him: "Caravan leader, she speaks of your good qualities in the highest terms. She says that one who is so well matched with you is like a mother to her too." The old woman replied: "Boys, is it not fine to meet one's child?" And they said: "Mother, we will do well by the caravan leader." Then they said to him: "Caravan leader, our mother wishes to come and visit you." He replied: "Excellent! Please go ahead," and so she went to his house.

She greeted him with a pleasant and welcoming form of address, saying: "Have you arrived comfortably?" and added: "My own son is just like you." He in turn told her his name. She said: "His name too is the same. In short, you and he are both my sons without any difference — do not think of yourself as a stranger." He replied: "Mother, if that is so, then it is just as you say — I am he, and I am no different from your son."

The wife of the householder then called her daughter over, saying: "Daughter, come here! Pay your respects to your elder brother." When the girl came out she was of the right age, and when he saw that her beauty was in full bloom and that she was lovely, the force of passion struck him like a gust of wind, and he found himself overcome before he could even take notice of it himself.

He gazed at her intently and asked: "Mother, who does this girl belong to?" She replied: "Son, she is your very own sister." He asked: "Mother, have you given her to someone else or not?" She said: "Son, I have not given her to anyone at all." He said: "If that is so, then why will you not give her to me?" She replied: "Son, to whom else would I give her if not to you? Though there is one small fault in you: you are unsteady in your friendships — you take a wife and then abandon her and leave." He said: "Mother, please grant her to me, and I will bring her along with me to high places and low alike, and will not abandon her." She said: "Son, if you were to deposit all your goods and possessions here first, then she could be confident that you would indeed take her along everywhere, high station and low." He said: "Mother, if that is what is required, then so be it." When he deposited the goods at her house — and that house had two doors — he brought them in through one door, but she was removing them out through the second door. Once he had deposited all his wealth and goods, she had removed them entirely through the other side, and only then did she give him the girl.

He arranged an auspicious day and date, and when the time came to receive his bride, she invited all the prostitutes, adorned with every kind of ornament, as the guests. While he was receiving his bride and the two were moving about and mingling together, the caravan leader said: "Mother, is it that among everyone here there is not a single man?" He was told. Then someone drew close to his ear and whispered: "Did you not know that the caravan leader had come to this? All of us here are prostitutes — where would there be a man?" Hearing this he thought to himself: "It seems I have taken a prostitute as my wife. In short, I have been deceived." Then the girl said: "I and he shall enjoy ourselves together for as long as we may — but master, please give me some gold coins." He said: "My good woman, I have deposited every single thing I possessed here. If I come to you now, where would I get other gold coins?" Thereupon he fell fast asleep, and she rolled him up inside a blanket and threw him out in the middle of the marketplace.

In the morning, as dawn broke, the many people who lived in the city came and went, and their movement roused him. When he woke and looked about, he saw that his own situation was disgraceful, and his mind and the mental factors born of mind collapsed. His eyes filled with tears, and he wandered about the ruined and dilapidated marketplace, through the streets, the crossroads, and the junctions, until hunger tormented him and he went to where the hired laborers gathered, seeking food, and sat down among them.

Now at that time the householder Gautama was building a wall on his house, and he was looking there for laborers. Another man brought him before the householder Gautama. When Gautama saw him he said: "This one is altogether young — far too young. He has never done such work before; he is looking for something else." Even as Gautama spoke, the young man looked back at the householder Gautama's face with eyes still brimming with tears.

The householder Gautama asked him: "Son, whose are you, and where have you come from? Tell me." Pitiable, of low station, and racked with suffering, his eyes filled with tears, and he struggled to speak, his voice breaking: "Father, I am from that city of Droṇa in the north. By the force of past karma I traveled here comfortably enough, but now I have searched everywhere and cannot find where to go, and even if the time comes to pass away destitute and abandoned midway, I cannot find it."

Hearing both his appearance and the train of his words, the householder Gautama felt his heart drawn to him with affection. "Son," he said, "do you know any of the many people who live in Droṇa?" "Father, I do." "Son, do you know one called this householder?" "Father, that is my poor unfortunate father — I know him." The householder Gautama felt yet deeper warmth and fondness rise in his heart and said: "Son, there is no need to be unhappy — do not weep."

"You shall become my son-in-law, and all these houses shall be yours." At these words the young man's spirits lifted, and his unhappiness fell away. The householder Gautama restored him with ointments, food, drink, clothing, ornaments, a house, a bed, and servants, and with words of warm encouragement. Then he spoke to his wife: "Good woman, your son-in-law has come — make ready and send our daughter to him as a bride." The householder had the auspicious day, date, moment, and stellar conjunction examined, and when all was properly arranged, he summoned his brothers, friends, and kinsmen and announced that the daughter should be given in marriage. The young man's father said that the wealth accumulated over a lifetime should not be seized all at once. The young man then said: "All the wealth there is in this house — all of it is yours. What need is there of wealth?" At this, the courtesan, wishing to take revenge on him, said: "Father, it may be as you say, but I, unlike a low-born woman, will not take a bride." He said nothing further to this. He left the circle of her company, wandered about aimlessly for a time, and eventually went to the riverbank. There a corpse came floating down the river. A crow was sitting on the bank and wished to eat the corpse, but its beak could not reach it. Then the crow rubbed its beak against a small piece of wood, and the beak grew very long, and with it the crow ate the corpse. After that, the crow rubbed its beak on another piece of wood, and things became as they had been before. The caravan leader then picked up those two pieces of wood with his hand and went home. He then took five hundred kārṣāpaṇas and went to the courtesan's house. "Good woman," he said, "you threw me out saying I had no kārṣāpaṇas — now take these kārṣāpaṇas and enjoy them fully, then come back." She, being attached to the money, spent them together with him. Then, as he spent time with her, he rubbed her nose with the second piece of wood, and it grew extremely long. He summoned every physician and had them examine her, but none of them was able to treat it. Thus, abandoned by all the physicians, she implored the caravan leader: "Master, please be patient — please find a cure for this." He replied: "If you vow to return everything you took, then and only then will I act." She said: "Master, I shall restore it all to you twofold." He then rubbed her with the second piece of wood, and just as before it returned to its former state, and she gave back to him everything she had taken. Then the caravan leader united the young woman, the slender Gautamī of great splendor, with himself and took her as his bride. The householder Gautama had a field in another village in the rocky hills, and he said to his son-in-law: "Son, take your wife and go to settle in that village in the rocky hills." He gave him all the fields in the rocky-hills village, and the slender Gautamī mounted a horse and went there to live. Together they enjoyed every pleasure and delight. While they were enjoying those pleasures, after some time had passed, the slender Gautamī became with child, and when the time for giving birth drew near, she said: "Master, the time for giving birth has come — let me go to my kinsmen's house. There they will attend to me as my mother's servants." He agreed, saying "Excellent," and escorted the young woman to the kinsmen's house. When she gave birth there, a boy was born. On the twenty-first day — the third seven-day period — after the birth, they held a great birth celebration, gave the child a name fitting to his lineage, and then she took the boy and returned to the village in the rocky hills. Later she again became with child, and when the time for giving birth drew near, she said: "Master, the time for giving birth has come — let me go to my kinsmen's house. There they will attend to me as mother's servants." He replied

He agreed, saying "Excellent — go safely," and loaded both mother and son onto a cart and set off. But she gave birth halfway along the road. Seeing that she had given birth, he descended from the cart and sat down beside another tree — and there fell fast asleep. As he lay in deep sleep, a venomous snake seized him, and he passed beyond his time. She, still up on the cart, gave birth to another boy; then she descended from the cart, went to the tree, and said, "My lord, I have given birth to a boy — rejoice!" But he was without consciousness and gave no reply. She shook him with her hand and, examining him, saw that he had passed beyond his time. She wept aloud. A cow, too — without being given — was snatched away by someone taking what was not theirs. Then she wept for a long while, grief arose in her, and looking in all four directions, she held the newborn in her arms and took the elder boy by the hand.

Just then, a great unseasonable storm arose, and ponds, marshes, and wells all filled with water; and along her road a river had to be crossed. She thought: "If I cross together with the boy, both I and the boy will be lost. Let me first cross the little one." She left the elder boy on the bank and carried the small one across. Then she left the small one on the far bank and crossed back for the elder, and when she had reached the middle of the river, a fox carried off the little boy. Then she stood in the middle of the river, waving her arms and calling out again and again. The elder boy, thinking "Mother is calling to me," leapt into the water. The bank, too, was crumbling at its edge, and he perished the moment he fell. Then she hurried along, swift and frantic, chasing after the fox; but it dropped the child and fled, and when she looked, she saw it was dead. She wept and flung herself into the water. Then, looking back, she saw the elder boy also being carried away by the current, and overcome with anguish she ran weeping — and saw that he too had passed beyond his time.

Bereft of husband and sons, she fell into despair. Alone, wrapped in a single cloth from the waist down, sitting on the river bank listening to the wind and the great forest and the sounds of the rivers and the calls of many birds, she wept with streaming tears full of grief and heartache, crying out, "Woe — my husband! Woe — my elder son! Woe — my little one!" and rolled back and forth upon the ground.

Since all karma will surely and inevitably ripen in full when it has entirely expanded and been completed, at that very moment her father and mother and many members of the household were struck by a thunderbolt and died. Of those inside, one man alone escaped. With tears streaming down his face and full of grief and heartache, he came quickly toward her and appeared before her. Seeing him running toward her, she thought he looked frightened, and asked: "Good man, why do you run in such a frenzy?" He threw himself down before her, weeping, his face wet with tears, and said: "Your father and your mother and all the many members of your household were struck by a falling thunderbolt and died — I alone escaped through karma."

Hearing this, she wept even more piteously, lamenting again and again:

"What evil did I do in lives gone by
that in a single moment I am parted
from husband, sons, and all my dearest kin?
What use was there in dwelling in a home?
Without good fortune — wherever I may turn —
I am again cut off from husband, kin.
It is not fitting that I stay at home.
Better to dwell in desolate hermitages
or empty houses, any one of those.
To remain in a home is harmful — it is wrong.
Only grief and suffering multiply there."

She set off in one direction and wandered here and there until she came to another village among the rocky crags. There she found an old woman sitting and spinning cotton thread, and she went up to her. The old woman gave her rest and let her join in the spinning. Now in that same place there was a young weaver boy who made his living at his craft, and the old woman would sell him her cotton thread from time to time.

One day Gautamī carried a fine thread to him and went to his door. He asked, "Mother, you used to bring thicker thread — where has this thin stuff come from?" She replied, "My son, I did not spin this." "Then who did, Mother?" "My son, there is a woman staying in my house — she spun it." He said, "Mother, why do you not give her to me? I have no wife. I will provide her with food, clothing, and all the means of livelihood." The old woman replied, "Son, wait a little. Let me ask her first, and whatever she says I will tell you afterward." He then paid a good price for the thread and gave her food as well, and sent her off adorned with scent and flowers.

When the lean Gautamī returned, the old woman said to her, "Daughter, you sold the thread for a good price — and who adorned you with scent and flowers?" She answered, "Mother, it was not only the adornment with scent and flowers — he gave food too." So the old woman asked, "How did all this come about?" Gautamī told her everything in detail, then spoke warmly of the young weaver's fine qualities: "Daughter, you should accept that young weaver. Agree to be his wife and all will be well." Gautamī replied, "Honoured mother, please do not speak of this again. I am weary of living in a home. However things may be, I will not lead that kind of life." The old woman said, "Daughter, a woman without support lives in a place of suffering, and men from outside will find occasion to take advantage of you. Think carefully, settle somewhere, and agree." Gautamī refused. The old woman pressed her again, pointing out the dangers, and at last Gautamī consented.

The weaver boy then, having chosen an auspicious day, month, and constellation, brought her home as his wife. Yet he was quarrelsome, wild, and quick to anger, and he constantly beat her with a stick and struck her with his fists. She said to the old woman, "Mother, you handed me over to a demon. He beats me with a stick and strikes me with his fists every single day, and I do not know what to do." The old woman replied, "Daughter, until you have borne him a child, he will beat you. But once you have brought him a son, you yourself will rule that household — do not be displeased."

In time she became pregnant, and the weaver boy grew fond of her. Yet she disdained him in return, and he tried to keep her there by coaxing. Then one day his weaver companions plied him with much wine, and he came home drunk and wild. The door was shut, for she was in the pains of labour, and when he called out for the door to be opened, she was so pierced all through by the agony of childbirth that she could not open it. He flew into a great rage, went and sat in a corner. When the child was born, she opened the door, and as he came inside she greeted him respectfully, saying, "My lord, be pleased — a son has been born to you." But he was entirely enveloped in anger, utterly covered over by unrelenting hostility, and he thought: "Even before this child was born she treated me with contempt. Now that her son has actually come into the world, she and her son together will —"

— certainly kill me." Thinking this, he said to her: "Good woman, stoke the fire in the hearth and set a bronze vessel on it." She stoked the fire and placed the bronze vessel on the hearth. He said, "Pour mustard oil in and bring it to a boil." She poured in the mustard oil and brought it to a boil. Then he said, "Put this infant in and cook him." At that she said, "My lord, this is your own son — what wrong has he done that you would kill him while he is still a child?" He beat her with a stick. Since there was nothing dearer to her than herself, she was terrified, and she put the child into the boiling mustard oil. He passed away in that instant. When the oil had cooked him through, he said, "Take him out," and she did. He said, "Eat." She said, "My lord, how can I eat the flesh of my own child?" At that he beat her all over her body, struck her again and again, and beaten like that, she ate the flesh of her son.

The Blessed One then said: Attachment is a minor fault but difficult to be free of. Anger is a grave fault but easy to be free of. And so it was that the weaver's boy, tormented afterward by the fire of remorse and unable to sleep for a long time, fell into a stupor of exhaustion. He slept so very deeply that Gautamī perceived it clearly and thought to herself: "This man killed my son and then made me eat the child's flesh. He is a demon. I must flee." She snatched up whatever she could carry and ran. She met some fellow travelers heading north and sold goods belonging to the locality called Khormo-jik, then took back the goods she had sold and set out along the northern road, traveling on — and she went along together with those companions.

In time the caravan leader caught sight of her beauty. Seeing her, he was drawn to her and asked, "Whose woman are you, and where are you going?" She said, "Caravan leader, my husband was devoured by a venomous snake. Of my two sons, one was carried off by a fox, and one perished in a river. My mother and father were killed by a thunderbolt. I am without protector — I go wherever I please — and I shall go wherever this great company of travelers goes." He thought to himself: "Wherever I travel, I shall enjoy the company of a woman such as this." And so he made her his wife.

Before long, that great company of travelers was attacked by bandits, and that caravan leader too was killed in the fighting. The lean Gautamī was taken as wife by the chief of the bandits, and that bandit chief was in turn killed by the king of the region. The lean Gautamī became the king's chief queen. In time that king too passed away, and the queen, the young attendants, the ministers, and the many people of the court honored the lean Gautamī greatly and placed her inside the royal tomb. But the northern people came as grave robbers and began digging into the tomb. Dust flew up into the lean Gautamī's nose and she sneezed. The grave robbers, terrified and thinking a corpse had risen, fled — and the lean Gautamī dug her way out through the excavated opening.

Reflecting on her suffering in all its many forms, she was utterly undone by the wind, and for lack of food she lost her mind. She cast off her lower garment, her hands and feet cracked, her matted hair grew long and pale, and she wandered here and there until she came at last to Śrāvastī.

Then the Blessed One said: The karmic maturation of sentient beings is inconceivable. Having experienced in this way the ripening of the fruit of the deeds she had performed in former times, she now arrived at the Jeta Grove through the force of her past karma.

At that time the Blessed One was seated before many hundreds and thousands of monks, teaching the Dharma. From a distance, the emaciated Gautamī caught sight of the Blessed One — the awakened one, the Blessed One — perfectly adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being, his body beautifully arrayed with the eighty minor marks of excellence, his surrounding aura of light surpassing the radiance of a thousand suns, filling a fathom's breadth all around, moving like a mountain of jewels. Upon seeing him, her own mind and memory were restored to her, and overcome with a sense of shame, she sat down to one side, huddled into herself.

Now, throughout all of this, there was not the slightest thing that the Blessed One did not know, did not see, did not discern, or did not perceive. By his very nature as the Blessed One, great compassion had become his way of benefiting the world. He is the sole protector, the sole hero; he speaks of non-duality and does not proclaim a second; he abides in calm abiding and insight; he is skilled in the three objects of discipline; he has crossed beyond the four rivers; the four bases of miraculous power are utterly firm beneath him; he is untroubled by the four fearlessnesses; he has fully abandoned the five limbs; he has genuinely transcended the five destinies; he is endowed with the six faculties; he has completely perfected the six perfections; he constantly abides in the six abodes; he is adorned with the flowers of the seven branches of awakening; he holds the eightfold path; he is skilled in the nine successive meditative absorptions; he is endowed with the strength of the ten powers; and he is absolutely certain — beyond all the hundreds of renowned ones who hold dominion in the ten directions. Three times by night and three times by day he surveys the world with the eye of a buddha, and his vision of primordial wisdom arises, beholding: who has declined, who has advanced, who has come to suffer, who is afflicted, who is harmed, who has come to suffer and be afflicted and harmed, who inclines toward the lower realms, who is falling toward the lower realms, who is plunging headlong into the lower realms — thinking: I shall draw such ones out of the lower realms and place them in the higher realms and in liberation. Those in whom the roots of virtue have not yet arisen — I shall cause them to arise. Those in whom they have arisen — I shall bring them to full maturation. Those in whom they have matured — I shall bring them to liberation.

He then spoke in verse:

Even the ocean, home of sea-creatures,
may at times transgress its season —
yet a buddha will never miss the hour
for those disciples who are ready to be tamed.

The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Ānanda: Ānanda, give an upper robe to Gautamī, the merchant's wife, and teach her the Dharma.

The venerable Ānanda gave an upper robe to Gautamī, the merchant's wife. Thereupon the emaciated Gautamī, wife of the merchant, having put on the robe, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and sat down to one side.

Once she was seated to one side, the Blessed One, having known her intention, her latent dispositions, her constitution, and her character, taught her the Dharma in such a way that she would thoroughly realize the four noble truths. Upon hearing this teaching, the emaciated Gautamī, wife of the merchant, shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection with the vajra of primordial wisdom, and manifestly attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Having thus seen the truth, she rose from her seat, and facing the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence, she prostrated and then addressed the Blessed One with these words: Reverend One, having gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, having received full ordination, and having become a fully ordained nun,

may I be permitted to practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One? Or would the Blessed One entrust me to the Great Matriarch, that she might grant me the going forth, bestow full ordination, give instructions in the Vinaya, and confer the scriptural transmission, so that under her I may strive with effort, apply myself with diligence, and accomplish the training?

Through striving, applying herself with diligence, and accomplishing the training, she came to know this wheel of saṃsāra in its motion and stillness. Having utterly vanquished, through the very nature of reality, all conditioned continuums as subject to decay, collapse, disintegration, and dissolution, she abandoned all mental afflictions, directly realized the fruit of arhatship, and became an arhat. She was freed from attachment to all three realms. Like clay and gold alike, like a hand that finds no purchase on the sky, her mind was utterly even. Like a thorn and sandalwood alike, she shattered the treasury of the storehouse of existence with the weapon of knowledge. She attained knowledge, the higher knowledges, and perfect individual discrimination. She turned her back on gain, attachment, and honor in this existence, and was venerated, prostrated to, and praised with pleasant words by those with controlling faculties and those approaching the controlling faculties, and by the gods.

She went to prostrate at the feet of the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: Monks, among my female śrāvaka nuns who uphold the Vinaya, the foremost is the nun Kṣemā Gautamī.

When the Blessed One had declared that the nun Gautamī was foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya, the nuns at that time came to her presence. She, in order to inspire weariness in them, recounted the threads of karma. The nuns in turn reported in full detail to the monks what had thus occurred. Then at a later time, Kṣemā Gautamī went to prostrate at the feet of the Blessed One. When the monks saw her, they recounted to one another the threads of her karma. Kṣemā Gautamī then prostrated with her head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

The following is a question asked knowingly by the Blessed One, the fully awakened Buddha. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: Why, Ānanda, did you allow the monks to whisper to one another? And Ānanda reported the matter in full.

The Blessed One then declared: Ānanda, the stream of being and the karmic maturation of sentient beings is inconceivable. For beings of the world, karma is their own possession. Karma is the womb of birth. Karma is the intermediate state. Karma is what follows and accompanies them. Whatever karma one has performed, one will experience that maturation individually.

When doubt arose among the monks, they asked the Blessed One, the buddha who cuts through all doubt: Venerable One, what karma did the nun Kṣemā Gautamī perform such that her husband was eaten by a serpent and died before his time; one son was killed by a fox; a second son was swept away by a river and died before his time; both her parents were killed by a meteorite; and then, after she had eaten her own son's flesh, wandered here and there out of her mind with distracted thoughts, she went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, abandoned all mental afflictions, and directly realized arhatship? And why did the Blessed One declare her foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya?

The Blessed One replied: Monks, the karma that the nun Kṣemā Gautamī herself performed, accumulated, and gathered, whose conditions have ripened, will necessarily come to manifest like a river. The karma that Kṣemā Gautamī performed and accumulated will not be experienced by another.

Monks, the karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, it is in these very appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases that virtuous and non-virtuous karma ripens.

Actions are never lost,
even after a hundred aeons have passed.
When the time and conditions meet,
they ripen as fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in a past time, in another village on a rocky hillside, there lived a certain householder who was wealthy, with great possessions and resources, whose dwelling was wide and spacious — his wealth was like wealth earned through toil. From that wealth earned through toil, he took a wife of equal family background, and together they enjoyed themselves in pleasure. Yet though they enjoyed themselves in pleasure, there was no son and no daughter. He thought: "Though much wealth is gathered in my house, there is no son and no daughter. When I am gone, all that I govern will be declared 'without an heir' and will pass into the royal treasury." And so he sat cheek resting in his hand, deeply absorbed in worry. His wife noticed this and said: "My lord, why do you sit with your cheek resting in your hand, so deeply absorbed in thought?"

He replied: "My dear, though much wealth is gathered in my house, there is no son and no daughter. When I am gone, all that I govern will be declared 'without an heir' and will pass into the royal treasury. That is why I sit so absorbed in thought."

She then thought: "Can it be that his fortune is small? There is no son and no daughter — can it be that my fortune is small? No, this is something else: he wishes to find fault with me and take another wife. That is why he sits before me, cheek in hand, so absorbed in thought, saying that though much wealth is gathered in his house there is no son and no daughter, and that when he is gone all he governs will be declared without an heir and will pass into the royal treasury. Therefore he intends to be rid of me."

With this in mind, she spoke: "My lord, since I am so unfortunate and you have no son and no daughter, take another wife, and from her sons and daughters will come."

He replied: "My dear, have you not heard it said that a man who has two wives can never drink the cold water of peace? His house is always filled with fighting, quarrelling, discord, and strife, and the people of the household are thrown into turmoil, so that he cannot attend to his own affairs."

She said: "My lord, please, go ahead and take one. If she turns out to be just like an elder or younger sister to me, I will care for her as a sister. And if she is just like a daughter, I will care for her as a daughter."

He was persuaded by her urging, and so he set out in search of a bride. Then, in another village on a rocky hillside, a daughter had been born to a certain householder, and both her parents had since passed away. He arranged with her kinsman to take her, and joined her in marriage to his great estate. And since it is the nature of things that the new overshadows the old, he came to feel very fond of and attached to the new wife.

In time, the old wife, by nature envious, caused her own womb to become barren. But then the new wife became pregnant, and the old wife, glad, said to her husband: "My lord, rejoice! I have become pregnant."

He replied: "My dear, excellent! If you give birth to a son, you will become my heir and the mistress of the household."

Then she said:

"My lord, your new wife has performed a ritual of miscarriage upon the child in her womb. If the child is not miscarried, she will become mistress of the household."

He replied: "My good woman, even before this I said something of the sort, and yet you had not even a little child to show for it. Did you have no answer to that?" She said nothing and fell silent.

Eight or nine months later, the new wife gave birth to a boy. A great birth celebration was held, and the child was given a name befitting his family line. Now the old wife thought to herself: "This child was born through the karma of a past life. If this mother does not kill him, it will be to my disadvantage. I must therefore make use of her." And so she said to her: "Sister, this boy belongs to both you and me — let us raise him together." The new wife gladly agreed, saying, "Very well, I shall do just that," and she took up his care.

But as the old wife nursed the child, a false notion arose in her mind: "Whichever woman's son he is, that is whose household it will be. Even though I am raising him, it will be she who becomes mistress of the house, and I shall be reduced to a slave. I must kill him." Moved by this perverse thought, she thrust a needle into the mouth of the boy. Tormented by the pain, he began to cry. The old wife said, "Why is this child crying?" The new wife replied: "Sister, why should he not cry?" She took the child up, trying to comfort him, held him, cooed at him, took him in her arms — but still he would not be calmed. Then she gave him her breast to nurse, and when she examined him more closely, she saw a needle had been thrust into his mouth. She quickly opened his mouth and pulled it out with her hand. But the child had no breath left. His time had passed, and he was dead.

The new wife beat her breast and wept, falling prostrate upon the ground. The people of the household came running and asked, "What is the matter?" She, her eyes streaming with tears of grief and sorrow, cried out: "Alas! That wicked woman of evil conduct, in her jealous rage, thrust a needle into my son's mouth and killed him!" They too began to weep. The neighbors of the household heard, and they too came running, saying: "What a sudden, terrible thing — this child, innocent and harmless, has been killed!" And many people surrounded her, calling out in lamentation. Then she beat her breast and wept, and made this sworn oath:

"If I have killed your son, may my husband be eaten by a snake and die. May one of my sons be eaten by a rat. May the second fall into a river and die. May my parents be struck by a thunderbolt and killed. And may I eat my son's flesh, go mad, and wander back and forth with a wandering, distracted mind!"

Now, monks, what do you think? The second wife of that householder was none other than the nun Sthavirā Gautamī (Skt. Gautamī) herself. Because she was utterly veiled by affliction, she not only killed the child but also spoke falsehood and swore that oath. And through the karmic maturation of those actions, her husband was eaten by a snake and died. One of her sons was killed by a rat. Another fell into a river and died. Her parents were crushed by a fallen meteorite and perished. She ate her son's flesh, went mad in her dotage, and wandered back and forth with a wandering, distracted mind.

Furthermore, the Blessed One Kāśyapa (the buddha Kāśyapa) had gone forth into the renunciant life, and she too went forth in that same lifetime and practised the holy celibate life, yet she gained not a single one of the many qualities it can bring. The preceptress under whom she had gone forth was declared by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened Kāśyapa, to be the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.

And at the time of her death, that one made this aspiration prayer:

"By whatever root of virtue I have accumulated through practising the holy celibate life for a single lifetime in the presence of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the unsurpassed field of merit — though I gained not even a single one of the many qualities it can bring — by this root of virtue, may I go forth into the teaching of the one whom the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, prophesied to the brahmin's son, his preceptor, saying: 'Brahmin's son, when beings live to the age of one hundred, Śākyamuni will become a Tathāgata, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha.' And having gone forth into that one's teaching, may I abandon all afflictions and realise arhatship. And just as this my preceptress was declared by the Blessed One, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha Kāśyapa, to be the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya, so too may I be declared the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the king of the Śākyas."

And because she had practised the holy celibate life for a single lifetime, she went forth into this one's teaching, abandoned all afflictions, and realised arhatship. And she made the aspiration prayer to be the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya — and by the power of that aspiration prayer, the Tathāgata has now declared her the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.

Furthermore, the monks put this question to the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, what karma did the parents of the nun Gautamī perform such that through the ripening of that karma they came to be struck by a meteorite and killed? What karma did her husband perform that he met his end through a snakebite? What karma did her two sons perform such that one was killed by a rat and the other fell into a river and perished?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the karma that those individuals themselves committed and accumulated, having gathered its collection and ripened its conditions, will without any doubt come to abide close at hand, like a river. What karma they themselves committed and accumulated, no one else will experience. Monks, karma committed and accumulated does not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind — rather, virtuous and non-virtuous karma committed ripens in these very appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

Actions are never lost,
though hundreds of aeons pass;
when the time comes and conditions meet,
they ripen as fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, long ago in this Fortunate Aeon, when human beings lived to the age of twenty thousand years, a Teacher called Kāśyapa appeared in the world — a Tathāgata, arhat, fully and perfectly awakened buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a blessed buddha — and he resided at the Deer Park of the sages near the city of Vārāṇasī. At that time there lived in Vārāṇasī another householder who was wealthy, with abundant resources and great possessions, whose dwelling was spacious and vast, whose riches were gathered in the manner of Vaiśravaṇa, and who was endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa. That householder built a monastery on the far bank of the river Varakā, and monks from various regions came to reside there. Men of the town had borrowed a loan from this householder and were leaving without repaying it. One of them was called to account three times by the householder, and when he heard the demand made three times, that man said to him: 'You ungrateful wretch, you have borrowed and heard my demand for repayment three times, yet you will not repay me — do not go until you have paid.' The other replied: 'Householder, grant me one repayment period, and then if I have not repaid, my three sons and —'"

"— together with my wife and children, accept as your servants." He then drew up a signed bond and gave it to the householder as surety. Being quite unable to do anything, he was heard out, and the householder then handed him over, along with his wife and sons, to serve in that monastery. Since he lived in a village nearby on the other side of the river, each day he would cross the river and cook rice for the monastic community of monks there, while his wife and sons did the sweeping. In that monastery there was a monk who was an arhat and who served as the community's steward.

Then, at a later time, rain fell and the river Varakā rose with water, so that the servant, together with his sons and wife, was long delayed. The monk who was an arhat came to him and said: "Hey, man — the sun has already moved this far across the sky and still you have not come. Are the cooked meals of the monastic community of monks to be cut short?" When he had spoken thus, the wife flew into a rage and said: "When he comes, why did no thunderbolt fall on his head?" The eldest son said: "Why did a venomous snake not eat him?" The middle son said: "Why did he not fall into the river and fail to come in time?" The youngest son said: "Why did no fox eat him?"

Monks, what do you think? Those two — the householder and his wife — are the father and mother of the nun Skaṃmā Gautamī. The eldest son is her husband. The middle son is her eldest son. The youngest son is her younger son. In that way, having directed harsh words with malicious intent at an arhat, through the karmic maturation of that action they were struck down by a thunderbolt, by a venomous snake, and by a fox and the like, and one fell into the river — and all four perished before their time.

Therefore, monks, the karmic maturation of extremely dark karma is likewise extremely dark. Extremely white karma is extremely white. Mixed karma is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon dark and mixed karma, and be diligent in extremely white karma. Train yourselves likewise in this way, monks.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those monks rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had said.

The Vinaya, the minor bases. The thirty-ninth fascicle.

The narrative context is Śrāvastī. Once, when the foolish man Āryaskanda killed members of the Śākya clan without fault or cause for harm, and the wives of the Śākyas became separated from their brothers, husbands, and fathers, and being tormented by suffering, they went forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma-Vinaya. Suffering is like the sound of a bell — at the time when those who have been parted from their grief are then, at that very moment, tormented by afflictions in which attachment is extremely strong, they are unable to bear it.

The Blessed One said: A black snake has five faults. What are the five? It is irascible, it is resentful, it is cold-hearted, it is ungrateful, and it has sharp venom. In just the same way, certain women also have five faults. What are the five? They are irascible, they are resentful, they are cold-hearted, they are ungrateful, and they have sharp venom. Now, what is the sharp venom of women? Women, for the most part, have great attachment.

Those women consulted one another and went to where the nun Sthūlanandā was. Having gone there and paid homage at Sthūlanandā's feet, they stood before her and said: "Noble one, afflictions are difficult to restrain. When they act to deceive women, please tell us how we may be turned away from them." She replied:

"Sisters, what is there to understand about this? You are in the bloom of youth. Submit yourselves to my authority, and go and enjoy yourselves freely with wealthy men, with merchants, with caravan leaders, and also with the sons of good families and with the sons of anyone at all without exception. And if I were young, I would go along with you." She deceived them with these words. They paid homage at her feet and departed, and then said: "How remarkable — the noble Sthūlanandā said, 'What is there to understand about this?'" Some among them said, "Excellent — she has spoken well; enjoy pleasures to the full." But others said: "Sisters, it is hard to find women who have gone forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. Let us go at once and ask the noble Gautamī as well." They said, "Excellent, let us do just that," and went to where Gautamī was. Having paid homage at her feet, they said: "Noble one, afflictions are difficult to restrain. When they act to deceive women, please tell us how we may be turned away from them." She replied:

"Noble ones, do not even take the name of desires upon your lips. Why so? Because desire yields little pleasure and great suffering, and has many objects of fault. The Blessed One declared: a wise person who truly sees the five objects of fault does not rightly indulge in desires. What are the five? A wise person who truly sees that desire yields little joy and great suffering, and has many objects of fault, does not rightly indulge in desires. A wise person who sees that indulging in desires leads to the proliferation of attachments does not rightly indulge in desires. A wise person who sees that indulging in desires brings restlessness, insatiability, and discontentment does not rightly indulge in desires. A wise person who sees that indulging in desires leaves no room whatsoever for refraining from harmful actions does not rightly indulge in desires. A wise person who sees, through many categories, that desires are condemned by the buddhas, by the śrāvakas of the buddhas, by the wise, and by noble persons of right conduct does not rightly indulge in desires.

A wise person who sees these five qualities does rightly aspire to the going-forth. What are the five? A wise person who sees that the going-forth offers one's own purpose unmixed does rightly aspire to it. A wise person who sees that while, as a householder, one is subject to servants, to those one has dispatched on errands, to weariness, to the power of others, and to going wherever one is bidden, those in the going-forth are honored and praised — such a wise person does rightly aspire to the going-forth. A wise person who sees that through the going-forth one will attain the supreme meditative bliss of yoga and the attainment of nirvāṇa does rightly aspire to it. A wise person who sees that even if one has not yet attained the supreme meditative bliss of yoga and nirvāṇa, one will at least be reborn among the gods — such a wise person does rightly aspire to the going-forth. A wise person who sees, through many categories, that the going-forth is praised by the buddhas, by the śrāvakas of the buddhas, by the wise, by those of right conduct, and by noble persons does rightly aspire to the going-forth.

Do you wish to hear about the suffering experienced on account of desires in future lives, or the suffering experienced in this very life?" They said: "Noble one, let the suffering experienced on account of desires in future lives wait for a moment — please speak first of what is experienced in this life." She then described to them in detail how it comes to pass: the suffering of separation from mother, father, husband, and children, and the suffering of one who has eaten the flesh of her own child.

Upon hearing this, they were so shaken that the hair all over their bodies stood on end. They raised their ears and looked, wan and dry, into the face of Gautamī. She, perceiving their thoughts, their latent tendencies, their faculties, and their temperaments, taught the Dharma in such a way that they would come to thoroughly realize the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones. Upon hearing it, those twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a self within the aggregates) were shattered by the vajra of primordial wisdom, and they actualized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, they said: "Noble one, we have been saved! We are utterly saved! This one called Bhomā has caused us to sink into the mud of desires." Gautamī then asked her sisters what had happened, and they recounted it to her in full detail. She said to her sisters: "What is to be done about this? She is engaged in a serious offense. She has cast aside the teaching of the Blessed One like riverbank grass." The nuns who were of little importance ridiculed her and spoke harshly, saying: "How could a nun possibly drive other nuns back into lay life?" Those nuns who had witnessed this reported the matter to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then declared: "Therefore, a nun must not send another nun back into lay life. If she does so, it will become a serious offense." The ancillary case took place at Śrāvastī. A certain nun had slandered a monk, and that monk became frightened. Those nuns who had witnessed it reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, if a nun slanders a monk, it shall entail a transgression. Just as a nun must not do this to a fully ordained monk, so too must she not do it to a fully ordained nun, a female trainee, a novice monk, or a novice nun. A female trainee must not do this to a fully ordained monk, a fully ordained nun, a female trainee, a novice monk, or a novice nun. A novice nun must not do this to a fully ordained monk, a fully ordained nun, a female trainee, a novice monk, or a novice nun."

In brief:
Do not go ahead unbidden —
rise to your feet, O nun.
Sit only when asked,
and cross-legged sitting is without category.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the venerable Mahākāśyapa was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the former pleasure grove, in the Deer-Sound Hall. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, in the early morning, donned his lower robe and his outer robe, took up his alms bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to go on alms round. The nun Bhomā likewise, in the early morning, donned her lower robe and outer robe, took up her alms bowl, and entered Śrāvastī on alms round. Seeing the venerable Mahākāśyapa, she thought to herself: "I must displease this fool." She went ahead of him to whatever household the venerable Mahākāśyapa was heading for, seated herself inside the doorway, and said: "Noble one, there is nothing at all prepared here right now — please move on." He then went to another household. There too she went on ahead and obstructed him as before. This she did repeatedly from house to house. Since he did not pay her any heed, the arhat's wisdom-eye did not engage; but when he turned his attention to the thought of who might be harassing him, he perceived that it was Bhomā, and he said: "Sister, it is not you who has erred — it is the venerable Ānanda who has erred, in that he gave women who engage in serious offenses the going-forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma-Vinaya and granted them full ordination, thereby establishing them as fully ordained nuns."

When the monks heard what had occurred, they informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter. Since any nun who goes on ahead into the alms-round domain of a monk becomes an object of offense, the Blessed One reflected: therefore nuns should not solicit alms in the domain of monks. He then declared: "Monks, the monk Kāśyapa justly rebuked the nun. Therefore let nuns not solicit alms in the domain of monks. Any nun who does so will incur a transgression."

When the Blessed One had spoken — saying that nuns should not solicit alms in the domain of monks — the nuns abandoned the monks' domain, and those nuns were left destitute of alms. The nuns who were in that situation told the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Therefore nuns should not go on ahead into the domain of monks who are going on alms-round. As for those domains that the monks have relinquished, let the nuns go there."

The occasion for what follows is this: it was at Śrāvastī. Bhomā was seated before an assembly of many hundreds, teaching the Dharma. The venerable Mahākāśyapa came along that road, and those in the assembly, seeing the venerable Mahākāśyapa, rose to their feet. Bhomā, however, did not stir even from her seat. When those people saw the noble Mahākāśyapa — honored by gods and humans alike — they said to her: "We stood up, yet you have not so much as risen from your seat. That is unseemly." She replied: "I went forth from among the tīrthikas. Fool upon fool, dullard upon dullard — I, a Śākyan nun, master of the Three Baskets, versed in doctrinal discourse, confident in knowledge and liberation: why should I rise from my seat upon seeing this one?" When the monks heard this, they informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, faithful brahmins and householders will rightly take offense. Therefore, the moment a nun sees a monk, let her rise from her seat. If she does not rise, she will incur a transgression." When the Blessed One had spoken — saying that the moment a nun sees a monk she should rise from her seat — some time later the nun Utpalavarṇā was seated outside the nuns' summer residence before an assembly of many hundreds, teaching the Dharma.

The venerable Ānanda, in the early morning, dressed in his lower robe and Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and set out from Śrāvastī on alms-round. Returning from the alms-round through Śrāvastī, he made his way to where the nuns' summer residence was. The nun Utpalavarṇā saw the venerable Ānanda, and the moment she saw him she rose from her seat. The venerable Ānanda sat down, and having sat, asked: "Sister, which sūtra have you been expounding?" She replied: "Noble one, this one, called such-and-such." The venerable Ānanda then began to explain the sūtra at length, and Utpalavarṇā stood listening with her ear turned toward him. Since the venerable Ānanda was engrossed in teaching the Dharma, he did not say to her "sit down." She stood there for a long time, and the heat of the sun's rays exhausted her. She fainted and fell to the ground. Then those without faith said: "The nun Utpalavarṇā, we hear, is free from attachment — yet upon seeing this handsome young Śākyan, her mind was moved by attachment and desire, and she fell to the ground." When the monks heard this slander, they informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, brahmins and householders slander according to what seems fitting to them. Therefore, monks, when the Dharma is being taught, you must say to the noble one, 'Please be seated.' And if a monk is occupied and forgets to do so, the nun herself should request it, saying: 'Noble one, please know that I am present.' The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. There the Blessed One declared to the monks: 'Monks, the sun rises; crows cry out; farmers till their fields; wild men weep. Therefore, monks, you should understand that this has the meaning of a simile. And the meaning should be understood as follows: When it is said that the sun has risen, that is an epithet for the speech of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha. When it is said that crows cry out, that is an epithet for the speech of those who teach the Dharma. When it is said that farmers till their fields, that is an epithet for the speech of those who give generously. When it is said that wild men weep, that is an epithet for the speech of Māra's retinue.
