Therefore, monks, the Teacher, who is affectionate, compassionate, and devoted to the welfare and benefit of his śrāvaka disciples, says: I have done what was to be done out of compassion for you. Now you, for your part, should dwell and meditate in remote forests, at the foot of trees, in empty houses, in valleys, in mountain caves, in piles of straw without cover, in charnel grounds, in groves, on mountains, and at the edges of ravines. Monks, do not be heedless! This is my teaching, lest you come to regret it later.' 'Monks, go to such places as lakes, marshes, mountain caves, pleasure groves, springs, and trees adorned with flowers and fruit — places of exceptional delight — and there apply yourselves to the cultivation of mental cultivation. Nuns too should go to dense thickets near the royal park, and to other places suitable for women, and there apply themselves to the cultivation of mental cultivation.' The Blessed One heard that, driven by the ripening of past karma, creatures had entered into what is called the wound that is womanhood, and declared: 'Therefore, monks, when a nun is engaged in mental cultivation, she should sit half cross-legged on a mat and practise mental cultivation in the proper manner, rather than sitting fully cross-legged.' The Blessed One said that nuns should sit half cross-legged on a mat and practise mental cultivation in the proper manner. When the nuns accordingly sat half cross-legged and began to apply themselves to mental cultivation, the Blessed One heard that during that night tiny creatures had entered there. The Blessed One therefore declared: 'In that place, after a leaf or a thin petal has fallen as a cushion, sit half cross-legged on it in the proper manner.'

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: 'Venerable one, if a nun who has fallen from the precepts wishes to go forth again, receive full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and be established in the status of a fully ordained nun, may she go forth, or may she not?' The Blessed One declared: 'Upāli, she may not go forth. Upāli, a nun who has once fallen may not be received back through going forth and full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, nor be established in the status of a fully ordained nun.'

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the buddha, the Blessed One: 'Venerable one, in the case where the Blessed One has here declared that a monk should adjudicate a nun's offence of deterioration in moral discipline, deterioration in view, and deterioration in conduct —'

— and deterioration in livelihood, he should not bring it up or call it to mind,' and the Blessed One declared this — Venerable one, is there then any category whatsoever in which a nun may bring up or call to mind a monk's deterioration in moral discipline, deterioration in view, deterioration in conduct, or deterioration in livelihood?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, there is no category whatsoever in which a nun may bring up or call to mind a monk's deterioration in moral discipline, deterioration in view, deterioration in conduct, or deterioration in livelihood."

In brief:

Even a merchant will not forgo
the leftover food set aside;
he does not ask about obstructions to the Dharma —
those are for others, and for the flow of blood.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī there lived another merchant who was wealthy, with abundant resources and great possessions. He took a wife from a family of equal standing, and he enjoyed her company with great delight. Yet although they enjoyed each other's company, no son was born and no daughter was born. Then in later times his wealth became exhausted, and his resources ran out. He said to his wife: "My good wife, I am now old and cannot go out to seek wealth, so I shall go to the Jeta Grove and go forth." When he said this, she replied: "Master, if you go forth, at whose side shall I stay? I too shall go forth." He said: "Good, my dear, let us go," and leading her there, he came before the noble lady Gautamī, the mother of the people, bowed at her feet, and said: "Noble lady, may your reverence grant this my wife going forth and full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, for I am going to the Jeta Grove to go forth." She replied: "My son, that you and your wife together have aroused the intention is excellent. As for going forth, the wise one who has seen the five qualities spoken of by the Blessed One ought to be drawn to going forth" — and then, just as before, she said: "Buddhas, the disciples of buddhas, the wise, those who have gone rightly, and holy persons have praised going forth in many ways; it is excellent. Go forth," — and she sent her forth. Then she went to the Jeta Grove and went forth among the monks. The merchant of Śrāvastī became known as one who had gone forth, and by great merit he obtained the requisites: robes, alms-food, a sleeping mat, and medicines and treatments for illness.

In later times he went out for alms. His wife too had gone on her alms round, and at that time a great famine arose, and she suffered from a lack of alms-food. He saw her and said: "Sister, how do you fare, how do you live?" She replied: "Noble one, since it is a time of famine, even alms-food is not given, and I live in hardship and suffering." He said: "Sister, I receive alms, and if the Blessed One permits it, I will give you half my alms-food." Without saying anything further, he went to the residence and told the nuns exactly how things stood. The nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "In the case of such a nun, if a monk obtains any alms-food, that monk should, in a time of famine, give her half his alms-food. Let there be no hesitation in this matter." The Blessed One declared: "In the case of such a nun, if a monk obtains any alms-food, and a time of famine has come upon her, let that monk give her half his alms-food." He then set aside for her half his alms-food; she ate it and went on her way. Then in later times he obtained some alms-food that came unexpectedly —

she did not come to that monk. The monk thought to himself: "She is certain to have found food elsewhere — and if she does not come here, for whose sake am I to set this aside?" Thinking thus, he did not set aside a portion for her. After some time the nun came after all. He said to her: "Sister, I thought you would not come, and so I did not set aside any alms-food. If this food I have here were permitted by the Blessed One, I would give it to you." She bowed at his feet and went to the nuns' quarters. She related to the nuns what had taken place. They reported it to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Whatever a monk has set aside, a nun may receive and eat. Whatever a nun has set aside, a monk may receive. In this matter there should be no hesitation: a nun may receive from a monk, and monks may receive from a nun."

The occasion arose at Śrāvastī. Monks asked a nun, in the midst of the nuns' Saṅgha, questions concerning matters of uncommon transgression. She grew ashamed and sat with her face cast down. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks must not ask nuns questions about matters of uncommon transgression. The nun herself should be questioned. If a monk asks a nun about uncommon transgressions belonging to nuns, he commits an offense with remainder. If elder monks have begun to ask common questions, and she nonetheless said nothing out of shame — " the Blessed One declared: "Place her before a nun and question her. That nun should speak to her, and that nun in turn should report to the monk."

The occasion arose at Śrāvastī. Another nun was being fully ordained by the venerable Śāriputra. In the course of his enjoining her thus — "Having received full ordination under the teaching of the supreme Wisdom, do not be disheartened at having obtained this precious and difficult-to-find leisure and endowment" — blood flowed from her during that time. The venerable Śāriputra said to her: "Sister, please leave." She, bleeding and burning with shame, arose with thoughts of self-harm, and the venerable Śāriputra, perceiving this, departed. Then the nuns said to her: "Sister, when you are right in the midst of the assembly and are told by the teacher to leave — why did you not rise?" She replied: "Older and younger sisters, were it not for such a great virtue as this, would you yourselves say such a thing? I was sitting alone and bleeding — how was I to rise?" They fell silent and said nothing further. They reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, a nun who is undergoing full ordination should not sit alone on the bare ground; she should be seated on a board, on grass, or on a mat set over a pure surface, on account of a woman's delivery of the afterbirth."

In sum: a surplus remnant is not permissible for a monk.
The unclean is held between the belt
and the nursing-cloth, together with the nursing-band —
these must not be kept as an obstruction.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time Gautamī, the great lady (prajāpatī), the mother of the people, was traveling the countryside with her retinue of five hundred, and as the sun sank to the west she came to the Jeta Grove. She thought: "It is too late now to proceed to Śrāvastī — I shall stay right here this night, in whatever manner I can, and set out at dawn in the morning."

She lay down on the ground there, and her robes became soiled with dust. In the morning, at dawn, she would have to return once more, and thinking, "I shall pay homage to the Teacher all at once before departing," she and her companions went to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, they bowed at the Blessed One's feet and stood in his presence. The Blessed One saw that her robes were soiled with dust and said, "Gautamī, who has soiled your robes with dust?" She explained to him in detail what had happened. The Blessed One then said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, have the monks given the nuns the leftover bedding of the monks, or have they not given it?" "They have not given it, Blessed One." The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, therefore let this be permitted: monks shall give nuns the leftover bedding of the monks. Have no hesitation in this." The Blessed One declared that monks should give nuns the leftover bedding of the monks. Then another monk took very fine bedding, and the monks gave that leftover bedding to those nuns. Thereupon the Blessed One declared: "Do not give from what is fine — give from old cloth, coarse wool, or the like."

The second narrative occasion is set at Śrāvastī. The venerable Mahākāśyapa, in the morning, dressed in his lower robe and outer robe, took up his almsbowl, and entered Śrāvastī to seek alms. The nun Sthūlanandā had also entered the monastery. Because it was the autumn season and the rivers were full of water, the venerable Mahākāśyapa crossed over a bridge. Sthūlanandā saw him, and she thought: "I shall do something to displease this fool." She went swiftly and quickly, and as he was crossing the bridge she shook it. The venerable Mahākāśyapa fell, his undergarments and lower robe were drenched with water, and his almsbowl slipped and sank into the river. Only his neck-cloth was saved. He said to her: "Sister, it is not you who have done wrong — it is the venerable Ānanda who has done wrong. Women who conduct themselves in such a gross manner have gone forth, taken full ordination, and become nuns within the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya (the discipline) — that is to be rejoiced in." When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One reflected: "Whoever — whether a nun or a monk — crosses a single bridge together, that is an occasion for transgression. Therefore a nun shall not cross a single bridge together with a monk her father in the Dharma. If she does so, she incurs a transgression." The Blessed One declared that a nun shall not cross a single bridge together with a monk. Then those nuns refrained from crossing even other bridges that were firm and broad, and the Blessed One declared: "Bridges that are firm and broad they may cross — have no hesitation about that."

The third narrative occasion is also set at Śrāvastī. The nun Sthūlanandā then, in the morning, dressed in her lower robe and outer robe, took up her almsbowl, and entered Śrāvastī to seek alms. In due course she went before the queen Mālagandha. Mālagandha welcomed her with pleasant words of greeting and set out a seat. While they were talking and sitting together for a moment, Sthūlanandā said, "Mālagandha, your waist is so very, very slender." Mālagandha replied: "Noble lady, why do you ask? Whatever it takes, I do what pleases my husband's mind." Sthūlanandā said: "Mālagandha, so it may be — but tell me, just enough to resolve my doubt."

She replied, "Noble lady, I wear a waist-cincher." Sthūlanandā said, "Good — that is why so many people find you pleasing and delightful." Mālagandha said nothing further.

Sthūlanandā went to her summer quarters and put on a waist-cincher. Some time later, Sthūlanandā was bathing together with other nuns at the river Aciravatī. When they saw her, they asked, "Noble lady, our waists are so very, very thick — why is yours so very, very slender?" She replied, "Sisters, I wear a waist-cincher. That is why my waist is like this." They asked, "Noble lady, is it fitting for you to wear a waist-cincher?" She replied, "Whether it is fitting or not, sisters, I have put one on." The nuns criticized and reproached her. The wicked ones said, "How could a nun possibly wear a waist-cincher?" When those who had witnessed this told the monks, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Therefore, a nun must not wear a waist-cincher. If a nun wears a waist-cincher, she shall incur an offense."

The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then the nun Sthūlanandā, in the morning, dressed in her lower robe and outer robe, took up her almsbowl, and went just as before. While they sat together talking for a moment, she asked, "Mālagandha, why are your breasts so high and firm?" Mālagandha replied, "Noble lady, why do you ask about this? Whatever it takes, I do what pleases my husband's mind." Sthūlanandā said, "So it may be, Mālagandha — but tell me, just enough to resolve my doubt." She replied, "Noble lady, I wear a breast-band." Sthūlanandā said, "Excellent! That being so, dear Mālagandha, you are truly a precious woman." Mālagandha said nothing further.

Sthūlanandā went to her summer quarters, and having put on a breast-band, the same sequence of events as before then followed. Therefore, monks, a nun must not wear a breast-band. If a nun wears a breast-band, she shall incur an offense.

The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then the nun Sthūlanandā, in the morning, dressed in her lower robe and outer robe, took up her almsbowl, and went just as before. While they sat talking together for a moment, she asked, "Mālagandha, why do your breasts hang down?" She replied, "Noble lady, why do you ask about this? Whatever I do, I do what pleases my husband's mind." Sthūlanandā said, "So it may be — but tell me, just enough to resolve my doubt." She replied, "Noble lady, I wear a breast-support." Sthūlanandā said, "Excellent! In that case, the ladies of the inner palace are pleased and delighted with you." Mālagandha said nothing further.

Sthūlanandā again went to her summer quarters, and having put on a breast-support there, the same sequence as before followed. Therefore, a nun must not wear a breast-support. If a nun wears a breast-support, she shall incur an offense.

The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

Now the Blessed One had declared that a nun must not wear a waist-cincher, whereupon Sthūlanandā bound her waist with whatever cloth she could find. Then some time later, Sthūlanandā was bathing at the river Aciravatī together with other nuns. When they saw her, they asked, "Noble lady, if the Blessed One has not permitted nuns to bind the waist with a waist-cincher, why is your waist so very, very slender?" She replied, "Sisters, I have wrapped it with whatever cloth was at hand."

They then asked her, "Sister, is it permissible to bind the waist with just any cloth?" She replied, "Sisters, whether it is permitted or not permitted — I have bound it." The nuns criticized and reproached her sharply: "How could a nun bind her waist with just any cloth?" And so those who had acted in this way were treated as in the previous case, up to the words: "A nun shall not bind her waist with just any cloth. If a nun binds her waist with just any cloth, she shall incur an offense."

In brief:

Do not discard it in an unclean place —
The womb, impurity, and foul drink,
One may touch one's own child,
But one must not touch another's child.

The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Mahākāśyapa, having dressed in his lower robe and outer robe in the morning, took up his alms bowl and entered Śrāvastī to collect alms. The nun Sthūlanandā had also gone out to collect alms. Now, the venerable Mahākāśyapa was coming down past a place near a cesspit, and Sthūlanandā saw him. She thought, "I shall do something to displease this fool," and she hurried along, going quickly and at length, and threw a bundle of refuse into the cesspit, fouling the outer robe and alms bowl of the venerable Mahākāśyapa. Then she said, "Sister, you have done no wrong" — and so forth as before. When monks who had witnessed what had happened reported it to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, a nun shall not defile a monk with filth. If a nun defiles a monk with filth, she shall incur an offense."

The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who was wealthy, with great riches and many possessions. He had taken a wife from a family of equal standing, and he enjoyed himself and lived together with her. Some time later he took up trade and traveled to another region. Before leaving, he said to his wife, "My dear, I am going away on a trading journey to another land. Do not be distracted; guard the household diligently and attentively, and send me news from time to time." She replied, "Very well, my lord; it shall be done as you say." So he left on his trading journey to another land.

After her husband had gone, his wife was tormented by affliction, craving fine clothing and food, and she consorted with another man. She became pregnant and thought to herself, "I shall kill the one dwelling in my womb. When my husband returns, it will bring disgrace upon me." Having thus decided to kill the one in her womb, she then thought about how to discard it, not knowing how or where. She was sitting there, absorbed in anxious thought, when Sthūlanandā came to that house to collect alms. The woman said, "Noble lady, please give alms." The woman, tormented by her own distress, said, "There is no one to give alms today; please move on." Sthūlanandā said, "Noble lady, has someone died, or is something amiss?" The woman replied, "Noble lady, no one has died, but a child has come forth from me and I do not know how to discard it or where." Sthūlanandā said, "Noble lady, if I dispose of it for you, will you give me alms?" The woman said, "Noble lady, yes I will." "And will you give alms to the nun who accompanies me?" "Yes, noble lady, I will." "And to the duty-assigner as well?" "Yes, I will." "Then I shall dispose of it properly." So she placed it in a large alms bowl, carried it to an empty house, and began to dispose of it there.

A man who had previously entered that empty house saw her and said, "What are you doing, ascetic woman?" She replied, "The likes of you — a worthless son of nobody — have no business questioning a woman of good family who has done such a thing. Begone!" And she rebuked him eight times and he left.

Then she encountered a nun, and that nun said to her, "You shameless, disobedient woman — Sthūlanandā has done such and such a thing." Sthūlanandā had no reply and said nothing.

When things had come to pass in this way, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: since it is an occasion for offense for a nun to carry a large alms bowl, the Blessed One, knowing that nuns should not carry large alms bowls, declared to the monks: "Monks, it was a woman who was not a nun who, with desire unbefitting one who is not a nun, acted as one who is not a nun. Therefore, a nun must not perform such an act. She must also not carry a large alms bowl. If a nun performs such an act or carries a large alms bowl, she incurs a transgression." The Blessed One declared: "A nun must not carry a large alms bowl." The Blessed One further declared: "Whatever counts as a small alms bowl for a monk counts as a large one for a nun."

The case arose in Śrāvastī. Once, the nun Guptā poured one drop of urine into her mouth and inserted one drop into the opening of her womb. By the inconceivable ripening of a sentient being's karma, the young Kāśyapa came into being. Since Guptā had not touched him, he cried. Her relatives and friends asked, "Guptā, why is this infant crying?" She said nothing. The nuns, recalling that the Blessed One had established the training rule that a nun must not touch a man, said, "He is not touching her, and that is why he is crying." Her relatives and friends said, "But the Blessed One is compassionate — why then would he prevent a mother from touching her own child? If this infant boy is not touched by his mother, he will surely die." They added, "Very well then, let the Blessed One be informed of this."

When things had come to pass in this way, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Then it is permitted to touch him, to nurse him, to care for him, to raise him."

The case arose in Śrāvastī. The Blessed One having declared, "She may nurse him, care for him, and raise him," women being by nature attached, the nuns passed the infant from lap to lap, and he grew thin and puny, his body wasted from being tossed about without rest. His relatives and friends saw this and asked, "Why has this infant become thin and puny, his body wasted and worn?" When Guptā explained it to them in detail, those relatives, out of affection, took to mocking the nuns.

When things had come to pass in this way, the monks heard of it and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, nuns must not touch another's child. If a nun touches another's child, she incurs a transgression."

The sixth chapter on minor matters is complete.

The Vinaya Garland, the fortieth fascicle. The collected sūtra passages: On doubt and the solitary retreat, on Saṃkākṣī, and on account of both — whether monks who sell liquor, or whether nuns and outsiders: in brief, also sleeping in the presence of doubt, and not dwelling alone elsewhere.

The same applies to boys and girls, as well as to novices and to Rādha.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that a nun must not sleep together with a man in a single room. Now, the nun Guptā had given birth to the young boy Kāśyapa, and she left him outside, where he cried alone. His kinfolk and friends heard this and asked Guptā why the young boy Kāśyapa was crying. She sat without saying a word, and the nuns said to the venerable ones: "Since the Blessed One has laid down the training rule that a nun must not sleep together with a man inside a single house, it is not permissible for her to sleep with this Guptā in the same room." Her kinfolk then said: "The noble Blessed One is compassionate — if the young Kāśyapa is not permitted to sleep together with Guptā, he will certainly and without question come to ruin." And they said further: "In that case, please let the Blessed One be informed." When things had come to pass in this way, they told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, it is permitted: let Guptā receive the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son from the community of nuns. The request is to be made as follows. Spread out a mat, strike the gong, and when the entire community of nuns is assembled and in order, let the nun Guptā bow according to seniority, seat herself before the elder nun on a piece of cloth, grass, a mat, or a pure surface, join her palms, and speak these words:

'Hail, noble community of nuns! I, Guptā, have given birth to a boy child. I request the noble community of nuns for the vow to sleep in a single room together with my son. May the noble community of nuns, out of compassion and for the sake of compassion, grant Guptā the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son.'

This is to be said a second time and a third time.

Thereupon, let one of the nuns move Guptā from the place of hearing to a place where she may be seen, and say: 'Hail, noble community of nuns! A boy child has been born to Guptā. She has requested from the noble community of nuns the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son. If it is timely and agreeable to the noble community of nuns, let it assent. The noble community of nuns grants Guptā the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son. This is the motion.'

The procedure is then as follows: 'Hail, noble community of nuns! A boy child has been born to this Guptā. She has requested from the noble community of nuns the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son. The noble community of nuns is granting Guptā the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son. Those among the noble community of nuns who consent to granting Guptā the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son: remain silent. Those who do not consent: speak.' The noble community of nuns has granted Guptā the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son. Since the community has consented and permitted, it remains silent; and so it is held to be.

Whatever nun has been given by the noble community of nuns the vow to sleep in a single room together with her son — she is permitted to sleep in a single room together with her son. On this point, let there be no doubt."

Guptā, however, continued to sleep there together with another nun as well, and the nuns who saw this told the monks. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Only the nun's own son may sleep together with her in a single room — no one else. Another nun must not stay there; if she does, she commits an offense. Guptā may sleep in a single room together with him even when he has grown up and become the great Kāśyapa the Elder." The nuns who witnessed this told the monks accordingly, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "When a nun's son has grown up, she may no longer sleep in a single room together with him. Train as the training has been prescribed."

The awakened one, the Blessed One, was residing at Rājagṛha in the bamboo grove of Kalandaka, in the cool forest. At that time, there dwelt in the city of Rājagṛha a yakṣa (Skt. yakṣa) named Sāta, who protected, guarded, and kept safe the learned, handsome, and eminent king of the land of Samānanda, together with his queens, the young princes, the ministers, and the people of the city and countryside. By that yakṣa's power, the wealth of the learned, handsome, and eminent king of Samānanda, of his queens, princes, ministers, and the people of the city and countryside increased and flourished; trees always bore flowers and fruit, rain fell in its proper seasons, the earth became laden with grain, and food offerings arrived in abundance. And from various villages, cities, provinces, royal residences, and outlying regions — ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and the destitute all gathered in Samānanda, and the yakṣa Sāta likewise protected, guarded, and kept safe all of them.

Sāta had taken a wife of equal birth, and together with her he lived in joyful delight.

In the land of Gāndhāra there likewise dwelt a yakṣa named Pañcāla, who protected, guarded, and kept safe the king of Gāndhāra, his queens, the princes, the ministers, and the people of the city and countryside. By that yakṣa's power, the wealth of the king of Gāndhāra, his queens, princes, ministers, and the people of the city and countryside increased and flourished; trees always bore flowers and fruit, rain fell in its proper seasons, the earth became laden with grain, and food offerings arrived in abundance. And from various villages, cities, provinces, royal residences, and outlying regions — ascetics, brahmins, the poor, and the destitute all gathered in Gāndhāra, and the yakṣa Pañcāla likewise protected, guarded, and kept safe all of them. Pañcāla too had taken a wife of equal birth, and together with her he lived in joyful delight.

Then, at a later time, the yakṣa Sāta and the yakṣa Pañcāla both went to a gathering of yakṣas, and there the two became close friends with one another. Thereafter, the yakṣa Sāta would from time to time send Pañcāla gifts of flowers, fruits, and other produce from the land of Samānanda; and the yakṣa Pañcāla would likewise send the yakṣa Sāta gifts of flowers and fruits from the land of Gāndhāra. Growing ever more deeply friendly with one another in this way, the two again went together to the yakṣa assembly. There, the yakṣa Sāta spoke of his friend: two generations had passed, and yet his son, grandson, great-grandson,

and great-grandchildren — how could friendship among them be kept unbroken? So he spoke. Then the yakṣa Pañcāla replied: "Friend, excellent! I too have been thinking the very same thing. Therefore let us become kinsmen even before any children are born. If I have a son and you have a daughter, you shall give her to my son; and if you have a son and I have a daughter, then I shall give her to your son." The other said: "Friend, excellent — let it be so!" The two of them thus pledged kinship to one another before any children had yet been born, and departed.

Then, at a later time, the wife of the yakṣa Sāta became with child. When nine months had passed she gave birth to a daughter — well-formed, beautiful to look upon, lovely. At her birth all the clans of the yakṣas rejoiced. Those of his own lineage and bloodline held a great birth-celebration and proceeded to the naming. When they deliberated on what name to give the girl, the kinsmen and friends said: "At the time of this girl's birth, all the clans of the yakṣas rejoiced; therefore let this girl be named Joymaker." And so she was named Joymaker.

The yakṣa Pañcāla of the land of Gāndhāra heard that a daughter had been born to the yakṣa Sāta in Rājagṛha, and he thought: "My friend has had a daughter — she will indeed become my daughter-in-law. It is proper that I send her gifts of clothing and ornaments." He then sent a letter to the yakṣa Sāta saying: "Dear friend, I have heard that you have had a daughter born to you and I am very glad. It is fitting that I send clothing and ornaments for my friend's daughter — please accept them." He also sent word: "Since we two are kinsmen, if you have a son, she is already promised to him." The yakṣa Pañcāla read the letter and thought constantly about when he would find a son, and took his pleasure in sport and enjoyment with his wife.

In their pleasurable enjoyment together a son was born to them. He too was of the same lineage and bloodline, and his kinsmen held a great birth-celebration and proceeded to the naming. When they deliberated on what name to give the boy, the kinsmen and friends said: "This boy is the son of the yakṣa Pañcāla; therefore let his name be Pāñcika." And so his name was set as Pāñcika.

The yakṣa Sāta of Rājagṛha heard that a son had been born to the yakṣa Pañcāla of the land of Gāndhāra, and he thought: "My friend has had a son — he will certainly become my son-in-law." He then sent him clothing and ornaments along with a letter: "Dear friend, I have heard that you have had a son born to you and I am very glad. It is fitting that I send clothing and ornaments for my friend's son — please accept them." Pañcāla read the letter and sent back word: "Then make ready the preparations for the wedding feast at which the bride will be received." The yakṣa Sāta read the letter and thought with satisfaction: "The girl Joymaker — I already gave her away before." He nurtured her and took his pleasure in sport and enjoyment with his wife. In their pleasurable enjoyment together his wife became with child, and on the very day she conceived, a crane cried out on the mountain. Nine months passed and she gave birth to a boy — handsome, beautiful to look upon, lovely — and at the very moment of his birth a crane again cried out from the mountain.

He held a great birth-feast befitting his lineage, of one blood with his own kind, and they proceeded to the naming ceremony. When it was deliberated what name the boy should be given, the kinsmen and friends said: "When he was conceived, a crane cried out from the mountain; when he was born, a crane cried out again; and his father is named Sāta. Therefore let this boy's name also be given in the line of Sāta" — and so his name was set as Sātakiri.

The boy Sātakiri was raised and nurtured and grew up. Then, some time later, the yakṣa Sāta passed away together with his wife, and Sātakiri became master of the household. Now the yakṣa girl Joymaker said to her brother Sātakiri that she wished to seize and devour the newborn children of the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha. He replied: "Sister, our father's home country is ruled by the wise, handsome, and noble king Manodatta, who constantly guards, protects, and shelters the queen, the youths, the ministers, the villages, the cities, and the people of the land. We belong to the class that must be thoroughly guarded. This is our own domain — and if others commit mischief here, it falls to us to stop them. Why then would it be fitting for you to act in this way? Turn back the resolve you have formed." But because she was possessed by the habitual tendency of a perverse aspiration from the past, she could not be restrained. Again she told Sātakiri that she wished to seize and devour the newborn children of the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha. Sātakiri recognized from the circumstances of the time that she could not be held back in this matter. He thought: "I cannot keep stopping this forever, and moreover, she was already given away earlier as a bride." So he sent a letter to the yakṣa Pañcāla, saying: "The girl Joymaker has now come of age — come here and take your bride." The yakṣa Pañcāla then arranged for the young yakṣa Pāñcika to take her as his bride, and she was led away to the land of Gandhāra. The young yakṣa Pāñcika sported and took his pleasure with her in every delight.

She was cheerful, bold, joyous, and grew greatly at ease. But at that time she told her husband that she wished to seize and devour the newborn children of the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha. He said: "Dear one, that is your home of kinship. If others commit mischief there, it is right that we should stop them — why then would you act in such a way? Turn back this improper resolve you have formed." But because she was driven by the habitual tendency of her former perverse aspiration, she merely sat in silence when he spoke, saying not a word.

She sported and took her pleasure with the young yakṣa Pāñcika, and gave birth to a son. A great birth-feast was held, and a name befitting their lineage was given. In like manner, a second time and a third, until she had borne five hundred sons, and the youngest of them all was named Joymaker. Now she had grown powerful through her sons, and when Pāñcika tried to restrain her he could not, and he became displeased and fell silent. Thereafter the yakṣa woman Joymaker went roaming and wandering wherever she wished, and she began to seize and devour the newborn children of the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha.

The many people dwelling in Rājagṛha went before King Bimbisāra and said: "Your Majesty, our newborn children are being seized. Whoever is doing us this harm is surely of the race of evil spirits." The king then commanded all those who held authority over every district: "Go and investigate who it is that is seizing the newborns of the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha." They set about searching with care and diligence. Yet even as they searched, the seizing continued and the harm grew great — and any woman who was with child was removed and placed in another district. The ministers then reported to King Bimbisāra: "Your Majesty, the harm has grown very great. Any woman who is with child is being removed and placed in another district." The king summoned his diviners and consulted them, and they replied: "Your Majesty, an enraged yakṣa is causing this harm. Make offering of torma at the yakṣa shrines and render worship and honor." The king then commanded his ministers: "Go and have proclamations made by drum throughout the city of Rājagṛha. Let all the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha, and all those who have come from other districts and towns, make torma offerings at the yakṣa shrines and render worship and honor." The ministers went and made the proclamation accordingly: "Hear, all you people of Rājagṛha, of the city, and of the various towns and districts who have come here — the king has declared: let all the many people dwelling in my realm, those who have come from cities and from every other district, make torma offerings at all the yakṣa shrines and render worship and honor." The many people dwelling in Rājagṛha then swept those city places clean of stones, pebbles, and dirt, sprinkled them with sandalwood water, and set out fragrant incense in individual bowls. They raised victory banners and divine victory-pennants, hung many silk streamers and garlands, and scattered diverse flowers, making those places as beautiful as the pleasure groves of the gods — like Joyous Heaven itself. Then torma offerings were made at all the yakṣa shrines, with full worship and honor. Yet even so, Joymaker was not pacified.

Then the gods dwelling in Rājagṛha revealed to the many people there: "The yakṣa woman Joymaker has been seizing your children. You must all go to the Blessed One — it is the Blessed One who will tame her." But the people said: "That is not Joymaker; that is the Seizer! She is the one who has been taking our newborns!" And so the name Joymaker was reversed, and she came to be known instead as the yakṣa woman the Seizer.

The many people dwelling in Rājagṛha then went to where the Blessed One was. They prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, touching their heads to the ground, and addressed him: "Blessed One, this yakṣa woman the Seizer has long harbored no enmity toward the many people of Rājagṛha — and now she bears enmity. She was no enemy — and now she has become an enemy. She was not estranged from them — and now she is estranged. She seizes newborns. Blessed One, out of compassion and loving concern, please do whatever is needed to tame the yakṣa woman the Seizer." The Blessed One, without saying a word, granted permission to the many people of Rājagṛha. Understanding that the Blessed One had granted permission by his silence, the many people prostrated at his feet, touching their heads to the ground, and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Then, in the early morning, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and his Dharma-robe,

took up his alms bowl, went into Rājagṛha for alms, and returning from his alms round in Rājagṛha, took his meal. Having declined the offer of a second serving, he departed and went to the place where the yakṣa woman the Seizer dwelt.

At that time, the yakṣa woman the Seizer had left her child Joymaker at home and gone out to roam her territory. The Blessed One placed his alms bowl over the child and concealed it there, and then bestowed a blessing such that, just as the boys could not see the Blessed One, so too the Blessed One would be visible to all of them — that is, he rendered the situation so that she could not see the child, yet the child would be seen by all others.

Immediately, the yakṣa woman the Seizer returned from her wanderings and, not finding Joymaker, left that spot and looked around the entire neighborhood of the house, yet still could not find him. The other children said: "Joymaker cannot be found. They have not seen him. We have not seen him either." At these words she beat her breast; her color faded and joy left her. Her eyes filled with tears, and she ran swiftly away, searching through the villages, the market districts, the streets, the crossroads, the three-way junctions, the pleasure parks, the gardens, the lakes, the ponds, the pools, the temples, the assembly halls, and all the other secluded dwellings of Rājagṛha — yet she did not find him.

Then, her hair disheveled and matted, she went mad, weeping and wailing: "Alas, my child! Alas, my father! Alas, Joymaker!" — calling out again and again. She searched through the villages, the towns, the outlying settlements, the royal palace, and all the palace precincts, yet still found him not.

Then she went to the great ocean in the east, and then to the oceans of the south, the west, and the north. In those four directions too, he was nowhere to be found.

Her hair now wild and matted, emaciated, she wandered aimlessly — leaping up, falling down, crawling on the ground, moving on her knees, crouching — and in this manner she crossed the seven black mountains of Jambudvīpa (the southern continent) and searched among the seven golden mountains, the snow mountains, the great lake Anavatapta, and the fragrant mountain ranges. Still weeping loudly, she searched through the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha, the western continent of Aparagodānīya, and the northern continent of Uttarakuru — yet she found him not.

Then she searched through the hells: the Sañjīva, the Kāḷasūtra, the Saṃghāta, the Raurava, the Mahāraurava, the Tapana, the Pratāpana, the Avīci, the Arbuda, the Nirarbuda, the Aṭaṭa, the Hahava, the Huhuva, the Utpala-like, the Padma-like, the Mahāpadma-like, and all the rest — yet she did not find him.

Then she climbed to the first terrace of Mount Meru, and from there to the second and the third. Without asking the lord of the yakṣas, Maṇibhadra, she searched the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods, going through the pleasure groves called Varied Chariots, Becoming Rough, Mingling, and Delight, and went as far as the pārijāta (coral tree) and the kuvīdāra tree.

Then she entered into the divine assembly known as Sudharmā, the beautiful city. Just as she was making her way toward Sudharma, the palace of Śakra (Indra), the lord of the gods, she was seized by the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi and many other yakṣas and a thousand gods, and was quickly and swiftly expelled from the beautiful city. She went off to another direction and wept at length until at last she was utterly exhausted and despairing. She went to the presence of Maṇibhadra, lord of the yakṣas, threw her body down upon a flat rock, and lamented, saying: "Alas, my child! Alas, my father! Alas, Joymaker!"

"Great chieftain, if someone has taken him and you are unhappy, please ask that your child be returned to you," she said. Then Maṇibhadra, the great king of the yakṣas, consoled her and said, "Come now, let go of your grief and wipe away your tears. Stay in your own dwelling and watch carefully to see who comes." She replied, "The chieftain is the ascetic Gautama." He then said to her, "Go to him, take refuge in the Blessed One, and he will show you your child Joymaker."

Like one who has found back what was thought to be lost with one's very life, she went quickly and swiftly to her own dwelling. The yakṣinī Aprāptā beheld the Blessed Buddha adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being, his body graced with the minor marks of excellence, ornamented with a radiant aura of light surpassing a thousand solar rays, moving in their midst like a mountain of precious jewels. The moment she saw him, joy arose in her, and thinking "I will find my Joymaker," she went to where the Blessed One was. She prostrated with her head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the yakṣinī Aprāptā addressed the Blessed One in these words: "O Gautama, please show me my son Joymaker. It has now been a long time since I last saw my son Joymaker."

The Blessed One said to the yakṣinī Aprāptā, "Aprāptā, if you have many children, how many do you have?"

She replied, "Blessed One, I have five hundred children."

The Blessed One said to Aprāptā, "You have five hundred children — what harm is it if you are missing just one?"

She then said, "Blessed One, if I cannot see my Joymaker, I will vomit hot blood and surely die."

The Blessed One said, "Aprāptā, even though you suffer so greatly at not seeing one of your five hundred children, you have yourself killed and eaten children who had only that one child — what must their suffering be like?"

She replied, "Blessed One, their suffering must be far greater than mine."

The Blessed One then declared, "Aprāptā, knowing what separation from a child feels like, why would you eat the children of others?"

She said, "Blessed One, please tell me what I should do."

The Blessed One said, "Come here, take refuge in me, accept the training precepts, grant fearlessness to the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha, and you will certainly see your son Joymaker right here before long."

She then said, "Venerable one, from this day forward I take refuge in the Blessed One, accept the training precepts, and grant fearlessness to the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha." And so it was that she took refuge in the Blessed One, accepted the training precepts, and granted fearlessness to the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha.

The Blessed One then showed her where her son Joymaker was, and he too took refuge in the Blessed One, accepted the training precepts, and granted fearlessness to the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha.

At the time when Aprāptā had taken refuge in the Blessed One, accepted the training precepts, and granted fearlessness to the many people dwelling in Rājagṛha, the monks arose with doubts, and to resolve all their doubts they asked the Blessed Buddha: "Venerable one, what karma did the yakṣinī Aprāptā perform? Through the maturation of what karma was she born as a yakṣinī with such a ravishing appearance, and in this life gave birth to five hundred children?"

The Blessed One declared, "Monks, the karma that Aprāptā performed and accumulated, and the conditions that have ripened — these stand close at hand like a river, and will inevitably come to pass. The karma that Aprāptā performed and accumulated cannot be experienced by another. Monks, karma performed and accumulated does not ripen within the external earth element, nor within the water element.

nor within the fire element, nor within the wind element. Rather, karma — whether virtuous or non-virtuous — that has been performed ripens within these very appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources. As it is said in verse:

Actions are never lost,
even after hundreds of aeons have passed.
When the time and conditions converge,
they ripen as fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in the distant past, in another city within this very Rājagṛha, there lived a cowherd. He took as his wife a woman of equal station, and together they enjoyed themselves in playful delight. Through that joyful union, after some time the wife became with child.

Now, in a period when no buddha appears in the world, a pratyekabuddha arises, dwelling in compassion for those who are weak and lowly — and in the end, a single worldly benefactor with warm devotion. At a certain point, another pratyekabuddha was wandering through the countryside and came to Rājagṛha. At that time, a festival was drawing near in the city of Rājagṛha. On the eve of the celebration, about five hundred revelers, carrying clean and well-prepared food and provisions, wrapped in garments of many colors, adorned with sweet-smelling flowers, dancing and singing and beating drums, were on their way to a pleasure grove — and along that path came a cowherding woman in the prime of her youth, carrying a brimming pot, walking down the road. The revelers, seeing her, called out, "Come, friend! Join the singing!" She, for her part, followed along with whatever they did, dancing exactly as they danced — and in doing so, her womb miscarried.

Enraged by this, she offered five hundred ripe mango fruits to the pratyekabuddha and made this aspiration: "By the root of this virtue, wherever and whenever I am born, may I be born as a ravishing yakṣinī, and may I seize and devour the sons and daughters of the people of Rājagṛha. And may I myself give birth to five hundred children."

Monks, the one who at that time was the wife of the cowherd is the very Aprāptā of the present. It is by the force of that aspiration that she has been born in such a manner.

The Vinaya Miscellany, the forty-first fascicle.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. The Blessed One had declared that nuns should not reside in forest hermitages. When those nuns entered into meditative concentration at market places, at the scales, and at crossroads, this too became an occasion for offense. When this had come about, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One thereupon declared, "Therefore let the nuns reside in a rain-season dwelling." When faithful brahmin householders and laymen heard that the Blessed One had granted permission for nuns to have rain-season dwellings, they built nuns' rain-season lodgings outside the city. But then ruffians, the sons of ferrymen, and uncouth young men took advantage of this to harass the nuns. When this had come about, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore let nuns' rain-season dwellings not be built outside the city, but within the city."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. The nun Sthūlanandā was sitting at the door of the rain-season dwelling and was mocking brahmins and householders, who in turn heaped insults and abuse upon her. When this had come about, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: the one who has become the occasion for offense is the nun who is sitting at the door of the rain-season dwelling. Therefore, having resolved that nuns should not sit at the door of the rain-season dwelling, the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, brahmins and

householders are given to mockery — therefore a nun must not sit at the door of the rain-season dwelling. If a nun sits at the door of the rain-season dwelling, she incurs a transgression.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. After the Blessed One had declared that a nun must not sit at the door of the rain-season dwelling, Sthūlanandā sat at a window and again mocked brahmins and householders, who in turn mocked her to her face, just as before. This continued until the rule was laid down: a nun must not sit at a window. If a nun sits at a window, she incurs a transgression.

In brief: the saṃkakṣikā garment is permitted. One must not bathe at a bathing place used by men. One must not go to market stalls. Through these, ordination is complete.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The nuns were wearing all five Dharma-robes in the rain-season dwelling while performing all their tasks, and they became distressed. When the nuns heard how things stood, they told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, let the nuns wear the saṃkakṣikā garment and perform all the tasks of the rain-season dwelling." Then when brahmins and householders came to the rain-season dwelling and saw the nuns working while wearing the saṃkakṣikā, they became attached. Others of different faith mocked them. When the monks heard how things had come about, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, brahmins and householders are given to mockery — therefore a nun must not wear the saṃkakṣikā and perform tasks in front of brahmins and householders. If a nun wears the saṃkakṣikā and performs tasks in front of brahmins and householders, she incurs a transgression. When performing tasks in the presence of brahmins and householders, she should cover her shoulders with the saṃkakṣikā and then, wearing the saṃkakṣikā, perform all her tasks."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. Sthūlanandā bathed at a bathing place used by men, and when young boys saw her, they pointed her out to one another, saying: "Look! That shaven-headed śramaṇī — her body is like a doe in the forest!" When the nuns heard how things had come about, they told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Whoever is a nun who bathes at a bathing place used by men is a basis for offense. Therefore, having resolved that a nun must not bathe at a bathing place used by men, he declared to the monks: Monks, brahmins and householders are given to mockery — therefore a nun must not bathe at a bathing place used by men. If a nun bathes at a bathing place used by men, she incurs a transgression.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. Sthūlanandā sat at a crossroads and jeered at brahmins and householders, and they mocked her in return, saying: "Look at this shaven-headed śramaṇī sitting at the crossroads — she is mocking us!" When the nuns heard how things had come about, they told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, brahmins and householders are given to mockery — therefore a nun must not go to market stalls. If she goes, she incurs a transgression."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that Gautamī, the great mistress of beings, went forth and received full ordination by accepting the eight chief rules, and thereby became a fully ordained nun. Does it follow that those five hundred nuns as well became fully ordained nuns by accepting the eight chief rules, going forth, and receiving full ordination?" Upāli replied: "Those five hundred nuns also went forth and received full ordination by accepting the eight chief rules, and thereby became fully ordained nuns."

In brief:

Just as in the case of one with the two marks,
and likewise one who is stopped up with mud,
and one who always discharges blood,
and finally one who has no blood at all.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. There at Śrāvastī, another nun gave full ordination to a person with two sex characteristics, and that person displayed those characteristics to the nuns. The nuns asked her, "Sister, what kind of being are you?" and she replied, "I am great — I have two sex characteristics." When things had come about in this way, the nuns reported it to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, a person with two sex characteristics is a hermaphrodite. You monks must expel that person with two sex characteristics. Monks, a person with two sex characteristics cannot undergo ordination in this Dharma-Vinaya. Therefore, when anyone who wishes to go forth comes before you, you must ask that person: 'Are you not a person with two sex characteristics?' If ordination is given without asking, it entails an offense."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. There at Śrāvastī, another nun gave full ordination to a woman who was stopped up, that is, whose internal passages were blocked. She went to the latrine to urinate, but defecation also occurred, and having evacuated both, she withdrew. Then another nun entered that place and, seeing that the latrine was defiled by excrement, asked her, "Sister, who has defiled this latrine with excrement?" That woman replied, "I am great — it was I who defiled it through carelessness." The nun asked her, "Sister, what careless thing did you do?" She replied, "I am great — I am a woman who is stopped up. When I intended to urinate, defecation came as well. What could I do?" When things had come about in this way, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, you must expel that stopped-up woman. Monks, this Dharma-Vinaya is not a place of ordination for a stopped-up woman. Therefore, when anyone who wishes to go forth comes forward, ask whether she is not a stopped-up woman. If ordination is given without asking, it entails an offense."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. There at Śrāvastī, another nun gave full ordination to a woman who always discharged blood. The place where her lower garment rested became defiled with blood and was filled with insects. A nun asked her, "Sister, do you always discharge blood?" She replied, "Elder sister, what is to be done? I always discharge blood." When things had come about in this way, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, a woman who always discharges blood is a hermaphrodite woman. You monks must expel her. One who always discharges blood cannot undergo ordination in this Dharma-Vinaya."

Therefore, whenever someone who wishes to go forth comes before a nun, that nun must ask her: "Are you a woman who always discharges blood?" If she gives full ordination without having asked, she incurs an offense carrying a remainder.

The originating case was at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī, another nun ordained a woman who had no menstrual flow. Because that nun had not abandoned attachment, the nuns would bleed at their time, and when she saw this, she said to the senior nuns: "What, are you thinking perverse thoughts? Why are you discharging blood? Sisters, what is wrong with you? Women by their very nature are this way — why do you not discharge?" She herself replied: "As for me, I have no blood — why would I discharge blood?" When things had come about in this way, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, a woman who has no menstrual flow is a hermaphrodite woman. You monks must expel her. Monks, one who has no menstrual flow cannot undergo ordination in this Dharma-Vinaya." Therefore, whenever someone who wishes to go forth comes before a nun, that nun must ask her: "Are you a woman who has no menstrual flow?" If she gives full ordination without having asked, she incurs an offense carrying a remainder.

In brief:

One who has only the mark of a woman, or a mole-mark,
must also be bound by the cord in that case.
She may not receive the gesture of spitting, nor take on the form of a monk,
nor may a nun give her confession.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī, another nun ordained a woman who had only the mark of a woman. That woman entered the privy for a long while and then came out. The nuns asked her: "Sister, you were in there a long time — what were you doing?" She replied: "Elder sisters, I have only the mark of a woman; I do not have complete female characteristics. What am I to do?" The nuns asked her: "Sister, are you not a woman who has only the mark?" She replied: "Elder sisters, I have only the mark." When things had come about in this way, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, a woman who has only the mark is a hermaphrodite. You monks must expel her. Monks, this Dharma-Vinaya cannot accommodate ordination for one who has only the mark." Therefore, whenever someone who wishes to go forth comes before a nun, that nun must ask her: "Are you not a woman who has only the mark?" If she gives full ordination without having asked, she incurs an offense carrying a remainder.

The originating case was at Śrāvastī. Because she had not abandoned attachment, by reason of previous karmic fault, a nun would from time to time discharge blood from her female organ, and the places where her lower garment rested became defiled, filled with insects, and unsightly. Although the nuns washed and treated the garment, it would return to the same state. When things had come about in this way, the nuns told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, let nuns wear a menstrual pad." When the Blessed One had said that nuns were to wear a menstrual pad, the nuns began to wear menstrual pads. Then at a later time, the joyful Nandā went out for her alms round, and her menstrual pad fell in the street. Some boys and girls who were playing in the street saw it and asked: "Noble one, what has fallen?" She was angered by what they said and replied: "Go and ask your mother's daughter and your sister about it right now, and they will show you." When the nuns heard what had happened, they told the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared:

Therefore, monks, a nun must not carry a menstrual pad in the bare manner described above. She should fasten it at the waist with a cord. In that way it will not become an occasion for offense.

The setting is Śrāvastī. On one occasion, the venerable Mahākāśyapa dressed in the morning, put on his lower robe and outer robe, took up his alms bowl, and entered Śrāvastī on his alms round. Pom-delight saw him from a distance and went to him quickly, hurrying along the road, and said "Utterly senseless fool!" and spat on him. He said to her, "Sister, you have done no wrong yourself, yet the venerable Ānanda has permitted women who engage in seriously improper conduct to go forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and discipline, receive full ordination, and be accorded the status of nuns — and that is the reply to your question." When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, Pom-delight is not a contemplative, not a nun. Even a prostitute would not do to a monk what Pom-delight did. Therefore, a nun must not spit at a monk." The Blessed One so declared. If a nun spits at a monk, she incurs a transgression.

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time another monk committed a transgression. He saw a nun and said, "Noble one, please wait a moment." She asked, "Noble one, what is it?" He said, "Noble one, I have committed a transgression and I confess it before you." She sat down, and he sat before her and said, "Please attend, noble one. I, the monk known by such-and-such a name, have committed such-and-such a transgression. I confess it before you, noble one. I acknowledge it, I do not conceal it. By confessing and acknowledging it I will come to ease; without confession and acknowledgment there is no ease." She asked, "Noble one, have you also committed such-and-such a transgression? What you have done is wrong." The monk was ashamed. When the monks heard what had happened and reported it to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, a monk must not confess a transgression in front of a nun. He should confess before a monk who holds a compatible pure view. If a monk confesses a transgression before a nun, he incurs a transgression."

The setting is Śrāvastī. At that time another nun committed a transgression. She saw a monk, and together with the act of paying respect she prostrated at his feet and said, "Noble one, please be compassionate and remain a moment." He asked, "Noble one, what is needed?" She said, "Noble one, I have committed a transgression, and I confess it before you, noble one." He sat down. She too prostrated at his feet, sat before him, joined her palms, and said, "Please attend, noble one. I, the nun known by such-and-such a name, have committed such-and-such a transgression. I confess this transgression before you, noble one. I acknowledge it, I do not conceal it. By confessing and acknowledging it I will come to ease; without confession and acknowledgment there is no ease." He said, "That you, noble one, should have committed a transgression of such a form — that the noble one has done wrongly." The nun was ashamed. When the monks heard what had happened and reported it to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, a nun must not confess a transgression before a monk who is her monastic father,

before a fully pure nun of compatible view. If a nun confesses a transgression before a monk, it becomes a matter of the past and is done with.

In brief:
Let the monks perform the formal act;
let the nuns examine it.
Seats and small seats shall be provided,
but cushioned ones are not to be given.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that the formal acts of the monastic fathers and the formal acts of the nuns were to be separate, with the exception of communal acts. When the nuns performed acts in the presence of the monastic fathers and then became frightened, they did not dare to perform those acts. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Let the monks perform the formal act; let the nuns examine it."

The Blessed One having declared, "Let the monks perform the formal act; let the nuns examine it," the nuns did not know how to carry out this examination. They reported this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns should attend carefully and know: this is the petition; this is the first proclamation; this is the second; this is the third."

The occasion for this was at Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One announced that a Dharma teaching was to be proclaimed and the monks had not laid out seats, the Blessed One said, "Lay out seats." Then on a later occasion, when a Dharma teaching was announced, nuns came and sat on cushioned small seats and began to listen to the Dharma. At that point, another nun who had not been mindful had a discharge of blood and soiled the cushioned small seat, rendering it unfit. When the teaching was finished and the officer in charge of seats began to gather them in, he found one small cushioned seat that had been rendered unfit, full of blood-stains. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, a cushioned small seat is not to be given to nuns who come to hear the Dharma, and they are not to sit on cushioned small seats."

The Blessed One having declared that cushioned small seats were not to be given to nuns who came to hear the Dharma, the monks accordingly gave those who came to hear the Dharma uncushioned small seats. Then it happened that a great lay patroness came to hear the Dharma, and they gave her too an uncushioned small seat. She said, "Noble ones, even when I lived in a household I never lacked for a cushioned small seat." The monks replied: "Gautamī, the Blessed One has not permitted it — he has declared that cushioned small seats are not to be given to nuns who come to hear the Dharma." She replied: "Noble ones, what fault of mine is the same as that of nuns who are not mindful?" When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, it is permitted: for those nuns who are mindful, when they come to hear the Dharma, cushioned small seats shall be given to them. Have no doubt in this matter."

In brief:
With women who sell liquor or sell their bodies,
or with servant women — one must not make contact.
One should not strike a person with a harmful garment or the chest.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the nun Sthūlanandā, in the early morning hours, having donned her lower robe and outer robe and taken up her alms bowl, entered Śrāvastī on alms round. While she was on her alms round, she saw a certain housewife who was well dressed, wearing a fine lower garment and fine ornaments. That woman, upon seeing her, asked: "Sister, where did you get your robes and ornaments?" She replied: "Noble one, I sell liquor — it is from that that I obtained all of these." Sthūlanandā thought to herself: "This is quite a good method — let me see whether it would work for me or not." With that in mind, she kept that woman in view and followed her mindfully. A little further on, she saw another woman in a dirty garment, with no food, walking slowly and staggering on her feet. She asked her: "Girl, whose are you?" The woman replied: "I belong to no one. I work for whoever gives me food and clothing." Sthūlanandā then said to her: "In that case, girl, why don't you engage in selling liquor?" The woman replied: "Noble one, is it really right to engage in selling liquor as things stand? To begin with, one needs a great deal of capital. And even if there is a supply of grain, there are no large comfortable premises where vessels and drinkers may be at ease." Sthūlanandā said: "Girl, I will arrange all of that, and I will give you food and clothing as well — just give me everything you earn." The woman replied: "Noble one, very well, I shall do so." Sthūlanandā had a building erected near the winter quarters and gave her grain, vessels, and supplies. The woman set up a liquor business there, and the liquor turned out to be excellent, so that drinkers gathered there in great numbers. Seeing this, the other liquor sellers became jealous. Sthūlanandā's own gains increased.

Then at another time, liquor was needed at the royal palace, and when the king's men rounded up all the liquor sellers, the jealous ones among them said to the king's men: "There is a liquor seller of Sthūlanandā's near the winter quarters — take that liquor seller too." The men seized her and took her away. She began to cry out: "Noble Sthūlanandā, the king's men are taking me away!" Sthūlanandā rushed off at a quick pace and said to the children of the grain merchants: "Where are they taking this girl of mine?" They replied: "Noble one, is she not a liquor seller who tramples on and presses down those who are unfriendly to her, and sells liquor? Does the noble one also have enemies?" She said: "You yourselves are my great enemies — that is why you have taken my girl away," and she began to quarrel with them. Brahmins and householders who witnessed the quarrel asked: "What is all this?" When those people explained the matter in detail, they mocked and reviled them, saying: "The ascetics who are sons of the Śākyas are truly disgraced! That an ascetic, a shaveling, should be engaged in selling liquor — ascetics and brahmacharins are utterly disgraced!"

When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Sthūlanandā has brought great disgrace upon the ascetic life. Therefore, monks, nuns must not sell liquor. If one does so, there is an offense with expiation."

The setting of this rule is Śrāvastī.

Then the nun Sthūlanandā, in the early morning hour, dressed in her lower robe and outer robe, took up her alms bowl, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. While she was going on her alms round, she saw a prostitute wearing a particularly fine dress and lower garment, adorned with excellent ornaments. When the prostitute saw her, she asked: "Sister, where did you come by such clothes and ornaments?" The prostitute replied: "Noble one, I obtained these things by practicing prostitution." Sthūlanandā thought to herself: "That method seems good — but will it succeed or not? I shall look into it," and she went on her way, keeping that woman in mind with full awareness.

After some time, in another place, she saw a girl whose clothes were soiled, who could not even obtain food, and who walked with a slow and listless gait, yet who had a beautiful face. She asked: "Girl, whose daughter are you?" The girl replied: "Noble one, whoever gives me food and clothing, for that person I will also do work." Sthūlanandā said to her: "Then, girl, why not become a prostitute?" The girl covered her ears and said: "Noble one, please do not speak like that! Such disgraceful things as that have never been done by anyone in my family before." Sthūlanandā said: "If that is the nature of a woman's way of life, then the daughter of so-and-so the king has done just that — she became a prostitute — and so it went for her. The daughter of so-and-so the brahmin likewise. Even among the highest families, many have done such things. Though a woman's mind turns toward men, if I had not gone forth into renunciation, I too would have done something like that — but having gone forth, it is uncomfortable." Thus deceiving her, she said: "Noble one, does one practice prostitution like this? Noble one, if one is to practice prostitution in this way, one needs many supplies: a large house where many men can gather, and many fine clothes, ornaments, ointments, food, and drink." Sthūlanandā said: "Girl, if I provide all of that, and you give me all the earnings you receive, then I will supply you with food, clothing, and everything else." The girl replied: "Noble one, very well — I will give the earnings just as you say."

Sthūlanandā had a house built for her near the winter quarters, gave her everything as she had promised, then had her bathed and given fine clothes and ornaments. After several days had passed, the girl, young and beautiful in form, was made into the figure of a prostitute and installed there. Driven and tormented by affliction, men all gathered there. When another prostitute saw her, jealousy arose in her heart and she could not bear it. Sthūlanandā's earnings grew greatly.

Then, at a later time, there was a great festival at the royal palace. A large quantity of perfumes was needed, and the king's men, in order to apply perfumes, gathered all the prostitutes together. Out of their jealousy, those other prostitutes said to the king's men: "Near the winter quarters there is one who prostitutes herself for Sthūlanandā — bring her along as well." The men seized that girl and took her away. She wept and cried out: "Noble one, Sthūlanandā, I am being taken away by the king's men!" Sthūlanandā ran quickly and shouted: "Sons of that slave woman! Where are you taking my girl?" They replied: "What? Does the noble one also practice prostitution? You crush others underfoot, trampling them under the heel of your enemies! What — does the noble one also have enemies? Since you have taken my girl, you yourself are the greatest among my enemies!" While they were quarreling, brahmins and householders saw them and —

They asked her what had happened, and she told them everything in detail. Thereupon they mocked and reviled her with harsh words: "The śramaṇas (renunciants) of the Śākya's sons are thoroughly disgraced! Both śramaṇas and those of pure life are disgraced! Now even a śramaṇa who has shaved her head is practicing prostitution!" So they mocked her.

When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter: Sthūlanandā has done something unbefitting a śramaṇa. Therefore, with the intention that nuns should not be allowed to practice prostitution, he thought: Monks, since Sthūlanandā has done something greatly unbefitting a śramaṇa, it is fitting that brahmins and householders should mock, revile, and speak ill of her. Therefore nuns shall not be permitted to practice prostitution. If a nun permits prostitution, it shall become a grave offense. The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

Then one morning Sthūlanandā dressed in her lower robe and outer robe, took up her alms bowl, and went into Śrāvastī on alms round. As she went on her alms round, she saw a maidservant wearing fine clothes, a fine lower garment, and fine ornaments. Seeing her, Sthūlanandā asked: "Sister, where did you find such fine clothes and ornaments?" The maidservant replied: "Noble one, I practice prostitution privately in a certain place, and that is how I obtained these." Sthūlanandā thought: That is a good method. Let me see whether this might work. Keeping that thought in mind, she went on her way mindfully observing the matter. Before long she saw a girl wearing soiled clothes, without food, walking slowly and looking worn, and she asked her: "Girl, whose are you?" The girl replied: "I belong to no one in particular. I work for whoever gives me food and clothing." Sthūlanandā said: "Girl, if that is so, why not practice prostitution privately?" The girl covered her ears and said: "Noble one, do not say such a thing! No one in our family has ever done anything like this before — it is wholly improper!" Sthūlanandā then said: "My girl, this is the nature of women. Even a king's daughter does it; even the daughter of such-and-such a brahmin does it; many women of great families have done likewise. Women set their minds on men. As for me, I have gone forth into renunciation, so it would not be fitting for me to do it." With these words she deceived the girl, and then said: "Noble one, as for how to practice prostitution privately — many supplies are needed for that. First, clothes and ornaments are needed. After that, a tent and a large net, and a man to act as a pimp. When rowdies come, one needs companions to deal with them. And to attract many men and keep them pleased, liquor, perfume, and cosmetics are needed." Sthūlanandā replied: "Very well then, I will provide everything — clothes, food, and all the rest. You give me everything you earn." The girl said: "Good, I will give it all." Then Sthūlanandā had her bathed, gave her clothes, ornaments, and the requisites of one dwelling in a monastery, kept her and looked after her for a few days, then provided a tent, sent a pimp to go with her, and directed her to go to the monastery and take up prostitution privately. Before long she was caught and arrested, and was brought before Sthūlanandā. Then Sthūlanandā ran quickly and cried out: "Sons of that slave woman! Where are you dragging my girl?"

They said to her: "Noble lady, are you also privately engaged in prostitution?" And pressing her down with the heel of the enemy, they forced her to do it. She replied: "Noble ones, do you also have enemies? It is you yourselves who are my great enemies, for you have carried off my girl." Brahmins and householders who saw them fighting asked: "Hey, what is all this?" And they explained in detail what had happened. Those people mocked and reviled them harshly, saying: "The asceticism of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyan is utterly scorched. The conduct of ascetics and those of holy life is utterly scorched. Now this ascetic, this shaved-head woman, is privately engaged in prostitution!" — and so they jeered.

When the monks heard what had occurred, they reported it to the Blessed One, the Buddha.
