The Blessed One, seeing that the nun Sthūlanandā had done something greatly unfitting for an ascetic, and intending thereby that nuns should not engage in private prostitution, declared: "Monks, it is an established fact that the brahmins and householders mocked, reviled, and spoke harshly — for Sthūlanandā did what is unfit for a nun. Therefore, monks, do not allow a nun to engage in private prostitution. If a nun allows private prostitution to take place, it becomes a grave transgression."

The basis for the minor Vinaya. The forty-second fascicle.

The setting is in Rājagṛha. At the time when some acrobats were levying fines against the Six Groups in the midst of a large crowd, the Six Groups conferred with one another among themselves. One of them said: "When the acrobats levy a fine against us here in the midst of a crowd — if the Twelve Groups do not give that fellow, the son of Buzanmo, a bowl and robe, and if he is thereby unable to pay the fine against us — then the time has now come. Tell us, what is the plan?" Neyagawa said: "What else is there to do? Let us go and give him a thorough beating." Another also said: "Yes, let us do exactly that." Having thus decided, they went to him. They caught sight of Sthūlanandā. Among themselves they said: "This is the chief among them — let us beat this one." And they struck her with open palms, sticks, clods of earth, cudgels, and fists. When the beating was done, she smeared her body with sesame oil and lay reclining upon a latticed couch.

When the nuns saw her, they asked: "Noble lady, what wrong have you done, that you should be like this?" She replied: "I have been beaten." They asked: "By whom?" She answered: "By the noble Six Groups." The nuns said: "What did you do?" She replied: "Sisters, those people who are of the clan of Dharma's kinsmen — it is wrong to speak ill of them. As for teaching and instructing a younger sister, there is surely no harm in that." Then the nuns felt indignant: "How could monks beat nuns?" When the nuns had said this to the monks, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter: "That which constitutes the wrongful act of which one can be accused is monks striking nuns." Therefore, intending that male monks should not be permitted to beat nuns, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is an established fact that the nuns felt indignant at what the Six Groups of ascetics did. Therefore, monks, it is not permitted for a monk to strike a nun. If a monk strikes a nun, he incurs a transgression along with what has already passed."

The setting is in Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One declared to the nuns that they should wear a menstrual cloth. When one of them wore the menstrual cloth, blood dripped through it, soaked the lower robe, and formed drops, and bees swarmed about her in every direction. She stood there overcome with shame and dread. When matters had come to this pass, the nun reported it to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, nuns should wear a protective cloth." When the Blessed One declared to the nuns that they should wear a protective cloth, they did not know how such a protective cloth should be made. The Blessed One then declared: "Wear an inner lower wrap." When they began wearing the inner lower wrap, blood dripped down even through that. When things came to this pass as well, the nuns reported it to the monks, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "At regular intervals wash it and dye it. Nuns should at all times maintain mindfulness and sleep with mindfulness in place. If a nun sleeps without mindfulness in place, she incurs a transgression along with what has already passed."

The setting is in Śrāvastī. At that time, a monk called Gunā of the Mūla group passed away. The Twelve Groups performed offerings for him, burned the body, and then struck their own chests in grief. The nuns mocked them, saying: "How could nuns strike their chests like that?" When matters had come to this pass, the nuns reported it to the monks, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered the matter: "The Twelve Groups of nuns have acted improperly. Therefore, intending that nuns should not strike their chests, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the Twelve Groups of nuns mocking the nuns for acting improperly is an established fact. Therefore, nuns should not strike their chests. If nuns do strike their chests, they incur a transgression along with what has already passed."

The setting is in Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, if a nun has become known by a name, what should be done regarding her ordination in relation to monks?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, place her among the monks according to however many years have elapsed since she first became known by that name. She will be fully ordained and will have the standing of a male monk."

In brief:
A nun is placed among monks as one who has come from the nuns.
She is not to be placed in every circumstance without qualification.
Even through a messenger, likewise, full ordination is permitted —
so has the great sage allowed.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you declared that if a nun has become known by a name, she should be placed among the monks from the beginning, according to the number of years that have elapsed. Does this mean that if a monk has become known by a name, he too should be placed among the nuns from the beginning, according to the number of years elapsed?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, if a monk has become known by a name, he should indeed be placed among the nuns according to the number of years elapsed. But Venerable One, if either a monk or a nun has been so placed, and then becomes known by a name again from that placement, what should be done in that case?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, place them again as is appropriate."

The setting is in Śrāvastī. Then the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you declared that if either a monk or a nun has become known by a name twice, they should be placed wherever is appropriate.

"Venerable One, if from that placement a person becomes known by a name a third time, what should be done in that case?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, in no circumstances whatsoever is such a person to be placed. Upāli, if someone has become known by a name a third time, the property of the monk and the property of the nun are immediately, in every respect, to be treated as forfeited. Have no doubt about this."

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In one part of Śrāvastī there lived a householder named Datta. He was very wealthy, with abundant riches and great means of enjoyment, prosperous and vast in his holdings, possessing wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, heaped up like the treasures of Vaiśravaṇa. He had taken a wife from a family of equal standing, and together with her he lived in delight and enjoyment. In another part of Śrāvastī there lived a householder named Mṛgadhvaja. He too was wealthy, with abundant riches and great means of enjoyment, prosperous and vast in his holdings, possessing wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, heaped up like the treasures of Vaiśravaṇa. He too had taken a wife from a family of equal standing, and together with her he lived in delight and enjoyment.

Each of the two was rivalrous with the other in wealth. One would say, "Your means of livelihood fall short of mine." The other would say, "Your means of livelihood fall short of mine." Thus they spoke. The two, however, became friends with one another, and from time to time the one would send gifts, and the other would likewise send gifts in return, and in this way the two became mutually dear friends.

Then some time later it happened that many people living in Śrāvastī had some business to attend to. They all went together to the pleasure grove, assembled there, conducted the affairs of the city, and then departed. The householder Datta and the one named Mṛgadhvaja sat together there exchanging affectionate conversation with one another. The householder Datta said: "Dear friend and companion, even after we ourselves have passed on, let us find a way to keep the bond of friendship unbroken, continuing among our children, our grandchildren, our great-grandchildren, and our great-great-grandchildren. What means shall we use to accomplish this?" Mṛgadhvaja replied: "Friend, excellent! I too have had that very thought. Come, let us arrange the kinship before the birth. If a son is born to me and a daughter is born to you, then you shall give her to my son. And if a son is born to you and a daughter is born to me, then I shall give her to your son." The other replied: "Friend, excellent! Let it be just so." And having arranged the kinship between each other before any birth had occurred, they departed.

Then some time later the wife of the householder Datta became with child, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a daughter — a child of fine form and pleasing to behold, well endowed with limbs and features, yet one who cried constantly. Then monks came to the home of the householder Datta to teach the Dharma, and at that time she pricked up her ears and listened. On the twenty-first day, the seventh day of the third week, a great birth-feast was given with lavish celebration, and they set about naming her. They deliberated: "What name shall we give this girl?" The family members said: "This girl always desires the Dharma, pricking up her ears to listen to it, and she is the daughter of the householder Datta; therefore let the girl be named Dharmadattā." The girl Dharmadattā was entrusted to eight nurses: two to suckle her, two to nourish her, two to bathe and cleanse her, and two to play with her. Raised and nurtured by those eight nurses, on milk, yogurt, fresh butter, and clarified butter,

and other special provisions of excellent food that had been properly prepared, she grew quickly, like a lotus born from the mud of a pond.

Now the householder Datta heard that a daughter had been born to his friend, the householder Mṛgaśabda. Thinking, "Since my friend's daughter has been born, I shall send her garments and ornaments" — for he had it in mind that she might become his daughter-in-law — he sent her garments and ornaments, along with this message: "Dear friend, I have heard that a daughter has been born to you, and I rejoice greatly. I send these garments and ornaments for my dear friend's daughter; it is fitting that you accept them." Mṛgaśabda accepted them and sent back the reply: "Dear friend, what you have done is excellent, and kinship has now been made. Should a son be born to you, I shall give her to him." When the householder Mṛgaśabda heard that reply, with a son in mind as his wish, he devoted himself fully to sporting pleasure with his wife. From that sporting pleasure, after some time his wife conceived a being in the womb, and when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a son. After his birth, a grand birth-feast was held for him with lavish celebration for twenty-one days, through three weeks of seven days each, and they deliberated: "What name shall we give this boy?" His family members said: "This boy was born under the lunar mansion Viśākhā, and so let his name be Viśākha." And so his name was set as Viśākha.

The boy Viśākha too was entrusted to eight nurses: two to suckle him, two to nourish him, two to bathe and cleanse him, and two to play with him. Raised and nurtured by those eight nurses on milk, yogurt, fresh butter, and clarified butter, and other special provisions of excellent food that had been properly prepared, he grew quickly, like a lotus born from the mud of a pond.

When the householder Datta heard that a son had been born to the householder Mṛgaśabda, he thought: "A son has been born to my dear friend. Before this slips away, he should become my son-in-law. I shall send him garments and ornaments." And so he sent him garments and ornaments along with this message: "Dear friend, I have heard that a son has been born to you, and I rejoice greatly. I send these garments and ornaments for my dear friend's son; it is fitting that you accept them." Mṛgaśabda accepted them and sent back the reply: "Dear friend, raise a daughter, and once she is born I will take her." Datta said: "It would be good to give a daughter. Let it be so." When the daughter Dharmadattā was born, she wished to go forth into homelessness, and she bowed at her father's feet and said: "Father, I request that you allow me to go forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma, the Vinaya." He replied: "Daughter, you were previously given to Mṛgaśabda's son Viśākha; he is your husband. It is no longer appropriate to grant this." And so he did not grant it.

At that household there came from time to time a fully ordained nun named Utpalavārṇā, who taught the Dharma to the assembled family. Dharmadattā said to her: "Noble one, I wish to go forth, to take full ordination, and to attain the state of a fully ordained nun in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, but my father does not permit it and keeps me back, and he will not let me go forth. Could you yourself bring about my going forth right here?" The nun replied: "Daughter, it is good that you have aroused such a mind. Sensual pleasures offer little happiness yet bring great suffering and many faults; to go forth is wholesome. The Blessed One, when a wise person sees five faults, declared that it is not fitting to resort to the five sensual pleasures. What are the five? When a wise person rightly sees that sensual pleasures offer little happiness yet bring great suffering and many faults, it is not fitting to resort to them.

When a wise person rightly sees that resorting to sensual pleasures causes the proliferation of binding tendencies (saṃskāras), it is not fitting to resort to sensual pleasures. When a wise person rightly sees that resorting to sensual pleasures brings no satisfaction whatsoever, no contentment, no sense of enough, it is not fitting to resort to sensual pleasures. When a wise person rightly sees that resorting to sensual pleasures leaves no evil deed undone, it is not fitting to resort to sensual pleasures. When a wise person sees that sensual pleasures are, by every account of this kind, what the buddhas, the śrāvakas of the buddhas, the learned, the rightly faring, and the holy persons have abandoned, it is not fitting to resort to sensual pleasures.

And when a wise person sees five virtues, it is fitting to have faith in going forth. What are the five? When a wise person sees that one will thereby attain a purpose unmixed with defilement, it is fitting to have faith in going forth. When a wise person sees that those who were once one's servants, one's commissioned agents, one's messengers, one's workers, and those who did whatever one pleased will in turn come to venerate and praise one, it is fitting to have faith in going forth. When a wise person sees that one will thereby attain the unsurpassed bliss of yogic practice and nirvāṇa, it is fitting for one to have faith in going forth. Even if one does not yet succeed in attaining the unsurpassed bliss of yogic practice and the passing beyond sorrow, when a wise person sees that one will be reborn among the gods, it is fitting to have faith in going forth. When a wise person sees that the virtues of the gone-forth life are praised by the buddhas, the śrāvakas of the buddhas, the learned, the rightly faring, and the holy persons, it is fitting to have faith in going forth.

"It is excellent that you have aroused such a mind. Go now and present your request to the Blessed One."

Thereupon the nun Utpalavarṇā went to where the Blessed One was. On arriving, she bowed her head to the Blessed One's feet, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the nun Utpalavarṇā addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable One, a girl named Dharmadinnā, daughter of the householder Datta, wishes to go forth into renunciation and receive full ordination in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, and to attain the full status of a nun. Yet the householder Mṛgasvara's son Sāga holds her under his authority and has not given his consent; he constantly guards her and will not allow her to go forth to freedom. I beg the Venerable One's permission."

The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell the nuns as follows: 'The daughter of the householder Datta, named Dharmadinnā, may be sent for by the nun Utpalavarṇā in that very house. Let her be given the three refuges and the five bases of training, and in that very place I grant permission for her to go forth into renunciation.'"

"Venerable One, so shall it be done," Ānanda replied. The venerable Ānanda then, having heard from the Blessed One, transmitted the instruction to the nuns. The community of nuns instructed the nun Utpalavarṇā and sent her as their messenger. She went there and told the girl that the Blessed One had also given his permission. The community of nuns then gave her the three refuges and the five bases of training for a laywoman. "You have now gone forth; the ten bases of training are also given to you. In regard to these and these particular bases of training, take them up and restrain yourself in accordance with how they are to be trained."

At this, she was filled with great joy. And as she was filled with great joy —

The nun Utpalavarṇā then preached the Dharma in such a way that the girl would perfectly realize the Four Noble Truths. The moment Dharmadattā heard this teaching, the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of a transitory collection were struck down by the vajra-like wisdom, and she actualized the fruit of stream-entry.

The nun Utpalavarṇā then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Go, venerable Ānanda, and convey this message to the community of nuns: let Dharmadattā remain there in that very place, and let Utpalavarṇā be sent as the messenger to give her, for two years, the training in the six rules and the six rules to be followed."

Venerable Ānanda replied, "So be it, Blessed One," and having heard the instruction from the Blessed One, he conveyed it to the community of nuns. The community of nuns then instructed the nun Utpalavarṇā and sent her as their messenger. She went there, and the community of nuns gave the girl the vow of training in the six rules and the six rules to be followed for two years, saying: "You have now become a probationary nun. You must do this and this. Restrain yourself in accordance with how each basis of training is to be trained."

Then, having heard such a Dharma teaching, Dharmadattā actualized the fruit of once-return.

And so it was that as Dharmadattā trained in the six rules and the six rules to be followed for those two years, she became youthful in form. She was fair and beautiful in appearance, and all the people of the household delighted in her and looked upon her with favor.

The householder Mṛgadhvaja then heard that the girl Dharmadattā had become youthful. He sent word to his friend, the householder Datta, saying: "Your son has become youthful, and the girl too has become youthful. Examine what day would be auspicious and take her as your son's wife." His friend replied in a message: "Very well, let it be so." The householder Datta assembled astrologers and had them determine what day would be auspicious for sending the girl as a bride. They calculated a favorable time and indicated the wedding day. Likewise, the householder Mṛgadhvaja also indicated the day for receiving the bride.

The householder Datta then sent word to his friends, brothers, and relatives: "At such and such a time, the girl Dharmadattā is to be sent as a bride. Come, brothers and relatives and kinsmen, to accompany her and give your support." The householder Mṛgadhvaja likewise sent the same message to his own friends, brothers, and relatives. The households of both families were filled, as their friends, brothers, relatives, and many attendants arrived and gathered in great numbers at Śrāvastī.

Word also spread that the queens, princes, ministers, many people, and the people of the provinces of Prasenajit, king of the land of Kosala, were giving the daughter of the householder Datta to Mṛgadhvaja to be his bride, and that friends, brothers, relatives, and many people were gathering there from their respective quarters. The king told his ministers: "You too, attend to the affairs of these two families." And those ministers sent messages to the local governors and those of royal lineage in each district, saying: "Bring together whatever provisions you have in your region; I myself will bring and assemble them. Let everyone gather here." As soon as they heard this, each one assembled their wealth and came to Śrāvastī. Hundreds upon thousands of sentient beings thus gathered there. The ministers then prepared the gardens, the nearby groves, and the parklands of Śrāvastī, and —

All the surroundings of that place were swept clean of the outside. Stones, weeds, and lumps of earth were cleared away and removed. The ground was sprinkled with sandal-scented water in even, measured strokes. Bowls of fragrant incense were purified and set to left and right. Banners and victory standards were raised, and silk streamers were hung out. Flowers of every variety were scattered about. The whole place was made to resemble the joyous groves and pleasure gardens of the delightful gods.

Then Dharmadattā, seeing that the preparations were being made, said to the household servants: "What is this festival that is happening out of season?" They replied: "By the power of your previously accumulated store of virtue, a great festival has been convened outside its proper time — it has been convened out of season in order to send you off as a bride. All these guests have come for that purpose." When she heard this, she was frightened and prostrated at her father's feet, saying: "Father, I ask a boon of you. Mother, may I go to the nunnery known as the Royal Garden, which serves as the rains retreat quarters for the nuns? Please allow it." He replied: "Daughter, before you were born, I gave you in betrothal to the householder's son Mṛgadhvaja of Sāgala. I no longer have authority in this matter. He is your husband. Moreover, King Prasenajit of the land of Kośala is here, along with his queen consort, young attendants, male servants, female servants, and many people, as well as many people who have come from various regions. If all this were known, how could I now grant you what you ask? Would I really want my beloved friends, brothers, and kinsmen to be imprisoned and put to death? You must go tomorrow as a bride. My dear ones, my people, my relatives, and many folk are assembled here — do not speak of this. You are very young and do not understand. Abandon the practice of the holy life." So he instructed her.

She, however, strove diligently and entered into the cultivation of the path, turning the mind toward the way, but she could not find the means to free herself from desire. Yet throughout all this, there was not even the slightest thing unknown, unseen, unrecognized, or unperceived by the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, endowed with great compassion, dwell for the benefit of the world. They are the single protector, the sole hero. They teach what is non-dual and beyond duality. They abide in calm abiding and special insight. They are skilled in the three objects of discipline and have crossed the four rivers. The soles of their feet are perfectly and permanently established in the four bases of miraculous power. They are unshaken by the four fearlessnesses. They have abandoned the five limbs. They have truly passed beyond the five births. They possess the six limbs. They have fully perfected the six perfections. They constantly engage in the six modes of conduct. They are adorned with the flowers of the seven branches of awakening. They hold the noble eightfold path. They are skilled in entering meditative absorption through the nine successive stages. They are endowed with the strength of the ten powers. Their renown resounds and spreads throughout the ten directions. They have attained supremacy over the thousand-fold realm. Three times by night and three times by day, with the eye of a buddha, they survey the world and engage their vision of primordial wisdom, looking to see: who is declining, who is increasing; who has come to suffer, who is in distress, who has been harmed; who is in difficulty, distress, and pain; who is tending toward the lower realms; who is falling into the lower realms; who has already fully fallen into the lower realms — and who among them they shall draw out of the lower realms and firmly establish in higher states and in liberation; whose roots of virtue have not yet arisen they shall cause to arise; those whose roots of virtue have arisen they shall bring to full maturation; and those who have matured they shall cause to be fully liberated. With this vision they looked.

And then it was spoken in verse:

That ocean, the dwelling of sea-monsters —

Though they may slip past their appointed time,
for those disciples who are yet to be trained,
a buddha does not pass beyond at the wrong moment.

Then the Blessed One smiled, and such being the nature of reality, whenever a blessed buddha smiles, rays of light in colors of blue, yellow, red, and white stream forth from his mouth. Some of these rays descend downward, and some ascend upward.

Those that descend enter the hells — the Hell of Revival, the Black Line Hell, the Hell of Crushing, the Hell of Crying, the Hell of Great Crying, the Hot Hell, the Very Hot Hell, the Hell of Ultimate Torment, the Blistering Hell, the Bursting-Blister Hell, the Ah-ha-ha Hell, the Ha-ha Hell, the Hu-hu Hell, the Blue-Lotus Hell, the Lotus Hell, and the Great-Lotus Hell — and when they descend into whichever hot hell it may be, that place becomes cool; and when they descend into whichever cold hell it may be, that place becomes warm. Through this, the particular suffering of those sentient beings is relieved and turned to ease, and those beings think to themselves: "Oh — have we died and passed away from here? Or have we been reborn somewhere else?" To arouse faith in them, an emanation of the Blessed One is sent to that place. When they behold the emanation, they think: "We have not died or been reborn elsewhere — yet through the power of this being, whom we have never before seen, our particular suffering has been turned to ease." From this direct and heartfelt faith in the emanation, those beings exhaust the karma of their suffering in the hells, and they then take rebirth, as gods or humans, wherever they are fit vessels for the noble ones' truths.

As for the rays that ascend upward, they proceed to the assemblies of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, and then to the gods of the Brahmā realms — the Brahma Retinue, the Brahma Ministers, the Great Brahma — and on to the gods of Lesser Light, Limitless Light, Radiant Light, the gods of Lesser Virtue, Limitless Virtue, Abundant Virtue, the Cloudless gods, the gods of Merit-Born, the Great-Result gods, the gods who are not too exalted, the gods without affliction, the gods of Clear Vision, the gods of Beautiful Sight, and the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Going to all these, the rays proclaim the words: "Impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness" — and also recite these two verses:

Seek out the occasion for arising;
apply yourselves with diligence to the Buddha's teaching.
Crush the armies of the lord of death
as a herd of yaks crushes a grass hut.
Whoever practices with heedfulness
in this Dharma and its discipline
will empty out the round of birth
and make an end of suffering.

Then those rays of light circle the great trichiliocosm, the realm of the three thousandfold worlds, and return to trail along behind the robe of the Blessed One.

Now, if the Blessed One intends to prophesy about the past, the light does not appear at the back of his robe. If he intends to prophesy about the future, it does not appear at the front. If he intends to prophesy a birth in hell, it does not appear at the soles of his feet. If he intends to prophesy a birth as an animal, it does not appear at the heels of his feet. If he intends to prophesy a birth as a hungry ghost, it does not appear at the toes of his feet. If he intends to prophesy a birth as a human, it does not appear at the knees. If he intends to prophesy birth as a wheel-turning king who rules by the power of force, it does not appear at the palm of the left hand. If he intends to prophesy birth as a wheel-turning king who rules by the Dharma-wheel, it does not appear at the palm of the right hand. If he intends to prophesy a birth as a god, it does not appear at the navel.

If he intends to prophesy awakening as a śrāvaka, it does not appear within his mouth. If he intends to prophesy awakening as a pratyekabuddha, it does not appear at his ūrṇā hair. If he intends to prophesy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, it does not appear within his uṣṇīṣa.

Then those rays of light circled the Blessed One three times and disappeared into his mouth. Thereupon the venerable Ānanda joined his palms together and addressed the Blessed One in verse:

Adorned with a thousand colors of varied hues,
many rays stream forth from within his mouth,
illuminating all directions as they blaze —
just as the rising sun lights up the world.

Then he spoke further in verse:

Without agitation, without displeasure, with pride cast away,
the buddha has become the supreme cause for beings.
Without cause, the roots of the white conch and the lotus —
the Protector, steadfast as the ocean and the mountains.
Without cause, the Victor who has vanquished the foe does not smile,
does not show a smile.
Now I myself have understood, and with an mind of discernment
I wish to hear from the king of victors.
O Sage, best of the herd, by your firm and excellent words,
please dispel the supreme doubt that has arisen.
For what reason did the Steadfast One show a smile?
These many beings here wish to hear.

The Blessed One declared: "It is so, Ānanda. Without cause and without condition, Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not smile.

Ānanda, you sent the girl Dharmadinnā away without transmitting the blue-lotus color, and by my word she was released from the community of nuns. Beginning with the three refuges she was ordained in stages, and for two years she was also given the vow of training in the six rules and the six rules that follow them. Tomorrow she will be sent away, and for that reason — do you see the multitude assembled there?" "Venerable one, I see them." "Ānanda, that girl has no occasion and no place to remain as a laywoman in a household, no place to fully indulge in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures for the sake of pleasure — she will not remain in such a state. Rather, she will now attain the fruit of non-return and will actualize arhatship.

Ānanda, go and instruct the nuns thus: Dharmadinnā has trained for two years in the six rules and the six rules that follow them; now release her, the one of blue-lotus color who has not been transmitted, and grant her the vow that generates pure conduct." "Venerable one, I shall do so."

The venerable Ānanda received this from the Blessed One, instructed the nuns accordingly, and the community of nuns sent off the one of blue-lotus color who had not been transmitted with the instruction: "Go, girl. The community of nuns grants you the vow that generates pure conduct; now you are to receive full ordination."

As soon as she heard this Dharma teaching of that kind, she immediately actualized the fruit of non-return and accomplished miraculous power. Utpalavarṇā then went and addressed the Blessed One. The Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and instruct the nuns thus: I have given leave; let the two assemblies of the Saṅgha release Utpalavarṇā who had not been transmitted, and fully ordain the girl Dharmadinnā." "Venerable one, it shall be done so." The venerable Ānanda received this from the Blessed One and gave the instruction to the nuns.

The assembly of nuns, having convened both assemblies of the Saṅgha together, fully ordained Dharmadinnā by messenger while she remained in that very house, through the agency of Utpalavarṇā. Utpalavarṇā then went to her and declared: "You have been given leave by the Blessed One and fully ordained by both assemblies of the Saṅgha." This Dharma teaching was also spoken to her, and upon hearing it, the nun Dharmadinnā came to know the turning and the non-turning of the five spokes of the wheel of cyclic existence. She fully broke through by means of the dharmatā — the nature of reality — in which all conditioned things disintegrate, all transgressions scatter and are destroyed, and all mental afflictions are abandoned. She actualized arhathood and became an arhat: freed from attachment to the three realms, equal in her regard for gold and clods of earth, her mind like open sky to which a palm cannot adhere, equally at ease with a thorn and with sandalwood. By her direct knowledge she broke the door-panel of the charnel ground. She attained the higher knowledges, the superknowledges, and the discriminating awarenesses; she turned her back on any desire for further existence and on all honors; and she became an object of offering, of reverence, and of words of praise from lords of the senses, their attendants, and the gods. An arhat nun with all defilements exhausted has no place remaining as a householder dwelling in a house; it is no place for her to enjoy the pleasures of desire for the sake of delight.

When Dharmadinnā actualized arhathood, she said at that very moment to her parents: "Father and mother, I have actualized arhathood. Please give me leave to go to the nuns' rains-retreat house in the king's pleasure garden." The householder Datta consulted with his wife, and the two of them spoke together, saying: "If it is like this with our daughter, surely the king would not reproach us. Let us proceed in due order, and let her go together with the Blessed One." She replied: "Excellent! I shall do so." Thereupon the householder Datta invited the Blessed One, the Buddha, together with the assembly of monks to his house. He sent word: "My dear friend, the householder Mṛgāradatta's daughter Dharmadinnā cannot remain in the house — she will certainly go forth — so come here, and do press her firmly to accept it." The householder Mṛgāradatta, for his part, went to report to Prasenajit, king of Kosala, and then set about gathering friends, brothers, relatives, and many people.

The householder Datta, that same evening, prepared pure and wholesome food and provisions. Rising early in the morning, he spread out seats, filled water vessels and set them in place. Having invited the Blessed One, he sent word: "Venerable one, come for the meal — but even by the time of the midday shadow, if it should fall, may the Blessed One please consider that the time has come." Then the Blessed One, in the forenoon, put on his lower robe and took up his bowl and outer robe, and surrounded by many monks, with the assembly of monks going before him, he proceeded to the dwelling of the householder Datta. Upon arriving there, he took the seat that had been spread out before the assembly of monks and sat down.

Then the householder Datta, surrounded by friends, siblings, and relatives, and knowing that the Buddha and the assembly of monks were seated comfortably, served and properly presented pure and wholesome food and provisions with his own hands until all were satisfied.

At that time the householder Mṛgāradatta, together with friends, siblings, relatives, young people, ministers, townspeople, and many people of the realm, celebrated the protection of the auspicious planetary conjunction, performed auspiciousness and peace ceremonies, and set out to claim the bride — and they took up their station right at the very gate of the householder Datta's house.

The householder Datta then served the Buddha and the community of monks with his own hands, giving them the rinse water and satisfying all. Having properly attended to them, he discerned that the Blessed One had finished eating and withdrawn his alms bowl, and placing a low seat, he settled down together with his friends, siblings, and relatives before the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One properly instructed, exhorted, gladdened, and rejoiced the householder Datta together with his friends, siblings, and relatives through a Dharma discourse. Having properly instructed, gladdened, and rejoiced them with the Dharma discourse in its many categories, he rose from his seat and departed.

The nun Dharmadattā, for her part, had attained the antidote to all three realms and attained fearlessness.

When the time for fetching the bride had arrived, the householder Mṛgāradatta, his son Puṣya, together with friends, siblings, relatives, young people, ministers, townspeople, and many people of the realm, offered various kinds of music there.

Dharmadattā, wishing to follow the Blessed One, and just then the householder Mṛgāradatta's son Puṣya suddenly extending his arm reached out to seize Dharmadattā by the hand — whereupon Dharmadattā, in full sight of countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, spread her wings like the king of geese and soared into the sky, displaying miracles of many kinds.

Then the householder Mṛgāradatta's friends, siblings, and relatives, young people, ministers, townspeople, many people of the realm, the householder Mṛgāradatta's son Puṣya, and all the other sentient beings who had gathered to watch were overcome with great amazement. Falling at her feet as if cut down from the root of a tree, they said: "If this sister has attained such abundant qualities, this is no time and no place for you to indulge in desire — we beg your forbearance."

Then Dharmadattā descended from the sky and sat down before the great multitude. She taught the Dharma in such a manner that the hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who heard it realized it with exceptional clarity. Some of them actualized the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, and some — having gone forth into renunciation under the Blessed One's teaching and abandoned all afflictions — actualized arhathood. Some aroused the awakening mind aimed at the awakening of a hearer, some at the awakening of a solitary buddha, and some at the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Of that entire assembly, the great majority were directed toward the Buddha, drawn toward the Dharma, and settled with firm faith in the Saṅgha.

Then the nun Dharmadattā, having obtained what she had obtained and found abundance, having accomplished this great benefit for sentient beings, went to where the Blessed One was. She prostrated with her head at the feet of the Blessed One and then departed from the Blessed One's presence.

The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Among my fully ordained nun-disciples, śrāvikā-nuns who are masters of Dharma discourse, this nun Dharmadattā is supreme."

The monks, having generated a doubt and wishing to have all doubts cut through, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, what did the nun Dharmadattā do that, while still living in a household, she went forth through her own power, received full ordination, attained the status of a nun, and right then and there actualized arhathood?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the merit that the nun Dharmadattā created and accumulated through her actions, and the conditions that supplied it, stand close at hand like a river — it is beyond doubt. What Dharmadattā created and accumulated through her actions cannot be experienced by another.

Monks, karma that has been created and accumulated does not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element. Rather, it is in these very appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases that virtuous and non-virtuous actions ripen into their results.

Actions are never lost,
Even across a hundred aeons.
When the time arrives and conditions meet,
Their fruit ripens for those who bear a body.

Monks, long ago, in this very fortunate aeon, when the life span of beings was twenty thousand years, a teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world — a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide and charioteer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, an awakened and blessed one — and he dwelt in the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park of the Hermitage of the Seers.

At that time there lived in Vārāṇasī another householder who had taken a wife of equal birth, and together the two of them lived in delight and enjoyment. While they thus enjoyed their delight, after some time his wife became pregnant. Eight or nine months passed, and a daughter was born to them. For twenty-one days — three sets of seven — a great birth celebration was held with great festivity, and a name fitting her lineage was given to her.

When she had grown up and her body was mature, she wished to go forth into renunciation, but her parents would not grant her permission to go forth. There was another, elderly nun who taught Dharma to that household and who came to that home from time to time. The young woman said to this elderly nun: "Noble one, I wish to go forth and receive full ordination in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya and attain the state of a fully ordained nun. But my parents do not permit it and will not let me leave the household. Is it possible for me to go forth right here in this very place?"

The elderly nun told the girl to request this of the Blessed One, and said it could be done. She then requested the perfectly and fully awakened Blessed One Kāśyapa, who sent a messenger. And so, while the girl remained in her home, she was caused to go forth, the vows of a fully ordained nun were conferred upon her, and full ordination was given by the dual assembly of the Saṅgha. The elderly nun then taught her the Dharma, and while still living in the household she actualized arhathood directly.

Then the elderly nun thought: "Everything that happened — this girl's going forth by means of a messenger while still in her home, her receiving the training vows and full ordination, her actualization of arhathood while still in the household — all of this came about through me. Through the roots of virtue from living the holy life during the time of the perfectly and fully awakened Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly and fully awakened Blessed One Kāśyapa gave this prophecy to the young brahmin student Guru: 'Brahmin's son, when the life span of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha named Śākyamuni.'

In the light of that teaching, it was I who, while still in a household, caused the going forth by messenger, and obtained the training vows and full ordination —

and obtained the status of a fully ordained nun, and while remaining in a household, she actualized the state of an arhat. Just as my own preceptress was praised as foremost among those who speak on the Dharma by the Blessed One, the perfectly and fully awakened Tathāgata Kāśyapa, so too may I be praised as foremost among those who speak on the Dharma by Śākyamuni, the Blessed One, the Śākya King." Thus she spoke.

"What do you think, monks? That elderly nun is none other than the nun Dharmadinnā here today. In a single lifetime she lived the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One, the perfectly and fully awakened Kāśyapa, and through the power of her aspiration she went forth from the household while still living there, by means of a messenger; she received the training vows and full ordination; she obtained the status of a fully ordained nun; while remaining in the household she abandoned all afflictions and actualized the state of an arhat; and the Tathāgata praised her as foremost among those who speak on the Dharma.

"Therefore, monks, karma that is wholly dark ripens in a wholly dark way. Karma that is wholly bright ripens in a wholly bright way. Karma that is mixed ripens in a mixed way. Therefore, monks, abandon karma that is wholly dark and mixed, and accomplish only karma that is wholly bright. Monks, train yourselves accordingly."

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, those monks, rejoicing in what the Blessed One had taught, were greatly pleased.

The Supplementary Rules of the Vinaya, the forty-third bundle. In brief:

A monk outside need not be asked for patience.
One who scrapes alone does not scrape.
A summer dwelling is not to be assigned to a secular person.
The body of a respectful son is not to be washed.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain nun was receiving reading instruction from a monk. Then on a later occasion she committed a fault, and he rebuked her for it. She went to the summer dwelling and sat there weeping. Her preceptress saw her and said, "Young one, what fault have you committed that you sit here weeping?" The nun replied, "I do not know what to do when my teacher and preceptress rebuke me." The preceptress said, "My child, what else is there to be done? The teacher and preceptress do so only to maintain the teaching. Go and ask for forbearance." She agreed and said, "Very well, I shall go and ask for forbearance," and she went to the Jeta Grove, but the monk was not to be seen. She searched for him, and after some time found him walking about in the walkway outside the shrine hall. She prostrated at his feet, and the monk went away disrespectfully. Some novices who saw this, impelled by their own afflictions, taunted her, saying, "Noble one, we know you intend to ask for his forbearance — if he will not accept it, come here, and we will accomplish your purpose for you." She, out of shame, went away without saying a word.

The monks, having heard what had happened, reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: when the one who has given rise to an offense is rebuked by a nun and she then goes to ask forbearance, the monk leaves without showing proper respect, and the novices, for their part, conceive unwholesome thoughts about the matter from the outside. Therefore the Blessed One, understanding and knowing that a nun should not ask a monk for forbearance outside the shrine hall, and that the monk should not go away showing disrespect toward the nun, declared: "Monks, the novices will conceive unwholesome thoughts about the matter from the outside. Therefore a nun shall not ask an angry monk for forbearance outside the shrine hall."

Even so, if a nun has asked a monk for forbearance and he has shown disrespect, she should not leave. A nun may ask a monk for forbearance outside the shrine hall. But if a monk shows disrespect toward a nun who is asking him for forbearance and then departs, both of them will have incurred a transgression.

The occasion for the next rule arose in Śrāvastī. Some monks had their hair cut by a barber, and afterward, when that barber became a youth, he was not applying mindfulness. He saw some of them and became attached. When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the mind is excitable; when mindfulness is not applied, one will be led astray. Women in general have very strong desire. Therefore, nuns shall not have their hair cut alone in the presence of a barber. Instead, let another nun be stationed with her. And if that barber becomes attached, the nun who is seated nearby should speak thus: 'Good friend, the body of this nun is a mechanism of bones; it is without adornment and the body is impure. She has gone forth — abandon such thoughts as these. How unfortunate it would be to fall into the hells!' And if the barber still becomes attached, speak to him again in these words: 'Sister, you have abandoned household work. Reflect on what you undertook before the Saṅgha of both orders at the time of your full ordination. The Blessed One has declared that sensual desire offers little pleasure but much suffering and is rife with faults for the objects it fixates upon. Abandon improper mental engagement and remain close in spirit to the going-forth.' If she speaks to him in that way, well and good. If she does not speak, then the nun who is seated nearby will have incurred a transgression."

The occasion for the next rule also arose in Śrāvastī. The nun Sthūlanandā converted another householder to faith and had him build a rain-season dwelling, and a large number of nuns came to stay there. Around that time, approximately five hundred merchants carrying goods arrived in Śrāvastī from the south. Those merchants looked throughout Śrāvastī for a house to store their goods but could not find one. They searched everywhere in the city and still found nothing. At the time of the market, they gathered and set out their goods at a crossroads of the bazaar and at the roadside. Then thunder rumbled, the sun was drawing near to setting, and a light rain fell. They were standing there agitated, supporting themselves by leaning on their arms against their sides. Sthūlanandā saw them and said: "Good friends, rain is falling — why are you standing at the roadside? Why not store your goods somewhere? What harm could there be?" They replied: "Noble one, we searched throughout all of Śrāvastī, but the people of the world are unfriendly and we could not find a house to rent — what are we to do?" She then said: "Boys, go seek a house for the night, find out what kind of conditions you need, and offer extra payment." And she added: "As for this market situation, it will not do, and if the rain soaks everything, who will buy?" They replied: "Noble one, these people here are unfriendly — we offered them double rent for their houses and still no one gave us even one." "That is my own doing," she said. "Whatever it may be, one night and then we move on." Then she said to them: "Boys, pay extra rent for the house and take shelter inside my rain-season dwelling." They replied: "Noble one, excellent — so be it." Thereupon Sthūlanandā drove the nuns out of the rain-season dwelling that evening and rented it out to those merchants. The nuns, with their Dharma robes soaking wet from the rain, went off to another rain-season dwelling.

The nuns of that place asked them: "Noble ones, why have you come here in the evening with your Dharma robes soaking wet?" And they explained it in full detail. The nuns of Doṇamatī rebuked and scolded her harshly: "How could it be fitting for a nun to rent out a house that a donor had built as her rain-season dwelling?" When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, it is indeed a case for rebuking nuns. Therefore, nuns must not rent out their rain-season dwellings. If a nun rents out her rain-season dwelling, she incurs a transgression."

The setting for the next matter is also in Śrāvastī. The nun Sthūlanandā entered the bathing place where some young boys were washing themselves, and dragged them and bathed them with a scrubbing cloth. Those boys became attached to her and kept looking at her, saying among themselves: "Look there — that female ascetic, with her shaved head, is like a great warrior wearing armor, yet she has been wiping and scrubbing her body outside." They ridiculed her, and because of their ridicule, those boys burst out laughing. When the monks heard what had happened, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, considering the matter and knowing that those young boys' behavior was a case for ridicule and that they had acted improperly, declared: "Monks, Sthūlanandā is unattractive and has acted badly, making herself an object of ridicule for those young boys. Therefore, nuns must not wipe their bodies with a scrubbing cloth. If nuns wipe their bodies with a scrubbing cloth, they incur a transgression."

In brief:
One must not wipe the body with a scrubbing cloth,
nor likewise with flat stones.
Nor with a cloth binding, nor with a fist —
by nothing whatsoever may one wipe.

The Blessed One, the awakened one, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One had declared that nuns must not wipe their bodies with a scrubbing cloth. When they wiped with a flat stone, that too became a basis for transgression. The Blessed One declared they must not wipe with a flat stone. When they wiped with a cloth binding, that also became a basis for transgression, and the Blessed One declared they must not wipe with a cloth binding. When they wiped with a fist, that too became a basis for transgression, and the Blessed One declared they must not wipe with a fist. When they wiped with whatever else they could find, that too became a basis for transgression. The Blessed One then declared: "Except with a single hand alone, by no means whatsoever may one wipe. If one does wipe in this way, one incurs a transgression."

Here ends the seventh chapter of the Vinaya on minor matters.

The summary verse:
Honor due to a nun — diminishing it,
giving instructions, and an iron vessel,
looking by two women,
and likewise the dark Udika.

In brief:
Without respect, and not universal,
except for the displaying of the body.
Not giving from what is snatched away;
from the restoration ceremony and from the training.

The Blessed One, the awakened one, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the garden of the Jeta Grove. At the time when the venerable Grelaskyé passed away, a group of twelve nuns gathered his bones together, and with great veneration they built a stūpa in a wide and spacious place. They adorned it with parasols, victory banners, and pennants, decorated it with fragrances and flowers, and appointed two eloquent nuns there, so that each day they would offer earth, water, incense, and flowers.

Then, for the monks who came from other regions, they washed their hands and provided them with flowers and incense, leading them in venerating the stūpa with the singing of verses. After some time had passed, the venerable Chutung, together with a retinue of five hundred, was travelling through that region and came to Śrāvastī. Arhats do not look with their wisdom-vision without first directing their attention, so it was only at a distance that he saw the stūpa, and he thought: "This is a stūpa built on a site containing the hair and nails of the Blessed One — let us go and pay our respects." When they arrived there, the two nuns provided them with the ground and water used for washing their hands and feet. They were then given flowers and incense, and they venerated the stūpa with the singing of verses. When he and the retinue of five hundred had paid their respects, they departed.

Not far from the stūpa, the venerable Utpalavarnā was sitting at the base of an utpala-colored tree, having settled there to pass the day. She saw them and said: "Venerable Chutung — whose stūpa have you just venerated? Please consider this." He reflected to himself: "Why is the venerable Utpalavarnā saying 'Venerable Chutung, whose stūpa have you just venerated? Please consider this'?" And so he replied: "Let me consider it for a moment." When he turned his attention inward, he saw that it was the stūpa built from the bones of the monk Grelaskyé. Immediately his mind-stream was overwhelmed by habitual tendencies rooted in aversion, and he turned back. He said to the venerable Utpalavarnā: "If a thorn has appeared in the Teaching, then while you are sitting right here you have let it go unaddressed" — and with that he said nothing more.

He then said to his own students and attendants: "Venerable ones, those who are devoted to the Teacher and who cause grief — for that reason take a thorn from this heap of bones and bone-splinters, one each, and scatter them about." As his retinue was large, they took one thorn each from the heap of bones and bone-splinters, cast them aside, and in an instant the stūpa was demolished.

The two nuns wept and, weeping as they walked, went to the nuns' summer residence and told the other nuns what had happened. The group of twelve nuns, along with others who were attached and devoted to him out of desire that had not yet been relinquished, heard this and wept and wailed, crying out as if their own brother had just died that very day. Then the senior nun Bhomgamo spoke: "Sisters, who was it that did this?" They replied: "It happened suddenly, and we do not know from the heart, but the noble Utpalavarnā was sitting in that direction — she was the one who spoke to them, and that is the truth." Bhomgamo said: "Sisters, she went forth from being a weaver, and she is herself of degenerate character — as for what she has done, I know only what I have been told. The Blessed One clearly declared that one who brings disgrace to the assembly must not be kept within the assembly. Therefore, whatever thought you have toward her, come now." Those who were consumed by rage took up weapons, needles, and acacia stakes and set off. Utpalavarnā saw them coming from a great distance, walking and weeping as they came, and she thought: "Coming with such force, they will surely do me harm. But let me consider what intention lies behind their coming." When she turned her attention inward, she saw that their intention was to kill her. She blessed her robe through her power of concentration and entered into the meditative absorption of cessation.

They stabbed her robe with weapons, needles, and acacia stakes, yet through the power of her meditative absorption she sat as though dead, with no breath moving in or out. They said to one another: "This woman who lived by bad conduct has now been killed and got what she deserved — let us go," and they departed.

After they had gone, the venerable Utpalavārṇā arose from that meditative absorption and, looking back, she saw what harm they had done to her. She then went straightaway to the monastery. When the monks saw her and saw what had happened to her, they asked: "Venerable Utpalavārṇā, why have you come to be in this state?" She replied: "Noble ones, please look — the nuns have killed me right here." They asked her to explain everything that had occurred in full detail. When she had told it all in detail, the monks of few desires were angered, and in various places the venerable elders, though furious at the nuns, said merely that they should not be shown respect, while mocking the affair: "To have had the venerable Utpalavārṇā actually killed — that is a marvel of contemptible behavior."

Then one of them said: "Come now, wise ones — having gotten this far, let us consider how to properly address the matter." Another said: "What is there to address? We need only report it to the Blessed One." Another said: "What need is there to report it to the Blessed One? Let us simply convene and make a rule that no nun whatsoever shall be permitted to enter the Jeta Grove." They assembled and enacted just such a rule — that nuns were not to be admitted to the monastery. Once the nuns were barred from entering the monastery, they lost the honor and respect they had previously received.

Now the great matron of beings (Skt. mahāprajāpatī) Gautamī had the daily practice of coming to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One, but on this occasion the monks said to her: "Gautamī, the monks' Saṅgha has enacted a rule that nuns are not to enter the monastery — remain here and do not go." She replied: "Noble ones, have I committed an offense of the kind they committed?" The monks said: "What can we do — the Saṅgha has determined it so." She turned back and went to her summer dwelling.

The blessed buddhas ask questions while already knowing the answer. Thus the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda: "Has the great matron of beings Gautamī been struck by illness, reverend one? Why has she not come?" Ānanda thereupon reported the whole matter to the Blessed One in full.

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, what the monks' Saṅgha has enacted is in order. However, the nuns depend greatly on the monks in many respects, and if they are not permitted to come they will lose all honor. Therefore, let a nun ask at the monks' gate and be admitted, but instruction shall not be given to her." The Blessed One declared: "Let it be established that a nun who has asked at the monks' gate may enter the monastery, but instruction is to be withheld."

Now the nuns did not know how to ask properly so as to be admitted inside, and so the Blessed One declared: "When a nun is not being allowed into the monastery, she should say thus: 'Noble ones, please be aware that we wish to enter the monastery and be admitted.' And the monk on his side should then ask: 'Sisters, you are not carrying weapons or needles out of hostility, are you?' If a nun enters without having been asked —"

— it becomes an offense. And if the monk has not spoken the question, it likewise becomes an offense. The Blessed One declared that the instruction should be recited, but the group of six monks did not recite it. The Blessed One then declared: "A monk should not give instruction to a nun who has an offense pending when the monks' Saṅgha has not yet consented. If a monk gives instruction to a nun who has an offense pending while the monks' Saṅgha has not consented, it becomes an offense. Just as with instruction, so too it is with the restoration ceremony (poṣadha) and the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā)."

Summary verse:

A nun's seeking of consent, and the invitation ceremony —
these are not the same as the restoration ceremony.
Each seeks the other's consent in turn,
and both proceed according to seniority.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park. A certain nun was studying under a certain monk. In time an offense arose in connection with her, and he rebuked her for it. She then went to the rains-retreat building and sat there weeping. The preceptress (upādhyāyā), seeing this, said: "Young woman, why are you sitting here weeping?" She replied: "Preceptress, my teacher has rebuked me — I did not know what to do." The preceptress said: "My daughter, a preceptress and a teacher give correction for the sake of the preservation of the teaching. You need only ask for forgiveness — what else is there for you to understand? Go and ask for forgiveness properly." She went to the Jeta Grove and prostrated at the feet of that monk, then asked his forgiveness. But that monk turned away and left. The nun, left without confidence, came back to the nuns' rains-retreat building, and the nuns said: "Sister, did you ask the teacher for forgiveness — did he grant it?" She replied: "May no such person ever again become a teacher!" They said: "What was the offense? Tell us what happened." When she had described what had occurred, the nuns said: "Sisters, daughters — in order to show contempt for women, he refused to grant forgiveness even when she asked for it once. And when she prostrated at his feet a second time and asked forgiveness, he turned away and walked off — look at this contemptuous behavior!" The nuns then told the monks about it, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, for a monk to show contempt for nuns in this way is blameworthy. Therefore, when a nun has prostrated at the feet of a monk and asked forgiveness, he must not turn away and leave. If a monk turns away and leaves when a nun has prostrated at his feet and asked forgiveness, it becomes an offense." Moreover, a nun need not ask forgiveness immediately on the spot; it may be done gradually. When the Blessed One declared that it should be done gradually, they did not know how to proceed gradually. The Blessed One then declared: "First, let her be thoroughly trained by another monk, nun, layman, or laywoman, and when she has become harmonious with that one, she may then ask forgiveness." The occasion for this ruling was at Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One declared that a monk who has observed the rains retreat should perform the invitation ceremony before the Saṅgha on three grounds: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what has been suspected. Having performed the invitation ceremony before the Saṅgha on these three grounds, the rains-retreat monk then conducts the restoration ceremony. Some among them said: "Venerable ones, just as the restoration ceremony is performed for the purpose of purification, I see that the invitation ceremony is likewise of the same nature. Therefore, that which is the restoration ceremony is also the invitation ceremony." Others said:

This was then put before the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is true that the restoration ceremony is one thing and the invitation ceremony is another. Yet, since there is nothing other to be done as a restoration ceremony beyond the invitation ceremony, therefore a monk need not perform the restoration ceremony after having performed the invitation ceremony. This is because the restoration ceremony is performed for the purpose of purification, and the invitation ceremony is itself entirely purification."

The occasion for this teaching arose in Śrāvastī.

Some monks, harboring resentment, abandoned equanimity of mind and began to look for fault in one another. At the time of the invitation ceremony they entered the midst of the Saṅgha and competed with one another there within, raising matters of degraded moral discipline, degraded views, degraded conduct in accordance with the rule, and degraded livelihood. They went about mixing others into their disputes, speaking of coming and going against one another, drawing in those who shared their aspirations, their companions, their teachers, their preceptors, those who shared the same teacher, and those who shared the same preceptor, until all were divided, each keeping to their respective sides. At that point a great schism arose in the Saṅgha: the Saṅgha broke into factions, the Saṅgha split in two, the Saṅgha fell into discord. Those who stood by watching then stirred things further, saying to the elders: "Venerable ones, there is no need to quarrel — rather, attain the individual states of mind belonging to those who have gone forth."

The Blessed One too declared: "Monks, in whatever quarter monks reside and there engage in fighting, in fault-finding, in abuse, in quarreling, and in acts of aggression — in such a quarter I have no wish even to hear much, let alone to go and dwell there. I will not go there.

"Monks, in whatever quarter monks abide and engage in fighting, fault-finding, abuse, quarreling, and acts of aggression — there, monks, these three things have been abandoned and these three things are cultivated in abundance. What are the three things that have been abandoned? The wholesome root of non-attachment has been abandoned, the wholesome root of non-aversion has been abandoned, and the wholesome root of non-delusion has been abandoned — these three things have been abandoned. And what are the three things cultivated in abundance? The unwholesome root of attachment is cultivated in abundance, the unwholesome root of aversion is cultivated in abundance, and the unwholesome root of delusion is cultivated in abundance — these three things are cultivated in abundance. In whatever quarter monks reside and fight, find fault, abuse one another, quarrel, and commit acts of aggression — monks, there these three things have been abandoned and these three things are cultivated in abundance: the wholesome root of non-attachment has been abandoned, the wholesome root of non-aversion has been abandoned, and the wholesome root of non-delusion has been abandoned — these three things abandoned; and monks, in whatever quarter monks reside and fight, find fault, abuse, quarrel, and commit acts of aggression — monks, there these three things have been abandoned and these three things are cultivated in abundance: what three? The unwholesome root of attachment is cultivated in abundance, the unwholesome root of aversion is cultivated in abundance, and the unwholesome root of delusion is cultivated in abundance — these three things cultivated in abundance. And monks, in whatever quarter monks reside and fight, find fault, abuse one another, quarrel, and commit acts of aggression —"

— commit acts of aggression. And monks, in whatever quarter these three things have been abandoned and three things are cultivated in abundance, there I have no wish even to hear of it, let alone to go and remain there. I will not go there." When this was declared, the venerable ones said: "There is no need to quarrel; rather, let each recover his own mind of renunciation." But at that point their entanglement had grown and spread so far that there was no reversing it. When brahmins and householders saw this and recognized it, those of discernment mocked them, saying: "These shaven-headed ascetics — though the invitation ceremony has been performed, they have not each recovered their minds of renunciation; they do nothing but fight on and on." They mocked them, disparaged them, and jeered at them. At that juncture the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, that brahmins and householders mock you is fitting. Therefore, monks, monks who hold grudges must not perform the invitation ceremony. Rather, they should first ask for forbearance and then perform it. But even if on the very day of the invitation ceremony they ask for forbearance, the entanglement has grown and spread, and at that moment they will be unable each to recover his own mind." The Blessed One declared: "One must not ask for forbearance on that very same day. Rather, when the invitation ceremony is to take place in seven or eight days, one should ask for forbearance then." When the Blessed One had declared that one should ask for forbearance when the invitation ceremony is to take place in seven or eight days, thereupon all of them asked for forbearance. The Blessed One declared: "All must not ask for forbearance. Rather, let those who are in disagreement ask for forbearance. As for the rest, let them delight in one another properly and then perform the invitation ceremony." The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One declared that in the fifth year and at the time of the topknot festival a great ceremony shall be held. The faithful brahmins and householders vied with one another in making offerings. At that time a great assembly of monks and nuns had gathered, and the Blessed One instructed them to be seated in order of seniority. When the nuns were seated in order of seniority and began calling out, the nuns spoke to the monks. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Let two or three be seated in order of seniority. As for the rest, let them be seated according to the retinue and according to the order of the aspirants."

A summary verse:

Being seated near the doorway,
the Restoration being received by two together,
even a learned nun
alone does not give the Restoration.

The awakened one, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, Prince Jeta's park. The Blessed One declared that, apart from common transactions, monks and nuns should perform their formal acts separately. All the nuns assembled and came to the Jeta Grove to perform the Restoration, and they performed it together with the monks in the same gatehouse. Brahmins and householders were sitting there watching. Upon learning of this, the Blessed One declared: "Monks and nuns must not perform the Restoration together in the same gatehouse."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks and nuns must not perform the Restoration together in the same gatehouse —

The monks went inside and performed the Restoration together with the nuns, and the two groups sat there for a long time exchanging conversation. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks and nuns must not perform the Restoration together in the same temple. Monks and nuns must not perform the Restoration together in the same temple."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks and nuns must not perform the Restoration together in the same temple, the nuns stopped coming to the temple for the Restoration altogether. The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, let the monks go halfway along the road and let the nuns also go halfway along the road, and there let them perform the Restoration together."

When the Blessed One had declared that the monks should go halfway along the road and the nuns should also go halfway along the road and perform the Restoration there together, they began conversing there as before. Then some brahmins and householders happened to travel along that road, and they saw the nuns performing the Restoration together with the monks. They then began to think improper thoughts and said to one another: "Friends, what are these shaven-headed nuns and these shaven-headed wanderers saying to one another?" One replied: "Friends, those two carry on secret talk at home — whatever secret things they do there, we have heard about it. Now they have gone to a deserted place and are simply telling one another whatever secrets there are to tell. What else could they be saying? And whatever punishment the king has inflicted on us because of reports made to him by these shaven-headed wanderers — all of that is being paid back in kind by these shaven-headed nuns."

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks and nuns shall not perform the Restoration halfway along the road. However, two nuns who receive the Restoration should be sent. They should go halfway along the road and then declare the complete purity of the community. The Blessed One declared that two nuns who receive the Restoration should be sent."

When nuns lacking confidence were sent and they were too timid to declare complete purity, the monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "A confident nun should be invited to do it." When there were not two confident nuns, the Blessed One declared: "One confident nun should be invited." When they came to the temple, and the one to whom they were to address the declaration did not understand what the large assembly of monks was saying to her, she turned back then and there, and the nuns' community performed the Restoration without having addressed the monks. The monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "A single monk should be invited, and when he arrives, the declaration should be made to him. When the monks had invited a single monk, he too did not understand, and the same fault arose again. The Blessed One declared: "The monk who has been invited must sit diligently in the gatehouse, and the nuns should go to him and make the declaration. He in turn should report to the monks' community, and the monks' community should appoint a teaching monk by the twofold act of request and formal motion. He should then give instruction to the nuns."

Here ends the summary verse.

Instructing them not to flee, asking their name and clan, the hat, the covered bowl, the rosary strand — these belong to the nun.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared: "Before the monk who has been invited, those nuns should make their declaration of purity." The invited monk sat in the gatehouse. But just as the nuns began to approach him, he cried out, "Do not touch me! Do not touch me!" and began to flee. They followed after him for a moment, then turned back and returned to the nuns' rains-retreat hall. The nuns thus failed to perform the restoration ceremony, and the nuns reported this to the monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "The invited monk must be instructed to remain without fleeing, and without letting the sisters touch him." If a monk, without giving such instruction to those nuns, were to flee far away just the same, he would be guilty of a serious offense. The Blessed One said: "One should request the monk who is appointed to give instruction to the nuns, and he too should remain diligently."

Then, at another time, a different monk who had been invited did not quickly go to the gatehouse; instead, a wandering ascetic who needed something came and sat in the gatehouse, examining the five-spoked wheel of a vehicle. The nuns thought, "This must be the one appointed to give us instruction," and went and touched his feet as they sat before him and said, "Noble one, please give us your attention. We wish to declare our purity to you by means of the restoration ceremony." He thought, "Let me first see what these shaven-headed female ascetics have to say," and said nothing. They spoke again: "Noble one, please give us your attention. The nuns' community of the garden of the king's son at the Jeta Grove bows with their heads at the feet of the monks' community of the Jeta Grove, and asks: are they well, free of affliction, free of distress, active, living, strong, comfortable, and dwelling without transgression? They also wish to declare their purity by means of the restoration ceremony." He did not know what he was supposed to say in reply and so said nothing at all. They said, "O noble one, will you not say at least 'It is well' or 'I will see'?" and he said, "I will see," and departed. The nuns also returned to the retreat hall.

The monk appointed to give instruction did arrive at the gatehouse on a later occasion, but stayed only a brief while before departing. Then, when the elder of the community had made only a single request and the monk appointed as overseer said to the monks, "Who accepted the declaration of purity from the nuns?" — no monk said, "I accepted it, I know of it." The monks concluded, "Surely no nun came at all, and no one accepted their declaration of purity." Without making a request to another monk, the elder of the community himself recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra and the community performed the restoration ceremony.

When the nuns who had come to make their declaration of purity arrived the following restoration day, they found no one there to receive the scriptural recitation, so they waited a long time and then returned to the retreat hall. The nuns' community also failed to perform the restoration ceremony. The next day all the nuns gathered and assembled together, and said:

"Why does the noble Saṅgha not send us a monk to recite the scripture?" The monks said: "Sisters, on that restoration day just past, to which monk who was present did you make your declaration of purity?"
