The nuns who had been receiving the declaration said: "There was a noble one of such-and-such a complexion and such-and-such a stature, sitting in the gatehouse turning the wheel of cyclic existence in his mind — to him we made our declaration of purity." The monks recognized from these marks that there had been a lay person present, and said: "That one is not a monk, yet it was indeed to the lay person who was sitting there that you made your declaration." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected that the fault lay in the monk who had been sent to recite the scripture not having been asked his name. He therefore thought: the name of the monk sent to recite the scripture for the nuns' community should be asked. He declared: "There is no transgression on the part of the nuns for what they said to those monks. Nevertheless, the nuns who are receiving the declaration of purity should ask the name of the monk who was sent to recite the scripture."

"If they speak without first asking the name of the preceptor sent to recite the scripture for us, it will become a serious offence." The Blessed One declared that the nuns who are receiving the declaration of purity should ask the name of the monk sent to recite the scripture. But then those nuns, while knowing the name of the monk sent to recite, still asked it anyway — and at that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "If they know his name, they should not ask. If they do not know it, they should ask."

The setting of the next rule is Śrāvastī. The Great Progenitress Gautamī was living in a certain place, and the nuns came to her and asked: "Noble one, how are you faring?" She replied: "Daughters, I am cold." They asked: "Noble one, what did you use to wear?" She said: "Daughters, when I was a laywoman and lived in a household, I used to wear a hat." "Noble one, why do you not wear one now?" "Daughters, I have gone forth, and unless the Blessed One permits it, how can I wear one?" — and at that point the nuns relayed this to the monks, and the monks to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Very well, it is permitted. Nuns may wear a hat in the retreat hall."

The setting of the next rule is Rājagṛha. A brahmin beggar woman of Rājagṛha was wandering about and entered another person's house, saying: "May you be well and fortunate — please give alms." The mistress of the house replied: "Brahmin, there is not even a little — be off with you." And so she departed and went away.

The great Progenitress Gautamī then also entered that house seeking alms. The brahmin thought to himself: "This shaven-headed renunciant has also entered — let me wait here a moment and see whether she too will be refused, or whether it is just me alone." And so he sought his opportunity and lingered there a little while. When he heard the words "The Buddha's mother has come," he rose up quickly, set out a seat, and with great joy went and filled her alms bowl with pure and fine food and drink and offered it to her. The brahmin, seized by jealousy and resentment, went off and said: "Noble one, please allow me to see what excellent things she has in her alms bowl." And being straightforward, she showed it to him. The brahmin spat into the alms bowl. The Great Progenitress Gautamī said:

"Child, why would you defile the alms round? Had you but asked, I would have given it to you just the same." The brahmin, having no boldness, said nothing and sat in silence. At that point the nuns reported it to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One reflected: "Ordinary men also harm women by their very nature, and so too this deluded brahmin fellow has in just this way generated a great deal of demerit." Knowing therefore that the nuns ought to carry a cover for their alms bowls, he declared: "Monks, ordinary men also harm women by their very nature, and this deluded brahmin fellow has in just this way generated a great deal of demerit. Therefore, I hereby permit it: the nuns shall carry a cover for their alms bowls."

When the Blessed One had spoken the words "The nuns shall carry a cover for their alms bowls," the nuns did not know what kind of alms-bowl cover was meant, and so they reported it to the monks. The monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "The alms-bowl cover is a vessel into which the alms bowl is placed, and the nuns shall take it when they go on their alms round."

The setting of this rule is at Śrāvastī. A great many people from the eastern regions were accustomed to gathering in the pleasure gardens. Now one day a festival fell at Śrāvastī, and those people took clean and fine food and drink and went to the pleasure gardens. They sent word to their wives: "Please string together garlands of flowers and send them." Their wives, thinking there were fine and varied flowers growing in the hedgerows and that they had been asked to send those, gathered flowers from the gardens along the long hedgerows but did not know how to string them into a garland. They sent word back: "Please send a garland-stringer to come." But that day the flower-sellers were there, and they had not yet arrived. Those people sat inwardly troubled, thinking: "When they asked us to send a garland of flowers, we who do not know how to string one called for a garland-stringer, and she could not come. How are we to manage this?"

Now Sthūlanandā was out going on her alms round and entered another house, where a pleasant-looking woman had gone to collect alms. The woman said: "Noble lady, please depart — we are inwardly troubled. We have no alms or words to give to anyone." Sthūlanandā said: "What is this you say? What small wrong have I done? Tell me in full how things stand." Sthūlanandā said: "Why don't you string them yourself?" The woman replied: "Noble lady, if we do not seek it, do you think we would know how?" Sthūlanandā said: "My good woman, I know how. Since the time has passed, there is not a craft or a trade I do not know." They presented it to the noble lady, and having strung it in just that way, what did she give? She said: "My good woman, will you give the price of some food?" The woman replied: "Noble lady, I shall offer it gladly. Please go around quickly and thoroughly." She put down her alms bowl, stretched out her legs and sat down, and quickly strung them just so. When the householders' wives saw this, they were astonished, and being thoroughly delighted with her, they gave Sthūlanandā a great deal of food in payment. Sthūlanandā, carried away by her success, strung garlands at another house as well, and there too she was given payment in food. Having thus obtained much in the way of gains, Sthūlanandā took what she had received and went to her seasonal dwelling.

Just then the garland-stringers arrived and said, "Please pass those flowers to us so that we may string them." She replied, "Where have you only just now come from? Those garlands have already been strung and sent to the pleasure garden." They asked, "Who strung them?" She replied, "The noble Sthūlanandā did." At this, they reviled the monks, the sons of the Śākyan contemplative: "The contemplatives are frauds, and their celibate life is a fraud, for they are now stealing the livelihood of others." And so they mocked, they reproached, and they slandered.

When the monks heard this, they reported the matter to the Blessed One at that time. The Blessed One, reflecting that whatever fault had arisen from the garland-stringers' slander had come about on account of the nun's stringing of garlands, and that therefore nuns should not string garlands, declared: "Monks, the garland-stringers have become a basis for slander. Therefore nuns are not to string garlands. If a nun strings garlands, she incurs an offense."

After the Blessed One had thus spoken, saying that nuns were not to string garlands, it came to pass that the festival of the top-knot, the great festival, and the five-year festival all occurred. King Prasenajit of Kosala, along with Queen Mallikā, the royal lady Vāsavadattā, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the mother of Mṛgāra named Visākhā, the elderly maidservant, the laywoman who was the mother of the supernaturally gifted one, the householder Ugra, the great Śākyan named Mahānāma, and many other faithful people all celebrated with increasingly magnificent and excellent festivities for the top-knot festival and the great festival. People dwelling in various regions, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen all assembled. Flowers were heaped up in abundance, and yet the garland-stringers were unable to string them well. Even when they were passed back and forth among other brahmin and householder faithful, the flowers still could not be strung properly.

Those people then said to the nuns, "Alas! If we are in need of garland-stringing, well now — noble ladies, you know the way of it. The time has come for you to honor the Teacher and string garlands." The nuns replied, "Wise ones, do you not know? The Blessed One has established a training rule that nuns are not to string garlands, so how could we string them?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Therefore I grant permission: nuns may string garlands for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha." After the Blessed One had thus spoken, granting that nuns might string garlands for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, the nuns sat in the gatehouse and in the corridors with their legs stretched out and began to string flowers. Faithless people, seeing this, taunted them: "Alas! Noble ladies, have you gone forth from nothing other than the garland-stringers' caste?" And the nuns sat there with their hair raised on end, unable to say a word.

At that point the monks again reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, those faithless ones have become a basis for slander through improper conduct. Therefore nuns are not to sit in the gatehouse or in the corridors and string flowers. If a nun sits in the gatehouse or in the corridors and strings garlands, she incurs an offense. Rather, if there is somewhere suitable, let them string garlands in a secluded area." Nuns are not to sit in the gatehouse or in the corridors and —

— string garlands incurs an offense.

The summary verse reads:

Pottery vessels and brewing,
Selling residential properties,
Likewise merchant shops and premises,
And images of divine form — none of these shall be held.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain nun named Sthūlanandā went to a potter and said, "Good man, can you make a begging bowl of clay?" He replied, "Noble one, if you know the proper size, I will make a large and good one." She said, "Noble one, what need has a nun of a great clay begging bowl? You are poor — if you will not make it for me free of charge, then I will pay the full price." He thought, "There is nothing in this for me," and so he made a large clay begging bowl. He then said, "Make yet another one that will fit inside it." He made another, and so on, one nested inside the other, until he had made seven in all.

Sthūlanandā then had the nuns clean them and strung them in a net of five-colored thread, placed them one by one on a nun's head, and set off for the place to which she had been invited as a guest. When she arrived and had spread them out and was sitting there, some brahmins and householders said, "Noble one, have you been visiting the potter's shop?" She replied, "You poor folk, what do you know? Here I took some rice, here I took up a load, here I took some cooked grain, here I took some vegetables — noble one, do set aside the rest in the same way. Even if you find a great quantity of vegetables, it may still be possible." And she sat there saying nothing more. At that point the monks heard of this and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, discerning that the fault lay in a nun's carrying pottery vessels, and knowing therefore that nuns should not carry pottery vessels, declared, "Monks, therefore nuns are not to carry pottery vessels. If a nun carries a pottery vessel, she incurs an offense. She may, however, carry a scraper, a salt container, and a drinking cup that has been offered."

The Basis for the Minor Vinaya, the forty-fourth fascicle. The occasion takes place in Śrāvastī.

In Śrāvastī there was a certain householder who took a wife from among those of equal caste, and with her he played, rejoiced, and enjoyed himself. From their playing and rejoicing and enjoyment a daughter was born on the right side — born laterally on the right — and because this girl was of ill omen, no one would take her. In Śrāvastī another householder took a wife, and she died in due course by her own karma. He then took a second, and then a third, up to a seventh; each of them likewise died by her own karma. He became universally known by the name "wife-killer," the wife-killer. He then sought the hand of another man's daughter, and that man said, "Would I give even my own daughter?" He sought the hand of a widow, and she said, "Would I myself be given away?" He then began to manage the household affairs on his own. A friend of his came to the house and asked him by name what was going on. The household folk replied, "He has gone inside and is managing the household affairs himself." The friend said, "Can you not feed your wives, give them instructions, and put them to work? Why is it that you are managing the household affairs yourself?" He said, "Friend, I could indeed manage,

but whenever I took a wife, she died in her own time by her own karma. The same happened with the second, the third, and up to the seventh wife I married — they all died in their own time by their own karma. Because of this I became widely known everywhere by the name 'wife-killer.' Would he seek anyone else? The people said, 'If he were to seek again, would we give him our own daughter?' He sought the hand of a widow, and she too said, 'Would I myself be given away?' As for taking a girl from a neighboring household — he had tried that too, but they said, 'Would we give away a girl of ours?' The friend said, 'Go ahead,' and so the householder, overcome by weariness, gave her. The friend urged him, went to that householder's home, said 'Good day, good day,' and the household folk replied, 'What are you asking for?' 'I am asking for the girl.' 'Which girl?' 'The neighbor's daughter.' 'She shall be given. Name the time of giving. Name the time of taking. Name the day auspicious for this.' Having said this, he departed.

Then the householder's wife, thinking she would send the girl off as a bride, brewed ale. The hot season had arrived, and the brew spoiled and became unfit. Then that householder's wife said to a female ale-seller, 'I am sending my daughter off as a bride and need just this much ale — prepare it.' The ale-seller replied, 'We shall supply it properly.' She began to make preparations with the ale when Plump-and-Joyful happened to be going on her alms round and entered that house. 'Lovely-featured one, please give alms.' The householder's wife, going back and forth looking at the ale in distraction, replied, 'Noble lady, please just go on your way. I am preoccupied with something in my mind, and as for alms — I am not going to offer them to anyone at all.' She said, 'Did I do something slightly wrong in saying what I said?' The wife then explained the matter in full, and Plump-and-Joyful said, 'Lovely-featured one, in that case why not have it fixed again?' She replied, 'Noble lady, if I had not sought help, would I have known how? What do I know of it?' Plump-and-Joyful said, 'Lovely-featured one, I do know — because the time has passed on it, there is no craft or trade matter that I do not know with certainty.' 'Noble lady, will you kindly fix it again for me?' She replied, 'Lovely-featured one, if I fix it again, will you give me the price of my food?' She said, 'Noble lady, I shall give it properly — give abundantly and fix it again.' Plump-and-Joyful said, 'Bring it here and let me look.' When she showed her the ale-jars, Plump-and-Joyful saw that the brew was spoiled. She examined the ale-jars against one another and, seeing from the warmth that the brew was unfit, she opened the air-holes, heaped much sand beneath the ale-jars, poured water over the outsides, wrapped them all about with fish-net weaving, then took up fans and began to fan them. Through this method of a distinctive cooling treatment, the ale was restored to fitness again.

The time to take the bride was near. Friends, companions, relatives, and people had assembled. The ale-seller had also made her ale preparations and sat ready, intending that whenever the wedding guests arrived she would give it to them. The householder had arranged with that very ale for the completion of sending off the bride. Then the ale-seller arrived and said, 'Householder, please take the ale.' He replied, 'Good woman, that is enough — the ale was fixed again and with that very ale the sending off of the bride has been completed.' She said, 'Householder, since that ale ran out there, who then fixed it again?' He explained: 'The noble Plump-and-Joyful fixed it again — that is her gift of benefit to us.' At this the fully ordained nuns of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are burned. The brahmin life is burned.

It was on account of this that they were now mocking, reviling, and slandering her, saying she was robbing others of their livelihood. The monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: the conduct of the nun Plump-and-Joyful is not the way of a contemplative. Therefore, knowing that nuns ought not to engage in the business of ale, he declared: "Monks, the conduct of the nun Plump-and-Joyful is not the way of a contemplative. Therefore, nuns must not engage in the business of ale. If a nun engages in the business of ale, it shall become a grave transgression."

The origin of this ruling is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī there lived a householder who delighted in generosity. At another time he was struck by illness, and as his bodily life was coming to its end he thought, "I am going to die." So he gave everything he owned and had in his home to contemplatives, brahmins, and also to friends, companions, and relatives, leaving only the house itself. When Plump-and-Joyful heard this, she came quickly, running to reach him in time. Upon her arrival she gave the householder a certain sign indicating that a woman of the household had been left with little to show for it. The householder understood and said: "Noble one, you have come late. Whatever there was, I have given it all away, and there is nothing left beyond the house alone — not even a little to give." She said: "Householder, you have praised me to the skies like an elephant's raised trunk, and now that I have come to you, how can I leave with all hope cut off?" He replied: "Noble one, did I not say that nothing remains beyond the house alone? If you wish it, take that house." She said: "Householder, so be it then." Then, saying "May you be free from illness," she departed.

Some time later, when that householder had passed away, his relatives wrapped the body in blue, yellow, red, and white cloth and carried it to the charnel ground. When Plump-and-Joyful heard that the householder had passed away, she came, taking her time, and sealed the door of his house with a lock and remained sitting there on one side.

After a while they came back from the cremation and said: "Who has sealed this house?" Plump-and-Joyful said: "The owner has sealed it." They said: "To whom was it given?" She said: "To me, Plump-and-Joyful." They said: "Noble one, if that is so, nonetheless pay a rental fee to enter." She said: "I will give it — I will give it," and having stamped a seal of agreement she let them in. Once they had entered and settled there, some brahmins and householders arrived, gathered among them, and the fully ordained monks who are the contemplatives, the sons of the Śākyas, were burned. The brahmin life was burned. For it was now being mocked, reviled, and slandered, saying she was renting out and taking in houses.

The monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, take the mockery of the brahmins and householders as the basis for this ruling. Therefore, nuns must not rent out or take in houses. If a nun rents out or takes in a house, it shall become a serious offense."

At Śrāvastī there lived another merchant who delighted in generosity. At another time he was struck by illness, and as his bodily life was coming to its end he thought, "I am going to die." So he gave everything he owned and had in his home to contemplatives, brahmins, and also to friends, companions, and relatives,

Only the shop remained. Stubborn Delightful, upon hearing this, traveled a great distance and came to that place, entered inside, and gave a signal to that merchant indicating that the female donor had but little gain. The householder, understanding this, said: "Noble one, you have come late. Whatever little I had, all of it I have given away. Nothing remained except the one shop alone, so there is nothing at all I can give." She replied: "Benefactor, you raised my hopes high as an elephant's trunk and drew me to your side — how can I go away with my hopes dashed like this?" He said: "Noble one, did I not say that nothing remained except the one shop? If that is what you wish, then take that house." She replied: "Householder, so be it, I accept." Then she said, "May you be free from illness," and departed.

Not long after, at another time, that householder passed away. His relatives wrapped him round and adorned him with blue, yellow, red, and white cloths, and carried him to the charnel ground. Stubborn Delightful, upon hearing that the householder had passed away, traveled a great distance, sealed the door of his shop and affixed a lock to it, then went off and sat in a corner by herself.

After some time, when the cremation was done and the relatives, friends, companions, and kinsmen had returned and were sitting together grieving for a while, another man going to the market came to that house and said to them: "The shop has been locked up by Stubborn Delightful." When they heard this, they went a great distance and said: "Who sealed this shop?" Stubborn Delightful replied: "The one to whom it was given sealed it." They asked: "To whom was it given?" She answered: "To me, Stubborn Delightful." They said: "Noble one, even if that is so, pay the rent and we shall open the storehouse for you." She replied: "Will you give it, or will you give it?" and they broke the seal and spread things out there.

Brahmins and householders who had gathered and were sitting there then mocked and criticized the monks, the ascetics who are sons of the Śākya: "The contemplatives are burning with shame! Those who practice the celibate life — burning with shame! For they now rent out and take in shops." And they continued to mock, revile, and slander them. The monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, take the mockery of the brahmins and householders as the basis for this ruling. Therefore, nuns must not rent out or take in shops. If a nun rents out or takes in a shop, it shall become a serious offense."

The case arose at Śrāvastī.

Stubborn Delightful, early in the morning, having arranged her inner robe and taken up her outer robe and bowl, entered Śrāvastī for alms. A female diviner carrying a bell was walking along and saw her. The diviner thought: "That is a fine method — I shall do the same myself." She then procured a bell for herself. The very next day she took the bell, entered Śrāvastī, and began bathing boys and girls; carrying incense and ringing the bell, she gave prophecies. Whichever boys and girls she bathed became well and at ease in their circumstances, and her prophecies likewise came true. The fame spread throughout Śrāvastī that this woman had obtained great spiritual attainment, and whenever anyone anywhere had need of a diviner they would seek her out.

Stubborn Delightful came to that woman and consulted her, and since no one else was approaching the diviner, she purposely went to the homes of brahmins and householders and said: "I shall perform offering-cake rites and give prophecies," and she visited whatever homes she went to.

Those various people said: "Our offering-cake rites and prophecies have already been performed." When those who had received prophecies said, "It was the noble Stubborn Delightful," abuse was directed at the monks, the sons of the Śākyan contemplative: "Contemplatives are burned out! The celibate life is burned out! For it is they who are now robbing others of their livelihood" — thus they mocked, reviled, and slandered them. When the monks heard this, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, reflecting that the fault lay in the nuns' adopting the appearance of a goddess, understood that nuns must not adopt the appearance of a goddess, and declared: "Monks, the basis for those women's mockery is Stubborn Delightful's improper conduct. And the fault lies in the nun's adopting the appearance of a goddess. Therefore nuns must not adopt the appearance of a goddess. If a nun adopts the appearance of a goddess, it shall constitute a serious offense."

The summary verse:

By a woman at the riverbank — not with bathing powder from the stream, not to be sought from the regular supply, a second alms-bowl carried along, and the gall-bladder vessel not to be held.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now at Śrāvastī a certain woman was sitting by the bathing place for women at the river Aciravatī, combing her hair. At that time Stubborn Delightful wished to bathe, and so she took her bathing powder and went to the river Aciravatī. From a distance she saw that woman combing her hair, and upon seeing her she was seized and gripped by jealousy, and she thought: "How could this slave-woman's daughter dare to rival me, sitting here combing her hair? Has Stubborn Delightful never before had hair? That woman will be displeased, and likewise in the future, so that when she sees me again she will not try to rival me in hair" — and she went up behind her and scattered terminalia powder into her hair.

She then said: "Noble one, what wrong have I done you that, after you had already bathed, you scatter terminalia powder on my head? Does the slave-woman not know? Has Stubborn Delightful never before had such hair? Therefore you have harmed me. Go and bathe again. Have I then defiled your hair with all manner of unclean things?"

When she began that abuse, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, these women have become a basis for mockery. Therefore nuns must not scatter bathing powder onto the head of a woman who has already bathed. If a nun scatters bathing powder onto the head of a woman who has already bathed, it shall constitute a serious offense."

The occasion is at Śrāvastī.

Stubborn Delightful wished to bathe, and she went to the Aciravatī together with the nuns. There they sat facing against the current of the water and amused themselves by splashing. The nuns said to them: "Noble ones, what are you doing?" They replied: "Great one, we are amusing ourselves by splashing." The nuns said: "Noble ones, is it fitting to sit facing against the current and amuse yourselves by splashing?" They replied: "It is perfectly fitting. It is most fitting. Who has forbidden it, and where has it been forbidden?" At that point the nuns told this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the nuns have become a basis for mockery.

Therefore, nuns must not sit facing against the current of the water and amuse themselves by splashing. If a nun sits facing against the current and amuses herself by splashing, it will become a serious transgression.

The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

The nuns set their alms bowls down wherever they happened to fall, and rodents ate from them, and they were struck by falling sticks. On that occasion the nuns told this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the nuns have become a basis for mockery. Therefore nuns must not set their alms bowls down wherever they happen to fall. Rather, they should secure their alms bowls with a cloth ring."

When the Blessed One had declared that alms bowls were to be secured with a cloth ring, the nuns wrapped all of their alms bowls entirely in cloth. Brahmins and householders saw this and asked: "Noble ones, what is this?" The nuns replied: "Worthy friends, the Blessed One has permitted it." The brahmins and householders said: "Noble ones, surely the Blessed One did not say to wrap all the alms bowls entirely in cloth!" and exclaimed: "Have you renunciants become attached to sensual pleasures?" The nuns, having no confidence, sat in silence and said nothing. On that occasion the monks heard of this, reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the brahmins and householders have become a basis for mockery. Therefore one must not wrap all the alms bowls entirely in cloth in that fashion. Rather, one should wrap just the foot of the alms bowl with a cloth ring in that same manner."

When the nuns wrapped the bowls with something resembling a mountain peak and something resembling a fence post, the Blessed One declared: "There are two fittings for the foot of the alms bowl: it should be done with leaves resembling the leaf of the awakening tree, or wrapped with leaves resembling the palm of a hand."

The origin of this rule is at Śrāvastī.

There was a certain nun named Stout-and-Glad who had a small water vessel. One day the husband of another woman came to her, approached Stout-and-Glad, and said: "Noble one, may I borrow your small water vessel for a short while?" She asked: "What for?" He said: "Noble one, I have a son-in-law, and he has no vessel from which to drink." Saying this, she gave it to him, and through carelessness he broke it. Later, on another occasion, when Stout-and-Glad came to take it back, he said: "Noble one, that one lacked care and was broken, so I will pay for it." Stout-and-Glad said: "Brother, I do not need payment from you — just give me that very replacement." He said: "Noble one, I have already given another one in its place and paid for it." She said: "Give me that very one." And so they fell into a dispute with one another. On that occasion the monks heard of this, reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One, having reflected that the fault lay in the nun's having kept possession of a small water vessel, knowing this, declared: "Monks, Stout-and-Glad has come to quarrel on account of the small water vessel. Therefore nuns must not keep a small water vessel." If a nun keeps a small water vessel, it will be a matter involving an offence.

The summary verse:

A woman involved in dance,
a senior monk who teaches Dharma,
or again one who petitions another —
these four are to be encompassed.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who was wealthy, of great means, and well-provided with enjoyments. His daughter-in-law gave birth to a son. Delighted to see the child, relatives, kinsmen, and other people came and held the naming ceremony on the very day of birth.

Afterward, that householder spent a long time feasting and making merry with the people of his household, and by the time dawn broke, he had lain down to sleep. His wife, too, overcome with drowsiness, had a dream in which she imagined herself lying together with her husband, and in that dream she experienced a nocturnal emission. Her robe and her lower garment became crumpled and fell to the ground.

Early the following morning at daybreak, a monk who was going on alms-round set out while it was still dark and came to that house. The house had many doors. He went to the first door and looked in — it was empty. He went to the second and third doors — they too were empty. When at last he came to the fourth door and looked in, he saw the householder's wife lying there in that unseemly condition. Startled, she immediately began to flee, but her faculties were clouded and she had no idea where to go, so she ran this way and that until she blundered into the householder's bedroom.

She began beating on the bed, and the householder woke up. Seeing a monk standing there, he asked, "Venerable one, where have you come from to be here?" But the monk, trembling and with his hair on end, was unable to give any reply.

Presently the householder came out of the bedroom and saw his wife in that unseemly state. He thought to himself, "This shameless monk has abused my wife." So he set upon the monk, striking him indiscriminately with the back of a stick, with a whip, with a clod of earth, and with his fists, until the noise of the beating woke the wife. She cried out, "My lord's son, why are you beating this monk like that?" He replied, "While you were lying in a stupor of sleep, this shameless wretch had his way with you." She said, "My lord's son, may the sin be calmed. This monk who has gone forth has done no such thing. I was deep asleep and overcome with drowsiness, and I had such a dream — dreaming that you and I were together, and that my lower garment was all crumpled and had fallen to the ground. This monk has done no wrong; let him go." So he broke the monk's alms-bowl and struck him on the head, tore his Dharma robe, and left him just as he was, in that unseemly state, his eyes streaming with tears, contemplating what had happened to him, as he made his way to the Jeta Grove.

The monks saw him, and asked, "Venerable one, who left you in such a condition as this?" He told them in full what had happened. The monks thereupon reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having reflected, understood that the fault lay in monks going indiscriminately from door to door in a house with many doors. Knowing this, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, therefore monks must not go indiscriminately from door to door in a house with many doors." He then added: "However, when going to a household one has visited before, if afterward one wishes to enter a house with many doors, one should first place a signal — flour or a pickle — at the doorway the previous evening and then proceed inside."

The Blessed One had thus said that a monk should place a signal of flour or a pickle at the doorway in the evening before going through the many doors of a house. But the monks set up the signal at the doorway and then went in without sweeping — and the men and women who were living there found lice in their lower and upper garments, and all the mothers...

A woman who was reclining with her body and voice at ease caught sight of this and, upon reflection, was deeply startled and alarmed. When the monks heard her cry of alarm, they reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you have become a cause of alarm for women. Therefore monks should not enter in that sudden manner. Rather, they should make a sound and then go in."

When the Blessed One had said that they should make a sound before going in, the monks went along calling out "a-la-la!" and when they arrived, the people of the household said: "Noble ones, why do you come calling out 'a-la-la!' like little children?" The monks replied: "Sisters, the Blessed One instructed us to make a sound and go — so we spoke a word as we came." The householders said: "Noble ones, is there no other way to make a sound? Why do you come like that?" The monks, having no ready answer, sat in silence.

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks should not go to a house calling out 'a-la-la!' They should make a different sound."

When the Blessed One had said they should make a different sound, the monks went and struck the door panels on their arrival, and the people of the household said: "Noble ones, why are you hitting the door panels?" The monks replied: "We are making a sound." "Did you break the door panels?" the householders asked. The monks, having no ready answer, sat in silence.

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "One should not strike the door panels. Rather, one should produce a sound with a staff."

The monks did not know what kind of staff was meant for producing such a sound, so the Blessed One declared: "One should carry a staff-bell (khakkhara), make a sound with it, and then enter."

When the Blessed One had said that one should make a sound with the staff-bell and enter, the monks went along making sound with their staff-bells, and dogs harassed them. Some monks, without paying attention, struck the staff-bell too many times, and the Blessed One declared: "One should not strike it repeatedly in that way; rather, one should simply give it a rattle."

When some dogs were rattled at in this way, they became all the more aggressive, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, give the dog a single morsel from the alms-food."

The monks then went to the house of someone who lacked faith, and when the monks rang their staff-bells, that person was displeased and no one came to the door. The Blessed One declared: "One should not ring it over and over again; one should ring it only two or three times."

Now the basis of the following rule is set at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī there was another householder, and to his house the community of monks headed by the buddha was invited for a midday meal, and the community of monks duly arrived. The Blessed One was staying in a room built up with materials, and he was also receiving alms-food. There are five reasons why a buddha, the Blessed One, stays in a room built up with materials while also receiving alms-food. What are the five? He wishes to establish the proper interior arrangement; he wishes to teach the Dharma to the gods; he wishes to look after those who are sick; he wishes to inspect the sleeping places; and he wishes to establish a basis for training in the Vinaya for the hearers. On this particular occasion, the Blessed One was staying in a room built up with materials and receiving alms-food because he wished to establish a basis for training in the Vinaya for the hearers.

That householder had constructed a bower of leaves, and the community of monks sat beneath it. Then the gods began to cause rain to fall, and at a certain winter moment it fell.

That householder served the community of monks with soup, porridge, rice-porridge, and turnips. When some monks drank the soup, they made a slurping sound. When some ate the rice-porridge, they made a crunching sound. When some ate the turnips, they made a chomping sound. Where the rain dripped down, it fell with a dripping, pattering sound. When monks drank water from a pot, there was a splashing, pouring sound. Now among those present was a monk who had gone forth from the life of a musician. He did not maintain mindfulness, and recalling what he had done before, conceptual thought proliferated within him. Carried along by the force of that discursive thinking, he fitted what he was doing to the sounds he heard and began to dance, calling out: "Reverend ones — chomp chomp! Reverend ones — crunch crunch! Reverend ones — munch munch! Reverend ones — clatter clatter! Reverend ones — splash splash!" At this, those monks who had not maintained mindfulness became pleased in mind and laughed. Those who had maintained mindfulness were undisturbed in their conduct and remained just as they were. Some of the attendants began to laugh out loud. Some began to jeer. The householder too became displeased. Then the monk who had gone to collect alms also became displeased. Having collected the alms-food, he went to where the Blessed One was staying, set the alms-food to one side, bowed his head to the Blessed One's feet, and sat down to one side.

It is the nature of things that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, delight in the monks who go to collect alms and speak words of rejoicing with them. So the Blessed One spoke words of rejoicing, asking: "Were the members of the community of monks satisfied and made content with food?" He spoke these words of rejoicing, and the Blessed One asked that monk: "Monks — ah, were the members of the community of monks satisfied and made content with food?" The monk replied: "Venerable One, it is so. The members of the community of monks were satisfied and made content with food. However, the householder has become displeased." He then reported in detail what had happened and how things had unfolded. Thereupon the Blessed One, having finished the business of eating, washed his feet outside the assembly hall, entered the hall, and sat down in inner composure within it. Then the Blessed One arose from inner composure in the late afternoon, and seated himself on a seat prepared for him before the community of monks. Seated there, he addressed those monks in these words: "Monks, from what intention did you act in this way?" They replied: "Venerable One, it arose from a slight intention to jeer, and a slight intention to laugh." Then the Blessed One addressed the monks in these words: "Any monk who acted in this way from an intention to laugh incurs an offense involving a transgression. If it arose from an intention to jeer, there is no downfall. Nevertheless, monks, the fault here is that monks ate their food making noise with their mouths. Therefore monks must not eat their food making noise with their mouths. A monk who eats his food making noise with his mouth incurs a transgression." When the Blessed One had said that monks must not eat their food making noise with their mouths, faithful brahmin householders offered the monks royal sugar-cane, rice-porridge, clarified-butter porridge, turnips, and sugar-cane stalks. The monks, having doubts, did not accept them. Those people said: "Noble ones, had the Blessed One, the buddha, not appeared in the world, our field of generosity would have been among the non-Buddhists. Now the Blessed One has appeared in the world, and you are our field of generosity.

"If you do not accept these offerings, we will be cut off from the provisions for the journey to the world beyond, and the Blessed One himself has taught in the Sūtra on Timely Giving that whatever crops are first-ripe and whatever fruits are first-ripe should be given first and foremost to those endowed with moral discipline, and only afterwards used for one's own purposes. These are timely gifts, and so out of compassion please accept them." When they had spoken thus, the Blessed One declared: "I permit it. Sugarcane stalks with the fruit-bearing ones and the grain-bearing ones are to be eaten together with flour. Turnips, royal sugar-cane, and clarified-butter stalks are to be cut into pieces and eaten."

The incident arose in Śrāvastī. In Śrāvastī, another householder invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to his home at midday. The monks came separately in groups without waiting for one another, and each group said: "Householder, serve us — we will eat." After they had eaten and gone, other groups came in the same way one after another, until the householder became worn out with serving and grew displeased. He said: "Oh! All of you should gather together and eat at the same time!" When the monks heard this, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, you must not eat separately at a busy household. Those who arrive first are to wait at the door, and when all have assembled and entered together, then eat. If one eats there while the household is still busy, it becomes an offence of wrongdoing."

When the Blessed One had taught that monks must not eat at a busy household, another monk fell ill, and his attendant went out to fetch food but did not return for a long time, and the monk became troubled with regret. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, I permit five categories of persons to eat sitting and receiving alms: one who has arrived unexpectedly, one who is departing, one who is sick, one who tends the sick, and one who is working. Giving is permitted to these."

The incident arose in Śrāvastī. In Śrāvastī there resided a householder who was wealthy, possessing great riches and abundant resources. At a certain time he came to have sincere faith in the Buddha and likewise in the Dharma and the Saṅgha. He invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha to his home at midday. The Saṅgha of monks went. The Blessed One, the Buddha, remained at a place prepared with requisites and also received alms. The text beginning with "For five reasons the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, remain at a place prepared with requisites and also receive alms" — on this occasion the Blessed One, wishing to establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the hearers, also remained at a place prepared with requisites and received alms, just as in the passage above.

When those monks had eaten their meal they left in the same way as before. The householder, wishing to hear the Dharma, looked about, but not a single monk remained, and he felt slighted. When the monks heard of this and reported it to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, you have become the basis for that householder's feeling slighted. Therefore, after eating, a monk must not leave in the same manner; he must teach the Dharma to a donor who desires it. If he departs without having taught, it becomes an offence of wrongdoing." When the Blessed One had instructed that the Dharma must be taught to a donor who desires it, the monks did not know who among them should teach. The Blessed One declared: "The elder of the Saṅgha is to teach."

If he is unable, then the second elder of the Saṅgha is to teach. If he too is unable, the monks are to be asked in order of seniority. Or, if there is another who is capable, that one is to be requested.

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī there lived a householder who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and of great means. He was also a man of faith, of good intention, and of virtue, and from time to time he would go to the Jeta Grove and listen to the words of the Buddha. On another occasion he invited the Saṅgha of monks, along with the Buddha and the rest, to his home for a midday meal, and the Saṅgha of monks went. The Blessed One, however, was occupied with a matter and remained behind, yet he did accept the alms-round. From the passage beginning "for five reasons" up through the words "the Blessed One the Buddha remained behind, occupied with a matter, yet also accepted the alms-round" — all of this is as stated above.

The Blessed One had declared: "If a donor wishes to hear the Dharma, the monk appointed for the purpose is to teach it." So the monks set out, leaving behind just the one monk who had been appointed, and the householder's friends, relatives, kinsmen, and those of great influence all gathered at the meal. Together with their wives they sat around that monk and said, "Noble one, please teach the Dharma." But the monk, seeing that assembly of powerful people seated around him, became overwhelmed with shyness and sat in silence without saying a word. The householder thought to himself: "It seems that this noble one has been overcome with shyness on account of me and my influential retinue. Let me myself teach the Dharma." And so he said: "Noble one, the Blessed One has declared: 'Through generosity one comes to possess great wealth; through moral discipline one is reborn in the higher realms; through meditation one comes to be free.' This is the Dharma — now please, be on your way." The monk, having lost all confidence, left without saying a word and went to the monastery. The monks asked him: "Venerable one, did you teach the Dharma to that donor?" He replied: "Venerable ones, what can I say? You left me there alone, and when I saw that powerful retinue of the householder's, I became so overcome with shyness sitting there alone that in the end it was he himself who taught me the Dharma." At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "That monk said something good. For the monk appointed to teach, four companion monks are to be appointed."

The Vinaya of Minor Matters, the forty-fifth fascicle.

The summary verse:

One is to go after checking,
the monk of brahmin lineage,
four are to copy,
and tooth-sticks too are to be washed.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove. The Blessed One had declared that four companion monks are to be appointed for a monk who is to teach the Dharma. So whenever monks went somewhere on an invitation to a meal, the monk requested to teach the Dharma had four companion monks appointed. But those companions, without having checked, went to relieve themselves — both for defecation and urination — at the homes of respectable families, and that very fact became a source of censure. At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Those who have been appointed as companions to the monk teaching the Dharma must not go elsewhere without having checked with him first. If they do go, it becomes a serious offence."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī a brahmin had taken a wife from a family of equal birth, and he sported with her, took pleasure with her, and enjoyed pleasures together with her. Through their sporting and pleasuring and enjoyment of pleasures together, his wife came to be with child.

After nine months she gave birth to a boy. Once he was born, they held an elaborate birth celebration and gave him a name befitting his clan.

Then at another time that boy grew up and went forth into renunciation in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. While he was ill, his bodily condition being as it was, he went to a physician and said: "Good sir, given the present state of my body, please prescribe a treatment." The physician said: "Noble one, apply such-and-such a poultice and you will recover." He applied the poultice, and after bathing once he washed himself with cold water, and it broke open. The physician asked: "Noble one, did the poultice work well?" He replied: "Good sir, it did not work well — I bathed only once." The physician said: "Noble one, did you not wash with cold water?" He replied: "Good sir, I did exactly as you said." The physician said: "Noble one, you have done something harmful — if it breaks open from cold water, how can one bathe? That part is finished now, so apply that same poultice again, and this time complete the full bathing before washing, and wash with warm water."

He replied: "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted it."

The physician said: "Noble one, then how am I to perform the procedure for the poultice?"

At that point the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I grant permission: outer wrappings are to be placed on, and after completing the full bathing, one may wash." When the Blessed One had said that outer wrappings are to be used, the monks did not know what kinds of things to use as outer wrappings. The Blessed One declared: "Sponge, or leaves, or pieces of cloth may be used as outer wrappings; after completing the full bathing, one washes with warm water."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī.

Then at that same time there was a venomous snake living in a forest. At some point the herders set fire to that forest, and the venomous snake, scorched by the fire, moved back and forth but was encircled again by the light of the flames and lay there barely alive. Leaping free from where it had been burned, it coiled and wound itself at the foot of a tree.

At some point the Venerable Śāriputra was wandering through the countryside and drew near to that spot. He went to the foot of the tree and looked, and he saw a venomous snake scorched by fire, severely burned, worn down by the sensation of suffering. Upon seeing it, he examined whether there were any roots of virtue at all in its stream of being, and he saw that there were. He also examined under whose influence it would fall, and he determined that it would be under his own. He sprinkled water on it and spoke three Dharma phrases:

"Good friend, all conditioned things are impermanent. All phenomena are without self. Nirvāṇa is peace. Bring your mind into a state of complete clarity toward me, and thus, free from the attachment of animals, you will be reborn in a happy destiny."

Having said this, he departed. Immediately a hawk seized the snake. At that moment, with a mind of strong faith toward the Venerable Śāriputra, it passed away, and was reborn in Śrāvastī in the family of a brahmin endowed with the six qualities.

The Venerable Śāriputra reflected: "If that venomous snake passed away without interruption, where has it been reborn?" Examining it in a single moment, he saw that it had been reborn in Śrāvastī in the family of a brahmin endowed with the six qualities. Seeing this, he set out to go to that house in order to train it. Having gone there, he established both the brahmin and his wife in the going for refuge and in the foundation of the training.

Then at another time he went alone to that house, and the brahmin said to him:

"Noble one, is there no monk who will follow after me?" The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Venerable sir, would a monk who follows after you spring up from elsewhere like kuśa grass or kaśa reeds? No — one who is born from someone such as yourself will become the monk who follows after me." The brahmin said: "Noble one, I have no boy who will come to be a monk following after a noble one. But if a son is born to the one who accompanies me with this longing in her heart, I will offer him to the noble one as a monk who follows after you." Śāriputra replied: "May it be so — may she be well. Take this and go." So saying, he departed.

In due course, after nine months had passed, the brahmin's wife gave birth to a boy. Twenty-one days after his birth — three times seven days — a great birth celebration was held and he was given a name suited to his lineage. He was nourished and raised on milk, yogurt, fresh butter, clarified butter, and the finest essence of butter, along with other principal provisions of every kind, and he grew quickly, like a lotus dwelling in a lake. When he drank from his mother's breast, if ever through carelessness a tooth or fingernail touched the breast, it would swell. As he grew older and played together with other boys and girls, whenever he was seized by a fit of anger and bit or scratched one of them, that place would swell up before long without delay.

In time, the Venerable Śāriputra, knowing that the moment had come to ordain him, went to that house and taught the Dharma to the brahmin's wife. He showed a sign, saying: "This boy is the monk who will follow after me." The brahmin then said: "Son, even before you were born I had offered you to the Venerable Śāriputra as the monk who would follow after him — go!" That being of his last existence gazed for a long while at the face of the Venerable Śāriputra, then followed behind him step by step. At that time the Venerable Śāriputra gave him the going forth and conferred full ordination upon him.

Now, this monk ate a tooth-cleaning twig, and having chewed it, set it down without washing it. A fly ate from it and passed away at its appointed time. Then a house-cricket ate a little of what remained there and also passed away at its appointed time. Then various birds ate from it and they too passed away at their appointed time. Then a cat ate from it and that one also passed away at its appointed time. Then yet another fly and many ants ate from it and all of them likewise passed away at their appointed time.

While the many creatures lay there having passed away at their appointed times, the next day some monks began eating tooth-cleaning twigs in that spot. They saw the many creatures that had passed away and one of them said: "Venerable ones, why have all these many creatures died?" Others replied: "We do not know." As they were examining it thus, another young monk arrived and said: "Venerable ones, the one who went forth from a brahmin family in this region — the one who dwelt together with the Venerable Śāriputra — ate a tooth-cleaning twig, chewed it, and set it down without washing it. Many creatures ate from it, and having eaten the filth from the chewed end, they passed away." On that occasion the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there exist some people of harmful character such as this. Therefore, monks must not discard a tooth-cleaning twig unwashed in just that way. If it is discarded, it becomes an offence involving a breach." The Blessed One taught that after eating a tooth-cleaning twig it must be washed.

Some other monks found themselves with too little water and did not know how to proceed. The Blessed One declared: "Whoever has too little water should first rub the tooth-cleaning twig on the ground so that it is free of the residue of the tongue."

On another occasion someone had begun to do laundry, and having boiled cloth for dyeing, he was wringing and drying it. Just then the Venerable Ānanda came that way, and seeing what was happening, he said, "Venerable one, let me help you." The man replied, "Elder, please do well — Ānanda naturally goes about practicing depravity everywhere: he dries the new cloths in the shade, dries the old ones in the sun, and leaves the damp ones in the shade. Elder, do not act like that." The Venerable Ānanda did this again and again, but could not be stopped. The man, completely beside himself with fury, rushed at Ānanda, and Ānanda began to flee.

Just then the Venerable Śāriputra came that way and asked, "Venerable one, what are you doing, what are you doing?" But the man, now wrapped in rage that only grew, could not stay still and pursued Ānanda as he ran away. When Ānanda began striking him with a banyan branch, the man could not stand it. The Venerable Śāriputra stepped forward, restrained and caught hold of him, and let Ānanda escape — yet even so the man turned back to the banyan tree and devoured all its leaves.

On that occasion the monks heard of this and reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not give way to anger like that."

After the Blessed One had declared that one must not give way to anger like that, on yet another occasion a monk's duty assignment fell to Ānanda. He went to him and said, "Venerable one, a task of this sort has fallen — please do it," and at that very moment of seeing him, the man flew into that same all-consuming fury. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "One must not in person directly assign a task to someone who has anger and resentment of this kind. Instead, a monk who is sitting near that person should convey the instruction: he should say to him, 'You are to do such-and-such a task.' That monk should go up to the man, take hold of him, and say clearly, 'Do such-and-such a task.'"

The man then, with thorough earnestness and fierce diligent effort, came to know this very wheel of existence, fivefold, moving and unmoving, and fully comprehending that all conditioned things are subject to decay, to falling, to dispersion, and to destruction, he abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship. Free of attachment to the three realms, his mind was like stone and gold alike — equanimous toward both; like the sky and like the palm of the hand — unimpeded and open; not distinguishing sandalwood from mud, he was one whose wisdom had burst open the door-panel of ignorance. He attained the higher knowledges and the individual perfect discriminative awarenesses. He had turned his back on the gains, honors, and acquisitions of further existence and desire. And he became one to be venerated, revered, and spoken of with praise by the gods together with Indra and the god-lords of the celestial hosts.

The monks then said to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, it is remarkable that even this one who lived alongside you in such extreme anger has attained arhatship itself." He then related at length to those monks the events that had occurred previously in that person's past. The monks gave rise to doubt, and wishing to have all doubts resolved, they asked the awakened Blessed One: "Reverend one, what deed did this monk do such that he was born as a venomous snake?" The Blessed One declared:

"Monks, the karmic accumulation this monk obtained — actions done and gathered that will inevitably come to maturation, abiding close like a flame whose conditions have been fully transformed — will certainly arise. No one other than this very monk can separately experience the actions he himself did and gathered. Monks, actions done and gathered do not ripen in the outer element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind. Rather, they ripen in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases. As the verse says:

Even were it a hundred aeons,
actions do not perish;
when the conditions and the time arrive,
they bear their fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in former times, in this very good aeon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world — one perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. He dwelt in the forest of the Deer Park of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī. A certain person went forth from that one's teaching and came to be known as a monk called 'Abiding in Loving-kindness.' When the other monks addressed him again and again as 'Abiding in Loving-kindness, Abiding in Loving-kindness,' he could not bear to remain silent at their teasing, and being thoroughly consumed by fierce anger he uttered to them, with malicious intent, these harsh words: 'I am the one abiding in loving-kindness — you are vicious men!'"

The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, what do you think? That monk in the teaching of the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa who was called 'Abiding in Loving-kindness' — that was none other than this very monk. At that time, in that era, he called the disciples of the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa 'vicious men' and acted accordingly. Through the karmic maturation of that deed, he was born as a venomous snake for five hundred lifetimes. And even now, by the remaining residue of that very karma, he was born as this venomous snake. But in that same existence he received scriptural transmission, recited and chanted it, and became skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is not possible. Therefore, having gone forth in my teaching, he abandoned all afflictions and directly realized arhatship.

Therefore, monks, the karmic maturation of wholly dark deeds is wholly dark; the maturation of wholly bright deeds is wholly bright; and the maturation of mixed deeds is mixed. Therefore, monks, abandon wholly dark deeds and mixed deeds, and strive after wholly bright deeds. Monks, train yourselves accordingly."

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, those monks were delighted and praised what the Blessed One had said.

Summary verse:

The patched robes were divided according to what was fitting —
the hermit and the subsistence-seeker,
the one carrying a load who makes no sound, who does not eat —
Vārāṇasī was not his domain.

The awakened Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The monks divided patched robes and, making a rustling sound, used soft, gentle implements to smooth and press them. They urinated and defecated in the latrine areas, and additionally performed cooking and other such tasks, and in the same way wore both upper and lower garments. The monks said: "Venerable ones, these monks use these Dharma robes without discrimination."

The Blessed One had declared the patched robe to be the finest of Dharma robes. How then could they use this supreme patched Dharma robe without discrimination? Another spoke up: "What the venerable one has said is true. There must be a reason that has not yet come to light. It ought to be investigated." At that point the monks submitted the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, take as the basis for what these monks have said this: monks, the patched robe is like a king. Therefore, when wearing the patched robe, one must not perform all tasks. The Blessed One having declared that when wearing the patched robe one must not perform all tasks, the monks, having distributed the patched robes, did not know what they should do and what they should not do. At that point the monks submitted the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, when going to the alms round, when taking the first seat at a meal, when paying respects at a stūpa, when receiving the Teacher's scriptural transmission and listening to it individually, when listening to the Dharma by day, when listening to the Dharma by night, when sitting in assembly to eat, when paying respects to the preceptor and the master, and furthermore when sitting together with those who keep the celibate life — at those times you shall put on the patched robe. The upper garment shall be put on neatly and in good order, and all tasks performed. The lower garment may be used freely as one pleases." The occasion of this instruction was at Śrāvastī.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, the sun has risen. The crow is cawing. The farmers are ploughing their fields. The bandits are weeping. Monks, 'the sun has risen' is a code phrase for the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha. 'The crow is cawing' is a code phrase for those persons who teach the Dharma. 'The farmers are ploughing their fields' is a code phrase for the donors and the givers. 'The bandits are weeping' is a code phrase for the host of Māra. Monks, the Teacher — whoever he is — acts out of loving care for the hearers, delighting in benefiting them out of compassion. I look upon you with compassion, and so what you must do is this: in forest hermitages, at the roots of trees, in empty houses, on mountains, in mountain retreats, in mountain caves, on seats of straw, in the open air, in charnel grounds, in forest groves, and in lodgings at the far edge of the wilderness, engage in meditative concentration. Monks, do not be heedless, and do not later come to regret it. This is my teaching." The Blessed One having said, "Monks, remain heedful and meditate in such lodgings," the monks set about meditating in the lodgings as they had been taught. Now, there was one monk of little learning who went off to a hermitage and sat there, not coming into the village in the evening and remaining in that same place during the day except at the time of the alms round. The cowherd, the livestock herder, the grass-cutter, the wood-cutter, those who lived by the road, and those who lived by the side roads all came to know of his dwelling there.

Then, at another time, some bandits went to raid another village by the rocky crags. There they beat and thoroughly thrashed the people, sacked the place, and fled it. Going off in another direction, they consulted together: "Wise ones, tell us — which direction should we head and where should we go?" At that one of them said, "I am severely wounded and cannot walk." Another said, "I am thirsty." Another said, "I am hungry."

Another among them said, "Wise ones, in this direction there dwells a monk, a son of the Śākyas. This son of the Śākyas is learned and compassionate, and in that hermitage there is nothing to fear. If you are willing, wise ones, let us go there." To this they agreed, saying, "Very well, wise ones — come then, let us go there." And so, like elephants lifting their trunks, they roused their hopes and made their way gradually to his presence. When they arrived, he greeted them with every word of genuine and heartfelt welcome, saying, "Have you come well?" They were greatly gladdened, and their minds grew quite at ease. They sat for a while, then spoke: "Noble one, we are stricken with cold — is there perhaps a little fire?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." Another said, "We are thirsty — is there perhaps a little water?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "Noble one, is there perhaps a little powder to dress our wounds?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "Noble one, is there perhaps a little cloth suitable for binding wounds?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "Is there perhaps a little butter to dress the wounds?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." "We are hungry — is there perhaps some cooked rice or hot porridge?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "What is today's date, what is the lunar day, what constellation prevails, and which day of the week is it?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." Then one among them, who knew the conduct of monks and who had examined the matter from all sides, said, "Noble one, since that is so, let me ask you this. Tell me first — are you an arhat, or a once-returner, or a non-returner, or a stream-enterer?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "Noble one, since that is so, let us ask you something else. Have you attained the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or the sense base of nothingness, or the sense base of infinite consciousness, or the sense base of infinite space, or the fourth dhyāna, or the third dhyāna, or the second dhyāna, or the first dhyāna?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "Noble one, since that is so — are you a master of the Three Baskets, or do you hold the Sūtra collection, or do you hold the Vinaya, or do you hold the Mātṛkā?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "Since that is so, let us ask you yet another thing — what is your name?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." They said, "Noble one, which direction is this?" He replied, "I am a forest-dweller." And so in every respect and in every matter he answered only, "I am a forest-dweller." Thereupon they grew extremely angry and said, "Wise ones, are we the thieves here? This is the real thief — one who does not even know his own name, who clings to a mere outward sign, and who deceives the world!" Intolerant of him, they beat him savagely. They smashed his begging bowl and staff, tore his Dharma-robe, and left him barely alive. Then that very night they departed in that direction.

When dawn broke, he made his way to the Jeta Grove in just that wretched and pitiable condition. The monks saw him and asked, "Venerable one, who left you in such a state? Tell us in detail exactly what happened." He then recounted everything in full. At that point the monks informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: Rules of conduct are to be established for forest-dwelling monks. A forest-dwelling monk must always keep a fire lit. He must carry a small amount of flour. He must keep clean cloths on hand. He must also keep on hand both any grain he has and leftover cooked food that has been eaten from. He must be knowledgeable about the stars, the reckoning of dates, and the sun. He must know the directions. He must know his own range of travel. He must keep water on hand. He must carry a small amount of oil and grain oil. He must be knowledgeable in sūtra, in Vinaya, in the Mātṛkā, and at minimum in pleasant speech. A forest-dwelling monk who does not properly uphold and practice the rules of conduct thus established for his way of life will have committed a serious offense. The origin of this ruling is in Śrāvastī.

Now there was a certain householder living in Śrāvastī who on another occasion fell ill. He went to a physician and asked for a diagnosis and treatment. The physician said to him, "Noble one, bathe in a hot-spring bath and you will recover." The man replied, "Good physician, I live by going on alms-rounds. How will I manage to get to a hot spring?" The physician said, "Noble one, the mendicant Śākya-sons bathe twice a month. Go there and take a bath." So the man began to go for a bath, and when he entered among the monks, he had put on a robe with the red-earth color turned to face outward, so all the monks assumed he too was a monk and no one stopped him. He quickly finished his bath, then sat there feeling unwell. After some time a group of monks came to that spot. When they saw him, one among them with a settled mind said, "Venerable ones, there is an elder monk sitting here — let him bathe." The others said, "Good, let it be so." They went to him and said, "Elder, come here and bathe." He shook his head, and they took him by the shoulder and helped him up. He then said, "Impure people who have not bathed are touching one who has already bathed — monks who are Śākya-sons." They replied, "We are the mendicant Śākya-sons. Who are you, to be like an elder monk?" He said, "I am a householder." They said, "Well then, householder, who gave you a bath?" — and at that point the monks reported this to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is therefore the case that when monks are bathing at the hot-spring bath, door-wardens are to be stationed, and those monks who enter from outside are to be asked their names." When they began asking monks for their names, the Blessed One then declared: "Do not ask for the names of monks who are known to you."

When the Blessed One Śākyamuni was touring the Kosala country and had arrived at Anupiya, he stayed in the Anupiya forest at Anupiya.

Now at that time a brahmin named Padmahṛdaya had been given by Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, a brahmin's benefice grant consisting of grass, wood, and water, and he enjoyed that great and prosperous property. Padmahṛdaya the brahmin had a student, a young brahmin called Maṣu, who was learned, of clear speech, and of unobstructed understanding. Padmahṛdaya the brahmin would instruct approximately five hundred brahmin youths in the recitation of brahmin sacred formularies.

Padmahṛdaya the brahmin had heard of the renown, the fame, the report, and the far-reaching praise of the wise Gautama — that the contemplative Gautama, son of the Śākyas, born of the Śākya clan, had shaved his hair and beard, put on saffron-coloured robes, and gone forth from home into homelessness out of pure and genuine faith, and had then fully awakened to the unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening; that this Blessed One Gautama is the Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassable guide of persons to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, an awakened and blessed one; that in this very visible teaching he, by his own direct knowledge, directly realised and accomplished the ending of his defilements: "My defilements are exhausted. I have dwelt in the holy life. What was to be done has been done. I know no further becoming beyond this." That his Dharma, too, is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end — of excellent meaning, excellent in word, unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, perfectly refined — and that it thoroughly reveals the holy life. This renown had also spread from the sacred brahmin formularies themselves, which say that a great man endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man can go one of only two ways: if he remains a householder, he will become a wheel-turning king who conquers in all four directions, a righteous king, a dharma-king possessed of the seven precious treasures. These seven precious treasures are as follows: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious woman, the precious householder, and the seventh is the precious minister. Such a king will have brave and valiant sons, splendid in their limbs, who will utterly defeat enemy forces; and the great earth extending to the ocean's edge will be his possession without division, free from annoyance and without violence, established well and securely in accordance with Dharma, and governed evenly. But if he shaves his hair and beard, puts on saffron-coloured robes, and goes forth from home into homelessness out of pure and genuine faith, he will become one renowned throughout the world as a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha.

He had heard that this one had toured the Kosala country and departed, had come to Anupiya, and was dwelling in the Anupiya forest at Anupiya.

Having heard this, Padmahṛdaya the brahmin said to the young brahmin Maṣu: "Maṣu, do you know? I have heard it said that the contemplative Gautama, son of the Śākyas, born of the Śākya clan, shaved his hair and beard, put on saffron-coloured robes, and went forth from home into homelessness out of pure and genuine faith" — and everything up to "he will become one renowned throughout the world" — "and I myself have drawn this from the sacred formularies: that a great man endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man can go one of only two ways: if he remains a householder he will become a wheel-turning king who conquers in all four directions" — and everything up to "he will become one renowned throughout the world" — "and that he has toured the Kosala country and departed, has come to Anupiya, and is dwelling in the Anupiya forest at Anupiya."

Having heard this, the brahmin youth Ambastha was told: "Go, young brahmin, to where the wise one Gautama is. Go and find out whether his virtue, renown, reputation, and the great verses of praise that have spread in all directions and to every quarter are exactly as reported or not, and whether the marks attributed to him are accurate or not."

The brahmin youth Ambastha listened to the brahmin Pokkharasāti and set out from the larger settlement accompanied by a great number of senior brahmins. He went to where the Blessed One was and, having arrived, sat down to one side. The senior brahmins then exchanged various pleasant and courteous words with the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Once they were seated, the Blessed One gave the senior brahmins a proper discourse on the Dharma, led them to take it up rightly, roused them to enthusiasm, and gladdened them thoroughly.

While the Blessed One was giving the senior brahmins this discourse on the Dharma, the brahmin youth Ambastha was walking about with his sandals on and breaking into the conversation with sudden remarks, refusing to stay until the topic was concluded — arrogant, disrespectful, and minded to contradict.

Then the Blessed One said this to the brahmin youth Ambastha: "Young brahmin, is it your habit to talk so abruptly like this in company with the three-knowledge brahmins?
