Or tell me, Gautama, what sort of talk is this — that while the Tathāgata is giving a Dharma discourse to the senior brahmins, you walk about with your sandals on, break in with sudden remarks, refuse to stay until the topic is concluded, and stand there arrogant, disrespectful, and minded to contradict?

"Young brahmin, those brahmins who walk — walk together with other walkers. Those who stand — stand together with other standers. Those who sit — sit together with other sitters. Those who lie down — lie down together with others who lie down. They speak well to one another. As for those shaven-headed ascetics, those dark-limbed menials born of Brahma's foot — with them it is fitting to hold such a sudden casual conversation, just as one might talk with the wise one Gautama now.

"Young brahmin, you have come here in pursuit of a purpose. Such lack of respect as this — no one else has shown it. Indeed, the brahmin youth Ambastha has shown no respect to the assembly of teachers."

When the Blessed One reproached the brahmin youth Ambastha with these words of disrespect, Ambastha became angry, agitated, and furious, his mind displeased. He wanted to rebuke the Blessed One, to be bold against him, to dispute with him, to call him to account, thinking: "With this alone I shall rebuke, be bold against, dispute with, and call to account the ascetic Gautama." Realizing this, the Blessed One spoke:

"Listen now, Gautama — these Śākyas are mere upstarts, upstarts by lineage. They do not show brahmins honor, respect, deference, or veneration. Does that mean, young brahmin, that the Śākyas have done you even the slightest harm?

"Indeed, Gautama, there was once an occasion when I and my preceptor went to the Śākya settlement of Kapilavatthu. There, the Śākyas and the Śākya maidens went up onto their fine upper terraces and pointed at me with their fingers, saying: 'That is Ambastha, the brahmin youth, pupil of the brahmin Pokkharasāti! That is Ambastha, the brahmin youth, pupil of the brahmin Pokkharasāti!' They pointed at me with nothing but their fingers; they did not show me honor, respect, deference, or veneration."

"Young brahmin, even a nestling sparrow chirps as it pleases in its own nest — so what need is there even to speak of the Śākyas? Young brahmin, the settlement of Kapilavatthu is the Śākyas' own. Gautama, there are four castes: brahmin, noble warrior, merchant, and commoner. These four castes all show honor, respect, deference, and veneration to the brahmins. But these Śākyas are upstarts — they are of upstart lineage — and so they show no honor, no respect, no deference, and no veneration to the brahmins."

Then the Blessed One thought to himself: "Ah, this disagreeable young brahmin is making such extravagant claims against the Śākyas — 'the Śākyas are upstarts, the Śākyas are of upstart lineage!' Let me therefore search out this young brahmin's ancestral lineage." And as the Blessed One searched out the ancestral lineage of the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, he saw that Ambaṭṭha was in fact the son of a slave woman of the Śākyas, and that the Śākyas were the sons of his masters.

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha: "Young brahmin, what is your lineage?"

"Gautama, I am the son of Icchanangala."

"Young brahmin, when your ancestral lineage is traced back from here, you are the son of a slave woman of the Śākyas, and the Śākyas are the sons of your masters — that is what I see."

Vinaya — the Minor Matters. The Forty-Sixth Bundle.

Then the senior brahmins said this to the Blessed One: "Gautama, please do not speak the word 'son of a slave woman' to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha. Why? Because the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is learned, eloquent, and speaks without hesitation. Moreover, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is confident that he can reply to the wise Gautama on this matter in a way that accords with the Dharma. Brahmins, if you think that the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is capable of giving a reply that accords with the Dharma, then say nothing yourselves and let the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha reply to him on this matter in a way that accords with the Dharma. Brahmins, if you think that the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha cannot give me a reply that accords with the Dharma on this matter, then let the young brahmin say nothing and let you, the learned ones, obtain from me a reply that accords with the Dharma on this matter. Gautama, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha himself is indeed learned, eloquent, and speaks without hesitation. The young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is confident that he can reply to the wise Gautama on this matter in a way that accords with the Dharma — it is not the case that others cannot."

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha: "Young brahmin, long ago there was a king named Okkāka. King Okkāka had four sons: Starface, Handear, Tamed by the Elephant, and Ornamented Feet. King Okkāka banished them for some offense or other, and they each took their own sisters and, leaving behind one territory and city after another, gradually went to a region near the Himalayas, to the bank of the river by the auspicious sal tree grove, not far from Kapilavatthu. There they made shelters from branches and leaves, and dwelt and settled there. There, in that place, they took their own sisters as wives, and —

in that place, setting aside the elder sisters, they lived together and settled there with the younger sisters. Living and dwelling there, they bore sons and daughters.

Then at another time, King Okkāka, remembering those beloved youths, spoke to his ministers: "Good people, where did those young men go?" The gods be praised — those youths were banished for some offense or other, and they took their own sisters and went from one territory and city to another, and gradually settled near the Himalayas by the bank of the river by the auspicious sal tree grove, bearing sons and daughters and dwelling there.

Then King Okkāka said to his ministers: "Good people, were those youths truly capable of this?" — "Indeed they were, Your Majesty!" Then King Okkāka bared his upper body, stretched out his right hand, and with a solemn utterance proclaimed: "Oh! Those youths were supremely capable!" — and by this cry, which resounded as far as beings of great power dwell — "Oh! Those youths were capable!" — this saying became a word, and they came to be known as "Śākya, Śākya."

Young brahmin, have you heard even a little of how it is that the Śākyas trace their origin to this and that this is the lineage and line of descent from which they come?

"O Gautama, I have indeed heard that the Śākyas trace their origin to this and that this is the lineage and line of descent from which they come."

Young brahmin, King Okkāka had a slave woman named Ngophödma — Dishnī by name — who was beautiful, lovely, and fair to behold. She came together with a man of the outcast sage lineage, and from their union together a son was born. The moment the boy was born, his mother said: "Wrap me for a while, and wash him, and free him from impurity." Then at another time, the Unblinking Ones — the rākṣasas — said, the moment the boy was born, in words: "Wrap me for a while and free him from impurity, and — oh! — a son of the Unblinking One has been born!" And so he came to be known as "Son of the Unblinking One, Son of the Unblinking One."

Young brahmin, have you heard even a little of how it is that the Sons of the Unblinking One trace their origin to this and that this is the lineage and line of descent from which they come?

When this was said, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha remained silent and said nothing. A second time, and a third time, the Blessed One said these very words to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha: "Young brahmin, have you heard even a little of how it is that the Sons of the Unblinking One trace their origin to this and that this is the lineage and line of descent from which they come?"

A second time and a third time, the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha said nothing at all.

Then the yakṣa (yakṣa) Vajrapāṇi, holding aloft a vajra blazing, fiercely blazing, blazing all around, burning with a single tongue of flame, stood over the head of the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, thinking: "If the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, having been asked by the Blessed One three times in succession, still plugs his ears and refuses to answer, may this vajra blazing, fiercely blazing, blazing all around, burning with a single tongue of flame split his head into seven pieces!"

The Blessed One saw Vajrapāṇi, and by the power of the Buddha the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha also saw him. Then the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, terrified and with his hair standing on end, said this to the Blessed One: "O Gautama, it is indeed so — the Sons of the Unblinking One trace their origin to this and this is

their lineage — that is what I have heard."

Then the elder brahmins and the householders who were present thought to themselves: "If what the venerable Gautama has said is true — that the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is the son of a slave woman and that the Śākyas are the sons of her masters — then we have simply failed to believe the wise Gautama when he spoke."

Then the Blessed One addressed the elder brahmins and the householders, saying: "You must not speak so harshly to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha as to call him the son of a slave woman. For at that time there was a great and mighty sage of great supernatural power, and King Okkāka had him expelled on account of some minor offense. A brahmin penalty was imposed upon him. And when that brahmin penalty had been imposed, King Okkāka, seized with terror and fright, his hair standing on end, took a great lady adorned with all her ornaments by the left hand and held a golden water-pot in his right hand, and offered her to that sage as a wife. But the sage did not accept her."

Then, because the Blessed One had declared in words that the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha was the son of a slave woman, Ambaṭṭha sank down in shame, hunched his shoulders, bowed his head, lost his composure, fell into deep consternation, and sat there without saying a word. The Blessed One thought: "Since I have spoken the words declaring that this young brahmin Ambaṭṭha is the son of a slave woman, he has sunk down in shame, hunched his shoulders, bowed his head, lost his composure, fallen into deep consternation, and will not speak. He will not rise from this — let me engage him further in conversation." And so the Blessed One addressed the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha with these words:

"Young brahmin, consider this example. Suppose a young man of the warrior caste (kṣatriya) and a brahmin girl were to come together, and a son were born from that union. Would that son receive a seat, water, or the secret words, or the recitation, from the brahmins? O Gautama, yes, he would receive them. And would he receive the anointing of the warrior caste from the warriors? O Gautama, yes, he would receive it. And why? Because he is the nephew — for this reason the warriors anoint the nephew with the warrior anointing.

"Young brahmin, consider another example. Suppose a young brahmin and a girl of the warrior caste were to come together, and a son were born from that union. Would that son receive a seat, water, or the secret words, or the recitation, from the brahmins? O Gautama, yes, he would receive them. And would he receive the warrior anointing from the warriors? O Gautama, yes, he would receive it. And why? Because he is the nephew — for this reason the warriors anoint the nephew with the warrior anointing.

"Young brahmin, consider yet another example. Suppose a young man of the warrior caste were expelled by the warriors on account of some minor offense. Would he receive a seat, water, or the secret words, or the recitation, from the brahmins? O Gautama, yes, he would receive them. And would he receive the warrior anointing from the warriors? O Gautama, yes, he would receive it. And why? Because he is a brother — for this reason the warriors anoint a brother with the warrior anointing.

"Young brahmin, consider yet another example. Suppose a young brahmin were expelled by the brahmins on account of some minor offense. Would he receive a seat, water, or the secret words, or the recitation, from the brahmins? O Gautama, no, he would not receive them. Would he receive the warrior anointing from the warriors? O Gautama, no, he would not receive it. And why? Because a brahmin is an outcaste — for this reason the warriors do not anoint a brahmin with the warrior anointing."

"Young brahmin, in that case, by blood, lineage, and oath, the warrior caste is supreme — not the brahmins."

The lord of the Mithilā brahmins, Brahmā, then spoke these verses:

Whoever stands connected by blood,
the warrior caste is most honored among two-legged beings.
Among gods and humans alike,
one endowed with lineage and virtue is most honored.

The young brahmin said that what the lord of the Mithilā brahmins, Brahmā, had spoken in verse was well spoken, not ill spoken; rightly expressed, not wrongly expressed. And so it was:

Whoever stands connected by blood,
the warrior caste is most honored among two-legged beings.
Among gods and humans alike,
one endowed with lineage and virtue is most honored.

"And why? Young brahmin, I myself once said these words:

Whoever stands connected by blood,
the warrior caste is most honored among two-legged beings.
Among gods and humans alike,
one endowed with lineage and virtue is most honored.

Young brahmin, what do you think? In a place where brides are taken and given in marriage, do the brahmins receive a seat, water, secret words, or recitation from there?"

"O Gautama, in a place where brides are taken and given in marriage, indeed the brahmins do receive a seat, water, secret words, and recitation from there."

"Young brahmin, in a place where brides are taken and given in marriage, there is pride of lineage, there is pride of blood, and there is pride of brahminhood.

Young brahmin, all those sentient beings who are bound by pride of lineage, bound by pride of blood, and bound by pride of brahminhood — so long as they have not directly realized this unsurpassed science endowed with virtue, they have no fortune to directly realize it. But a brahmin's son who has abandoned pride of lineage, abandoned pride of blood, and abandoned pride of brahminhood — he will come to directly realize this unsurpassed science endowed with virtue that he has not yet directly realized.

I myself, O wise Gautama, have never before encountered, nor shall encounter hereafter, nor do I now encounter anything like unto this — I am filled with conviction. O wise Gautama, please teach the Dharma to me in such a way that I may come to be endowed with science and virtue."

"Young brahmin, therefore listen well, attend carefully, and I shall teach."

"Young brahmin, the Teacher — the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with science and virtue, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed guide of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Blessed One — has appeared in this world. He teaches the Dharma that is good at the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end, with noble meaning and noble words, unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and thoroughly clarified — and he reveals the holy life. A householder or a householder's son hears that Dharma. Having heard that Dharma, he attains genuine faith. Possessed of that genuine faith, he reflects thus: 'The household life is confined and dusty; going forth is unsurpassed. While dwelling in a home, it is difficult to live the holy life in a way that is singular, bright, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and thoroughly clarified for as long as one lives. Let me shave off hair and beard, don the saffron-colored robes, and go forth from home into homelessness out of genuine faith alone.' And so, having thus reflected and examined, he abandons his many goods and possessions and his circle of relatives, shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron-colored robes, and, going forth from home into homelessness out of genuine faith alone, he takes up residence in moral discipline. He is restrained by the vows of individual liberation (Skt. pratimokṣa)."

He is one of proper conduct and perfect comportment, seeing danger in even the subtlest transgression. He undertakes and trains in the bases of training. Having abandoned the taking of life, he has turned back from the taking of life: he has renounced violence, renounced weapons, and is possessed of conscientious shame. Toward all sentient beings — toward every creature — even down to the smallest living thing, even a worm or an ant, he has turned back from the taking of life.

Having abandoned taking what is not given, he has turned back from taking what is not given. He accepts only what is given, he rejoices in accepting what is given, and he rejoices in freely releasing through generosity. He is no thief; he is not one of great craving; he is pure, he is open-handed, he is blameless, and by guarding himself he has turned back from taking what is not given.

Having abandoned unchaste conduct, he has turned back from unchaste conduct. He is one who lives a chaste life; pure through abandoning base conduct, he is clean, free from foul odor, free from coupling, free from the ways of the lower region, and has turned back from unchaste conduct.

Having abandoned false speech, he has turned back from false speech. He speaks truthfully, he delights in truth, he is faithful, trustworthy, and steadfast, not a deceiver of the world, and he has turned back from false speech.

Having abandoned divisive speech, he has turned back from divisive speech. What he has heard on this side he does not repeat to those on that side in order to divide them; what he has heard on that side he does not repeat to those on this side in order to divide them. He reconciles those who are divided, encourages those who are in harmony, delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, and speaks words that bring about harmony — and thus he has turned back from divisive speech.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he has turned back from harsh speech. He abandons any such words that are harmful and rough, unpleasant to others, offensive to others, unacceptable to the minds of many people, disagreeable to the hearts of many people, displeasing to many people, unwelcome to the minds of many people, not peaceful, and not conducive to settling the mind in peace. Instead he speaks such words as are inoffensive, pleasant to the ear, satisfying to the heart, delightful, like the sound of a royal court assembly, melodious and sweet, clear and distinct, worth listening to, not contrary to what one relies upon, boundless, dear to many people, pleasing to many people, delightful to many people, welcome to the minds of many people, peaceful, and conducive to settling the mind in peace — and thus he has turned back from harsh speech.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he has turned back from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, he speaks truthfully, he speaks about suchness, he speaks about what is meaningful, he speaks about the Dharma, he speaks with certainty, he speaks about what can be understood, and he speaks words that lead to comprehension. What he says is timely, has a basis and a point of reference, is accompanied by purpose and reason, is grounded in the Dharma — and thus he has abandoned idle chatter and turned back from idle chatter.

Having abandoned fraudulent trading, he has turned back from fraudulent trading. He has abandoned falsifying measures of volume, falsifying scales, and falsifying measures of weight, and he has turned back from falsifying measures of volume, scales, and measures of weight.

He has abandoned taking bribes, embezzlement, and seizing things by force and making them his own, and he has turned back from taking bribes, embezzlement, and seizing things by force and making them his own.

He has abandoned the intention to kill, to bind, to cut, to stab, and to beat, and he has turned back from the intention to kill, to bind, to cut, to stab, and to beat.

He has abandoned lying down together with one who has a light and with a woman, and he has turned back from lying down together with one who has a light and with a woman.

He has abandoned taking plots of farmland, plots for houses, and plots for shops, and he has turned back from taking plots of farmland, plots for houses, and plots for shops.

He has abandoned taking elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, fowl, and pigs, and he has turned back from taking elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, fowl, and pigs.

He has abandoned taking male slaves, female slaves, workers, and those who subsist on whey, and he has turned back from taking male slaves, female slaves, workers, and those who subsist on whey.

He has abandoned taking women, men, boys, and girls, and he has turned back from taking women, men, boys, and girls.

He has abandoned taking gold and silver, and he has turned back from taking gold and silver.

He has abandoned taking undamaged grain, and he has turned back from taking undamaged grain.

He eats but one meal a day, having relinquished eating in the evening and relinquished eating food at an improper time. He is devoted to practice at the proper time and to engagement at the proper time. He is content and knows his measure with robes sufficient for the body. He is content and knows his measure with alms food sufficient to fill his belly. Because he is content and knows his measure with robes sufficient for the body, and content and knows his measure with alms food sufficient to fill his belly, wherever he goes he goes carrying only his bowl and his robes. Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies carrying only its feathers and its wings — so too he is content and knows his measure with robes sufficient for the body, content and knows his measure with alms food sufficient to fill his belly, and wherever he goes he goes carrying only his bowl and his robes.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves with diligence to undertaking various kinds of seed-collections and plant-collections in the following manner: root seeds, stem seeds, node seeds, cutting seeds, and fifth, seed-seeds. From such application and diligence on the part of ascetics and brahmins in undertaking various kinds of seed-collections and plant-collections, he has turned back.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves with diligence to undertaking various kinds of storing, in the following manner: storing food, storing drink, storing cloth, storing fragrance, storing flavors, storing leaves, storing flowers, and storing fruits. From such application and diligence on the part of ascetics and brahmins in undertaking various kinds of storing, he has turned back.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves with diligence to acquiring high seats and great furnishings, and who dwell in the following manner: cushioned seats, thrones, thrones with wool coverings, thrones with cotton coverings, seats with inner padding, great lengths of cloth, variegated cloth, cloth woven with pālelā fiber, elephant battle-mats, horse battle-mats, single-sided wool, double-sided wool, fleece-wool,

wool worked from the back, coverings of Kāliṅga cloth, cloth with upper covers, cloth worked with red dye on both sides — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in acquiring high seats and great furnishings in just such ways.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves with diligence to acquiring various kinds of adornments and accessories, and who dwell in the following manner: massaging and bathing, rubbing and anointing, garlands and perfumes, unguents and cosmetics, coloring of nails, coloring of teeth, mouth-powder, face-scrubbing, gazing into mirrors, adorning the hands with bangles, binding the topknot, parasol-handles with fringe, swords, yak-tail fans with jeweled handles, embroidered slippers, new cloth, and fresh cotton cloth with long edges to be worn and carried — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in applying themselves to acquiring various kinds of adornments and accessories in just such ways.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves with diligence to attending various kinds of spectacles, and who dwell in the following manner: elephant fights, horse fights, chariot fights, contests with young soldiers, fights with staves, fights with fists, contests among champion bulls, buffalo fights, ram fights, cock fights, fights of quail, fights among boars, fights between women, fights between men, fights between young men, fights between young women, climbing trees, gatherings for song and dance, leaping from shoulders, the tops of victory banners, the foremost feats of strength, viewing large armies, and desiring to see large assemblies — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in applying themselves to attending various kinds of spectacles in just such ways.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves with diligence to listening to various kinds of sounds, and who dwell in the following manner: the sounds of elephants, the sounds of horses, the sounds of chariots, the sounds of young soldiers, the sound of conches, the sound of paṭaha drums, the sound of great drums, the sounds of various musical instruments, the singing voice of dancers, the sounds of music, the sound of cymbals, the sound of bells, the sound of clapping hands, the sound of vases being struck, the sound of amateur performances, poetry, various writings, various words, and desiring to hear the talk of fame connected with proclamations of the world — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in applying themselves to listening to various kinds of sounds in just such ways.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves with diligence to games of dice, gambling, and sports, and who dwell in the following manner: boards with eight squares, boards with ten squares, the eye of nāya, contests from all sides, pot-games, trials of strength, walking-games, bouncing games, sports, dice, substitution-moves, needle-games, hand-ornament games, and contests played with pieces inserted in various ways — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in applying themselves to games of dice, gambling, and sports in just such ways.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith,

consume, living on food given out of faith, apply themselves to composing various kinds of talk — that is to say, talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of armies, talk of food, talk of drink, talk of clothing, talk of marketplaces, talk of courtesans, talk of bad roads, talk of seas, talk of lands and great continents — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in applying themselves to composing various kinds of such talk.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, dwell applying themselves to engaging in various kinds of dispute, such as: "I know this Dharma and discipline thoroughly. You do not know this Dharma and discipline. As I know this Dharma and discipline in full, so you do not know this Dharma and discipline in full. My position is consistent with reason; yours is not. My position is relevant; yours is not. You said last what ought to have been said first, and said first what ought to have been said last. You spoke too quickly and your point was not answered. You have been defeated in argument and your case has been overthrown — abandon that statement you made in the course of argument! If you think you can counter it, ask and speak!" — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in applying themselves to engaging in various kinds of such dispute.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, earn their livelihood by the wrong means of carrying and delivering messages — acting as messengers for kings, or for great ministers, or for brahmins, or for householders, or for townspeople, or for country-folk, or for merchants, or for caravan leaders, carrying messages hence thither and leading the way, and carrying messages thither back hence — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in earning their livelihood by such wrong means of carrying and delivering messages.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, engage in dissembling, flattery, canvassing, and measuring gain to gain further gain — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in engaging in such dissembling, flattery, canvassing, and measuring gain to gain further gain.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, earn their livelihood by the wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading — that is: reading of violent weather, reading of birthmarks, reading of dream signs, reading of burns from fire, reading of contact with water, reading of marks left by mice, making of auspicious offerings, reciting of pleasing words, reading the sounds of all manner of spirits, reading of bodily signs, reading of house-sites, reading of fields, reading of birds, reading of finger-signs, and the making of various applications — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in earning their livelihood by such wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, earn their livelihood by the wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading — that is: making of momentary conjunctions, reading of the rising of constellations, examination of portents of all kinds, performance of pacifying rites, performance of enriching rites, performance of fierce rites,

performance of fire-offering rites, recitation of syllables, calculation of astrological charts, counting of numbers, finger-reckoning, and examination by mirror — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in earning their livelihood by such wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, earn their livelihood by the wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading — that is: the practice of healing examination, the giving of root medicines, the giving of eye medicines, the giving of emetics, the giving of medicines, the examination of women, the examination of men, the examination of boys, the examination of girls, and the application of medicinal treatments — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in earning their livelihood by such wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, earn their livelihood by the wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading — that is: reading the marks of precious gems, reading the marks of staffs, reading the marks of swords, reading the marks of arrows, reading the marks of weapons, reading the marks of elephants, reading the marks of horses, reading the marks of excellent bulls, reading the marks of buffaloes, reading the marks of goats, reading the marks of sheep, reading the marks of roosters, reading the marks of tortoises, reading the marks of hares, reading the marks of women, reading the marks of men, reading the marks of youths, reading the marks of maidens, reading the signs of a short life, reading the signs of a long life, reading the signs of little fortune, reading the signs of great fortune, reading the signs of little merit, reading the signs of great merit, reading the signs of little power, reading the signs of great power, reading the marks of masters, and reading the marks of servants — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in earning their livelihood by such wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, earn their livelihood by the wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading — that is: the simultaneous purging of medicinal food upward and downward, purging by means of swelling, the administration of enemas, inducing vomiting, purgation downward, nasal infusions, inhalation of smoke, procedures involving bile, examination of phlegm, examination of the stomach, examination of moles, examination of eyes that are underdeveloped, divination by the circling of deer, divination by the circling of crows, examining the movement of the shoulder blades, determining by taste with the tongue, and the application of procedures involving corpses and half-corpses — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in earning their livelihood by such wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who, living on food given out of faith, earn their livelihood by the wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading — that is: summoning spirits, full summoning, particular summoning, causing bewilderment, full bewilderment, particular bewilderment, bringing about scattering and destruction, causing well-being, causing suffering, causing conception in the womb, fire-offerings with sesame, fire-offerings with rice, fire-offerings with butter, fire-offerings with substances, fire-offerings of the fire-offering itself, paying homage to the sun, paying homage to the stars, paying homage to the gods, and paying homage to the great objects of veneration — he has turned back from the diligence of ascetics and brahmins in earning their livelihood by such wrong means of the debased arts of omen-reading.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who,

living off the full use of what was given in faith and sustaining themselves through the debased livelihood of the crooked arts of omen-reading — namely: predicting that there will be danger, predicting that there will be well-being, predicting that the harvest will be poor, predicting that the harvest will be good, predicting that rainfall will be scarce, predicting that rainfall will be plentiful, predicting that epidemic disease will arise, predicting that epidemic disease will not arise. He has turned back from such a debased livelihood of the crooked arts as is practiced by ascetics and brahmins.

The forty-seventh fascicle of the minor bases of Vinaya.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who live off the full use of what was given in faith and sustain themselves through the debased livelihood of the crooked arts of omen-reading — namely: predicting that the inner king will be victorious and the outer king will be defeated, that the outer king will be victorious and the inner king will be defeated, that the inner king will flee and the outer king will advance, that the outer king will flee and the inner king will advance. He has turned back from such a debased livelihood of sustaining oneself through the crooked arts.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who live off the full use of what was given in faith and sustain themselves through the debased livelihood of the crooked arts of omen-reading — namely: predicting from such occurrences as the sun and moon straying from their courses; the path of the sun through a planetary conjunction; the path of the moon through a planetary conjunction; the falling of meteors; the appearance of lights on the horizon; the blazing of lights on the horizon; the drumming of the gods in the sky; the sun not being in conjunction with a planet; the moon not being in conjunction with a planet; the falling of meteors; the appearance of lights on the horizon; the blazing of lights on the horizon; the drumming of the gods in the sky; how the sun and moon, being of such great magic power and great might, rise on such a path or stray from the path, set on such a path or set from other than the path — and when the path is thus, predicting what will be affliction and what will be purification. He has turned back from such a debased livelihood of sustaining oneself through the crooked arts.

O friend, there are also certain ascetics and brahmins who live off the full use of what was given in faith and sustain themselves through the debased livelihood of the crooked arts of omen-reading — teaching such things as: if the sun and moon stray from their course in such a way, such and such a karmic maturation will result; such a karmic maturation of such a kind arises when solar and lunar conjunctions are entered in such a way, when meteors fall, when lights appear on the horizon, when lights blaze on the horizon, when the gods drum in the sky, the maturation will ripen in such a form; the sun and moon, being of such great magic power and great might, rise on such a path and set on such a path; when the path is thus, such will be the maturation of affliction and such the pleasant maturation of purification. He has turned back from such a debased livelihood of sustaining oneself through the crooked arts.

Endowed with such an aggregate of noble moral discipline, he is inwardly blameless and thus experiences well-being. He turns the sense faculties back from their objects and so dwells with mindfulness fully guarded. His mindfulness is clear; acting mindfully, he dwells in a place of mental composure. Though he sees forms with the eye, he does not grasp at their marks, nor does he grasp at their secondary features. Because dwelling without being restrained by the restraint of the eye faculty allows attachment, low-mindedness, and the unwholesome and non-virtuous states of worldly wrongdoing to flow into the mind, he applies himself to restraint for the sake of that restraint, and by guarding the eye faculty he achieves restraint of the eye faculty. In the same way, with the ear he guards sounds; with the nose he guards smells; with the tongue he guards tastes;

with the body he guards touches; and with the mind he guards phenomena. Though he knows phenomena with the mind, he does not grasp at their marks, nor does he grasp at their secondary features. Because dwelling without being restrained by the restraint of the mind faculty allows attachment, low-mindedness, and the unwholesome and non-virtuous states of worldly wrongdoing to flow into the mind, by restraining the mind he achieves restraint of the mind faculty.

Being endowed with this noble moral discipline, and turning the faculties away from their objects, he is inwardly blameless and experiences happiness in his own right. He becomes fully aware of his coming and going, and dwelling in that awareness he knows and remains mindful of looking ahead and looking around, of drawing in and stretching out the limbs, of wearing the patch-robe and outer robe, of holding the alms bowl, of going, standing, sitting, lying down, and not lying down, of speaking and keeping silent, of falling asleep and of dispelling drowsiness.

Endowed with this aggregate of noble moral discipline, and with faculties turned inward, and being possessed of thorough mindfulness and clear introspective awareness, he feels inward blamelessness as genuine happiness. Then he resorts to seclusion and sits in a forest grove, at the root of a tree, in an empty house, or in any secluded or remote place. Sitting cross-legged, holding the body upright, and establishing mindfulness before him, he abandons the attachment of the world and dwells again and again in a mind free from attachment, purifying the mind of attachment. He abandons ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt in the world, and becomes free from expectation and free from doubt. He thoroughly purifies the mind of the doubtful thought: "Is this wholesome quality of such a kind, or of what kind?"

It is like this. An unfortunate man takes out a loan and applies it to a business. That business prospers, and with the proceeds he repays the loan and moreover has enough wealth remaining to support his wife and family. He then thinks to himself: "Before, I was an unfortunate man who had taken out a loan and applied it to a business. That business prospered, and so I repaid the loan and moreover I have enough wealth to support my wife and family." Because of that he becomes happy and joyful.

It is like this. An unfortunate man is sick, suffering, and gravely ill; when he eats food it harms his body, and when he drinks water his stomach becomes uncomfortable. Then at a later time he becomes well, free from illness, and strong; when he eats food it benefits his body, and when he drinks water his stomach is not troubled. He then thinks to himself: "Before, I was sick, suffering, and gravely ill; because of that, when I ate food it harmed my body, and when I drank water my stomach was uncomfortable. Now I am well and free from illness, endowed with strength; when I eat food it benefits my body, and when I drink water my stomach is not troubled." Because of that he becomes happy and joyful.

It is like this. An unfortunate man was a slave, under the command of others, at the bidding of others, in service to others — one who could not go where he himself wished. Then at another time he is no longer a slave, no longer under the command of others, no longer at the bidding of others, no longer in service to others — he can go where he himself wishes. He then thinks to himself: "Before, I was a slave, under the command of others, at the bidding of others, in service to others — one who could not go where I myself wished. Now I am no longer a slave, no longer under the command of others, no longer in service to others — I can go where I myself wish."

He became happy and glad on account of that. Just so — a miserable man who has been bound in chains with his hands tied behind his back, and who is then freed from that, becomes fortunate, happy, and untroubled. He thinks to himself: "Before, I was bound in chains with my hands tied behind my back. Now I am freed from that — I am fortunate, happy, and untroubled." He becomes glad on account of that. Just so — a miserable man who passes from danger to safety, and from a bad year to a good year, thinks to himself: "I have passed from danger to safety, and from a bad year to a good year." He becomes happy and glad on account of that.

In precisely the same way — just as with debt, just as with illness, just as with slavery, just as with bondage, just as with danger — he sees himself freed from these five obstacles (nīvaraṇas). He sees that these five, which afflict sentient beings, which diminish wisdom, which are on the side of harm, which obstruct passage beyond suffering — these five unfavorable obstacles — have been abandoned. Withdrawn from desire, withdrawn from negative and unwholesome phenomena, he dwells having directly accomplished the first meditative concentration (dhyāna), which is born of seclusion, accompanied by applied thought and sustained examination, with joy and bliss.

He thoroughly saturates, pervades, fills, and suffuses this very body with the joy and bliss born of seclusion. He drenches it, soaks it completely, satisfies it utterly, and permeates it throughout — so that there is not the slightest part of this entire body that is not reached and pervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion.

It is just as when a skilled bathman or a bathman's apprentice pours fine bathing powder into a bronze basin or bowl or bathing trough, works it through with water, kneading it again and again until it is moist — so that the ball of bathing paste becomes oily, permeated with oil, saturated with oil, gleaming — moistened evenly within and without, neither separating nor seeping. In precisely that same way, he saturates, pervades, fills, and suffuses this very body with the joy and bliss born of seclusion, thoroughly saturating and permeating it — so that there is not the slightest part of this entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion.

Then, in order to still applied thought and sustained examination, with the mind inwardly settled and focused upon a single object of joy, he dwells having directly accomplished the second meditative concentration — which is born of meditative absorption (samādhi), free from applied thought and sustained examination, with joy and bliss.

He thoroughly saturates, pervades, fills, and suffuses this very body with the joy and bliss born of meditative absorption — so that there is not the slightest part of his entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of meditative absorption.

It is just as a natural spring lake set upon a mountaintop, into which no water flows from the east, no water from the south, no water from the west, and no rain falls into it from the north at any time — yet from within the lake itself, a great upwelling of water rises from a great opening in the floor of the pool, so that the entire pool is saturated, pervaded, filled, and suffused with cool water — so that there is not the slightest part of that pool that is not pervaded by cool water throughout. In precisely that same way, he saturates, pervades, fills, and suffuses this very body with the joy and bliss born of meditative absorption — so that there is not the slightest part of this entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of meditative absorption.

Having abandoned joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and full awareness, experiencing pleasure throughout the body — and, as the noble ones declare, he dwells at ease with equanimity accompanied by mindfulness. Thus he enters and abides in the third meditative concentration, having directly accomplished it.

This very body of his he saturates, pervades, fills, and suffuses with a bliss free of joy — so that there is not the slightest part of this entire body that is not pervaded by the bliss free of joy.

It is just as with a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white water lily, or a white lotus, each born from the water, grown in the water, with its roots sunk in the water and resting there — from root to tip there is not the slightest part that is not pervaded by cool water throughout. In precisely that same way, he saturates, pervades, fills, and suffuses this very body with the bliss free of joy — so that there is not the slightest part of this entire body that is not pervaded and suffused by the bliss free of joy.

Then, having relinquished pleasure and having relinquished suffering — and since mental ease and mental discomfort have already been set aside before — he enters and abides in the fourth meditative concentration, which is neither suffering nor pleasure, and in which equanimity and mindfulness are perfectly pure, having directly accomplished it.

He dwells suffusing this very body, having entered into and being devoted to a state of complete purity and utter luminosity, and he directly accomplishes this pervading presence. It is just as when a householder or the son of a householder, having been wrapped from head to foot — from head to hand to foot — in cloth that is fastened with eight or nine folds, so that from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet there is not the slightest part of the entire body that is not covered and enveloped by that perfectly pure, utterly white cloth. In precisely that same way, he enters and abides directly accomplishing this pervading, devoting himself to this very body with a mind of complete purity and utter luminosity — so that there is not the slightest part of this entire body that is not pervaded and suffused by a mind of complete joy and utter purity.

Dear one, it is just as the noble śrāvakas declare: having relinquished pleasure and having relinquished suffering, and since both mental ease and mental discomfort have already ceased before, he dwells having directly accomplished the fourth meditative concentration — which is neither suffering nor pleasure, in which equanimity and mindfulness are perfectly pure. His mind at that time becomes neither elevated nor depressed. Dwelling neither elevated nor depressed, it attains unshakeable stillness.

It is just as a flame of mustard-oil butter burning in an upper chamber or a great upper chamber — when that flame is not stirred or moved by wind, birds, people, or non-human beings — at that time it becomes neither elevated nor depressed, and, dwelling neither elevated nor depressed, it burns without wavering.

In precisely the same way, dear one, when the noble śrāvakas have relinquished pleasure and have relinquished suffering, and since both mental ease and mental discomfort have already ceased before, they dwell having directly accomplished the fourth meditative concentration — which is neither suffering nor pleasure, in which equanimity and mindfulness are perfectly pure. His mind at that time becomes neither elevated nor depressed. Dwelling neither elevated nor depressed, it attains unshakeable stillness, and this thought arises in him:

"This body of mine is form — it is great, being composed of the four great elements, and in it consciousness dwells, on it consciousness depends, and into it consciousness has entered. Now let me shift the mind from this body and accomplish a body of another kind — a form body, mind-made, complete, with its faculties unimpaired."

And so he does shift the mind from that body and directly accomplishes a mind-made form body, complete and with its faculties unimpaired.

It is just as a beryl gem — eight-sided, of fine quality, clear, and perfectly translucent —

threaded on a cord of four colours — blue, yellow, red, and white. A person with good eyes, seeing it, would know: "This is the cord; this is the gem; and the gem is threaded upon the cord." In just the same way, he shifts the mind from that body and directly accomplishes another body — a form body, mind-made, complete, with its faculties unimpaired.

It is just as a person with good eyes, seeing a skillful man draw a single reed from a bundle of reeds, would know: "This is the bundle of reeds; this is the reed; and the reed has been drawn out from the bundle." In just the same way, he shifts the mind from that body and directly accomplishes another body — a form body, mind-made, complete, with its faculties unimpaired.

It is just as a person with good eyes, seeing a skillful man draw a snake out from a snake-basket, would know: "This is the basket; this is the snake; and the snake has been drawn out from the basket." In just the same way, he shifts the mind from that body and directly accomplishes another body — a form body, mind-made, complete, with its faculties unimpaired.

It is just as a person with good eyes, seeing a skillful man draw a sword from its scabbard, would know: "This is the scabbard; this is the sword; and the sword has been drawn from the scabbard." In just the same way, he shifts the mind from that body and directly accomplishes another body — a form body, mind-made, complete, with its faculties unimpaired.

With a mind thus undistracted, utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, free from fault, free from the near afflictions, and having become straight and pliant, he attains imperturbability. Then, directing his mind toward the domain of miraculous power, the gnosis of that domain blazes forth, and his mind enters into the superknowledges.

He then directly experiences the various domains of miraculous power one by one: from one he becomes many; from many he becomes one; he passes from the manifest into the unmanifest; he directly experiences the luminosity of gnosis — passing through walls, through mountains, through enclosures, unobstructed, as though through open space; sinking into the earth and rising from it as though it were water; walking upon the surface of water without sinking as though upon solid ground; travelling through the sky cross-legged as though he were a winged bird; touching and stroking with his hand even the sun and moon, so mighty and so powerful; and exercising mastery of body as far as the Brahmā world.

It is just as a skilled goldsmith, or the able apprentice of a skilled goldsmith, who, knowing gold to be thoroughly refined, works it by whatever means and for whatever purpose he desires — fashioning from it a tablet, or an earring, or a necklace, or an armlet, or a bracelet, or a finger-ring, or a garland of silver and gold — swiftly and at length. In just the same way, with a mind in meditative equipoise, utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, free from fault, free from the near afflictions, having become straight and pliant, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind into the superknowledges in order to manifest gnosis in the domain of miraculous power. Thus, from one becoming many, and so forth as before, he exercises mastery of body as far as the Brahmā world.

It is just as a skilled potter, or the able apprentice of a skilled potter —

knowing how to work a lump of clay that has been thoroughly prepared, he swiftly and at length produces whatever particular vessel he desires, in whatever way he desires. Just so, in exactly the same way, with a mind in meditative equipoise, utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, having become straight and pliant, and having attained imperturbability, he exercises mastery of body as far as the Brahmā world, just as before.

It is just as a skilled ivory-worker, or the able apprentice of a skilled ivory-worker — knowing how to work ivory that has been thoroughly prepared, he produces whatever particular form he desires, in whatever way he desires, swiftly and at length. Just so, in exactly the same way, with a mind in meditative equipoise, utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, and so forth as before, he exercises mastery of body as far as the Brahmā world.

Then, with that same mind in meditative equipoise, utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, free from fault, freed from the near afflictions, having become straight and pliant, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind into the superknowledges in order to manifest gnosis in the domain of the divine ear. With the divine ear, pure and surpassing that of ordinary human beings, he hears both kinds of sound — those of humans and those of non-humans, those far away and those near.

It is just as a man who blows a conch shell climbs to the summit of a high mountain, and at the hour of midnight blows the conch, so that the sound of that blowing resounds and spreads in all directions. Just so, in exactly the same way, with a mind in meditative equipoise, utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, free from fault, freed from the near afflictions, having become straight and pliant, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind into those superknowledges in order to manifest gnosis in the domain of the divine ear. With the divine ear, pure and surpassing that of ordinary human beings, he hears both kinds of sound — those of humans and those of non-humans, those far away and those near.

Then, with that same mind in meditative equipoise, utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, free from fault, freed from the near afflictions, having become straight and pliant, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind into the superknowledges in order to manifest gnosis in the domain of the enumeration of minds. He fully and correctly knows the minds of other sentient beings and other persons, having examined and investigated them as they truly are. A mind with attachment he fully knows as it truly is — namely, as a mind with attachment. A mind free from attachment he fully knows as it truly is — namely, as a mind free from attachment. A mind with aversion, a mind free from aversion, a mind with delusion, a mind free from delusion, a distracted mind and an undistracted mind, a contracted mind and a grasping mind, an exalted mind and an unexalted mind, a pacified mind and an unpacified mind, a mind in meditative equipoise and a mind not in meditative equipoise, an uncultivated mind and a cultivated mind, an unliberated mind — he fully knows as it truly is, namely, as an unliberated mind. A thoroughly and completely liberated mind he fully knows as it truly is — namely, as a thoroughly and completely liberated mind.

It is just as a sighted person who takes hold of a perfectly clear mirror and observes the features of his own face. Just so, in exactly the same way, with a mind in meditative equipoise, utterly pure,

thoroughly purified, flawless, freed from the proximate afflictions, straightened and abiding in a serviceable state, having attained imperturbability — in order to directly know the synonyms of mind through direct knowledge, one directs the mind toward those direct knowledges — proceeding just as before, up to fully knowing a thoroughly and completely liberated mind as it truly is, namely, as a thoroughly and completely liberated mind. This is called "the foot."

Now, what is knowledge? With a mind in meditative equipoise that is fully pure in just this way, thoroughly purified, flawless, freed even from the proximate afflictions, straightened and abiding in a serviceable state, having attained imperturbability — in order to directly manifest the gnosis of recollecting previous abodes, one directs the mind toward those direct knowledges. One then recollects manifold previous abodes in many forms, thus: one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten; twenty, thirty, forty, fifty; a hundred births, a thousand births, many hundreds of thousands of births; a kalpa of destruction, a kalpa of arising, a kalpa of destruction and arising; many kalpas of destruction, many kalpas of arising, many kalpas of destruction and arising — all these one recollects. Those sentient beings who were born there — they were called such-and-such; I too had such-and-such a name, such-and-such a clan, such-and-such a lineage; my food was of such-and-such a kind; I experienced such-and-such pleasures and sufferings; my lifespan was of such-and-such a length; I dwelt for so long; and when the limit of that life was reached, I died and passed away, then was born in a certain place. From there too I died and passed away and was born in a certain place; from there too I died and passed away and was born right here. In this way, with specific details of appearance and location, one recollects manifold previous abodes in many forms.

It is just as a certain person who goes from one village to another village, then from that village on to another still, and thinks to himself: I went from such-and-such a village to such-and-such a village, and from there again to another place, and from there I arrived at this very village. In just the same way, with a mind in meditative equipoise that is fully pure, thoroughly purified, flawless, freed from the proximate afflictions, straightened and abiding in a serviceable state, having attained imperturbability — in order to directly manifest the gnosis of recollecting previous abodes, one directs the mind toward those direct knowledges. One recollects manifold previous abodes — beginning with "one," and so forth just as before, with specific details of appearance and location — all the way through to the recollection of manifold previous abodes.

Then, in just that same way, with a mind in meditative equipoise that is fully pure, thoroughly purified, flawless, freed from the proximate afflictions, straightened and abiding in a serviceable state, having attained imperturbability — in order to directly manifest the knowledge of death and birth, one directs the mind toward those direct knowledges. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of ordinary human beings, one sees sentient beings dying and being born, with beautiful forms and with ugly forms, with inferior and with excellent forms, going to fortunate realms and going to unfortunate realms. One fully knows them just as they fare according to their karma: Alas, these sentient beings — endowed with misconduct in body, endowed with misconduct in speech and mind, reviling and bearing wrong views toward the noble ones, engaging in the deeds of wrong view, and intent on the Dharma in such a wrong spirit — by reason of that cause and that condition, upon the dissolution of the body, after death, fall into unfortunate realms, into a bad destination, and are born among hell-beings.

Alas, yet these sentient beings are endowed with virtuous conduct in body, endowed with virtuous conduct in speech and mind; they do not revile the noble ones, they hold right views, and they are intent upon the Dharma with right views and right-view deeds. By reason of that cause and that condition, upon the dissolution of the body, after death, they go to fortunate realms and are born as gods in the heavens.

It is like this: a man with good eyesight, standing at the great crossroads where four main roads meet, sees the many people coming and going, standing and sitting and lying down, dwelling in all their various forms. And so, just as it is here — with his purified divine eye, surpassing that of ordinary humans — up to the point of "they are born as gods," as stated before. With a mind in meditative equipoise that is utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, without blemish, free from proximate afflictions, become straight and workable, he attains imperturbability; and in order to see the wisdom born of the exhaustion of defilements, he applies his mind to the higher knowledges. He then fully knows as it really is: "This is suffering, a noble truth. This is the origin of suffering. This is the cessation of suffering. This is the noble truth of the path that leads to the cessation of suffering." Knowing it thus as it really is, and seeing it thus as it really is, his mind is fully liberated from the defilement of desire, fully liberated from the defilement of existence, and fully liberated from the defilement of ignorance. Being fully liberated, there arises the wisdom of knowing: "I am fully liberated." He knows: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. There is no more of this existence."

As an example: not far from a village or a town there is a pool of water, deep, unmuddied, clear, and pellucid. A man with good eyesight, sitting on the bank, sees shrimp or crabs or fish or turtles or a crocodile. So too, with a mind in meditative equipoise that is utterly pure, thoroughly cleansed, without blemish, free from proximate afflictions, become straight and workable, he attains imperturbability — and so on as before, up to "there is no more of this existence."

This is called knowledge. Together with the former knowledge, the two combined are called knowledge and conduct. Young man, in order to actualize this unsurpassable knowledge and conduct which has not yet been actualized, one should understand it by way of four methods. What are the four?

Here, young man, some ascetic or brahmin, failing to actualize this very unsurpassable knowledge and conduct, goes from the village to the wilderness, makes a shelter of branches and leaves, and dwells there, saying: "We shall live here on roots and fruits." And they do indeed live on roots and fruits. That young brahmin who, in order to actualize this unsurpassable knowledge and conduct which has not yet been actualized, follows this first method — young brahmin, what do you think? Have you, together with your teachers, ever lived according to that first method of unsurpassable knowledge and conduct which I have taught? "O Gautama, I have not."

Furthermore, young man, some ascetic or brahmin, failing to actualize this very unsurpassable knowledge and conduct, abandons that food of roots and fruits, goes off to one side, makes a shelter of leaves and branches, and dwells there.

"We shall live here on a diet of leaves," they declare, and so they sustain themselves there on leaves alone as their food. Young brahmin, know that this, the second method, is the means for actualizing this unsurpassable knowledge and conduct which has not yet been actualized.

Furthermore, young brahmin, some ascetic or brahmin, failing to actualize this very unsurpassable knowledge and conduct, abandons both that food of roots and fruits and that food of leaves, goes off to one side, makes a shelter of branches and leaves, and dwells there. "Here we shall memorize the mantras and compose the incantations," they declare, and so they diligently memorize the mantras and compose the incantations of old. Young brahmin, know that this, the third method, is the means for actualizing this unsurpassable knowledge and conduct which has not yet been actualized.

Furthermore, young brahmin, some ascetic or brahmin, failing to actualize this very unsurpassable knowledge and conduct, abandons that food of roots and fruits, that food of leaves, and the memorizing of mantras and composing of incantations, and, still without having actualized it, enters a village, builds a four-doored house, and dwells there. They then announce: "Here we shall give gifts, make merit, and offer alms to whatever ascetics and brahmins pass by, to the best of our ability and according to our means." And so they give gifts, make merit, and offer alms to whatever ascetics and brahmins pass by, according to their ability and whatever resources they have. Young brahmin, know that this, the fourth method, is the means for actualizing this unsurpassable knowledge and conduct which has not yet been actualized.

Young brahmin, what do you think? I have taught four methods for actualizing this unsurpassable knowledge and conduct. Have you, together with your teachers, ever lived according to any of those methods?

"O Gautama, I have not."

Young brahmin, since you have not completed any of those methods, why then do you speak these words to the Śākyas: 'Alas for the Śākyas, they are new! Alas, the Śākyas are upstarts!'?

Young brahmin, what do you think? Those brahmins of former times, the brahmin seers — Aṣṭaka, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Aṅgiras, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu — they composed the mantras and brought forth the incantations. The brahmins of today, just as those of old, chant, praise, intone, compose, and recite those very mantra words and hymns. Is it the case that you, together with your teachers, live as one who is now surrounded by a moat, with iron stakes planted around, dwelling in a city under blockade? Is it like that for them too?

"O Gautama, it is not so."

Is it the case that you, together with your teachers, are the kind who gird on armor, survey the finest battle standards and supreme shows of strength, and witness many battles arrayed? Is it like that for them too?

"O Gautama, it is not so."

Is it the case that you, together with your teachers, mount a chariot drawn entirely by grey mares, take up golden whip and rein, and ride out through the countryside surrounded by many brahmin youths, with many brahmin youths going before you? Is it like that for them too?

"O Gautama, it is not so."

Is it the case that you, together with your teachers, are anointed, bathed, and attended in this manner — by women with their hair bound up on their heads, wandering about, with bracelets on their wrists, their breasts swelling like those of a young male buffalo —

— and the pleasures and so forth practised in that way: is it the same for them too?

"O Gautama, it is not so."

Is it the case that you, together with your teachers, wearing golden armlets, adorned with golden necklaces, stretch out your legs and lie abed with women so bedecked until the sun has risen? Is it the same for them too?

"O Gautama, it is not so."

O brahmin youth, now listen to the faults of your own teacher. O brahmin youth, the brahmin's son called Padmaśīrṣa — his going before the king of the Kosala country was no different from going behind a wall or behind a curtain. Why? Is it fitting that a man who is known to be of such a kind would not show his face openly to the very person by whose cooking he eats? O brahmin youth, now listen also to your own faults. Once upon a time, O brahmin youth, Prasenajit, king of the Kosala country, was seated on his own throne and was issuing instructions to another man, saying: "O man, the matter is such and such; do this and this, conduct yourself thus and thus." Having given those instructions, the king rose from his throne and departed. Then that man, in secret, sat down on the king's throne and proceeded to issue instructions to yet another man, saying: "O man, do this and this, conduct yourself thus and thus." O brahmin youth, what do you think? If a man were to sit secretly on the king's throne in that way, and were to speak the words the king had spoken and repeat what the king had said — would he thereby be the king? Would he become a king?

"O Gautama, it is not so."

In just the same way, O brahmin youth: if you were to teach what has been taught by a sage, and to say what a sage has said — would you thereby be a sage? Would you become a sage?

"O Gautama, it is not so."

O brahmin youth, nevertheless, take the purpose for which you have come very well to heart, for it will bring you long-lasting benefit, meaning, and happiness.

Thereupon the brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha began to examine the thirty-two marks of a great man on the body of the Blessed One. Of the thirty-two he could see thirty; but as to two of them he was of two minds and had doubts — namely, the concealed male organ, which is withdrawn below, and the tongue, thin yet great. And so he spoke in verse:

I have heard there are thirty-two marks of a man,
marks of a great man said to be upon you, O Great Sage.
Of the thirty-two marks, O Gautama, I have heard you possess them all upon your person —
yet as to two of them I cannot find them there.
O foremost of men, your concealed male organ —
is it truly withdrawn below?
And the words of your voice, like a woman's —
can it be that your tongue is not short?
Pray extend it swiftly, that slender tongue,
and dispel my doubt.
To behold the buddhas of widespread renown
is exceedingly rare to find.

Then the Blessed One thought: "The brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha, having examined the thirty-two marks of a great man on my body, has seen thirty of the thirty-two, but has two minds and doubts about two — the concealed male organ that is withdrawn, and the tongue that is great yet slender. How shall I show him a sign by which he, Ambāṣṭha, may see that my concealed male organ is withdrawn and that my tongue is large yet slender?" And so the Blessed One displayed those signs so that the brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha could see that the Blessed One's concealed male organ was withdrawn into a sheath. Then, extending his tongue from his mouth as far as the hairline of his face, stretching it to cover that space, he showed it. Upon seeing this, Ambāṣṭha thought to himself: "The ascetic Gautama is indeed endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man. And one endowed with the marks of a great man has two paths before him — no other."

If he were to remain a householder and dwell at home, he would become a wheel-turning king — and so on, as before, down to becoming famous throughout the world with a name that has spread everywhere.

Then the brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha, rejoicing and delighting in what the Blessed One had declared, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

The Minor Matters of Discipline. The forty-eighth section.

Now at that time, the brahmin Pokkharasādi was assembled and seated together with the eldest and most senior brahmins in the high place of a distinguished brahmin household. The brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha was also seated there among them. The brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha caught sight of Pokkharasādi from a distance. Seeing him, he went to where Pokkharasādi was, and upon arriving he prostrated with his head at Pokkharasādi's feet, bowed to the other senior brahmins as well, and sat down to one side.

Once he was seated to one side, Pokkharasādi addressed the brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha with these words: "Brahmin youth, is what is heard of the virtuous qualities, the fame, the renown, and the verses of the wise Gautama — spread far and wide in all directions and quarters — truly as it is said? Are the reports about his marks accurate?"

"It is so, learned teacher. The virtuous qualities, the fame, the renown, and the verses of the wise Gautama, spread far and wide in all directions and quarters, are indeed exactly as reported, and the accounts of his marks are indeed accurate."

"Brahmin youth, did you have an exchange of words with the wise Gautama?"

"I did, learned teacher."

"Brahmin youth, tell us fully everything that was said in the conversation you had with the wise Gautama."

Then the brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha related to Pokkharasādi in full everything that had been said in the conversation with the Blessed One.

When this was said, Pokkharasādi became furious, agitated, and enraged, his mind thrown into turmoil. He struck the brahmin youth Ambāṣṭha on the head with a sandaled foot, saying: "Ah, what a messenger! Ah, what an envoy! Such conduct, such a messenger, such a bearer of messages — even this alone could cause me to fall into a lower state of existence! Brahmin youth, in whatever way you intended to disparage and refute the wise Gautama, the wise Gautama has understood you to be reckoned among his own kind in each and every such instance. Wise sirs, even now I myself wish to go to see and pay homage to the wise Gautama, yet today it has simply not been possible for me to do so. Nevertheless, tomorrow I will go to see and pay homage to the wise Gautama."

Then, starting from that very evening, Pokkharasādi had pure and fine foods and delicacies prepared. Rising early the next morning, he had a carriage loaded with pure and fine foods and delicacies and departed in the direction of where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he exchanged various words of cordial greeting and mutual rejoicing with the Blessed One, then sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, Pokkharasādi addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Wise Gautama, I have had a carriage loaded with pure and fine foods and delicacies, and I offer it."

The Blessed One, wise Gautama, accepted this offering out of compassion. At that time the venerable Ānanda was standing to one side of the Blessed One holding a fan, fanning the Blessed One as he sat. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and gather together all the monks who are dwelling in the vicinity of Kosambī into the dining hall." "Reverend sir, I will do as you command," said the venerable Ānanda, and having heeded the Blessed One's word, he gathered all the monks dwelling in the vicinity of Kosambī into the dining hall, then went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet, then sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend sir, all the monks dwelling in the vicinity of Kosambī have been assembled and are present in the dining hall. Blessed One, may it now please you to consider that the time has come." Then the Blessed One went and arrived at the dining hall and took the seat that had been arranged in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, and sat down. Then the brahmin Pokkharasādi, perceiving that the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, served and satisfied them with his own hands with pure and fine foods and delicacies, and in many ways he served and satisfied them with pure and fine foods and delicacies with his own hands. When the Blessed One had finished eating and had set aside his bowl, Pokkharasādi took a low seat and sat down before the Blessed One to listen to the Dharma. Then the Blessed One rejoiced in the brahmin Pokkharasādi's gift of generosity with this verse of rejoicing:

The best among fire-offerings and oblations,
the best of metres is the sun-deity,
the best among people is a king,
the best of oceans is among rivers,
the moon is chief among stars,
the sun is chief among those that give light,
and in all the worlds with their gods,
among whatever beings travel
above, below, and across,
the best of speakers is the fully awakened buddha.

At that moment, while the brahmin Pokkharasādi was making the dedication of merit, he saw an old man drinking sesame oil. Seeing this, he addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend sir, do all hearers act to please the wise Gautama?" "Brahmin, that is not certain. Some do please him, some do not please him." "Gautama, some seek the Dharma, it seems, while others seek to drink sesame oil." "Gautama, is my student, the young brahmin Māsuka, here?" "Brahmin, he has come." "Wise Gautama, did you have an exchange of pleasantries with him?" "Brahmin, we did." "Gautama, please tell me in full everything that passed in that exchange between you and him." Then the Blessed One told the brahmin Pokkharasādi everything that had passed in the exchange between himself and the young brahmin Māsuka. Then the brahmin Pokkharasādi addressed the Blessed One thus: "Gautama, the young brahmin Māsuka has a nature that is unruly by temperament. Gautama, please be patient with the young brahmin Māsuka." "Brahmin, I am patient."

"Wise Gautama, whenever you see me entering a carriage, or taking up a whip, or raising a goad, or calling out loudly, at such a time please regard it as the brahmin Pokkharasādi bowing his head at your two feet, and please understand it as his asking after you: 'Are your ailments few? Is your discomfort slight? Do you live well, are you active, do you dwell in strength and ease?' O Wise Gautama, whenever you see me coming from the middle of the market square, or removing my sandals, or drawing back my robe, or stretching out my hand — at such a time, please consider it as my paying homage to the Wise Gautama" — and from that point the passage continues as before, up to "do you dwell in strength and ease?" O Wise Gautama, whenever you see me in the midst of a retinue, or seated on a couch or throne, or wearing a turban — at such a time, please consider it as my paying homage to the Wise Gautama" — and from that point the passage continues as before, up to "do you dwell in strength and ease?" And why is this? O Wise Gautama, brahmins live by their reputation, and it is from reputation alone that they seek their livelihood.

Then the Blessed One reflected thus: "How remarkable — this brahmin Pokkharasādi is extremely proud. Let me teach him the Dharma in order to abandon that pride." And so the Blessed One taught the brahmin Pokkharasādi thoroughly and rightly with a Dharma-endowed discourse, exalted him rightly, engaged him rightly, and gladdened him rightly.

The preliminary Dharma-endowed discourse given by the blessed buddhas is this: the talk on generosity, the talk on moral discipline, the talk on the higher realms, the drawbacks, the defilement, and the corruption of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation, of seclusion, and of the qualities on the side of purification — all of these he expounded fully and thoroughly.
