When the Blessed One saw that the brahmin had become joyful at heart, with a wholesome mind, a pleased mind, a mind free from obscuration, that he was endowed with good fortune and power and was capable of understanding the supreme teaching of Dharma — at that very moment the Blessed One taught the supreme teaching of Dharma: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path — the Four Noble Truths — expounding them broadly and thoroughly. Just as a clean cloth free of stains is fit to receive dye, and when placed in dye takes the colour well — so too did the brahmin Pokkharasādi, seated right there on that seat, directly realise the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Then the brahmin Pokkharasādi, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, understood the Dharma, known the categories of the Dharma, reached the depth of the Dharma, crossed beyond doubt, crossed beyond uncertainty, placed his reliance on no other, was carried along by no other, and having attained fearlessness with respect to the teachings in the Teacher's doctrine — he rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward where the Blessed One was, joined his palms in reverence with a bow, and spoke these words to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, I am one who has risen. I am one who has fully risen. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha for refuge. May the Blessed One please accept me as a layman. From this day forward, for as long as I live, I am committed even at the cost of my life, and I go to refuge with complete faith."

Then the brahmin Padmasnying (Lotus-Heart) rejoiced and was gladdened at what the Blessed One had said. He bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed.

The Blessed One reflected: the fault of which the brahmin Padmasnying is accused is that the monks were eating food while dedicating merit. Therefore, knowing that monks should not eat food while dedicating merit, he declared to the monks: "Monks, take the case of the brahmin Padmasnying as the basis for this rule. Monks are not to eat food while dedicating merit. If monks eat food while dedicating merit, it becomes a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks are not to eat food while dedicating merit, a certain young monk found himself eating past the proper hour. At that time the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, if a monk was already eating beforehand and he neither understands the meaning nor hears the sound of the declaration, he may eat, and there is no offense for him. If he hears the sound but does not understand the meaning, he may also eat, and there is no offense for him either. But one who both hears the sound and understands the meaning should not eat; if he does, it becomes a serious offense."

When the Blessed One had declared that those who both hear the sound and understand the meaning commit a serious offense if they continue to eat, a great many monks assembled in another monastery. There the monks were seated in two rows, the younger monks together and the elder monks together. At that point the younger monks were eating, and they both heard the sound and understood the meaning. They felt remorse, stopped eating, and sat fasting. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Wait until two or three verses have been recited, then eat — and there is no need for remorse."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Sages' Retreat.

Then, at the time of morning, the Blessed One put on his lower robe and outer Dharma robe, took up his alms bowl, and went into Vārāṇasī for alms. A certain other monk likewise put on his lower robe and outer Dharma robe at the time of morning, took up his alms bowl, and went into Vārāṇasī for alms.

This other monk sat down at the foot of a thicket tree, turning things over in unwholesome conceptual thought, his mind fixed upon and dwelling in sinfulness. The Blessed One saw that monk sitting at the foot of the thicket tree, his mind turning over in unwholesome conceptual thought, fixed upon and dwelling in sinfulness. Having seen this, the Blessed One addressed that monk with these words:

"Monk! Monk! Do not make yourself like a hot seed — rank and festering. Monk, know that if you make yourself here like a hot seed, rank and festering, you will become a place where bees will neither alight nor lick."

Then that monk thought to himself: the Blessed One knows the thoughts and reflections of my mind. Filled with fear and terror, his hair standing on end, he rose from the foot of the thicket tree and departed.

The Blessed One reflected:

"The fault arose from dwelling in a place that is not a monk's proper domain. Therefore, knowing that one should not dwell in a place that is not a monk's proper domain, I went on alms-round in Vārāṇasī, completed the matter of food, set aside the remainder of the alms-food, put down my bowl and robes, washed both feet, and entered the assembly hall to settle into inner composure. Then the Blessed One rose from his inner composure and took the seat that had been arranged for him before the community of monks. Having taken his seat, the Blessed One addressed the monks with these words:

"Monks, today, in the morning hour, I robed myself, took my bowl, and went to Vārāṇasī for alms. Another monk also, in the morning hour, robed himself and took his bowl, and set out for Vārāṇasī for alms. That monk sat down at the foot of another thicket tree, engaged in unwholesome conceptual thought, fixed upon and dwelling in sinfulness. I saw that monk sitting at the foot of that other thicket tree, engaged in unwholesome conceptual thought, fixed upon and dwelling in sinfulness. Having seen him, I addressed that monk with these words: 'Monk! Monk! Do not make yourself like a hot seed — rank and festering. Monk, know that if you make yourself here like a hot seed, rank and festering, you will become a place where bees will neither alight nor lick.' Then that monk thought to himself: the Blessed One knows the thoughts and reflections of my mind. Filled with fear and terror, his hair standing on end, he departed hastily from the foot of that very thicket tree.

"Therefore, monks, this is the fault: it is dwelling in a place that is not a monk's proper domain. Therefore, monks, do not dwell in a place that is not your proper domain. If you dwell in a place that is not your proper domain, trouble will come of it."

Then another monk rose from his seat, drew his outer robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, bowed in that direction, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, in the noble Dharma and Vinaya, what is called a hot seed? What is called rank? What is called festering? And what are called the bees of that festering?"

"Monks, what is called a hot seed is a term of elevation for conceptual thought directed toward sinful, unwholesome things — namely, conceptual thought directed toward sensual desire, conceptual thought directed toward malice, and conceptual thought directed toward harm.

"What is called rank is a term of elevation for the five qualities of sensual pleasure — form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Yet, monks, it is not these qualities of sensual pleasure themselves that are meant; rather, it is the longing and attachment for them that is called desire.

"What is called festering is what some people do, dwelling in a state of seeping contact with the six sense bases — the sense base of eye-contact, the sense base of ear-contact, the sense base of nose-contact, the sense base of tongue-contact, and the sense base of body-contact.

"What are called the bees of the festering are what some people do, dwelling without restraint over the six sense bases — the mind seeping after the sinful, unwholesome phenomena of the world through attachment and discontent."

Having spoken these words, the Blessed One then —

The Teacher, the Sugata, then spoke these further words:

One who stirs up the desire of craving,
who guards neither eye nor ear,
who is intoxicated by conceptual thought —
that monk scorches his own seed.
He dwells attached to the foul,
abiding with defilement and the festering.
Whether in a village or in a wilderness,
by night or in the light of day,
he remains far from every happiness,
and wretchedness draws ever near.

But one who strives in inner calm abiding
and cultivates direct knowledge by himself —
such a one has done away with those bees
and dwells in ease within this world.

To rely on a person of virtue
is what the noble ones have called fair speech.
If one truly knows those words,
one will not go forth into rebirth again.

When the Blessed One had said that monks must not dwell in domains that are not their proper sphere, the monks, not knowing how many kinds of improper domain there were, asked the Blessed One about this. The Blessed One declared: "There are five kinds of improper domain — the places of music and entertainment, the places of prostitutes, the places of those who sell liquor, the gateway to the royal palace with its surrounding court, and the places of inferior castes."

Summary verse: Do not sleep where a black snake lies in the bed; do not bow with a single robe. One should bow to four who are senior, and likewise bow to the assembly.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Now, a certain monk who was living at Śrāvastī asked a monk companion to watch over his sleeping mat, and then went off wandering about the district. That monk left the sleeping mat just as it had been spread out, and no one slept on it or looked after it. As the mat lay there empty, a venomous snake came down at dusk and moved about at will, gliding back and forth, until it reached the mat and coiled itself up beneath it.

Before long, another monk came suddenly to the dwelling of the first monk. The second monk rested from his fatigue, and after he had recovered from the weariness of the road, he was brought to pay homage at the stūpa and to bow before those of pure conduct comparable to Brahma. When he had bowed before the stūpas the sun set. The first monk then said to him: "Venerable one, here is water, earth, and mustard oil — and here is the sleeping mat, spread out just as it is. You are weary from the road, so wash your feet and lie down."

Driven by the power of his former karma, the newcomer lay down without examining the mat and, overcome by sleep, fell into slumber. As he lay there sleeping, he pressed down upon the venomous snake, and the snake, finding no way to move back and forth, was tormented by the pain of being crushed and seized hold of the monk's body. The agony of its bite arose; the monk twisted and turned, and he died — and both of them had passed beyond their time.

When night gave way to dawn, the first monk came to the other's dwelling and knocked gently on the door, again and again. Since the other had passed beyond his time, how could he possibly answer? The first monk thought to himself: "He is tired from the journey and is surely lying in and feels cold." After a while the sun rose, and the monk went again to the dwelling and knocked hard on the door, calling out: "Venerable one, rise up — the morning sun is here!" But as the room was empty of any answer, how could there be a reply? The other monks said: "Why are you knocking on the door?" and he explained to them in full what had happened. The monks then took a crooked key and opened the door, and there they found the other monk had passed beyond his time. Looking around they saw that a venomous snake had pressed itself down beneath the bedding and had also perished. Some of them then said: "This venerable one was devoured by this venomous snake — that is how he passed beyond his time."

At that point, some said: "This venerable one passed beyond his time because he transformed his body." The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected and perceived that the fault lay in this: the monk, having been entrusted with the bedding, had not handed it over to the attendant of the bedding and had not examined it at regular intervals, and on that account the mishap had occurred. Knowing this, the Blessed One declared: therefore, a monk who has been entrusted with the bedding should hand it over to the bedding attendant, shake it out, and lay it on the rod of a robe.

The Blessed One spoke: "Monks, that monk acted with heedlessness and so incurred a fault. Therefore, monks, whatever monk has been entrusted with bedding should, as best he can, shake it out when it is damp and hand it over to the bedding attendant; or else shake it out and place it on the rod of a robe. And whoever is about to sleep should first inspect the bedding and then lie down."

The Blessed One declared: "Whoever wishes to sleep on a bed should inspect the bed and then lie down."

The monks then began inspecting beds by lamplight. The Blessed One declared: "One should not inspect a bed by lamplight; rather, one should inspect a bed during the daytime."

The monks then shook out all the bedding. The Blessed One declared: "Those that have been stored for a long time should be shaken out from the base and inspected. Other bedding that has been laid out need only be shaken lightly before one lies down."

The occasion is at Śrāvastī.

Two monks were staying together in one dwelling. Of the two, one had ordained a certain young man as a novice. Now this novice was a very heavy sleeper and rose only after a long while, and his preceptor would constantly scold him for it. Then one time, after sleeping very long, he awoke, startled, and got up, put on his sweat-cloth as a lower robe, and went in that state to his preceptor's side. The preceptor too had risen from his bed and was sitting there, wearing his lower robe. The novice prostrated with his head at the preceptor's feet. Since his hair and beard had only recently been shaved, as he rose up the preceptor's lower robe caught on his head and fell off, leaving him uncovered. The sweat-cloth of the novice also fell away. Both were thus left uncovered, sitting in an indecorous manner, when another monk who was dwelling in the same room caught sight of them. He called out: "Well now, good sirs! Only now do I know you for what you are — that you bear the marks of a man born as such!" Both were mortified and fell silent, overwhelmed with shame. He then reproached that monk, and the other monks said to him: "Venerable one, if he scolds you constantly like that, what did you do?" The monk replied: "Venerable ones, in the past we could still be reconciled, but now we can no longer be, so I will go and confront him alone." The others asked: "What happened?" and he explained to them in full what had occurred. They said: "Venerable one, his scolding you for that fault was justified." The monk then said nothing more.

At that juncture the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected and declared: "That monk's reproach was justified."

"Monks, therefore the fault lies here: one who wears but a single robe making prostrations, and one wearing a single robe making prostrations, taking that as one's own affair. Therefore, monks, one wearing a single robe should not make prostrations, and one wearing a single robe making prostrations should not be taken as one's own concern."

Knowing this, the Blessed One declared: "That monk's reproach was justified. Monks, therefore, let the one wearing a single robe not make prostrations, and let not one wearing a single robe make prostrations to another wearing a single robe, and making prostrations while wearing a single robe should not be taken as one's own affair."

Monks, if one wearing a single robe makes prostrations, or makes prostrations to one wearing a single robe, or takes the prostrations of one wearing a single robe as one's own concern, that becomes a serious offense. The setting for this rule is Rājagṛha.

The Blessed One had declared to the monks that a monk should not rest without knowing the discipline. Monks dwelling in various localities came from their villages, towns, outlying districts, and the surrounding royal palaces to pay their respects at a stūpa. No one offered them rest, and having been turned away, they stayed in the cloisters, gatehouse, on the stairs, in the gatehouse corridors, and at the foot of trees. Certain brahmins and householders of little faith, seeing this, said to them: "Noble ones, have you been expelled from the monastery? Why are you staying like this?" The monks replied: "Good sirs, we have not been expelled from the monastery; we have simply arrived as visitors." Those people said: "Noble ones, did your fellow practitioners of the holy life not give you a room?" The monks replied: "Good sirs, since our discipline is not known, who would open a room for us? In any case, we will stay here however we can, pay our respects at the stūpa, and then return to our own dwelling places."

When those brahmins and householders heard that the discipline of the monks, the sons of the Śākya, was equal and uniform, they said: "How is it that this uniform discipline still results in monks who have arrived as visitors not being given a room?" And they reproached, criticized, and derided them. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I shall establish a rule of conduct for monks who arrive as visitors. A monk who arrives as a visitor should make prostrations to the four elders and sit before them. Those elders, for their part, should show him respect, allow him to rest, and, through the keeper of rooms and beds, provide him with a bed."

The Blessed One had declared that a monk who arrives as a visitor should make prostrations to the four elders and sit before them. Now it happened that another monk, while traveling on a journey through the countryside, arrived at Rājagṛha and asked the monks: "Where is the venerable elder Kuṇḍinya (Skt. Kauṇḍinya), he who knows all?" They replied: "He is in the Timber Grove." He went to the Timber Grove and knocked gently, gently on the door of his dwelling. The venerable Kauṇḍinya, who knows all, said: "Who is knocking at the door?" The monk replied: "Venerable elder, I am a visitor who has just arrived; my name is such and such." Kauṇḍinya said: "Venerable one, come inside and rest." The monk replied: "If I am to make prostrations to the venerable elder, the great Kāśyapa, please tell me where he is staying." Kauṇḍinya said: "The venerable one is staying in the cave of the Pippala tree; go there." He went to the cave of the Pippala tree and knocked gently, gently on the door. The venerable great Kāśyapa said: "Who is knocking at the door?" The monk replied: "Noble one, I am a visitor who has just arrived; my name is such and such." Kāśyapa said: "Venerable one, come inside and rest." The monk replied: "If I am also to make prostrations to the venerable elder, the great Maudgalyāyana, please tell me where he is staying." Kāśyapa replied: "The venerable one is staying on Vulture Peak Mountain; go there." He went to Vulture Peak Mountain and knocked gently, gently on the door of his dwelling. The venerable great Maudgalyāyana said: "Who is knocking at the door?" The monk replied: "Venerable elder, I am a visitor who has just arrived; my name is such and such." Maudgalyāyana also said: "Venerable one, come inside and rest."

The monk said: "Elder, I wish to make prostrations to the venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers — please tell me where he is staying." The other replied: "The venerable one is staying in the Pippala Cave; go there." The monk went to the Pippala Cave and knocked gently, gently on the door. The venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers said: "Who is knocking at the door?" The monk replied: "I am a visitor who has just arrived; my name is such and such." Kāśyapa also said: "Venerable one, come inside and rest." At that the monk said: "Elder, it is already late in the night and we must soon go on alms round — how can I rest? The Blessed One has declared that, since we visitors have arrived wearied by the journey, one should go to pay respects to the four elders who have come from afar, in order to perform the act of reviving those exhausted by the penalty." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, I said that one should make prostrations to elders seated on the ground everywhere without exception — yet one should, all the same, make prostrations to the elder who is residing in that same temple."

The summary verse:
At the Teacher's request, the eloquent one
presented it, and then practised according to the preceptor.
At Mṛgadāva there were five hundred,
and at the end seven hundred.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in the prince's Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the venerable Vāgīśa rose from the composure of resting in inward absorption at dusk, went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet in prostration, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Vāgīśa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend one, how should co-residents and attendants serve their preceptor and teacher?" The Blessed One replied: "Vāgīśa, I shall properly establish the Dharma that co-resident monks and attendants should practise throughout. Co-resident monks and attendants should rise early in the morning and enquire of the preceptor and teacher: 'Are you in good health?' If the preceptor says he is not well, one should enquire about the illness and speak to a physician thus: 'My preceptor is afflicted with such and such an ailment — please prescribe medicine.' Then one should act as instructed. If it goes well, good. If medicine is not obtained in that way, one should send to his relatives. If there are many relatives, one should ask: 'From which of the preceptor's relatives should I obtain medicine?' and then obtain it from the one indicated. If there are no relatives, one should obtain it from whichever brahmin or householder is indicated. If there is no such person either, one should obtain it from the infirmary. If it cannot be obtained even there, one should attend to one's own work and remain content with just food, drink, and what one can taste. If it is something other than that — if a tooth-stick is to be used — one should sweep with a cloth and make a circle in the direction in which the preceptor has cast his tooth-stick; one should prepare a seat-spread, set out a water vessel, a rinsing basin, a spittoon, and a tooth-stick; then take up the rinsing basin. If there is one with an eye ailment, one should prepare the eye medicine as directed by a physician, and having prepared it, present it, and then take it back again. Dharma robes too should be presented; and whenever Dharma robes have been distributed and one goes to make prostrations at stūpas, one should set out the dwelling room with care and wipe it with a cloth. If there is dust, one should smear it to whatever extent is needed with cow dung or green leaves. Then one should make prostrations at the stūpas and, to those living the brahma-conduct, also make prostrations as best one can. After that one should remain in application to meditative concentration and recitation. Knowing the time, one should wash both bowls. If one is a wandering almsman, one should oneself carry the heavy bowl,

and whichever is the lighter one, that one should be given to the preceptor. If it is the cold season, whichever blanket-robe is the heavier one should be given to the preceptor, and whichever is lighter, that one should be worn by oneself. If it is the warm season, whichever is the lighter one should be given to the preceptor, and whichever is the heavier one should be carried by oneself. If the road is rough, one should go ahead; if it is smooth, one should follow behind. If a stream is to be crossed, one should take hold of the preceptor's hand. When going on alms round, one should ask the preceptor: "Venerable sir, shall we go on alms round together or separately?" If he says "together," one should go along together; and if, while going, one finds flour, one should take it into one's own bowl. If something with rice is found, one should say: "Please put it into the preceptor's bowl." If food made from beans and lentils, or food made from ground rice, is found, one should take it into one's own bowl. If something that is a richer dish is found, one should say: "Please put it into the preceptor's bowl." If boiled butter-milk or a thick broth is found, one should take it into one's own bowl. If there is milk, or curds, or something prepared with cream, one should say: "Please put it into the preceptor's bowl." Then, having gone to the dwelling room, one should prepare two circles on the ground and, having removed any fallen leaves, set out two seats. Then one should sit and attend to the business of the meal. If one has gone on alms round separately and has received alms, one should say to the preceptor: "Venerable sir, this is what I have obtained on alms round. Please take from it whatever you wish." And the preceptor too should be mindful of what is fitting. If something is to be received from the Saṅgha, one should wash the vessels, go to the assembly, and inquire about the distribution, saying: "Venerable ones, what portion of the Saṅgha's share has been prepared today?" And one should do so respectfully and report it back. Then one should say to the preceptor: "Venerable sir, the Saṅgha has prepared such-and-such a portion. Please take from it whatever you wish." And the preceptor too should be mindful of what is fitting. Then, in whatever place the preceptor has washed his hands, one should prepare a circle on the ground there and set out a seat, a water vessel for rinsing the head, a spittoon, and tooth-wood; and one should also wash the preceptor's feet. After washing his feet, one should dry them and then offer the sandals. If no foot-washing is being done, one should offer water, earth, and a vessel of sesame oil. Then, when the meal is finished, one should ask the preceptor: "Venerable sir, will you devote yourself to virtue right here, or will you go to rest for the midday?" If he says he will go to rest for the midday, one should take up the seat; and while he goes and rests at midday, one should wipe it with a cloth and dust it off, and arrange the cushion, and at the appropriate times anoint it with the dung of a young bull. If he engages in extensive recitation, one should show him the text. If he engages in extended meditative concentration, one should demonstrate to him the mental application. When he returns from midday rest, one should examine the bed and seat, wash one's hands and feet, and make prostrations at the stūpa. One should also make prostrations to those practising the brahma-conduct; and one should place nearby the preceptor's small seat, water, sandals, and a vessel of sesame oil. If he washes his feet, one should wash them for him and anoint them. If not, one should offer water and earth. If it is the cold season, one should kindle fire and stoke the embers. If it is the warm season, one should set out a fan to cool the air.

He should also have him learn at the proper times to recite and chant by heart. In all matters concerning the alms bowl and the like, whatever is to be done, the preceptor and ācārya should do it first, and only afterwards should one do it oneself. Those who live in community and the personal attendants should serve the preceptor and ācārya in just this way. When those who live in community and the personal attendants serve the preceptor and ācārya in such a manner, the virtuous qualities of such a person will flourish abundantly, like a blue lotus (utpala) flower blossoming in water.

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, the forty-ninth fascicle. The occasion for this is in Rājagṛha.

Then at that time, monks by the name of "Swift-walker" and "Nabso," and reddish-grey monks who were a disgrace to householders, who practiced every manner of evil, were dwelling on the Black Mountain. They sat together with women, exchanged conversation with them, played together, made noise together, were restless and carelessly swung their bodies about, sat together on the same seat, enjoyed things from the same vessel, drank many kinds of liquor from the same cup, plucked flowers and had them plucked, threaded garlands and had them strung, tied flower ornaments and had them tied, sang songs, played musical instruments and had others play them. They gave wages to skilled dancers, pleasant singers, and those adept at playing musical instruments. Hitching up their robes, they ran, leaped, and jumped over things. Drawing up one leg, they turned about; they also turned about doing a hand-walk, and turned about in a fish-leap. They dammed up water and released it, made frog sounds in the water, made drumming sounds in the water, made the sound of an elephant, made the cry of a crane, made the sound of a horse, made the strutting sounds of a fine stallion, made the sound of a clay drum, made sounds imitating a conch, a drum, and a peacock's cry, and made the sound of a cuckoo. They staged fights between elephants, fights between horses, fights between stallions, fights between buffalo, fights between rams, fights between sheep, fights between women, fights between men, fights between girls, fights between cocks, fights between goats, and fights between rams — and they also instigated such fights between cocks, goats, and rams. They also performed other acts unworthy of a contemplative.

On account of their conduct, their behavior, and these corrupt activities, monks who had not yet come to the Black Mountain did not come, and those who had come did not remain, so that the community abandoned the Black Mountain as a dwelling place. The brahmins and householders residing on the Black Mountain spoke thus: "These monks perform acts unworthy of contemplatives," and they mocked, derided, and disparaged them.

When the monks heard of this, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is indeed the case that brahmins and householders mock, deride, and disparage them. Therefore, a monk should not perform such acts unworthy of a contemplative, nor should he cause others to do them. If monks perform or cause others to perform such acts unworthy of a contemplative, it will constitute a serious offense."

The Blessed Śākyamuni Buddha was dwelling on the Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha. At that time, Ajātaśatru, the son of Queen Vaidehī, king of the land of Magadha,

the Vajjians fell into mutual discord. Ajātaśatru said to his retinue: "I shall crush, reduce to dust, and utterly destroy without trace these Vajjians, who are prosperous and flourishing, at ease, enjoying good harvests, populous, and filled with many people."

Then Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, king of the land of Magadha, addressed the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of Magadha, with these words: "Come here, Vassakāra. Go to where the Blessed One is, and when you have gone, bow your head at the feet of the Blessed One on my behalf, and inquire after his health, saying: 'Does he have little discomfort? Does he have little affliction? Is he in good spirits? Does he dwell touching strength and ease? Is he free from blame?' After conveying these greetings, say this: 'Venerable sir, Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, king of the land of Magadha, and the Vajjians have come into mutual conflict, and he has said to his retinue: "I shall crush, reduce to dust, and utterly destroy without trace these Vajjians, who are prosperous and flourishing, at ease, enjoying good harvests, populous, and filled with many people." What does the Blessed One declare in this matter?' And whatever the Blessed One prophesies, remember it just as it is. For Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and fully awakened buddhas do not speak falsely."

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of Magadha, answered Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, king of the land of Magadha: "As your majesty commands," and he entered a white carriage drawn among all carriages by swift mares, taking a golden whip and a garland-vessel for anointing, and departed from Rājagṛha. He went as far as the ground was passable by carriage, then descended from the carriage and climbed Vulture Peak Mountain on foot, and went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he exchanged with the Blessed One the various words of cordial and pleasant greeting, and then sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One: "O Gautama, Blessed Gautama, Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, king of the land of Magadha, bows his head at your feet and inquires after your health: does you have little discomfort? Does you have little affliction? Are you in good spirits? Do you dwell touching strength and ease? Are you free from blame? These are his greetings, Blessed One.

"And further: may Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, king of the land of Magadha, and you, Vassakāra, likewise be well.

"O Gautama, Ajātaśatru, son of Queen Vaidehī, king of the land of Magadha, and the Vajjians have come into mutual conflict, and he has said to his retinue: 'I shall crush, reduce to dust, and utterly destroy without trace these Vajjians, who are prosperous and flourishing, at ease, enjoying good harvests, populous, and filled with many people.' O Blessed One, O Gautama, what do you declare in this matter?"

"Vassakāra, this matter is not to be determined once and for all. Vassakāra, at one time when I was dwelling near the Vajjian stūpa at Capal, I taught the seven principles of non-decline for the Vajjians. Vassakāra, as long as the Vajjians rightly take up and practise these seven principles of non-decline, and

as long as the seven principles of non-decline are manifest among the Vajjians, the wholesome qualities desired by the Vajjians will grow and not decline.

"Gautama has spoken thus in brief, but if he has not yet expanded upon it and I have not understood the meaning in full, then let Gautama unfold what he has spoken in brief and explain it at length — in that way I shall come to understand well the meaning that the Blessed One Gautama has unfolded and explained in full."

Then at that very moment the venerable Ānanda was seated to one side of the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke to the venerable Ānanda:

"What do you say, Ānanda? Have you heard that the Vajjians meet together often and attend their assemblies in full?"

"Venerable sir, I have heard it: the Vajjians do indeed meet together often and attend their assemblies in full."

"Ānanda, for as long as the Vajjians meet together often and attend their assemblies in full, one should know that the wholesome qualities of the Vajjians will not decline but will grow.

"What do you say, Ānanda? Have you heard that the Vajjians sit together in harmony and rise together in harmony, and that they conduct the affairs and business of the Vajjians in harmony?"

"Venerable sir, I have heard it: the Vajjians are indeed in harmony" — and so on in the same way as above.

"Ānanda, for as long as the Vajjians sit together in harmony and rise together in harmony, and conduct the affairs and business of the Vajjians in harmony, one should know that the wholesome qualities of the Vajjians will not decline but will grow.

"What do you say, Ānanda? Have you heard that the Vajjians do not establish what has not been established as a rule, and do not discard what has already been established, but live and conduct themselves in accordance with the rules that the Vajjians have laid down and properly adopted?"

"Venerable sir, I have heard it: the Vajjians do not establish what has not been established as a rule, and do not discard what has already been established, but live and conduct themselves in accordance with the rules that the Vajjians have properly adopted."

"Ānanda, for as long as the Vajjians do not establish what has not been established as a rule, do not discard what has been established, and live and conduct themselves throughout in accordance with the rules that the Vajjians have properly adopted, one should know that the wholesome qualities of the Vajjians will not decline but will grow.

"What do you say, Ānanda? Have you heard that the Vajjians do not seize by force or coerce women and girls of the Vajjians — those guarded by their fathers, guarded by their mothers, guarded by their brothers, guarded by their sisters, guarded by relatives, guarded by their clan, protected by the law, kept under guard, those who are the wives of others and are claimed by others, and even those who in their youth have cast but a garland of flowers — that the Vajjians do not immediately cast them aside and do not pursue their desires by force?"

"Venerable sir, I have heard it. The Vajjians do not seize by force or coerce women and girls of the Vajjians — those guarded by their fathers, guarded by their mothers," and so on as above, "and even those who in their youth have cast but a garland of flowers — the Vajjians do not immediately cast them aside and do not pursue their desires by force."

"Ānanda, for as long as the Vajjians do not seize by force women and girls of the Vajjians —

— those girls of the Vajjians who in their youth have cast but a garland of flowers — the Vajjians do not immediately cast them aside and do not pursue their desires by force. For as long as the Vajjians do not do so, it should be known that the virtuous qualities of the Vajjians will not decline but will grow and flourish.

"Ānanda, have you heard whether the Vajjians honor, revere, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian elders, the nobility, and those of distinguished family lineage whom the Vajjians hold in respect, and whether they listen with confidence to their words and take them to heart?"

"Venerable sir, I have heard it. The Vajjians do honor, revere, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian elders, the nobility, and those of distinguished family lineage whom the Vajjians hold in respect, and they do listen with confidence to their words and take them to heart."

"Ānanda, for as long as the Vajjians honor, revere, esteem, and venerate the Vajjian elders, the nobility, and those of distinguished family lineage whom the Vajjians hold in respect, and listen with confidence to their words and take them to heart — it should be known that the virtuous qualities of the Vajjians will not decline but will grow and flourish.

"Ānanda, have you heard whether the Vajjians, in the four regions of the Vajjians wherever Vajjian shrines are found, honor, revere, esteem, and venerate those shrines, and whether they do not abandon the offerings formerly consecrated at them?"

"Venerable sir, I have heard it. The Vajjians, in the four regions of the Vajjians wherever Vajjian shrines are found, do honor, revere, esteem, and venerate those shrines, and they do not abandon the offerings formerly consecrated at them."

"Ānanda, for as long as the Vajjians, in the four regions of the Vajjians wherever Vajjian shrines are found, honor, revere, esteem, and venerate those shrines, and do not abandon the offerings formerly consecrated at them — it should be known that the virtuous qualities of the Vajjians will not decline but will grow and flourish.

"Ānanda, have you heard whether the Vajjians keep close and unwavering mindfulness toward the arhats with a mind of strong faith, invite those arhats who have not yet come, and rejoice in the presence of those who have come, and do not leave them without robes, almsfood, lodging, medicines for the sick, and other requisites?"

"Venerable sir, I have heard it. The Vajjians do keep close and unwavering mindfulness toward the arhats with a mind of strong faith, they invite those arhats who have not yet come, and they rejoice in the presence of those who have come, and they do not leave them without robes, almsfood, lodging, medicines for the sick, and other requisites."

"Ānanda, for as long as the Vajjians keep close and unwavering mindfulness toward the arhats with a mind of strong faith, invite those arhats who have not yet come, rejoice in the presence of those who have come, and do not leave them without robes, almsfood, lodging, medicines for the sick, and other requisites — it should be known that the virtuous qualities of the Vajjians will not decline but will grow and flourish."

For as long as the monastics who undertake the rains retreat take up and practice in full these seven qualities that prevent decline, and for as long as these seven qualities that prevent decline are seen to be present among those who undertake the rains retreat — it should be known that the virtuous qualities of those who undertake the rains retreat will not decline but will grow and flourish.

"O Gautama, even if the monastics possessed but one of these qualities, the army of Ajātaśatru, king of Magadha, would not be able to overcome them — how much less so when they possess all of them. And now, O Gautama, since I have many matters to attend to and many duties that await me, I shall take my leave."

"Brahmin Vassakāra, you know yourself that the time has come. You may go."

Then Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, rejoiced and was glad at what the Blessed One had said, and rising from before the Blessed One he departed.

When Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, had not long gone, the Blessed One knew this, and he spoke to the venerable Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda, go and assemble all the monks who are dwelling in dependence at Vulture Peak and gather them here at the assembly hall."

"Reverend sir, I shall do as you command," said the venerable Ānanda, and having listened to the Blessed One, he went to Vulture Peak, assembled all the monks who were dwelling there in dependence, and then went to where the Blessed One was. He arrived and, bowing with his head to the Blessed One's feet, sat down to one side. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus: "Reverend sir, all the monks who were dwelling in dependence at Vulture Peak have assembled here and are present together. Blessed One, please consider that the time for this has now come."

Then the Blessed One proceeded to the assembly hall and sat down on the seat that had been prepared in the midst of the community of monks. Once seated, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I shall teach you seven qualities that prevent decline. Listen well, take them to heart, and I shall speak."

"What are the seven qualities that prevent decline? Monks, for as long as the monks assemble again and again, and remain from that repeated assembly without departing — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish. For as long as the monks gather in harmony, depart in harmony, and conduct the affairs and business of the Saṅgha in harmony — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish. Monks, for as long as the monks do not promulgate what has not been promulgated, do not abandon what has been promulgated, and live in accordance with the trainings as they have been established, taking up and practicing whatever additional rules are rightly undertaken — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish. Monks, for as long as the monks are not dominated by delight in things arising from craving — that craving for renewed existence, born of joyful desire and arising moment by moment in this or that form — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish. Monks, for as long as the monks honor, revere, esteem, and venerate those elder monks who are like kings among long-dwellers in the community, who went forth long ago, who have made the holy life a habit, who have been praised by the Teacher, who have fully cultivated and clearly perfected the practice of the holy life — and for as long as they listen to such elder monks with faith in their words —

— it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish. Monks, for as long as the monks take up their dwelling in remote forest hermitages, woodland groves, and lodgings at the edges of settlements, it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish. Monks, for as long as the monks, guarding themselves continuously with a strong mind of faith toward those who live the holy life as their peers, remain with mindfulness close at hand — calling out to those living the holy life who have not yet come, rejoicing in those who have come, and not troubling those who have come with concern for robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, for as long as the monks properly take up and live by these seven principles of non-decline, and for as long as these seven principles of non-decline are fully evident among the monks, it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, I shall now teach you yet another set of seven principles of complete non-decline. Listen carefully, take them to heart, and I shall explain them. What are these seven principles of complete non-decline?

Monks, for as long as the monks honor, revere, esteem, and venerate the Teacher, and dwelling in reliance upon the Teacher whom they have honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish. For as long as they cultivate meditative absorption, honor it, revere it, esteem it, and venerate it, demonstrating through it careful heedfulness in the trainings and thorough discernment, and dwelling in reliance upon that meditative absorption which they have honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, for as long as the monks properly take up and live by these seven principles of complete non-decline, and for as long as these seven principles of complete non-decline are fully evident among the monks, it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, I shall now teach you yet another set of seven principles of complete non-decline. Listen carefully, take them to heart, and I shall explain them. What are these seven principles of complete non-decline?

Monks, for as long as the monks take no delight in busyness, take no delight in idle chatter, take no delight in sleep, take no delight in gossip, take no delight in gatherings, take no delight in socializing, and dwelling thus, setting aside other preoccupations, remain in steady pursuit of endeavor, content with the smallest and most meager of things, and through that contentment press ever further onward in accomplishing what is to be done — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, for as long as the monks properly take up and live by these seven principles of complete non-decline, and for as long as these seven principles of complete non-decline are fully evident among the monks, it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, I shall now teach you yet another set of seven principles of complete non-decline.

Listen well, take it to heart, and I shall speak. What are these seven principles of complete non-decline? Monks, for as long as the monks come to possess faith, a sense of shame, a sense of conscience, applied diligence, the establishment of mindfulness, the establishment of meditative equipoise, and wisdom — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, for as long as the monks properly take up and live by these seven principles of complete non-decline, and for as long as these seven principles of complete non-decline are fully evident among the monks, it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, I shall now teach you yet another set of seven principles of complete non-decline. Listen well, take it to heart, and I shall speak. What are these seven principles of complete non-decline? Monks, for as long as the monks come to possess knowledge of the Dharma, knowledge of its meaning, knowledge of the proper time, knowledge of measure, knowledge of themselves, knowledge of the assembly, and knowledge of persons — whether supreme or not supreme — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, for as long as the monks properly take up and live by these seven principles of complete non-decline, and for as long as these seven principles of complete non-decline are fully evident among the monks, it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, I shall now explain to you yet another set of seven principles of complete non-decline. Listen well, take it to heart, and I shall speak. What are these seven principles of complete non-decline? Monks, for as long as the monks cultivate the limb of awakening that is correct mindfulness — abiding in seclusion, abiding in dispassion, abiding in cessation, transforming the mind through complete relinquishment — and for as long as they cultivate the limbs of awakening that are discrimination of phenomena, diligence, joy, thorough pliancy, meditative absorption, and equanimity — each abiding in seclusion, abiding in dispassion, abiding in cessation, transforming the mind through complete relinquishment — it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, for as long as the monks properly take up and live by these seven principles of complete non-decline, and for as long as these seven principles of complete non-decline are fully evident among the monks, it should be known that their virtuous qualities will not decline but will grow and flourish.

Monks, I shall now teach you six principles that lead to universal delight. Listen well, take it to heart, and I shall speak. What are these six principles that lead to universal delight?

One who, with acts of loving-kindness in body, constantly abides and cultivates in the presence of the Teacher and those who practice the holy life — rejoicing in the wise, honoring them, gladly welcoming them, having welcomed them with gladness, having honored them, having held them in reverence — gathers all together in unity, and having truly gathered them, lives and practices in harmony without conflict and as one: this is a principle that leads to universal delight. Likewise, acts of loving-kindness in speech and acts of loving-kindness in mind.

Whatever is obtained in accordance with the Dharma — even if only a little, even something that comes into the begging bowl, even such a small gain as that — one does not consume it alone in seclusion, but shares it in common with joy together with those who practice the holy life, eating in fellowship. One rejoices in them, honors them, gladly welcomes them, having welcomed them with gladness, having honored them, having held them in reverence.

Having cultivated and fully gathered them together, and having completely assembled them, one acts without conflict and as one, practicing them in common: this is a principle that leads to universal delight. Whatever moral discipline is unimpaired and flawless, not dragged along, not patched together, self-governed, not blackened or mottled, thoroughly undertaken, completely perfected, praised by the wise, and such that those who live the holy life are not censured by the wise — moral discipline of that kind one holds in common together with those wise ones who live the holy life, practicing it as one and practicing it in common with them. All the rest follows as before, up to "practicing them in common": this is a principle that leads to universal delight. Whatever noble view is one of definite emergence, of definite distinction, of genuine deliverance — a view that by its very cause brings suffering to a thorough end and leads to the final cessation of suffering — that kind of view one holds in common together with those wise ones who live the holy life, sharing the same view, acting as one and practicing it in common with them. All the rest follows as before, up to "practicing them in common": this is a principle that leads to universal delight.

Monks, so long as you rightly take up and practice these six principles of universal delight, monks, when these principles of universal delight are everywhere apparent, know that the wholesome qualities of the monks will not decline but will increase and flourish.

The intermediate summary in verse:
The Teacher, and the Vinaya,
Livelihood and faith and the nature of reality,
The limbs of awakening — universal delight,
The rains retreat, and the full exposition.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us go to the village of Nāḍa." "Venerable sir, as you command," said the venerable Ānanda, and he complied with what the Blessed One said.

Then the Blessed One, traveling with the community of monks through the country of Magadha, spent the night at a royal resting place called Ambalaṭṭhikā, lying between the village of Nāḍa and Rājagṛha.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, it is because you and I did not know, did not see, did not penetrate, and did not individually realize the Four Noble Truths that we have been running and wandering for so long upon this lengthy road. What are those four truths? It is because you and I did not know, did not see, did not penetrate, and did not individually realize suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path that leads to the cessation of suffering, that we have been running and wandering for so long upon this lengthy road. But now, having followed and individually realized the noble truth of suffering, having cut off the craving for existence, the births of cyclic existence are exhausted, and there is no further existence. And likewise having followed and individually realized the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering — having cut off the craving for existence, the births of cyclic existence are exhausted, and there is no further existence."

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the Sugata, the Well-Gone, having said this, the Teacher then spoke further in verse:

Because you and I alone
did not see as they truly are
the four noble truths,
we wandered for long upon the lengthy road.

Now, having seen those truths
and having cut off the craving for existence,
the births of cyclic existence are exhausted:
there is no further existence now.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Now, Ānanda, let us go to the village of Nāḍa."

"As you command, Venerable One," said the venerable Ānanda, and he did as the Blessed One directed. Then the Blessed One, travelling on tour through the land of Magadha, arrived at the village of Nādika and took up residence at the Nādika stūpa in the village of Nādika. The brahmins and householders of the village of Nādika heard that the Blessed One, travelling on tour through the land of Magadha, had arrived at the village of Nādika and was residing at the Nādika stūpa. Having heard this, they gathered in groups and assembled in crowds, and coming out from the village of Nādika they went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One spoke these words to the brahmins and householders of the village of Nādika:

"Brahmins and householders, these five are the faults of heedlessness. What five?

"Brahmins and householders, one who is heedless and who abides in heedlessness will, on account of that, fall away from great wealth. That a brahmin or householder who is heedless and abides in heedlessness falls away from great wealth on account of that — this is the first fault of heedlessness.

"Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedless and who abides in heedlessness will, on account of that, go into whatever assembly it may be — whether the assembly of the warrior-nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, or the assembly of ascetics — and in each and every such assembly they will arrive timid and joyless, going about in shame and embarrassment. That a brahmin or householder who is heedless and abides in heedlessness goes into whatever assembly it may be and arrives timid, joyless, going about in shame and embarrassment — this, as stated above, is the second fault of heedlessness.

"Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedless and who abides in heedlessness will, on account of that, become known in all directions and throughout all quarters by a bad, unflattering, and ignoble report and reputation in verse. That a brahmin or householder who is heedless and abides in heedlessness becomes known in all directions and throughout all quarters by a bad, unflattering, and ignoble report and reputation in verse — this is the third fault of heedlessness.

"Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedless and who abides in heedlessness will, on account of that, come to die confused in mind. That a brahmin or householder who is heedless and abides in heedlessness comes to die confused in mind — this is the fourth fault of heedlessness.

"Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedless and who abides in heedlessness will, on account of that, at the breaking up of the body after death, fall into a miserable state, a bad destination, a downfall, and be reborn among the hell-beings. That a brahmin or householder who is heedless and abides in heedlessness at the breaking up of the body after death falls into a miserable state, a bad destination, a downfall, and is reborn among the hell-beings — this is the fifth fault of heedlessness.

"Brahmins and householders, these five are the benefits of heedfulness. What five?

"Brahmins and householders, one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, not fall away from great wealth. Brahmins and householders —"

Brahmins and householders, that one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, not fall away from great wealth — this is the first benefit of heedfulness.

Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, enter whatever assembly — whether an assembly of the warrior-nobles, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics — without timidity, with joy, and without embarrassment. Brahmins and householders, that one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will enter whatever assembly — as stated above from "on account of that" through "without embarrassment" — this is the second benefit of heedfulness.

Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, become renowned in all directions and quarters through virtue, fame, repute, and verses of praise spread far and wide. Brahmins and householders, that one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, become renowned in all directions and quarters through virtue, fame, repute, and verses of praise spread far and wide — this is the third benefit of heedfulness.

Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, pass the time without worry. Brahmins and householders, that one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, pass the time without worry — this is the fourth benefit of heedfulness.

Furthermore, brahmins and householders, one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, at the breaking up of the body after death, be reborn among the gods of the heavenly realms, a happy destination and a higher world. Brahmins and householders, that one who is heedful and who abides in heedfulness will, on account of that, at the breaking up of the body after death, be reborn among the gods of the heavenly realms, a happy destination and a higher world — this is the fifth benefit of heedfulness.

Then the Blessed One instructed, engaged, inspired, and delighted the brahmins and householders of Roruka with a Dharma-talk, in many ways instructing them, engaging them, inspiring them, and delighting them with a Dharma-talk; and then he fell silent.

Then the brahmins and householders of Roruka rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, knelt on their right knees, and with palms joined in the direction of the Blessed One, bowed in reverence, and said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, may you consent to remain here in our place for a day."

The Blessed One consented to the brahmins and householders of the village of Roruka by remaining silent.

Then the brahmins and householders of Roruka, understanding by the Blessed One's silence that he had consented, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said and expressed their approval. They prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

Then, not long after the brahmins and householders of Roruka had departed, the Blessed One knew the time and rose, going to where his dwelling was. He washed both feet at the outer entrance of the dwelling and went inside the dwelling in order to sit in proper meditation.

Then at that time, the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, was striving to build a city wall around the village of Pāṭaligāma in order to crush the Vajjian brahmins and householders. And at that time, the powerful and mighty gods were mingling in that place, dwelling by dwelling, throughout Pāṭaligāma. While the Blessed One was dwelling there engaged in his daytime practice, with his divine eye, purified beyond that of ordinary human beings, he saw the powerful and mighty gods mingling in that place, dwelling by dwelling, throughout Pāṭaligāma. Having seen this, he rose from the meditative equipoise in which he had rested during the afternoon, came forth from his dwelling, and took his seat on a prepared cushion in the shadow of the dwelling, in the midst of the community of monks.

When he was seated, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, who is it that you have heard is striving to build a city wall around Pāṭaligāma?"

"Venerable Sir, I have heard that it is the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, who is striving to build a city wall around the village of Pāṭaligāma in order to crush the Vajjian brahmins and householders."

"Excellent, Ānanda, excellent! Ānanda, the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, is skilled. He has, as it were, deliberated together with the gods of the Thirty-Three. Ānanda, while I was dwelling here engaged in my daytime practice, with my divine eye, purified beyond that of ordinary human beings, I saw the powerful and mighty gods mingling in that place, dwelling by dwelling, throughout Pāṭaligāma. Ānanda, in whatever direction the powerful and mighty gods have mingled by dwelling, in that direction the minds of powerful and mighty people will incline — it is on account of the dwellings. In whatever direction middling gods and common gods have mingled by dwelling, in that direction the minds of middling people and common people will incline — it is on account of the dwellings. Ānanda, here in this Pāṭaligāma, in this direction where the powerful and mighty gods have mingled by dwelling, the minds of powerful and mighty people will incline — it is on account of the dwellings. Ānanda, there will be as many noble dwelling places, as many noble designations, and as many roads for noble merchants, and it will become a great trading center — that is to say, this city of Pāṭaligāma will become supreme. Yet know that three dangers will arise for it: from fire, from water, and from internal strife."

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, heard that the ascetic Gautama, having journeyed through the realm of Magadha, had come to the village of Pāṭaligāma and was dwelling near the Pāṭaligāma shrine in Pāṭaligāma, and that the brahmins and householders of Pāṭaligāma were attending upon him. Having heard this, he came out from Pāṭaligāma, went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arriving exchanged with the Blessed One various words of joyful and cordial greeting, and then sat down to one side.

Once he was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, with Dharma-connected discourse, roused him, established him in it, encouraged him, and filled him with delight. Having in many ways instructed him with Dharma-connected discourse, roused him, encouraged him, and filled him with delight, the Blessed One fell silent.

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and bowed,

said the following to the Blessed One: "Wise Gautama, if it would be permitted for us to take our midday meal together with the community of monks, please grant your consent." The Blessed One consented to the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, by remaining silent.

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, fiftieth bundle.

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, rejoiced at what the Blessed One had said, praised him, rose from his seat, and departed.

That same night the brahmin Vassakāra prepared pure and choice food and drink, and rising early the following morning, he spread out seats and set out a water vessel adorned with jewels. He then sent word to the Blessed One of the hour, saying: "Gautama, it is midday. Wise Gautama, if the time has come, may he be pleased to know that the time has come."

Then the Blessed One, at the morning hour, dressed in his lower robe and robes, took up his bowl, and with the community of monks before him, went to the dwelling of the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha. He arrived and sat down in the seat that had been laid out in the midst of the community of monks.

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, having seen that the Blessed One and the community of monks were comfortably seated, served them with pure and choice food and drink with his own hands, satisfying them to the full. Again and again with his own hands he served them with pure and choice food and drink, and satisfied them to the full.

When the Blessed One had finished his meal and withdrawn his hands, Vassakāra, knowing that the bowl had been set aside, took up a golden water-sprinkler, sat before the Blessed One, and said: "O Gautama, whatever source of merit, source of virtue, and foundation of happiness arises from this act of giving — may it be dedicated here and now for the long-term benefit, welfare, and happiness of the gods who dwell in the city of Rājagṛha." He thus requested the Blessed One to dedicate the merit of the gift there and then.

Then the Blessed One rejoiced in the gift of the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, with this rejoicing:

A person of faith,
whoever makes offerings to the gods,
who acts in accordance with the word of the buddhas —
such a one is praised by the buddhas.

One who is wise and of settled mind,
in whatever quarter he takes up his abode,
having offered food to those endowed with moral discipline,
let him dedicate the merit beneath them.

Those honored by such honoring shall be honored,
and worshipped by such worship shall be worshipped.
Then, as a mother to the child born of her womb,
let him show love to these.
The person whom the gods love
will come to see great happiness.

Then the Blessed One, having in many ways instructed the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, with Dharma-connected discourse, roused him, established him in it, encouraged him, and filled him with delight. Rising from his seat, he departed.

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, gave away all the remaining food as a gift, and followed after the Blessed One, reflecting inwardly and forming this thought: "The gate through which the ascetic Gautama departed from the city of Rājagṛha — I shall name it Gautama's Gate."

"And the ford of the Ganges River by which he crossed — that too I shall name Gautama's Ford."

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thoughts of the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, passed directly through the midst of the town of Ambalaṭṭhikā, emerged by the western gate, traveled northward, and arrived at the bank of the Ganges River. At that time the people of Magadha were crossing the Ganges back and forth: some on planks of sal wood, some on wooden rafts, some in boats, and some by swimming.

Then the Blessed One considered: "Shall I cross against the current of the Ganges, or shall I disappear from this bank and appear on the far bank?" Then the Blessed One entered into such a meditative absorption that, together with the community of monks, he disappeared from this near bank and appeared on the far bank — just as one places the mind in equipoise. And thereupon another monk spoke these verses:

Some build a bridge and, casting aside the shallows, cross the sea.
The wise among beings cross by means of rafts.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, having crossed while the brahmin still waded, stands upon the far shore dry.
Here the monks who bathe — those hearers — are the ones making use of rafts.

If water is everywhere found,
what use then is the water of a well?
Having cut the root of craving,
who would still go seeking what to consume?

Then the brahmin Vassakāra, chief minister of the realm of Magadha, named the gate of the town of Ambalaṭṭhikā by which the Blessed One had departed "Gautama's Gate," and named the ford of the Ganges by which he had crossed "Gautama's Ford."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us go to the city of Pāṭaliputta." "As the Venerable One commands," replied the venerable Ānanda, and he listened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One traveled through the countryside, departing from that region, and arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputta, where he took up residence in a grove of śāpa trees to the north of the city.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, moral discipline is of this kind; meditative absorption is of this kind; wisdom is of this kind. When moral discipline is thoroughly cultivated, one comes to dwell long in meditative absorption. When meditative absorption is thoroughly cultivated, one comes to dwell long in wisdom. When wisdom is thoroughly cultivated, the mind becomes completely liberated from attachment, aversion, and delusion, exactly as they are. Monks, when the noble hearers (śrāvakas) are thus completely liberated in mind, they directly and truly know: 'Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what had to be done has been done; there is no further existence beyond this.'"

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us go to the city of Vaiśālī." "As the Venerable One commands," replied the venerable Ānanda, and he listened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One traveled through the countryside, departing from that region, and arrived at Vaiśālī, where he took up residence at the Kundaka's Grove in Vaiśālī.

At that time a great fear arose among the common people of Vaiśālī. It was reported that the lay practitioner Udraka had passed away at his appointed time; and likewise the lay practitioners Neyya, Rabhassona, Kātyāyana's Bull of the Herd, Subhadda, Neyya-subhadda, Āciravata, Neyya-āciravata, Bhadra, Subhadra, Yasa, and

Yaśodatta and Yaśottara had also passed away at their appointed time. Then a great many monks, in the early morning hour, put on their lower robes, took up their outer robes and alms bowls, and entered Vaiśālī for the sake of alms. As a great many monks were making their alms round in Vaiśālī, they heard that a great many common people of that city had died — that the lay practitioner Udraka had passed away at his appointed time, and likewise the lay practitioners Neyya, Rabhassona, Kātyāyana's Bull of the Herd, Subhadda, Neyya-subhadda, Āciravata, Neyya-āciravata, Bhadra, Subhadra, Yaśa, Yaśodatta, and Yaśottara had all passed away at their appointed time. Having heard this, they completed their alms round in Vaiśālī, finished the meal, set aside the alms bowl after the meal, put away their bowls and robes in order, washed their two feet, went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side.

Sitting to one side, the great many monks addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, we — a great many monks — in the early morning hour, having put on our lower robes and taken up our alms bowls and outer robes, entered this Vaiśālī for the sake of alms. Venerable One, as we, a great many monks, were going on our alms round through Vaiśālī, we heard that a great many common people of this city had died — that the lay practitioner Udraka had passed away at his appointed time, and likewise the lay practitioners Neyya, Rabhassona, Kātyāyana's Bull of the Herd, Subhadda, Neyya-subhadda, Āciravata, Neyya-āciravata, Bhadra, Subhadra, Yaśa, Yaśodatta, and Yaśottara had also passed away at their appointed time. Venerable One, where have they gone? In what place of the other world were they reborn?"

"Monks, the lay practitioner Udraka abandoned the five fetters that are not in conformity with the higher part, was born spontaneously in that very realm, attained complete nirvāṇa there, and entered the nature of one who does not return to this world and does not arise in it again. The lay practitioners Neyya, Rabhassona, Kātyāyana's Bull of the Herd, Subhadda, Neyya-subhadda, Āciravata, Neyya-āciravata, Bhadra, Subhadra, Yaśa, Yaśodatta, and Yaśottara likewise abandoned the five fetters that are not in conformity with the higher part, were born spontaneously in that very realm, attained complete nirvāṇa, and entered the nature of those who do not return to this world and do not arise in it again.

"Monks, as for the two hundred and fifty-one lay practitioners of Vaiśālī who have passed away at their appointed time — they too abandoned the five fetters that are not in conformity with the higher part, were born spontaneously in that very realm, attained complete nirvāṇa, and entered the nature of those who do not return to this world and do not arise in it again.

"Monks, as for the more than three hundred lay practitioners of Vaiśālī who have passed away — they abandoned the three fetters, thinned out attachment, aversion, and delusion, and became once-returners, who will return to this world one more time and, having returned once, will make an end of suffering.

"Monks, as for the more than five hundred lay practitioners of Vaiśālī who have passed away — they abandoned the three fetters and, having entered the stream, entered the nature of those who do not fall back, and are certain to attain perfect and complete awakening.

at most, one will not pass beyond seven existences, and having taken birth seven times among gods or humans, one will make an end of suffering.

"Monks, you have asked the Tathāgata about the time of passing. To ask the Tathāgata 'when the time of passing has come' is to show disrespect to the Tathāgata. That it is uncomfortable for the Tathāgata is one thing; but that where there is birth there will certainly come a time of death — in that there is no great wonder. What is wonderful is this: whether or not Tathāgatas appear in the world, the way of the Dharma abides. These very dharmadhātus abide as the nature of reality — the Tathāgata himself knows and fully comprehends them, and then teaches, sets forth, establishes, analyzes, makes clear, reveals, and fully expounds them. And what he expounds is this:

When this exists, that arises; with the arising of this, that is born. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance, formations arise; conditioned by formations, consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, becoming arises; conditioned by becoming, birth arises; conditioned by birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation arise. Thus this entire great mass of suffering comes to be.

And this: When this is absent, that does not arise; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation cease. Thus this entire great mass of suffering ceases.

"Monks, such being the case, I have now taught the Dharma teaching that is a category of the Dharma Mirror. Listen to it well, take it to heart, and I will explain it. What is the Dharma teaching that is a category of the Dharma Mirror? Faith founded on knowing the Buddha — that is the Dharma teaching that is a category of the Dharma Mirror. Faith founded on knowing the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the noble ones' beloved moral discipline — that too is the Dharma teaching that is a category of the Dharma Mirror. Monks, I have spoken to you of the Dharma teaching that is a category of the Dharma Mirror, and in that saying it has been said."

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us go to Vaiśālī." "Venerable one, as you command," said the venerable Ānanda, and he followed the Blessed One's lead. Then the Blessed One departed from that district, traveled through the countryside, and arrived at Vaiśālī, where he took up residence in the Āmrapālī Grove of Vaiśālī.

Āmrapālī heard that the Blessed One had departed from that district, traveled through the countryside, arrived at Vaiśālī, and was residing in the grove that was her own garden at Vaiśālī.
