Upon hearing this, she adorned herself with all her ornaments, surrounded herself with a retinue of women, mounted a fine carriage, and set out from Vaiśālī to behold the Blessed One.

She went into the Blessed One's presence to pay him honor and reverence. She rode in her carriage as far as the road was passable for carriages, then dismounted and went on foot to the pleasure grove.

At that time the Blessed One was seated in the midst of an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma. The Blessed One saw Āmrapālī coming from a distance. Seeing her, he addressed the monks: "Monks, as Āmrapālī approaches, remain steadfast in diligence, vigilance, and mindfulness."

"Monks," he continued, "what is it that I am teaching when I say 'remain steadfast in diligence'? Monks, here one generates the intention to abandon sinful and unwholesome phenomena that have already arisen; one strives, initiates diligence, grasps the mind, and applies it. One generates the intention not to give rise to sinful and unwholesome phenomena that have not yet arisen; one strives, initiates diligence, grasps the mind, and applies it. One generates the intention to give rise to virtuous phenomena that have not yet arisen; one strives, initiates diligence, grasps the mind, and applies it. One generates the intention to maintain virtuous phenomena that have already arisen, so that they do not decline, so that they become fully complete, so that they grow and expand; one strives, initiates diligence, grasps the mind, and applies it. Monks, this is what it means to remain steadfast in diligence.

"Monks, what is it to remain steadfast in vigilance? Monks, here one acts with vigilance when looking ahead and looking around, when drawing in and stretching out the limbs, when wearing one's robes and carrying one's bowl, when walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, when rising, speaking, and keeping silent, when drowsy, fatigued, and resting. Monks, this is what it means to remain steadfast in vigilance.

"Monks, what is it to remain steadfast in mindfulness? Monks, here one dwells observing the body as body in relation to the inner body, endowed with diligence, vigilance, and mindfulness, having abandoned ill-will and discontent with regard to the world. One dwells observing the outer body, the inner and outer body. One dwells observing feelings as feelings in relation to outer feelings, inner feelings, and inner and outer feelings. One dwells observing mind as mind in relation to outer mind, inner mind, and inner and outer mind. One dwells observing phenomena as phenomena in relation to outer phenomena, inner phenomena, and inner and outer phenomena, endowed with diligence, vigilance, and mindfulness, having abandoned ill-will and discontent with regard to the world. Monks, this is what it means to remain steadfast in mindfulness.

"Monks, when I said 'as Āmrapālī approaches, remain steadfast in diligence, vigilance, and mindfulness,' that is what I meant."

Then Āmrapālī went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, and bowed her head to the Blessed One's feet; then she sat down to one side. Once she was seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed her fully with a Dharma-endowed discourse, established her fully in it, praised her fully, and gladdened her fully. With many different categories of Dharma-endowed discourse he instructed her fully, established her fully, praised her fully, and gladdened her fully; and then he fell silent.

Then Āmrapālī rose from her seat, faced toward the Blessed One, joined her palms, bowed, and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, may it please you to grant me the honor of accepting tomorrow's meal together with the community of monks." The Blessed One consented to Āmrapālī by remaining silent. Perceiving by his silence that the Blessed One had granted her request, Āmrapālī rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said, praised it openly, bowed her head to the Blessed One's two feet, and departed from his presence.

Now the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī heard that the Blessed One had set out, was traveling through the countryside, had arrived at Vaiśālī, and was residing in Āmrapālī's grove there in Vaiśālī. Hearing this, each of them mounted his own chariot. Some had blue horses, blue chariots, blue harnesses, blue whips, blue crests, blue parasols, blue sword-scabbards, blue yak-tail fans with jeweled handles, blue garments, blue ornaments, blue ointments, and blue retinues. Some had yellow horses, yellow chariots, yellow harnesses, yellow whips, yellow crests, yellow parasols, yellow sword-scabbards, yak-tail fans with jeweled handles, yellow garments, yellow ornaments, yellow ointments, and yellow retinues. Some had red horses, red chariots, red harnesses, red whips, red crests, red parasols, red sword-scabbards, yak-tail fans with jeweled handles, red garments, red ornaments, red ointments, and red retinues. Some had white horses, white chariots, white harnesses, white whips, white crests, white parasols, white sword-scabbards, yak-tail fans with jeweled handles, white garments, white ornaments, white ointments, and white retinues. Calling out loudly and with great noise, "Make way! Make way!", they set out from Vaiśālī and proceeded into the presence of the Blessed One to see him and pay their respects.

The Blessed One saw the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī approaching from a great distance. Seeing them, he addressed the monks: "Monks, any of you who has not seen the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three (Skt. Trāyastriṃśa) going to their pleasure grove — look upon the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī. For monks, just as the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī appear right now, with such splendor, such richness, and such magnificence of dress as they go to a pleasure grove — so too do the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three go to their pleasure grove."

The Licchavīs rode as far as the road allowed for riding, then dismounted and entered the park on foot, went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, bowed their heads to the Blessed One's two feet, and sat down to one side. Once they were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī fully with a Dharma-endowed discourse, established them fully in it, praised them fully, and gladdened them fully. With many different categories of Dharma-endowed discourse he instructed them fully, established them fully, praised them fully, and gladdened them fully.

Now at that very time the brahmin youth Serkya was present there among that assembly. Then the brahmin youth Serkya rose from his seat and —

draped his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined his palms, bowed, and addressed him thus: "Blessed One, I am bold enough to speak. Sugata, I am bold enough to speak."

The Blessed One declared, "Brahmin youth Serkya, speak boldly." And then the brahmin youth Serkya addressed him in verse:

The king of Aṅga who wears the jewel-crown —
through the power of his mother he has gained a fortunate gain.
The buddha who appeared in that land
is like the sound of fame that stands like a snow mountain.

Just as a beautiful lotus that has bloomed well,
opening at dawn, bearing sweet fragrance —
look to the stream of the sun that, in the sky,
shines with a light surpassing the sun itself.

Just so, look to the power of wisdom of the Tathāgatas,
like a blazing fire in the night:
it is that which opens the eye and brings light,
and dispels entirely the doubts of those who have come.

The five hundred Licchavīs praised the brahmin youth Serkya for having spoken well. "The brahmin youth Serkya has spoken well!" they said, and gave him five hundred upper robes in honor of his having spoken so well. Then the Blessed One instructed the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī once more fully with a Dharma-endowed discourse, established them fully in it, praised them fully, and gladdened them fully, and then fell silent.

Then the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined their palms, bowed, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, may it please you to grant us permission to invite the community of monks together with yourself to our home tomorrow for a midday meal. The lodging-keepers, however, were first invited by Āmrapālī. Venerable Āmrapālī is a woman of low standing, of inferior wisdom; she has deceived us. We had hoped from the very first to see and honor the Blessed One, but even so, even though she got there before us, we still wish to offer honor and service to the Blessed One and the community of monks."

The Blessed One declared to them, "The lodging-keepers have spoken well." Then the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī, praising what the Blessed One had said and rejoicing, bowed their heads to the Blessed One's two feet and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

The brahmin youth Serkya, however, remained right there. Then the brahmin youth Serkya, knowing that the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī had not gone far after departing, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined his palms, bowed, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable one, these five hundred upper robes given to me here by the five hundred Licchavīs for having spoken well — may the Blessed One, out of compassion, be pleased to accept them."

The Blessed One, out of compassion for the brahmin youth Serkya, accepted the five hundred upper robes.

Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin youth Serkya: "Serkya's son, when a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha appears in the world, five wondrous and marvelous phenomena arise in the world. What are the five? Serkya's son, in this regard, when the Teacher — the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed one, the guide who tames beings, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Awakened Blessed One — appears in the world, the Dharma he teaches is wholesome at the beginning, wholesome in the middle,

wholesome at the end, good in meaning, good in words, unmixed, complete, perfectly pure, perfectly clear, and it fully reveals the holy life. Serkya's son, when a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha appears in the world, this is the first wondrous and marvelous phenomenon that arises in the world.

Serkya's son, furthermore, those who listen to that Dharma with reverence, who regard it as supreme, who regard it as sacred, who take it to heart, who have made their minds one-pointed, who lend their ears and gather all their attention to listen — Serkya's son, when a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha appears in the world, this is the second wondrous and marvelous phenomenon that arises in the world.

Serkya's son, furthermore, those who, having heard that Dharma, experience joy, delight, and the great wholesome quality of listening that is accompanied by renunciation — Serkya's son, when a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha appears in the world, this is the third wondrous and marvelous phenomenon that arises in the world.

Serkya's son, furthermore, those who, having heard that Dharma, practice accordingly, just as it was taught — Serkya's son, when a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha appears in the world, this is the fourth wondrous and marvelous phenomenon that arises in the world.

Serkya's son, furthermore, those who, having heard that Dharma, individually discern the ground of its profound meaning — Serkya's son, when a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha appears in the world, this is the fifth wondrous and marvelous phenomenon that arises in the world.

Serkya's son, noble persons are those who appreciate what has been done for them and who feel what has been done for them. If they do not let even the slightest good deed go to waste, how much more so with great deeds? Serkya's son, therefore, train yourselves to be ones who appreciate what has been done and who feel what has been done — not letting even the slightest good deed go to waste, let alone great ones. Serkya's son, you should train yourselves in just this way.

Then the brahmin youth Serkya's son, rejoicing in and approving of what the Blessed One had said, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and departed from his presence.

Then, that very same night, Ambapālī prepared pure and excellent food and drink, and rising early the next morning, she spread out seats, set out jeweled water vessels, and then sent word to the Blessed One to inform him that the time of the invitation had come, saying: "Venerable One, the seats are prepared; please consider that the hour is now right."

Then the Blessed One, in the early morning, put on his lower robe, took his outer Dharma robe and his alms bowl, and surrounded by the assembly of monks, with the community of monks before him, went to Ambapālī's grove, the place where she resided. Having arrived, he took his seat on the prepared seat in the midst of the community of monks.

Then Ambapālī, perceiving that the Buddha and the community of monks were comfortably seated, served pure and excellent food and drink with her own hands, satisfying them to the full. In many ways she served and fully satisfied them with pure and excellent food and drink with her own hands.

When the Blessed One had finished eating and had set aside his bowl, Ambapālī took a low seat and sat down in the Blessed One's presence in order to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One, rejoicing in Ambapālī's act of generosity, expressed his rejoicing, and

Those who delight in giving are relied upon by others;
they gain a good name, and their renown increases.
Free from miserliness, entering any assembly,
they do not shrink but become fearless.
Therefore the wise who desire happiness
should relinquish the stain of miserliness and practice giving.
Those who have given dwell for a long age of thirty-three
and rejoice in a state equal to that of the gods.
One who gives and acts virtuously, on passing away,
wanders in the grove of delight in their own radiance.
There they play and make merry,
endowed with the many pleasures of sensuous enjoyment.
Having heard the words of the Unbound Protector,
the Sugata's śrāvakas rejoice in the higher realms.

Then the Blessed One, having instructed Ambapālī thoroughly with words rich in Dharma, having established her firmly in them, having praised her, and having fully gladdened her, rose from his seat and departed.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us proceed to the town of Beluva." "As you command, Blessed One," replied the venerable Ānanda, and he complied with the Blessed One's words. Then the Blessed One, leaving that region and touring the land, came to the town of Beluva and stayed in a grove of beluva trees to the north of the town.

Now at that time a severe drought had fallen upon the region, bringing hardship and scarcity of food for the wandering mendicants. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, at present a harsh drought has come upon this region, bringing scarcity of food for the wandering mendicants. Therefore, monks, disperse now among whatever acquaintances, companions, and friends you each have in the vicinity of Vaiśālī, and undertake the rains retreat there. I myself shall remain here in this very town of Beluva for the rains retreat, attended by the venerable Ānanda, and thus all of you will not go without alms." "As you command, Blessed One," those monks replied, complying with the Blessed One's words, and they dispersed among their various acquaintances, companions, and friends in the vicinity of Vaiśālī, undertaking the rains retreat there. And the Blessed One, attended by the venerable Ānanda, undertook the rains retreat in that very town of Beluva.

During that rains retreat, the Blessed One was struck by a severe, violent, and acute illness bordering on death. Then the Blessed One reflected: "I am afflicted by a severe, violent, and acute illness bordering on death, and the community of monks is dispersed. It would not be right for me to pass into final nirvāṇa while the community of monks is dispersed and without having addressed them. Let me instead, with vigorous effort, hold this feeling in check, attend to no signs whatsoever, and dwell having realized directly in the body the signless meditative absorption of the mind." Then the Blessed One, with vigorous effort, held that very feeling in check, attended to no signs whatsoever, and, having realized directly in the body the signless meditative absorption of the mind, dwelt therein. And thus the Blessed One recovered and regained his health.

Then the venerable Ānanda, rising from meditative composure deep in the night, went to where the Blessed One was, and having prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Reverend Blessed One, you were struck by a great and grievous illness, fierce and verging on death, and I, reeling from that blow as though dazed by poison, found my body unsteady, my sense of direction confused, and even what I had learned of the Dharma was driven from my mind. Yet one thought gave me some comfort: that the Blessed One would surely not pass into complete nirvāṇa without first delivering even the briefest of final instructions to the community of monks."

"Ānanda, whoever thinks, 'The community of monks is mine; I shall instruct the community of monks; I shall lead the community of monks' — it is such a one who might leave some final instruction for the sake of the community. As for me, Ānanda, I do not think, 'The community of monks is mine; I shall instruct the community of monks; I shall lead the community of monks.' What reason would I have, then, to leave any final instructions at all for the community of monks? Moreover, Ānanda, what more is there that remains for me with regard to the community of monks? I have already taught the Dharma that is to be practiced unceasingly: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven branches of awakening, and the noble eightfold path. All of these have already been taught.

Ānanda, the Tathāgata does not have the closed fist of a teacher who holds something back, thinking, 'This is something others should not know, so the Tathāgata will conceal it.' Yet, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata was struck by that great and grievous illness, fierce and verging on death, this thought arose in me: 'I am afflicted by a severe and terrible illness, one that touches the very brink of death. The community of monks has also dispersed. When the community of monks is dispersed, it is not fitting for me to pass into complete nirvāṇa. Let me, by vigorous effort, hold that very feeling in check, attend to no signs whatsoever, and, having realized directly in the body the signless meditative absorption of the mind, dwell therein.' And so, by vigorous effort, I held that very feeling in check, attended to no signs whatsoever, and, having realized directly in the body the signless meditative absorption of the mind, dwelt therein. And it was through this that the Tathāgata continued to live and to sustain himself.

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata is now eighty years of age, and this body has grown old and worn. Just as a worn-out old cart keeps going by being held together with straps, so too the Tathāgata, now eighty years of age, with this body grown old and worn, keeps going by relying on these two means.

Therefore, Ānanda, do not grieve, do not be troubled, do not lament. For whatever has been born, has come into being, has been made, is conditioned, is compounded, and has been accumulated — being subject to dependent origination, it has the nature of dissolution. That such a thing should not fall apart — this is impossible; there is no such possibility.

Ānanda, whatever I have spoken to you of before — all that is dear and beloved, pleasant and agreeable — all of it is subject to separation, destruction, dissolution, and impermanence.

Therefore, Ānanda, whether now or hereafter, whoever dwells making themselves their own island, their own refuge, making the Dharma their island and the Dharma their refuge, not resorting to any other island or any other refuge — it is they who shall remain. And why is this so? Ānanda, whether now or hereafter, whoever dwells making themselves their own island, their own refuge, making the Dharma their island and the Dharma their refuge —"

the Dharma as their refuge — not resorting to any other island or any other refuge — they are the very best among all my śrāvaka disciples who desire training.

And how, Ānanda, is it that a monk should dwell making himself his own island, his own refuge, the Dharma his island and the Dharma his refuge, not resorting to any other island or any other refuge?

Here, Ānanda, a monk abides observing the body in the body internally, dwelling with diligence, vigilance, and mindfulness, having abandoned ill-will and discontent with regard to the world. He abides observing the body externally, the body both internally and externally, feelings internally, feelings externally, feelings both internally and externally, mind internally, mind externally, mind both internally and externally, phenomena internally, phenomena externally, and phenomena both internally and externally, dwelling with diligence, vigilance, and mindfulness, having abandoned ill-will and discontent with regard to the world.

It is a monk such as this, Ānanda, who dwells making himself his own island, his own refuge, the Dharma his island and the Dharma his refuge, not resorting to any other island or any other refuge.

The basis of the minor matters of the Vinaya, the fifty-first fascicle. A summary verse: the rains retreat at the city of Pāṭali, the commissioned work and the Ganges, Koṭigāma and Nāṭikā, Vaiśālī and the Ambapāli Grove.

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda, "Let us go, Ānanda, to the city of Vaiśālī." "So be it, Venerable One," replied the venerable Ānanda, and he listened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then journeyed through the region of Bṛijī and came to the city of Vaiśālī, where he took up residence near the Monkey Pool in Vaiśālī, at the Kūṭāgāraśālā.

Then in the morning the Blessed One dressed, took his robe and alms-bowl, and entered Vaiśālī for alms, with the monk Ānanda following behind as his attendant. After going for alms, when the meal was done, having declined the invitation for a further meal, he set down his alms-bowl and robe, washed his feet, and proceeded to the Cāpāla Shrine. Having arrived, he settled at the foot of a certain tree to spend the day in repose.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, Vaiśālī is a delight, and so too the region of Bṛijī, the Cāpāla Shrine, the seven Āmra trees, the Bahuputraka Shrine, the Gautama Nyagrodha tree, the pair of Sāla trees, the Udena Shrine, the shrine where the Mallas crown their kings, and the many varied beauty-spots of Jambudvīpa — all these are dear to people who cherish life.

Ānanda, whoever has cultivated and repeatedly practised the four bases of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda) could, if they wished, remain for a world-age or for what remains beyond a world-age. The Tathāgata too, Ānanda, having cultivated and repeatedly practised the four bases of supernatural power, could, if he so wished, remain for a world-age or for what remains beyond a world-age."

When this was said, the venerable Ānanda made no reply. A second time and a third time the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda:

"Ānanda, Vaiśālī is a delight, and so too the region of Bṛijī, the Cāpāla Shrine, the seven Āmra trees, the Bahuputraka Shrine, the Gautama Nyagrodha tree, the pair of Sāla trees, the Udena Shrine, the shrine where the Mallas crown their kings, and the many varied beauty-spots of Jambudvīpa — all these are dear to people who cherish life.

"Ānanda, whoever has cultivated and repeatedly practiced the four bases of supernatural power may, if he so wishes, remain for a world-age or for what remains beyond a world-age. The Tathāgata, too, has cultivated and repeatedly practiced the four bases of supernatural power; therefore the Tathāgata, if he so wishes, may remain for a world-age or for what remains beyond a world-age." Even though the Blessed One spoke thus a second and a third time, the venerable Ānanda said nothing at all.

Then the Blessed One reflected: "Alas, this monk Ānanda has surely been obscured by Māra the Evil One. That is why, even though I have three times made this great and luminous indication, he has been unable to take the meaning of it to heart." Knowing that Ānanda had been obscured by Māra the Evil One, and in order that neither of the two of them be disturbed, he declared: "Go now and sit for a while near another tree." "As you command, Venerable One," replied the venerable Ānanda, and having heard the Blessed One's words, he went and sat near another tree to spend the day there.

Then Māra the Evil One went to where the Blessed One was. On arriving, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Māra the Evil One addressed the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One now pass fully into nirvāṇa. May the Sugata pass fully into nirvāṇa — the time for passing has come."

The Blessed One reflected: "This is surely Māra the Evil One, who has come here in an emanated body." Knowing this, he said to Māra the Evil One: "Evil Māra, why do you say, 'May the Blessed One now pass fully into nirvāṇa; may the Sugata pass fully into nirvāṇa — the time for passing has come'? Wicked One, not long after I had fully and perfectly awakened on the bank of the Nairañjanā river at Uruvilā beneath the Awakening Tree, you came to me and said exactly this: 'May the Blessed One pass fully into nirvāṇa; may the Sugata pass fully into nirvāṇa — the time for passing has come.' And at that time the Blessed One replied: 'Evil Māra, I will not pass into nirvāṇa until my śrāvaka disciples — monks, nuns, male laypeople, and female laypeople — have become learned, clear, and endowed with wisdom, capable of refuting opponents' arguments according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, and of thoroughly purifying those who put forward challenges; and until the holy life has been widely proclaimed and spread, greatly beneficial to the many, to gods and humans alike.' But now, Evil One, the Blessed One's śrāvaka disciples — monks, nuns, male laypeople, and female laypeople — have indeed become learned, clear, and endowed with wisdom, capable of refuting opponents' arguments according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, and of thoroughly purifying those who put forward challenges; and you yourself have proclaimed the holy life to be widely spread and greatly beneficial to the many, to gods and humans alike. Therefore I now petition the Blessed One to pass fully into nirvāṇa. May the Sugata pass fully into nirvāṇa — the time for passing has come."

The Blessed One replied: "Do not press so urgently, Evil One. The Tathāgata will not be long — after three months have passed he will pass into nirvāṇa in the element of nirvāṇa with no remainder of the aggregates."

Then Māra the Evil One thought to himself:

Knowing for certain that the ascetic Gautama would pass fully into nirvāṇa, Māra the Evil One was filled with delight and great rejoicing, and in that very instant vanished from sight.

Then the Blessed One reflected to himself: "How might I, with an undistracted mind, perform such a feat of supernatural power as this — by blessing the life-formations and relinquishing the death-formations?" So thinking, the Blessed One entered into meditative absorption of that kind, and with a mind in equipoise he blessed the life-formations and relinquished the death-formations. The moment the death-formations were relinquished, at that very instant the great earth trembled. Shooting stars fell. Directions blazed. And from the sky the gods beat their drums.

Then the Blessed One arose from that absorption and at that moment proclaimed this verse:

Existence — balanced and unbalanced alike —
the Sage has relinquished all the formations of existence.
Inwardly joyful, abiding in equipoise,
he has burst open his own shell, as a creature breaks forth from its egg.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his afternoon sitting meditation, went to where the Blessed One was, and when he had arrived, he bowed with his head to the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what was the cause, what was the condition, that the great earth trembled?"

"Ānanda, this great earth trembled on account of eight causes and eight conditions. What are those eight? Ānanda, this great earth rests upon water; water rests upon wind; wind rests upon space. Ānanda, at a certain time great winds arise in space. When great winds rise up from space, they stir the water. When the water is stirred, the earth is shaken. Ānanda, this is the first cause and first condition for the trembling of the great earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, there may be a monk of great supernatural power and great might who, having blessed the earth with the perception of it as small, applies to the water the perception of it as boundless — and then, should he wish, the earth trembles. Likewise a fully ordained nun, or a god endowed with great supernatural power and great might, who blesses the earth with the perception of it as small and applies to the water the perception of it as boundless — should they wish, the earth trembles. Ānanda, this is the second cause and second condition for the trembling of the great earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, at a certain time when a bodhisattva passes away from the assembly of the Tuṣita gods and enters his mother's womb, the great earth trembles most violently. A vast radiance pervades this entire world, outshining by its divine splendour the power and brilliance of the gods, so that even in those dark abysses between worlds and between world-systems — lightless, pitch-black places where the sun and moon, though possessed of such great supernatural power and might, cannot shed their light separately — even there at that time a great radiance appears. The beings born in those places, who cannot see even their own hand held before them, become aware: 'Other beings too have been born here! Other beings too have been born here!' Ānanda, this is the third cause and third condition for the trembling of the great earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, at a certain time when that bodhisattva issues forth from his mother's womb, the great earth also trembles most violently" — and from there the account continues as before, up to and including the awareness: "Other beings too have been born here! Other beings too have been born here!" — "Ānanda, this is the fourth cause and fourth condition for the trembling of the great earth."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, at a certain time when the bodhisattva fully and completely awakens to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, the great earth also trembles most violently" — and from there the account continues as before, up to and including the awareness: "Other beings too have been born here! Other beings too have been born here!" — "Ānanda, this is the fifth cause and fifth condition for the trembling of the great earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, at a certain time when the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects and three rounds, the great earth also trembles most violently" — and from there the account continues as before, up to and including the awareness: "Other beings too have been born here! Other beings too have been born here!" — "Ānanda, this is the sixth cause and sixth condition for the trembling of the great earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, at a certain time when the Tathāgata intentionally reinforces the life-sustaining formations and relinquishes the will-to-live, at that moment the great earth trembles most violently, meteors fall, fires blaze in every direction, and the gods in the sky beat their drums. Ānanda, this is the seventh cause and seventh condition for the trembling of the great earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, before long — when three months have elapsed and the Tathāgata passes into the nirvāṇa-element that is without remainder of the aggregates — at that moment the great earth trembles most violently, meteors fall, fires blaze in every direction, and the gods in the sky beat their drums. Ānanda, this is the eighth cause and eighth condition for the trembling of the great earth."

Then the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, having understood the meaning of what you have declared, I ask whether, just now, the Blessed One has indeed reinforced the life-sustaining formations and relinquished the will-to-live." The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, it is exactly so. It is exactly so, Ānanda. Just now the Tathāgata has reinforced the life-sustaining formations and relinquished the will-to-live."

Then the venerable Ānanda said: "Venerable one, I heard directly from the Blessed One and received it directly from him that whoever cultivates and develops the four bases of miraculous power assiduously could, if he wished, remain for a kalpa or beyond a kalpa. Venerable Blessed One, since you have cultivated and developed the four bases of miraculous power assiduously, if the Blessed One so wishes, he could remain for a kalpa or beyond a kalpa. May the Blessed One remain for a kalpa! May the Sugata remain for a kalpa!"

The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, the fault is yours. Ānanda, you have committed a fault. For when I gave you the broad and clear indication three times, you could not grasp its meaning — so thoroughly had the māra of evil overcome you. Ānanda, what do you think: would the Tathāgata ever speak words that would later prove otherwise? — "No, venerable one." — "Excellent! Excellent! Ānanda, there is no basis, no occasion, for the Tathāgata to speak words that would prove otherwise. That is simply impossible."

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and gather together in one place all the monks who are staying and dwelling at the Cāpāla Shrine." "Venerable one, so be it," said the venerable Ānanda, and having received this instruction from the Blessed One, he gathered together in one place all the monks who were staying and dwelling at the Cāpāla Shrine. He then went to where the Blessed One was, and having bowed with his head to the Blessed One's feet, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, if you consider that the time has now come —"

"All the monks who are staying and dwelling at the Cāpāla Shrine have been gathered together in one place," he reported. Then the Blessed One went to where that gathered assembly was, and upon a seat that had been laid out before the community of monks, he sat down. Having sat down, the Blessed One spoke to the monks:

"Monks, all conditioned things are impermanent, unstable, subject to change. Monks, it is fitting to grow weary of all conditioned things, to become disenchanted with them — they are proper objects of liberation. Therefore, monks, whatever Dharma teachings are beneficial in this present life, bring happiness in this present life, are beneficial in future lives, and will bring happiness in future lives — such teachings, monks, should be taken up, fully mastered, and in just that way upheld, practiced, and recited. Let this holy life (brahmacarya) abide here for a long time, for the benefit and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and human beings.

"And what, monks, are the Dharma teachings that are beneficial in this present life, bring happiness in this present life, are beneficial in future lives, and will bring happiness in future lives? They are those which the monks have taken up and fully mastered, upheld in just that way, practiced, and recited — and through which this holy life will abide for a long time, bringing benefit to the many, happiness to the many, and compassion for the world. They are these: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right abandonings, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven limbs of awakening, and the noble eightfold path. Monks, these Dharma teachings are beneficial in this present life, bring happiness in this present life, are beneficial in future lives, and will bring happiness in future lives. These, monks, are to be taken up, fully mastered, and in just that way upheld, practiced, and recited. Let this holy life abide here for a long time — for the benefit of the many, the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of gods and human beings."

Then the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us go to Kuśinagara." "Venerable one, so be it," said the venerable Ānanda, and he received the Blessed One's instruction.

Then the Blessed One, departing from the grove of Vaiśālī, turned his entire body to the right and gazed back as an elephant looks back. And the venerable Ānanda saw the Blessed One turn his entire body to the right and gaze back as an elephant looks back. Having seen this, he said to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, without cause, without condition, a Tathāgata, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, does not turn his entire body to the right and gaze back as an elephant gazes. What then is the cause, what is the condition, for this gaze like that of an elephant?"

"Ānanda, it is so. It is so, Ānanda — without cause, without condition, a Tathāgata, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, does not turn his entire body to the right and gaze back as an elephant gazes. Ānanda, this is the last time the Tathāgata, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, looks upon this city of Vaiśālī."

The Tathāgata would not come to Vaiśālī again. He departed thence toward the twin śāla trees in the grove near the Malla territory, in order to pass into nirvāṇa.

Then another monk, at that very moment, spoke these words in verse:

O Sage, this is the last time
you have looked upon Vaiśālī.
The perfectly and fully awakened buddha
shall return to Vaiśālī no more.
Near the territory of the Mallas,
by the twin śāla trees,
today he departs to pass beyond sorrow.

Then the Blessed One traveled through the land of Bṛijī, passing through village after village, and came to the village of Ruṭa. There, in the śāpa tree grove to the north of that village, he took up residence.

There the Blessed One declared to the monks: "This is moral discipline. This is meditative absorption. This is wisdom. When moral discipline is thoroughly cultivated, meditative absorption will long endure. When meditative absorption long endures, wisdom will be thoroughly cultivated. When wisdom is thoroughly cultivated, it is like this: the mind becomes fully liberated from attachment, from aversion, and from delusion. Just so, monks, those noble śrāvakas who possess minds that are completely and utterly liberated know directly: 'My birth is exhausted. The holy life has been lived. What had to be done has been done. There is no further existence beyond this.'"

In summary in verse:

Ruṭa, Dumpa, Āmra,
Jambu, Śurva, Balaglaṅ,
the two towns Bṛijī and Mallā —
such too is the prosperous city.

Just as Ruṭa village, so too the village of Dumpa, the village of Āmra, the village of Jambu, the village of Jī, the village of Śurva, the village of Balaglaṅ, the village of Bṛijī, and the village of Mallā — from each of these he journeyed onward to the prosperous city, and from the prosperous city he took up residence in the śāpa tree grove to the north of the city.

At that time the great earth trembled. Shooting stars fell. In all directions there were flashes of light. And in the sky the gods beat their drums.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his afternoon meditation, went to where the Blessed One was, and having placed his head at the feet of the Blessed One in prostration, sat down to one side.

Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable one, what is the cause, what is the condition, for this trembling of the great earth?"

"Ānanda, there are three causes and three conditions for the trembling of the great earth. What are the three? Ānanda, the great earth rests upon water; water rests upon wind; wind rests upon space. Ānanda, there comes a time when a great wind rises from space. When a great wind rises from space, the water is set in motion. When the water is set in motion, the earth trembles. Ānanda, this is the first cause and condition for the trembling of the earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk who has become of great power and great supernatural ability — such a one, making the perception of earth small and suffusing the perception of water boundlessly, can, if he wishes, cause the earth to tremble. A nun or even a deity who has become of great supernatural ability and great power — such a one likewise, making the perception of earth small and suffusing the perception of water boundlessly, can, if he or she so wishes, cause the earth to tremble. Ānanda, this is the second cause and the second condition for the trembling of the earth.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, when before long a Tathāgata is about to pass completely beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa — the nirvāṇa without remainder — at that time the great earth will tremble violently. Shooting stars will fall. In all directions there will be flashes of light. And from the sky the gods will beat their drums. Ānanda, this is the third cause and the third condition for the trembling of the great earth."

Then the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, how wondrous!"

"Such, then, are the wondrous and marvellous qualities that belong to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas. And so it is: before long the Tathāgata will pass completely beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa — the nirvāṇa without remainder — and at that time the great earth will tremble violently, shooting stars will fall, there will be flashes of light in all directions, and from the sky the gods will beat their drums. So it is, Ānanda. Thus, such great wondrous and marvellous qualities belong to the Tathāgatas, the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas.

"Ānanda, I will go to visit the many hundreds of retinues of the warrior class. Having gone, just as their dominion and majesty are such, so too shall my dominion and majesty become the same. Just as their complexion is beautiful, so too shall my complexion be beautiful in the same way. Just as the sound of their voices resounds, so too shall the sound of my voice resound in the same way. Whatever meaning they speak to, I too shall speak to that meaning. Whatever they do not speak to, I too shall not speak to that. And beyond that, I shall teach them the discourse of Dharma properly, urge them properly, praise them properly, and gladden them fully — and then vanish from that very spot. And when I have vanished, I shall directly know whether whoever is present there, whether god or human, is without a trace of conceit.

"Just as I shall do with the retinue of the warrior class, so likewise shall I do with the retinue of the brahmin class, with the retinue of the householders, with the retinue of monks, with the assembly of the Four Great Kings, with the gods of the Thirty-Three, with those of Yāma, with those of Tuṣita, with those of Nirmāṇarati, with those of Paranirmitavaśavartin, with those of the Brahma class, with the gods of Brahma's retinue, with those of the Universal Brahma, with the Great Brahma, with those of Minor Radiance, with those of Immeasurable Radiance, with those of Resplendent Light, with those of Minor Virtue, with those of Immeasurable Virtue, with those of Pervasive Virtue, with those of Cloudless, with those of Merit-Increasing, with those of Great Fruit, with those of Not-Great, with those of Non-Afflicted, with those of Great Perception, with those of Sublime Vision, and with the gods of Akaniṣṭha. Having gone to each of them, just as their dominion and majesty are such, so too shall my dominion and majesty become the same. Just as their complexion is beautiful, so too shall my complexion be beautiful in the same way. Just as the sound of their voices resounds, so too shall the sound of my voice resound in the same way. Whatever meaning they speak to, I too shall speak to that meaning. Whatever they do not speak to, I too shall not speak to that. And beyond that, I shall teach them the discourse of Dharma properly, urge them properly, praise them properly, and gladden them fully — and then vanish from that very spot. And when I have vanished, I shall directly know whether whoever is present there, whether god or human, is without a trace of conceit.

"Such are the wondrous and marvellous qualities of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Therefore, Ānanda, from now on one should engage with the limits of the sūtras rather than engaging with the person. Ānanda, how is it that monks engage with the limits of the sūtras rather than with the person? Here, Ānanda, a monk comes and says the following: 'I heard this directly from the Blessed One and received it directly — this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.' That monk's words should neither be praised nor disparaged. Without praising or disparaging, one should listen carefully, take up the words and letters of the Dharma, and check them against the sūtras.

One should also properly examine it against the Vinaya. When it is checked against the sūtras and the Vinaya, if it is discordant with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and furthermore contradicts the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, the Blessed One did not teach this Dharma in that way. It is a mistake, venerable one, to take up this Dharma as your own. Therefore, since this Dharma, when checked against the sūtras and properly examined against the Vinaya, is discordant with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality, know it to be not Dharma, not Vinaya, not what the Teacher taught, and set it aside.'

Furthermore, Ānanda, another monk comes and says the following: 'Venerable one, in a certain great monastery there reside elder monks who hold the Prātimokṣa, and a large community of monks dwells there. Venerable one, I heard this directly and received it directly from that large community of monks: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.' That monk's words should neither be praised nor disparaged. Without praising or disparaging, one should listen carefully, take up the words and letters of the Dharma, check them against the sūtras, and properly examine them against the Vinaya. If, when checked against the sūtras and examined against the Vinaya, it is discordant with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, that large community of monks perceives this as Dharma and perceives it as Vinaya; but if what they have declared is not Dharma and not Vinaya, then, venerable one, it is a mistake to take up this Dharma as your own. Since this Dharma, when checked against the sūtras and properly examined against the Vinaya, is discordant with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality, know it to be not Dharma, not Vinaya, not what the Teacher taught, and set it aside.'

Furthermore, Ānanda, another monk comes and says the following: 'Venerable one, in a certain great monastery there dwell many monks — monks who hold the sūtras, monks who hold the Vinaya, and monks who hold the Mātṛkā. Venerable one, I heard this directly and received it directly from those many monks: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.' That monk's words should neither be praised nor disparaged. Without praising or disparaging, one should listen carefully, take up the words and letters of the Dharma, check them against the sūtras, and properly examine them against the Vinaya. If, when checked against the sūtras and the Vinaya, it is discordant with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, those many monks perceive this as Dharma and perceive it as Vinaya; but if what they have declared is not Dharma and not Vinaya, then, venerable one, it is a mistake to take up this Dharma as your own. Since this Dharma, when checked against the sūtras and properly examined against the Vinaya, is discordant with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality, know it to be not Dharma, not Vinaya, not what the Teacher taught, and set it aside.'

Furthermore, Ānanda, another monk comes and says the following: 'Venerable one, in a certain great monastery there dwell elder monks, those who learned from the elders, those who learned from them in turn, and others of principal standing. Venerable one, I heard this directly and received it directly from those elder monks: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.'

Do not praise or disparage what that monk has said. Without praising or disparaging it, lend an ear, take hold of the words and syllables of the Dharma, and examine them against the sūtras and check them properly against the Vinaya. If, upon being examined against the sūtras and properly checked against the Vinaya, they are discordant with the sūtras, do not appear in the Vinaya, and are contradicted by the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, that elder monk has understood this as Dharma and understood it as Vinaya; but if you speak of what is not Dharma and not Vinaya, then it is wrong for the venerable one himself to take hold of this teaching.' Say further: 'Since this teaching, when examined against the sūtras and properly checked against the Vinaya, is discordant with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality, know it to be not Dharma, not Vinaya, not what the Teacher taught, and set it aside.'

Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk comes and says the following: 'Venerable one, I heard this directly and received it directly from the Blessed One himself: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.' Do not praise or disparage what that monk has said. Without praising or disparaging it, lend an ear, take hold of the words and syllables of the Dharma, and examine them against the sūtras and check them properly against the Vinaya. If, upon being examined against the sūtras and properly checked against the Vinaya, they are concordant with the sūtras, do appear in the Vinaya, and are not contradicted by the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, this teaching was indeed spoken by the Blessed One, and the venerable one himself has taken hold of it well. Since this teaching, when examined against the sūtras and properly checked against the Vinaya, is concordant with the sūtras, appears in the Vinaya, and is not contradicted by the nature of reality, know it to be Dharma, know it to be Vinaya, know it to be what the Teacher taught, and hold it fast.'

Furthermore, Ānanda, another monk comes and says the following: 'Venerable one, in a certain great monastery there dwell elders, along with a great community of monks possessing individual liberation. I heard this directly and received it directly from that great community of monks: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.' Do not praise or disparage what that monk has said. Without praising or disparaging it, lend an ear, take hold of the words and syllables of the Dharma, examine them against the sūtras, and check them properly against the Vinaya. If, upon being examined against the sūtras and properly checked against the Vinaya, they are concordant with the sūtras, do appear in the Vinaya, and are not contradicted by the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, that great community of monks has spoken thus as Dharma and Vinaya, and the venerable one too has taken hold of this teaching well. Since this teaching, when examined against the sūtras and properly checked against the Vinaya, is concordant with the sūtras, appears in the Vinaya, and is not contradicted by the nature of reality, know it to be Dharma, know it to be Vinaya, know it to be what the Teacher taught, and hold it fast.'

Furthermore, Ānanda, another monk comes and says the following: 'Venerable one, in a certain great monastery there dwell many monks — monks who uphold the sūtras, monks who uphold the Vinaya, and monks who uphold the Mātṛkā. I have received directly from those many monks this: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.' Do not praise or disparage what that monk has said. Without praising or disparaging it,

listen with open ears. Take up the words and letters of the Dharma, compare them with the sūtras, and examine them carefully against the Vinaya. If, upon comparison with the sūtras and careful examination against the Vinaya, they accord with the sūtras, appear consistent with the Vinaya, and are not contradicted by the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, those many monks have indeed taught the Dharma and the Vinaya, and the venerable one has received these teachings well. Therefore, since these teachings, when compared with the sūtras and carefully examined against the Vinaya, accord with the sūtras, appear consistent with the Vinaya, and are not contradicted by the nature of reality, know them to be Dharma, know them to be Vinaya, know them to be what the Teacher taught, and hold them fast.'

Furthermore, Ānanda, another monk comes and says the following: 'Venerable one, in a certain place there dwell monks — elder monks, other elder monks, senior monks, and other senior monks. I have received directly from those elder monks of that monastic community this: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught.' Do not praise or disparage what that monk has said. Without praising or disparaging it, listen with open ears. Take up the words and letters of the Dharma, compare them with the sūtras, and examine them carefully against the Vinaya. If, upon comparison with the sūtras and careful examination against the Vinaya, they accord with the sūtras, appear consistent with the Vinaya, and are not contradicted by the nature of reality, then say this to that monk: 'Venerable one, those elder monks of that monastic community have indeed taught the Dharma and the Vinaya, and the venerable one has received these teachings well. Therefore, since these teachings, when compared with the sūtras and carefully examined against the Vinaya, accord with the sūtras, appear consistent with the Vinaya, and are not contradicted by the nature of reality, know them to be Dharma, know them to be Vinaya, know them to be what the Teacher taught, and hold them fast.'

Now, Ānanda, as for whichever of the first four great declarations was spoken on the side of the dark — that is, on the side of what is not Dharma — the monks, having applied their wholesome faculties and examined it carefully, shall know it to be not Dharma, not Vinaya, not what the Teacher taught, and cast it aside. As for whichever of the latter four great declarations was spoken on the side of the bright — that is, on the side of what is Dharma — the monks, having applied their wholesome faculties and examined it carefully, shall know it to be Dharma, Vinaya, what the Teacher taught, and hold it fast. Thus, Ānanda, monks are to rely upon the sūtras and not upon persons.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, let us travel to the town of Sāpa.' 'So be it, Blessed One,' replied the venerable Ānanda upon hearing the Blessed One's words. And so the Blessed One set out from Mallā on a journey through the region and came to the town of Sāpa, where he took up residence in a great Jālikā grove near the town of Sāpa.

When the Mallās of Sāpa heard that the Blessed One had set out from Mallā on a journey through the region and had come to the town of Sāpa, taking up residence in the great Jālikā grove of Sāpa, they gathered together from their assemblies, assembled from their congregations, and, coming out from the town of Sāpa, proceeded to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet, did reverence, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One taught them the Dharma in full, urged them in full, praised them in full, and gladdened them fully. And at that very time, the smith's son Cunda was also gathered there in that very retinue, seated among them.

Then the Blessed One taught the Mallians of Sāpa the Dharma by means of many categories of teaching, urged them in full, praised them in full, and gladdened them fully, and then fell silent. The Mallians of Sāpa, delighted and rejoicing in what the Blessed One had said, bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet and departed from his presence. The smith's son Cunda had also been seated there all along. Then, not long after the Mallians of Sāpa had departed, the smith's son Cunda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, turned toward the Blessed One, joined his palms together, bowed in reverence, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, may it please you to come tomorrow to my dwelling with the Saṅgha of monks, for your midday meal." The Blessed One said nothing in reply to the smith's son Cunda, and by that silence he consented. The smith's son Cunda, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that consent had been given, delighted and rejoicing in what the Blessed One had said, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and departed from his presence.

That very evening, the smith's son Cunda prepared excellent food with good rice, made ready fine dishes of food, and gathered together pure and choice food and accompaniments for the Saṅgha of monks. The next morning he rose early, spread out seats, set out water vessels, and then sent word to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, the preparation for the meal is complete. Please know that the midday hour is now upon us." Then the Blessed One, in the early morning, dressed in his robes and lower garment, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by many monks, went forth at the head of the Saṅgha of monks to the dwelling of the smith's son Cunda. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat placed before the Saṅgha of monks.

Then the smith's son Cunda, knowing that the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks were comfortably seated, served the Blessed One with excellent food, well prepared and placed in an iron vessel, with his own hand, offering and distributing it. He also served the Saṅgha of monks, with his own hand offering and distributing pure and choice food and accompaniments. At that time, another wicked monk seized an iron vessel and tucked it under his arm. The Blessed One saw that wicked monk, and through the power of the Buddha, the smith's son Cunda saw him too. Then the smith's son Cunda, having well prepared excellent food in many bowls, served it with his own hands, offering and distributing it. He also served the Saṅgha of monks, with his own hands offering and distributing pure and choice food and accompaniments. Knowing that the Blessed One had finished eating, he offered water for washing the hands. Then, taking up his alms bowl, he took a low seat and sat before the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One with a request in verse:

To the Sage of vast knowledge I address my petition.
You who have crossed over, gone to the far shore, who have crossed beyond all doubt,
supreme helmsman, most excellent guide —
please declare that there are many true ascetics in the world.

There are four kinds of ascetic; there is no fifth.
Knowing this, I declare it to you.
The victor of the path, the teacher of the path,
the one who lives by the path, and the one who corrupts the path —
what did the Buddha say of the victor of the path?
How is the one who teaches the path said to be without equal?
I ask you: please speak of the one who lives by the path,
and speak to me too of the one who corrupts the path.

The one who cuts off the speech of doubt, freed from affliction,
not led astray by others, rejoicing in the passing beyond sorrow,
teacher of the world together with its gods —
that one, it is said, the Buddha calls the victor of the path.

The one who has thoroughly and supremely understood...

...who has thoroughly and supremely understood the Dharma the Buddha proclaimed in just the same way — that one is said to be the sage who cuts off doubt, not led astray by others, not of two minds. By means of austerity, that one is said to be the teacher of the path.

The one who teaches the words of the Dharma well, who lives by the path, who is the master of austerity and mindfulness, and who trains in blameless speech — these three things are said, through austerity, to be how one lives by the path.

One who harbors pleasure in excellence while concealing it inwardly, who is utterly desiccated, who disgraces the clan and claims to be a victor, who is deceitful, without restraint, and yet a great proclaimer, whose conduct is improper — that one corrupts the path.

Whatever householder reflects carefully, and who is possessed of learning and is thoroughly known by noble śrāvakas — all who truly understand will not become like that. Knowing such a one, their faith in him will not grow.

How can one treat as equal the discordant and the harmonious, the pure and the impure? When one person has done evil deeds, even those who do no evil become suspect among beings. One should not judge a person by complexion and form; one whose breeding is low, the moment one sees him the mind cannot rely on him. One who is utterly without restraint, full of many outward signs of virtue, and yet incapable — such a one moves through this world. Like an earring coated with gold, like a pin of iron coated with gold — inwardly full of aversion, outwardly bearing the appearance of a noble one: some who are possessed of deceit move through this world in just this way.

Then the Blessed One expressed his rejoicing in the gift of the smith's son Cunda with these words of rejoicing:

When one gives, merit increases greatly.
Through right restraint, no resentment grows.
One of virtue abandons evil deeds.
When afflictions are exhausted, one passes beyond sorrow.

Then the Blessed One taught Dharma to the smith's son Cunda, exhorted him rightly, praised him rightly, and filled him with joy rightly; and having exhorted him, praised him, and filled him with joy rightly by means of Dharma in many ways, he rose from his seat and departed.

Here ends the fifty-second section of the Vinaya of minor matters.

Summary verse: He performed the formations of Cāpāla and of life; he gazed upon the Great Elephant; and the ten towns including Rurutā and the rest; the stirred sūtras; and the sinful one.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us go to the town of Kushinagar." The venerable Ānanda replied, "As the Reverend One commands," and listened to the Blessed One. Then, as the Blessed One was passing through the district of the Mallas, from the sinful one as far as the river Kakuṭṭhā, the Blessed One, having gone ahead, turned back from the way and spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, my back is uncomfortable. Let me rest. Fold the Tathāgata's outer robe into four layers and spread it out."

"As the Reverend One commands," said the venerable Ānanda, and following the Blessed One's instruction, he folded the outer robe carefully into four layers, spread it out, and laid it down. Then he said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Tathāgata's outer robe has been folded into four layers and laid out. May the Blessed One now consider that the time has come."

Then the Blessed One made many folds of his patched garment and placed it beneath him. Lying down on his right side, placing his feet one upon the other, he cultivated in his mind the perception of light, mindfulness, vigilance, and the intention to rise, and he rested.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and bring a bowlful of water from the river Kakuṭṭhā. I will drink it and pour it over my body." "As the Reverend One commands," said the venerable Ānanda, and following the Blessed One's instruction he took his bowl and went toward the river Kakuṭṭhā. At that time, the river Kakuṭṭhā had been crossed by a distance of about five hundred carts, and not long after...

they had stirred up the river, churned it, and made it turbid. Then the venerable Ānanda took a bowlful of water from the river Kakuṭṭhā and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he said to the Blessed One: "Reverend One, not long ago, a distance of about five hundred carts across, those carts had crossed the river Kakuṭṭhā and stirred it, churned it, and made it turbid. Reverend One, let the Blessed One rinse his mouth and wash his feet with this water. Not far from here, Reverend One, there is the river Kakuddhā. Let the Blessed One drink from it and pour it over his body as well."

Then the Blessed One rinsed his feet and washed his mouth with the water from the bowl. And thereupon the Blessed One found relief and ease. Then the Blessed One rose, sat cross-legged, held his body upright, and remained seated with mindfulness clearly established.

Now at that very time, a wandering ascetic belonging to the great Mallian clan had entered upon that same road. And this wandering ascetic of the great Mallian clan saw the Blessed One — beautiful, inspiring faith, his faculties serene, his mind at peace, supremely tamed and perfectly tranquil, blazing with splendor like a golden pillar — seated, leaning against the trunk of another tree. Seeing him, he went toward the Blessed One, and arriving there, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side.

As he sat to one side, the Blessed One said to the wandering ascetic of the great Mallian clan: "Wandering ascetic, which purity of conduct — that of a śramaṇa or that of a brahmin — do you delight in?"

"Reverend One, I am the son of Silāyin the Magician, I travel far through the air, and it is in purity of conduct that I delight."

"Wandering ascetic, why is it that you, the son of Silāyin the Magician, who travel far through the air, delight in purity of conduct?"

"Reverend One, on one occasion, while I had set out traveling far through the air on the path of Silāyin the Magician, I turned aside from the road and remained by the trunk of another tree, spending the day in the practice of one who rests. At that very time, on that same road, a distance of about five hundred carts had also passed, not long before. Then another man, who had been left behind on account of those carts, came to where I, the son of Silāyin the Magician, was, and said to me: 'Did you not see the passage of a distance of about five hundred carts?' 'Friend, I did not see them.' 'Did you not even hear the sound of about five hundred carts passing?' 'Friend, I did not hear them.' 'Have you been asleep?' 'Friend, I was not asleep.' 'Then with the perception of one not asleep, did you fail to hear the sound of about five hundred carts passing?' 'Friend, with the perception of one not asleep, I indeed did not hear the sound of about five hundred carts passing.'

Then that man thought to himself: 'Remarkable — a renunciant who dwells in peace, who with the perception of one not asleep has not even heard the sound of about five hundred carts passing, and whose robes he could see were covered in a fine dust.' That man was filled with wonder and, having placed his faith in me, the son of Silāyin the Magician, he became devoted. Reverend One, that is why I delight in the conduct of purity that belongs to Silāyin the Magician, who travels far through the air."

"Wandering ascetic, what do you think? Which sound is greater — the sound of about five hundred carts passing, or the sound they call a thunderclap, or the sound of a thunderbolt that has fallen? Which of these two is the greater?"

"Reverend One, what is there to say? Setting aside five hundred carts, even a thousand carts, even a hundred thousand carts — none of them approaches what is called a thunderclap,

the sound of a thunderbolt that has fallen is the greater."

"Wandering ascetic, at one time I was dwelling in the courtyard of the spirit-house in the town of Ātumā. In the morning I dressed in my under-robe and outer robe, took my alms-bowl and robes, and went into the town of Ātumā to gather alms. Having gathered alms through the town of Ātumā and completed the meal, I set aside the alms of the subsequent meal, put away my bowl and robes, washed my feet, entered the courtyard of the spirit-house, and sat down within, composing myself in inner stillness.

"Now at that very time, in the town of Ātumā, what is called a great clap of thunder rang out, a thunderbolt fell, four oxen died, and two brothers, householders and farmers, died as well. As a result, many people in the town of Ātumā began crying out with a great din and much noise. I too rose from my inner stillness and composure at evening, came out from the courtyard of the spirit-house, and was walking back and forth in a place sheltered from the shadow of the spirit-house, without cover, when another man came toward me from among that crowd of people, approached me, prostrated with his head at my two feet, and walked along after me as I walked.

"I said to him: 'Good man, why is it that many people in the town of Ātumā are crying out with this great din and so much noise?'

"He said: 'Reverend One, it is thus: in the town of Ātumā there was what is called a great clap of thunder, a thunderbolt fell, four oxen died, and two brothers, householders and farmers, died. That is why the many people of the town of Ātumā have been crying out with a great din and much noise.' Then he said: 'Blessed One, did you not hear what is called the great clap of thunder and the thunderbolt that fell?'

"I said to him: 'Good man, I did not hear it.'

"He said: 'What then, Blessed One — were you asleep?'

"I said: 'Good man, I was not asleep.'

"He said: 'Then, Blessed One, could it be that you did not hear the thunder-clap and the falling thunderbolt because you had the perception of one who is asleep?'

"I said: 'Good man, I did not hear what is called the thunderclap and the thunderbolt that fell, yet I had the perception of one who is not asleep.'

"Then that man thought to himself: 'How remarkable it is that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, remained so peacefully still that, with the perception of one who is not asleep, he did not hear the sound of the thunderclap and the thunderbolt that fell.' And so that man came to have faith in me, and, moved by that faith, he said: 'Reverend One, who could fail to have faith in the Blessed One? As for myself, I have deep and extensive faith in the Reverend Blessed One.'

"Thereupon the wandering ascetic belonging to the great Gyad clan said to his attendant: 'Good man, give me a pair of fine bleached cloth, yellow as the color of gold, and I shall offer it to the Blessed One.' And that man gave to the wandering ascetic belonging to the great Gyad clan a pair of fine bleached cloth, yellow as the color of gold.

"Then the wandering ascetic belonging to the great Gyad clan took that pair of fine bleached cloth, yellow as the color of gold, and addressed the Blessed One thus: 'Blessed One, out of compassion please accept this pair of fine bleached cloth, yellow as the color of gold — it is something that brings us joy and gladness, something worthy to be cherished.' The Blessed One, looking with compassion upon the wandering ascetic belonging to the great Gyad clan, accepted the pair of fine bleached cloth, yellow as the color of gold."

Then the wandering ascetic belonging to the great Gyad clan, Gyungpo, addressed the Blessed One thus: "I would furthermore, Venerable Blessed One, render service to the Blessed One and to the Saṅgha of monks." And the Blessed One declared, "Gyungpo, this is said well."

Then Gyungpo, belonging to the great Gyad clan, was filled with delight and joy at what the Blessed One had said, bowed his head to the two feet of the Blessed One, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

Not long after Gyungpo of the great Gyad clan had departed, the Blessed One, knowing this, addressed the venerable Ānanda thus: "Ānanda, give me that pair of fine bleached cloth, yellow as the color of gold, trimmed and cut at the edges — I will divide it."

The venerable Ānanda, cutting the pair of fine bleached cloth, yellow as the color of gold, along the edge of its hem, offered it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One received it. The radiant color of the Blessed One's body shone with an equal brilliance.

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, I have been in attendance at the feet of the Blessed One for more than twenty years, yet never before have I witnessed such a radiance as this arising in the body of the Blessed One. Venerable one, by what cause and by what condition has such a radiance arisen in the body?"

"Ānanda, a radiance such as this arises from two causes and two conditions. What are the two? The night on which a bodhisattva fully awakens to the unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening — and the night on which a Tathāgata passes utterly into nirvāṇa in the element of nirvāṇa that is without remainder of the aggregates. This is the second cause and the second condition for the arising of such a radiance in the body."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, go to the river Kakudhā." "As you command," said the venerable Ānanda, and he complied with the Blessed One's word.

Then the Blessed One went to the river Kakudhā, and arriving at one bank of the river Kakudhā, he set down his outer robe and Dharma robe and remained there. He then entered the river Kakudhā, bathed well, crossed the river Kakudhā, and remained with only his inner robe and Dharma robe, his body refreshed.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, the smith's son Cunda has given rise to remorse. Others have aroused remorse in him, saying: 'You have not obtained good fortune — you have obtained misfortune — you have not obtained happiness,' because the Teacher passed into nirvāṇa in the element without remainder of the aggregates after accepting Cunda the smith's son's final meal offering. Ānanda, you should dispel the remorse that has arisen in Cunda the smith's son by means of two points. Say to him: 'Cunda, I heard directly from the Blessed One and received it directly from him, that the karmic maturation of a meal offering is equal and unequalled in two respects: the meal after receiving which a bodhisattva fully awakens to the unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, and the meal after receiving which a Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa in the element without remainder of the aggregates. These two are the equal and unequalled karmic maturations of a meal offering.'"

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is karma that has been done and accumulated by Cunda the smith's son — karma that will ripen as long life, as beautiful complexion, as strength, as prosperity, as fortunate rebirth, and as wealth together with a retinue."

The summary verse reads:

Long life, complexion, strength,
prosperity, fortunate rebirth, and wealth —

Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, this monk Sunakkhatta is fierce, shameless, insolent, angry, and constantly abusive toward us monks. After you have passed away, how shall we deal with him?"

The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, after my passing, that monk Sunakkhatta is to be censured by brahmic penalty. Having censured him with brahmic penalty, he should be made to feel ashamed. And once that complete sense of shame has arisen in him, he is to be placed under the guidance of Kātyāyana."

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, let us proceed to the city of Kuśinagara." "As you command, venerable one," replied the venerable Ānanda, and he complied with the Blessed One's word.

Then, as the Blessed One was travelling through the Malla country, he stopped short of the city of Kuśinagara and of the river Hiraññavatī, stepped aside from the path, and declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, my back is uncomfortable. Let me rest. Fold the Tathāgata's outer robe fourfold and lay it down." "As you command, venerable one," replied the venerable Ānanda. And duly folding the outer robe fourfold, he laid it down.

The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Ānanda again: "The outer robe of the Tathāgata has been folded fourfold and laid down. Blessed One, may you now see fit that the moment has come." Then the Blessed One made of his patchwork robe a many-layered cushion, and having let down his right side and placed foot upon foot, he applied to his mind the perception of light, mindfulness, vigilance, and the perception of rising, and lay down to rest.

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, recite the limbs of awakening." The Blessed One himself, having fully known and perfectly understood mindfulness as a limb of awakening, taught it thus: dwelling in seclusion, dwelling in dispassion, dwelling in cessation, thoroughly transformed by relinquishment — the discrimination of phenomena (Skt. dharmapravicaya), diligence, joy, thorough pliancy, meditative absorption, and equanimity are the limbs of awakening. "Venerable one, it is the Blessed One himself who fully knows and perfectly understands them, having taught them thus: dwelling in seclusion, dwelling in dispassion, dwelling in cessation, thoroughly transformed by relinquishment." "Ānanda, was diligence spoken of?" "Blessed One, diligence was spoken of." "Ānanda, if diligence is relied upon, cultivated, and made abundant many times over, it will lead to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening."

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose, sat cross-legged, straightened his body upright, established mindfulness fully present, and remained seated.

Then another monk spoke this verse:

Though the Teacher himself lay ill,
he requested the teaching for the sake of hearing much Dharma.
The monk himself then taught the Dharma —
through those limbs of awakening, he became a teacher.
The wise one, endowed with intelligence, who understands —

The elder Ānanda spoke well:
from the utterly pure words of the Sage,
one will attain those very teachings themselves.
Right mindfulness, thorough discernment,
diligence, joy, a thoroughly trained body,
mind, meditative absorption, and equanimity —
these, brave ones, are the limbs of awakening.
Having heard the teaching on the limbs of awakening,
