and knowing by omniscience the taste of the limbs of awakening,
the Blessed One, whose mind was in very great discomfort,
arose from that grave and severe illness.
Therefore, even that lord of Dharma
wished to hear Dharma as this precious teaching was being explained.
As for others who also wish to hear the Dharma —
why should any one of them not listen to this?
The one who has been shown to be supreme in wisdom,
shown so by one possessed of the ten powers of wisdom —
even that attendant, though himself ill,
goes for the sake of hearing the sacred Dharma.
Those who hold the sūtras, those who hold the Vinaya, those who hold the Abhidharma,
the learned ones who know the ways of the Dharma —
if they listen to the teachings, what of others?
Why should anyone not listen to this?
Having heard and understood the Dharma's word with the mind,
and having settled it within —
through joy one will attain suchness
through this teaching of the Buddha, which is without taint.
With a mind filled with joy, the body is thoroughly trained,
and bliss too arises in just the same way.
A mind that has become blissful is one-pointed,
and through it one reaches and touches upon meditative absorption.
A mind that has become equanimous does not take refuge in formations,
and being wearied, one becomes free of attachments,
so that the mind arrives at thorough liberation.
Wearied of wandering in existence,
not clinging even to gods and humans —
just as a fire dies when there is no more fuel,
one becomes an arhat and passes into complete nirvāṇa.
The benefits of hearing the Dharma are many and various;
the Victors have explained them all throughout.
Therefore, with earnest effort,
one should listen most attentively to the Teacher's words.

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to the city of Kuśinagara." "As you command, Venerable One," said the venerable Ānanda, and he attended upon the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One passed through the land of the Mallas and arrived at the city of Kuśinagara, and dwelt in the grove of twin śāla trees near the territory of the Mallas. Then, at the very moment the Blessed One was to pass into complete nirvāṇa there, he declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, between the two śāla trees, set up the Tathāgata's bed with its head toward the north. The Tathāgata will pass into complete nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates at this very midnight watch of tonight." "As you command, Venerable One," said the venerable Ānanda, and he attended upon the Blessed One. He set up the bed between the twin śāla trees with its head toward the north, then went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's two feet and sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I have set up the Tathāgata's bed between the twin śāla trees with its head toward the north."

Then the Blessed One went to where the bed was, and having arrived, he lay down on his right side, foot placed upon foot, and held in mind the perception of luminosity, mindfulness, vigilance, and the perception of passing into nirvāṇa.

Then again, at that time, the venerable Ānanda, sitting to the side of the Blessed One, grasped the bed and wept with tears streaming, and said these words: "The Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa far too soon! The Sugata has passed into nirvāṇa far too soon! Far too soon has the eye of the world become blind! In former times, monks, from such and such directions and from such and such lands, they came to where the Blessed One was. To those who came, the Blessed One taught the holy life, good at the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end, with excellent meaning, excellent phrasing, unmixed, perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and perfectly refined. Because of this, from time to time they also heard and obtained the deep discourse on profound Dharma — but now, having heard that the Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa, they will not come, and in this way this great feast of Dharma, this singular thing, has set in the world."

Then the Blessed One said to the monks: "Monks, where is Ānanda sitting?" "Blessed One, the venerable Ānanda is here, to this side of the Blessed One, grasping the bed and weeping with tears streaming, saying these words: 'The Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa far too soon! The Sugata has passed into nirvāṇa far too soon! Far too soon has the eye of the world become blind! In former times, monks' — and so on as before, up to — 'this great feast of Dharma has set in the world.'"

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do not grieve, do not be distraught, do not lament. And why is that? Ānanda, the service you have rendered in attendance upon the Tathāgata has been of benefit, of ease, non-dual, and immeasurable, through loving physical action, through loving verbal action, and through loving mental action. Ānanda, all those who in past times were Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas — their attendants served those Blessed Buddhas in just such a manner as you have served me. And all those who in future times will be Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas — their attendants will serve those Blessed Buddhas in just such a manner as you now serve me. Therefore, Ānanda, do not grieve, do not be distraught, do not lament. Whatever is born, whatever has arisen, whatever has been made, whatever is conditioned, whatever has come about through dependent origination — all such things are subject to disintegration. That they should not disintegrate: this is not possible; it cannot be conceived. Ānanda, I have said this before as well: all things dear and beloved, pleasing and agreeable — all of them come to separation, to parting, to dissolution, to non-existence."

Then the Blessed One, wishing to delight the venerable Ānanda, addressed the monks: "Monks, there are four wondrous and marvellous qualities in a wheel-turning king. What are the four? If the retinue of a noble warrior class comes to behold a wheel-turning king and sees him, they rejoice.

If Dharma is taught to those who have come near, they rejoice upon hearing it. If the retinue of brahmins, the retinue of householders, and the retinue of ascetics come to behold the wheel-turning king and see him, they rejoice. If Dharma is taught to those who have come near, they rejoice upon hearing it.

Monks, in the same way, the monk Ānanda also possesses four wondrous and marvellous qualities. What are the four? If the retinue of monks comes to behold the monk Ānanda and sees him, they rejoice. If Dharma is taught to those who have come, they rejoice upon hearing it. If the retinue of nuns, the retinue of laymen, and the retinue of laywomen come to behold the monk Ānanda and see him, they rejoice. If Dharma is taught to those who have come, they rejoice upon hearing it.

Monks, furthermore, the monk Ānanda possesses yet another four wondrous and marvellous qualities. What are the four? When the monk Ānanda teaches Dharma to the assembly of monks, he teaches with reverence and not without reverence. Then the assembly of monks thinks to themselves: "Ah, the venerable Ānanda never ceases to speak, and moreover he teaches only Dharma — how fitting this is!" And though the assembly of monks never tires of listening to Dharma from the monk Ānanda, still the monk Ānanda falls silent. When the monk Ānanda teaches Dharma to the assembly of nuns, the assembly of laymen, and the assembly of laywomen, he teaches with reverence and not without reverence. Then the assembly of laymen and the rest think to themselves: "Ah, the venerable Ānanda never ceases to speak, and moreover he teaches only Dharma — how fitting this is!" And though the assembly of laymen and the rest never tire of listening to Dharma from the monk Ānanda, still the monk Ānanda remains silent.

Then the venerable Ānanda, having been truly delighted by the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend One, for what reason, setting aside the six great cities of the different regions of the world — Śrāvastī, Sāketa, Campā, Vārāṇasī, Vaiśālī, Rājagṛha, and others, those six great cities — did you intend to pass into nirvāṇa here in this wretched town, this wilderness, this miserable fort, this branch of a town, this mere remnant of a city? Ānanda, do not say that this city of Kuśinārā is a wretched town, a wilderness, a miserable fort, a branch settlement, or a mere remnant of a city. For why? In former times, Ānanda, this city of Kuśinārā was the palace of King Kuśavat — prosperous, flourishing, happy, blessed with good harvests, full of people, thronging with many inhabitants — twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in breadth. Ānanda, the enclosure of King Kuśavat was fourfold: made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl (vaiḍūrya), and made of crystal; surrounded on all sides by seven enclosures. Ānanda, the four gates of the palace of King Kuśavat were made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal. Ānanda, the four staircases of those gates were made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal.

In height, the pillars were set to the depth that seven men standing could reach, with a quarter and a half of a man's height sunk into the ground as a foundation, and they were erected in sets of three. Ānanda, the four ponds of the palace of King Kuśavat — made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal — were surrounded on all sides by seven enclosures of paneled walls. Ānanda, the four palm trees of the palace of King Kuśavat — made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal — were surrounded on all sides by seven rows of palm trees made of those same four materials. Ānanda, the golden palm trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits fashioned from silver. Ānanda, the silver ones had leaves, flowers, and fruits of gold, beryl, and crystal. Ānanda, the crystal palm trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits fashioned from beryl. Ānanda, when those palm trees were stirred by the wind, they gave forth a pleasing sound of this kind — like a skilled musician giving a full and perfect performance on a five-part instrument. Ānanda, between those palm trees there were beautiful ponds, and those ponds too were fashioned of panels of the four kinds: gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. Ānanda, the four kinds of steps of those beautiful ponds were made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal. The parapets of those ponds were also surrounded on all sides by parapets of the four kinds: made of gold, made of silver, made of beryl, and made of crystal. Ānanda, the pins, rafters, and supports of the golden parapets were made of silver. Those of the silver parapets were made of gold. Those of the beryl parapets were made of crystal. And those of the crystal parapets — their pins, rafters, and supports — were made of beryl. Ānanda, within those beautiful ponds there grew various kinds of water-born flowers: the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, the white lotus, the supremely fragrant, the gently fragrant, and those that bloom in every season and flower at all times — yielding the causes for garlands of flowers, without obstruction, for all people. Ānanda, on both banks of those beautiful ponds there grew various kinds of flowers that grow on dry land: the atimukta, the campaka, the yellow jasmine, the pāriśāka, the mālikā, the navamālikā, the pleasing one, the yūthikā, the dhānuskari, and those that bloom in every season and flower at all times — yielding the causes for garlands of flowers, without obstruction, for all people. Ānanda, King Mahāsudarśana had placed in the spaces between those beautiful palm trees young attendants adorned with all manner of ornaments, who gave food to those who desired food, drink to those who desired drink, clothing to those who desired clothing, and garlands, perfumes, and unguents to those who desired garlands, perfumes, and unguents. Ānanda, those in the palace of King Kuśavat who wished to play, to rejoice, and to make merry — gamblers, dancers, and those who sell wine — played and rejoiced and made merry in great delight among those palm trees. Ānanda, in the palace of King Kuśavat, from those palm trees, there came pleasing sounds of this kind: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of small drums, the sound of conches, the sound of great kettledrums, the sound of assemblies,

the sound of the paṭaha drum, the sound of music, the sound of song, the sound of the flute, the sound of "Generosity has been given!", the sound of "Merit has been made!", the sound of "Those who fast on one meal have undertaken fasting and have taken up ethical conduct rightly!" — and so it became endowed with these twelve kinds of sound.

Ānanda, in the palace of King Kuśavat there dwelt a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) by the name of Great Sudassana, endowed with the seven precious things and the four kinds of human prosperity. What were the seven precious things he possessed? They were these: the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious gem, the precious woman, the precious householder, and the seventh, the precious minister.

Ānanda, what were the four kinds of human prosperity with which King Great Sudassana was endowed? He was long-lived and dwelt for a great span of time. He reached eighty-four thousand years playing the games of youth. He reached eighty-four thousand years acting as regent. He reached eighty-four thousand years acting as a great king. And he reached eighty-four thousand years living the royal sage's life of holy celibacy.

Ānanda, King Great Sudassana was long-lived and dwelt for a great span of time. He spent eighty-four thousand years in the joy of youth, playing games; eighty-four thousand years as regent; eighty-four thousand years as a great king; and eighty-four thousand years living the holy celibate life of a royal sage. This, Ānanda, is called the prosperity of King Great Sudassana.

Ānanda, furthermore, King Great Sudassana was handsome, beautiful, and lovely to behold — surpassing human complexion, though not yet attaining the complexion of the gods. Ānanda, King Great Sudassana was handsome, beautiful, and lovely to behold, surpassing human complexion though not yet attaining the complexion of the gods. This, Ānanda, is called the prosperity of King Great Sudassana.

Ānanda, furthermore, King Great Sudassana was of a constitution afflicted by little and free from illness. His stomach was neither too cold nor too hot; it was temperate, ever comfortable and free from distress, so that whatever he ate, drank, chewed, or tasted was well and easily digested. Ānanda, King Great Sudassana was of a constitution afflicted by little and free from illness — his stomach neither too cold nor too hot, temperate, ever comfortable and free from distress — so that whatever he ate, drank, chewed, or tasted was well and easily digested. This, Ānanda, is called the prosperity of King Great Sudassana.

Ānanda, furthermore, King Great Sudassana was beloved and pleasing to the townspeople and the country folk, just as a father is to his children. King Great Sudassana was beloved and pleasing to the townspeople and the country folk, just as children are to a father.

Ānanda, on one occasion, as King Great Sudassana was going to the pleasure grove, he said to the charioteer: "Charioteer, drive the chariot slowly, step by step — I wish to gaze long upon the townspeople and the country folk." And the townspeople and the country folk also said to the charioteer: "Charioteer, drive the chariot slowly, step by step — we too wish to gaze long upon our lord."

Ānanda, thus it was that King Great Sudassana was beloved and pleasing to the townspeople and the country folk, just as a father is to his children.

That King Great Sudassana was beloved and pleasing to the townspeople and the country folk, just as children are to a father — this, Ānanda, is called the prosperity of King Great Sudassana.

Then the townspeople and the country folk took up great quantities of gold and silver and precious jewels and rare gems, went to where King Great Sudassana was, and said to him: "O lord, we have come bringing great quantities of gold and silver and precious jewels and rare gems for your majesty's sake. May your majesty, out of gracious compassion, accept them." But he said: "Friends, in my land there is wealth of this kind in abundance — I have no need of it." And he would not accept it.

Then the townspeople and the country folk said again to King Great Sudassana: "O lord, these great quantities of gold and silver and precious jewels and rare gems that we have brought for your majesty's sake — may your majesty accept them out of gracious compassion." And King Great Sudassana said to the townspeople and the country folk two and three times: "Friends, in my land there is wealth of this kind in abundance — I have no need of it." And he would not accept.

Then the townspeople and the country folk thought to themselves: "We have come bringing gold and silver and precious jewels and rare gems for the lord's sake. For us now to take these back and go each to our own place would not be fitting for us. Rather, let us heap up great mounds of gold and silver before King Great Sudassana, and set the precious jewels and rare gems all around, and say: 'These are the lord's treasury,' and then leave them behind and depart." And so they laid the gold and silver and precious jewels and rare gems down before King Great Sudassana, left them there, and departed.

Then King Great Sudassana thought to himself: "My wealth has been acquired in accordance with the Dharma and not otherwise. Therefore let me build a Dharma-fitting palace." And he heard that the eighty-four thousand border vassal kings wished to assist King Great Sudassana in building a Dharma-fitting palace. Hearing this, they went to where King Great Sudassana was and said to him: "O lord, please be graciously pleased to undertake the task of building a Dharma-fitting palace. We shall build a Dharma-fitting palace for your majesty." But he said: "Friends, in my land there is wealth of this kind in abundance — there is no need." And he did not grant it.

The eighty-four thousand border vassal kings said to King Great Sudassana two and three times: "O lord, please be graciously pleased to undertake the task of building a Dharma-fitting palace. We shall build a Dharma-fitting palace for your majesty." And King Great Sudassana said to the eighty-four thousand border vassal kings two and three times: "Friends, in my land there is wealth of this kind in abundance — there is no need." And he did not grant it.

Then the eighty-four thousand border vassal kings prostrated at the feet of King Great Sudassana, some taking hold of his hands, some taking hold of the hem of his garment, and some, from whatever direction they faced King Great Sudassana, joining their palms and bowing in reverence.

They said to King Great Sudassana: "Your majesty, please be pleased to give your mind to the task of building a Dharma-fitting palace. We shall build a Dharma-fitting palace for your majesty." King Great Sudassana granted it to the eighty-four thousand border vassal kings with silence. Then the eighty-four thousand border vassal kings, understanding that King Great Sudassana had granted it with silence, departed each to their own lands and, carrying gold, much silver, and precious pillars one by one, went to the place where King Great Sudassana was. When they arrived there, they said to King Great Sudassana: "Your majesty, where and of what size shall we build the Dharma-fitting palace?" The king said to them: "Friends, for that purpose, build to the east of Kuśavati a Dharma-fitting palace one league in length and one league in breadth." "As your majesty commands," replied the eighty-four thousand border vassal kings, and in obedience to King Great Sudassana they built to the east of Kuśavati a Dharma-fitting palace one league in length and one league in breadth.

Ānanda, the four foundations of the Dharma-fitting palace were made, respectively, of gold, of silver, of beryl (vaiḍūrya), and of crystal. The four base-supports of the pillars of the Dharma-fitting palace were fashioned, respectively, of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. The four kinds of pillars of the Dharma-fitting palace were erected, respectively, of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. Ānanda, the golden pillars had their base-supports, column-caps, bracket-blocks, and crossbeams made of silver. Those of silver had theirs of gold. Those of beryl had theirs of crystal. Those of crystal had their base-supports, column-caps, bracket-blocks, and crossbeams made of beryl.

Ānanda, the four kinds of secondary rafters of the Dharma-fitting palace were laid of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. The four kinds of front beams of the Dharma-fitting palace were laid of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. The four kinds of main roof beams of the Dharma-fitting palace were laid of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal.

The fifty-third fascicle of the Vinaya Kṣudrakavastu.

Ānanda, the four kinds of wall-panels of the Dharma-fitting palace were hung of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. The four kinds of wall-slabs cladding the Dharma-fitting palace were fashioned of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. The four kinds of steps of the Dharma-fitting palace were built of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. The four kinds of railings encircling the Dharma-fitting palace were fashioned of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. Ānanda, the dowel-pins, support-posts, and baluster-shafts of the golden railings were made of silver. Those of silver had theirs of gold. Those of beryl had theirs of crystal. Ānanda, the crystal railings had their dowel-pins, baluster-shafts, and

support-posts made of beryl. Ānanda, the four kinds of multi-storied pavilions of the Dharma-fitting palace were built of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. Ānanda, in the golden multi-storied pavilion there were placed, on both sides, thrones made of silver, fitted with divine canopies, spread with Golika cloth, furnished with inner cushions of Brahma-quality fabric, with owl-feather cushions, with Mentri cushions, with Armonig cushions, and with cushions of fine Kāliṅga cloth — all covered with coverings and having red borders. For the silver pavilion, these were of gold. For the beryl pavilion, they were of crystal. For the crystal multi-storied pavilion, beginning from "thrones made of beryl, fitted with divine canopies" down to "placed on both sides with red borders" — all is as stated above. Ānanda, in front of the golden multi-storied pavilion there were strung silver palm-leaf fronds, flowers, and golden fruits. For the silver pavilion, these were of gold. For the beryl pavilion, they were of crystal. In front of the crystal multi-storied pavilion there were strung beryl palm-leaf fronds, flowers, and crystal fruits. When those palm fronds were stirred by the wind, delightful sounds arose — like, for example, a skilled person playing beautifully upon a lute furnished with five strings. Ānanda, the Dharma-fitting palace was spread with golden sand and sprinkled with sandalwood water, and adorned with golden nets and golden bells threaded on loops of wire.

The summary verse:

The foundations, column-bases, pillars,
the smaller rafters, fore-rafters, and great beams,
the eave-boards, wall-slabs, steps,
the railings, pavilions, and palm-trees — all of gold.

Then, knowing that all the construction of the eighty-four thousand Dharma-fitting palaces of the frontier kings was complete, in front of the Dharma-fitting palace a Dharma-fitting pool was made, one league in length and one league in breadth. Ānanda, the four wall-sides of the Dharma-fitting pool were built of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. Ānanda, the four kinds of steps of the Dharma-fitting pool were built of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. Ānanda, the Dharma-fitting pool was encircled by four kinds of railings made of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. The dowel-pins, baluster-shafts, and support-posts of the golden railings were made of silver. Those of silver had theirs of gold. Those of beryl had theirs of crystal. The crystal railings had their dowel-pins, baluster-shafts, and support-posts made of beryl. Ānanda, within the Dharma-fitting pool there grew various kinds of water-born flowers, namely: blue lotus (utpala), pink lotus (padma), white night-lotus (kumuda), white day-lotus (puṇḍarīka), flowers of supreme fragrance, flowers of mild fragrance, flowers in season for all occasions, and flowers for all times — producing, without obstruction for all people, the material for garlands of flowers. Ānanda, on both banks of the Dharma-fitting pool there grew land-born flowers, namely: atimuktaka, campaka, sky-blue lotus, pāriśāka, mālikā, navamālikā, the pleasing flower, yuṣṭika, dhanuṣkarī, flowers in season for all occasions, and flowers for all times — producing, without obstruction for all people, the material for garlands of flowers. Ānanda, the Dharma-fitting pool was spread with golden sand and sprinkled with sandalwood water,

and hung with golden nets and golden bells threaded on wire. Then the eighty-four thousand vassal kings, having learned that all the tasks pertaining to the Dharma-fitting pool were complete, planted before the Dharma-fitting pool a Dharma-fitting grove of tāla palms, one league in length and one league in breadth. Ānanda, in that Dharma-fitting grove of tāla palms there were planted tāla palms of four kinds: those made of gold, those made of silver, those made of vaidūrya, and those made of crystal. Ānanda, the tāla palms made of gold had leaves, flowers, and fruits made of silver fitted to them. Those made of silver had their fittings made of gold. Those made of vaidūrya had their fittings made of crystal. The tāla palms made of crystal had leaves, flowers, and fruits made of vaidūrya fitted to them. Ānanda, when those groves of tāla palms were stirred by the wind, a pleasing sound arose from them like that of a skilled musician performing a perfectly rendered melody on a five-part instrument. Ānanda, that Dharma-fitting grove of tāla palms was entirely enclosed by four balustrades — one made of gold, one made of silver, one made of vaidūrya, and one made of crystal. Ānanda, the balustrade made of gold had its pins, crossbars, and supports made of silver. The one made of silver had its fittings made of gold. The one made of vaidūrya had its fittings made of crystal. The balustrade made of crystal had its pins, crossbars, and supports made of vaidūrya. Ānanda, the Dharma-fitting grove of tāla palms was spread with golden sand and sprinkled with sandalwood water, and hung with golden nets and golden bells threaded on wire.

Then the eighty-four thousand vassal kings, having learned that all the tasks pertaining to the Dharma-fitting palace, the Dharma-fitting pool, and the Dharma-fitting grove of tāla palms were complete, went to where King Mahāsudarśana was, approached him, and spoke to him thus: "Your Majesty, all the works of the Dharma-fitting palace, the Dharma-fitting pool, and the Dharma-fitting grove of tāla palms have been accomplished. Your Majesty, please now consider that the time has come."

Then King Mahāsudarśana thought to himself: "It would not be fitting for me alone to dwell first in this Dharma-fitting palace. Rather, let me first give food in the Dharma-fitting palace to whatever ascetics, brahmins, and those of good conduct and worthy of veneration dwell in my realm, and let me present each one of them with a pair of fine woven cloth garments." Then King Mahāsudarśana did indeed first give food in the Dharma-fitting palace to whatever ascetics, brahmins, and those of good conduct and worthy of veneration dwelt in his realm, and presented each one with a pair of fine woven cloth garments.

Then King Mahāsudarśana thought to himself again: "It would not be fitting for me to sport and play and take delight in the Dharma-fitting palace amid the fully supplied five qualities of sensual pleasure. Rather, let me in the Dharma-fitting palace practice, together with a single close attendant, the royal sage's holy celibate life." And so King Mahāsudarśana did practice in the Dharma-fitting palace, together with a single close attendant, the royal sage's holy celibate life.

Then King Mahāsudarśana entered the golden multi-storied palace and sat upon a silver throne. Seated upon that throne, withdrawn from sensual desires, withdrawn from non-virtuous and unwholesome phenomena, with applied thought and sustained thought, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he dwelt having completed the first meditative concentration.

Descending from the silver throne, he departed from the golden multi-storied palace, entered the silver multi-storied palace, and sat upon a golden throne. Seated upon that throne — from "withdrawn from sensual desires" up to "he dwelt having completed the first meditative concentration" — all is as stated above.

Descending from the golden throne, he departed from the silver multi-storied palace, entered the vaidūrya multi-storied palace, and sat upon a crystal throne. Seated upon that throne — from "withdrawn from sensual desires" up to "he dwelt having completed the first meditative concentration" — all is as stated above.

Descending from the crystal throne, he departed from the vaidūrya multi-storied palace, entered the crystal multi-storied palace, and sat upon a vaidūrya throne. Seated upon that throne — from "withdrawn from sensual desires" up to "he dwelt having completed the first meditative concentration" — all is as stated above.

Then the eighty-four thousand women of the court went to where the jewel queen was, approached her, and addressed her thus: "May your ladyship please know: it has been a long time since we have seen our lord the king. We are deeply thirsting to see him. We wish to behold our lord."

"Sisters, wait here for a moment while I inquire of the jewel minister." The jewel queen then summoned the jewel minister by messenger and said: "General, know this: it has been a long time since I have seen our lord, and I am deeply thirsting to see him. Today I wish to behold him. Therefore, sisters, let all of you adorn yourselves with golden ornaments, golden garments, garlands, pendants, and golden unguents, and let the retinue too be arrayed in gold. In the meanwhile, let me assemble the eighty-four thousand frontier vassal kings, the eighty-four thousand elephants led by the elephant king Nearby Restoration and the others, the eighty-four thousand horses led by the horse king Cloud-Force and the others, and the eighty-four thousand chariots led by the chariot Joyful Sound and the others."

Then all the queens adorned themselves with golden ornaments, golden garments, garlands, pendants, and golden unguents, and the retinue too was arrayed in gold. Then the jewel minister assembled the eighty-four thousand frontier vassal kings, the eighty-four thousand elephants led by the elephant king Nearby Restoration and the others, the eighty-four thousand horses led by the horse king Cloud-Force and the others, and the eighty-four thousand chariots led by the chariot Joyful Sound and the others.

When all had been assembled, the jewel queen mounted the chariot Joyful Sound, and all the other women each mounted their own chariots, and they set out toward the Dharma-fitting palace.

At that moment, the noise and great clamor of the common crowd was heard from below the Dharma-fitting palace, and King Mahāsudarśana, from inside the Dharma-fitting palace, heard the noise of the common crowd rising from below. Having heard it, he spoke to his close attendant thus:

"Ho there, good man — what is this great noise and clamor of the common crowd that is heard below this Dharma-fitting palace?"

"Your Majesty, it is the jewel queen and the eighty-four thousand women who desire to look upon the king from below the Dharma-fitting palace, together with the eighty-four thousand border kings led by the jewel minister and the others, the eighty-four thousand elephants led by the elephant king Near-Observance and the others, the eighty-four thousand horses led by the horse king Cloud-Force and the others, and the eighty-four thousand chariots led by the chariot Joyful Sound and the others — all of them have come from below this Dharma-fitting palace, Your Majesty."

"In that case, good man, go and arrange a fine golden throne on the lower veranda of the Dharma-fitting palace, where I may sit and be seen by the many people."

"As Your Majesty commands," the man replied, and heeding the words of King Mahāsudarśana, he arranged a fine golden throne on the lower veranda of the Dharma-fitting palace. Then he went to where King Mahāsudarśana was and spoke to him thus: "Your Majesty, a fine throne of gold has been arranged on the lower veranda of the Dharma-fitting palace. Your Majesty, please be pleased to consider that the time has now come."

Then, as King Mahāsudarśana descended from the Dharma-fitting palace, he saw that all the women were adorned in yellow ornaments, yellow robes, garlands, pendants, yellow unguents, and yellow retinue-dress. Seeing this, he thought to himself, "Alas — these women will give rise to attachment in me," and so he sat looking upward toward the sky. The jewel queen then saw King Mahāsudarśana sitting there with his gaze directed upward toward the sky, and she thought: "Since the king sees us and yet sits looking up at the sky, he must surely be thinking that we will bring him some harm."

Then King Mahāsudarśana descended from the Dharma-fitting palace and took his seat on the fine golden throne that had been arranged. The jewel queen went to where King Mahāsudarśana was, and prostrating with her head at his feet, she sat to one side. Having sat to one side, the jewel queen spoke to King Mahāsudarśana in these words:

"Your Majesty, these eighty-four thousand women belong to Your Majesty — may Your Majesty be pleased to look upon them with delight and sustain them. The eighty-four thousand border kings led by the jewel minister and the others, the eighty-four thousand elephants led by the elephant king Near-Observance and the others, the eighty-four thousand horses led by the horse king Cloud-Force and the others, the eighty-four thousand chariots led by the chariot Joyful Sound and the others, the eighty-four thousand cities led by the royal palace Grassy and the others, and the eighty-four thousand multi-storied mansions led by the mansion Three-Balconied and the others — all of these, Your Majesty, belong to Your Majesty. May Your Majesty be pleased to look upon them with delight and sustain them. Sister — whereas before you treated me as a friend and companion, now you have made yourself my rival."

Then, at being addressed by King Mahāsudarśana with the word "sister," the jewel queen wept, and with tears flowing she spoke thus:

"How is it that Your Majesty has called us 'sister' and summoned us? Before long we shall no longer be together with Your Majesty — we shall be parted, separated, and sundered."

Then the jewel queen took hold of King Mahāsudarśana's robe at its hem, and with tears flowing she spoke thus: "How has Your Majesty — who before treated us as a friend and companion — now made yourself our rival? 'Sister, come here,' you say. Human beings live but a short while, and none are free from death; they pass on to other lives. Therefore do virtue and practice the holy life." Then she said: "Your Majesty, those eighty-four thousand divine women toward whom desire, attachment, affection, delight, and longing arise — please abandon them for the sake of your living on. And those eighty-four thousand frontier lords led by the jewel minister, the eighty-four thousand elephants led by the elephant-king Nearby Poṣadha, the eighty-four thousand horses led by the horse-king Cloud-Force, the eighty-four thousand chariots led by the chariot Joyful Sound, the eighty-four thousand cities led by the royal palace Grassy, and the eighty-four thousand multi-storied mansions led by the mansion Three-Balconied — toward all of these, toward those places where desire, attachment, affection, delight, and longing arise — please abandon them and set them aside utterly, for the sake of your living on. For Your Majesty will perish entirely and in every part in but a single instant, a single moment — and that will bring you no joy."

They then replied: "Since we are treating Your Majesty as a friend and companion, and not as a rival, if Your Majesty so wishes — human beings live but a short while, and none are free from death; they pass on to other lives — then let us do virtue and practice the holy life. Your Majesty will perish entirely and in every part in but a single instant, a single moment, and that will bring no joy. Those eighty-four thousand divine women toward whom desire, attachment, affection, delight, and longing arise — please abandon them and regard them with equanimity for the sake of your living on. And those eighty-four thousand frontier lords led by the jewel minister, the eighty-four thousand elephants led by the elephant-king Nearby Poṣadha, the eighty-four thousand horses led by the horse-king Cloud-Force, the eighty-four thousand chariots led by the chariot Joyful Sound, the eighty-four thousand cities led by the royal palace Grassy, and the eighty-four thousand multi-storied mansions led by the mansion Three-Balconied — toward all of these, toward those places where desire, attachment, affection, delight, and longing arise — please abandon them and regard them with equanimity for the sake of your living on."

Then, when the jewel queen had given this counsel to King Mahāsudarśana, he ascended the Dharma-concordant palace, entered the golden multi-storied mansion, and sat upon a silver throne. Seated upon that throne, he cultivated a mind of loving-kindness — without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction with it, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained. In the same way he then cultivated the second direction, and in the same way the third,

and in the same way the fourth, and above, and below, and across — pervading every direction, suffusing this entire world complete in all its aspects with a mind of loving-kindness, without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained.

Then he descended from the silver throne, left the golden multi-storied mansion, entered the silver multi-storied mansion, and sat upon a golden throne. Seated upon that throne, he cultivated a mind of compassion — without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction with it, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained. In the same way the second direction, and in the same way the third, and in the same way the fourth, and above, and below, and across — pervading every direction, suffusing this entire world complete in all its aspects with a mind of compassion, without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained.

Then he descended from the golden throne, left the silver multi-storied mansion, entered the lapis lazuli multi-storied mansion, and sat upon a crystal throne. Seated upon that throne, he cultivated a mind of joy — without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction with it, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained. In the same way the second direction, and in the same way the third, and in the same way the fourth, and above, and below, and across — pervading every direction, suffusing this entire world complete in all its aspects with a mind of joy, without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained.

Then he descended from the crystal throne, left the lapis lazuli multi-storied mansion, entered the crystal multi-storied mansion, and sat upon a lapis lazuli throne. Seated upon that throne, he cultivated a mind of equanimity — without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction with it, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained. In the same way the second direction, and in the same way the third, and in the same way the fourth, and above, and below, and across — pervading every direction, suffusing this entire world complete in all its aspects with a mind of equanimity, without ill-will, without rivalry, without harm, vast, expansive, boundless, and very well developed — pervading one direction, suffusing it, filling it, and completing it, and there he remained.

Then King Mahāsudarśana, having dwelt in and cultivated the four divine abodes many times over, relinquished sensual pleasures and attachment to them, and was reborn on an equal footing in the Brahmā world.

Ānanda, at the time of his death, King Mahāsudarśana experienced a feeling of that very kind — just as a strong man who has eaten a fine meal feels, in that very moment, wearied and sated by the food.

Ānanda, from the city of Kuśāvatī to the river Anomā, to the paired śāla trees,

to the Caitya Adorned by the Champion, a distance of twelve leagues all around — in all these places the body of a Tathāgata, functioning as a wheel-turning king, was reborn six times. And, Ānanda, up to and including that very place, there were seven times that a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha appeared. As for an eighth occasion on which the body of a Tathāgata would be cast aside in some eastward, southward, westward, or northward direction from that place — I have not seen such a one. Why so? Because the craving for existence has been cut, births in cyclic existence are exhausted, and from this no further existence will arise.

At that time the venerable Upavāṇa was sitting in the presence of the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said to the venerable Upavāṇa: "Step aside, monk; do not stand before me."

Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Reverend one, for more than twenty years I have served as the Blessed One's personal attendant, and yet I have never before heard such a sharp and rebuking word spoken to the venerable Upavāṇa as this. What is the reason, reverend one, for the Blessed One speaking so harshly and censuring him?"

"Ānanda, the gods of the many hundreds of kalpas' duration of the capable — thinking to themselves: 'A Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha appears in this world only rarely, like the udumbara flower — and this Blessed One will pass into the nirvāṇa without remainder this very night at midnight; and that monk, the one renowned for his great power, is sitting right here in the presence of the Blessed One, and by standing with his back to us he blocks us from going to see and attend upon the Blessed One' — they are resentful, they censure, they murmur against him. Reverend one, may the Blessed One be pleased to take note of however many gods there are." "Ānanda, from the city of Kuśāvatī to the river Anomā, and from the grove of the paired śāla trees to the Caitya Adorned by the Champion, within a circle of twelve leagues — there is not even the tiniest space, even as small as the point of a blade of grass pressed into the earth, that is not filled and pervaded by great and renowned gods. The monks, having arisen in doubt, and wishing to have all those doubts cut through, asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: 'Reverend one, what is it? What action did the venerable Upavāṇa perform that made him become renowned for great power?' The Blessed One declared: 'Monks, this monk Upavāṇa performed and accumulated actions that bring about the acquisition of a retinue, the full transformation of conditions, and the certain arising of radiant proximity. The actions performed and accumulated by monk Upavāṇa — who else would experience their fruits? Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth; they do not ripen in the element of water; they do not ripen in the element of fire; they do not ripen in the element of wind. Rather, virtuous and non-virtuous actions performed and accumulated ripen in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense sources.

Actions, though a hundred kalpas pass,
are never lost; when the conditions and the time arrive,
they bear their fruit for embodied beings.

Monks, in this very auspicious kalpa, when the lifespan of living beings was twenty thousand years, the Teacher named Kāśyapa — fully endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One — arose in the world.

He dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park forest at Ṛṣivadana near the city of Vārāṇasī, and at that time he went forth under that one's teaching. Then, on another occasion, it was the turn of the duty-monk, and the monks, in the early morning hour, donned their lower robes, took up their bowls and dharma robes, and entered Vārāṇasī on the alms round. At that time, in the winter season, a great storm arose out of season and rain fell. He thought: "Those who live the celibate life have been soaked by this unseasonable rain and are endangered by the cold; when they return I must kindle a fire." So he entered a fire-shelter and lit a fire, then strung ropes all around the courtyard, and sat by the door of the assembly hall watching for their return. When the monks returned, he laid down seats in the fire-shelter. Those monks gave their robes to one another, and those that had been soaked by the rain were hung on the ropes to dry. Then those monks entered the fire-shelter, gathered around the fire, and sat warming themselves. When the cold had passed, they turned their backs to the warmth of the fire and sat facing away from it.

Then the duty-monk felt faith arise, bowed at the feet of those monks, and began to make an aspiration: "By the root of virtue from this act of sheltering these celibate practitioners who were endangered by the cold, may I — whoever I may be — receive a prophecy from the fully and perfectly awakened buddha named Kāśyapa to the brahmin youth called Guru, and at the time when the lifespan of beings reaches one hundred years may I become a Tathāgata, arhat, fully and perfectly awakened buddha named Śākyamuni. Having received that prophecy, may I go forth under that one's teaching, abandon all afflictions completely, and actualize arhatship directly. And just as those monks could not bear the bright heat of the fire, so may the gods themselves be unable to bear the brilliance of my splendour." By the power of that aspiration he made, he went forth under my teaching, abandoned all afflictions, actualized arhatship directly, and became renowned for great power, so that even the gods are unable to outshine him with their radiance.

Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend Blessed One, after you have passed, how much effort should we devote to veneration of your bodily relics?" "Ānanda, concern yourself with this but little. This is something that brahmins and faithful householders will accomplish." "Reverend one, how do brahmins and faithful householders accomplish this?" "Ānanda, they do it in the manner done for a wheel-turning king." "Reverend one, how is it done for a wheel-turning king?" "Ānanda, the body of a wheel-turning king is wrapped in cotton wool, wound round with cotton wool, and then swathed in five hundred pairs of cloth. Wrapped in five hundred pairs of cloth, he is placed in an iron casket, filled with sesame oil, and covered above with a sealed iron lid. Then all fragrant woods are heaped up, he is cremated with these, the fire is quenched with milk, and his bones are placed inside a golden urn. At the crossroads of a great highway a bone stūpa is built, and parasols, victory banners, and pennants are erected; incense, garlands, burnt offerings, powders, and the sound of music are offered; he is honoured, exalted, portrayed in painting, and worshipped, and a great festival is held. Ānanda, just as it is done for a wheel-turning king, so for a Tathāgata, arhat, and fully and perfectly awakened buddha it should be done even more and beyond that."

"Ānanda, go and tell the warrior-nobles of the city of Kuśinagara to make their preparations: your Teacher will pass into nirvāṇa, the nirvāṇa-element without remainder, at the middle watch of this very night. Warriors, perform your tasks and duties there, and do not afterwards lament, saying: 'Our Teacher has passed into nirvāṇa, the nirvāṇa-element without remainder, and we who dwell nearby in the city are unable to go and see him or pay him reverence.'"

The venerable Ānanda replied, "As you command," and having listened to the Blessed One, he took up his outer robe and, together with other monks and wandering ascetics who were following behind, went straight to the assembly hall of the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara. When he arrived, there were in that assembly hall some five hundred warrior-nobles gathered together for a certain matter.

Then the venerable Ānanda spoke to the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara as follows: "O great assembly of warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara, gathered here in numbers, wise ones who are keepers of the place, hear this! The Teacher will pass into nirvāṇa, the nirvāṇa-element without remainder, at the middle watch of this very night. Warriors, perform your tasks and duties there, and do not afterwards lament, saying: 'Our Teacher has passed into nirvāṇa, the nirvāṇa-element without remainder, and we who dwell nearby in the city are unable to go and see him or pay him reverence.'"

Then the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara, having listened to the venerable Ānanda, departed from Kuśinagara along with their sons, their wives, their male servants, their female servants, their workers, those who lived on dairy produce, their friends and companions, their ministers, their relatives, and their kinsmen by marriage, and went straight to the grove of twin sāl trees. Having arrived, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. The Blessed One then rightly taught the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara with talk in accordance with the Dharma, rightly guided them to uphold it, rightly praised them, and rightly caused them to rejoice.

Then the leading warrior-nobles among the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara rose from their seats, arranged their robes over one shoulder, turned and bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and spoke to the Blessed One thus: "Venerable One, we are the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara. We go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks, and we shall undertake the foundations of training."

Then the venerable Ānanda thought to himself: "If each of the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara were to sit individually before the Blessed One to make their lay refuge declaration, the warrior-nobles would have to leave again at midnight without having made their declarations individually. Therefore I should sit before the Blessed One and administer the lay refuge declaration to all the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara simultaneously."

Here begins the fifty-fourth section, the basis of the minor matters of the Vinaya.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, turned and bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and spoke to the Blessed One thus: "Venerable One, the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara, together with their sons, their wives, their male servants, their female servants, their female workers, those who lived on dairy produce, their friends, their ministers, their relatives, and their kinsmen by marriage — these ones go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and

the Saṅgha of monks, and we ask you to grant us the foundations of the training." Then the venerable Ānanda, together with those warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara, sat before the Blessed One, and before that night's middle watch had passed, they performed the individual confession of lay practitioners.

Then the warrior-nobles of Kuśinagara, delighted and rejoicing at the words the Blessed One had spoken, bowed with their heads at the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

At the time when the bodhisattva was dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven and looked out with the five kinds of seeing, he surveyed the six classes of gods of the desire realm three times, manifested a great elephant, and entered the womb of his mother. At that time Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), said to Rabjā (Pramudita), king of the gandharvas, these words: "Know this, Rabjā: the Blessed One, dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven, has looked out with the five kinds of seeing, surveyed the six classes of gods of the desire realm three times, manifested a great elephant, and entered the womb of his mother. I am going forth to guard and protect him." Rabjā replied: "Let me first take up a song, O Kauśika — then go." At the time when the bodhisattva emerged from the womb of his mother, Śakra, lord of the gods, again said to Rabjā, king of the gandharvas, these words: "Know this, Rabjā: the Blessed One, the bodhisattva, has emerged from the womb of his mother. I am going forth to serve and attend upon him." Rabjā replied: "Let me first take up a song, O Kauśika — then go." At the time when the Blessed One, as bodhisattva in his youth, was at play and sport, Śakra, lord of the gods, again said to Rabjā, king of the gandharvas, these words: "Know this, Rabjā: the Blessed One, as a young bodhisattva, continues at play and sport. We are going forth to pay him honour and service." Rabjā replied: "Let me first take up a song, O Kauśika — then go."

At the time when the bodhisattva saw old age, sickness, and death, felt renunciation arise in his heart, and entered the forest of ascetic practice — and then, having accomplished the austerities, arose from that austerity — the village girls Gayā and Sujātā offered him a sweet milk-porridge like honey, prepared with sixteen rounds of boiling down to its essence, and a coarse meal of easy inhalation and easy exhalation, of comfortable grains and warm food. They then anointed his body with sesame oil and clarified butter, and bathed him with cool water.

At that time Śakra, lord of the gods, said to Rabjā, king of the gandharvas, these words: "Know this, Rabjā: the Blessed One, the bodhisattva, saw old age, sickness, and death, felt renunciation arise, entered the forest of ascetic practice, and performed austerities. Now the village girls Gayā and Sujātā have offered him sweet milk-porridge like honey, prepared with sixteen rounds of boiling, and a coarse meal of easy breath and comfortable grains and warm food, and have anointed his body with sesame oil and clarified butter and bathed him with cool water. I am going forth to pay him honour and service." Rabjā replied: "Let me first take up a song, O Kauśika — then go."

At the time when the Blessed One subdued the thirty-six billion hosts of Māra's demons and realized unsurpassable gnosis, Brahmā implored him, he proceeded to Vārāṇasī, and turning the wheel of Dharma in twelve aspects, reciting it three times — at that time, the Blessed One, in whatever directions there were villages, towns, and

royal precincts, and regions of every kind — wherever beings were to be tamed, he tamed them — and then proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara and entered his final resting place. Therefore, you should set out to that place to hear the Dharma." Rabjā replied: "Let me first take up a song, O Kauśika — then go."

Then once again Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) spoke these words to Rabjā, king of the gandharvas (celestial musicians): "Know this, Rabjā — the Blessed One has entered his final resting place and is about to pass fully into nirvāṇa. Let us set out to pay him honour and service." Rabjā replied: "Let me first take up a song, O Kauśika — then go."

The Blessed One then reflected: "The wanderer Supriya is one whom I can tame, but Rabjā, king of the gandharvas, is difficult to tame. Those who are to be tamed by śrāvakas the Tathāgata proceeds to tame; but those who are to be tamed by a buddha cannot be tamed by śrāvakas. For that reason, the knowledge by which the Tathāgata knows what beings are to be tamed is unsurpassable. I must not miss the moment for taming this one." With this thought, he entered into a meditative absorption of such a kind that, while remaining in equipoise, he left an emanation on the final resting place, took up a hollow lute with a thousand strings, its body made of lapis lazuli, rose from the final resting place, and came to stand at the door of Rabjā, king of the gandharvas, among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

Rabjā, king of the gandharvas, had grown proud, thinking: "There is no one like me." He had taken up his melodious lute, and sat there utterly delighted in mind. Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the doorkeeper: "Go and tell Rabjā, king of the gandharvas, that a gandharva who understands has come to the gate, wishing to see him." The doorkeeper went and announced this. Rabjā, intoxicated with pride, replied: "What does that person say? Is there really another gandharva besides me?" The doorkeeper said: "I shall not mention others for the moment — there is simply one here at this very gate." The gandharva, carried along by the force of his intoxicating pride, came to the door in an instant and said: "Are you a gandharva, good man?" The Blessed One declared: "I am indeed a gandharva, and more." Rabjā said: "If that is so, take up your song and come in." The Blessed One declared: "Very well, so be it" — and for as long as the Blessed One played alongside him, when the Blessed One plucked one string, Rabjā also plucked one string, and the sound and melody of both lutes were equal. When the Blessed One plucked two strings, likewise the sound and melody were indistinguishable. So too with three strings, and from four strings down to a single string — and when Rabjā left it at two, three, and from four down to a single string, likewise both lutes were indistinguishable in sound and melody.

Then the Blessed One plucked even that one remaining string, and in the sky itself the sound and melody arose just as before.

Rabjā, the king of gandharvas, was filled with wonder and, his pride entirely deflated, thought to himself: "Is there truly another noble gandharva who surpasses me?" Then the Blessed One caused his gandharva appearance to vanish, and he stood revealed in his own true form — adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty minor excellent features, his body graced with an aura of light a fathom wide surpassing the radiance of a thousand suns, beautiful on all sides like a mountain of precious jewels. When Rabjā, the king of gandharvas, beheld this, faith arose in him. He prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat in his presence to hear the Dharma.

The Blessed One, knowing his disposition, his latent tendencies, his elemental constitution, and his intrinsic nature, taught the Dharma in a manner suited to bring about realization of the Four Noble Truths. Upon hearing it, Rabjā, the king of gandharvas, shattered with the vajra of gnosis the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection — and thereby directly actualized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, he uttered this solemn declaration three times:

"Venerable one, no such gift as this has ever been given to me — not by my mother, not by a king, not by a god, not by a friend, not by my own people and the assembly of my kin, not by those gone before me, not by ascetics or brahmins. What the Blessed One has done for me is this: he has dried the ocean of blood and tears, he has freed me from the mountain of bones, he has closed the door to the lower realms, and he has opened the door to the higher states and to liberation, establishing me in a place fitting for gods and humans. Venerable one, I now go to the Blessed One, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha for refuge. Please receive me as a lay practitioner. From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I turn away from the taking of life and go to refuge with sincere faith and devotion."

Then the Blessed One, with words endowed with Dharma, thoroughly instructed Rabjā, the king of gandharvas, caused him to retain it thoroughly, praised him thoroughly, and caused him to rejoice thoroughly.

And just as the Blessed One entered meditative equipoise, he became invisible to the gods of the Thirty-Three and entered into such a meditative absorption as is the final resting place, the last couch.

At that time, in the city of Kuśinagara, there dwelt one called Suprabha, a wandering ascetic — old, ancient, decrepit, one hundred and twenty years of age — revered, honored, esteemed, and worshipped by the warriors of Kuśinagara as a reputed arhat. He was dwelling in his daytime abode beside a gently flowing pond at the foot of an udumbara grove in Kuśinagara.

At the time when the Blessed One, dwelling in the Tuṣita realm as a bodhisattva, surveyed with his five forms of vision, trained three times among the six classes of gods of the desire realm, manifested as a great elephant, and entered the womb of his mother — at that very moment the udumbara grove came to be covered with buds like frog-eyes.

At the time when he emerged from his mother's womb, those buds opened wide.

At the time when he played the sports of youth, the flowers were in full bloom.

At the time when, having seen old age, sickness, and death, his mind turned away and he entered the forest of austerities, the open flowers began to close again.

At the time when he was practicing austerities, the formerly open flowers became withered.

At the time when he recognized that the practice of austerities was without purpose, began to breathe as he pleased and breathe out as he pleased, and took coarse food of gruel and warm rice and fed his body with sesame oil —

— anointed with butter and sesame oil — up through and including the words "he awoke to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening": all as before. At that time, all the udumbara flowers burst into full bloom.

At the time when Brahmā petitioned the Blessed One and he set out for the city of Vārāṇasī, and having proclaimed it three times, turned the wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects — at that time the grove of udumbara flowers blazed with a brilliant, clear radiance.

At the time when the Blessed One, in whatever directions there were — in villages, cities, towns, royal palaces and their surroundings, and in various provinces — had tamed those who were to be tamed, and had come to rest on his final bed in the city of Kuśinagara: at that time the udumbara grove began to wither. All of this was witnessed as an auspicious sign by the wanderer Supriyā. And a deity dwelling in the city of Kuśinagara spoke to the inhabitants of that city, saying: "The Tathāgata will tonight, at the middle watch of the night, pass completely beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder."

Supriyā the wanderer heard this. And having heard it, she thought: "If the ascetic Gautama passes beyond sorrow tonight at the middle watch of the night into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, I have doubts about certain teachings. These doubts of mine are such that the Blessed One Gautama would dispel them for me — he would engage in clearing my doubts. Let me therefore go to where the Blessed One Gautama is, and if I am given the opportunity, after asking my questions and receiving his prediction, I shall ask about several points." And so she set out from the city of Kuśinagara and went to where the twin sāla trees stood.

At that moment, the venerable Ānanda had come outside and was walking and sitting in the open, in a place without cover. Supriyā the wanderer saw the venerable Ānanda from a considerable distance — walking and sitting in that exposed place outside. Having seen him, she went to where the venerable Ānanda was, and when she had arrived, she said to him: "O Ānanda, having heard that the ascetic Gautama will tonight, at the middle watch of the night, pass completely beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder, I have come to have doubts about certain teachings. These doubts of mine are such that the Blessed One Gautama would dispel them — he would engage in clearing my doubts. If the venerable Ānanda would allow me to enter within, and if an opportunity were given after I present my questions seeking his prediction, I would ask about several points."

"Supriyā, do not disturb the Tathāgata. It is enough. The body of the Blessed One is weary. The body of the Sugata is weary."

Yet Supriyā repeated her words to the venerable Ānanda a second and a third time: "O Ānanda, I have heard from elderly wandering teachers and masters of former times that a Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly complete buddha arises in the world only rarely — at most perhaps once in a hundred — like the udumbara flower. The Blessed One Gautama will tonight, at the middle watch of the night, pass beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder. I have come to have doubts about certain teachings, and these doubts of mine are such that the Blessed One Gautama would dispel them for me — he would engage in clearing my doubts. I have come thinking this, and so —"

"If the venerable Ānanda would permit me to enter, and if an opportunity were granted for me to put a question and receive instruction on it, I would ask about one matter" — so spoke the wanderer Subhadra to the venerable Ānanda, a second time and then a third. And Ānanda replied: "Enough, Subhadra. Do not trouble the Tathāgata. The body of the Blessed One is weary. The body of the Sugata is spent."

So it was that the two of them — the venerable Ānanda and the wanderer Subhadra — were speaking together in this way, the one urging and the other refusing, when the Blessed One heard them with his divine hearing, pure and surpassing that of human beings. Having heard, he spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do not prevent this wanderer Subhadra. Let him come and ask whatever he wishes. For this will be the last conversation I shall hold with a tīrthika. And this is how it is: this very wanderer Subhadra, once I have summoned him to my presence, will become the last among my disciples — the monks who have gone forth and taken ordination."

Then the wanderer Subhadra, delighted and greatly rejoiced that the Blessed One had granted him the opportunity, arose with joy and gladness in his heart and went to where the Blessed One was. Having arrived, he exchanged with the Blessed One various words of greeting and mutual rejoicing, and then sat down to one side.

Seated to one side, the wanderer Subhadra addressed the Blessed One thus: "O Gautama, if an opportunity is granted for me to put a question and receive instruction on it, I would ask about one matter."

"Subhadra, ask whatever you wish."

"O Gautama, in this world there are various tīrthikas — namely: Pūraṇa Kassapa, the wanderer Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya the son of the Belaṭṭha woman, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, and the naked Kassapa — each with their own doctrines and each claiming their own form of knowledge. Have they, as they claim, truly known, or have none of them truly known?"

Then the Blessed One at that time declared these verses:

"Subhadra, I was twenty-nine years of age when I went forth,
and for more than fifty years since then
I have sought whatever is virtuous and good.
Subhadra, from the time of that going forth of mine,
in moral discipline, in meditative absorption, in conduct and awareness,
I have cultivated one-pointed concentration throughout,
and if I have set forth even a portion of the teaching of right reasoning —
beyond this, there is no other ascetic.

In whatever teaching and discipline the noble eightfold path does not appear, there no first ascetic is to be found, no second ascetic, no third ascetic, no fourth ascetic. But in whatever teaching and discipline the noble eightfold path does appear, there a first ascetic is to be found, a second, a third, and a fourth ascetic. Subhadra, in whatever teaching and discipline the noble eightfold path appears, here is the first ascetic, here is the second, here is the third, and here is the fourth. In what lies beyond this teaching, there is neither ascetic nor brahmin. Thus do I roar the lion's roar rightly before this assembly, emptying it of the rival claims of others' ascetics and brahmins."

When this presentation of the Dharma had been taught, the eye of Dharma — free of dust and stainless — arose in the wanderer Subhadra with regard to all phenomena. Then the wanderer Subhadra, having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, having realized the Dharma, having reached the very depth of the Dharma, having crossed beyond doubt, having crossed beyond uncertainty, having nothing more to ask of another, having no need to rely on another's guidance —

having gained fearlessness with regard to the teachings the Teacher had taught, he rose from his seat, arranged his outer robe over one shoulder, turned toward where the venerable Ānanda was, joined his palms, bowed, and spoke these words to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda has indeed obtained a great gain — for the venerable Ānanda was ordained by the great master and received full ordination. May I too obtain a great gain, in that I too shall go forth and receive full ordination in the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, and attain the state of a monk." Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable sir, this wanderer Subhadra wishes to go forth into the well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and attain the state of a monk. May the Blessed One, moved by compassion, grant him the going forth and full ordination." Then the Blessed One spoke to the wanderer Subhadra: "Come, monk — live the holy life (brahmacarya)." With that, that venerable one went forth and received full ordination, and attained the state of a monk.

Having thus gone forth, that venerable one dwelt in seclusion, with vigilance, with diligence, and in austerity — dwelling in seclusion, with vigilance, with diligence, and in austerity. He accomplished precisely that for which sons of good family shave their hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and go forth from home into homelessness with perfect faith — bringing to completion the unsurpassed holy life. In this very life he realized it directly through his own higher knowledge, actualized it, and dwelt in it, and proclaimed: "Birth is exhausted. The holy life has been fulfilled. What had to be done has been done. I know of no further becoming beyond this." That venerable one's mind was utterly liberated, and he became an arhat endowed with perfect knowledge.

Then the venerable Subhadra, having attained arhatship and experiencing throughout himself the joy and happiness of liberation, thought to himself: "It is not fitting for me to witness the Teacher's complete passing into nirvāṇa. I must by all means pass into complete nirvāṇa beforehand." So thinking, he went to where the Blessed One was, arrived, and having bowed his head to the Blessed One's two feet, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Subhadra addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable sir, I wish to pass into complete nirvāṇa beforehand."

When he said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhadra: "Subhadra, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa — or in order for the Blessed One to pass into nirvāṇa?" "For the Blessed One to pass into nirvāṇa, venerable sir." "Subhadra, do you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa — or in order for the Sugata to pass into nirvāṇa?" "For the Sugata to pass into nirvāṇa, venerable sir." "Subhadra, if you speak in order to pass into nirvāṇa, what is there for me to say? It is the very nature of all conditioned things."

Then the venerable Subhadra thought: "I shall bless five places and then pass into nirvāṇa." He envisioned that those who live the holy life equally with himself would be seen with shaven heads wearing patched robes, while the tīrthikas would be seen bearing the banners of their own tradition — that those rival tīrthikas would be unable to raise his bier, while those who live the holy life equally with himself would be able to raise it. He conjured up a small pond, envisioning it thus: that the tīrthikas would be unable to walk into the pond or move about in it —

while those who live the holy life equally with himself would be able to move about in it freely; that the fish and turtles would be able to harm the tīrthikas, but would not be able to harm those who live the holy life equally with himself; that the tīrthikas would be unable to kindle a fire or light a funeral pyre, while those who live the holy life equally with himself would be able to light it. Having thus blessed these five places, he passed fully into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.

When the other wandering tīrthikas heard that the wanderer Rabzang had passed fully into nirvāṇa, they raised great banners of white cloth and paraded through the broad avenues, colonnades, crossroads, and intersections of the city of Kusināra, proclaiming in this manner: "This is the first among renunciants. This is the second. This is the third. The fourth — beyond him there is no renunciant or brahmin whatsoever. The renunciants and brahmins who challenge him as rivals are utterly empty." Roaring thus with the true lion's roar before the assembly, they declared: "Our companion in the holy life, the wanderer Rabzang, has passed into nirvāṇa."

At this the monks said to them: "Friends, if this one was indeed your companion in the holy life, bring him here, place him upon a bier, carry him, and let us see." When those wanderers placed him upon the bier and began to lift it, they could not move it at all. Then the monks said: "Friends, shall we lift him? Let us try." And when the monks lifted him, the wanderers, having no confidence, said nothing and stood in silence.

When those wanderers then entered the small pond, the monks again said to them: "Friends, if this one was your companion in the holy life, come in here — enter the pond and let us see." They entered, and sank; the fish and turtles harmed them and they could not move about, so they retreated, coming out step by step from a distance. Then the monks said: "Watch while we enter." The monks entered and did not sink; the fish and turtles could not harm them, and they moved about freely. The wanderers again had no confidence, said nothing, and stood in silence.

Then the monks said further: "Friends, if this one was your companion in the holy life, light the pyre and cremate him — let us see." When those wanderers kindled the fire and began to cremate him, they could not light it. The monks then said: "Friends, let us light it." The monks lit the fire, and it blazed. And those wanderers, just as before, had no confidence, said nothing, and stood in silence.

Then many people, having witnessed all this, departed. The warriors of Kusināra were filled with great wonder and came to have deep faith in the Blessed One.

At the very time when the Blessed One lay upon his final resting-bed, his joints severed and his articulations splitting — with that piercing sensation having come upon him — even while he remained thus lying, Rabzang was established in the state of arhatship. At that moment, as many warriors of Kusināra were being established in the Dharma, doubts arose among the monks. They brought all their doubts to be resolved and addressed the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, at the very time when the Blessed One lay with his joints severed and his articulations splitting, with that piercing sensation having come upon him, even while lying thus — he drew the wanderer Rabzang out from the ocean of saṃsāra, made him perfectly accomplished and brought him to the consummation of happiness, and established him for nirvāṇa. Look upon this!" The Blessed One then declared:

"Monks, consider this: now I, who am fully free from attachment, fully free from aversion, fully free from delusion — free from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation — having attained the knowledge of all things, the knowledge of all aspects, the wisdom of omniscience, drew the wanderer Rabzang out from the ocean of saṃsāra, made him perfectly accomplished, brought him to the consummation of happiness, and established him for nirvāṇa. How wondrous, how marvelous is that!

Yet in a former time, I had not yet freed myself from attachment, aversion, and delusion; I had not freed myself from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and agitation. I was without the power to examine and to save. I was born in the realm of animals. Without even regard for my own life, I became a refuge for the wanderer Rabzang, and I became a refuge for the warriors of the city of Kuśa — a refuge precious as life itself — and I protected all of them utterly from affliction. Listen well to this, take it to heart, and I shall tell it.

Monks, in a time long gone by, in a certain region there dwelt a deer king, surrounded by a herd of a thousand deer. He was wise, clear of mind, and composed. A hunter noticed that deer king and reported him to the king. Then the king set out with an army of fourfold forces and surrounded that deer king on every side.

Then the deer king thought: 'Mother, if I do not protect these deer, they will all be destroyed.' So the deer king looked to see in which direction the herd might escape. He saw a river flowing through that region, and its current was violent and swift in the extreme. The deer, too, were weak and small. So at once the deer king himself entered the river, stood in the middle, and called out: 'Come here, all of you! Step upon my back from this bank, place your feet upon me, and cross to the other shore. There is no other way to survive; otherwise you will certainly perish.' The deer did as he said, and the hooves of those deer struck his back. His skin was torn open, flesh, blood, and bone were exposed — and yet he did not abandon his diligence.

When all had crossed, he felt compassion and looked back, wondering whether any had failed to cross. He saw that one young deer had not yet crossed. And then the body of the deer king was stricken to its joints, his articulations splitting, with that piercing sensation having come upon him — and yet, a refuge precious as life itself to the assembled ones on this riverbank, he carried the young deer upon his back, rescued it from the river, and set it down on the shore.
