Knowing that he had led the great herd of deer across, as his time of death approached he began to make an aspiration prayer: 'Just as I have been a refuge precious as life itself to these deer and to this young deer, and have wholly protected them from affliction — by this merit, may I fully awaken to the unsurpassable, genuine, perfect awakening, and then draw them again from the ocean of saṃsāra, make them perfectly accomplished, bring them to the consummation of happiness, and establish them in nirvāṇa.' Thus he made his aspiration.

The Blessed One then declared: 'Monks, what do you think? He who was the deer king at that time in that place — that was I. Those deer were these very warriors of the city of Kuśa. And the young deer who had not yet crossed — that was this very Rabzang.'"

"Monks, hear further this account of how, at another time when I had been struck through and was unable to move, when I had been born in an animal body, with my joints severed and my limbs split apart, pierced to the vitals by a sensation of agony, yet as I lay there, the wandering mendicant Rabzang took refuge in me. Listen to this.

Monks, long ago, in a time gone by, in the land of Vārāṇasī there was a king by the name of Brahmadatta who was ruling as king — wealthy, prosperous, happy, with fine harvests, full of people, thronged with a great multitude — with quarrels, disputes, attacks from enemies, and conflicts thoroughly pacified, free from thieves and disease, abounding in grain, molasses, cattle, and buffalo: a Dharma-king endowed with the Dharma, governing as a king ought to govern according to the Dharma. His horse, named Wise-Knowing, died. And the tributary kings of the border regions, hearing that the horse named Wise-Knowing belonging to King Brahmadatta had died, sent messengers there with this instruction: 'Either exact a tribute from him, or let him not emerge from the city gate; otherwise, once a new one has certainly been born and harnessed, summon it here.' But no tribute was exacted, nor did he come out through the city gate. Nevertheless, he remained within the city itself and went searching for a horse as fine as Wise-Knowing. Then at another time he found such a horse, and mounted it. It happened to be the spring season, and the trees were in full bloom. To a garden grove where geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, Indian cuckoos, common cuckoos, and śaṅkhaśaṭha birds were giving voice, he went forth surrounded by his queen's retinue. There he amused himself in pleasure, dwelling heedlessly in a state of delight, given over to the pursuit of various diversions, and did not enter the city. The tributary kings of the border regions heard how King Brahmadatta was dwelling heedlessly in the garden grove and not entering the city. They took counsel together, arrayed themselves with a fourfold army, and surrounded the gate of the city of Vārāṇasī. A minister then said to King Brahmadatta: 'Your Majesty, the tributary kings have surrounded the city gate. Please consider what is to be done for our welfare.' The king, upon hearing this, commanded: 'Seek out wherever the wise horse Wise-Knowing is to be found. Have the fourfold army equipped as well. We shall give battle together with them.' So the horse Wise-Knowing was also readied, the fourfold army was equipped, the forces were arrayed together with them, and battle was joined. Then another of the tributary kings thrust a single lance into the flank of King Brahmadatta's horse Wise-Knowing, so that its entrails spilled forth. Pierced by the sensation of suffering, with its joints severed and its limbs split apart, a sensation that penetrated to the very vitals had come upon it — and yet, as this was happening, it braced its mind and thought thus: 'The king, beset by anguish and distress, has come to a pitiable pass; for me to abandon him is not in accordance with my nature. With diligence I will ward off the suffering and by whatever means possible I will go through the small gate and enter the city.' Thinking this, it watched for an opening to make its way into the city. And in between, within the pleasure-grove of Vārāṇasī, there lay the pool of King Brahmadatta, known as the Brahmā-Endowed Pool, adorned with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water-lilies, and white lotuses, with its islets beautified by geese, kāraṇḍava ducks, and herons, ringed all about with flowering and fruit-bearing trees and dense thickets, resounding with the calls of many kinds of birds. With great force it plunged into that dense grove, placed its hooves upon a lotus leaf on the surface of the Brahmā-Endowed Pool, crossed over, came out through the small gate, and then the king dismounted."

Then it fell to the ground and passed away. Thereupon the king and those ministers began to search for it everywhere. Some went into the pleasure-grove, others ran off in the four directions, but none of them found it. Each took hold of his own horse or elephant and turned back.

King Brahmadatta, in order to perform the life-ransoming rite, assembled the townspeople and country-folk of Vārāṇasī together with the remaining ministers and said: "Since the one to be ransomed is a being who has been anointed at the crown as a royal heir, how shall this be accomplished?" They replied: "Your Majesty, we shall offer half the kingdom." He said: "The one whose life I would ransom was the horse Cañjaśa, and it has passed away. Even if we gave half the kingdom to it, what could it do with it?" They replied: "Your Majesty, for its sake we shall establish houses of giving at the four gates of the city, hold a festival of merit-making outside the normal festival season, and accumulate merit." The king said: "Wise ones, that is good. Let it be done accordingly."

Then the queen, the young nobles, the ministers, and the people of the land gathered together all the finest fragrant woods and burned the body. Moreover, they erected houses of giving at the four gates of the city; they had the city cleared of stones, gravel, and rubbish; sprinkled it with sandalwood water; set out bowls of fragrant incense; raised parasols and victory banners; hung many silk streamers; and spread throughout it a delightful carpet of many kinds of flowers like the pleasure-groves of the gods' gardens. Having held a festival outside the normal season, they had this proclamation announced by drum throughout the city: "Hear, wise ones — townspeople of Vārāṇasī and you crowds of people who have come from various lands! Here, for the sake of the divine horse Cañjaśa, giving is being dispensed at the four gates of the city, and a merit-festival is being held outside the regular festival season. Therefore let each of you come forth to the Dharma, adorned with various garments, ornaments, garlands, and the finest wealth." Then the townspeople and country-folk came and held a great festival outside the regular season, and at the four gates of the city they gave gifts of many kinds of desired things.

O monks, what do you think? That horse Cañjaśa was none other than myself. Even then, at that very time, though my joints were severed and my sinews and tendons were struck through with a sensation piercing as ten millions of blows, still I protected that being's life.

Here ends the fifty-fifth fascicle of the Vinaya Kṣudrakavastu.

Then again the monks were assailed by doubt, and in order to resolve all their doubts they put a question to the buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, what deed did the long-lived Supriya perform such that he was made manifest as the last, the lowliest, among the hearers?" The Blessed One declared: "O monks, the very karma that the monk Supriya himself performed and accumulated, having gathered its conditions and fully transformed them — karma ripening and waiting like a flame near at hand, certain to be experienced — that karma which Supriya himself performed and accumulated, who else would experience it? O monks, karma that has been performed and accumulated does not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element; but in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense bases, virtuous and non-virtuous karma that has been performed does ripen.

Actions do not perish even in a hundred aeons;
they do not decay, and when the assembly and the time
come together, they ripen into their full result
for those who bear a body.

O monks, in this very same Good Aeon, in a past and gone age, when the lifespan of beings endured for twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Teacher named Kāśyapa — one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, a buddha, a Blessed One. That Blessed One dwelt in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the deer park of Ṛṣipatana.

Now, a householder of the Blessed One Kāśyapa named Anāthapiṇḍada — Sorrowless — went forth from the household life under the Blessed One Kāśyapa for the sake of liberation. Thinking "I am liberated, I have attained independence," he made no effort. For a very long time, Sorrowless wandered about and remained in the countryside. Then the Blessed One, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa, having accomplished without remainder all the deeds of a buddha, passed into his final rest like a fire whose fuel is spent.

O monks, Sorrowless was staying near an aśoka tree, dwelling inwardly in correct meditation. A god who dwelt in that aśoka tree heard that the Blessed One Kāśyapa had passed into nirvāṇa and wept. As the god wept, a single teardrop fell upon the body of Sorrowless. Sorrowless looked up and saw the god sitting there weeping, and said: "God, why do you weep?" The god replied: "Tonight, at the midnight hour, the Blessed One Kāśyapa passes into nirvāṇa."

Then Sorrowless, upon hearing the god's words, fell as though struck to the heart, and sat there weeping with cries of lamentation. The god asked: "Why do you weep?" Sorrowless replied: "Because I am parted from a kinsman, parted from my teacher. The perfectly and fully awakened buddha Kāśyapa is my uncle. Because I did not strive in training and practice, I have remained an ordinary person, and the path is so very long that I am unable to behold him."

The god said: "Venerable one, if that is so, if I were to bring you into the presence of the Blessed One, would you be able to gain some distinction?" Sorrowless replied: "If the god were to arrange for me to behold the face of the Blessed One, my mind would fully ripen, and I would indeed attain distinction."

Then the god, by miraculous power, brought Sorrowless into the presence of the Blessed One. And upon seeing the Blessed One, faith arose in him. With faith arisen, the Blessed One Kāśyapa taught Dharma of such and such a kind, and immediately upon hearing it, Sorrowless actualized arhatship directly. And so the venerable Sorrowless was the first to pass into nirvāṇa, before the Blessed One. Then the perfectly and fully awakened Blessed One Kāśyapa passed into nirvāṇa.

Then that god saw that the venerable Sorrowless had passed into nirvāṇa, and joy arose in him. He thought: "Whatever distinction the venerable one attained — all of that was owing to me. Therefore, in a future time, when the Blessed One Kāśyapa at his final rest prophesied to that brahmin boy, his disciple, saying: 'Brahmin boy, when the lifespan of beings endures for one hundred years, you will become the Teacher Śākyamuni, a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha' — at that very time I shall be the last among that Blessed One's hearers to actualize arhatship directly, and I shall pass into nirvāṇa before the Blessed One. And may it come to pass that the Blessed One Śākyamuni then passes into nirvāṇa." Thus did he make an aspiration.

The Blessed One then declared: O monks, what do you think?

That god was none other than Subhadrā himself. Therefore, monks, train yourselves in the following way: because one should rely upon a virtuous spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), dwell together with the virtuous, and depend upon virtue; and should not rely upon wicked companions, not dwell together with the wicked, and not depend upon wickedness — monks, train yourselves in precisely this way.

Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Reverend One, while I had gone alone into seclusion and was dwelling in inner stillness, a thought of this kind arose in my mind: that relying upon a virtuous spiritual friend, dwelling together with the virtuous, and depending upon virtue, while not relying upon wicked companions, not dwelling together with the wicked, and not depending upon wickedness — this is half of the holy life." The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, do not say that relying upon a virtuous spiritual friend, dwelling together with the virtuous, depending upon virtue, not relying upon wicked companions, not dwelling together with the wicked, and not depending upon wickedness is half of the holy life. Why is that? Ānanda, this is the holy life in its entirety, fulfilled to the utmost, unmixed, completely perfect, completely pure, completely purified — namely: relying upon a virtuous spiritual friend, dwelling together with the virtuous, depending upon virtue, not relying upon wicked companions, not dwelling together with the wicked, and not depending upon wicked companions. And why, Ānanda? Because through relying upon a virtuous spiritual friend, those sentient beings who are subject to birth become fully liberated from the nature of birth; and those who are subject to old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, mental unhappiness, and agitation become fully liberated from the nature of agitation. Ānanda, by means of such a category of reasoning you should understand this. This holy life that is fulfilled to the utmost, unmixed, completely perfect, and completely purified is precisely this: relying upon a virtuous spiritual friend, dwelling together with the virtuous, depending upon virtue, not relying upon wicked companions, not dwelling together with the wicked, and not depending upon wicked companions. Ānanda, train yourself accordingly."

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, therefore from this day forward, apart from Śākya kinsmen and those bearing matted fiery hair, none of the other wandering non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) shall be given the going forth or full ordination. Should Śākya kinsmen come bearing the banner of the non-Buddhists and wish to go forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and to receive full ordination and obtain the status of a monk, the monks shall give them the going forth and grant them full ordination. Why is that? Monks, it is because this is a concession to kinship granted to our own kindred. If other wandering non-Buddhists come and wish to go forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and to receive full ordination and obtain the status of a monk, the monks shall place them under the care of a preceptor, providing robes, for a period of four months. If during that time they render service and are able to satisfy the minds of the monks, the monks shall then grant them the going forth and full ordination. As for those bearing matted fiery hair, monks shall give them the going forth and grant them full ordination as well."

"And why is that, monks? Those who bear matted fiery hair are ones who speak of action. Monks, those who bear matted fiery hair are ones who speak of action, who speak of cause, who speak of diligence. Therefore, monks, you shall train in this way: 'One who speaks of action, who speaks of cause, who speaks of diligence — you too, monk, shall train to be just such a one.'

Therefore, monks, whatever Dharma you perceive that brings benefit and happiness in this present life, and benefit and happiness in future lives, that the monks shall uphold and bring to complete fulfillment. In whatever way they take it up, retain it, and recite it, the holy life will long endure, bringing benefit to the many, happiness to the many, compassion toward the world, benefit and happiness to gods and humans alike. These are the following: the category of sūtras, the category of mixed prose and verse, the category of prophetic declarations, the category of verse, the category of intentional sayings, the category of origin narratives, the category of stories of spiritual attainment, the category of accounts of past deeds, the category of birth stories, the category of extensive teachings, the category of marvellous Dharma, and the category of established doctrines. These, monks, are what bring benefit and happiness in this present life, benefit and happiness in future lives. The monks shall uphold them and bring them to complete fulfillment. In whatever way they take them up, retain them, and recite them, the holy life will long endure, bringing benefit to the many, happiness to the many, compassion toward the world, benefit and happiness to gods and humans alike.

Monks, after I, your Teacher, have passed into complete nirvāṇa and am no more, you shall not think: 'We have no Teacher, our Teacher is gone.' For the reason that I have taught the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra every fortnight — from this day forward, that shall be your Teacher; that is your Teacher.

Monks, as for the minor and petty rules of training, the Saṅgha community may set them aside and abide in ease and comfort.

Monks, from this day forward, newly ordained monks shall not address senior monks by name or by clan. They may address them only as 'Venerable' or as 'Venerable One,' and not otherwise. And senior monks shall gather in junior monks with gifts of alms-bowls, robes, nets, bowls, and belts; they shall keep them close, have them recite, have them chant, transmit the scriptural teachings to them, and lead them to engage in yogic practice in mind.

Monks, the faithful sons and daughters of good family throughout these four directions shall be mindful of the following for as long as they live. What are the four? 'The Blessed One was born here. The Blessed One here fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Here the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma three times in its twelve aspects. Here the Blessed One passed into the utter nirvāṇa of the element beyond all remainders of the aggregates.' Monks, after I have passed on, those who come here to circumambulate the stūpa and to pay homage to the stūpa — to them you shall say these words: 'The Blessed One was born here.'"

"The Blessed One here fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Here the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma three times in its twelve aspects. Here the Blessed One passed into the utter nirvāṇa of the element beyond all remainders of the aggregates." All of these things are to be recalled. Those among them who die with a mind of faith in me — all of them shall go to a higher realm. Some shall go with a remainder of the aggregates still present. Monks, those from these four directions — sons of good family or daughters of good family who have faith — shall make their pilgrimage here for as long as they live. What are the four? "The Blessed One was born here. The Blessed One here fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Here the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma three times in its twelve aspects. Here the Blessed One passed into the utter nirvāṇa of the element beyond all remainders of the aggregates." Monks, after I have passed on, those who come here to circumambulate the stūpa and to pay homage to the stūpa — to them you shall say these words: "The Blessed One was born here. The Blessed One here fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Here the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma three times in its twelve aspects. Here the Blessed One passed into the utter nirvāṇa of the element without any remainder of the aggregates whatsoever." All of these things are to be recalled. Those who die with a mind of faith in me — all of them shall go to a higher realm. Some shall go with a remainder of the aggregates still present. Thus shall you be mindful of them exactly as they are to be approached in practice.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks in these words: "Monks, if any among you have doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, or the path, do not suppress those questions — ask them, and I shall prophesy the answer for you. Do not think: 'We would not dare to answer directly in the presence of our Teacher.' Monks shall speak to monks, and companions shall speak to companions, and whatever is asked shall be prophesied in response."

Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, so far as I can understand the meaning of what you, the Venerable Blessed One, have taught — among all these monks of the assembly gathered here, there is not a single monk who has doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, or the path."

"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! You say this out of faith, Ānanda. But the Tathāgata's gnosis, which sees without remainder, is unsurpassed. Indeed, among all the monks of the assembly gathered here, there is not a single monk who has doubt or uncertainty regarding suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, or the path. Yet the Tathāgata's purpose in this is his compassion for the sentient beings of future times."

Then the Blessed One removed the upper robe from his own body and declared to the monks: "Monks, look upon the body of the Tathāgata. Monks, look well upon the body of the Tathāgata. And why is that?"

To behold a Tathāgata, a foe-destroyer, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, is rare — like the udumbara flower.

"Monks, now say nothing. Know this: all conditioned phenomena are subject to disintegration." Having declared these, his final words as the Tathāgata, the Blessed One entered meditative absorption in the first dhyāna. Rising from the first dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the second dhyāna. Rising from the second dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the third dhyāna. Rising from the third dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the fourth dhyāna. Rising from the fourth dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the sphere of infinite space. Rising from the sphere of infinite space, he entered meditative absorption in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Rising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he entered meditative absorption in the sphere of nothingness. Rising from the sphere of nothingness, he entered meditative absorption in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Rising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered meditative absorption in the cessation of perception and feeling.

Then the venerable Ānanda said to the venerable Anuruddha: "Venerable Anuruddha, has the Blessed One passed into complete nirvāṇa?"

"No, venerable Ānanda. The Blessed One, the Buddha, has entered meditative absorption in the cessation of perception and feeling."

"Venerable Anuruddha, the Blessed One, the Buddha, has entered meditative absorption in the fourth dhyāna, has obtained the eye of peaceful, unmoving stillness, and will pass into complete nirvāṇa." Thus did I hear directly from the Blessed One, and directly did I receive it.

Then the Blessed One arose from the cessation of perception and feeling and entered meditative absorption in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Rising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered meditative absorption in the sphere of nothingness. Rising from the sphere of nothingness, he entered meditative absorption in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Rising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he entered meditative absorption in the sphere of infinite space. Rising from the sphere of infinite space, he entered meditative absorption in the fourth dhyāna. Rising from the fourth dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the third dhyāna. Rising from the third dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the second dhyāna. Rising from the second dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the first dhyāna. Rising from the first dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the second dhyāna. Rising from the second dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the third dhyāna. Rising from the third dhyāna, he entered meditative absorption in the fourth dhyāna. And the Blessed One, the Buddha, having entered meditative absorption in the fourth dhyāna and having obtained the eye of peaceful, unmoving stillness, passed into complete nirvāṇa.

The very moment the Blessed One, the Buddha, passed into complete nirvāṇa, the great earth trembled, shooting stars fell, the directions blazed, and from the sky the gods sounded the roll of drums.

At that time the venerable Mahākāśyapa, who was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, was roused by the earthquake and wondered: "What has happened?" He perceived that the Blessed One had passed into complete nirvāṇa. And he reflected, grounding himself in the nature of reality: "All conditioned phenomena are thus."

Now, the body-servant Ajātaśatru — a man of royal birth and genuine, rootless faith — upon hearing that the Blessed One had passed into complete nirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa understood, would vomit warm blood and fall into a mortal crisis. He therefore thought: "I must devise some means to deal with this." And so he spoke to Varṣakāra, one of the great ministers of the land of Magadha, saying: "Varṣakāra, know this: the Blessed One has passed into complete nirvāṇa. If that body-servant, King Ajātaśatru of genuine, rootless faith, hears that the Blessed One has passed into complete nirvāṇa, he will vomit warm blood and fall into a mortal crisis. You must understand that a means must be devised for him."

Varṣakāra replied: "Noble one, please describe in order what the means should be."

Mahākāśyapa said: "Varṣakāra, come here. Go quickly, as fast as you can, to the king's pleasure grove. There you shall paint images depicting how the Blessed One, while residing as a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita heaven and surveying the world with his five kinds of vision, trained the gods of the six classes of the desire realm three times, then appeared in the form of an elephant and descended into his mother's womb; how, after descending, he fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassed complete awakening at the foot of the tree of awakening; how the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects, proclaiming it three times, at Vārāṇasī; how he displayed the great miracle at Śrāvastī; how he ascended to the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three to teach the Dharma to his mother, face to face, and then descended to the city of Sāṃkāśya; how he tamed those who were to be tamed in whatever direction they dwelt; and how, having thus completed all the deeds of a buddha, he departed to his final resting place in the city of Kuśinagara. Paint images of all these things.

As for the seven long-stemmed offering bowls, fill them with butter, arranged level at the bottom; and the eighth, fill it with sandalwood gosirṣa, and place it in that part of the pleasure grove.

As soon as the king comes through the gate, have someone say that a certain deity has gone to visit the pleasure grove. When the king sees the paintings and asks, 'Varṣakāra, what is this?' you shall explain at length: 'Sire, this is the city of Kapilavastu — it was in this direction that the Blessed One was born. This is the bank of the Nairañjanā river — it was in this direction that the Blessed One, seated at the Vajrāsana, fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassed complete awakening. This is the city of Vārāṇasī — it was in this direction that the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects, proclaiming it three times. This is the city of Śrāvastī — it was in this direction that the Blessed One displayed the great miracle. This is the city of Sāṃkāśya — it was here that the Blessed One descended from the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three. This is the city of Kuśinagara — it was in this direction that, having tamed those who were to be tamed in whatever direction they dwelt and having completed all the deeds of a buddha, he departed to his final resting place.' And then, as soon as the king hears this and before the words have even passed, he will faint and fall to the ground. At that moment, you shall lower him into the long-stemmed bowl filled with butter. When that butter melts, transfer him from the second bowl, and so on through to the seventh. Then, lifting him out, place him in the long-stemmed bowl filled with sandalwood gosirṣa. He will recover."

Having said this, the venerable Mahākāśyapa departed for the city of Kuśinagara.

The painter, working with great haste, drew all the paintings on a large scale. When he had finished, the king came outside, and the painter said, "Your Majesty has come to the pleasure grove." As the king entered the pleasure grove and saw the paintings, he asked, "Painter, what is this?" The painter then explained in detail, just as before, up to the words: "It was in this very direction that the Blessed One departed to his final resting place." Then the king said, "Painter, what are you saying? Has the Blessed One passed completely into nirvāṇa?" But the painter sat there and said nothing.

Then King Ajātaśatru fainted and fell to the ground. The painter lowered him into the long-stemmed bowl filled with butter and immersed him seven times in succession. He then lifted him out and placed him in the long-stemmed bowl filled with sandalwood gosirṣa, and the king recovered.

Now, immediately after the Blessed One, the buddha and bhagavān, had passed into nirvāṇa, beneath a supreme śāla tree in the grove of twin śāla trees, where flowers were falling, the Blessed One lay in repose like a lion. At that moment, another monk spoke these verses:

Here in this grove of twin śāla trees, most beautiful,
amid these supreme flowering boughs,
upon the Teacher who has passed into nirvāṇa
flowers have fallen and scattered all around.

Immediately after the Blessed One, the buddha and bhagavān, had passed into nirvāṇa, Śakra, lord of the gods and ruler of the hundred powers, spoke these verses:

Alas! Formations are impermanent,
their nature is to arise and to pass away.
Having arisen, they cease —
their coming to rest is peace and bliss.

Immediately after the Blessed One, the buddha and bhagavān, had passed into nirvāṇa, Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, spoke these verses:

All beings in this world have come to the end of what they have accumulated.
In this world that passes away, he was a person without equal,
a Tathāgata endowed with vision, who had attained the powers —
even a Teacher such as this has passed fully into nirvāṇa.

Immediately after the Blessed One, the buddha and bhagavān, had passed into nirvāṇa, the venerable Aniruddha spoke these verses:

With a mind of steadiness he protected beings,
and attained the unshakeable peace.
His exhalation and inhalation ceased,
and the one endowed with vision passed fully into nirvāṇa.

He who was endowed with excellence in every regard —
when the Teacher made his time,
then there arose a great trembling,
and even the hairs of the body stood on end.
With a mind free of despondency,
he remained especially present in his feelings.
His mind was completely liberated —
that lamp, just so, has passed into nirvāṇa.

Immediately after the Blessed One, the buddha and bhagavān, had passed into nirvāṇa, some monks flung themselves on the ground; some seized their shoulders and cried out in lamentation; some sat pierced with pain; and some, grounding themselves in the nature of reality, reflected in this way: "That which the Blessed One taught to us so thoroughly — all that was dear and precious, a source of joy and delight — has now departed, has ceased, has been scattered and dispersed."

Then the venerable Aniruddha said to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, if the monks do not gradually and gently restrain themselves, then the gods of the Mighty One who, through countless hundreds of eons, have gone forth into the monastic life in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, will taunt them, mock them, and speak ill of them, saying: 'See how these monks who have gone forth remain long in unthinking indolence.'" Aniruddha then asked how many gods were present. Ānanda, from the distance between the city of Kuśinagara and the river Hiraṇyavatī, and from the distance to the grove of twin śāla trees, to the stupa crowned with a warrior's diadem — within a radius of twelve yojanas all around, those of great power...

there was not the slightest space left uncovered or unfilled by gods of great renown — not even a gap the size of a mustard seed. Some of those gods fell prostrate upon the ground. Some beat their shoulders and wailed aloud. Some sat with minds pierced by grief. And some, reflecting upon the nature of reality, thought: "Thus has the Blessed One taught us again and again, in countless ways, that all which is dear and beloved to the heart must be separated from, lost, gone, dissolved, and dispersed."

That evening, the venerable Anuruddha spoke to the venerable Ānanda words of decisive Dharma, and then sat in silence with the composure of a noble one. Then, when that night had passed and dawn had come, the venerable Anuruddha said this to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, go to the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara and say to the leading men there: 'Tonight, at the middle watch of the night, the Teacher passed into the final nirvāṇa, the nirvāṇa without remainder, into the realm of complete cessation. Whatever you have to do and to accomplish, do it now, so that you do not afterward fall into the thought: "Our Teacher passed into final nirvāṇa, into the realm of complete cessation without remainder, and we were not able to honor him and to exert ourselves in his service."'"

After the venerable Anuruddha had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda heeded him, took up his robe, and went to the assembly hall of the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara, together with other monks and with wandering ascetics who were in attendance. At that time, in the assembly hall of the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara, there were gathered about five hundred Mallas who had come together for some affair.

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara: "O wise leading men, great assembly gathered together — you Mallas of many retinues — hear this. Tonight, at the middle watch of the night, the Teacher has passed into final nirvāṇa, into the realm of complete cessation without remainder. Whatever you have to do and to accomplish, do it now, so that you do not afterward fall into the thought: 'Our Teacher passed into the realm of complete cessation without remainder, and we were not able to honor him and to exert ourselves in his service.'"

After this was said, some of the Mallas of Kuśinagara fell prostrate upon the ground. Some beat their shoulders and wailed aloud. Some sat with minds pierced by grief. And some, reflecting upon the nature of reality, thought: "Thus has the Blessed One taught us again and again, in countless ways, that all which is dear and beloved to the heart must be separated from, lost, gone, dissolved, and dispersed."

Then the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara, taking as much perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and musical instruments as there was, together with their sons, wives, male servants, female servants, workers, those who lived on wages, their friends and companions, kinsmen, ministers, and blood relations, came forth from the city of Kuśinagara and went to the grove of twin śāla trees. There they paid homage and honor to the Blessed One as he lay in the lion's posture — with perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and music — paying him reverence, doing him honor, venerating and adorning him.

Then again, the leading chiefs of the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara spoke to the venerable Ānanda, saying: "Venerable Ānanda, how should we pay homage to the remains of the Blessed One, and with what diligence should we carry it out? The proper arrangement is this: it should be done as it is done for a wheel-turning king (cakravartin). Venerable Ānanda, how exactly is it done for a wheel-turning king?"

"The proper arrangement for a wheel-turning king is this: the body is wrapped in cotton wool, and having been wrapped in cotton wool, it is then wound with five hundred pairs of cloth. Having been wound with five hundred pairs of cloth, it is placed in an iron vessel, which is filled with sesame oil, and covered on top with two iron lids. All manner of fragrant woods are piled up, and the body is cremated with these. The fire is then extinguished with milk. The bones are placed inside a golden urn, and at the crossroads of a great highway a bone stūpa is erected, with parasols, victory banners, and pennants set up, and it is venerated, exalted, adorned, and honored with perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and music, and great festivals are also held. That, good people, is what is done for a wheel-turning king — and for a Tathāgata, an arhat, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha, it should be done even more excellently than that."

Having heard from the venerable Ānanda what he had said, they understood what was being asked of them. Since assembling one, or two, or three canopies together proved difficult, within seven days the Mallas gathered cotton wool, and having gathered the cotton wool, they also gathered five hundred pairs of cloth. Having gathered five hundred pairs of cloth, they prepared an iron vessel. Having prepared the iron vessel, they piled up all manner of fragrant woods. Having piled up all manner of fragrant woods, they made ready the golden urn. Having made ready the golden urn, they arranged the golden bier. Having arranged the golden bier, from the city of Kuśinagara as far as the Hiraṇyavatī River, and from the grove of twin śāla trees as far as the stūpa crowned by the Mallas with a jeweled diadem — a distance of twelve yojanas — all along that length they took up supplies of perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and musical instruments, and set forth from the city of Kuśinagara. They went to the grove of twin śāla trees, and there they paid reverence, honor, respect, and homage to the Blessed One as he lay in the lion's posture, with perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and music.

Then the leading chiefs of the Mallas of Kuśinagara spoke to the assembled Mallas, saying: "Let the great multitude of the Mallas of Kuśinagara, you who are gathered and assembled, you men of understanding — listen well! Let the wives of the Mallas and the daughters of the Mallas each spread a layer of cloth over the Blessed One. Let the Mallas and the young Malla men carry the bier of the Blessed One. And let us pay reverence, honor, respect, and homage with perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and music."

They would enter through the western gate of the city of Kuśinagara, pass straight through the middle, emerge from the eastern gate of the city of Kuśinagara, cross the river Hiraṇyavatī, and place the bier of the Blessed One at the shrine adorned with a diadem by the Mallas, and there it should rest.

Then the Mallas of Kuśinagara agreed, saying "We shall do so." And the wives of the Mallas and the daughters of the Mallas spread layers of cloth over the Blessed One. The Mallas and the young Malla men then wished to lift the bier of the Blessed One, but they were unable to lift it. Since the venerable Ānanda had not yet spoken, he said this to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, the Mallas of Kuśinagara have been unable to lift the bier of the Blessed One. Why is that?" "Because it is the intention of the gods." "Venerable Ānanda, what then is the intention of the gods?" "It is the intention of the gods that the wives of the Mallas and the daughters of the Mallas should spread layers of cloth over the Blessed One, and that the Mallas and the young Malla men should lift the bier of the Blessed One, and that we ourselves should pay reverence, honor, respect, and homage with divine perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and music; that we should enter through the western gate of the city of Kuśinagara, pass straight through the middle, emerge from the eastern gate of the city of Kuśinagara, cross the river Hiraṇyavatī, and place the bier at the shrine adorned with a diadem by the Mallas, and there let it rest." This was the intention the gods had formed.

"Venerable Ānanda, let it be done as the gods have intended."

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Mallas of Kuśinagara: "Men of understanding, you who are assembled — the reason you were unable to lift the bier of the Blessed One is that it is the intention of the gods." "Venerable Ānanda, what is the intention of the gods?" "The gods have intended this: that the wives of the Mallas and the daughters of the Mallas should spread layers of cloth over the Blessed One, that the Mallas and the young Malla men should lift the bier of the Blessed One, and that we ourselves should pay reverence, honor, respect, and homage with divine perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and music; that we should enter through the western gate of the city of Kuśinagara, pass straight through the middle, emerge from the eastern gate of the city of Kuśinagara, cross the river Hiraṇyavatī, and place the bier at the shrine adorned with a diadem by the Mallas, and there let it rest. This is what the gods have intended." "Venerable Ānanda, let it be done as the gods have intended."

Then the wives of the Mallas and the daughters of the Mallas spread layers of cloth over the Blessed One. The Mallas and the young Malla men lifted the bier of the Blessed One, and at the very moment they lifted it, the gods dwelling in the sky scattered divine flowers — utpalas, lotuses, white lotuses, kumudas — as well as powder of agaru and tamāla wood, and divine māndārava flowers and other such blooms; they raised the sounds of divine music, and they cast down many garments.

Moreover, the leading chiefs of the Mallas of Kuśinagara spoke to the assembled Mallas of Kuśinagara, saying: "Men of understanding, you who are assembled — let us set aside our human musical instruments, and let us ourselves pay reverence, honor, respect, and homage with divine perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and music.

They said: "Let us proceed through the western gate of the city of Kuśinagara, pass straight through the city, exit by the eastern gate, cross the river Hiraṇyavatī, and place the remains to rest at the stūpa crowned with the garland raised by the champion."

The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, the fifty-sixth fascicle.

Then the champions of Kuśinagara set aside their human musical instruments, and with divine perfume, garlands, incense, powder, and the sound of music they paid reverence, honor, respect, and homage. They entered through the western gate of the city of Kuśinagara, passed straight through the middle of the city, emerged from the eastern gate, crossed the river Hiraṇyavatī, and placed the remains to rest at the stūpa crowned with the garland raised by the champion.

At that time, divine māndārava flowers fell upon the city of Kuśinagara to the depth of a person's knees.

At that time, a certain wandering ascetic (ājīvika) took up a great quantity of those divine māndārava flowers and set out for the land of Malla with some business in mind. And at that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, accompanied by five hundred attendants, was traveling the road from the land of Malla toward the city of Kuśinagara, wishing to pay homage to the uncorrupted bodily relics of the Blessed One. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa saw that wandering ascetic there on the road, and seeing him, he said to him: "Venerable wandering ascetic, from where have you come, and where are you going?"

"Reverend Mahākāśyapa, I have come from the city of Kuśinagara and am going to the land of Malla on a certain errand."

"Venerable wandering ascetic, do you know of my Teacher?"

"Noble one, indeed — it is the monk Gautama."

"Noble Mahākāśyapa, that Teacher passed into complete nirvāṇa seven days ago today. These divine māndārava flowers that I have taken are ones that were offered in reverence to his bodily relics."

At that moment, a certain elder of another group began to speak improper words, saying: "Thus, racked with regret and the infirmity of age, I used to say to the monks, 'This is what should be done; this is what should not be done' — but now I am freed from that. Let us now do what we are able to do, and not do what we are not able to do." And as he was speaking these unseemly words, the gods dwelling in the sky obscured them so that not one member of the assembly of monks heard them — none, that is, except the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, in order to tame the one who had spoken such improper words, turned aside from the road and took his seat on a prepared seat in the midst of the assembly of monks. Having seated himself, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the monks thus: "Venerable ones, all conditioned things are impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change. For so long as this is so, one should turn away from all conditioned phenomena and win liberation from them. Venerable ones, I shall now go far to look upon the uncorrupted bodily relics of the Blessed One."

Then the champions of Kuśinagara wrapped the bodily relics of the Blessed One in cotton batting, and having wrapped them in cotton batting, they wound them in five hundred pairs of cloth. Having wound them in five hundred pairs of cloth, they placed them in an iron casket and filled it with sesame oil. Having placed them in the iron casket and filled it with sesame oil, they covered it from above with two iron lids.

They piled up all the fragrant wood and tried to light the fire for the cremation, but they were unable to do so.

Then the Venerable Aniruddha spoke to the Venerable Ānanda, saying: "Venerable Ānanda, the champions of Kuśinagara have been unable to light the fire for the cremation of the bodily relics of the Blessed One. Why is that? Because the gods have so intended it. Venerable Aniruddha, what is it that the gods have intended? It is this: the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, has set out on the road from the region of the sinful country and is journeying toward Kuśinagara, intending to come and pay homage to the uncorrupted bodily relics of the Blessed One. Venerable Aniruddha, you should act in accordance with what the gods have intended."

Then the Venerable Ānanda spoke to the champions of Kuśinagara, saying: "O champions of Kuśinagara, you who are assembled here in your great multitude — you who are wise and well-composed — hear this. The reason you have been unable to light the fire for the cremation of the bodily relics of the Blessed One is that the gods have so intended it. Venerable Ānanda, what is it that the gods have intended? It is this: the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, has set out on the road from the region of the sinful country and is journeying to Kuśinagara, intending to come and pay homage to the uncorrupted bodily relics of the Blessed One."

They replied: "Venerable Ānanda, we shall act in accordance with what the gods have intended."

Then when the Venerable Mahākāśyapa arrived at Kuśinagara, his retinue saw him from a great distance. Seeing him, they took up perfumes, garlands, incense, powders, and musical instruments, and went to where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was. Having gone there, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and followed along behind him as he went forward.

The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, surrounded by many hundreds of attendants, many thousands of attendants, and many hundreds of thousands of attendants, proceeded to where the Blessed One was. All the fragrant wood was then removed. Having removed all the fragrant wood, the lid of the iron casket was opened. Having opened the lid of the iron casket, the five hundred pairs of cloth were unwound. Having unwound the five hundred pairs of cloth, the cotton batting was also removed. Having removed the cotton batting, they paid homage to the uncorrupted bodily relics of the Blessed One.

At that time on this great earth there were four great śrāvakas: the Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Daśabala Kāśyapa, and the Venerable Mahākāśyapa. Among them, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was endowed with wisdom and great merit, and he obtained robes, alms-food, a resting place, and medicines and necessities for the sick.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa thought to himself: "I myself should perform the act of making offerings to the Blessed One." Having generated enthusiasm for this, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa prepared fresh cotton batting, and having prepared fresh cotton batting, he also prepared another five hundred pairs of cloth. Having prepared another five hundred pairs of cloth, he wrapped the bodily relics of the Blessed One in the cotton batting. Having wrapped them in the cotton batting, he wound them in the five hundred pairs of cloth. Having wound them in the five hundred pairs of cloth,

he placed them in an iron casket and filled it with sesame oil. Having placed them in the iron casket and filled it with sesame oil, he covered the top with two iron lids and piled up all manner of fragrant woods. Having piled them up, he withdrew to one side, and then, just as it happens through the buddha-power of the buddhas and the divine power of the gods, the pyre ignited of itself.

Then the Venerable Ānanda circumambulated the piled-up bodily relics of the Blessed One, and at that moment he spoke these verses:

The guide who possessed the precious body,
who went with great miraculous power to the Brahmā world —
the buddha's body wound about with five hundred pairs of cloth
and with a thousand robes throughout:
by his own resplendence, the bodily relics
and all the wrappings were utterly consumed.
Of those robes, only two were not burned —
these two, the innermost and the outermost.

Then the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara extinguished those fires with milk, and from that milk four trees arose, namely: the Golden One, the Pale Yellow One, the Horse-Wish, and that called the Udumbara.

Then the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara placed those bodily relics in a golden urn, set them upon a golden palanquin, and paid them honor with fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powdered offerings, and the sounds of music; they held them high, they adorned them with ornament, they made offerings. They proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara and, having had the relics installed in the very center of that chief city, they paid them honor with fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powdered offerings, and the sounds of music; they held them high, they adorned them with ornament, they made offerings.

Then the warriors of the wicked country heard that, seven days having now passed since the Blessed One had passed into nirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara, the warriors there were performing relic-worship with the bodily relics. Upon hearing this, they equipped a fourfold army — a host of elephants, a host of horses, a host of chariots, and a host of foot soldiers — went to where the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara were, and spoke to them thus: "You many gathered and assembled retainers of the warriors of Kuśinagara, listen well, you who are wise. The Blessed One was for us from long ago our cherished and beloved one. Since he passed into nirvāṇa while dwelling in the vicinity of your city, give us a share of the bodily relics of the Blessed One, a portion of the relics. We will erect a stūpa for the bodily relics of the Blessed One in the wicked country and honor it with parasols, victory banners, and flags; with fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powdered offerings, and the sounds of music; we will hold it high, adorn it with ornament, make offerings — and having made offerings, we will also hold a great festival."

The warriors of Kuśinagara replied: "The Blessed One was indeed from long ago our cherished and beloved one as well, and since he passed away while dwelling in the vicinity of our city, we will not give you a share of the bodily relics of the Blessed One, a portion of the relics. If you accept this, then well and good. But if you do not, we will ravage you with our armies."

The warriors of Kuśinagara held firm to this position.

The Kṣatriya prince Buluka dwelling in the rolling country of Ṭoka, the Kṣatriyas of the city of Rāmagāma, the brahmins dwelling in Viṣṇudvīpa, the Kṣatriya Śākyas dwelling in the city of Kapilavastu, and the Kṣatriya Licchavīs dwelling in Vaiśālī also heard the news, as did Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, the king of the country of Magadha — that the Blessed One had passed into nirvāṇa, and that the warriors of the wicked country and

the Kṣatriya prince Buluka dwelling in the rolling country of Ṭoka, the Kṣatriyas of the city of Rāmagāma, the brahmins dwelling in Viṣṇudvīpa, the Kṣatriya Śākyas dwelling in the city of Kapilavastu, and the Kṣatriya Licchavīs dwelling in Vaiśālī had all armed their fourfold armies and marched to Kuśinagara to pay homage to the relics and to receive a share of the relics there.

Upon hearing this news, the brahmin Vassakāra, who was the great minister of the country of Magadha, spoke to him thus: "Vassakāra, I am unable to act. Go yourself, arm the fourfold army, and march to the warriors of Kuśinagara bearing my message. Ask after their welfare — whether their afflictions are few, whether their distress is slight, whether they are active, whether they are well, whether they dwell in contact with strength and ease — and speak these words: 'O wise ones, the Blessed One was long my cherished and beloved teacher. Now that he has passed into nirvāṇa in the vicinity of your city, O wise ones, grant me a share of the relics, the bodily remains of the Blessed One. I shall erect a stūpa for the relics of the Blessed One in Rājagṛha and honour, exalt, adorn, and make offering to them with parasols, victory banners, pennants, forms, fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sounds of music. Having made such offerings, I shall also hold a great festival.' Thus instruct them."

Vassakāra replied, "It shall be done, my lord." Then Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, the king of the country of Magadha, mounted an elephant, and as he did so his mind turned to recollecting the qualities of the Blessed One, and he fell into a swoon. He was then taken down from the elephant and placed upon a horse, and upon that horse he swooned again. Then he said: "Vassakāra, I am unable to go. Go yourself, arm the fourfold army, and march to the warriors of Kuśinagara. Ask after their welfare on my behalf — whether their afflictions are few, whether their distress is slight, whether they are active, whether they are well, whether they dwell in contact with strength and ease — and then speak these words: 'O wise ones, the Blessed One was long my cherished and beloved teacher. Now that he has passed into nirvāṇa in the vicinity of your city, O wise ones, grant me a share of the relics, the bodily remains of the Blessed One. I shall erect a stūpa for the relics of the Blessed One in Rājagṛha and honour, exalt, adorn, and make offering to them with parasols, victory banners, pennants, forms, fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sounds of music. Having made such offerings, I shall also hold a great festival.' Thus instruct them."

Vassakāra replied, "It shall be done, my lord." Having received these instructions from King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, the brahmin Vassakāra, great minister of the country of Magadha, armed the fourfold army and set out for Kuśinagara. Upon arriving there, he addressed the warriors of Kuśinagara before a large and assembled gathering of that city's warriors: "O wise ones, let the many warriors and retinue of Kuśinagara hearken. O wise ones, we bring the greetings of King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, king of Magadha — whether your afflictions are few, whether your distress is slight, whether you are active, whether you are well, whether you dwell in contact with strength and ease. And he speaks these words: 'O wise ones, the Blessed One was long my cherished and beloved teacher. Now that he has passed into nirvāṇa in the vicinity of your city, O wise ones, grant me a share of the relics, the bodily remains of the Blessed One. I shall erect a stūpa for the relics of the Blessed One in Rājagṛha and honour, exalt, adorn, and make offering to them with parasols, victory banners, pennants, forms, fragrant substances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sounds of music.

I shall make offerings and hold a great festival as well.' The brahmin Vassakāra, who was in the service of the great minister of the land of Magadha, spoke these words to the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara: 'If you grant a share, then well and good. If you do not grant a share, we shall come against you with our army.' The Mallas of Kuśinagara heard this and agreed to do so. But when they saw the great host of the royal retinue assembling, the wives and young men of the Mallas also began to practice archery. Now when the Mallas of the wicked land, the Pāva-dwelling Kṣatriya Buluka, the Kṣatriya Kroḍya of the city of Rāmagāma, the brahmins of Viṣṇudvīpa, the Kṣatriyas of the Śākya clan dwelling in Kapilavastu, the Kṣatriyas of the Licchavī clan of Vaiśālī, and the brahmin Vassakāra belonging to the great minister of the land of Magadha — when all of these had equipped their four-limbed armies with their troops of elephants, their troops of horses, their troops of chariots, and their troops of foot soldiers, they came to the Mallas of Kuśinagara in order to give battle. Then the Mallas of Kuśinagara arrayed their wives and young men outside the city, equipped their own four-limbed armies with their troops of elephants, their troops of horses, their troops of chariots, and their troops of foot soldiers, and marched out to meet the seven opposing armies in battle.

At that very moment, one who was equal to a brahmin of the brahmin lineage came to that very place. Knowing that if the two sides were to face each other in a great many battles, they would quickly slay one another, he made a wide circuit around them and went to where the Mallas of Kuśinagara were. He arrived and spoke these words to the Mallas of Kuśinagara:

'O wise ones, you great assembly of Kuśinagara's Malla community gathered here, listen well. The Blessed One Gautama has for a long time been one endowed with patience, one who taught the praise of patience. O wise ones, if the Blessed One Gautama was indeed endowed with patience and taught the praise of patience, then it is not fitting that for the sake of his relics you should slay one another. Therefore I, being glad to divide the relics of the Blessed One Gautama into eight portions, ask that the urn in which the relics were placed be given to me. I shall then erect a stūpa for the relics of the Blessed One Gautama in the brahmin city, and I shall honour, exalt, adorn, and make offering to them with parasols, victory banners, pennants, forms, fragrant substances, garlands, incense, and the sounds of music, and I shall hold a great festival as well.'

The Mallas of Kuśinagara heard him and agreed to do so. Then the one equal to a brahmin of the brahmin lineage went to where the Mallas of the wicked land, the Kṣatriya Buluka of the land of Pāvā, the Kṣatriya Kroḍya of the city of Rāmagāma, the brahmins of Viṣṇudvīpa, the Kṣatriyas of the Śākya clan dwelling in Kapilavastu, the Kṣatriyas of the Licchavī clan of Vaiśālī, and the brahmin Vassakāra belonging to the great minister of the land of Magadha were gathered, arrived there, and spoke these words to the brahmin Vassakāra, belonging to the great minister of the land of Magadha:

'O Vassakāra, hear this well.

The Blessed One Gautama, for a long time, possessed patience and was praised for his patience. Since the Blessed One Gautama possessed patience and was praised for his patience, it is not fitting, O wise Vassakāra, that you kill one another for the sake of his bodily relics. Therefore I am pleased to divide the relics of the Blessed One Gautama into eight portions. And give to me the urn in which the relics were placed, so that I may erect a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One Gautama in the city of Droṇa, and honor it with parasols, victory banners, and pennants, with fragrances, garlands, incense, and the sound of music; and hold it in the highest esteem, adorn it with images, make offerings to it, and also hold a great festival.' The brahmin Vassakāra, belonging to the great minister of the land of Magadha, and those equal to the brahmin lineage of Droṇa, agreed to do likewise.

Then the one equal to a brahmin of the brahmin lineage of Droṇa divided the relics of the Blessed One into eight portions. The first portion he gave to the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara. And so the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One, raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and honored it with fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sound of music; they held it in highest esteem, adorned it with images, made offerings, and held a great festival. The second portion went to the Mallas of the wicked land. The third portion went to the Kṣatriya Buluka of the land of Pāvā. The fourth portion went to the Kṣatriya Kroḍya of the city of Rāmagāma. The fifth portion went to the brahmins of Viṣṇudvīpa. The sixth portion went to the Kṣatriyas of the Śākya clan dwelling in Kapilavastu. The seventh portion went to the Kṣatriyas of the Licchavī clan dwelling in Vaiśālī. The eighth portion went to the brahmin Vassakāra, belonging to the great minister of the land of Magadha. And so the king Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, of the land of Magadha, erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One, raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and honored it with fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sound of music; he held it in highest esteem, adorned it with images, made offerings, and held a great festival.

Then the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara gave to the one equal to a brahmin of the brahmin lineage the urn in which the relics had been placed. Then the one equal to the brahmin lineage of Droṇa erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One in the city of Droṇa, raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and honored it with fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sound of music; he held it in highest esteem, adorned it with images, made offerings, and held a great festival.

Then at that time the brahmin youth Nyagrodhajāta came to that very assembly. And the brahmin youth Nyagrodhajāta spoke these words to the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara: 'O wise ones, great multitudes of the retinue of the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara are gathered and assembled — hear this! The Blessed One Gautama has long been beloved and dear to me. He passed into complete nirvāṇa in your city. O wise ones, give to me the charcoal that remains from the burning of the relics of the Blessed One, so that I may erect a stupa of the charcoal of the Blessed One Gautama in the land of Nyagrodhajāta, and raise parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and honor it with fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sound of music, hold it in highest esteem, and adorn it with images.'

'May we offer worship, and having offered worship, may a great festival be held.'

The Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara gave the charcoal of the relics to the brahmin youth Nyagrodhajāta. The brahmin youth Nyagrodhajāta then erected a stupa of the charcoal of the Blessed One in the land of Nyagrodhajāta, raised parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and honored it with fragrances, garlands, incense, powder, and the sound of music, held it in highest esteem, and adorned it with images. He offered worship to it and held a great festival.

At that time, in Jambudvīpa there came to be eight stupas of the relics of the Blessed One, and nine with the stupa of the urn, and ten with the stupa of the charcoal.

Of the eight measures of the glorious relics,
seven were obtained for the worship of those dwelling in Jambudvīpa.
One measure of the relics of that supreme being
was worshipped by the nāga king whose city is resounding with sound.
Of the four canine teeth of that supreme being,
one is worshipped in the world of the three summits.
The second is in the delightful city of Tsig-dzin.
The third is in the land of the king of Kaliṅga.
The fourth canine tooth of that supreme being
was worshipped by the nāga king whose city resounds with sound.
The sorrowless victor, abiding at Skar-snar,
caused the seven stupas to be greatly multiplied,
and through that power Indra also here
was adorned and fulfilled through aspirational prayer.
Thus, to those glorious relics,
the lord of gods, the lord of nāgas, and the lords of men,
as well as humans, nāgas, and yakṣas,
paid the highest honor and offered worship.

He who possessed supreme knowledge, endowed with compassion, master of power,
born of the Śākyas, was awakened in Magadha.
In Kāśī he turned the wheel of Dharma,
and relying on the city of Kuśinagara, he passed into nirvāṇa.

At the time when the venerable Śāriputra passed into complete nirvāṇa, eighty thousand monks also passed into complete nirvāṇa. At the time when the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana passed into complete nirvāṇa, seventy thousand monks also passed into complete nirvāṇa. At the time when the Blessed One passed into complete nirvāṇa, eighteen thousand monks passed into complete nirvāṇa as well. Then, over the course of many hundreds of divine aeons, whatever teachings the Blessed One had spoken dwindled to a mere wisp of smoke, and those monks who possessed authority, having passed into complete nirvāṇa, jeered and mocked and slandered, saying: 'The sūtras and Vinaya and the mahāmāyā texts of the Blessed One — they are not recited.'

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke these words to the monks: 'Venerable ones, know this: at the time when the venerable Śāriputra passed into complete nirvāṇa, eighty thousand monks also passed into complete nirvāṇa. At the time when the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana passed into complete nirvāṇa, seventy thousand monks also passed into complete nirvāṇa. Now here, at the time when the Blessed One has passed into complete nirvāṇa, eighteen thousand monks have also passed into complete nirvāṇa. Because so many monks have passed into complete nirvāṇa, divine sons who live for many hundreds of aeons — whatever teachings the Blessed One had spoken have dwindled to a mere wisp of smoke — and those monks who possessed authority, having passed into complete nirvāṇa, jeer and mock and slander, saying: "The sūtras, the Vinaya, and the mahāmāyā texts of the Blessed One are no longer recited." Therefore, let us come together and assemble here.'

The monks replied: 'Venerable one, it shall be done exactly so.'

Now, whoever serves as the disciplinary officer of the Saṅgha —

It was the venerable Gaṅgapoṣa.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the venerable Gaṅgapoṣa: "Gaṅgapoṣa, come here. Strike the gong and assemble the Saṅgha of monks."

When the venerable Mahākāśyapa had spoken those words, the venerable Gaṅgapoṣa listened to the venerable Kāśyapa and, having entered into equipoise in the four perfected dhyānas, gazed out to the full extent that his sight of gnosis could reach. Then, rising from that meditative absorption, he began to strike the gong. When he struck it, five hundred arhat monks of the Saṅgha who were dwelling in various regions — all but one — assembled together.

When the monks had gathered and were sitting assembled, the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this: "Venerable ones, take note of which monks from the Saṅgha have not yet come." The monks who had come from various regions looked at one another, and then said to the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "Venerable one, all the many monks are assembled and present here, with the sole exception of the venerable Vāṇadatta."

At that time, the venerable Vāṇadatta was sitting in an empty mansion of śirīṣa wood.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the venerable Gaṅgapoṣa: "Gaṅgapoṣa, come here. Go to where the venerable Vāṇadatta is, and when you have arrived, say this to the venerable Vāṇadatta: 'The Saṅgha of monks, Kāśyapa and the others, wish you good health, venerable Vāṇadatta. There is a small matter of Saṅgha business; please come quickly.'"

When the venerable Kāśyapa had spoken those words, the venerable Gaṅgapoṣa listened to the venerable Kāśyapa and entered into just such a meditative absorption — one in which the city of Tṛṇāvatī became invisible, and he appeared to be sitting in an empty mansion of śirīṣa wood with mind placed in equanimity.

Then the venerable Gaṅgapoṣa went to where the venerable Vāṇadatta was. Having arrived, he bowed his head to the venerable Vāṇadatta's two feet, and said to the venerable Vāṇadatta: "The Saṅgha of monks, Kāśyapa and the others, wish you good health, venerable Vāṇadatta. There is a small matter of Saṅgha business; please come quickly."

Though Vāṇadatta was free from attachment, he was permeated by the habitual tendency of loving-kindness, and so the venerable Gaṅgapoṣa reflected: "Has not the Blessed One departed to another world to tame beings? Has not strife, contention, and discord arisen within the Saṅgha of monks, or have they been slandering one another? Has not the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata been deflected by non-Buddhists? Have those people assembled and done harm to the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's śrāvakas? Has not the Tathāgata — who is like the sun — been scorned by mendicants, brahmins, wanderers, and itinerants who are under the power of mental afflictions that wrap around them like clouds? Have those of poor understanding, darkened by the gloom of ignorance, not caused a schism in the assembled Saṅgha? Have there not arisen words, letters, and webs of view similar to the Dharma, yet opposed to the Dharma and Vinaya as taught by the Tathāgata? Have those who practice the pure life not been turned away from reciting, chanting, and taking to heart those teachings, and come instead to gather and make idle chatter? Have those with doubting, wavering minds not taught what is non-Dharma as Dharma and Dharma as non-Dharma, what is non-Vinaya as Vinaya and Vinaya as non-Vinaya?"

"Monks, have they not failed to practice the six principles of harmony (sāraṇīyadharma) and the like toward those living the chaste life who have arrived suddenly, and have they not shown them contempt? Have corrupt renunciants caused brahmins and faithful householders to lose faith in the teaching and come to rely on non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) instead? Have some fallen into wrong livelihood, ploughing fields, engaging in trade, and looking to kings for their sustenance? Have those who had properly taken up the qualities of training and dwelt in remote forest lodgings come to abandon those very qualities of training? Have those who are not true ascetics, claiming to be ascetics, not come to disturb the community's practice of the pure life? Yet even so, has the monk Saṅgha spoken of the worthy Gaṅgāpāla and others who are called 'buddha and so forth,' as Kāśyapa and the like? Has the Teacher, who dwelt in great compassion and entered into practice, not passed into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of aggregates? Has the world been thrown into confusion because there is no one to lead the migrating beings? Has the one possessed of the ten powers (daśabala) been overpowered by the force of impermanence? Has the guardian who awakens us, the Teacher of all sentient beings, gone to sleep? Has the buddha, the sun, set? Has the sovereign sage, the moon, been vanquished by Rāhu and lost his light? In the Heaven of Thirty-three, has the lordly wish-fulfilling tree, fragrant and adorned with the blossoms of the limbs of awakening, been broken by a maddened wild elephant of impermanence that possessed the four good fruits of the ascetic life? Has the lamp of primordial wisdom been extinguished by the wind of impermanence, and has it fully passed beyond sorrow?"

Thus they spoke. Then at that time the venerable Gaṅgāpāla spoke these verses:

Those wise ones, for the sake of preserving the teaching,
gathered from the śrāvaka Saṅgha and assembled there,
remaining with you and striving in that very effort.
The great ship of the Victor has been destroyed.
The very mountain of primordial wisdom has crumbled.
The many monks of that most excellent teaching
have now fully passed into peace.
O Lady of gracious virtue,
I have come here as a messenger.
For the sake of preserving the teaching,
you must therefore now set forth without delay.

Then the venerable Vālambhaka spoke thus to the venerable Gaṅgāpāla: "Gaṅgāpāla, enough — do not speak so. It is not yet time to go. And yet, noble Gaṅgāpāla:"

Though my mind intends to go to that place
where the guardian, the lamp of beings, still dwells,
once he has gone from there to supreme peace on the other shore,
what wise one will go to those worlds?
These finest of the three robes — bowl, Dharma robe, and all —
offer them yourself to the Saṅgha.
I will go where there is no peace, nor any further existence.
I ask the noble one to bear with what I have resolved.

Then the venerable Vālambhaka displayed a great miracle of lightning, warmth, rainfall, and supreme radiance, and passed into nirvāṇa in the realm without remainder of aggregates. His body was consumed by the element of fire arisen from within itself, and from it four streams of water flowed down.

From one stream of water came a teaching proclaimed in a melodious voice resounding:

Now the times have grown degenerate.
Sentient beings depend upon their own karma.
That lamp of beings has passed away —
know that all beings now proceed to their going.

A second spoke:

Conditioned and accumulated things are destroyed in an instant,
bearing the afflictions and suffering of birth and all the rest.
Ordinary persons are proud with a sense of self —
let them know that these things have no maker.

A third spoke:

One who is wise is always vigilant with care,
and should strive with mind devoted to merit.

All the hosts of elemental beings are gone and will perish,
and the glory of those who have life has grown unstable.

A fourth spoke:

To that Sage the finest disciples made perfect obeisance,
and accomplished, without remainder, everything that was needed.
With reverence and deep faith in that teacher,
I, Valandhara, followed after him just as a calf does.

Then the Venerable Gaṅgha performed a bone-relic offering at the bones of the Venerable Valandhara, took up his bowl and his robes, and entered into a meditative absorption of this kind: just as when the mind settles into equipoise, it is no longer seen within the palace of the śirīṣa tree, and the warriors of the city of Kuśinagara draw near, and one comes to dwell in the grove of the twin śāla trees — he entered into that very samādhi.

Then the Venerable Gaṅgha went to where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the other five hundred monks were, approached them, and bowed to them in order of seniority. He then gave to an elder monk his bowl and robe, and spoke these words in verse:

Having heard that the body of the Protector is no more,
Valandhara, his mind supremely still through the karma of merit, passed away in perfect peace.
This is his bowl and robe —
with this in mind, he asks forbearance of the Saṅgha.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the monks as follows:

Listen, you who lead the holy life (brahmacārins)!
In the noble manner he too has passed beyond.
Let others not likewise go to such a sudden peace.
Therefore, for as long as there is need, carry out the necessary work,
and as long as is needed, deliberate in the great assembly.

And then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke again, in order to strengthen those monks:

Just as Valandhara of the śirīṣa tree, his mind most noble,
passed away calmed through the karma of merit —
let none of you think likewise,
but for the sake of benefiting beings, apply your intelligence in the assembly.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa laid down a rule for those five hundred monks and said: Venerable ones, listen to what I say. Let us teach the Dharma just as it is, and when monks who are in anguish having been separated from the Tathāgata — wherever in whatever direction and region they dwell — hear of it and come here, even though they may distract our minds, nevertheless, it is where the Blessed One attained awakening in the region of Magadha, and where the Blessed One obtained the dharmakāya, that we should deliberate on the manner of the Dharma. One monk then said, "Excellent, we will do exactly so." But another said, "Venerable one, are we then going to the foot of the tree of awakening?" The Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied: Venerable ones, the faithful one — the king of Magadha, the son of the Licchavī lady, Ajātaśatru, whose root of faith is unimpaired — will provide the monastic community with the requisites of sustenance and will fully attend to the proper conduct of the Dharma, and will serve as patron; so we shall go to Rājagṛha. They said, "Excellent, we shall do just so." Then they said, "But the Venerable Ānanda has training duties still to complete, and the Blessed One entrusted all the sūtras to him — how are we to accomplish this?" The Venerable Mahākāśyapa then said: Venerable ones, if that is so, then the other monks still in training who are here present will also be disturbed. So let a skillful arrangement be made: let Ānanda be appointed with joy to serve as water-bearer for the monastic community, and let the rest be sent back. They said, "Excellent, we shall do exactly so." Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the Venerable Ānanda and said: Venerable Ānanda, are you willing to serve as water-bearer for the monastic community? He replied: Venerable Mahākāśyapa, I am willing.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa made the formal motion and the two-fold act of the Saṅgha began. "Let the venerable members of the Saṅgha please listen. The Venerable Ānanda has been the personal attendant of the Blessed One, has stayed close to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One has entrusted all the sūtras to him. Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda is to be appointed by the Saṅgha as water-bearer to the Saṅgha. If the time is right for the Saṅgha and the Saṅgha consents to appointing the Venerable Ānanda as water-bearer, and to the monk Ānanda's serving as water-bearer and drawing water, let the Saṅgha please approve. This is the motion. The act is to be performed as follows: Let the venerable members of the Saṅgha please listen. The Venerable Ānanda is the personal attendant of the Blessed One, has stayed close to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One has entrusted to him all the sūtras. Therefore, the Saṅgha appoints the Venerable Ānanda to draw water for the Saṅgha. The monk Ānanda is to draw water for the Saṅgha.
