Those venerable ones who consent to the Venerable Ānanda's drawing water for the Saṅgha should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak." The Saṅgha consented and approved, and the Venerable Ānanda was appointed to draw water for the Saṅgha. Since no one spoke, so it was held to be.

Here ends the section on minor Vinaya matters. The fifty-seventh fascicle.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the Venerable Ānanda: Ānanda, come here. Travel at your leisure together with the community of monks and go to Rājagṛha. I shall go by the direct route. The Venerable Ānanda replied: Venerable one, so be it. And the Venerable Ānanda traveled at leisure together with the community of monks and went on. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa likewise went to Rājagṛha by the direct route as before.

Now it was the custom of Ajātaśatru, king of Magadha and son of Vaidehī, that whenever he saw the Blessed One while riding an elephant, he would immediately dismount of his own accord, and the power of the Blessed One would cause him to alight upon the ground unharmed. When King Ajātaśatru of Magadha saw the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, he was reminded of the Blessed One and in the same way fell to the ground of his own accord. At that moment the Venerable Mahākāśyapa caught him with his supernatural power and said: Great king, buddhas and blessed ones are always abiding in meditative equipoise. Śrāvakas, however, do not enter into the vision of gnosis without meditative equipoise; sometimes they abide having entered equipoise, and sometimes they abide without having entered it. Therefore, from now on, when you see a śrāvaka of the Blessed One, do not fall of your own accord from elephants or horses. And he established this as a rule for him.

The king replied: Noble one, I shall do exactly as the noble one has commanded. Noble one, while the Blessed One was living I paid reverence to the Blessed One; but now that the Blessed One has passed into complete nirvāṇa, to whom am I to pay reverence? The Blessed One himself has entrusted the teaching of the Blessed One to me. And so saying, he commanded his ministers: Provide the wise and noble Mahākāśyapa with everything he needs.

The Venerable Mahākāśyapa then said:

Great King, the Blessed One attained awakening in the land of Magadha. There the Blessed One obtained the dharmakāya, and the community of monks has set out on the road, wishing to deliberate on the manner of the Dharma at this divine abode. The king replied: Noble one, I shall gladly provide the community of monks with all requisites.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the five hundred arhats set out for Rājagṛha in order to compile the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma. The king of Magadha, the son of the Vaidehī queen, Ajātaśatru, heard that the five hundred arhats had come to Rājagṛha. Upon hearing this, he had the towns swept and cleaned, the roads prepared, and then the queen, the young princes, the ministers, and the palace retinue went out to receive them. Then a thousand good men served as attendants, and having arranged everything splendidly, they entered the city; and the community of monks was provided with all requisites. Then they sat in order of seniority, and someone spoke to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa thus: Noble one, in which direction shall we deliberate?

He replied: Great King, here in the Kalandaka bamboo grove of Veḷuvana, the monks who have been separated from the Tathāgata have arisen in suffering, and from whatever regions and districts they had been residing in they have come here, and this causes the fault of distraction to our minds. At Vulture Peak likewise there is this drawback. And though this cave of the nyagrodha tree is quite secluded, it nevertheless lacks bedding and seats.

The king said: Noble one, please be of good cheer — there are seats. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said: Venerable ones, the king says thus: let us go to this cave of the nyagrodha tree. The five hundred arhats said nothing and consented. The king said: Noble one, Mahākāśyapa, the Blessed One passed into complete nirvāṇa without entrusting me with anything at all. Do not you also pass into complete nirvāṇa without first considering. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa likewise consented to this.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa first repaired the fraying and damage of the early rains retreat boundary, and then undertook to spend the later rains retreat there, thinking to deliberate on the Dharma. He first repaired the fraying and damage of the early rains retreat, and then undertook the later rains retreat. Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having surveyed the minds of the venerable ones and examined them all thoroughly, said this to the Venerable Ananda, who had not yet attained cessation: Venerable Ananda, take heed. Among this retinue who have been so praised by the Tathāgata, there are monks who are still in training — those with attachment, those with aversion, those with delusion, those with craving, those with clinging.

Then the Venerable Ananda, having entered into the absorption of the fourth dhyāna and examined carefully, saw that the Venerable Ananda alone was still in training — possessed of attachment, possessed of aversion, possessed of delusion, possessed of craving, possessed of clinging. Having seen this, he said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: Venerable Mahākāśyapa, please be aware. The community of monks is free of what is without essence, pure, clean, having essence, unsurpassed, a field of merit, a fit object of offering for the world — yet the Venerable Ananda is one with attachment, with aversion, with delusion, with craving, with clinging: he is still in training.

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa considered whether the Venerable Ānanda could be tamed by being treated gently, or whether he would be tamed by being treated harshly. Having examined this, and having seen how much harshness was needed to tame him, he said to him: "I am the foremost of the assembly, and you, Ānanda, have never discussed the Dharma together with me. Be gone!"

At this, as though struck to the quick, the Venerable Ānanda trembled violently and said: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, enough! I have not broken my moral discipline, I have not broken my view, I have not broken my conduct, I have not broken my livelihood. I have committed no offense whatsoever against the Saṅgha. Venerable Mahākāśyapa, please bear with me."

Then Mahākāśyapa said to him: "Venerable Ānanda, you who have served so close to the feet of the Blessed One — that you have not broken your moral discipline, not broken your view, not broken your conduct, not broken your livelihood — how remarkable is that? And yet you would say 'I have committed no offense at all against the Saṅgha'? Come now, take up a sīla-wood, and I shall show you your offenses."

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose. The very moment he stood up, the great trichiliocosm shook three times — it shook, shook greatly, shook entirely; it trembled, trembled greatly, trembled utterly. The gods dwelling in the sky were filled with wonder and, opening their eyes wide, exclaimed "Ah!" Then they said: "Alas! The noble Mahākāśyapa speaks truth, he speaks for the good — and yet here in this very place, now that the Sage has passed from among us, he treats the noble Ānanda with such excessive harshness!"

Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke these words to the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, you say, 'I have done no harm whatsoever to the Saṅgha.' But how can it be that you have done no harm to the Saṅgha? When the Blessed One did not wish to give full ordination to women who were living every day in corrupt conduct, you entreated him, and the Blessed One then gave Ānanda ordination to women, granting them full ordination and conferring the state of fully ordained nuns — do not speak to me of that! Why? Because when women are admitted to going forth in the Dharma and Vinaya, the Dharma and Vinaya do not endure for long. Just as when hail falls upon a field of excellent ripened rice, whatever rice there is is ruined and gone — so too, when women are admitted to going forth in the Dharma and Vinaya, the Dharma and Vinaya do not endure for long. Did he not say this? Venerable Mahākāśyapa, enough — please bear with me. It is not that I lacked conscience or lacked shame. But the great mother of the Blessed One's being, the great Gautamī, endured hardship — she who had nursed and raised the very one whose own mother had passed from this world before her time. Moreover, thinking that, just as the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas of former times each had a fourfold retinue, so too would this Blessed One have the same — and wishing to repay what had been done for me, I entreated the Blessed One to grant ordination to women on behalf of my relative and kin. In this one matter alone I ask forgiveness for my fault."

Then Mahākāśyapa said: "Venerable Ānanda, by doing what you did in this way — by repaying a debt — you have caused harm to the dharmakāya. How can you say it was for the sake of relatives and kin? You acted like hail falling upon the perfectly endowed buddha-field, cutting short by a mere residue what would have endured for a full thousand years. To grant ordination on account of relatives and kin — that is improper, it is not good, it is an offense."

"Just as I have heard that fully awakened buddhas of former times had four assemblies, and just as I declared that this Blessed One too would have it so — in those earlier times people were of few desires, few faults, little attachment, little aversion, little delusion, and their underlying tendencies were thin. Those of that sort are appropriate in that way; this, however, is not appropriate. For in this manner, however much you entreated the Blessed One — even against his wish — it was granted accordingly. Therefore this is the first offense. Set down the disciplinary staff. You have yet another offense as well.

The Blessed One said: 'Ānanda, wherever one cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices the four bases of miraculous power, one could, if one wished, remain for a full eon or even beyond.' Yet you did not entreat the Blessed One, saying: 'Blessed One, please remain for a full eon for the benefit of the world; Sugata, please remain beyond a full eon.' This is your second great offense.

Furthermore, you have this offense as well: when the Blessed One had issued a pronouncement — when the Blessed One had declared to the venerable Ānanda, 'It is to be thus' — you gave a different reply to what another said. This too is your third offense.

You have yet further offenses: you stepped upon the Blessed One's robe of golden hue with your foot. Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is not that I was without shame or without profound shame — but at that moment there was no monk companion at my side on either left or right."

To which he replied: "Why did you not toss it into the air? The gods would have caught it." This is your fourth offense.

You have yet further offenses: when the Blessed One had entered upon his final passing and lay between the twin śāla trees, thirsty and asking for water — the water was turbid. Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is not that I was without shame or without deep shame — but at that time some five hundred carts had crossed the river Kakuṭṭhā and stirred it into muddiness. Because of that it was indeed your fault; yet why did you not hold up your begging bowl into the sky? The gods would have filled it with water endowed with eight fine qualities. This is your fifth offense.

You have yet further offenses: the Blessed One had declared that at the time of reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra every fortnight, whoever recited the minor and lesser rules, the Saṅgha of monks would set them aside and take ease in comfortable contact. At that time you failed to ask the Blessed One: 'What are the minor and lesser training rules?' Therefore this is your sixth offense.

"As for what I say here: the four rules entailing defeat, the thirteen rules entailing the Saṅgha's remainder, the two indeterminate rules, the thirty rules entailing confession with forfeiture, the ninety rules entailing confession, the four rules requiring individual acknowledgment, and the many further rules of training — those that remain beyond these are the minor and lesser rules."

There is also this that is said: from the four rules entailing defeat through the four rules requiring individual acknowledgment inclusive —

those that remain beyond these are the minor and lesser rules. There is also this that is said: beyond the four rules entailing defeat, the thirteen rules entailing the Saṅgha's remainder, the two indeterminate rules, and the thirty rules entailing confession with forfeiture, and the ninety rules entailing confession — those that remain are the minor and lesser rules. There is also this that is said: beyond the four rules entailing defeat, the thirteen rules entailing the Saṅgha's remainder, the two indeterminate rules, and the thirty rules entailing confession with forfeiture — those that remain are the minor and lesser rules. There is also this that is said: beyond the four rules entailing defeat, the thirteen rules entailing the Saṅgha's remainder, and the two indeterminate rules — those that remain are the minor and lesser rules.

Thus it is that while monks, having fully understood them from within, abide by the four rules entailing defeat, some who abide by the thirteen rules entailing the Saṅgha's remainder have given opportunity to non-Buddhists, so that the Dharma of the monk Gautama has become like smoke dissipated into the air. When the ascetic Gautama was alive, the training of the hearers was properly observed under restraint; but now they conduct themselves as they please and have grown lax — if they wish, they do it; if they do not wish, they do not. Therefore it was your fault that you did not petition the Blessed One for the sake of benefiting people in the future.

Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is not that I was shameless or utterly shameless. Rather, at that time I was tormented by the suffering of grief at being separated from the Tathāgata. And yet that too was your fault: you who served as an attendant to the Tathāgata — since all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, your lamenting too was an offense. Moreover, there are these further offenses: you showed women of bad conduct in the household retinue the concealed and sunken places of the Tathāgata's body. Venerable Ānanda, it is not that I was shameless or utterly shameless — yet I reasoned thus in my mind: women, by nature greatly prone to attachment, if they see the concealed and sunken places of the Blessed One's body, will be rid of their womanly marks. Venerable Ānanda, from where did such an excellence of wisdom come to you — that if the concealed and sunken places were shown, women would thereby be rid of their womanly marks? This is the seventh offense.

Moreover, there are these further offenses against you: you showed women the Blessed One's body with its golden complexion, and that body was thus stained with their tears. Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is not that I was shameless or utterly shameless — yet this thought arose in my mind: if sentient beings see the Blessed One possessed of such a complexion, great numbers of them will form the aspiration in their minds to be possessed of such a complexion. Ānanda, you who have no such single-pointed knowledge and no knowledge of others' minds — this is the eighth offense.

Since you are possessed of a measure of attachment, rise up and depart from this assembly of the supreme ones who are free from attachment. We shall not recite together with you.

Thus it was that the venerable Mahākāśyapa enumerated eight offenses committed by the venerable Ānanda, and having done so, gazed in all four directions and spoke slowly, with words of compassion and grief: Alas, my time has come to this — I have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, and there is no protector, no refuge.

Then, after the venerable Mahākāśyapa had enumerated the eight offenses of the venerable Ānanda, the gods who were dwelling in the expanse of the sky cried out "Ālālā!" and said: Now the bodies of the gods shall flourish, and the bodies of the asuras shall be wounded. The teaching of the Blessed One shall flourish — for so it is when a great śrāvaka who is the equal of the Teacher enumerates the offenses of another great śrāvaka who is the equal of the Teacher.

Then the venerable Ānanda spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa in these words: Great venerable Kāśyapa, it is as you say — please grant your forbearance. I will act in accordance with the Dharma and shall not do so again. But the Blessed One had entrusted me to you. At the time when the Blessed One passed completely beyond sorrow, he said: Ānanda, do not grieve, do not be downcast, do not lament. I entrust you to the monk Mahākāśyapa. Ānanda, though it is hard, be patient with minor offenses and do not be unable to bear them. Ānanda, do not weep — your wholesome qualities will grow and not diminish. Rise up and depart from this assembly of the supreme ones, so that I may apply myself to the teaching. I shall not recite together with you — and with this he pronounced the formal censure.

Then the venerable Aniruddha spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa in these words: Venerable Mahākāśyapa, without the venerable Ānanda, how shall we recite correctly? He replied: Although the venerable monk Ānanda possesses good qualities, he cannot remain here with us. He is one who must still train while possessed of attachment, aversion, and delusion — and so I shall not recite together with you. And then he said to the venerable Ānanda: Venerable Ānanda, rise up and go. When you have striven with great diligence and become an arhat, we shall recite together.

Then the venerable Ānanda's eyes filled with tears. Remembering that he was parted from the Teacher, his heart was heavy with sorrow. He then rose from the midst of the assembly of the supreme ones and went to the city of Vṛjī, and there he entered properly into the rains retreat.

Now at that time, when Ānanda's attendant, the venerable Vṛjīputra, was serving him, the venerable Ānanda was teaching the Dharma to the four assemblies with great diligence. Then the venerable Vṛjīputra thought to himself: Does my preceptor train while free from the attachment of desire, or does he train while not yet free from the attachment of desire? I shall enter a meditative absorption such as this, and with the mind of one thus absorbed I shall look into my preceptor's mind. The venerable Vṛjīputra then entered into just such a meditative absorption, and with the mind of one thus absorbed he examined the mind of the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Vṛjīputra discerned the mind of the venerable Ānanda and saw that the venerable Ānanda was still training while not free from the attachment of desire. He then arose from the meditative absorption, went to where the venerable Ānanda was, approached him, sat before him, and spoke these verses:

Gautama, do not be heedless.
Lean upon the dense shade of a tree and pass into peace.
Set your mind to it and enter into meditation —
before long you will attain the abode of tranquility.

Then the venerable Ānanda, taking up this instruction given by the venerable Vṛjīputra, purified his mind of all those phenomena that are obstructive when one walks and sits during the day. He purified his mind of those phenomena that are obstructive when one walks and sits during the day. During the first watch of the night he purified his mind of those phenomena that are obstructive when one walks and sits. He purified his mind of those phenomena that are obstructive when one walks and sits during the first watch of the night. At the middle watch of the night he washed his feet outside the assembly hall, entered within the assembly hall, lay down on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, and rested with only the perception of light, possessed of mindfulness and vigilance. The venerable Ānanda had not yet laid his head upon the pillow when, just so, the mind of the venerable Ānanda became liberated from the defilements without clinging. Then the venerable Ānanda, having individually experienced joy and happiness, was fully liberated and attained the state of arhat. He then went to Rājagṛha, to the place where the venerable Kāśyapa and the five hundred arhats were gathering and assembling the Dharma in the grotto of the Nyagrodha tree.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the monks as follows: "Venerable ones, in a future time, when monks have become forgetful and their physical capacities have declined, they will be unable to retain the sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma in the form of sūtra verses. Therefore, in the morning hours the sūtra verses should be recited, and in the afternoon the sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma should be discussed." When the venerable Mahākāśyapa had spoken thus, those monks, having heard the venerable Mahākāśyapa, spoke to him as follows: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, of the sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, which should be discussed first?" He said: "Venerable ones, for the time being let the sūtras be discussed first." "So be it."

The five hundred arhats then requested the venerable Mahākāśyapa to compile the Dharma. He sat upon a lion throne and encouraged the venerable Ānanda, saying: "Venerable Ānanda, if you are willing, are you then willing to compile the sūtras of the Tathāgata? Yes, be willing." Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa began the act of petition and motion. He addressed the noble Saṅgha as follows: "Venerable ones of the Saṅgha, please hear. If the venerable Ānanda is willing to undertake the compilation of the sūtras of the Blessed One, and if the time is right for the Saṅgha and it meets with approval, let the Saṅgha grant its consent. This is the proposal: let the Saṅgha appoint the venerable Ānanda to undertake the compilation of the sūtras, and let the venerable Ānanda accomplish the compilation of the sūtras of the Blessed One. This is the proposal."

The motion is to be carried out as follows. The venerable ones of the Saṅgha, please hear. The venerable Ānanda is willing to undertake the compilation of the sūtras of the Blessed One. The Saṅgha appoints the venerable Ānanda, and the venerable Ānanda is to accomplish the compilation of the sūtras of the Blessed One. Those venerable ones who consent to the venerable Ānanda being appointed to accomplish the compilation of the sūtras of the Blessed One should remain silent, and those who do not consent should speak. The Saṅgha has consented and approved, and the Saṅgha has appointed the venerable Ānanda to accomplish the compilation of the sūtras of the Blessed One. Since no one has spoken, it is so held.

Five hundred patchwork robes were arranged by the five hundred arhats upon the lion throne of the venerable Ānanda, the Dharma-speaking lion. Then the venerable Ānanda gazed out in the four directions, aroused a mind of compassion toward sentient beings, generated reverence toward the Dharma, and, fixing his attention on those who live the holy life with reverent regard, circumambulated the lion throne to the right, touched it with his head, and paid homage in due order according to seniority. Holding impermanence in mind, he took his seat, overcoming the lion throne with his radiance.

Then, gazing upon that assembly, deep as the ocean, unmoving, he thought: "If I were to recite all the sūtras that the Blessed One taught without exception as I have retained them — among them there are sūtras that the Blessed One taught in the dwelling places of the nāgas, sūtras taught in the dwelling places of the gods, and sūtras taught directly to me, those which came transmitted one to another and were heard and retained in just that way — all of these that I have thus heard, I shall recite." And since the knowledge and vision of the gods is inferior, each one cried out to the others: "O noble Sage, the noble Ānanda, the mightiest of the noble ones — listen with one-pointed mind as he expounds the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata!"

Then at that moment another divine son spoke these verses:

In whom the phenomena are well established,
whom the three worlds honor always —
this noble one, free of all hesitation,
roars out the Dharma like a lion.
O wonderful! When he speaks of the peaceful,
you who wish for happiness:
hearken with reverence and devotion
to the essence, the supreme of essences, the pure.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke to the venerable Ānanda in these words:

The Teacher, who intends benefit for the world —
of the Dharma taught by the Victor,
the most excellent form, declared where?
The venerable one shall recite the sūtras.

Having deeply understood the recollection of the Buddha — arising from what the Teacher had fully proclaimed — and holding it in mind, the venerable Ānanda gazed intently in the direction where the Blessed One had entered perfect peace and had been received into the heart, then sat with palms joined together and, making his voice resound throughout the assembly, he declared:

"Thus did I hear. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park of the Sages."

The very instant those words were spoken, thousands of divine beings dwelling in the middle of the sky and in palaces, and many hundreds of monks and others who had not been separated from attachment, were stricken and overwhelmed with distress, and, feeling suffering, they cried out in lamentation:

Alas! Among these worlds,
in impermanence there is no distinction.
He who was that treasury of jewels —
the ocean of his qualities, too, is dried.
From him I directly heard
the Dharma that brings the bliss of liberation.
Having heard these words and joined them with wisdom,
that too is proclaimed this very day.

Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the five monks:

"O monks, this teaching not heard before — it is the noble truth of suffering" — and so, turning the wheel of Dharma in full, he expounded the sūtras.

Then the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya spoke to the venerable Mahākāśyapa in these words: "O venerable Mahākāśyapa, I heard this category of Dharma directly, and through the recitation and teaching of this sūtra for my own benefit, the ocean of my blood and tears has dried up, the mountain of my bones has been surmounted, the door to the lower realms has been closed, and the door to the higher realms and liberation has been opened.

Through the teaching of this precious sūtra, the stainless and immaculate eye of Dharma arose in me and in eight thousand gods. Today, upon hearing this, he spoke: "Alas, all things are without distinction, for they are impermanent." Having said this, he descended from his seat, sat upon the ground, and all those arhats, their minds steeped in habitual tendencies of attachment, descended one by one from their own seats and sat upon the ground, saying these words: "Alas, we who have beheld the Blessed One teaching Dharma face to face — even he has now gone by the path of hearing, carried away by the power of impermanence."

They then spoke these words:

When he who was the sovereign of gods, humans, asuras, and nāgas has passed into peace,
why do you remain alive and not enter the abode of peace?
When the omniscient one has visibly departed from among beings,
what person of wholesome mind clings to life and holds it dear?

Then, one less than five hundred arhats entered into meditative equipoise in the four dhyānas at their respective lodgings at the edge of the world, and with the awareness born of aspirational prayer they looked out, and with joyful minds rose from meditative absorption and spoke to the venerable Ānanda these words: "Venerable Ānanda, is that your scriptural transmission?" The venerable ones answered: "That is my scriptural transmission, venerable ones." "Is it similar to our scriptural transmission, venerable ones?" "Venerable Ānanda, it is exactly so."

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa thought to himself: "When I compiled the first sūtra collection of the Blessed One, not a single person practicing the holy life objected or rebuked it. Therefore, this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this was taught by the Teacher." And he spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, where did the Blessed One teach the second sūtra? Clarify this." He replied: "It was at Vārāṇasī itself, for the sake of the five monks." And the content of it was thus: "Thus did I hear. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park of the Sages Who Speak Truth. There the Blessed One declared to the monks: 'O monks, these are the Four Noble Truths — the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. What is the noble truth of suffering? The suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is dear, the suffering of meeting with what is unpleasant, the suffering of seeking what one desires and not finding it, and in short, the five aggregates of clinging — these are suffering. This is called the noble truth of suffering. What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is craving that leads to renewed existence, born from the impulse of joyful desire, taking delight in this and that. This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete abandonment of that very craving that leads to renewed existence, born from the impulse of joyful desire, taking delight in this and that — its relinquishment, its utter termination, its exhaustion, its freedom from desire, its cessation, its nirvāṇa. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is the noble eightfold path — that is to say, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood,

right effort, right mindfulness, and right meditative absorption — this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering." When this enumeration of the Dharma had been taught, the venerable Kauṇḍinya, without any clinging, was liberated in mind from all defilements. As for the remaining four monks, the dust-free and stainless eye of Dharma with respect to all phenomena arose in them — so it was declared.

At that time the venerable Kauṇḍinya spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "O venerable Mahākāśyapa, I myself heard this enumeration of the Dharma directly, and at the very moment this enumeration of the Dharma was taught, without clinging I was liberated in mind from all defilements. As for the remaining four monks, the dust-free and stainless eye of Dharma with respect to all phenomena arose in them."

Then, from the passage beginning "one who finds it incomplete" down to "I summarize a second discourse of the Blessed One, by which no one who leads the pure life is turned back or reproached" — all of this proceeds as before.

Knowing thereby, "This is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher has taught," the venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the venerable Kauṇḍinya: "O venerable Kauṇḍinya, where did the Blessed One teach the third discourse? Indicate clearly that it was in Vārāṇasī alone, and for the sake of the five monks — and what, then, is it?"

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. At that time the Blessed One spoke thus to the remaining four monks:

"Monks, form is not self. Monks, if form were the self, form would not be subject to harm or suffering, and it would be possible to say of form: 'May form be thus; may form not be thus.' Monks, precisely because form is not self, form is subject to harm and suffering, and it is not possible to say: 'May form be thus; may form not be thus.'

"Monks, feeling, perception, and formations are not self — monks, if perception and the rest were the self" — and so on, as before — "it would not be possible to say: 'May such consciousness be thus.'"

"Monks, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?" "Venerable one, it is impermanent." "And further, that which is impermanent — is it suffering or not suffering?" "Venerable one, it is suffering." "And further, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change — would a learned noble hearer regard it as: 'This is mine, this am I, this is my self'?" "Venerable one, that is not so."

"Monks, what do you think? Are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness" — as before — "'this is mine, this am I, this is my self'?" "Venerable one, that is not so."

"Therefore, monks, with respect to all form whatsoever — whether past, future, or present; whether internal or external; whether gross or subtle; whether inferior or superior; whether far or near — all of it should be viewed with correct wisdom exactly as it is: 'This is not mine, this am I not, this is not my self.'

In the same way, with respect to all feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness whatsoever — whether past, future, or present,

whether internal or external; whether gross or subtle; whether inferior or superior; whether far or near — all of it should be viewed with correct wisdom exactly as it is, as before.

Monks, it is because the learned noble śrāvakas see the five clinging aggregates exactly as they truly are — as without self and without anything belonging to a self — that, having thus seen them exactly as they truly are, they do not cling in the slightest to anything in the world. Not having clung, they are not tormented. Not being tormented, they themselves attain nirvāṇa. They know with full understanding: "My birth is exhausted; the holy life has been lived; what had to be done has been done; there is no further existence beyond this."

When this exposition of the Dharma had been spoken, the five remaining monks were liberated from defilement, their minds freed without clinging.

From the passage beginning "The one arhat who was absent" through "that none who practiced the holy life turned away or spoke in reproach" — all of that is as before, as in the third sūtra of the Blessed One.

Knowing thus — "This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught" — the venerable Ānanda then recited the sūtras that the Blessed One had taught in various villages, cities, districts, and royal palaces, at their respective times, and compiled them together with the five hundred arhats, with one absent. Those sūtras that dealt chiefly with the aggregates were gathered and arranged under the heading of the aggregates. Those that dealt chiefly with the sense bases were gathered under the six sense bases. Those that dealt chiefly with dependent origination and the noble truths were gathered under the heading of originating conditions. Those in which śrāvakas spoke most extensively were gathered under the heading of śrāvaka teachings. Those in which the buddha spoke most extensively were gathered under the heading of buddha teachings. Those that dealt chiefly with the four applications of mindfulness, the four right abandonments, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the limbs of awakening, and the limbs of the path were gathered under the heading of the limbs of the path. Sūtras with a great deal of precise and correct statement were gathered under the section of precise and correct statement. Those containing verse, together with properly elaborated material, were gathered under the heading of scriptures with proper elaboration. Long sūtras were placed under the heading of long scriptures. Medium-length sūtras were placed under the heading of medium-length scriptures. Those entitled "of one phrase," "of two phrases," through "of ten phrases" were designated the scriptures derived from the one, the numerically arranged collection.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, is this the full extent of your scriptural transmission?" The venerable Ānanda replied: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, this is the full extent — there is nothing beyond this." And so saying, he descended from the lion throne.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke: "Venerable ones, the sūtras of the Blessed One have now been compiled in their entirety. Let us now take up the discussion of the Vinaya." All replied: "So be it."

At that time the venerable Upāli had already become skilled in the Vinaya, learned in its occasioning circumstances and the stories behind its rules. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, seated on the lion throne, spoke: "Venerable ones, the venerable Upāli is skilled in the Vinaya, learned in its occasioning circumstances and the stories behind its rules, and the Blessed One himself prophesied him as the foremost upholder of the Vinaya. Therefore, with great enthusiasm, let him be appointed to compile the Vinaya." All replied: "So be it."

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the venerable Upāli: "Venerable Upāli, you are a practitioner —"

"— are you willing to compile all the Tathāgata's Vinaya without remainder?" "I am willing."

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa descended from the lion throne, and the venerable Upāli took his seat upon it. The venerable Mahākāśyapa then began the formal act of the Saṅgha, addressing the assembly: "Venerable ones, please listen. The venerable Upāli is willing and undertaking to compile all the Blessed One's Vinaya without remainder" — and from there, through the words "since no one speaks against it, so it is accepted," all proceeded as before.

The venerable Mahākāśyapa descended from the lion throne, and the venerable Upāli took his seat upon the lion throne. Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the venerable Upāli:

This is the fifty-eighth fascicle of the section on minor rules.

Venerable Upāli, where did the Blessed One establish the first training rule? He replied clearly: In the city of Vārāṇasī. For whose sake? For the sake of the five monks. And the reason? Because the rule was established thus: "The lower robe is to be worn in a circular fashion." Then those among the five hundred arhats who had not yet been born entered into the four dhyānas perfected to their highest limit, and with the knowledge of aspiration they surveyed — and so forth as before, through the words "the venerable Mahākāśyapa thought to himself" — that when the Blessed One's first training rule had been properly compiled in this way, no practitioner of the holy life objected to it or found fault with it. Therefore they recognized: "This is the Dharma. This is the Vinaya. This is what the Teacher taught." The venerable Mahākāśyapa then said to the venerable Upāli: "Venerable Upāli, tell us where the Blessed One established the second training rule." He replied clearly: In the city of Vārāṇasī. For whose sake? For the sake of the five monks. And when the rule was established thus: "The upper robe too is to be worn in a circular fashion." Then those among the five hundred arhats who had not yet been born entered the four dhyānas perfected to their highest limit — and so forth as before for the second training rule — and no practitioner of the holy life objected to it or found fault with it. Therefore they recognized: "This is the Dharma. This is the Vinaya. This is what the Teacher taught." The venerable Mahākāśyapa then said to the venerable Upāli: "Venerable Upāli, tell us where the Blessed One established the third training rule." He replied clearly: In the village of Kalandaka. For whose sake? For the sake of Supriya, son of Kalandaka. And the reason? Because the rule was established thus: "Furthermore, if a monk who shares the same training and stands equal with the other monks — without having relinquished the training and without having declared his weakness in the training — engages in sexual conduct, the practice of unchastity, even with an animal born in a lowly state of existence, that monk has incurred a defeat and may not remain." Then those among the five hundred arhats who had not yet been born entered the four dhyānas perfected to their highest limit — and so forth as before, through the words "this is what the Teacher taught."

The remaining training rules of the Blessed One — those spoken in whichever villages, cities, districts, and royal residences — the venerable Upāli recited one by one for the monks, and those among the five hundred arhats who were not yet present made them into a canonical text. These are the defeats. These are the residues for the Saṅgha. These are the two undetermined rules, the thirty rules entailing forfeiture, the ninety rules entailing confession,

the four rules entailing individual confession, the many rules of training, and the seven rules for settling disputes. This is what was prescribed. This is what was subsequently prescribed. This is what is to be individually abandoned. This is what is permitted. Ordination by going forth and full ordination are to be performed in this way. The act of a single motion is to be performed in this way. The acts of a motion with two proclamations and a motion with four proclamations are to be performed in this way. One of this kind is to be expelled. One of this kind is not to be expelled. The restoration ceremony is to be performed in this way. The invitation ceremony is to be performed in this way. From rules of this sort — this is the detail, this is the origin story, this is the intention — he compiled the Vinaya in full, point by point in just this manner. Then the venerable Upāli Sengge descended from the lion throne.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, foreseeing that in times to come people would be of weak wisdom and would follow mere letters, and that among those who aspired to the profound meaning there would be some who needed only him to protect the meaning of the sūtras and the Vinaya — thinking "I shall set forth what is called the Māmakī," and so desiring that purpose, he performed the act of a motion with two proclamations, seated himself on the lion throne, and addressed the monks in these words:

"Venerable ones, what is called 'Māmakī, Māmakī' — that I alone shall now teach. The Māmakī is what makes the defining characteristics of all that is to be known perfectly clear: namely, the four close applications of mindfulness, the four correct abandonments, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the noble eightfold path, the four specific knowledges, the four fruits of the contemplative life, the four Dharma-summaries, the absence of affliction, knowledge arising from aspiration, supreme culmination, emptiness that is emptiness, signlessness that is signless, the concentration cultivated through familiarity, what arises from the summit of direct realization, conventional knowledge, calm abiding, special insight, and the thorough compilation and analysis of the aggregates of Dharma-categories — all of these are what is called the Māmakī."

Then, those among the five hundred arhats who had not yet been present, beginning from "supreme culmination," recited all that follows — "This is the Dharma. This is the Vinaya. This is what the Teacher taught" — just as before.

Then the earth-dwelling yakṣas, having compiled and drawn forth the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, proclaimed aloud with melodious voice: "Wondrous! The noble Mahākāśyapa and the five hundred arhats have fully compiled the three scriptural collections of the Sugata. The bodies of the gods have thereby increased, and the bodies of the asuras have altogether diminished!" Thus they spoke. The earth-dwelling yakṣas' cry was heard by the yakṣas moving through the sky, and from these it resounded instantly, in that very moment, in that very instant — in a single moment, in a single flash — all the way to the realm of Akaniṣṭha. When the gods of Akaniṣṭha in turn proclaimed it, the announcement spread back down, and the bodies of the asuras had altogether diminished — and so forth as before, just as it was recounted.

Because it was compiled by five hundred arhats, it came to be known by the name "compiled by five hundred, compiled by five hundred."

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, having completed the compilation, spoke these words:

The speech of the one who holds the ten powers is boundless.
For the benefit of beings, I have compiled this treatise on the Dharma.
Where the world is darkened by feeble minds and wasted away,
it stands as a lamp that clears the dimness from the intellect.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa reflected thus: "Having compiled the three scriptural collections, I examined with the wisdom of aspirational awareness how long they should be preserved so that the teaching of the Blessed One would endure" — and everything that was said to that effect, I have fulfilled in every way. Whatever the Blessed One declared and prophesied, I have accomplished to the best of my ability. I have regarded the Blessed One, the nature of reality, the lord of the Dharma, as a dear friend, looked to him closely, repaired what needed to be repaired, and rendered even a small measure of benefit in return. Yet who can fully requite that protector of the world — repaying him without remainder? I have practiced the holy life in conformity with the Dharma and have rendered benefit to the worlds. Having long ago been appointed by my teacher, I am now weary of this burden of the aggregates and this body full of filth. I have come to the moment of passing fully into nirvāṇa; it is time for me to go.

And having so reflected, he spoke:

I have compiled the sūtras of the Sage
and set the path of the Dharma in place.
From one to the next, through long ages,
these scriptures of the Teacher shall endure.
The shameless have been cut off by severance;
the conscientious have been thoroughly embraced.
Because I have brought benefit and virtue,
the time of my nirvāṇa has now come.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the venerable Ānanda and said: "Venerable Ānanda, know this: the Blessed One entrusted the teaching to me and passed into nirvāṇa. Now I too shall pass into nirvāṇa — so guard the teaching. In Rājagṛha there will be born the son of another merchant, and because he will be wrapped in a garment of linen he will be given the name Linen-Clad. He shall cross the great ocean and return, and he will serve the teaching of the Blessed One for a period of five years. Ordain him as a monk and entrust the teaching fully to him." So he spoke.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa thought to himself: "Now, before I go, I wish to make offering for the last time at the relics and bodily marks of the Blessed One, who strove with great compassion and was nourished by a spiritual teacher of boundless qualities. I will go and rest at peace wherever his relics may be." With that thought, he went to the four great stūpas and, after paying reverence and making excellent offerings at the eight relic stūpas, he went to the dwelling place of the nāgas, made offering at the Blessed One's tooth relic, then rose upward into the sky and went to the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods.

There Śakra, the lord of the gods (Indra), and many other gods rejoiced and made offerings, and asked: "Why have you come? If you have a wish, please speak it."

"Kauśika," he replied, "I have come wishing to make offering for the last time at the tooth and other marks of the Blessed One."

When Śakra, the lord of the gods, and the other gods heard the word "last," they became downcast; and having stirred up that feeling, they said nothing at all. They then brought it forth. And then the elder Mahākāśyapa took the tooth relic in his hand, gazed at it without blinking, placed it upon his crown, and scattered over it an abundance of māndārava flowers, blue lotuses, and powdered heartwood of sandalwood and serpent-wood. He gave a brief teaching to Śakra and the many hundreds and thousands of gods, urging them to be heedful. Then he vanished from the summit of Mount Meru and departed for Rājagṛha.

He thought to himself: "When the time comes for me to pass into nirvāṇa, I should send word to King Ajātaśatru." So he went to the royal palace and said to the doorkeeper: "My good man, go and let King Ajātaśatru know that Kāśyapa is standing at the gate and wishes to pay his respects to the king."

He entered inside. Now the king happened to be asleep, and the doorkeeper said: "Noble sir, the king is sleeping." The elder said: "Go and rouse him." The doorkeeper replied: "Noble sir, the king is fierce-tempered; he will have me punished with execution." "Very well, then — when he has woken from sleep, tell him this: Kāśyapa is about to pass into nirvāṇa."

Meanwhile, the venerable Mahākāśyapa ascended the Vulture Peak, the southern mountain of Rājagṛha. In the midst of the three hills he made a grass seat, and he reflected: "The robe-cloth given to me by the Blessed One has been apportioned over my body and blessed until the time when Maitreya's teaching shall spread. All those beings who were foremost among the Blessed One's assembly of disciples have been caused to feel sorrow. Now I shall enter such a meditative absorption that my body will remain here within this chamber enclosed by the three hills, undecayed until the teaching of Maitreya has spread wide. When King Ajātaśatru comes, the door will open. If he does not see my body, I know that he will vomit warm blood and reach the point of death." And so he relinquished the life-formations. The very instant he relinquished the life-formations, the earth trembled in six ways, shooting stars fell, the directions blazed, and the gods beat their drums in the sky — or so he had foreseen.

Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa, having performed a joining together, a burning, a drawing of lightning, and various great miracles, blessed his own body, lay down on his right side, placed one foot upon the other, and passed fully into nirvāṇa in the sphere of nirvāṇa without remainder.

Then Śakra (Indra, the lord of the gods) and Brahmā and the other gods thought to themselves: "Why has this trembling arisen for us?" And when they understood that the venerable Mahākāśyapa had passed into nirvāṇa, Śakra and Brahmā and the other gods, together with many hundreds and thousands of gods, took up blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and other such flowers, along with finest sandalwood and powdered aloe-wood, went to the place where the remains of the venerable Mahākāśyapa lay, and arrived there. They honored and strewed upon the elder's body blue lotuses, red lotuses, kumuda lotuses, fine white lotuses, finest sandalwood, and powdered aloe-wood, and then sealed the three hills together and covered him over.

Then the gods, bereft of the elder, were overcome with grief. They thought: "The grief we felt at being parted from the Blessed One had not yet subsided, and now, before it could clear, this too has come to pass." The gods dwelling in this Nyagrodha cave suffered obstruction to their wholesome practice of the Dharma. The kingdom of the ruler of the land of Magadha became empty and devoid of light. "Now there is no protector," they thought, "to care for the poor, the destitute, and the helpless with loving-kindness, no guardian to benefit them. People are impoverished of virtue. Now two Blessed Ones alone have passed into nirvāṇa." They thought: "Now the peak of the mountain of the holy Dharma has crumbled. Now the boat of the holy Dharma is wildly rocking. Now the light of the holy Dharma has faded. Now the ocean of the holy Dharma is churned into turmoil."

"Now the Teacher who bestows benefit is nowhere to be seen, and even the māras rejoice." With these words and many other such lamentations, the people paid their respects and disappeared from sight.

Now, as for King Ajātaśatru: in a dream he saw the lineage of the Kṣatriya clan severed. Seeing this, he woke in fright, and then heard the doorkeeper announce that the Elder Mahākāśyapa was about to pass fully into nirvāṇa. Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground. When he had been revived with water and helped to his feet, he went to the Jeta Grove, prostrated himself with his whole body at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda, and wept, saying: "I have heard today that the Elder Mahākāśyapa has passed into nirvāṇa."

Then the Venerable Ānanda led King Ajātaśatru up to Kukkuṭapādagiri, the mountain of the rooster's foot. There the yakṣas split open the mountain, and the king saw the body of the Elder arrayed in robes of mandārava flowers, kuśeśaya blossoms, and the finest sandalwood powder. Seeing this, he stretched out his arms and, like a tree felled at the root, prostrated himself with his whole body at those feet; then he rose and was about to begin gathering wood to cremate the body.

The Elder Ānanda said: "Great king, what do you intend?"

The king replied: "I intend to consume the Elder's body in cremation."

The Elder said: "Great king, this body has been blessed to remain until the scripture of Maitreya arrives. The bodhisattva Maitreya will come to this very place surrounded by sixty-nine million śrāvakas, take up the body of the Elder Mahākāśyapa, and show it to those śrāvakas, saying: 'This one called Kāśyapa was a śrāvaka of the Blessed One Śākyamuni — foremost among those who are content with little, who know sufficiency, and who uphold the quality of training — and he it was who properly gathered together the holy Dharma of that Blessed One Śākyamuni.'" Then, the Elder showed this to the assembled śrāvakas.

The people of that future time, it is thought, will have smaller bodies, and they will surely regard the body of the Blessed One Śākyamuni as having been immense. Then that Blessed One will take the patchwork robe from the Elder's body and show it to the śrāvakas, saying: "This is the patchwork robe of the perfectly and fully awakened Blessed One Śākyamuni." Hearing this, those very śrāvakas — sixty-nine million monks — having properly received the qualities of training, and having striven and accomplished as much as was possible, were blessed by him so as to actualize the state of arhat directly. Although this body cannot be consumed by fire, a stūpa is to be erected upon it.

Then the king arrived at the entrance, the mountain closed in and covered the Elder's body. Afterward the king erected a stūpa on top and made offerings.

Then King Ajātaśatru prostrated himself at the feet of the Venerable Ānanda and said: "Elder, I have not witnessed the Blessed One's passing into nirvāṇa, nor have I seen the Elder Mahākāśyapa. Now I should like to behold the Elder passing into nirvāṇa."

"So be it," the Elder agreed.

Now, a man wearing linen garments arrived in ease and good fortune from the great ocean. He had hidden his wealth as a hoard and then came to the Jeta Grove. He bowed to the Venerable Ānanda, who was walking at the door of the fragrant house, and said: "Venerable one, please know this: I am holding a five-year festival. I have crossed the great ocean and arrived in ease and good fortune. Therefore I wish to hold a five-year festival for the Saṅgha of monks, beginning with the buddhas. Where does the Blessed One reside?"

The Elder said, "My son, the Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa." When the man wearing linen garments heard this, he fainted and fell to the ground. After some time, water was sprinkled on him and he was revived. When he had regained his senses, he said, "Elder, where is Śāriputra? He too has passed into nirvāṇa. And the Great Maudgalyāyana, and the Great Kāśyapa — they likewise." Then, with great sorrow arising in him, he made his offering of the five-year festival out of faith, and completed it fully. Afterward, the Elder said to him, "My son, you have already drawn people to the teaching of the Blessed One through material gifts. Now gather them through the Dharma itself."

The man wearing linen garments said, "Elder, what do you command? How long before the Elder Ānanda tells someone to go forth into the Blessed One's teaching?" The man said he would do just so. And after a time, the Venerable Ānanda caused him to go forth and, through the formal act of entreaty and of the four-fold procedure, had him fully ordained, and accepted him, for the rest of his life, as one who wears and bears the linen robe.

He was one who upheld what he had heard. All that the Venerable Ānanda had heard and retained from the Blessed One — and everything the Venerable Ānanda had heard and kept among both communities of monks and nuns — the Venerable man of linen garments also retained, and he expanded the three knowledges and the three scriptural collections in full.

Now, the Elder Ānanda was dwelling in the Añjana Grove when a monk recited this verse:

One who lives a hundred years
is, without doubt, like a water-crane before a pool —
as the crane merely gazes at the pool,
a solitary life, lived well, excels it.

When the Venerable Ānanda heard this, he went to that place and said, "My son, the Blessed One did not say it in that way. Rather:

One who lives a hundred years
is, without doubt, subject to arising and perishing.
For one who teaches both kinds of person,
to proclaim it forever on this earth
is for one with faithlessness and aversion in mind,
or for one whose faith has gone utterly astray.

One who has grasped the sūtras wrongly
is like a cow that has wandered into a swamp —
that one is drawing near to ruin,
bereft of wisdom's own discernment:
one who does not know what has been heard bears no fruit,
and wrong understanding is like poison.
One who knows what has been heard truly
is the wise one who has gone beyond."

Then the monk's teacher said to him, "Ānanda has grown old, and his memory has declined." The Elder replied:

Tormented by old age,
the memory of the one with a body may falter.
One who no longer recollects correctly —
that one's mind is crushed by age.

"Go there and say this." The Elder Ānanda then returned, and when the monk recited those words again, the Elder said, "Did I not say that the Blessed One did not say it in that way?" And the monk spoke as the teacher had instructed.

Then the Venerable Ānanda considered: "If I myself were to speak to the monk, it would come to a dispute. It would not be fitting for him to come before me, nor is it proper that I should go to him." He then thought: "All those great ones — Śāriputra, the Great Maudgalyāyana, the Great Kāśyapa and the rest — have already passed. Before long I too shall pass into nirvāṇa, and the holy Dharma of the Blessed One will remain in the world for a thousand years." And he spoke:

Those who were old have gone before,
and I am not in harmony with the new and young.
I dwell alone in meditative concentration,
remaining here like a hatching egg.
All my companions and dear friends
have gone on and passed away before me.
One who remembers how to rest in meditative concentration —
a spiritual friend such as that is no longer to be found here.

Purified of stain, gone to peace — a lamp for wandering beings,
the great ones who, with their greatness of being, dispelled the pitch-black darkness of delusion.
Having tamed immeasurable beings to be tamed,
they stand alone, like what remains in a deserted hermitage grove of stūpas.

Then the Blessed One, clad in robes of hemp, having entrusted the teaching to the Great Kāśyapa, passed utterly into nirvāṇa. He in turn had entrusted it to me, saying: "Now I entrust the teaching to you; I shall pass into nirvāṇa. Guard it everywhere." And the Blessed One had given a prophecy that in the land of Broached-Ruin, at the place called Rimurunda, the sons of a merchant — Nata and Phata by name — would build a temple and become patrons of that temple. The temple at Rimurunda being already built, the Blessed One further prophesied that in the land of Broached-Ruin there would come to be a son named Nyesba, born to a man known as the Hidden Incense Seller; that this boy should be ordained; and that one hundred years after the Blessed One had passed into nirvāṇa he would become a buddha without marks, and would perform all the activities of a buddha.

When the venerable Śāṇavāsin said this, the venerable Ānanda replied: "I shall do as the preceptor has instructed."

Then Śāṇavāsin said: "I too shall now pass into nirvāṇa, and I entrust you with this."

The elder Ānanda then thought: "If I pass into nirvāṇa here, King Ajātaśatru and the Vriji-subduer will quarrel with one another, and the people of Vaiśālī will not receive a share of the relics. If I pass into nirvāṇa in Vaiśālī, those others will not receive a share either. Therefore let me pass into nirvāṇa in the middle of the river Gaṅgā." And so he went there.

Now King Ajātaśatru dreamed that he saw the handle of the parasol held over the king become cracked. He woke in terror, and his doorkeeper told him: "O god, the elder Ānanda is about to pass into nirvāṇa."

On hearing this the king fainted and fell. After a time he was revived with water, regained his senses, and the king said: "Where is the venerable Ānanda passing into nirvāṇa?"

The venerable Śāṇavāsin replied:

Great King, this one who arose manifestly as the devoted son who followed the Blessed One,
the certain guardian of the treasury of the holy Dharma,
who brought conditioned existence to cessation, of utterly pure intelligence —
he has gone forth manifestly to the city of Vaiśālī.

Then King Ajātaśatru armed a fourfold host of troops and marched to the bank of the river Gaṅgā. And the gods addressed the people of Vaiśālī:

The noble Ānanda, lamp of wandering beings,
showed compassion to the multitude of common folk.
This sage, having dispelled the darkness of sorrow,
has gone to Vaiśālī, firm and at peace.

Then the Licchavīs of Vaiśālī likewise armed a fourfold host and came to the bank of the river Gaṅgā. The elder Ānanda, meanwhile, had boarded a boat and was seated in the middle of the river Gaṅgā.

Then King Ajātaśatru prostrated at the feet of the elder Ānanda, touching his head to the ground, and spoke:

His eyes as wide-open as a lotus of a hundred petals, the awakened one of Vaiśālī —
he who was the lamp of the three realms of existence, now gone to peace.
We have come to you for refuge; yet if you are going to peace,
come back here for our sake — let your body linger here awhile.

The people of Vaiśālī spoke likewise. And then the venerable Ānanda gave rise to this thought:

If I leave my body in the town of Māgadhā,
the Licchavīs will certainly fall into suffering.
If I leave my body in the city of the Vajjians,
the lord of Māgadhā will surely be displeased.
Therefore I shall give half my body to the lord of men,
and give half my body to the assembly —
and thus, for both of them alike,
it will become a worthy object of veneration forever.

At the very moment the elder Ānanda passed into nirvāṇa, the great earth shook in six ways. At that time another ascetic (ṛṣi), accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, came by supernormal power to where the venerable Ānanda was. Joining his palms together in reverence, he addressed the elder Ānanda: "We wish to go forth and receive full ordination in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and to be established in the state of a fully ordained monk."

No sooner had the elder Ānanda given rise to the thought — "Let the disciples come together and approach me" — than, even as he formed that intention, five hundred disciples arrived there. The elder Ānanda conjured solid ground in the middle of the river, rendering it impassable by boat.

Thereupon the five hundred ascetics who had gone forth and requested full ordination — all five hundred attained the fruit of non-return. Having declared the third karma ceremony and abandoned all afflictions, they attained the fruit of arhatship. Since they had gone forth in the middle of the river Gaṅgā, at the midpoint between sun and water — some in the midst of the river and some at the solar midpoint — they became known accordingly. Having accomplished what was to be done, they prostrated at the feet of the venerable Ānanda, touching their heads to the ground, and spoke: "The Blessed One last ordained the foremost Supriya and then passed into nirvāṇa first. Now please, preceptor, grant us your command — for we too are about to pass into nirvāṇa before you, and we have no wish to witness the preceptor's own passing into nirvāṇa."

The elder replied: "Children, the Blessed One, having entrusted the teaching to the venerable Mahākāśyapa, passed into nirvāṇa. The elder Mahākāśyapa in turn entrusted it to me. Now, as I am about to pass into nirvāṇa, you must guard this teaching well. The Blessed One prophesied concerning the land of Kaśmīr as follows: 'The land of Kaśmīr is supremely suited to meditative concentration and is the finest of dwelling places.' And the Blessed One also prophesied: 'One hundred years after my nirvāṇa, a fully ordained monk called Madhyāntika will arise, and he will establish the teaching there.' Therefore, children, you too should take up the teaching." They replied: "We shall do so."

Then the venerable Ānanda began to display various miraculous manifestations. The people of Māgadha wept with compassion, calling out: "O Protector, come back to us!" The Vajjians too wept with compassion, calling out: "O Protector, come back to us!" Both peoples on either bank of the river cried out these words. Hearing them, the one of great wisdom divided his former body in two.

Then the venerable Ānanda, his body transformed by blessing, displayed various miraculous manifestations, and, like water being cast into fire, he passed into nirvāṇa. Half his body was received by the people of Vaiśālī, and half was obtained by King Ajātaśatru, who then declared:

With the sharp vajra of wisdom
he cleft the mountain of his own body.
Half he gave to the lord of men,
and half the Sage gave to the assembly.

Thereupon the Licchavīs erected a stūpa in Vaiśālī and established it there. And King Ajātaśatru likewise erected a stūpa at the southern gate of the city and established it there.

Then the thought arose in the venerable Madhyantika that his own preceptor had charged him, saying, "Go and establish the Dharma in the land of Kashmir." The Blessed One had likewise prophesied: "There shall arise a monk named Madhyantika, who will subdue the nāgas (Skt. nāga) hostile to humans in the land of Kashmir and establish the Dharma there." And so, thinking, "I must fulfil the Teacher's intention entirely," the venerable Madhyantika journeyed to the land of Kashmir and sat down cross-legged.

Then Madhyantika, intending to overpower the nāgas of Kashmir and thinking, "If I agitate those nāgas, they will be tamed," entered into the appropriate meditative absorption. The land of Kashmir shook in six ways, and the nāgas, disturbed and furiously enraged, unleashed fierce hailstorms and advanced to do harm to the elder. But the elder entered into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, and the nāgas were unable to stir even the hem of the elder's Dharma robe.

Next the nāgas sent a rain of arrows, and the elder caused shining flowers to fall — blue lotuses, red lotuses, kumuda lotuses, and white lotuses. The nāgas began to hurl single-pointed vajras, great bolts, single-tipped weapons, and enemy-axes, and upon the elder there rained down a shower of kusuma flowers, as they declared in verse:

Just as the peak of a snow mountain,
melted wholly by the sun's radiance,
is seen to vanish entirely away,
so too let all the mountain peaks be gone.

Raining down a shower of silk banners,
making fall a varied rain of kusuma flowers,
raining from the sky a shower of arrows —
all transformed into garlands of blossoms wherever they settled.

Then, through the elder's entering into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, fire did not burn his body, weapons could not pierce him, and poison could not touch him. The nāgas were filled with wonder.

The nāgas then approached the elder and said, "Noble one, what do you command?" The elder said, "Give me this place." The nāgas replied, "We do not grudge to give it." The elder said, "This place was prophesied by the Blessed One as my residence: inasmuch as this land of Kashmir is a dwelling suited to meditation, from this day forward it is mine." The nāgas said, "Did the Blessed One truly declare this?" The elder replied, "The Blessed One declared it." The nāgas asked, "How large a place shall we give?" The elder answered, "Only so much as I occupy sitting cross-legged." The nāgas said, "Venerable one, we shall give it," and the elder, sitting cross-legged, pressed down with his crossed legs upon the confluence of nine valleys. The nāgas then asked, "How great a retinue does the elder possess?" The elder thought, "How many monks will gather?" and reckoning, "Perhaps five hundred arhats," the elder declared: "Five hundred arhats." The nāgas said, "So be it — but if even a single arhat is missing, then at that time we shall reclaim the land of Kashmir for ourselves." The elder Madhyantika then said to the nāgas of Kashmir: "That being so, yet since wherever a patron dwells there must be recipients to receive offerings, I shall also bring in householders." The nāgas said, "So be it." And the elder himself established villages, towns, and districts, and groups of people entered in. These people then asked the elder, "How shall we prosper?"

Thereupon the elder led the assembled people to the saffron fields, told them to go in and harvest saffron, and they did so. But the nāgas of the saffron fields grew enraged. The elder then tamed them as well, and they declared: "How long will the teaching of the Blessed One endure?" The elder replied, "One thousand years." The nāgas then pledged: "For as long as the teaching of the Blessed One endures, we shall allow it to remain." The elder said, "So be it," and then he consecrated Kashmir for the planting of saffron.

Now, in the space of a single day, the elder established the teaching of the Blessed One in Kashmir, spread it widely, and gladdened both householders and those who lived the holy life by performing miraculous displays of many kinds. Then, like fire quenched by water, he passed into nirvāṇa, and his body was burned with supreme sandalwood and aloe and other such fragrant woods, and a stūpa was built and set in place.

After that, the venerable Śāṇavāsin himself gave the going-forth to the venerable Upagupta, spread the teaching broadly, and said to him: "Venerable Upagupta, know this: the Blessed One entrusted the teaching to the venerable Mahākāśyapa and passed into complete nirvāṇa; the venerable Mahākāśyapa entrusted the teaching to his preceptor and passed into complete nirvāṇa; my preceptor entrusted the teaching to me and passed into complete nirvāṇa. My son, I too shall now pass into complete nirvāṇa. Henceforth you must guard the teaching well and apply yourself diligently to all that the Blessed One has declared."

Thereupon the venerable Śāṇavāsin gladdened both householders and those who lived the holy life by performing miraculous displays of many kinds — blazing with fire, burning, causing rain to fall, and causing lightning to strike — and passed into complete nirvāṇa in the element that leaves no aggregates remaining.

The elder Upagupta then transmitted the teaching's purpose to the venerable Dhītika; the venerable Dhītika to the venerable Kṛṣṇa; and the venerable Kṛṣṇa to the venerable Sudarśana. In this way those great elephants passed into complete nirvāṇa.

One hundred and ten years had passed since the Blessed One, the fully awakened one, had passed into complete nirvāṇa, and the sun of the Victor had set. The monks of Vaiśālī then overstepped ten improper rules — transgressing the sūtras, transgressing the Vinaya, departing from the teaching of the Teacher, not in accord with the sūtras, not appearing in the Vinaya, contradicting the nature of reality — and they presented these as proper, practiced them, and actively followed them. As for what these ten were:

The monks of Vaiśālī made allowable a practice called "A-la-la," and then, both in discord and in accord, they acted contrary to the Dharma, and in a state of discord performed Dharmic acts. This is the first rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, contradicted the nature of reality, and which the monks of Vaiśālī presented as proper, practiced, and actively followed.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī urged the resident monks, saying, "Venerable ones, you should rejoice along with us — come, rejoice with us," and having induced them to rejoice and having made such rejoicing allowable, they then, both in discord and in accord, acted contrary to the Dharma, and in a state of discord performed Dharmic acts. This is the second rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, and did not appear in the Vinaya.

and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī made it allowable to dig the ground and have others dig it with their own hands. This is the third rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī mixed salt that had been consecrated for lifetime use together with salt that was allowable only at the proper time, consumed it, and declared that mixed salt was allowable. This is the fourth rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī traveled a league and a half, assembled together, ate a meal, and declared that eating in such a manner while on the road was allowable. This is the fifth rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī ate food and provisions that had not been set aside as a remainder, doing so by means of a two-fingered gesture, and then declared that the two-fingered practice was allowable. This is the sixth rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī strained fermented drink through a water-straining cloth as though filtering through a lotus, drank it, and declared it allowable for the sick. This is the seventh rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī churned together a full measure of milk and a full measure of curds, ate them outside the proper time, and declared that what had been mixed in this way was allowable. This is the eighth rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of the city of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī took an old sitting mat that was trimmed with a border the width of a Sugata's span, used it without replacing it with a new mat, and declared that the use of such a sitting mat was allowable. This is the ninth rule, one that overstepped the sūtras, overstepped the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, was not in accord with the sūtras, did not appear in the Vinaya, and was contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Furthermore, the monks of Vaiśālī took their round and pure alms bowls — ones fit for use — washed and rinsed them, perfumed them with fine incense, adorned them with various sweet-smelling flowers, placed them on a throne-cushion atop a seat, and then set them out on the main road, at the market, and

at the four crossroads, and made this proclamation: "Let the many people who have come from various towns and cities and are dwelling in Vaiśālī — let those who are wise listen! This is a fine alms bowl. Give here, give generously! Whoever makes an offering into it, by that act of offering they will obtain great fruit, great benefit, great striving, and great breadth of result." And having thus acquired and obtained silver, gold, and other precious things, they made use of them and treated gold and silver as permissible. This was beyond the sūtras, beyond the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, not appearing in the sūtras, not evident in the Vinaya, and contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, the monks of Vaiśālī presented as allowable what was not allowable, and practiced and actively followed it.

Now at that time, the venerable Ānanda was dwelling in Vaiśālī, and dwelling alongside him was an elder called Sarvatrāma — an arhat who cultivated the eight liberations — and he lived there humbly, in modest circumstances. And in the city of Kosambi there was an elder named Yaśas who likewise dwelt together with others, who was also an arhat who cultivated the eight liberations. He was traveling about with a retinue of five hundred, wandering through the countryside, and he came to the city of Vaiśālī. When the various gains were being distributed upon his arrival, the monastery steward said to him: "Elder, the gains of the elder Saṅgha have been distributed — please take your share." He replied: "Venerable one, what gains have arisen, and who gave them?" The steward described it in detail, and Yaśas then reflected: "Is this solitary incident the only one of its kind, or are there others as well?" He then saw that the slackening of the training and the practice of all ten non-allowable matters was growing, and, wishing to make the teaching endure, he went to where the venerable Sarvatrāma was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the venerable Sarvatrāma's feet and said to him: "Elder, is it allowable — the thing they are calling allowable with the word 'Alala'?
