Venerable one, what is this that they call 'allowable by the Alala [word]'? Elder, the monks of Vaiśālī perform Dharma-acts by non-conformity through what is not Dharma by non-conformity, and what is not Dharma by conformity, and they make it allowable saying 'Alala.'"

Vinaya: minor matters, fascicle fifty-nine. The venerable one: it is not allowable. The elder: it was established at the city of Campā. What it depends on: the group of six monks. What transgression it becomes: an offense of wrongdoing. This elder matter is beyond the first root sūtras, beyond the Vinaya, departed from the teaching of the Teacher, not appearing in the sūtras, not evident in the Vinaya, and contrary to the nature of reality. With respect to these, if the monks of Vaiśālī present as allowable what is not allowable, and practice and actively follow it, then he said to them: "Have you set aside your equanimity over such things?" And they said nothing in reply.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is this practice of making things allowable by the word of approval — 'allowable by approval' — itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'allowable by approval'? Elder, the monks of Vaiśālī perform Dharma-acts by non-conformity through what is not Dharma by non-conformity, and what is not Dharma by conformity, and by non-conformity perform Dharma-acts, saying, 'Let the venerable ones approve by approval!' — and they cause the surrounding monks to approve and make things allowable by approval."

"Elder, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In the city of Vaiśālī." "On the basis of whom?" "On the basis of the six groups of monks." "What transgression does it entail?" "A wrongdoing."

"Elder, this is the second basis. It has gone beyond the sūtras, gone beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not enter into the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality. Regarding these matters, when the monks of Vaiśālī fully teach what is not allowable as allowable and practice it and thoroughly practice it — did you remain in equanimity toward all that?" And the elder said nothing.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is this practice of making things allowable by communal practice itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'allowable by communal practice'? Elder, the monks of Vaiśālī dig the ground and excavate it with their own hands, and make it allowable by communal practice."

"Venerable one, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In Śrāvastī." "On the basis of whom?" "On the basis of the six groups of monks." "What transgression does it entail?" "A transgression entailing expiation."

"Elder, this is the third basis. It has gone beyond the sūtras, gone beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not enter into the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality. Regarding these matters, when the monks of Vaiśālī fully teach what is not allowable as allowable and practice it and thoroughly practice it — did you remain in equanimity toward that?" And the elder said nothing.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is this practice of making salt allowable itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'allowable salt'? Elder, the monks of Vaiśālī mix salt that is allowable at its proper time together with other salt and consume it throughout their entire lives, and in this way make salt allowable at its time."

"Venerable one, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In Rājagṛha." "On the basis of whom?" "On the basis of the venerable Śāriputra." "What transgression does it entail?" "A transgression entailing expiation."

"Elder, this is the fourth basis. It has gone beyond the sūtras, gone beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not enter into the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality. Regarding these matters, when the monks of Vaiśālī fully teach what is not allowable as allowable and practice it and thoroughly practice it — did you remain in equanimity toward that?" And the elder said nothing.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is this practice of making things allowable by the road itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'allowable by the road'? Elder, the monks of Vaiśālī travel a league and a half, gather together, eat their meal, and then make things allowable by the road."

"Venerable one, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In Rājagṛha." "On the basis of whom?" "On the basis of Deva-datta." "What transgression does it entail?" "A transgression entailing expiation."

"Elder, this is the fifth basis. It has gone beyond the sūtras, gone beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not enter into the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality. Regarding these matters, when the monks of Vaiśālī fully teach what is not allowable as allowable and practice it and thoroughly practice it — did you remain in equanimity toward that?" And the elder said nothing.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is this practice of making things allowable by two fingers itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'allowable by two fingers'? Elder, the monks of Vaiśālī eat food and drink that has not been formally made a remainder — making it allowable by two fingers — and after eating they make things allowable by two fingers."

"Venerable one, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In Śrāvastī." "On the basis of whom?"

"On the basis of many monks." "What transgression does it incur?" "It incurs a transgression." "Elder, this sixth point goes beyond the sūtras, goes beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not appear in the sūtras, is not found in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality. To teach openly and practice habitually that what is not allowable is allowable — as those monks of Vaiśālī do in regard to these matters — did you remain in equanimity toward that?" And he said nothing.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is the practice of making things allowable for the sick itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'making allowable for the sick'? Elder, the monks of Vaiśālī filter fermented drink through a lotus-fibre strainer and drink it, then make it allowable as medicine for the sick." "Venerable one, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In Śrāvastī." "On the basis of whom?" "On the basis of the venerable Legsong." "What transgression does it incur?" "It incurs a transgression." "Elder, this seventh point is the same as the earlier ones."

"It is for that very reason that I make this request. Is the practice of making things allowable by mixing itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'making allowable by mixing'? Elder, this is how it is: the monks of Vaiśālī stir together a full measure of milk and a full measure of curds and eat it at an improper time, making it allowable by means of the mixing." "Venerable one, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In Śrāvastī." "On the basis of whom?" "On the basis of many monks." "What transgression does it incur?" "It incurs a transgression." "Elder, this eighth point goes beyond the sūtras, goes beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not appear in the sūtras, is not found in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality. To teach openly and practice habitually that what is not allowable is allowable — as those monks of Vaiśālī do in regard to these matters — did you remain in equanimity toward that?" And he said nothing.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is the practice of making things allowable by means of a seat-mat itself allowable? Venerable one, what is this that they call 'making allowable by means of a seat-mat'? Elder, this is how it is: the monks of Vaiśālī make use of an old seat-mat whose circumference measures a Sugata's span, without patching its worn border, and make it allowable on account of the mat." "Venerable one, it is not allowable." "Where was it established?" "In Śrāvastī." "On the basis of whom?" "On the basis of many monks." "What transgression does it incur?" "It incurs a transgression." "Elder, this ninth point goes beyond the sūtras, goes beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not appear in the sūtras, is not found in the Vinaya, and contradicts the nature of reality. To teach openly and practice habitually that what is not allowable is allowable — as those monks of Vaiśālī do in regard to these matters — did you remain in equanimity toward that?" And he said nothing.

Then he said: "Elder, it is for that very reason that I make this request. Is the practice of making things allowable by means of gold and silver itself allowable? What is this that they call 'making allowable by means of gold and silver'? Elder, this is how it is: the monks of Vaiśālī take alms-bowls that are round and clean and fit for use, smear them with lac, fumigate them with fine-smelling incense, adorn them with various fragrant and beautiful flowers, place them on a small throne with a cushion-seat upon the head of a monastic, and then circulate through the main roads, the marketplaces, and the crossroads, proclaiming aloud these words: 'Let the wise persons dwelling in Vaiśālī who have come from various towns and regions, listen!'

'This alms-bowl is a fine alms-bowl. Whoever gives here, gives abundantly, or pours offerings into it, will obtain great fruit, great benefit, great endeavor, and great extent of result.' By these words, coins, gold, and other precious things were obtained and received, and they lived off those and used gold and silver to make things allowable.

Elder, that is not allowable.

Where is this established? In the Vinaya, in the sections treating the offenses requiring abandonment and in the scriptures dealing with proper conduct; it is included among what the Buddha has taught; it is found in the Norbu on the Crown sūtras; it occurs in the longer scriptural transmissions; it belongs to the collection dealing with moral discipline; it is in the middle-length scriptures; it occurs in paired scriptures; it appears in the Strengthening sūtras; in scriptures derived from the one preceding; and in those belonging to the fourth and fifth. From whom does it depend? From the group of six monks, from other monks, and from householders. This elder, then, exceeds the text of the Ten Grounds Sūtra, exceeds the Vinaya, and is separated from the teaching of the Teacher; it does not accord with the sūtras, it does not appear in the Vinaya, and it contradicts the nature of reality. Fully expounding these points to them and putting them into constant and thorough practice — are you going to remain indifferent to this? Go now, Elder, and search for an ally, and I shall assist you in accordance with the Dharma.

The elder replied that he would do just so. The venerable Yaśas, having heard that elder comply with all that was desired, then entered into and remained in the most excellent meditative absorption and abided there.

At that time, in the city of Norcan, the venerable elder Cayala was residing together with the venerable Ānanda — an arhat who cultivated the eight liberations. Then the venerable Yaśas went to where the venerable Cayala was, arrived there, and having prostrated with his head at the venerable Cayala's feet, spoke these words: 'Elder, is making allowable by means of "A-la-la" allowable? What is this that is called making allowable by "A-la-la"? Elder, in Vaiśālī the monks of Vaiśālī, by means of a discordant act that is not in accordance with the Dharma, or a concordant act that is not in accordance with the Dharma, or a discordant act performed as a legal act of the Saṅgha, make things allowable by declaring "A-la-la."'

Elder, that is not allowable. Where is this established? In Campā. From whom does it depend? From the group of six monks. What transgression does it become? A wrongdoing. This elder, then, exceeds the text of the first ground sūtra, exceeds the Vinaya, and is separated from the teaching of the Teacher; it does not accord with the sūtras, it does not appear in the Vinaya, and it contradicts the nature of reality. Fully expounding these points to them and putting them into constant and thorough practice — are you going to remain indifferent to this? Elder, therefore I ask: is it allowable to express approval? What is this that is called the venerable one expressing approval? — and so on, as before, with the ten points set out in detail.

Then he said: Go and seek an ally, and I shall take sides in accordance with the Dharma.

Then the venerable Yaśas prostrated with his head at the venerable Cayala's feet and went to the city called Sāṃkāśya.

At that time in the city called Sāṃkāśya, the venerable elder Dhanakas was residing together with the venerable Ānanda — an arhat who cultivated the eight liberations. Then the venerable Yaśas prostrated with his head at the venerable Dhanakas's feet and spoke to the venerable Dhanakas these words:

"Elder, is the expression of approval by saying 'Alala' permissible? Venerable one, what does it mean to express approval by saying 'Alala'? Elder, in the city of Vaiśālī, the monks of Vaiśālī perform a monastic act without harmony and without Dharma, or with harmony but without Dharma, or with disharmony in performing a Dharma act, and then express approval by saying 'Alala.' Venerable one, it is not permissible. Where was it established? In Campā. On what basis? From the group of six monks. What is the transgression? A wrongdoing. Elder, this first basis goes beyond the sūtras, goes beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not accord with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and is contrary to the nature of reality. Given that the monks of Vaiśālī are fully teaching and practicing what is not permissible as though it were permissible, will you remain indifferent to this? Elder, for this very reason I make this request: is it permissible to express approval by saying 'Alala' through rejoicing? Venerable one, what does it mean to express approval through rejoicing?" — and so on, as before, setting out the ten points in detail.

Then he said: Go and seek an ally, and I shall take sides in accordance with the Dharma.

Then the venerable Yaśas prostrated with his head at the venerable Dhanakas's feet and went to the city called Sāṃkāśya. At that time in the city called Sāṃkāśya, the venerable Priyadatta and the venerable Zlagur were residing there, and at that time they had entered into the meditative absorption of cessation. Then the venerable Yaśas set out the ten points in detail to the venerable Priyadatta, prostrated with his head at the venerable Priyadatta's feet, and went on to Srughna. At that time in Srughna, the venerable Aparājita was residing there, and he set out the ten points in detail to him as well, then prostrated with his head at his feet and went on to Mahela. At that time in Mahela, the venerable Sambhūtasanavāsin was residing there, and he set out the ten points in detail to him as well, then prostrated with his head at his feet and went on to Sahajāta. At that time in Sahajāta, the venerable Namgru was residing there, and he prostrated with his head at that elder's feet and said:

"Elder, is the expression of approval by saying 'Alala' permissible? Venerable one, what does it mean to express approval by saying 'Alala'? Elder, in Vaiśālī, the monks of Vaiśālī perform a monastic act without harmony and without Dharma, or with harmony but without Dharma, or with disharmony in performing a Dharma act, and then express approval by saying 'Alala.' Venerable one, it is not permissible. Where was it established? In Campā. On what basis? From the group of six. What is the transgression? A wrongdoing. Elder, this first basis goes beyond the sūtras, goes beyond the Vinaya, is divorced from the Teacher's teaching, does not accord with the sūtras, does not appear in the Vinaya, and is contrary to the nature of reality. Given that the monks of Vaiśālī are fully teaching and practicing what is not permissible as though it were permissible, will you remain indifferent to this? Elder, for this very reason I make this request: is it permissible to express approval by saying 'Alala' through rejoicing? Venerable one, what does it mean to express approval through rejoicing?" — and so on, as before, setting out the ten points in detail.

Now the venerable Namgru, wondering whether this venerable one had first come to him or had gone elsewhere, and then seeing that he had indeed gone to others as well, thought to himself: This venerable one has come from a long journey and must be weary; I shall let him rest and go out myself to seek allies. With this in mind, he spoke to the venerable Yaśas:

"Venerable Yaśas, you have come from a long journey and must be weary; rest here, and I shall go out to seek allies." With these words he let him rest, and the venerable Namgru departed to seek allies.

Then the monks of Vaiśālī went to the monk who was the attendant dwelling with the venerable Yaśas, came to him, and asked: "Venerable one, where has the venerable one's preceptor gone?" He replied: "The venerable one has gone to seek allies." "But why has he gone to seek allies?" "Because he intends to carry out a formal act of expulsion against us from our residence." "What must we do to prevent him from carrying out this formal act of expulsion against us?" He explained it to them at length. And they said: "Venerable one, what he is doing is not right. If such and such things are permissible to live by according to the scriptures of the Teacher who has passed away, why should we be thought inferior? Then someone else, from among them, with an honest mind and well-meaning words, spoke to them: "Venerable ones, you are behaving in a way that is discordant, improper, and unbecoming of ascetics. It was heard before that the Blessed One's teaching would endure for a thousand years; yet now you are engaged in conduct that makes the future teaching itself invisible — and just as others too have entered into lax training and produced these bubble-like formations, it is precisely in order to preserve the teaching that a formal act of expulsion is certainly being undertaken against you." Upon hearing this, they were frightened and, losing their courage, sat in silence.

Then they began to pass the news from one to another: "The venerable Yaśas has gone seeking allies and intends to carry out a formal act of expulsion against us — why do we sit here with such faint hearts? Tell us how we should proceed." Then one of them said: "What is there to accomplish? If he has gone seeking allies, we too can seek allies. Why should we be the ones to leave?" Another said: "Let us flee and go away before we come into conflict with that venerable one." Another said: "But wherever we go, the same fault will follow us there in the same way. We should ask for pardon." Another said: "We cannot ask for pardon; we are already hemmed in on all sides." Another said: "Here is what we should do: all those many attendants who dwell with him have their alms-bowls, robes, nets, bowls, and belts gathered together — let us bind them up and put them away somewhere to be retrieved later." Another said: "Good, let it be so." And so they distributed things among themselves: to some they gave a patched robe; to some they gave an upper robe; to some they gave a lower robe; to some they gave a sweat-cloth; to some they gave a sitting cloth; to some they gave an alms-bowl; and to some they gave a water-strainer. In this way they gathered everything together and took up a position in the middle.

Now by the time the venerable Yaśas had gradually sought allies and returned to Vaiśālī, his attendants who had come with him arrived there but had not yet entered the town of Vaiśālī — they were resting from the journey — when those attendants said to him: "Preceptor, were those allies found? Master, they will come without long delay. Well sought, preceptor." He thought: "Such a disposition as that is one to be entirely turned away. If such and such things are permissible to live by according to the scriptures of the Teacher who has passed away, why should I do harm to those people?" Then he thought: "What were those unprecedented words they spoke? Certainly these ones must have taken possession of what belongs to those others" — and realizing this,

The venerable ones spoke words without precedent, saying: "The venerable ones have taken into their own possession what belongs to those others" — and upon saying this, those others sat in complete silence.

Then the venerable Yaśas spoke in verse to those who had deliberated together with him:

Since the aspects of laxity in the training have multiplied,
it is fitting that they be distant from what is proper —
do not neglect the purpose of the teaching.

Whoever neglects what is proper, makes distance fitting, makes laxity fitting,
who utterly abandons right conduct — that childish one goes to suffering.
He is one abandoned by fortunate companions of good repute.
His benefit does not increase, like the moon in its waning fortnight.

Whoever thinks in accordance with that intention, who is wise, who does not neglect,
who abandons what is not proper — that skilled one attains happiness.
He will not be abandoned by companions who are fortunate and of good repute.
His benefit increases, like the moon in its waxing fortnight.

Then the venerable Yaśas entered the walking hall of the monastery and, entering into meditative absorption in the four dhyānas perfected to their ultimate degree, he surveyed with aspiration and examined through his knowledge. When the wooden signal board was struck, all of those — the arhats falling one short of seven hundred — who were dwelling together with the venerable Ānanda assembled.

At that time, however, the venerable Candragiri had entered into the meditative absorption of cessation and did not hear the sound of the board. Then, when the community of monks had gathered and assembled, the venerable Yaśas thought: "If I were to call out those ones by name, it would cause great disruption — therefore I will speak without naming them by name." So thinking, he bowed in order of seniority, and standing to the side of the eldest with hands joined in reverence, he took his seat.

Since the arhats fell one short of seven hundred and it was desired to fulfil that number, at that moment the venerable Candragiri too rose from his meditative absorption in cessation. Then a god said to him: "Noble Candragiri, why do you remain with a mind of lesser scope? Those arhats who share your preceptor, falling one short of seven hundred, are gathering together in Vaiśālī in order to establish the teaching — you should go quickly." With that, by means of miraculous power, he vanished from the city of Kuśāgāra and traveled to Vaiśālī, where he sat at the gate of the walking hall of the monastery and knocked at the door.

The monks asked: "Who are you?"

He spoke in verse:

Among those dwelling in Kuśāgāra —
monks learned in much scripture, upholders of the Vinaya —
one other than those has arrived here:
one called Conqueror of the Faculties stands at the gate.

The monks said: "There are others called Conqueror of the Faculties as well — tell us who you are."

He again spoke in verse:

Among those dwelling in Kuśāgāra —
ascetics learned in much scripture, upholders of the Vinaya —
one other than those has arrived here:
one called Doubt-Severer stands at the gate.

The monks said: "There are others called Doubt-Severer as well."

He again spoke in verse:

Among those dwelling in Kuśāgāra —
ascetics learned in much scripture, upholders of the Vinaya —
one other than those has arrived here:
one called Without-Remorse stands at the gate.

The monks said: "There are others called Without-Remorse as well — tell us who you are."

He again spoke in verse:

Among those dwelling in Kuśāgāra —
ascetics learned in much scripture, upholders of the Vinaya —
one other than those has arrived here:
one called Candragiri stands at the gate.

The monks said: "Welcome, welcome — please come inside."

He entered inside. The monks then came out from the surrounding courtyard and circumambulated the venerable Candragiri as a mark of respect. After that they entered the courtyard and took their seats, each in his proper place. The venerable Yaśas then formally recited the ten points before those seated in order of seniority, saying: "Venerable ones, is it permissible to give approval by the exclamation 'Alala'? What is meant by 'approval by the exclamation Alala'? Venerable ones, there are certain monks who have performed what is contrary to the Dharma through discord, what is contrary to the Dharma through concord, and what constitutes a formal act of the Saṅgha contrary to the Dharma through discord, and thereby give approval by the exclamation 'Alala.' Venerable ones, this is not permissible. Where was it established? At Campā. On what basis? In connection with the group of six monks. What transgression does it constitute? A wrongdoing. Venerable ones, this first point departs from the sūtras and departs from the Vinaya; it is severed from the Teacher's dispensation, it finds no entry in the sūtras, it finds no place in the Vinaya, and it is at variance with the nature of reality. Regarding these matters, the monks of Vaiśālī have proclaimed publicly that what is not permissible is permissible, practiced and continued to practice it — these we shall reject. Venerable ones, that being so, we now put this question to the others: is it permissible to give approval by rejoicing?"

Up to the phrase "What is meant by giving approval by rejoicing?" the ten points were then set forth in full just as before. Having recited them correctly, they came out from the surrounding courtyard, and then after the gong had been struck and the monks dwelling in Vaiśālī had gathered together in a body, seated together with them, the venerable Yaśas once again, before those seated in order of seniority, began to recite the ten points by name, saying: "Venerable ones, is it permissible to give approval by the exclamation 'Alala'? What is meant by giving approval by the exclamation 'Alala'? Venerable ones, the monks of Vaiśālī have performed what is contrary to the Dharma through discord, what is contrary to the Dharma through concord, and what constitutes a formal act of the Saṅgha contrary to the Dharma through discord, and thereby give approval by the exclamation 'Alala.' Venerable ones, this is not permissible. Where was it established? At Campā. On what basis? In connection with the group of six monks. What transgression does it constitute? A wrongdoing. Venerable ones, this first point departs from the sūtras and departs from the Vinaya; it is severed from the Teacher's dispensation, it finds no entry in the sūtras, it finds no place in the Vinaya, and it is at variance with the nature of reality. Regarding these matters, the monks of Vaiśālī have proclaimed publicly that what is not permissible is permissible, practiced and continued to practice it — these we shall reject. Venerable ones, that being so, we now put this question: is it permissible to give approval by rejoicing? What is meant by giving approval by rejoicing?"

Up to this phrase, the ten points were set forth in full just as before, together with the conclusion "these we shall reject." When the seven hundred arhats had thus recited it correctly, it became known by the name "The Correct Recitation by Seven Hundred," "The Correct Recitation by Seven Hundred," "The Correct Recitation by Seven Hundred."

A summary verse:

The Alala, the practice of approval by rejoicing,
the examination, the salt, the path,
the two-finger permission, the stirring, and the certainty,
and the matter of gold and silver — these are the true summary of the intermediate section.

The city of Vaiśālī and the possessor of wealth,
the one descended from the gods and likewise the red-robed one,
Sarvagāmin and the one who possesses a buffalo,
and the one who arose simultaneously — these are the latter ones.

All those of Doṣa, of Yaśas, of Guile,
of Dhaniya, and of Priya,
Candragiri and likewise Aparājita,
Samudra, Nāvagiri, and the rest.

Here, the commentary has completed what is called the Eighth Chapter of Karmagroups, fulfilling all eight chapters. The Vinaya of the Minor Matters (Skt. kṣudrakavastu) is complete.

This was translated by the Indian masters Vidyākaraprabha and Dharmaśrīprabha, together with the Tibetan translator, the monk Paljyor.

At the time this Vinaya Scripture of the Minor Matters was translated, many translators divided it into many portions and rendered each portion separately. When these were compiled into a volume, the sections became scattered in the wrong order and were assembled in an incomplete state, so that much of the Scripture of the Minor Matters remained deficient. Later, when the Elder Dharmasiṃha, residing at the temple of La-stod Ol-rgod, erected the four canonical collections, the virtuous spiritual friend and great Vinaya-holder Byang-chub Seng-ge undertook the practical work. He searched with great effort and the offering of manuscript fees among those dwelling in temples throughout Ü and Tsang in general, and in particular among those at Samyé and Chimpu — including the junior monk Dagchungwa and the monk Tsulkrim Yönten — for the copies they had obtained, and by comparing the texts against one another, those passages of the Scripture of the Minor Matters that were absent from some copies but present in others were used to fill the gaps and restore the text. What was supplied and corrected amounts to this: beginning from the passage in the thirty-third fascicle (Skt. bāmpo), in the context of the story of the Great Physician, where the Great Physician says, "If that is so, vomit it out! Let us see whether it is true or false" — and continuing to the beginning of the thirty-fourth fascicle — one fascicle that had been cut was restored. As for the verse summary: below the line "I too, by the medicine, it was likewise" — one line that had been cut was restored. Then, at the end of the thirty-fourth fascicle, upon the completion of the context of the conduct of the Niṭhyodha — from the passage "Alas, to have met one such as you who is truly learned is a blessing for one who possesses merit" — continuing to the upper portion of the forty-third fascicle — this is the general summary. The gap from the lower portion of the thirty-fourth fascicle to the upper portion of the forty-third fascicle — nine fascicles that had been cut — were restored. Below that summary verse, one line of the summary verse that had been cut was restored. Then, at the end of the forty-sixth fascicle, in the context of the narrative episode of the brahmin boy Masdug: from the passage "Such a return from that kind of wrong livelihood, the crooked practice of those ascetics" — continuing to the beginning of the forty-eighth fascicle, where it reads: "Then at that time, the brahmin Padmasnying-po was gathered and assembled together with the elder brahmins at a high and prominent place of a great householder" — the forty-seventh fascicle, which had been cut, was restored. Then, at the end of the fiftieth fascicle, in the context of the instruction given to Ānanda: from the passage "Ānanda, a monk of this kind should dwell with oneself as an island, oneself as a refuge, the Dharma as an island, and the Dharma as a refuge — not with another island, not with another refuge" — continuing to the upper portion of the fifty-second fascicle — this is the intermediate summary. From the passage ending "Capāla and performing the conditioning factors of life" — one fascicle that had been cut was restored.

In total, what was supplied amounts to twelve fascicles and two lines of summary verse. This very restoration has become the crown jewel of the great Elders of the Tibetan lineage who hold their vows and are learned. It was accomplished by Chimpa Thams-cad Mkhyen-pa — a monk of the Śākya order who holds the Vinaya, the Sūtras, and the mother of the Piṭakas, whose maṇḍala of knowledge extends across the sky of all that is to be known, and whose rays of renown pervade every direction.

A manuscript copy was summoned from the great temple of Ol-god in Upper Latö, and at the glorious temple of Narthang — that source and wellspring of the Dharma — a pure and complete edition was compiled encompassing all four scriptural divisions. From that very edition a copy was made, and in particular a copy was made of those very supplementary passages that had filled the missing portions. Then, summoning the manuscript copy of the Kangyur compiled by the Śākya monk Jampa'i Dbyangs, the glorious community of Victors, in order to cause the teaching of the Victor to spread and flourish in every direction and at all times, compiled at the glorious temple of Gung-thang a full and complete set of these supplementary scriptural portions — which supply what is missing in the great Sage's word, in the root canonical texts, in the two divisions of the monastic codes of monks and nuns, and in the principal treatises. Those who subsequently compile scriptural editions should also write the fascicle-count in sequence from the beginning of each aṣṭaka, just as the numbering is given here.

Here abides the Vinaya.

Translator's notes

The three opening summary verses are standard mnemonic verse-summaries of chapters to come. Their translation necessarily requires supplying some context from the commentarial tradition; individual items such as "elder's body-wash," "mirror-born matter," and "ring impression" are technical headings for stories that follow in the text and are deliberately terse in the original. The phrase rendered "pressed down by the round of your throat" is a somewhat obscure insult in the original, likely mocking the monks' shaved heads or round bowls; the exact idiomatic force is uncertain. The phrase rendered "speak with contempt" and then "spoke with contempt, saying: 'Speak with contempt!'" reflects a slightly awkward textual moment in the Tibetan where the terms for mockery and contemptuous speech appear in close succession. The passage appears to describe bystanders mocking the group of six, who then respond — the sequence is preserved faithfully though the Tibetan is slightly elliptical at that point. The term rendered throughout as "Giu Wanggi Thig Le" is a Tibetan transcription of what appears to be a foreign — possibly Indic or Central Asian — cosmetic or ritual substance associated with elaborate body-markings or dots. Its precise Sanskrit equivalent is not established with certainty in this context; it may refer to a style of decorative body-marking associated with brahminical or festival practice. This uncertainty does not affect the sense of the legal rulings, which concern self-adornment with such markings as a monastic offense. The phrase rendered "the hill of the Jīvaka's Children's Killing — the grove that strikes terror into the heart" is unusual and the Tibetan toponym is obscure. The passage reads ཆུ་སྲིན་བྱིས་པ་གསོད་ཀྱི་རི་ལ་འཇིགས་འཇིགས་ལྟའི་ཚལ་རི་དགས་ཀྱི་ནགས. This likely refers to a known locale described in Vinaya narratives, possibly Jīvaka's mango grove near Rājagṛha or a related site; the literal rendering has been preserved here since the exact identification is uncertain and a smooth paraphrase would risk misidentifying the place. The name Ānanda does not appear explicitly in the Tibetan at the close of this passage — ཉེ་དགའ་བོ is rendered "the beloved Ānanda" following standard Vinaya usage where this term refers to Ānanda as a named disciple. The term rendered "offense entailing a meeting of the community" translates a Vinaya technical expression for a saṅghādisesa, a class of offense that requires formal confession before the assembled community. The Tibetan does not spell out the term in full in each instance but the context is consistently that of this category of transgression.

The phrase rendered "hungry ghosts with goiters" refers to a class of pretas characterized by swollen throats or goiters, a standard subdivision within the preta realm in Abhidharma literature.

The personal name "Rtogs-byed" has been left in the translation as it appears in the preceding passage; it is a Tibetan rendering of a proper name (possibly Sanskrit Bodhanaka or similar) whose precise Sanskrit original is uncertain. The phrase rendered "non-humans" translates a term used in Vinaya literature for spirits, yakṣas, and similar beings — here the physician's promise of recovery through a mantra-cord implies the curing agent was a spirit, and so the mockery at the cord's casual disposal comes from that being. The rendering "non-humans" follows standard Vinaya usage.

The phrase "pillar's joint" refers to the hollow junction between stacked pillar sections, a common monastic architectural feature used as a discrete storage location. The summary verse is a mnemonic colophon-style gāthā listing the topics covered in the preceding section of Vinaya rules; "āmra" refers to the mango, and "myrobalan" renders skyu ru ra, the fruit of Terminalia chebula, a common Vinaya medicinal item. The phrase rendered "those who take what has not been given" is a standard Vinaya idiom for thieves, using the technical expression for theft as defined in the pārājika rule. The phrase "ring-shaped seal ornaments" for sor gdub rgya renders a compound meaning finger-ring-style seal or signet fittings on a lock, which is the most plausible reading in this Vinaya context. The passage uses a stock narrative device of abbreviated repetition, signaled in Tibetan by "everything is exactly as before" and a resumption mid-narrative. The translation makes this seamless for a listener by rendering the abbreviated section as a smooth continuation rather than a scribal shorthand note.

The series of similes for nail shapes — tip of a grain, ledge of a fence, razor's edge, crescent, first sliver of the new moon — are Vinaya technical descriptions of nail-trimming styles; they are rendered descriptively rather than left as bare Tibetan images. The "Group of Six" monks refers to the notorious sextet of ill-disciplined monks who appear repeatedly in Vinaya narratives as foils illustrating misconduct; no further gloss is needed for a Vinaya-literate audience, but listeners unfamiliar with the tradition should know this is a stock Vinaya cast of characters whose habitual misuse of communal resources is the narrative point here.

The phrase rendered "a garden of a thousand mango trees" follows the Tibetan literally; the gift is of the garden as a whole containing a thousand trees, donated to the four-directional Saṅgha in perpetuity, with a festival attached to it. The phrase rendered "the Ānanda Garden" follows the preceding context where Ānanda was shown overseeing a mango garden. The Tibetan "སྟོང་གི་ཀུན་དགའ་ར་བ" at this point likely means the garden associated with Ānanda, consistent with the narrative. The term "སྐྱུ་རུ་ར" is āmalaka, the myrobalan or Indian gooseberry fruit, rendered here as "myrobalan fruit" for clarity and consistency with traditional Vinaya translation conventions. The "sahakāra tree" is another variety in the mango family; the Tibetan "ཤིང་ས་ཧ་ཀ་ར" is a transliteration of Sanskrit sahakāra, which can denote the champaka mango or a related species. The householder's name "ཤིན་ཏུ་བཟང་པོ" (Shintu Zangpo) is a Tibetan rendering meaning "extremely good" or "very excellent," likely a translation of a Sanskrit name such as Sudarśana or Supriya. It has been retained in phonetic Tibetan form rather than translated, as it functions as a proper name throughout the passage.

The five medicinal fruits listed correspond to the classical Āyurvedic group known as the three myrobalans (triphalā) plus long pepper and black pepper. The Tibetan terms "ན་ལེ་ཤམ" for black pepper is somewhat unusual; "marica" is the standard Sanskrit equivalent offered here as a best reading. The naked ascetic's wordplay on "luster" rests on a classical Indian pun: the term rendered "luster" or "to illuminate" shares its root with the word for fire, allowing him to reinterpret the prophecy as foretelling a house fire rather than family glory. This is preserved in the translation by glossing his explanation in context.

The phrase "being in his final existence" refers to a being who will attain liberation in this very life and will not be reborn again, a standard technical usage in Abhidharma and narrative literature. The "naked wanderers" renders the Tibetan term for the Nirgrantha ascetics (followers of Jainism), who are depicted as rivals celebrating what they believe to be a failure of the Buddha's prophecy.

The phrase rendered "the white road of existence" is literally "the bright path of existence" and may carry a specific cosmological or metaphorical nuance that is contextually uncertain; it likely indicates the long, difficult road of wandering through saṃsāra.

The lists of numerical qualities of the Buddha — the four bases of miraculous power, the seven limbs of awakening, the ten powers, and so forth — are standard doctrinal enumerations and are rendered here without expansion, as the text itself does not gloss them. The list of cold hells in the downward-ray passage follows the standard Abhidharma enumeration of eight cold hells, here rendered by their descriptive meanings rather than transliterated Sanskrit names (Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, Mahāpadma) since the Tibetan text gives Tibetan descriptive equivalents throughout. The distinction between "powerful wheel-turning kingship" (associated with the left hand) and "wheel-turning kingship" (right hand) likely refers to a cakravartin of the highest and a lower grade respectively, though the Tibetan distinction here is subtle and the commentarial tradition varies. The final figures in the list require brief clarification. "Dhṛtarāṣṭra" renders ཡུལ་འཁོར་སྲུང་, the guardian king of the East (Skt. Dhṛtarāṣṭra), whose domain is the gandharvas (དྲི་ཟའི་ཚོགས་). The "noble man surrounded by kumbhāṇḍas" renders འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ་གྲུལ་བུམ་གྱི་ཚོགས་: འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ is an epithet likely referring to the guardian king Virūḍhaka, whose domain is the kumbhāṇḍas (a class of spirits, Skt. kumbhāṇḍa). The passage ends mid-sentence in the supplied Tibetan, and the translation reflects this. The eighteen "benefits of the Buddha's arrival" is an unusual formulation. The list mixes freedom from physical dangers with positive omens, suggesting this text belongs to a genre of popular sūtra literature enumerating auspicious qualities rather than a standard Abhidharma or Prajñāpāramitā context.

The name rendered "Virūpākṣa" for མིག་མི་བཟང་ is the standard Tibetan translation-equivalent of that lokapāla's name, meaning "Ill-eyed" or "Deformed-eyed." Similarly, "Virūḍhaka" for ཐགས་ཟངས་རིས follows the standard identification of that lokapāla.

The term བསེལ་རྔན ("false accusation" or "unjust charge") is rendered contextually; it can also mean "bribery" or "inducement to false witness." The term rendered "womb-vessel" translates the Tibetan "lto'i nyen kor," a compound referring to the womb or uterine container, here depicted as surviving intact after the cremation before miraculously bursting to produce the lotus. This is a stock miraculous-birth motif, and the rendering follows the sense of a contained vessel associated with the abdomen.

The naked ascetics here are almost certainly Jains (Nigaṇṭhas or Nirgrantha followers), and the one who speaks to Supriya appears to be a Jain teacher bound by his own code, explaining why he refuses to enter the fire himself despite urging Supriya to act. The name "Agnijāta" is a Sanskrit reconstruction of the Tibetan "me skyes" — literally "fire-born." The text gives the Tibetan folk-etymology explanation explicitly, so rendering the name in Sanskrit with its meaning conveyed by context is appropriate here.

The closing sentence is grammatically compressed and its referent slightly ambiguous: "his maternal uncle" is the brother of the boy's mother who had earlier left for another region, and the passage appears to be transitioning to a new narrative thread explaining that he had learned by some means of the birth and its auspicious signs. This is a genuine structural ambiguity in the Tibetan at this point.

The sequence of attainments — "warm roots," "highest intensity," "lesser and middling patience" — reflects the standard Abhidharma schema of the four phases of the path of preparation, rendered here in their doctrinal order. The name Śin-tu Bzang-po is a Tibetan personal name meaning "Utterly Good" or "Excellent" and likely renders an Indic name such as Supriya or Subhadra; it is retained in transliteration here since no Sanskrit original is provided and it functions as a proper name throughout the narrative. Similarly, Meskyes (Me-skyes, "Fire-born") is retained as a proper name. The passage's use of "lord" for the king renders the Tibetan honorific lha (literally "god/deity") applied to royalty, which is a standard convention; the gloss "O lord" captures the royal address without importing theological content. The greeting "Aroga" is a conventional salutation meaning something like "Be well" or "In good health" — a term of address used when conveying a superior's message to a king, functioning here as a formal honorific opening rather than a personal name or title. It is left transliterated in keeping with the preceding passage's convention.

The phrase rendered "Kalandakanivāpa grove" follows the standard sūtra colophon formula for Rājagṛha; Kalandakanivāpa means the Squirrel-Feeding Ground or Squirrel Park, a well-known location associated with the bamboo grove there. The Tibetan here reads "ku myed pa'i tshal" which is the standard rendering of that name. The phrase "the venerable Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers" renders Tshe dang ldan pa 'Od srung Stobs bcu pa. This appears to be a distinct monk named Kāśyapa ("Ösung") with the epithet "of the Ten Powers," not Mahākāśyapa. The epithet "of the Ten Powers" (daśabala) is ordinarily reserved for a buddha; its application to this monk here is unusual and may reflect a nickname or a textual peculiarity in this Vinaya narrative context.

The ruling that display of supernatural power before a layman incurs a "serious offense" renders 'gal tshabs can, meaning an offense of grave consequence — in Vinaya technical terms this falls short of a pārājika but is nonetheless a weighty transgression. The term kārṣāpaṇa is a standard Indian monetary unit (a silver or copper coin); it is retained untranslated as a proper currency name, consistent with standard Vinaya translations. The phrase rendered "cut off the road" for demanding toll or dice-fee reflects the dice-house practice of blocking passage until travelers pay a transit levy, a well-attested motif in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narratives. The name Agnidatta is rendered from the Tibetan མེ་སྐྱེས, literally "born of fire," which is a standard Tibetan calque of the Sanskrit Agnidatta or Agnija. The narrative context strongly supports Agnidatta.

The term kārṣāpaṇa is kept in transliteration throughout as it is a specific ancient Indian monetary unit with no natural English equivalent.

The phrase rendered "let me examine it by touching it" translates a somewhat compressed Tibetan idiom; the sense is that Agnidatta reaches out to feel the cloth while mentally deliberating whether the king intends to give it to him. The phrase rendered "Māra" for "གཞོན་ནུ་མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲ་" — literally "Young man, the Unborn Foe (Māra)" — reflects a stock epithet of Māra in this narrative context. The passage appears to shift, somewhat abruptly, from Agnidatta's perspective to a scene where ministers address the king (who has been identified with Māra or a māra-figure in the broader narrative). The referent of "he" in the dialogue involving the ministers is ambiguous in the Tibetan and may require the reader to consult the wider story context.

The phrase "dguṅ bdun" (rendered "seven high" for the heavens) is a Tibetan idiomatic expression for counting stories or levels of a building; Agnidatta is describing the storeys of his residence, not cosmological heavens. The translation "the heavens to be seven high" approximates the sense. The figure "Agni" here renders མེ་སྐྱེས (literally "fire-born"), used as a personal name throughout this narrative; it is a Tibetan calque of the Sanskrit name Agni or possibly Agnidatta. "Ajātaśatru" renders མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲ (literally "unborn enemy"), the well-known king of Magadha. These names are sustained from the preceding passage per the continuity instruction.

The phrase དེ་དག་གང་ནས་ཇི་ལྟར་འཛེགས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ན་དེ་བཞིན་འཁོད་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ describes the thieves being supernaturally immobilized in whatever posture and position they occupied on the wall — rendered accordingly. The phrase rendered as "he moved and then stilled the five-spoked wheel of saṃsāric existence" reflects the Tibetan "འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ཆ་ལྔ་པ་གཡོ་བ་དང་མི་གཡོ་བ་འདི་ཉིད་རིག་སྟེ," literally "knowing both the moving and the not-moving of this five-spoked wheel of saṃsāra." The "five spokes" likely refer to the five aggregates or five realms; the precise referent is not spelled out in the text, and interpretations may vary across commentaries.

The verse at the close of the passage is a well-known canonical stanza on the indestructibility of karma, appearing in multiple sūtras. The rendering follows the standard doctrinal understanding. The Buddha's name here rendered as Vipaśyin is the Sanskrit equivalent of Tibetan Rnam par gzigs, one of the seven buddhas of antiquity. The epithet means "He Who Sees Clearly" or "All-Seeing."

The name Anāparin is a back-reconstruction; the Tibetan Nyes med ("Anāparin" or "Anāgāmin"-adjacent) may represent a Sanskrit name not fully transparent from this form alone; "Anāparin" follows the standard Tibetan spelling nyes med used here.

The palace name Mūlāga renders Tibetan Rtsa lag can, literally "having roots and branches," which likely represents a Sanskrit name such as Mūlaka or similar; this is a conventional restoration and the exact Sanskrit is uncertain. The phrase rendered "drawing lots" translates a term literally meaning "by the size of the canopy" or "by competing canopy measures," which appears to be an idiomatic expression in this Vinaya narrative for a competitive draw or contest to determine precedence. The narrative logic — that whoever wins goes first — confirms this reading, though the precise mechanism of the contest is not entirely clear from the text alone. The phrase rendered "set in motion with incense-wood" describes Anāparin stoking or agitating the canopy-steaming apparatus using fragrant wood; the exact mechanical operation is not entirely clear from the Tibetan alone, but the general sense — that he used aromatic wood to perfume cloths — is evident from context.

The final sentence breaks off mid-description (the passage ends mid-enumeration of furnishings), which is consistent with the source text being a continuation. The buddha's name rendered here as "Namaparīkṣit" corresponds to Tibetan རྣམ་པར་གཟིགས, which literally means "the All-Seeing" or "He Who Surveys All Aspects." This is likely a Sanskrit name such as Vipaśyin or a related epithet; the Tibetan matches a known convention for rendering such a name, and the translation of the preceding passage used "Namaparīkṣit" — consistency is maintained, though the exact Sanskrit behind this particular buddha's name in this narrative context warrants scholarly verification. The divine son's name rendered here as "Lasthamsadpa" is a transcription of the Tibetan lha'i bu las thams cad pa, which literally means "the divine son who is all-tasks" or "the divine son Sarvakārya." This is a proper name that should ideally be rendered by its Sanskrit equivalent Sarvakārya; the Tibetan here treats it as a name throughout. Likewise, the buddha's name rendered as "Namapar Zikyi" corresponds to Tibetan rnam par gzigs, Sanskrit Vipaśyin — the first of the seven ancient buddhas. A consistent rendering as "Vipaśyin" would be standard, and the passage should be understood as referring to the buddha Vipaśyin throughout.

King Nyendan corresponds to Tibetan rgyal po gnyen ldan, which may be a rendering of Sanskrit Bandhumant, the father of the buddha Vipaśyin — a detail consistent with the Vipaśyin cycle of narratives found in the Dīrghāgama and related sources.

The goddess Bde (Tibetan bde) heading the list of Śakra's queens likely stands for Sanskrit Śacī or a similar name; the text as given appears abbreviated with "sogs" ("and others") following. The summary verse at the passage's midpoint is a colophon-style mnemonic verse listing items whose use was formally permitted, followed by the opening of a new legal narrative. "Namapar Zik" renders the Tibetan buddha-name throughout, consistent with the preceding translation. The final saying — that truthful craftsmen are rare — is a proverbial remark by the friend, anticipating the story that follows about the blacksmith's evasiveness. The phrase rendered "variegated or ornamented" translates two Tibetan terms meaning literally "spotted/multicolored" and "bright/beautiful," describing decorated knife handles. The rendering captures the sense of ornamental elaboration that prompted the Blessed One's ruling. The two types of needle case described — one with a hollow tube and one with a stopper or plug — reflect standard Vinaya technical vocabulary. The rendering of the second type as "like a container with a stopper" is an interpretation of the somewhat compressed Tibetan; the contrast is between a tubular open-ended case and one that is closed or sealed at one end.

The phrase translated "wooden pins" for སྒྲོ་གཟུངས is literally something like "feather-holder" or "pin-holder," here interpreted as a wooden peg or pin used to hold the fabric taut in the frame, which fits the context.

The summary verse at the end is a mnemonic gāthā listing topics treated in this section of the Vinaya. "Warm gown and great fever" likely refer to a subsequent rule about a garment worn during illness or fever, which would appear in the text immediately following.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the source text is a continuing passage. The account of Anāthapiṇḍada offering the Jeta Grove and the episode of "the sweeper" refers to a fuller story told earlier in the Vinaya text; this passage explicitly cross-references that prior narrative with the phrase "just as it was told before."

The bird identified here as "śaṅkaśāṭika" is rendered as "kalavinka birds" following conventional Vinaya translation practice, though the precise species intended by the Tibetan "ཤང་ཤང་ཏེའུ" is debated; some translators render it simply as a type of melodious bird.

The name rendered "Vakkha" for "བལང་གནས" (literally "dwelling among cattle") may alternatively correspond to the monk Vakula or another figure with a similar epithet; the identification is uncertain but does not affect the narrative materially. "King Udayana" renders "འཆར་བྱེད" (literally "the one who causes to appear," a standard Tibetan rendering of Udayana). The text identifies the monk as Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja only by context carried from the preceding passage. The five stages of spiritual attainment the king enumerates follow canonical Pāli and Sanskrit tradition: arhat, non-returner, once-returner, stream-enterer, and then the four dhyānas in descending order. The king's questioning in descending order is a narrative device revealing his ignorance of the path: he works from highest to lowest, hoping to find some redeeming attainment in the monk. The name rendered "Vālanasin" follows the Tibetan phonetic form; the Sanskrit original is uncertain and may be a corruption or regional variant. The phrase regarding the physician's advice is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan, and the final exchange is syntactically elliptical; the rendering follows the most contextually coherent reading. "Udayana, king of Vatsa" expands the Tibetan's "king of Vatsa, Udayana" (བད་སའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་འཆར་བྱེད) for clarity; བད་ས is Vatsa and འཆར་བྱེད reconstructs as Udayana (Sanskrit: Udayana, the well-known king of Kauśāmbī). The phrase rendered "in the shape of a sea" for the window's interior width is a somewhat unusual simile. The Tibetan suggests the interior opening should be broad like the expanse of an ocean — meaning the window splays wide inward. This is an architectural detail typical of early monastic construction rules preserved in Vinaya literature.

The term rendered "barley-beer" and "āmalaka berry-beer" translates Tibetan forms of medicinal rinses used for the eyes; these are likely dilute medicinal infusions rather than intoxicating beverages, the word "beer" (Tibetan chang) being used loosely for any fermented or steeped liquid preparation in this medical context. The phrase rendered "gift of words" translates a Tibetan expression meaning a verbal offering or piece of news to report — here used with a clearly ironic and manipulative intent by the two monks, who are inducing the Licchavi to falsely accuse a third monk before the Buddha. The idiom is somewhat idiomatic and the rendering captures the sense within its narrative context.

The name "Jātanora" is a phonetic rendering of the Tibetan "གྱད་བུ་ནོར" (gyad bu nor); the Sanskrit original is uncertain, but this appears to be a personal name of a monk, treated here as such.

The phrase "born of the earth" is a standard epithet or stock description in Vinaya narratives referring to beings who arose spontaneously from the ground — here applied to the wandering monk in passing, possibly as a formulaic description of his origin or simply as a narrative detail about his nature. The Tibetan phrase rendered as "bowl-overturning ceremony" reflects the Vinaya procedure of turning one's alms bowl upside down as a formal sanction against a lay supporter who has wronged the Saṅgha — a recognized ecclesiastical act of censure in multiple Vinaya traditions (Skt. pātranikkujjana). The term is kept descriptive throughout for clarity in audio narration.

The phrase translated as "words of inquiry" for the formal motion procedure reflects the standard羯磨 (Skt. karman) Vinaya procedure; only a single motion (without a vote) is required in this case, as indicated in the text. The phrase rendered "limbs became fit for service" translates a technical Vinaya euphemism for erection or involuntary sexual arousal; this is standard canonical language in Vinaya contexts and requires no further gloss for informed listeners, but general audiences should be aware the summary verse and the narrative that follows pertain to a case of self-stimulation, which will presumably be treated in the next passage.

The opening sentence presents a slight syntactic difficulty: it appears to be the woman's closing ultimatum to the Licchavī (from the preceding passage), and the rendering follows that reading.

The phrase rendered "the two earth-born ones" likely refers to two specific figures known from the broader narrative context; the Tibetan ས་ལས་སྐྱེས (earth-born, i.e., born from the earth) may be an epithet or name, and its precise referent is uncertain without more context. The opening passage refers to the monk from the preceding section who was struggling with bodily arousal. The term rendered "his limbs became fit for service" is a discreet canonical idiom for sexual arousal; this continues directly from the preceding passage. The act of striking his member on a stone is an ancient canonical account (found in Pāli parallels) of a monk attempting self-castration, here described with characteristic Vinaya restraint. The Blessed One's remark that "the one who should be beaten is the deluded one" is a standard Vinaya doctrinal pun: the correct antidote to desire is meditation on unattractiveness, not physical self-harm. The phrase rendered "festive assembly" translates a term for communal festival gatherings; the two groups — merchants and soldiers — are stock characters in Vinaya narrative. The final lines set up a new narrative episode. The "group of six" refers to the notorious six monks who repeatedly appear in Vinaya narratives as the instigators of misconduct that prompts new rules. The Tibetan "འཕགས་པ་དྲུག་སྡེ" here is the soldiers' honorific address to them, not a doctrinal use of "noble ones," though the irony is evident in context. The names Supriya rendered from the Tibetan phonetic བཟང་ལྡན (bzang ldan) are retained consistently as Supriya throughout, following the Sanskrit reconstruction: bzang ldan is a direct calque of Supriya ("endowed with the good / beautiful"). The child's name སྙན་པ་བཟང་ལྡན (snyan pa bzang ldan) appears to add the qualifier "snyan pa" (beautiful-voiced / melodious) to the family name, and the relatives' reasoning in the text ties the name to both the voice quality and the father's name; this double nuance is preserved in the translation. The phrase rendered "wheel of cyclic existence with its five spokes" translates a somewhat unusual expression. The five spokes likely refer to the five aggregates or the five realms of rebirth, both common in this kind of formulation. This is a genuine point of doctrinal ambiguity but does not alter the sense of the passage as a whole.

The expression rendered "split open the shell of the cave of his rebirth-door" is a vivid metaphor for breaking the bonds of continued existence; the precise Tibetan idiom here is unusual but the doctrinal meaning is clear in context. The phrase "སྐད་ཀྱི་གཏང་རག" is rendered throughout as "the resonance of his voice," following the established convention of the preceding passage. The term suggests the carrying or projecting quality of the voice used in Dharma teaching, possibly with connotations of formal proclamation or announcement.

The final verse is mid-sentence in the source, as the passage breaks off after the conditional "If one knows inwardly." This is faithfully reproduced as an incomplete verse, consistent with the passage being a continuation. The buddha named in the Tibetan as "Saṃvartanīya" (འཁོར་བ་འཇིག, literally "destroyer of saṃsāra" or "dissolver of the world") is rendered by its Tibetan meaning rendered into likely Sanskrit equivalent. The name is an epithet-style buddha-name common in this genre of canonical narrative; no single universally attested Sanskrit form exists in the secondary literature, so the reading given here is a plausible reconstruction based on the Tibetan.

The phrase rendered "found a collection of karma, gathered conditions like a flame drawing close, and caused things that were inevitably going to arise" reflects a technically dense passage on the mechanics of karmic maturation. The simile "like a flame drawing close" is unusual and may indicate a variant reading; it is translated as it stands. The epithet "the sage who speaks truth" renders "drang srong smra ba," which in the context of Vārāṇasī and the Deer Park is a Tibetan rendering of the name Ṛṣipatana (literally "the place of the sage who speaks truth," a standard alternative name for the site otherwise called Mṛgadāva, the Deer Park at Sarnath). This is a genuine textual identification worth flagging.

The phrase "ལས་དྲུག་ལ་མཁས་པའི་བྲམ་ཟེ" refers to a brahmin learned in the six Vedic ancillary sciences (the ṣaḍaṅgas); rendered here as "skilled in the six branches of learning" to capture the sense without inserting a technical list. The term rendered "brahmin youth Blama" follows the Tibetan bram ze'i khye'u bla ma, where bla ma here appears to function as a proper name or title for a brahmin student figure, not as the later Tibetan religious title "lama." The passage is recounting the prophecy given to a brahmin youth in the time of Kāśyapa, and the name or epithet Blama (literally "superior/upper") seems to designate a specific individual whose identity is not further elaborated in this excerpt.

The phrase rendered "scattering the words about like a shower of pine seeds" translates the Tibetan image of rgya shug gi 'bras bu'i tshogs gtor ba bzhin, which describes a disorganized, scattered manner of recitation — the pine seeds (or cypress seeds) being flung about without order, implying a lack of melodic cohesion or formal chanting. The phrase rendered "scattering a heap of pine cones" translates a simile involving rgya shug gi 'bras bu (the fruits, i.e. cones, of a cypress or similar conifer). The image is of something spilling out randomly and without order, describing the young monk's tuneless and disorganized recitation. The rendering "jumble" attempts to preserve this sense for a listening audience.

The royal name "Rtogs ldan" (meaning "the Discerning" or "the Insightful") and its epithet "Gzhon nu" (Young or Youthful) have been kept as a transliteration here because no standard Sanskrit equivalent is firmly established for this figure in the Vinaya narrative and the name as a proper noun is more accurate than a rendered meaning in context.

The location described as "the land of crocodiles, on a frightful mountain, the haunt of wild beasts, in the place of the slaughter of children" (chu srin byis pa gsod kyi ri) is a Vinaya section-marker giving a place name used to indicate a new episode; it is somewhat formulaic and its precise identification as a real place is uncertain. The opening location "ངན་སྤོང་གི་བུ་དག་ན་ཆུ་སྲིན་བྱིས་པ་གསོད་ཀྱི་རི་" is ambiguous and difficult. The literal reading yields something like "the mountain of the Aṅga boys' crocodile-child-killing," which is likely a place name or descriptive toponym for a mountain near Aṅga (a region in eastern India). The translation renders it as a descriptive place-name phrase, acknowledging the compound's uncertain referent.

The term "ཞུམ་ནས" rendered as "chafed them" reflects the sense of the wide straps causing a different kind of discomfort, likely rubbing or pressing uncomfortably; the precise nature of the problem is not entirely explicit in the text. The five textile types prohibited for weaving into robes present some terminological difficulty. The Tibetan terms describe various grades of fiber or weave. "Young animal wool" for བེའུ་རས, "goat hair" for ལ་བ, "plain raw cloth" for ཕྱིང་པ, "hemp fiber" for ཀླམ, and "coarse jute fiber" for སེང་བ are reasonable renderings, though the precise material referents of ཀླམ and སེང་བ are not entirely certain from context alone; the point is that these are base or unworked materials unsuitable for robes. The passage ending "monks, other monasteries and" is a deliberate cutoff at the boundary of the supplied text. The phrase rendered "consecrate them by means of the mental act of one who previously took them out" is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The sense is that the mental intention alone, performed by the person who originally removed the robes from consecrated status, suffices to re-consecrate them. This reading follows the commentarial tradition on consecration of robes by mental resolve.

The verse spoken by the second monk contains a slight doctrinal nuance: the compound rendered "gives up one's own life, but does not take the life of living creatures" reflects a strict reading of the precept against taking life even at the cost of one's own death, rather than drink water containing living organisms.

The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, suggesting the passage continues in the next folio. The phrase rendered as "the view of the transitory collection" refers to the technical Abhidharma term satkāyadṛṣṭi, the view that grasps at a self among the five aggregates. The image of a "twenty-peak mountain" for this view, shattered by the "vajra of gnosis," is a vivid Abhidharmic metaphor: twenty peaks correspond to the twenty modes of the satkāyadṛṣṭi (viewing each of the five aggregates as self in four ways). The "fruit of stream-entry" confirms that this is the moment of first seeing the truth directly on the path of seeing.

The phrase rendered as "divine daughter" at the opening reflects the doctrinal convention that the son of the gods (lha'i bu) reborn in that heaven spontaneously possesses three kinds of knowledge shortly after birth; the Tibetan here switches to the feminine form (lha'i bu mo), possibly referring to a separate figure mentioned earlier or reflecting a textual inconsistency. This may warrant checking against a Sanskrit or alternative Tibetan witness. The verse concerning Kāśyapa and the ālā leaf is doctrinally dense. The reference is to the great elder Mahākāśyapa having, in a past life, broken his training and been reborn among the nāgas. The "ālā leaf" is a plant associated in Vinaya narrative with the nāga realm; the verse implies that the consequences of his past infraction still bound him to nāga rebirths for a time. This is an established narrative in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, reflecting that the Tibetan provided is itself incomplete at that point. The speaker identified here as Upavāna (Tib. ཉེ་བ་འཁོར) takes the unusual structural role of both questioner and respondent in the same dialogue sequence. This format, where a named elder poses a question and then immediately supplies the answer himself, is a recognizable Vinaya literary convention recording settled rulings rather than live debate; no textual corruption need be assumed.

The term rendered "one fathom" for འདོམ་གང translates a standard Indic unit of measure (approximately the span of outstretched arms), used in Vinaya texts to define a monk's immediate vicinity. The phrase rendered "just enough to fill a cart of six oxen loaded with bamboo" is a measurement simile for the degree of visual examination required; the image conveys that monks need only inspect water sufficiently to be reasonably confident of its purity, not exhaustively. The Tibetan is slightly compressed here and the precise image is somewhat unusual, but this reading is the most defensible.

The phrase translated "fingerbowls" renders སྡེར་སྤྱད, literally "claw-use" implements, which in Vinaya context refers to small bowls or vessels used for washing the fingers after eating — commonly called fingerbowls in English Vinaya literature. The gaṇḍī is a wooden plank or board struck as a signal to assemble the Saṅgha; it is the standard monastic convening instrument and is here rendered descriptively on first use.

The formal motion-and-act (羯磨, Skt. karman) structure reproduced here is the standard single-announcement single-act (ñattidutiakamma) procedure of Vinaya law; the formulaic repetition is deliberate and has been preserved faithfully.

The phrase rendered "horse dung" refers to the monks of the group of six beating the broken pieces with a clod or lump of horse dung, apparently in mockery or frustration; the passage is intentionally comic and the bystander monks' sarcastic exchange that follows reflects that tone. The term rendered "eating utensils" throughout translates a Tibetan term literally meaning something like "individual implements" or "personal vessels" — contextually it refers to individual bowls or containers for food. The detail about "softened and moistened rice" renders a term for a porridge-like or softened preparation, appropriate for the infirm. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end as given; this is noted for continuity. The summary verse is a mnemonic stanza listing the topics covered in the preceding section. Its terms are terse and elliptical by design; the rendering reflects the telegraphic nature of such verse summaries in the Vinaya tradition.

The phrase rendered "the rule about seeds" translates sa bon gyi chos, literally "the Dharma of seeds," referring here to the Vinaya rule prohibiting monks from damaging or consuming seeds in a way that violates their germinating life; the episode turns on an accidental encounter with such seeds.

"Dyeing with seed-varieties" renders sa bon gyi rigs tshos dka' ba, a technical Vinaya term for a procedure of rendering seeds ritually permissible through heating or boiling until they are no longer viable — here confirmed by the appearance of steam. The river name "Dṛkṣā" is an approximation of the Tibetan "chu bo dregs ldan," which literally means "the proud river" or "the river of pride." This may be a proper name or a descriptive epithet; it does not correspond with certainty to a known Sanskrit river name, and "Dṛkṣā" is offered as a plausible reconstruction only.

The "six duties" of a brahmin is a standard reference to the six traditional brahminical occupations: studying, teaching, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving, and receiving gifts.

"Vatsadāsa" (literally "servant of the calf" or "he who belongs to the bull-calf") is the reconstructed Sanskrit for the Tibetan name "ba lang bdag," meaning "lord of the bull" or "possessor of the bull." The phrase rendered as "the wheel of cyclic existence moves, yet in this fifth aspect it does not move" is a technical and somewhat obscure formulation in the Tibetan. The compound "འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་གཡོ་བ་དང་མི་གཡོ་བ་ཆ་ལྔ་པ་འདི་ཉིད" is a Vinaya-context doctrinal reference that is not fully transparent; the translation renders it as literally as possible while preserving readability. Some commentarial tradition would be needed to explain the precise doctrinal referent of "the fifth aspect of non-movement" here.

The epithets "ཙན་དན་དང་སྟེའུར་འདྲ་བ" — sandalwood and camphor — are standard similes in Vinaya literature for a mind that is fragrant and purified, rendered here in their natural sense. The verse on karma's indestructibility is closely parallel to a canonical verse found in several Buddhist traditions, including the Pāli and Chinese parallel canons, often attributed to the Buddha in various contexts. The rendering follows the standard interpretation in Tibetan commentarial tradition.

The phrase rendered "seized upon" in "aggregates, sense bases, and elements that have been seized upon" translates a technical term indicating the appropriated or grasped psychophysical complex — the basis of experience in a given life — distinguishing it from these constituents as abstract categories. This is a significant doctrinal nuance indicating that karma ripens in the living, appropriated continuum of a being, not in inert physical elements.

The episode of the monk stealing food from his preceptor while distracted by another's recitation is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan and the sequence of events requires careful reading; the translation follows the most coherent narrative reading. The phrase rendered "field of offering unsurpassable" reflects the Tibetan honorific compound for the buddha as the supreme object of offering and veneration; this is a standard epithet in the tradition. The term "received gift" for the Tibetan "byin len byas pa" conveys that food which falls into one's vessel by accident counts as properly received alms, thus permitting consumption without transgression. The phrase "purely dark," "purely bright," and "mixed" are the three standard categories of karma in the Abhidharma schema. The rendering of "entailing a formal proceeding" for "nyes pa" with " འགལ་ཚབས་ཅན" reflects a Vinaya technical term for a class of offense requiring a formal act of the Saṅgha. The phrase rendered "a scraper, a salt-pouch, and an offered drinking cup" refers to specific small implements exempted from the prohibition on tin bowls; the precise identification of the first item (ཁ་གཟར, literally a "mouth-scraper" or tongue-scraper) is secure in Vinaya context. The summary verse is a brief mnemonic gāthā recapitulating the rulings just given. The passage breaks off mid-sentence with the Blessed One's final declaration, as the source text ends there. The phrase rendered "it is crushing your throats with a stone" is a terse colloquial insult meaning roughly "that is a lie that chokes you" or "your words are strangling you." The exact idiomatic force is somewhat obscure; the rendering given captures the hostile, dismissive tone directed at the monks.

The term translated "copper basin" at the opening continues the established context; the Tibetan ཤོལ་ཟངས can denote a basin or vessel of mixed metal, but "copper basin" is consistent with the preceding passage. The phrase rendered "groin and genitals exposed" translates a compressed Tibetan euphemism indicating that the monk's private parts were visible. The term "group of six monks" refers to the notorious Chaddhagga, a recurring group in the Vinaya whose misconduct prompts new rules. The summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā enumerating the rulings of the preceding section; the items listed correspond to the cases treated in the passage. The phrase rendered "wind-illness" refers to a classical Indian medical condition, vātavyādhi in Sanskrit, involving the wind humor; it is associated with weakness of the limbs and poor balance, which explains why these monks were prone to falling. The "nets" in question are carrying nets or bag-nets used to hold and protect vessels during travel on mountain paths; the Tibetan term dra ba encompasses such woven or netted carrying bags. The phrase rendered "sits respectfully" translates a reduplicative form suggesting a posture of humble, attentive sitting at the periphery of the assembly, which is a standard Vinaya convention for a petitioner approaching the Saṅgha.

The "wooden sounding board" renders the Sanskrit term gaṇḍī, a wooden plank or board struck to summon the community, standard Vinaya terminology.

The formal羯磨 (karma, i.e., Saṅgha legal act) structure here — motion followed by three announcements — is the standard single-motion, triple-announcement form used for granting Vinaya permissions. The "twenty peak-summits of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" renders a technical Abhidharma image: the view of the transitory collection as a personal self produces twenty subsidiary views (regarding each of the five aggregates as fourfold: as self, as belonging to self, as containing self, as contained in self), which stream-entry eliminates. The vajra of wisdom shattering them is a standard metaphor.

The "fourth dhyāna of the pinnacle of existence" renders a somewhat compressed phrase; the "pinnacle of existence" normally refers to the peak of the formless realm, but here the text specifies the fourth dhyāna, which may indicate Śāriputra examined the matter from the highest level of the form realm accessible to his concentration, or it may be a textual compression. This is a genuine minor uncertainty. The two summary verses appear to be mnemonic colophon verses listing topics covered in the preceding section and topics to be covered in the next, in the standard Vinaya style. Several items in the second verse, such as "not sharing" and "residing in a house," refer to specific rules whose full titles are compressed; the rendering follows what the Tibetan text itself provides without expanding beyond it.
