The terms rendered "heated water" and "razor" in the summary verses and the narrative are the same Tibetan words as in the preceding context, maintaining consistency with the established translation of those terms. "ཀུན་དོང" and "ཀིའུ" in the duration rules refer to specific types of facial sores or eruptions; "ཀུན་དོང" is rendered "sore on the face" and "ཀིའུ" as "cold sore," though the precise medical identification of these terms remains uncertain. The passage distinguishes three body-hair rules that arise sequentially: head hair shaved with scissors, pubic hair, and armpit hair. Each follows the same narrative template: the barber is sent, kept all day, people complain, a rule is laid down, then an exception for medical necessity is added. The term rendered "private parts" is a standard Vinaya euphemism for the pubic region. "Hair-scissors" renders a term for a scissor-like implement distinct from the razor used for tonsure. The phrase "elder monks" renders the standard Vinaya term for senior ordained monks qualified to act as witnesses or advisors. The passage ends mid-sentence, breaking off just as the monks are about to report the armpit-hair incident to the Blessed One. The phrase rendered "gabled hall" for ཁང་པ་བརྩེགས་པ refers to the Kūṭāgāraśālā, the famous two-storied or peaked-roof hall at Vaiśālī; some translators render it "multi-storied building" or simply leave it in Sanskrit. "Gabled Hall" is a reasonable functional rendering, and readers should note it is the well-known Kūṭāgāraśālā of the Vinaya narratives.

The "Six Group monks" are the notorious Chaddasvaggiyā bhikkhus, a recurring group of wayward monastics in Vinaya literature who serve as the foil prompting disciplinary rules. The term rendered "close friend" or "companion" is Ānanda, the well-known attendant of the Buddha. In the Tibetan the name appears as ཉེ་དགའ, which is the standard Tibetan rendering of the name Ānanda. The narrative context and the address "Venerable Ānanda" confirm this identification, though the passage is here using the name as a character in a Vinaya story and may refer to a different individual of the same name who happens to be a monastic companion rather than the famous disciple.

The summary verse presents some compression; the phrase rendered "worldly javelin throw" reflects རྒྱང་འཕེན, literally "a throw-distance," a conventional unit of distance, here used in the sense of walking within a cast's-throw of a settlement. The verse is a mnemonic condensing the preceding case-rulings about when walking while wearing a shared robe is or is not permitted. The phrase rendered "produces a kind of transparent outlining of the body" translates a compound describing how the wet robes clung so as to reveal the body's contours, likened to the silhouette visible through a tent or screen. The imagery is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan but the meaning is clear from context: the soaked cloth outlined the monks' bodies in a manner the brahmin found unseemly. The names of the group of five companions of the Buddha — Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman — appear here, and the Tibetan list also includes Bhadrajit, Vimala, and Gavāṃpati, suggesting a larger group in this narrative context. The exact identification of some of these latter names with standard Sanskrit forms is inferred from comparable Vinaya lists and may warrant verification against the Sanskrit or Chinese parallels. The wanderer's name, rendered here as Bright World-Hurler, is a translation of the Tibetan "འཇིག་རྟེན་རྒྱང་འཕེན་པ་འཆར་བ," meaning roughly "Appearing/Bright One who hurls the world"; this is likely a Tibetan rendering of an Indian name whose Sanskrit original is not immediately recoverable from this context. The phrase "the wheel of saṃsāra in its fifth part, moving and unmoving" is an internal cross-reference to a passage not included in this excerpt; the translation preserves the reference formula as given. The Tibetan "གསལ་བའི་དུས" literally means "the bright/clear period" and most likely refers to daylight hours or perhaps the bright fortnight, but in context the three-part division of the day makes daylight the most natural reading. The name "བལང་འབྱོར" is rendered here as Vālendriya, a tentative reconstruction; the Tibetan may reflect a corrupt or uncertain Sanskrit original. The list of monks named in this passage — Aśva, Bhadra, Revatī, Mahānāman, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, and Hastaka — are Tibetan epithets and name-forms rendered into their standard Sanskrit equivalents by convention. The Tibetan forms (རྟ་ཐུལ, བཟང་པོ, རླངས་པ, མིང་ཆེན, གྲགས་པ, གང་པོ, དྲི་མེད, བ་ལང་བདག, ལག་བཟངས) are well attested in Vinaya literature as members of the Group of Seventeen or other named disciples; identification of all nine with their exact Sanskrit names is conventional but certain members admit some variation in different recensions.

The phrase rendered "black-bowled, rope-belted paupers" reflects a derogatory taunt by the Group of Six directed at Ānanda and Upānanda, whose black bowls and rope belts apparently marked a simpler or more austere style associated with their status. The reading is secure; it is included here as a doctrinal-contextual note since the insult is somewhat opaque to a general listener. The sentence beginning "Śakra's awareness and perception extends downward, and so he thought" is left deliberately incomplete in the source text at this point, indicating the passage breaks off mid-sentence. No content has been added or suppressed; the translation reflects exactly where the Tibetan ends.

The elder monk's speech to the junior near the end of the confrontation is grammatically compressed and the logic of the argument is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan; the translation renders the most defensible reading, which is that the elder is saying: even without the Saṅgha's rule, he himself as the senior possessor of lodging would have the upper hand, and the junior, having been disrespectful, should nonetheless pay respects to whoever grants him lodging. The term rendered "wool-strip garment" (be'u ras) refers to a small piece or strip of woolen cloth — a specific textile item in Vinaya contexts whose exact form is uncertain, but "wool-strip garment" is a workable approximation. The summary verse is a mnemonic listing permitted textile articles; the phrase "waistbands — these make three" reflects that the preceding list enumerates three types of items. The final three paragraphs are formulaic repetitions announcing permissions for three successive cloth items. The episode of Venerable Nāgapāla (klu skyong) is unusual: he misinterprets the Blessed One's extended outdoor walking as being caused by fear of the yakṣa Bakula, and his crude attempt to "test" this by impersonating the yakṣa draws a rebuke both from the Blessed One and, implicitly, from Śakra. The text ends mid-sentence; this is a continuity break at the fascicle boundary and the narrative will resume in the following passage.

The term rendered "stick-fastener" for ལྕག་པོད་བཅང is literally something like "a holder with a rod or stick," referring to a toggle or stick-clasp device used to secure a belt; the precise implement is uncertain but the general sense of a fastening device is clear.

The phrase རི་བྲགས་ན་གནས་པའི་སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཚོགས, rendered "a group of people dwelling in the rocky hills," likely refers to a local community or tenant population living in a particular rocky or cliff-side district under the administration of the great man Śākya's household. The name rendered "Candravatī" appears in the text as "Zla ba" (literally "Moon") used as a proper name. The longer form Candravatī is a reasonable Sanskrit reconstruction for a female name in this narrative context. Similarly, "Mālyavatī" renders "Phreng ldan ma," literally "the one possessing garlands," which is explicitly glossed as such in the text itself. The phrase rendered "the householder Mingchen" reflects a proper name in the Tibetan that appears to be a transliteration of a Sanskrit name not fully recoverable from context alone; it is kept as a name throughout for consistency with the preceding passage. The passage "beginning from 'because the awakened buddhas...' down to 'ripens as a fruit for embodied beings'" is a textual shorthand indicating that a formulaic passage appearing earlier in the sūtra is to be understood as repeated in full here; this is rendered as a summary reference in keeping with the text's own instruction. The girl's name rendered here as "Phreng-ldan-ma" (meaning "she who bears a garland") is left in transliteration during the proclamation passage since it functions as a proper name and no Sanskrit equivalent is established in context. A translator working with a fuller edition may find a Sanskrit form such as Mālikā or similar.

The phrase rendered "jealousy arose in him" translates "kun nas dkris pa," literally "he was bound all around," a standard idiom for being seized by jealousy or indignation; the subject here is the great Śākya chief, who is troubled upon learning his daughter has been received merely as a junior wife rather than chief queen, apparently suspecting her low status was announced. The shang-shang-teu bird is a semi-mythical creature of Indian origin appearing in Tibetan literature, sometimes associated with a bird of melodious song. Its exact zoological identification is uncertain, but it functions here as one of a list of auspicious garden birds.

The aśoka tree renders Tibetan "shing mya ngan 'tsang," literally "the grief-dispelling tree," a standard equivalent for the Sanskrit aśoka, Saraca asoca, a tree of great symbolic significance in Indian literature and Buddhism.

The epithet "daughter of a woman who eats grain" renders "bu zan ma'i bu mo," literally "daughter of a grain-eating woman," referring back to the earlier context in which the mother was identified as a maidservant of low birth. The phrase carries the implication of ordinary human stock, setting up the irony of the lineage nonetheless flourishing through this union. The verse "Even across a hundred aeons, karma does not perish..." is a well-known canonical gāthā found in several Āgama and Vinaya sources, often attributed to the Buddha as a summary teaching on karma. Its rendering here follows the standard doctrinal sense.

The phrase rendered "appropriated aggregates" translates "zin pa'i phung po" (upādānaskandha), meaning the aggregates seized upon or appropriated through clinging — a standard Abhidharma technical term indicating that karma ripens in the psychophysical continuum of the being who performed it, not in the external elements. The name rendered "Mālyā" for "ལྷ་མོ་ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ" is a reasonable reconstruction: the Tibetan literally means "the goddess Garland-bearer," which corresponds to Sanskrit Mālyā or Mālinī; the exact Sanskrit name of this figure would depend on the source text.

The name rendered "Āyuśmāna of royal lineage" for "རྒྱལ་རིགས་དབྱར་ཚུལ་མ" is uncertain; the Tibetan literally reads something like "she of the manner of the summer, of royal lineage," which may be a phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name now unclear from context alone. This is flagged as genuinely uncertain.

The term "རེག་བྱ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ" rendered as "excellent texture" or "endowed with excellent texture" refers to the quality of pleasant or exquisite touch, a recognized category of physical excellence in Buddhist canonical literature (Skt. sparśa). The passage contains a narrative sequence with several proper names whose Sanskrit forms are reconstructed from Tibetan phonetic approximations: Mālyā appears as the garland-goddess introduced in the preceding passage; Āryajāta is reconstructed from the Tibetan gloss "Phags skyes po," literally "noble-born"; Mātṛdatta ("given to the mother" or here ironically "affliction to the mother") is reconstructed from "ma la gnod." The Tibetan "ma la gnod" literally means "harm or affliction to the mother," which is an unusual folk etymology for a Sanskrit name; the name Mātṛdatta normally means "given by the mother," suggesting a deliberate wordplay or alternative folk etymology in this narrative context. The list of martial and craft arts at the end of the passage is clearly incomplete, as the text breaks off mid-enumeration. The passage refers to "the eight mothers" and the preceding lotus simile without reproducing them, signaling an explicit cross-reference to an earlier section of the narrative; the translation follows the text's own shorthand accordingly. The six terminal duties of a Brahmin listed here correspond closely to the standard Sanskrit formula: yajana, yājana, adhyayana, adhyāpana, dāna, and pratigraha. The figures "Gārgya" and "Māthara" appear as Brahminic sages whose names are being invoked ritually or typologically; the exact referent of "making" them (Tibetan: byas pa) may indicate a ritual identification or initiation rite — this is somewhat obscure and may be context-dependent within the larger text. "The noble young man" (Tibetan: 'phags skyes po) is a recurring epithet in this narrative, likely rendering Sanskrit āryajanman, "one born noble," and has been rendered consistently throughout. The town name "Meḍuludī" (Tibetan: མེ་ཙུ་རུ་དི) is a phonetic rendering of an Indic place-name; the Sanskrit form is not fully recoverable from the Tibetan alone. It appears consistently throughout the passage and is rendered phonetically each time.

The name Mālagandhā (Tibetan: མ་ལ་གནོད) appears to be a phonetic rendering of a proper name; the reading "Mālagandhā" is a plausible reconstruction but is noted here as uncertain. The phrase rendered "faith in the Dharma arising from the Dharma itself" translates chos las byung ba'i dad pa, which could also be rendered "faith arising from the Dharma" or "Dharma-born faith." This is a standard category in Buddhist soteriology referring to confidence grounded in reasoned understanding of the teaching rather than mere devotion; the rendering chosen preserves this nuance.

The expression "more humble than the most humble" renders shin tu dman pa bas kyang ches dman pa byed, literally "you act even lower than the lowest." This is the Blessed One gently chiding the king for extreme prostration, and the idiomatic English rendering is intentional.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan as given; the translation follows accordingly. The passage contains several instances where the Tibetan explicitly instructs the reader to repeat earlier formulaic passages rather than restating them in full — "as before" or "the same as what preceded." These have been rendered as cross-references to what preceded, following the text's own convention. The phrase translated as "before they were even fully posed" reflects an important textual nuance: the Blessed One answers questions that are still in the process of being asked, which is a sign of his omniscience. The self-reproach of the newly ordained monks — "we were improper" — reflects their recognition that they had falsely claimed spiritual attainments they did not possess; this is a standard doctrinal trope illustrating the danger of pride and the transformative power of authentic realization. The phrase rendered as "living in complete dependence on others" translates a clause meaning that monks depend entirely on alms for their livelihood, which is the standard reading in this context. The positive force of the phrase is that such dependence on alms — far from causing bodily deterioration — is associated with the monks' flourishing appearance, the implicit contrast being with the emaciated ascetics who pursue self-mortification. The phrase rendered "I deprive them of wealth" describes Prasenajit withdrawing patronage or financial support from certain ascetics and brahmins, causing them to disrobe and return to lay life. The Tibetan is elliptical here, and the contrast being drawn is between these figures who abandon the holy life once deprived of material support and the Blessed One's śrāvakas who persist without wavering.

The section break "The Minor Matters of the Vinaya, the Eighth Fascicle" is a scribal colophon mid-passage marking the textual source and division; it interrupts the continuous speech of King Prasenajit. The names Viḍūḍabha, Mālikā, Vāsabhā-khattiyā, Medaḷumpa, and Ajātaśatru are Pāli forms of the names well-known from the Pāli parallel of this narrative in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. The Tibetan preserves phonetic approximations of these Indic names. Viḍūḍabha is rendered as "Prince Viḍūḍabha" following the Pāli; the Tibetan reads "spyod pa'i bu ring po," a calque. Medaḷumpa appears in the Tibetan as "me tsu ru di," a phonetic rendering. Ajātaśatru, "the unborn foe" (literally "Ma-skyes dgra"), is rendered by his proper Sanskrit name. The sentence "Prasenajit had left Viḍūḍabha in charge of the kingdom" and the later redundant phrasing "placed Viḍūḍabha in charge" reflect a slight awkwardness in the Tibetan that mirrors probable source ambiguity. The passage "as before, up to the passage: like the pleasure garden of delight among the gods" reflects a deliberate ellipsis in the Tibetan source itself, which abbreviates a repeated stock description by referring back to an earlier occurrence. This is standard in Tibetan narrative literature and has been rendered transparently.

The phrase rendered "the quarters of the young" translates a term suggesting a place or station appropriate to a youth or junior — the implication being that Ajātaśatru, perhaps feeling unworthy or awkward, withdraws to a subordinate position rather than the royal throne, though some traditional readings understand this differently. The ambiguity is minor and does not affect the narrative. The phrase rendered "a bowlful of grain husks" translates "la phug spar gang" — literally "a full measure of husks from a mountain pass," likely meaning the rough grain or chaff husks obtainable in such a locale; the precise grain is unspecified in the text and the rendering captures the sense adequately.

The phrase "abiding close like a shadow that never departs" renders the simile "dba' rgal bzhin du nye bar gnas pa," which is a conventional simile in karmic discourse; the image is of karma as inseparable as a shadow.

The teaching that pratyekabuddhas teach through their body rather than through speech is a standard doctrinal point in texts concerning these solitary buddhas, and the rendering follows the Tibetan precisely. The śākoṭaka tree is a scrubby or thorny tree, identified in some commentarial sources with a variety of acacia or similar species with thin foliage; it is left in transliterated form as the precise identification is uncertain and the descriptive qualifiers in the text convey the meaning. The detail of the Blessed One choosing shade under this unprepossessing tree in preference to finer trees is deliberate: the Blessed One's reply that "the shade of kinsmen is cool" forms the dramatic and doctrinal pivot of the episode, signaling his compassionate intervention on behalf of the Śākyas despite the inexorability of their karma. The narrative as a whole traces the massacre of the Śākyas by Virūḍhaka, a well-known episode found across multiple Vinaya and Avadāna sources. The passage "ལྷའི་ཉི་མ་ཡང་བཟང་། ཡུད་ཙམ་ཡང་བཟང་། སྐར་མ་ཡང་བཟང་། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་གདུགས་ཀྱང་བཟང་" is rhetorically compressed and somewhat elliptical. The sense appears to be that, since Gautama has no regard for kinsmen, from this day forward any moment is equally auspicious — the divine sun, a mere instant, a star, or the canopy of merit are all equally good — meaning there is no reason to delay the attack. The translation renders this sense, though the exact rhetorical force is slightly ambiguous in context.

The phrase "དབའ་རྒལ་བཞིན་ཉེ་བར་གནས་པ" literally means something like "abiding close like a dam-breaking flood" or "standing by like a ford about to be crossed." The translation renders the image as a welling flood for clarity in a TTS context. The name rendered "Virūḍhaka" does not appear explicitly in this passage but is clearly the referent of the repeated phrase "the man born of a woman of low birth" and the recurring pronoun. Contextually this is Virūḍhaka, king of Kosala, well known from parallel accounts of the destruction of the Śākyas. The Tibetan phrase literally means "a man of great delusion, born of a noble/elevated woman," which is an unusual circumlocution; it likely reflects a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit epithet or proper name. The name Śambhaka for the Śākya outcast is given directly in the text. The name rendered "Ārya-jaṭa" translates the Tibetan འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ, literally "noble-born man." This may be a personal name or an epithet; without broader context it is difficult to determine whether this refers to a specific named character or is a general epithet for Virūḍhaka, whose narrative is running in parallel. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, suggesting the text continues beyond this excerpt. The phrase rendered "dwelling of the yellow-robed ones" translates སེར་སྐྱའི་གནས, literally "abode of the yellow-robed," a common designation for a monastic community or monastery. The communal act referred to (ཚོགས་པ་ཅན་གྱི་ལས) is a formal legal act of the Saṅgha (saṃghakārman) in the Vinaya sense — a binding resolution requiring the full assembly; those who absented themselves were not bound by it, which explains the distinction in the narrative.

The curious detail of Śākyas circulating in and out of different gates — entering one and emerging from another — appears to describe a miraculous or supernatural evasion; the text is compressed and the full sense may depend on surrounding narrative context. The epithet "Mālanod" renders མ་ལ་གནོད, which appears to be a personal name or title of a minister or counselor figure. Its meaning and identity are not entirely clear from the passage alone; it may be a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit or Prakrit name.

The phrase སེར་སྐྱ་ན་གནས་པའི་ཤཱཀྱ་རྣམས — literally "the Śākyas dwelling in the yellow-grey" — is here rendered "those who dwelled among the yellow-robed ones," understood as Śākya monastics. The expression is slightly ambiguous; it could also mean Śākyas who had gone forth into the renunciant life more broadly. The phrase rendered "of ignoble birth and low lineage" translates a compound meaning literally "a brahmin who is in accord with vileness and with bone-lineage," which is a pointed inversion of the brahminic claim to pure lineage: the narrator uses this to mark the brahmin as socially low despite his caste designation. The irony is intentional — a self-identified brahmin is described in terms that subvert his pretension to high birth.

The repeated refrain structure in the original is explicitly marked by the Tibetan "as before" (snga ma bzhin), indicating a liturgical or recitative abbreviation of stock phrases. The translation preserves this abbreviated refrain device in faithful rendering. The phrase rendered "present like a creditor who has reached the threshold" translates the term "dba' rgal bzhin nye bar gnas pa," an idiom comparing ripening karma to a creditor standing at the door demanding repayment. This is a well-attested metaphor in karma teachings.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, which reflects the actual state of the Tibetan as given; the fish's thought is left incomplete. This is a genuine textual feature, not a translation error. The passage uses "Āryaskanda" (འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ) literally meaning "noble-born one," and "Mālāgandha" (མ་ལ་གནོད), which is a proper name rendered consistently from the preceding context. The text's narrative is identifying the figures Āryaskanda and Mālāgandha as the reincarnations of the two fish and two householders in past lives, and the five hundred Śākyas as the reincarnations of the five hundred fishermen and bandits, establishing karmic continuity across lives — a central doctrinal point of this passage.

The term གཡོན་ཅན་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་པོ ("five hundred who had deceit/crookedness") in reference to the bandits is rendered simply as "five hundred bandits" in the main translation for smooth narration, since the context already identifies them as robbers; the nuance of "deceitful ones" is absorbed into the narrative. The phrase rendered "arrogant-born man" (Āryaskanda) reflects a play in the Tibetan between the name Āryaskanda and the epithet ངོམ་ཞིང་རྣམ་པར་ངོམ ("boasting and preening") used just below; the epithet འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ་ lit. "noble-born man" is used for Āryaskanda throughout, but here the irony is clearly intentional given his actions. The rendering "arrogant-born" is interpretive; the literal sense is simply "Āryaskanda, a man of delusion," and the epithet འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ is his standard designation.

The final sentence "The Blessed One considered:" is left open because the Tibetan passage breaks off mid-sentence (བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དགོངས་པ། without completing the object), indicating the text continues in the next passage. The phrase rendered "breathe freely" translates a Tibetan idiom literally meaning "to release the breath" or "to take a breath" — here used in the sense of allowing the distressed women relief and recovery from their ordeal. The doctrinal image of the "mountain peak of the view of the transitory collection, twenty heights high" reflects a standard scholastic enumeration: the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi) comprises twenty sub-views (five aggregates each taken in four ways as self or as belonging to self), and stream-entry involves their complete uprooting. The epithet "Viḍūḍabha" (Tibetan: འཕགས་སྐྱེས་པོ) literally means "nobly born" and is the name of the Kosalan prince famous in Buddhist narrative for massacring the Śākyas; it is here rendered by name throughout since context makes identification clear.

The phrase rendered "struck down like a serpent's gaze" (སྦྲུལ་གྱིས་བལྟས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་རབས་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ) is somewhat unusual; the image appears to be of death coming suddenly and inevitably, as prey is paralyzed by a snake's look. This could alternatively refer to destruction "as if stared down by a serpent," a literary expression for utter doom.

The passage "as before" (སྔ་མ་བཞིན་ནོ) indicates that the text is abbreviating sections already given in full earlier in the same scripture, a standard compositional device in Tibetan canonical collections. The "group of six monks" refers to the well-known six wayward monks who appear throughout the Vinaya literature as exemplars of improper conduct. The phrase "Serkya" renders a Tibetan toponym that may correspond to a locale otherwise known as Sāketa or a similarly named place; the exact identification is uncertain but not consequential to the narrative.

The phrase rendered "spirits had already blocked all the exits" translates a term for non-human beings who obstruct escape, consistent with the fulfillment of the Blessed One's prophecy about inescapable karmic consequences. The summary verse appears to be a mnemonic encoding the topics of a set of Vinaya rules; the precise referent of each item (incense, orpiment, salve, cup, raw grain, etc.) is clear as a list but the verse's compressed telegraphic syntax is characteristic of Vinaya uddāna verses and is rendered accordingly.

The phrase rendered "which deer do not avoid as they avoid hunters" is a stock Śrāvastī epithet meaning the city is so safe and pleasant that even deer roam there freely; the Tibetan literally says "deer-saviors do not avoid deer in broad Śrāvastī," a compressed idiomatic phrase conveying that the city is without danger even for wild animals. The phrase rendered "coins and kārṣāpaṇas" translates a compound that appears to list two kinds of currency: a general term for coin and the specific denomination kārṣāpaṇa. The doubling may be a hendiadys for "money in general," but both terms are preserved in the translation for accuracy.

The phrase rendered "a poison to the touch" is a morally loaded narratorial comment in the original, presenting women as inherently dangerous to the male renunciant. It is a standard trope in Vinaya literature and has been translated literally as the text demands, without softening. The passage shifts between two distinct episodes. The first concerns a member of the Group of Six who tricks the old monk into revealing his transgression and then manipulates him further; the Blessed One's ruling culminates in ordering the formal promulgation of the four pārājika rules to be given immediately upon ordination. The second episode introduces a new character, the monk Priyadatta, who is harassed by a māra-goddess while meditating. The phrase rendered "she engaged in sexual intercourse with him" is the text's direct narrative statement; the monk's subsequent anguish and self-assessment reflect the Vinaya's technical question of whether involuntary sexual contact constitutes a pārājika offence — the point the episode is building toward. The name rendered throughout as "Nandaka" translates the Tibetan "dga' ba can," which literally means "one possessing joy" or "the joyful one" — a standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Nandaka. The bitter wordplay when he says he is now "mi dga' ba can," one without joy or gladness, is deliberate and has been preserved in the translation.

The procedural text here is a verbatim Vinaya (monastic discipline) formula for the formal Saṅgha act of re-granting the training precepts. The passage reproduces the standard tripartite structure of Vinaya acts: the preliminary motion (gsol ba), the formal motion (las bsgrags pa), and the act proper (las), here read at its first recitation, with the implication that it is to be repeated three times in full. This structure has been rendered with the technical precision the Vinaya tradition requires. The phrase rendered "request-and-two" and "request-and-four" translates formulaic Vinaya expressions for formal acts of the Saṅgha that require one announcement plus two affirmations, or one announcement plus four affirmations, respectively — standard technical categories of Vinaya procedure.

The "shrine-hall's lord" is ambiguous; it may refer to a patron or donor of the vihāra rather than a deity, but in context it appears alongside "deities of the shrine-hall," suggesting a presiding protective deity of the building. This reflects standard Vinaya liturgical usage. The verse at the end is a mnemonic summary verse listing topics covered in the preceding section. The items are enumerated tersely and some terms are technical Vinaya shorthand; "what has been accumulated" likely refers to items set aside or stored, and "nasal pouring" refers to the nasal-oil procedure described in adjacent sections of the Vinaya. The overall list signals the scope of regulations just covered rather than constituting independent doctrine.

The name of the plant whose smoke Pilindavatsa relies on is not specified in the Tibetan; the text uses only a generic term. The identity of the plant is not determinable from this passage alone. The phrase rendered "accumulated-herbs bath" translates a technical medical term for a therapeutic herbal decoction bath. The precise Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain; it may correspond to something like a sarvauṣadhi or kaṣāya preparation, but the text does not specify and the physician himself admits ignorance of the details.

The term rendered "wheel-turning physicians" translates a phrase suggesting a lineage of royal or authoritative medical practitioners; it may refer to the tradition of a cakravartin-associated medical corpus, but the exact referent is uncertain.

"Pilindavatsa" is the Tibetan rendering of a known disciple's name; kept as is for consistency with standard scholarly usage. The phrase rendered "you have come with the fruit of the buddha's arising" is a somewhat cryptic compliment: the wives mean that by listening to the Dharma, their husbands have come home bearing the very fruit for which a buddha appears in the world, namely, the teaching of Dharma. The Tibetan is compressed and the exact nuance is slightly elliptical, but this reading is consistent with the context.

The name Pilindavatsa renders the Tibetan ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་པི་ལིན་དའི་བུ, literally "the Venerable son of Pilinda," which is a standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit proper name Pilindavatsa; it is treated throughout as a personal name. The final sentence renders the idiom "བཤང་བའི་ས་བྱའོ" literally as "a latrine pit should be made," understanding this as an instruction to construct a designated toilet facility. The precise form of this structure is not specified in the text; the translation follows what is contextually implied by the narrative. The compound "རིལ་བ་སྤྱི་བླུགས" in the latrine construction passage refers to a rinsing pot together with a communal ladle or scoop for pouring water, a standard pair of ablution implements in Vinaya contexts. The rendering reflects this pairing.

The phrase "སོ་གའི་དུས" rendered as "the hot season" follows the standard Vinaya reckoning of the three seasons, where this term denotes the warm or hot period before the rains. The phrase rendered "as before, down to 'and let him consent'" follows a common Vinaya literary convention of abbreviating repeated procedural formulas by referencing an earlier full version; the abbreviation is in the source itself. The phrase rendered "Those who are in residence are to pour the water" refers to monks who are currently staying at the monastery, distinguishing them from visitors or those passing through. The text at this point is a regular Vinaya narrative and the term gnас pa (those residing, residents) carries this technical sense.

The passage "from the words beginning ... up to ... everything proceeds as before" is a standard Vinaya scribal abbreviation indicating that a previously recounted exchange between the Blessed One and Prajāpatī Gautamī is to be understood as occurring here in full without being repeated in the manuscript.

The epithet skye dgu'i bdag mo chen mo (great mistress of creatures) renders the Sanskrit Mahāprajāpatī; the personal name Gautamī follows. The verse rendering of the penultimate stanza, particularly the line rendered "hearers who dwell in harmony, viewing one another as kin," involves some compression. The Tibetan phrase ཉན་ཐོས་མཐུན་པ་ལྟ་ཕྱེད་པ is syntactically dense; "ལྟ་ཕྱེད་པ" most naturally suggests something like "regarding each other well" or "looking upon one another with goodwill," which the translation approximates. The exact metrical and syntactic structure of the verse section is loosely rendered in the interest of natural spoken English, as required for TTS delivery. The names rendered "Ānanda, Anupama, Selā" in the middle passage are uncertain. The Tibetan gives "Tshe dang ldan pa dga' bo" (the venerable Ānanda), "ma 'gags pa" (possibly "Unobstructed" — perhaps the nun Utpalavārṇā or another figure; the name is unclear), and "sgra can zin" (literally "one who has caught a sound/tone," possibly Selā or another nun's name). Because these names are not perfectly transparent and the passage appears to conflate the monks Ānanda and others with the nuns in a textually difficult stretch, this is flagged as a point of genuine uncertainty. The dialogue structure, however, is clear. The passage describes the canonical "twin miracle" (yugaṃnadhā) of fire and water issuing simultaneously from the upper and lower body, a standard display of supernormal power in Pāli and Sanskrit sources, here applied to Prajāpatī. The sequence of nine meditative attainments traversed in both forward and reverse order, culminating in nirvāṇa from the first dhyāna, matches the classical account found in Pāli nibbāna-parinibbāna narratives. The name rendered "Lāṅgika" (རླངས་པ) and "Nāmavān" (མིང་ཆེན) are less common śrāvaka names; the identifications are reasonable but not certain. "Mṛgāramātā Viśākhā" (རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་ག) follows the standard Tibetan rendering of the well-known female lay disciple Viśākhā, also called Mṛgāramātā. The four names rendered as "Ānanda, Avighna, Nandaka, and Sundarananda" correspond to Tibetan དགའ་བོ, མ་འགགས་པ, ཀུན་དགའ་བོ, and སྒྲ་ཅན་ཟིན respectively. The last name, སྒྲ་ཅན་ཟིན, literally means "one who has caught a sound" and is a standard Tibetan rendering of Sundarananda or possibly Nandopananda; the identification as Sundarananda follows common Tibetan usage though some manuscripts differ.

The phrase rendered "abided like a flame" translates འོད་པ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉེ་བར་གནས་པ, which is somewhat elliptical. The simile likely indicates that karma, like a flame, persists and functions continuously until its fuel is spent — a common doctrinal illustration of karma's ongoing potential. The phrase rendered "Great Mistress of Beings" translates a Tibetan epithet for a senior nun figure who serves as the head of the group of five hundred nuns; the precise identity is not given in this passage but she is presented as their leader. The passage about "karma thoroughly dark" and the closing formula are deliberate abbreviations in the canonical text itself, referring back to a standard doctrinal section treated earlier in the sūtra. The final two verse lines are the opening of a verse summary section embedded in Vinaya text, listing structural or material items. The full meaning becomes clear only with the following lines, so these opening lines read as fragmentary. No doctrinal uncertainty attaches to the preceding prose; the enumeration of foods follows standard Vinaya categories and presents no difficulty. The terms traymabuka and trailata are transliterations of obscure Indic insect or creature names that do not have standard English equivalents; they are rendered here in approximate phonetic form.

The passage describes the incremental development of Vinaya rules for the construction and fittings of monastic dwelling-houses, progressing through a series of practical problems encountered by the monks and their solutions as authorized by the Blessed One. The window-lattice instruction describing the shape as resembling "the ocean" likely refers to a flared or wide-mouthed profile, deeper on the inside than the outside. The plant name uṣatu is left in approximate transliteration; the Tibetan ཨུ་ཥ་ཏུ་ is clearly a rendering of a Sanskrit botanical name, but the exact identification is uncertain enough to warrant flagging. It may refer to a grass used for polishing metal, sometimes identified with darbha or a related species, but the precise referent cannot be confirmed from this passage alone. The term rendered "couches with decorative legs" translates a compound describing couches or seats featuring carved or ornamented legs, a standard Vinaya category. The precise ornamental style is not specified beyond this in the text. The summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā listing items previously permitted: peg, three kinds of ladder, latch, interior support-bar, and tread-boards of wood, stone, and earth — with a final line recapitulating permission for ladders in three types. The verse is deliberately compressed and telegraphic, as is normal for Vinaya summary verses.

The term rendered "latch" translates a word for a door-fastening device; "interior support-bar" renders a term for an internal bracing element. The exact carpentry referents of these Vinaya technical terms are somewhat conventional in translation. The phrase rendered as "dried off this mark" refers to Sundarī's action in the preceding passage of marking Nanda before he departs, so that she can tell upon his return whether he has been near the Blessed One, whose presence was understood to radiate a golden or luminous quality. The drying of the mark serves as a test of how close he came. This is a well-known motif in the Nanda avadāna cycle.

The sentence about the Blessed One not breaking "a single word of Dharma" across generations with parents, teachers, and so forth is doctrinally dense. It means the Blessed One had never resorted to a direct Dharma teaching as a form of social pressure or obligation in any of those relational roles across his previous lives — yet here he uses the indirect method of feeding Nanda the bowl-remnants and simply asking why he does not go forth, which is gentle and therefore irresistible. This is a standard commentarial point in the Nanda ordination narrative. The text identifies the woman as "Mṛgāramat's mother of Sundarī" (རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་གའི་ཁྱིམ), meaning the household of Mṛgāramat, mother of Sundarī — a well-known lay patroness of Śrāvastī; the syntax is slightly compressed in Tibetan but the referent is standard in Vinaya literature.

Turushka (ཏུ་རུཥྐ) is a fragrant resinous substance used as incense, sometimes identified as frankincense or a related aromatic resin imported from Central Asia.

The phrase that Nanda bears the thirty marks but falls "four finger-breadths short" reflects the tradition that Nanda possessed thirty of the thirty-two major marks of a great being and was slightly shorter in stature than the Buddha, falling short by four finger-breadths. The term rendered "receptacle for the outflow" translates འཛག་སྣོད་ (a container for seminal fluid / nocturnal emission), and སྒྲེའུ་བཅང་བར་བྱ as "carry a receptacle" or "wear a pouch" — both refer to the same object described in what follows as a skin pouch stuffed with wadding. The progression of rulings here is a standard Vinaya legislative sequence and has been rendered accordingly.

The phrase གདོན་པ rendered as "recitation" refers to the chanting or vocalization of texts, a standard paired duty with meditation in the monastic context. The phrase rendered "arrive directly" translates a somewhat terse Tibetan that may simply mean "straightaway" or "at once"; the general sense of immediate arrival in the heaven of the Thirty-Three is clear. The list of divine pleasures and architectural and musical details is somewhat formulaic and some terms, particularly the names of musical instruments such as the three-stringed lute, the flute, and the lute, are Tibetan transliterations of Indic terms whose precise identification is uncertain; this does not affect the doctrinal content. The passage lists six forms of communal avoidance imposed on Nanda by the Saṅgha at the Buddha's instruction: shared seating, shared walking ground, shared robe-rack, shared bowl-stand, shared water-stand, and shared liturgical recitation or chanting. These are well-attested disciplinary measures in Vinaya literature for isolating a monk whose conduct or motivation is considered unwholesome, intended here to produce shame and reform rather than permanent exclusion. The exchange between Nanda and Ānanda at the close sets up the continuation of the narrative. The phrase rendered "rivers without fords" translates a Tibetan term for one of the classic hell-realm features, likely corresponding to the Vaitaraṇī river in Sanskrit sources; the Tibetan here simply says "rivers without fords" without naming it, so no Sanskrit name has been supplied. The location at the end is given as "grong khyer tsampa," which corresponds to the city of Campā with its famous hot springs, a recognized site in the Nanda cycle narratives. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, in the middle of a comparison being drawn between women whose fertile seasons last long and those whose do not; the text is clearly continuing into a subsequent passage.

The term rendered "gandharva" refers here specifically to the being inhabiting the intermediate state between death and rebirth. The text's own gloss — "the designation for a being of the intermediate existence" — reflects the standard Abhidharmic understanding used in this sūtra context. The term "gandharva" here refers to the being who enters the womb at conception — a being between death and rebirth, called in Tibetan "dri za" (literally "scent-eater"). This is a significant doctrinal term in Abhidharma and Vinaya embryology: the gandharva is the intermediate-state being whose entry is the third necessary condition for conception, alongside the union of father and mother. The text's insistence on its "mind" being male or female is an important detail for understanding sex determination in traditional Buddhist embryology.

The architectural and anatomical vocabulary describing womb defects is highly technical and several terms admit multiple interpretations. The renderings offered reflect the most contextually plausible readings; a specialist in Āyurvedic and early Buddhist medical literature might refine several of these. The creature name "besaraka" is a transliteration of an unidentified Sanskrit term rendered phonetically in Tibetan as be sa ra ka. It likely refers to a specific insect or small animal in the context of examining whether the womb is a suitable vessel; the exact species is uncertain.

The "worm born from green grass" that takes on the color of a green leaf is a classical Indian biological observation used repeatedly in embryological texts as an analogy for dependent origination without identity or total difference; it is a stock example found in several Indic sources. The term rendered "cedar wood" translates rgya shug, which refers to a coniferous tree, likely cypress or a related species. "Cedar" is an approximation; the exact species is uncertain, but it is consistently described as producing red-colored worms in the analogy, which fits the context. The passage on the butter-lamp carrier and the lotus stalk is a simile for how breath and heat within the womb cause the embryo to develop; the exact mechanics of the image are somewhat obscure in the Tibetan, but the doctrinal point — that the wind element animates growth — is clear.

The final phrase, "I do not praise even the slightest accomplished existence," renders a standard Pāli and Sanskrit formula in which the Buddha declares that he finds no good in continued becoming in saṃsāra, however small. This is a well-attested doctrinal refrain and is rendered accordingly. The three Tibetan embryological terms for the developmental stages of the fetus — nur nur po, mer mer po, and nar nar po — are standard Āyurvedic and Abhidharma embryological categories (kalala, arbuda, peśī in Sanskrit). They are rendered here descriptively as "viscous mass," "firmer mass," and "lumpy mass" respectively, following the context of the analogies given. The Sanskrit equivalents are well-attested in parallel texts. The wind named "gathering" (kun sdud) and "storehouse-door" (mdzod sgo) are among the named winds of karmic-embryological tradition; no standard English equivalents exist, so they are transliterated by meaning. The passage opens with "and in suffering," which is the completion of the sentence broken off at the end of the preceding passage, preserved here as instructed for continuity.

The Tibetan term rendered "thorn of the womb" is mngal gyi zug rngu, a standard technical expression in this genre meaning the embryo conceived as a painful thorn or affliction lodged in the womb; the translation preserves this striking image faithfully rather than smoothing it to "embryo."

The term rendered "rounded mass" in this week corresponds to the preceding passage's "lumpy mass" from the prior stage; the Tibetan here uses gor gor po, a slightly different shape term indicating a rounder, more globular form than the preceding week's stage. The verse embedded in the thirteenth-week passage is rendered as verse in the translation, consistent with the Tibetan metrical form. The channel-count of nine hundred (225 × 4) is numerically consistent within the text and is rendered as given. The term translated as "mesentery" for གཉེ་མ is a reasonable anatomical equivalent in context; some traditions gloss it differently, but this is the most defensible rendering for a general audience. The phrase rendered as "the hollow around the heart" translates a term that literally refers to the region or cavity around the heart, understood in this embryological context as a bodily chamber or receptacle. The series of verbs for placing and arranging — five synonymous or near-synonymous terms — follows a formulaic pattern common to Abhidharmic and embryological sūtra literature and has been rendered with corresponding English synonyms to preserve the rhetorical texture without excessive repetition. The phrase rendered "the face of the draw-string" translates a wind name that appears to describe a pulling or tightening action associated with the clarification of the sense organs; the precise anatomical imagery is idiomatic to this embryological genre and the Tibetan is translated literally.

The section marker "This is the twelfth fascicle of the basis of the minor Vinaya" is an editorial colophon embedded in the text marking a manuscript division; it interrupts the discourse and has been rendered plainly as it appears. The verse on bodily form is cryptic and likely represents a mnemonic summary of ideal physical proportions, presented here in inverted form to indicate what the being born of bad karma will lack. The Tibetan is terse and the verse's precise sense turns on context within the larger treatise; the translation renders the most natural reading.

The term rendered "the arising of all" (Tib. kun du 'byung ba), "the all-victorious" (yongs su rgyal ba), "the holder of purity" (gtsang 'dzin), "the all-floating" (yongs su 'phyo ba), "the carrier of dissolution" (khyer 'jig), and "the great medicinal offering" (sman yon chen po) are technical names of specific embryological winds; no standard Sanskrit equivalents are recoverable from this passage alone. The phrase rendered "blood-kin" translates a compound meaning relatives by blood lineage on the paternal side, as distinct from relatives more broadly. The distinction is preserved here by pairing "relatives and blood-kin." The term "a hundredfold equal in fortune" renders a comparative expression indicating a human rebirth incomparably superior; the precise quantification follows the Tibetan literally. The phrase "the bark of kuśa grass" renders རྩྭ་དཱུར་བའི་ཤུན་པ. The Sanskrit botanical term dūrvā refers to a type of sacred grass commonly found in Indian ritual contexts; its bark or fiber has a characteristic pale greenish-gray color. The repetition in the Tibetan is deliberate and formulaic, and has been preserved faithfully.

The "five cords" with which the being is said to be bound is a standard Abhidharma and womb-description formula for the physical constraints of the fetal position; it is rendered literally as the tradition intends. The phrase rendered "the thirty-eighth day of the seventh week" and the parallel references to "days" within "weeks" follow the Tibetan literally. The text counts gestational periods in units of seven-day weeks (ཞག་བདུན་པ), and the ordinal number within that unit refers to the numbered day of the given week. The transition at the end to "the thirty-eighth week" uses the same Tibetan formula but the context makes clear a shift has occurred from day-counts within the final week to the week-count overall; this is a common feature of such embryological sūtra literature and the translation follows the Tibetan as given.

The śalmali plant (Skt. śālmalī) is the silk-cotton tree, whose soft fibers were used medicinally; this is the plant referred to by the Tibetan ཤིང་ཤལ་མ་ལི. The phrase rendered as "nourished, sustained, and kept alive by the impurity of its own blood" refers to the newborn being sustained by mother's milk, which the text itself immediately glosses: in this noble Dharma discipline, blood-impurity is the term used for mother's milk. This is a standard doctrinal motif found in Āgama literature emphasizing the painful and impure nature of birth and bodily existence.

The final sentence breaks off mid-enumeration, as the source passage itself is incomplete at that point. The names of the parasitic worm-kinds are rendered by their semantic meaning from the Tibetan, as the underlying Sanskrit is not recoverable from this passage. Some anatomical terms admit minor uncertainty: "ལྐོག་མ" is rendered "sides" (flanks), though it can also denote the area around the ribs or armpits; "དཀན་" is rendered "palate" following the most common gloss in medical lexica; "ལོང་ཀ་" is rendered "bladder," though some sources gloss it as a section of the lower abdomen. These choices are consistent with the medical-anatomical context of the passage. The list of afflictions includes several terms that denote classes of spirits or supernatural forces whose names are rendered here by their descriptive meanings, as many lack established Sanskrit equivalents in this context. "Māmō spirits" renders མ་མོ, a class of wrathful female spirits well known in Tibetan tradition, left in transliterated form since no standard English or Sanskrit equivalent is in common use. "Garuḍas" renders གནམ་ལྡིང, and "kinnaras" renders མིའམ་ཅི, both standard Indo-Tibetan mythological categories. "Those of the sky-corner" renders ནམ་གྲུ, a less common term possibly referring to spirits of the cardinal or intermediate directions; its exact referent is uncertain. The tenfold division of life phases is a well-known literary scheme in Indian Buddhist literature. The translation of the eighth phase as "steadiness like that of a king" reflects the Tibetan comparison of the peak of mature stability to royal dignity.

The medical terminology in the final list presents some interpretive choices. The term rendered "lipoma" or "fatty disease" translates a term for a growth of fatty tissue. "Night-sweat" renders a term that can also mean nocturnal emission or nocturnal discharge; the medical context supports the broader rendering. The passage is clearly a catalogue and breaks off mid-list, consistent with the Tibetan text as given. The sequence "མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར། སོ་སོར་མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར། ཚོར་བར་འགྱུར། སོ་སོར་ཚོར་བར་འགྱུར།" uses four verbs for experiencing and feeling, likely a formulaic quadruple expression emphasizing the fullness and intimacy of that experience. The translation renders them as a natural foursome without being pedantic about each nuance. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source; the translation reflects this faithfully. The passage enumerates the four types of womb-entry found in several Āgama and Abhidharma sources. The Tibetan term "ཤེས་བཞིན་དུ" here rendered "with full awareness" literally means "with clear knowing" or "consciously," corresponding to the Pali "sampajāno" and Sanskrit "saṃprajānan." This is a standard Abhidharma category and the rendering is consistent with commentarial usage.

The phrase rendered "one who has not yet attained any result" translates a list that appears slightly compressed in this portion of the text; the full list of attainment levels is picked up in the subsequent sentence. No significant doctrinal uncertainty arises from this. The extended womb description is a close parallel to similar passages in the Śrāvakabhūmi and related Yogācāra literature cataloguing the sufferings of gestation. The list of bodily substances and the physiological details follow a well-established Indian Buddhist genre of meditating on the repulsiveness of the body. The phrase rendered "grub-releasing vessel" translates a Tibetan compound describing an unclean fluid distributed like the fluid that releases or drips from worms; the precise image is that of a container oozing vermin-fluid, used as an analogy for the nourishment received in the womb. The five bonds mentioned are a standard Indian image for the constriction of the fetus in the womb rather than the five bonds to the lower realms (the orambhāgīya-saṃyojana), and context makes this clear. The text is structured as a discourse addressed to "Nanda," identifiable as the sūtra Nanda-garbhāvakrānti-nirdeśa context, in which the Buddha describes to his half-brother Nanda the sufferings of existence beginning from conception. The repeated vocative rendered here as "Nanda" corresponds to "དགའ་བོ" in Tibetan, literally "Beloved One" or "Dear One," which is a standard honorific form of address for Nanda in this text. The choice to render it as "Nanda" rather than "Beloved" follows the convention established by the surrounding context; a reader should know that the Tibetan literally means something like "Joyful One" or "Dear One."

The phrase rendered as "mechanism of bones" for "རུས་པའི་འཁྲུལ་འཁོར་" is a graphic anatomical metaphor for the pelvic birth canal; "འཁྲུལ་འཁོར་" ordinarily means a machine or mechanism driven by contrivance, here applied metaphorically to the skeletal frame of the pelvis. The phrase "The minor Vinaya matters. The thirteenth fascicle" is a scribal colophon dividing the text into fascicles and appears mid-passage in the Tibetan; it has been rendered as a brief interlude exactly where it occurs in the text, as it belongs to the manuscript structure rather than the narrative itself. A TTS producer may wish to omit or pause around it.

The term rendered "inverted womb" refers to a malpresentation of the fetus; the Tibetan is describing obstetric complications and the manipulation required to correct fetal position, which a skilled midwife performs. The phrase rendered "seven-times-returner," "one born from noble family to noble family," "once-returner," and "one with a single intervening existence" reflects the standard Abhidharmic enumeration of levels of stream-enterers, and the text is structuring a distinction between those who die and enter the next womb with mindfulness intact versus those who do not — the former being practitioners of established virtue or those who have attained one of the lower stages of the path of liberation.

The concluding section, beginning with the description of the womb as supremely hot and running through the enumeration of impurities, appears to be an extended catalogue of the body's repulsive characteristics that continues beyond this passage; the abrupt end mid-list reflects the passage as supplied. The passage contains a sequence of four iterative Tibetan onomatopoeic or descriptive terms for the embryo's developing physical states: nur nur po, mer mer po, nar nar po, and gor gor po. These are technical embryological terms describing successive stages of the embryo's texture and shape, rendered here as "soft and tender, then firming, then hardening, then rounding out," following the traditional commentarial sequence of embryonic development. The precise correspondence of each term to a specific classical Indian embryological stage is a specialist matter but does not affect the overall sense.

The phrase rendered "the lower wound" translates a term literally meaning "the lower mouth-wound," a graphic designation for the birth canal or uterine opening, consistent with the text's sustained rhetoric of bodily impurity. The phrase rendered "consciousness that is of one flavor with suffering" translates a construction in which the consciousness at the moment of death is said to be characterized entirely by or identified with suffering — a somewhat unusual formulation that may reflect a specific doctrinal point about the quality of consciousness at death for those with heavy unwholesome karma. The Tibetan "sdu g bsngal du ro gcig pa'i rnam par shes pa" literally means "consciousness that is of one taste/flavor with suffering," and this is rendered faithfully rather than smoothed over. The terms traima-buka and traila-ta appear to be transcriptions of Sanskrit insect or worm names that remain unidentified in standard sources; they are rendered here in approximate phonetic form rather than translated, as their precise referents are uncertain.

The phrase rendered "young crocodiles who kill" translates a compound that literally suggests a chu-srin of the kind that kills young; the exact zoological referent is unclear but points to a crocodilian or similar aquatic predator. The phrase rendered "through the form of one who has the fortune" translates a passage that is somewhat compressed and difficult. The Tibetan reads "not through speculative tolerance of views, nor through the form of one who is fortunate" — this appears to be the Buddha distinguishing his mode of teaching from philosophical debate or the posturing of a fortunate individual. The exact doctrinal referent is mildly uncertain but the overall sense — that he speaks only from direct experience — is clear from context.

The closing injunction "understand directly just what you yourself see with the eye of flesh" is striking and rhetorically abrupt; it appears to be a rhetorical challenge directed at Ānanda, inviting him to trust even ordinary sense-perception as a starting point. No further gloss is supplied here as the passage continues. The closing sentence is syntactically incomplete in the passage provided, breaking off mid-construction. The translation renders as much as the text supplies and ends where the Tibetan ends.

The fourfold mindfulness passage follows the standard Pali satipaṭṭhāna formula closely. The rendering of "bdag nyid gling" as "one's own island" follows the well-attested reading of attadīpa as "island" rather than "lamp," which is the traditional Indic interpretation reflected in this Tibetan text.

The phrase rendered "go off alone to a secluded place and reflect" translates a compressed imperative construction; the sense of solitary retreat and sustained contemplation is clearly intended. The final verse line breaks off mid-sentence, as the source passage ends there. The translation preserves this open ending faithfully.

The phrase rendered "without remainder" for "len pa med par" literally means "without grasping" or "without taking up" (anupādāya in Sanskrit), a technical Vinaya and Abhidharma expression indicating liberation that leaves no residue of clinging; both senses are present but "without remainder" captures the doctrinal import for listeners. The embryological sequence near the opening — "glutinous mass," "foam-like substance," and so on — reflects the classical Indian five-stage account of embryonic development (kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, śākhā), rendered here from the Tibetan descriptive terms rather than imported Sanskrit labels, since the text itself uses Tibetan phonological approximations of the stages rather than the Sanskrit names directly.

The bone-count passage is a highly technical anatomical enumeration common to Abhidharma and related Buddhist medical literature; the numbers given follow the Tibetan text precisely, though some totals are internally complex and the counting scheme reflects a traditional Indian anatomical schema rather than modern anatomy. The epithet Vipaśyin, one of the seven buddhas of antiquity, is retained in Sanskrit throughout. The Tibetan "རྣམ་པར་གཟིགས" is a standard Tibetan rendering of Vipaśyin. The phrase "གཡས་ཁྱིམ་གྱི་གཅུང" literally "the younger brother of the house to the right" is somewhat unusual; it likely refers to a neighboring household or a junior kinsman living to the right of the palace, and this literal rendering is preserved rather than smoothed over. The verse on the experience of pleasures is likely Nanda's recollection of his former life of comfort before renunciation; the translation preserves this reading. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, so the translation ends at the same point. The phrase rendered "taking hold of his face" or "holding him by the face" translates a verb meaning something like physically grasping or cupping the face to steer someone — a slightly unusual detail suggesting he was brought along by mild physical coaxing. The meaning is contextually clear but the precise gesture is somewhat idiomatically opaque in the original. The phrase rendered "forcibly separated" translates a term suggesting vigorous, determined intervention — the younger brother had to be pulled away from his attachments against his will, which the aspiration then mirrors for the aspirant's own future liberation. This reading is doctrinally consistent with the narrative of the Blessed One rescuing a deeply attached relative through compassionate compulsion, paralleling well-known stories in the canon.

The epithet "Vipaśyin" is the buddha of the preceding world-age, one of the seven buddhas of antiquity. The narrative is situating Ānanda's deep karmic connection to the Blessed One Śākyamuni within this distant past life, explaining why Ānanda became the Buddha's attendant in the present age. The phrase rendered "came to abide as though at the water's edge" translates the Tibetan idiom "dba' rgal bzhin nye bar gnas par gyur pa," which describes being at the very threshold of a result — like someone who has waded to the bank and stands ready to cross. This is a standard karmic-fruition idiom indicating that conditions have fully ripened.

The passage "ཕུང་པོའི་ལྷག་མ་མ་ལུས་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ" refers to nirvāṇa without remainder (Skt. nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa), the parinirvāṇa at death, as distinct from nirvāṇa with remainder. This distinction is preserved in the translation. The epithet string "rig pa dang zhabs su ldan pa" renders the Sanskrit vidyācaraṇasampanna, "endowed with knowledge and conduct," a standard Tathāgata epithet. The phrase "dba' rgal bzhin nye bar gnas pa" literally "standing near like one who has crossed [the stream, i.e., an arrow]" is an unusual idiom for karmic inevitability; it is rendered here as "drawing near like a crossbow bolt ready to fly," following commentarial tradition that glosses it as an image of inescapable momentum. The name of the forest, "rang srang smra ba," is rendered as the Sanskrit Ṛṣivadana, the standard equivalent for the Deer Park at Varanasi (Mṛgadāva / Ṛṣivadana). The passage ends mid-sentence as given. The name "Blama" rendered here as a proper name for the brahmin youth is the Tibetan "བླ་མ," which in this context functions as a personal name rather than the common noun "lama" or "teacher." The text reads that the Blessed One Kāśyapa prophesied to "the brahmin youth Blama," addressing him directly as a named individual.

The phrase "those who guard the gates of the sense faculties" renders the Tibetan "དབང་པོའི་སྒོ་བསྡམས་པ," meaning those who are restrained or controlled at the doors of the sense faculties — a recognized category in monastic virtue rankings, here designating Priya as the foremost among the community in this discipline.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text; the translation faithfully reflects this incompleteness. The two summary verses at the opening are colophon-style mnemonic verses listing topics covered in the preceding section of the Vinaya; they are rendered as verse accordingly. The term rendered "patches" and "patch-tent" refer to the patchwork panels of the monastic robe and a small canopy or shade-cloth used during the sewing of robes. The "crow's wing" measure is a standard traditional unit of finger-widths used in Vinaya robe measurements. The phrase "clay paste" renders a term for a sizing or smoothing agent applied to cloth before sewing to keep it flat. The term rendered "verger" is the Tibetan disciplinarian or caretaker-monk of the monastery, the dge skos, whose role is to maintain order and care for the communal spaces and furnishings. "Verger" approximates this custodial function for a general audience, though the role is more precisely a monastic chant-master and disciplinarian. The sequence of rulings in this passage belongs to a Vinaya narrative establishing regulations about the sweeping and maintenance of monastic seating and walking meditation areas. The passage concerning paving stones is the beginning of a new narrative episode that continues in the following passage. The term rendered "container with a lid" translates a Tibetan phrase for a vessel or bowl together with its cover; the precise object is a medicine bowl with lid, which is a standard monastic requisite item. The rendering follows the natural sense.

The phrase "given distinguishing marks and that the Dharma was to be listened to at night" renders the closing sentence, which is syntactically incomplete as it stands in the passage; the text appears to continue beyond what has been provided here. The phrase rendered "a hundred holes" refers to a kind of perforated lantern cover or lamp shade. The Tibetan "bu ga brgya pa" is literal — "having a hundred holes" — and the passage describes improvised versions made from pierced pottery. This is a practical Vinaya ruling on lamp use during Dharma teachings, and no doctrinal ambiguity arises.

The "sweat cloth" (rngul gzan) is a cloth worn to absorb perspiration, a practical monastic garment permitted under heat conditions; it is distinct from the formal robes. The river name rendered throughout as "Sundarī" follows the Tibetan phonetic form; the Sanskrit is Nairañjanā in some parallels, but "Sundarī" (literally "the pleasant/beautiful one") appears to be the intended river here and is kept as given.

The phrase rendered "water vessels and pots" translates a Tibetan compound referring to physical ascetic practice using containers; the exact nature of the practice is unclear from context alone, but it appears to describe a form of meditative austerity associated with the riverbank setting.

The summary verse near the beginning is a mnemonic verse (uddāna) listing topics; it is rendered as verse accordingly, though its relationship to the surrounding narrative suggests it belongs to a preceding section's colophon rather than the present passage. The passage contains a compressed repetition formula ("and the passage continues as before, down through…") rendering the Tibetan shorthand that recalls earlier material verbatim without restating it in full. This is standard sūtra redactional practice, and the translation renders it as such rather than expanding the repeated passage, which is consistent with the preceding context. The phrase rendered "that first meditative concentration which surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" translates a technical expression indicating a uniquely superior form of the first dhyāna accessible only to a buddha; the term "rdug pa" (literally "to beat" or "surpass") is here used in a comparative sense meaning this concentration transcends or exceeds what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can attain. The phrase rendered "that which surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" translates a construction meaning a first meditative concentration that is complete and excels or outstrips all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. The term "རྡུགས་པ" is read here in the sense of "surpassing" or "that which exceeds," indicating a superlative quality of the Tathāgata's dhyāna compared to that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This is a genuinely difficult term and some uncertainty remains about its precise nuance in this context. The term rendered "tooth-wood" refers to the wooden stick used for dental hygiene in ancient India, equivalent to a tooth-cleaning twig. The Tibetan "so shing" is the standard Vinaya term for this implement, corresponding to Sanskrit dantakāṣṭha. The passage is a standard Vinaya narrative establishing a rule, and the sequence of events — report, permission, incident, further restriction — is a typical Vinaya legislative pattern.

The phrase rendered "genuine noble joy in the noble Dharma and discipline" translates 'phags pa'i yang dag par dga' ba, literally "the perfectly genuine joy of the noble ones." The repetition in the source is deliberate and has been preserved as faithfully as readability allows. The phrase rendered "blowing soot under a pot and striking ascetics" is the Group of Six monks sarcastically listing other supposed "advantages" of having a long piece of tooth-wood. The Tibetan is terse and the sarcasm is contextually inferred from the narrative pattern; the precise meaning of these two activities as pretexts or mockeries is clear from context in similar Vinaya passages.

The term translated "bundle" for བམ་པོ is a standard Tibetan canonical division marker equivalent to a fascicle or chapter-unit; it is left as "bundle" to match Vinaya translation conventions. The name rendered "Cāraka" represents the Tibetan "Char ka," which in this Vinaya narrative context is a personal name. The identification is contextually straightforward but the precise Sanskrit form is uncertain; "Cāraka" is the most plausible reconstruction.

The phrase rendered "the mother of beings" translates "Skye dgu'i bdag mo chen mo," a standard epithet of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, meaning the great mistress or mother of all creatures. The term rendered "act of exclusion" translates Tibetan ཐུལ་གཞུག་པ / ཐུལ་འཇུག་པ, a Vinaya procedural act imposed on recalcitrant monks. The Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain in this precise Mūlasarvāstivāda context; taghanīyakarman is one reconstruction offered by Vinaya scholars, but the text does not supply the Sanskrit here, so the gloss is given parenthetically only on first occurrence and should be understood as provisional.

The phrase "grandson of the Buddha" (སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྲུ) reflects the Vinaya's generational metaphor: the Buddha's direct disciples are his "sons," and their disciples are his "grandsons." This is a standard Mūlasarvāstivāda idiom, not a biological claim. The Tibetan term rendered as "ball of food" for རིལ་བ refers to a traveling provision, a small ball of compacted food given to someone being sent on their way; the precise nature of this provision is conventional in the Vinaya context.

The construction terminology in the architectural passage presents several interpretive challenges. The term ཀ་ཞུ is rendered as "column caps" or capitals placed atop the columns, following the most plausible reading in a building context. The overall sequence describes a standard post-and-lintel structure with a raised platform, columns, horizontal beams, rafters, planking, and a brick and plaster covering. The phrase rendered "food rack" translates a term meaning a kind of platform or shelf on which food is placed for animals — the precise form is not entirely certain from context, but "rack" conveys the sense adequately. The monk's "waiting in expectation" of giving food to the dog is a small technical Vinaya point: the meal period had elapsed, making a proper offering impossible, hence the transgression of the moment passing its proper time. The crow's communication to the thief leader in "crow language" is presented in the text as literal, consistent with the tradition of certain humans understanding animal speech. The passage contains a philosophically significant distinction between two modes of the Buddha's intention: "worldly intention" and "mind that transcends the world." The text states that when the buddhas give rise to worldly intention even animals perceive it, but when they give rise to transcendent intention even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom it. This is a standard doctrinal point about the inscrutability of buddha-mind at its deepest level and is rendered accordingly.

The name Nāmadru rendered here corresponds to the Tibetan "nam gru," which may represent a Tibetan equivalent of a disciple name; the identification is not entirely certain but is rendered in the most natural phonetic form given the context of the standard list of great śrāvakas. The phrase rendered as "twenty-one weeks of seven days" translates the Tibetan "zhag bdun gsum nyi shu rtsa gcig," which is a somewhat unusual construction. It most likely means "on the twenty-first set of seven days," i.e., after twenty-one weeks, though it could also be read as simply indicating a specific ceremonial day count. The meaning is contextually clear as a birth-celebration naming ceremony held after a fixed auspicious interval. The verse at the end is incomplete in the source passage as given; it breaks off mid-sentence at the final line. This is almost certainly a passage boundary, and the continuation would follow in the next segment. No emendation has been made.

The term rendered "Mysterious one" for གསང་བ་པོ is literally "Keeper of Secrets" or "Secret One," a common epithet of Vajrapāṇi, but here it appears to be used by the king as an address to the disguised yakṣa, possibly recognizing something uncanny about him, or as a conventional polite address to a being of uncertain identity. The translation preserves the sense without importing the full Vajrapāṇi association. The opening half-verse completes the verse begun in the preceding passage; the rendering "cool as a lake of water infused with sandalwood and blue lotus" follows the Tibetan literally, where "mtsho chu tsandan 'de gus bcin pa lta bur bsil ba" describes the fire-pit becoming cool like a lake scented with sandalwood and blue lotus.

The term rendered "wooden board" is the Sanskrit gaṇḍī, a sounding board struck to summon the Saṅgha; it is left as a functional description here for natural listening.

The phrase "noble silence" renders the Tibetan literally as "not speaking the words of noble ones," which in Vinaya context is the standard expression for maintaining silence rather than speaking, here contrasted with speaking appropriate Dharma words while working. The passage concerning the two boys' exchange about the next world and arhats is doctrinally notable: the king misidentifies their views. From the tradition's standpoint, affirming the next world corresponds to the view of permanence (eternalism), while affirming the existence of arhats is here taken as implying the view of annihilation (since an arhat attains nirvāṇa and in that sense "ceases"). This is a subtle and somewhat paradoxical point the narrative is making, and the translation preserves the king's characterization faithfully. The name rendered "Skyongwa" is a transliteration of the Tibetan name; no Sanskrit equivalent is recoverable from this context. The phrase rendered "the absorptive dwelling in equipoise by which they abide" translates "gnas pa'i snyoms par 'jug pa" — a meditative absorption that constitutes a stabilized dwelling state. The instruction is for whichever monk has attained that particular samādhi to communicate with or guide the two boys through it, presumably as a means of correcting their wrong views through direct meditative demonstration rather than verbal teaching. This is a somewhat unusual instruction and the precise mechanism is left implicit in the text. The closing line "འདུལ་བ་ཕྲན་ཚེགས་ཀྱི་གཞི།" is a colophon-like editorial marker indicating that this narrative episode serves as the originating story for a particular category of minor Vinaya rules. It is rendered as a plain prose label rather than integrated into the verse, as it stands apart from the narrative body. The four kinds of individual discriminating awareness render so-so yang-dag-par rig-pa, the four pratisaṃvids — discrimination of phenomena, meaning, etymology, and ready speech — a standard arhat attainment list. The term is rendered descriptively since unpacking each member would interrupt the flow; the doctrinal content is preserved in the collective phrase.

The phrase "gods of the sense faculties and the faculties' near-dependents" renders dbang-po dang nye-dbang-du bcas-pa'i lha-rnams, a formulaic list of deity classes organized by their relationship to the sense faculties; the rendering is literal and the precise classification is standard Abhidharma cosmology. The two monks named in this passage are Śroṇa and Pāṃśukūlika. Their Tibetan forms are ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་བྲན་བུ and ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་སྐྱོང་བ respectively. The Sanskrit equivalents are not fully certain from this passage alone; these renderings follow standard identifications from parallel Vinaya narratives where these names appear. The passage concludes with a formula indicating that the karmic backstory to follow is to be narrated "as before," referring the reader or listener back to an earlier section of the same text.
