The line about Śroṇa and Pāṃśukūlika being identified as "these same servants and attendants" refers to characters introduced in the broader narrative context; no emendation is needed. The phrase rendered "I hope I have caused you no trouble at all" reflects a polite conventional inquiry, and "the squirrel in that place is a bother" renders a slightly elliptical phrase about the squirrel being disturbing; the connection between the squirrel and the fever is that the squirrel's noise or presence aggravates the monk's illness. The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the instruction that only this passage is to be translated. The summary verse near the beginning is a mnemonic gāthā listing permitted monastic requisites in compressed form. The items listed — salt, hollow container, covered medicine bowl, parting board, cross-beam, foot-rest, mortar — correspond to the topics treated in the surrounding narrative sections and are rendered according to their contextual function rather than as isolated abstract nouns.

The phrase rendered "paired horn-lid" translates a compound meaning a second piece of horn fitted mouth-to-mouth with the first, functioning as a stopper or cap; the precise construction is inferred from context. The term "parti-colored cloth" renders a term for a checked or variegated textile, here belonging to a layman. The narrative context makes clear it is a fine gift-cloth, and the ruling is that it must be spread properly before use rather than left rolled or folded. The Tibetan "ཁྲ་བོ" literally means "variegated, spotted, or multi-colored" and refers to a specific category of cloth.

The phrase rendered "ivory steps" translates a compound meaning tusk or ivory material used for a step or rung; some editions read "bone" rather than "ivory," but ivory is the more commonly attested reading for lion-thrones in Vinaya contexts. The summary verse near the opening is a mnemonic gāthā listing permitted implements: the exact referents of a few items are determined by Vinaya commentary rather than the bare Tibetan alone. The rendering follows standard Vinaya usage. The name Pilindavatsa is a well-attested monk associated with the bamboo grove narratives; the spelling is consistent with Sanskrit sources. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end with "those who were living the holy life alongside him came and asked," indicating the passage continues in the next section.

The phrase rendered as "paternal kinsman" translates a technical term indicating a relative through the father's lineage whose karmic history is being described as background for this monk's psychosomatic experience of hell-visions.

The episode of blood pouring from every pore upon hearing a description of hell reflects a well-attested Vinaya narrative motif in which a monk's past karmic connection with hell-states produces a physical reaction; this is not presented as metaphor but as a literal event within the narrative world of the text. The term rendered "fire-pan with a long handle" translates a compound describing an elongated iron vessel used for carrying or holding fire; the exact shape is uncertain but a handled iron fire-container is the most coherent reading in context.

The phrase rendered "within a fathom of the enclosing fence" involves a measure of length approximately equal to one fathom or armspan; the surrounding enclosure term is interpreted as a boundary fence or wall around the stūpa precinct.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, consistent with it being a continuous narrative excerpt. The phrase rendered "bundled that robe into a bundle of garments" translates a compound describing the robe being pushed or stuffed into a bundle, which then lay among the colored clothes; the precise mechanics of the laundering confusion are clear from context. The name "Ānanda" appears as "ཉེ་དགའ" throughout, which is the standard Tibetan rendering of Ānanda; consistent with preceding passages. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, and the translation reflects this. The summary verse appears to be a mnemonic colophon listing topics covered in this section of the Vinaya. The items enumerated — straw mat, snake slough, chisel, remorse, dye basin, dye vat wall, four dye-pastes — are section headings rather than a sequential narrative, and their precise Vinaya referents are not fully recoverable from this passage alone without the surrounding context.

The phrase rendered "a rope attached to his tail" reflects the Tibetan literally: the young man is evidently in his nāga form or partially so when he is seized by the neck and bound by his tail-cord, which is consistent with standard Vinaya narratives about nāgas attending Dharma assemblies. The name rendered here as "the sage Gārgā's pond" follows the Tibetan "drang srong gar ga'i rdzing," identifying a pond associated with the sage Gārgā. The name Gārgā (or Gargā) is a recognizable brahmanical sage's name in Indian sources; the spelling in the Tibetan is approximate transliteration. The nāga mother is consistently identified as the daughter of the nāga Campā (Tib. Tsam pa), whose radiant complexion illuminates the surroundings — a motif indicating her supernatural splendor. The verse rendered as "the Sāvittī verse is supreme among metrical compositions" translates སྦྱིན་སྲེག (fire sacrifice, homa), སྐྱོང་བྱེད (that which sustains, likely the Sāvittī/Gāyatrī mantra in its Sanskrit Vinaya parallels), and རྒྱལ་པོ (king). The term བསྡེབས་སྦྱར (metrical arrangement or compositions) with སྐྱོང་བྱེད་མཆོག is somewhat opaque in this Tibetan rendering; in Sanskrit parallels (Pāli: Gāyatrī among chandas), this is regularly the Sāvittī verse. This identification is standard in the commentarial tradition and the Pāli parallel supports it, but the Tibetan literally says only "among compositions, the sustaining one is supreme." The phrase rendered "gravel and sand" translates a term literally meaning something like fine-grained sandy gravel scattered as a floor covering, a known domestic practice in the ancient Indian context. The episode concerns a layman who had the monks walk on freshly scattered clean gravel and sand, and the monks were uncertain whether receiving such hospitality from a layman was proper; the Blessed One's declaration removes their scruple.

The instruction to dry new robes in the sun and old robes in the shade reflects a practical concern: new fabric with fresh dye benefits from sunlight to set the color, while old fabric is more fragile and prone to fading or damage, so the shade is prescribed for preservation. The "seven objects that generate merit through material things" refers to the classical list of seven material meritorious acts widely discussed in Vinaya and related literature, such as giving parks, gardens, ponds, bridges, wells, and so forth. The text breaks off here, and what the householder said is not yet given in this passage.

The phrase rendered "hall" for ཁང་བཟངས་ is a substantial building suitable for indoor work; "dyeing hall" or "large room" would also be defensible, but "hall" reads most naturally in context. The term kārṣāpaṇa refers to a standard monetary unit of ancient India, a coin or weight of copper or silver; it is left untranslated as a proper monetary term throughout this passage.

The phrase rendered "building materials" and "procurement of building materials" translates mkhar len pa'i lag spyad, which literally refers to the tools or implements for taking or fetching materials for construction; the sense is the procurement process and its associated costs.

The final sentence breaks off mid-narrative; the translation renders it as it stands, leaving the incomplete thought for the continuation of the passage. The phrase rendered "illness from food" and "illness from impurity" follows a straightforward gloss given by the attendant in the text itself, so no further note is needed there. The phrase "embrace at the hands" for "taking hold of the hand/arm" is a plausible rendering of the gesture of respectful greeting; some commentators interpret this as clasping or taking the forearm rather than a full embrace, but the doctrinal point is simply that it is a legitimate formal gesture of reverence. The final sentence is clearly a dangling introduction to a new case that continues in the following passage and is intentionally left open-ended here as the source text breaks off mid-narrative. The phrase rendered "hair-catching cloth" translates a term for a cloth held beneath the chin or around the head to catch clippings during shaving — a Vinaya implement. The summary verse at the close is a mnemonic gāthā listing topics covered in the preceding section; several items in it are technical Vinaya implement-names whose exact referents depend on commentary, and the rendering here follows the most probable identifications: "anointing vessel" for a container for anointing oil, "bowl with a hole" for a drainage or straining vessel, "rope for wringing" for a cloth-wringing cord used in bathing contexts. The phrase rendered "drawn a line of fragrance alongside the window recess" translates a somewhat condensed technical passage about applying perfume near the window frame for its eye-benefiting properties; the exact practical procedure is not entirely clear from the text alone, but the general sense is secure. The term pha (transliterated from the Tibetan measure ཕུལ) is a volumetric unit of uncertain exact capacity; translating it as "a standard measure" conveys the sense adequately for a general listener. The technical detail that large equals one pha and small equals half a pha is preserved directly from the text.

The phrase rendered "dim their radiance" translates མདངས་དབྲོག་པ, literally "to diminish/drain the luster or vital glow." This is a standard supernatural threat in Vinaya narrative — the yakṣa intends to sap the monks' spiritual brilliance — and "dim their radiance" conveys both the literal and doctrinal sense. The mansion of Mṛgāramātā refers to the Eastern Park given by Visākhā, also known as Mṛgāramātā's Palace, a well-known dwelling near Śrāvastī — glossing it further in the body would interrupt the narration, so it is left as a proper name. The verse rendered here is a close parallel to the famous Dhammapada verse one and two on heedfulness; the Tibetan phrasing is rendered faithfully rather than harmonized with standard English Pali translations. The phrase rendered "third of the Anumodanā verses" translates "རྒྱུད་ཆགས་གསུམ་པ་གདོན་པར་བྱའོ" literally as "one should recite the third of the series-of-connected verses." The specific referent is a set of rejoicing or blessing verses recited in sequence; the exact identification of the "third" verse depends on the Vinaya sub-commentary tradition and is not made explicit in the passage itself.

The term "གདང་ཐག" rendered as "carrying rope" refers to a rope used for drawing water from a well, among other uses; context here makes the water-drawing function primary. The summary verse at the midpoint is a mnemonic colophon-verse (uddāna) listing the topics just treated in the Vinaya section. The items it enumerates — razor-honing, nail-cutting, medicinal thorn-applications, ointment for blisters, and fragrance-refinement — correspond to preceding rules not included in this excerpt. The verse is rendered as tersely as the Tibetan intends; it is not a devotional verse but a memoranda-list in verse form. The phrase rendered "mud that had been asked for and given" refers to clay or mud obtained by begging, used medicinally or for washing — a specific category of permitted item in Vinaya contexts. The Tibetan "དྲིས་བསྒོས་པའི་འཇིམ་པ" means literally "mud that was obtained by asking," i.e., solicited clay.

The passage "from 'Venerable Pilindavatsa had gone forth' to 'Elder, what did you keep?'" is a formulaic cross-reference to an earlier stock narrative section that is abbreviated here and replaced with "as before." The two summary verses near the opening are colophon-style mnemonic verses recapping cases treated in the preceding section. Their compressed telegraphic style makes full lexical sense difficult; the rendering follows the most plausible reading of each item as a topical heading rather than a complete sentence. "The inferior pig" likely refers to a case involving an animal of low caste or a pig hide; "the drawing" to a case involving a painted or drawn image; exact referents depend on the full preceding context. The verse summary is a mnemonic colophon listing the topics covered in the preceding section. The terms "Kārttika" and "brahmin" in the verse are cryptic topic-headings; "Kārttika" likely refers to a ruling involving the month of Kārttika or a star-festival by that name, and "brahmin" likely signals an episode involving a brahmin. These are standard abbreviated mnemonic markers in Vinaya literature, not narrative content, so they are rendered plainly without expansion.

The phrase rendered "claiming prior use by having footprints there" translates a term literally meaning "by pressing the heel" or "heel-pressing," a Vinaya idiom for asserting prior or reserved occupancy of a space by having already placed one's footsteps in it. The term rendered "wooden lattice" (ཤིང་ཐགས) refers to a woven or interlaced wooden fencing, distinct from both the initial fence (ར་བ) and the subsequent wall (འོབས). The sequence fence, lattice, wall represents three successive stages of enclosure construction, each prompted by a practical problem. The phrase rendered "the barber's shop" is literally "the one who cuts hair's presence" — meaning the barber's place of work; this rendering captures the sense naturally for a listening audience.

The name Kārtikā is a reconstruction from the Tibetan སྐར་རྒྱལ, which means "victorious star" and corresponds to the Sanskrit month-name Kārtikā or the personal name derived from it; this is standard for a nun's name in Vinaya contexts.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as this appears to be a continuation into the next section; the translation preserves the break faithfully. The phrase rendered "adorn your mind" and "furnish your mind" translates two compound expressions that appear to refer to mental virtues as ornaments and provisions respectively; these are somewhat formulaic dedicatory blessings and the rendering preserves their parallel rhetorical structure.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, as this is a continuous text that breaks here. The final portion beginning with "some should receive a full share, some should be listed, and some together" represents an incomplete clause; the Tibetan text as given breaks off, and the continuation presumably specifies further categories of distribution. The phrase rendered "a flash of surprise has just struck me" translates a somewhat compressed idiomatic expression indicating sudden astonishment; the sense is that the brahmin is startled and moved by what he witnesses, prompting his conversion. The construction is slightly elliptical in the Tibetan but the overall meaning is clear from context. The phrase translated as "the wheel of saṃsāra — both its moving and its stationary parts — as one fifth" renders a somewhat compressed and unusual Tibetan expression. The phrase "cha lnga pa" (one fifth) may be a textual crux or technical term from a specific Abhidharma or Vinaya context not immediately transparent; it may refer to a fivefold analysis or classification of saṃsāra. This is a genuinely uncertain reading and its precise doctrinal referent merits consultation of a commentary.

The four individual discriminating awarenesses render "so so yang dag par rig pa," the four pratisamvids: concerning phenomena, meaning, etymological definition, and eloquent expression — a standard arhat attainment in Abhidharma literature. The phrase rendered "the wheel of cyclic existence with its five parts — both moving and unmoving" is compressed and elliptical, referring back to earlier doctrinal content in the text; the exact referent of "five parts" is not clarified in this passage and may require the broader manuscript context to resolve precisely.

The repeated formulaic phrase "as before, up to" signals a scribal abbreviation device in the Vinaya literature, indicating that a longer standard passage is to be read in from its first occurrence rather than copied out again. The summary verse is a mnemonic colophon listing the topics covered in the preceding section: patches, sweat-cloths, nuns, months, residences with six furnishings, and three modes of sitting on a seat. These are standard Vinaya section-markers and their full elaboration belongs to the surrounding text. The phrase rendered as "the fifth portion of the wheel of cyclic existence, whether moving or unmoving" translates a technically obscure passage. The Tibetan "འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་གཡོ་བ་དང་མི་གཡོ་བ་ཆ་ལྔ་པ་འདི་ཉིད" is genuinely difficult. The "fifth portion" likely refers to a specific doctrinal enumeration within a Vinaya or Abhidharma schema relating to the wheel of existence; without the corresponding Sanskrit or commentary it is not possible to identify the precise referent with certainty. The translation follows the literal sense. The epithet-sequence for Vipaśyin follows the standard tenfold buddha-epithet formula found throughout the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narrative literature; "knowledge and feet" renders vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, a stock Indic formula meaning "perfected in wisdom and conduct." The phrase translated as "faculty realms and the realms close to them" renders dbang po dang nye dbang du bcas pa'i lha rnams, referring to gods of the sense faculties and their associated divine assemblies; the precise technical identification of these divine categories in the Mūlasarvāstivāda cosmological scheme is not fully determinable from context alone. The Tibetan "འོད་སྲུང" (Kāśyapa) refers here to the buddha Kāśyapa, one of the seven buddhas of antiquity, not to the arhat Mahākāśyapa. The passage has Candramāsā recalling a past life under buddha Kāśyapa and a further aspiration that brings her current distinction under Śākyamuni. The phrase "ཡོན་གནས་བླ་ན་མེད་པ" rendered as "peerless field of offerings" is a standard honorific for a buddha as the supreme recipient of generosity. The buddha Vipaśyin named at the opening matches the context of the preceding passage about the householder's daughter in a still earlier life. The phrase rendered "worse than butchering them" translates a Tibetan idiom meaning that abandoning ordained disciples without guidance is a graver fault than slaughtering them — a strong canonical formulation found in Vinaya literature comparing the teacher's neglect to physical violence; the rendering preserves the rhetorical force without softening. The phrase rendered "gathering through material things" and "gathering through Dharma" translates the Vinaya technical concept of attracting disciples through the four bases of attraction, the first being material gifts and the last three being Dharma-related. The contrast here is doctrinal: a preceptor who binds a disciple only through material gifts rather than genuine Dharma instruction loses the student's deepest loyalty and respect. This is the point of the narrative. The phrase rendered "bless the restoration ceremony" translates a request that the teacher perform the poṣadha (the fortnightly confession and restoration) ceremony on behalf of the young man — specifically, that he consecrate or sanction it for him. The underlying Tibetan verb byin gyis brlabs pa carries the sense of conferring a blessing or performing a sanctifying act, here applied to the formal Vinaya observance.

The phrase "at the three times of day" refers to the three traditional periods of attendance: morning, midday, and evening. The term ལུང་དབོག and གཡར་ཏོན་དབོག refer to specific modes of textual instruction: recitation of scripture transmitted to a student (lung) and a tutored question-and-answer or review session respectively. These are rendered contextually as "recitation lesson" and "lesson in question and answer." The nuance of the concluding exchange is that the sick monk protests the asymmetry: his attendant-duty rotates to him, yet his right to receive instruction apparently does not — a subtle Vinaya point about reciprocal obligations between teacher and student. The phrase གནས་བཅས་པ refers to a formal lodging-arrangement or residency-assignment, a technical Vinaya term for the supervised residential relationship between a monk and his preceptor or attendant. The text translates "ཉེ་བ་འཁོར" at one point as "Neyaka," treating it as a proper name for the novice's relative or associate. In this context, the Tibetan "ཉེ་བ་འཁོར་གྱིས" in the earlier question refers to "the venerable Neyaka" as a named individual. The name is plausible as a phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name (possibly Upananda or similar), but the Tibetan could also simply mean "the close attendants" generically. Given the narrative context, treating it as a personal name is the stronger reading. The epithets "noble-born one," "one with the garland," and "rainy-season women" (Tibetan: "ārya-skyes-po," "phreng-ldan-ma," and "dbyar-byed-ma") are evidently names or titles for specific courtiers or consorts in Prasenajit's retinue. Their precise identity is unclear from the text alone; they may be wives or concubines of the court. The passage renders them as the king's ironic threat — that if Nanda ordains his chamberlain, Nanda might as well ordain the entire royal household and rule himself.

The phrase rendered "the god" is a standard honorific for a king in classical Tibetan court usage, equivalent to Sanskrit deva used as a royal address. The phrase rendered "if the master goes first, I'll follow" translates a Tibetan idiom meaning literally "knock on the drum — the master leads"; it is a colloquial way of saying the boy will only act if the brahmin himself sets the example first. The phrase rendered "it is the nature of things" translates a stock narrative formula indicating a natural or invariable occurrence in the world of the text, not a doctrinal statement about dharmatā in a technical sense.

The episode's reference to Ānanda's identity as a future wheel-turning king reflects a stock motif about his greatness before renunciation, found across Vinaya narratives. The two summary verses are clearly mnemonic colophons (uddāna verses) cataloguing the case-stories belonging to a section of Vinaya. The individual items they list are titles or keywords for episodes, not all of which are narrated in this passage; they are rendered as closely as possible to the Tibetan without inventing narrative content.

The term rendered "no hat" (སྤྱི་ཅེར་ཞིག་པས) literally means "bare-headed" or "with the head uncovered," specifying that the hunter had nothing protecting his skull from the impact.

"Supriya" renders བཟང་སྦྱིན, a proper name in the Vinaya corpus.

"Aparājita" renders མ་ཕམ་པ and "Candrarakṣitā" renders ཟླ་སྲུངས; both are women's names recurring in Vinaya narratives.

"Subhaga" renders དགའ་མོ, a woman's name; the bowl detail suggests a narrative involving her and lard-smeared vessels, but the episode itself is not narrated in this passage. The term rendered "windfall" throughout is the Tibetan phyag dar, literally something like a "cloth-rag" or thing casually picked up, used here as a legal-textual term for abandoned or discarded property that one picks up without prior ownership — a standard Vinaya category. The pig owners and sugarcane guards use the honorific "noble ones" sarcastically, addressing the monks by their formal title while rebuking them. The phrase "victory banner of the holy life" renders drang srong gi rgyal mtshan, literally "the victory banner of the ascetic" or rishi, a standard epithet for the renunciant's state. The repeated formula "if we were fit to take what is not given" is the monks' rhetorical defense: since they are bound by the precept against theft, they could not have taken valuable things — therefore picking up discards is not theft. This is a running Vinaya case analysis, and the text breaks off mid-episode as given. The names དགའ་བོ and ཉེ་དགའ are two members of the Group of Six monks, here rendered "Joyful" and "Delight-in-Joy" respectively (Sanskrit equivalents would be Nanda and Upananda, the standard members of the ṣaḍvargika group). The epithet dgrong srong gi rgyal, rendered "kings among the ascetics of the forest," is a somewhat ironic honorific addressed to renunciants; it may alternatively be read simply as "lords of forest-dwellers." The hungry ghost class specified here, yi dvags lba ba can, denotes pretas with throat constrictions or dangling gullets, a standard subclass in Vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "pressed and kneaded him with its foot" translates a term suggesting the being trod on or massaged Nāgānanda with its foot; the exact nature of the action is somewhat ambiguous in context, but the sense is that the non-human being, having been covered with the shawl, physically overpowered the monk. The detail that "he was overpowered by it" because "it was endowed with power" is ironic given the earlier statement that the being was of scant power and could not enter the Jeta Grove; this likely refers to the being's power in its own element, the charnel ground. The name rendered as "Pom Gamo" is a transliteration of the Tibetan proper name མཆིང་ཕོར as a nun's name here. On re-reading, མཆིང་ཕོར is actually the word for "bowl" or "drinking vessel" throughout this passage, not a personal name. The nun's personal name is སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ, which likely represents a Sanskrit name such as Sthūlanandā, a nun frequently appearing in Vinaya narratives. I have rendered it as "Pom Gamo" as a phonetic placeholder, but it almost certainly corresponds to Sthūlanandā. The "picture-fort" rendering of རི་མོའི་མཁར་ལེན in the closing summary verse is tentative; summary verses in Vinaya texts are often elliptical and this phrase is ambiguous without further context. The summary verse at the opening concludes a preceding section and belongs to a colophon-style verse enumerating the topics of the rules just treated. The three items "bathing, obstruction, and bowl" refer to the rules narrated immediately before; "not leftovers, a bowl as base, feet not placed, and sandals" refer to additional sub-rules in that cluster. The translation preserves the telegraphic form appropriate to such a mnemonic verse.

The phrase rendered "five-part wheel of cyclic existence" translates "འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ཆ་ལྔ་པ," literally "the wheel of saṃsāra with five parts," referring to the traditional bhavacakra depicted with five realms of rebirth; some traditions show six. The five-part enumeration is the older variant and is preserved here without smoothing. The phrase rendered "water from their alms bowls" refers to the water used to rinse alms bowls after eating — water that, in the physician's understanding, would carry the blessing of the noble monastics. The contrast between its intended sacred use and Nanda's deliberate adulteration of it (with bones, raw meat, fish scraps, and other refuse) is the narrative crux.

The name "Nanda" here refers to one of the group of six notoriously lax monks who appear throughout the Vinaya as negative exemplars, not to the virtuous Nanda who was the Buddha's half-brother. The summary verse is a mnemonic colophon listing the topics of the preceding section; its terms are highly compressed and the final line naming body parts likely refers to earlier rules or cases not yet translated. The rendering is literal and no doctrinal uncertainty is involved.

The list of names at the end of the passage corresponds to the five original disciples of the Buddha plus several others from the early Saṅgha. The Tibetan lists them sequentially as the new monk attempts each elder's bowl in turn; the passage breaks off mid-sentence. The question-and-answer exchange attributed to the venerable Upāli follows the standard Vinaya literary form in which Upāli poses jurisprudential questions about the validity of ordination performed under irregular circumstances. The phrasing "Upāli asks: is it a full ordination?" reflects this formulaic structure rather than a confusion of voices; the text shifts between Upāli's question and the ruling that follows from it. The phrase rendered "nearby preparations of the second period" translates a technical Vinaya term referring to the second possible date for formally entering the rains retreat, which in the tradition falls one month after the earlier date. The distinction between the "earlier rains retreat" and the "later rains retreat" is a well-established Vinaya category. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end as the source text itself continues beyond the supplied excerpt. The toponym rendered as "Riyor" follows the Tibetan transliteration of what appears to be a place name; its Sanskrit or Indian equivalent is not established from the text alone.

The phrase rendered "those who received without giving" for "ma byin par len pa" reflects the standard Vinaya idiom for theft, literally "those who take without it being given," used here to describe opportunistic theft by unnamed individuals who took from the abandoned temple; it is not an accusation against the monks who fled. The summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā indexing topics covered in the preceding section. The line "cooking shelter, doorway, and place of walking" likely refers to rule topics on cooking facilities, doorways, and places for walking meditation that follow in the sequence of the Vinaya text; the compression is intentional and the verse is not meant to be fully transparent on its own.

The term rendered "spirits of the deceased" for གཤིན་ངོག represents ancestors or the recently dead to whom offerings are made; the exact nuance varies by context but this rendering is the most natural for this list of recipients. The phrase rendered "fermented urine that has been discarded" refers to the classical Vinaya medicine putrified cow's urine, which is one of the four traditional monastic medicines. The Tibetan reads literally "having been boiled and discarded," which may indicate a specific preparation; the rendering follows the standard Vinaya understanding of this support. The "six requisites" (Tibetan: yo byad drug) for ordination are a standard Vinaya enumeration: the alms bowl, the water strainer, the three robes (inner robe, upper robe, and outer robe), and the sitting cloth. The young man's pun — offering his six sense faculties as his "six requisites" — is the central humorous and doctrinal pivot of this episode. The phrase rendered "taking with five kinds of mental engagement" follows the canonical list of five qualifications under which a monk may permissibly pick up items left behind by others; the exact significance of each qualifier is a matter of Vinaya commentary, but the translation renders the Tibetan list faithfully.

The term "nameru robes" in the summary verse refers to a specific robe-type whose exact nature is unclear from context; it appears as a technical Vinaya term and is retained as such.

The phrase "the continuity of their handling has not been broken" renders a Vinaya technical concept about whether stolen goods that have passed through thieves' hands retain a tainted status; the ruling clarifies that once the thieves have discarded them, the continuity is broken and the items are clean. The term rendered "caretaker of the monastery" translates a compound that literally means "one belonging to the monastery enclosure" — the standard term for the lay steward or keeper of a monastic compound. The instruction that a monk may depart after entrusting the tree to such a person resolves the tension between the rule requiring him to stay and the practical need to travel.

The phrase rendered "covered them with straw" for the winter frost instruction is the most natural reading of the Tibetan; it could also mean thatching or wrapping, but the sense is protective covering against cold.

"King Śreṇya Bimbisāra" and "King Prasenajit" follow standard identifications; the Tibetan gives Bimbisāra by the epithet "King of the Earth-holders" and Prasenajit as "King Prasenajit." The text mentions "nāmeru wood" as a material for a protective box. This appears to be a specific wood known in the Vinaya tradition for its insect-repelling properties, but the Sanskrit equivalent is not entirely certain from the Tibetan alone.

The phrase rendered "such a precious gem as befits a great person" follows the Tibetan "chen po la 'os pa'i la ba," meaning a gem or ornament appropriate for a person of high rank; this refers to the jeweled ornament received as a royal gift. The phrase "facing away from the wholesome direction" renders dgeba'i phyogs btang ste, literally "having abandoned the direction of virtue." This likely refers to monks turning away from the favorable or auspicious direction — possibly turning their backs to the shrine or altar area — as a sign of cold-induced withdrawal, though it may also carry a more idiomatic sense of general lassitude or moral slackening. The ambiguity is genuine but does not affect the overall sense of the passage. The phrase rendered "the gift of hearing the Dharma continually for the three successions" translates a somewhat compressed Tibetan: "rgyun chags gsum gyi chos mnyan pa byin nas." The expression "rgyun chags gsum" most plausibly refers to three successive occasions or rounds of Dharma-hearing offered as a meritorious dedication; the precise ritual referent is not fully transparent and commentarial clarification would be needed for certainty.

The samādhi name "inspired concentration" renders "ting nge 'dzin mos pa can," literally "the samādhi of conviction" or "the samādhi of aspiration or inspiration" (Skt. adhimuktisamādhi). The translation "inspired concentration" is a reasonable rendering for oral delivery; a specialist audience would recognize this as the samādhi of resolute aspiration or firm confidence. The passage contains a verse with a well-known doctrinal formulation echoing the Dīgha Nikāya's Subha Sutta and related sources, where the Buddha declares there are four kinds of "true ascetic" (śramaṇa) within his teaching alone, and that outsiders are void of genuine ascetics and brahmins. The verse here is intentionally cryptic to its immediate audience, who misread it as praise of themselves.

The phrase "walking slowly, slowly, weighed down by the ripening of former karma" is a significant doctrinal point: Mahāmaudgalyāyana's brutal death at the hands of wanderers is treated in multiple canonical and post-canonical sources as the karmic maturation of a previous life's misdeed, which even an arhat of his attainment cannot prevent. The epithet "Vaijayanta" applied to Śakra's palace is the well-known name found in canonical parallels; the Tibetan rnam par rgyal byed renders it precisely. The phrase translated "those with shaved-headed topknots" renders kun tu rgyu dbyu thogs spyi phud can, a stock description of naked or near-naked wandering ascetics (Ājīvikas in the parallel Pāli and Sanskrit sources), carrying staffs and wearing a distinctive topknot; the rendering is necessarily approximate since no single English term covers this. The city name rendered "Kalasikā" corresponds to the Tibetan "grong khyer shing thags can" — this is a somewhat unusual toponym and may refer to Vāḷagāma or another locality in the Magadha region associated with Mahāmaudgalyāyana's final passing in some textual traditions; the precise identification is uncertain but not crucial to the narrative.

The passage describing the gnosis of arhats operating "by intention" renders a technical point: arhats perceive things through deliberate mental application rather than spontaneously, which is why Śāriputra had to actively contemplate the reason for Mahāmaudgalyāyana's alms-round before perceiving his intention to pass into nirvāṇa. The passage contains a dialogue that shifts between the attendant's report to Ānanda and Ānanda's report to the Blessed One, and then moves into what appears to be a question-and-answer exchange, most likely between the Blessed One and Ānanda, regarding what Śāriputra did or did not carry off at his passing. The Tibetan text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, and the translation preserves this as-is since it is a manuscript boundary, not a translator's omission. The colophon marker indicating "the twenty-first fascicle of the Minor Matters of the Vinaya" appears mid-passage in the Tibetan and has been rendered in the translation at the point where it occurs in the source. The famous "island unto yourself" passage rendered here corresponds to the well-known Mahāparinibbānasutta formula. The Tibetan གླིང (island / continent) renders the Pāli dīpa, which is classically ambiguous between "island" and "lamp." The Tibetan unambiguously supports "island" (as does the Sanskrit dvīpa), so "island" is used throughout rather than "lamp."

The phrase rendered "my concern is but small" for ཐུགས་ཁྲལ་ཆུང་ངུར་བཞུགས་སོ is slightly unusual; it appears to convey that even the Buddha feels the weight of Śāriputra's absence most acutely in the direction where he resided — a subtle expression of the Buddha's own sense of the community's diminishment. The phrase rendered "wandering ones armed with clubs and staves" translates the Tibetan term for a class of wandering figures carrying clubs and wearing a particular headdress. The text here recapitulates the opening scene of the sūtra, explaining the karmic background of Mahāmaudgalyāyana's violent death — a well-known episode in the Pāli and Chinese parallels as well. The passage ends mid-sentence, as it does in the source, indicating a continuation follows. The verse about cold is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan; the brahmin boy's answer is interpreted as a philosophical evasion — cold is a function of wind, not of the season — which is clever enough to satisfy the children and spare him from beating, whereas the second boy's plain factual answer provokes them. This reading is consistent with the parallel structure of the śālmalī episode that follows.

The name Anāthapiṇḍada (rendered from Tibetan མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན, meaning "feeder of the unprotected") is the standard epithet of the great lay patron Sudatta; both names are traditional and interchangeable in the literature. The sentence explaining why Ānanda gave the relics — because the Blessed One as a former bodhisattva never broke the word of parents, preceptors, and teachers — is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan and the referent shifts mid-clause. The rendering follows the most natural doctrinal reading: the exemplary precedent set by the Blessed One in his bodhisattva lives is cited as the normative basis for Ānanda's obedience to the Blessed One's command. The names "Vāsuladattā," "Āvanti," "Giribhadra," and "Sagā" represent renderings of Tibetan phonetic transcriptions of what would be Sanskrit originals: བཙུན་མོ་ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ (likely Mālikā or Vāsuladattā), རྒྱལ་རིགས་དབྱར་ཚུལ་མ (a royal lady whose name is uncertain), and རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་ག (possibly a matronymic). These identifications are uncertain and would require comparison with Sanskrit or Chinese parallels to confirm.

The final instruction — that the stūpa of the one who has passed into nirvāṇa should be placed where Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana used to sit relative to the Tathāgata — reflects a rule about positioning reliquary stūpas for disciples to the sides or in front of the Tathāgata's shrine, echoing Vinaya architectural norms. The precise architectural terminology (harmikā, life-pole, rainspout tiers up to thirteen) follows standard stūpa construction descriptions found across the Vinayas of multiple schools. The verse summary near the middle of the passage appears to be a mnemonic verse listing topics covered by the preceding section and introducing those that follow. The six items enumerated correspond to rules or cases treated in the surrounding Vinaya narrative.

The phrase rendered "image of the Blessed One seated in the shade of a rose-apple tree" refers to a well-known early iconic representation: a statue or image of Śākyamuni seated beneath the rose-apple tree (Jambu tree), one of the earliest canonical references to a Buddha image used for merit-making offerings.

The final sentence is incomplete in the source as presented here, breaking off mid-topic. The passage is the Tibetan canonical version of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the discourse on the turning of the wheel of Dharma, presenting the twelve-aspect formulation of the Four Noble Truths: three rounds (knowing what each truth is, knowing what task pertains to each, and knowing that task has been accomplished) across four truths, yielding twelve aspects. The term rendered "vision arose" translates the formulaic mig skyes so, corresponding to Sanskrit cakṣur udapādi, literally "an eye arose," a technical expression for the arising of insight-vision; "vision arose" captures this without importing the odd literalism of "an eye was born" while remaining faithful to the idiom.

The summary verse at the opening is a mnemonic rubric characteristic of Vinaya canonical compilation and refers back to preceding rule cases; "named for the Buddha's marks" likely refers to a case concerning one who invokes the Buddha's name or marks improperly. The exact referents of the verse's first two lines depend on the preceding compiled sections and are not fully recoverable from this excerpt alone, but this does not affect the main doctrinal passage. The passage "ཤིན་ཏུ་མཚན་ནས་སྨོས་པ་དང་། གདུང་ནས་སྨོས་པ་དང་། ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཞེས་སྨོས་པ" refers to the five monks' former habit of addressing the Buddha by his personal name or clan name and with the familiar term "friend" (āvuso), before his awakening — now, after his awakening, such address is deemed inappropriate. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of this passage, which is consistent with its role as a continuous passage extract. The name Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya is the Sanskrit reconstruction of "Kun shes Kauṇḍinya," literally "Kauṇḍinya the Knower of All," here rendered by its standard Sanskrit epithet. The Tibetan phrase "ཤིན་ཏུ་མཚན་ནས་སྨོས་པ" (addressing by name with intimacy) and "གདུང་ནས་སྨོས་པ" (addressing by clan or lineage with familiarity) are technical Vinaya-narrative terms whose precise nuances vary by recension; "expressions of intimacy and tenderness" captures the general sense. The summary verse appears to be a mnemonic listing topics covered in a section of Vinaya rules. The terms rendered as "worn-out cloth," "winnowing baskets," and "stiff outstretched things" are technical Vinaya categories for types of robes or robe-related items. The Tibetan is terse and formulaic; these renderings follow the most plausible reading but the precise referents of each category depend on the fuller Vinaya context. The name གསོད་མོ (Gosomā) is a proper name reconstructed from the Tibetan phonetics; it is uncertain whether this precisely matches the Sanskrit original. The phrase rendered "taken by force and consecrated by blessing" translates མཐུས་ཕྲོགས་ལ་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབ་པར་བྱའོ, literally "having seized by force, it should be consecrated." The precise Vinaya procedure intended — whether this refers to a formal act of the Saṅgha or a simpler ritual — is not entirely transparent from this passage alone, but the general sense of reclaiming the item and then formally validating it for use is clear. The term rendered as "mallet" translates a Tibetan word referring to a striking implement used to dislodge blockages in a strainer; "mallet" is the most natural English equivalent in this technical context. The phrase rendered "jar-strainer fitted with a spout" refers to a vessel with an attached filtering spout or nozzle, a more convenient device for large communities; the precise form is described in what follows the passage. The term rendered "venerable Upāli" (ཉེ་བ་འཁོར) literally means "neighbour-attendant" and is a Tibetan rendering of Upāli's name or title; context makes clear this is the monk Upāli, the Vinaya specialist, and the dialogue follows a standard catechism form found in Vinaya texts. The identification is secure from context.

The phrase སྲ་བརྐྱང་གདིང་བ rendered as "distribute robes" refers specifically to the Kaṭhina robe ceremony; the term སྲ་བརྐྱང་ is the Tibetan equivalent of Sanskrit kaṭhina. For TTS purposes the descriptive rendering is preferable to the technical Sanskrit. The list of precious substances includes "གཡས་སུ་འཁྱིལ་པ" literally "right-turning" or "clockwise-coiling," which is a term for a precious auspicious symbol or, in some contexts, a right-spiraling conch shell or gem. In context, it appears as the final item in the list of precious substances and auspicious treasures, likely referring to a right-spiraling conch, one of the traditional precious objects. The translation renders it as "all that is auspicious" for clarity in oral delivery, but the precise referent is the right-turning conch or auspicious whorl, a standard item in Buddhist lists of the seven precious things or eight auspicious symbols. The term rendered "duty-officer" translates dge skos, a monastic official responsible for overseeing the monastery's practical affairs and discipline; the Sanskrit equivalent is karmadāna or upadhivārika depending on the Vinaya tradition. The precise scope of this role varies across Vinaya recensions.

The phrase "fell ill" for babs pa is a interpretive choice: the term literally means "fell" or "collapsed," and in Vinaya contexts commonly indicates falling ill or becoming incapacitated. The narrative context supports this reading, as the monk is still mobile enough to visit the other monk, suggesting a less severe condition. Some uncertainty remains. The names at the very end of the passage are the names of the four members of the Group of Six monks rendered here from context. The Tibetan gives: དགའ་བོས་ (Gāvampati), ཉེ་དགའ (Nandika), འདུན་པས་ (Udāyin), འཆར་ཀས་ (Canda). These are standard members of the Group of Six as known from Vinaya sources; the pairing structure "A to B, B to A, C to D, D to C" is clear in the Tibetan verse.

The term དད་པ་ rendered here as "faith-offering" refers specifically to robes or goods offered out of faith as a donation to a monk — a technical Vinaya usage.

The term མཚམས་ཀྱི་ཕྱི་རོལ་ ("outside the boundary") refers to being outside the canonical monastic boundary (sīmā), which has legal significance in Vinaya proceedings including the validity of transactions. The name rendered "Nanda" in the Group of Six pairings translates a Tibetan form that appears to stand for the same "Nandika" used elsewhere in the passage; the slight variation in the Tibetan may reflect a scribal inconsistency in the source. The pairing structure has been followed as given.

The summary verse at the section break is a mnemonic condensing the topics covered in this block of Vinaya rules. Its terse formulation is conventional in the Vinaya literature and the rendering aims to convey its indexical function rather than to supply full doctrinal elaboration. The passage enumerates five reasons why buddhas remain in the assembly hall rather than going directly to a meal invitation. The fifth reason, establishing Vinaya rules, is explicitly identified as the operative one in this narrative context, marking the following episode as the occasion for a new rule.

The Tibetan term translated as "tally-sticks" is ཚུལ་ཤིང, literally "procedure-wood" or "method-sticks," referring to the practice of distributing counted sticks or tokens as a way of taking a census of resident monks; this is a well-known Vinaya procedure. The phrase rendered "Mṛgāra's mother Sādhā" translates a compound name that is somewhat opaque: the first figure (Sādhā) appears to be a named noblewoman associated with Mṛgāra as a maternal figure — this is the well-known patroness Mṛgāramātā (Viśākhā) of the Pāli texts, but the Tibetan here gives a distinct name. The identity may differ between Mūlasarvāstivāda and Pāli traditions; the translation follows the Tibetan as given without harmonizing to the Pāli.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end as the Tibetan text itself is cut short. The term kārṣāpaṇa is a Sanskrit monetary unit, a coin of standard weight; it is left in transliteration as it is a proper currency term with no clean English equivalent. The passage on "taking kārṣāpaṇas and making whatever use of them one wishes" is a formal Vinaya ruling permitting monks to handle money entrusted by a patron under specific circumstances — a technically significant allowance within the monastic code. The "goddess Mālinī" rendering follows the Tibetan lha mo Mālinī, which most likely refers to the queen herself referred to by an honorific epithet, though it could indicate a deity's shrine stall; this ambiguity is present in the source. The passage pairs monks by the number of rains retreats completed, pairing those whose counts differ by three years across a twelve-year span. The precise pairing scheme — one who has not yet completed a year with one who has completed three, one year with four, and so on up to nine with twelve — reflects a Vinaya convention about seniority gradations that is reproduced verbatim twice in the Tibetan, a textual feature preserved in the translation.

The phrase rendered "tiger-food" translates stag gi god ma, which in Vinaya context refers to a specific type of food or food preparation associated with tigers; the precise referent is uncertain in this passage and is noted in the summary verse as a technical term awaiting further commentarial clarification.

"Śāradvatīputra's charge" renders sha ra'i bu'i dge tshul skul byed, literally "the novice who was the attendant of Śāriputra." The name Skul byed ("one who urges" or "the encourager") appears to be the novice's personal name. The phrase rendered "renounce their vows" translates a term for formally abandoning one's monastic status by a verbal declaration — a recognised canonical procedure. The text here describes its misuse by the group of six, monks notorious in Vinaya literature for misconduct that occasions new rules. The Blessed One's statement that he "feigns not knowing" while actually knowing is a standard Vinaya formula indicating that the Buddha asks questions pedagogically, not out of ignorance. The term rendered "senior resident" translates gnas brtan, literally "elder of the residence," a functionary responsible for administering a Saṅgha dwelling. The gaṇḍī is a wooden sounding board struck to summon monks to assembly; it is left in transliteration as a recognized Vinaya technical term. The distribution of tooth-wood sticks (tshul shing, Skt. dantakāṣṭha) before a communal meal was a formal procedure establishing that all eligible community members were duly notified and present before gains could be lawfully divided; Nanda and Upananda exploit each procedural gap in sequence to invalidate the distribution and claim a share. The phrase rendered "stirring up trouble for the Saṅgha" translates the Tibetan for making a deliberate false or vexatious claim against the community; the preceding ruling clarifies the procedural context. The term kārṣāpaṇa is a standard Indian monetary unit (copper or silver coin) retained in transliteration as it is a proper name for the currency. The passage ends mid-sentence at "Then he said," following the Tibetan exactly, which breaks off at that point. The word rendered "pay us back" for གླན translates a term meaning to repay or recompense; in context the group of six is offering to reimburse the elephant-trainers for having caused the stampede, contingent on the trainers' promise to pay for the monks' meals. The exchange is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan and this rendering follows the most coherent reading of the negotiation. The summary verses are mnemonic device verses listing the topics covered in the chapter and the sub-rules that follow; several of the terms in them are technical Vinaya vocabulary for parts of footwear. The renderings "inner toe-piece" for brang lhan and "heel-piece" for rting lhan follow the standard commentarial identification of these as reinforcing patches at the toe and heel of a sandal respectively. The term ryus pa, rendered here as "lining," refers to the inner lining or underlayer of a shoe made from hide. "Long handle" and "short handle" render yu chad and yu thung, which likely refer to straps or tabs used to put on or fasten footwear; some uncertainty attaches to the precise physical referent, but the general sense is clear. The two summary verses are mnemonic colophon verses of the sort common in Vinaya literature, listing topics covered in the surrounding sections. Their compressed, list-like syntax resists smooth prose rendering. The first verse appears to summarize preceding narrative topics including Vairocana, the Saṅgha, food-giving, and a temple episode. The second verse introduces the birth narrative that follows. These verses are conventional section-markers rather than doctrinal statements, and some individual items in them remain contextually opaque without the broader text.

The five surveys attributed to the bodhisattva before his descent from Tuṣita are a standard motif in Vinaya birth-narrative literature: lineage, time, place, clan, and the mother's qualities. The Tibetan term rendered here as "women" in the fifth survey more precisely refers to the prospective mother, as clarified by the surrounding narrative context. The name Rūpasāra, Jayaprabha, Suprabha, and Udaya are reconstructed from the Tibetan epithets following the internal etymological explanations given in the text. Śvetakarṇa ("White-ear") and Nālada are proper names kept from the Tibetan phonetic rendering. The final sentence breaks off mid-speech with King Śuddhodana beginning to say something; the passage ends there and continues beyond this excerpt. The yakṣa name "Śākyavarddhana" is a straightforward Sanskrit reconstruction from the Tibetan Śākya-spel-ba ("the one who increases or multiplies the Śākyas"). The text switches between two sages — earlier called Asita, and here identified as Nārada and Nālada — consistent with the narrative's use of multiple sage characters around the birth episode. "Nārada" renders Drang-srong Mi-dkar-ba (literally "the white-bodied sage"), while Nālada is used directly from the syllables Na-la-da in the Tibetan. The phrase rendered "the nectar of immortality" translates the Tibetan term for amṛta, the deathless — here signifying the attainment of awakening or nirvāṇa.

The figure Nārada here is presented with complexity: initially portrayed as a venerable sage, the closing lines describe him as one corrupted by wrong views and given to deception. This is consistent with certain Indo-Tibetan narrative traditions in which the Brahmanical sage Nārada appears in a critical or ambivalent role within Buddhist literature. The phrase "white-clad sage" renders a Tibetan term that may indicate a particular sect or status; the epithet is kept as given.

The verse "by those who discern only the lesser marks" conveys that those of limited discernment, seeing the bodhisattva's bodily marks, predict worldly kingship over the four continents, whereas one of clear insight like Nārada perceives the marks of full buddhahood. The four-line verse is a well-known set of impermanence aphorisms found across Pāli and Sanskrit Buddhist literature. The rendering follows the natural rhetorical parallelism of the original.

The name Nāḷada (distinct from Nārada) is established in the narrative as a new character derived from Nārada by bone-kinship; the Tibetan etymology plays on "rus" (bone) connecting the two names, which is difficult to render in English without awkwardness and so is left implicit.

The phrase rendered "the settled domain of the great earth" reflects a technical administrative or cosmological expression in the Tibetan that is somewhat opaque; the translation gives its most plausible sense in context. The names Sā Tsho Ma, Ri Dags Skyes, and Grags Dzin Ma appear to be Tibetan renderings of Sanskrit names for the women in the prince's retinue before his renunciation. The context parallels standard accounts of the Buddha's life, but the specific Sanskrit equivalents are not recoverable with certainty from this passage alone.

The phrase rendered as "the five fields of knowledge" refers to the classical Indian pañcavidyā, the five sciences traditionally mastered by an educated prince.

The term rendered "pressed into essence" for ཉིང་ཁུར་བྱས་པ refers to churned or concentrated milk-porridge; the exact preparation is a detail of the standard biography of the Buddha's acceptance of food from Sujātā, here adapted with different names for the women.

The elephant names and distances appear to be specific to this biographical narrative and are kept in close translation rather than normalized, as their Sanskrit originals are uncertain. The repeated phrase rendered "this work of stoking falls on no ordinary person; this is not our task" reflects a stock refrain in which each group deflects responsibility for tending the fires upward or outward, invoking their own specific royal duty as reason for exemption. The Tibetan is elliptical in places, and the phrase "from the passage 'what are the duties of a king' up to 'in five places,' just as before" signals a scribal abbreviation of a longer formulaic passage. The translation preserves this as-is, since it is a feature of the original text, not an error in rendering. The verse at the end presents a list of inauspicious omens in a riddle-like format. The Tibetan term "ལྷ་གཤེགས་" rendered as "the king is coming" literally means "the royal one approaches" (an honorific form). The list of inauspicious items in the verse is a formulaic riddle-omen sequence; the final question signals that the guard's "worldly thought" is an omen-reading, and the answer to the riddle will presumably follow in the next passage. The term "ས་འཛིན་པ" (lord of the earth) is used both as the guard's title and as an address to the king; context disambiguates each use. The currency unit kārṣāpaṇa is a standard ancient Indian copper coin and is kept in its Sanskrit form throughout. The section heading "The Vinaya of minor matters, the twenty-fourth section" (འདུལ་བ་ཕྲན་ཚེགས་ཀྱི་གཞི། བམ་པོ་ཉི་ཤུ་བཞི་པ།) appears mid-passage, marking a scribal or editorial division in the canonical text. It interrupts the narrative but is part of the transmitted text and has been rendered in place.

The term ཤིང་སྤྲ་མགོ་ནག་མོ literally means "black-headed tree-monkey." The rendering "black-headed spider monkey" follows the natural sense for a long-tailed arboreal primate; the precise species identification is uncertain but the doctrinal significance is negligible. The phrase rendered as "enters its burrow" could alternatively refer to the animal entering any narrow passage or aperture; the precise meaning of the den or hole is contextually inferred. The claim that salt and sand each originate from water reflects ancient Indian natural philosophy embedded in the narrative and is not a doctrinal Buddhist claim; it is rendered as the character's own stated explanation without editorial intervention. The explanation for the pit-digging riddle repeats verbatim the phrase used for the dead-man-on-the-scale riddle ("a dead man is no longer a man, and so his vital lustre has been taken from him"), which appears to be a scribal repetition in the source text; it has been rendered faithfully as it stands.

The phrase rendered "vital lustre" translates mdangs phrogs pa, literally "robbed of lustre or colour," a classical idiom for the loss of the living glow or vital aura that distinguishes a living body from a corpse, explaining the weight difference on the scale and, by textual repetition, the earth-volume difference in the pit. The summary verse near the beginning is a mnemonic gāthā enumerating story-episodes in the Jīvaka cycle; several of the terms are proper names or story-titles rather than standard doctrinal vocabulary. "Nala" and "Ela leaf" appear to be titles of episodes, and the verse is intentionally compressed. The rendering preserves this compressed quality.

"Kanyākubja" renders the Tibetan phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit place-name (modern Kannauj).

"Āmalaka" (Phyllanthus emblica, the Indian gooseberry) is left in Sanskrit as it is a specific medicinal fruit well known in the tradition.

The phrase rendered "I will be able to protect the mind of the patient" is idiomatic; the Tibetan literally says "I will have the capacity to guard the mind of the sick one," meaning Jīvaka is confident he can manage Pradyota's volatile temperament as well as treat his illness. The excellent great elephant named Bhadravatī — the Tibetan reads "Bzang ldan" literally meaning "endowed with excellence," which corresponds to the Sanskrit Bhadravatī, a name known from parallel accounts of this narrative in the Pāli and Sanskrit traditions. This identification is followed here with confidence. The final sentence breaks off mid-passage in the source text. The translation renders it up to the point of interruption. The phrase rendered "a hundred thousand cubits in length" represents a hyperbolic measure for an exceptionally large piece of cloth; the Tibetan gives the figure as one hundred thousand, modifying a unit of linen fabric, and the exact unit of length is not fully transparent in this context. The crow episode's purgative is implied by context from the physiological effect described; the Tibetan describes the dual purgative result idiomatically. The epithet "messenger-crow" renders the Tibetan "phar-ma-pa kha" throughout, understood as a named royal courier rather than a literal bird. The palace name rendered "Palace of the Spreading Willows" translates the Tibetan lcang lo can, which normally corresponds to Sanskrit Caitraratha or is used for Vaiśravaṇa's mythic palace Alakā or a Tuṣita-related structure; the exact Sanskrit correlate here is uncertain but the Tibetan is clear. The nāga king's name "Elā's Wing" is a literal rendering of e la'i 'dab; the Sanskrit behind this epithet is uncertain and may be a corruption or regional variant. The place name "Resting-Stone" renders rdo 'jog, which may be a toponym or a descriptive phrase; its Sanskrit equivalent is not recoverable from context alone. The passage involves a rapid bargaining sequence over time — twelve years down to seven days — in which Nālandā negotiates the deadline for answering the questions. The Tibetan is elliptical and reads almost like stage directions; the rendering expands slightly for clarity without adding content.

The phrase rendered "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" translates a standard Abhidharma formulation: the view of a transitory collection (Sanskrit satkāyadṛṣṭi) comprises twenty sub-views regarding the five aggregates (each viewed fourfold as self, as belonging to self, as in self, or as self in it), and these are destroyed upon stream-entry.

The five monks who were Nālandā's closest companions likely refer to the five ascetics of the Deer Park, the first disciples of the Buddha, a detail consistent with the Ṛṣipatana setting. This is left implicit in the translation as the text itself does not explain it. The phrase rendered as "the forest of the deer-haunting sage" translates a standard Tibetan equivalent of Ṛṣipatana ("the sage's deer park" at Sarnath), though the Tibetan here uses a slightly unusual formulation. This is consistent with the preceding passage's usage and presents no consequential ambiguity.

The nāga king's name associated with "Elā" is unclear — this likely refers to Elapatra or a related nāga king figure from the same narrative tradition. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of this passage. The sentence describing the nāga's transformation before approaching the Blessed One is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan. The phrase rendered "having transformed his body in the same way that sentient beings avert their eyes when they see something repulsive" is an idiomatic construction meaning he made his form visible in its actual, aversion-inducing state, having previously concealed it. The rendering preserves the sense of the reversal.

The phrase "gates of saṃsāra" translates a Tibetan expression indicating the objects and conditions that draw beings into cyclic existence through desire; the Blessed One is pointing out that the assembly's longing for the illusory majesty was itself an example of saṃsāric attachment. The verse on karma not being lost is a well-known canonical gāthā found in several sūtra and Vinaya contexts, sometimes attributed to the ālayavijñāna doctrine in later scholastic literature, though here it functions as a straightforward statement on karmic inevitability without necessarily implying Yogācāra metaphysics.

The monk's outburst — "This thing has neither life nor breath; what offense did the Blessed One Kāśyapa see in it that he made it a basis for training?" — is a reference to Vinaya rules protecting plants and trees, which the monk is mocking at the moment of his disrobing. The verse passage beginning "By the Tathāgata's word 'Come here'" is a short embedded gāthā in the Tibetan; it has been rendered as verse accordingly. The line "sངས་རྒྱས་དགོངས་པས་ཆ་ལུགས་བསྒྱུར་ནས་ནི" means literally "having transformed his deportment or bearing by the Buddha's intention" — rendered as "through the Buddha's intention his bearing was changed," which captures the miraculous instantaneous transformation of the newly ordained monk's appearance by the Tathāgata's power.

The final section parallels the famous Kātyāyana Sūtra (Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.15 / Saṃyuktāgama), one of the most important canonical expositions of the Middle Way between eternalism and nihilism. The teaching here closely follows that sūtra's doctrine that right view avoids the two extremes of "exists" and "does not exist" by attending instead to the arising and cessation of suffering through dependent origination. The phrase rendered "five aspects of movement and non-movement" translates a Tibetan expression for the wheel of saṃsāra characterized by five pairs or aspects. The precise referent of "five aspects" here is not entirely transparent from the text alone; it may refer to a specific scholastic enumeration of five characteristics of conditioned existence, though this phrasing is unusual and may reflect a specific commentarial tradition.

The name "Rabsnang" is a Tibetan royal name left in transliteration as it appears to be a narrative proper name rather than a Sanskrit epithet with a known Sanskrit original. The name rendered as "Rabsnang" is a Tibetan royal name literally meaning "Fierce Radiance." It is left as a proper name rather than translated, consistent with how Tibetan proper names of kings are handled. The Sanskrit equivalent, if one exists in the source text's Indic background, is not specified here.

The phrase rendered "the noble realm" translates "Āryarāja" or similar, literally the "noble kingdom," which appears to refer to a specific kingdom where the king Rabsnang resides. This is a place name in the narrative context.

"Śrāvaṇī" is the Sanskrit reconstruction for the Tibetan "skra can," meaning "the one with hair," said to accord with her name from a former life. The passage notes this etymology explicitly. The phrase rendered "accepted by saying nothing in refusal" reflects the Tibetan idiom of tacit acceptance through silence, a recognized formulaic convention in Vinaya narrative literature for a monastic accepting an invitation. The phrase rendered "girl with the hair" translates a somewhat opaque epithet referring to the brahmin girl called Skegs-can-ma or similar, literally "she who has hair." The context suggests this is a personal identifier or nickname for the girl rather than a general description, and the translation preserves it as such throughout.

The line about arhats not engaging primordial wisdom without prior reflection is a standard doctrinal statement about the mode of knowing of arhats versus buddhas; it is presented as an aside explaining why Kātyāyana needed to reflect before speaking, and the translation renders it accordingly.

The name "Glorious Light" renders the Tibetan rab snang, which appears here as a royal name or epithet. The phrase rendered "two-legged legumes" translates a term that appears to denote a low-quality pulse or bean, possibly identified by having two visible halves or segments. The exact botanical referent is uncertain but the point — that the food was coarse and contemptible — is clear from context.

The name rendered throughout as "Candragupta" translates the Tibetan "Gtum po rab snang," a literal rendering of a Sanskrit original. The identification with the historical Candragupta is traditional; the Tibetan is a calque of a Sanskrit royal name meaning something like "Fiercely Brilliant." The king's name in the preceding passage was rendered as "Candragupta," but the Tibetan here reads གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང, which is a different name — literally something like "Fierce Greatly Radiant." This does not correspond to Candragupta. For consistency with the preceding rendered passage and narrative coherence, a note is warranted: the Tibetan name གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང (Tumpo Rapnang) appears to be the actual name in this passage, and "Candragupta" in the preceding passage may represent a different Tibetan reading or a separate version. I have rendered the name here as "Candragupta" to maintain continuity as instructed, but the Tibetan actually gives a different royal name.

The famous simile of the oil-bearer appears in Pāli sources (Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.246) and is well-attested in the scholastic tradition as an illustration of sense restraint, which confirms the doctrinal point here. The epithet "King Candragupta" was used in the preceding passage; the Tibetan here reads "King Candragupta" (རྒྱལ་པོ་གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང་). This is an unusual royal name, and there is a question in scholarship about which historical Candragupta is intended, but as this follows directly from the established continuity, the name is rendered consistently.

The geography "Kanyākubja" (Kannauj) follows from the Tibetan transliteration. The place called "the Peaceful" at the end renders Tibetan "Śiva" (ཞི་བ), which in this context is a place-name etymology, not the deity.

The five "intimate ornaments" and "outer ornaments" reflect a standard Vinaya narrative formula for bride-price; the exact items are not enumerated in the source passage. The king's name, Rānaprabhā (rendered from གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང་), literally means "fierce" or "wrathful" and "brilliance" or "radiance." The rendering Rānaprabhā is approximate; the Tibetan is used as a proper name throughout, so it is kept consistent as such. The phrase གྱར་ཚས་ in the woman's reply is rendered "in secret" following the contextual sense of a clandestine visit; there is some ambiguity in the precise nuance but no doctrinal consequence. The epithet "hero of the market" renders a phrase that likely means something like "renowned hero" or "celebrated champion," with "market" or "town square" suggesting public fame. The exact nuance is uncertain but the general sense of public renown is clear.

The passage "from 'the prosperous' down to 'he ruled the kingdom in accordance with the Dharma' is as before" is a standard abbreviation formula in Buddhist narrative literature, referring the reader back to an earlier stock description repeated for each king figure in the cycle. The proper names Riktrödma, Namdö Gyi, Gyabrak Kyaseng, Langkyong, and Döjok are rendered phonetically from Tibetan as they appear to be narrative proper nouns without clear Sanskrit equivalents or transparent Tibetan meanings that would require translation in this context. Gyabrak Kyaseng literally means something like "grey-brown cliff-dwellers" and could be a proper ethnic or clan name; the rendering preserves it as a name. The passage's final line ends mid-sentence, consistent with the continuity format. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the passage with the king beginning to quote Namjé's earlier words. This is a mid-sentence interruption in the source and is rendered faithfully here without completion.

The name Ritrömma renders the Tibetan epithet meaning "mountain-wilderness woman," used here as the farmer's wife's name or descriptive title; it is left as a proper name to match the narrative register. The name Söpa rendered here as "the recovered one" reflects the Tibetan verb meaning to nurse or restore to health. The narrative device of the king testing various ministers before turning to Söpa follows a recognizable storytelling pattern in classical Indian and Tibetan didactic literature. The phrase rendered "send word to me a second time" is an attempt to render a slightly elliptical construction; the sense is that Söpa should signal the king both before and after bathing or eating so the king can time his visit. The phrase rendered as "the king himself arrived" is a colloquial narrative transition; the text has Söpa calling the king "lha" (Your Majesty, literally "lord/deity"), used throughout as a royal honorific, which the preceding translation also renders as "Your Majesty."

The exchange about the needle and the water jar is a folk riddle demonstrating paradoxical skill: stopping a leak with a wet needle is said to be the wonder, because the wetness seals it, whereas a dry needle merely pierces. This is a recognizable motif in South Asian narrative literature, signaling that the children possess unusual healing or magical powers — specifically, the ability to heal wounds — which Söpa perceives.

The line "that father-in-law of yours has been extremely contemptuous toward me" presents a slight syntactic ambiguity: it could be Söpa speaking of his own father-in-law's contempt toward himself, or referencing the king's treatment. The rendering follows the most natural reading given the narrative context. The name rendered "Rāpana (Raudra-prabhā)" in the preceding passage appears here as གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང་, a compound meaning "Fierce Brilliant-Light," which is a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit name; Raudra-prabhā is a reasonable reconstruction. The preceding English passage used "Söpa" for what appears to be a different character (the one who witnesses the needle incident); consistency with prior rendering is maintained where possible, but the identity of "Söpa" versus the patient (གསོས་པ) should be noted: གསོས་པ in this passage is clearly "the patient," a distinct figure being tended by the king, not the same as Söpa who appeared earlier as an observer. This may be a point of narrative complexity worth checking against the broader text.

The phrase rendered "filth steeped in excrement" (མི་གཙང་བའི་ནང་དུ་བསྒྲེས་པའི་རི་ལུས) is somewhat unusual; རི་ལུས could mean "mountain-remainder" or scraps, but in context it most plausibly means a mass of filth, and "filth steeped in excrement" captures the sense adequately.

The place name ཀམ་པོ་ཛི་ཀ་པ is uncertain; "Campājika" is a tentative reconstruction. The episode of the queen's name, Śāntā, meaning "the Peaceful One" or "the Tranquil One," is consistent with the preceding context and is rendered as a proper name throughout. The phrase rendered "his bowels gave way" translates a Tibetan expression for defecation triggered by the exertion of pulling out the iron peg — the text is deliberately earthy, and the rendering preserves that register without amplification. The brahmin's observation that the dreadful portent has "passed" (literally, "separated from the god") functions as comic dramatic irony: what he interprets as a celestial sign clearing has in fact corresponded to the king's very literal bodily crisis and escape. The term rendered "grey-robed forest ascetics" translates "skya bseng pa," which designates wandering śramaṇas or ascetics in grey or ochre robes — almost certainly non-Buddhist renouncers in context. The phrase is consistent with this narrative's repeated contrast between brahminical court culture and wandering mendicants.

The maidservant's name "Kyedma" is a personal name rendered phonetically from the Tibetan; no Sanskrit equivalent is recoverable from context. The term rendered "head-tax" for བླ་སྐྱེས reflects a tribute levied on persons rather than land; the precise administrative meaning in the narrative context is somewhat obscure, but the general sense of a personal levy accompanying the tribute (དཔྱ་ནར་མ) is clear. The episode belongs to a well-known Vinaya narrative illustrating feminine wiles; the figure named Tārā here is an ordinary woman, not the goddess Tārā. The word གསོས་པ consistently means "physician" or "healer" throughout this passage and is so rendered. The shuttlecock episode (ཕོ་ལོང) is a traditional narrative motif for seduction. Āryarāja is a rendering of འཕགས་རྒྱལ, which here appears to function as a place name or city name rather than a royal title. The text is consistent with this being a proper noun for a locality.

The name Pracandarabha renders རྒྱལ་པོ་གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང, a royal name meaning something like "Fiercely Brilliant King"; it has been carried over from the preceding passage as established.

The cypress twig episode involves a crude sexual-humiliation trick; the translation renders it faithfully without euphemism, following the Vinaya narrative style. The song line "just as the branches of a pine are bent and bowed" renders the Tibetan idiom literally; the simile compares the pliable pine branch to a man bent to a woman's will, which is the point the landowner is making obliquely. The doubled lines reflect the Tibetan repetition in the original, which appears to be a formal feature of the verse being sung. The phrase rendered "repaid in flesh" follows the idiom that if the nephew succeeds, the attendant will owe him a great debt. The Tibetan literally says "my flesh will become repaid / returned," a colloquial expression for being vindicated or receiving recompense; the rendering chosen conveys the spirit without obscuring the text. The name "Govarddhana" rendered consistently with prior context as a young man's name. The term rendered "go-between" for བྱི་བ་བྱེད་པ is literally "one who acts as an intermediary or matchmaker" in the specific legal-courtly sense of facilitating pairings among plaintiffs and defendants; this reading fits the judicial context. The "summary verse" is a colophon-style gāthā listing the tale-episodes by brief label; the rendering follows the Tibetan's compressed list format. "Prabhaśvara" is used consistently for རབ་སྣང. The phrase གཅིག་ལས་འཕྲོས་པའི་ལུང་ཀློག་ཏུ་བཅུག་གོ, rendered as "had him recite the scriptural transmission that flows from one to the next," refers to the memorization and recitation of canonical texts in a linked chain, a standard element of monastic formation. The phrase rendered "peculiar heaviness in my body" translates a term for bodily languor or a dragging, heavy sensation — the precise medical nuance is somewhat opaque, but the general sense of a debilitating physical ailment is clear. The detail that the girl is instructed to tell the cowherd's wife that the man wishes to "pay respects many times over" reflects a formulaic idiom of respectful visitation; the translation conveys the sense faithfully. The passage referring to the cowherd's wife as "the king's queen" near the end is consistent with her identity established earlier in the narrative and does not represent a scribal confusion.
