The phrase rendered as "your thread — is it still in that condition" reflects the Tibetan idiom for asking after the patient's condition; the word for "thread" here likely refers to the pulse or a medical gauge rather than literal thread, though the text is elliptical and the exact meaning is slightly uncertain. The passage moves between speakers rapidly and without always marking the shift; attribution has been inferred from context throughout. The passage renders "Āryāvarta" for འཕགས་རྒྱལ, the standard Tibetan translation of the Sanskrit name for the sacred heartland of northern India.

The phrase rendered "royally consecrated king of the warrior caste" reflects the Tibetan reference to the king anointed (དབང་བསྐུར་བ) from among the royal class (རྒྱལ་རིགས), i.e., the kṣatriya lineage.

The name "Rabsang" (རབ་སྣང) is left as a Tibetan proper name; it may represent a Tibetan coinage rather than a translation of a known Sanskrit royal name. The epithet "Tumpo Rabsang" rendered consistently with the preceding passage. The phrase translated as "the gray-robed ascetic" renders skya bseng, literally "gray/ash-clothed mendicant," likely indicating a non-Buddhist wandering ascetic; the rendering follows the contextual register throughout. The name rendered "Gosā" throughout corresponds to Tibetan "གསོས་པ" in this passage, which appears to be a proper name in context rather than the past-tense verb "revived." This reading is consistent with the preceding narrative where a counselor or general figure is addressed. The ring inscription episode, and the identification of "གསོས་པ" as a named official rather than a verbal form, is a genuine interpretive point worth flagging. The term rendered "guards" throughout for གསོས་པ is a contextually driven choice: in this narrative the གསོས་པ (literally "the one who fed" or "the keeper") appears to function as a royal officer or chamberlain assigned to keep watch; the translation treats them collectively as guards or the guard-keeper in accordance with the dramatic situation.

The phrase འཁྲུལ་འཁོར་གྱི་སྒྱུ་རྩལ (yantra-craft or the art of mechanical automata) refers to the classical Indian tradition of constructing mechanical devices or automata, well attested in Sanskrit literature; "automaton" is chosen as the closest natural English equivalent. The name Damburi Mountain renders the Tibetan Damburi Ri, the proper name of the elephant chief used consistently in the preceding passages. Tumpo Rabnang is likewise carried over from prior context as the name of the king of the noble realm. The phrase rendered "critical distance" translates sa tshigs das par gyur pa, literally "when a certain fixed point or interval had been passed," indicating a pre-arranged distance beyond which pursuit would be futile; this is the most consequential interpretive choice in the passage. The names Norha Jin (nor lha'i byin, "Gift of the Wealth-God"), Rab Nang (rab tu snang, "Greatly Radiant"), Jungwa Chang (sbyor ba 'chang, "Bearer of Method / Schemes"), and Sertrengchen (gser phreng can, "She of the Golden Garland") are rendered in phonetic approximation as character names in a narrative context; their literal meanings are transparent in Tibetan but function as proper names here. The epithet "old woman" at the end is Jungwa Chang's sister still in her wanderer disguise, addressing the disguised prince — the shift is intentional in the source. The names in this passage are rendered from a mix of Sanskrit originals and Tibetan translations. "Nora Lhé Jin" is a Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Dattā (meaning "given by the god of wealth," i.e., Dhanadattā or similar); I have supplied the Sanskrit "Dattā" for clarity. "Suvarṇamālā" (Golden Garland One) translates the Tibetan epithet gsер phreṅ can. "Vasantī" (Spring One) translates dpyid ldan. King Caṇḍapradyota renders gtum po rab snaṅ, a well-known king of Kauśāmbī in Vinaya narrative literature. The phrase rendered "sacred food" and "libation" involves deliberate comic absurdity: the madwoman claims elephant dung and urine are royal offerings, which the grooms dismiss as insanity — the humor is integral to the narrative's plot of escape. The fascicle and chapter headings in the middle of the passage are scribal colophon insertions marking a text division; I have rendered them plainly in the translation. The song sung by Holder-of-the-Bow is metrically structured in the original and is rendered here as verse accordingly. The names throughout — Śarva, Holder-of-the-Bow (Skt. Dharmadhara or similar), Golden-Garland (Skt. Suvarṇamālā), Bhadravatī, Dhanavardhana, Pradyota — are kept consistent with the preceding passage. The epithet translated as "the noble realm" renders 'phags rgyal, which may refer to Magadha or a realm of noble status; the precise identification is contextually uncertain but does not affect the narrative sense. The song's four lines present some compression. The line rendered "Vaiśravaṇa's steward drove him on" refers to Pradyota being driven like a draft animal; "the steward of Vaiśravaṇa" is an epithet playing on the name Dhanavardhana, who is elsewhere identified with the yakṣa treasurer figure. The line "Earth and forest soared into the sky" is a riddle-kenning for the palanquin carrying Pradyota. These are intentional riddles sung by the bystanders, and the opacity is original to the text.

The phrase rendered "the god Dhanavardhana has given this" reflects a deliberate fiction Śarva orders to be maintained: that Pradyota's arrival was a divine gift rather than a kidnapping, to protect the political secret. The passage describes Dhanavardhana's elaborate plot to fulfill — or appear to fulfill — the queen's vow while engineering the death of King Śarva's son. The queen's vow involves a seven-day fast and a ritual wrapping in flower garlands followed by being seated at the enclosure gate; Dhanavardhana exploits this vow as the mechanism for throwing the prince from the enclosure wall. The identity of "the god" in the queen's speech refers to the captive king, using the honorific "lha" as a form of royal address, not to a divine being. This dual usage of "lha" — both as the deity Dhanavardhana's name-element and as a royal honorific in the queen's speech — is a notable feature of the passage; the translation renders each instance according to context. The closing epithet applied to the new king renders three Tibetan terms together: "fierce" (gtum po), "supremely radiant" (rab snang), and "without rival" (gran zla med pa). These appear to be epithets embedded in or functioning as a proper name or a descriptive title for the successor king; the text does not give a separate personal name here, so they are rendered as descriptive epithets. The name rendered "Rabhasa Prabhā" corresponds to the Tibetan "གཏུམ་པོ་རབ་སྣང་" (fierce, supremely radiant), which is the king introduced at the end of the preceding passage. This is the same king described there as fierce and radiant as the sun.

The name "Lotus-Hearted" renders "པད་མའི་སྙིང་པོ་ཅན་" (one who has a lotus heart/core), which appears to be a personal name or epithet of the king's antagonist.

"Āryā" renders "'འཕགས་རྒྱལ་," a term for the noble realm or country; this may be a place name requiring identification from the broader textual context.

"Dambha" renders "'འདམ་བུ་," treated here as a proper name for the elephant.

The final sentence is cut off mid-passage in the source text; the translation ends accordingly. The phrase rendered "the land of setting-down-stones" translates the toponym that has been consistently used in the preceding context for Balaṅkya's destination; it is a proper place-name in this narrative, not a descriptive phrase, but the Tibetan is rendered literally as no Sanskrit or standard equivalent is established in the passage.

The minister's remarks to the potter and the dung beetle are deliberately ambiguous, each capable of being heard as a general moral maxim or as a pointed personal jibe at the king — which is precisely the dramatic irony the text exploits. The translation preserves this ambiguity. The term rendered as "god" throughout this passage is an honorific form of address from the minister to the king, a standard idiom of Indian courtly speech in which a king is addressed as "divine majesty" or simply "god." It is not a reference to a deity.

The phrase rendered "unfired pottery vessels" (སྣོད་སོ་མ) refers to raw, sun-dried but not yet kiln-fired pots, which are fragile; this detail is essential to the meaning of the minister's first explanation. The passage presents several interpretive challenges. The term translated throughout as "spy-women" or "eavesdroppers" (Tibetan: phra men ma) refers to female spies or informants — possibly also understood as demonesses or she-demons (srin mo) in the proclamation at the close, which conflates the two groups deliberately in the ruse. The final line's proclamation invokes "the pledge of the mother of the gods" (lha ni ma'i dam tshig) as the authoritative summons, a ritual fiction designed to gather the targets together. The text breaks off mid-sentence at "And they thought," indicating the passage continues beyond the excerpt provided. The phrase rendered "those who lived by the chopper's trade" translates a term literally meaning "those who live by the chopper or cleaver," that is, butchers or slaughtermen, here serving as executioners — the point being that the king employed men already habituated to killing for this mass beheading.

The six opening syllables of the dream-verses are given as a mnemonic device in the text: each monosyllabic word is the first syllable of the corresponding verse. The verses appear to be laments spoken by the slain brahmins — now recognizing in the dream-speech of the dead that they have been cast into hell as a consequence of their previous evil deeds as she-demons. This doctrinal interpretation should be understood in the context of the narrative. The six verses keyed to the six sky-sounds form an embedded literary structure; each verse is introduced by its opening syllable or word, which serves as a mnemonic heading. The translation preserves this structure while making it natural for listening.

The phrase rendered "five finest limbs nourished there" translates a term literally meaning "the five best limbs fattened/nourished," which in the context of blood-sacrifice likely refers to five prime sacrificial victims selected and prepared. The exact referent is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, which is reflected in the translation. The six earth-sounds and six sky-sounds function as acrostics: each word names the opening syllable of the verse that follows. This is a recognized literary device in Indian narrative and the Tibetan text signals it explicitly. The rendering preserves the acrostic frame by heading each verse with its key word.

The name Kātyāyanī's son refers to Mahākātyāyana, one of the principal disciples of the Buddha, renowned for his skill in doctrinal exposition. The cow's counsel to seek him out is a pivot in the narrative. The term rendered "otters" translates a Tibetan word that can refer to otters or similar water-dwelling creatures; the precise species is contextually uncertain but "otter" is the standard identification in Vinaya commentarial literature. The mountain name "Tumldän" renders the Tibetan Ri bo Gtum ldan. The literal meaning is something like "the mountain possessing fierceness," but as it functions as a proper place name in context it is left in transliterated form rather than translated. If a conventional Sanskrit or standard English rendering exists in the source text's tradition it has not been preserved here.

The phrase rendered "procures even a single eye's worth" is genuinely difficult. The Tibetan reads mig ya gcig kyang 'jor byed pa, literally "one who acquires even a single eye." In context the crow appears to be saying that even someone who takes so little as a single egg or morsel — or, alternatively, one who profits by a single eye's amount through dishonest means — has caused her loss. The intended sense within the verse is that the horse-keeper's destructive act, however small it might seem, ultimately freed her (and her young) from some form of suffering, perhaps meaning that death ended their distress. The doctrinal or narrative logic here is somewhat opaque and may reflect a variant reading. The place-names Yavana, Siṃhala, Vaṅgāla, and Kaliṅga are left in approximate Sanskrit equivalents as they appear in the text and denote, respectively, the Greek or western lands, Sri Lanka, Bengal, and the Kaliṅga region of eastern India. The Tibetan for Vaṅgāla is rendered as such rather than "Bengal" to preserve the proper-name register of the passage.

The phrase rendered "a different person in the funeral litter" follows the context established in the preceding passage about the litter-bearer; the Tibetan gdung ma yang gzhan zhig bcug literally means "he also put another person in the gdung ma," where gdung ma refers to the funeral or carrying litter referenced earlier.

The phrase skya bseng gi bu mo is rendered "daughter of the śramaṇa woman" literally; it could also mean "daughter of a poor woman" or "daughter of a mendicant woman." The context does not fully resolve this. The passage distinguishes between the Blessed One's "worldly thought" and his "supramundane thought" — a doctrinal point about the range of the buddha's cognition: his ordinary operational awareness is perceptible even to insects, whereas his transcendent awareness is beyond the reach of even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This is a standard teaching on the incomprehensibility of a buddha's highest gnosis.

The term rendered "Śivā" for Gopālā's mother comes from the preceding context where "Gopālā's mother, Śivā" appears; here the Tibetan has only "Gopālā's mother, Śivā," consistent with the preceding passage rendering.

The term མ་ཧེ (mahe) is a loanword for the water buffalo (Skt. mahiṣa), rendered accordingly. The epithet rendered "Bimbisāra, the artisan-king of Rājagṛha" translates a Tibetan phrase meaning literally "the artisan-skilled, form-possessing essence of Rājagṛha," which appears to be a circumlocution identifying Bimbisāra as a patron of fine craftsmanship. The Tibetan name བཟོ་སྦྱངས་གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ is unusual and may be a descriptive epithet rather than the king's proper name; the identification with Bimbisāra rests on context (king of Rājagṛha, first to offer cooked food to the Saṅgha), which is a well-attested distinction of Bimbisāra in the tradition.

The name Supriya (བཟང་ལྡན) for the householder of Vārāṇasī follows the probable Sanskrit reconstruction; the Tibetan literally means "possessing excellence/goodness." The creature called "thī-ba" is a small bird (likely a wren or similar passerine) whose Tibetan name lacks a clean English equivalent. Rather than invent a misleading common name, I have retained "thī-ba" throughout as a proper name for the creature, treating it as the story treats it — as a named narrative character. Listeners familiar with Jātaka literature will recognize the type.

The attendant's speech beginning "Indeed, Your Majesty, I sought her out and killed her" is a continuation of his ruse from the preceding passage: he has not actually killed Śāntā but hidden her, and he now speaks deceptively to the king before telling the parable to cool the king's fury. This dramatic irony is clear in context. The verse on the "two kinds of blind" hinges on a contrast between those who are physically blind from birth and those who are morally blind through rejecting the Dharma or the law — a standard didactic trope in Buddhist narrative literature. The second set adds those who hold sinful views and those who disregard civil or moral law.

The phrase rendered "plays the go-between" for ཕོ་ཉའི་ཕོ་ཉ is literally "a messenger of a messenger," meaning one who acts as an intermediary courier, here condemned in the context of carrying illicit communications. The specific nuance of ཕོ་ཉའི་ཕོ་ཉ alongside མངག་གཞུག་པ་ཡི་མངག་གཞུག and འཕྱོན་མ is that all three involve deceptive or exploitative use of a role of trust; the rendering attempts to capture this social sense. The final two lines are the opening of a summary verse that breaks off mid-passage; they are translated as they stand without completion.

The verse about the net plays on a sustained pun in the Tibetan: the word rendered as "net" also carries the sense of "by means of" or "through connections," creating a deliberate double meaning that the original exploits in each line. The translation attempts to preserve this where possible.

The line about the wrestler's son is rendered as "for one who is to slay, there is always the means to do it without fail," reflecting the sense that a trained killer naturally finds a way; the exact force of the final line is slightly compressed in the Tibetan and this reading is the most defensible. The verse on the four kinds of deceivers presents some syntactic ambiguity. The fourth item, "dividing what belongs to the powerful," could alternatively be rendered as "scattering among the powerful" or "dispersing to those of strength," depending on whether the object is what is distributed or to whom it goes. The rendering chosen fits the proverbial pattern of futile or absurd actions best.

The summary verse near the middle of the passage appears to be a mnemonic colophon enumerating the topics of the entire dialogue sequence, and its terms are intentionally compressed. "Grief and its attendants" renders a compound that literally means "craving, unconsidered action, grief-class," which fits the list of topics covered by the king's accusations. The summary verse near the end is metrically and syntactically compressed; its four paired objects read as a list of things that are paradoxically trustworthy or worth attending to despite their problematic qualities. The precise pairing of each quality with its subject is ambiguous in the Tibetan, and the verse appears to function as a transitional summary of the preceding exchanges rather than a self-contained logical unit. The rendering given here follows the most natural reading of the grammatical structure. The summary verse beginning "Sleeplessness, unwished-for things" appears to function as a colophon-like mnemonic enumerating the topics of the section just completed and those to follow; its terse compression makes the precise sequence of referents somewhat ambiguous, but the rendering reflects the most natural reading. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the attendant's explanation of the nine torments, corresponding to the Tibetan text ending mid-construction. The passage's threefold repetition of the nine-things formula appears to present three distinct psychological cases that are structurally parallel but doctrinally distinct. The second and third iterations appear to reverse the relational valence between the two parties involved, which produces some interpretive difficulty in the Tibetan. The rendering follows the most natural reading of the syntax as it stands.

The list of "ten without compassion" is a standard folk-ethical enumeration found in Vinaya-adjacent narrative literature; the rendering of each occupation follows established parallels in similar canonical lists.

The phrase rendered "fallow ground" for སླད་ས is somewhat uncertain; it may refer specifically to land that has been cultivated but left barren, and the explanation of why it "turns things away" is contained in the portion of text yet to be translated. The phrase rendered "tamer of persons to be tamed, a charioteer, unsurpassed" reflects a standard epithet cluster for a buddha: one who tames those to be tamed and is the supreme charioteer or guide. The Tibetan here runs several epithets together without fully separating them, but they correspond to standard Sanskrit formulae found throughout the Vinaya and sūtra literature.

The expression "station of the finest bull of the herd" translates a standard epithet of the Buddha as foremost among beings, corresponding to Sanskrit vṛṣabhasthāna or similar. The Tibetan term rendered as "the path that leads everywhere" is "kun du 'gro ba'i lam," which in the parallel Sanskrit lists of the ten powers corresponds to "sarvatragāminīṃ pratipadaṃ," the path leading to all destinations or the path to all rebirths. The rendering "the path that leads everywhere" preserves both the literal meaning and the technical doctrinal sense of knowing which karma leads to which realm of rebirth.

The passage ends mid-sentence as the Tibetan source text itself is cut off at that point. The phrase rendered "having taken up actions and dharmas rooted in wrong view" (and its positive parallel) reflects a formulaic Pali-Tibetan locution meaning that these persons have adopted a course of conduct fully consonant with wrong or right view respectively. The term "dharmas" here means doctrines or principles (the things one upholds), not phenomena in a philosophical sense.

The name "Gośa" (Tibetan: གསོས་པ, literally "one who nourishes" or possibly a proper name transcription) appears here as the character who leads the cow-herder's mother to the king; the Tibetan is ambiguous as to whether this is a proper name or a descriptive epithet. The reading as a proper name is adopted here as contextually more natural, but a note on this is warranted. The name Kanyākubja rendered from the Tibetan transliteration "ka nyā kub dza" — this is the city in northern India also known as Kanauj, and its appearance here as a gift from the king is consistent with the narrative's royal setting. The summary verse is a mnemonic colophon listing characters from the preceding story cycle; its terseness is intentional and the rendering is accordingly spare. The phrase rendered "the way of the Dharma of permanence" reflects the Tibetan "rtag chos kyi tshul," where "rtag" may mean "eternal" or "constant" in the sense of the Dharma's abiding character — the point is that the Dharma's way endures and is to be followed continually. The phrase rendered "as a way of testing them" translates brtag pa'i bsam pas, literally "with a mind of examination or testing." The contrast between this wording in the Blessed One's speech and the slightly different phrasing bgam pa'i bsam pas, "with a mind of deceiving or entrapping them," in Ānanda's retelling to the monks is noteworthy and may reflect a deliberate distinction in the Tibetan: the Blessed One frames it neutrally as a test, while Ānanda characterizes the householder's intent as more adversarial. Both renderings follow the text as given. The passage moves between two distinct narrative episodes without a marked break: the Vaiśālī episode concludes with the Vinaya ruling on precious vessels, and a new episode then opens in Śrāvastī. This abrupt transition is in the original and is not a translation error.

The phrase rendered "knowing moderation" translates a term meaning awareness of measure or restraint in eating and receiving, a standard Vinaya virtue; the context confirms this reading. The name Prabhāvatī is a Sanskrit reconstruction of the Tibetan འོད་བཟང་མ (od bzang ma), meaning "she who is radiant with fine light." The text's own folk etymology connects it to the blazing of the house at birth. The rendering "Radiant with Light" reflects the Tibetan form; the Sanskrit Prabhāvatī is the standard equivalent found in parallel Sanskrit recensions.

The phrase "sages who had renounced attachment by the ordinary worldly path" renders the Tibetan འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་ལམ་གྱིས་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བའི་དྲང་སྲོང, referring to non-Buddhist ascetics or worldly meditators who have suppressed but not eradicated desire through mundane meditative paths — a standard doctrinal distinction. The epithet "Wife-killer" renders the Tibetan "chung ma gsod pa," literally "killer of wives," which functions as a stigmatizing nickname in the narrative. The rendering "fined and penalized" for "dpya bar 'gyur ba'i las" reflects a probable legal or social penalty associated with the repeated deaths of his wives; the precise nature of this penalty is not specified in the text. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, mid-enumeration of the body parts Śrī-prabhā is mentally cataloguing. This is a continuation passage and the list is clearly unfinished at the manuscript break point; the translation renders exactly what is present.

The phrase rendered "the keys and the crooked keys" reflects a distinction in the Tibetan between two types of keys; the precise technical difference is unclear from the text alone, but both terms appear to denote household keys of different kinds, symbolizing Śrī-prabhā's installation as household mistress. The phrase "the fire of attachment at the tenth ground" is doctrinally striking: it says the fire of desire characteristic of beings at the tenth bodhisattva ground arose in her, which is an unusual formulation. In context it likely means an intensity of desire surpassing even the highest level — a hyperbolic expression indicating overwhelming passion rather than a technical claim that she was a tenth-ground bodhisattva. This is worth flagging as a doctrinal curiosity.

The closing phrase rendered as "what abided near her like a weapon's thrust" translates a term literally meaning "that which was present like a dagger" or "ready at hand like a weapon." The exact idiomatic force of this final clause is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan and likely signals that her karmic fruits were ripe and unavoidable — the image of a weapon poised to strike conveying inevitability. The verse "Even across hundreds of aeons..." is a well-known canonical gāthā that appears in several Vinaya and Āgama sources; it is here rendered as verse consistent with its formulaic status.

The epithet translated as "Grove of Sages Who Speak Truth" renders a Tibetan gloss of the standard Isipatana (Pāli) or Ṛṣivadana (Sanskrit), the deer park at Vārāṇasī. The Tibetan phrase here is a semantic rendering rather than the usual transliteration.

The phrase rendered "maternal uncles" (Tibetan zhangpo) is a specific kinship term; it may refer more broadly to senior male relatives on the mother's side. The precise social relationship is not entirely clear from context, but "maternal uncles" is the most natural reading. The name rendered as "Sudarśanā" continues from the preceding passage. The Tibetan "བཟང་མོ" (literally "the good/beautiful one") is used throughout as her name or epithet; it corresponds to Sudarśanā established in the prior context, and is here rendered consistently as such.

The wife's name "འོད་བཟང་མ" literally means "she of beautiful light" and is here rendered as "Prabhāvatī" with the Tibetan gloss provided in parentheses for listener clarity, as this is her first named introduction.

The phrase "teaches the Dharma by body, not by word" is a standard formula for pratyekabuddhas in canonical Vinaya narrative literature, indicating they demonstrate the Dharma through miraculous displays rather than verbal exposition. The phrase rendered as "dangerous and treacherous resting place" translates གདུག་པ་མང་པོ་ཅན་གྱི་གནས་མལ, literally "a resting place with many harmful things," which in the Vinaya context refers to a place of moral and physical danger, particularly where improper conduct could occur or be alleged. The term གདུག་པ is broader than "dangerous" alone, encompassing malice, harm, and treachery.

The disease name འབྲས ("the fruit of wrong food and conduct") is a Tibetan rendering of a condition associated with dietary or behavioral impropriety; the precise Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain in this context. The proper name rendered "Viśākhā" appears in the Tibetan as "རྒྱལ་རིགས་དབྱར་ཚུལ་མ," which is an unusual formulation; the identification with Viśākhā (a famous lay devotee at Śrāvastī) is plausible from context and parallel Vinaya accounts, though the Tibetan phrase is not a standard rendering of that name. Similarly, "ཕྱ་མཁན་དྲང་སྲོང་བྱིན" is rendered as "the brahmin ascetic Dīrghanakha," which is a conjecture based on context; the Tibetan may refer to a different figure. The name "རི་དགས་འཛིན་གྱི་མ་ས་ག" is rendered as "the mother of Mṛgāra," following the well-known identification of Viśākhā as "Mṛgāramātā," though the Tibetan phrasing suggests this may be a distinct person listed alongside her. The passage about "those with black bowls" is an idiomatic reference to non-Buddhist wanderers who carried black begging bowls, distinguishing them from Buddhist monks. The Venerable Ānanda worries this green-haired being might fall into their hands rather than be properly ordained in the Dharma. This is a standard narrative motif in Vinaya literature.

The phrase rendered "deer do not feed deer" is a proverbial expression meaning that fellow monastics are not obliged to support one another materially; each monk must sustain himself through his own alms-round.

The "Group of Six monks" are a notorious group repeatedly referenced in Vinaya literature as exemplars of misconduct, whose bad behavior prompts the Buddha to establish new rules of discipline. The verse catalogue of physical disqualifications for ordination is a standard Vinaya list; the renderings of anatomical and pathological terms follow the most defensible readings, though several Tibetan terms for specific conditions (notably མཛེ་, འབྲས་, ཕོལ་མིག་, གཏའ་གམ་, ཤུ་བ་, གྱེན་པ་) admit some latitude in precise medical identification. The rendering of ཤ་མདོག་ཁ་དོག་བཞི་པ as "the fourth colour" reflects the Vinaya tradition of four recognized skin tones, with the fourth being an inauspicious or aberrant hue; this is left deliberately literal as the precise referent is a matter of commentarial tradition. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the source text breaks off. The passage contains a Vinaya narrative in mixed verse and prose typical of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. The term rendered "kept woman" translates སྐྱོང་བ, meaning a woman maintained as a concubine or ward; "pledged woman" translates གཏའ་གམ, a woman given as a surety or pledge. The term སྲིན་བུ་རི rendered "a mountain of worms" in the summary verse is cryptic and likely refers to a case-narrative heading in the original compendium; its precise referent is uncertain. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, so the translation ends correspondingly. The six teachers named here are the classical "six heterodox teachers" (Skt. ṣaṭ śāstāraḥ) of the Pāli and Sanskrit Buddhist tradition: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośāla (here "son of the dark-roaming god Kāḷa" renders ཀུན་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་གནག་ལྷས་ཀྱི་བུ, a somewhat literal Tibetan rendering of Maskarin Gośāla's name and epithet), Sañjaya Vairatīputra ( སྨྲ་འདོད་ཀྱི་བུ་མོའི་བུ་ཡང་དག་རྒྱལ་བ་ཅན), Ajita Keśakambala (མི་ཕམ་སྐྲའི་ལ་བ་ཅན), Kakuda Kātyāyana (ཀ་ཏྱའི་བུ་ནོག་ཅན), and Nirgrantha Jñātaputra (གཉེན་གྱི་བུ་གཅེར་བུ་པ, rendered as "Nirgrantha's son" — Nirgrantha Jñātaputra, i.e., Mahāvīra). The Tibetan epithets are literal translations of the names as found in Pāli and Sanskrit sources. The epithet "Bimbisāra the artisan — Śreṇya" renders the Tibetan "bzo sbyaṅs gzugs can sñiṅ po," which is a Tibetan transcription-rendering of the king's name and epithets. "Gzugs can sñiṅ po" is Bimbisāra and "bzo sbyaṅs" corresponds to Śreṇya or Seniya, a well-known epithet of the Magadhan king; some editions differ in the ordering.

The phrase rendered "the Nirgrantha's son" at the opening corresponds to the series of six non-Buddhist teachers being impersonated; this continues the list from the preceding passage. The Tibetan reads "gcer bu pa gñen gyi bu," meaning the son of the Nirgrantha (i.e., the naked ascetic Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's tradition), consistent with the continuation of the earlier list. The term rendered "bystander" or "one who stands apart" for གཟུ་བོ་ལྟ་བུ་ translates a Tibetan expression meaning something like "one who watches from the sidelines" or "an uninvolved onlooker" — the implication being that Prasenajit, unlike the partisan Bimbisāra, might be a more neutral or susceptible audience for their challenge. The precise nuance is contextually inferred. The phrase rendered "confess wrongdoing and be purified of it" translates a terse construction meaning literally "accumulate evil deeds and then acknowledge them" — the classical idiom for formal confession leading to purification, which is the standard doctrinal sense here.

The "empowerment as regents" renders a phrase in which hearers who have accumulated wholesome roots are given a kind of authorization or investiture to act as stand-ins or deputies of the buddha; this is a specific technical concept within the sūtra's own framing and the rendering follows the literal sense while preserving the doctrinal strangeness.

"Kuśa" as the city name is what the Tibetan spells; this may correspond to another city name in a Sanskrit Vorlage, but the Tibetan is consistent and is rendered as given. The name "Nagnaja" is a reconstructed Sanskrit equivalent of the Tibetan "na gu" (likely གཞོན་ནུ་ན་གུ), which may mean "the naked-born" or similar. The Tibetan is not entirely transparent here and the exact identity of this prince is uncertain.

The phrase rendered "the great lake Anavatapta" corresponds to མཚོ་ཆེན་པོ་མ་དྲོས་པ, a legendary lake in the Himalayas associated in Buddhist cosmology with cool, pure waters and inhabited by the nāga king Anavatapta. The compound "Anavatapta" is not spelled out in Tibetan but is the standard Sanskrit identification. The passage contains a formal "truth declaration" or act of truth, a well-attested Indian literary and religious device in which a solemn assertion of a known truth is held to have miraculous efficacy. The Tibetan term rendered here as "truth declaration" is bden pa'i tshig, literally "words of truth." The Blessed One's injunction constitutes a hierarchical enumeration of the Three Jewels and their respective supremacies as the content of the declaration. The phrase rendered "the noble Vinaya in which the noble ones delight" translates 'phags pa dgyes pa'i tshul khrims, a slightly unusual formulation; it refers to the monastic code as cherished or rejoiced in by the noble ones, functioning here as the supreme among those who abide in ethical conduct. The name of the grove formed from the prince's story presents a minor textual-etymological point. The Tibetan reads "Khaṇḍa-Ānandavana" — a grove named after the episode of the scattered and rejoined limbs, rendered here as "Grove of Rejoining" to make the origin of the name clear to a listening audience. The name is given twice in the Tibetan, likely a scribal repetition.

The stone or gem rendered "andara crystal" is uncertain; it appears to be a transliteration of a Sanskrit gem-name not easily identified; this rendering is provisional. The passage identifies the one who conjures the mango tree as "Cullapanthaka of the Jeta Grove" — the Tibetan reads "dum bu'i kun dga' ra ba pa," literally "the one of the joyful grove of the grove." This is a somewhat compressed epithet; the figure is likely Cullapanthaka (Cūḍapanthaka), a disciple associated with the Jeta Grove, though the precise referent of this name-form in the Tibetan merits verification against the Sanskrit or Chinese parallel. The householder rendered as Anāthapiṇḍika corresponds to the Tibetan "ngan legs sbyin," which is a standard Tibetan rendering of that name. The names Vimalā, Yārtsulma, Jyin, Nyingpa, and Migdak Dré'i Masa are Tibetan phonetic renderings of Indian names that are difficult to identify with certainty from the Tibetan alone; they are rendered here as transliterations of their Tibetan forms. Anāthapiṇḍada is the standard Sanskrit restoration of the householder whose name literally means "giver of food to the destitute," well attested in the sources.

The kurandaka and kunda are flowering plants and the campaka a fragrant tree, all well known in Sanskrit literary and Buddhist contexts as symbols of beauty and purity.

The final sentence of the passage is syntactically incomplete in the source, ending in a list of qualifiers without a main verb; the translation renders it accordingly, leaving it open as the passage does. The phrase "the fifth part of the wheel of saṃsāra — its moving and its still" renders a condensed technical expression referring to the five constituents or sections of saṃsāric existence, described through the pair of moving and unmoving phenomena. The precise doctrinal referent is somewhat unusual and may reflect a specific Vinaya or Abhidharma enumeration that the commentarial tradition would clarify; the rendering follows the literal Tibetan closely. The laywoman's name is left in transliterated Tibetan as it appears in the source; a Sanskrit equivalent is not established from context alone. The names of the novice monk and novice nun rendered here are Kulabhadra and Amogha, the expected Sanskrit behind the Tibetan སྐུལ་བྱེད and བརྗེད་མེད respectively. The exact Sanskrit equivalents of these two minor figures' names involve some uncertainty, as the Tibetan renderings are functional epithets rather than straightforward phonetic transcriptions. This is noted but does not affect the doctrinal content. The phrase rendered "the thirty-second fascicle of the Minor Bases of Discipline" is a section colophon within the Vinaya text (Kṣudrakavastu) marking the end of a bam-po (fascicle) division; it interrupts the narrative but is part of the canonical text as preserved and is therefore included.

The "twin miracle" (Tibetan: zung gi cho 'phrul) is the classical Buddhist miracle in which fire and water issue simultaneously from different parts of the body, traditionally associated with the Śrāvastī miracle of the Buddha. The fourfold deportment display within the sky (walking, standing, sitting, lying) preceding the twin miracle is also a standard element of this narrative.

The word rendered "worldly intention" versus "supramundane intention" translates 'jig rten pa'i thugs bskyed pa and 'jig rten las 'das pa'i thugs bskyed pa respectively. The doctrinal point is that a buddha's ordinary or accessible mental acts can be perceived even by insects through the buddha's mind-radiance, whereas his transcendent, supramundane cognitive acts surpass even the comprehension of arhats. The verse rendering "logicians" for རྟོག་གེ་ཅན translates a term meaning those who rely on logical reasoning or speculation, often used to refer to Brahmanical or non-Buddhist dialecticians, whose intellectual light is shown to be eclipsed by the Buddha's appearance — a classic polemical image.

The phrase འདམ་བུའི་ཁྱིམ་ལ་གླང་ཆེན་བཞིན translates as "like a great elephant at a house of reeds," which is a standard simile for unstoppable, crushing force — the elephant effortlessly demolishing the fragile dwelling. The chain of passing the challenge — Pūraṇa Kassapa to Kṛṣṇadeva's son to Vijayaputra and so on — follows a well-known sequence of the six non-Buddhist teachers (the ṣaṭ-śāstṛs) of the Buddha's era. The Tibetan names are rendered as close phonetic equivalents of their standard Sanskrit identifications: Pūraṇa Kassapa, Ajita Keśakambala's disciple, Kātyāyanī's son (Pakudha Kaccāyana), and the naked ascetic Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's disciple. The precise one-to-one mapping in this particular list is slightly irregular compared to the canonical six, so the identifications follow the Tibetan as given rather than forcing a canonical list. The term rendered "eunuch" translates མ་ནིང (ma ning), a person of indeterminate or third gender in Indian classificatory thought; "eunuch" is the traditional Tibetan Buddhist commentarial rendering, though some scholars prefer "hermaphrodite" or "third-gender person." The choice here follows classical usage without interrupting the text.

The verse exchange is a rare dramatic interlude; the identity of the young woman in the second exchange is left ambiguous in the Tibetan, likely a female renunciant or ascetic given her Dharma robe. The epithet rendered "King Vaishravana" translates the Tibetan rgyal po rnam thos bu, which is the standard Tibetan for Vaiśravaṇa, one of the four great guardian kings, associated with the north, wealth, and yakṣas. The verse's meaning is essentially: "Such a person deserves to be executed by Vaiśravaṇa's soldiers." The crossbow rendering follows the Tibetan steu ka, a small bow or crossbow used for executing criminals in some Indian and Central Asian traditions.

The phrase "completing vessel" renders rdzogs byed bum pa, a vessel used in a ritual of completion or death — filled with sand and tied around the neck as a means of weighted drowning. This is consistent with the narrative context of mass suicide by drowning. The phrase rendered "means of succession" or "means of kingship" translates a term that in context refers to the formal investiture or regency authority granted to a prince or heir — the political mechanism by which a nephew would be made heir apparent or regent. The repeated construction is intentional in the source and has been rendered consistently throughout. The name "Rgyal-srid-la-Mngon-par-dga'-ba" is rendered in its full translated form throughout ("Rejoicing-in-the-Royal-Throne") as a story-name whose meaning is plot-significant. The names "Skyed-pa" (the ruling king) and the framing "king beneath the sun" are preserved consistently with the preceding passage. The phrase "king beneath the sun" renders Tibetan "ཉི་འོག་གི་རྒྱལ་པོ" literally; this is a royal title, possibly meaning a subordinate king or a king of a southern realm — the exact geographical or political referent is not certain, but the translation follows the established rendering from the preceding passage. The verse at the close is a gāthā of lament; the third line's "bare ground" renders "ས་སྟེང་ཐང་བུ་ལ," literally "on the flat plain of the earth-surface," which in context conveys the contrast between the royal bed and destitute wandering. The name "Bzabtung" (spelled bza' btung in Tibetan, literally "food and drink") is a narrative proper name used consistently in this text. It is kept as a phonetic rendering throughout for consistency with the preceding passage's conventions.

The phrase rendered "the lord of men follows the way of his kind" translates mi dbang rigs rjes 'gro ba'i rtags yin no — literally "it is the sign that the sovereign of men goes following his lineage/nature," meaning that even the mightiest of men are subject to the alternation of fortune. This is the young man's philosophical consolation to his mother.

The passage ends mid-sentence with "the king of the five territories reflected —" because the Tibetan breaks off at that point, clearly continuing in the next section. The phrase rendered "the one who had rejoiced in royal sovereignty" refers to the king of the five territories mentioned in the preceding passage, who delighted in his kingship and is now said to have died without an heir, extinguishing the royal line. The Tibetan is somewhat elliptical here, but context makes this the only coherent reading.

The idiom "sounding out the mother's own feelings" translates a compressed Tibetan phrase about taking the warmth of the mother's sentiment — a colloquial expression for gauging how someone truly feels before acting. The names Bha-tung and Bha-tung Mangpo appear to be transcriptions of indigenous (likely non-Sanskrit, possibly Old Tibetan or regional) names meaning something like "Eater" and "Great Eater" or "Much-Eater." The text itself plays on this etymology when it says the prior name "ceased to exist" in favour of the coronation epithet. I have rendered them as proper names throughout rather than translating the apparent folk-etymology, since the text treats them as names. The epithet "Vaiśravaṇa's son" in the verse addressed to Gangpo is puzzling, as Gangpo is a village headman, not Vaiśravaṇa. The Tibetan reads "rnam thos bu," literally "son of Vaiśravaṇa." This may be a form of address meaning something like "dear fortunate one" or could reflect an honorific convention, or it may be a textual peculiarity. It is rendered literally here. The term "ཆུ་སྐྱར" is rendered "water-bird" as a general term; "ཆུ་སྲེགས" is rendered "crane," and "ངང་མོ" as "goose," though the precise species identification of these birds is uncertain. The phrase rendered "arrow reversed at the brahmin's wife" translates a Tibetan expression of public shaming or mockery whose precise idiomatic force is not entirely recoverable from context alone. It appears to be a taunt directed at the brahmin for his humiliation, possibly invoking a proverbial image; the rendering preserves its function as a cry of ridicule without overstating its literal content. The term rendered "flatbread" is dar ba, literally thin or flat cake. The list of foods here differs from the rogue's list in the preceding passage, which is the narrative's point: the brahmin's vomit confirms his account and the rogue's lie. The phrase "buried up to his neck" renders the idiom mgrin pa man chad dong du bcug, literally "placed into the pit from the throat downward." The name Pūrṇakacchana appears to designate both a person (the headman Pūrṇa) and the locality named after him; this double reference is present in the Tibetan and is preserved here. The term rendered "hermaphrodite" is ma ning, which in Buddhist canonical literature designates a third-gender category (Sanskrit paṇḍaka or napuṃsaka). The precise meaning is debated in the tradition, but "hermaphrodite" or "person of indeterminate sex" best captures the contextual logic here, namely someone who is neither male nor female and can therefore satisfy the king's impossible condition.

The king is referred to throughout as rgyal po skyed pa, literally "King who begets" or "the procreating king," which is a Tibetan rendering of Ajātaśatru ("unborn enemy"), the well-known king of Magadha. The name is given in its Tibetan descriptive paraphrase rather than transliterated; I have supplied "Ajātaśatru" for clarity at the one point where his identity as king becomes salient. The name rendered throughout as "Jīvaka" corresponds to the Tibetan "Gang po," which in this narrative context appears to be Jīvaka the father (the elder physician figure), while "the great physician" (sman chen po) refers to the young Jīvaka, his son. The text consistently distinguishes these two figures, and the translation preserves this distinction. The plant identified as "a-ra-nd-a" (Tibetan transliteration of Sanskrit araṇḍa) is the castor-oil plant (Ricinus communis), which is indeed known in Indian botanical and medical literature for producing flowers and fruit within a single year. The names Gaṅgapa (gang po, literally "the full one" or a proper name), Pūrṇakaccha, and Prasenajit (rgyal po skyed pa) are rendered from context and standard identification; Prasenajit is the well-known king of Kosala, though the Tibetan here uses an unusual epithet form. Vāsava is an epithet of Indra; "gods of rest" renders ngal bso po, a deity type associated with repose or comfort, not a fully standard term — the rendering is approximate. The verse functions as a colophon-summary listing the episodes of the tale in sequence. The term rendered "clifftop village" translates a compound meaning literally "a village of cliffs and crags," likely a specific named settlement in the story's geography. The phrase rendered "humiliation" and then reinterpreted as "homage" plays on a deliberate ambiguity in the Tibetan (མཐོ་བཙམ་པ), meaning something like "putting on a level above," which can read as either demotion/mockery or exaltation depending on context — this wordplay is the pivot of the physician's argument, and is preserved as best the English allows. The name rendered as "Karṇabhadra" translates the Tibetan "rna bo che" literally as "great ear" or "large ear," but in context it functions as a personal name. The Sanskrit equivalent Karṇabhadra is a reasonable reconstruction, though the text may simply be using the Tibetan loan-translation of a Sanskrit name; this does not affect the narrative meaning. The phrase rendered "the god Indra" translates "lha dbang phyug" which is a Tibetan epithet for Śakra or Indra; this is the first occurrence and is glossed accordingly. The passage about "the brahmin woman" serving is slightly ambiguous in the Tibetan — it could mean the brahmin's wife is to serve the guests, with the observer watching her behavior toward the male brahmin guests; this reading has been adopted as the most contextually coherent one. The name rendered "Raṇabadra" represents a Tibetan transcription of a Sanskrit name and is kept in that form for consistency; the orthography of the Tibetan spelling (རྣ་བོ་ཆེ) is, however, the ordinary word for "earring," and this has created an intentional wordplay in the narrative — the man's name and the recovered object are both referred to by the same Tibetan term. The translation differentiates them by context: "Raṇabadra" as the person and "earring" as the object. This is a genuine textual ambiguity worth noting. The name "Pūrṇakaccha" and "Gaṅgapa" are phonetic renderings from the Tibetan; the Sanskrit forms of the place-name and personal name may vary in other witnesses. The phrase rendered "the king who had engendered the realm" translates རྒྱལ་པོ་སྐྱེད་པ, which is slightly ambiguous — it may mean "the king who fathered him" (i.e., the minister's father, the king) or "the king who generated/produced the realm"; context suggests it refers to the reigning king who has been reduced to powerlessness, and "engendered" is used in the sense of one who established or originated his royal line. The passage about "keeping you in the womb" is a striking idiom implying that the minister was raised and sustained by the king precisely for this destined purpose. The proper name Skyedpa appears throughout as the king's name and is retained in transliteration as it was established in the preceding passage. The social title rendered "maternal uncle" for the Tibetan term ming po reflects the specific kinship term rather than the more generic "uncle," as the maternal uncle holds a distinct and honored role in Tibetan social structure — the comparison here carries a specific warmth of that relationship. The phrase "fourfold military strength" renders the standard classical Indian and Tibetan military division of forces into elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry, though the text does not enumerate them explicitly. The name rendered "Mongtul" follows the Tibetan transliteration; the Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain. The term "karavīra" (Tibetan: shing ka ra bī ra) refers to the oleander plant (Nerium oleander), whose flowers were used in executions or shaming processions in Indian custom. The passage shifts mid-section into a standard Vinaya colophon marking the thirty-fourth fascicle of the Kṣudraka-vastu, and the narrative then continues without a new heading. The final dialogue about "a king becomes no true friend" is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan; the Great Minister appears to be explaining to the executioners that his verse was not about the present king personally but about the general truth that kings cannot be relied upon as lasting friends — and that his hearers had missed this meaning. The term rendered "candāla" glosses the Tibetan གདོལ་པ, which denotes the lowest caste group in the Indian social hierarchy; the text plays on the social stigma attached to this group in its proverb. The phrase ལུས་འཕགས་པའི་ལྗོངས (literally "the noble land of the body") is rendered as "the noble land of Āryāvarta," which is the conventional Sanskrit referent for this Tibetan circumlocution meaning the land of the noble ones or Āryāvarta, the heartland of brahminical India. There is some ambiguity as to whether this is a proper place name or a descriptor; given the brahmin context, Āryāvarta is the most plausible reading. The name "Sa-ga" renders the Tibetan sa ga, left untranslated as it functions as a proper name throughout the narrative. It may carry the sense of "earth" or "ground," but the text treats it purely as a personal name.

The phrase rendered "forest of grain" translates zan gyi nags, literally "forest of cooked food" or "forest of provisions." The verse appears to speak in riddle-form, consistent with Sa-ga's character as a girl who speaks in enigmatic verses, so the translation preserves the oblique quality.

The verse "One who wears no woven woolen cloth / who wears unwoven, unspun cloth" likely refers to Sa-ga having removed her clothing and sitting unclad by the pond, described just before — she is "wearing" nothing woven, only unspun skin, so to speak. This is consistent with her testing him with riddles. The phrase rendered "the house of the one who causes the body to flourish" translates a technical or idiomatic expression for a physician or perhaps a ritual officiant who oversees a coming-of-age or marital rite; the exact referent is contextually uncertain but most likely a wedding officiant or a physician-host. The barley and deer-skin episode is part of an elaborate comic-didactic folk narrative involving double entendre; the translation preserves the surface level of the literal text without suppressing the evident allegorical undercurrent, which is standard for this genre. The phrase "tucked the full measure of barley into the hem of his garment" renders a carrying gesture implied by the Tibetan. The identity of the new brahmin who arrives from another village and the brahmin woman appear to form a subplot; the narrative shifts of subject are somewhat compressed in the Tibetan and have been resolved as clearly as the grammar allows. The name "Sāgā" is a transliteration of the Tibetan "ས་ག," which functions here as a proper name. Its identity and etymology within the larger narrative are unclear from this passage alone, but it has been rendered consistently as a proper name throughout.

The verse passage presents a slightly condensed legal idiom: the meaning is that if the full four-hundred-coin share is not delivered intact, a punitive measure (the wooden skewer) will be applied. The rendering follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan.

The epithet "king who nourishes the Noble Ones" renders "རྒྱལ་པོ་སྐྱེད་པ," a title that recurs in the narrative; it may refer to a specific royal figure whose name has not yet been made explicit in the translated portions. The place name Lus 'phags pa'i ljongs is the Tibetan rendering of Uttarakuru, the northern continent in traditional Buddhist cosmology. It is here functioning simply as a geographic setting rather than a cosmological symbol, so it has been rendered with its Tibetan pronunciation alongside the standard identification.

The figure Gyopo (Gyos po) is the hunter-father of Sāgā introduced in the preceding passage; the name is retained as established there.

The phrase rendered "from the opening of proceedings until the sun set" translates a passage describing the formal legal session (literally "from the spreading of the mat/carpet") lasting until sunset without resolution — a standard narrative idiom for an intractable legal dispute before a king. The phrase rendered "a merchant from the northern regions" translates byang phyogs kyi tshong pa, literally "a merchant of the northern direction." The two birds are rgod ma, wild geese or possibly adjutant birds; "wild geese" is adopted as a reasonable rendering consistent with the narrative register.

The passage "yong rgyal po go blon po" is syntactically awkward in the Tibetan and may reflect a minor scribal irregularity; it has been read as "a minister of a great and learned king," which suits the context of Sagā's mild reproach. The term rendered "physician" throughout is སྨན་ཆེན་པོ, literally "the great physician" or "great doctor," and in context it appears to be a title for one of the ministers rather than a separate character; the narrative logic suggests these six ministers collectively approached Sagā, and "the great physician" is the one who is impersonated by the wooden effigy. The final sentence breaks off mid-narrative, matching the source text's abrupt ending at that point. The verse summary near the middle of the passage is a mnemonic colophon recapping story elements: the udumbara flower is a standard Buddhist image for something rarely or illusorily seen. The term rendered "necklace" for སེ་མོ་དོ is an ornament-type; "mynah bird" for ནེ་ཙོ follows standard identification of this bird in classical Tibetan narrative contexts.

The name ལྔ་ལེན (Ngalen) is a kingdom name kept in transliteration throughout for consistency. རྒྱལ་པོ་སྐྱེད་པ (king Skyedpa) likewise. The passage contains two bird characters whose conversation serves as an intelligence-gathering device: the parakeet Caryāprakāśa (Tibetan: spyod gsal, "Conduct-Illuminating") acts as the spy sent by the physician to Ngalen's court. The name "Lnalen" in the verse is a reconstructed form of the kingdom name Ngalen as it appears in the story context; the verse seems to present a hypothetical rumor scenario used to test the mynah's knowledge of the true situation.

The foods mentioned — "finest honey" (sbrang rtsi'i mchog), "sorrow-free sweets" (mya ngan med sgyur), fried puffed grain (phe'u te'u), and sugar-based dishes — are rendered as best as the context allows; some of these food names may be playful or archaic terms whose exact referents are uncertain, though the doctrinal content is unaffected. The name "Smanchen" (blon po sman chen po) is a title meaning "the great minister" or "chief minister" rendered throughout the preceding translation as a proper name for consistency; it is in origin an honorific title. The passage's narrative logic concerning the five hundred ministers — who are simultaneously said to be suborned by gifts, then reported killed — reflects a condensed court-intrigue sequence that is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan; the translation follows the text as given without smoothing. The name "Lnalen" for the opposing king's realm is carried over from the preceding passage per the continuity instruction. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end of the source text, so the translation likewise ends there. The bird's name, rendered here as "Chösal," is a Tibetan phonetic rendering of the bird's human-language name; it is best understood as a myna bird capable of speech, a common motif in Indian story literature. The text's reference to "Lnalen" preserves the name as established in the preceding passage. The verse translated "The doer is repaid in kind — look back, and the scorned one scorns in turn. Here it was one alone, a despised one, who swept out every last queen perfectly" is metrically and syntactically compressed in the original. The word rendered "swept out" or "expelled" is from a root meaning to clean or clear out, playing on the earlier temple-cleaning scene; the verse is intentionally ironic and the rendering preserves that tone as best the English allows. The phrase rendered as "the eighteen branches of the fields of knowledge" translates a standard Sanskrit scholastic category, vidyāsthāna, here listed as eighteen, which is an unusually expanded enumeration; the standard count is eighteen limbs of the Vedas or the traditional four or ten fields of knowledge. This may reflect a specific regional or textual tradition, and the number eighteen here most likely refers to the eighteen auxiliary sciences or the limbs of the Vedas as counted in certain Brahmanical curricula. The translation follows the Tibetan literally without imposing a fixed Sanskrit equivalent.

The floating stone is likely a pumice stone, used here as a proof of wit — the Great Physician knew it would float, while others assumed all stones sink. This is not marked in the text but is the natural reading. The phrase rendered "like a lizard, to starve unfed" translates a Tibetan expression that compares the woman's situation to a reptile left to go hungry; the comparison is idiomatic and the precise nuance is somewhat colloquial, but the gist is clear from context.

The "eighteen inauspicious signs" is a standard enumeration in classical Indian literature of physical marks considered ill-omened; the text treats this as a well-known category requiring no elaboration. The rendering of "ཨུག་ཤུད་བརྒྱ་ཞིང་འདུག་གོ" is genuinely uncertain. The phrase literally suggests something like rocking or swaying together a hundredfold in close physical proximity, most likely an idiom for intimate embrace or amorous sport. This rendering is interpretive.

The opening paragraph of this passage is somewhat ambiguous in the Tibetan, as it appears to re-narrate events already described in the preceding passage from a slightly different angle before moving into the verse retelling. This structural feature, common in Buddhist narrative literature, is preserved rather than smoothed over. The verse section at the opening is deeply elliptical and fragmentary in character, resembling riddle-speech exchanged between estranged spouses who allude to shared memories. Several lines resist transparent syntax. The rendering follows the most contextually plausible reading of each line, taking the recurring motifs — the udumbara tree, the Gaṅgā, the carpenter and stone, the brahmin woman, the owl, the mountain, poison, unripe and ripe fruit, harsh words — as allusive references to events in the earlier narrative. Readers should be aware that a fully literal rendering of some lines would be nearly unintelligible, and some editorial reconstruction of sense has been necessary.

The name "King Prasenajit" (Skt. Prasenajit) is inferred from context as the king in question; the Tibetan uses only "རྒྱལ་པོ་སྐྱེད་པ" (lit. "King Prasenajit"), consistent with the Prasenajit narrative cycle in which this story appears. The verse spoken by the brahmin as he leads away the servant woman is metrically and lexically somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The rendering preserves the rhetorical pattern of the original: each line plays on pairing by social rank or appearance, culminating in the brahmin's self-deprecating identification with a demon as a way of addressing the servant. The final two lines shift into a kind of invitation or declaration of mutual joy, consistent with the comic and somewhat ribald tone of the episode.

The phrase rendered "bound to the pillory" translates a term meaning literally "bound to the wood," which in the context of Vinaya narratives refers to being fastened to a wooden restraint or stocks rather than crucifixion; this is the standard reading in such contexts.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, indicating this is a continuous excerpt. The term translated as "great physician" renders སྨན་ཆེན་པོ literally; in context this clearly refers to a man who is a physician of great repute, not a physician named "Great Physician," though the Tibetan could in principle be a title. The narrative logic supports reading it as an occupational descriptor rather than a proper name. The name "Mātarā" renders the Tibetan "ne tso ma ta ra," which appears to be a female servant's name. The exact Sanskrit form is uncertain, but it is treated here as a proper name throughout, consistent with the preceding rendering convention.

The phrase rendered "ate together from one vessel" follows the Tibetan idiom of communal eating as a seal of sworn brotherhood or conspiracy. The pārijāta (Skt. pārijāta) and kovidāra (Skt. kovidāra) are trees found in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three; the pārijāta is the great divine coral tree associated with that realm. The Tibetan "la ba rdo dkar" rendered as "white stone slope" is a topographical descriptor qualifying the location near these trees; it may alternatively refer to a specific place-name, but the rendering given is the most natural reading of the Tibetan.

The phrase rendered "cut off the arising of gain and honour" follows the Tibetan idiom of the Blessed One withdrawing to diminish the excessive reverence and material offerings that had been accumulating. The passage mentions the Pāṇḍukambala rock and the Pārijāta and Kovidaraka trees, which are well-known features of the traditional heaven of the Thirty-Three (Trāyastriṃśa). The Blessed One is here said to be teaching Dharma to his mother, an episode widely attested across Pāli and Sanskrit sources, referring to the tradition that after his awakening the Buddha ascended to Trāyastriṃśa to preach to his mother Māyā (reborn there). The health-inquiry formula rendered here is a standard Indian epistolary convention found throughout the canon. The simile at the passage's end — extending a drawn-in arm — is a classical canonical formula for the speed of supernatural travel; the passage breaks off mid-simile. The Pārijāta and Kovidaraka are well-known divine trees of the heaven of the Thirty-Three. The Pārijāta is the celebrated coral tree of that realm; the Kovidaraka is a related flowering tree. Both names are transliterated from Sanskrit via Tibetan phonetic rendering.

The phrase rendered "knowledge of and faith in the Buddha" translates a compound meaning discernment or recognition of the Buddha together with faith; the Tibetan "sangs rgyas shes shing dad pa dang ldan pa" carries both cognitive and devotional senses, and both are intended.

The passage ends mid-sentence as the text breaks off; the final line is a fragment in which additional gods begin individually to declare their own grounds of rebirth in the divine realm. The place name "Apaṇajarī" renders the Tibetan "ཨ་པ་ཛ་རི" as a phonetic transcription of what is likely a Sanskrit toponym associated with Sāṃkāśya (the traditional site of the Buddha's descent from Tuṣita — here rendered as the Thirty-Three Gods' realm, which is Trāyastriṃśa). The pairing with the udumbara tree is a well-known motif at Sāṃkāśya. The exact Sanskrit form of "Apaṇajarī" is not fully certain from this transcription alone.

The passage states the Blessed One taught the Dharma in the Yāma heavens on his way down — this downward sequence through the divine realms is a standard narrative element of the Sāṃkāśya descent story found in Vinaya and other sources. The sequence of heavenly realms listed here follows the standard Abhidharma cosmology of the form realm: the three Brahmic heavens, three radiance heavens, three virtue heavens, and the five Pure Abodes capped by Akaniṣṭha, which the Blessed One visits in descending reverse order. The text's unusual feature of having him descend from Akaniṣṭha downward through the realms — rather than simply descending from the Thirty-Three — is preserved faithfully.

The name "Sarvārthasiddha" (lhas bcu cad dang ldan pa, literally "endowed with all purposes" or "accomplishing all aims") is the same name as Siddhārtha in its fuller form; here it refers to a divine youth in the assembly, not the bodhisattva who became the Buddha.

The phrase rendered "vomit warm blood and die on the spot" reflects a classical Indian literary idiom for death from overwhelming shock or overpowering splendor, attested in other sūtra contexts. The Tibetan reads "ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་འཆར་ཀ" at the passage where the retort about the nun's identity is made. "འཆར་ཀ" is a phonetic rendering of Śāriputra in some Tibetan sources. The passage unambiguously identifies this figure by his recognizing the scent of the blue lotus — a detail attributed to Śāriputra in parallel versions of this narrative. The translation renders accordingly.

The phrase "བློན་པོ་སྟོབས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ས་ཡ་ཕྲག་བདུན་བཅུ་རྩ་དགུ" is parsed as seventy-nine hundred-thousands (i.e., 7,900,000) ministers of supreme strength, a common hyperbolic retinue number in such narrative contexts. The sequence of spiritual fruits listed — stream-entry, non-return, once-return, arhatship — follows a slightly non-standard order in the Tibetan (stream-entry, non-return, once-return rather than the canonical ascending order: stream-entry, once-return, non-return, arhatship). The translation preserves the order as it stands in the Tibetan text.

The verse is terse and its syntax somewhat compressed. The rendering given follows the most natural doctrinal reading: that each of the three options in the first three lines is surpassed by the fruit of stream-entry named in the fourth. The term rendered "grounds" in the first line is the Tibetan "sa" (bhūmi), which here likely refers to stages or levels of spiritual attainment rather than the bodhisattva grounds specifically.

The city name "Camkarmojik" is a transliteration of the Tibetan འཁོར་མོ་འཇིག; its Sanskrit original, if any, is uncertain. The island name rendered here as "Kāśeru" (Tibetan: གླིང་ཀཱ་ཤེ་རུར) is uncertain. It may refer to a legendary island in the narrative geography of this jātaka cycle; no confident Sanskrit reconstruction is possible without further witnesses. The bird "གཤོག་བཟངས" literally means "fine-wings" or "good-wings" and is a standard Tibetan rendering of Suparṇa, a name for the mythical bird-king (often identified with Garuḍa). It is rendered here as "the Golden Wing (Suparṇa)" on first use for clarity, though the Tibetan epithet more literally means "fine-winged." The name "Śoṣumā" for ཤོ་ཤུམ་པ is a phonetic reconstruction; the exact Sanskrit is uncertain but this is a plausible reading. The kinnara woman (མི་འམ་ཅི་མོ) is a female being of the kinnara class, half-human and half-animal in Indian mythology; she is rendered simply as "a kinnara woman." The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, so the translation likewise ends there. The two instructions about which string not to touch are textually inconsistent: the first giver says "do not touch the highest string" and the second says "do not touch the lowest string." This appears to be a deliberate narrative detail rather than a scribal error, and is translated as it stands.

The phrase rendered "that wrathful woman" translates "མ་འབར་མ་མོ," literally something like "fire-mother" or "the blazing one / the fierce one" — an epithet applied to the boy's mother, suggesting she has a fierce or dangerous character. The name rendered "Crocodile-Woman" translates ཤོ་ཤུམ་པ, which literally means "she of the crocodile kind" or simply "Crocodile-Woman," a yakṣiṇī or spirit being associated with crocodiles in the narrative context; the precise species intended is uncertain but the crocodile or a similar aquatic creature is the standard understanding in the Vinaya story tradition.

The passage shifts pronoun logic in the final section: the narrative has the woman consorting with a king named Brahmadatta by night and with Swift-Going by day, but the Tibetan syntax is compressed and the question "where do you go at night?" is directed at the woman by someone, most naturally Swift-Going; the translation reflects the most coherent reading. The bird named śārikā is a species of myna or starling-like bird frequently listed in Indian literary and Buddhist narrative contexts alongside the cuckoo (kokilā, here kā ko ki la). "Tīmira" and "kāśeru" are Indian plant names; tīmira is likely a fragrant flowering plant and kāśeru a sedge or similar water-plant, both appearing as loanwords or transcriptions in the Tibetan. The svastika auspicious mark on the thigh is a standard mark of beauty in Indian narrative literature. The term rendered "god-eyes" translates lha mig, literally "divine eyes," referring here not to supernatural vision but to his eyes in an elevated or honorific sense, possibly meaning simply "fine eyes" or "bright eyes" in context — the phrase picks up from the preceding narrative where he was blinded. The river name "Kāradā" is a transliteration of the Tibetan "ཀ་ར་ད་བ་" and its exact Sanskrit or geographical referent is uncertain. It has been retained as a proper noun throughout for consistency.

The final verse breaks off mid-sentence, as the source passage itself ends incompletely with "when someday a snake and a mongoose, both —". This is not a translation error but an artifact of the passage provided. The name "Thāskaryesd" and "Nābso" are rendered phonetically from ཐ་སྐར་སྐྱེས and ནབ་སོ, which appear to be monk names. Their exact Sanskrit equivalents or identification is uncertain. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, reflecting an incomplete source text for this unit.

The river name ཀ་ར་ན་ད་ན is rendered as Karanadana, a phonetic approximation; its Sanskrit form is uncertain. Similarly ཆུ་བོ་བལ་གུ་མ་ཏི is the river Vaṅgumatī, a well-known Vinaya locus.

The phrase ཤ་དུམ་བུ, literally "a piece of meat," is translated straightforwardly; in the Vinaya context this is understood as raw meat given to a fox, consistent with the narrative frame. The four-line verse in the middle of the passage appears to be a colophon or transitional summary verse bridging sections of the Vinaya text. The referent of "the nun who has descended again" is contextually unclear from this passage alone and likely refers to a narrative figure treated in the immediately preceding section.

The list of animal and human contests reflects standard Vinaya proscriptions against monks attending or organizing spectator events and competitions; the term rendered "wool-sheep" follows the literal Tibetan for sheep raised for wool, as distinct from ordinary sheep. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the Tibetan source text itself ends mid-phrase. The continuation would complete the Blessed One's third refusal in the same formulaic terms as the preceding two. This is preserved faithfully rather than completed by conjecture.

The Guñja residence at Nādikā is a known early canonical location; Nādikā (also rendered Nāḍika in some traditions) is the village of that name frequently mentioned in the Pāli parallels. The three similes employed by the Blessed One here, depicting the harmful effects of women's admission to the order, are standard in the Vinaya literature and appear across multiple recensions (Pāli Cullavagga, Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, and others). Their doctrinal and historical significance is well recognised in scholarship; the translation renders them faithfully without softening.

The term "sālu" refers to a specific grain (possibly Oryza sativa or a related variety); it is retained as a proper name since no single transparent English equivalent exists. The phrase rendered "status as a fully ordained person" translates a term literally meaning "the reality or substance of one who has transgressions" — that is, a person who now stands under the Vinaya's rules governing transgressions, which is the technical definition of a fully ordained monastic. This is a technical Vinaya usage: the acceptance of the rules, including liability for downfalls, is itself the conferral of full ordination status upon Gautamī. The phrase rendered "seek the scriptural transmission of the Teacher's instruction" translates a formulation concerning the fortnightly exhortation of nuns by monks — the formal teaching and Vinaya instruction. The three grounds of the invitation ceremony, "what was seen, what was heard, and what was suspected," are the standard Vinaya formulation for the pravāraṇā, preserved here precisely as they appear in the parallel passages of other Vinaya traditions. The phrase rendered "from under the preceptorship" translates the Tibetan term for a nun who has arisen or emerged in dependence on a preceptor-teacher, referring to nuns under the system of the chief rules. The precise procedural force of this phrase in Vinaya context is that such a nun is newly established under the rules rather than fully independent.

The flowers named — campaka, jasmine (varṣikā), and atimuktaka — are standard Indian garland flowers appearing frequently in Sanskrit Vinaya literature; the Tibetan transliterations correspond to these identifications with confidence. The phrase rendered "from this day on" in the second set of training rules contains a reading "ཉི་གཉིས་" which literally could mean "these two days" or "day two," but in context it is best understood as simply "from this very day," consistent with the standard formula; this minor oddity may reflect a scribal variant.

The announcement formula at the end breaks off mid-sentence in the source passage, as the text continues beyond what was provided for translation here. The phrase rendered as "without characteristics, or has ambiguous characteristics, or is hermaphroditic" translates three Tibetan terms referring to canonical categories of physical sex anomalies relevant to monastic ordination validity: one who lacks the defining physical mark, one who has a secondary or double mark, and one who is intersex. These are technical Vinaya categories and the translation follows standard scholarly renderings.

The shadow-measuring ceremony near the end is a classical Vinaya procedure for establishing the precise time of ordination, which must be recorded as part of the valid ordination record. The phrase rendered "six rules and the six rules that accompany them" refers to the śikṣamāṇā (probationary nun) training: six primary rules and six secondary or attendant rules to be kept for two years before full ordination. The distinction between the candidate approaching a "preceptor nun" (mkhan mo) and an "acharya nun" (slob dpon ma) reflects a situation where the acharya serves as intermediary in requesting ordination from the preceptor, which is a recognized procedural variant in the Vinaya for nuns. The phrase rendered "the six rules that accompany them" translates the Tibetan for rules that are ancillary or subordinate to the six main training rules; some editions distinguish these terminologically as "the six rules to be followed in accordance," but "accompanying rules" preserves the sense and parallelism of the text.

The verse section presents the six main rules and six ancillary rules in gāthā form; the translation renders these as verse lines accordingly.

The final sentence breaks off mid-construction in the source passage, corresponding to the continuation of a list of robe items; this is reflected in the translation ending with "upper robe and," which is where the passage ends. The passage distinguishes between a "place of hearing" and a "place of seeing" as the technical Vinaya boundaries governing where the candidate stands during the private examination versus where she is presented to the assembly. This is a standard procedural distinction in Mūlasarvāstivāda ordination texts.

The series of disqualifying conditions — including "not one who bears the banner of a thief," "not one who lives separately," and "not one who does not abide" — are obscure Vinaya technical categories whose precise referents are debated even in the commentarial tradition. The translations given follow the most broadly accepted interpretations. The list of diseases presents several terms whose precise clinical identification is uncertain. The renderings given follow standard Tibetan medical lexical conventions and Vinaya parallels where available, but some remain approximate: "dappled flesh" for ཤ་བཀྲ་ཅན, "aggregative fever" for འདུས་པའི་རིམས, and "fever accompanied by exhaustion and collapse" for རིམས་ལྡང་དུབ་པ are interpretive. The term མཚན་པར་རྡོལ་བ, rendered "nocturnal discharge," refers literally to a condition that erupts or breaks out at night, and may indicate a specific gynaecological condition; the Vinaya context suggests this reading. The phrase rendered "householder of twelve years' standing" refers to a woman who has been married for twelve years, a standard Vinaya qualification for ordination at a younger age than the otherwise required twenty years. The text presents two alternative qualifications: either a married woman of twelve years, or a young woman who has reached age twenty.
