The passage is the interrogation of a candidate for full ordination as a bhikṣuṇī. The list of physical impediments at the end is a standard canonical enumeration; many medical terms in the Tibetan Vinaya correspond to Indian medical categories whose exact Sanskrit equivalents are debated, and the English renderings given here follow the established scholarly consensus for Vinaya translations. The passage breaks off mid-list in the source text, and the translation accurately reflects that the list continues beyond what is given. The passage is a Vinaya ordination ritual formula for the full ordination of a nun from both Saṅghas simultaneously, the dual-Saṅgha ordination procedure characteristic of the bhikṣuṇī ordination rite. The phrase "ཆོས་དྲུག་དང་རྗེས་སུ་འབྲང་བའི་ཆོས་དྲུག" refers to the śikṣamāṇā training: the six qualities to train in and the six attendant or accompanying qualities, a standard twofold set in the probationary nun's preparation, rendered accordingly. The five Dharma-robes and alms bowl are the standard requisites of full ordination. "ཚངས་པར་སྤྱད་པ་སྐྱེད་པའི་སྡོམ་པ" is the vow that gives rise to or produces the celibate holy life, i.e., the śikṣamāṇā vow conferring the basis for ordination. The enumeration of robe-fabrics contains several loanwords from Sanskrit and Indic languages rendered phonetically in Tibetan. "Ami-la," "so-mi-la," "dugulaka" (Skt. dukūla, a fine cloth), and "kotampaka" (Skt. kauṭumbaka or similar) are textile names whose precise identification in the Indian textile tradition is uncertain; they are transcribed as close to the Tibetan phonetic forms as possible. The phrase rendered "dust-heap robes" refers to the ascetic practice of collecting discarded rags from rubbish heaps or cremation grounds. The meal-festival names (fifth, eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth) refer to specific communal feast days in the lunar calendar. The sequence of synonyms for sensual desire — "clinging, attachment, intention, fondness, dwelling, certainty, deep infatuation" — renders a standard Vinaya listing of terms (similar to Pali counterparts such as chanda, rāga, citta, pema, etc.) that appears elsewhere in the canon as an enumeration of the aspects or synonyms of kāma. The translation follows the most natural doctrinal reading of each term in context.

The phrase rendered "without having formally prepared the ground" translates མ་བཤམས་པར, literally "without having arranged/laid out." In Vinaya context this refers to the preparatory act of formally setting aside one's precepts through the proper procedure; it is paired with "without having surrendered her training," yielding the standard dual condition that marks a pārājika offense as distinct from mere lapse. The text closes mid-sentence with the rule on false speech being introduced. This is a continuous Vinaya exposition of the four root downfalls for nuns, running parallel to the monks' pārājika rules. The phrase rendered "one who has come to be in a human body" translates the Tibetan mi'i lus su gyur pa, a standard Vinaya formulation distinguishing a fully human person from a fetus or ambiguous case; I have rendered it literally rather than interpreting it more narrowly, as the commentarial tradition treats it as referring to any being possessing a human form. The monetary unit māśa is left in Sanskrit as it is a technical legal measure in the Vinaya theft rule. The enumeration of the supernatural beings follows Vinaya convention. The term rendered "garuḍas" translates nam mkha' lding, literally "sky-flyers," the standard Tibetan for Skt. garuḍa. The term "flesh-eaters" renders sha za, Skt. rākṣasa or piśāca; "putrefying bodies" renders lus srul po, Skt. vetāla or a related class of corpse-spirit; and "great serpents" renders lto 'phye chen po, Skt. mahoraga. The elaborate list of perceptions near the end of the passage is a standard enumerative sequence from Vinaya literature cataloguing the meditation objects and attainments which an unqualified claimant might falsely assert; the passage breaks off mid-sentence continuing into the next segment. The eight qualities in the passage on the nun who has "become subject to a man" appear to be a reference to a standard Vinaya list of eight characteristics of a woman who has surrendered her will to a man. The Tibetan is technical Vinaya language here and the precise enumeration in this sub-list (body-leaning, signal-setting, pleasure in the man's coming and going, etc.) corresponds to known Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya categories.

The phrase rendered "liberation from both aspects" translates Tibetan phyogs gnyis las rnam par grol ba, likely referring to the liberation that is free from both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, or in some Vinaya contexts the one liberated in both mind and body — a technical term whose precise referent in this Vinaya context warrants attention. The passage contains highly technical Vinaya procedural language governing the formal admonition of a nun who pays improper respect to an expelled monk. The phrases involving lying prostrate with hair unbound and stretching out flat before the Saṅgha are stock Vinaya formulas for prostration protocol; the translation renders them as literally as readability permits. The phrase rendered as "shows readiness to make obeisance" and "prepares to rise" reflect conventional Vinaya sequences of deferential behavior whose precise physical choreography varies across commentarial traditions. The repeated injunction to supply the nun with alms-bowl, robes, strainer, cup, waist-band, reading, recitation, and meditative engagement is a formulaic list of practical supports used as an inducement or assurance within the admonition procedure. The term translated as "chief rules" is gurudharma (the eight "weighty rules" or "rules of respect" for nuns), a standard technical term in Vinaya literature. The passage describes the formal proclamation of each rule within a legal Vinaya act, with the nun's name inserted at each announcement, consistent with the standard Tibetan Vinaya formulaic style. The phrase "instruction that shows them the teaching" renders a slightly elliptical construction meaning the fortnightly exhortation from the monks' community. The "probationary practice" in the seventh rule renders the standard penance period (Skt. mānatta) incumbent on one who has committed a saṅghāvaśeṣa offense, here adapted for nuns under the gurudharma framework. The phrase rendered "what is a proper case and what is not" translates "gnas dang gnas ma yin pa," literally "the possible and the impossible" or "the fitting and the unfitting" — a standard doctrinal dyad referring to knowledge of what circumstances are and are not conditioned to produce certain results. This is a well-recognized category in the canon and requires no special flag, but listeners should note it carries a semi-technical sense.

The verse contains the name "the buddha called Satya" (bden zhes bya ba'i sangs rgyas), meaning a buddha of that name who endorsed or declared the ordination valid. This is an unusual phrase; it may refer to a formulaic appeal to truthfulness or to a specific buddha-name in the ordination liturgy's poetic register.

The four rules added here (not speaking back, not returning anger, not striking back, not reviling in return) are presented as appended to the eight chief rules but connected in a separate transmission until recognized by a perfectly awakened buddha — this reflects a liturgical convention that certain rules are provisional until confirmed by full buddhological authority. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the source text is incomplete at this point. The term rendered "monks" in the seniority-salutation context translates a Tibetan term that refers to fully ordained monks (bhikṣu); the parallel structure of the passage makes clear that the question at issue is cross-gender seniority-salutation between monks and nuns, not salutation among nuns alone, though the framing is somewhat ambiguous. The conditional clauses about women not having gone forth are a well-known passage found across Vinaya traditions and are rendered here following the standard form of the argument. The town names Khormo Jig and Donjog are transliterations of Tibetan place names that appear to be rendering Sanskrit originals now unrecoverable from this passage alone; they are rendered phonetically here. Sthulanandā is a well-known nun in Vinaya narratives and her name is kept in Sanskrit. The verse summarizing the rule is terse and compressed; the rendering follows the standard Vinaya verse style. The phrase rendered "without power" reflects the Tibetan sense that a nun who has once disrobed lacks the canonical standing to be re-ordained by another nun. The final sentence contains a grammatical difficulty. The Tibetan says the householder of Donjog entrusted his son's education to women who had formerly kept company with courtesans, and then says "let this girl be taught." The shift from "boy" to "girl" may reflect a scribal confusion in the source text, or the referent of "this girl" may be Gauthami the Thin, whose education the householder of Donjog is also arranging by proxy. The translation renders the text as it stands without smoothing the difficulty, though the narrative logic here is somewhat strained. The phrase rendered "the Āvantī quarter" translates a term that can mean either a neighborhood or district named Āvantī or simply a surrounding area; the exact toponym is uncertain but does not substantially affect the narrative. The term rendered "distinguished friend" is a polite honorific address used between the courtesans and warrants no special note. The district name "Roḍa" renders Tibetan "yul rdo 'jog," a transcription of an Indic place name; its exact Sanskrit form is uncertain but it recurs from the preceding passage. The currency "kārṣāpaṇa" is a standard Indian coin mentioned frequently in Vinaya literature. The gold coin unit rendered as "gold coins" reflects the Indic monetary term kārṣāpaṇa (a standard copper or gold coin of ancient India), which appears transliterated in the Tibetan as ཀཱར་ཥཱ་པ་ཎ. Since the text is for audio narration, "gold coins" is used for naturalness; the technical term is kārṣāpaṇa.

The city name རྡོ་འཇོག (literally "Stone-placing") is rendered as Droṇa, its standard Sanskrit equivalent in Buddhist narrative literature.

The phrase rendered "his mind and the mental factors born of mind collapsed" (སེམས་དང་སེམས་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྒྱུ་བ་རྣམས་ཉམས་ཏེ) is a deliberate doctrinal formulation using the classical Abhidharma pairing of mind (citta) and mental factors (caitasika); it signals a total psychological breakdown expressed in scholastic idiom. The term kārṣāpaṇa is a standard ancient Indian monetary unit (a copper or silver coin); it is left in its Sanskrit form as it appears transliterated in the Tibetan throughout. The name "slender Gautamī" renders སྐེམ་མོ་གཽ་ཏ་མཱི, literally "the thin or lean Gautamī," a personal name used consistently. The passage ends mid-sentence in the supplied Tibetan; the translation breaks off accordingly without completion of the final speech. The phrase rendered "a cow was snatched away by someone taking what was not theirs" translates a compact passage indicating theft without a named agent. The reading is straightforward but the agent is entirely absent from the Tibetan, so the rendering reflects that ambiguity without forcing a subject. The name rendered throughout as "Gautamī" — literally "the lean Gautamī" — is a stock narrative epithet in this text, combining a clan name with a physical descriptor. The preceding passage established this as the same Gautamī figure; the epithet "the lean one" likely distinguishes her within the story tradition.

The final sentence is syntactically incomplete in the Tibetan as transmitted — the construction breaks off mid-thought, indicating either a lacuna in the manuscript or a deliberate cliff-hanger at a section boundary. This is noted here rather than flagged in the body. The phrase rendered "the locality called Khormo-jik" translates a proper place name that appears in the Tibetan as a toponym. Its exact identification is uncertain; it may be a transliteration of an Indian place name now obscure, and is retained here in descriptive form rather than left as an untranslatable string.

The expression rendered "beaten like that, she ate the flesh of her son" follows the Tibetan closely; the passage is deliberately harrowing and the syntax confirms she acted under coercion. The list of buddha-qualities in the middle section is a stock encomium drawing on canonical Abhidharma and Mahāyāna lists. "The three objects of discipline" renders Tibetan dul ba'i dngos po gsum, a technical triad (body, speech, mind, or alternatively the three trainings in discipline); the exact referent varies by commentarial tradition and is not doctrinally certain here. "The four rivers" most likely refers to the four floods or āsravas in their river metaphor. "The six abodes" and "six faculties" are less standard terms whose precise referent in this particular text's tradition is uncertain; the rendering follows the most natural reading. The "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a standard Abhidharma image for the twenty forms of the belief in a personal self, here dissolved at stream-entry. The phrase rendered "like clay and gold alike" translates the Tibetan bong ba dang gser du 'dra, literally "resembling clay and gold." This is a standard image for equipoise or non-discrimination — indifference to pleasant and unpleasant, of which various commentarial explanations exist. Some editions read this as referring to the even-minded saint who regards coarse and refined things without preference.

The phrase "treasury of the storehouse of existence" renders rig pas sgo nga'i mdzod bcom pa, which is literally "shattered the treasury of the egg of existence with knowledge." The image of the cosmic egg (sgo nga) as a container of cyclic existence is a classical Indian and Tibetan motif; "shattered the egg-shell treasury of existence" would be equally valid, and listeners should understand this as the destruction of the shell of ignorance encasing saṃsāric existence.

The phrase rendered "those with controlling faculties and those approaching the controlling faculties" follows dbang po dang nye dbang po, which in a Vinaya context likely refers to kings and their ministers or senior courtiers; the translation given is a literal doctrinal rendering, but a contextual rendering of "rulers and those close to rulers" is also defensible. The phrase rendered "caused her own womb to become barren" translates a Tibetan passage in which the old wife's jealousy causes the new wife's womb to be made pure or empty of a being — in other words, the old wife, acting out of natural jealousy, causes the new wife to miscarry or prevents conception. This is a narratively pivotal moment and the passage is slightly ambiguous: it is the old wife who acts out of jealousy, and the result is that the new wife's womb is affected. The rendering follows the most natural reading given the narrative context, but a case could be made that the new wife's womb subsequently becomes receptive after this episode. The passage cuts off mid-sentence. The phrase rendered "the nun Sthavirā Gautamī" represents the Tibetan dge slong ma skem mo gau ta mī. The epithet skem mo ("dried up / withered") appears to be a Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Sthūlanandā in some recensions but here is more likely a descriptive epithet, possibly translating Kṣemā or another name. Given the narrative context and the Vinaya tradition, this figure is most plausibly the nun Sthavirā Gautamī, though the exact identification warrants consultation of the Sanskrit or Chinese parallels of this Vinaya story.

The "thunderbolt" rendering of gnam lcags (literally "sky-iron") is contextually warranted; it can mean meteorite or lightning-bolt. Both readings are attested in the commentarial tradition. The epithet rendered as "perfect in knowledge and conduct" translates the standard Tibetan equivalent of the Sanskrit vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, one of the ten epithets of a buddha; this is its first full appearance in the passage and the rendering follows standard convention.

The river name is transliterated from the Tibetan as Varakā; the Sanskrit original is uncertain, and this may be a Tibetan phonetic rendering of an Indic toponym no longer securely identifiable.

The phrase rendered "gathered in the manner of Vaiśravaṇa, endowed with the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa" reflects the Tibetan idiom comparing a wealthy householder's riches to those of Vaiśravaṇa, the deity of wealth; the expression is conventional and idiomatic rather than literal. The name "Skaṃmā Gautamī" renders སྐེམ་མོ་གཽ་ཏ་མཱི, which corresponds to Sanskrit Kṣemā Gautamī or possibly Śyāmā Gautamī. The first syllable སྐེམ་མོ is uncertain; it may be a Tibetan phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name not easily recoverable from this form alone. This is consequential because it identifies a specific nun.

The phrase འཕགས་མ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་གཟུང་བར་དཀའ་སྟེ is somewhat elliptical. Rendered here as "afflictions are difficult to restrain," it could also mean "noble ones are difficult to grasp or take hold of" — the doctrinal point being that the afflictions seize women in ways that are hard to check. The translation follows the contextual sense of the women's petition to the nun for guidance. The phrase rendered "submit yourselves to my authority" translates a construction meaning literally "offer the law to me" or "hand authority over to me," which in context means placing themselves under Sthūlanandā's direction or management — a euphemism for her acting as a procuress. The translation conveys this pragmatic meaning without editorializing.

The closing reference to "one who has eaten the flesh of her own child" alludes to a canonical story, likely the tale of Kuntī or a similar narrative of extreme suffering due to famine or karmic consequence, which the text is about to recount. No textual corruption is suspected; the allusion is left to context. The phrase rendered "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a standard Abhidharma metaphor: the twenty-peak mountain represents the twenty modes of the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), comprising the fivefold attribution of self and mine to each of the five aggregates. The image of the vajra of primordial wisdom shattering these peaks signals the attainment of stream-entry (srotāpatti), which cuts the fetter of the view of the transitory collection entirely.

The verse stanza near the middle of the passage is terse and possibly mnemonic in character; "cross-legged sitting is without category" renders a phrase that may mean the rule about sitting cross-legged in the presence of a monk has no enumerated exception — a minor point of Vinaya procedure. This reading is defensible but the exact nuance is not certain. The epithet of Bhomā rendered "master of the Three Baskets" translates the Tibetan phrase indicating she claims command of the Tripiṭaka, used here with clear irony given the context of her arrogance. The phrase "fool upon fool, dullard upon dullard" renders a double intensification in the Tibetan, indicating degrees of stupidity. The phrase rendered "what is called the wound that is womanhood" reflects a difficult and anatomically crude expression in the Vinaya literature. The Tibetan "བུད་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་རྨའི་སྒོར་སྲོག་ཆགས་དག་ཞུགས་པར" literally means "creatures entered into the opening of the wound called woman." This is an archaic Vinaya idiom, likely reflecting a canonical Indian view of the female body; the rendering preserves it faithfully without softening.

The phrase rendered "half cross-legged on a mat" for "སྐྱིལ་མོ་ཀྲུང་ཕྱེད་དུ་ཆོས་ལ་འདུག་པས" involves some interpretive difficulty. The compound "ཆོས་ལ་འདུག་པ" could mean "sitting in the proper or lawful manner" or "sitting in accordance with the rule." The translation "in the proper manner" is chosen to capture both the posture and the Vinaya connotation. The verse in the middle of the passage presents a compressed, aphoristic quality. The phrase rendered "the flow of blood" for "khrag 'dzag pa" is a standard Vinaya idiom indicating menstruation, contextually used to mark the specific restrictions applicable to nuns; the verse as a whole appears to be a mnemonic summarizing the rules just discussed regarding what a monk will not forgo and what a nun may not inquire about. The verse quatrain near the end is terse and the Tibetan is somewhat compressed. The rendering "unclean" refers to menstrual or parturition blood; "nursing-cloth" and "nursing-band" render ནུ་རྟེན and ནུ་མཆིངས, terms for garments or supports used in breastfeeding or postpartum care. The precise referents of these Vinaya technical terms are debated in the commentarial tradition, and the translation renders the plain sense.

The epithet Gautamī for Mahāprajāpatī (here གཽ་ཏ་མཱི་སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ) is her clan name; "mother of the people" renders སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ literally, though it is also an honorific epithet for Mahāprajāpatī as foster-mother of the Buddha. The phrase rendered "monk her father in the Dharma" translates the Tibetan literally: the monk is the nun's senior male counterpart in the Vinaya relationship, here expressed as "father monk" (dge slong pha). This is a standard Vinaya category denoting a senior monk in a quasi-parental disciplinary relationship to a nun.

The name Sthūlanandā is the standard Sanskrit reconstruction for the Tibetan "Sbom dga' mo" (meaning "Fat Joyful One"). The queen's name Mālagandha (Tibetan: phreng ldan ma, "Garland-fragrant") is reconstructed on the same basis. The three garments in this passage present a terminological sequence: the waist-cincher (Tib. rkyed chings), the breast-band (nu rten), and the breast-support or breast-separator (nu ma'i bar chad, literally "that which occupies the interval between the breasts," likely a garment that lifts or separates the breasts). The distinctions among these three items are clear in the Tibetan and have been rendered accordingly. The Vinaya narrative follows a formulaic pattern in which the same episode is repeated with a new garment each time; the translation preserves that repetitive structure deliberately, as it reflects the canonical form of rule-origination stories. The verse summary in this passage is a mnemonic tag condensing the preceding rules into shorthand. The line rendered as "Do not discard it in an unclean place — the womb, impurity, and foul drink" is terse and deliberately abbreviated; the full legal content is in the narrative prose around it. The reference to "the womb" alludes to the rule about not discarding waste in a womb-related place, while "foul drink" likely points to a separate rule not yet fully narrated at this point in the text.

The phrase rendered as "the one dwelling in my womb" translates the Tibetan term for a being already conceived, making clear the child was still in utero when the decision to abort was made. The narrative is heading toward a rule about a nun acting as an abortionist, a serious transgression in the Vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "she rebuked him eight times" translates a Tibetan idiom for a strong, emphatic rebuke; the number eight here likely reflects a formulaic expression of repeated insistence rather than a literal count of eight utterances.

The name Guptā renders the Tibetan "གུབ་ཏས," and young Kāśyapa renders "གཞོན་ནུ་འོད་སྲུང." The story of Kāśyapa's miraculous conception from a drop of urine, without physical contact, is a well-known narrative in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya literature.

The closing verse summary is a colophon-style mnemonic listing topics covered in or adjacent to this section of the Vinaya; the rendering attempts to follow the compressed, list-like Tibetan closely, though the final lines are deliberately terse in the original. The phrase rendered "Rādha" at the opening refers to the same Rādha mentioned in the immediately preceding passage; the text here is a brief verse-like summary line indicating that the rules just stated apply equally to boys, girls, novices, and Rādha. The transition from this summary into the main narrative is abrupt, which is characteristic of Vinaya compilation style.

The name "Guptā" renders Tibetan "Gub ta" and the boy's name "Kāśyapa" renders "Od srung gzhon nu" (literally "young Kāśyapa / young Protector of Light"), a standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name Kāśyapa meaning "one who protects brilliance." The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, rendering the final passage about the two generations incomplete. The phrase "གྲོགས་པོ་ཡུ་བུ་གཉིས་དུས་ལས་འདས་ཀྱང་" is somewhat elliptical. The reading taken here is that Sāta reports that though two generations of time have elapsed for his friend Pañcāla, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons are mentioned — suggesting a conversation about the longevity or family circumstances of one of the yakṣas. The exact syntactic completion of this sentence depends on the continuation of the passage.

The name rendered "Guptā" follows the established rendering from the preceding passage. The epithet "Kāśyapa the Elder" renders "འོད་སྲུང་ཆེན་པོ," literally "great Kāśyapa," and refers to Mahākāśyapa, one of the principal disciples of the Buddha. The identification of the son as Mahākāśyapa is an unusual hagiographical detail preserved in this Vinaya narrative context. The name Joymaker renders the Tibetan "Dga' byed ma," a feminine name meaning "she who makes joy" or "she who causes delight" — a transparent formation chosen to reflect the narrative etymology given in the text. The boy's name Pāñcika is a Sanskrit patronymic from Pañcāla, and is kept in its Sanskrit form as it becomes a proper name in the tradition. The crane cry at the moment of conception and birth is a folk-omen motif whose significance will presumably be developed in the narrative that follows. The name Sātakiri is a compound formed from Sāta (the father's name) and giri (mountain), yielding something like "Sāta-of-the-mountain" or "Mountain-Sāta," reflecting the text's own folk etymology linking the father's name and the crane's cry from the mountain. The Tibetan ས་ཏ་གི་རི literally renders this compound.

The yakṣa Pañcāla and the young yakṣa Pāñcika appear to be distinct figures: Pañcāla is the elder to whom the earlier betrothal was made, while Pāñcika is the young yakṣa to whom Pañcāla gives Joymaker in marriage. This distinction is maintained in the translation. The phrase rendered "the Blessed One granted permission by his silence" follows the standard canonical idiom in which a Tathāgata's silence in response to a request constitutes assent; this is a well-established convention in Vinaya and sūtra narrative literature and requires no special comment beyond noting the deliberate wordlessness. The names of the hell realms listed follow the standard Sanskrit series: Sañjīva, Kāḷasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, Avīci (the eight hot hells), followed by the cold hells Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. The Tibetan here renders most of these by translation or partial transcription; the Sanskrit names are restored for clarity.

The child's name, rendered here as "Joymaker," translates the Tibetan Dga' byed, which corresponds to Sanskrit Priyaṃkara or a similar form meaning "one who makes delight."

Maṇibhadra is identified here as the lord of the yakṣas (gnod sbyin gyi bdag po ngal bso po); the epithet ngal bso po, meaning "the one who gives rest" or "the refresher," is a standard Tibetan rendering of Maṇibhadra's name and function. The yakṣinī's name, rendered in the preceding passage as "Aprāptā" (from Tibetan འཕྲོག་མ), literally means "she who seizes" or "snatching-one." The consistency with the preceding rendering has been maintained throughout.

The speech by Maṇibhadra identifies the "chieftain" (སྡེ་དཔོན་, sde dpon) as the ascetic Gautama — meaning the Buddha — which is an unusual construction in which Aprāptā herself seems to name Gautama as the chieftain she has been told about, or Maṇibhadra identifies Gautama as the chieftain who can help. The syntax is somewhat compressed in the original, and the reading adopted here is the most coherent one. The phrase rendered "in the end, a single worldly benefactor with warm devotion" translates a compressed and difficult clause. The Tibetan reads literally something like "because compassion dwells toward the weak and lowly, in the end a single worldly donor of heat." The precise sense is obscure; this rendering reflects the most plausible reading — that the pratyekabuddha accepts alms from humble donors out of compassion — but the clause is genuinely difficult and may be corrupt or elliptical. The term saṃkakṣikā refers to a half-garment or underrobe covering the torso and upper arms, worn during physical work or bathing to preserve decency. The Tibetan transliteration is preserved throughout the passage as a technical Vinaya term without a fully transparent Tibetan rendering.

The phrase rendered as "others of different faith mocked them" translates a brief clause indicating that those who were not followers of the Buddha took the opportunity to ridicule the nuns — a stock Vinaya scenario contrasting the reactions of the laypeople who became attached with those who expressed disapproval. The term rendered "person with two sex characteristics" translates a technical Vinaya category referring to individuals with ambiguous or combined sexual anatomy, in Sanskrit pandaka or ubhayavyañjanaka depending on the specific context. Here the Tibetan uses a term literally meaning "one having two marks/signs," which corresponds most precisely to ubhayavyañjanaka in the broader Vinaya taxonomy of those excluded from ordination. The category "hermaphrodite" is used as the closest conventional rendering, though the Vinaya taxonomy is more nuanced than any single modern term captures.

The verse summarizes four categories of persons ineligible for ordination that the surrounding narrative sections address: those with two sex characteristics, those whose passages are blocked, those who always discharge blood, and those who have no menstrual blood at all. The final category, one with no blood, is introduced in the verse but its narrative case is not yet rendered here, as the source passage ends before it.

The phrase rendered "stopped up" or "whose passages were blocked" refers to a physiological condition in which urinary and intestinal passages are abnormally connected or obstructed, causing involuntary simultaneous evacuation. The verse passage in the middle of this text is terse and somewhat cryptic. The rendering "the gesture of spitting" for ཐུ་མི་བྱ is based on the Vinaya context where spitting (or making a gesture of contempt or dismissal) is a recognized ceremonial act; the exact referent may be a specific ritual gesture of reception or rejection in the ordination procedure. The line དགེ་སློང་འཆགས meaning "take on the form of a monk" is interpretive; it may refer to a hermaphrodite adopting monks' robes or status. These are genuinely uncertain phrases in a condensed verse summary that likely presupposes a fuller prose commentary.

The figure ཞིང་དགའ་མོ་བསོད་སྙོམས་ is rendered as "the joyful Nandā" following the standard identification of this stock character in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya narrative. The term rendered "Pom-delight" follows the preceding passage's established rendering of སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ. The epithet applied to Mahākāśyapa — venerable Ānanda is named in the Tibetan as the one who permitted the ordination of women — this reflects the well-known Vinaya account in which Ānanda interceded with the Buddha on behalf of Mahāprajāpatī. The phrase "monk who is her monastic father" renders དགེ་སློང་ཕ, literally "monk-father," a recognized Vinaya term for the monk under whose authority or in relation to whom a nun stands in a particular institutional relationship; the precise technical meaning of this term as the passage continues would benefit from seeing the following sentence, which is where the ruling is completed. The phrase rendered "communal acts" translates སྤྱི་ལས, meaning acts that are held jointly between the two communities rather than separately by each order. The distinction between separate and shared Vinaya acts is a standard feature of dual-ordination Vinaya procedure.

The figure translated as "great lay patroness" renders སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ, literally "great mistress of beings" — a title for a prominent lay female donor or patroness of high social standing.

The final verse lines are the closing summary verse of a Vinaya section; the last line ("one should not strike a person with a harmful garment or the chest") is terse and likely refers to rules against using clothing or physical contact as forms of assault or inappropriate touching — the precise referent is unclear without the fuller Vinaya context. The phrase rendered "an offense with expiation" translates a standard Vinaya term for a pācittiya-class transgression, meaning a downfall that requires confession and expiation before the community but does not constitute a root defeat. The text does not spell out the Tibetan term in full here but it is implied by the formula "འདས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ," which in Vinaya contexts consistently marks this category of offense.

The name "Sthūlanandā" is the Sanskrit reconstruction of the Tibetan སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ, literally "Fat Joyful One," a well-known nun in the Vinaya narratives notorious for misconduct. The phrase rendered "sons of that slave woman" translates a Tibetan insult directed at the king's men. The term "bzan mo'i bu" literally means "son of a female slave" or "son of a maidservant," and is a harsh term of abuse; the translation preserves its force. The winter quarters mentioned here likely refers to a building or compound used during the cold season, which Sthūlanandā had built adjacent to it as a venue for the girl's activities. The phrase rendered "a man to act as a pimp" translates a term literally meaning "a man who guards or watches" in the context of the sex trade; the rendering is a contextual interpretation consistent with the narrative logic. The passage uses "noble one" as a form of address between women, reflecting the Tibetan honorific convention in Vinaya narratives. The expression "sons of that slave woman" is a term of abuse, identical to the one used in the preceding passage, and has been rendered consistently. The phrase rendered "along with what has already passed" translates a formulaic Vinaya expression indicating that the offense also retroactively implicates prior related conduct; this is a standard technical idiom in Vinaya literature and not a scribal error.

The name "Buzanmo" is a proper name in the Tibetan that does not correspond to a well-known Sanskrit equivalent in this context; it is retained in transliteration.

"Neyagawa" likewise appears to be a phonetic rendering of a personal name in the source; it is retained as transliterated. The phrase rendered as "became known by a name" translates the Tibetan "mtshan gyur na," literally "if one has become named" or "if one has come to be identified by a sign or name." In the Vinaya context this appears to refer to a situation where a monastic's gender identity or biological sex has become a matter of public knowledge or formal recognition — likely referring to cases of sexual transformation or ambiguity, a well-attested Vinaya topic. The precise technical sense cannot be determined from this passage alone, and the rendering is deliberately neutral to preserve that ambiguity.

The verse summary uses "great sage" to render "drang srong chen po," literally "great ṛṣi," a standard epithet applied to the Buddha in Vinaya verse summaries.

The monk named Gunā (spelled "gu na" in the Tibetan) and his affiliation with the "Mūla group" (mu la pa) are as in the text. "Mūla" here may refer to a sub-grouping within the community rather than the Mūlasarvāstivāda school as such. The epithet translated as "wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, heaped up like the treasures of Vaiśravaṇa" renders a formulaic phrase comparing the householder's wealth to that of the god of wealth. The Tibetan reads "ngal bso po'i nor dang 'dra ba ngal bso po'i nor la sdo ba," where ngal bso po is the standard Tibetan rendering of Vaiśravaṇa (Kubera), the deity of wealth.

The name Dharmadattā is given in the Tibetan as Chos sbyin ma, meaning "she who is given by the Dharma" or "gift of the Dharma," which matches the Sanskrit Dharmadattā. The passage's explanation of the name connects it to the girl's listening to the Dharma. The nun's name rendered here is Utpalavārṇā, the standard Sanskrit reconstruction for the Tibetan transcription given. This is the celebrated arhat nun famous in the canon.

The lunar mansion "Viśākha" (Tibetan sa ga) is the sixteenth nakṣatra; the boy is named after the asterism under which he was born. This is a standard Indian naming convention.

The five faults of sensual pleasure are introduced here but the list is cut off at the first item in the passage as given; the enumeration continues beyond the supplied text. The phrase "ཡང་དག་པར་སོང་བ་སྐྱེས་བུ་དམ་པ" is rendered "rightly faring holy persons," a stock phrase indicating spiritually accomplished individuals who have gone the right way; this is a standard honorific formula in such lists and does not designate a specific technical category. The name "སྒྲིབ" in the compound "མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདའ་བ" is rendered as "passing beyond sorrow," consistent with the house gloss for nirvāṇa throughout. The phrase "བླ་ན་མེད་པ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་བདེ་བ" is rendered "the unsurpassed bliss of yogic practice," which may be a summary phrase for a specific meditative state; the doctrinal referent in this sūtra context is likely the highest dhyāna or liberation, not necessarily a tantric category. The "six rules and six rules to be followed" refers to the training period prescribed for a śikṣamāṇā, a probationary nun, which in the Vinaya tradition involves six primary rules and six ancillary rules observed for two years before full ordination as a nun. This technical category is rendered descriptively here, as is standard when Tibetan follows the Sanskrit formula without giving the individual rules. The list of qualities attributed to the buddhas draws on standard scholastic enumerations: the four bases of miraculous power, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers, and so forth. "Five limbs abandoned" and "five births transcended" refer to specific Abhidharma categories; the exact referents vary by tradition and are not glossed here to keep the narration flowing, as both are standard items in such buddha-quality lists.

"Mṛgadhvaja of Sāgala" renders the name given in the Tibetan; the preceding passage used "Mṛgadhvaja" for the same figure, so the rendering is kept consistent. The list of cold hells follows a standard Indic taxonomy preserved in Abhidharma literature: Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma — rendered here by their descriptive Tibetan equivalents rather than reconstructed Sanskrit names, since the Tibetan text presents them in descriptive form. The Tibetan "རྒྱལ་ཆེན་བཞིའི་རིས" and the subsequent enumeration of divine realms follow the standard cosmological sequence through the desire realm and into the Brahma realms of the form realm. The distinction between the wheel-turning king who rules "by the power of force" (སྟོབས་ཀྱི་འཁོར་ལོས་སྒྱུར་བ) and the ordinary wheel-turning king (འཁོར་ལོས་སྒྱུར་བ) is a recognized sub-category in some sūtra traditions and is rendered accordingly. The narrative in this passage is somewhat compressed and moves quickly between two distinct ordination sequences involving Dharmadinnā and Utpalavarṇā (Tib. Utpala'i kha dog ma, "she of blue-lotus color"). The sequence of events — first Dharmadinnā is sent away with the two-year probationary training, then Utpalavarṇā goes to the Blessed One and a second instruction is given — reflects a dual ordination procedure. The narrative logic is condensed in the Tibetan and slightly elliptical; the rendering follows the most coherent reading of the sequence.

The term mdzod spu (ūrṇā) refers to the tuft of white hair between the eyebrows, one of the thirty-two major marks of a great being; it is rendered here by its Sanskrit term for clarity, as "ūrṇā hair." The phrase rendered "the five spokes of the wheel of cyclic existence, its turning and non-turning" follows the Tibetan closely but is an unusual formulation. The five spokes likely refer to the five aggregates or the five destinies; the commentary tradition is not uniform here, and the precise doctrinal referent of this image is not entirely transparent from the text alone.

The passage "broke the door-panel of the charnel ground by direct knowledge" is a striking metaphor. The Tibetan reads "rig pa s sgo nga'i sbubs bcom pa," which likely renders a Sanskrit expression for shattering the enclosure of the charnel ground through gnosis — a standard image for the arhat's breaking free from rebirth and death. This is a genuine crux where the exact Sanskrit Vorlage is uncertain. The passage lists the attainments of the audience using the standard Abhidharmic scheme of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path: stream-entry (Skt. srotāpatti), once-returning (Skt. sakṛdāgāmin), non-returning (Skt. anāgāmin), and arhathood. The arousing of the awakening mind then branches into the three vehicles, a standard Mahāyāna narrative device.

The phrase rendered "went forth through her own power" translates a somewhat condensed construction that indicates her renunciation occurred spontaneously or supernaturally, without an external ordaining community performing the rite in the normal way — a recognized narrative motif in early Mahāyāna sūtras concerning spiritually advanced women. The city name rendered here as Vārāṇasī translates the Tibetan "Khormo-jig" which is the standard Tibetan equivalent of Vārāṇasī. The Deer Park at the Hermitage of the Seers is the well-known Ṛṣipatana-Mṛgadāva (Deer Park of Sarnath), rendered accordingly. The passage ends mid-sentence in the supplied Tibetan, indicating the text is incomplete as provided; the translation faithfully follows the Tibetan to its ending point without supplying further material. The phrase rendered "the forty-third bundle" follows the standard Vinaya section-marker in the Tibetan text. The verse summary at that point is a mnemonic rubric listing the four topics of the bundle in telegraphic form; the translation gives the sense of each line as precisely as the compressed style allows, but these rubrics are often cryptic and the exact referents of rules two and four depend on broader Vinaya context not given here. The term rendered "barber" (Tib. འབྲེག་མཁན) literally means "one who cuts" and clearly refers to a barber or hair-dresser; the subsequent narrative confirms this. The phrase གྱུར་ཏ་རེ in the speech of the nearby nun is an optative of wishing or alarm and has been rendered as an exclamatory "How unfortunate it would be," which preserves the idiomatic force. The nun Sthūlanandā (Tib. སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ, literally "the greatly joyful fat one," a well-known problematic figure in Vinaya narratives) is kept by her Sanskrit name as is standard. The phrase བདག་གི་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ལྟ་སྟེ is an idiomatic expression of resignation, here rendered "That is my own doing," though it could also be translated as "such is my situation" or "this is the result of my karma" — the exact nuance is mildly uncertain, but the sense of accepting responsibility or one's own predicament is clear. The term rendered "Doṇamatī" (Tibetan: དོན་ཆུང་ངུ་མ) is uncertain. This appears to be an epithet or place-name for a group of nuns, literally meaning "those of little benefit" or possibly a proper name; the rendering follows the most natural reading of the text as a group designation. Some editions may read this differently.

The name གྲེ་ལས་སྐྱེས (Grelaskyé) is a Tibetan transcription of a Sanskrit proper name that cannot be securely reconstructed without access to a parallel Sanskrit recension. It appears to be a monk whose remains are honored by the twelve nuns.

The phrase དུས་ལས་འདས་པ ("passed beyond his time") is a standard Tibetan euphemism for death, rendered here as "passed away." The name "Chutung" appears to be a Tibetan rendering of a proper name (literally meaning "water-drinker"), which was also used in the preceding passage as the name of the venerable elder arriving with five hundred monks. The text is consistent in using this name, and it is preserved as such for continuity with the previous rendering.

The expression translated as "she blessed her robe through her power of concentration" renders a compact phrase indicating that Utpalavarnā used her supernormal ability to imbue her robe with a protective quality before entering the absorption of cessation. The precise mechanism is left elliptical in the Tibetan. The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan as given, breaking off at the conditional clause about what happens if a nun enters without having been asked. The translation reflects this open ending faithfully.

The epithet སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ, literally "great mistress of beings," is a standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Mahāprajāpatī, the name of the Buddha's aunt and the first Buddhist nun. It has been rendered accordingly. The summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā condensing the preceding legal rulings on the poṣadha and pravāraṇā ceremonies and the procedure for nuns seeking consent. The verse's compressed syntax follows standard Vinaya mnemonic style.

The term rendered "gradually" (Tibetan: bgags kyis) in the forgiveness procedure is a procedural term indicating a staged or mediated reconciliation rather than an immediate, direct confrontation — a nuance preserved in the translation. The passage contains a characteristically repetitive Vinaya-style enumeration of the three unwholesome and three wholesome roots, repeated in slightly varying formulations as part of an oral-formulaic structure. The text appears to break off mid-sentence at the end; the translation renders what is present in the passage without supplying missing text.

The phrase rendered "acts of aggression" translates a cluster of terms including fighting, fault-finding, abuse, quarreling, and a fifth term suggesting aggressive confrontation or incitement; these have been rendered as a unified list throughout for naturalness in speech. The term rendered "invitation ceremony" throughout is the Pravāraṇā, the formal ceremony at the end of the rains retreat in which monastics invite correction from their fellows. The term rendered "Restoration" in the final section is Poṣadha, the fortnightly confession and recitation of the Prātimokṣa; both terms appear in the house glossary and are used consistently.

The phrase "recover his own mind of renunciation" renders the Tibetan idiom for the re-establishing of each individual's proper monastic resolve or composure after conflict — literally "separately obtaining his mind of renunciation." The rendering is interpretive but doctrinal.

The "topknot festival" is a calendrical observance whose exact identification in this Vinaya context is uncertain; it may refer to a specific Indian festival associated with hair-offering rites. The phrase rendered as "shaven-headed nuns" and "shaven-headed wanderers" translates the Tibetan terms for nuns and monastics in the mouths of the brahmins and householders, who use the colloquial derogatory expression for shaven-headed renunciants. The scornful tone is deliberate and belongs to the speakers, not to the text itself.

The final line, "Here ends the summary verse," renders the Tibetan closing marker indicating that a mnemonic summary verse follows, though the verse itself does not appear in this passage. The phrase rendered as "the five-spoked wheel of a vehicle" reflects a somewhat unusual image in this narrative context; the Tibetan reads "sgo khang na 'khor ba'i 'khor lo cha lnga pa la rtog cing 'dug go," which literally means he sat in the gatehouse examining a five-part or five-spoked wheel. This detail appears to be a narrative flourish establishing that the man is a wandering craftsman or trader, not a monk, and the translation follows the literal reading. Some commentators may read 'khor ba here differently, but the sense of a wheeled conveyance or cartwheel seems most natural in context. The phrase rendered "turning the wheel of cyclic existence in his mind" translates the idiom for a non-monk lay person sitting in a gatehouse being preoccupied with worldly affairs — the nuns described him only by his appearance and posture, not knowing he was a layman. The "wheel of cyclic existence" here is a vivid way of characterizing his mental state as worldly, not a technical Dharma usage.

The title "Great Progenitress" for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī renders སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ་ཆེན་མོ་གཽ་ཏ་མཱི, where སྐྱེ་དགུའི་བདག་མོ means "mistress of beings" or "progenitress of beings," an honorific for Mahāprajāpatī. The passage alternates between her full title and the shorter གཽ་ཏ་མཱི alone. The phrase rendered "My good woman, I know how. Since the time has passed, there is not a craft or a trade I do not know" is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The speaker is Sthūlanandā boasting of her skills; the sense is that over time she has come to know every craft and trade, and the translation reflects that confident self-assertion. The list of named individuals in the festival passage is slightly compressed in the Tibetan and some names are abbreviated or variant forms. "Queen Mallikā" renders བཙུན་མོ་ཕྲེང་ལྡན་མ, literally "Queen Garland-Bearer," which is a standard Tibetan rendering of Mallikā. "Vāsavadattā" renders རྒྱལ་རིགས་དབྱར་བྱེད་མ, a royal lady whose name is uncertain from this epithet alone; the rendering is tentative. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, reflecting an abrupt cut in the supplied Tibetan. The phrase rendered "born laterally on the right side" translates a compound indicating an oblique or lateral birth position on the right side, understood in the narrative as an inauspicious birth sign. The exact medical or cultural referent is not further specified in the text.

The nested-bowl episode involves Sthūlanandā commissioning progressively smaller bowls that nest inside one another; the text's phrasing is somewhat compressed but the sense of a graduated set of seven nesting bowls is clear from context. The final two sentences mark a sharp transition to a formulaic legal declaration within the Vinaya narrative frame. The phrase rendered "the fully ordained nuns of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are burned — the brahmin life is burned" reflects the stock Vinaya expression used when a monk or nun has committed a breach: "burned" here means their celibate religious life has been compromised or violated. The term "brahmin life" renders tshangs par spyod pa, literally "pure conduct" or "brahmic conduct," the standard term for the celibate religious life (Sanskrit brahmacaryā). The passage signals that a Vinaya offense is being narrated. The phrase rendered "praised me to the skies like an elephant's raised trunk" is an idiomatic Tibetan expression of flattery or grand proclamation; the simile of the elephant's uplifted trunk conveys lofty, public praise. The rendering preserves the figurative sense for a listening audience.

The repeated narrative frame, "The brahmin life was burned" and "the contemplatives, the sons of the Śākyas, were burned," is a formulaic Vinaya expression indicating that the reputation and good name of the monastic community was damaged or inflamed by public scandal. The phrase rendered "Stubborn Delightful" translates the nun's name སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ (Stubborn-Joyful or Obstinate Delight); it is preserved consistently from the preceding passage. The signal she gives indicating "the female donor had but little gain" is a somewhat compressed idiom; the Tibetan མཚན་མ་ཞིག་ཉེ་བར་བསྟན་པ refers to her making a sign or giving a hint — the precise nature of the sign is not specified in the text. The summary verse appears to be a mnemonic listing several Vinaya rules in compressed form. The individual terms are elliptical, and the rendering given follows the most natural reading of each phrase as a rule-heading rather than a complete sentence — this is standard for such verse summaries in Vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "gall-bladder vessel" translates a term for a kind of container; the precise referent is a minor point of Vinaya material culture and is not consequential for the doctrinal content. The name rendered "Stout-and-Glad" translates the Tibetan "སྦོམ་དགའ་མོ" (Sbom dga' mo), literally "Fat-Joy" or "Stout-Delighted." This is a personal name of a nun and has been rendered in a natural English compound reflecting its literal meaning. Some editions may read this differently.

The phrase "འགལ་ཚབས་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ" rendered as "it will be a matter involving an offence" is a Vinaya technical formula; the exact grade of offence is not specified in this passage.

The summary verse at the close is a standard mnemonic (uddāna) marking the end of a section; the four items it enumerates summarize preceding rules. The referent of "these four" is the four cases treated in the preceding section, which is conventional in Vinaya uddāna verses. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end ("མ་ཀུན་དག་ཐུ" — literally "all the mothers..."), indicating the supplied Tibetan is incomplete. The translation reflects this abrupt ending faithfully.

The phrase rendered "nocturnal emission" translates "mi gtsang ba yang byung," literally "something unclean also arose/occurred," a standard Vinaya euphemism for seminal or vaginal discharge during sleep; the context makes the meaning clear.

The signal left at the doorway (flour or pickles/condiments) is a standard Vinaya device to indicate prior arrival and avoid entering a household unannounced; "ཚོད་མ" (tshod ma) here likely means condiments or pickled vegetables rather than fresh vegetables, functioning as a recognizable marker. The term rendered "staff-bell" (Tibetan: khar gsil) corresponds to the Sanskrit khakkhara, the ringed walking staff traditionally carried by monks, which jingles as they walk and can be shaken to announce one's arrival. This is its standard Vinaya identification.

The phrase rendered "a room built up with materials" translates rdzas kyis bsgrubs pa, literally "accomplished or constructed by means of requisites or materials." This is a technical Vinaya designation for a temporary dwelling or cell assembled from donated supplies; the exact nature of the structure is deliberately left in plain descriptive language rather than over-specified. The passage contains a string of onomatopoeic Tibetan syllables rendered here as approximations in English, since the original clearly intends to evoke the actual sounds of eating and drinking. The precise onomatopoeia differs between languages, but the general sense is preserved. The term translated as "rice-porridge" for འབྲས་ཁུར་ covers a thick rice dish; "porridge" for ཐུག་པ covers a general thick soup or congee. The phrase ནང་དུ་ཡང་དག་འཇོག is rendered as "inner composure," a standard Vinaya idiom for the Buddha's afternoon period of meditative rest. The phrase rendered "a place prepared with requisites" translates the Tibetan for a dwelling or setting arranged with the four requisites offered to the Buddha; this is a standard Vinaya context indicating the Buddha accepted an invitation and sat within a formally prepared space while also going on alms round, a juxtaposition that the text itself flags as requiring explanation through the "five reasons" passage referenced but not quoted here. The phrase rendered "occupied with a matter" for རྫས་ཀྱིས་བསྒྲུབས་པ་ན་བཞུགས is a Vinaya technical idiom; it refers to the Blessed One remaining behind to attend to some business or matter rather than going with the assembly. The passage cross-references an earlier section of the Vinaya narrative (the "five reasons" passage) which is not reproduced here; the instruction "as stated above" reflects the Tibetan's own cross-referential shorthand.

The closing summary verse is a mnemonic gāthā listing topics covered in the fascicle; the four items enumerated correspond to four separate narrative sections, of which only the last two appear in this passage. The phrase rendered "bathing" throughout refers to a therapeutic soaking or irrigation of a wound, not ordinary bathing. The Tibetan verb "khrus byed" normally means to bathe, but in this medical context it describes rinsing or washing a treated wound — the poultice procedure requires the wound to be fully irrigated before rinsing with cold or warm water. The narrative logic makes clear that the problem was applying cold water too soon and only once.

The expression "brahmin endowed with the six qualities" refers to a brahmin of full hereditary qualification according to traditional Indian brahminical reckoning: noble birth on both sides for seven generations, expertise in the Vedas, handsome appearance, good character, learning, and so forth. The specific six qualities vary by source. The phrase rendered "being of his last existence" translates "srid pa tha ma pa'i sems can," literally "the sentient being of the last existence," a technical term for one whose current life will be their final rebirth before nirvāṇa — here the child who is about to be ordained.

The term rendered "house-cricket" for "srog chags khyim sbyong" is uncertain; the compound could refer to various small domestic insects or vermin. The identity of the creature is not doctrinally significant. The phrase rendered "wheel of existence, fivefold, moving and unmoving" translates a technical Vinaya formula for the five aggregates or the constituents of conditioned existence; the exact doctrinal referent is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan and may allude to a stock phrase from Abhidharma enumeration. The rendering is faithful to the Tibetan syntax while keeping it intelligible in context.

The phrase "like stone and gold alike" and "like the sky and like the palm of the hand" are stock simile-pairs for an arhat's equanimity, well attested in Vinaya narrative literature; they are rendered literally as the tradition intends them. The verse "Even were it a hundred aeons..." is a well-known canonical gāthā attested in multiple Āgama and Vinaya sources; it is cited here in the standard form.

The summary verse at the close is a colophon-style mnemonic gāthā listing key narrative elements of the story. The phrase rendered "the one carrying a load who makes no sound, who does not eat" corresponds to the image of the snake (which carried its karmic burden silently), and these compressed summaries are conventional in this genre. The precise referents of each phrase within the mnemonic are intentionally condensed and some ambiguity is inherent to the genre.

The transition after the summary verse marks a new sūtra episode beginning with a fresh setting, which is standard in this collection. The phrase rendered as "code phrase" translates a term literally meaning something like "a word that conceals" or "a substitute expression," used here in the sense of a veiled or encoded expression, where each ordinary image stands for a doctrinal reality. The rendering "code phrase" is chosen for clarity in a spoken context.

The passage about the monk of little learning and the bandits sets up a narrative of danger in the wilderness — a typical Vinaya illustrative story establishing the context for a subsequent rule. The phrase rendered as "master of the Three Baskets" refers to one who has mastered the Tripiṭaka. The term མ་མོ་འཛིན་པ, literally "holder of the Mātṛkā," refers to the Abhidharma matrix-texts or numerical summaries; this is an older designation for what became the Abhidharma Piṭaka, rendered here by its Sanskrit technical name to preserve the scholastic sense. The repeated formula "I am a forest-dweller" is the monk's consistent and almost absurdist self-identification, likely conveying either a vow of strict forest renunciation that precluded all social knowledge, or a deliberate meditative refusal of conventional categories; the narrative presents this without irony as the cause of the bandits' outrage. The term translated as "Mātṛkā" refers to the Abhidharma matrix texts or their proto-forms. It sits alongside Sūtra and Vinaya as the third division of the canon, though in this early Vinaya context it likely refers to summary doctrinal lists rather than the fully developed Abhidharma.

The place name "Anupiya" renders Tibetan "འདོད་པ་མཐུན་པ" three times. This is the standard Tibetan rendering of the toponym Anupiya (also spelled Anupiyā), a town and mango grove near Kapilavāstu associated with early Buddhist narratives. The repeated phrase in the Tibetan is formulaic, establishing arrival at and residence in that locale.

The young brahmin's name "Maṣu" is a tentative rendering of "མ་སྡུག." The name is unclear and may be a Tibetan phonetic rendering of an Indic original not easily recovered. The passage employs the standard ten epithets of a buddha, here rendered according to their established canonical meanings. The repeated phrase "from home into homelessness" renders the classical going-forth formula. The phrase translated "sacred brahmin formularies" or "secret formularies" renders gsang tshig, literally "secret words," referring to the esoteric Vedic or brahminical texts in which the marks of a great man are said to be described — a detail common to parallel Pāli sūtra passages. The name Maṣu corresponds to the young brahmin introduced as Ma su in the preceding passage. The phrase rendered "dark-limbed menials born of Brahma's foot" (dge sbyong mgo reg nag po'i rtsa lag pho reng) is a derogatory epithet that the brahmin youth Ambastha appears to be applying to ascetics of low birth, reflecting the Brahmanical varna ideology in which śūdras are said to originate from Brahma's feet. The Blessed One is turning this language back on Ambastha ironically, noting that even with such menials a brahmin does not behave with such rudeness. The syntax here is compressed and the passage is echoing the Ambaṭṭha Sutta (DN 3); the translation follows that context. The section heading "Vinaya — the Minor Matters. The Forty-Sixth Bundle" appears mid-passage as a Tibetan canonical colophon marker indicating a fascicle division within the Vinaya Kṣudrakavastu; it interrupts the narrative and is rendered plainly as it stands in the source, since it is present in the text.

The name "Icchanangala" renders the Tibetan མིག་མི་འཛུམས་ཀྱི་བུ, literally "son of the Unblinking Eye," which corresponds to the Pāli Icchānangala or, in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta context, a patronymic. The exact Sanskrit form is uncertain; the rendering follows contextual identification with the Pāli tradition's Cankī or related figures, though the Tibetan here is likely a rendering of a name meaning something like "son of the unblinking one."

The four sons' names — Starface, Handear, Tamed by the Elephant, and Ornamented Feet — render Tibetan སྐར་མདའི་གདོང, ལག་རྣ, གླང་པོ་ཆེས་འདུལ་བ, and རྐང་རྒྱན་ལྡན respectively. These correspond to the Pāli Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍa, Hatthinīka, and Sinipura, though the Tibetan renderings diverge somewhat from the Pāli names; the translation follows the literal Tibetan meaning. The name "Ngophödma" is a transliteration of a Tibetan rendering of a Pāli name (likely Dishnī or a similar slave woman's name from the Ambaṭṭha Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya). The Tibetan text gives it as a proper name without further gloss; I have retained the Tibetan form and added the likely Pāli equivalent parenthetically in a light way. The rākṣasa passage is rendered following the Tibetan closely; in the Pāli source this episode concerns the Kaṇhāyana lineage differently, but the Tibetan here reads "Unblinking Ones" as a class of beings equivalent to rākṣasas.

The phrase "splitting the head into seven pieces" is a standard formulaic expression in these sūtra accounts for the consequence of refusing to answer a teacher's question three times. The fourfold sequence of hypothetical cases about caste-mixing and ritual privilege follows the structure of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. The term rendered "secret words" renders གསང་ཚིག, which in the Pali corresponds to mantras or sacred formulae transmitted within brahmin lineages. "Seat" and "water" refer to the customary hospitality honours due to qualified brahmins. "Anointing" renders དབང་བསྐུར, literally "empowerment," but here used in the sense of the royal or kṣatriya consecration rite. The figure of King Okkāka and the sage expelled by brahmin penalty appear in the extended narrative context of the sutta; the Tibetan here follows the standard account. The figure called "the lord of the Mithilā brahmins, Brahmā" renders མི་མཇེད་ཀྱི་བདག་པོ་ཚངས་པ. This is a brahmin named or epithetized Brahmā who is lord of the Mithilā region; the text presents him as a human brahmin lord, not the deity Brahmā. This is consistent with similar passages in related Pāli sūtra literature where a brahmin is compared to or named after Brahmā.

The repeated verse citation, appearing three times in the passage, is a standard rhetorical feature of this type of sūtra dialogue affirming the authority of a verse by attributing it to oneself and to the interlocutor in sequence. The compound rendered "like the sound of a royal court assembly" translates a phrase that literally suggests speech resembling the resonant sound within a royal palace and its surrounding assembly — conveying a quality of dignified, well-rounded sonic fullness. The rendering captures the simile's intended sense.

The terms for fraudulent commercial practices (falsifying measures of volume, scales, and weights) reflect standard Vinaya and sūtra enumerations of merchant dishonesty. The phrase rendered as "one who has a light and with a woman" reflects the Tibetan literally: འོད་དང་བུད་མེད་ཅན་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཉལ་བ. The term འོད་ཅན ("one who has a light") is ambiguous and may refer to sleeping in a room with a lamp lit, or alongside a person carrying a light — the exact sense is uncertain and likely reflects a Vinaya-context prohibition against sharing sleeping quarters in these circumstances. This is a genuine exegetical uncertainty worth flagging.

The term ཞོ་ཤས་འཚོ་བ (those who subsist on whey) may be a social category of dependent laborers or bondspeople identified by their meager subsistence.

The passage ends mid-sentence, enumerating types of luxurious furnishings; the translation faithfully follows the text to its terminus. The passage contains an extended catalogue of games and entertainments that closely parallels the Brahmajāla Sutta list of wrong livelihood. Several terms in the games section are obscure and their exact referents uncertain. "Miig brgyad pa" and "miig bcu pa" likely refer to board games played on eight-square and ten-square grids respectively, analogous to Pali "aṭṭhapada" and "dasapada." "Na ya'i mig" is rendered "the eye of nāya," following a conventional reading but the precise game is unclear. "Gul tshab," rendered "substitution-moves," and "pheg," rendered "bouncing games," are also of uncertain precise meaning. "Rang bzo'i sgra," rendered "the sound of amateur performances," may alternatively refer to improvised or spontaneous sounds. These uncertainties do not affect the doctrinal substance of the passage. The list of omen-reading and ritual arts in the final two paragraphs presents some cataloguing challenges. The term rendered "momentary conjunctions" translates a compound referring to brief astrological configurations. "Reading of fields" renders a term that could also denote reading of the character of one's natal land or surroundings; the precise referent is uncertain but contextually consistent with a list of geomantic arts. The three final ritual categories — pacifying, enriching, and fierce — are the standard three (sometimes four) tantric ritual activities and appear here in a pre-tantric Vinaya context simply as types of ritual manipulation, not technical tantric rites. The passage on medical practices is a classical list of Āyurvedic and quasi-medical procedures. Several terms in the medical and ritual sections present interpretive challenges. The term rendered "excellent bulls" for ཁྱུ་མཆོག is literally "supreme of the herd" and almost certainly refers to a bull, though some traditions read it as referring to a fine horse or similar creature. The term མ་ཧེ (rendered "buffaloes") may refer to a specific breed or type of large bovine animal; this is the standard reading in comparative Pāli sources. The term རི་དགས་འཁྱིལ་པ and བྱ་རོག་འཁྱིལ་པ, rendered as divination by the circling of deer and crows respectively, follow the Pāli parallel closely. The term ཕོལ་མིག (rendered "eyes that are underdeveloped") is uncertain and may refer to cataracts, half-formed eyes, or similar ocular conditions in a medical-diagnostic context. The phrase rendered "inner king" and "outer king" refers to the practice of predicting the outcomes of conflicts between a patron's own king and a rival or foreign king — a standard item in the canonical lists of wrong livelihood through political divination. The Tibetan nang gi rgyal po and phyi'i rgyal po carry exactly this sense.

The repeated astronomical list — solar and lunar deviations, conjunctions, meteors, horizon lights, and celestial drumming — appears to be a deliberate canonical enumeration and is rendered accordingly without condensation. The sequence of similes here — the debtor, the sick man, the slave — belongs to the classical Nīvaraṇa-abandonment passage found in the Sāmaññaphala-sutta and parallel texts. The Tibetan at several points is formulaic and slightly elliptical; the translation follows the natural expansion the formula requires for coherent oral delivery. The term rendered "low-mindedness" throughout continues the rendering established in the preceding passage. The five obstacles mentioned here are the five hindrances (nīvaraṇas): sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and regret, and doubt. The Tibetan does not enumerate them by name in this passage, so they are rendered collectively as "five obstacles" in accordance with the text.

The simile of the mountaintop lake is a classical canonical simile for the second dhyāna; it appears in the Pāli parallels (e.g., Sāmaññaphala Sutta, DN 2) and the correspondence is here well-preserved. The passage moves through the third and fourth meditative concentrations (dhyānas) and then introduces the practice of creating a mind-made body, a topic that will continue in the following passage. The phrase rendered "complete purity and utter luminosity" translates a compound describing the quality of the fourth dhyāna; the Tibetan "kun du dag pa yongs su dkar ba" literally means "thoroughly pure and completely white," which in context denotes the mental radiance and purity characteristic of the fourth absorption. The simile of the gem at the end is left incomplete as the Tibetan passage breaks off mid-sentence; its continuation presumably follows in the next passage. The phrase rendered "near afflictions" translates the Tibetan term for upakleśas, secondary or proximate afflictions, distinguished from the root afflictions. This is a standard Abhidharma technical usage and no emendation is required, though a general listener may understand it simply as "lesser defilements."

The simile of the snake and basket renders a term that could also be "snake-basket" or "wicker cage for snakes"; the exact implement is a container from which a snake is extracted, and "snake-basket" is the most natural rendering. The passage contains two consecutive similes introducing the same superknowledge of the divine ear, which is not an error in translation but reflects the text's own repetitive structure. The second simile set appears to be a continuation or fuller version of the same teaching.

The term rendered "ivory-worker" translates a word that more literally means "bone-worker" or "craftsman working with a hard material such as tusk or bone." In context, the parallel with a potter suggests an artisan shaping a prepared material; ivory-worker is the standard interpretation. The phrase rendered "intent on the Dharma in such a wrong spirit" translates "chos la yid dam bcas pa," which is somewhat elliptical. The most natural reading in this karmic context is that it refers to holding views or commitments toward the Dharma in the wrong way — possibly denying or misrepresenting it — consistent with the preceding description of calumny toward the noble ones and wrong view. This is a consequential interpretive choice worth flagging.

The term "proximate afflictions" renders "nye ba'i nyon mongs pa," referring to secondary or adjacent mental afflictions as distinct from the root afflictions, a standard Abhidharma category. The phrase rendered "knowledge and conduct" translates the compound that corresponds to the Sanskrit vijjācaraṇasampanna, a standard epithet of the Buddha meaning "perfect in knowledge and conduct." The text is structured as a dialogue, apparently between the Buddha (speaking as Gautama) and a young brahmin, likely drawing on a sūtra parallel to the Tevijja-vacchagotta or a related discourse. The sequence of the four methods is introduced but the fourth portion is not yet complete in the passage given. The list of brahmin seers follows the Tibetan transliteration closely. The Sanskrit names reconstructed are: Aṣṭaka, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni (Tibetan: Ja ma dag ni), Aṅgiras, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu. The Tibetan rendering of some names is slightly irregular but the identifications are standard.

The image of the "four-doored house" built in the village is a recurring textual marker in this discourse for householder-style merit-making practice distinguished from forest or ascetic modes.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, consistent with the supplied Tibetan which ends mid-description; the translation faithfully reproduces this open ending. The name rendered "Padmaśīrṣa" (Tib. པདྨའི་སྙིང་པོ, literally "Essence/Heart of a Lotus") may alternatively be read as "Padmahṛdaya." The passage is somewhat elliptical here; the reference appears to be to the brahmin youth's own teacher, who approached the king only indirectly, hence the comparison to being hidden behind a wall or curtain.

The final phrase — that one bearing the marks of a great man has "two paths" — refers to the classical teaching that a mahāpuruṣa must become either a universal monarch or a fully awakened buddha; this thought is left suspended in the text at this point, clearly to be completed in a subsequent passage. The name rendered "Pokkharasādi" transliterates the Tibetan Pad+ma'i snying po, which is a Tibetan rendering of the Pāli Pokkharasādi, also known in Sanskrit as Puṣkarasārin or Puṣkarasādi. The text is a Tibetan version of the Ambāṭṭha-sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya. The name is kept consistent as Pokkharasādi throughout, as this is the established identification in scholarship, though the Tibetan literally means "Lotus Heart."

The phrase rendered "fallen into a lower state of existence" translates the Tibetan for a downfall or bad rebirth destiny, here in the context of Pokkharasādi's distress that his messenger behaved so poorly toward a genuinely great being. The phrase rendered "drinking sesame oil" is literal; commentarial context suggests this old man was consuming sesame oil as part of some ritual or ascetic practice, and the brahmin's remark contrasts sincere Dharma-seekers with those pursuing worldly or ritualistic ends. The point of the anecdote is clear from context even without further gloss.

The name translated as "Māsuka" is rendered from the Tibetan "ma sdug" (literally "not agreeable" or "unpleasant"), which in this Pāli sūtra context corresponds to the brahmin student named Ambaṭṭha in the Pāli canon. The Tibetan translator appears to have rendered the name semantically rather than phonetically. This is a genuinely consequential philological point for identification of the text. The repeated phrase rendered "continues as before, up to…" reflects a standard Indic and Tibetan abbreviated repetition formula in sūtra texts, signalling that the full wording of the enquiry after health is to be understood as repeated in each scenario.

The expression rendered "I am one who has risen / fully risen" translates the Tibetan "འཕགས་སོ / མངོན་པར་འཕགས་སོ," which in this context means the brahmin is affirming his attainment: he has risen, gone forth, or been elevated in a spiritual sense. This may reflect the Pali formula "aññāto 'mhi" or a similar declaration of spiritual realisation, and the exact nuance is somewhat uncertain; some interpret it as a declaration of having "understood" or "penetrated" the truth. The phrase rendered "Lotus-Heart" for Padmasnying is a translation of the Tibetan name pad+ma'i snying po; the text uses the Tibetan throughout and no Sanskrit equivalent is given, but the name corresponds to Sanskrit Padmasnying or Padmahṛdaya. The translation keeps it as "the brahmin Padmasnying" for consistency with the preceding passage.

The simile of the "hot seed" that is "rank and festering" and from which bees stay away is a somewhat cryptic condemnation of moral corruption: a foul seed attracts no beneficial contact. The triple characterization — hot, rank, festering — follows the Tibetan exactly.

The closing "The Blessed One reflected:" mirrors the Tibetan དབཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དགོངས་པ at the end of the passage, indicating the passage breaks here and the Blessed One's subsequent reflection will follow in the next portion of the text. The phrase rendered "a term of elevation" translates the Tibetan "tshig bla dags," which means a metaphorical or figurative expression, a term used in an elevated or indirect sense to denote something else. This is a standard Abhidharma-style explanatory formula.

The final sentence is left incomplete as the source passage itself ends mid-sentence, indicating a continuation follows. The phrase rendered "wash your feet and lie down" is a conventional Indic hospitality formula; "earth" in the list alongside water and mustard oil likely refers to cleansing clay or ash used for foot-washing, a standard Vinaya-narrative detail.

The "summary verse" is a colophon-style mnemonic gāthā recapping the rules just given; its compressed syntax makes the precise referents of "four who are senior" and "the assembly" depend on the wider Vinaya context. The passage contains two interleaved Vinaya rulings woven together: the first concerns bedding inspection and safety after the death of the monk found with the snake; the second is a separate incident involving a novice and preceptor who are both left without proper robe cover during an accidental prostration, and the resulting ruling about not making prostrations when wearing only a single robe, meaning when not properly robed. The final paragraph repeats the ruling in slightly amplified form, which is typical of Vinaya canonical redaction. The phrase rendered "takes that as one's own affair" reflects a Vinaya idiom meaning treating the act as a personal matter, i.e., as something that does or should concern oneself.
