The Tibetan "གནས་བརྟན་ཀུན་ཤེས་ཀཽཎྜི་ནྱས" identifies the elder as Kauṇḍinya with the epithet "Kun-shes" (he who knows all), the traditional Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (he who has come to know), the first disciple of the Buddha. This has been rendered as "Kauṇḍinya, he who knows all" to preserve both elements.

The name "སྐུལ་བྱེད་ཆེན་པོ" rendered as Maudgalyāyana follows the Tibetan epithet meaning "great Maudgalyāyana"; the Tibetan here uses the epithet rather than the Sanskrit name directly, but the identification is standard. The summary verse is a colophon-style verse (uddeśa or uddāna) summarizing preceding narrative content. The "five hundred" and "seven hundred" refer to the numbers of monks in the assembly narratives, and "Mṛgadāva" is Deer Park (the standard Tibetan ri dags is read here as sde can, a known variant name for Vārāṇasī's Deer Park). The phrase rendered "Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers" (stobs bcu 'od srung) is an epithet combining "Ten Powers" (daśabala) with the name Kāśyapa ('od srung), designating the elder Mahākāśyapa. "Pippala Cave" (sde can gyi phug) — the Tibetan sde can is unusual here; it most likely renders Pippalā (Pippala Cave on Vulture Peak), the known residence of Mahākāśyapa; the reading is consistent with the narrative context. The act of "reviving those exhausted by the penalty" (chad pas dgum pa'i las) refers to a Vinaya regulation involving a penance or suspension — the precise technical circumstance is not entirely clear from context alone but concerns a formal act of discipline requiring attendance by senior elders. The term rendered throughout as "circle on the ground" translates the Tibetan dkyil 'khor, which in this Vinaya context denotes a prepared, demarcated area on the floor rather than the ritual maṇḍala of tantric usage. This is a well-attested Vinaya usage and the translation reflects it accordingly.

The phrase "earth" offered alongside water likely refers to cleansing earth or clay used for ritual purification of the feet, a standard Vinaya practice. The name "Nabso" is a phonetic rendering of an Indian name not easily reconstructed with certainty; it appears to be a personal name of a monk and is retained as found.

The phrase rendered "Swift-walker" translates the Tibetan literally; it functions as a monk's name or epithet.

"Khyas rdza rnga" rendered as "clay drum" is an interpretation of what appears to be a type of percussion instrument; the exact instrument is uncertain.

"Kha dpya zer" and related expressions in the sequence of the monks' behavior are idiomatic and rendered according to their natural sense in context. The name "Vassakāra" (Tibetan dbyar byed, literally "one who makes rain" or "rain-maker") is the chief minister referred to throughout. The passage is clearly from the Mahāparinibbāna-sūtra context. The greeting formula rendered as "bowing your head at my feet" and the health-inquiry sequence follow standard sūtra conventions. The phrase rendered "garland-vessel for anointing" (ril ba spyi blugs) refers to a vessel used for ceremonial sprinkling; some uncertainty attaches to the precise nature of the object, but it is a standard royal accoutrement in this narrative. The Capal stūpa (Tibetan tsā pa la'i mchod rten) is the well-known Cāpāla shrine of the Pāli parallel. The phrase rendered "do not establish what has not been established as a rule, and do not discard what has been established" follows the standard Pāli parallel closely. The Tibetan "smon pa" here most naturally corresponds to what in the Pāli is rendered as existing ordinances or conventions; the translation reflects this political-legal sense rather than any devotional meaning of "aspiration."

The phrase "even those who in their youth have cast but a garland of flowers" is a conventional idiom from the Pāli parallel meaning girls of marriageable age who have received even the most token of betrothal tokens; the translation preserves this idiomatic force. The term rendered throughout as "the Vajjians" translates ཡུལ་སྤོང་བྱེད་པ (lit. "those who act as the Vajjians" or "the Vajji country-people"), which corresponds consistently to the Pāli Vajjī. The word མཆོད་རྟེན in this context does not mean a stūpa in the usual Buddhist sense but rather a pre-Buddhist or civic "shrine" or sacred site of the Vajjians, corresponding to Pāli cetiya, here rendered "shrine" to avoid doctrinal confusion. The phrase rendered "kings among long-dwellers" translates a compound in which "gnas brtan rgyal po lta bu" means those who are like kings among the elders, i.e., the most senior and venerable monks. This is a stock simile in early Buddhist canonical texts for the most experienced members of the community.

The phrase "born of joyful desire and arising moment by moment" renders a dense compound about craving for becoming; the Pali parallel (nandirāga) confirms this is craving accompanied by delight. The passage is mid-sentence at its conclusion, as the Tibetan continues directly into further conditions; it has been left open accordingly to signal continuation. The phrase rendered "not troubling those who have come with concern for robes, alms-food" etc. reflects a reading in which arriving practitioners of the holy life are welcomed and not burdened with material anxiety. The Tibetan construction here is slightly compressed, but the sense is clear from parallel Pāli versions of this discourse, where the monks are praised for ensuring visiting brethren are well provided for rather than left to worry over requisites.

The list item translated as "gossip" renders a Tibetan term literally meaning "speech about towns and villages," a standard idiom in the Vinaya literature for worldly gossip and frivolous talk about mundane affairs. The seven limbs of awakening passage presents a compressed syntactic structure in which each limb is implicitly qualified by the same four characteristics — abiding in seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and transformation through relinquishment — that are explicitly stated for mindfulness and equanimity. The translation reflects this parallelism as the Tibetan intends it, consistent with the standard Pāli and Sanskrit presentations of the seven bodhyaṅgas (Sanskrit: saptabodhyaṅga).

The phrase rendered "knowledge of measure" (Tibetan: ཚོད་ཤེས་པ) can also mean knowing moderation or knowing the right amount, a standard term in Buddhist ethical literature referring especially to moderation in eating and in one's activities generally. The village name rendered in Tibetan as "Nāḍa" (དམར་བུ་ཅན) is literally "the reddish one" in Tibetan. This appears to be a rendering of the Pali "Nāḷandā" or possibly "Nādika," depending on the Sanskrit source text. Given the narrative context — traveling between Magadha and Rājagṛha — "Nādika" (the village known from parallel Pali passages such as the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta) is most likely the intended referent, though the Tibetan epithet "the reddish one" does not transparently match either name. The translation preserves "Nāḍa" as a neutrally transliterated placeholder; scholars consulting the source should verify against parallel recensions.

The phrase "Ambalaṭṭhikā" (rendered from the royal resting place description) follows the Pali parallel; the Tibetan reads འོད་མའི་དབྱུག་པ་ཅན, literally "having a staff of light" or "mango-grove-staff" — the correspondence to Ambalaṭṭhikā is contextually plausible but the Tibetan form is unusual. The village name rendered "Nādika" (Tibetan: dmar bu can, literally "the one having red offspring" or "the reddish one") is a Tibetan translation-rendering of the toponym Nādika or Nāḍika, well attested in Pāli parallels (e.g., the Mahāparinibbānasutta) as Nādika or Nāṭika. The Tibetan translates rather than transliterates the place-name, which is a recognized feature of certain canonical translations.

The phrase rendered "confused in mind" for "yid la gcags bzhin du dus byed" is slightly idiomatic; the literal sense is "to die with the mind as though seized or obstructed," meaning to die in a state of mental confusion or distraction, without clarity or composure at the moment of death. This rendering captures the established doctrinal sense. The place name rendered as "Roruka" reflects the Tibetan "དམར་བུ་ཅན," a toponym that likely corresponds to a locality known from Pāli parallels; its exact Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain but the name is kept consistent with the preceding rendering convention. The phrase "pass the time without worry" for "ཡིད་ལ་གཅགས་པ་མེད་པར་དུས་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར" is a reasonable rendering; the Tibetan literally suggests spending time free of mental anguish or brooding concern. The text contains several Pāli technical proper nouns in Tibetan phonetic rendering. "Pāṭaligāma" is the Pāli village name rendered as "དམར་བུ་ཅན་གྱི་གྲོང" in Tibetan. "Vassakāra" is rendered from "དབྱར་བྱེད." The passage is from the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta tradition. The phrase "གནས་ཀྱིས་འདྲེ་བར་གྱུར་ཏོ" meaning that the gods "mingled" or "were intermingled" place by place is a somewhat unusual cosmological observation about auspicious dwelling presence; the translation follows the standard reading. The "Thirty-Three" refers to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the realm of Śakra (Indra) and his thirty-two companion gods. The phrase rendered "city of Rājagṛha" translates a Tibetan term meaning literally "the city of the red-dwelling" or "the city with the red village" — this is the conventional Tibetan rendering of Rājagṛha, and the translation follows the standard identification. The term for the gate dedication at the close is a characteristic narrative flourish found in several Vinaya accounts of the Buddha visiting Rājagṛha; no doctrinal ambiguity arises.

The verse section presents compressed syntax; the rendering follows the most natural reading supported by the commentarial tradition, in which each stanza addresses the merit of the faithful donor who gives to monastics and dedicates the resulting merit to others, including deities. The verse section is terse and somewhat cryptic in the original, and the metaphor of crossing the Ganges functions on two levels simultaneously: the literal crossing and liberation from craving. The rendering attempts to preserve both levels. The final verse couplet about cutting the root of craving is a discrete doctrinal statement appended to the water-crossing image.

The list of names at the very end of the passage is a series of personal names of lay practitioners who have died; the passage breaks off mid-list. Several of these names are phonetically transcribed Tibetan renderings of Sanskrit or Pali originals and some are uncertain in their precise reconstruction. The name rendered "Udraka" is དགེ་བསྙེན་ཨུད་ཀ་ཏ, which likely corresponds to the Pali Uggata. The other names in the list are given in their closest reconstructed form. The full identification of each individual in the list would require collation with the Pali parallel in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. The phrase rendered "fetters that are not in conformity with the higher part" translates the Tibetan for the Pali/Sanskrit distinction between the five lower fetters (orambhāgīya saṃyojana) and the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgīya saṃyojana). Those who abandon the five higher fetters are non-returners (anāgāmin), reborn in pure-abode realms and attaining nirvāṇa there without returning to the desire realm; those who abandon only the three fetters and thin out desire are once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin); those who abandon the three fetters entirely and enter the stream are stream-enterers (srotāpanna). The Tibetan here presents these soteriological categories by description rather than by the standard Sanskrit technical names, and the translation follows the Tibetan phrasing while preserving the doctrinal referents.

The name "Rabhassona" in the preceding passage corresponds here in the Tibetan to "Rab brtson," which literally means "Diligent" or "Supremely Striving." The names in this list are Tibetan translations or transliterations of Indian originals and the exact Sanskrit equivalents are not always certain. The passage on the "Dharma Mirror" presents a notable doctrinal framing: the four factors of confirmed faith in the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and noble discipline serve here as a kind of interior "mirror" by which a noble disciple can verify their own attainment of stream-entry. This is consistent with the standard Pāli parallel in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, where the same teaching is called the Dhammādāsa. The Tibetan term here rendered "category" is rnam grangs, which strictly means "synonym" or "enumeration," but in this stock phrase it functions as a name-category or class-designation for the teaching. The four-fold formula of diligence rendered here corresponds to the classical teaching on the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), presented here in an expanded, repetitive sūtra style. The fourfold application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is similarly given in the abbreviated form standard in Pāli and Sanskrit sūtra parallels. The phrase rendered "grasps the mind and applies it" translates a stock formula for mental effort and sustained engagement. The name rendered "Serkya" is a Tibetan phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name not transparently reconstructable from this passage alone; it may correspond to a name such as Ambapālī's son or another figure known from parallel Pali sources. The Pali parallel (Dīgha Nikāya 16) features a young man named Sīha or a similar figure at Vaiśālī, but "Serkya" (སེར་སྐྱ) most likely renders a Sanskrit name meaning something like "tawny-grey" or may be a personal name; listeners should note this is a proper name rendered phonetically. The verses present some interpretive challenges. The opening image of "the king of Aṅga who wears the jewel-crown" gaining something "through the power of his mother" is an allusion whose precise referent is not entirely clear from the Tibetan alone; it may be an encomiastic comparison to the Blessed One or a genealogical praise-trope. The translation renders it faithfully without over-interpreting. The phrase rendered "the sun that shines surpassing the sun itself in the sky" is deliberately paradoxical in the original and is preserved as such. The term "lodging-keepers" translates a Tibetan term that may refer specifically to those who had arranged or accepted prior hospitality arrangements; the doctrinal point is that the Licchavīs acknowledge Āmrapālī's prior invitation as valid, which reflects a Vinaya-related principle of honoring prior invitations. The phrase rendered "appreciate what has been done and feel what has been done" translates a paired expression indicating gratitude and sensitivity to kindness received — a classical virtue in Pāli and Sanskrit Buddhist literature (kataññu / katavedī). The translation preserves the deliberate repetition of the formula, which is rhetorically significant.

The name Ambapālī is a well-known figure from the Pāli canon; the Tibetan renders her name as "Amra Skyongma," meaning "guardian of the mango grove," which is the exact semantic equivalent. The epithet rendered "Unbound Protector" translates a compound meaning one who is a protector and who is unbound or unfettered, used here as a verse epithet for the Buddha. This is a relatively transparent rendering of the Tibetan; the doctrinal nuance is that the Buddha protects beings while himself being free from all bondage.

The town name "Beluva" translates the Tibetan "Öd ma can" which corresponds to the Pali "Beḷuva" or Sanskrit "Veṇugrāma." The grove in which the Buddha stays is identified as a grove of beluva trees matching the name of the town.

The phrase rendered "hold this feeling in check" refers to the Blessed One suppressing or containing the painful feeling of illness through meditative power, a significant moment in the Mahāparinirvāṇa narrative. The "signless meditative absorption" is the formless samādhi in which no characteristic marks are taken as object. The phrase rendered "held together with straps" translates a term meaning the Tathāgata's body survives by relying on two means (Tib. rnam pa gnyis la brten nas). The precise identity of the "two means" is not specified in this passage; parallel Pāli sources (Dīgha Nikāya, Mahāparinibbānasutta) suggest they are: ordinary meditative states and the signless meditative absorption, though some commentaries differ. This ambiguity is inherent in the source passage.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, consistent with it being a segment of a longer text. The text contains two slightly variant lists of the local shrines and landmarks. In the first occurrence the text reads "Āmra" trees as ཤིང་ཨ་ཀྲ (reading uncertain, possibly a scribal variant of Āmra), while the second occurrence clearly reads ཤིང་ཨ་མྲ, which is the standard rendering of Āmra. The translation harmonises both to Āmra in keeping with the parallel Pāli passage in the Mahāparinibbānasutta, where the same list appears. The summary verse at the head of this portion is a mnemonic colophon marking the end of a fascicle of the Tibetan Vinaya; it is translated as found rather than omitted, since it belongs to the transmitted text. The sentence structure in the Tibetan at the point where the Blessed One recapitulates his earlier exchange with Māra (the Uruvilā passage) is somewhat complex and syntactically embedded. The translation renders this as a flashback quotation for clarity in speech, which is supported by the Pāli parallel. The phrase "thoroughly purifying those who put forward challenges" renders the Tibetan for refuting and purifying one's own position when questioned, and follows the standard commentarial reading. The verse presents a notable interpretive challenge. The image of "bursting open his shell" translates a term evoking a creature emerging from an egg, here applied to the Blessed One's relinquishing of the life-formations through absorbed equipoise. This is a recognized metaphor in the Pāli parallel (the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta context) for breaking free from conditioned existence. The Tibetan term rendered "death-formations" and "life-formations" (tshe'i 'du byed and 'tsho ba'i 'du byed) refers to the volitional formations sustaining life — the Blessed One intentionally withdrawing his supernatural extension of the life-span, an act described in the parallel Pāli narrative as relinquishing the life-principle (āyusaṃkhāra). The phrase rendered "reinforces the life-sustaining formations and relinquishes the will-to-live" translates a technically precise Pāli/Sanskrit concept: the Tathāgata, through meditative power, deliberately suspends the life-force (āyusaṃskāra) rather than allowing it to continue naturally. The Tibetan "tshe kyi 'du byed spangs" (relinquishing the life-formation) is the counterpart of the Pāli āyusaṃkhāraṃ ossajji, a pivotal moment in the parinirvāṇa narrative. The rendering "meteors fall, fires blaze in every direction" for "skar mda' lhung, phyogs tshig" reflects the standard portents listed in the parinirvāṇa sūtra tradition. The phrase rendered "four right abandonings" translates yang dag par spong ba bzhi, the standard Tibetan for the four right efforts or four perfect abandonments (Skt. catvāri samyakprahāṇāni). The rendering "four bases of miraculous power" follows standard tradition for rdzu 'phrul gyi rkang pa bzhi (Skt. catvāri ṛddhipādāḥ). The seven and eight factors (limbs of awakening and the noble eightfold path) are the standard thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyadharma), listed here in part. The verse summary of the route (beginning "Ruṭa, Dumpa, Āmra…") is a mnemonic gāthā listing the sequence of villages traversed; the Tibetan here is compressed and the place-name identifications follow the standard list in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition. "Balaglaṅ" and "Śurva" are Tibetan phonetic renderings of Indic place-names whose exact Sanskrit forms are uncertain; they are rendered here as transliterations.

The phrase rendered "the prosperous city" translates a Tibetan term that in context refers to Pāvā or a similarly named settlement on the route to Kuśinagara; the Tibetan does not make this identification explicit at this point in the text. The long enumeration of divine assemblies corresponds to the standard cosmological list of desire-realm and form-realm deities found across Pāli and Sanskrit sources. The Tibetan names rendered here follow standard Tibetan-to-Sanskrit equivalences: Yāma (མཚེ་མ), Tuṣita (དགའ་ལྡན), Nirmāṇarati (འཕྲུལ་དགའ), Paranirmitavaśavartin (གཞན་འཕྲུལ་དབང་བྱེད), and the form-realm heavens from Brahma's retinue (ཚངས་ལྷ་ཉེ་ཕན) through Akaniṣṭha (འོག་མིན). The rendering of སྲིད་དང་ཞེང as "dominion and majesty" is a considered choice; the phrase likely renders Sanskrit sthāna and vaibhava or similar, referring to a being's rank, stature, and magnificence. The final section, beginning "Therefore, Ānanda, from now on one should engage with the limits of the sūtras," is the locus classicus of the "four great references" (Pāli: cattāri mahāpadesa) teaching on textual authority; this passage corresponds closely to the Mahāparinibbānasutta. The term rendered as "Mātṛkā" in the third scenario refers to the Abhidharma matrix-texts or numerical summary lists — sometimes rendered "doctrinal summaries" — and is paired here with sūtra-holders and Vinaya-holders as the third category of specialist monk. The Tibetan "མ་ལྟ་བུ་འཛིན་པ" is a rendering of Sanskrit mātṛkādhara, a technical term for monks who memorize the Abhidharma or numerical doctrinal lists. This is a genuinely significant textual-historical point.

The fourth scenario introduces a hierarchy of transmission — elders, those who learned from elders, and so on — corresponding to what Indian sources describe as the lineage of oral transmission within a monastery. The passage breaks off mid-scenario as the source text ends here. The term rendered "monks who uphold the Mātṛkā" translates a phrase that in Tibetan reads literally "those who uphold the mother-like" or "those who uphold the matrix text." Mātṛkā here refers to the Abhidharma or proto-Abhidharma summaries, the numerical and categorical lists that formed the basis of doctrinal analysis, a standard third category alongside sūtra and Vinaya in early canonical classification. The passage breaks off mid-sentence in the supplied text, and the continuation follows in the next block. The fourfold structure here is the teaching of the "four great references" or "four great proclamations" (mahāpadesa in Pali), which authenticates teachings by checking them against sūtra, Vinaya, and the nature of reality. The text divides these into a dark side (teachings to be rejected) and a bright side (teachings to be accepted), which is a somewhat condensed presentation compared to the parallel Pali text in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.

The town name rendered "Sāpa" and grove name "Jālikā" are transcribed from the Tibetan phonetics; these correspond to the Pali "Bhoganagara" and grove "Ānanda" in the parallel passage, but I have followed the Tibetan readings rather than harmonizing with the Pali, as the Tibetan may reflect a distinct Sanskrit recension.

The smith's son Cunda here should be distinguished from Cunda the smith who offered the Blessed One his final meal; this appears to be a different individual or the same person introduced in a different narrative context. The Tibetan does not clarify this, and the identification is not certain. The verse section at the end of this passage is a well-known exchange between Cunda and the Buddha found in Pali parallels (Subha Sutta area, DN 29 type material), where four types of "ascetic" (Skt. śramaṇa, here rendered from Tibetan དགེ་སྦྱོང) are enumerated: the path-victor, the path-teacher, the path-liver, and the path-corrupter. The last verse is incomplete in the source as given; the translation renders it up to the point the Tibetan breaks off.

The gesture of placing the robe over one shoulder before addressing the Buddha is a standard Vinaya posture of respectful supplication and is rendered accordingly. The summary verse near the middle of the passage is a colophon-style mnemonic listing the topics of the fifty-second section. The names "Cāpāla" and "Rurutā" are rendered from the Tibetan phonetics; the Sanskrit forms may vary by recension. The river name "Kakuṭṭhā" is the standard Pāli form; the Tibetan reads "Kakusta," which corresponds to it. The phrase rendered "Great Elephant" likely refers to the Blessed One himself, as "great elephant" (mahānāga) is a standard epithet of the Buddha in Vinaya literature. The name "Silāyin" renders the Tibetan sgyu rtsal shes kyi bu ring du 'phur, which is a somewhat unusual construction. The Tibetan appears to preserve the name of a wandering ascetic teacher known in Pāli sources as Pukkusa Mallaputta's teacher, Āḷāra Kālāma in some parallels, but the specific name here — "Silāyin the Magician" — translates sgyu rtsal shes as "one who knows magical arts" and bu ring du 'phur as "son who travels far through the air." It is possible the full phrase is an epithet or title rather than a personal name with patronymic; the rendering here treats it as a name-cum-epithet consistent with the narrative context. The parallel Pāli passage in the Mahāparinibbānasutta (DN 16) names this figure as Pukkusa Mallaputta, a disciple of Āḷāra Kālāma, which confirms the general identification but does not resolve the specific Tibetan nomenclature with certainty. The town name rendered throughout as "Ātumā" corresponds to the Pāli Āṭumā, a known location in canonical texts. The Tibetan spelling ཨ་དུ་མ་ཡ and ཨ་དུ་མན་དུར reflects this place name with case suffixes.

The proper name "Gyad" renders a Tibetan transcription of what in Pāli sources is the Oḍḍhaddha or similar clan affiliation; the exact Sanskrit or Pāli identification of this clan name in the Tibetan transmission is uncertain and may warrant further comparison with parallel Pāli versions of this sūtra episode, which appears to correspond to the Aṭṭhaka-sutta or a related account of the storm at Āṭumā. The river name rendered as "Kakudhā" is the standard Sanskrit equivalent of the Tibetan "dbyig ldan" — this is the river near Kuśinagara where, according to the Mahāparinirvāṇa accounts, the Buddha bathed before his final passing.

The phrase translated as "equal and unequalled" renders Tibetan "mnyam pa dang mi mnyam pa," a classical paradoxical formulation meaning that these two meal offerings are equal to each other and yet unequalled by any other — a standard doctrinal expression found in Pali and Sanskrit parinirvāṇa literature (Pali: "samasama"). The monk named "Sunakkhatta" appears here as "འདུན་པ" in the Tibetan. This is a Pali name rendered into Tibetan; the form given here follows the name as it appears in the context. The identification is reasonably secure from parallel passages in the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra tradition.

The "brahmic penalty" (tshangs pa'i chad pa) refers to a specific formal disciplinary measure in the Vinaya tradition: the community collectively ceases to speak with the offending monk, effectively cutting off all normal interaction. It is the inverse of a proclamation and is called "brahmic" because Brahmā himself is said to observe this form of silent withdrawal.

The final verse ends mid-sentence in the source passage as given; the translation preserves this incompleteness, as the text breaks off at that point. The phrase rendered "those who hold the Abhidharma" translates a term literally meaning "those who hold the Mātṛkā," an early term for the Abhidharma matrix texts; this is a standard identification in the tradition and requires no further gloss.

The "ten powers of wisdom" refers to the ten powers (daśabala) of a Tathāgata, here specifically characterized in terms of wisdom. The verse line identifies the monk who taught as one whom the Buddha himself had declared to be foremost in wisdom, a reference consistent with the figure of Śāriputra in comparable narrative contexts, though the text does not name him explicitly here. The phrase rendered "this great feast of Dharma, this singular thing" translates a construction in which "great feast of Dharma" and "singular" describe the Buddha's unsurpassed Dharma teaching as a unique and peerless treasure now lost to the world. The Tibetan "ཆོས་ཀྱི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཆེན་པོ་འབའ་ཞིག་པོ" could also be rendered "this one sole great enjoyment of Dharma," with "sole" or "singular" emphasizing its irreplaceability; the rendering above preserves that sense. The passage's rhetorical structure is slightly irregular in the Tibetan, repeating the formula about the wheel-turning king's retinue partway through the Ānanda parallel before the second set of four qualities. This appears to be a textual feature of the Tibetan rather than a translational issue, and the translation follows it faithfully.

"Sāketa" renders གནས་བཅས, which is a standard Tibetan equivalent for that city. "Campā" renders ཙམ་པ.

The term རྩང (staircase or landing of a gate) is rendered as "staircase" in context with gate architecture, though "pillar" or "post" is occasionally proposed; "staircase" is the more standard reading here and fits the architectural list. The passage lists several Sanskrit flower names transliterated into Tibetan. Where standard Sanskrit equivalents are well-attested — utpala (blue lotus), padma (lotus), kumuda (white water lily), puṇḍarīka-class whites, campaka, mālikā, navamālikā, yūthikā — they have been rendered accordingly. The term rendered "yellow jasmine" for skya snar is an approximation; the Sanskrit equivalent may be tagara or a related aromatic. Dhānuskari is a phonetic transliteration whose botanical identification is uncertain.

The phrase "King Mahāsudarśana" appears here for the first time by name in this passage — in the Tibetan it reads rgyal po legs mthong chen po, literally "the great king of excellent appearance," the standard Tibetan rendering of Mahāsudarśana. This name was used in the preceding portion already, so it has been rendered consistently.

The section ends mid-sentence in the source text; the translation breaks at exactly the same point. The term rendered "lord" in the people's address to the charioteer is literally "the god" (lha), used here as a royal honorific for the king — a common usage in Tibetan sūtra literature for a cakravartin monarch, not a reference to a divine being. This honorific flavor is preserved contextually without cluttering the prose.

The twelve sounds: the text explicitly numbers them as twelve (sounded in the prior passage and the count closed here). The list in the preceding passage contains ten items; this passage adds the paṭaha drum, music, song, and flute (four more), but also includes three proclamatory sounds ("Generosity has been given," "Merit has been made," "Those who fast have taken up ethical conduct"), bringing the total to twelve as stated. The grouping is internally consistent in the Tibetan. The phrase rendered "Dharma-fitting palace" translates a compound meaning a palace built in accordance with the Dharma, that is, through righteous means. The repetition of the offering and refusal cycle two and three times is a standard formulaic trope in this literature indicating persistent, earnest entreaty. The honorific verbal forms directed at the king have been rendered with appropriate dignity without being archaic. The passage includes a standard fascicle-division colophon marking the boundary between the fifty-third and fifty-fourth fascicles of the Vinaya Kṣudrakavastu; it has been rendered in plain prose as it appears in the text.

The architectural terminology presents consistent interpretive challenges. Terms such as ཀ་རྟེན, ཀ་ཞུ, བྲེ་ཕུལ, གདུང་, གདུང་ཕྲན, མདུན་གདུང, གདུང་པོ་ཆེ, བ་གམ, སྤང་ལེབ, ལན་ཀན, གཟུངས་གཟེར, རྟེན་མ, and གདུང་བུ refer to specific structural elements of a multi-story palace. The renderings given — base-support, column-cap, bracket-block, crossbeam, secondary rafter, front beam, main roof beam, wall-panel, wall-slab, railing, dowel-pin, support-post, baluster-shaft — reflect reasonable correspondences to traditional South Asian timber architecture but cannot be verified with certainty against the original Sanskrit architectural vocabulary. The throne furnishings — Golika cloth, Mentri cushions, Armonig cushions, Kāliṅga cloth — are Sanskrit loanwords transcribed into Tibetan (go li ka, men tri, ar mo nig, kā liṅ ka) referring to specific luxury textiles and furnishing styles known in the Indian courtly tradition; their precise identification is uncertain, and they are rendered here by approximate transliteration following scholarly convention.

The term rendered "owl-feather cushions" (za 'ug gi stan) literally means a cushion made of or styled after the owl; this may refer to a particular style of soft cushioning rather than literal feathers, but the exact referent is uncertain. The phrase rendered "five-part instrument" translates a term referring to a musical instrument with five components or registers — likely the classical Indian vīṇā or similar; the exact instrument is not specified in the text. The phrase "fine woven cloth garments" renders a term for a type of high-quality textile; the precise identification is uncertain but the rendering conveys the general sense adequately. The "royal sage's holy celibate life" renders a compound meaning the brahmacarya practiced by a royal ṛṣi — a life of celibacy and renunciation while remaining nominally a king, a recognized category in Indian Buddhist narrative literature. The elephant king's name, rendered here as "Nearby Restoration," translates the Tibetan ཉེ་བའི་གསོ་སྦྱོང་, literally "the nearby poṣadha," where གསོ་སྦྱོང་ (poṣadha) can refer to the Buddhist observance day but in this cosmological context is a proper epithet of the elephant king. The rendering follows the literal meaning and may correspond to a Sanskrit epithet such as Upapoṣadha; this is a well-known name in wheel-turning monarch narratives. The chariot name དགའ་དབྱངས་ (Joyful Sound) and the horse king སྤྲིན་གྱི་ཤུགས་ཅན་ (Cloud-Force) are straightforward literal renderings of Tibetan epithets. The term rendered "Near-Observance" for the elephant king's name (Tibetan: ཉེ་བའི་གསོ་སྦྱོང) literally means "near poṣadha" or "approaching the observance day." It is a proper name in this narrative context and the rendering attempts to convey its literal sense. The exact Sanskrit original is uncertain; some versions read differently.

The phrase rendered "Three-Balconied" for the mansion name (ཁང་པ་རྩེག་མ་བ་གམ་ཅན) literally means "the multi-storied mansion possessing three balconies/terraces," treated here as a proper epithet of that category's lead example. The phrase rendered "frontier lords" translates a compound meaning lords of the border regions or districts, here prefaced by "jewel minister" as the lead exemplar; this matches the preceding passage's usage. The repetition of the full list of possessions in both the queen's speech and the retinue's reply is faithful to the Tibetan, which genuinely repeats the catalogue twice. The phrase "ཁམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་ཕྲན་" in the queen's initial speech and "མཐའི་རྒྱལ་ཕྲན་" in the retinue's reply differ slightly in wording but appear to refer to the same category; "frontier lords" is used for both. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, describing distances from Kuśāvatī. This is simply where the supplied passage ends and is not a translation problem.

The phrase rendered "reborn on an equal footing" translates a term meaning "born equally" or "born in parity" in the Brahmā world, indicating rebirth at the same level as the Brahmā gods — a standard doctrinal point about the fruit of the four divine abodes. The epithet "the capable" (Tib. thub pa) applied to the gods of many hundreds of kalpas is unusual. It likely refers to gods who have accumulated the power (thub pa = capable/enduring) over vast cosmic time, but it may be a compressed reference to gods associated with a particular class of long-lived beings. The rendering reflects the literal Tibetan without over-interpreting.

The phrase rendered "radiant proximity" translates 'od pa bzhin nye bar gnas pa, literally "dwelling near, like light" — a slightly opaque phrase likely referring to the supernatural quality of being luminously present and accessible. This is a genuinely uncertain reading. The passage moves between two distinct narrative threads: first, a past-life story set during the time of buddha Kāśyapa, in which the duty-monk's aspiration leads to his eventual rebirth as an arhat under Śākyamuni; and second, the Blessed One's instructions to Ānanda on relic veneration after his passing. The shift is abrupt in the Tibetan and has been rendered accordingly.

The phrase rendered "duty-monk" translates dge skos, the monk assigned rotating administrative duties in a monastery; this technical Vinaya term has been rendered descriptively for clarity in speech.

The aspiration prayer is syntactically complex in the Tibetan and involves an embedded prophecy (lung bstan) within the aspirational frame; the rendering preserves this structure as faithfully as readability permits. The phrase rendered "warrior-nobles" translates a term referring to the Malla clan, the ruling warrior aristocracy of Kuśinagara (Sanskrit: Malla), who in Pāli sources are consistently called Mallā. The Tibetan renders this as "gyad," a term for powerful warriors or heroes. Keeping "warrior-nobles" maintains the social register without importing the Sanskrit clan name mid-sentence, which would interrupt the flow.

The phrase "foundations of training" renders the standard formula for lay refuge and the five precepts. The Tibetan here gives only the refuge formula explicitly; the precepts are implied by "foundations of training."

The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the passage supplied ends there; no content has been added or invented beyond what the Tibetan provides. The name rendered "Rabjā" is Tibetan for "Pramudita," meaning "Greatly Joyful," and functions as a proper name for the gandharva king. The epithet Kauśika is a standard name for Śakra (Indra). The five kinds of seeing refers to the five considerations by which a bodhisattva in Tuṣita surveys before taking his final birth: the right time, the right continent, the right land, the right clan, and the right mother. The "thirty-six billion" renders bye ba phrag sum bcu rtsa drug, literally thirty-six sets of ten thousand, i.e., 360,000,000; some editions may vary in this figure. The epithet "gandharva and more" renders ང་དྲི་ཟ་ཏེ་པོར་ཡིན་ནོ, where ཏེ་པོ conveys "and something beyond" or "and more besides" — a pointed double meaning, since the Blessed One is both literally playing the role of a gandharva musician and is, of course, far more than that. This wordplay is integral to the narrative's irony and is preserved in the rendering. The phrase rendered "the last couch" for ཐ་མའི་གཟིམས་མལ is a reference to the Blessed One's final resting place before parinirvāṇa, a standard Pali and Sanskrit idiom. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, which reflects the source text's continuation into the next segment. The phrase rendered as "blazed with a brilliant, clear radiance" translates the Tibetan idiom me lhan ne lhang nger gyur, a vivid sensory expression suggesting the grove lit up or shone brightly; the exact nuance is picturesque rather than technically doctrinal.

The city rendered "Kuśinagara" appears in the Tibetan as grong khyer rtsa can, literally "the city with grass," which is a Tibetan calque for Kuśinagara (Pāli: Kusinārā); context and tradition confirm the identification. The six teachers named are the well-known "six heterodox teachers" of the Pāli tradition. The Tibetan names correspond to Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (the Jain leader Mahāvīra), and Ajita Kesakambalī or Kaccāyana. The rendering follows standard identifications from parallel Pāli sources (Dīgha Nikāya, Mahāparinibbānasutta). The verse section is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan and the passage ends mid-sentence in the source, which is reflected faithfully by ending the translation at the same point. The passage contains Subhadra's parinirvāṇa blessing-visions, which are part of a canonical narrative preserved in several Vinaya and sūtra traditions. The "five places" Subhadra intends to bless are enumerated in what follows; only the first part of the list appears in the passage translated here, so the full sequence is not yet visible.

The exchange between Subhadra and the Blessed One — "do you speak in order for yourself to pass into nirvāṇa, or for the Blessed One to pass into nirvāṇa?" — reflects a delicate grammatical ambiguity in classical Tibetan that the dialogue format itself resolves: Subhadra clarifies that he is requesting the Blessed One's consent to his own prior nirvāṇa, not commenting on the Buddha's. The name "Rabzang" renders the Tibetan kun du rgyu rab bzang, which is a Tibetan translation of what is likely a Sanskrit name meaning something like "excellent wanderer" or "supremely good peripatetic." In the preceding passage it was rendered "Rabzang" for consistency; the full meaning is "the Excellent Wanderer." This is the figure known in Pali sources as Subhadda, the last direct disciple of the historical Buddha — though the narrative here differs from the Pali account in significant ways.

The phrase "joints severed and articulations splitting" renders gnad rnams ni chad, tshigs rnams ni 'bye ba, a description of the severe physical pain the dying Buddha was experiencing, understood in the tradition as signaling the approach of parinirvāṇa. The epithet "the city of Kuśa" renders གྲོང་ཁྱེར་རྩྭ་ཅན, literally "the city of grass," which most probably corresponds to Kuśinagara (Kuśa being the sacred grass); the earlier passage rendered it as "Kusināra," so consistency is maintained by the phrase "city of Kuśa." The phrase སྲོག་སྡུག་པའི་སྐྱབས, "refuge precious as life itself," is a somewhat unusual compound meaning shelter that is as dear to them as their own lives, or alternatively that he offered refuge at the cost of his own life; both meanings are in play and the translation preserves the resonance without choosing artificially between them. The horse's name, literally "Knows-the-Art-of-War" or "Knows-Military-Craft," is rendered "Wise-Knowing" throughout for consistency with the established translation. The precise nuance of the Tibetan compound (རྟ་ཅང་ཤེས, "horse knowing the art") is one of military skill rather than generic wisdom, but "Wise-Knowing" is preserved here as the established proper name rendering. A note on the pool's bird species: kāraṇḍava is a standard Sanskrit waterfowl name retained in the text; ངུར་པ (heron) follows the most common identification. The bird ཤང་ཤང་ཏེའུ is an uncertain compound; it may refer to a type of flycatcher or similar bird and is rendered generically. The verse near the end is the well-known karma-stanza found across several Vinaya and Abhidharma contexts; it is rendered here according to its standard doctrinal meaning. The phrase rendered "waiting like a flame near at hand" translates a metaphor implying that the karma is present and luminous, poised for inevitable fruition — a standard image for karma that is "definite to be experienced" in this very life or in a near future life. The term rendered "long-lived Supriya" (Tibetan: tshe dang ldan pa Rab bzang) is a standard honorific form of address for an elder monk; "long-lived" renders the formulaic tshe dang ldan pa (Sanskrit āyuṣman). "Cañjaśa" is kept consistent with the preceding passage's rendering of the horse's name. The epithet "Anāthapiṇḍada" rendered here as "Sorrowless" follows the Tibetan mya ngan med, which means "without sorrow." This is distinct from the famous lay patron Anāthapiṇḍada of the Pāli and Sanskrit traditions; in the Tibetan, the name given is mya ngan med, meaning "sorrowless" or "Anātha" in the sense of being free from grief. The rendering follows the Tibetan literally throughout.

The phrase rendered "knower of the world" translates 'jig rten mkhyen pa, a standard epithet of the Buddha corresponding to Sanskrit lokavid.

The syntax of the god's aspiration prayer at the close is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan; the translation unpacks it to make the sequence of intended events clear for the listener. The phrase "matted fiery hair" renders the Tibetan me ba ral pa can literally. This is most likely a reference to the Jaṭilas, the fire-worshipping ascetics with matted hair, such as the Kāśyapa brothers and their followers, who were among the earliest converts. The Vinaya tradition preserves a specific exemption for this group from the four-month probationary period required of other non-Buddhist wanderers. The identity of "Subhadrā" as the god named Supriya or Subhadra, the brahmin boy disciple of Kāśyapa referenced in the preceding passage, is consistent with the narrative logic of the prophecy section immediately prior. The twelve-fold wheel of Dharma refers to the standard formulation of the Four Noble Truths each presented in three aspects of recognition, application, and attainment, yielding twelve aspects in total.

The list of twelve textual categories corresponds to the traditional twelvefold classification of canonical literature known in Sanskrit as the dvādaśāṅga-pravacana. The rendering of individual categories follows their standard Tibetan-Sanskrit correspondences: sūtra, geya (mixed prose and verse), vyākaraṇa (prophetic declaration), gāthā (verse), udāna (intentional saying), nidāna (origin narrative), avadāna (story of spiritual attainment), itivṛttaka (account of past deeds), jātaka (birth story), vaipulya (extensive teaching), adbhutadharma (marvellous Dharma), and upadeśa (established doctrine).

The phrase rendered "nets" in the list of monastic requisites is genuinely uncertain; this term may refer to a kind of filtering cloth or strainer used by monks, and its precise identification is debated among commentators. The phrase rendered "some shall go with a remainder of the aggregates still present" refers to rebirth in a higher realm rather than nirvāṇa — that is, they attain a fortunate rebirth but not yet final liberation. This reflects the classical distinction between those who attain liberation at death versus those reborn in higher realms due to faith. The repetition of the four sacred sites formula in this passage is faithful to the source, which genuinely repeats the full formula multiple times in succession. The phrase "prophesy the answer" renders lung bstan pa, which in this conversational context means "to give an authoritative declaration or answer," not eschatological prophecy in a narrow sense — though the same term covers both meanings elsewhere. The phrase rendered "the eye of peaceful, unmoving stillness" translates a description of the physical eyes of the deceased body — the Blessed One's eyes remain open and still, serene and motionless. This is a recognized Indian literary and doctrinal topos for the moment of parinirvāṇa; the Tibetan zhiba mi g.yo ba'i spyan refers literally to eyes that are peaceful and unmoving, a sign the body has entered final cessation.

The sequence of absorptions described here — ascending through the four dhyānas and four formless spheres to the cessation of perception and feeling, then descending in reverse, and finally ascending again to the fourth dhyāna where parinirvāṇa occurs — is the canonical account found across multiple recensions of the Mahāparinirvāṇa literature and is doctrinally significant: the Buddha's final passing occurs from the fourth dhyāna, not from the cessation attainment. The phrase "body-servant" for ལུས་འཕགས་མའི་བུ" is textually odd and may reflect a title or epithet of Ajātaśatru that is obscure; the Tibetan literally reads "son of the one whose body is noble" or possibly "son of Vaidehī" (a known epithet of Ajātaśatru's mother Queen Vaidehī). The rendering here follows context and parallel passages in this genre. Some translators render this as "son of Vaidehī," which is doctrinally standard in accounts of Ajātaśatru.

The term "rootless faith" (རྩ་བ་མེད་པའི་དད་པ) is a technical term from Vinaya and narrative literature describing Ajātaśatru's particular form of devotion, rooted in remorse for parricide rather than in prior spiritual accumulation — it is left as a doctrinal term of art here.

The gosirṣa sandalwood treatment across seven bowls of butter is a resuscitation procedure attested in other versions of the Mahāparinirvāṇa narrative cycle. The phrase rendered "gods of the Mighty One" translates a compound that literally reads "the gods, as many as exist, of the Capable One / the Mighty One" — a standard epithet for the Buddha as "the Sage" or "Capable One." The syntax here is compressed and the sentence structure slightly irregular; the taunt that follows is attributed to those gods, directed at the lamenting monks.

The stupa described as "crowned with a warrior's diadem" renders a compound suggesting a commemorative or reliquary monument ornamented in the manner of a warrior's crown — the precise referent is a specific stupa in the Kuśinagara region, named by the manner of its construction or ornamentation.

The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the provided text being a fragment; no translation is invented beyond what is given. The phrase rendered "those who lived on wages" translates a term for those maintained by milk-whey or similar provisions, indicating a class of dependents or hired servants in the household; the exact social category is context-dependent but the general sense of household dependents is clear. The phrase "into the realm of complete cessation without remainder" renders the standard technical compound for the nirvāṇa without residue, literally the "nirvāṇa-realm without remaining aggregates," which is the parinirvāṇa. The final phrase "venerating and adorning him" renders a sequence of three terms of veneration that slightly overlap; the translation condenses them naturally for oral delivery. The phrase rendered "golden bier" translates a term meaning golden stretcher or carrying frame, used to bear the body in procession; "bier" is the most natural English equivalent in a funerary context. The distance of twelve yojanas is given in the text as a measurement along the processional route, which is notably large; this is a standard hagiographic amplification and is rendered faithfully without reduction. The phrase rendered "shrine adorned with a diadem by the Mallas" translates a Tibetan expression referring to a stūpa (caitya) crowned or decorated with a diadem-like finial by the Mallas. The Pāli parallel (Mahāparinibbānasutta, DN 16) identifies this as the Makuṭabandhana shrine of the Mallas, and "diadem-bound" is its standard epithet. This is preserved in the translation as "shrine adorned with a diadem by the Mallas" to reflect both the Tibetan wording and the known referent. The "champion" who raised the garland on the stūpa is the same figure referenced in the preceding passage as a hero or strong-man among the Mallas; the term rendered "champion" translates the Tibetan word for a warrior of exceptional strength.

The elder who speaks the improper words is understood by the tradition to be Subhadra the Elder, distinct from Subhadra the last personal disciple of the Buddha; the passage becomes the canonical occasion that motivates Mahākāśyapa to convene the First Council. This is doctrinally significant context, though the name does not appear in the passage itself. The epithet ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་སྐུལ་བྱེད་ཆེན་པོ rendered as "Mahāmaudgalyāyana" follows the standard identification in this narrative context, though the Tibetan literally means "the great impeller" or "the great instigator," which corresponds to Maudgalyāyana's epithet in some traditions. This identification should be verified against the broader textual tradition if the full name matters for the critical edition.

The phrase ཡུལ་སྡིག་པ་ཅན, rendered "the region of the sinful country," is a toponym of uncertain precise location; it appears to refer to a place name rather than a generic moral description, but no Sanskrit equivalent is recoverable from this passage alone. The four trees arising from the milk used to extinguish the funeral pyre is a striking narrative detail with no standard Sanskrit parallel immediately to hand; the names given in Tibetan are rendered interpretively. "The Golden One" translates gser can; "the Pale Yellow One" renders ser skya; "the Horse-Wish" renders rta don; and Udumbara is the fig tree Ficus racemosa, kept as a proper name throughout the tradition.

"The wicked country" renders yul sdig pa can throughout, likely a translation of a place name such as Pāpīyans or Pāpa, a republic mentioned in Pāli accounts of the relic distribution (the Mallas of Pāvā). The rendering follows the Tibetan literally, as the doctrinal context is a narrative account of territorial claims to the Buddha's relics.

Buluka and Ṭoka represent Tibetan transliterations of names corresponding to Pāli Buḷi and Alakappa in the parallel Pāli account. Viṣṇudvīpa renders kha byab 'jug gling, literally "the island of Viṣṇu," identified with Vethadīpa in Pāli sources. The passage presents a narrative repetition characteristic of the Āgama style, in which instructions are given and then repeated verbatim when carried out. The translation preserves this repetition faithfully rather than condensing it, as it is structurally and doctrinally intentional.

The phrase rendered "fourfold army" refers to the classical Indian army of four divisions: elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. The figure described as "equal to a brahmin of the brahmin lineage" (bram ze'i rigs bre bo dang mnyam pa) is a slightly puzzling designation. In parallel Sanskrit and Pāli accounts of the distribution of the Buddha's relics, the mediator is Droṇa (Pāli: Doṇa), a brahmin. The Tibetan phrase may be a rendering of a name or epithet that has been rendered somewhat opaquely in transmission. The term "bre bo" could indicate a specific measure or title; taken in context with parallel accounts, this figure is most plausibly Droṇa the brahmin, though the Tibetan phrase is rendered literally here rather than substituting the Sanskrit name, since the text itself does not explicitly give that name in this passage. The Tibetan ཡུལ་མ་ག་དྷཱའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལུས་འཕགས་མའི་བུ་མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲ is a rendering of Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī (Skt. Vaidehīputra Ajātaśatru), king of Magadha. The name Ajātaśatru is not spelled out in the Tibetan but is given through its semantic components: མ་སྐྱེས་དགྲ means "enemy not yet born" (Ajātaśatru) and ལུས་འཕགས་མའི་བུ means "son of Vaidehī." This is the standard identification.

The term སོལ་བ rendered as "charcoal" refers to the embers or charcoal remaining after the cremation fire — a standard element of the relic-distribution narrative in the Mahāparinirvāṇa literature. The phrase rendered "the world of the three summits" translates "rtsa gsum 'jig rten" which is a somewhat cryptic geographical or cosmological reference. It may indicate the three peaks of the cosmic world-mountain or a specific location known to the tradition; the exact identity is uncertain.

The term rendered "mahāmāyā texts" translates "ma mo dag," which literally means "mahāmāyā" or possibly "the māyā texts." In some manuscript traditions this refers to a class of texts associated with the teaching; its precise meaning in this context is uncertain and may be a technical term for a specific category of Dharma literature.

"Tsig-dzin" is a transliteration of the Tibetan place name "tsig 'dzin grong khyer"; its Sanskrit equivalent is not established here.

"Skar-snar" likewise is a Tibetan toponym without a clear Sanskrit equivalent in this context. The long sequence of rhetorical questions near the end is attributed in the Tibetan grammar to Vāṇadatta's inner reflection as he receives the message, prompted by the habitual imprint of loving-kindness. The syntax is ambiguous about whether these are Gaṅgapoṣa's thoughts or Vāṇadatta's; the passage most naturally reads as Vāṇadatta's concerned inner deliberation upon hearing the summons, and the translation renders it accordingly.

The city name rendered as "Tṛṇāvatī" corresponds to the Tibetan "རྩྭ་ཅན," meaning "having grass," a standard equivalent of that Sanskrit toponym. The passage names "ཇོ་བོ་གང་པོ" and "ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་གང་པོ" as one figure (a senior monk named Gaṅgāpāla), and "ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་བ་ལང་བདག" as another (Vālambhaka). These names are reconstructed from the Tibetan phonetic rendering; the Sanskrit originals are uncertain, and scholars may propose alternatives. The identification of "ཇོ་བོ་གང་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་སོགས་པ་དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ཞེས་སྨྲས་པའི་རིགས་ན་འོད་སྲུང་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཞེས་སྨྲའམ" is syntactically compressed and concerns a polemical question about whether certain monks equate their community with that of the Buddha — the rendering given reflects the most plausible reading. The self-immolation of Vālambhaka, consuming his body by inner fire with water flowing from the relics, is a standard hagiographic motif for the passing of a great elder. The epithet rendered here as "Valandhara" represents the figure called bā laṅ bdag in Tibetan, a name meaning "lord of oxen" or "master of cattle," used consistently in the preceding passage as a monk's name or byname. The Sanskrit form would likely be Vṛṣabhadatta or similar; the Tibetan is left as "Valandhara" per the preceding rendering for consistency.

The phrase describing Ajātaśatru as "son of the Licchavī lady" renders lus 'phags ma'i bu, literally "son of the Licchavī woman," a standard way of referring to his maternal lineage in certain textual traditions, though some traditions identify his mother differently. This is a genuine doctrinal-historical point worth flagging.

The appointment of Ānanda as chu'i zhal ta ba, "water-bearer" or "one who oversees the water," is a detail specific to accounts of the First Council (Rājagṛha council) and refers to a humble preparatory role assigned to Ānanda before the council convened, consistent with the narrative that he was still a learner (śaikṣa) at that time. The phrase rendered "the Blessed One himself has entrusted the teaching of the Blessed One to me" is spoken by Ajātaśatru and is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan. The king appears to mean that because the Blessed One entrusted his teaching to disciples like Mahākāśyapa, honouring Mahākāśyapa is the proper continuation of his devotion to the Blessed One. The translation follows this reading.

The two-fold Vinaya act (formal motion plus single recitation of the act) is a standard Vinaya procedure; the translation preserves its repetitive, formulaic character, which is intentional and canonical, not an error. The passage contains a narrative curiosity: Mahākāśyapa addresses Ananda and declares him still "in training" (a learner, Skt. śaikṣa, as opposed to an arhat), and then Ananda himself enters the fourth dhyāna and upon examination also perceives that Ananda alone among the assembly is still in training. The Tibetan syntax at that point uses a third-person construction even while reporting Ananda's own examination, which is consistent with the tradition that Ananda attained arhatship only after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa and just before the First Council — this episode is part of that narrative. The slightly awkward self-reference in the Tibetan is preserved in the translation as faithfully as possible.

The term translated "the Vaidehī queen" renders ལུས་འཕགས་མའི་བུ, literally "son of Vaidehī," the standard epithet of Ajātaśatru; "Vaidehī" is the name of his mother. The phrase rendered "take up a sīla-wood" translates ཚུལ་ཤིང་ཟུང་ཤིག. The term ཚུལ་ཤིང (literally "rule-stick" or "tally-stick") refers to a voting or confession tally used in Vinaya procedures. The full expression here likely means "come and take up the formal tally," that is, submit to a formal Vinaya examination of offenses. This is a technical Vinaya term and its precise procedural meaning in context — whether it refers to a tally-stick vote, a formal charge, or a public confession procedure — is not entirely certain from this passage alone.

The phrase ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལ་གནོད་པ ("harm to the dharmakāya") is striking. In this narrative context, dharmakāya most likely refers to the body of the Dharma-teaching in its totality rather than the ontological truth-body of a buddha, though the double resonance may be intentional. The passage lists the five offenses attributed to Ānanda during the First Council, a standard enumeration found in Vinaya literature. The sixth offense concerning the Prātimokṣa and minor rules is the canonical account from the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition, which this text follows.

The river name rendered "Kakuṭṭhā" (Tibetan: ཀ་ཀུས་སྟ) is the river near Kuśinagara where the Buddha drank before his passing; the spelling follows standard Sanskrit attestation.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the input ("from the four rules entailing defeat through the four rules requiring individual acknowledgment inclusive —"), indicating the Tibetan source itself breaks off here and the translation faithfully reflects that incompleteness. The passage contains a series of alternative formulations defining "minor and lesser rules" by progressively shorter lists of named rule-categories. This repetitive structure is characteristic of Vinaya textual composition and is faithfully rendered here in sequence.

The phrase rendered "the concealed and sunken places of the Tathāgata's body" refers to the retracted or hidden physical marks of the Buddha — specifically those among the thirty-two major marks or eighty minor marks that are concealed, such as the retracted male organ. This is a standard Vinaya narrative detail. The exclamation "Ālālā" is a Tibetan transliteration of an Indic expression of astonishment or acclamation, here used by the gods. It is not a term of grief but of admiring wonder, which the context of the subsequent proclamation confirms.

The passage involves two distinct speeches interleaved: Ānanda addresses Mahākāśyapa, recalling the Buddha's own parting words to him; the narration is compressed and the boundaries between Ānanda's current speech and the quoted words of the Buddha can be difficult to parse cleanly. The rendering follows the most natural reading given the doctrinal context of the First Council narrative. The term rendered "Abhidharma" translates མ་མོ, which is an unusual orthography; it most likely represents a phonetic rendering of "Abhidharma" in this context of the canonical threefold division of scripture (sūtra, Vinaya, Abhidharma), though the spelling is irregular and worth noting for text-critical purposes.

The phrase describing Ānanda's liberation — "not yet having laid his head upon the pillow" — follows the well-known narrative in which Ānanda attains arhatship at the precise moment of lying down, between sitting and lying, and is a doctrinally significant detail preserved here faithfully. The phrase rendered "overcoming the lion throne with his radiance" translates a Tibetan idiom meaning that the brilliance of the person sitting upon it eclipses the throne itself — a conventional expression of the sitter's spiritual eminence. This is a recognized literary formula rather than a doubtful reading.

The passage contains an abrupt shift: Ānanda's recitation of the sūtra opening triggers grief among those not yet free of attachment, and then — following their lament — the text quotes directly from the First Turning of the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī, beginning with the noble truth of suffering. The juxtaposition is in the source text and is not a translation anomaly. The phrase rendered "one less than five hundred arhats" translates a group just short of five hundred, meaning four hundred and ninety-nine. The syntax in context suggests this is a formulaic way of indicating nearly the full complement of arhats gathered for the council, with one position unfilled — almost certainly referring to the absence of Ānanda, who as a stream-enterer at the time of the first council was technically not yet an arhat. This is a well-known episode in the Vinaya accounts of the first Buddhist council.

The phrase rendered "the Sages Who Speak Truth" is a translation of the Tibetan name for the Ṛṣipatana or Mṛgadāva deer park at Sarnath; the Tibetan gives it as "the grove of the sage who speaks truth," a standard Tibetan rendering of Ṛṣipatana or a related epithet for Sarnath. The passage contains a transitional summary section indicating that the compiler is condensing and cross-referencing material from other discourses, using the conventions of Vinaya or sūtra compilation. The phrase rendered "from the passage beginning 'one who finds it incomplete' down to..." reflects a standard Tibetan editorial convention of indicating abbreviated repetition by citing the opening and closing phrases of a passage that is to be understood as reproduced in full from elsewhere. The final sentence breaks off mid-construction in the Tibetan, consistent with an interrupted passage; the translation reflects this faithfully. The classification of sūtras in this passage follows the traditional scheme of the Āgama collections and their Tibetan equivalents; the categories rendered here correspond to the skandhaka, āyatana, nidāna, śrāvakabhāṣita, buddhabhāṣita, bodhipakṣya, uddāna, sūtra, dīrgha, madhyama, and ekottarika groupings known from the Sarvāstivāda transmission. The phrase rendered "those among the five hundred arhats who had not yet been born" is a somewhat elliptical Tibetan idiom referring to arhats who had not yet taken rebirth after parinirvāṇa, or more likely those among the five hundred who were not yet fully assembled or present in that moment. The exact nuance is debated in commentarial literature; contextually it refers to those of the assembly who participated by entering meditative absorption to verify the recitation.

The "circular fashion" of wearing robes translates a technical Vinaya term describing the proper mode of wearing the lower and upper monastic robes with the hem forming an even, level line around the body. The term "Māmakī" is used here in an unusual technical sense within the Vinaya narrative: it does not refer to the tantric deity Māmakī but appears to designate a specific compilation or recension of doctrinal categories, described as making "the defining characteristics of all that is to be known perfectly clear." The passage is somewhat opaque, and the framing "I alone shall speak what is called Māmakī" may reflect a sectarian or textual-historical claim embedded in this version of the council narrative. The exact doctrinal identity of "Māmakī" in this context is genuinely uncertain.

The progression of celestial realms listed — from earth-dwelling yakṣas upward through the heavens of the desire realm and form realm, culminating in Akaniṣṭha — follows a standard cosmological sequence, with the joyful proclamation rippling upward through the entire universe at the moment of the Dharma's compilation. The name rendered "Linen-Clad" translates the Tibetan phrase meaning "one wearing a garment of śāṇa-cloth" — a kind of hemp or linen fiber. The individual is understood in the tradition to be Madhyāntika, one of the early patriarchs who spread the Dharma, though the text here gives only the descriptive epithet rather than the proper name. The identification is contextually secure but the Tibetan gives only the epithet, so the name is not supplied in the translation body.

The phrase "dwelling place of the nāgas" renders a location where a relic of the Buddha was enshrined and venerated — a well-attested element of early Buddhist relic-cult narrative. The passage describing what Mahākāśyapa does with his body before dying — "a joining together, a burning, a drawing of lightning" — renders Tibetan terms for specific tantric or supernormal physical acts whose precise technical meaning is debated in commentarial literature. The rendering is literal; the sequence likely describes a meditative process of gathering vital energies, applying inner heat, and releasing them before death, but the exact referents are not fully transparent from the Tibetan alone.

The phrase rendered "two Blessed Ones alone have passed into nirvāṇa" reflects the gods' lament that both the Buddha and now Mahākāśyapa — the latter treated here with an honorific elevation approaching that of a second "Blessed One" — have departed. This is an unusual formulation and may be a hyperbolic expression of grief rather than a doctrinal claim. The mountain name "Kukkuṭapādagiri" (the Tibetan ri bya gag rkang, "mountain of the rooster's foot") is the traditional site in Indian Buddhist narrative where Mahākāśyapa is said to be in a state of meditative absorption, awaiting Maitreya's future appearance. This detail is doctrinally significant and reflects a well-known tradition preserved across multiple canonical sources.

The phrase "linen garments" renders sha na'i gos, which likely corresponds to Sanskrit śāṇa or kṣauma cloth, a type of rough or bast fiber textile. The precise identification is uncertain but the general meaning of a cloth garment worn by the merchant figure is clear.

The passage transitions somewhat abruptly from the Mahākāśyapa narrative to the merchant arrival, as it does in the Tibetan; no text appears missing. The verse rendering of "like a water-crane before a pool" translates the simile in the first verse quoted by the wandering monk. The point of the verse is that a long life spent merely watching, without genuine practice, is like a crane that gazes at a pool but does not enter it — this standard sūtra passage is known from the Pali Dhammapada (verse 114) and parallel Āgama sources, and Ānanda's correction concerns a garbled version of the canonical text.

The phrase rendered "both kinds of person" refers to those with faith and those without, as the following lines make clear.

"Remaining here like a hatching egg" translates a simile in the final verse whose Tibetan literally means "dwelling as from a nest-egg" or "dwelling as though hatching from an egg," suggesting isolated, solitary remaining — a somewhat unusual image that may reflect an underlying Sanskrit or Prākrit idiom for a solitary or quietly gestating existence. The epithet "buddha without marks" renders མཚན་མེད་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས, literally "a buddha without characteristics/marks." This is a known designation in certain Vinaya narrative traditions for a type of buddha who does not display the major physical marks of a great being; the term is preserved as rendered.

The place names Broached-Ruin (བཅོམ་བརླག) and Rimurunda (རི་མུ་རུན་ད) are Tibetan phonetic renderings of what appear to be Indic place names; their exact Sanskrit or Prākrit forms are uncertain, so they are rendered phonetically here.

The phrase "the Vriji-subduer" (ཡུལ་སྤོང་བྱེད་པ) refers to a king or leader who suppresses or contests the Vriji (Vajji) confederacy — likely a reference to a political rival or ally of Ajātaśatru in the historical narrative of the period. The phrase rendered "the city of the Vajjians" translates Tibetan "grong khyer spong byed pa," where "spong byed" is an unusual rendering; in context it refers to the Vajjian capital (Vaiśālī). The passage may preserve an alternate epithet or a slightly corrupt reading, but the referent is clear from context.

The name "Supriya" renders Tibetan "rab bzangs" (literally "most excellent / supremely good"), which is a standard Tibetan translation of Sanskrit Supriya or Sudarśana; the identification is conventional in this narrative context.

"Midpoint between sun and water" and the epithets "midst of the river" and "solar midpoint" render obscure Tibetan geographic or ceremonial designations that became monastic names for the newly ordained community; their precise meaning is uncertain, but the passage is clearly an etiology for those monastic names.

"The third karma ceremony" refers to the threefold formal proclamation (ñatti-catuttha-kamma in Pāli, equivalent Sanskrit karmavācanā) required for valid ordination; "declaring the third" means the full ordination procedure was completed. The monk's name rendered here as "Madhyantika" appears in the Tibetan as Nyimé Gung, a calque of the Sanskrit Madhyantika (literally "midday" or "middle"). This is the standard identification in the Vinaya tradition: Madhyantika is the disciple of Ānanda commissioned to propagate the Dharma in Kashmir. The name is kept as Madhyantika throughout for consistency with historical usage.

The verse's imagery in lines three and four is compressed and the syntax somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan; the rendering preserves the parallelism of the original while clarifying the transformation of weapons into flowers, which is the evident doctrinal point. The term "A-la-la" is a transliteration of an indistinct Tibetan phonetic rendering of what is likely a Pali or Sanskrit technical term for one of the ten disputed practices at the Council of Vaiśālī. Classical sources identify the first disputed practice as the "salt in a horn" practice (Pali: siṅgiloṇakappaṃ), but the Tibetan here renders the term phonetically rather than translating it, making a firm identification uncertain. The ten disputed points correspond to the famous schism-related Council of Vaiśālī narrative preserved across Vinaya traditions.

The phrase rendered "like fire quenched by water" describes a mode of passing into nirvāṇa — the imagery of natural extinction is standard for parinirvāṇa descriptions in this genre. The passage enumerates rules three through nine of what is evidently the canonical list of the Ten Points of Vaiśālī, the disputed practices that prompted the Second Buddhist Council. The text breaks off mid-sentence in rule ten, which concerns the public display of alms bowls to solicit gold and silver coin.

The "two-fingered practice" in rule six refers to a Vinaya dispute about eating food that had not been formally designated as a "remainder" after the midday meal: monks indicated by a two-fingered gesture that they wished to eat more, without the food having been properly set aside. The precise Vinaya technicality is debated across traditions.

The phrase rendered "strained fermented drink through a water-straining cloth as though filtering through a lotus" reflects a disputed practice concerning the consumption of a mildly fermented beverage; some traditions interpret this as unfermented palm juice. The Tibetan ཆང་བཞིབས suggests straining of chang, a fermented drink, and the allowance claimed was for medicinal use by the sick. The term "Alala" is a technical Vinaya term that appears to be a procedural word — possibly an Indic exclamation or ritual formula — used by the Vaiśālī monks to ratify non-allowable matters by acclamation. Its precise original-language form and exact procedural meaning in this specific Vinaya tradition is uncertain; it may represent a corrupt or specialized form of an approval formula.

The section break marker mid-passage ("Vinaya: minor matters, fascicle fifty-nine...") is a brief scholastic gloss or summary rubric embedded in the Tibetan text itself, not a later editorial addition, and has been rendered accordingly in plain prose rather than set off, to preserve TTS flow.

"Sarvatrāma" renders the Tibetan ཐམས་ཅད་འདོད་པ, literally "desiring/wishing for everything," which may correspond to a Sanskrit name; the identification is tentative. The phrase rendered "allowable by the road" refers to a practice of declaring leftover food permissible to eat again by virtue of having traveled a certain distance — a disputed extension of allowances for monks on journey. The source of the rule cited as "the venerable Śāriputra" for the salt ruling is taken at face value from the text; it is unusual to attribute an illicit practice to so eminent a disciple, and the text may mean that the rule against it was established in connection with a case involving Śāriputra rather than originating with him as its author.

The "two-finger" allowance refers to a practice of indicating with two fingers that food already eaten from counts as a remainder, making it permissible for a second round — a rule concerning the formal declaration of leftovers in the Vinaya. The term rendered "seat-mat" is a felt or woolen sitting-mat; the rule refers to the Vinaya regulation on the size of such mats, measured by a "Sugata's span." The phrase "without patching its worn border" translates a Tibetan expression indicating the mat was used past its proper condition without the required repair to its edging. This is a Vinaya technical matter; the exact nature of the permissibility being claimed is that the old mat's size exempts it from the standard measurement rule.

The passage on gold and silver is the tenth contested point and is left mid-sentence as the Tibetan text itself breaks off with the proclamation just beginning, continuing into the next passage. The proper names Norcan, Cayala, and Dhanakas are transliterations of the Tibetan renderings of Sanskrit names: Norcan represents a Tibetan translation of a name meaning "possessing wealth" (likely Dhaniya or similar), Cayala likely represents a Sanskrit name now difficult to reconstruct with certainty, and Dhanakas is similarly reconstructed. The Tibetan name rendered "Cayala" as གཡོ་ལྡན (literally "possessing agility or movement") could correspond to Sanskrit Śalha or Sambhūta-Sāṇavāsī; and the passage refers to the Second Buddhist Council at Vaiśālī, where these elders are the traditional participants. The elder Yaśas (Tibetan: Yaśas = གྲགས་པ) is the principal protagonist of this account.

The phrase "A-la-la" rendered in transliteration represents a Tibetan phonetic rendering of a proclamation used to validate monastic acts — its exact Sanskrit equivalent and precise procedural meaning within the specific Vinaya tradition is uncertain and would warrant specialist Vinaya consultation.

The categorization of sūtra collections (Norbu on the Crown, longer transmissions, middle-length, paired, strengthening, derived, fourth and fifth) reflects a Vinaya-specific classification system that does not map neatly onto the standard Pāli or Sanskrit canonical divisions; these are rendered descriptively following the Tibetan. The Tibetan names ཡིད་དགའ (Priyadatta), ཟླ་སྒུར (Zlagur), མ་ཕམ་པ (Aparājita), ཡང་དག་སྐྱེས (Sambhūtasanavāsin), ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས (Sahajāta), and ནམ་གྲུ (Namgru) are Tibetan renderings of Indian names. Sambhūtasanavāsin and Revata (not yet named) are historically attested figures in the Second Council narrative; Namgru likely corresponds to Revata, though the text does not yet make this explicit at this point in the passage. The rendering of ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས as a place name "Sahajāta" follows the grammatical reading, though it may be a toponym or a monk's name; context suggests a place name here. "Srughna" renders སྲུག་ན and "Mahela" renders མ་ཧེ་ལྡན, both attested place names in the Second Council accounts. The phrase rendered "nets" for དྲ་བ is uncertain in context; it may refer to a type of straining cloth or filter used by monastics, related to the water-strainer mentioned separately. The precise distinction between the various textile and vessel items listed here reflects Vinaya technical vocabulary for monastic requisites, and the exact referent of each term can vary by tradition. The name rendered "Candragiri" throughout is literally "Crescent Moon Suppressor" or "Moon-Peak" in Tibetan, but the Tibetan here appears to be a phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit name — Candragiri is the most plausible reconstruction. The same figure is called "one who entered the absorption of cessation" and "one called Crescent Moon" in the boarding-scene verses; consistency with prior text is maintained by using Candragiri throughout. If the preceding translation used a different rendering for this figure, that rendering should be adopted here.

The phrase rendered "falling one short of seven hundred" reflects the Tibetan construction throughout, indicating the assembly was to consist of seven hundred arhats but was not yet complete by one.

The city name rendered "Kuśāgāra" reflects "གྲོང་ཁྱེར་དམར་བུ་ཅན" — this is Rājagṛha's alternative identification in some Vinaya accounts; "Kuśāgāra" or "Kuśāgārapura" is the Sanskrit equivalent sometimes used for this locale. If the prior translation used "Rājagṛha," that should be adopted for consistency. The term rendered "approval by the exclamation 'Alala'" translates the Tibetan "a la la zhes rung bar byed pa." The syllable "a la la" is an exclamation of wonder or approval; in this Vinaya context it refers to a practice of sanctioning the ten disputed points by an informal vocalized assent rather than through proper formal procedure. The passage is from the narrative of the Second Council at Vaiśālī, recounting the deliberations over the ten points introduced by the Vaiśālī monks.

The phrase rendered "the group of six monks" refers to the notorious "Shadvaggiya" monks frequently cited in Vinaya literature as the originators of improper practices.

The closing summary verse contains a series of proper names of participants or places associated with the ten points and the council; some of these names, including "Sarvagāmin" and "Nāvagiri," are here rendered by their apparent Sanskrit equivalents reconstructed from the Tibetan forms "ཐམས་ཅད་འདོད" and "ནམ་གྲུ." "Dhaniya" for "ནོར་ཅན" and "Priya" for "ཡིད་དགའ" are similarly reconstructed. The identification of all persons named in the verse is not entirely certain from this passage alone. The text is a colophon and editorial postscript rather than a doctrinal passage; it is largely administrative in character. Several proper names are Tibetan personal and place names that have been retained in transliteration as they appear: La-stod Ol-rgod (a temple locality), Dharmasiṃha (Tib. Dar-ma Seng-ge), Byang-chub Seng-ge, Dagchungwa, Tsulkrim Yönten, Chimpa Thams-cad Mkhyen-pa (Chim Omniscient), and Samyé and Chimpu (meditation hermitage above Samyé). The term bāmpo, rendered throughout as "fascicle," is a unit of text division used in the Tibetan canon roughly equivalent to a chapter-length section.

The phrase translated as "the mother of the Piṭakas" refers to the Abhidharma Piṭaka, traditionally called the "mother" because it generates wisdom; this is a conventional Tibetan honorific usage.
